m-c-ricklefs: Merle Calvin Ricklefs was born in Fort Dodge, Iowa, on 17 July 1943. He took his doctorate at Cornell University in 1973 under the supervision of O. W. Wolters, with a dissertation on Jogjakarta under Sultan Mangkubumi from 1749 to 1792. It appeared in 1974 from Oxford University Press as a history of the division of Java, and later in a revised Indonesian edition.

Ricklefs held posts at the School of Oriental and African Studies, All Souls College, Monash University, the Australian National University and the University of Melbourne, and retired from the professorship of Southeast Asian history at the National University of Singapore. He was emeritus professor of history at both the Australian National University and Monash. He was elected a fellow of the Australian Academy of the Humanities in 1989, received the Centenary Medal in 2001 and was made a member of the Order of Australia in June 2017. He died on 29 December 2019, aged 76.

In the early 1980s he was the driving force behind the Monash Orientation Scheme for Aborigines, which he co-founded as the first bridging programme for Aboriginal people at an Australian university. By the time he left Monash in 1993 it had roughly doubled the number of Aboriginal university graduates. He also took part in the immigration debate of the 1980s, which began when Geoffrey Blainey of the University of Melbourne argued that Australia should limit Asian immigration.

His research centred on Mataram, Kartasura, Yogyakarta and Surakarta in Central Java, and he regularly revised his survey of modern Indonesia. His books include a study of an original Kartasura chronicle (1978), War, Culture and Economy in Java, 1677–1726 (1993), The Seen and Unseen Worlds in Java, 1726–49 (1998), on the court of Pakubuwana II, and a series on the Islamisation of Java: Mystic Synthesis in Java (2006), Polarizing Javanese Society (2007) and Islamisation and Its Opponents in Java (2012). His last book, Soul Catcher (2018), is a life of Prince Mangkunagara I. With P. Voorhoeve he catalogued the Indonesian manuscripts in British public collections.
m-s-subbulakshmi: Madurai Shanmukhavadivu Subbulakshmi, known as Kunjamma in her family, was born in Madurai in the Madras Presidency on 16 September 1916, to the veena player Shanmukhavadivu Ammal and Subramania Iyer. Her grandmother Akkammal was a violinist, and her mother, from the devadasi community, was a regular stage performer, so she grew up in an environment conducive to musical learning. She trained in Carnatic music under Semmangudi Srinivasa Iyer and later in Hindustani music under Pandit Narayanrao Vyas.

She gave her first public performance in 1927, aged eleven, in the 100-pillar hall of the Rockfort Temple in Tiruchirappalli, with Mysore Chowdiah on the violin and Dakshinamurthy Pillai on the mridangam, organised by the Congress leader F. G. Natesa Iyer. In 1936 she moved to Madras.

In 1929, aged 13, she sang bhajans at the Madras Music Academy, which broke with tradition in inviting a young girl as a key performer. Critics called her performance spellbinding and her a musical genius, and she soon became one of the leading Carnatic vocalists. Her concerts included the Edinburgh International Festival in 1963, Carnegie Hall, the UN General Assembly on UN Day in 1966, the Royal Albert Hall in 1982 and the Festival of India in Moscow in 1987. On 21 June 1963 she recorded the Venkateswara Suprabhatam. With D. K. Pattammal and M. L. Vasanthakumari she formed what is called the Trinity of Carnatic Music.

She acted in four Tamil films in her youth. Sevasadanam (released 2 May 1938, directed by K. Subramanyam, opposite F. G. Natesa Iyer) was an early Tamil film set in contemporary society, advocating reform and taking marriages between young girls and old men as its subject. In 1941 she played the male role of Narada in Savitri to raise money for Kalki, her husband's nationalist Tamil weekly, and her title role in Meera (1945) gave her national prominence. She gave more than 200 charity concerts, including five benefit performances in 1944 for a fund in memory of Mahatma Gandhi's late wife, and she donated royalties of records such as the Suprabhatam.

After her husband Kalki Sadasivam died in 1997 she stopped all public performance. Her honours included the Padma Bhushan in 1954, the Sangita Kalanidhi in 1968, the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 1974, the Padma Vibhushan in 1975 and the Bharat Ratna in 1998. Jawaharlal Nehru is quoted as asking who he, a mere prime minister, was before a queen of music, and Sarojini Naidu called her the Nightingale of India. She died at her home in Kotturpuram, Chennai, on 11 December 2004, aged 88. A bronze statue of her stands in Tirupati, and a commemorative stamp was issued on 18 December 2005.
m-visvesvaraya: Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya was born on 15 September 1861 at Muddenahalli in the Kingdom of Mysore, now in Chikkaballapura district, Karnataka, into a Telugu speaking family. His ancestors came from Mokshagundam, a village in present-day Prakasam district of Andhra Pradesh, and had migrated to Mysore before his birth. He was educated at Bangalore, took a Bachelor of Science at the University of Madras, and graduated in civil engineering from the College of Engineering, Pune. There he helped found the Deccan Club and was its first secretary, knowing progressives of Pune such as R. G. Bhandarkar, Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Mahadev Govind Ranade.

He became an assistant engineer in the Public Works Department of Bombay in 1885 and worked in the Bombay Presidency. Invited to join the Indian Irrigation Commission in 1899, he introduced an irrigation system on the Deccan Plateau and designed and patented automatic weir floodgates, first installed in 1903 at the Khadakvasla Dam near Pune and later at the Tigra Dam in Gwalior and the Krishna Raja Sagar dam in Mysore. Around 1906 or 1907 he was sent to Aden to study water supply and drainage, and his project was carried out there.

After retiring from British service he toured industrial countries, worked for the Nizam of Hyderabad on flood protection against the Musi river, and in 1909 became chief engineer of Mysore, where he directed the Krishna Raja Sagar dam.

In 1912 Maharaja Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV appointed him Dewan of Mysore, an office he held for nearly seven years until 1918. With the maharaja's support he founded factories and institutions, among them the Mysore Soap Factory, the Mysore Iron and Steel Works at Bhadravathi, the State Bank of Mysore, the Mysore Chamber of Commerce and, in 1917, the Government Engineering College at Bangalore. He commissioned new railway lines and encouraged private investment in industry.

He was made a Companion of the Order of the Indian Empire in 1911, knighted in 1915, and awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1955. He wrote Reconstructing India (1920) and Planned Economy for India (1936), and died in April 1962 aged 100. His birthday is observed as Engineer's Day.
ma-al-aynayn: His given name was Muhammad al-Mustafa al-Qalqami. He was born in the Hawdh region, a son of Muhammad Fadil wuld Mamin, founder of the Fadiliyya, a sub-order of the Qadiriyya Sufi brotherhood. His nickname, meaning water of two eyes, was given by his mother because he was her only living son. He studied under his father, memorised the Quran by the age of seven, and at sixteen left to study under other scholars.

In 1858 he set out on the Hajj, passing through Essaouira, Marrakesh and Meknes, where he met Sultan Abd al-Rahman of Morocco and his heir, Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman. The meeting began his close links with the Moroccan court. He returned home in 1861 with a reputation for mastery of the religious sciences, and his father gave him a turban and the title of Shaykh.

By 1870 he had moved to the Saqiyat al-Hamra, where in 1871 and 1872 he established the zawiya of Dar al-Hamra as his first headquarters. In 1879 Sultan Moulay Hassan I issued a dahir naming him his representative over a territory from the Souss to the Saguia el Hamra and Tarfaya. From 1888, with arms supplied by the Makhzen, he began to assert administrative and military authority, and after 1894 the Moroccan government resupplied him by sea at Tarfaya.

In 1904 he proclaimed a jihad against the colonisers and gathered a large coalition of tribes, acquiring firearms through Morocco and from rival European powers such as Germany. A member of his brotherhood may have assassinated Xavier Coppolani, leader of the French conquest of Mauritania, in 1905. When Sultan Abdelaziz ratified the Algeciras Conference in 1906, he called it a betrayal and in 1907 backed the sultan's brother Abdelhafid.

Pushed back by French forces under Colonel Gouraud, he withdrew to Tiznit. In 1910 he led an army of 6,000 men north against Abdelhafid, now sultan, and was defeated by General Moinier on 23 June. He died at Tiznit on 23 October, and his tomb there became a place of pilgrimage. Biographers attribute to him between 140 and 314 books. His son Ahmad al-Hiba, known as the Blue Sultan, continued the war against the French, and his name is invoked both in Morocco and by the Polisario Front.
ma-huan: Ma Huan, courtesy name Zongdao, wrote under the pen name Mountain-woodcutter. He was born in Kuaiji Commandery in Zhejiang, an area within the modern borders of Shaoxing. He knew several Classical Chinese and Buddhist texts and learned Arabic so that he could serve as a translator on the voyages of Admiral Zheng He to the Western Oceans.

On the expedition that sailed in 1413 he went south and west into the Indian Ocean, visiting Champa, Java, Sumatra, Palembang, Siam, Kochi and Hormuz. His voyage of 1421 took him to Malacca, Aru, Sumatra, Trincomalee, Ceylon, Kochi, Calicut, Zufar and Hormuz. The voyage of 1431 brought him to Bengal, Chittagong, Sonargaon, Gaur and Calicut, and from Calicut the eunuch Hong Bao sent him as an emissary to Mecca.

Throughout the voyages Ma Huan took notes on geography, politics, weather, the environment, trade, local customs and even the punishment of criminals. He began writing on the way home from his first voyage and had a first draft ready around 1416, which he enlarged and revised on the later voyages.

The Yingya Shenglan circulated in many printed and hand-copied editions under the Ming and Qing dynasties. The historian Feng Chengjun edited and annotated a printed text, and a newer edition based on Ming hand copies was published by Ocean Publishing House in China. J. V. G. Mills's annotated English translation, based on Feng's edition, was published by the Hakluyt Society in 1970 and reprinted in Bangkok in 1997.

Sinologists treat the book as a primary source for Ming naval exploration and for the history of South East Asia and India. Scholars who have studied Ma Huan include J. J. L. Duyvendak, F. Hirth, Paul Pelliot, Xiang Da and Mills.
ma-xie: Ma Xi'e was the 30th son of Ma Yin, his mother unnamed in the sources. In 947 he was military governor of Wuping Circuit and acting prefect of Yong Prefecture under his half-brother Ma Xifan. When Ma Xifan died without naming an heir, officers argued that Ma Yin had wanted his sons to succeed by age, but the faction of Liu Yantao put Ma Xifan's full brother Ma Xiguang, the 35th son, on the throne. Ma Xi'e was disarmed on his way to the mourning, then allowed back to Lang Prefecture, where his brother Ma Xichong secretly urged him to rebel.

He asked the Later Han emperor Liu Chengyou to let him send tribute separately, in effect dividing Chu; the court refused. In the autumn of 949 he rose openly with 700 ships, against the urging of his wife, Lady Yuan, who drowned herself in a well after his first defeat. He then won over the non-Han tribes of Chen, Xu and Meishan and submitted as a vassal to the Southern Tang emperor Li Jing, who sent troops to help him.

After crushing Liu Yantao's attack on Lang, Ma Xi'e marched on Changsha, having secretly won over Ma Xiguang's commander Xu Keqiong with an offer to share the kingdom. The city fell when Xu surrendered and was pillaged. Ma Xi'e took the title Prince of Chu, had several of his brother's officials executed and their bodies eaten by the soldiers, and ordered Ma Xiguang to commit suicide.

He then spent his days feasting, leaving government to Ma Xichong, under whom the legal system broke down. With the treasury looted, wealth was taken from civilians to pay the soldiers, who stayed discontented, and his favourite, the guard officer Xie Yanyong, was resented by the generals. Soldiers set to rebuild the burned offices without pay left for Lang, which then went its own way. On 22 October 951 officers mutinied with Ma Xichong's knowledge; Ma Xi'e was captured and Xie cut to pieces.

Peng Shigao, whom Ma Xi'e had once caned, refused to murder him and escorted him safely to Hengshan, where the garrison commander Liao Yan proclaimed him Prince of Hengshan and gathered over 10,000 men. When Ma Xichong surrendered Chu to the Southern Tang, the people of Changsha asked Li Jing not to give the city to Ma Xi'e. Taken to Jinling, he was made governor of Jiangnan West Circuit, but after paying homage around the new year of 953 he was kept at Jinling, where he died several years later.
ma-xiguang: Ma Xiguang, courtesy name Depi, was Ma Yin's 35th son and a full younger brother of Ma Xifan, both born to the concubine Lady Chen; his birth date is not known. Ma Yin had ordered that his sons succeed one another by age, and Ma Xifan, who came to the throne in 932, was especially fond of the careful and obedient Ma Xiguang and had him oversee headquarters affairs. When Ma Xifan died suddenly in 947 without naming an heir, Zhang Shaodi and Tuoba Heng urged the claim of the 30th son, Ma Xi'e, but Liu Yantao and his partisans announced that it was Ma Xifan's will that Ma Xiguang succeed.

Liu Zhiyuan, emperor of Later Han, made him Prince of Chu in 947. When Ma Xi'e came to Changsha to mourn, Ma Xiguang had his soldiers disarmed and kept him at Bixiang Palace, but refused advice to kill him and let him return to Lang Prefecture with many gifts. In 948 he refused a marriage proposal from Liu Sheng of Southern Han, who then sent the eunuch general Wu Huai'en to take He and Zhao Prefectures.

In 949 Ma Xi'e rose openly, building 700 ships. Ma Xiguang's general Wang Yun defeated him and took 300 of them, but Ma Xiguang recalled the army, telling Wang not to harm his brother. Ma Xi'e then won over the non-Han tribes of Chen and Xu and the Meishan Tribes, who killed several of Ma Xiguang's officers, and submitted as a vassal to Southern Tang, which sent the general He Jingzhu to his aid. Liu Yantao's attack on Lang ended in an ambush that crushed his army.

As Ma Xi'e advanced on Changsha, Ma Xiguang gave his main army to Xu Keqiong, who was secretly negotiating with Ma Xi'e, and ignored the warnings of the loyal officer Peng Shigao. Snow halted the armies, and Ma Xiguang turned to sorcerers and Buddhist monks, wearing monk's robes himself. When the attack came, non-Han soldiers set fire to the east wall, Xu surrendered and the city fell. Ma Xi'e had several of Ma Xiguang's officials executed and their bodies eaten by the soldiers. Urged by Zhu Jinzhong that a state cannot have two lords, he ordered Ma Xiguang to commit suicide, and Peng Shigao buried him outside the Liuyang Gate.
ma-yin: Ma Yin's family came from Yanling, in modern Xuchang in Henan, and claimed descent from the Han dynasty general Ma Yuan; of his ancestors little is known beyond the names of his father Ma Yuanfeng, his grandfather and his great-grandfather. He worked as a carpenter in his youth. He then served in the army of Zhongwu Circuit stationed at Cai Prefecture against the rebel Huang Chao, under the officers Sun Ru and Liu Jianfeng, and became known for his ability and bravery.

In 887 Ma Yin and Liu Jianfeng marched with an army sent into Huainan Circuit, where Sun Ru seized command and made himself military governor. Sun's campaign against Yang Xingmi ended in 892 with his defeat and death near Xuan Prefecture. Liu and Ma then led 7,000 soldiers south, Liu as leader and Ma as forward commander, and the force grew to over 100,000. In 894 Ma persuaded the defenders of Longhui Pass to disband, and Liu's men, wearing their uniforms, took Tan Prefecture, the capital of Wu'an Circuit, by surprise.

When Ma Yin took command of Wu'an, he was advised by his strategist Gao Yu not to buy off his stronger neighbours but to settle the people and train his army. In 897 he held only Tan and Shao of the circuit's seven prefectures, the other five being in the hands of rebels. By the end of 899 his generals had taken Heng, Yong, Dao, Chēn and Lian, and Emperor Zhaozong of Tang formally named him military governor.

When Zhu Quanzhong ended the Tang and founded the Later Liang in 907, Ma Yin recognised the new emperor, who created him Prince of Chu. That year his general Qin Yanhui defeated an invasion sent by Yang Wo of Hongnong, and in 908 Ma took Lang and Li Prefectures. After the fall of the Later Liang he sent tribute to the Later Tang, whose Emperor Mingzong gave him the title King of Chu in 927; Ma then called his residence a palace and set up offices on the imperial model.

At Gao Yu's suggestion Ma Yin drew merchants by collecting no transaction taxes and coined money of iron and lead, which could only be spent inside Chu, and he allowed his subjects to pay taxes in silk, so that Chu became a major producer of silk. He had at least 35 sons, several of whom ruled Chu after him.
ma-zhongying: Ma Zhongying, born Ma Buying and nicknamed Commander Ga, joined a Muslim militia in 1924 at the age of 14. He took part in the rebellion in Gansu against the Guominjun forces of Feng Yuxiang, fighting even his own relatives, among them his great-uncle, the warlord Ma Lin, and massacred Tibetans during the rising. In his 1928 revolt, in a time of famine and heavy taxation, he besieged and seized Hezhou, and in April 1929 he took the provincial capital Lanzhou before the Guominjun drove him out. He attended the Whampoa Military Academy in Nanjing in 1929.

Through his alliance with the Kuomintang, his mainly Chinese Muslim troops became the New 36th Division of the National Revolutionary Army. When Yulbars Khan asked for help after the governor Jin Shuren abolished the Kumul Khanate, Ma entered Xinjiang, was wounded and went back to Gansu, where he forced Mildred Cable and Francesca and Eva French to tend his wounds; he returned in the summer of 1933. His campaigns included atrocities against Han and Uyghur civilians, and local men were conscripted and sent to the front lines under heavy cannon fire.

The Soviets and Sheng Shicai claimed that Ma was backed by Japan, but he proclaimed his allegiance to the Nanjing government and used the Kuomintang's Blue Sky with a White Sun banners. The Han general Zhang Peiyuan and his Ili army went over to him. During the Soviet invasion of Xinjiang his troops withdrew again and again; in April 1934, after they had stormed Kashgar, he spoke at the Id Kah Mosque, denouncing Sheng as a Soviet puppet and urging the Uyghurs to be loyal to Nanjing. His last line of defence was set up around Khotan.

From Khotan he was generally believed to have fled to Soviet territory, and he was not seen again in Xinjiang. The Soviet agent Vladimir Petrov later wrote that Ma had been lured onto a plane by Soviet agents, made to issue false orders to his troops and flown to Moscow. Nothing more was heard of him after 1936. Accounts of his end include a crash, execution in Moscow, death in the Great Purge, and, in Sheng Shicai's memoir, execution with his staff on the orders of Joseph Stalin in 1937. Sven Hedin, whom Ma's forces detained during their retreat, wrote that he dreamt of an empire reaching across Central Asia to the Caspian Sea.
maamme: The music was composed by Fredrik Pacius, a German immigrant, to the Swedish words of Johan Ludvig Runeberg. It is said that Pacius composed the tune in four days. The song was written for the 500th anniversary of Porvoo and was first performed on 13 May 1848.

The poem formed the prologue to the verse cycle The Tales of Ensign Stål (Fänrik Ståhls sägner), a classic example of Romantic nationalism. The Finnish text now in use is usually attributed to Paavo Cajander's 1889 translation of the cycle, but it in fact originates from the 1867 translation by Julius Krohn.

The song was popular throughout the 19th century but established its present position only after Pacius's death. There were attempts in the 1880s and the 1920s to replace it with a version in Finnish, but these ceased by the 1930s. Some Finns have proposed the Finlandia piece by Jean Sibelius as the anthem instead.

Finland has no law naming an official national anthem, unlike its coat of arms and flag, which are legally defined. The position of Maamme was established gradually by convention, and in use it fills the function of a national anthem: it is played during state visits and used to represent Finland at international sporting fixtures. It is customary to sing only the first and the last verse, unless the people gathered are a mix of Finnish and Swedish speakers. In that case three verses are sung: the first in Finnish, the first in Swedish and the last in Finnish.

The melody of Maamme is also used for two other anthems: the Estonian anthem Mu isamaa, mu õnn ja rõõm (My Fatherland, My Happiness and Joy) and the Livonian anthem Min izāmō (My Fatherland). Both borrow the tune that Pacius wrote for Runeberg's poem.
maan-jordan: Ma'an lies in southern Jordan, 218 kilometres south-west of Amman, at a height above 1,000 metres. The climate is a cold desert one, with hot summers, mild to cold winters and rainfall averaging only 44 millimetres a year. The modern city stands just north-west of the ancient town of the same name, which dates at least to the Nabatean period. It lies on the old King's Highway and on the modern Desert Highway, and it is the capital of the Ma'an Governorate.

Ma'an was founded, according to the account given for it, by the Minaeans, an ancient Arab people based in Yemen, between the 2nd and 4th century BCE, on a major trade route. Local tradition holds that it was named after Ma'an, the son of Lot. Under Byzantine rule it lay in the territory of the Arab Christian tribe of Banu Judham. Its governor in the early 7th century, Farwa ibn Amr al-Judhami, converted to Islam and was executed by crucifixion on the Byzantine emperor's order. The Muslim state in Medina then sent an army under Usama ibn Zayd to conquer the town.

The Hajj route to Mecca ran through Ma'an, and its economy depended on the pilgrim caravans. Its main trade partner was Gaza, and it sold livestock, above all camels and sheep, to pilgrims. Most residents were literate and many served as imams or advisers to the Bedouin, with whom the town had unusually good relations. The Ottomans annexed Transjordan in 1517 and in 1559 built a fort to protect the pilgrim road; in the late nineteenth century they tried several times to raise Ma'an's rank, but al-Karak was preferred as district capital. The railway station opened in 1902, connecting the city to Damascus and Medina.

In April 1918 the Arab Northern Army besieged the Ottoman garrison at the Battle of Maan, from 13 to 17 April. It failed to take the city but wrecked the Hejaz railway to the south. In 1920 the Hashemite emir Abdullah I arrived with several hundred fighters in an attempt to restore the Sharifian throne in Damascus after its overthrow by France. Ma'an was annexed to the Transjordanian state in 1925.

Ma'an is the seat of Al-Hussein Bin Talal University and of the Ma'an Development Area, a special economic zone whose industrial park began construction in 2008. A railway building at the station, used by Abdullah I as the seat of the first government, is now called the Ma'an Palace and appears on the reverse of the 5 dinar note. Most of the inhabitants are Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school.
maarten-tromp: Maarten Harpertszoon Tromp was born in Brielle and baptised on 3 May 1598, the oldest son of Harpert Maertensz, a naval officer and captain of the frigate Olifantstromp. The surname Tromp probably comes from the name of the ship. At the age of nine he went to sea with his father, and in 1610 his father was killed by a cannonball when English pirates under Peter Easton attacked their merchantman. The pirates seized the boy and sold him at the slave market of Salé, where he served as a cabin boy until Easton ordered his release about two years later.

He supported his mother and sisters by working in a Rotterdam shipyard. In 1621 Barbary corsairs captured him off Tunis, and he was kept as a slave until 1622, when the Bey of Tunis, impressed by his gunnery and navigation, allowed him to leave as a free man.

Tromp joined the Dutch navy as a lieutenant in July 1622 and was flag captain to Lieutenant-Admiral Piet Hein in the fight with Ostend privateers in 1629, in which Hein was killed. He left the service in disappointment in 1634 but was asked back in 1637, when he became Lieutenant-Admiral of Holland and West Frisia after the dismissal of officers for incompetence. He insisted on more ships, well supplied and well manned, and blockaded Dunkirk. On 21 October 1639 he attacked the Spanish fleet of Antonio de Oquendo at the Battle of the Downs and destroyed much of it.

In the First Anglo-Dutch War he commanded at Dover, Dungeness, Portland, the Gabbard and Scheveningen. The Battle of Dover on 19 May 1652 began when he refused to lower his flag to Robert Blake. He won at Dungeness on 30 November 1652, but at the Gabbard on 2 and 3 June 1653 the Dutch lost seventeen ships and the English none.

At the Battle of Scheveningen on 31 July 1653 an English sharpshooter killed Tromp. His flag captain, Egbert Bartholomeusz Kortenaer, kept the standard flying to sustain morale. He received a state funeral in August 1653 and was buried in the Oude Kerk in Delft, where a monument honours him, and the poet Joost van den Vondel wrote a poem about it. His second son, Cornelis Maartenszoon Tromp, also became a distinguished naval officer, and several ships of the Royal Netherlands Navy have carried the name HNLMS Tromp.
maasai-people: The Maasai are an Eastern Nilotic people whose language, Maa, belongs to the Nilo-Saharan family. They arrived in the African Great Lakes region by way of South Sudan. Like other groups in East Africa, they adopted customs and vocabulary from neighbouring Cushitic-speaking peoples, including the age-set system of social organisation and circumcision. Groups already settled in the region were forcibly displaced by the incoming Maasai, while other, mainly Southern Cushitic, groups were assimilated into Maasai society. They are pastoralists and have a reputation as fearsome warriors and cattle raiders.

The Maasai territory reached its largest size in the mid-19th century, covering almost the whole Great Rift Valley and adjacent lands from Mount Marsabit in the north to Dodoma in the south. Raiders used spears and shields but were most feared for their throwing clubs. In 1857, after depopulating what was called the Wakuafi wilderness in south-eastern Kenya, Maasai warriors threatened Mombasa.

The period of expansion was followed by the Emutai of 1883 to 1902, marked by epidemics of cattle pleuropneumonia, rinderpest and smallpox, and by drought. A German lieutenant estimated that 90 per cent of cattle died of rinderpest, and by one estimate two thirds of the Maasai themselves died. Later, Maasai in Tanganyika were displaced in the 1940s from fertile lands between Mount Meru and Mount Kilimanjaro. In 1951 British colonial policymakers removed all Maasai from the Serengeti National Park and moved them to the Ngorongoro Conservation Area. More land was taken for wildlife reserves and national parks in both Kenya and Tanzania, among them Amboseli, Maasai Mara and Lake Manyara.

There are twenty-two geographic sectors of the Maasai, called iloshon, each with its own customs, leadership and dialect. The Maasai are monotheistic and worship a single deity, Enkai, who has a benevolent aspect, Engai Narok, the Black God, and a vengeful one, Engai Na-nyokie, the Red God. The laibon is the central human figure of their religion, with roles that include healing, divination and prophecy. Many Maasai have also adopted Christianity or Islam.

Their way of life has centred on cattle, which are the main source of food, and a man's wealth is measured in cattle, wives and children. Warriors are the only members of the community who wear long hair, and at the Eunoto ceremony a warrior becomes a junior elder and has it shaved off. Boys are circumcised as a rite of passage, and girls undergo a female rite, a form of genital mutilation, which activists such as Agnes Pareyio campaign against.
maastricht: Maastricht lies on both sides of the Meuse, at the point where the river is joined by the Jeker, close to the border with Belgium. Mount Saint Peter is largely within the municipal borders, and the city belongs to the Meuse-Rhine Euroregion, which includes Aachen, Liège and Hasselt. Neanderthal remains have been found to the west of the city, and Celts lived here around 500 BCE at a spot where the Meuse was shallow and easy to cross. The Roman settlement, Trajectum ad Mosam, developed into a medieval centre of river trade and religion.

In the early Middle Ages Maastricht, with Aachen and Liège, formed part of the heartland of the Carolingian dynasty, and was an important centre of river trade and manufacturing; Merovingian coins minted there have been found throughout Europe. The Vikings plundered the town in 881, and in the tenth century it was briefly the capital of the duchy of Lower Lorraine. Its position at a major river crossing led to an array of fortifications from the sixteenth century, and the Spanish and Dutch garrisons shaped its economy. In 1579 the Spanish army under the Duke of Parma sacked the city.

For over fifty years the Spanish crown held the joint sovereignty that the dukes of Brabant had held before; in 1632 Prince Frederick Henry of Orange conquered the city, and the Dutch States General took the Spanish crown's place. A Spanish attempt to retake it in 1634 failed.

In 1815 Maastricht became part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands and the capital of the new province of Limburg. When the southern provinces seceded in 1830, the Dutch garrison stayed loyal to King William I, although most of the townspeople sided with the Belgian revolutionaries. The arbitration of 1831 gave the city to the Netherlands, but neither side accepted it until the Treaty of London of 1839. In this isolation Maastricht became an early industrial town. Traditional industries such as its potteries declined in the later twentieth century, and Maastricht University was founded in 1976.

Maastricht is the capital and largest city of the province of Limburg. European Councils were held there in 1981 and 1991, and the second led a year later to the signing of the Maastricht Treaty, which created the European Union and the euro. The city has 1,677 national heritage buildings, the second highest number in the Netherlands after Amsterdam, and its whole centre is a conservation area. The Bonnefanten Museum shows old masters and contemporary art.
maastricht-treaty: The treaty was negotiated against the end of the Cold War and the reunification of Germany, and had to reconcile member states seeking deeper integration with those wishing to keep national control. French President François Mitterrand had been forced to abandon his Socialist programme in 1983 because of speculation against the franc, and he was afterwards committed to drawing Germany into a currency partnership. When Chancellor Helmut Kohl asked for reunification in 1990, Mitterrand would accept it only if Germany agreed to give up the Deutsche Mark for a common currency.

The twelve members of the European Communities signed the treaty on 7 February 1992. It was signed in Maastricht because the Netherlands held the presidency of the Council during the six months of negotiation.

Title I established the European Union on the foundation of the three partly merged communities, the European Economic Community, the European Coal and Steel Community and Euratom. Its objectives were a citizenship of the Union, economic and monetary union ultimately with a single currency, and a common foreign and security policy. Title II renamed the European Economic Community the European Community and set a staged path to monetary union, with criteria for adopting the single currency and a future European Central Bank.

Every national of a member state became a citizen of the Union, with the right to vote and stand in local and European elections where they lived. The European Parliament gained co-decision on some legislation and the power to confirm the Council's nominations for the Commission. Foreign policy and justice and home affairs stayed intergovernmental, and the United Kingdom obtained opt-outs from the social protocol and the final stage of monetary union.

Ratification required referendums in Denmark, France and Ireland. Danish voters rejected the treaty on 2 June 1992 by 50.7 to 49.3 percent, but after concessions agreed at Edinburgh, including an exemption from the single currency like the British one, a second referendum on 18 May 1993 approved it with 56.7 percent. Ireland approved it on 18 June 1992 with 69.1 percent, and France narrowly in September 1992 with 50.8 percent. In Britain Prime Minister John Major overcame Conservative rebels only by tying ratification to a vote of confidence. The German Federal Constitutional Court ruled it compatible with the Basic Law on 12 October 1993.
maba-diakhou-ba: Maba was born in 1809 in the region of Rip, also called Badibu, into a family descended from the Fulani Denianke dynasty; his grandfather had come from Futa Toro, and the family were teachers of the Quran. He studied in Cayor and taught in the Kingdom of Jolof, his mother's homeland, where he married into the royal family. In 1846 he probably met El Hadj Umar Tall, who named him the Tijani leader for the region, and around 1850 he returned to Rip, spending ten years teaching near Kaolack while the French under Governor Faidherbe waged a scorched-earth campaign against resistance in Senegambia.

As court marabout to the weak king of Rip, Maba stockpiled weapons, and when the ceddo warriors attacked the marabouts his students defeated them. By 1861 he controlled all of Rip, and his jihad soon took most of Saloum and part of Niumi; he founded Nioro as his capital. He enforced his reading of Islam by burning and enslaving villages that resisted, and he was a prominent slave trader. In May 1864 he gave refuge to Lat Dior, the deposed Damel of Cayor, and converted him, and later the Buur of Jolof, Alboury Ndiaye, a turning point for Islam among the Wolof.

With up to 11,000 fighting men, he was recognised by the French in October 1864 as Almamy of Baddibu and Saloum. When Governor Émile Pinet-Laprade marched on Saloum with 1,600 regulars, 2,000 cavalry and 4,000 volunteers and foot soldiers, Maba's forces under Lat Dior drove him back at the Battle of Pathé Badiane outside Nioro. His movement also sought to abolish the caste system of the Wolof and Serer states.

Maba invaded Sine, ruled by the Serer king Kumba Ndoffene Diouf, burned its capital Diakhao, and on 20 April 1867 killed the French captain Le Creurer at Thiofack. On 18 July 1867, at Fandane-Thiouthioune, a rainstorm made his men's guns useless, and he was killed in the rout. Sine's resistance kept much of Serer country outside Islam into the 20th century. The Tijani centres of Tivaouane and Kaolack both arose from his short-lived state, and his tomb at Fandène is a place of pilgrimage.
mabo-v-queensland-no-2: The case concerned the Murray Islands Group, Mer, Waua Islet and Daua Island, home of the Meriam people. Land on Mer is held under Malo's Law, a set of religiously sanctioned laws under which the whole island belongs to Meriam owners, with no public ownership; land passes orally, held by the eldest son on behalf of a lineage. The arrival of the London Missionary Society in 1871 brought Christianity without displacing these customs, and Queensland annexed the islands in 1879.

Australian law had not recognised pre-colonial property interests: in Milirrpum v Nabalco Pty Ltd in the 1970s native title was held never to have existed. In 1982 the plaintiffs, led by Eddie Mabo and represented by the barrister Ron Castan, asked the High Court to declare the Meriam owners of their land. Queensland's attempt to extinguish any such title by the Queensland Coast Islands Declaratory Act 1985 was struck down in Mabo No 1 in 1988 as inconsistent with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975.

Decided on 3 June 1992, the judgment held that native title exists as part of the common law of Australia, that its source is the traditional laws and customs of Indigenous groups rather than a grant from the Crown, and that its content depends on those continuing laws and customs. The Crown acquired radical title with sovereignty, but that did not by itself extinguish native title, which could be ended only by a valid exercise of government power inconsistent with it. Justice Brennan endorsed a three-part test of Indigenous identity: biological descent from the people, the person's own recognition of membership, and recognition by the elders or others holding traditional authority.

Prime Minister Paul Keating praised the decision in his Redfern Speech as establishing a fundamental truth, while Richard Court, premier of Western Australia, and mining and pastoral groups opposed it. The Native Title Act 1993 set up the National Native Title Tribunal to hear claims, and the Howard government later amended it after the Wik decision. In 2005 the historian Michael Connor argued in The Invention of Terra Nullius that the case was wrongly decided, since Britain had annexed Australia rather than treating it as terra nullius. Brennan's test of Indigenous identity has since been used in later cases, among them Love v Commonwealth. Mabo Day, 3 June, is a holiday in the Torres Shire.
mac-cuu: Mạc Cửu was born in Leizhou, Guangdong, then under the Southern Ming dynasty. His birth name was Mạc Kính Cửu, which was easily confused with the names of several rulers of the Mạc dynasty of Vietnam, such as Mạc Kính Chỉ and Mạc Kính Cung, so he changed it. He later left China to expand his business, and sometime between 1687 and 1695 the Cambodian king granted him the Khmer title Okna and sponsored his move to southern Cambodia, where he first served as chief of a small Chinese and Vietnamese community.

He grew rich from a casino he built and drew more Chinese and Vietnamese settlers, founding seven villages at places including Phú Quốc, Lũng Kỳ (Kep), Cần Bột (Kampot), Hương Úc (Sihanoukville), Giá Khê (Rạch Giá) and Cà Mau. The town the newcomers built at Peam, a Khmer word for port or river mouth, was called Gangkou in Chinese and Pontomeas by Europeans. Rule there was divided: Mạc Cửu governed the Chinese and Vietnamese, while the Khmer inhabitants kept a Khmer governor, the Okna Reachea Setthi, until a Siamese expedition of 1771 overthrew that system.

When the Siamese army invaded Cambodia, Mạc Cửu was captured and taken to Bangkok, returning only when civil strife broke out in Siam. He then turned to the Nguyễn lords, sending them a tribute mission in 1708 and receiving the title of Tong Binh of Hà Tiên and the noble rank of Marquess Cửu Ngọc. In 1715 the Cambodian king Thommo Reachea III, backed by Siam, invaded to regain the territory; Mạc Cửu fled to Lũng Kỳ, and after Cambodia sacked Hà Tiên and withdrew he returned and built several castles to defend it.

His son Mạc Thiên Tứ was born in 1718 to a lady from Biên Hòa, and his daughter Mac Kim Dinh married a son of the exiled Chinese general Trần Thượng Xuyên. His descendants governed Hà Tiên until the Nguyễn dynasty abolished the title in 1832. The clan's genealogy survives as the Hà Tiên trấn Hiệp trấn Mạc thị gia phả.
mac-dang-dung: Mạc Đăng Dung was born on 23 November 1483 at the village of Cổ Trai in Nghi Dương district, now Kiến Thụy in Haiphong, the son of a fisherman. He began as a bodyguard to Emperor Lê Uy Mục and rose through the military ranks while both Lê Uy Mục and his successor Lê Tương Dực were assassinated. After the young Lê Chiêu Tông was enthroned in 1516, court rivalries and the rebellion of Trần Cao brought the country to civil war, as the warlords Nguyễn Hoàng Dụ, Trịnh Duy Sản, Nguyễn Kính and Trần Cao fought for power until 1520.

Leading the forces loyal to Lê Chiêu Tông, Mạc Đăng Dung defeated the warlords and grew strong enough to force the emperor to abdicate in 1522 in favour of Lê Cung Hoàng. Lê Chiêu Tông fled to Thanh Hóa with the warlord Trịnh Tuy and fought on until he was captured in 1526. In 1527 Mạc Đăng Dung had both emperors killed and proclaimed himself emperor under the name Minh Đức. He forced Lê officials to recognise him and murdered the Lê family members left in the north; some officials killed themselves rather than accept him, and others fled south to the resistance.

Through submissive behaviour and bribery he won temporary recognition from the Ming in 1528, and in 1529 he abdicated in favour of his son Mạc Đăng Doanh, living on as retired emperor. Nguyễn Kim and his son-in-law Trịnh Kiểm led a new rising, and in 1533 Nguyễn Kim installed Lê Trang Tông, a son of Lê Chiêu Tông, from Thanh Hóa; Mạc Đăng Doanh lost the provinces south of the Red River. A Chinese delegation then judged the usurpation unjustified, and in 1537 the Ming sent a large army. That summer Mạc Đăng Doanh died, and his father took the throne again.

Faced in 1540 with 110,000 Ming troops ready to invade from Guangxi, Mạc Đăng Dung accepted harsh terms: he crawled barefoot before the Chinese, gave up land and tax registers, and saw his realm downgraded from a country to a chieftaincy. He died on 22 August 1541, and de facto power passed to his grandson Mạc Hiến Tông. Later Vietnamese historians questioned the legitimacy of his reign; the Mạc held the north while the Lê, backed by the Trịnh and Nguyễn lords, held the south.
mac-giolla-phadraig: The name, in Old Irish Mac Gilla Pátraic, means son of the devotee of Patrick. Giolla Phádraig first appears in the annals at the end of the 10th century in connection with the Christianized Uí Ímair dynasty of Waterford, and, probably through intermarriage, it came to be borne by the leading medieval branch of the Dál Birn, the ruling lineage of neighbouring Osraige; some scholars suspect a Norse influence on the name. It was adopted by the descendants of Gilla Patráic mac Donnchada, king of Osraige from 976 to 996.

A genealogy of Domnall mac Donnchada mac Gilla Patric, preserved in the Bodleian Library as MS Rawlinson B 502, traces the dynasty back to Óengus Osrithe, who supposedly flourished in the first or second century, and further back to Noah, which scholars regard as an attachment of the accounts in Genesis to native tradition. Another early Ossorian genealogy is found in the Book of Leinster.

Donnchad mac Gilla Pátraic, son of the dynasty's namesake, was king of Osraige from 1003 to 1039 and also king of Leinster from 1033 to 1039, and he was the first king to bear the surname. When the ruling chief of Upper Ossory submitted to Henry VIII, he took the anglicised name Fitz-Patrick, and most of the clan followed. His successors held the title of Baron Upper Ossory until the seventh baron was attainted on 11 May 1691 and the barony forfeited. In the 18th century John FitzPatrick was created 1st Earl of Upper Ossory, and in the 19th John FitzPatrick, a Liberal politician, became 1st Baron Castletown.

Fitzpatrick arms carry a white saltire on a black field, with a lion and dragon crest; some bear the French augmentation of three fleurs-de-lis, a gift of Henri II to the second Baron Upper Ossory while he served as ambassador for Edward VI. Places linked with the family include Jerpoint Abbey, Aghaboe Abbey, Gowran, Grangefertagh, Ballaghmore Castle and Cullahill Castle. In April 2004 a ground-penetrating radar survey found what were probably the foundations of the twelfth-century cathedral of the diocese of Ossory and a very large structure, possibly a royal Mac Giolla Phádraig palace.
mac-thien-tu: Mạc Thiên Tứ, also known as Mạc Thiên Tích or Mạc Tông, was the eldest son of Mạc Cửu and a Vietnamese woman from Biên Hòa. The Veritable Records of the Qing dynasty call him Mo Shilin. After his father's death the Nguyễn lord gave him the title of Tổng binh of Hà Tiên and the noble title Marquess Tông Đức. In a letter of 1742 to the Tokugawa shogunate, written in Khmer, he styled himself king of Cambodia.

His rule is remembered as the golden age of Hà Tiên. He set up a regular bureaucracy, enlarged the army, and built castles and business streets, and the town became the trade centre of the Mekong Delta and the best-known port of the Gulf of Siam. He built many schools, treated all religions evenhandedly, and allowed the French priest Pierre Pigneau de Behaine to preach. Vietnamese sources record that in 1739 he defeated a Cambodian invasion, after which Hà Tiên was free of Cambodia.

In Cambodian affairs he adopted the prince Ang Ton, escorted him home and crowned him king as Outey II, receiving in return Hương Úc, Cần Bột, Trực Sâm, Sài Mạt and Linh Quỳnh. After the second fall of Ayutthaya he sheltered the Siamese prince Chao Chui, refused to hand him to Taksin, sent a fleet against Chantaburi in 1769 and told Qing officials that Taksin was a usurper. In 1771 Taksin took Hà Tiên and he fled to Gia Định, returning two years later with the Nguyễn lord's help.

When the Tây Sơn defeated Nguyễn Phúc Thuần, who was executed in 1777, Tứ refused to surrender to Nguyễn Huệ and fled by way of Phú Quốc to Siam, where Taksin received him and gave him the title Phraya Rachasethi Yuan. In 1780 Taksin imprisoned him, according to Vietnamese records because of a letter forged by Nguyễn Huệ, according to Thai records because he planned to flee to Hà Tiên. He killed himself in prison, and two of his sons and his wife were executed. Three other sons were hidden and later lived in Bangkok, and in 1789 his grandson Mạc Công Bính brought his body back to Hà Tiên for burial.
macario-sakay: Macario Sakay y de León was born along Tabora Street in Tondo, Manila. He first worked as an apprentice in a kalesa, or carriage, workshop, and was also a tailor and a stage actor in plays such as Principe Baldovino and Doce Pares de Francia. He joined the Katipunan in 1894 and fought beside Andrés Bonifacio against the Spanish. Early in the Philippine–American War he was jailed for seditious activities and later released under an amnesty.

Sakay helped found the Partido Nacionalista, which sought independence by legal means, but when the Philippine Commission passed the Sedition Law forbidding propaganda for independence he took up arms again. Resistance had not ended with the capture of General Emilio Aguinaldo: Sakay declared himself Supreme President of the Tagalog Republic, which he said included all the islands from Luzon to Mindanao, and wrote a constitution under which supporters of the enemy were to be punished with exile, imprisonment or death. From May 1902 his men carried on guerrilla raids for five years.

His presidential and military orders survive from 1903. Military circular No. 7, of 19 June 1903, set out an army of squads, companies of 117 men and battalions of 801, though his Second Manifesto of 5 April 1904 said its strength could not be known. To obtain weapons he offered military rank to citizens who handed in firearms, a lieutenancy for 10 to 15. According to General León Villafuerte, Sakay's and allied forces planned to kidnap Alice Roosevelt Longworth, daughter of President Theodore Roosevelt, but she postponed her trip.

The labour leader Dominador Gómez, authorised by Governor-General Henry Clay Ide, persuaded Sakay that his resistance was delaying a Filipino national assembly. Sakay came down from the mountains on promises of amnesty, but at a party in Cavite he and his lieutenants were disarmed and arrested. Tried for bandolerismo under the Brigandage Act of 1902, he was hanged on 13 September 1907, declaring that his men were not bandits but revolutionaries. A statue of him stands at Plaza Morga in Tondo, and a camp in Los Baños bears his name.
macarius-metropolitan-of-moscow: Macarius was born in the region around Moscow; his secular name is thought to have been Mikhail. In the late 15th century he became a monk at the St. Paphnutius Monastery in Borovsk, where he served as reader, deacon and priest and learned icon painting, and he supported Joseph Volotsky and his disciples. In 1523 Metropolitan Daniel made him archimandrite of a monastery in Mozhaisk, where he came to know Grand Prince Vasili III, whose divorce from Solomonia Saburova and second marriage to Elena Glinskaya he supported.

Appointed archbishop of Novgorod in 1526, he followed pro-Muscovite policies and in 1533 and 1535 sent the monk Ilya and others as missionaries to the Finno-Ugric peoples along the Neva, Lakes Ladoga and Onega and into the Kola Peninsula. In 1541 he and his companions finished the first edition of the Great Menaion Reader, twelve volumes arranged by month; further editions followed in 1552 and 1554. With the support of Prince Andrey Shuisky he was elected metropolitan on 16 March 1542.

His independence brought attempts to remove him during Ivan IV's minority, and in 1544 he escaped the fire in the Moscow Kremlin. He took part in removing the Glinskys from government, blessed Ivan's marriage to Anastasia Zakharyina-Yuriyeva, and at the zemsky sobors of 1547, 1549 and 1550 urged conciliation between boyar factions. At his synods 39 all-Russian saints were canonised. He blessed the army before the Kazan campaign of 1552, supported heresy charges against Matvei Bashkin, starets Artemiy and Feodosiy Kosoy at the councils of 1553–1555, and conducted diplomatic business when the tsar was away.

Late in life Macarius withdrew from affairs of state, supervising the Stepennaya kniga, which traced Ivan's lineage to a fictitious brother of Augustus named Prus, supporting Ivan Fyodorov's printing and renovating icons. He died on 12 January 1563 and was buried in the Cathedral of the Dormition of the Moscow Kremlin. The Russian Orthodox Church canonised him in 1988, though his name appears in lists of saints from the 18th century.
macau: Macau lies on China's southern coast, 60 km west of Hong Kong, on the south shore of Zhongshan Island on the western side of the Pearl River estuary. It consists of the Macau Peninsula, Taipa, Coloane and the Cotai reclamation zone between them. The peninsula was originally a separate island with hilly terrain that became a tombolo as a sandbar formed, and natural sedimentation and land reclamation have enlarged it. The land area grew from 10.28 square kilometres in the late 19th century to 32.9 square kilometres in 2018.

During the Qin dynasty (221–206 BCE) the region came under Panyu County, Nanhai Commandery, and it is first known to have been settled in the Han dynasty. In 1152, under the Song, it fell under the new Xiangshan County. In 1277 about 50,000 refugees fleeing the Mongol conquest of China settled on the coast. The earliest written record of the name, A Ma Gang, is in a letter of 20 November 1555. It refers to the sea goddess Matsu, or A-Ma, whose temple the local people took the Portuguese to be asking about when they gave the name Ma Kok.

The explorer Jorge Álvares, the first European to reach China by sea, arrived in 1513. Portuguese merchants set up a trading post at Tamão, now Tuen Mun, but after their expulsion in 1521 the Ming and Portuguese navies clashed. Portugal lost two ships at the Battle of Tamão in 1521 and two more at the Battle of Sincouwaan; later defeats came at Shuangyu in 1548 and near Dongshan County in 1549. Merchants kept trying to settle on the Pearl River estuary and finally settled at Macau.

The Ming dynasty first leased the territory to Portugal as a trading post in 1557. Portugal paid an annual rent and administered it under Chinese sovereignty until 1887, when the Sino-Portuguese Treaty of Peking gave it perpetual colonial rights. Portuguese rule lasted until the handover to China in 1999. The Sino-Portuguese Joint Declaration provided for economic and administrative continuity, and the Basic Law of Macao, under the principle of one country, two systems, serves as the regional constitution.

Macau is a special administrative region of China, with a population of about 720,000 and one of the highest densities in the world. Its economy rests largely on casino gaming and tourism. More than four centuries of Chinese and Portuguese contact have left a mixed culture, with Macanese people of mixed Portuguese ancestry, and a downtown that blends Portuguese, French, English, Italian and Chinese architecture. The historic centre was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
macbeth-king-of-scotland: Little is known of Macbeth's early life. He was the son of Findláech of Moray, who had been killed by Gille Coemgáin, and may have been a grandson of Malcolm II, presumably through the king's daughter Donada. His name, Mac Bethad, means son of life, and implies a righteous or religious man. When Cnut the Great came north in 1031 to accept the submission of Malcolm II, Macbeth also submitted to him.

He became Mormaer of Moray, a semi-autonomous province, in 1032, and was probably responsible for the death of Gille Coemgáin. He then married Gille Coemgáin's widow, Gruoch, who may herself have had a claim to the throne. They had no children together, and Macbeth accepted her son Lulach as his heir.

Duncan I was acclaimed king of Alba on 30 November 1034, apparently without opposition. In 1039 the Northumbrians attacked Strathclyde and a retaliatory raid by Duncan against Durham ended in disaster. The next year he led an army into Moray, apparently on a punitive expedition, and was killed in action at Bothnagowan, near Elgin, by the men of Moray led by Macbeth, probably on 14 August 1040. Macbeth became king and no resistance to his accession is known.

In 1045 Duncan's father Crínán of Dunkeld was killed in a battle between two Scottish armies, and Duncan's brother Maldred is believed to have died there too, fighting Macbeth in defence of Duncan's young son Máel Coluim, later Malcolm III. Marianus Scotus records that Macbeth made a pilgrimage to Rome in 1050 and gave money to the poor as if it were seed.

In 1052 he received Norman exiles from England at his court. In 1054 Siward, Earl of Northumbria, led a very large invasion of Scotland. The Annals of Ulster report 3,000 Scots and 1,500 English dead in the bloody battle at Dunsinane. Macbeth did not survive the English invasion for long: he was defeated and mortally wounded or killed by the future Malcolm III at Lumphanan in 1057. The Prophecy of Berchán says he died at Scone some days later. His stepson Lulach was installed as king but was soon killed by Malcolm.

Unlike later writers, no near-contemporary source calls Macbeth a tyrant. The Duan Albanach calls him Mac Bethad of fame, and the Prophecy of Berchán calls him the generous king of Fortriu. His life had moved far towards legend by the end of the 14th century, when John of Fordun and Andrew of Wyntoun wrote. William Shakespeare's tragedy, probably first performed in 1606 and based on Holinshed's Chronicles, is not historically accurate. A likely reason for its unflattering portrait is that James VI and I descended from Malcolm III, while Macbeth's line died out with Lulach.
maccabean-revolt: Alexander the Great's Macedonian forces conquered the Levant in 333 and 332 BCE. Judea passed to Ptolemaic Egypt in 302 and 301 BCE and was then conquered by the Seleucid Empire in campaigns between 235 and 198 BCE. Under both dynasties many Jews, especially in the upper class, learned Greek, and many adopted a Greek name beside a Hebrew one.

In 168 BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes began a campaign of repression against the Jewish religion. His reasons are not entirely clear, but he seems to have mistaken a conflict within the Jewish priesthood for a full rebellion. Jewish practices were banned, Jerusalem was placed under direct Seleucid control and the Temple became the site of a mixed pagan and Jewish cult.

In 167 BCE a rural priest of the Hasmonean family, Mattathias of Modein, refused to sacrifice at a new altar there, killed a Jew who stepped forward to do so and the Greek officer sent to enforce it, and fled to the hills with his five sons. After his death his son Judas Maccabeus led a band that grew into an army. It raided the countryside, destroyed Greek altars and attacked Hellenized Jews.

In 164 BCE the rebels captured Jerusalem. The cleansing of the Temple and rededication of the altar on 25 Kislev is the origin of Hanukkah. Judas died in 160 BCE at the Battle of Elasa against the Seleucid general Bacchides. His brother Jonathan Apphus kept a rival government in the countryside, and Seleucid civil wars let him bargain: Alexander Balas made Jonathan high priest.

In 141 BCE Simon Thassi expelled the Greek garrison from the citadel in Jerusalem, and an alliance with the Roman Republic helped guarantee independence. When Antiochus VII besieged Jerusalem in 134 BCE, John Hyrcanus paid a ransom and the Seleucids left. After Antiochus VII died in 129 BCE the Hasmoneans paid no more tribute, and Hyrcanus's son Aristobulus I took the title of king.

The main sources, 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees, favour the Maccabees and present the war as a divinely sanctioned struggle. A later view, popularised by Elias Bickerman in 1937, holds that it was also a civil war between traditionalist Jews in the countryside and Hellenized Jews in the cities.
maccabees: Maccabee was a personal epithet of Judas Maccabeus, and the name is often used for the whole Hasmonean dynasty, though strictly it refers to Judas and his brothers, since later generations were not his direct descendants. One explanation derives it from the Aramaic maqqəḇa, the hammer, for his ferocity in battle. The traditional Jewish explanation reads it as an acronym of the verse of Exodus 15:11, the battle cry of the Maccabees.

In the 2nd century BCE Judea lay between the Ptolemaic Kingdom and the Seleucid Empire and fell to the Seleucids around 197 BCE. Some Hellenizing Jews, mainly of the urban upper class, wished to adopt a Greek way of life. When Antiochus IV Epiphanes took power in 175 BCE the office of high priest became a matter of bribery between Jason and Menelaus, and in 168 BCE Antiochus pillaged the Temple. According to 1 Maccabees he then banned Jewish practices, including circumcision and the sabbath. Most modern scholars see a civil war between traditionalists and Hellenizers that Seleucid intervention turned into a revolt.

In the narrative of 1 Maccabees, Mattathias the Hasmonean, a rural priest from Modi'in, started the revolt by refusing to worship the Greek gods. He and his five sons fled to the wilderness of Judah. After he died in 166 BCE his son Judas led a guerrilla war, entered Jerusalem, ritually cleansed the Temple and restored traditional worship, an event marked at Hanukkah. Judas was killed in battle in 160 BCE and was succeeded as army commander by his brother Jonathan, who was already high priest.

Jonathan was assassinated in 142 BCE by Diodotus Tryphon, and the last remaining son of Mattathias, Simon, was recognised in 140 BCE by an assembly as high priest, military commander and ruler. Simon was murdered in 134 BCE by his son-in-law Ptolemy, and his son John Hyrcanus I succeeded him. Independent Hasmonean rule lasted until 63 BCE, when the Roman general Pompeius intervened in a Hasmonean civil war. The dynasty ended in 37 BCE when Herod the Great became king.

The story is told in the books of First and Second Maccabees. They are not part of the Tanakh but belong to the Septuagint, and the Catholic and Orthodox churches count them as deuterocanonical, while most Protestants regard them as apocryphal. The miracle of the oil lasting eight days is first described in the Talmud, about 600 years after the events. Christians also venerate the Holy Maccabean Martyrs, seven brothers, their mother and their teacher, who are not said to belong to the family; their feast day is 1 August.
macdonnells-of-antrim: The family descends from John Mor MacDonald, chief of the Clan MacDonald of Dunnyveg and second son of Good John of Islay, Lord of the Isles, by his second marriage to Princess Margaret Stewart, daughter of King Robert II of Scotland. John Mor married Margery Byset, daughter of the Mac Eoin Bissett, Lord of the Glens of Antrim. The family already held Dunnyvaig Castle on the Isle of Islay and lands in Kintyre.

A century and a half later the MacDonnells claimed that Margery's dowry had included the lordship of the Glens, but the Mac Eoin Bissetts kept it into the 16th century. After the last known Mac Eoin Bissett was killed in 1522, fighting for the O'Neills against the O'Donnells, the MacDonnells made gains in the region and used the old marriage to claim the Bissett lordship. The Antrim line became a branch of its own in 1558, when Sorley Boy MacDonnell obtained the lordship in Ireland from James MacDonald, 6th chief of Dunnyveg.

In Scotland John Mor was assassinated by James Campbell in 1427, and his son Donald Balloch MacDonald led the clan to victory at the first Battle of Inverlochy in 1431. In Ireland Sorley Boy resisted the efforts of Shane O'Neill and the English crown to expel the family, fighting Shane at the Battle of Glentasie in 1565. In 1583 he turned on his allies of the Clan McQuillan, and Edward McQuillan's death at the Battle of Aura ended McQuillan rule over the Route and Dunluce Castle. His eldest son Alaster was killed in 1585 and his head set on a spike at Dublin.

In the 17th century Randal MacDonnell, a friend and courtier of King Charles I, offered to lead an expedition against the Scottish Covenanters. A force under Alasdair MacColla sailed from Waterford to Scotland, joined the Marquess of Montrose and defeated Clan Campbell at the Battle of Inverlochy, though the royalist defeat in England undid these gains. MacDonnell troops later opposed the Cromwellian invasion of Ireland and supported King James II in the Williamite War in Ireland.

Dunluce Castle became the seat of the Earl of Antrim in Ireland, while Dunnyvaig Castle was his seat in Scotland. The surname is now mostly spelled McDonnell, and many McConnells belong to the same family, since that form follows the Gaelic pronunciation of Mac Domhnaill.
macedonia-region: Macedonia is a geographical and historical region of the Balkan Peninsula in Southeast Europe. In the 19th century the name was revived for a region bounded by Mount Olympus, the Pindus range, the mountains Shar and Osogovo, the western Rhodopes, the lower course of the river Mesta and the Aegean Sea. The ancient kingdom of Macedonia, which gave the region its name, lay before the expansion of Philip II within the central and western parts of what is now Greek Macedonia.

The earliest known settlements, such as Nea Nikomedeia in Imathia, date back about 9,000 years. Rome ended Macedonian sovereignty in the 2nd century BCE: Philip V was defeated in the Second Macedonian War, and Perseus lost his kingdom in the Third. The land was divided into four districts and annexed as a Roman province in 146 BCE.

From the beginning of the 6th century Slavic tribes raided the Byzantine Balkan provinces, and great parts of Macedonia came to be controlled by Slavic-speaking communities, though Thessaloniki held out. The parts ruled by the First Bulgarian Empire in the 9th and 10th centuries were taken into the Byzantine Empire in 1018. After the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Maritsa in 1371 most of Macedonia accepted vassalage, and the Ottomans took Thessalonica in 1430. The region remained Ottoman for nearly 500 years and became multicultural, with Greeks, Bulgarians, Turks, Albanians, Jews and Aromanians among its peoples.

In the 19th century Greece, Serbia and Bulgaria contested the region, and the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization organised the Ilinden-Preobrazhenie Uprising in 1903. In the First Balkan War, begun in August 1912, Greek forces entered Thessalonica first. In the Second World War about 60,000 Jews from Thessaloniki were deported to extermination camps in occupied Poland.

The modern region at its maximum extent spans the largest part of Northern Greece, known as Greek Macedonia, all of North Macedonia, a large part of southwestern Bulgaria, known as Pirin Macedonia, and small parts of Albania, Serbia and Kosovo. Greek Macedonia's largest city, Thessaloniki, is the second largest in Greece.
macedonia-roman-province: After the Third Macedonian War Rome abolished the Macedonian monarchy and divided the country into four client republics, called merides, with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia. They belonged to a federal league, the League of the Macedonians, and both the merides and the league continued as parts of the province. Its northern border notionally ran from Lissus on the Adriatic east to the Hebrus river, but was loosely defined: Cicero claimed that for the governors of Macedonia the borders were always those marked by swords and shields.

The Via Egnatia, begun by Gnaeus Egnatius, ran from Dyrrhachium on the Adriatic across the Pindus mountains and through Macedonia to Thessalonica and on to Cypsela on the Hebrus. This stretch was finished by 120 BCE. It followed an older route but was a more solid, level road, three to six metres wide, and its eastern end was later extended to Byzantium.

In the first decades the Romans fought nearly constant campaigns against the Dardani, the Thracians and above all the Scordisci, a Celtic people who first invaded in the Fourth Macedonian War. Two pretenders also tried to restore the kingdom. In 114 BCE Gaius Porcius Cato invaded the Scordisci but was defeated and nearly his whole army was killed. After the Mithridatic Wars the governors were consuls or proconsuls, often holding command for several years, and Gaius Scribonius Curio became the first Roman commander to lead an army to the Danube.

Macedonia was a main arena of the civil wars. Pompey and about two hundred senators withdrew to it in 49 BCE and set up a Senate in exile at Thessalonica. Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus in August 48 BCE, and in 42 BCE Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius at Philippi. Six Roman colonies were then founded for veterans, among them Cassandrea, Philippi, Dium and Pella.

Under Augustus the northern lands became the provinces of Moesia, Dalmatia and Pannonia, and the territories south of Thermopylae became Achaia. Macedonia lost much of its military role but stayed important for supplies and manpower. Greek remained the main language, with Latin used officially and in the colonies, and there were substantial Christian communities by the mid-first century CE. Around 293 CE Diocletian's reforms split the province into smaller units, including Macedonia Prima, governed from Thessalonica, and Macedonia Salutaris, with its capital at Stobi. The provincial system faded until the themes replaced it in the mid-seventh century.
macedonian-dynasty: The dynasty is named after its founder, Basil I the Macedonian, who came from the theme of Macedonia in the region of Thrace, and it followed the Amorian dynasty. Its ethnic origin is unknown and has been debated. During Basil's reign an elaborate genealogy was produced that claimed his ancestors were not mere peasants, as everyone believed, but descendants of the Arsacid kings of Armenia, of Alexander the Great and of Constantine the Great.

Some Persian writers, such as Hamza al-Isfahani and al-Tabari, called Basil a Saqlabi, a term usually denoting Slavs but which can mean the inhabitants of the region between Constantinople and Bulgaria. Claims have therefore been made for Armenian, Slavonic or mixed descent. The author of the only dedicated English biography of Basil concludes that his origins cannot be established with certainty, though he relied on the support of Armenians in prominent positions.

Basil I ruled from 867 to 886 and married Eudokia Ingerina, mistress of Michael III; he died in a hunting accident. His son Leo VI the Wise, possibly the natural son of Michael III, caused a church crisis by his fourth marriage, to Zoe Karbonopsina, who ruled as regent for their son Constantine VII from 914 to 919. Romanos I Lekapenos staged a coup in 919 and became senior emperor in 920, until he was deposed and exiled in 944. Constantine VII, born in the purple, ruled again from 945 to 959.

After Romanos II (959–963) came two successful generals: Nikephoros II Phokas (963–969), who was assassinated, and John I Tzimiskes (969–976), the regents for Basil II. Basil II, the Bulgar-slayer, reigned from 976 to 1025. His brother Constantine VIII followed as sole emperor until 1028, and then Constantine's daughter Zoe ruled until 1050 with a succession of husbands: Romanos III Argyros, who was murdered, Michael IV the Paphlagonian and Constantine IX Monomachos.

Michael V the Caulker, Zoe's adopted son, reigned in 1041–1042. Zoe's sister Theodora ruled jointly with her in 1042 and alone from 1055 to 1056. Michael VI, chosen by Theodora, was a non-dynastic ruler who was deposed and entered a monastery.

Under the dynasty the Byzantine state reached its largest extent since the early Muslim conquests, and the Macedonian Renaissance in letters and arts began. The dynasty's family ties reached beyond the empire: Basil's daughter Anna was betrothed to Louis the Blind, and Basil II's sister Anna Porphyrogeneta married Vladimir I of Kiev.
macedonian-front: After Austria-Hungary's attack on Serbia in August 1914 failed, Bulgaria's attitude became decisive in the Balkans. Bulgaria had fought Serbia in 1885 and in the Second Balkan War of 1913, and felt that Serbia had seized land that was rightfully Bulgarian. The Allies could offer only small concessions, whereas the Central Powers promised most of what Bulgaria claimed. After the Allied defeat at Gallipoli and the Russian defeat at Gorlice-Tarnów, King Ferdinand signed a treaty with Germany, and on 21 September 1915 Bulgaria began to mobilise. Two Bulgarian armies attacked on 15 October, cutting the Serbian army off from the Greek border, and only about 125,000 Serbian soldiers reached the Adriatic coast after a retreat through Montenegro and Albania.

The first Allied troops, two divisions sent from Gallipoli under the French commander Maurice Sarrail, landed at Salonika on 5 October 1915, too late to help Serbia. Pushed back by the Bulgarians, they were all back in Greece by 12 December and entrenched around Thessaloniki, earning the mocking name Gardeners of Salonika. The Serbian army, rested on Corfu, was brought to the front by the French. Greece was officially neutral, but King Constantine I was pro-German and Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos pro-Allied. After the Bulgarian offensive of August 1916 took Greek territory east of the Struma, Venizelist officers staged a coup, and Greece had two governments, a division known as the National Schism.

By spring 1917 the Allied Army of the Orient had grown to 24 divisions, but its April offensive failed. In June Constantine was exiled and Greece declared war on the Central Powers. The Greek army, a third of the Allied force, took part in the Battle of Skra-di-Legen on 30 May 1918.

General Franchet d'Espèrey won agreement for a grand offensive in September 1918. After the bombardment for the Battle of Dobro Pole began on 14 September, the French and Serbians attacked and captured their objective the next day, while the Greeks and the British were stopped at Doiran on 18 September. Some Bulgarian units then surrendered positions without a fight and the Bulgarian command ordered a retreat.

Mutinous Bulgarian troops gathered at Radomir, and on 27 September leaders of the Bulgarian Agrarian National Union proclaimed a republic. Bulgaria was granted the Armistice of Salonica on 29 September, in force from noon on 30 September, and Ferdinand I abdicated on 3 October. Winston Churchill, in The World Crisis, saw the defeat of Bulgaria as the start of events that led to Germany's defeat in November 1918.
macehualtin: Most mācēhualtin were rural farmers, and on their plots they built small dams and terraces to raise their yields, projects probably organised by local communities rather than by the state. The Aztecs held a locative view of the world in which everyone had a correct place: the pipiltin, the nobles, were thought made by the gods to rule, and the commoners to work for the good of society. Rituals and teachings reinforced this, as did separate sets of laws for commoners and nobles, which punished the nobility more harshly for a comparable offence.

Mobility, though uncommon, existed before Moctezuma II. Commoners who rose through military deeds were called yāōtequihuah, while nobles who fell in rank were pillaquīztīltin. Commoners could also become slaves or sell their children into slavery. Every boy received some military instruction, beginning with his father at about three years of age. Taking captives marked a man's passage to full warrior status, and failing to do so later in life brought dishonour, a heavier social blow for nobles than for commoners, though less damaging materially.

At the telpochcalli, the House of Youths, boys and girls were taught separately. Young men learned warfare and did hard physical labour, such as hauling ever larger loads of firewood as a test of strength, while young women attended the cuicalco, the House of Song, where they learned ritual dance and song. Gender divisions began at birth: a boy's umbilical cord was given to warriors to bury on fields where battles might be fought, while a girl's was buried near the hearth.

After the Spanish conquest the Nahuatl word mācēhualli was adopted into colonial Spanish as macehual. It was used all over New Spain as a synonym for commoner, for subject and for native, and so outlived the Aztec order of ranks in which it had named the farmers who worked the lands of the calpolli.
machado-de-assis: Joaquim Maria Machado de Assis was born on 21 June 1839 in Rio de Janeiro, then the capital of the Empire of Brazil. His father, Francisco José de Assis, was a wall painter and the son of freed slaves; his mother, Maria Leopoldina da Câmara Machado, was a Portuguese washerwoman from the Azores. He was born in a country house owned by a senator's widow, who protected his parents and became his godmother. His mother died when he was ten.

He barely studied in public schools and never attended university, learning French from an immigrant baker and Latin from a priest he met while serving at mass. His first poem, Ela, was published on 12 January 1855, when he was fifteen, and the next year he became a typographer's apprentice at the Imprensa Oficial.

In 1858 Francisco Otaviano hired him as a proofreader at the Correio Mercantil. The writer José de Alencar, a friend, taught him English, and he later learned German and, in old age, Greek. Emperor Dom Pedro II hired him as an assistant director of the Diário Oficial in 1867 and knighted him. He married the Portuguese Carolina Augusta Xavier de Novais on 12 November 1869; her family disapproved because he was of African descent, and the couple had no children. He rose through the bureaucracy, beginning in the Agriculture Department.

He published the poetry books Falenas in 1870 and Americanas in 1875, but their weak reception made him try other genres, and his romantic novels, among them Helena and Iaiá Garcia, pleased the public but not the critics. Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas, in 1881, brought a sceptical and realistic tone and is widely considered a masterpiece. The overthrow of the monarchy on 15 November 1889 took him by surprise, since he considered himself a liberal monarchist. Quincas Borba followed in 1891, Dom Casmurro in 1899, Esaú e Jacó in 1904 and Memorial de Aires in 1908. In 1893 he published the short story A Missa do Galo.

With fellow writers and intellectuals including Joaquim Nabuco, Machado helped found the Brazilian Academy of Letters in 1897 and was its president until his death. In 1905 he obtained a proper headquarters for it. His wife died on 20 October 1904, and he died on 29 September 1908.

Critics are divided about his writing. Abel Barros Baptista sees an anti-realist who attacks Realism, John Gledson a faithful description of Brazilian reality executed with daring technique, and Roberto Schwarz a prose that exposes the hypocrisies and dysfunction of 19th-century Brazil. His work has been adapted for television, theatre and cinema and translated into many languages, though his books have never sold widely in the English-speaking world.
machanidas: Machanidas served in a band of Tarentine mercenaries in the pay of the Spartan government, perhaps as their leader. The history of Lacedaemon at this time is obscure, and how he gained the tyranny is unknown. He was probably first associated with Pelops, son and successor of Lycurgus on the double throne of Sparta, and he either eclipsed or expelled Lycurgus. Livy calls him the tyrant of the Lacedaemonians. Like his predecessor he had no hereditary or other claim to the crown, but unlike Lycurgus he respected neither the ephors nor the laws and ruled by the swords of his followers.

Argos and the Achaean League found him a restless and relentless neighbour whom they could not resist without the aid of Macedonia, while Rome, anxious in the 11th year of the Second Punic War to keep Philip V of Macedon occupied, used him as an ally. Towards the close of the Aetolian War in 207 BCE, while the Greek states were negotiating peace and the Eleans were preparing the next Olympic festival, he planned an inroad into the sacred territory of Elis. The arrival of the king of Macedon in the Peloponnesus frustrated the plan, and Machanidas withdrew to Sparta.

In the same year, after eight months of preparation, Philopoemen, captain-general of the cavalry of the Achaean League, led the Achaean army against him, and the two armies met between Mantineia and Tegea. In the Battle of Mantinea the Tarentine mercenaries of Machanidas routed those of Philopoemen and chased them from the field, while the Achaeans stood entrenched behind a deep ditch. Machanidas was killed by Philopoemen as he jumped his horse over the ditch. The Achaeans later set up a brass statue at Delphi showing Philopoemen giving Machanidas the death-wound.
machilipatnam: Machilipatnam lies on the south-eastern, or Coromandel, coast of India at the mouth of the River Krishna on the Bay of Bengal, about 60 kilometres from Vijayawada. In the 17th century it was known as Masulipatnam, Masulipatam, Masula and Bandar, the last from the Persian word for port. In ancient times it was also called Maesolia. It is the administrative headquarters of Krishna district.

The town has existed since at least the 3rd century BCE, the Satavahana period, when according to Ptolemy it was known as Maisolos. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea calls it Masalia.
