Sea trade flourished at the port, and the word muslin is derived from the name Maisolos. Muslin was a significant source of income and a favourite of Roman traders, and several Roman coins have been found in excavations of Buddhist towns near the town.

Machilipatnam served as the primary sea port of the Kingdom of Golkonda, an outlet for textiles produced in the Godavari Delta. It was a major source of income for the kingdom and contributed to its prosperity in the 1620s and 1630s. From the 16th century European traders settled there, and in the 17th century it was a major trading port for the Portuguese, British, Dutch and French. It was known for minting copper coins and for exporting diamonds and textiles. By the end of the 17th century the port had fallen into decline, which coincided with the Mughal conquest of Golkonda, though mismanagement before the conquest may also have been a factor.

Salabat Jung, the son of Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, owed his throne to the French East India Company and granted it in return the district of Kondavid, or Guntur, and soon afterwards the remainder of the Circars. The British captured the Circars from the French in 1759 and returned them to the Nizam, but the East India Company kept Masulipatnam, which it had taken in the Siege of Masulipatam. The town became the headquarters of Masulipatnam district, from which the Krishna district was formed in 1859 in Madras state. On 1 November 1864 a giant wave damaged the port, and the cyclone of that year is said to have killed at least 30,000 people.

Machilipatnam is known for its handloom industry and for Machilipatnam Kalamkari, hand-dyed block-painting on cloth, which is carried out at the nearby town of Pedana and has a geographical indication. Boat building and fishing are other local trades. The town has the ruined buildings built by the Europeans who settled there, and it is home to Shia Muslim imambargahs, some more than 600 years old, where Ashura is observed.
machimoi: The earliest use of the word for native Egyptian warriors comes from Herodotus, who visited Egypt during the first Persian domination, the 27th Dynasty of Manetho's list. Since then the term has usually been translated simply as warriors or fighting men; Herodotus also used it for Asiatic troops in Persian service. He claimed that the hermotybies numbered 160,000 and the kalasiries 250,000 soldiers, and that the two groups were told apart by their districts of origin.

Greek writers such as Plato and Diodorus Siculus also report the machimoi in many battles of the Late Period. Pharaoh Apries sent them against Cyrene; after their defeat they proclaimed the general Amasis pharaoh and served him against Apries in 570 BCE. Egyptian machimoi fought at the Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE. Under the 30th Dynasty they were used widely against the Achaemenid Empire: according to Diodorus, Pharaoh Teos sent 80,000 of them on his expedition into the Near East in about 360 or 358 BCE, with his nephew Nakhthorheb, the future Nectanebo II, as their commander, and Nectanebo II later relied on them before the second Persian conquest of Egypt.

Most scholars see the Ptolemaic machimoi as direct successors of the Late Period warriors. Their name appears only in documents under the Ptolemies, whereas in the Late Period it occurs only in Greek literary works. The earliest Ptolemaic mention, from 261 BCE under Ptolemy II Philadelphus, concerns guard duty. They are thought to have put growing social pressure on the Ptolemies and to have taken part in various rebellions and uprisings.

Christelle Fischer-Bovet's 2013 paper challenged most of Herodotus' account. She pointed out that the ancient Egyptians had no comparable caste system and that his numbers of men and of land were almost certainly unsustainable, suggesting that he had merged professional officers with a militia of commoners called up when needed and given the whole group a status like that of the Spartiates. She also found Greek machimoi in Ptolemaic documents, so the term described a military role, as with the pike-bearing machimoi epilektoi and the mounted machimoi hippeis, or the size of a land grant, as with a pentarouros holding five arourai, rather than an ethnic group.
machu-picchu: Machu Picchu stands in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru, on a narrow saddle between two peaks, Machu Picchu and Huayna Picchu, at about 2,430 metres. It lies some 80 kilometres north-west of Cusco and more than 1,000 metres lower than the Inca capital, so its climate was milder. The Urubamba River bends round the site on three sides, and cliffs drop 450 metres to the water. A study of 2021 suggests that its builders called it Huayna Picchu, or simply Picchu.

The dating is debated. Models based on John H. Rowe's reconstruction of the reign of Pachacuti put the start of building around 1450, while radiocarbon measurements on human remains, reported in a 2021 study led by Richard L. Burger, indicate occupation from about 1420 to 1530. Archaeologists generally hold that Pachacuti ordered the royal estate after conquering the middle and lower Urubamba, as part of a programme of royal estates along the river, though no contemporary written record confirms it.

The estate seems to have been a seasonal retreat. About 750 people are estimated to have lived there, most of them permanent support staff known as yanaconas, with religious specialists and temporary workers. The site was abandoned in the mid-16th century, around the time of the Spanish conquest, probably because Inca rule collapsed and disease followed European contact; smallpox may have killed most of its inhabitants before the conquistadors arrived.

The forest overgrew the ruins, and few outside the area knew of them. The Peruvian explorer Agustín Lizárraga reached the site in the early 20th century, but the American historian Hiram Bingham III brought it to international attention in 1911.

The citadel is built in the classical Inca style, with finely worked dry-stone walls. About 200 buildings stand on parallel terraces round a central square, divided into an agricultural sector and an urban sector with an upper and a lower town. Its main structures include the Temple of the Sun, the Temple of the Three Windows and the Intihuatana stone. Peru declared a Historic Sanctuary there in 1981, and UNESCO listed Machu Picchu as a World Heritage Site in 1983.
machynlleth: Machynlleth is a market town, community and electoral ward in Powys, within the historic boundaries of Montgomeryshire. It lies in the Dyfi Valley at the intersection of the A487 and A489 roads. The name derives from ma, meaning field or plain, and Cynllaith, a personal name. Radiocarbon dating in the late 1990s showed that copper was mined in the Early Bronze Age within a mile of the town centre. The Romans built a fort at Cefn Caer, near Pennal, and are reputed to have had another, called Maglona, at Machynlleth.

One of the earliest written references is the royal charter of 1291 in which Edward I granted Owen de la Pole, Lord of Powys, a market every Wednesday and two fairs a year. The market and fair thrived, and in 1613 other towns complained that they were damaging their cloth trade. The Dyfi Bridge was first mentioned in 1533. In 1404 Owain Glyndŵr, who rebelled against the English in the reign of Henry IV, held a parliament at Machynlleth and was crowned Prince of Wales near the Parliament House, one of three medieval houses in the town, in the presence of foreign envoys.

For this the town claims to be the ancient capital of Wales, although it has never had official recognition as one. Glyndŵr held his last parliament at nearby Pennal. By local tradition the Royal House held the Welsh ally of the English kings Dafydd Gam prisoner from 1404 to 1412.

In the English Civil War Rowland Pugh of Mathafarn supported the Royalist side and ambushed a Parliamentarian force under Sir Thomas Myddleton on 2 November 1644; on 29 November Myddleton burned Mathafarn and several houses in the town. In the nineteenth century Plas Machynlleth was the home of the Londonderry family, whose townspeople-funded clock tower, designed by Henry Kennedy of Bangor, became the symbol of the town. The Corris Railway carried slate from 1859 to 1948, and Laura Ashley opened her first shop in the town in 1961.

Machynlleth has a population of 2,098. Welsh is spoken alongside English: in the 2021 Census 62 per cent of residents had some knowledge of it. The town hosted the National Eisteddfod in 1937 and 1981 and applied unsuccessfully for city status in 2000 and 2002. It lies in the Dyfi Biosphere, designated by UNESCO in 2009, and near the Centre for Alternative Technology, and it is home to MoMA Wales, an arts centre that began in 1986 in an old chapel.
maciej-sulkiewicz: Sulkiewicz was born on 20 June 1865 to parents of Lipka Tatar origin. He joined the Imperial Russian Army in 1883 and became an officer in 1886. From 1894 to 1905 he served in the Odessa Military District, where he was chief of staff at the Ochakov Fortress. He was promoted to major general in 1910 and to lieutenant general in 1915.

He took part in the Chinese expedition against the Boxers and in the Russo-Japanese War, in which he fought at the Battle of Mukden with the 8th Army Corps of the 2nd Manchurian Army, commanding the 57th Modlin Infantry Regiment. For his service in the Far East he received the Order of Saint Anna, the Order of Saint Vladimir and the Golden Weapon for Bravery. After the war he stayed in Asian Russia, serving in the Irkutsk Military District.

In World War I he fought on the Romanian Front, and late in 1917 he was involved in creating the 1st Muslim Army Corps while remaining in the service of the front's administration. After the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk between Soviet Russia and the Central Powers, he came to Crimea with the occupying forces of the Central Powers, which drove Bolshevik irregulars out of the peninsula, and headed the Crimean Regional Government formed as an interim government under German occupation. As provisional governor he negotiated with the Ukrainian government over federative relations between mainland Ukraine and Crimea.

When the Central Powers withdrew their troops from Crimea at the end of 1918, Sulkiewicz moved to Azerbaijan and became chief of staff of the armed forces of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic. There he changed his name to Mohammad, and in Azerbaijan he is still known as Suleyman bey and Mammad bey Sulkiewicz. After the Bolshevik invasion of Azerbaijan in 1920 he was executed by the Bolsheviks, on 15 July 1920.
macon: Mâcon lies on the western bank of the river Saône, between Bresse to the east and the Beaujolais hills to the south, about 65 kilometres north of Lyon. It is the southernmost city of the department of Saône-et-Loire. The town controlled access to the present-day Lamartinien Valley, where the southern end of the Côte de Bourgogne joins the first foothills of the Beaujolais hills and opens the way to the plains of the Loire.

The settlement began as an oppidum and river port established by Celts from the Aedui, probably at the start of the 1st century BCE. Known as Matisco, it grew considerably under the Roman Empire, as the large hoard called the Mâcon Treasure shows: it was found in 1764, and its remains are in the British Museum. The town was fortified in the 4th century.

In the Middle Ages Mâcon was the administrative centre of a county belonging to the Duchy of Burgundy, at the end of the bridge over the Saône that led to Bresse, which belonged to the Duchy of Savoy. Its position made it a possible entrance into the kingdom for Swiss or German mercenaries during the French Wars of Religion. On 3 June 1564 Charles IX stopped there during his Royal Tour of France, and was welcomed by Queen Jeanne III of Navarre and 1,500 Huguenots.

In 1790 the Revolutionary government made Mâcon the chef-lieu of the new department of Saône-et-Loire. Austrian troops invaded in 1814 and captured the town again after the Hundred Days. In the Second World War it was the northernmost town of the unoccupied zone between Paris and Lyon; nearly eight hundred German soldiers settled there on 11 November 1942, and it was liberated on 4 September 1944.

Mâcon has about 35,000 residents. Its sights include the Cathedral of Saint-Vincent, the old Saint-Vincent in the town centre, the Hôtel de Senecé, which houses the Lamartine museum, and a town hall finished in 1751. Alphonse de Lamartine was born in the town on 21 October 1790. The vineyards around it, of about 5,000 hectares, grow mostly Chardonnay, and the best-known appellation of the Mâconnais is Pouilly-Fuissé. The Saône gives the town a river port.
macquarie-harbour: Macquarie Harbour is a shallow fjord of about 315 square kilometres in the West Coast region of Tasmania, with an average depth of 15 metres and deeper places up to 50 metres; a reported Aboriginal name for it is Parralaongatek. The Gordon River and the King River, which cuts through the West Coast Range, empty into it. So much fresh water pours in through the narrow exit that the harbour has barometric tides, rising with rain in the mountains around it. A man-made rock wall keeps the entrance channel deep and narrow.

The harbour was named after Major General Lachlan Macquarie, the fifth governor of New South Wales. James Kelly wrote that he reached it in a five-oared whaleboat from Hobart on 28 December 1815, but other accounts differ: T. W. Birch told a commission of inquiry in 1820 that Kelly came by boat from Port Davey, and a letter of Birch's dated the discovery to 26 December 1815. Surveyor-General Oxley of New South Wales battled the seas at the heads in March 1820.

The first settlement was on Sarah Island, named after Birch's wife, chosen for its isolation and harsh climate. The prison held British convicts, among them Irish patriots, and many Aboriginal Tasmanians were detained there. Later the port of Strahan grew up to serve the mining settlements, chiefly Queenstown, and a short-lived port and townsite at Pillinger in Kelly Basin was built by the North Mount Lyell company. Mine waste from the Mount Lyell Mining and Railway Company polluted the Queen and King rivers and the harbour until the company closed in 1994; an estimated 100 million tonnes of tailings went into the Queen River.

Strahan is the departure point for tourism on the west coast, with boats to Hell's Gates, Sarah Island and the lower Gordon River, and the West Coast Wilderness Railway runs along part of the north-eastern shore. Salmon farms, first set up in the 1980s, have brought de-oxygenated zones beneath their pens and concern for the endangered Maugean skate.
macva: Mačva lies on the southern edge of the Pannonian Plain, between the Cer mountain and the Sava river, and a small part of it falls in the province of Vojvodina. It takes its name from a medieval town of Mačva near the Sava, whose site has not been clearly established; it may have stood a few kilometres downriver from Šabac. In the past the region was also called Lower Syrmia, while the lands north of the Sava were Upper Syrmia. The Kitog forest covered part of it until the mid-19th century.

Before the Roman conquest of the first century BCE the region was home to Illyrians and the Celtic Scordisces, and under Roman rule it belonged to the provinces of Moesia and Pannonia. After Roman rule ended in the 5th century it was taken by Sarmatians, Huns, Goths, Gepids, Lombards and Avars, and Slavic tribes settled there in the 6th century. In the 11th century it formed part of the Byzantine Theme of Sirmium.

Under Hungarian rule King Béla IV gave Mačva to the Russian prince Rostislav Mikhailovich. From 1282 to 1316 the Serbian king Stefan Dragutin ruled a Kingdom of Syrmia that included Mačva, with his capitals at Debrc and Belgrade. After Stefan Dečanski defeated Dragutin's son Vladislaus II in 1324, Mačva was disputed between Serbia and Hungary. It later belonged to the Serbian Empire of Stefan Dušan, the Serbian Despotate and, from 1459, the Ottoman Empire, apart from Habsburg rule between 1718 and 1739.

Mačva joined Karađorđe's Serbia between 1804 and 1815 and the autonomous Principality of Serbia in 1817. In the First World War the Austro-Hungarian army occupied it and committed war crimes against Serb civilians. From 1918 it belonged to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia, and after the breakup of Yugoslavia to an independent Serbia.

The region is divided among the municipalities of Šabac, Bogatić and Sremska Mitrovica and has 39 settlements, two of them urban, Šabac and Mačvanska Mitrovica. Šabac, with 51,163 inhabitants, is by far the largest town.
mad-war: The name Mad War was coined by Paul Emile in his Histoire des faicts, gestes et conquestes des roys de France, published in 1581. The conflict followed a long series of struggles between the crown and the great lords of France after the formation of the League of the Public Weal. Besides Louis II of Orléans and Francis II of Brittany, the rebels included René II, Duke of Lorraine, Alain d'Albret, Jean de Châlon, Prince of Orange, and Charles, Count of Angoulême, and they had the support of England, Spain and Austria.

Historians disagree whether the events form a single war. Some call the phase from June 1486 to November 1488 the War of Brittany, and Breton nationalist writers treat it as a Franco-Breton war or even a Breton war of independence.

The States General of Tours refused Louis of Orléans the regency in 1484, and he went to Brittany, asking the pope to annul his marriage so that he could marry Anne of Brittany, the duke's heir. Anne de Beaujeu broke this first revolt mostly by diplomacy and shows of force, and the Peace of Bourges suspended the fighting on 2 November 1485. When war resumed, Louis escaped from Blois on 11 January 1487 and fled again to Brittany, while the royal army subdued Guyenne and the Lord de Candale defeated Alain d'Albret at the Battle of Nontron.

On 20 January 1488 the Parlement of Paris declared the Dukes of Orléans and Brittany rebels, guilty of lèse-majesté. D'Albret joined Francis II with 5,000 men paid for by a subsidy from the court of Spain, Maximilian I of Austria sent 1,500 and the English leader Lord Scales landed more, but the allies were outnumbered and quarrelled over the hand of Anne of Brittany. Under Louis II de la Trémoille the royal army took Fougères and Dinan, and on 28 July 1488 it defeated the Breton forces under Marshal de Rieux and captured Louis of Orléans.

By the Treaty of Sablé of 20 August 1488 Francis acknowledged himself the king's vassal, promised to send away foreign troops and accepted that his daughters could marry only with the king's consent. He died on 9 September 1488. Anne of Brittany's marriage by proxy to Maximilian on 19 December 1490 broke the treaty and war resumed. After Rennes fell in 1491, Anne married Charles VIII on 6 December 1491, a marriage Pope Innocent VIII validated on 15 February 1492.
madagascar: Madagascar covers 592,800 square kilometres and is the world's fourth-largest island and second-largest island country. It split from Africa around 180 million years ago and from the Indian subcontinent approximately 90 million years ago, so that its plants and animals evolved in relative isolation; over 90 per cent of its wildlife is endemic. A narrow, steep escarpment with tropical lowland forest runs along the east coast, and west of it lies a central plateau of terraced, rice-growing valleys between 750 and 1,500 metres high. The highest point is Maromokotro, at 2,876 metres.

Madagascar was first permanently settled during or before the mid-first millennium CE by Austronesian peoples, presumably arriving by outrigger canoe from present-day Indonesia, and scholars are cautious about dates earlier than 250 CE. The first settlers met giant lemurs, elephant birds and Malagasy hippopotamuses, which later became extinct through hunting and habitat destruction. Arab traders reached the island between the 7th and 9th centuries and brought Islam and the Arabic script, adapted as sorabe. Bantu-speaking migrants from south-eastern Africa arrived around the year 1000, and zebu cattle from South India were brought about then.

Until the late 18th century a fragmented set of shifting alliances ruled the island. King Andrianjaka founded Antananarivo as capital of the Imerina Kingdom around 1610 or 1625. From the early 19th century a series of Merina nobles united most of the island as the Kingdom of Madagascar. France's annexation ended the monarchy, and the country became independent in 1960.

Madagascar has had four republics and has been a constitutional democracy since 1992. A political crisis and coup in 2009 led to a long transition, and constitutional governance returned in January 2014. Malagasy and French are the official languages.

The Malagasy form over 90 per cent of the population, divided into 18 ethnic subgroups, of which the Merina of the highlands are the largest at about 26 per cent. The Malagasy language is of Malayo-Polynesian origin, closest to Ma'anyan of Borneo. The valiha, the most emblematic instrument, is a bamboo tube zither carried by early settlers from southern Borneo.
madakari-nayaka-v: The Chitradurga Nayakas had begun as local governors under the Vijayanagara Empire and became effectively independent after that empire lost control of its heartland in the late 16th century. Their kingdom in central Karnataka was organised around Chitradurga Fort, its political and military centre. Madakari, also known as Veera Madakari Nayaka, succeeded Kasturi Rangappa Nayaka II. He is numbered the fifth of his name in the conventional list of the dynasty's rulers, although the numbering of the rulers called Madakari varies between accounts.

His reign fell during the struggle between the expanding Kingdom of Mysore and the Maratha Empire for central Karnataka. Chitradurga's rulers negotiated with the Marathas in the hope that their support would keep the kingdom independent, while at other times Madakari cooperated with Hyder Ali. Hyder Ali's forces clashed with Chitradurga repeatedly in the 1760s and 1770s, and the hill fort, with its successive lines of walls, gateways, storehouses and reservoirs built into the rocky ground, withstood these earlier attacks.

The campaign of 1779 ended Nayaka rule. After the fort was taken the kingdom became a province of Mysore, and Madakari and members of his family were taken to Srirangapatna as prisoners. Hyder Ali also moved a large number of Bedar soldiers and their families from Chitradurga to Srirangapatna, and many of the men were taken into the Mysore army. Chitradurga stayed under Mysore after the death of Tipu Sultan in 1799, when the Wadiyars were restored.

Madakari died in captivity at Srirangapatna. In Karnataka he is remembered as Veera Madakari Nayaka, the last defender of Chitradurga's independence. In the best-known tradition of the sieges, Onake Obavva, the wife of a soldier on guard, found enemy soldiers entering through a narrow gap in the rocks and killed several with a wooden pestle before help came; the gap is called Onake Obavvana Kindi, though accounts differ over which attack it was. The surviving walls, parts of them built under earlier dynasties or under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, are the chief remains of the Nayaka state. T. R. Subba Rao's novel Durgaasthamaana, which received the Sahitya Akademi Award for Kannada posthumously in 1985, and B. L. Venu's Gandugali Madakari Nayaka tell his story.
madame-de-pompadour: Jeanne Antoinette Poisson was the daughter of François Poisson, a steward to the Paris brothers who financed the French state. It was suspected that her biological father was a financier or the tax collector Charles François Paul Le Normant de Tournehem, who became her guardian and paid for an expensive education, with tutors including the dramatist Crébillon and the singer Jélyotte. At twenty she married his nephew Charles Guillaume Le Normant d'Étiolles. She attended Paris salons, held her own at Étiolles, and met Voltaire, Montesquieu and Helvétius there. In 1744 she contrived to be seen by Louis XV while he hunted, and at a masked ball at Versailles on 25 February 1745 he declared his interest in her.

By March 1745 she was the king's mistress. The king bought her the marquisate of Pompadour in June, and she was presented at court on 14 September. She won the favour of Queen Marie Leszczyńska, became a duchess in 1752 and lady-in-waiting to the queen in 1756. She acted in effect as a prime minister, handling appointments, favours and dismissals, and in 1755 the Austrian diplomat Kaunitz approached her during the talks leading to the Treaty of Versailles, which allied France with Austria. Later she brought the duc de Choiseul into office. France was diminished by the Seven Years' War, and she was widely blamed. Around 1750 her sexual relationship with the king ended, and she remained his confidante.

Libels called poissonnades, a pun on her name, attacked her. Historians stress that the Parc-aux-Cerfs, a house at Versailles where the king later met young women, was not the harem of legend, and that she only accepted it.

Pompadour was a major patron of architecture, painting and the decorative arts, supporting Boucher, Nattier and the engraver Jacques Guay, who taught her to engrave gems. In 1759 she bought the porcelain factory at Sèvres. She protected the physician and economist François Quesnay and defended the Encyclopédie of Diderot and d'Alembert against those who wished to suppress it. She made 52 prints after Guay's engraved stones and acted in plays at her private theatres. She died of tuberculosis on 15 April 1764, aged 42.
madang: Nicholai Miklukho-Maklai was probably the first European to visit the area. In 1871 he stayed for 15 months at Astrolabe Bay, south of present-day Madang, and left on good terms with the local communities, suffering from malaria. In April 1884 an expedition of the German New Guinea Company led by Otto Finsch and Eduard Dallmann reached the landing point and named it Friedrich Wilhelmshafen, though the explorers thought the area unsuitable for settlement. A survey in 1888 noted good soil for a coffee plantation. A station was built in the summer of 1891, and by September 1892 it was the seat of the provincial administration, although the Imperial Government Commissioner stayed at Stephansort, some 23 kilometres away, because of malaria.

The name Madang was used by Papuan natives who had come with the German administrators, after their home island, and became official only towards the end of German rule. The settlement was expanded in 1893 and 1894 with warehouses, a sawmill, a hospital and an ox-drawn railway to Stephansort, but the coffee plantations and atap palm processing proved ruinous because of malaria and the climate. In 1895 and 1896 several German warships were stationed there for a survey, and 295 men fell ill with malaria. In 1899 the New Guinea Company moved its capital to Herbertshöhe on New Pomerania, now New Britain.

After the First World War the area passed to Australia as part of the Territory of New Guinea, mandated by the League of Nations. The Imperial Japanese Army captured Madang without a fight in 1942. Australian forces began a sustained campaign in September 1943 to retake the Finisterre Range and Madang, and took the town on 24 April 1944. It was virtually destroyed in the fighting and had to be rebuilt. It is the capital of Madang Province and had a population of 27,420 in 2005. Divine Word University and a small museum of natural science and ethnographic objects are there, and 173 languages are spoken in the province.
madaoua: Madaoua, also written Madoua or Madawa, is an agricultural town in the fertile plain of the Tarka Valley in the Sahel, its centre at an altitude of 322 metres. It is the seat of the Madaoua Department, which forms the south-west corner of the Tahoua Region. Its neighbouring communes include Bouza and Karofane to the north and Bangui to the south. The urban commune has eleven urban districts, among them Sabon Gari and Dar Es Salam, and a rural area of 73 villages, 80 hamlets and two camps, the largest villages including Tounfafi and Nakoni.

In the last third of the 19th century, before the arrival of French rule, Madaoua belonged to the territory of the Kel Gres, a Tuareg subgroup. At the beginning of the 20th century the French administration authorised a small market at Tounfafi, and in 1909 Madaoua became the capital of a large district of the French military territory of Niger, which had been run from Tahoua and included Maradi and Tibiri. In the 1920s the riders' tracks to Tahoua and Tessaoua and the road from Niamey to N'Guigmi, which ran through Madaoua, were the main routes of the colony.

The town later lost its national importance, though in the 1960s its market became an important transhipment centre for peanuts, then Niger's most important export. In 1988 Madaoua became an independent municipality together with nine other towns of Niger; until then the country had twelve municipalities. Floods in July 2008 destroyed 24 houses, and in 2023 large numbers of refugees displaced by conflict in northern Nigeria reached the town.

Madaoua is an urban commune with a population of 127,254 at the 2012 census. Its sights include the palace of the traditional ruler of Madaoua, and the town is an important centre of lutte traditionnelle, a martial art popular in Niger.
madara-rider: The Madara Rider is a large early medieval rock relief on the Madara Plateau east of Shumen in north-eastern Bulgaria, dated to the very late 7th or, more often, the very early 8th century, in the reign of the Bulgar khan Tervel. The relief shows a horseman, almost life-size, about 23 metres above the ground on an almost vertical cliff 100 metres high. He faces right and thrusts a spear into a lion lying at his horse's feet, while a dog runs after him on the left. Erosion and the poor condition of the monument have left his halo, his garments and the bird before his face barely recognisable. The relief was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.

Its meaning and symbolism are uncertain, as are its masonry tradition and cultural source. The relief probably combines elements of Thracian cults and those of the newly arrived Bulgars. Its monumental size and many details, the stirrup, halo, skull-cup and bird among them, belong to Bulgar tradition, while the rightward direction and the lion are more typical of Thracian. Some early researchers took it for a Thracian horseman, a recurring figure of a deity in Paleo-Balkanic mythology, but this view was rejected because of differences in iconography. Others see a resemblance to Sasanian rock reliefs, or link the horseman to the Bulgar deity Tangra or to the Iranian deity Mithra. A simpler suggestion is that it represents Khan Tervel.

Three partly preserved texts in medieval Greek are carved in the rock around the rider. The oldest is by Tervel, so the relief is thought to date from his rule or soon after the Bulgars settled the region in 680–681. The others name Khan Krum and Khan Omurtag. The first mentions a treaty with the emperor Justinian, whom it calls the emperor with the cut-off nose.

In 1924–1935, some 250 metres north beneath the relief, excavators found the remains of a complex believed to have been a pagan shrine and a rectangular building, probably the ruler's dwelling, where he performed rituals to Tangra, together with a damaged inscription of Omurtag mentioning Tangra. The relief appeared on Bulgarian coins of 1 to 50 stotinki issued in 1999 and 2000.
madeira: Madeira lies in the North Atlantic, in the region of Macaronesia, just under 400 kilometres north of the Canary Islands, 520 kilometres west of Morocco and 805 kilometres south-west of mainland Portugal. The archipelago includes the islands of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas, administered together with the separate Savage Islands. The main island is mountainous, with Pico Ruivo reaching 1,862 metres. It is wet in the north-west and dry in the south-east. The Portuguese name means wood, after the forest that once covered the island; settlers burned much of it to clear land, though laurel forests survive on the northern slopes. From the 16th century the settlers built levadas, irrigation channels carrying water to the dry south.

Ancient authors and legend hint at earlier knowledge of the islands. Plutarch, in his life of Sertorius, reports sailors' tales of two Atlantic islands called the Isles of the Blessed, and archaeological evidence suggests the Vikings may have visited between 900 and 1030. A legend of the lovers Robert Machim and Anna d'Arfet, driven ashore in 1346, is said to have given Machico its name. Medieval atlases such as the Medici-Laurentian Atlas of 1351 show the islands. The uninhabited archipelago was claimed in 1419 by Portuguese sailors in the service of Prince Henry the Navigator and settled after 1420.

Sicilian advisers and Genoese capital transformed its sugar industry, with water-driven mills and the levadas, and by 1490 Madeira was the principal source of European sugar. The sugar was cultivated by enslaved labour. In the 18th century vineyards replaced the sugar plantations, in a wine trade dominated by English merchants, and British forces first occupied the island in 1801. On 3 December 1916 the German submarine SM U-38 sank three ships in Funchal harbour and bombarded the city. In April 1931 the garrison joined a military uprising against the National Dictatorship, crushed by mainland forces after seven days. After the 1974 Carnation Revolution a separatist front carried out about 200 bomb attacks before the 1976 Constitution granted Madeira its own administration and legislature.

Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal and an outermost region of the European Union. Its capital and largest city is Funchal, on the south coast of the main island, and about half the population lives there. The population was 251,060 in 2021, mostly descended from Portuguese settlers. Madeira wine, a fortified wine, goes back to the Age of Exploration, when the islands were a standard port of call for ships bound for the New World and the East Indies. Its laurel forest is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
madeira-mamore-railway: In 1846 José Augustin Palácios and Rudolf Oscar Kesselring convinced the Bolivian authorities that the best way to the Atlantic Ocean lay through the Amazon, since the lucrative trade with the United States and Europe ran across the Atlantic. In 1851 the government of the United States, interested in Bolivian products, above all rubber, hired Lieutenant Lardner Gibbon to study a rail link between the navigable Amazon and the Bolivian centres of production. He concluded that a railroad along the rapids of the Madeira River would carry goods efficiently from La Paz to American markets.

In the 1870s the American George Earl Church made two attempts to get round the rapids, both defeated by the terrain and by heavy loss of life to malaria, accidents and violence. The successful bid began with the Treaty of Petrópolis of 1903, under which Bolivia gave Brazil the territory of Acre, 191,000 km², in return for land, money and the railway. Built during the rubber boom, it linked Porto Velho and Guajará-Mirim, and its final leg was opened on 30 April 1912.

The line became known as the Devil's Railroad, but there are no accurate figures for the dead. The novelist Errol Lincoln Uys puts them at 7,000 to 10,000, the Brazilian government estimates 6,000, and Fiorelo Picoli, in O Capital e a Devastação da Amazônica, gives more than 30,000. Much of the legend rests on Church's deadlier failed attempts and on the rubber boom itself, which cost tens of thousands of lives.

The South American rubber boom ended under competition from Asian producers and synthetic rubber, and the railway became redundant, though Brazil had to keep it running under the treaty. In 1972 Brazil completed the BR-364 highway linking Bolivia to navigable parts of the Amazon, and the railroad was abandoned. Later dams on the Madeira, the Santo Antônio Dam and the Jirau Dam among them, were built under the IIRSA South American integration project to turn the rapids into navigable lakes.
madeleine-de-la-tour-dauvergne: Madeleine was a younger daughter of Jean III de La Tour, Count of Auvergne and Lauraguais, who died on 28 March 1501, and his wife Jeanne de Bourbon, Duchess of Bourbon, who died in 1511. She was the penultimate member of the senior branch of the House of La Tour d'Auvergne. With both parents dead, she and her elder sister Anne shared wide properties in Auvergne, Clermont, Berry and Castres. Anne inherited Auvergne and in 1505 married John Stewart, 2nd Duke of Albany.
Her betrothal to Lorenzo II de' Medici formed part of an alliance between Francis I of France and Pope Leo X, and her family welcomed the tie to the Pope's own circle.

The couple married at the Château d'Amboise on 5 May 1518 in a lavish festival that also marked the birth of a dauphin to Francis I. Dancing, mostly in the Italian style, filled the celebrations, with seventy-two ladies in Italian, German and other costumes; Francis gave Madeleine 10,000 gold coins, and Lorenzo gave rich gifts to the French nobility.

Their daughter Catherine, later the consort of King Henry II of France, was born on 13 April 1519, and both parents were said to be as pleased as if she had been a boy. Madeleine died in Italy on 28 April 1519, shortly before her husband, probably of plague, though some speculate that she had syphilis from Lorenzo. Anne outlived her by five years and died childless, so the counties of Auvergne and Boulogne and the barony of La Tour passed to Catherine and later to the French crown.
madhab: The Arabic word madhhab means way to act. Early Islamic law grew out of administrative and community practice in the conquered territories, shaped by Islamic religious and ethical principles, and it developed in circles of learning where students gathered round a local master. In the 8th century the schools of fiqh were regional, and their jurists were loyal to the practice of their own community, whether Mecca, Kufa, Basra or Syria.

Joseph Schacht held that the real basis of doctrine in these ancient schools was the living tradition of the school, expressed in the consensus of its scholars, rather than reports of Muhammad's sayings.

The four main Sunni schools, the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali, are named after classical jurists and emerged in the 9th and 10th centuries. By the 12th century almost all jurists aligned themselves with one of them, and the schools recognise each other's validity.

Each ranks its sources of law differently: the Maliki school, for example, gives weight to the practice of the people of Medina, and the Hanafi school to istihsan and custom. Each came to dominate in different regions: the Maliki in North and West Africa, the Hanafi in South and Central Asia, the Shafi'i in East Africa and Southeast Asia, and the Hanbali in central and northern Arabia.

Shia law followed theological lines and produced the Ja'fari school of the Twelver Shia, named after the sixth Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, and the Ismaili and Zaydi schools. The Ibadi school, derived from the moderate wing of the Kharijite movement, is distinct from both and predominates in Oman. The Zahiri school survives with fewer followers, and the Jariri, Awza'i, Laythi and Thawri schools died out.

Why some schools survived is attributed to state support for particular scholars, success in debate and numbers of students. Historians differ on the sequence, but one account has the Jarirites excluded by dynasties and the Zahirites by the Mamluk Sultanate, which set up four independent judicial posts for the Maliki, Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools. The Ottoman Empire later reaffirmed the official status of the four in reaction to Shia Persia.

The schools were often in political and academic conflict, vying for the favour of rulers so that their representatives would be appointed to legislative and judicial posts. Ibn al-Nadim in the 10th century named eight groups, and by the 12th century the Jariri and Zahiri schools had been absorbed by the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools respectively.
madhavrao-i: Madhavrao was born at Savnur on 15 February 1745, the second son of Peshwa Balaji Bajirao, known as Nanasaheb, and Gopikabai, and a grandson of Bajirao I. In 1753 he married Ramabai, daughter of Trimbakrao Bapusaheb Patwardhan. His elder brother Vishwasrao and his uncle Sadashivrao Bhau were killed at the Third Battle of Panipat, and his father died shortly afterwards. He was declared Peshwa on 21 June 1761, at sixteen, with his paternal uncle Raghunathrao at first acting as regent.

In 1762 Raghunathrao raised an army against him, broke a peace treaty and defeated him at the Battle of Alegaon on 12 November 1762, taking control of the administration with Sakharam Bapu Bokil. When the Nizam of Hyderabad, Raghunathrao's ally, encroached on Maratha lands, Madhavrao took command again and defeated the Nizam's army at the Battle of Rakshasbhuvan on 10 August 1763. He later met Nizam Ali Khan at Kurumkhed in 1766 and reconciled with him. In 1768 he defeated his uncle, captured him and placed him under house arrest at the Shaniwar Wada.

From January 1764 his armies campaigned against Hyder Ali of Mysore, taking Dharwad Fort and winning at Rattihalli. A second expedition in 1767 won at Sira and Madhugiri, where he freed Queen Virammaji of the Keladi Nayaka Kingdom, and the Sira Subah was annexed. He declined an East India Company proposal for British forces at Vasai and Sashti. His northern armies took tribute from Udaipur, defeated the Jats of Bharatpur in 1770, and in 1771 brought the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II back to Delhi under Maratha protection. At Shukratal in 1772 they defeated the Rohillas, of whom over 70,000 were killed.

He fell ill with tuberculosis and spent his last days at the Ganesha Chintamani Temple in Theur, where he died on 18 November 1772; Ramabai committed sati on his funeral pyre. The historian James Grant Duff argued that his death did more to bring about the decline of the Maratha Empire than the defeat at Panipat.
madho-rao-scindia: Born on 20 October 1876, Madho Rao came to the throne in 1886 as the sixth Maharaja of Gwalior of the Scindia dynasty of the Marathas, and the British government regarded him as a progressive ruler of a princely state. He invested his wealth in shares and bonds of many Indian companies, most prominently TISCO, which his investment helped to grow, and he was the only ruler of his time to hold such investments.

He was appointed honorary aide-de-camp to King Edward VII in 1901 in recognition of his support during the Boxer Rebellion in China, received an honorary doctorate of laws from the University of Cambridge in May 1902, and was made a Knight Grand Cross of the Royal Victorian Order on 2 February 1903, during a visit to Gwalior by the Duke and Duchess of Connaught. His later honours included the Order of the British Empire in 1917, and he rose to the rank of lieutenant-general.

Princess Indira of Baroda broke off her engagement to him by letter, and he married Gajararaje of the Rane family of Goa, whose sisters married into the Angre, Shitole and Mahadik families of Gwalior. He married twice but had children only with his second wife: a son and a daughter, for whom King George V and Queen Mary stood sponsors. The daughter died without children in 1934.

He paid for the last phase of a set of mosaics in the Church of the Ascension at Timoleague in County Cork, Ireland, as a memorial to his friend and physician Lieutenant Colonel Crofts, who had saved his son's life; Italian workmen completed them in 1925. The architect Jeremy Williams called the church a hidden masterpiece of the Arts and Crafts Movement in Ireland. Madho Rao died on 5 June 1925 and was succeeded by his son, Jivaji Rao Scindia.
madhura-vijayam: The poem is a mahākāvya in nine cantos with some 500 verses; some verses are incomplete or lost, and an entire canto may be missing between the eighth and the last. Its early cantos describe the background of the Vijayanagara Empire, the rule of Bukka Raya I, whose second son Kumara Kampana was, and the prince's birth and youth. The city of Vijayanagara, its temples and suburbs are described at length, and the army then marches to Kanchipuram, where it winters.

After taking Kanchipuram and subduing the Sambuvaraya chieftain, Kampana is visited by a strange woman, described as the goddess Meenakshi in disguise, who urges him to free the south from the Madurai Sultanate. He marches on Madurai, destroys the Muslim armies, kills the last sultan in single combat and restores the temple of Srirangam. A passage translated by Henry Heras tells how the temples of Siva and Vishnu were reopened and the prince granted villages and jewels to the temple at Madurai.

M. Krishnamachariar, in his History of Classical Sanskrit Literature, praised its melodious verses. S. K. De, writing with S. N. Dasgupta, placed it among poems on historical themes beside the later Raghunāthābhyudaya of Rāmabhadrāmbā, called Gangadevi a more gifted poet than Tirumalāmbā and found the poem simple in style and comparatively free of pedantry. Its praise of Līlāśuka's Kṛṣṇa-karṇāmṛta, placed after Daṇḍin and Bhavabhūti, has been used to date that author. Historians use the poem with Ibn Battuta's memoirs and with inscriptions and coins to reconstruct the conquest. Salman Rushdie's novel Victory City is framed as a fictional retelling of it and of Gangadevi's life.

Pandit N. Ramasvami Sastriar found the poem in a private library at Thiruvananthapuram, on a single manuscript of sixty-one palm leaves bound between two unrelated works. The printed editions rest on that manuscript, though three others were found later, two in Trivandrum and one in Lahore with only seven cantos. G. Harihara Sastri and V. Srinivasa Sastri published the Sanskrit text in 1916, S. Thiruvenkatachari added an English translation in 1957, and Shankar Rajaraman and Venetia Kotamraju translated about 200 verses in 2013.
madhvacharya: Madhvacharya was born at Pajaka near Udupi on the west coast of Karnataka, in a Shivalli Brahmin household, and was named Vāsudeva. His father's name is traditionally given as Naduillaya, while sources variously name his mother as Satyavati or Vedavati. The year of his birth is unclear: many sources date him to 1238–1317, and some to 1199–1278. As a teenager he took sannyasa, or renunciation, and received the name Pūrnaprajña; the name Ānanda Tīrtha was conferred when he became head of his monastery, and Madhva or Madhvacharya is the name most used today. Several hagiographies were written by his disciples, of which the most authentic is Narayana Panditacharya's Madhvavijaya, in sixteen cantos.

Thirty-seven Dvaita texts are attributed to him. They include thirteen commentaries on the principal Upanishads, a commentary on the Brahma Sutras, a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, a commentary on forty hymns of the Rigveda and the Bhagavata-tatparya-nirnaya on the Bhagavata Purana. His Anu-Vyakhyana, a supplement to his Brahma Sutras commentary, is regarded as his masterpiece. In several texts he proclaims himself the third incarnation of Vayu, the wind god, after Hanuman and Bhima, and he claimed that his commentary rested on his personal encounter with Vishnu. His disciples told of miracles, such as crossing the Ganga without wetting his clothes.

Madhva called his philosophy Tattvavada, arguments from a realist viewpoint. Reality is of two kinds, independent and dependent, and Vishnu, whom he also names Krishna, is the only independent reality. Individual souls and matter are dependent, and he describes a fivefold difference between God, souls and matter that is neither temporary nor merely practical. He accepted three means of knowledge: perception, inference and testimony. He held that knowledge alone does not liberate; liberation comes through devotion and the grace of God, and Vishnu can be reached only through Vayu. Each soul has real agency and free will, though it is influenced by its nature and past karma.

Madhva was a fierce critic of rival schools. He accused Shankara and the Advaitins of teaching Buddhism under the cover of Vedanta, and he wrote arguments against twenty-one ancient and medieval scholars to establish his own school. His reading of the saying Tat Tvam Asi stressed difference rather than identity. Dvaita became one of three influential Vedanta philosophies, with Advaita and Vishishtadvaita, and influenced Vaishnavism and the Bhakti movement. Kulandran and Kraemer judged his historical influence salutary but not extensive. His lineage of students produced scholars such as Jayatirtha, Vyasatirtha and Raghavendra Tirtha.
madhya-pradesh: Madhya Pradesh, whose name means Central Province, lies in the geographic heart of India. It borders Rajasthan to the northwest, Uttar Pradesh to the northeast, Chhattisgarh to the east, Maharashtra to the south and Gujarat to the west. The state straddles the Narmada River, which runs east and west between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges; these ranges and the river are the traditional boundary between the north and south of India. The Narmada is considered very sacred and is worshipped throughout the region, and the Tapti runs parallel to it. The highest point is Dhupgarh, at 1,350 m.

Isolated remains of Homo erectus found at Hathnora in the Narmada Valley suggest the area may have been inhabited in the Middle Pleistocene. Painted pottery of the later Mesolithic period has been found in the Bhimbetka rock shelters, and Chalcolithic sites of the Kayatha culture (2100-1800 BCE) and the Malwa culture (1700-1500 BCE) lie in the west. The region includes the area of the ancient Avanti Mahajanapada, whose capital Ujjain arose as a major city in the sixth century BCE.

Major dynasties of India ruled the region in later centuries, and the Maratha Empire dominated most of it in the 18th century. After the Third Anglo-Maratha War it was divided into several princely states under the British. After independence, the Central Provinces and Berar was renamed Madhya Pradesh, with Nagpur as its capital, and the Central India Agency became Madhya Bharat, with Gwalior as its capital. In 1956 these states were reorganised and combined with Vindhya Pradesh and Bhopal into the new Madhya Pradesh. The state was the largest in India by area until 2000, when its southeastern Chhattisgarh region became a separate state.

Bhopal is the capital, and other major cities include Indore, Gwalior, Jabalpur and Sagar. The state has over 72 million residents, and Hindi is its official language. Tribal groups such as the Gondi, Bhil, Baiga and Korku form a significant part of the population. UNESCO has declared three sites in the state World Heritage Sites: the Khajuraho Group of Monuments (1986), the Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi (1989) and the Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka (2003). Buddhism and Jainism were once prominent here, especially on the central plateau near Raisen and Bhopal, and Malwa still has a significant Jain minority.
madikeri: Madikeri lies in the Western Ghats at an elevation of 1,170 metres and has a tropical highland climate. It is a popular hill station. The nearest large cities are Hassan, 110 kilometres to the north, Mysore, 120 kilometres to the east, and Mangalore, 138 kilometres to the north-west. Rainfall is heavy: the Madikeri hobli received 3,957 millimetres in 2022. The lowest temperature recorded is 4.5 degrees, and the monsoon makes the weather chilly from June.

The town was known as Muddu Raja Keri, meaning Mudduraja's town, after the Haleri king Mudduraja, who ruled Kodagu from 1633 to 1687. From 1834, under the British Raj, it was called Mercara, and the Government of Mysore later renamed it Madikeri. Its history is bound up with that of Kodagu. Kadambas ruled the northern part from the 2nd to the 6th century, Gangas the southern part from the 4th to the 11th, and then came the Cholas, the Hoysalas in the 12th century and the Vijayanagar kings in the 14th.

After Vijayanagar fell, local Kodava chieftains, the Palegars, ruled their own areas and appointed Veeraraju, founder of the Haleri dynasty, as ruler. His descendants ruled Kodagu from 1600 to 1834. Mudduraja, the third Haleri king, began levelling the land around Madikeri and built a fort in 1681, making the town the capital. The fort was first built of mud and was later replaced by Tipu Sultan. Kodagu became part of British India after 1834.

Madikeri is the headquarters of Kodagu district in Karnataka. Its attractions include Madikeri Fort, Raja's Seat, the Sri Omkareshwara Temple, the Gaddide, which is the tomb of the rajas, the General Thimmaiah War Museum and Abbey Falls. The census of 2011 counted 33,381 inhabitants. A national highway links it eastward to Mysore and Bengaluru and westward to Mangalore.
madinat-al-zahira: The name means the resplendent city. Almanzor built it east of Córdoba along the Guadalquivir, deliberately mirroring Madinat al-Zahra, the caliph's palace city to the west, to display his magnificence, secure his person and rival the caliph. Traditional accounts, chiefly that of the chronicler and poet Al-Fath ibn Khaqan, say the building went quickly, though modern scholarship suggests he may have reused existing structures. Legend held that the site was chosen after an omen foretold that a city there would become the centre of power but doom the Umayyad dynasty.

The historian Laura Bariani describes a small but heavily fortified palace, with key administrative buildings outside the walls that enclosed Almanzor, his household and his troops. Its single gate, the Gate of Victory, is where Almanzor reportedly displayed the head of the general Galib. Foreign envoys were received there rather than in the caliphal palaces, and Almanzor tried without success in 981 to make its mosque the city's principal one. Officials, artisans, merchants and poets settled around it.

Almanzor's sons ruled from it as emirs. According to a later chronicle, Muhammad al-Mahdi ordered the city razed on 15 February 1009, and the people of Córdoba looted it for three days; Arab chroniclers put the plunder at 1,500,000 gold coins and 2,100,000 silver pieces. On 19 February the ruins were set on fire. Ibn Hayyan, however, notes a prefect living there in 1023, which suggests a slower decline. Its mosque survived into Almohad times, and the Sufi Abu al-Qasim, who died in 1182, preached in a still-inhabited quarter.

The search for the site goes back to Sánchez de Feria in 1772, and at least 21 locations have been studied. The only object certainly from the palace is a broken marble ablution basin with an inscription of 987–988, found in Seville and now in Madrid's Archaeological Museum. A LiDAR study has tentatively placed the city at the La Pendolilla estate, about 12 km east of Córdoba near Alcolea.
madinat-al-zahra: Madinat al-Zahra, or Medina Azahara, meaning the radiant city, was a fortified palace-city on the western outskirts of Córdoba. Abd ar-Rahman III, a member of the Umayyad dynasty, built it, and the reason was chiefly politico-ideological. The Umayyads had been overthrown in the east by the Abbasids in 750, and Abd ar-Rahman I re-established the dynasty in Al-Andalus in 756, but its rulers governed as emirs. Abd ar-Rahman III declared himself caliph in 929, and the dignity of the title called for a new city, a symbol of his power that imitated the eastern caliphates and showed his superiority over his rivals, the Fatimid caliphs of Ifriqiya and the Abbasid caliphs of Baghdad.

According to historical sources the city was founded in 936, about 5 km west of Córdoba, and Abd ar-Rahman's son and heir al-Hakam II oversaw the work. The mosque was finished in 941 to 942 or 944 to 945, the caliph was living there by 945, the road to Córdoba was paved in 946, and in 947 the apparatus of state, including the mint, moved there. Building continued through the reign of al-Hakam II (961 to 976).

The palaces housed the caliph's household and a large body of slaves, including eunuchs, mostly of European origin. The city held a throne hall, the Salón Rico, government offices, workshops making luxury objects, officials' residences and, on the lower levels, markets and districts for common workers. Under al-Hakam II there was a library said by some accounts to hold hundreds of thousands of volumes.

Al-Hakam II was succeeded by his son Hisham II, aged 14 or 15, and real power passed to Ibn Abi Amir, who took the title al-Mansur, or Almanzor. In 978 or 979 he began his own palace-city, Madinat az-Zahira, and when it was ready, in two years, he moved the government there, leaving Madinat al-Zahra in disuse. After al-Mansur's family lost power in 1009 and the civil war known as the Fitna began, Berber factions besieged Córdoba, and Madinat al-Zahra was pillaged and left in ruins.

The city lies on the slopes of Jabal al-Arus, Bride Hill, in the foothills of the Sierra Morena, facing the Guadalquivir valley, and its rectangular area of 112 hectares is laid out in three terraces. Excavations began in 1911, and only about 10 hectares have been excavated and partly restored, though they include the main palaces. An archaeological museum opened at the edge of the site in 2009, and on 1 July 2018 the site was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site under the name Caliphate City of Medina Azahara.
madiun: Madiun lies in the western part of East Java, 169 kilometres south-west of Surabaya and 38 kilometres south-east of Ngawi. It stands on the Madiun River, a tributary of the Bengawan Solo River, at an average height of 63 metres above sea level. The city is surrounded by mountains: Mount Wilis, 2,169 metres high, to the east, the Kapur Selatan range to the south and Mount Lawu, 3,285 metres high, to the west. Its climate is a tropical monsoon one, with moderate to little rain from June to October and heavy rain from November to May.

The best-known episode in the city's modern history is the Madiun Affair of 1948. After the signing of the Renville Agreement that year, guerrilla units and militias under the influence of the Communist Party of Indonesia (PKI) were ordered to disband. In Madiun a group of PKI militia refused to disarm and were killed in September. The killings set off a violent uprising. Army sources claimed that the PKI announced the proclamation of a Soviet Republic of Indonesia on 18 September, with Musso as its president and Amir Sjarifuddin as its prime minister.

Republican troops suppressed the uprising. On 30 September the Silwangi Division took over Madiun. Thousands of party cadres were killed and 36,000 were imprisoned. Among the executed were several leaders, including Muso, who was killed on 31 October, allegedly while trying to escape from prison. Other PKI leaders, such as D. N. Aidit, went into exile in China.

Madiun has been administratively separate from the surrounding Madiun Regency since the two bodies were formed in 1950, although it remained the seat of the regency administration until 2010. It covers 33.23 square kilometres, is divided into three districts (Manguharjo, Taman and Kartoharjo) and had 195,175 inhabitants at the 2020 census. It is known for its agricultural role and is nicknamed Kota Gadis, an acronym for Trading, Education and Industrial City in Indonesian; the Dutch sometimes called it Milaan van Java. A railway station serves the city, and the Solo-Kertosono Toll Road and Indonesian National Route 20 reach it.
madiun-affair: Amir Sjarifuddin's cabinet fell on 28 January 1948, and his left-wing faction refused posts in Hatta's new cabinet unless it kept key ministries, including defence. In February the left regrouped at Surakarta as the People's Democratic Front (FDR), led by Sjarifuddin and joining the Partai Sosialis, the PKI, Pesindo and the labour federation SOBSI. It opposed the Renville Agreement, which Hatta meant to carry out, and Hatta's rationalisation of the army, which cut excess troops and demobilised the TNI Masjarakat, a local force that had been a base of Sjarifuddin's strength.

Tension grew through mid-1948: the Senopati Division of Solo resisted rationalisation, its commander Colonel Sutarto was murdered on 2 July, and some 20,000 workers struck at the Delanggu cotton plantations for about 35 days. On 11 August Suripno returned from Prague with Musso, who became chairman of a new political bureau of the left late in August. In September kidnappings and clashes between pro-government units such as the Siliwangi Division and leftist groups left Solo in government hands and Madiun the FDR's last important stronghold.

At 3 am on 18 September 1948 FDR forces under Sumarsono and Djoko Sujono seized Madiun's government offices, telephone exchange and army headquarters; two loyal officers were killed. Setyadjit and Wikana set up a regional National Front government, and Sumarsono announced on the radio, From Madiun victory begins. On the night of 19 September President Sukarno called the revolt an attempt to overthrow the Republic and told Indonesians to choose between him and Hatta or Musso, backed by Sultan Hamengkubuwono IX; Musso answered by declaring war on the government. Some FDR leaders, including Sumarsono and Sjarifuddin, then insisted that it was no coup.

The government used the revolt to crack down on the left. Troops under Colonel Gatot Soebroto and Nasution moved in, and Lieutenant Colonel Sadikin of the Siliwangi Division was sent to take Madiun on 30 September. The FDR leaders retreated towards the hills. On 28 October the government arrested 1,500 men of the last rebel unit, and Musso was shot dead three days later; his body was displayed at Ponorogo and burned. Sjarifuddin was captured on 4 December and executed with other FDR leaders on 19 December. About 35,000 people were arrested, and casualties were estimated at 24,000 across Madiun, Cepu and Ponorogo. Sumarsono escaped, and was arrested again in the anti-communist campaign of 1965.
madockawando: Madockawando was born in Maine around 1630 and was the adopted son of Assaminasqua, whom he succeeded as sachem of the Penobscot. The Penobscot lands east of the Penobscot River formed part of the French colony of Acadia, which the English returned to France in the 1667 Treaty of Breda, although the English claimed that the land between the Penobscot and St. Croix rivers fell within the Duke of York's patent. Jean-Vincent d'Abbadie de Saint-Castin, a trader who settled among the Penobscot, drew them into the French interest.

When the war of King Philip's confederacy with the Plymouth Colony spread to Maine and New Hampshire, the Penobscot were the first of the Native peoples to sue for peace, and Madockawando ratified the articles subscribed at Boston on 6 November 1676. The English renewed hostilities, and the Penobscot destroyed the English settlements in that part of Maine. A treaty made at Casco in 1678 let English settlers return to their farms on condition of paying rent to the Penobscot.

The peace lasted until 1688, when Edmund Andros arrived in a frigate and sacked Saint-Castin's house. The Penobscot chiefs, supplied with arms by Saint-Castin, attacked English settlements, one of the causes of King William's War, and Madockawando took a prominent part in every stage of the conflict. When the English built Fort William Henry at Pemaquid he hurried to Quebec to tell Louis de Buade de Frontenac, and his messengers warned Boston of Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville's expedition. After agreeing to peace in 1693 he could not persuade the chiefs under the influence of French Jesuit emissaries and had to resume hostilities.

The war went on for more than a year after the Peace of Ryswick. Madockawando moved to Meductic, a Maliseet-Abenaki mission village on the St. John River, where he died in a smallpox epidemic in 1698. A plaque in Castine, Maine, recorded that in 1692 an English boy taken captive at Casco and held by Madockawando was tortured and burned at the stake for trying to escape, a form of ritual torture used against enemies taken in war.
madog-ap-maredudd: Madog was the son of King Maredudd ap Bleddyn and grandson of King Bleddyn ap Cynfyn, and followed his father on the throne of Powys in 1132. He married Susanna, sister of Owain Gwynedd. In 1141 he is recorded fighting at the Battle of Lincoln for Ranulf de Gernon, 4th Earl of Chester, alongside Cadwaladr ap Gruffydd, Owain's brother, and a large army of Welshmen.

He seems to have gained the fortresses of Oswestry and Whittington from William Fitzalan in 1146, and in 1149 he rebuilt Oswestry Castle and gave the commote of Cyfeiliog to his nephews Owain Cyfeiliog and Meurig. Owain, King of Gwynedd, was then pressing on the borders of Powys. Around 1150 Madog allied with the Earl of Chester, but Owain defeated them near Ewloe and took his lands in the Lordship of Iâl.

When King Henry II of England invaded Gwynedd in 1157, Madog supported him, and although Henry was defeated at the Battle of Ewloe, Madog regained many of his Welsh lands. In 1159 he seems to have been the Welsh prince who went with Henry on the campaign to Toulouse, which ended in failure. The Mabinogion tale The Dream of Rhonabwy is set in his reign: its hero is one of his retainers, sent to bring in Madog's rebellious brother Iorwerth Goch ap Maredudd.

Returning home, Madog died about 9 February 1160 at Whittington Castle and was buried in the church of St Tysilio at Meifod, the mother church of Powys. His eldest son, Llywelyn, was killed soon afterwards, and Powys was shared between his sons Gruffydd Maelor, Owain Fychan and Owain Brogyntyn, his nephew Owain Cyfeiliog and his half-brother Iorwerth Goch. It was never reunited. His death let Owain Gwynedd force the homage of Owain Brogyntyn and annex part of northern Powys.

The poet Cynddelw Brydydd Mawr lamented in his elegy that while Madog lived no man dared ravage his borders. Madog's daughter Marared married Iorwerth Drwyndwn and was the mother of Llywelyn the Great; another daughter, Gwenllian, married Rhys ap Gruffydd, prince of Deheubarth.
madra-kingdom: Hindu tradition gives the Madras more than one founder. The Vayu Purana names King Ushinara Shibi of the Anu line, Anu being a son of Yayati, while the Bhagavata Purana names Madra, a son of the Anu king Shibi. A myth in the Mahabharata gives the Madra and Salwa tribes a common origin in the seven sons of Bhadra, wife of the Puru king Vyushitaswa: three became kings of Salwa and four kings of Madra. Besides the kingdom with its capital at Sagala, sometimes called Eastern Madra, a Western and a Northern Madra are believed to have existed.

In the epic, Bhishma obtained Madri as a bride for Pandu by paying wealth to her kinsmen, as Madra custom required, and her sons were the Pandava twins Nakula and Sahadeva. Nakula later came to Sakala on his western campaign and received jewels and gems from Shalya. Though Shalya set out with his army to join the Pandavas, Duryodhana's men received and paid his troops on the way, and he fought for the Kauravas, drove Karna's chariot for a day and, as their commander on the last day of the Kurukshetra War, was killed by Yudhishthira.
Outside the epic, the Allahabad Pillar inscription of Samudragupta (r. c. 350–375 CE) names the Madrakas among the frontier peoples who paid him tribute, obeyed his orders and came to his court.

The epic counts Madra among the Bahlika or western countries, which it describes as cold lands where people used blankets, reared sheep and drank their milk, knew camels and bred horses of excellent quality. Their horses and horsemen served in the wars of the kings of Aryavarta, and their soldiers are said to have fought for either side for payment. These western lands were also called Arashtra or Aratta, a kingless country, which raises the question whether they were republics ruled by elected chiefs. Some passages place the Madrakas among the tribes beyond the kingdoms of Aryavarta.
madras-state: The region had long been ruled by the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas and later by the Kalabhras, Pallavas, Hoysalas and Vijayanagara. After the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War of 1799 and the Second Polygar War, the British consolidated their power there with Madras as the capital, and the famines of 1876–1878 and 1896–97 killed millions. At first the state covered present-day Tamil Nadu, the Malabar district, Rayalaseema, Coastal Andhra and South Canara, about 331,000 square kilometres, and the 1951 census counted 57,016,002 people.

In the 1952 elections to the 375-seat assembly the Indian National Congress formed the government under Chakravarti Rajagopalachari. Potti Sriramulu's fast to the death for a Telugu state was followed by riots. Rajagopalachari's education policy of 1953, under which pupils learned their parents' vocation after school, was opposed as casteist, by Periyar among others, and dropped on 18 May 1954.

K. Kamaraj became chief minister on 13 April 1954. He made school education free, extended the Midday Meal Scheme to all public schools and introduced free uniforms, and literacy rose from 19% to 37%. Dams, industrial estates and institutions such as BHEL at Trichy and IIT Madras followed. He resigned on 2 October 1963 under what became the Kamaraj Plan. Under his successor M. Bhaktavatsalam the state saw anti-Hindi agitations against the Official Languages Act of 1963.

The agitations helped the rise of the Dravidian parties. In 1967 the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam, founded by C. N. Annadurai in 1949, won the elections and formed the first non-Congress government; it legalised self-respect marriages and sold rice at subsidised prices. The renaming of the state as Tamil Nadu on 14 January 1969 was proposed by that government.
madrasa: Madrasa is the Arabic word for any educational institution, secular or religious, and means a place where learning and studying take place. In Arabic it can refer to a primary or secondary school as well as a university-level school. In English it usually refers to Islamic institutions of learning, and historians use it for a college where Islamic law was taught along with other subjects. In medieval usage the term was usually specific to higher learning, as opposed to elementary schools, which were known as kuttab, khalwa or maktab.

Tradition holds that the first madrasa education took place under Muhammad at the estate of Zayd ibn Arqam, and that after the Hijrah a school known as Suffa was set up beside the mosque at Medina. The formal madrasa developed in the late 11th century under the Abbasid caliphs, when the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk created a system of state madrasas, called the Nizamiyahs after him, in cities from Mesopotamia to Khorasan. Nizam al-Mulk was later murdered by the Assassins.

Madrasa-type institutions appear to have existed in Iran before him, but his period is considered by many to be the starting point for the spread of the formal madrasa across the Muslim world, adapted to all four Sunni legal schools and to Sufi orders. Part of the motive of Sunni rulers and elites in adopting it was a wish to counter the influence of Shi'ism by spreading Sunni teachings.

In its formative period the madrasa curriculum included only the religious sciences, and philosophy and the secular sciences were often excluded. The curriculum slowly diversified, and many later madrasas taught logic, mathematics and philosophy, and some history, ethics, medicine, astronomy and chemistry. The founder usually set the curriculum. Between 1155 and 1260 there were 75 madrasas in Cairo, 51 in Damascus and up to 44 in Aleppo.

Architecturally, the classical madrasa was centred on an interior courtyard with four iwans, vaulted chambers open on one side, arranged symmetrically around it. Practically none of the first Nizamiyah madrasas survives. Many Seljuk madrasas of Anatolia survive, often with an attached mausoleum, a minaret and an ornate entrance portal, and some courtyards were covered by a dome, as at the Karatay Madrasa in Konya, founded in 1279.

In the Maghreb madrasas flourished only in the 13th century under the Marinid and Hafsid dynasties, which followed the Almohad dynasty. The earliest Hafsid madrasa was founded in Tunis in 1252, and the first in Morocco was built in Fes in 1271. In the Ottoman Empire madrasas trained doctors, engineers, lawyers and religious officials, among other members of the governing elite, for nearly six centuries. Muhammad the Conqueror built eight higher madrasas for specialised studies and eight lower ones beside a mosque.
madrasa-of-granada: Madrasas, colleges of Islamic learning, arose in Seljuk Iran in the 11th century and spread west, reaching Marinid Morocco in the late 13th century, where colleges such as the Madrasa al-Attarin in Fes may have influenced the Nasrid design. The Madrasa of Yusuf I is the only major madrasa known to have been built in al-Andalus; a smaller private one had existed earlier in Malaga. It stood in the centre of the city beside the main mosque, now the site of Granada Cathedral, and near the Alcaicería, the bazaar of silk, gold and linen.

The founders meant it to train scholars who could also serve as state officials, to attract established teachers and to enhance the Nasrid rulers' reputation for piety. Besides law and Arabic grammar, its subjects included medicine, astronomy, logic, mathematics and mechanics. Ibn Marzuq taught there in 1354, and Ibn al-Khatib studied there under teachers who included the poet Ibn al-Jayyab.

Under the Treaty of Granada of 1491 the madrasa continued to work after the conquest of 1492, until late 1499 or early 1500. After the Muslim uprising in the Alpujarras in 1499, Gonzalo Jimenez de Cisneros intervened in the diocese, and the madrasa's library was carried to the plaza of Bib-Rambla and burned in a public bonfire. In 1500 Ferdinand II made the building the Casa del Cabildo. Most of the original structure was demolished between 1722 and 1729 and replaced by a baroque building designed by José de Bada.

The town hall moved to the Plaza del Carmen in 1858 and the building was sold as a textile warehouse. Two years later the main inscription of the mihrab was found, and after a fire its owners, the Echeverría family, hired Rafael Contreras, restorer of the Alhambra, to repair the building. The city bought the building back in the early 20th century, and in 1976 it passed to the University of Granada.

Of the Nasrid building only the prayer hall survives. Square, 6.84 metres a side, it turns octagonal halfway up through four muqarnas squinches, and its upper walls carry arabesque and calligraphic stucco, 16 windows and a muqarnas cornice beneath a wooden cupola. Pieces of the white marble façade are in the Archaeological Museum of Granada. Excavations in 2006–2007 found traces of buildings from as early as the 11th century, and the building was opened to the public in 2011.
madrid: Madrid lies in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula on the southern Meseta Central, 60 kilometres south of the Guadarrama mountain range, at an average altitude of about 650 metres. It straddles the Jarama and Manzanares river sub-drainage basins, within the wider catchment of the Tagus. The oldest urban core stands on hills beside the left bank of the Manzanares. The city grew eastwards to the creek now followed by the Paseo de la Castellana and on to the Abroñigal Creek, and also by annexing neighbouring settlements.

The origin of the name is unknown. Theories include a Latin derivation from matrix, a Celtic form meaning 'ford', and an Arabic word for a water stream, majrā. All have difficulty explaining the phonetic change fully. Nicknames include Los Madriles and La Villa y Corte, 'the town and court'.

The site has been occupied since prehistoric times. Archaeological remains include a settlement of the Celtic Carpetani, Roman villas, a Visigoth basilica near the church of Santa María de la Almudena and three Visigoth necropolises. The first historical document of an established settlement dates from the Muslim period. In the second half of the 9th century the Umayyad emir Muhammad I built a fortress on a headland near the Manzanares, one of many on the border between Al-Andalus and the kingdoms of León and Castile, to protect Toledo from attack from the north.

After the Caliphate of Córdoba broke up in the early 11th century, Madrid became part of the Taifa of Toledo. In 1083 Alfonso VI of León and Castile seized it as an outpost against Toledo, which he took in 1085. Christians then occupied the centre of the town, while Muslims and Jews were displaced to the suburbs. Madrid remained a borderland for a time and suffered raids during the Almoravid period; its walls were destroyed in 1110. Philip II moved his court to Madrid in 1561 and transformed the town into a capital city.

Madrid is the capital and largest city of Spain and of the autonomous community of Madrid, with about 3.4 million people in the city proper. Its landmarks include the Plaza Mayor, built in 1617 to 1619 and attributed to Juan Gómez de Mora, the Royal Palace, the Buen Retiro Park, founded in 1631, and the Prado, Reina Sofía and Thyssen-Bornemisza museums along the Paseo del Prado, which form a UNESCO World Heritage site called the Golden Triangle of Art.
madriu-perafita-claror-valley: The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley is a glacial valley in the south-east of Andorra, covering 42.47 km2, about 9 per cent of the country, and part of its second largest watershed basin. It has high pastures, craggy cliffs and steep wooded valleys, bounded by ridges to the south, east and west, the southern edge running along the border with Spain, and by an escarpment dropping to the Valira valley in the north. It is isolated from the rest of Andorra and can be reached only by tracks passable on foot. It is recognised as a haven for rare or endangered wildlife, and has recently been considered the spiritual heart of Andorra.

The dwellings, field terraces, tracks and remains of ironworking show how the natural resources of the high Pyrenees were used by the local people over many centuries, through changes in climate, prosperity and social structure. Two small settlements, Entremesaigües and Ramio, lie on the narrow valley floor; both were occupied all year until about the last fifty years. The twelve houses are built of local granite with schist roofs, each with a barn for grain and hay. The settlements are surrounded by terraced fields, once used for wheat and rye and now mostly for grazing, and the slopes held vines in the Middle Ages. The forests, owned communally, were managed to produce charcoal until the nineteenth century.

Iron was smelted from local ore on the banks of the Madriu River, in a Catalan forge of the kind typical of the Pyrenees, which was abandoned in 1790. The high pasture has been grazed in summer by sheep, cows and horses on land owned communally since the Middle Ages, and shepherds spent the summer in borders, small stone huts with turf roofs. Milk was made into cheese.

The valley became Andorra's first and only UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004, with a small extension in 2006. Tracks link it to Roussillon, Languedoc and Catalonia, and paved tracks connect it to the centre of Andorra.
