Many shepherds' huts, trackways and field walls have been restored, no access road is planned, and the land is intended for farming high-quality livestock and for limited tourism.
mads-lange: Mads Johansen Lange was born in Rudkøbing on 18 September 1807, the second son of the merchant Lorents Lange Pedersen and Maren Hansen, who ran a tavern and a shop she had inherited. He went to sea at fourteen and from 1824 served on the ship North under Captain John Burd, sailing with him for many years, including to the Danish trading post of Tranquebar in India. After a stay in Denmark in 1833 and 1834 he and Burd bought the ship South and sailed for India and China, with Burd as captain, Lange as first mate and three of Lange's younger brothers aboard. None of the four brothers saw Denmark again.

In 1835 he settled on Lombok, where the Raja of Karangasem Lombok let him trade from Tanjungkarang for a yearly fee; he exported coffee, rice, spices and tobacco and imported textiles and weapons. When war between the island's states culminated in his patron's defeat in 1839, he fled to Bali in his schooner Venus. Invited by Raja Kassiman of Badung, he built his factorij near Kotta, now Kuta, on a narrow peninsula where ships could load on either side, profiting from a rice shortage in Asia and Bali's three harvests a year.

When the Dutch sent the First Dutch Expedition to Bali in 1846 and took Buleleng and Singaraja, Lange negotiated with the Rajas of Buleleng and Karangasem a peace under which the Rajas paid small damages and the Dutch kept a small force on the island. The war, blockades and the rise of steamers, which drew trade to Hong Kong and Singapore, left his business in decline, and his oil mill stopped for want of coconuts.

Lange sent artefacts to the Royal Ethnographic Museum in Copenhagen, for which Frederik VII awarded him the Danish Golden Medal of Merit on 28 July 1854, and money to Denmark during the First Danish-German War. He died on 13 May 1856; his daughter Cecilia and his English physician suspected poison, which was never proved. His brother Hans and nephew Peter Christian kept the business going until Raja Kassiman's death in 1863, after which it was sold to a Chinese merchant. With the Balinese princess Nyai Kenyèr and a Chinese woman he had three children; Cecilia's son Ibrahim became Sultan of Johor. The Dutch government raised an obelisk over his grave in 1927.
madura: Madura is an island off the north-eastern coast of Java, part of the province of East Java and separated from Java by the narrow Madura Strait. The island itself covers about 4,471 square kilometres; the administered area is about 5,408 square kilometres because it includes smaller islands, which belong to the easternmost regency, Sumenep. The island is relatively flat, and its limestone hills are lower and rounder than those of northern Java. It is warmer and drier than the Javanese mainland. It is named for Madurai, the home of the Hindu deity Azhagar.

In 1624 Sultan Agung of Mataram conquered Madura, and its government was brought under the Cakraningrats, a single princely line. The family often opposed Central Javanese rule. After the First Javanese War of Succession the Dutch gained control of the eastern half of Madura in 1705. In 1743 Pakubuwono II ceded full sovereignty over Madura to the Dutch, which Cakraningrat IV contested; he fled to Banjarmasin, was betrayed by the sultan there, and was captured and exiled to the Cape of Good Hope.

The Dutch kept Madura's four states, each with its own regent. The island was at first important as a source of colonial troops, and in the second half of the 19th century it became the main source of salt for Dutch-controlled territories in the archipelago. The Dutch gradually sidelined the Sultan and took over direct control of the whole island in the 1880s, governing it as the Madoera Residency. From 1948 to 1950, under the United States of Indonesia, it was a federative state called the State of Madura.

Madura has about four million inhabitants, most of them Madurese, who speak Madurese, an Austronesian language. The Madurese number around seven million, and many live elsewhere, especially in eastern Java. The soil is not fertile enough for major agriculture, and maize, cattle, small-scale fishing and tobacco and cloves for the kretek industry are mainstays, with salt exported since the Dutch era. The island is well known for karapan sapi, bull racing, in which a jockey rides a wooden sled pulled by two bulls over about 100 metres in ten to fifteen seconds. Its theatre includes masked topeng performances of the Ramayana and Mahabharata, and the Madurese are regarded as excellent sailors. The Suramadu Bridge to Surabaya opened in 2009.
madurai: Madurai stands on the flat, fertile plain of the river Vaigai, which runs through the city and divides it into two almost equal halves. The Sirumalai and Nagamalai hills lie to the north and west. A 2nd-century BCE Tamil-Brahmi inscription refers to the city as matiray, an Old Tamil word that Iravatham Mahadevan reads as meaning a walled city. Tradition holds that the site was once a forest of Kadamba trees, and the city has also been called Koodal and Thirualavai. Vaishnava texts call it the southern Mathura.

The recorded history of Madurai goes back to the 3rd century BCE. Megasthenes may have visited it as Methora, though some scholars believe he meant the northern city of Mathura. Sangam literature such as Maturaikkāñci records its importance as the capital of the Pandyan dynasty, and the third Tamil Sangam, an assembly of poets, is said to have been held there. The second book of the Tamil epic Silappatikaram is set in the city. Over the centuries it was ruled by the Pandyan Kingdom, the Chola Empire, the Madurai Sultanate, the Vijayanagar Empire, the Madurai Nayaks and the Carnatic kingdom.

The first Madurai Nayak king, Viswanatha Nayak (1529–64), redesigned the city according to the Shilpa Shastras. It is built around the Koodal Azhagar and Meenakshi temples, in concentric quadrangular streets named after Tamil months and their festivals, such as the Aadi, Chittirai and Masi streets.

In 1801 the East India Company took direct control of Madurai and annexed it to the Madras Presidency. In 1837 the British demolished the fortifications around the temple, drained the moat and used the debris to build new streets. The municipality was constituted on 1 November 1866. In 1921 Mahatma Gandhi first adopted the loincloth in Madurai, after seeing agricultural labourers wearing it. In 1939 the Madras Presidency passed the Temple Entry Authorization and Indemnity Act, and the temple entry movement was led at the Meenakshi temple by A. Vaidyanatha Iyer.

Madurai is the administrative headquarters of Madurai district in Tamil Nadu and is called the cultural capital of the state. It had a population of 1,470,755 in 2011, and Tamil is the main language. Its best-known monuments are the Koodal Azhagar temple, the Meenakshi Temple and the Thirumalai Nayakkar Mahal. The surrounding land is farmed mainly for paddy, and the city is a centre of learning and of industries such as automobile and granite manufacturing.
madurai-nayak-dynasty: The Nayaks were Telugu-speaking Balija warriors from the Rayalaseema region of present-day Andhra Pradesh. Nagama Nayaka, a general of Emperor Krishnadevaraya, was sent to reassert Vijayanagara authority over the Pandya territories, but his strict rule alienated the local chieftains, and in the late 1520s he began to defy the capital. The emperor sent his son Viswanatha Nayaka, who defeated his father and sent him under guard to the capital, where Nagama was pardoned. Viswanatha was appointed governor of Madurai in 1529. A traditional chronicle tells of Nagama usurping the Pandyan throne instead, but it lacks contemporary inscriptions to support it.

Viswanatha rebuilt the fort of Madurai and abdicated in 1564 in favour of Krishnappa Nayaka I, whose troops sent to the Battle of Talikota in 1565 arrived too late; the defeat of Rama Raya left the southern Nayak kingdoms practically autonomous. Muttu Krishnappa Nayaka recognised Sadeika Thevar as Sethupathi at Ramanathapuram in 1604, and Muttu Virappa Nayaka I backed Gobburi Jagga Raya in the Vijayanagara civil war, lost at the Battle of Toppur in 1616, and moved the capital to Tiruchirappalli. Tirumala Nayaka took it back to Madurai in 1635, enlarged the army to about 30,000 troops and stopped all payments to the empire.

Chokkanatha Nayaka captured Thanjavur in 1673, but in 1675 the Maratha general Venkoji took it and founded the Thanjavur Maratha kingdom. Rani Mangammal, regent from 1689 to 1704, paid tribute to the advancing Mughal army under Zulfiqar Khan and helped it at the siege of Jinji. After Vijaya Ranga Chokkanatha died without issue in 1732, his widow and the claimant Bangaru Tirumala fought over the succession, and the queen turned to Chanda Sahib, who was acting for the Nawab of Arcot.

Viswanatha and his dalavay, Ariyanatha Mudaliar, divided the kingdom into 72 palayams, each held by a hereditary palayakkarar, anglicised as polygar, who kept armed retainers and judged local cases. A chief sent one third of his revenue to the treasury, kept one third for his troops and retained the rest. The court used Telugu, while most of the people spoke Tamil. The Nayaks enlarged the Meenakshi-Sundaraswarar temple with enclosures, pillared halls and gateway towers up to 50 metres high, and a related line ruled the Kingdom of Kandy from 1739 to 1815.
madurai-sultanate: In 1325 Fakhruddin Jauna Khan took the throne of Delhi as Muhammad bin Tughluq. His plans to invade Iran and Greater Khorasan emptied his treasury, his token currency invited counterfeiting, and unpaid soldiers in distant provinces revolted. Bengal broke away first and Ma'bar, the Muslim chroniclers' name for the Tamil region, soon followed. Its ruler, Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan, described as a Sayyid from Kaithal and also as an Afghan, declared independence; the date of the revolt is uncertain, and the sultanate's founding year rests on its coins. The kingdom ruled Madurai, Tiruchirapalli and parts of South Arcot.

Jalaluddin's daughter married the traveller Ibn Battuta, and when Muhammad bin Tughluq heard of the rebellion he had Jalaluddin's son Ibrahim, his own purse bearer, killed. An expedition from Delhi in 1337 failed when the sultan fell ill at Bidar, and his army was defeated. Jalaluddin was killed by one of his nobles in 1340, and Ala-ud-Din Udauji Shah and Qutb-ud-Din Firuz Shah followed within that year before Ghiyas-ud-din Damghani seized power.

Ghiyasuddin, defeated at first by the Hoysala king Veera Ballala III, captured him during the siege of Kannanur Koppam in 1343, robbed him, had him killed and displayed his stuffed body on the walls of Madurai. He died in 1344 from the effects of an aphrodisiac, and his nephew Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Damghan Shah killed many officers and nobles before being killed himself. Eight rulers reigned in 43 years.

No coins survive from 1344 to 1357, which suggests a time of infighting, but coins of Shams-ud-Din Adil Shah, Fakhr-ud-Din Mubarak Shah and Ala-ud-Din Sikandar Shah show a revival until 1378. The contemporary accounts of Ibn Battuta and of Gangadevi, wife of the conqueror Kumara Kampana, describe the sultans as tyrants who impaled Hindu prisoners and killed women and children. Gangadevi's Sanskrit poem Madhura Vijayam celebrates the conquest, after which the Srirangam Ranganatha temple was restored in 1371 and the Madurai Nayakas later rose.
madyes: In the 8th and 7th centuries BCE a movement of steppe nomads brought the Scythians south of the Caucasus, where eastern Transcaucasia, in the region of present-day Azerbaijan, became the centre of their operations in West Asia. Madyes's father, the previous Scythian king, made an alliance with the Neo-Assyrian Empire and asked for the hand of the Assyrian princess Šērūʾa-ēṭirat, daughter of Esarhaddon; she was probably Madyes's mother, which would make Ashurbanipal his uncle. The marriage made the Scythians vassals of Assyria, and their power in West Asia came to rest on that alliance. The scholar Mikhail Bukharin derives his name, which reached the Greek authors through Persian sources, from a Western Iranic word meaning Median.

When Shamash-shum-ukin of Babylon revolted against his brother Ashurbanipal in 652 BCE, the Medes supported him, and Madyes helped suppress the revolt by invading Media. He then imposed Scythian rule over Media for twenty-eight years on behalf of the Assyrians, the period Greek writers called the Scythian rule over Asia, and extended it to Urartu, while Media, Mannai and Urartu continued as kingdoms under Scythian overlordship.

The Cimmerians, who had sacked the Lydian capital Sardis in 644 BCE under Tugdammi, and the Thracian Treres, who took Sardis again in 637 BCE, threatened Assyria's north-west. Soon after 635 BCE Madyes entered Anatolia with Assyrian approval and in alliance with Lydia, expelled the Treres and broke the Cimmerians for good. Strabo credits Madyes with the victory, while Herodotus and Polyaenus credit Alyattes of Lydia. Scythian power then reached from the Halys river to the Caspian Sea and from Transcaucasia to the borders of Assyria.

After Ashurbanipal died in 631 BCE the Assyrian empire began to unravel. In 625 BCE Cyaxares, son of the Median king Phraortes, invited the Scythian rulers to a banquet, made them drunk and murdered them, Madyes among them. His successor is unknown. Graeco-Roman writers later merged him with earlier and later kings into one figure who drove the Cimmerians from their homeland and defeated the Medes and the Egyptian king Sesostris of Greek tradition.
maeatae: The sources are vague about where the Maeatae lived. The fort near the summit of Dumyat in the Ochils, whose Gaelic name Dùn Mhèad is believed to mean hill of the Maeatae, may have marked their northern boundary, and Myot Hill near Fankerton plausibly their southern limit. Excavations at Dumyat led by Murray Cook found an outer ditch with a radiocarbon date of the 5th to 7th centuries. Three other possible place names, Dalmeny in West Lothian, Cremannan near Balfron and Rummond at St Andrews, would give them a wider territory.

John Rhys placed them between the Firth of Forth and the Firth of Tay, in parts of what are now Clackmannanshire, Fife and Stirlingshire, and suggested that the Isle of May was named after them. Cassius Dio put them between the wall and the Caledonians, but it is disputed whether he meant the Antonine Wall or Hadrian's Wall.

The confederation appears to have formed through the treaties the Roman Empire made with the frontier tribes in the 180s, under the governor Ulpius Marcellus. At the end of the second century the governor Virius Lupus was obliged to buy peace from them. In 210 they began a serious revolt, reportedly very bloody on both sides, and another revolt followed the next year. In 213, according to Joseph Ritson, they received money from the Romans to keep the peace.
The Miathi of Adomnán's Life of Columba, probably to be identified with the Southern Picts, have been taken as the same people, which would carry their identity into the 6th or 7th centuries.
maeda-clan: The Maeda claimed descent from the Sugawara clan through Sugawara no Kiyotomo and Sugawara no Michizane in the 8th and 9th centuries, though the line is uncertain. Their name comes from Maeda, a place in Kaitō District of western Owari Province, seat of the senior branch in the Azuchi-Momoyama period. A cadet branch held the castle of Arako, now part of Nakagawa-ku in Nagoya. Its head Maeda Toshimasa served Oda Nobuhide, and his son Maeda Toshihisa served the Oda in turn until he was made to retire in favour of his brother Maeda Toshiie.

Maeda Toshiie began as a page of Oda Nobunaga and rose as a member of the akahoro-shū under Nobunaga's personal command to become an infantry captain. A friend of Toyotomi Hideyoshi from his youth, he fought at the Battle of Anegawa in 1570 and the Battle of Tedorigawa in 1577 and, under Shibata Katsuie, against the Ikkō-ikki in Hokuriku. He received Fuchu in Etchū Province, then Noto Province in 1581, and after Nobunaga's death served Hideyoshi, who extended his lands over all of Noto, Kaga and Etchū. Toshiie divided the fief among his sons; the eldest, Maeda Toshinaga, fought at the Battle of Sekigahara, built Kanazawa Castle and was confirmed by the Tokugawa.

The Maeda ruled from Kanazawa from 1583 until the Meiji Restoration of 1868. Though a tozama clan, they kept good relations with the Tokugawa through marriage and were allowed the honorific name Matsudaira. Maeda Toshitsune founded cadet branches at Toyama and Daishōji, and Toshiie's fifth son Maeda Toshitaka another at Nanokaichi in Kōzuke Province. The clan was often beset by O-Ie Sōdō incidents, and many heads died young or without heirs.

The clan took no prominent part in the Meiji Restoration. Afterwards the heads of its branches were made peers under the kazoku system, and the descendants of Maeda Nagatane, who had entered Toshiie's service and whose line served the Kaga Maeda as hereditary retainers, received the title of baron. Among the family's other members, Maeda Toshimasu, known as Maeda Keiji, a son of Takigawa Kazumasu adopted by Toshihisa, was remembered as a warrior; legend has him breaking the Mogami line with eight riders.
maeda-toshiie: Maeda Toshiie was born on 15 January 1538 in the village of Arako, in present-day Nagoya, the fourth of seven brothers of Maeda Toshimasa, who held Arako Castle. His childhood name was Inuchiyo. He served Oda Nobunaga from childhood, first as a page, and like Nobunaga dressed in the outlandish style of a kabukimono. His loyalty was rewarded when he was allowed to head the Maeda clan, unusual for a fourth son. His preferred weapon was the yari, a spear, and he became known as Yari no Mataza. He is believed to have been a friend of Kinoshita Tokichiro, later Toyotomi Hideyoshi, in their youth.

Toshiie began in Nobunaga's personal unit, the akahoro-shū, whose members wore a red cloak, and later led it and became an infantry captain. In 1559 he killed Nobunaga's attendant Jūami in a quarrel over a stolen hairpin and was dismissed as a rōnin. He fought secretly at Okehazama in 1560 and at Moribe in 1561, and after Moribe Nobunaga pardoned him. In 1569 Nobunaga ordered his elder brother Toshihisa, who was in frail health, to give up the headship, and Toshiie succeeded. He fought at Anegawa, Nagashino and Tedorigawa, and was granted the fief of Fuchū and a domain spanning Noto and Kaga, which became the richest han of the Edo period, rated at a million koku.

After Nobunaga's death at Honnō-ji in 1582 Toshiie first backed Shibata Katsuie, and in 1583 he changed sides to Hideyoshi during the Battle of Shizugatake. In 1584 he defeated his friend Sassa Narimasa at Suemori Castle. In 1590 he and Uesugi Kagekatsu led a force of 35,000 through the Usui Pass in the Odawara Campaign, taking a series of Hōjō strongholds, and in 1591 he helped suppress the Kunohe rebellion. In 1587 he sheltered the Christian daimyo Dom Justo Takayama.

Before dying in 1598 Hideyoshi named Toshiie to the council of Five Elders to support his heir Toyotomi Hideyori. When Tokugawa Ieyasu arranged forbidden marriage alliances, Ishida Mitsunari and others relied on Toshiie and many daimyo supported him, so Ieyasu apologised. Toshiie died on 27 April 1599, himself ailing. His son Toshinaga was then accused by Ieyasu of an assassination plot, and Toshiie's widow Matsu persuaded the clan to submit by going as a hostage to the Tokugawa; the Maeda fought on the Tokugawa side at Sekigahara in 1600. A sword, the Ōdenta, once held by the Ashikaga shoguns, passed to Toshiie, and a legend says it healed his daughter.
maeda-toshinaga: Toshinaga, whose childhood name was Inuchiyo, was born in what is now part of Nagoya in Owari Province, where his father served Oda Nobunaga. In 1581 he married one of Nobunaga's daughters, Ei-hime. Nobunaga was assassinated the following year in the Honnō-ji Incident. In 1583 Toshinaga fought beside his father at the Battle of Shizugatake, and after the death of Shibata Katsuie he swore fealty to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who gave him a fief of 40,000 koku in Kaga Province.

In 1585 he took a leading part in Hideyoshi's campaign against Sassa Narimasa, and his holdings grew to 320,000 koku across Kaga and Etchū. He led some 3,000 men in the Kyūshū Campaign of 1587 and at the Siege of Odawara in 1590. In 1598 he received his father's Kanazawa holdings, and after Toshiie's death Hosokawa Tadaoki persuaded him to back Tokugawa Ieyasu against Ishida Mitsunari and Toyotomi Hideyori.

During the Sekigahara campaign his task was to hold back the forces of Uesugi Kagekatsu and Niwa Nagashige, whom he met at the Battle of Asainawate, and to keep his younger brother Maeda Toshimasa, ruler of Noto, from joining the western army. Under the Tokugawa shogunate his domain reached 1,025,000 koku, exceeded only by the shogun's own house. He built and lived in Kanazawa Castle, and under the system of alternate attendance he was the first daimyō to set up a residence in Edo.

Having no son, Toshinaga adopted his younger brother Maeda Toshitsune as heir and retired in 1605 to Toyama Castle, keeping 220,000 koku for his expenses. When Toyama Castle burned in 1609 he moved to Uozu and then to Takaoka. Suffering from complications of syphilis, he withdrew more and more from public life, and in 1614 he took his own life by poison at Takaoka Castle. His mortuary temple is Zuiryū-ji in Takaoka.
maeda-tsunanori: Maeda Tsunanori was born on 26 December 1643 at the Maeda clan residence in Edo, the eldest son of Maeda Mitsutaka; his childhood name was Inuchiyo. His father died in 1645 at the age of 29, leaving the domain to a two-year-old, and by order of the Tokugawa shogunate his grandfather Maeda Toshitsune became regent. In 1654 he came of age in a genpuku ceremony over which Shōgun Tokugawa Ietsuna presided, receiving court rank and the title Kaga-no-kami.

In 1658 he was married for political reasons to Suma-hime, the ten-year-old daughter of Hoshina Masayuki of Aizu Domain; she died in 1666 at 18, and he never formally remarried. The same year Toshitsune died, and at 15 Tsunanori took full control of the domain. He grouped villages in tens to ease tax collection and the opening of new rice land, put famine relief and medical care on a more systematic footing, and revised the domain's laws, which had been severe since Maeda Toshiie's suppression of the Ikkō-ikki. He also settled a long border dispute with Fukui Domain over the holy mountain of Hakusan.

He patronised the arts, above all Noh performances, and built up a major collection of Japanese and Chinese literature, though he is best known for developing the Kenroku-en gardens in Kanazawa. In 1689, under Shōgun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, the domain was granted the same courtesy at audiences in Edo Castle as the Gosanke, and its assessed yield was set at 1 million koku.

Tsunanori had children by several concubines, and his daughters married into the Asano, Ikeda and Nijō families among others. He was raised to the court rank of Sangi in 1693 and to Senior Third Grade in 1707. He retired from public life in 1723 and died on 29 June 1724 at the age of 80. In 1909 he was posthumously raised to the Second Grade of court rank.
maedoc-of-ferns: Irish tradition places his birth around 558 at Inisbrefny, an island in Templeport Lake in what is now County Cavan, and makes him a son of Sedna, a chieftain of Connaught, and his wife Eithne. Welsh genealogies instead call him a son of Gildas or Aneurin. Because of these separate origins, the long span of his activity and two dates of death, some scholars, such as Sabine Baring-Gould, have proposed that his stories join two men named Aed, one Welsh and one Irish.

According to his lives, he was held as a youth as a hostage of Ainmuire mac Sétnai, High King of Ireland, and won the release of all the hostages. He studied at the school of Saint Finnian at Clonard Abbey, where he befriended Molaise of Devenish, and then went to Wales. The Welsh triads list him as one of the three most faithful disciples of Saint David.

Tradition says he returned to Ireland in 570, landing on the Wexford coast with hives of bees, and settled at Brentrocht in Leinster. His hagiographers credit his prayers with the victory of King Brandubh of Leinster over the High King Áed mac Ainmuirech at the Battle of Dún Bolg in 598, though the Aidan named in that tale may be another man. Brandubh granted him Ferns, and a synod made Ferns a see and gave its bishop nominal supremacy over the other Leinster bishops. Stories tell of his hospitality and meekness, and his lives record many miracles in Wales and Ireland.

He is credited with founding thirty churches and several monasteries, among them one on the island of his birth, Drumlane in County Cavan, Dissert-Nairbre in County Waterford and Rosinver in County Leitrim, as well as a church at Haroldston West in Pembrokeshire. He died on the shore of Lough Melvin, and his relics are claimed by St Edan's Cathedral in Ferns. His shrine, the Breac Maodhóg, dates from the 9th century, was used for swearing oaths and is now in the National Museum of Ireland. He is the patron saint of Wexford, Ferns and Templeport.
mael-sechnaill-mac-domnaill: Máel Sechnaill, also called Máel Sechnaill Mór, belonged to the Clann Cholmáin branch of the Uí Néill. He was a grandson of Donnchad Donn, a great-grandson of Flann Sinna and a great-great-grandson of the first Máel Sechnaill, Máel Sechnaill mac Máele Ruanaid. By his time the kingship of Tara alternated between Clann Cholmáin in the south and the Cenél nEógain in the north, a system that had survived the kings of Ulster, Munster and Leinster and the Viking invasions, and so he succeeded Domnall ua Néill in 980.

In 980 Olaf Cuaran, King of Dublin, attacked Meath with auxiliaries from the Scottish Isles and Mann, and was defeated at the Battle of Tara, where his heir Reginald was killed. Dublin surrendered after a siege of three days and nights, and according to the Annals of Tigernach Máel Sechnaill freed the slaves held there. At a meeting near Clonfert in 997 he made a truce with his rival Brian Boru, King of Munster, leaving Brian the southern half of Ireland and himself the north and the high kingship; the two exchanged hostages.

When the Leinstermen and the Norse of Dublin revolted against Brian late in 999, the two kings joined forces and, according to the Annals of Ulster, defeated them at Glenmama on 30 December 999, opening the road to Dublin. In 1002 Brian displaced him as high king, a bloodless change that came about because his northern kinsmen failed to support him. After Brian, his son and grandson died at the Battle of Clontarf in 1014, Máel Sechnaill regained the title with the aid of Flaithbertach Ua Néill.

He died on 2 September 1022. His two known wives were Gormflaith ingen Murchada and Máel Muire ingen Amlaíb, and his six known children included Conchobar, Flann, Congalach and Domnall. Brian's rise had ended the alternating succession of the Uí Néill, and Clann Cholmáin provided no further high kings, though the Cenél nEógain later gave two, Domnall Ua Lochlainn and Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn.
mael-sechnaill-mac-maele-ruanaid: Máel Sechnaill was the son of Máel Ruanaid and grandson of Donnchad Midi mac Domnaill, King of Tara from around 778 to 797. Clann Cholmáin, a sept of the southern Uí Néill, ruled Mide in east central Ireland, and the largely symbolic Kingship of Tara alternated between it and the Cenél nEógain of the northern Uí Néill. He appears in the annals in 839 and in 841, when he killed his cousin Diarmait, who had tried to depose his father. He became king of Mide after killing his brother Flann in 845.

He became king of Tara in 846 on the death of Niall Caille mac Áeda, who drowned in the Callan River. Later sources such as the Cogadh Gaedhil re Gallaibh portray his reign as constant war with the Vikings, but he was at times allied with the Norse-Gaels. His real achievements lay in Ulster and Munster. The Ulster king Matudán mac Muiredaig and Diarmait, Abbot of Armagh, acknowledged him as High King, and his army is called the men of Ireland in 858.

He led expeditions into Munster for tribute and hostages in 854, 856 and 858. His rival there was Cerball mac Dúnlainge, king of Osraige, who drew allies from the Norse of southern Ireland and in 859 entered Mide with Amlaíb and Ivar. An assembly of kings and clerics at Rahugh in County Westmeath in 859 detached Osraige from Munster. His last years were spent fighting the northern Uí Néill under Áed Findliath, whose night attack on his camp near Armagh in 860 was beaten off.

Máel Sechnaill died peacefully on 27 November 862. The Annals of Ulster call him rí hÉrenn uile, king of all Ireland, a title that sets him apart from the usual Kings of Tara, who are called High Kings only in late sources. His achievements did not outlast him: Áed Findliath could neither keep peace among the Uí Néill nor obtain the submission of Munster. His son Flann Sinna later became King of Mide and High King.
maelgwn-gwynedd: Maelgwn was the son of Cadwallon Lawhir ap Einion and Meddyf, a daughter of Maeldaf, and a great-grandson of Cunedda. His Middle Welsh name means Princely Hound. After Roman authority collapsed, north Wales had been settled by Gaelic tribes from Ireland; Cunedda's northern Britons reconquered the coast, and Cadwallon destroyed the last Irish settlements on Anglesey. Maelgwn was the first king to enjoy the fruits of that conquest and is considered the founder of the royal family of medieval Gwynedd.

The only contemporary account is the De Excidio et Conquestu Britanniae of Gildas, written around 540, which condemns five British kings in images from the Book of Revelation. Gildas says Maelgwn overthrew his maternal uncle to take the throne, became a monk and returned to the world, and married the widow of a nephew for whose death he was responsible. Gildas's choice of only these kings has led historians to suspect a motive beyond the moral outrage he claims.

Maelgwn gave generously to the church, supporting the saints Brynach in Dyfed, Cadoc in Gwynllwg, Cybi in Anglesey, Padarn in Ceredigion and Tydecho in Powys; the claim that he founded the see of Bangor lacks hard evidence. That his gifts reached across the lands ruled by Cunedda's descendants suggests he held a regional pre-eminence among them, perhaps as a kind of high king, though nothing points to a wider rule.

He died in a great mortality a few years after the Plague of Justinian broke out in Constantinople; historians debate whether this was that plague or a severe relapsing fever. Tradition buries him at Llanrhos or on Ynys Seiriol, now Puffin Island, though no record confirms either. His son Rhun succeeded him. Later writers, from Geoffrey of Monmouth to the forged Iolo Manuscripts, added fictions to his story. Through the House of Gwynedd and later the House of Tudor, his descendants are recorded to the present.
maelor: The Maelor is an area of north-east Wales along the border with England. Its name is an old Welsh word that can be translated as land of the prince, from mael, prince, and llawr, low ground or region. Maelor Gymraeg, known in English as Bromfield, lay west of the river Dee, and Maelor Saesneg, the English Maelor, lay east of it and reached almost to Whitchurch.

The Maelor began as a cantref of the Kingdom of Powys centred on the monastic settlement of Bangor-on-Dee, with the commotes of Maelor, Yale (Iâl), the Alyn Valley (Ystrad Alun) and Hope (Yr Hob). Most of it fell to the Kingdom of Mercia in the 8th century, with Offa's Dyke marking the new border. At the Norman conquest of 1066 its eastern lands were held by Edwin, Earl of Mercia, and later granted to Hugh d'Avranches, Earl of Chester. Madog ap Maredudd brought it back into Powys in the reign of Stephen of England (1135–54).

By the early 13th century the Maelor belonged to Madog ap Gruffydd, Prince of Powys Fadog, and was divided in two; Malaur Saisnec appears in a document as early as 1202. The word English is thought to reflect church rather than language, as the area lay in the Diocese of Lichfield and Chester, while the Welsh Maelor stayed in the Diocese of St Asaph. After Edward I's conquest of 1282-3 the English Maelor became crown property and in 1284 part of the new county of Flintshire, while the Welsh Maelor went to the Marcher Lordship of Bromfield and Yale, granted to Earl John de Warenne.

In 1397 the English Maelor was attached to the County Palatine of Chester to form the Principality of Chester. After 1536 it remained a detached part of Flintshire, centred on Overton and surrounded by Cheshire, Shropshire and Denbighshire, until 1974, while the Welsh Maelor became the Hundred of Bromfield in Denbighshire.

The Maelor is now entirely part of Wrexham County Borough. When local government in Wales was reorganised in 1974, both halves were included in Wrexham Maelor, one of six districts of the new county of Clwyd, and they passed to the newly created county borough of Wrexham at a further reorganisation in 1996.
maeotians: The name comes from the sea: Maeotian was at first a label for the tribes living around the Maeotis, above all on its eastern coast. In sources of the 4th century BCE it has three senses: a broad term for the peoples around the sea, the name of the coastal tribes later listed by Strabo, and, in the usage of the Bosporan chancery, the lesser tribes of the Kuban region as distinct from the Sindi.

Their language, and even its family, is uncertain; the place names of their country suggest that they were not of Iranian stock. The Cambridge Ancient History reports two main views, that they were of Cimmerian ancestry, akin to the Thracians, or that they were Caucasian natives under Iranian overlordship. Soviet scholars concluded that they were among the ancestors of the Circassian, or Adyghe, people.

Strabo names among them the Sindi, Dandarii, Toreatae, Agri, Arrechi, Tarpetes, Obidiaceni, Sittaceni and Dosci, and adds that there were many others. Which peoples counted as Maeotian was disputed already in antiquity: Hellanicus of Lesbos and Pseudo-Scylax set the Sindi apart, while Pseudo-Scymnus and Strabo include them. The Sindi are the best attested and were probably the dominant people of the region.

The Maeotians lived in earthworks and open settlements on the Taman Peninsula and along the middle Kuban. According to Strabo they were as warlike as their nomadic neighbours, paid tribute at times to the rulers of Tanais and at times to the Bosporans, and rose in revolt from time to time. In the Kuban region they lived under successive steppe overlords. The graves show it: the ruling Scythians, and in Sindica the Sindian elite, were buried in richly furnished kurgans, while the Maeotian population used poorly equipped flat cemeteries.

In the early 4th century BCE Maeotian tribes fought a major war against the Bosporan Kingdom and its Sindian subjects. When the Sindian king Hecataeus repudiated his Maeotian wife Tirgatao, she roused her people, the Ixomatae, and other tribes to a destructive war on both kingdoms, which ended only under Gorgippus through supplication and gifts.

After Leucon I annexed Sindica, probably in the 380s BCE, the tribes of the Kuban were brought into the Bosporan state by stages. Leucon ruled the Toretae, Dandarii and Psessi as king, and under Paerisades I the royal style became king of the Sindi and all the Maeotians. Under Aspurgus, in the early 1st century CE, the royal titles still listed the Sindi and Maeotians, now with the Tarpetes and the people of Tanais.
mafra-national-palace: King John V of Portugal made a vow in 1711 to build a convent if his wife, Maria Anna of Austria, bore him a child, and the birth of his first daughter, the Infanta Barbara, led to construction. The site was chosen in 1713 and bought in 1716, and the first stone was laid on 17 November 1717 before the king, his court and the Cardinal Patriarch of Lisbon. It began as a small friary for 13 Capuchin friars who were to live in strict poverty. When gold and diamonds from Brazil arrived in Lisbon in abundance, the king announced a sumptuous palace and a much larger friary instead.

He made João Frederico Ludovice director of the royal works. Several other architects took part, including Carlos Baptista Garbo, Custódio Vieira and Manuel da Maia, but one style runs through the whole building. Construction lasted 13 years and employed on average 15,000 workers daily, up to 45,000 at the peak, with 7,000 soldiers keeping order. A total of 1,383 workers died. The basilica and convent were inaugurated on 22 October 1730, the king's 41st birthday, with eight days of festivities.

The facade is 220 metres long, with a square domed tower at each end and the white marble basilica at the centre, flanked by the royal palace. John V had sought advice from his ambassador in Rome, and the central balcony echoes that of St Peter's Basilica. The towers and the dome were inspired by Sant'Agnese in Agone by Francesco Borromini. The complex has about 1,200 rooms and housed up to 330 friars. The basilica has 58 marble statues by Roman sculptors, six organs built between 1792 and 1807, and carillons cast in Antwerp. The Rococo library, 88 metres long, houses bats that protect the books from insects.

The palace was never lived in permanently, since the royal family found it gloomy, but it served for hunting. Work stopped in 1755, when workers were needed in Lisbon after the earthquake. The royal family fled to Brazil in 1807, and Jean-Andoche Junot, driven out by Wellington, used the palace. The Franciscans left in 1834 and the monastery was given to the military in 1849; the last king, Manuel II, left from Mafra on 5 October 1910 for exile. A Mafra School of Sculpture, headed by Alessandro Giusti, trained Portuguese sculptors, among them Joaquim Machado de Castro. José Saramago's novel Baltasar and Blimunda describes its building. On 7 July 2019 it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
magadha: Magadha was a region and kingdom of ancient India in the eastern Ganges plain, one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas of the period of the second urbanisation. Before it expanded, its territory was bounded on the north, west and east by the Ganga, Son and Campa rivers, with the eastern spurs of the Vindhya mountains to the south, and corresponded to the modern Patna and Gaya districts of Bihar. Its first capital was Rajagriha, now Rajgir, and later Pataliputra, now Patna. A wider Greater Magadha, covering neighbouring parts of the eastern Gangetic plain, had a distinct culture.

The Atharvaveda, composed about 1200 to 900 BCE, lists the Magadhas among non-Vedic tribes outside the Kuru-Panchala cultural sphere, and according to the Puranas the Brihadratha dynasty was the first to rule. Information on early rulers is scarce; the main sources are the Buddhist Pali Canon, the Jain Agamas and the Puranas, all written long after the events. The Haryanka dynasty is said to have ruled for some 130 years, with dates that are uncertain and could be significantly later. Its notable kings, Bimbisara and his son Ajatashatru, appear in Buddhist and Jain literature as contemporaries of the Buddha and Mahavira. Magadha grew to include most of Bihar and Bengal by conquering the Vajjika League and Anga.

Mahapadma Nanda took the throne and founded the Nanda dynasty, which conquered much of north India from about 345 to about 322 BCE. Chandragupta Maurya overthrew it and founded the Maurya Empire, which lasted from about 322 to 185 BCE. The Shunga Empire and the Kanva dynasty followed, then rule from outside and later the Gupta Empire, from about 240 to about 579, centred in Magadha. The Later Guptas and the Maukharis ruled parts of the region afterwards, and from the 11th to the late 13th century Buddhist kings known as the Pithipatis called themselves Lords of Magadha.

Magadha was a centre of the sramana movements, which rejected Vedic authority and gave rise to Jainism, Buddhism and Ajivika. The Buddha lived much of his life in Magadha, attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, and the first Buddhist council was held at Rajgriha. Early Magadhan kings supported Buddhism and Jainism. Its language, Magadhi Prakrit, later evolved into Magahi, Maithili and Bhojpuri, and the Pali language has traditionally been identified with Magadhi. Two UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the region: the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya and the Nalanda monastery.
magar-people: The first home of the Magars lay west of the Gandaki River, around Gulmi, Arghakhanchi and Palpa. This country was divided into twelve districts known as the Bahra Magarat, a confederation of twelve Magar villages, while another confederation of eighteen Magar kingdoms, the Athara Magarat, was originally inhabited by Kham Magars. In the medieval period the whole area from Palpa to Rukum and Rolpa was called the Magarat. Several mythical stories tell of their origin, and the first written history of the Magars dates back to about 1100 CE.

In the 1750s Prithvi Narayan Shah relied heavily on his Magar soldiers as he brought the small kingdoms of the region together. Magars held high office at the court: Biraj Thapa Magar was the first army chief, and Abhiman Singh Rana Magar and Sarbajit Rana Magar headed the army. Their influence ended with the Kot Massacre, of which Abhiman Singh Rana Magar was the first victim, and under the Rana dynasty they held almost no government posts. The British began recruiting them into Gurkha regiments from 1815. During the Nepalese Civil War of 1996 to 2006, Magars formed a large part of the Maoist People's Liberation Army, and Magar villages gave the insurgents food and shelter.

The Magars are divided into eight clans, Ale, Budha, Chitorey, Gharti, Pun, Rana, Roka and Thapa, which intermarry, share the same customs and are equal in social standing. In the 2021 census 2,013,498 people in Nepal identified as Magar, of whom about 810,315 spoke Magar Dhut and 91,753 Magar Kham as their mother tongue, the rest mostly Nepali. Most follow Hinduism, with much blending of Buddhism, animism and ancestor worship. Maghe Sankranti in mid-January marks the turn from udheli to ubheli, the down and up halves of the year that probably follow the herding of livestock between pastures. The Sorathi or Maruni dance originated among them.
magas-of-cyrene: Magas was the first-born son of the Macedonian noblewoman Berenice and her first husband Philip, an officer in the campaigns of Alexander the Great who commanded one division of the phalanx. He had two younger sisters, Antigone of Epirus and Theoxena of Syracuse. Philip died of natural causes about 318 BCE, and Berenice took her children to the Ptolemaic Kingdom, to the entourage of her cousin Eurydice, wife of Ptolemy I. By 317 BCE Ptolemy had repudiated Eurydice to marry Berenice, so that Magas became a stepson of Ptolemy I and a member of the Ptolemaic dynasty. His mother bore Ptolemy three children, Arsinoe II, Philotera and the future Ptolemy II.

After Agathocles of Syracuse had Ophellas, the governor of Cyrene, put to death in November 308 BCE, Ptolemy ruled Cyrene directly, but the Cyrenaeans rebelled soon after he declared himself king. Around 300 BCE Ptolemy sent Magas, then about twenty, to reconquer the city, and he stayed on as governor. After Ptolemy I's death in 283 BCE, Magas tried to win independence from his half-brother Ptolemy II and crowned himself king; the date of his coronation is disputed, with proposals between 283 and 280 BCE and a later date of 276 or 274 BCE.

He married Apama II, a daughter of the Seleucid king Antiochus I Soter, and Antiochus used the alliance to plan an invasion of Egypt. Magas attacked Egypt from the west while Antiochus attacked Palestine, but Magas had to cancel his operations because the nomadic Libyan Marmaridae revolted, and Antiochus was defeated by Ptolemy II.

Afterwards his reign was largely peaceful and he favoured the arts and sciences, and the Cyrenaic philosophical school. In a treaty of the 260s with the Cretan League of the Oreioi he is called basileus, while Cyrenaica is called an eparchia, a province. After 259 BCE he betrothed his only child, Berenice II, to Ptolemy II's son, the future Ptolemy III.

Magas died in 250 BCE. Agatharchides, as reported by Athenaeus, records that he spent his rule in luxury and avoided war, and grew so corpulent that he choked on his own fat. His widow Apama II broke the engagement and offered her daughter and the throne to Demetrius the Fair, son of Demetrius I Poliorcetes, who became king of Cyrene; Berenice II had Demetrius killed and returned to Egypt to marry Ptolemy III. The Edicts of Ashoka name Magas among the Hellenistic kings to whom the Indian emperor's Buddhist teaching reached, although no Western source records such envoys.
magdalena-river: The Magdalena rises in the south of Colombia, in Huila Department, where the Cordillera Central and the Cordillera Oriental separate. It runs east and then north in a great valley between the two ranges, reaches the coastal plain at about nine degrees north, runs west for about 100 kilometres, and turns north again to enter the Caribbean at Barranquilla, in the zone called Bocas de Ceniza. Its length is 1,528 kilometres, and it is the largest river system of the northern Andes. It is navigable through much of its lower reaches, despite shifting sand bars at the mouth of its delta, as far as Honda, at the foot of its rapids.

Its basin covers 273,000 square kilometres, 24 percent of the area of Colombia, and 66 percent of the country's people live there. The valley was formed by tectonic depressions that filled with sediment from the Central Ranges in the Tertiary period. The river takes its name from Mary Magdalene.

Since pre-Columbian times the river has been a route into the interior of present-day Colombia and Ecuador. Carib-speaking peoples such as the Panche and the Yariguí went up its western bank, while the Muisca civilisation lived on the eastern side and called the river Yuma. Rodrigo de Bastidas discovered and named it on 1 April 1501. Spanish conquistadors used it in the 16th century to push into the mountainous interior, and during the colonial period it was the only transport link between Bogotá and the port of Cartagena de Indias, and so with Europe.

The Magdalena Campaign of Pierre Labatut and Simón Bolívar took place along the river. In 1825 the Congress of Colombia awarded Juan Bernardo Elbers a concession for steam navigation, but his company closed soon after. By 1845 steamboats ran regularly, and they continued until 1961, when the last steamers stopped. The first recorded European contact with the potato was in 1537 in the Magdalena Valley, and potatoes probably reached Europe by Spanish ship around 1570.

The valley crosses ecosystems from páramo at the headwaters through dry forest and rainforest to swamps and wetlands in the lower course. The basin, which includes the Cauca River, is very rich in fish, and about 55 percent of its species are endemic. The Magdalena Valley is also an important area for oil exploration. Gabriel García Márquez's novel The General in His Labyrinth is a fictionalised account of Bolívar's last voyage down the river.
magdeburg: Magdeburg stands on the Elbe river and is the capital of the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. It is first mentioned in a document as Magadoburg in the Capitulary of Diedenhofen issued by Charlemagne in 805, and the name probably comes from Old High German magado, big or mighty, and burg, fortress. The city marked its 1,200th anniversary in 2005.

King Henry the Fowler fortified the town in 919 against the Magyars and Slavs. In 929 King Otto I granted it to his English-born wife Edith as dower, and Otto himself was buried in the cathedral. The archbishops played a prominent part in the German colonisation of the Slavic lands east of the Elbe. In 1035 the city received a patent giving it the right to hold trade exhibitions, which formed the basis of the Magdeburg rights. In the thirteenth century Magdeburg joined the Hanseatic League. Fires in 1188 and 1207 destroyed much of it.

Martin Luther preached there in 1524, after which the city left Roman Catholicism, and Matthias Flacius and his companions wrote the Magdeburg Centuries there. The city withstood a siege by Albrecht von Wallenstein in 1629. In 1631 imperial troops under Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, stormed it, massacred the inhabitants and burned it, and only about 4,000 people remained after the war. Otto von Guericke, its mayor and a scientist, led the recovery. Under the Peace of Westphalia the city passed to Brandenburg-Prussia in 1680.

Magdeburg surrendered to French troops in 1806 and in 1815 became the capital of the Prussian Province of Saxony. A British air raid on 16 January 1945 destroyed much of the city centre. It belonged to East Germany from 1949 to 1990, and in 1990 became the capital of Saxony-Anhalt.
magdeburg-borde: The Magdeburg Börde is the central landscape unit of Saxony-Anhalt, part of a loess belt along the south-eastern rim of the North German Plain. Its boundaries are ill-defined. To the west it meets the East Brunswick hill country near the Hohes Holz forest and Oschersleben, where its border north of the town roughly follows the Weser-Elbe watershed along the Druxberge hills. To the north the river Ohre and the Mittelland Canal divide it from the Altmark, and to the east the Elbe and the lower Saale mark its edge.

In the south the lower Bode river below Oschersleben forms the border, and the northern foothills of the Harz east of the Selke river are sometimes counted as part of the Börde. The landscape is gently undulating and largely treeless. Beneath a cover of wind-blown loess lies loose morainic material of the Saale glaciation, with outcrops of older rock. The Börde lies in the rain shadow of the Harz Mountains and is one of the driest regions of Germany. Its highest point is the Großer Wartberg near Niederndodeleben, at 145.7 m.

The soils are very fertile, partly of black earth, on loess laid over the glacial debris. In 1934 the soil of Eickendorf, now part of Bördeland, was given a soil value of 100, the richest in Germany, and served as the yardstick for German soils until the division of the country in 1945.

Sugar beet and wheat are the main crops on these soils. Its towns include Wanzleben, Irxleben and Egeln, with Staßfurt and Aschersleben in the Harz foothills, and a variant of West Low German known as Bördeplatt is traditionally spoken there, though by fewer and fewer people. The A 2 and A 14 motorways and the railway from Hanover through Magdeburg to Berlin serve the region.
magellans-cross: The cross stands in Magellan's Cross Pavilion, an octagonal stone kiosk of coral stone on Plaza Sugbo, beside the Basilica del Santo Niño in Cebu City. The pavilion was built in 1834 under Spanish colonial rule to house the cross that men of Ferdinand Magellan's expedition, the first to sail around the world, had planted in 1521.

In 1835 the original cross was encased in another cross of tindalo wood, to protect it from people who chipped off pieces in the belief that they had miraculous powers. A mural by Jess Roa and Serry M. Josol on the pavilion's ceiling shows the baptism of Rajah Humabon and his household by the priest Pedro Valderrama and Magellan planting a wooden cross.

The pavilion and the tindalo cross were cracked in the Bohol earthquake of 2013, and in 2015 the original cross was found to have been damaged by termites. The pavilion was closed for renovation and reopened in March 2016. It was closed to the public again after cracks caused by the Cebu earthquake of 2025, when worshippers prayed outside and placed Sinug candles inside through its doors and windows.

For the quincentennial commemorations of 2021 the cross was named the 2021 Jubilee Cross. On 14 April 2021 the National Museum of the Philippines declared the pavilion, together with the church and convent of the Basilica del Santo Niño, a National Cultural Treasure of the Philippines.
maghreb: The word maghrib is an Arabic term that the first Muslim Arab settlers gave in the 7th century to the recently conquered area west of the Umayyad capital of Damascus. It means both the western land and the place where the sun sets, in contrast to the Mashriq in the east. The Atlas Mountains and the Sahara isolate its northern parts from the rest of the continent, and these have long had commercial and cultural ties across the Mediterranean to Southern Europe and Western Asia.

The extent of the term has changed. Before the 20th century it most commonly meant Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia between the Mediterranean and the Atlas Mountains, often with eastern Libya and never with Mauritania. It has since widened to include Mauritania and the disputed territory of Western Sahara. During the era of al-Andalus its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants were known to Europeans as the Moors.

The Berber people have inhabited western North Africa since at least 10,000 BCE. Trade with the Phoenicians dates back to the 1st millennium BCE, and tradition holds that they founded Carthage around 800 BCE. The region was somewhat unified under the kingdom of Numidia, then briefly under the Kingdom of Mauretania, and then under Roman rule. The Vandals invaded afterwards, and the Byzantine Empire briefly re-established a weak Roman rule.

The Arabs reached the Maghreb in early Umayyad times. The founding of Kairouan in 667 gave Islam its first permanent foothold, Carthage fell in 698 and the rest of the region by 709. The Umayyad, Abbasid and Fatimid caliphates held power, but the longest-lasting rule was that of local dynasties such as the Idrisids, Almoravids, Almohads, Zirids and Marinids. Trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold, ivory and slaves was costly and dangerous but highly profitable. In the 19th and early 20th centuries France, Italy and Spain administered the region, and decolonisation followed after the Second World War.

Jewish communities have a long presence there. The earliest documented one dates to the third century BCE, when Ptolemaic rulers of Egypt settled Jews in eastern Libya, and after the expulsion of Jews from Spain in 1492 many Sephardic Jews settled in North Africa. The region is primarily inhabited by peoples of Arab and Berber ancestry, and couscous was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2020.
magi: The word appears only twice in Iranian texts from before the 5th century BCE, and only one of those can be dated precisely. It occurs in the trilingual Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great, of about 520 BCE, where certain rebels are called magian; in the Old Persian portion the word is maγu-, generally assumed to be a loanword from Median, and its meaning there is uncertain.

The other instance, in the Younger Avesta, is the word moghu.tbiš, meaning hostile to the moghu, where moghu seems to mean a member of the tribe or a social class rather than a magus. A common Iranian term for a member of the tribe may have taken, among the Medes, the sense of a member of the priestly tribe, and so a priest.

In the mid-5th century BCE Herodotus used the word in two senses: for one of the tribes of the Medes, and for a sacerdotal caste whose ethnic origin is never mentioned again. He also showed the magi as interpreters of omens and dreams. In the early 4th century BCE Xenophon, who had seen the Persian court, depicted them as authorities on all religious matters and as responsible for educating the future king. Magi are recorded in Persia, Parthia, Bactria, Media and elsewhere, and in non-Iranian lands such as Arabia, Ethiopia and Egypt.

Greek mageia soon came to mean something close to magic in the modern sense, often with a pejorative tone, and magos came to mean a conjurer or charlatan. The Greeks made Pseudo-Zoroaster the founder of the magi and the inventor of astrology and magic, and Pliny the Elder, in the first century, named Zoroaster as the inventor of magic and called it a monstrous craft. The word magos displaced the older Greek goēs for a practitioner of magic.

In the Gospel of Matthew, magi from the east, guided by a star, pay homage to the infant Jesus and present gold, frankincense and myrrh; the plural magi entered English from Latin in this context around 1200, and the word is often rendered as kings or wise men. The Talmud depicts the magi as sorcerers who obstructed Jewish practice.

In Arabic, majus is the term for Zoroastrians, and it occurs in the Qur'an, in sura 22 verse 17. In India the Sakaldwipiya Brahmins are held to descend from Maga priests invited to worship Mitra at Multan. A hereditary Zoroastrian priesthood survives in India and Iran, with ranks called Herbad, Mobad and Dastur.
magna-carta: England was ruled by King John, the third of the Angevin kings. John and his predecessors had ruled by the principle of vis et voluntas, force and will, taking executive and sometimes arbitrary decisions, often on the basis that a king was above the law. Many contemporary writers believed that monarchs should rule in accordance with custom and law, with the counsel of the leading men of the realm, but there was no model for what should happen if a king refused to do so.

John had lost most of his ancestral lands in France to King Philip II in 1204 and spent years trying to regain them, raising heavy taxes on the barons to pay for a war that ended in costly failure in 1214. After the defeat of his allies at the Battle of Bouvines he had to sue for peace and pay compensation. Rebel barons in the north and east began to organise resistance.

The charter was first drafted by Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, and sealed by John at Runnymede on 15 June 1215. It promised the protection of church rights, protection for the barons from illegal imprisonment, swift and impartial justice and limits on feudal payments to the Crown, to be carried out through a council of 25 barons. Most of it governed the feudal rights of the Crown over the barons. Clauses 39 and 40 demanded due process in royal justice, which John had used to extort large sums.

At least thirteen copies were issued in 1215, and four survive: two at the British Library, one at Salisbury Cathedral and one at Lincoln Castle. There were no signatures, and the numbering of clauses used today was introduced by William Blackstone in 1759.

Neither side stood by its commitments, and Pope Innocent III annulled the charter, which led to the First Barons' War. After John's death the regency of his young son Henry III reissued it in 1216 without some of its more radical content, and again in 1217 as part of the peace agreed at Lambeth. Henry reissued it in 1225 in exchange for new taxes, and Edward I confirmed it in 1297 as part of England's statute law.

In the early 17th century lawyers such as Sir Edward Coke argued against the divine right of kings, claiming that an ancient English constitution had been restored by the charter. Victorian historians showed that the 1215 charter concerned the king and the barons, not ordinary subjects, and most historians now call its reading as a charter of universal rights a later myth. Only three clauses remain in force in England and Wales.
magna-graecia: The Greek expression Megale Hellas, later translated into Latin as Magna Graecia, is first attested in the historian Polybius, writing around 150 BCE, who ascribed it to Pythagoras and his school. Ancient authors used it for different parts of southern Italy, with or without Sicily. The sense that spread was the Greek cities of southern Italy along the coast between Cumae and Taras. The settlements lay in what are now Calabria, Apulia, Basilicata, Campania and, where Sicily is included, Sicily. Their inhabitants are called Italiotes and Siceliotes.

Greeks founded colonies because of famine and overcrowding, civil strife, a need for new ports and markets, and expulsion after wars. Unlike Roman colonies, they were not dependent on their mother cities but were independent city-states.

Greeks began to settle in southern Italy in the 8th century BCE. The first great wave, by Euboeans, went to the Gulf of Naples and the Strait of Messina; Pithecusae on Ischia is considered the oldest Greek settlement in Italy and Cumae the first on the mainland. A second wave of Achaeans, shortly before 720 BCE, settled the Ionian coast at Metapontion, Poseidonia, Sybaris and Kroton. Governments were typically aristocratic, though Syracuse had tyrants such as Dionysius.

By the 6th century BCE the Ionian cities were wealthy enough to fight one another. The Battle of the Sagra river set Locri Epizefiri against Kroton, Siris was destroyed by Sybaris and Metapontum, and Kroton destroyed Sybaris, which had an estimated population of 300,000 to 500,000 between 600 and 510 BCE. Pythagoras moved to Crotone and founded his school there in 530 BCE.

Neapolis was the first Greek city absorbed by the Roman Republic, in 327 BCE. Threatened by the Bruttii and Lucanians, other cities asked Rome for help, and it sent garrisons in the 280s BCE. Their independence ended when the Roman Republic annexed them during the Second Punic War, in 205 BCE.

Ruins of several cities remain, among them Syracuse, Agrigento, Taranto, Reggio Calabria and Crotone. The Valley of the Temples at Agrigento, with seven Doric temples, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, and Syracuse is also listed. Poseidonia and Elea are part of the Cilento World Heritage Site, listed in 1998. South Italian Greek pottery, especially of the 4th century BCE, is a notable legacy, and athletes of Crotone alone won 18 titles at the Olympic Games over 25 Olympiads. The Griko language, spoken by Griko communities in Calabria and Apulia, is the last living trace of the Greek presence.
magnentius: Magnus Magnentius was born in Samarobriva, now Amiens, in Gaul, purportedly the son of a British father and a Frankish mother, though some scholars suspect that these origins were exaggerated or invented by Constantinian propaganda. He served in the protectores, a bodyguard corps attached to the imperial court, and rose to command the Herculians and Jovians, two guard units. He was well liked by important court officials, notably Marcellinus, the comes rerum privatarum, who backed his bid for power against the emperor Constans, whom the ancient sources describe as unpopular.

At Augustodunum, now Autun, on 18 January 350 Magnentius stepped out of a dinner party and came back in a purple toga, and the guests hailed him Augustus. Constans, hunting near the Pyrenees away from his troops, was pursued and killed at Helena, near Perpignan. Magnentius quickly won the loyalty of Britannia, Gaul and Hispania, took Italy within a month and secured Africa, but Illyria came under Vetranio. Lacking any link to the dynasty of Constantine, he married Justina, possibly a great-granddaughter of Constantine, presented himself on coins as liberator of the Roman world, and for six months spoke of Constantius II as his senior. Libanius conceded that he governed in accordance with the laws.

Constantius, whose brother Constans he had killed, would not recognise him. In the early months of 351 Constantius offered him control of Gaul, which he refused. The armies met at the Battle of Mursa Major, a victory for Constantius at great cost and one of the largest battles ever fought among Romans, with low estimates of over 50,000 dead. Zosimus says Constantius feared Rome could no longer hold off barbarian invaders.

Magnentius withdrew across the Alps. In 352 his offers of peace, even to step down and take a soldier's post, were refused, and his legions along the Rhine began to defect. After a final defeat at the Battle of Mons Seleucus in July 353 he fled to Lugdunum, now Lyon, where on 10 August 353 most sources say he fell on his sword. His brother Decentius, whom he had made caesar to hold Gaul, hanged himself on hearing the news. Constantius then rooted out his followers, using the notary Paulus Catena, called Paul the Chain, for the purpose.

Almost all of Magnentius' acts were repealed, and the succeeding regime condemned his rule as an illegitimate barbarian usurpation, which is why historians call him a usurper. His religion is disputed: some see him as a nominal Christian, others point to his allowing night sacrifices, and his coinage includes a series bearing a Christogram.
magnetic-compass: Early references to lodestone and its attraction of iron come from several cultures. The Greek philosopher Thales of Miletus, in the 6th century BCE, was credited with discovering that a lodestone attracts iron, and the Sushruta Samhita, an ancient Indian medical text, describes using it to remove arrows from a body. The earliest Chinese literary reference to magnetism is in the 4th-century BCE Guiguzi, and the Lüshi Chunqiu of the 2nd century BCE states that the lodestone makes iron come to it. The Lunheng, composed between 20 and 100 CE, says that a lodestone attracts a needle.

The first devices to use these properties may date to Han China. In the 2nd century BCE Chinese geomancers were experimenting with a south-pointing spoon of lodestone for divination, which turns to a north–south axis on a smooth bronze plate, though archaeologists have not found a magnetite spoon in a Han tomb. Some historians believe that a compass using an iron fish floating in a vessel of oil was in use in southern India in the 4th century, while others think the evidence for compasses before the 11th century is very weak.

The first compasses used for navigation appeared in China by 1088, under the Song dynasty, as described by Shen Kuo. They were made of iron needles magnetised by striking them with a lodestone. The first use recorded in Western Europe dates to around 1190 and in the Islamic world to the 13th century. Such needles, set in a cork or a piece of wood and floated in a bowl of water, were universally used until the box-like compass with a dry pivoting needle appeared around 1300. The dry compass was supplanted in the early 20th century by the liquid-filled compass.

Compass cards were originally marked only with north or with the four cardinal points. These were later divided into 24 points in China and 32 in Europe, and in the modern era the 360-degree system took hold. Mariners also learned that a compass needle does not point exactly to true north: variation values for most of the oceans had been calculated and published by 1914. Iron in a ship causes further error, called deviation, and navigators made correction tables by comparing compass bearings with landmarks of known magnetic bearing.

A magnetic compass has a magnetised needle that aligns itself with the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field and so points approximately to the north magnetic pole. The needle turns on a low-friction pivot, in better compasses a jewel bearing. The angle between true north and magnetic north is called magnetic declination, and it varies widely from place to place and changes slowly over time. The compass is counted among the Four Great Inventions of China.
magnificat: The Magnificat is recorded only in Luke's Gospel, as one of four hymns, distilled from a collection of early Jewish-Christian canticles, that complement the theme of promise and fulfilment in Luke's infancy narrative. The others are Zechariah's Benedictus, the angels' Gloria in Excelsis Deo and Simeon's Nunc dimittis. They are patterned on the hymns of praise in Israel's Psalter and reflect pre-Christian Jewish hymnology. The oldest and likely original version was written in Koine Greek. Scholars discuss whether the historical Mary herself proclaimed it, though Luke portrays her as its singer. Adolf von Harnack argued in 1900 that Luke 1:46 should read And Elizabeth said, following several ancient readings.

The canticle echoes several biblical passages, above all the Song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2:1 to 10. Its first stanza shows the Hebrew device of synonymous parallelism, in which my soul mirrors my spirit and of the Lord mirrors in God my Savior. The third stanza sets three contrasts: the proud are reversed by those of low estate, the mighty by those of low degree, and the rich by the hungry.

Its structure has four parts: Mary rejoices that she is to bear the promised Messiah (Luke 1:46 to 48); she glorifies God for his power, holiness and mercy (1:49 to 50); she looks forward to God transforming the world, bringing the proud low and feeding the hungry (1:51 to 53); and she exalts him for his faithfulness to his promise to Abraham (1:54 to 55).

The Magnificat is the most popular canticle, and is used in the liturgies of the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Lutheran churches and the Anglican Communion. In the West it is most often sung or recited at the main evening service: Vespers in Catholic and Lutheran churches and Evening Prayer, or Evensong, in Anglicanism, where it is usually paired with the Nunc dimittis. Western tradition usually adds the doxology Gloria Patri, which is not part of the original text. In the Eastern Orthodox Church it is always sung at Matins, with a refrain sung after each verse. Lutherans commonly use it at the Feast of the Visitation on 2 July.

Many composers, beginning in the Renaissance, set it to music, among them Claudio Monteverdi in his Vespro della Beata Vergine of 1610, Johann Sebastian Bach in 1723, Vivaldi, Anton Bruckner and Arvo Pärt. Charles Villiers Stanford wrote a Magnificat in every major key.
magnitogorsk: Magnitogorsk lies in Chelyabinsk Oblast, on the eastern side of the southern Ural Mountains beside the Ural River. Its name means city of the magnetic mountain, after Mount Magnitnaya, a geological anomaly that once consisted almost completely of iron ore, around 55 to 60 percent iron. The city straddles von Strahlenberg's line, the boundary between Europe and Asia, and its official motto calls it the place where Europe and Asia meet. It is one of a small number of planned socialist realist settlements of the Soviet bloc, alongside Nowa Huta in Poland, Havířov in Czechoslovakia and Eisenhüttenstadt in the GDR.

A settlement was founded in 1743 as part of the Orenburg Line of forts built under Empress Elizabeth, and it had a small wooden chapel by 1747. Iron-ore mining dates from 1752, when two entrepreneurs named Tverdysh and Myasnikov, taking advantage of the fact that the mountain belonged to no one, petitioned the empress for it. The petition was accepted in 1759 and they began to produce ore.

In 1928 a Soviet delegation went to Cleveland, Ohio, to ask the American consulting firm Arthur G. McKee to plan a copy of the U.S. Steel mill at Gary, Indiana. The contract was enlarged four times, and the new plant eventually had a capacity of over four million tons a year. Many of the workers were former peasants with little industrial experience, so several hundred foreign specialists came to direct the work, including a team of architects headed by the German Ernst May. His plan for a linear city had to be altered because factory and housing construction had already begun. John Scott's book Behind the Urals documents the city's development in the 1930s. It received city status in 1931.

In 1937 foreigners were told to leave and the city was declared closed. Little reliable information survives from the closed period. In the Second World War it supplied much of the steel for the Soviet war effort, and its position east of the Urals kept it out of reach of the German army. The closed status was lifted under perestroika, and the steelworks later became a joint-stock company. With local ore depleted, raw materials are brought from northern Kazakhstan.

Magnitogorsk contains the largest iron and steel works in Russia, the Magnitogorsk Iron and Steel Works. It has the Magnitogorsk State Technical University and the Magnitogorsk State Conservatory, three theatres, and a monument called The First Tent to the first builders of the works. It is served by an airport and a railway.
magnus-barefoot: Magnus was born around the end of 1073 as the only son of King Olaf Kyrre. Most of what is known comes from Norse sagas and chronicles that began to appear in the twelfth century; the later sagas are the most detailed but are generally considered the least reliable, and since they chiefly describe warfare they may have made the image of kings like Magnus one-sided. Olaf died in September 1093 after a long period of peace, and Magnus was probably proclaimed king at the assembly of Viken. In the north his cousin Haakon Magnusson contested his claim, and the two ruled uneasily together until Haakon died in 1095.

Under Magnus, Norway came to resemble other European kingdoms more closely: royal rule became established, he consolidated power through a network of noblemen, and church organisation developed, though in practice he ruled the church. His main effort lay in the west. In 1098 he sailed into the Western Sea and reached Orkney with a large fleet, of which the sources give sizes from 60 to 160 ships. He raided Orkney, the Hebrides and Mann, secured Norwegian control by a treaty with the Scottish king and built forts and houses on Mann. Norwegian and Scottish historians generally believe his chief aim was to control the Norse communities around the Irish Sea.

After his return he campaigned in the Swedish provinces of Dalsland and Västergötland, claiming an ancient border at the Göta älv. The Danish king Eric Evergood arranged talks, and in 1101 Magnus made peace by agreeing to marry Margaret, daughter of King Inge Stenkilsson, and received Dalsland as her dowry.

In 1101 or 1102 Magnus again set out for Ireland. He allied with Muirchertach Ua Briain, king of Munster, whose daughter married Magnus's son Sigurd, and Muirchertach recognised his control of Dublin and Fingal. The next year Magnus was killed in an ambush by the Ulaid while obtaining food supplies, in unclear circumstances. He was the last Norwegian king to fall in battle abroad. His sons Sigurd, Eystein and Olaf succeeded him peacefully. His memory is stronger in Ireland and Scotland than in Norway, and he is the subject of Gaelic ballads as Manus Mór.
magnus-duke-of-holstein: Magnus was born at Copenhagen Castle on 5 September 1540, the second son of King Christian III of Denmark and Norway and Dorothea of Saxe-Lauenburg. At seventeen he was sent to Germany to be educated at various German courts, and he returned to Denmark after his father's death in 1559 for the coronation of his older brother, Frederick II. That year the prince-bishop Johannes V von Münchhausen sold his lands of Ösel-Wiek and Courland in Old Livonia to Frederick for 30,000 thalers. To avoid dividing his own lands, Frederick gave the territory to Magnus on condition that he renounced his claim to Schleswig and Holstein. In 1560 Magnus landed on Ösel with an army and was at once elected bishop by the cathedral chapter.

During the Livonian War Magnus arrived in Moscow on 10 June 1570 with his brother's approval, and Ivan IV crowned him King of Livonia. He swore allegiance to Ivan and received a charter for the vassal kingdom. The territories still had to be conquered, though Põltsamaa Castle was named the future residence. He left Moscow with 20,000 Russian soldiers to take Swedish-controlled Reval, but Ivan's hope of support from Frederick II failed, and by the end of March 1571 Magnus gave up the siege. In 1574 he married Maria Vladimirovna of Staritsa, and they had two daughters, who died young.

In 1577, having lost Ivan's favour and with no help from his brother, Magnus called on the Livonian nobility to rally against foreign occupation. Ivan's forces attacked him and took him prisoner. After his release he renounced his royal title, and the rights to the throne passed to Stephen Báthory.

Magnus spent his last six years at the castle of Pilten in the Bishopric of Courland as a pensioner of the Polish crown, and he died on 28 March 1583. In 1662 his body was returned to Denmark and buried again in Roskilde Cathedral. He had been titular King of Livonia from 1570 to 1578.
magnus-eriksson: Magnus was born in Norway, in April or May 1316. His father was Duke Erik Magnusson, son of King Magnus Ladulås of Sweden, and his mother was Ingeborg, daughter of King Haakon V of Norway. He was elected king of Sweden on 8 July 1319 at Mora Thing to prevent his uncle, the previous king Birger Magnusson, from returning to power, and in August of the same year he was acknowledged as hereditary king of Norway at Haugating in Tønsberg. After his mother was removed from the regency in 1322–1323, local magnates ruled both countries until he came of age.

Magnus was declared of age at 15 in 1331, which provoked resistance in Norway, where a statute of 1302 set the age at 20. In 1332 he bought Scania, Blekinge and Ven from Duke Johan of Holstein for 34,000 marks of silver, and after the Kalundborg War King Valdemar renounced his claims at Varberg in 1343. In 1335 he outlawed thralldom for thralls born to Christian parents in Västergötland and Värend, the last parts of Sweden where slavery was still legal. He was crowned king of both realms in Stockholm on 21 July 1336, and Norwegian nobles rose again in 1338.

In 1348 Magnus led a crusade against Novgorod up the Neva, briefly took the fortress of Orekhov, and fell back after the Novgorodians retook it in February 1349, largely because of the plague in the west. Taxes raised to pay for Scania led some Swedish nobles, backed by the Church, to set up his elder son Erik as king; Erik died in 1359. In 1363 nobles banished after a revolt went to Mecklenburg, and Albert of Mecklenburg was crowned king of Sweden on 18 February 1364. Magnus took refuge in Norway with his younger son and drowned in a shipwreck in Bømlafjorden on 1 December 1374, according to Icelandic annals.

Contemporaries and later chroniclers judged his rule a period of decline, and Bridget of Sweden was among his most prominent critics. Accusations about his relations with his favourite Bengt Algotsson formed part of the political attacks on him, though there is no firm historical evidence for them; the later epithet Magnus Smek has an uncertain meaning. Historians from the eighteenth century onward questioned the hostile tradition. His legislation included Magnus Erikssons landslag, the first law code meant to apply throughout the Swedish countryside, and he issued charters for mining at Norberg and Stora Kopparberget in Falun, which supplied much of the state's later revenue.
magnus-erlendsson: Magnus was the eldest son of Erlend Thorfinnsson, who ruled Orkney jointly with his twin brother Paul, and of Thora, a daughter of Sumarlidi Ospaksson; through his grandmother Ingibiorg Finnsdottir the family was related to the Norwegian kings Olav II and Harald II. The rivalry of his brother Aerling and his cousin Haakon Paulsson led to the earldom being split in two. In 1098 King Magnus Barefoot of Norway, invited by Haakon, took the islands, sent both earls to Norway as prisoners and kept the young cousins as hostages.

According to the Orkneyinga saga, Magnus refused on religious grounds to fight when the king's fleet raided Anglesey, and stayed aboard singing psalms during the Battle of Menai Straits. He then took refuge in Scotland.
