Returning to Orkney in 1105, he disputed the succession with Haakon, and King Eystein I of Norway granted him the earldom, which he shared amicably with his cousin until 1114.

When their followers fell out, the earls agreed to meet on Egilsay at Easter with two ships each, but Haakon came with eight. Magnus spent the night in the island's church and offered to go into exile or prison, but, in the saga's account, the chieftains insisted that one earl must die. Haakon's standard bearer Ofeigr refused, and Haakon made his cook Lifolf kill Magnus with an axe on 16 April. The historian Thomson argues that the assembly was invented or stressed to shift blame from Haakon, whose grandson was earl when the saga was written.

Magnus was buried where he fell and then at Christchurch in Birsay, and reports of healings followed. Bishop William of Orkney, who had called such tales heresy, declared him a saint in 1136. When the cathedral at Kirkwall was ready, his relics were moved there, and in 1919 bones with a damaged skull were found hidden in one of its columns. Twenty-one churches in Europe are dedicated to him, and George Mackay Brown's novel Magnus became Peter Maxwell Davies's opera The Martyrdom of St Magnus in 1977.
magnus-maximus: Magnus Maximus was born in Gallaecia, Hispania, on the estates of Count Theodosius the Elder, to whom he claimed to be related. In their youth he and the future emperor Theodosius I served together in the army of Theodosius the Elder in Britannia. He served under the Count in Africa in 373 and was assigned to Britain in 380, where he defeated an incursion of the Picts and Scots in 381. He gained the support of his soldiers and the admiration of the Romano-Britons he defended.

In the spring of 383 the discontented Roman army proclaimed Maximus emperor in place of Gratian, who was accused of favouring Alans in his bodyguard. He took at least part of the garrison of Britain to Gaul, and after skirmishing near Paris Gratian fled and was killed at Lyon on 25 August 383. An accord seems to have been reached in 384 in which Valentinian II and Theodosius I recognised Maximus as Augustus in the West, while he acknowledged Valentinian's rule of Italy, Africa and Illyricum. He ruled Britain, Gaul and Spain from Trier and ordered the execution of Priscillian and six companions for heresy, despite protests from Ambrose and Martin of Tours.

In 387 he invaded Italy and drove Valentinian II out of Mediolanum. Theodosius I, who had married Valentinian's sister Galla, invaded with Valentinian in 388, and Maximus was defeated at the Battle of Poetovio, retreated to Aquileia, surrendered and was executed. The Senate decreed damnatio memoriae against him, and his son Victor was executed at Trier.

In the view of some historians his death marked the end of direct imperial presence in northern Gaul and Britain. Gildas wrote that he took from Britain its troops, governors and the flower of its youth, and the ninth-century Historia Brittonum says he settled his British soldiers in Armorica, which modern historians think may reflect a real settlement in Brittany. In Welsh legend he is Macsen Wledig, who in The Dream of Macsen Wledig marries the Welsh princess Elen. The earliest Welsh genealogies make him founding father of the dynasties of Powys, Gwynedd and Gwent.
magnus-olafsson: Magnús was a son of Óláfr Guðrøðarson, King of the Isles, and possibly of his second wife Cairistíona, daughter of Fearchar, Earl of Ross. His elder brother Haraldr succeeded their father in 1237 but drowned in 1248, and his brother Rǫgnvaldr was killed on Mann weeks after his accession in 1249. The kingship was seized by Haraldr Guðrøðarson, of the rival line of Óláfr's half-brother, until King Hákon Hákonarson of Norway summoned him away in 1250. That year Magnús and Eóghan Mac Dubhghaill landed at Ronaldsway with Norwegians, but the Manx took offence at Eóghan's royal style and routed them on St Michael's Isle.

Magnús later returned and, according to the Chronicle of Mann, began his reign with the consent of the people; Hákon gave him the title of king in 1254, and Henry III of England knighted him in 1256. The chronicle, the only narrative source for the kingdom, was compiled on Mann in his reign and favours his father's line, depicting Haraldr Guðrøðarson as a usurper.

When Hákon brought a great fleet against Scotland in 1263, Magnús was one of the few vassals who backed him wholeheartedly. With Dubhghall mac Ruaidhrí and others he led a detachment through Loch Long, hauled the ships overland to Loch Lomond and wasted its islands and shores, while the main fleet fought the inconclusive skirmishes at Largs. In 1264, with no protection from Norway or England, Magnús met Alexander III at Dumfries, resigned his crown, did homage and surrendered hostages and ten galleys.

He died at Castle Rushen on 24 November 1265 and was buried at the Abbey of St Mary of Rushen, leaving his widow Máire, Eóghan's daughter. A continuation of Historia rerum Anglicarum says that on his death kings ceased to reign on Mann. Under the Treaty of Perth of 2 July 1266 Norway ceded Mann and the Hebrides to Scotland for 4,000 merks and 100 merks a year. In 1275 his illegitimate son Guðrøðr rose on Mann, but a Scottish fleet crushed the revolt at the Battle of Ronaldsway.
magnus-the-good: Magnus Olafsson was born around 1024, an illegitimate son of King Olaf Haraldsson, later Saint Olaf, and Alfhild, an English slave of Olaf's queen Astrid Olofsdotter. Born prematurely and weak, he was hastily baptised by the skald Sigvatr Þórðarson, who named him after Charlemagne. When Cnut the Great dethroned Olaf in 1028 the family fled through Sweden and the Baltic to Kievan Rus', where Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise sheltered them. In 1031 Magnus's uncle Harald Sigurdsson brought news of Olaf's death at the Battle of Stiklestad. The boy was educated in Old Russian and some Greek and trained as a warrior.

Cnut had appointed his first wife Ælfgifu and their son Svein as regents of Norway, but the Norwegians found their rule oppressive and drove them out before Cnut died in 1035. Einar Thambarskelfir and Kalf Arnesson went to Kievan Rus' to bring the boy back, and Magnus was established as king at the age of eleven. He first sought revenge on his father's enemies, but on Sigvatr's advice stopped, and so became known as the Good.

Harthacnut, king of Denmark, wanted the two kingdoms reunited, and Magnus began a campaign against Denmark around 1040, but nobles of both countries brought the kings together at the Göta älv, where they agreed that the first to die would be succeeded by the other. When Harthacnut died in England in 1042 Magnus also became king of Denmark, against the claim of Cnut's nephew Sweyn Estridsson. He destroyed Jomsborg, the headquarters of the Jomsvikings, and in 1043 decisively defeated an invasion by the Wends at the Battle of Lyrskov Heath, near Hedeby, with up to 15,000 killed. He also wrote to Edward, the new English king, that he meant to attack England, but never did so.

Harald Sigurdsson returned to Norway from the east and contested Magnus's rule there, allying himself with Sweyn, and in 1046 Magnus made him co-king of Norway. By late 1046 Magnus had driven Sweyn out of Denmark. He died suddenly in Denmark on 25 October 1047; accounts vary between an accident, such as falling overboard or from a horse, and disease. He is said to have named Sweyn his heir in Denmark and Harald in Norway, and he was buried with his father in the cathedral at Nidaros, now Trondheim.

His line ended with his death. In 1280 Eric II of Norway, descended through his mother from Magnus's legitimate sister Wulfhild, was crowned king. Heimskringla describes Magnus as a man of middle height, light-haired, well spoken and generous.
magnus-vi-of-norway: Magnus Haakonsson was born in Tunsberg and baptised in May 1238, the youngest son of King Håkon Håkonsson and Margaret Skulesdatter. He grew up mostly in Bergen. In 1257 his older brother Håkon died, leaving Magnus heir to the kingdom, and his father gave him the title of king the same year. On 11 September 1261 he married Ingeborg, daughter of King Eric IV of Denmark, Håkon died on 16 December 1263 during a campaign against the Scottish king over the Hebrides, and Magnus became ruler of Norway.

Magnus abandoned his father's aggressive foreign policy. Under the Treaty of Perth in 1266 he gave up the Hebrides and the Isle of Man to Scotland for a large sum of silver and a yearly payment, while the Scots recognised Norwegian rule over Shetland and Orkney. In the 1260s the border with Sweden was officially defined for the first time. In 1275 he gathered a leidang fleet, for the only time in his reign, when the deposed Swedish king Valdemar Birgersson fled to Norway, but he failed to reconcile Valdemar's brothers and withdrew without fighting.

His main work was the law. Helped by legal scholars and advisers, he had a modernised code adopted at the Things in 1274 (the Landslov), applying to the whole country including the Faroe Islands and Shetland and replacing the regional laws, and a town law (the Bylov) in 1276. The code treated crime as an offence against the state rather than the individual, narrowed personal vengeance and made the throne the source of justice. In 1273 he gave his five-year-old son Eric the title of king and his brother Håkon that of duke, settling the succession. The Tønsberg Concord of 1277 with Archbishop Jon Raude of Nidaros confirmed certain privileges of the clergy but ended the Church's claim that the kingdom was its fief.

Magnus fell ill in Bergen in the spring of 1280, planned to have Eric crowned co-ruler at midsummer, and died on 9 May. Eric succeeded at the age of 12, with real power in the hands of advisers, among them the widow Ingeborg. Magnus was buried in the Franciscan monastery church in Bergen, later Bergen Cathedral. He was remembered as a good ruler who ruled by law rather than by the sword, and he is mostly considered wise for sparing the kingdom needless wars. His saga, commissioned from Sturla Þórðarson, survives only as a short fragment.
mago-agricultural-writer: Mago wrote his manual in Punic, and it recorded the farming knowledge of Carthage, which was then the granary of the central Mediterranean. It drew on local Berber and Punic practice and covered both agriculture and the care of animals. The Roman writer Columella summarised its opening advice: a man who buys land should sell his town house, so that he will not prefer the household gods of the city to those of the country, since one who delights more in his city residence has no need of a country estate.

The surviving fragments show the range of the work. They deal with which way the most productive vineyards face, how to plant and prune vines, how to plant olives and fruit trees, how to harvest marsh plants and how to prepare grains and pulses for grinding. Others concern choosing bullocks, the health of cattle, farmyard animals, bees and beekeeping, preserving pomegranates and making passum, a raisin wine.

Nothing of Mago's own Punic text survives. After Rome destroyed Carthage, the Carthaginian libraries were given to the kings of Numidia, but Mago's book alone was taken to Rome. Cassius Dionysius adapted it into Greek, and D. Junius Silanus translated it in full into Latin. The Greek version was later shortened by Diophanes of Nicaea into six books.

What is known of the work comes from quotations of these translations by Roman writers on agriculture, among them Varro, Columella, Pliny the Elder and Gargilius Martialis. Their extracts preserve even small observations, such as the remark that mules sometimes foal in Africa and that mules and mares foal in the twelfth month after conception, as well as the advice that a beekeeper should not kill drones.
magonid-dynasty: The Magonids held power in Carthage from about 550 BCE to 340 BCE. According to Justin, Mago I was chosen as general after his predecessor had been ousted for seeking royal power. Under him Carthaginian policy appears to have changed sharply: where Carthage had earlier colonised the island of Ibiza tentatively, it now took the lead and became the dominant Phoenician military power in the western Mediterranean. About 540 BCE a Carthaginian and Etruscan alliance drove the Greeks from Corsica after the Battle of Alalia.

Leading historians of Carthage doubt whether its internal history can be reconstructed at all. Mago and his heirs probably ruled less like kings than like tyrants or political strongmen. Diodorus, however, calls them kings according to the law, which suggests a legal procedure rather than a seizure of power, and Herodotus says Hamilcar I was king by valour, implying selection rather than inheritance. Mago's son Hasdrubal I is said to have been invested eleven times with the office of dictator. After Hamilcar's death in 480 BCE the ruler lost most of his power to an aristocratic Council of Elders.

Mago was followed by Hasdrubal I, who with his brother Hamilcar led an expedition against Sardinia, and then by Hamilcar I. A treaty with Rome in 509 BCE is the first known evidence of Carthaginian control over Sicily and Sardinia. Carthage may have allied with the Persian king Xerxes against the Greeks, though the accounts are unsure. Herodotus reports the belief that the Battle of Himera was fought on the same day as the Battle of Salamis in 480 BCE; the Greeks won both, and Hamilcar was killed.

Under Hamilcar's son Hanno, whom some have conjectured to be Hanno the Navigator, much of Carthage's African territory was conquered and the Atlantic coast of Africa explored. Hannibal I, Hamilcar's grandson, invaded Sicily in 410 BCE and destroyed Selinus in 409 BCE, slaughtering thousands of prisoners, before dying of an epidemic at the siege of Agrigentum. His cousin Himilco II warred against Dionysius I of Syracuse until his disastrous defeat in 396 BCE, after which he killed himself. Mago II put down a Libyan revolt that nearly ended Carthaginian rule before falling at the Battle of Cabala. The line ended when Hanno III tried in 340 BCE to restore full royal power against the Council of Elders, failed and was executed.
magway-region: Magway Region, formerly Magway Division, is a first-level administrative division of central Myanmar and the second largest of its seven regions, with an area of 44,820 square kilometres. It is bordered by Sagaing Region to the north, Mandalay Region to the east, Bago Region to the south and Rakhine State and Chin State to the west. The capital and second largest city is Magway, and the largest is Pakokku. At the 2014 census the region had 3,912,711 inhabitants, mostly Bamar, with the Chin as the largest minority; 98.8 per cent were Buddhists.

Fossils of early primates more than 40 million years old were excavated at Pondaung and Ponnya in Pakokku District. An ancient city of the Pyu, Peikthano-myo, about 2,000 years old, lies in Taungdwingyi Township. The region's older name was Minbu Region, or Minbu Province, established with three districts, Minbu, Thayet and Yenangyaung, and its capital was Yenangyaung. Late in the Konbaung era two forts, Fort Min Hla and Fort Kway Chaung, were built on opposite banks of the Irrawaddy to resist a British invasion.

After the military coup of 2 March 1962 under General Ne Win and the constitution of 1974, Minbu Region was renamed Magway Region and Yenangyaung District was abolished. Pakokku District was added, while Mindat District went to Chin State, and the capital moved from Yenangyaung to Magway. In 1996 Pakokku District was divided into Pakokku and Gangaw, giving five districts, with 25 townships.

The Irrawaddy is the main transport route, and most major towns, among them Magway, Pakokku, Minbu, Yenangyaung and Chauk, are river ports. Pakokku Bridge, the longest in the country, is part of the India–Myanmar–Thailand Trilateral Highway. The principal product of the region is petroleum, and it yields most of Myanmar's oil and natural gas, from fields at Yenangyaung, Chauk and elsewhere, which has earned it the name oil pot of Myanmar. Sesame and groundnut are the major crops, and Pakokku is the largest rice market of Upper Myanmar. The Thihoshin Pagoda in Pakokku was built by King Alaungsithu.
magyarisation: Smaller ethnic groups had been assimilated into a common Hungarian culture throughout the Middle Ages, among them Turkic Kabars, Pechenegs and Cumans, and some Romanian knezes ennobled by the crown took on the Hungarian language and the Catholic faith. Latin remained the language of administration until 1784, and again from 1790 to 1844. Joseph II's attempt to replace it with German provoked a national awakening among the lesser Hungarian nobility. Magyarization as a social policy began in the 1830s, when Hungarian started to replace Latin and German in education. In the early 1840s Lajos Kossuth urged the country to hurry to Magyarize the Croats, the Romanians and the Saxons, and wrote in 1842 that Hungary must have one language, Hungarian.

The term usually refers to the policies of Austro-Hungarian Transleithania after the Compromise of 1867, especially after Count Menyhért Lónyay became prime minister in 1871. It rested on classical liberal ideas of individual citizenship and civic nationalism. The Nationalities Act of 1868 declared all citizens of Hungary one indivisible political nation with equal rights, yet in practice Hungarian was almost the only language of administration, the courts and higher education. Leaders of the Romanian, Serb and Slovak minorities sought territorial autonomy, which Hungarian politicians, remembering the revolution of 1848, saw as dismemberment of the kingdom.

From the Primary Education Act of 1879 and the Secondary Education Act of 1883 the state worked to reduce the use of non-Magyar languages in schools. All Slovak secondary schools were closed in 1874 and the Matica slovenská in 1875, and a law of 1897 required that village names be Hungarian. Hungarian names replaced others, especially in towns. At Černová in 1907, 15 people were killed and 52 injured in a shooting; whether this shows violent Magyarization is disputed.

Romanians, Slovaks, Ruthenians, Croats and Serbs perceived Magyarization as cultural aggression or discrimination, above all where they formed the local majority. Its results were uneven: between 1880 and 1910 the share of the population speaking Hungarian as a first language rose from 46.6 to 54.5 per cent, mostly in central Hungary and the educated middle classes, while rural and peripheral populations hardly changed, and the 1910 census found that about 87 per cent of the minorities could not speak Hungarian. Most Jews adopted Hungarian as their main language. After the Treaty of Trianon about 10.4 per cent of the population of post-Trianon Hungary still spoke a minority language as its mother tongue in 1920.
maha-bandula: Maha Bandula was born Maung Yit on 6 November 1782 at Dabayin, the eldest son of a minor gentry family. He studied at the local Buddhist monastery from the age of six, but left before he was 13 when his father died, and worked the sesame fields with his mother. He later moved to Amarapura, then the capital, as a low-ranking retainer of Crown Prince Thado Minsaw, became one of his bodyguards in 1806, and learned military strategy there. After a bold act in 1812 caught the notice of the new crown prince, the Prince of Sagaing, he was made a messenger of the Privy Council and in June 1813 governor of Dabayin.

He first saw battle in the invasion of Manipur in 1814 and served as a regimental commander in the Assam campaigns of 1817 and 1819. When the Prince of Sagaing became King Bagyidaw, he made him governor of Ahlon-Monywa and on 3 November 1819 gave him the title Maha Bandula. In December 1819, as a deputy commander, he took the nearly impregnable Manipuri fort by sending commandos over the hills at night to open its gates. From February 1821 he led 20,000 men into Assam and defeated Chandrakanta Singha in July 1822; the British refused to surrender the king, who had fled to Bengal.

Bandula belonged to the war party at court with Queen Me Nu and her brother, the lord of Salin. The war broke out on 5 March 1824. His forces won at Ramu in May, but he stopped short of Chittagong. When a British force of over 10,000 under General Archibald Campbell seized Yangon on 11 May 1824, he led his army across the Arakan Yoma in the monsoon and was granted the rank Agga Maha Thenapati. On 30 November he sent about 30,000 men, only half with muskets, against the British lines at the Shwedagon. British shells and Congreve rockets cut them down, and only 7,000 returned.

He fell back to the teak stockade at Danubyu, where a first British attack in March 1825 failed. On 1 April a mortar shell killed him as he walked the fort in full insignia under a golden umbrella, ignoring his generals' warnings. Burmese tradition credits his leadership with making this the only one of the three Anglo-Burmese wars in which Burma put up a real fight. A school team, a Yangon road, park and bridge, and a navy frigate bear his name, and the army's infantry badge shows his helmet.
maha-manikya: His original name was probably Chhengthung Fa. Historians identify his son Dharma Manikya I with the ruler whom the Rajmala, the royal chronicle of Tripura, calls Dangar Fa, and so equate Maha Manikya with Dangar Fa's predecessor in the text, Chhengthung Fa. Maha Manikya, literally Great Manikya, would be an unusual personal name, and Maha is a prefix that does not work as a given name.

The Rajmala says little about his life. It makes him the son of Mukut Manikya and grandson of Ratna Manikya I, the dynasty's supposed founder and a descendant of the mythical Lunar dynasty, and presents him as a virtuous ruler and scholar who fought no wars. Coins show that this cannot be right: Mukut only began to rule in 1489, and Ratna Manikya reigned more than thirty years after Maha's death.

Historians believe that Chhengthung Fa was a Tripuri chief who established the kingdom by subjugating neighbouring tribes, among them the Kukis, Jamatias and Reangs. This was possible because the Tripuri had the largest tribal population and held the productive valleys bordering Bengal, between Sylhet and Chittagong. These events are thought to have taken place while Raja Ganesha held temporary sovereignty over Bengal and the Sultan's influence was weak.

According to the Rajmala, an unidentified ruler of Bengal sent a large army against him after a man carrying a gift for the Sultan was robbed while passing through Tripura. Chhengthung Fa was ready to sue for peace, but his queen, Tripura Sundari, called submission cowardice, took command of the soldiers herself and led them to victory. He probably took the title Maha Manikya after this triumph. Because coins of Sultan Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah resemble those of a later Tripura ruler, it has been suggested that part or all of the kingdom submitted to Bengal for a time during his reign, though historians dispute this.

Maha Manikya died in 1431. After a brief struggle among his children and generals, he was succeeded by his eldest son, Dharma Manikya I. The descendants of another son, Gagan Fa, inherited the throne in later centuries, beginning with Kalyan Manikya in 1626, and the Manikya suffix he had taken was carried by all his successors.
maha-singh: Maha Singh, also spelt Mahan Singh, was the eldest son of Charat Singh, chief of the Sukerchakia Misl, and Desan Kaur; sources give his birth as 1756 or 1760. He grew up in the family's martial tradition and went with his father on campaign from an early age, and before Charat Singh's death, when his own matchlock exploded, he was married to Mai Man Kaur, daughter of Sardar Jai Singh Mann. His mother helped him govern and built alliances through her children's marriages, arranging his second marriage, to Raj Kaur of Jind, in 1774.

He took Rohtas Fort from Nur-ud-din Bamezai, a general of Ahmad Shah Durrani, and after a four-month siege of Rasool Nagar defeated Pir Muhammad of the Chathas. On his return he named his newborn son Ranjit, victor in battle, in honour of the victory. In 1777 he entered the Sialkot district, held mostly by the Bhangi Misl, imprisoned twenty-two Bhangi chiefs who came to meet him and freed them once they accepted his overlordship and paid tribute.

In January 1784 he plundered Jammu alone for three days and nights, though he had agreed with Haqiqat Singh Kanhaiya to share the attack; thousands of men were killed and the booty was worth more than a crore. When Jai Singh Kanhaiya insulted him at Amritsar that Diwali, Maha Singh allied with Jassa Singh Ramgarhia and Raja Sansar Chand Katoch. At the Battle of Achal near Batala Jai Singh's son Gurbaksh Singh was killed, and the Kanhaiya territories Maha Singh seized were worth three lakhs a year.

Peace with the Kanhaiyas followed the betrothal in 1786 of Ranjit Singh to Mehtab Kaur, daughter of Gurbaksh Singh's widow Sada Kaur, and Ranjit was also betrothed to Raj Kaur Nakai. When Sahib Singh of the Bhangis refused tribute, Maha Singh besieged Sodhra with his young son, but fell ill, handed command to Ranjit and withdrew to Gujranwala, where he died while Ranjit went on to win the siege. The historian Hari Ram Gupta held that, had he lived ten years longer, he would have become sole ruler of northern India.
maha-sura-singhanat: Bunma was born on 1 November 1744, the youngest child of Daoreung and of Thongdi, Royal Secretary of Northern Siam and Keeper of the Royal Seal, a descendant of Kosa Pan, who led the Siamese mission to France in the 17th century. He entered the Ayutthaya court as a mahadlek, a royal page. After the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767 he joined the forces of Phraya Tak, the future King Taksin, in the campaigns to seize Chanthaburi and drive the Burmese from Thonburi, and he brought his elder brother Thongduang, the future Rama I, into the king's inner circle.

In 1770 he led a land force north against the rebellion of Chao Phra Fang and was then made Chao Phraya Surasi Phitsanuwathirat, governor of Phitsanulok, with charge of the northern frontier. Working with Kawila of Lampang, he helped restore Chiang Mai under Siamese suzerainty, and earned the name Phraya Suea, the Tiger Lord. Accounts of the conquest of Vientiane place him in charge of the Lao captives brought to the capital.

After the coup of April 1782 that ended Taksin's reign, Rama I made him Front Palace, and he lived in the Front Palace complex north of the Grand Palace. When King Bodawpaya of the Konbaung dynasty invaded in 1785, he commanded at the Battle of Lat Ya in Kanchanaburi against far larger numbers, harassing Burmese supply lines until they retreated. In 1786 he drove the Burmese from the provinces of the Malay Peninsula and won the Tha Din Daeng campaign. In 1802, marching to help Kawila at Chiang Mai, he fell ill with gallstones at Thoen.

He was also a poet. His works include a poem on the southern campaign of 1786, another written on the expedition to Tavoy in 1787, and a poem of 1795 on the enshrinement of the Phra Phuttha Sihing image in the Front Palace. He died on 3 November 1803 and was cremated at Sanam Luang. A later tradition holds that he cursed anyone who held the Front Palace without being his descendant. He had 43 children, and the royal houses of Asuni, Sangkhatat, Patamasingh and Neerasingh descend from him.
maha-thammaracha-iii: Born Sai Luthai about 1380, he was the son of King Maha Thammaracha II and a great-great-grandson of King Ram Khamhaeng. His mother was a daughter of King Li Thai, Maha Thammaracha I, and was married to her own brother, Maha Thammaracha II. Much of what is known of the king comes from stone inscriptions that she had written in his name, among them the Asokārāma inscription and inscription No. 46, in which she bears long royal titles. He had a full brother, Prince Asoka, of whom nothing more is known.

According to inscription No. 46, the Queen Mother and her son, styled Mahādharrmarājādhipati Śrī Surīyavaṅsa, recaptured Phra Bang, the present-day Nakhon Sawan, and Phrae with her army in 1400, and then enjoyed dominion over all of Sri Satchanalai and Sukhothai. Holding Phra Bang interrupted the north-south transport of goods from Ayutthaya.

After the death of King Saen Mueang Ma of Lan Na, the kingdom to the north, in 1401, Sai Luthai intervened in the succession dispute on the side of the late king's eldest son, Thao Yi Kum Kam, and marched into Lan Na. Having seen a bad omen, he withdrew, taking Yi Kum Kam with him and giving him one of his provinces, possibly Kamphaeng Phet, as an appanage, while Lan Na passed to Yi Kum Kam's younger brother Sam Fang Kaen.

When King Intharacha came to the throne of Ayutthaya in 1409, one of his first acts was to reassert Ayutthaya's hold on Sukhothai as a vassal state. The date is unknown, but inscription 49 was written in 1412 by Nai Inthara Sorasak, probably the resident sent by the king of Ayutthaya to watch over his vassal. On Maha Thammaracha III's death in 1419 the throne passed to his son, Maha Thammaracha IV.
maha-yazawin: Before the Maha Yazawin, Burmese histories were biographies and brief local chronicles. Work on it began around 1712 to 1720, early in the reign of King Taninganway. Its author, U Kala, was a wealthy descendant of court and regional officials on both sides of his family, his mother being of mixed Shan and Burman noble descent, and he apparently had access to court documents going back to the reign of Bayinnaung. He prefaced the work with an apology, since Buddhist scriptures held the writing of history to be inimical to religious development, and argued that studying the past showed the impermanence of all things, political power included.

Kala compiled the chronicle in three versions: the Great Chronicle in twenty-one volumes, the Shorter Chronicle in ten and the Brief Chronicle in one. He drew on court records and more than 70 regional and foreign texts, among them the Thaton, Mon, Ayutthaya and Chiang Mai chronicles and the Mahavamsa. The first two parts deal with the origin of the universe and the Buddhist kings of ancient India; the third covers the founding of Threhkittara and Pagan and the Pinya, Sagaing, Ava and Toungoo dynasties down to 1711. He left out the Tagaung Kingdom, which the Hmannan Yazawin later presented as the beginning of the Burmese monarchy.

Its account of 16th-century Toungoo Burma, also seen by many Europeans, has been found largely factual. The earlier periods are sketchier, often giving only the year, because Kala lacked the full earlier chronicles and did not consult inscriptions. It is also the first text to tell of King Anawrahta's conquest of the Thaton Kingdom in 1057, a story the historian Michael Aung-Thwin has argued appears in no earlier text or inscription.

Many of Kala's sources were destroyed in a fire at Ava some twenty years later, which made the chronicle all the more important. The pre-1712 portions of Yazawin Thit (1798), Maha Yazawin Kyaw (1831) and the Hmannan Yazawin largely reproduce it, though they corrected many Pagan and pre-Pagan dates from inscriptions. The historian Victor Lieberman wrote that rarely has a national tradition depended so heavily on a single author. The last sections, from 1597 to 1711, have been translated into English by Tun Aung Chain.
mahabad: Mahabad lies south of Lake Urmia in a narrow valley 1,300 metres above sea level, and is the capital of Mahabad County in West Azerbaijan province. By road it is 122 kilometres from the provincial capital Urmia and 679 kilometres from Tehran. Most of its people are Kurds who follow Sunni Islam, and many also speak Persian and Azeri Turkic. Neo-Aramaic-speaking Jews once lived in the city as well. Because of its place in Kurdish nationalism, the Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization treats it as the capital of Iranian Kurdistan.

The city's older name, Savojbolagh, is a Persian corruption of the Turkic soghuk bulak, meaning cold spring; the Kurdish form was Sablagh. It is first attested in the 16th century, in the Safavid era, when the Mukri Kurds took part in the wars between the Safavid dynasty and the Ottoman Empire and gained prominence. In the 17th century it became the seat of the Mukri principality. Many believe that Budaq Sultan Mukri, who built the congregational mosque, founded the present town. The name Mahabad came into use after the First World War, in the reign of Reza Shah, who ruled from 1925 to 1941.

Mahabad was the capital of the short-lived Republic of Mahabad, declared on 1 January 1946 under the Kurdish nationalist Qazi Muhammad. It had strong Soviet support, as the Soviet Union had occupied northern Iran during the Second World War, and it included the mainly Kurdish-speaking towns of Bukan, Piranshahr, Sardasht and Oshnavieh. After an agreement brokered by the United States, the Soviets agreed to leave Iran. The Shah's government then moved against the republic, and its leaders were arrested. Qazi Muhammad was hanged on 31 March 1947.

The 2016 census counted 168,393 people in the city. The Mahabad dialect is the literary standard of Kurdish in western Iran and is very close to the Sorani used in Iraqi Kurdistan. Several poets and writers came from the city, among them Hejar (Abdurrahman Sharafkandi), who wrote the first Kurdish-Kurdish-Persian dictionary in Iran, and Hemin, and both were given the title of Kurdistan's national poet under the republic. The translator Mohammad Ghazi, who rendered more than 70 literary works into Persian, was also from Mahabad.
mahabharata: Tradition ascribes the Mahabharata to the sage Vyasa, who is also a major figure in the epic and who described it as itihasa, history. Scholars regard the story of the scribe Ganesha writing down Vyasa's dictation as a later interpolation, and the Critical Edition does not include it. The epic began as an orally transmitted tale of charioteer bards. Unlike the Vedas, which had to be preserved letter-perfect, it was a popular work whose reciters conformed to changes in language and style, so its earliest surviving components are believed to be no older than the earliest external references to it, among them Panini's grammar of the 4th century BCE. The text probably reached its final form by the early Gupta period.

The core story is a dynastic struggle for the throne of Hastinapura, ruled by the Kuru clan, between two collateral branches, the Kauravas and the Pandavas. The eldest Kaurava, Duryodhana, is younger than the eldest Pandava, Yudhishthira, and both claim to be first in line. The Pandavas build the capital of Indraprastha, but Duryodhana's uncle Shakuni wins their wealth and kingdom from Yudhishthira with loaded dice. They spend thirteen years in exile, and when negotiations through Krishna fail, both sides summon vast armies to Kurukshetra.

The epic runs to over 100,000 shlokas, about 1.8 million words, roughly ten times the length of the Iliad and the Odyssey combined. It is divided into 18 parvas and holds many other stories, including those of Damayanti, Shakuntala and Savitri and Satyavan, as well as discussions of philosophy and of dharmayuddha, just war, which sets criteria such as proportionality, just means and fair treatment of captives and the wounded. Its best-known part, the Bhagavad Gita, is a dialogue between the Pandava prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna.

Within the Indian tradition the Mahabharata is sometimes called the fifth Veda. Between 1919 and 1966 scholars at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune compared manuscripts from India and abroad and produced the Critical Edition, in 19 volumes on 13,000 pages, which is the text usually used in current studies. The epic was translated into Tamil and Javanese, where part of a Kawi prose version survives from the late 10th century. It inspired plays by Bhasa and many later works, and in the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand villagers still perform the Pandav Lila, a ritual re-enactment of episodes from it. Swami Vivekananda, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Mahatma Gandhi, among others, drew on the text in the Indian independence movement.
mahadji-scindia: Mahadji was the fifth and youngest son of Ranoji Rao Scindia, the founder of the Scindia dynasty, and was injured at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. He became Maharaja of Gwalior in 1768 and a trusted lieutenant of the Peshwa, the leader of the Maratha Confederacy. With Madhavrao I and Nana Fadnavis he is counted among the three pillars of the Maratha revival. He was also a scholar of Sanskrit.

Mahadji fought about 50 battles. He escorted Shah Alam II from Allahabad to Delhi, which the emperor reached in January 1772, and during 1772 and the following year he invaded Rohilkhand to punish the Rohillas for their part at Panipat: he captured Najibabad and the family of Zabita Khan, desecrated the grave of Najib ad-Dawlah and looted his fort, and the rest of the country was burnt. In the First Anglo-Maratha War he defeated the British at the Battle of Wadgaon and in Central India, and he mediated the Treaty of Salbai of 1782, which returned to him his lands west of the Ganges.

In 1784 he was made Vakil-i-Mutlaq, regent of Mughal affairs. The historian R.S. Chaurasia judged that Shah Alam II was sovereign only in name and in practice a puppet overseen by Mahadji. A treaty with the Sikhs in 1785 made the Cis-Sutlej states his protectorate. When the Rohilla warlord Ghulam Qadir seized Delhi and blinded Shah Alam, Mahadji retook the city on 2 October 1788, killed Ghulam Qadir and restored the emperor. Repulsed by the Rajput armies at Lalsot in 1787, he defeated Jodhpur and Jaipur at Patan and Merta in 1790.

Mahadji died in February 1794 at his military camp at Wanawdi near Pune. He left no male heir and was succeeded by Daulat Rao Scindia. His role was instrumental in establishing Maratha supremacy over North India. The Shinde Chhatri at Wanawadi, a three-storeyed memorial in Rajput style, marks the place of his cremation.
mahajanga: Since the 10th century the ports of northern Madagascar, home to an Islamized population, had drawn merchants and migrants from East Africa, the Middle East and the Far East; by the late 15th century the Arab geographer Ibn Mājid identified at least a dozen of them. In the early eighteenth century Andriamandisoarivo, backed by an army of eight hundred men, founded a new Sakalava dynasty in the north called Volamena. He died at Bezavo around 1710. His kingdom held the established trading port of Mazalagem Nova and the new ports of Boina and Mahajanga.

An English captain described Mahajanga in 1764 as a bustling, cosmopolitan port, built after the Indian fashion, with many stone buildings and mosques, and with Muslim inhabitants from Surate, Johana, Mosembeck and the Commoro islands. The Sakalava rulers let Muslims practise their religion freely and in return imposed trading controls through a purser who traded in the king's name. Sakalava kings and queens also allowed European merchants to trade, and some incorporated Islamic beliefs into their divine kingship and had converted to Islam by the early nineteenth century.

In the 1780s, according to the French traveller Dumaine, about 200 Muslim traders from the Indian subcontinent had settled at Mahajanga at the mouth of the Betsiboka River, mostly Khojas, Ismailis and Da'udi Bohras, with some Hindus coming later. Their legal status was confused: they often declared themselves Malagasy subjects to avoid laws against slave-holding and stone houses that bound British subjects, and their dhows flew French flags. The 1911 census found 4,480 Indians in Madagascar. The word Mahajanga may have an Indic etymology. In 1977 the city saw ethnic unrest that forced the evacuation of the Comorian minority living there.

Mahajanga is a seaport on the north-west coast of Madagascar and the capital of the Boeny Region; the district, which is identical with the city, had 258,068 inhabitants in 2020. Only small ships can reach the wharf, and deeper ships anchor off and transfer cargo by barge. The city is the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese and has a large Muslim population and a university. Its symbol is an African baobab near the coast, 21 metres round, said to be 700 to 800 years old; it was once used for important meetings and, in the nineteenth century, for executions. The climate is tropical savanna, with a wet season from November to mid-April.
mahakam-river: The Mahakam is the third longest river in Borneo, after the Kapuas and the Barito, and the largest river of East Kalimantan, with a catchment of about 77,100 square kilometres. It rises at Cemaru in the highlands of the island, flows south-east to Muara Pahu and then east through a low, flat lake region with about 30 shallow lakes, of which Jempang, Semayang and Melintang are the largest.

Below the lakes it is joined by the Belayan, Kedang Kepala and Kedang Rantau and enters the Makassar Strait through a delta of about 1,800 square kilometres, with mangroves near the shore, Nypa swamps in the middle and lowland forest near the apex. Samarinda lies about 48 kilometres from the mouth.

The Mahakam has served as a waterway and as a source of fish and fresh water since ancient times. The kingdom of Kutai grew up in its basin, and its history is divided into two periods. Kutai Martadipura, about 350 to 400 CE, was a Hindu kingdom founded by Mulawarman at Muara Kaman and is regarded as the oldest kingdom in Indonesia.

Kutai Kartanegara, about 1300, was founded by settlers from Java at Kutai Lama near the river's mouth. About 1565 two preachers from Java, Tunggang Parangan and Ri Bandang, spread Islam widely in Kartanegara. The Kutais, the Banjars and the Dayaks are the peoples of the region.
Geological investigations began in the lower Mahakam in 1888, and in 1897 exploration drilling found oil at a depth of 46 metres on the Louise structure; production began in 1898.

The Mahakam and its floodplain are an ecologically important region, with 147 freshwater fish species and the Irrawaddy dolphin, called pesut locally, and 298 bird species have been recorded in the basin. Fishing is the main livelihood in the lakes area. From the 1970s the Indonesian government moved people from Java, Bali and Madura to East Kalimantan, especially near the river, and by 1973 almost 26 per cent of the cultivated land of the province was worked by migrants. The Kutai Kartanegara Bridge over the river collapsed on 26 November 2011, and a new bridge opened on 8 December 2015.
mahakuta-group-of-temples: The temples stand in the village of Mahakuta in the Bagalkot district of Karnataka. The site remains an important place of Hindu worship and the seat of a well-known Shaiva monastery. A natural mountain spring flows within the complex and feeds a large tank called the Vishnu Pushkarni, the lotus pool of Vishnu, and an ablution tank, the Papavinasha Tirtha. The largest of its several shrines are the Mahakuteshvara temple, built in the dravida style, and the Mallikarjuna temple. A small shrine in the middle of the Vishnu Pushkarni holds a Panchamukha linga, a five-faced Shiva linga with one face for each direction and one on top.

The temples are dated to the 6th or 7th century CE from their architecture, which resembles that of the temples at nearby Aihole, and from two inscriptions in the complex. Their builders, Karnataka artisans of the 7th century, set south Indian dravida temples, with a tiered tower capped by a dome-like top, beside north Indian nagara temples, with a curvilinear tower over a square shrine capped by a ribbed stone. Both were local variants, unrelated to the styles of Tamil Nadu or Central India, and the builders combined the plan of one with features of the other. This hybrid is regarded as a peculiarity of the region and as the beginning of the Vesara style.

The Mahakuta Pillar inscription, written in Sanskrit in the Kannada script, records a grant by Durlabhadevi, a queen of Pulakeshin I, the father of King Mangalesha, who added an endowment of ten villages, among them Pattadakal and Aihole, to the god Mahakuteshvara Natha. It also gives historians information on the Chalukya lineage, their campaigns, conquests and early monuments. Called the Dharma-jayastambha, the pillar of victory of religion, it is shown in an archaeological museum at Bijapur. A second inscription, in the porch of the Mahakuteshvara temple and written in Kannada, records the gift of rubies, a silver umbrella and land by Vinapoti, a concubine of King Vijayaditya, and is dated between 696 and 733 CE.
mahalia-jackson: Mahalia Jackson was born Mahala Jackson on 26 October 1911 to Charity Clark and Johnny Jackson, a stevedore and weekend barber who lived elsewhere and never joined Charity as a parent. Both sets of her grandparents were born into slavery. She grew up in the leaky three-room house of her aunt Mahala, called Duke, in New Orleans, the thirteenth person living there.

In a very cold December around 1928 she arrived in Chicago. Her aunts took her to Greater Salem Baptist Church, where she felt at home at once. She sang Hand Me Down My Silver Trumpet, Gabriel, joined the choir, and became part of the Johnson Singers, Chicago's first black gospel group.

From about 1931 the Johnson Singers were asked to other church services and revivals, often by small storefront churches whose members were newly arrived migrants, one of whom called her a fresh wind from the down-home religion. The Great Depression drove church attendance, and larger churches gradually became more open to her style as they sought ways to attract members. In 1946 she appeared at the Golden Gate Ballroom in Harlem, where a scout for Apollo Records heard her.

Her first two Apollo releases sold poorly, and when the company asked her to record blues she refused. The song she had sung as a warm-up, Move On Up a Little Higher, was recorded in two parts, and the 1947 release sold two million copies and reached number two on the Billboard charts, both firsts for gospel music.

In 1954 she learned that Apollo's chief executive had withheld royalties and became the first gospel artist to sign with Columbia Records. When Mitch Miller asked her to record ballads and classical songs she again refused. She sang the national anthem at John F. Kennedy's Inaugural Ball in 1961, became the first gospel recording artist to tour Europe, and sang at the March on Washington in 1963. She was a loyal supporter of Martin Luther King Jr.

Completely self-taught, she never learned to read or write musical notation. She adapted the style of Bessie Smith to Protestant hymns and drew on Thomas Dorsey. Asked how she sang, she answered that she sang the way she felt, off-beat, on the beat, between beats. She sold an estimated 22 million records. The historian Robert Marovich identifies her success with Move On Up a Little Higher as the event that launched gospel from a niche movement in Chicago churches to a commercially viable nationwide genre, in the period called the Golden Age of Gospel, from 1945 to 1965. She died on 27 January 1972.
mahamatra: The word means officer of high rank. The Edicts of Ashoka, inscribed on rocks and pillars in the reign of the Maurya emperor Ashoka (269–233 BCE), mention Mahamatras repeatedly, and they appear to have been an essential part of his government: a class of senior officials in charge of various aspects of administration and justice. The edicts name groups with particular duties: Amta-mahamatras, in charge of foreigners, Stri-adhyaksha mahamatras, in charge of women, and the Dharma-Mahamatras, whose full title, Dhaṃma Mahāmātā, means inspectors of dharma.

According to Major Rock Edict 5, there had been no Dharma-Mahamatras in the past; Ashoka appointed them thirteen years after his coronation, in the fourteenth year of his reign (256 BCE). They worked among all religions to establish and promote dharma and for the welfare and happiness of all devoted to it, including among the Greeks, the Kambojas, the Gandharas, the Rastrikas, the Pitinikas and other peoples on the western borders.

Major Rock Edict 12 names them beside the Mahamatras in charge of the women's quarters and the officers of outlying areas, all working for growth in the essentials of all religions, which the king says he values more than gifts and honours. The 7th Major Pillar Edict, in E. Hultzsch's translation of 1925, records that Ashoka set up pillars of morality, appointed Mahamatras of morality and issued proclamations on morality.

The same edict describes these officers as busy with affairs beneficial to ascetics and householders alike. Some were ordered to attend to the Sangha, others to the Brahmanas and Ajivikas, others to the Nirgranthas and others to various sects, so that different Mahamatras dealt with different congregations, while all of them attended to every sect.
mahamuni-buddha: Arakanese legend holds that the Buddha visited Dhanyawadi, the capital of Arakan, with Shin Ananda and 500 disciples, and that King Candrasurya asked him to leave an image for the people to worship. In the story, Sakka, ruler of the Tavatimsa heaven, and his assistant Vissakamma moulded a lifelike image from ornaments given by the king and his people while the Buddha meditated under a Bodhi tree for a week. The Buddha then imbued it with his spiritual essence, named it Candasara and said it would last for five thousand years.

Tradition counts only five likenesses made in the Buddha's lifetime, two in India, two in paradise and this one. King Anawratha of Pagan is said to have tried to move the image to Bagan without success. When the Konbaung forces of Crown Prince Thado Minsaw took it from Mrauk U, it was too large to carry whole, so it was cut into sections and reassembled in a new temple at Amarapura.

The bronze image weighs 6.5 tonnes and reaches 3.82 metres on a pedestal 1.84 metres high, seated in the Bhumisparsa Mudra, the right hand touching the ground. It wears royal costume with Brahmanic cords and regalia across the chest and a crown set with diamonds, rubies and sapphires. Male devotees press gold leaf onto it, and the coating, about 15 centimetres thick, has blurred its outline. The right hand and crown are free of gold leaf, which suggests they were added later.

Fires in 1879 and 1884 destroyed the spire and halls, though the image was saved, and gold recovered after the fire was made into a robe for it. Minister Kinwun Mingyi U Kaung built the present temple in 1896 around the original shrine of King Bodawpaya.

Under the Burmese kings, food and other offerings were carried to the image each day in a procession from the palace under a royal white umbrella, escorted by a minister, as was due to a sovereign. Since 17 February 1988 monks have washed its face and brushed its teeth every morning at dawn, a ritual begun by Sayadaw Bhaddanta Paññavaṃsa of Htilin Monastery; the towels used are returned to devotees for their home shrines. The Mahamuni Paya Pwe festival in early February includes several days of recitation of the Paṭṭhāna.
mahanadi: The name Mahanadi combines the Sanskrit words maha, great, and nadi, river. The river drains around 132,100 square kilometres of east-central India and flows through Chhattisgarh and Odisha to the Bay of Bengal. Like many seasonal Indian rivers it is a combination of mountain streams, so its precise source cannot be pinpointed. Its farthest headwaters lie in forest south of Sihawa town in Dhamtari district of Chhattisgarh, in hills that extend the Eastern Ghats.

It first flows north through Raipur district, then east after the Shivnath joins it, and enters Odisha after about half its length. Near Sambalpur it is dammed at Hirakud. It then forces its way through the Eastern Ghats by the 64-kilometre Satkosia Gorge and reaches the plain at Naraj, near Cuttack.

Cuttack and Sambalpur were prominent trading places in the ancient world, and Ptolemy refers to the river as the Manada. Before the Hirakud Dam the Mahanadi was navigable from its mouth up to Arrang, but barrages have ended that.

The river was notorious for devastating floods for much of recorded history and was called the sorrow of Orissa. It deposits more silt than any other river of the Indian subcontinent, and before the dam it was about a mile wide at Sambalpur. At its monsoon peak its discharge is almost as great as that of the much larger Ganges, but for most of the year it is a narrow channel between wide sand banks. The Hirakud Dam was the first major multipurpose river valley project after India's independence in 1947. It is the longest earthen dam in the world, measuring 26 kilometres including its dykes.

Just before Cuttack the river gives off a large distributary, the Kathjori, and the city stands on the spit between the two channels. The Mahanadi proper enters the sea by several channels near Paradeep. The combined delta of its distributaries and the Brahmani is one of the largest in India, and the valley is best known for its fertile soil and agriculture.
mahanaim: The name Mahanaim means camps in Hebrew. The Bible places the town near the Jabbok river, beyond the Jordan River, in the same general area as Jabesh-gilead. Two possible sites have been identified, and the western of the twin Tulul adh-Dhahab tells, Tell edh-Dhahab el-Gharbi, is one proposed identification; the precise location remains uncertain.

In the Book of Genesis, Jacob, returning from Padan-aram to southern Canaan, has a vision of the angels of God at the place and names it Mahanaim, God's camp. Later in the story, afraid of the approach of his brother Esau, he divides his company into two hosts, and the town built on the site took its name from them.

According to the Book of Joshua and 1 Chronicles, Mahanaim became a Levitical city and had lain on the southern boundary of Bashan until the Israelite conquest of Canaan. In the narrative of 2 Samuel it was a stronghold that served as a sanctuary for important fugitives. There Abner, commander of King Saul's army, set up Saul's son Ish-bosheth as king of Israel after Saul's death.

In the story of Absalom's revolt, David reaches Mahanaim, shelters with a man named Barzillai and musters forces there against his son's army, and it is at Mahanaim that he learns of the victory and of Absalom's death. Some translations of the Song of Songs mention a dance of Mahanaim.

Gaston Maspero identified Mahanaim with the Ma'hanema' of the towns plundered by Shishak during his invasion of the Levant, a view shared by Champollion, Rosellini and Budge. The town is not mentioned again, and Maspero thought it not improbable that resistance to Shishak or another invader led to its destruction.
mahapadma-nanda: What is told of Mahapadma comes from the Puranas, which make him the first Nanda king and the son of Mahanandin, the last king of the preceding Shaishunaga line, by a Shudra woman. His name, also given as Mahapadma-pati, means lord of the great lotus. Other traditions about the founder of the dynasty do not use this name at all.

Buddhist texts call the first Nanda king Ugrasena and describe him as of unknown lineage. According to the Mahavamsa-tika he came from the frontier region, was captured by a gang of robbers and later became their leader. One theory holds that Ugrasena was probably another name for Mahapadma. Jain texts such as the Parishishtaparvan and the Avashyaka sutra say that the Nanda king was the son of a courtesan by a barber and that he succeeded Udayin, with Kalpaka, a Jain, as his chief minister.

The Puranas describe him as ekarat, sole sovereign, and as sarva-kshatrantaka, destroyer of all the Kshatriyas, the warriors and rulers. The lines he is said to have exterminated include the Maithalas, Kasheyas, Ikshvakus, Panchalas, Shurasenas, Kurus, Haihayas, Vitihotras, Kalingas and Ashmakas.

The length of his reign is uncertain. The Matsya Purana assigns him 88 years, the Vayu Purana only 28. Modern estimates of his coronation also differ: the Indologist F. E. Pargiter put it in 382 BCE, the historian R. K. Mukherjee in 364 BCE and the historian H. C. Raychaudhuri about 345 BCE, and the beginning of Nanda rule has been placed as early as the 5th century BCE.

According to the Puranas, eight sons of Mahapadma ruled in succession after him for twelve years in all; only one, Sukalpa, is named. The Buddhist texts instead make the next eight kings brothers of the first, give the dynasty 22 years in total and name the last of them as Dhana Nanda.

Greek and Roman writers call the Nanda king of the time of Alexander's invasion Agrammes, possibly a corruption of the Sanskrit Augraseniya, son or descendant of Ugrasena. They suggest that the founder was a barber who took the throne from the last king of the earlier dynasty. The Roman historian Curtius, of the 1st century CE, reports on the authority of Porus that this barber became the queen's lover, murdered the king, seized power while pretending to act as guardian of the princes and later killed them, and that the king reigning in Alexander's day was his son.
mahaparinirvana-sutra: The history of the text is extremely complex, but the consensus is that its core was compiled in South India, possibly in Andhra or the Deccan, in the time of the Śātavāhana dynasty, whose rulers gave rich patronage to Buddhism. Stephen Hodge places the core between 100 CE and 220 CE, in a Mahāsāṃghika environment such as Karli or Amaravatī, and Masahiro Shimoda distinguishes several stages of growth from a short proto-sutra. The original title was Mahāparinirvāṇamahāsūtra, and the earliest version was associated with the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravāda school. Only fragments of the Sanskrit survive, found in Central Asia, Afghanistan and Japan.

The sutra is set in the final hours of the Buddha's life, but its main interlocutor is Mañjuśrī rather than Ananda, and it ends with the Buddha lying down, without describing his death, cremation or the division of relics. Its most important innovation, according to Sallie B. King, is linking buddha-nature with tathāgatagarbha, presented as an eternal, pure Self, a radical idea that caused much controversy. It treats not-self and emptiness as skilful means leading to that teaching, promotes vegetarianism and describes a coming age of decline with false monks and false teachings.

The sutra also discusses the icchantikas, people hostile to its teaching who are either barred from Buddhahood or find it very hard to reach. Scholars such as Mark Blum note that the text treats them in different ways: some passages compare them to scorched seeds, while others say they too have buddha-nature.

The shortest and earliest Chinese version, the six fascicle text, was made between 416 and 418 and is conventionally ascribed to Faxian, although the earliest catalogue credits Buddhabhadra and his assistant Baoyun. The far longer translation of Dharmakṣema became the most popular in China, Japan and Korea, and some scholars think its later parts were composed in China. In the Southern Dynasties period a Nirvana School devoted to it taught that even icchantikas could reach Buddhahood; it thrived under the Liang and many of its teachings passed into the Tiantai school. Baoliang compiled the chief Chinese commentary in 509, and Tibetan translations were made from the early 9th century.
maharaja-sayajirao-university-of-baroda: Baroda College was founded by Baroda State in 1881, one of the first public acts of Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III, and taught arts and science. Its main building, now the Faculty of Arts, was designed by Robert Fellowes Chisholm in the Indo-Saracenic style, with Indian and Byzantine arches and domes in brick and polychrome stone; the dome of its convocation hall was modelled on the Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur. In 1949 Pratap Singh Gaekwad, the last Maharaja of Baroda, founded the university on his grandfather's wishes and settled the Sir Sayajirao Diamond Jubilee and Memorial Trust for the education of the people of the former state.

Several faculties are older than the university. The Academy of Indian Music, founded by Ustad Moula Bux under Sayajirao's patronage on 26 February 1886, became the Music College and then the Faculty of Performing Arts; after Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande's curriculum was introduced there, Madhusudan Joshi received a diploma in music in 1932. Bharatanatyam came to Baroda with Maharani Chimnabai I of Tanjore, who married Sayajirao in 1880, and in 1950 the university began the first dance programme in India.

The Department of Education dates from 1935, when it grew out of a teacher training college. The Faculty of Science became independent in March 1951 under its first dean, C. S. Patel, and the Department of Biochemistry was set up in 1955 under C. V. Ramakrishnan. The Baroda Medical College, attached to the Sir Sayajirao General Hospital, began in 1949, and the Faculty of Management Studies in 1984.

The university has 89 departments on six campuses, two rural and four urban, covering 275 acres. The Hansa Mehta Library was founded in 1950 and keeps a number of titles now out of print. The Oriental Institute, founded on 1 September 1927 from a plan Sayajirao made in 1893, keeps his collection of more than 10,000 manuscripts and published a critical edition of the Ramayana in seven volumes between 1951 and 1975. Its teachers have included the sociologist M. N. Srinivas and the political scientist Rajni Kothari, and its alumni the film-maker Dadasaheb Phalke and Vinoba Bhave.
maharana-pratap: Pratap Singh was born in 1540, the year his father Udai Singh II took the throne of Mewar. His mother was Jaiwanta Bai, and his younger brothers included Shakti Singh, Vikram Singh and Jagmal Singh. After Udai Singh's death in 1572 his wife Rani Dheer Bai Bhatiyani wanted her son Jagmal to succeed, but senior courtiers preferred Pratap as the eldest son. He was crowned at Gogunda on the day of Holi as the 54th ruler of Mewar in the line of the Sisodia Rajputs. Jagmal swore revenge and went to join Akbar's armies at Ajmer.

The siege of Chittorgarh in 1567 and 1568 had cost Mewar its fertile eastern belt, but the wooded hills of the Aravalli range were still held by Pratap. Akbar wanted a stable route to Gujarat through Mewar and sent envoys, among them Man Singh I of Amber, Bhagwant Das and Todar Mal, asking Pratap to become a vassal. Pratap consistently refused, either with vague promises or by declining to meet them. Akbar's demands probably included attendance at court, tribute, allegiance or a marriage alliance, none of which he would accept.

On 18 June 1576 Pratap, with about 3,000 cavalry and 400 Bhil archers, met Man Singh, who commanded about 10,000 men, at Haldighati near Gogunda. After more than three hours Pratap was wounded and the day was lost, but he escaped to the hills and the Mughals did not capture him or his family. Akbar himself campaigned against him in September 1576, and Gogunda, Udaipur and Kumbhalgarh came under Mughal control. Shahbaz Khan Kamboh's later invasions weakened Pratap further and forced him to take refuge in the hills, where he fought as a guerrilla.

Mughal pressure eased after 1579 because of rebellions in Bengal and Bihar. A Mughal expedition under Jagannath Kachhwaha in 1584 was driven back, and in 1585 Akbar moved to Lahore for twelve years. Pratap recovered thirty-six outposts, including Udaipur, Gogunda and Mandal, and by his death he had regained a large part of Mewar. He could not retake Chittor itself. His court at Chavand sheltered poets and artists, and the Chavand school of art developed there.

Pratap reportedly died of injuries from a hunting accident at Chavand on 19 January 1597, aged 56, and his eldest son Amar Singh I succeeded him. He is a folk hero in Rajasthan and across India. The historian Satish Chandra wrote that his defiance of the Mughal empire, almost alone and unaided by the other Rajput states, was a saga of Rajput valour, and that his guerrilla methods were later elaborated by Malik Ambar and by Shivaji.
maharashtra: Maharashtra covers 307,713 square kilometres of the western peninsular region of India and occupies a substantial part of the Deccan Plateau. It has a coastline of 840 kilometres on the Arabian Sea. The dominant feature is the plateau, separated from the narrow Konkan coastal plains by the Western Ghats, also called the Sahyadri Range, which run parallel to the coast and average 1,200 metres in height. The Satpura Hills form its northern border. The Godavari and Krishna are its two major rivers. Its main regions are North Maharashtra, Konkan, Marathwada, Vidarbha and Desh, or Western Maharashtra.

The region has a history of many thousands of years. Late Harappan or Chalcolithic sites of the Jorwe culture, c. 1300 to 700 BCE, have been found throughout the state, the largest at Daimabad, which had a mud fortification and an elliptical temple with fire pits. In the Late Harappan period many people migrated from Gujarat to northern Maharashtra. Among the dynasties that ruled the region were the Asmakas, the Mauryas, the Western Satraps, the Abhiras, the Vakatakas, the Chalukyas, the Western Chalukyas, the Khaljis, the Tughlaqs, the Bahamanis and the Mughals, besides the Satavahanas, Rashtrakutas and Seuna Yadavas.

In the early 19th century the region was divided between the Peshwa's dominions in the Maratha Confederacy and the Nizamate of Hyderabad. The British East India Company then defeated the Marathas and brought most of present-day Maharashtra under its control, directly and through many princely states, and from 1858 the British crown took over. The region was divided among the Bombay Presidency, the Central Provinces, Berar and princely states including Hyderabad. After independence in 1947 the Bombay Presidency became Bombay State, which gained Berar, the Deccan states and the Gujarat states between 1950 and 1956. The United Maharashtra Movement campaigned for a separate state for Marathi speakers, and on 1 May 1960 Bombay State was divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat.

Mumbai is the capital of Maharashtra, with Nagpur as its winter capital, and the state has 36 districts in six divisions. Marathi, written in the Devanagari script, is the official language and is spoken by about 69 per cent of the people. Its earliest literature is the Dnyaneshwari, a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita by the 13th-century Bhakti saint Dnyaneshwar. Seven UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the state, among them the Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta Caves and the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus.
maharero: Maharero kaTjamuaha was born about 1820 at Okahandja. In 1843 he went with his father Tjamuaha to Windhoek to stay with Jonker Afrikaner, Captain of the Oorlam Afrikaners. Tjamuaha remained Jonker Afrikaner's ally, though in a subordinate position, until his death in 1861. When Jonker Afrikaner died and was succeeded by Christian Afrikaner, Maharero rebelled, and on 15 June 1863 the Afrikaners attacked his men at Otjimbingwe in a battle in which Christian Afrikaner was killed.

Christian's successor, Jan Jonker Afrikaner, would not let the Herero escape his overlordship, and fighting went on for years. Traders at Otjimbingwe, among them Charles John Andersson and Frederick Thomas Green, thought the war bad for trade and helped organise and lead the Herero army; Green's force captured most of the Oorlam cattle, and Jan Jonker's forces were decisively beaten on 22 June 1864. Maharero went on to take control of Damaraland and sent forces into Namaqualand, until the missionary Carl Hugo Hahn of the Rhenish Missionary Society brokered a peace in 1870.

More traders from the Cape Colony and Boers from the east then entered Herero lands. Maharero complained to the Cape governor, who sent the Palgrave Commission; the Cape annexed Walvis Bay in 1878. In 1880 a grazing dispute with Jan Jonker Afrikaner became a pogrom against all Nama in Maharero's territory, in which over 200 were killed. Hendrik Witbooi, who escaped, then led the opposition to him. Under attack from Witbooi's ǀKhowesin, Maharero signed a protection treaty with the German governor Heinrich Ernst Göring on 21 October 1885, without ceding Herero land.

Finding no German help against Witbooi, Maharero renounced the treaty in 1888 and reopened talks with the Cape Colony, but the European powers had by then recognised South West Africa as a German sphere of influence, and he reaffirmed the treaty in May 1890. He died at Okahandja on 7 October 1890. The historian Heinrich Vedder claims that his main wife Kataree poisoned him to stop him changing his choice of successor. His eldest son, Samuel Maharero, became chief of the Herero.
mahasi-sayadaw: Mahāsī Sayādaw U Sobhana was born on 29 July 1904 in Seikkhun village in Upper Burma. He became a novice at twelve and was ordained at twenty with the name Sobhana. Over decades of study he passed the government examinations in the Theravāda texts, gaining the newly introduced Dhammācariya, or dhamma teacher, degree in 1941. In 1931 he left his teaching of scriptural studies in Moulmein to practise intensive meditation at Thaton under Mingun Jetawun Sayādaw, also known as U Nārada.

He first taught Vipassana meditation in 1938 in his home village, at a monastery named after its great drum, Mahāsi, and became known by its name. At the invitation of Prime Minister U Nu he became resident teacher of a new meditation centre in Yangon, the Mahāsi Sāsana Yeiktha. At the Sixth Buddhist Council, on 17 May 1954, he served as questioner and final editor.

He helped found meditation centres across Burma and in Sri Lanka, Indonesia and Thailand, and by 1972 those under his guidance had trained more than 700,000 meditators. In 1979 he travelled to the West, leading retreats at new centres such as the Insight Meditation Society in Barre, Massachusetts. His students included Sayādaw U Paṇḍita, Nyanaponika Thera, Dipa Ma, Joseph Goldstein, Sharon Salzberg and Jack Kornfield. He died after a massive stroke on 14 August 1982, and thousands of devotees came through monsoon rains to pay their respects.

His method derived from the New Burmese Method of U Nārada and rests on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. The meditator first keeps Buddhist morality, sīla, then anchors attention on the rising and falling of the abdomen in breathing, noting each physical or mental event as it arises without further thought. Joined to reflection on causation, this is held to bring insight into anicca, dukkha and anattā. He published nearly seventy volumes in Burmese, translated the Visuddhimagga of Buddhaghosa into Burmese and wrote a Manual of Vipassana Meditation.
mahatma-gandhi: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 in Porbandar, a coastal town on the Kathiawar Peninsula and then part of a small princely state. His father Karamchand Uttamchand Gandhi was the dewan, or chief minister, of Porbandar and later of Rajkot. A family friend advised that he study law in London, and to win his mother's consent he vowed to abstain from meat, alcohol and women. The elders of the Modh Bania community excommunicated him from his caste, but he sailed on 4 September 1888 and was called to the bar at 22.

After two uncertain years in India, Gandhi went to South Africa in April 1893 to represent an Indian merchant in a lawsuit, and stayed for 21 years. He faced discrimination at once: he was thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg for refusing to leave the first-class compartment. He had thought of himself as a Briton first and an Indian second, but the prejudice he saw made him question his people's standing in the British Empire. There he first used nonviolent resistance, in a campaign for civil rights.

Gandhi returned to India in 1915 at the request of Gopal Krishna Gokhale. He took leadership of the Indian National Congress in 1920 and formulated satyagraha as a political movement in a Resolution on Non-cooperation that September. Congress declared the independence of India on 26 January 1930, and that year he led the 400 km Dandi Salt March against the British salt tax. In 1942 he demanded immediate independence, and the British imprisoned him and tens of thousands of Congress leaders. He was imprisoned many times in both South Africa and India.

The Muslim League moved, against Gandhi's strong opposition, to demand a separate Muslim state. In August 1947 the British partitioned the land, and India and Pakistan each became independent on terms Gandhi disapproved. Religious violence followed, especially in Punjab and Bengal. He visited the affected areas and undertook several hunger strikes to stop the violence.

On 30 January 1948 Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who opposed Gandhi's advocacy of nonviolence and his friendship with Indian Muslims, shot him three times in the chest in the garden of Birla House in Delhi on his way to a prayer meeting. Gandhi's birthday, 2 October, is a national holiday in India, Gandhi Jayanti, and is marked worldwide as the International Day of Nonviolence. He is regarded as the Father of the Nation in India and was often called Bapu. His pamphlet Hind Swaraj of 1909 became the intellectual blueprint of the independence movement. Writers differ on him, some presenting a paragon of ethical living and others a more complex, contradictory and changing figure.
mahaut-countess-of-artois: Mahaut, also called Mathilda, was the eldest child and only daughter of Robert II, Count of Artois, and Amicie of Courtenay; her paternal grandparents were Robert I of Artois and Matilda of Brabant. In 1291 she married Otto IV, Count of Burgundy. They had three children: Joan, who married the future Philip V of France, Blanche, who married Charles IV of France, and Robert, who died in 1317.

Her brother Philip died in 1298, before their father, so at Robert II's death in 1302 Mahaut inherited Artois by proximity of blood rather than Philip's son Robert III. He challenged the decision repeatedly, but the Parlement of Paris and the royal court upheld her rights each time. She proved an able administrator, defeated many rebellions by members of the nobility, and relied on Thierry de Hérisson, bishop of Arras, as her senior administrator.

When Otto died in 1303 their under-age daughter Joan succeeded him in the County of Burgundy, and Mahaut governed it as regent. After Joan married the future Philip V in 1307, Mahaut continued to rule her absent daughter's lands until 1315. Her daughters Joan and Blanche, with their cousin Margaret of Burgundy, were caught up in the Tour de Nesle affair, in which Joan was briefly imprisoned for concealing her sisters' adultery and Philip was said to have become estranged from her.

In 1316, on the claims of Robert III, Mahaut was accused of bewitching Philip V and poisoning Louis X; a repudiation of Joan would have threatened her standing, while a quick succession favoured her son-in-law, then regent. She died on 27 November 1329 and Artois passed to Joan. Maurice Druon made her a central figure of his novel series The Accursed Kings, as the poisoner of Louis X and his infant son Jean I, and she was played by Hélène Duc in the television adaptation of 1972 and by Jeanne Moreau in that of 2005.
mahavamsa: The Buddhist monks of the Anuradhapura Maha Viharaya kept chronicles of the island's history from the 3rd century BCE. These annals were combined into a single document while King Dhatusena ruled the Anuradhapura Kingdom, on the basis of earlier commentaries in Sinhala known as the Atthakatha. The simpler Dipavamsa, or Chronicles of the Island, probably served as the nucleus of an oral tradition that was incorporated into the written text. The Mahavamsa-tika attributes the work to an otherwise unknown monk, Mahānāma, who lived in a monastery affiliated with the Mahavihara.

The text is written in Pali verse and holds four kinds of material. The first recounts three visits, told as tradition, of the Buddha to the island, which are not mentioned in the Pali Canon or other early sources. The second consists of genealogies of Sri Lankan kings. The third deals with the history of the Buddhist sangha, including the mission sent by Emperor Ashoka, the transplanting of the bodhi tree and the founding of the Mahavihara. The fourth begins with the arrival of Prince Vijaya from India and continues to the reign of King Mahasena. Its account of the war between the Sinhala king Dutthagamani and the Tamil invader Elara runs to 861 verses, against 13 in the Dipavamsa.

Early Western scholars such as Otto Franke doubted that the chronicle held reliable history, but inscriptions and archaeological finds have since confirmed much of it, including Ashoka's missionary work and the founders of monasteries and stupas. G. C. Mendis was sceptical of the story of Vijaya, whose arrival seems to have been fixed to coincide with the Buddha's death around 543 BCE. The work travelled along the Silk Road, and an Extended Mahavamsa survives in Southeast Asia.

The Culavamsa, compiled by several authors, continues the chronicle to 1815. In modern Sri Lanka many Sinhalese cite the text as proof that the island has been a Sinhalese nation since ancient times, while Tamil nationalists contested that view from the 1930s. In 2023 it was listed on UNESCO's Memory of the World International Register.
mahavira: Historical information about Mahavira is scarce, and traditional accounts vary by sect, but scholars do not dispute that he lived in ancient India. Both Jain sects agree that he was born in 599 BCE. The Śvetāmbaras say that he died in 527 BCE and the Digambaras in 510 BCE. Historians place him in the 6th or 5th century BCE, reviving and reforming an earlier community that was probably led by Parshvanatha, whom Jains consider his predecessor.

According to the Kalpa Sūtra and the Uttarapurana, he was born at Kundagrama in the Kingdom of the Videhas, in present-day Bihar, though its exact location is disputed. His father was King Siddhartha of the Nāya tribe and his mother Queen Trishala of the Licchavi republic. His parents were lay followers of Parshvanatha. The Digambaras hold that he refused to marry, while the Śvetāmbaras say that he married Yashoda and had a daughter.

At about thirty, or twenty-eight according to some accounts, Mahavira abandoned royal life and became an ascetic. He undertook severe fasts, meditated under the Ashoka tree and discarded his clothes. The Ācārāṅga Sūtra describes his hardships and self-mortification in graphic terms. After about twelve and a half years of penance he is said to have attained Kevala Jnana, or omniscience, under a Sāla tree on the bank of the river Rijuvalika.

He then preached for thirty years. Jain texts name eleven Brahmanas as his first disciples, the Ganadharas, led by Indrabhuti Gautama. According to the Kalpa Sūtra his followers numbered 14,000 monks and 36,000 nuns, with 159,000 male and 318,000 female lay followers. Tradition names Srenika and Kunika of the Haryanka dynasty, popularly known as Bimbisara and Ajatashatru, and Chetaka of Videha among his royal followers. He died at Pawapuri in present-day Bihar, now a pilgrimage site, and Jains commemorate the night of his nirvana as Diwali.

Mahavira taught that the observance of five vows is necessary for liberation: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity and non-attachment. Non-violence was already an established rule among the followers of Parshvanatha. He also taught Anekantavada, the doctrine of many-sided reality. Moriz Winternitz notes that his teaching contains a very elaborate belief in the soul, unlike that of the Buddhists.
