Gautama Swami compiled his teachings as the Jain Agamas, which monks passed on orally. According to Jain tradition they were gradually lost after about 300 BCE, when a severe famine in Magadha dispersed the monks. In the early centuries of the common era the surviving teachings were written on palm-leaf manuscripts, and the Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions each hold their own incomplete and somewhat different versions.
mahaviracharya: Mahāvīra, whose title Mahaviracharya means Mahavira the Teacher, was possibly born in Mysore. His Gaṇita-sāra-saṅgraha, the Compendium on the gist of Mathematics, separated astrology from mathematics and is the earliest Indian text entirely devoted to mathematics. It treats the subjects that Aryabhata and Brahmagupta had discussed, but more clearly, and takes a highly syncopated approach to algebra, with much of the text given to the techniques needed to solve algebraic problems. It established terms for the equilateral and isosceles triangle, the rhombus, the circle and the semicircle.

Its arithmetic uses the decimal place-value system and zero, though it wrongly states that a number divided by zero is unchanged. Mahāvīra asserted that the square root of a negative number does not exist, gave a formula approximating the area and perimeter of the ellipse, methods for squares and cube roots, and the general formula for choosing r things from n. He also stated algebraic identities, among them one for the cube of a number. The chapter on the reduction of fractions gives, in verses 55 to 98, systematic rules for writing a fraction as a sum of unit fractions.

Mahāvīra is highly respected among Indian mathematicians, above all for the terms he established, and his reputation spread through southern India, where his books inspired later mathematicians. Pavuluri Mallana translated the compendium into Telugu as Saara Sangraha Ganitamu. One of his rules for unit fractions, applied with the smallest suitable integer each time, is identical to the greedy algorithm for Egyptian fractions, and further rules of the kind were given in the 14th century in the Gaṇita-kaumudi of Nārāyaṇa.
mahavyutpatti: The Sanskrit name means roughly great etymology, and the Tibetan title is Bye-brag-tu rtogs-par byed-pa chen-po. Tradition attributes the work to the reign of Ralpacan, about 838, but Professor Tucci argued that it goes back to his predecessor Sadnalegs, who reigned about 800 to 815, and perhaps in conception to the time of Khri Srong-lde-brtsan, when the problems of translation were first seriously faced. Indian pandits were consulted, and a committee of three Tibetan translators, 'Bro Ka.ba dPal.brtsegs, Cog.ro kLu'i rgyal.mtshan and sNa.nam Ye.she.sde, did the work. Final amendments were made by Indian pandits including Jinamitra, Surendrabodhi and Dhanashila.

The original dictionary held 9,565 entries in 277 chapters and three volumes, one on the Hinayana, one on the Mahayana and one of indexes. Three copies were installed at pho.brang lDan.mkhar, 'Phang-thang and mChims.phu. It is included in the Tibetan Tengyur and is the earliest substantial bilingual dictionary known.

A companion work produced in the reign of Sadnalegs, the sGra-sbyor bam-po gnyis-pa, describes how it was made: terms used by earlier translators that did not accord with religious criteria or grammar were revised, difficult terms were broken into their parts and given a fixed meaning by reference to Mahayana and Hinayana texts and to masters such as Nāgārjuna and Vasubandhu, and simple terms were rendered by their ordinary sense. Translators were ordered never to depart from this standard, and tantras and mantras were not to be translated without permission. With it, older translations were corrected and completed.

Chinese was later added to the Sanskrit and Tibetan, and by the 17th century versions gave Chinese, Mongolian and Manchu equivalents as well. The first English translation was made by the Hungarian Tibetologist Sándor Kőrösi Csoma, whose work the Asiatic Society of Bengal in Calcutta published in three parts, in 1834, 1910 and 1944. The dictionary is still used, usually in reverse, to find the Sanskrit behind Tibetan Buddhist terms and to reconstruct Sanskrit texts whose originals survive only in Tibetan translation.
mahayana-buddhism: Mahāyāna, Sanskrit for Great Vehicle, is a broad group of Buddhist traditions, texts, philosophies and practices that developed in ancient India from about the 1st century BCE. Its origins are still not completely understood, and there are many competing theories. The earliest textual evidence comes from sutras originating around the beginning of the common era. According to Jan Nattier, the term was at first an honorary synonym for Bodhisattvayāna, the vehicle of a bodhisattva who seeks buddhahood for the benefit of all beings, and in the earliest sources it meant the rigorous emulation of the path of Gautama Buddha. The movement remained quite small until it grew strongly in the 5th century, when manuscripts and inscriptions begin to show popular and some royal support.

Mahāyāna accepts the main scriptures and teachings of early Buddhism but also recognises sutras that Theravāda does not accept as canonical, such as the Lotus Sutra and the Vajra-cutter Sutra. These emphasise the ideal of the bodhisattva, who vows to attain buddhahood to save all living beings, an attitude called bodhicitta. Mahāyānists hold that the bodhisattva path is superior to the path of those seeking only their own release from suffering, which they call a lesser aspiration. Its teachings include the Perfection of Wisdom, Buddha-nature and skilful means, the idea that the Buddha adapts his teaching to each hearer. Its cosmology includes buddhas such as Amitābha and Vairocana, and philosophical schools such as Madhyamaka and its theory of emptiness.

Mahāyāna texts and philosophy reached Central Asia and China along trade routes such as the Silk Road. Translators from Central Asia, among them Lokakṣema, Dharmarakṣa, Kumārajīva and Dharmakṣema, were central to this transmission, and Dunhuang was an important place of study. In India the great scholastic centres of Nalanda and Vikramashila thrived between the 7th and 12th centuries. From the Gupta period a new tantric movement grew within it, called Vajrayāna, which dominated Indian Buddhism in the Pala era. Mahāyāna traditions such as Zen, Pure Land and Tiantai are the main forms of Buddhism in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam, and tantric forms are dominant in Tibet, Mongolia and Bhutan.
mahdi: The Arabic word al-Mahdī means the guided one. It comes from the root h-d-y, which indicates divine guidance, but the word does not occur in the Quran. From the beginning of Islam it was an honorific without messianic meaning, applied to Muhammad, to Abraham, to al-Husayn and to some Umayyad caliphs. During the Second Muslim Civil War (680 to 692) it came to mean a ruler who would restore Islam and justice after oppression. Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who claimed the caliphate against the Umayyads, presented himself in this role, and a hadith was circulated in which Muhammad foretells a just ruler.

Some historians suggest that southern Arabian tribes settled in Syria in the mid-7th century introduced the term. The idea is also linked to the Christian Second Coming, the Jewish Mashiach ben David and the Zoroastrian Saoshyant; Islamic scholars reject a Zoroastrian influence and defend the traditions. They appear in Sunan Abi Dawud and Sunan al-Tirmidhi but not in the early works of al-Bukhari and Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj.

The Mahdi is the Islamic messianic figure expected to appear before the end of time, alongside Jesus, to restore justice and defeat tyranny. In Sunni Islam he is a descendant of Muhammad through Fatima who has not yet appeared and is not identified with any historical person. In Twelver Shia Islam he is the twelfth and last Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, born in 869, who entered occultation and remains alive until his return. Shia writers often call him al-Qa'im, he who will rise.

Traditions about the occultation of a future imam circulated for about a century before the death of the eleventh Imam in 260 AH (874 CE). Sects now extinct, such as the Kaysanites, who said Ibn al-Hanafiyya was hiding near Medina, used them, and the Twelver doctrine took shape in the first half of the tenth century in the works of al-Qummi, al-Kulayni and Ibn Babawayh.

Belief in the Mahdi has had a central place in Islamic theology, devotional literature and popular piety for over a millennium, and it has influenced many religious, political and messianic movements. There have been a vast number of Mahdi claimants. Many Muslims hold that the Mahdi appears occasionally to pious individuals, and every year millions celebrate Mid-Sha'ban, the birth of Muhammad al-Mahdi.
mahdia: Mahdia is a Tunisian coastal city, south of Monastir and south-east of Sousse, and the capital of Mahdia Governorate. Its old part corresponds to the Roman city called Aphrodisium and later Africa, or Cape Africa. A bishopric called Africa is supposed to have been established when the city was held by the Kingdom of Sicily, within the Kingdom of Africa from 1147 to 1160, and Pope Eugene III consecrated a bishop for it in 1148. A ship carrying Greek art treasures, dated to about 80 BCE and found sunk off the shore, is known as the Mahdia shipwreck.

The Fatimid caliph Abdallah al-Mahdi founded the city and made it the capital of Ifriqiya. Since the new Fatimid Caliphate was a Shi'a regime backed by a Berber Kutama army, he may have wished to put distance between his power base and Kairouan, a mainly Sunni city and the traditional capital. Construction began in 916, and the city was inaugurated on 20 February 921. It had heavy walls, the Fatimid palaces, an artificial harbour and the Great Mosque of Mahdia. Most of the Fatimid city has not survived, but the mosque is among the best-preserved Fatimid monuments in the Maghreb, though much of it was rebuilt by archaeologists in the 1960s.

The Zirid dynasty, successors of the Fatimids in the Maghreb, moved their capital to Mahdia in 1057. In 1087 ships from Genoa and Pisa raided it and burned the Muslim fleet in the harbour, which helped Christians take control of the western Mediterranean and supply the First Crusade by sea. The city fell to the Norman conquest in 1148 and came under Almohad rule in 1160. The role of capital passed to Tunis in the 12th century. In 1390 a French army besieged Mahdia in the Barbary Crusade and failed to take it.

The Spaniards captured the city in 1550. Charles V offered it to the Order of Saint John, who refused as too costly, and he ordered the Viceroy of Sicily, Juan de Vega, to dismantle it. The Ottomans then reoccupied it, but it lived only by fishing and oil-works and lost its commercial importance. It remained under Turkish rule until the 19th century.

The city, with 76,513 inhabitants, is a provincial centre north of Sfax and is known for fish processing and weaving. Its railway station is the southern terminus of the Sahel Metro line from Sousse and Monastir. The Great Mosque and fragments of mosaic pavements from the Fatimid palaces are what remain of its early history.
mahdist-state: Egypt had conquered Sudan from the early 19th century, a period known locally as the Turkiyya. After the Suez Canal opened in 1869 Britain sought a greater role in Egyptian affairs, and Khedive Ismail appointed the Briton Charles George Gordon governor-general of Sudan, whose opposition to the slave trade bankrupted many merchants. After Gordon resigned, discontent grew and tax collectors raised taxes arbitrarily. Muhammad Ahmad, the son of a Danagla boatbuilder and a sheikh of the Sammaniyah Sufi order, called for a jihad that found great appeal among the poorest communities along the Nile.

To avoid arrest the Mahdi and his followers, the Ansar, marched to Kurdufan and won recruits, especially among the Baggara. Early in 1882 the Ansar overwhelmed a 7,000-man Egyptian force near Al Ubayyid; the Mahdi then starved the town into submission after four months, and the Ansar later defeated an 8,000-man relief force at Sheikan. In Darfur, Baggara rebels besieged the governor-general Rudolf Carl von Slatin, who was captured in 1883. Gordon, sent back to evacuate the garrisons, chose to hold Khartoum. The Ansar stormed it in January 1885, killed him and destroyed the town, building a new capital at Omdurman.

The Mahdi died, probably of typhus, on 22 June 1885. His deputy Abdallahi ibn Muhammad, the Khalifa, gained unchallenged supremacy in 1891 with the help of the Baqqara Arabs, purged the Mahdi's family and early disciples and met any hint of tribal disloyalty with reprisals, among them the massacre of the Juhaina. A 60,000-man army invaded Ethiopia in 1887, but an invasion of Egypt was defeated at Tushkah in 1889, and after an 1888 drought the country fell into famine. On 2 September 1898 Herbert Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian force destroyed the Khalifa's 52,000-man army outside Omdurman, where about 11,000 Mahdists died.

The Khalifa died fighting at Umm Diwaykarat in November 1899, and Osman Digna resisted until January 1900. In Darfur, where the Mahdist era became known as the umkowakia, the period of chaos and anarchy, rule had already been collapsing amid rebellions led by Abu Jimeiza of the Tama, and the restored Sultanate of Darfur destroyed the last holdout, at Kabkabiya, in 1909.

Famine, disease, persecution and war had roughly halved the population: about 8 million people lived in Sudan before the revolt, and an Egyptian census afterwards recorded barely 2.5 million. The Mahdiyah has become known as the first genuine Sudanese nationalist government. It imposed Sharia, added a declaration of the Mahdi to the creed and severely persecuted Christians, including Copts.
mahdist-war: After Muhammad Ali's invasion of 1820 to 1821, Sudan was governed as part of the Ottoman-Egyptian state, known locally as the Turkiyah. Large sections of the population suffered heavy taxation, forced labour and coercion, and many people left the Nile Valley for Kordofan and Darfur. The slave trade remained a major part of the economy. Egypt's debts under Isma'il Pasha led to his forced abdication in 1879. In 1873 Isma'il had appointed Charles George Gordon governor of the Equatorial Provinces, and Gordon tried to suppress the slave trade, but resigned in 1880. Resentment of Turco-Egyptian rule grew among merchants, tribal leaders and religious figures, and the British government refused to assume direct responsibility.

In the 1870s the cleric Muhammad Ahmad preached renewal of the faith and proclaimed himself the Mahdi, the promised redeemer. In August 1881 two Egyptian companies sent to arrest him fired on each other in the dark and were destroyed in turn at the Battle of Aba. He retreated to Kordofan and declared a jihad, calling his followers the Ansar. On 7 June 1882 his army surprised an Egyptian force of 4,000 under Yusef Pasha and destroyed it. In November 1883 the Mahdi, with about 40,000 men, defeated the army of the retired colonel William Hicks at the Battle of Shaykan, and only about 500 Egyptians survived.

Britain then decided that Egypt should evacuate Sudan and sent Gordon, who reached Khartoum on 18 February 1884. He grew reluctant to leave while any who wished to go had not been able to, and it is debated whether he deliberately stayed too long. The telegraph lines were cut on 15 March. A relief column of 9,000 under Sir Garnet Wolseley won at Abu Klea and Abu Kru in January 1885, but Khartoum fell on 26 January 1885, after a siege of 313 days, and Gordon and the garrison were killed. Muhammad Ahmad died on 22 June 1885 and was succeeded by the Khalifa Abdallahi ibn Muhammad.

The Mahdist state fought Ethiopia in the 1880s and Italian troops in the 1890s. In 1898 Herbert Kitchener led an Anglo-Egyptian force of 8,200 British soldiers and 17,600 Egyptian and Sudanese soldiers up the Nile with railways and gunboats. After the Battle of Atbara in April the force reached Omdurman, the Mahdist capital, on 2 September, where the Mahdist army of more than 60,000 attacked and was cut down by machine guns and rifles. Organised resistance ended the next year, and Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, a condominium in which Britain held de facto control, was created in 1899.
mahe-de-la-bourdonnais: La Bourdonnais, born on 11 February 1699, entered the service of the French Indies Company as a lieutenant and was promoted to captain in 1724. His bravery in the capture of Mahé on the Malabar Coast supposedly added the town's name to his own, though another account holds that the town took his name instead. He then spent two years in the service of the Portuguese Viceroy.

He returned to French service in 1735 as governor of Isle de France, present-day Mauritius, and Île de Bourbon, present-day Réunion, and his first five years of administration were vigorous and successful. He greatly enlarged the enslaved African population of Isle de France, which numbered only 638 in 1735 and grew by around 1,300 a year, and brought 70 enslaved people for his own estate. In March and April 1738 two of his children died, and in May his wife died on the island.

A visit to France in 1740 was interrupted by war with Great Britain, and he was given command of a fleet in Indian waters. He assembled a squadron of 3,342 men, 720 of them enslaved, for an expedition from Isle de France to Madras. His victory sharpened his rivalry with Joseph François Dupleix, Governor of Pondicherry, and he was accused of taking money from the British East India Company. Forced back to France in 1746 to face trial, he was held in the Bastille for three years and replaced by Pierre Félix Barthelemy David.

He was tried in 1751 and acquitted, but imprisonment and the loss of his property broke his health, and he accused Dupleix to the last. He died on 10 November 1753. The main island of the Seychelles, Mahé, was named after him in 1742 by the French explorer Lazare Picault, and General Decaen founded Mahébourg in his honour in 1806. Statues of him stand in Port Louis, erected on 30 August 1859, in Saint-Malo and in Saint-Denis, Réunion, where the statue has been a target of anti-slavery protesters since 2020. His grandson Louis-Charles Mahé de La Bourdonnais was a strong chess player.
mahe-india: Mahé, also known as Mayyazhi, is a municipality and small town in the Mahe district of the Puducherry Union Territory. It lies at the mouth of the Mahe River and is surrounded by the State of Kerala: the district of Kannur encloses it on three sides and Kozhikode district on one. The name derives from Mayyazhi, the Malayalam name of the local river and region. French documents of the early 1720s spell it Mayé, and the spelling Mahe became the norm only in the early 19th century, so the belief that the town was named for Bertrand François Mahé de La Bourdonnais is incorrect.

Before European trading companies arrived, the area belonged to Kolathu Nadu. The French East India Company built a fort here under an accord made between André Mollandin and Raja Vazhunnavar of Vatakara. In 1741 La Bourdonnais retook the town after a short occupation by the Marathas. The British captured it in 1761 and handed it to the Rajah of Kadathanadu, and restored it to the French by the 1763 Treaty of Paris. It was lost again in the Anglo-French war of 1779 and returned in 1785.

A British force under James Hartley captured Mahe in 1793, and it was restored to the French in 1816 under the 1814 Treaty of Paris. For the long period that followed it was a small French colony, an enclave within British India. Hyder Ali of Mysore had earlier given Naluthara to the French in appreciation of their help in war. After Indian independence in 1947 Gandhians such as I. K. Kumaran led the movement for union with India. On 21 October 1948 the French flag was removed from the municipal building and the Indian flag raised, but a French navy ship arrived on 26 October and French control returned. The struggle ended with the town's union with India in 1954.

Mahe is one of the four districts of the Union Territory of Puducherry and has one representative in its Legislative Assembly. The 2011 census counted 41,816 people, mostly Malayalis, of whom 66.8 per cent were Hindu and 30.7 per cent Muslim. Malayalam is the main language, and fewer than 100 people speak French. French influence survives mainly in buildings, among them St. Teresa's Shrine, built in 1736, the Government House, the Mahe Lighthouse and a statue of Marianne commemorating the French Revolution.
mahendra-of-nepal: Mahendra was born on 11 June 1920 at the Narayanhiti Palace, the eldest child of King Tribhuvan and Queen Kanti. Under the Rana dynasty the king had been reduced to a figurehead, and the royal family was held captive in the palace. The Rana rule ended in 1951. Mahendra became king on 13 March 1955.

Mahendra appointed Tanka Prasad Acharya prime minister on 27 January 1956, and in 1957 he appointed Kunwar Indrajit Singh, who was dismissed after, it is said, trying a coup with the army. The constitution announced on 12 February 1959 provided an elected House of Representatives of 109 members. The Nepali Congress won a two-thirds majority in the election of 18 February to 4 April 1959, and B. P. Koirala took the oath as prime minister on 27 May.

On 15 December 1960 Mahendra used emergency powers, claiming that the Congress government had encouraged corruption and failed to keep order. He suspended the constitution, dissolved parliament, imprisoned Koirala and his colleagues, and outlawed political parties. On 13 April 1961 he introduced the Panchayat, a partyless system of village, district and national councils. The constitution of 16 December 1962 made it a four-tier system in which sovereign power lay with the king, who could amend the constitution by proclamation. A bomb was thrown at his car at Janakpur on 22 January 1962; one of three men found guilty, Durgananda Jha, was hanged in 1964.

Mahendra promoted a single Nepali identity through the Nepali language, a Nepali currency and a Hindu kingdom named in the constitution. He founded the Nepal Rastra Bank in 1956 to reduce dependence on the Indian rupee. The Mahendra Highway was begun in 1961 with help from several foreign donors, and the Kodari road to Tibet was finished with Chinese aid in 1967. He established diplomatic relations with 45 countries. A new legal code of 17 August 1963 replaced the Muluki Ain of 1854 and sought to end caste discrimination. Tribhuvan University was founded in his reign. He died on 31 January 1972.
mahendradatta: Mahendradatta, also known as Gunapriya Dharmapatni, was born in 961 and grew up in the Watugaluh Palace in eastern Java. She was a daughter of King Sri Makutawangsawarddhana of the late Mataram kingdom, a descendant of Mpu Sindok, founder of the Isyana dynasty in the 10th century, and a sister of King Dharmawangsa of Mataram. Betrothed to King Udayana Warmadewa of Bali, she moved to the island as his wife and took the name Mahendradatta.

The marriage was a political arrangement binding Bali, whose Warmadewa rulers were vassals of Mataram, to the East Javanese realm, and her standing as a princess of the ruling house has led a historian to suggest that she was queen regnant. Old Balinese inscriptions, among them the Serahi inscription of 993 and the Buahan inscription of 994, were issued in the names of both rulers, often with hers before Udayana's. The Balinese court is said to have respected and even feared her, and the marriage was probably not a smooth one.

Besides Airlangga, who was sent back to Java as a youth, her sons were Marakata, who became king of Bali after Udayana's death, and Anak Wungçu, who succeeded Marakata. Remains of the period, among them the temples of Gunung Kawi, Kerobokan, Kelebutan and Jukut Paku, lie in the Pakerisan and Petanu valleys and the highlands of Tampaksiring, Pejeng, Bedulu and Kintamani.

Mahendradatta was devoted to Durga and is believed to have brought her cult to Bali from Java; in Javanese and Balinese tradition Durga has a fierce nature, and her cult was linked with sacrifice and witchcraft. Balinese folklore connects the queen with Rangda, the witch of Balinese mythology, telling of a queen exiled for witchcraft who as a widow sent a plague on the kingdom until a holy man overcame her. The tale may reflect a troubled marriage or court efforts to discredit a foreign queen. After her death in 1011 she was deified as Durga Mahisashuramardini and entombed at Pura Bukit Dharma Kutri in Buruan village, Gianyar.
mahendravarman-i: Mahendravarman I was the son of Simhavishnu, who had defeated the Kalabhras and re-established the Pallava kingdom. His realm covered the southern part of the present-day Andhra region and the north of present-day Tamil Nadu. When the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II attacked, the Pallavas fought a series of wars in the northern Vengi region, and according to the Pallava grants at Kuram, Kasakudi and Tadantottam Mahendravarman routed his chief enemies at Pullalur.

He saved his capital but lost the northern provinces to Pulakeshin. His son Narasimhavarman I, who succeeded him in 630, later defeated Pulakeshin II and sacked the Chalukya capital of Vatapi, also known as Badami. Mahendravarman was at first a patron of Jainism; according to tradition he turned to the Shaiva faith under the influence of the saint Appar. A 12th-century Sanskrit work, the Divyacharitam, tells that Tirumalisai Alvar, a devotee of Vishnu, was persecuted and exiled by the king while he was under Jain influence, and that the image of Vishnu enshrined at Kanchipuram left the city with him.

Mahendravarman was the first Pallava ruler to excavate rock-cut temples. The inscription of the Mandagapattu Tirumurti Temple calls him Vichitrachitta and says the temple was made without wood, brick, mortar or metal. Temples of his reign include the five-celled cave at Pallavaram, the Avanibhajana Pallaveswaram temple at Seeyamangalam, the upper rock-cut temple at Trichy and the Vishnu caves at Mahendravadi and Singavaram. Paintings attributed to his time survive in the Sittanavasal Cave.

Besides the Mattavilasa Prahasana, a farce about Buddhist and Shaiva ascetics, he is claimed as the author of another satire, the Bhagavadajjuka, which is named with it in an inscription at the Mamandur cave shrines near Kanchipuram; another view attributes that play to Bodhayana. Tamil devotional literature flourished in his reign, with the Tevaram hymns of Appar and Sambandhar.

Mahendravarman began most of the monuments of Mahabalipuram, now grouped as the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, a UNESCO World Heritage site. He is a prominent figure in Tamil historical fiction, above all in Kalki Krishnamurthy's novel Sivagamiyin Sapatham, which tells of the Chalukya invasion and his defence of the fort of Kanchi.
maheshwar: Maheshwar lies on the northern bank of the Narmada River in Khargone district of Madhya Pradesh, central India. It is 91 km from Indore, and its name in Hindi means Great God, an epithet of Shiva. Several writers, among them H. D. Sankalia, P. N. Bose and Francis Wilford, identify it with the ancient town of Mahishmati, also known as Minnagara.

Hindu tradition describes the site as the capital of the king Kartavirya Arjuna, who is mentioned in the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. By a popular legend he held back the Narmada with his thousand arms, and when the demon king Ravana was swept from his sand Shivalinga by the released water, Kartavirya Arjuna captured him. The Mahabharata also tells of a king Nila of Mahishmati, whose realm Agni protected on condition that love be treated as lawful, so that women there had a freedom unknown elsewhere.

In the late 18th century Maheshwar was the capital of the Maratha queen Rajmata Ahilya Devi Holkar. She embellished it with a palace, temples, a fort and riverfront ghats. It remained the Holkar capital of Malwa until 6 January 1818, when Malhar Rao Holkar III moved the capital to Indore. Maheshwar has been a centre of handloom weaving since the 5th century. According to local accounts, Ahilya Bai hired weavers from Mandu and Surat to make saris and turbans for royal guests, and it is said she designed the first Maheshwari sari.

The town has a fort, ghats and more than 100 temples, most along the river near the ghat and the fort, among them the Sahastra Arjun Temple and the Kashi Vishwanath Mandir. Maheshwari saris are cotton, with stripes, checks and floral borders. The Rehwa Society, founded by the Holkars in 1979, employs about 130 weavers and runs a free school for weavers' children. Ahilya Fort is now a heritage hotel. Nearby are the medieval fortress-town of Mandu, the Chalcolithic site of Navdatoli and the Omkareshwar jyotirlinga.
mahi-kantha-agency: The Mahi Kantha states came within the British sphere of influence after the Second Anglo-Maratha War of 1803 to 1805. In 1811, as Maratha power declined, the British government undertook to collect the yearly tribute of the states and pay it over to the ruler of Baroda. In 1820 it took over the management of the whole territory, collecting the tribute for Baroda free of expense, while Baroda pledged not to send troops into the country or interfere in its administration.

There were disturbances in the 1830s, in 1857-58 and in 1867. After that the region was at peace until 1881, when the Bhils of Pol rose against their chief and forced him to settle their claims. The agency lay within the Gujarat Division of the Bombay Presidency and covered 8,094 square kilometres, with a population of 361,545 in 1901.

The states were ranked in seven classes. Idar, a state with a 15-gun salute, covered more than half of the agency's territory. Danta, under a Maharana with an 11-gun salute, was the only other salute state. Below them came the third-class states of Malpur, Mansa and Mohanpur and dozens of smaller chiefships of the fourth to seventh classes, among them Pethapur, Ambliara, Sathamba and Satlasna. The agency also held many estates of Rajput thakurs, once feudatories of Baroda; some, classed as non-jurisdictional talukdars, were administered by the British.

In 1933 the states of the agency, except Danta, were placed in the Western India States Agency, and Mahi Kantha was merged with the Banas Kantha Agency, known until 1925 as the Palanpur Agency; Palanpur State itself went to the Rajputana Agency. After the independence of India in 1947 the rulers acceded to the Government of India and the area was reorganised into districts of Bombay State. When Bombay State was divided along linguistic lines in 1960, Mahi Kantha became part of the new state of Gujarat.
mahikeng: Mahikeng, in the classic Setswana language, means place of rocks, or place among rocks, and refers to volcanic rocks that gave temporary shelter to Stone Age people hunting animals that came to drink at the Molopo River. The town lies close to South Africa's border with Botswana, built on open veld at about 1,500 metres by the banks of the Upper Molopo, 1,400 km northeast of Cape Town and 260 km west of Johannesburg. It was long written Mafeking by British settlers, a spelling still used for the siege of 1899–1900, and it later became Mafikeng, the form in common speech.

The town began as Molema's town. In 1857 Molema Tawana led an advance guard of the Barolong to scout the Molopo River and settled there, while the main body under his brother Montshiwa followed. Montshiwa felt unsafe because of the nearby Boers of the Transvaal and moved to Moshaneng, but Molema stayed and used diplomacy to keep the Boers from settling near the town. Montshiwa returned in 1876. Molema was a firm believer in Western education and opened a school for the Barolong; he died in 1882.

In 1882 the Boers set up the Republic of Stellaland and the State of Goshen in Bechuanaland. Tswana chiefs sought British protection, and a force of 4,000 troops under Major General Charles Warren dissolved the two states in a campaign of 1884–1885. Bechuanaland was proclaimed a British protectorate with Mafeking as its capital, though the protectorate was later divided and Mafeking lay south of its boundary, in British Bechuanaland, later passed to the Cape Colony. It remained the protectorate's administrative capital until Gaborone was established in 1965.

When the Second Boer War broke out in 1899 the Boers besieged the town. The siege lasted 217 days, from October 1899 to May 1900, and made Robert Baden-Powell a national hero; the use of adolescent boys as military auxiliaries helped lay the groundwork for the Scouting movement. British losses were 212 killed, soldiers and civilians, and more than 600 wounded, and Boer losses were significantly higher. In 1900 the British also built a concentration camp there for Boer women and children. A local referendum took the town into the Bantustan of Bophuthatswana in 1980.

After the end of apartheid in 1994 Bophuthatswana was reincorporated into South Africa, and the merged Mafikeng and Mmabatho became the capital of the new North-West Province. The provincial legislature stands in the New Parliament Building in Mmabatho. The North-West University has a campus there, and the town has a museum, a railway station and the Mafikeng Game Reserve on its edge.
mahinda-buddhist-monk: According to Sri Lankan tradition Mahinda was a Mauryan prince, the first-born son of Emperor Ashoka and his first wife Queen Devi, and the older brother of Princess Sanghamitta. The Dipavamsa and the Mahavamsa, Sri Lanka's two great religious chronicles, are the main sources for his life. An early Brahmi inscription of about 200 BCE at Rajagala records a stupa of the elders Ittiya and Mahinda, who came to the island. The texts give a spiritual motive for his journey, but some historians argue that it was political: Ashoka feared that he would be killed, as another son had been, and sent him away to avoid a succession war.

The chronicles record the arrival of the party on the full moon of Jettha. King Devanampiya Tissa was on a hunting expedition in the Mihintale hills when Mahinda preached to him the Chulahatthipadopama Sutra, and the royal hunting party converted to Buddhism. Invited to Anuradhapura, Mahinda gave two public talks, in the Royal Hall and in the Nandana Garden. The royal park Mahamegha was set aside for his party and later became the Mahavihara, and the Chetiyagirivihara monastery was established at Mihintale.

Mahinda sent for his sister Sanghamitta from Magadha to found an order of nuns. A sapling of the original Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya was planted in the Mahavihara, and part of the bodily relics of the Buddha were brought from the Maurya Empire.

Mahinda outlived Devanampiya Tissa and died in Sri Lanka. King Uttiya, who succeeded his brother, gave him a state funeral and built a stupa for his relics at Mihintale, now an important pilgrimage site visited in June, the month of Poson, when Mahinda is believed to have arrived. The 20th-century monk Walpola Rahula called him the father of Sinhalese literature because he translated the Tripitaka into Sinhala and wrote commentary on it. He is also credited with introducing the culture and architecture of the Mauryan Empire to the island.
mahishmati: The ancient sources place Mahishmati on the Narmada, south of Ujjayini and north of Pratishthana, on the road between the two. The Sutta Nipata names it among the towns that Bavari's disciples passed on that journey, and Patanjali mentions that a traveller leaving Ujjayini saw the sunrise at Mahishmati. Avanti was divided by the Vindhyas, with Ujjayini in its northern part and Mahishmati in the southern.

Its exact site is uncertain. F. E. Pargiter and G. C. Mendis identify it with the island of Mandhata, or Omkareshwar, arguing that the Raghuvamsa describes an island city; an inscription of 1225 found there records a land grant made by the Paramara king Devapala while he stayed at Mahishmati. H. D. Sankalia and others identify it with Maheshwar, an identification Pargiter criticised. Older proposals, such as Alexander Cunningham's Mandla or B. Lewis Rice's site in Mysore, are no longer accepted.

In the Sanskrit texts the city belongs to the Haihayas. The Ramayana tells of the Rakshasa king Ravana attacking it, and the Mahabharata makes it the capital from which the Haihaya king Kartavirya Arjuna ruled the earth until Parashurama killed him. In the Sabha Parva the Pandava general Sahadeva defeats its ruler Nila, who later fights in the Kurukshetra War. The Harivamsha names its founder as Mahishmant, a descendant of Yadu through Haihaya, and elsewhere as Muchukunda; the Raghuvamsa makes it the capital of the Anupa country.

Buddhist texts disagree on Avanti's capital: the Digha Nikaya names Mahishmati, the Anguttara Nikaya Ujjaini, which may mean the capital moved for a time. Inscriptions at Sanchi record pilgrims from Mahishmati visiting the stupa. In the 6th and 7th centuries it may have been the capital of the Kalachuri kingdom, and rulers of some 11th- and 12th-century kingdoms in southern India styled themselves Lord of Mahishmati to claim Haihaya descent. Devapala's inscription shows the city still flourishing in the 13th century.
mahmud-badaruddin-i: Mahmud Badaruddin I, also known as Jayo Wikramo, was the fourth Sultan of Palembang. His coronation ended a struggle for power among the royal families that had gone on since the death of Sultan Abdurrahman in 1706.

During his reign tin gradually took the place of pepper as Palembang's main commodity. He secured the sultanate's sovereignty over the tin-producing islands of Bangka and Belitung, which the Bugis had formerly managed, and in 1731, with the help of the Dutch East India Company, he defeated a revolt begun by the Bugis on Bangka. He then brought Chinese miners to the islands and appointed several Chinese Muslims as officials of the tin mines; one of his own wives was a Peranakan Chinese. By the end of his reign some 25,000 to 30,000 Chinese lived on Bangka.

He ruled in peace, improved the sultanate's trade and kept the support of the nobles through regular exchange and communication with them. The company did not interfere in his government, as its own finances were declining and it faced stronger competition from the British and the growing power of the Bugis in the western Indies. His largest conflict was with the Banten Sultanate over Lampung, which produced pepper and, from the 1730s, gold. The company mediated in 1738 and awarded Lampung to Banten, but he kept such close ties with the ponggawa, the chiefs, of the Tulang Bawang Kingdom and other rulers of Lampung that they went on trading with the merchants of Palembang.

Mahmud Badaruddin I was buried in the cemetery complex of Kawang Tengkurep, on Belabak Street in 3 Ilir, Palembang. He had himself ordered the complex built for his family, his relatives and the high officials of the sultanate, and several later Sultans of Palembang were buried there as well.
mahmud-barzanji: Mahmud Barzanji, also known as Mahmud Hafid Zadeh, was born in 1878 in Sulaymaniyah to parents of the Barzanji clan, a family of the Qadiriyya Sufi order whose sheikh he later became. He was among the notables exiled to Istanbul with Sheikh Ubeydullah after Ubeydullah's uprising of 1880 for Kurdish autonomy was suppressed. During the First World War the British promised the Kurdish tribal leaders a state of their own, a promise they did not keep.

When the Ottoman Empire collapsed in October 1918, a council of Kurdish notables in the Sulaimaniya region elected him head of government. After the British took Kirkuk on 25 October 1918 he captured the Ottoman troops in his district, declared Ottoman rule at an end and pledged allegiance to Britain, which made him governor of Kurdish area B, from south of the Lesser Zab River to the old Ottoman-Persian frontier. He used British subsidies to buy the loyalty of chieftains, and relations soured.

On 23 May 1919 he raised 300 tribal fighters, expelled the British supervisors and proclaimed himself ruler of all Kurdistan. Tribes from Iran and Iraq joined him, among them the 16-year-old Mustafa Barzani, but two British brigades defeated his 500-strong force at the Bazyan Pass on 18 June. Wounded and captured, he was sentenced to death but imprisoned in a British fort in Lahore.

With Turkish nationalists under Mustafa Kemal pressing on Mosul, Sir Percy Cox brought him back as governor of southern Kurdistan, and on his return he proclaimed himself King of the Kingdom of Kurdistan. He rejected the British terms, worked with the Turks, and Cox withdrew the offer of a Kurdish state in 1923.

He later made peace with the Iraqi government and died in Baghdad on 9 October 1956. He is remembered with displays across Iraqi Kurdistan, above all in Sulaimaniah, as a pioneer of Kurdish nationalism, and Kurdish nationalists in the diaspora draw on his memory.
mahmud-begada: Born Fateh Khan in Ahmedabad on 20 December 1445, he was the son of Muhammad Shah II and Bibi Mughali, a daughter of Jam Tughlaq of the Samma dynasty of Thatta in Sindh. When the nobles deposed his uncle Daud Khan after a reign of only days, they placed Fateh Khan on the throne at little more than thirteen as Mahmud Shah I. His surname Begada is explained either by his moustaches, twisted like a bullock's horns, or by the Gujarati words for two forts, after his capture of Junagadh and Pavagadh. He styled himself sultan of the land and sultan of the sea.

In 1462 he twice marched to help Nizam Shah Bahmani against Sultan Mahmud Khalji of Malwa, who withdrew each time. In 1464 he took the pirate hill fort of Barur near Daman and left its chief in place under tribute. At Junagadh he forced the Chudasama ruler Ra Mandalika III to submit in 1467, and after a siege of nearly two years the Ra surrendered Girnar in 1472-73 and converted to Islam; Sorath became a crown possession. In 1473 he took Dwarka and Bet Dwarka, destroying temples, and Raja Bhim was later captured and killed at Ahmedabad.

In 1487 his army sacked Kuva, the Jhala capital, after the death of Vaghoji Jhala, an event remembered as Kuva-no-Kehr. Against the Portuguese he allied with the Zamorin of Calicut and the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt. In 1508 his squadron under Malik Ayyaz and the Mamluk fleet won the Battle of Chaul, but in 1509 the Portuguese won the Battle of Diu, an event that marks the start of European colonialism in Asia.

Mahmud doubled the army, ousted landholders only for proved oppression, forbade soldiers to borrow at interest, kept the roads safe and opened hospitals. He founded Mustafabad at Junagadh, Muhammadabad at Champaner and Mehmudabad, and his court's nobles built suburbs of Ahmedabad and the fortress of Diu. A staunch Sunni, he died on 23 November 1511 before a Shia embassy from Shah Ismail Safavi entered the city. Later writers gave him the highest place among the Gujarat kings, and Udayaraja's Sanskrit Rājavinoda presented him as an Indic king. European travellers spread exaggerated tales of his appetite and of his being fed poison from childhood.
mahmud-gawan: Born Imadu'd-din Mahmud in 1411 in the village of Gawan, he came, according to the historian Firishta, from a family of ministers of a kingdom in Gilan; by his own account it had included viziers at Rasht. After intrigues undermined the family, he and his brother Shihabu'd-din Ahmad left Gilan on their mother's advice. For more than a decade he travelled as far as Anatolia and Egypt, trading in horses and other goods and studying in Cairo and Damascus. In 1453 he landed at Dabhol to sell horses to the Bahmanis, and Sultan Ahmad Shah II received him at Bidar and made him a noble.

Humayun Shah made him chief minister, Wakil-us-Sultanat, with the title Prince of Merchants. After Humayun's death he sat with the queen mother and the noble Jahan Turk on the regency council of the boy sultans Nizam Shah and Muhammad III, which helped repel a Gajapati invasion and, with Mahmud Begada of Gujarat, the attacks of Mahmud Khalji of Malwa. When the queen mother had Jahan Turk killed in 1466, she gave Mahmud supervision of all the provinces and the title of prime minister.

From 1469 he campaigned against the Vijayanagara Empire, taking the Konkan and in February 1472 the port of Goa, partly to curb piracy against the horse trade and Muslim pilgrims. At Belgaum he made the first known use of gunpowder in the Deccan. In 1473 he divided the provinces from four into eight, shared between the local Deccani and foreign Afaqi nobles, and limited each governor to a single fort, reforms that many nobles resented. He wrote poetry and letters, 148 of which survive, corresponding with Mehmed II, the Timurid Husayn Bayqara and the poet Jami. His madrasa at Bidar held a library of 3,000 manuscripts.

Rival nobles forged letters, apparently in Mahmud's hand, inviting the Gajapati king Purushottamadeva to invade. Muhammad Shah III, partly drunk, rejected Mahmud's plea that they were forged and had him executed on 5 April 1481. The sultan later regretted it and died a year afterwards; Malik Hasan Bahri, one of the plot's chief architects, succeeded Mahmud as prime minister. The disorder that followed led to the independence of the Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Berar sultanates in 1490 and of the Bidar Sultanate in 1492.
mahmud-hotak: Mahmud Hotak was born in 1697, the eldest son of Mirwais Hotak, chief of the Ghilji Pashtuns, who made the Kandahar region independent of Safavid rule in 1709. When Mirwais died in 1715 his brother Abdul Aziz succeeded him and returned to Safavid suzerainty, which was unpopular among the Afghans. Mahmud gathered his father's loyal followers, entered the royal palace, killed Abdul Aziz himself and took the throne at the age of 18.

Mahmud began to wage war on the Safavids in 1720 with a siege of Kerman. In October 1721 the Ghilzais took the town but not its citadel, and lost one thousand five hundred men because they lacked experience of siege tactics. In 1722 he marched on Isfahan with 20,000 men, bypassing Kerman and being fended off near Yazd. On 8 March 1722 the Afghans met the Persian army at the Battle of Gulnabad and, though outnumbered and worse equipped, routed it.

They then besieged Isfahan, beginning with the capture of Julfa. Lacking siege equipment, they took until 23 October 1722, and it is believed that over 80,000 of the city's inhabitants died. Shah Soltan Hoseyn went to the Afghan camp at Farahabad, took off his crown and placed it on Mahmud's turban. Mahmud at first treated the royal family well and brought food to the starving capital, and his forces took Shiraz and Kashan.

In November 1722 Hoseyn's son Tahmasp declared himself shah. Mahmud's army took Qazvin, but its people rose against the Pashtuns in January 1723. Fearing revolt, Mahmud invited Persian ministers and nobles to a meeting and had them killed, and executed up to 3,000 of the Persian royal guards. The Ottomans and Russians seized land while Persia was in chaos. In February 1725 he ordered the other Safavid princes put to death, sparing two young children when Hoseyn tried to stop the killing.

His health and reason failed. On 22 April 1725 Afghan officers freed his cousin Ashraf from prison and placed him on the throne. Mahmud was killed by Ashraf, though other sources say he died of his insanity. He was twenty-seven. Afterwards the Ghilji chiefs, who had served as kalantars of Kandahar, rebuilt the bureaucracy, and Mirza Sami'a wrote the Tazkerat al-Moluk, a manual of how the state was administered.
mahmud-ii: Mahmud II was born on 20 July 1785, the youngest son of Sultan Abdul Hamid I and his consort Nakşidil Kadın. According to tradition he was confined in the Kafes after his father's death. In 1808 his half-brother Mustafa IV ordered his execution along with that of the deposed Sultan Selim III. Selim was killed, but Mahmud was kept hidden by his mother and placed on the throne after rebels deposed Mustafa IV. Their leader, Alemdar Mustafa Pasha, became his vizier and resumed reforms, but he was killed in a rebellion that year and Mahmud temporarily abandoned reform.

The Russo-Turkish War of 1806 to 1812 ended in the Treaty of Bucharest, by which the empire ceded the eastern half of Moldavia to Russia, which renamed it Bessarabia. His governor of Egypt, Muhammad Ali, reconquered the Hejaz, taking Medina in 1812 and Mecca in 1813. A Greek rebellion began in 1821, and after the combined British, French and Russian navies defeated the Ottoman fleet at Navarino in 1827 the empire had to recognise Greece in July 1832. France began the conquest of Ottoman Algeria in 1830.

In June 1826 he carried out the Auspicious Incident. When the Janissaries demonstrated against his proposed military reforms, he had their barracks fired upon, and many were executed or exiled. This allowed a European-style conscript army. With it he subdued the derebeys and ayans, hereditary local chiefs who had become petty princes, until only Cyprus kept such power. He closed the Court of Confiscations and forbade governors to execute anyone without a sentence signed by a judge.

Mahmud reformed the bureaucracy, raised salaries to end bribery, and in 1831 founded the first Ottoman Turkish newspaper, the official gazette Takvim-i Vekayi. In 1838 he established the Supreme Council of Judicial Ordinances and in 1839 a Council of Ministers. He died of tuberculosis on 1 July 1839 and was succeeded by his son Abdülmecid I, who announced the Tanzimat. He is often called the Peter the Great of Turkey, and the abolition of the Janissaries removed a major obstacle to later reforms, although his reign also brought military defeats and loss of territory.
mahmud-ii-seljuk-sultan: Mughith al-Dunya wa'l-Din Mahmud bin Muhammad, known as Mahmud II, became Seljuk sultan of Iraq in 1118 on the death of his father Muhammad I Tapar, while still a youth, and he ruled over Iraq and Persia. Early in his reign he sent a force to Yazd against his vassal Garshasp II, a favourite of his father, who had fallen into disgrace after slander at court. Garshasp was arrested, escaped and returned to Yazd, and then sought the protection of Mahmud's rival Ahmad Sanjar, whose sister was Garshasp's wife.

Garshasp urged Sanjar to invade Mahmud's domains in central Persia. Sanjar had ambitions of his own and wished to restore the unity of the Great Seljuks under one sultan, as it had been before the death of Malikshah. Mahmud's offer of a tribute of 200,000 dinars and the cession of Mazandaran failed to appease him. Sanjar used the excuse of his nephew's youth, and the manipulation of his viziers, to advance west and meet him at the Battle of Saveh. Outnumbered, on unfamiliar ground and with the water supply in Mahmud's hands, he nearly faltered, and the day was won only by the last-minute intervention of his 18 war elephants, which frightened Mahmud's cavalry.

Sanjar pushed on to Baghdad. Mahmud was married to one of Sanjar's daughters and made his uncle's heir. Because the victory had been so narrow, Sanjar returned everything to Mahmud except Rayy, restored the lands of Garshasp II and went back east. Mahmud's younger brother Mas'ud revolted in 1120, and the civil war ended the next year through the intervention of Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, atabeg of Mosul, after which Mas'ud was pardoned. In 1126 al-Bursuqi was murdered by Assassins, believed to have acted on Mahmud's orders.

Mahmud ruled from Isfahan, while Shihna military governors for Iraq were based in Baghdad. In 1126 he personally led a campaign against the caliph of Baghdad. In 1127 he appointed Anushirvan ibn Khalid as his vizier and removed him the next year. In 1129 he formally recognised the authority of Imad al-Din Zengi, who had supported him against a revolt led by the caliph al-Mustarshid in Syria and northern Iraq. He died on 11 September 1131. His death was followed by a civil war between his son Dawud and his brothers Mas'ud, Suleiman-Shah and Toghrul II, while his other son Alp Arslan ruled Mosul under the protection of Zengi.
mahmud-khalji: Mahmud Khalji was distantly related to the Khalji dynasty of Delhi: his ancestor Malik Nasiruddin was a cousin of Sultan Jalaluddin Khalji. He was also a grandnephew of Dilawar Khan, the first sultan of Malwa. His father, Malik Mughlith, helped restore Hoshang Shah to the throne after Ahmad Shah I had seized it and was given the title Khan-i-Jahan. Mahmud proved a capable commander early; in 1419, at sixteen, Hoshang Shah made him a Khan and gave him his daughter in marriage.

After Hoshang's death Mahmud supported the accession of his eldest surviving son, Ghazni Khan, as Muhammad Shah. The new sultan grew suspicious of him, and when Muhammad Shah was said to be plotting his murder, Mahmud had him poisoned. Muhammad's thirteen-year-old son Masud was briefly placed on the throne, but Mahmud attacked the palace, deposed him and became sultan on 14 May 1436, taking titles that included Sikandar-us-Sani.

Much of Mahmud's reign was spent at war with Rana Kumbha of Mewar. Battles between 1442 and 1446 left the sultan unwilling to attack Mewar again for ten years. In February 1444 he besieged Gagron, held by Palhan Singh Khichi, who was killed trying to flee. When Kumbha moved north against Gujarat in December 1456, Mahmud attacked Mandalgarh once more and took the fort in October 1457 after a long siege.

During the reign of Muhammad Shah II of Gujarat, Mahmud invaded Gujarat, took Champaner and advanced with 80,000 cavalry. Muhammad Shah II died and was succeeded by Qutb-ud-Din Ahmad Shah II. Mahmud took Sultanpur, plundered Baroda and reached Nadiad, but was defeated at Kapadvanj after a battle of several hours and forced to retreat; Muzaffar Khan, said to have urged the invasion, was captured and beheaded. In the same year an attempt on Nagore ended when Mahmud retreated before a Gujarat army near Sambhar. He also campaigned unsuccessfully against the Delhi Sultanate. He died on 1 June 1469.
mahmud-of-ghazni: Mahmud was born in Ghazni, in the region of Zabulistan, on 2 October 971. His father, Sabuktigin, was a Karluk Turkic slave who founded the Ghaznavid dynasty in 977, ruling as a subordinate of the Samanids. His mother was a local woman of possible Iranian descent. As a young man he served his father against the Hindu Shahi ruler Jayapala and in the capture of Khorasan in 994, and received the title Saifu'd-Dawlah, Sword of the State.

Sabuktigin died in August 997 and was succeeded by Mahmud's brother Ismail, for reasons that are uncertain. Mahmud revolted and defeated Ismail at the battle of Ghazni, taking the throne at the age of 27.

In 999 Mahmud took Khorasan from the Samanids, defeating their army near Merv on 16 May, and the Oxus was fixed as the border with the Kara-Khanids. In 1002 he ended the Saffarid dynasty by deposing Khalaf ibn Ahmad in Sistan. He defeated the Kara-Khanids at the Battle of Katar on 5 January 1008, and in 1017 he conquered Khwarazm and captured Gurganj. In 1029 and 1030 his forces took Ray and Isfahan.

In the Indian subcontinent he defeated Jayapala at Peshawar on 28 November 1001 and later fought Jayapala's son Anandapala. He took Multan in 1006, where the Ismailis were massacred. His coinage from Lahore called him the breaker of idols, and he presented his wars as the defence of the Sunni Abbasid caliphate against Shia rivals.

Mahmud contracted malaria on his last Indian campaign in 1027, which led to tuberculosis. He returned to Ghazni about 22 April 1030 and died on 30 April. His sultanate was served by departments of finance, war, correspondence, intelligence and household, with a postal service that carried news to the ruler. Dawlatshah reckoned that he had 400 poets at court, and Ghazni drew al-Biruni and Ferdowsi. Many Indian Muslim scholars regard him as a founder of Muslim rule in the subcontinent's interior.
mahmud-shah-ii-of-johor: Mahmud Shah II succeeded his father, Sultan Ibrahim Shah, in 1685. Ibrahim had extended Johor's territory and prosperity until the state held much of the southern Strait of Malacca and the Malay Peninsula as well as eastern Sumatra. Because the new sultan was a young child, Johor was governed by a joint regency of his mother and the Bendahara Paduka Raja. Only when the bendahara died on 27 July 1697 did Mahmud take on all the duties of sultan himself.

European trading company records and local texts alike describe an erratic ruler of cruel nature and a state they called ungovernable. Local texts tell of violence against women, some ordered to be executed for minor offences. The Scottish country trader Alexander Hamilton, who visited Johor in 1695, recorded the sultan firing a gun into a man in the street to test the weapon, and in his A New Account of the East Indies of 1727 described him as preferring men. Traders began to avoid the main port, and the economic damage, together with violence against women of the orang kaya, the Malay nobility, led the high officials to move against him.

According to Dutch East India Company reports his body lay exposed at the bendahara's residence until late afternoon and was buried that night with little ceremony; his grave survives in a village near Kota Tinggi still called Kampung Makam, the village of the tomb. Because regicide was unthinkable in Malay culture, legends soon arose about his death, and the name Sultan Mahmud Mangkat Dijulang recalls that he died while carried in a royal litter. The story was retold in court texts such as the Tuhfat al-Nafis and the Hikayat Siak, and in the 1961 film Sultan Mahmud Mangkat Dijulang.

With the line of the Malacca sultans ended, the Bendahara dynasty struggled for two decades to win support. By 1718 Raja Kecil of eastern Sumatra, who claimed to be Mahmud's son, conceived on the eve of the murder, attacked Johor with Orang Laut support. After four years he withdrew and founded the Siak Sultanate in 1722, and the bendahara's descendants returned with Bugis mercenaries, laying the foundation of the Johor-Riau-Lingga sultanate.
mahmud-shah-iii-of-johor: Mahmud Shah III was born on 24 March 1756, the younger son of Sultan Abdul Jalil Muazzam Shah of Johor and his second wife, Tengku Puteh binti Daeng Chelak, and a grandson of Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah. The Bugis, who held de facto control of the Johor Empire, kept puppet rulers on the throne, and he succeeded his elder brother Ahmad Riayat Shah while still young. In the early years of his reign the office of Yamtuan Muda was held by the powerful Bugis chief Daeng Kemboja.

Mahmud came of age as the trade rivalry between the Bugis and the Dutch grew. After the Bugis were defeated in the Riau War of 1783–1784, he concluded a treaty of protection with the Dutch East India Company aboard the Utrecht on 10 November 1784, which styled him Most Serene Prince. It ended the Bugis hold on the office of Yamtuan Muda, barred other Bugis from office, ordered the expulsion of those not born or raised in Riau and allowed a Dutch Resident in Johor. Mahmud soon withdrew to Pahang, and fighting between the Dutch and the Bugis went on until 1795, when the Dutch drove the Bugis chief Raja Ali from Riau and the sultan returned.

That same year the Netherlands fell under French occupation and the British took over Dutch territories in the Malay world for a time, which let Raja Ali return; Mahmud had to accept him in 1803. To balance the factions he married his son Tengku Hussein to a daughter of the Malay Yamtuan Muda, Tengku Muda, and made his other son, Tengku Abdul Rahman, Raja Ali's ward. To keep his distance from the Bugis he set up his capital at Daik on Lingga.

From Lingga he had little power. The Temenggong Abdul Rahman, installed in 1806, controlled the Johor mainland, Singapore and the Riau islands, while in Pahang the Bendahara Tun Abdul Majid took the title Raja Bendahara, and the sultanate's parts became in effect separate principalities. Mahmud died at Fort Tanna, Bukit Chengah, on Lingga, without naming a successor, and was buried at the Masjid Jamie' in Daik. The Tuhfat al-Nafis presents him as an able statesman facing insurmountable odds, and Abdullah Abdul Kadir attests to his good character.
mahmud-shah-of-malacca: Mahmud Shah was the son of Sultan Alauddin Riayat Shah and was installed at a very young age after his father's early death. The government lay in the hands of the bendahara, or prime minister, Tun Perak, who acted as regent. As a young man the sultan was known as a ruthless ruler. He is associated with the Malay legend of Puteri Gunung Ledang, the story of his failed courtship of a celestial princess, and with warriors of his court such as Hang Tuah and Hang Nadim.

Tun Perak's death in 1498 is said to have made Mahmud a more responsible ruler, but his later years were turbulent. The new bendahara, Tun Mutahir, took bribes and appointed ministers on a whim, and factions formed at court. Deceived by one faction, which accused Tun Mutahir of planning a rebellion, the sultan had him and his whole family executed; Tun Mutahir had also refused to let him marry his daughter, Tun Fatimah. The defences of Malacca weakened, its army being largely made up of mercenaries who were disloyal to the sultan.

During the visit of the Portuguese admiral Diogo Lopes de Sequeira in 1509–1510 the sultan planned to have him killed, but Sequeira learned of the plot and escaped. The episode gave Afonso de Albuquerque a reason for the attack that ended in the Capture of Malacca in 1511.

Mahmud fled to Pahang, where he sought Chinese aid in vain, then moved south to Bintan, where he still received tribute from states that had owed allegiance to Malacca. He led a Malay Muslim confederacy that attacked Portuguese Malacca several times between 1515 and 1519 without success. His son Ahmad Shah, who had succeeded him, was judged incompetent and was killed by Mahmud himself in 1513 after a failed attempt to retake the city, and Mahmud took the title again as a pretender. In 1526 the Portuguese destroyed his capital on Bintan, and he fled to Kampar, where he died two years later.
His son Raja Ali, as Alauddin Riayat Shah II, founded the Johor Sultanate, and another son, Muzaffar, was invited by the Perak ministers Tun Saban and Nakhoda Kassim to found the Perak Sultanate.
mahmud-yalavach: Yalavach came from Khwarazm and began as a merchant and an official of the Qara Khitai; some historians identify him with Mahmud Bey, vizier of the last Gur-Khan Yelü Zhilugu, while others dispute this. He first met Genghis Khan as a representative of the Khwarazmian Empire and became his emissary. Muhammad II of Khwarazm also used him as a spy, though Yalavach may have been a double agent, since he sometimes gave false information and did not report the capture of Zhongdu.

Under Genghis Khan he was made governor of Ghazni and then of Transoxiana, and as darughachi of Turkestan he repaired cities, rebuilt irrigation and resettled scattered people. Ögedei Khan gave Turkestan to his son Masʿud Beg and sent Yalavach to northern China, perhaps because of his unpopularity in Central Asia or a dispute with Chagatai Khan over Transoxiana, which ended in Chagatai's apology. During the religious uprising of Mahmud Tarabi in 1238–39 he tried to prevent a mass slaughter of the population by the Mongols.

When Töregene Khatun took power in 1242 she dismissed him, perhaps through a grudge held by her adviser Fatima Khatun, and replaced his taxes with tax farming. Sent to arrest him, Ogal Qorchi was treated as an honoured guest and made drunk, and Yalavach escaped to the camp of Godan Khan, who refused to hand him over. Güyük Khan executed Fatima and ʿAbd al-Rahman and restored Yalavach in northern China, and Möngke Khan kept him there and made him yeke jaruchi as well.

To refill a treasury drained by war, Ögedei introduced regular taxation under Yalavach's influence, with Yelü Chucai, in place of plunder. Yalavach's system, based on the qubchur, a poll tax on adult men paid in cash, and perhaps influenced by the jizya, was later made the standard for the whole empire and, under Möngke, was applied to sedentary peoples everywhere. Under Yalavach and Masʿud Beg, Bukhara became one of the most prosperous cities of the Muslim world. In Möngke's reign he was regarded as an elder statesman.
mahon: Mahón stands on the eastern coast of Menorca. Its harbour is one of the longest natural harbours in the world, 5 kilometres long and up to 900 metres wide, deep and mostly clear because it is so enclosed. It was one of the most strategically important harbours of the western Mediterranean.

The name is attributed to the Carthaginian general Mago Barca, brother of Hannibal, who is thought to have taken refuge there in 205 BCE. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the island became part of the Eastern Roman Empire. It suffered raids from Vikings and Arabs until the Caliphate of Córdoba conquered it in 903. Alfonso III of Aragon took Mahón from the Moors in 1287 and made it part of the Kingdom of Majorca, and the harbour was refortified. In 1535 Ottoman forces under Hayreddin Barbarossa attacked Mahón and carried 600 captives to Algiers as slaves.

A British and Dutch force captured Menorca in 1708, in the War of the Spanish Succession, and the Treaty of Utrecht confirmed British possession in 1713. The capital moved from Ciutadella to Mahón, which housed the governor, the best known being General Richard Kane. A Royal Navy dockyard was set up on the north side of the harbour in 1715 and served as the principal Mediterranean base for much of the century.

France took the island in 1756, returned it in 1763, and Spain regained it in 1782, confirmed in 1783. Britain retook it in 1798, and under the Treaty of Amiens in 1802 it passed to Spain. In the Spanish Civil War the island stayed loyal to the Republic until the Nationalists captured it in 1939.

Mahón, officially Maó in Catalan, is the capital and second largest city of Menorca and the seat of the Island Council of Menorca. Mahón cheese takes its name from the city, and in Spanish mahón is also the word for nankeen cloth. Buildings of the British dockyard from the 1760s survive on the island of Illa Pinto, and the ruins of the Royal Naval Hospital, founded in 1711, stand on Illa del Rei.
mai-thuc-loan: His date of birth is unknown, but he came from Mai Phụ village, in the modern Thạch Hà District of Hà Tĩnh. The Chinese histories record his name differently: Mai Thúc Loan in the Basic Records of the New Book of Tang, Mai Huyền Thành in the Old Book of Tang and Mai Thúc Yên in the Zizhi Tongjian. According to the Khâm định Việt sử Thông giám cương mục, the title Black Emperor came from his notably dark skin.

The rising began in what is now Hà Tĩnh Province and spread through Hoan Châu and Ái Châu, now Thanh Hóa and Nghệ An, rallying people from 23 counties with a reported 400,000 followers, many of them peasants who roamed the countryside plundering food. It took Songping, the capital of the Tang protectorate of Annan, on the site of modern Hanoi. He allied with Champa, Chenla, an unknown kingdom called Jinlin and others.

On the order of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, the general Yang Zixu marched an army of 100,000 from Guangdong, with many loyal mountain tribesmen, along the old coastal road built by Ma Yuan, and took the rebels by surprise. The bodies of the emperor and his followers were piled into a great mound and left on display as a warning against further revolt.

The dynastic chronicles treat the rising briefly. Ngô Sĩ Liên's Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư gives his army as 30,000 and calls him a rebel, while the compilers of the Cương mục doubted their own figure of 40,000. Ngô Thì Sĩ, writing under the Tây Sơn dynasty, praised the rising as a sign of Vietnamese independence and criticised Lê Văn Hưu and Ngô Sĩ Liên for misjudging it.

A temple stands on the site of his citadel of Vạn An, and a shrine in Haiphong honours his children of folk legend, Mai Thị Cầu and Mai Kỳ Sơn. The historian John D. Phan notes that his place as a national leader came from a later revisionist project, although he came from a periphery that included Cham and Khmer elements.
maiden-castle-dorset: Maiden Castle stands 2.6 km south-west of Dorchester on a ridge north of the South Winterborne valley, which drains to the River Frome. The earliest activity on the hill is a Neolithic causewayed enclosure of around 4000 BCE, two interrupted ditches that were not defensive and probably served as a ritual and meeting place; pottery from the coast and from far to the east and west was found there, and radiocarbon dating shows it was abandoned some six centuries later. A bank barrow 546 m long was then built over it. Around 1800 BCE the hill was cleared for crops, but the soil was soon exhausted.

The first hill fort, built on a territorial boundary around 600 BCE, enclosed 6.4 ha within a single ditch and rampart, with a double entrance in the east that is unique among British hill forts. Around 450 BCE it was extended west over Hog Hill to 19 ha, and four ramparts with three ditches were added on the south, more than defence alone required and probably a statement of power. Rows of roundhouses and granaries, bronze objects brought from afar and pottery from around Poole Harbour point to trade and growing control by elites. Around 100 BCE the western half was abandoned and settlement moved east, where the archaeologist Mortimer Wheeler later found an iron-working site and a cemetery.

Wheeler took fourteen violent burials there, one with a Roman catapult bolt in its back, as evidence that a Roman legion stormed the fort during Vespasian's campaign of 43–47. Later archaeologists find little support for a siege or massacre, and no proof that those people died at Maiden Castle. The fort was abandoned by the end of the 1st century. Sometime after 367 a Romano-Celtic temple with a mosaic floor was built in its eastern half, and after it fell into disuse the hill served as pasture, with a short spell of ploughing in the 17th century.

Wheeler and Tessa Verney Wheeler excavated the site from 1934 to 1937, and Niall Sharples dug again in 1985 and 1986 while visitor damage was repaired. It became a Scheduled Monument in 1981, is maintained by English Heritage and is open all year. Thomas Hardy, John Ireland and John Cowper Powys drew on it in their work.
maiduguri: Maiduguri lies along the seasonal Ngadda River, which disappears into the Firki swamps in the country around Lake Chad. The climate is hot and semi-arid, and the colonial administration made tree planting a priority, so that large trees along the main roads give shelter from the sun. The region had been home to the Kanem-Bornu Empire for centuries.

The city consists of two parts: Yerwa to the west and Old Maiduguri to the east. Yerwa was founded in 1907 by Abubakar Garbai of Borno as the capital of the kingdom of Bornu, replacing Kukawa as the capital of the Kanuri people. The site had been a small village called Kalwa. In 1908 the British chose Old Maiduguri, in place of Mafoni, as their military headquarters, and in the same year it became the seat of the British Resident Commissioner for British Bornu. In 1957 the name Yerwa was officially given to the urban centre and Maiduguri to the surrounding rural area. When the railway was extended to the city in 1964, it began to rise as a major commercial centre of the region.

Maiduguri has also been known as a centre of Islamic scholarship in West Africa. Since the mid-1960s it has seen riots between religious groups, in 1982 and 2001 among others. In 2002 the cleric Mohammed Yusuf founded the group later known as Boko Haram there, with a mosque and a madrasa that drew children from poor Muslim families in Nigeria and neighbouring countries. In 1975 the University of Maiduguri was founded.

Maiduguri is the capital and largest city of Borno State and is one of the local government areas of the traditional Borno Emirate. Its residents are mostly Muslim and include Kanuri, Hausa, Shuwa, Bura, Marghi and Fulani, with a considerable Christian population and people from southern Nigerian states such as the Igbo, Ijaw and Yoruba. A railway line links it with Port Harcourt, Enugu, Kafanchan and Bauchi, and it has an international airport. It is the principal trading hub of north-eastern Nigeria, with an economy based mainly on services and trade, and has three large markets, among them the Monday Market. The city is also home to the El-Kanemi Warriors football club and to Kyarimi Park, the oldest and largest zoo in Nigeria.
maimonides: Moses ben Maimon, known in Hebrew by the acronym Rambam, was born in Córdoba under the Almoravid dynasty, at the end of the Golden Age of Jewish culture in Spain. His father, Maimon ben Joseph, was a dayyan, or rabbinic judge, and taught him Torah. At an early age he took an interest in contemporary science and philosophy, reading ancient Greek philosophy through Arabic translations.

The Almohads conquered Córdoba in 1148 and abolished the protected status of non-Muslims in some territories. Jewish and Christian communities faced a choice between conversion, martyrdom and exile. Many Jews were forced to convert and had to wear identifying clothing, because the authorities suspected false conversions. Maimonides' family chose exile. For ten years he moved about southern Spain and North Africa before settling in Fez, and he wrote his commentary on the Mishnah in 1166-1168.

Around 1171 Maimonides was appointed nagid, or head, of the Egyptian Jewish community; Shelomo Dov Goitein believes his leadership during the ransoming of Crusader captives led to the appointment. He was replaced by Sar Shalom ben Moses in 1173, excommunicated him and quarrelled with him for years, and was appointed nagid again in 1195. After the family's funds were lost in a business venture, he took up medicine, which he had studied in Spain and in Fez. He became court physician to Qadi al-Fadil, the chief secretary to Sultan Saladin, then to Saladin himself, and he remained a physician to the Ayyubid dynasty after Saladin's death.

He died in Fustat on 12 December 1204. Medieval sources beginning with al-Qifti say he was buried near the Sea of Galilee, though there is no contemporary evidence that his body was moved from Egypt. A tomb in Tiberias is a pilgrimage site and bears the inscription 'From Moses to Moses arose none like Moses.'

The Mishneh Torah is a code of Jewish law in fourteen books that gathers the binding laws of the Talmud and the positions of the Geonim. It is still regarded as one of the chief authoritative codifications of Jewish law and is closely studied in yeshivot. In his Mishnah commentary he set out thirteen principles of faith, which he saw as the required beliefs of Judaism. His Guide for the Perplexed sought to reconcile Aristotelianism and science with the Torah, and French rabbis banned it and burnt copies in Montpellier.

He also wrote on medicine, including a Guide to Good Health composed in Arabic for Sultan al-Afdal, son of Saladin, who suffered from depression. Translated into Latin, it was printed in Florence in 1477. His writings influenced the Scholastic philosophers Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus.
main-neckar-railway: Plans for the line date from 1835, but the three states took years to agree on its route and organisation. A treaty of 1838 for a line from Frankfurt to Mannheim via Darmstadt failed when the Hessian Railway Company could not raise the capital. A second treaty, signed on 21 and 23 March 1843, had the line built at government expense as a condominium railway, its cost shared by length: 6.9 km in Frankfurt, 49.4 km in Hesse-Darmstadt and 38.8 km in Baden. As a compromise between Mannheim and Heidelberg it met Baden's line at Friedrichsfeld.

Work began in June 1843 under the engineer Remigius Eyssen, and the line opened in sections between 22 June and 1 August 1846. Because Baden's own line used a broad gauge of 1600 mm while the Main-Neckar line was built to standard gauge, separate tracks had to be laid from Friedrichsfeld to Heidelberg and Mannheim. Georg Moller designed the station buildings at Bensheim and Heppenheim.

The railway began with 18 locomotives and 252 cars, twelve of the engines from the Sharp works in Manchester. Freight began on 9 August 1847, and in the first fifteen years freight grew thirtyfold while passenger numbers rose by half. The link to the Main-Weser Railway in Frankfurt, opened in 1851, made the line part of a major north-south route. During the Baden Revolution traffic south of Heppenheim stopped from 18 May 1849, and in early June the line carried only troops.

After Prussia annexed Frankfurt in 1866 it took over the city's share, and in 1896 the Prussian and Hessian shares passed to the Prussian-Hessian Railway Company. A treaty of 1902 divided the line between the Baden State Railways and the Mainz railway directorate, ending the company's independent existence.

The Main-Neckar bridge in Frankfurt was blown up by the German Army in the last days of the Second World War, and steam trains ran over the repaired bridge from 23 November 1946. The line was electrified in stages in 1956 and 1957. From 1997 lines of the Rhine-Main S-Bahn ran on its northern part, which was widened to three and four tracks, and most of the original station buildings still stand in the old Main-Neckar style.
mainz: Mainz lies on the left bank of the Rhine at the northern end of the Upper Rhine Plain, opposite the mouth of the Main. Its name does not come from the river but is a simplification of Mogontiacum, a name that appears to be Celtic, probably linked to the Gallic god Mogons whom Roman soldiers had adopted. The city is in one of Germany's important wine regions.

The Roman general Nero Claudius Drusus founded the stronghold of Mogontiacum, perhaps as early as 13 or 12 BCE, on the northern frontier of the empire, and it became the capital of the province of Germania Superior. The Emperor Julian liberated the city in 357, and in 451 Attila's Huns sacked it. The Franks settled there from 459.

In the early Middle Ages Mainz played a significant part in the Christianisation of the German and Slavic peoples. Its first archbishop, Boniface, was killed in 754 while trying to convert the Frisians. The archbishopric was established in 781, when Boniface's successor Lullus received the pallium from Pope Adrian I, and the archbishops held high office in the Holy Roman Empire as archchancellors. A Jewish community existed from the 10th century and was known for its teaching, notably that of Rabbi Gershom ben Judah (960–1040). From the 12th century Mainz belonged to the ShUM cities with Speyer and Worms.

French revolutionary troops occupied the city in 1792, and on 18 March 1793 the Jacobins of Mainz proclaimed a Republic of Mainz under Georg Forster. After an 18-week siege the French surrendered to the Prussians on 23 July 1793. In 1816 Mainz became the capital of Rhenish Hesse, and until 1866 it was the chief fortress of the German Confederation against France.

Mainz is the capital and largest city of Rhineland-Palatinate, with about 223,000 inhabitants. It is the birthplace of Johannes Gutenberg, and its cathedral, one of the three Rhenish Imperial Cathedrals, is over a thousand years old. Roman remains include Jupiter's column, and the ShUM sites of Speyer, Worms and Mainz are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
mainz-diocesan-feud: In 1459 Diether of Isenburg, the cathedral's Domkustos, narrowly defeated Adolph of Nassau in the election for Archbishop of Mainz.
