He soon lost the Battle of Pfeddersheim to Frederick I, Count Palatine, in July 1460, and he won papal confirmation only with difficulty and the payment of 20,000 guilders. Opposing the demands of Emperor Frederick III and the papacy, and calling for the abolition of papal annates, he was declared deposed by Pope Pius II on 21 August 1461. Adolph was enthroned on 1 October 1461, but the city of Mainz stood by Diether, who refused to give up the see.

Adolph's allies were John II of Baden, Archbishop of Trier, George of Baden, Bishop of Metz, the Bishop of Speyer and Count Ulrich V of Württemberg, and Margrave Charles I of Baden joined them after first trying to mediate; the war is also called the Baden-Palatine War. Diether had the Mainz city council, his brother Louis and his former enemy Frederick I, who was given Lorsch, Heppenheim and Bensheim for his help. Baden troops devastated the Palatine lands on both banks of the Rhine.

In summer 1462, believing Frederick away in Bavaria, 8,000 Baden and Württemberg troops marched from Bretten, burning and plundering, but were routed near Seckenheim, where their mounted vanguard had ridden far ahead of the foot. Charles I and Bishop George were captured, Ulrich V soon after, and Frederick held them in chains at Heidelberg until ransoms of 25,000 and 45,000 guilders were paid. The victory earned him the name the Victorious. On the night of 28 October 1462, through the betrayal of some citizens, Adolph entered Mainz by the Gautor with 500 men; after 12 hours of street fighting 400 men were dead and parts of the town were sacked.

Adolph took away the town's privileges, placing it under a vicedominus appointed by the archbishop, and drove out the 800 citizens who answered his summons to the Dietmarkt, though about 400 were later allowed back. By the Treaty of Zeilsheim Diether recognised Adolph and received money and a small principality of Höchst, Steinheim and Dieburg. Both sides' alliances left the archbishopric deep in debt. After Adolph's death in 1475 Diether was elected again and ruled until his death in 1482.
maio-of-bari: Maio was born in the first decades of the twelfth century to Leo of Rayza and Kuraza, members of the urban upper class of Bari. Leo is documented as a judge in Bari between 1119 and 1135, as a royal justice from 1141 and as protoiudex, or first judge, from 1142 to 1147. The contemporary Liber de regno sicilie, a partisan source, falsely claims that Maio was the son of an oil merchant, while Romuald Guarna, a partisan of the other side, called him an eloquent, honest and discreet man.

Maio first appears in October 1144 as royal scriniarius, keeper of the archive of the royal court. In 1149 he was given the title of vice-chancellor, apparently created for him, and from May 1152 he headed the chancery as chancellor. After the execution of the admiral Philip of Mahdia in 1153, King William I appointed him admiral of admirals shortly after his coronation on 4 April 1154. The title came from the Arabic amir al-umarā' and was then an administrative office; the Arabic writer Ibn al-Athīr rendered it as vizier.

Maio was unpopular with the baronage. In 1155 Robert de Bassonville, count of Loritello and the king's cousin, joined a Byzantine army under Michael Palaeologus and took Bari, and while William lay ill Maio and Hugh, Archbishop of Palermo, ran the kingdom. Rebels who seized Butera demanded the removal of both men, but William kept Maio. In 1156 Maio was chiefly responsible for the Treaty of Benevento, which ended hostilities with the Holy See. When Mahdia surrendered on 11 January 1160, he was blamed for the loss.

Rumours spread that Maio meant to seize the crown. Matthew Bonnellus, whom Maio wished to marry to his daughter, planned his murder while Maio prepared the wedding, and the conspirators stabbed him to death in the street called Via Coperta, also wounding his protégé Matthew of Ajello. A mob descended on his palace, and his wife and children were taken away to safety.

Maio's administration consolidated the centralisation of the kingdom begun under the first two Rogers. His enemy the chronicler Hugo Falcandus called him a monster, more loathsome and damaging to the kingdom than any vermin. Maio himself wrote an Exposition of the Lord's Prayer in the scholastic tradition.
maison-carree: The Maison carrée, French for square house, is an ancient Roman temple in Nîmes in southern France and one of the best-preserved Roman temples to survive in the territory of the former Roman Empire. It is a mid-sized Augustan provincial temple of the imperial cult, a caesareum. The temple dominated the forum of the Roman city. It stands on a podium 2.85 m high and measures 26.42 m by 13.54 m, a rectangle almost twice as long as it is wide. Its deep portico, almost a third of the building's length, emphasises the temple front and distinguishes the layout from Greek temples.

The temple was dedicated or rededicated to Gaius and Lucius Caesar, grandsons and adopted heirs of Augustus who both died young. The dedicatory inscription was removed in medieval times, but a local scholar, Jean-François Séguier, reconstructed it in 1758 from the order and number of the holes in the frieze and architrave to which bronze letters had been fixed. In his reconstruction it reads: to Gaius Caesar, son of Augustus, consul; to Lucius Caesar, son of Augustus, consul designate; to the princes of youth.

The temple is similar to the Tuscan-style Roman temple described by the contemporary writer Vitruvius, though it uses the Corinthian order. It is hexastyle, with six Corinthian columns under the pediment at each end, and pseudoperipteral, with twenty engaged columns along the walls of the cella. A large door leads to the small windowless interior, which has no ancient decoration. The carving is not as precise as that of the Parthenon.

Until the nineteenth century the temple formed part of a larger complex of adjoining buildings, which were demolished when it housed, from 1821 to 1907, what is now the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Nîmes. The present door dates from 1824, and a restoration between 1988 and 1992 re-roofed it and cleared the square, revealing the outlines of the forum. Thomas Jefferson had a stucco model made of the temple in 1785 while minister to France, and it inspired the Virginia State Capitol he designed, as well as the Église de la Madeleine in Paris and St Marcellinus Church in Rogalin, Poland. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in September 2023.
maitraka-dynasty: Bhaṭārka had been the Gupta military governor of Saurashtra. He and his successor Dharasena I used only the title Senapati, general, while the third ruler, Droṇasiṁha, called himself Maharaja. Early scholars such as Fleet misread a copperplate grant and took the Maitrakas for a foreign tribe Bhaṭārka had defeated; later readings showed he was himself a Maitraka. The grants say only that the family came of a warlike tribe with its capital at Vallabhi. The Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang called the ruler a Kshatriya, and Virji, followed by D. R. Bhandarkar and others, traced them to the Mitra dynasty of the Mathura region.

Guhasena dropped the phrase that had shown nominal allegiance to the Gupta overlords, and his son Dharasena II took the title Mahadhiraja. Hiuen Tsang, who visited in 640, described Śilāditya I Dharmāditya as a monarch of great administrative ability and rare kindness. A copperplate grant of 616 shows that Kharagraha I held Ujjain. Dhruvasena II Balāditya married a daughter of Harṣavardhana, under whose rule the Maitrakas came in the mid-7th century while keeping local autonomy, and they regained their independence after his death. Dharasena IV took full imperial titles, and the Sanskrit poet Bhatti served at his court. Arabs probably invaded under Śilāditya V, and repeated attacks from the sea weakened the kingdom; the last known king was Śilāditya VI.

The kings were Shaivas who styled themselves parama-maheshwara and used the bull Nandi and the trident on their coins and inscriptions; only Dhruvasena I, a Vaiṣnava, and Dharapaṭṭa, a sun-worshipper, stood apart. They gave grants to all faiths, and the kingdom had many Buddhist viharas. Vallabhi's university was compared with Nalanda: the traveller I-Tsing found it a great centre of learning late in the 7th century, the Buddhist scholars Gunamati and Sthiramati worked there, and students came from across India. More than a hundred temples of the period are known, mostly along the western coast of Saurashtra.
maitreya: Maitreya, in Pali Metteyya, is regarded in all schools of Buddhism as the future Buddha of this world and the direct successor of Gautama Buddha. His name comes from the Sanskrit maitrī, meaning loving-kindness, and is related to the Indo-Iranian name Mitra. In Tibetan Buddhism he is called the Lord of Love. Tradition counts him as the fifth and final Buddha of the present eon. He is expected to appear in an age of decline, when the teachings of Gautama have been forgotten, and to re-establish the dharma, 5,670,000,000 years from now. Meanwhile he lives as a bodhisattva in the Tushita heaven, where Gautama also lived before his birth.

The Cakkavatti Sutta says that Maitreya will be born in the city of Ketumatī, when humans live for eighty thousand years, to the chief priest Brahmayu and his wife Brahmavati. He will live as a householder, have a son, then renounce the world and attain Buddhahood, and the wheel-turning emperor Sankha will give away his palace and follow him. Jan Nattier distinguishes four kinds of Maitreya myth: meeting him in this life, meeting him in a later life, seeing him in a vision of his court, and rebirth in his Tushita palace.

Mahayana Buddhists hold that Maitreya revealed five scriptures to the Indian master Asanga in the 4th century, texts important to the Yogacara tradition. Chinese Buddhists regard the monk Budai, traditionally dated to the tenth century, as an emanation of Maitreya, which gave rise to the image of the Laughing Buddha.

Maitreya devotion in China goes back at least to Dao'an in the 4th century and was popular under the Northern Wei. Masters such as Xuanzang, Wonhyo and Yijing hoped to be reborn in his Inner Court. In Japan the Hossō school treats him as its founder.

The prophecy was also used by secret societies and rebels. Three people declared themselves incarnations of Maitreya under the Sui dynasty in failed attempts to overthrow it, and in 515 the monk Faqing proclaimed himself the New Buddha and raised an army against the Northern Wei. The White Lotus Society, whose roots go back to the 12th century, and later Chinese salvationist religions made Maitreya a saviour sent by the Eternal Venerable Mother.
maize: Maize, Zea mays, is a tall annual grass with a single stem, ranging in height from 1.2 to 4 m. The tassel at the top bears the male flowers, and a female inflorescence lower down develops into an ear wrapped in husks. The grains are usually yellow or white in modern varieties but can be orange, red, brown, blue, purple or black. Maize relies on humans for its propagation, since its kernels, unlike those of its wild ancestor teosinte, do not fall off the cob on their own.

The teosinte origin theory was proposed by the botanist Nikolai Vavilov in 1931 and by George Beadle in 1932. In 2004 John Doebley identified Balsas teosinte, native to the Balsas River valley in Mexico's south-western highlands, as the wild relative most similar to maize. All maize arose from a single domestication in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. Stone milling tools with maize residue have been found in an 8,700-year-old layer in a cave near Iguala, Guerrero, and maize reached highland Ecuador at least 8,000 years ago.
The Olmec and Maya cultivated it in numerous varieties and processed it by nixtamalisation, and by 3,000 years ago it was central to Olmec culture, including their calendar, language and myths.

The niacin in maize is not available without nixtamalisation, the alkali treatment, and the Maya made nixtamal meal into porridges and tamales. After 1492 explorers and traders carried maize to Europe. Spanish settlers preferred wheat bread, and maize flour could not replace wheat in communion bread, since only wheat was believed able to undergo transubstantiation. Maize was nevertheless grown in Spain within a few decades of Columbus's voyages, and by the 18th century it was the chief food of the southern French and Italian peasantry, especially as polenta.
majapahit-empire: Majapahit, also called Wilwatikta, was a Javanese Hindu-Buddhist empire based on the island of Java. The name means bitter maja, after the fruit of a tree; the 16th-century chronicle Pararaton says that workers clearing the forest of Trik for Raden Wijaya found maja trees and ate their bitter fruit. Before it, the kingdom of Singhasari had become the most powerful polity of the region after the Pamalayu campaign against the Melayu Kingdom in Sumatra. Its king Kertanagara refused tribute to Kublai Khan and sent a Yuan envoy back to China with his face mutilated. In response the khan sent a punitive expedition of 30,000 soldiers and 1,000 ships to Java in 1293, and Majapahit rose to power in the aftermath of the Mongol invasion.

After the reign of King Jayanegara, his stepmother Gayatri Rajapatni, who had become a Buddhist nun, appointed her daughter Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi queen. In 1336 the queen made Gajah Mada her prime minister, and at his inauguration he swore the Palapa oath, vowing to take no rest until he had united the archipelago under Majapahit. Under Tribhuwana and her son Hayam Wuruk, in the mid-14th century, conquests extended Majapahit's authority through Southeast Asia. The Nagarakretagama, written in 1365, describes an empire of 98 tributaries stretching from Sumatra to New Guinea, although historians still debate how far its influence reached and the nature of its relations with its overseas vassals.

After Hayam Wuruk died in 1389, a dispute over the succession began. His nephew and son-in-law Prince Vikramavardhana succeeded him, but Bhre Wirabhumi, a son by a concubine, also claimed the throne, and this led to the Regreg Civil War of 1405 to 1406. The war weakened control over the vassal states and the empire slowly declined, until it collapsed in 1527 when the Sultanate of Demak invaded. Its fall saw the rise of Islamic kingdoms in Java.

The capital Trowulan was known for its annual festivities. On the first day of the month of Caitra, in March or April, representatives of all the territories that paid tax or tribute came to court. The realm was divided into the palace and its vicinity, the parts of east Java and Bali administered directly by royal officials, and outer dependencies with considerable internal autonomy. Buddhism, Shaivism and Vaishnavism were all practised, and the king was regarded as the incarnation of the three; there were certainly Muslim courtiers by this period.

Poets wrote kakawin in Old Javanese, among them Prapanca's Nagarakretagama and Tantular's Sutasoma. The ruins of the capital lie around Trowulan, which Sir Thomas Stamford Raffles described in the 19th century, and aerial and satellite images have shown a wide network of canals. Chinese accounts, such as the 1451 work of Zheng He's translator Ma Huan, also describe Majapahit.
majd-al-dawla: Abu Talib Rustam, known by his honorific Majd al-Dawla, was the eldest son of Fakhr al-Dawla, Buyid ruler of Jibal, Tabaristan and Gurgan, and of Sayyida Shirin, a princess of the Bavand dynasty. He was tutored by Ibn Faris, a Persian scholar and grammarian from Hamadan. When his father died in 997, Jibal was divided: Majd al-Dawla received Ray and its surroundings, and his younger brother Shams al-Dawla, as his subordinate, Hamadan and Qirmisin, with their mother as regent. In 998 the caliph al-Qadir gave him his title.

Early in the reign the Ziyarid ruler Qabus retook Tabaristan and Gurgan, and the Sallarids of Azerbaijan seized western towns including Zanjan. In 1005 Majd al-Dawla took the title shahanshah, and from 1009/10 his coins recognised Baha al-Dawla as senior amir. In 1008 he tried with his vizier Abu 'Ali ibn 'Ali to end his mother's regency, but she and Shams al-Dawla besieged Ray, took him prisoner and held him in the fort of Tabarak until she reinstated him a year later.

From 1014 the polymath Avicenna served at the court as physician, treating him for melancholia. In 1016 the Daylamite officer Ibn Fuladh, refused the governorship of Qazvin, besieged Ray with 2,000 troops of the Ziyarid Manuchihr and forced his appointment to Isfahan. Ala al-Dawla Muhammad, whom Sayyida Shirin had made governor of Isfahan, ruled almost independently, taking Hamadan in 1023, though his coins still named Majd al-Dawla as suzerain.

Facing a revolt of his Daylamite soldiers, Majd al-Dawla asked the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud for help, a decision the historian Clifford Edmund Bosworth called foolish. Mahmud took Ray in March or April 1029 and sacked it; much of its great library was burned and many inhabitants were stoned as heretics. Majd al-Dawla was reportedly sent to Ghazni, where he died. His son Fana-Khusrau later tried and failed to restore Buyid power. Under his rule Ray had flourished as a centre of learning, and Persian literature from Khurasan gained ground at his court.
majdanek-concentration-camp: The camp stood on the outskirts of Lublin, next to the Lublin Ghetto of Majdan Tatarski, from which local residents gave it the nickname Majdanek, "little Majdan", in 1941. Nazi documents first described it as a prisoner-of-war camp of the Waffen-SS. On 9 April 1943 the Reich Security Main Office renamed it Konzentrationslager Lublin, but the Polish name remained the more common one. It covered about 2.7 square kilometres, with some 227 structures, three gas chambers and two wooden gallows.

Heinrich Himmler ordered the camp after a visit to Lublin on 17 to 20 July 1941. It was planned for 25,000 prisoners of war, a figure raised several times as Soviet prisoners were taken, to 250,000 by March 1942. Building began on 1 October 1941 with 150 Jewish forced labourers, later joined by 2,000 Red Army prisoners who slept in the open. By mid-November only 500 of them were alive, and a typhus epidemic had killed all the slave labourers by January 1942.

Around March 1942 the camp was refurbished as a killing centre within Operation Reinhard, the plan to murder the Jews of the occupied Polish territory. Prisoners were killed with Zyklon B and by shooting squads of Trawniki men. Until June 1942 the dead were buried in mass graves; afterwards they were burned, and the graves were later opened by prisoners of Sonderkommando 1005. On 3 November 1943, the first day of Aktion Erntefest, 18,400 Jews were shot at the main camp. Estimates of the total dead have ranged from 360,000, given in 1948, to the figure of 78,000 reached in research published in 2005.

The Red Army reached the camp on 24 July 1944. The Germans had evacuated it in haste and partly destroyed the crematoria, but most of it stood. The Soviet NKVD then held soldiers of the Polish Home Army there. A museum was founded on the grounds in autumn 1944, the site became a monument of martyrdom by a decree of the Polish Parliament in 1947, and in 1965 it became a national museum.

A mound holding some 1,300 cubic metres of soil mixed with ashes and bone fragments was raised in 1947. A large monument designed by Wiktor Tołkin was built in July 1969, with a gate at the entrance and a mausoleum for the ashes. The camp now occupies about half its original area and lies within the boundaries of Lublin, with houses overlooking it. The Majdanek State Museum also runs branches at Sobibór and Bełżec.
majeerteen: The Majeerteen, also known as Mohammed Harti, belong to the Harti branch of the Darod. They traditionally inhabit the Bari, Nugaal and Mudug regions, from Bosaso to Garacad, between the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, and are most numerous in the regional capitals of Bosaso, Garowe and Galkacyo. Migrations that began in the 19th century took some to Kismayo in the south, and some live in the Dollo Zone of the Somali Region of Ethiopia. Historically the clan formed part of a coastal trading network around the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.

The first recorded mention of the clan in English is by Henry Salt, who described them as living on the coast of Hafun under a Sultan Hassan. Salt relates that the Imam of Muscat had sent gifts and asked leave to build a small fort there, and that both the request and the gifts were refused. In the 19th century Majeerteen merchants were active across the Red Sea. One of them, Ahmed Muhammad, was granted the island of Baka by the Damoheita Afar, and his family ruled it as sultans into the period of Italian rule in Eritrea.

The Majeerteen Sultanate was founded in the 15th or 16th century and rose to prominence in the 19th under Boqor Osman Mahamuud. It was nearly destroyed by his struggle with his cousin Yusuf Ali Kenadid, who was forced into exile in Yemen, returned with a band of Hadhrami musketeers, overpowered the local Hawiye clans and founded the Sultanate of Hobyo in 1878.

Kenadid signed a protectorate treaty with Italy, and Boqor Osman followed in late 1889. Each hoped to use Italian support against the other and to avoid direct occupation. When Kenadid refused to let British troops land in his territory to fight the Dervish forces of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, the Italians exiled him to Aden and then to Eritrea. After two years of resistance by Boqor Osman and Majeerteen rebels, which Italian forces put down with long coastal bombardments of towns and naval blockades, the territory came under the full authority of Rome by late 1927.

Osman Yusuf Kenadid, a son of the first sultan of Hobyo, devised the Osmanya script for the Somali language in the 1920s. Members of the clan held many government posts in the 1960s and 1970s, among them Abdirashid Shermarke, the first prime minister and second president of Somalia. In the 1980s and 1990s the Somali Salvation Democratic Front was a predominantly Majeerteen political group.
majolus-of-cluny: Majolus came from a wealthy family of Avignon; his father was named Fulcher and his mother Raimodis, and he had a brother, Cynricus. Around 916 feudal wars drove him from the family estates near Rietz to relatives at Mâcon, and both his parents died while he was young. He studied the liberal arts at Lyon, became canon and later archdeacon of Mâcon and was ordained priest there, teaching a large body of clerks without charge. When Besançon needed a new bishop many called for him, but he refused.

He entered Cluny Abbey under Abbot Aymard, who made him armarius and later librarian. Around 948 he became Aymard's coadjutor, and when the blind abbot resigned Majolus at first refused, then accepted, becoming abbot about 954. Cluny II was built from about 955, after the Hungarian raids of 953, and its church was consecrated in 981. The houses reformed under earlier abbots had stayed independent of Cluny, but under Majolus a network of dependent monasteries took shape: Payerne Priory was placed under Cluny in 965, Paray-le-Monial was founded as a Cluniac house in 973, and the Abbey of St. Benignus in Dijon was resettled from 989.

Otto I and his wife Adelheid of Burgundy held him in favour; with her support he founded the Monastery of San Salvatore in Lombardy in 971, and Otto made him abbot of Sant'Apollinare in Classe in 972. In 974 Adelheid and Otto II summoned him to Italy to make him pope, which he refused, and around 980 at Pavia he helped reconcile the emperor with his mother. Returning across the Alps from Pavia in 972, he was captured by Arabs from Fraxinet; after a ransom was paid, anger in Provence moved William, Count of Provence, to defeat the raiders at the Battle of Tourtour.

Majolus died at Souvigny Priory on his way to reform Saint-Denis in Paris, and was buried there, though the monks of Cluny wanted his body. His tomb became a place of pilgrimage, visited by Hugh Capet, King of France, in 994. Two lives were written, by Syrius, a monk of Cluny, and by his successor Odilo, and the Vita S. Maioli credits him with many miracles. His feast is on 11 May, and he is also commemorated on 29 April with Odo, Odilo and Hugh of Cluny.
maka-satrapy: Maka has been identified with the barren coastal region of Makran in present-day Iran and Pakistan, Greek Gedrosia, and alternatively with the lands across the Persian Gulf, now Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and the northern half of Oman, which correspond to Magan. The historian Fleming counts Maka, in the area of Gedrosia, among the Indian satrapies of the Achaemenid Empire. Babylonian voyages to India passed by way of Maka.

Maka already belonged to the empire when Darius I came to power in 522 BCE, as the Behistun inscription shows. As neither Cambyses nor Smerdis is known to have campaigned there, it may have been conquered by Cyrus the Great. Herodotus places the Mykians in the same tax district as the Drangians, Thamanaeans, Utians, Sagartians and those deported to the Persian Gulf, and Achaemenid inscriptions, among them the Daiva inscription, name the men from Maka among the empire's peoples.

The Mykians served in the army of Xerxes the Great, and they are thought to have been responsible for the qanats, underground galleries that carry water from an aquifer at the foot of the hills to gardens and palm groves on the plains. The satrapy remained part of the empire until Alexander the Great's conquest, when it became independent. Alexander's army crossed Makran by a harsh desert route and lost a large number of soldiers.

The Mykians of the eastern side, in the present-day regions of Balochistan and Sindh, are thought to have become independent, since Arrian of Nicomedia's account of Alexander's campaigns mentions only the Omani side, which he calls Maketa. Maka later survived as a satrapy of the Parthian and Sasanian empires, under the name Makuran or Mazun depending on its identification.
makaba-ii: Makaba was born about 1760, the son of Moleta, kgosi of the Bangwaketse, and succeeded his father about 1790. He was often in conflict with the peoples of the region and launched numerous cattle raids against neighbouring tribes, above all the Bakwena, the Barolong and the Batlhaping. He also targeted the Mmanaana Kgatla, over whom he seized control from 1820 to 1824. These raids made the Bangwaketse the strongest tribe of the surrounding area, and Makaba used the tribe's wealth in cattle to encourage immigration into its territory.

He had three children: Tshosa and Segotshane by one wife and Sebego by another. When the Difaqane conflicts began in the 1820s, his control over the Bangwaketse slipped, as his sons worked with the Bakwena to undermine him. Tshosa rebelled openly against his father in 1823 and was killed, and Segotshane, who had also joined the rebellion, fled after its defeat to the Barolong, one of the peoples his father had raided. Tshosa had been Makaba's heir. In July or August 1824, in the last months of his life, Makaba welcomed Robert Moffat of the London Missionary Society to Kgwakgwe.

Makaba was killed in 1824 while fighting against a Bakololo invasion. It has been suggested that his son Sebego played a part in his father's death. Because Tshosa had died before his father, the succession passed to Tshosa's son Gaseitsiwe, for whom Sebego and Segotshane both served as regents. Makaba's death opened a period of strife among the Bangwaketse, whose strength under him had rested on the raids and the cattle wealth he had gathered.
makahiki: The ancient Hawaiians divided the year into two seasons: Makahiki, and eight lunar months in which the rituals of the god Kū were practised. In the Hawaiian language makahiki means year, and also the change from the harvest season to the planting season. The word probably comes from Makaliʻi hiki, the rising of the Pleiades, though it may also come from ma Kahiki, roughly as in Tahiti, since the legend of Lono is tied to voyages to and from Tahiti. The festival's origins are linked to the return of Lono in the form of a mortal man during an early migration.

On Oʻahu the season might begin when the Pleiades rose above Puʻu o Mahuka Heiau as seen from Kaena Point, or when the star ʻAʻa, Sirius, appeared above a particular cliff. Hawaiians gave thanks to Lono-ika-makahiki, who brought life, peace and victory, prayed for the death of their enemies, and commoners prayed that their chiefs' lands would grow. Since there was no money, offerings were also left at ahu, stone altars on the boundaries of each ahupuaʻa. The king placed a niho palaoa necklace on the Akua Loa, which was adorned with white kapa streamers.

The contests included boxing, hōlua sledding on lava courses, foot racing, wrestling, javelin throwing, surfing and canoe races, alongside games of the mind: riddles, proverbs and the recitation of genealogies. A contestant's showing reflected on the family, and people bet on their favourites. When the chief came back to shore at the festival's end, warriors threw spears at him, and he had to parry them to prove himself worthy to rule. A royal child born during the season was sometimes named Lono i ka makahiki.

The sails and masts of Captain James Cook's ship resembled the Akua Loa, and his vessel anchored in Kealakekua Bay near a large heiau to Lono. The Keauhou Holua National Historic Landmark preserves one of the best-kept lava sled courses. The traditional games are still played to teach younger generations about their ancestors, and the Aloha Festivals, first held as Aloha Week, celebrate the Makahiki tradition.
makan-ibn-kaki: Abu Mansur Makan ibn Kaki served, like his father, as an officer of the Alids of Tabaristan, a Zaydi branch of the Alids who ruled an independent emirate on the southern shore of the Caspian Sea. He was tied to them by marriage: Ja'far, son of the imam Hasan ibn Ali al-Utrush, was his son-in-law. After Ja'far and his brother Ahmad ousted al-Utrush's successor, the Da'i ila'l-Haqq Hasan ibn Qasim, in 923, Makan became governor of Gurgan, the easternmost province of the emirate.

When Ja'far died in 924, Makan deposed his heir Abu Ali Muhammad and set up his own grand-nephew Ismail, but Muhammad escaped and, with Asfar ibn Shiruya, defeated him. Makan held out in a mountain fortress near Sari until Muhammad's death in 926 or 927, then defeated the Alid army and recalled the Da'i. In 928 the two took Rayy and advanced as far as Qum, but Asfar seized Tabaristan in their absence, the Da'i was mortally wounded before Amul, and Asfar drove Makan from Rayy.

In 930 Makan recovered Tabaristan, took most of Gurgan and even Nishapur, which he gave up in 931 under pressure from the Samanid ruler Nasr II. Mardavij, who had overthrown Asfar, then conquered Tabaristan. Makan went to the Samanids, who made him governor of Kirman, which he held until Mardavij was killed by his own Turkish ghilman in 935. He then became governor of Gurgan, and after fighting with Mardavij's brother Vushmgir he was left in possession of it when Vushmgir recognised Samanid overlordship.

As relations with Vushmgir improved, Makan felt secure enough to drop his dependence on the Samanids. In 939 a Samanid army under Abu Ali ibn Muhtaj attacked him at Gurgan, and after a seven-month siege of his capital he fled to Rayy. The Samanids pursued him, and on 25 December 940 they defeated him at Iskhabad near Rayy. Makan was killed by an arrow and beheaded, and his head was sent to Nasr in Bukhara.
makarios-iii: Makarios III was born Michael Christodoulou Mouskos on 13 August 1913 in Panayia village in the Paphos District of Cyprus, then a British protectorate. At thirteen he entered Kykkos Monastery as a novice. He finished secondary school at the Pancyprian Gymnasium in Nicosia in 1936 and studied theology and law at the University of Athens, graduating in 1942. A World Council of Churches scholarship took him to Boston University. In 1948, still a student there, he was elected Bishop of Kition against his will and took the name Makarios, meaning happy or blessed. Like many Greek Cypriot public figures he supported enosis, union with Greece.

Elected Archbishop on 18 September 1950, aged 37, Makarios became both head of the Church and Ethnarch, the de facto national leader of Cypriots. He argued for enosis and encouraged Greece to take the question to the United Nations in 1954. His relation to the insurgent organisation EOKA, led by George Grivas, is unclear and disputed, and he later denied any involvement in its violence. In March 1956 British Special Branch officers seized him at Nicosia airport and exiled him to the Seychelles. Released after a year but barred from Cyprus, he worked from Athens. Greece gradually dropped enosis for independence, and after the Zurich Agreement of 1958 he agreed, at first reluctantly, to the terms for independence.

He returned to Cyprus on 1 March 1959 and won the presidential election on 13 December 1959 with two-thirds of the vote against Ioannis Clerides. Taking office on 16 August 1960 with Fazıl Küçük as vice-president, he followed non-alignment and attended the first Non-Aligned Movement summit at Belgrade in 1961. In November 1963 he proposed thirteen constitutional amendments to ease the ethnic restrictions on public office. Many Turkish Cypriots saw a threat to their protections, most in public office resigned, and intercommunal violence broke out again by the end of 1963. UN peacekeepers arrived in 1964. In the 1968 election he won about 96 per cent of the votes.

During the early 1970s the Greek junta backed Grivas and his EOKA B, and in July 1974 Makarios demanded that Greek officers leave the island. On 15 July Dimitrios Ioannidis organised a coup in Nicosia; Makarios escaped to Paphos and was taken off by a British helicopter, and Nikos Sampson was installed as president. Turkey invaded on 20 July and captured roughly 36 per cent of the island, where the unrecognised state of Northern Cyprus was later established. Makarios returned in December 1974. He died of a heart attack on 3 August 1977 and is buried on Mount Throni, near Kykkos Monastery. An estimated 250,000 people filed past his coffin.
makassan-contact-with-australia: Trepang live on the sea floor and are exposed at low tide. They were gathered by hand, by spearing, diving or dredging. At the height of the trade the Makassan fleets, whose perahu could carry crews of thirty, arrived with the north-west monsoon each December and ranged thousands of kilometres along the coast; Campbell Macknight estimated about a thousand men a year. They called Arnhem Land Marege', the wild country, and the Kimberley fishing grounds Kayu Jawa. In 1803 Matthew Flinders met a fleet near present-day Nhulunbuy and spoke at length with its captain, Pobasso.

The crews camped at semi-permanent sites to process the catch and sailed home four months later. Remains of their processing places survive at Port Essington, Anuru Bay and Groote Eylandt, with stands of the tamarind trees they introduced. Aboriginal people traded turtle-shell, pearls and cypress pine for cloth, tobacco, metal axes and knives, rice and gin, and some worked as trepangers or sailed to Sulawesi. Most contact was peaceful, but some was hostile.

In 1883 Using Daeng Rangka became the first trepanger to pay South Australia for a licence; fees, customs duties and probably overfishing made the trade less viable. After a Makassan crew was massacred at Cape Wilberforce in May 1902, South Australia stopped issuing licences in July 1906, and Rangka's perahu, the last, left Arnhem Land in 1907.

The Yolngu of Arnhem Land took up the dug-out canoe and learned ironworking from the visitors, which let them hunt dugongs and turtles at sea. A Makassan pidgin became a trade language along the coast, and words such as rupiah, jama and balanda, white person, remain in Aboriginal languages. Regina Ganter and Peta Stephenson suggest that the Yolngu adapted aspects of Islam, which still appear in some ceremonies, while the anthropologist Ian McIntosh has argued that contact also brought strife. In 1988 the prau Hati Marege sailed from Makassar to Arnhem Land under Rangka's great-grandson.
makassar-war: From 1607 the sultans of Makassar welcomed all foreign traders, and an English factory was built there in 1613. Gowa also dominated its Bugis neighbours: Bone rose against it in 1644 and was defeated at the Battle of Passempe, and in 1660 Arung Palakka, a prince of Bone, led a Bugis revolt whose army grew to 10,000 men by August 1660. The rebellion was crushed and Palakka fled South Sulawesi. Sultan Hasanuddin, the 16th sultan of Gowa, tried to unite the small kingdoms of eastern Indonesia against the VOC.

On 24 November 1666 a VOC expedition under Admiral Cornelis Speelman set sail: the flagship Tertholen and twenty other vessels with some 1,860 people, among them 818 Dutch sailors, 578 Dutch soldiers and 395 native troops from Ambon under Captain Joncker and Bugis under Arung Palakka and Arung Belo Tosa'deng. Palakka's arrival roused the Bugis of Bone and Soppeng against Gowa, and while Speelman fought Gowa's fleet, Palakka led a difficult campaign on land.

The Treaty of Bongaya, signed on 18 November 1667, did not end the war. Feeling aggrieved, Hasanuddin took up arms again, and the VOC asked Batavia for more troops. In August 1668 the Bugis beat Gowa's forces at Siang and Maros, and on 12 October 1668 the allies won a major battle at Makassar, marred by the death of Arung Belo Tosa'deng.

The assault on Somba Opu began on 14 June 1669, when explosives in a secret tunnel opened a breach of about 27.5 metres in its wall. The defenders held it for days, and the attackers lost 50 dead and 68 wounded. On 22 June Palakka led Bugis, Bacan and Ambon soldiers through the breach, and fires fanned by a strong wind forced Hasanuddin to leave the fort, which 8,000 Bugis then plundered.

Speelman destroyed Somba Opu and built Fort Rotterdam, named after his birthplace, as the VOC's headquarters in Sulawesi. Palakka was the most powerful man in South Sulawesi until his death in 1696; in 1672 he was formally made arung, king, of Bone, which replaced Gowa as the leading principality, and he and the VOC divided power, Palakka holding internal affairs and the company external ones. Bands of Makassarese soldiers fled to Banten, were expelled in 1674 and turned to piracy on the coasts of Java and Nusa Tenggara; some later fought as allies of Trunajaya's rebellion, and other refugees went to Jambi and Palembang.
makatea: Makatea, also called Mangaia-te-vai-tamae, lies in the north-western Tuamotus, 79 kilometres south-west of Rangiroa. It is a raised coral atoll, about 7.5 kilometres long and 24 square kilometres in area, and one of only four islands of the archipelago that do not form a typical atoll. Cliffs 60 to 75 metres high ring its northern and eastern coasts and rise to a plateau about 80 metres above the sea, while the southern coast slopes more gently. It formed during the Miocene as an atoll-like platform on an older reef. Phases of emergence opened karst cavities that later filled with phosphate, thought to derive from weathered volcanic material carried from nearby volcanic islands.

Makatea is one of the few islands of the Tuamotus with drinking water, which people brought out of its dark caves. Later Polynesians called it Papa Tea, white rock. Pedro Fernandes de Queirós named it Sagitario in 1606 during a Spanish expedition from Peru, and the Dutch mariner Jakob Roggeveen named it Aurora in 1722.

Makatea was one of three major Pacific raised coral islands with large phosphate deposits, the others being Nauru and Banaba. The Pacific Phosphate Company, active on Nauru and Banaba, formed the Compagnie des Phosphates de l'Océanie with a Tahitian syndicate to mine it. During World War II, after Japanese forces cut off other phosphate islands, Cook Islanders were sent to Makatea to maintain New Zealand's supply of phosphate for agriculture. After the war about 3,000 labour contracts were signed, and many workers used their wages to help their families migrate to New Zealand.

Mining left thousands of hand-dug cylindrical holes across the plateau, each about 2.4 metres wide and 15 to 23 metres deep. The ghost town of Vaitepaua and the abandoned port of Temao on the north-west coast date from the mining years. Once the phosphate ran out, only a few families remained.

Makatea is an associated commune within the commune of Rangiroa, with 95 inhabitants at the 2022 census and its main village at Moumu. People live from agriculture, copra, some fishing and the trade in coconut crabs. It is the only home of the Polynesian imperial pigeon Ducula aurorae aurorae and the Makatea fruit dove.
makea-takau-ariki: Makea Takau was born around 1839, the daughter of Makea Te Vaerua Ariki, eldest daughter of Makea Pori Ariki, and was adopted by her mother's brother Makea Davida. The Makea title of Makea Nui, one of the three chiefdoms of Te Au O Tonga, passed among her mother's generation: Davida held it from 1839 to 1849, then Te Vaerua until 1857, Makea Daniela until 1866 and Makea Abera until his death in 1871, when she succeeded him. In the 1860s she married Ngamaru Rongotini Ariki, a high chief of Atiu, Mauke and Mitiaro. The marriage was childless, and Beatrice Grimshaw, a journalist from Ireland who visited in 1907, described it as happy despite Ngamaru's violent temper.

France's armed takeover of Tahiti in 1843 had left the ariki of the Cook Islands anxious for British protection. In the 1870s the islands were prosperous and peaceful under Makea, a shrewd negotiator who won good prices for exports and cut the debts that had built up before her accession. By 1882 four of the five ariki of Rarotonga were women. Fearing a French invasion, she petitioned Britain for a protectorate in 1888 and signed the treaty at the Para O Tane Palace in Avarua on 26 October 1888.

The first British Resident, the New Zealand politician Frederick Moss, tried to help the chiefs form a central government. In 1898 Major W. E. Gudgeon was sent to prepare a takeover by New Zealand, in line with the ambitions of its prime minister Richard Seddon. Makea preferred annexation to Britain, but the islands were annexed by New Zealand through a deed of cession signed by five ariki and seven lesser chiefs.

After a long illness Makea died at midnight on 1 May 1911, aged 72, and was buried in the family graveyard in the palace grounds. Her chosen successor, Rangi Makea, was installed on 24 October 1911 but was not made head of government. The palace later fell into ruin, and from 1990 students of Auckland University and local volunteers restored it over three years.
makerere-university: The trade school that became Makerere began operating in 1921 with classes in carpentry, building construction and mechanics. In 1922 it was founded as the Uganda Technical College, with added courses in the arts, education, agriculture and medicine, and in the same year renamed Makerere College. In 1928 the vocational classes were separated and renamed Kampala Technical School. In 1937 the college began offering post-secondary certificate courses that awarded diplomas, not degrees. It is the oldest currently active university in East Africa.

The Asquith Commission, set up by the British government in 1943, recommended raising Makerere to full university level. It noted that in 1943 the student roll was still modest, with 114 resident students. The protectorate government's proposal for a university led to a controversial struggle: the Bataka Party described it as a plot to steal African soil for European settlement, and rioting broke out in Kampala. In 1949 the college was granted university status, and in the same year the Bataka Party was banned after riot and arson.

Makerere became an independent national university in 1970. After Uganda's independence it was a focal point of the literary activity central to African nationalist culture, and writers including Nuruddin Farah, Ali Mazrui, David Rubadiri and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o were there at some point in their careers.

Student unrest and faculty disenchantment closed it three times between 2006 and 2016. After a strike over unpaid pay in 2016, President Yoweri Museveni closed it indefinitely, and it reopened in January 2017.

Makerere is the alma mater of many post-independence African leaders, among them Milton Obote of Uganda, Julius Nyerere and Benjamin Mkapa of Tanzania, Joseph Kabila of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Mwai Kibaki of Kenya. It also did much to develop primatology and wildlife field studies. In September 2020 a fire gutted its main building, the Ivory Tower, built in the 1930s and commissioned in 1941; an investigation could not establish the cause but pointed to an electric fault. Reconstruction of a building designed to look like the original began in April 2022. In 2022 the university marked the centenary of its establishment as Makerere College.
makhachkala: Makhachkala stands on the Caspian Sea and has been a major Russian seaport and a transport hub. Its historic predecessors were the towns of Tarki and Anji, or Anji-kala, which according to some sources date back to Khazar times; some chronicles suggest Anji-kala was the name of a citadel of the Khazar capital Semender. Anji was a port town in Kumykia and part of the possessions of the Tarki state, known as the Kumyk capital from the 8th century. Among the Kumyks the place was still called Anzhi-Qala, the Pearl Fortress, after the Russian town was founded.

Dagestan was long contested. Muslim armies arrived under the Umayyad Caliph Hisham, the Khazars captured Derbent in 796, and the region later fell under Seljuk, Mongol, Timurid, Safavid and, between 1578 and 1606, Ottoman influence. From the 17th century Iranians, Russians and Ottomans struggled for it. In the 1840s, after the Russian Empire seized the Kumyk plateau, the fort of Petrovskoye was founded at Anji-kala, named for Tsar Peter the Great, who had waged war in the region in 1722. The fortress received town status in 1857 and was renamed Petrovsk-Port. A railway linked it to Vladikavkaz and Baku in 1894.

During the Russian Civil War two British Royal Air Force squadrons were based at Petrovsk in 1919 and bombed Bolshevik forces. The Red Army took the city in March 1920. On 14 May 1921 it was renamed Makhachkala, after the Dagestani revolutionary Magomed-Ali Makhach Dakhadaev, and became the capital of the new Dagestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic. An earthquake on 14 May 1970 did major damage.

Makhachkala is the capital of the Republic of Dagestan and has 623,254 residents. It is ethnically very diverse: the Avar, Kumyk, Dargin, Lezgin and Lak nations each make up a substantial part of the population, with Russians a minority. Oil refining, mechanical engineering and textiles are the main industries, and the city is a centre of education, research and the regional press. Its commercial port handles oil, grain, timber and other cargo, and it is linked by rail to the North Caucasus network.
makhambet-otemisuly: Makhambet was first educated at a Russian language school in Orenburg, and from 1824 to 1828 he lived there with Zulkarnaiyn, a son of Jangir-Kerey Khan. In 1829 he was arrested for secretly crossing the Ural River into the Inner Horde and spent nearly two years in Kalmykov's prison; he escaped in 1831 and was later acquitted. His poetry drew on Kazakh literary tradition rather than his schooling, and its themes were of two kinds: political attacks on Russia or the khan, and verse on human existence and life.

In 1834 he joined Isatay Taymanuly. Jangir Khan offered him the post of starshina on 9 June that year to win him over, but land disputes, the scarcity of pasture, Russian pressure on the Kazakh Khanate, the khan's favour to his relatives and the power of his father-in-law Karauylkhozha Babazhanov fed wide unrest. In March 1836 the khan ordered the arrest of the two leaders, but on 4 April Karauylkhozha, with 522 men, retreated from their force of about 200 near Kieli Mola.

In autumn 1837 Isatay and Makhambet surrounded the khan's horde with more than 2,000 men, a siege his poem Ey, Makhambet, My Comrade! recalls. In November they were defeated by Geke's troops in the Beketai sands, a defeat told in his poem War and mourned in Jabigu. The rebels crossed the Ural to the Kishi Zhuz, and Isatay was killed at the battle of Akbulak on 12 July 1838.

Makhambet spent about two years trying to raise forces in the Khiva region, then returned in secret to the Bukey Horde. He was captured on 4 March 1841 in the home of a Kazakh named Tilekeev and sent to Orenburg, where a military court released him on 7 July with a warning not to cross the border again. When he came to Orenburg in February 1846 to put his son Nursultan in school, the case was reopened. B. Aishuakov, administrator of the western Kishi Zhuz, put a bounty of 1,000 rubles on his head and sent a detachment after him, and on 20 October 1846 Makhambet was killed by one of its members.
makhanda-prophet: Makhanda was born near the coast around 1780 in the Uitenhage area. His father, Gwala, was a Xhosa of the Cwerha clan, and his mother a Khoikhoi of the Gqunukhwebe clan. After his father died when Makhanda was a boy, he was raised by his mother, a spiritual diviner and medicine woman, and was later recognised as an inyanga. It is unclear when he first met Christianity; the missionary Dr James van der Kemp had founded a mission at Bethelsdorp in 1799, and Makhanda may have known him.

As an itinerant preacher he advocated peace and denounced the use of magic. Around 1812 Chief Ndlambe appointed him an advisor and military doctor, and he discussed theology with the chaplain at Grahamstown and the missionary John Read, who described him as a stout and handsome man who commanded respect. In 1816 his view of the missionaries changed. He had seen the mistreatment of Khoikhoi by Afrikaner farmers, and the Xhosa had suffered the expulsion of 20,000 people from the Zuurveld in 1812. He came to see the conflict as a contest between Thixo, the god of the whites, and Mdalidiphu, the god of the Xhosa, and preached a fusion of the two that leaned toward Xhosa belief.

In 1818 he fought at the Battle of Amalinde against Chief Ngqika, an ally of the Cape Colony. After a force under Colonel Thomas Brereton seized 23,000 head of cattle from Ndlambe's people, Makhanda urged the Xhosa to unite and drive out the British, promising that their bullets would turn to water. The attack of 22 April 1819, under the overall command of Ndlambe's son Mdushane, was made in daylight, with women and children following to occupy the town; about 350 British troops and a Khoikhoi group led by Jan Boesak repulsed it.

He was held on Robben Island with private quarters, food and furniture. On 25 December 1820 he tried to escape with thirty other prisoners; only four survived the crossing. Because he had promised never to abandon his people, they waited about fifty years before holding his funeral rites. He is regarded as one of the first Africans to attempt a synthesis of African and European beliefs, and political prisoners on Robben Island, Robert Mangaliso Sobukwe among them, later petitioned for the island to be renamed after him.
makhzan-al-asrar: The poem is a mathnawi, the first of the five long poems that make up the Khamsa of Nizami Ganjavi, and is divided into 60 sections. It opens with the traditional invocation of the name of God, the basmala, and turns at once to a central principle of Sufism, the unity and necessary existence of God. Its aim is to lead readers to self-knowledge, theology and good habits, and its advice is given through short stories.

The scholar Hamidreza Shayeganfar groups its themes under five heads: human neglect in the world, the instability of the world, the relation of man to God, social questions, and politics and government. In one passage Nizami tells how the archangel warned him that whoever would write poetry for people must first know what to sing, and he then describes nights of meditation in which he followed the heart as his teacher. Section 15, on describing the night and knowing the heart, urges the reader to escape the bandits of the senses and learn the path the heart knows.

The poem gives no date, directly or indirectly, and no early authority records one. Working from the precise dates Nizami gives in his other works, from the history of Azerbaijan and Arran and from comparative study, scholars place its composition between 1165 and 1173, probably close to 1173. Nizami, who lived from 1141 to 1209, dedicated it to Fakhr al-Din Bahramshah, who then governed Erzincan.

The poem has been counted ever since among the most important works of Persian literature, and its verses on the inner journey of the heart, complex and dense, have been compared to surrealist writing. It has been translated into English, German, Turkish, Kurdish and Russian.
maki-izumi: Maki Yasuomi, known by his court title Maki Izumi no kami or simply Maki Izumi, was born in Kurume in northern Kyushu in 1813. His father, Maki Toshiomi, headed the hereditary line of Shinto priests who cared for the Suitengu shrine, and during Maki's childhood he was made a full samurai by Arima Yorinori, lord of Kurume. When Maki was eleven his father died, leaving him in charge of both the family and the shrine. He served as a retainer of the Arima clan of Kurume.

Maki studied the sonno-joi ideology of the Mito school, and in particular the philosophy of Aizawa Seishisai. Combining what he had learnt from the Mito teachings and elsewhere, he founded a school of thought of his own, called Tenpogaku after the era in which it began. In Kyoto he worked with Okubo Toshimichi of the Satsuma domain to arrange Shimazu Hisamitsu's journey to the capital. In 1862 he was implicated in the Teradaya incident and briefly imprisoned.

In the Kinmon Incident of 1864 Maki joined the attack of the Choshu domain on the allied forces of Aizu and Satsuma in Kyoto, and was beaten back. Surrounded on Mount Tennozan by Aizu troops under Hayashi Gonsuke and Jinbo Kuranosuke and by Shinsengumi forces under Kondo Isami, he killed himself together with his men. His death poem speaks of his years and his Japanese spirit coming to an end among the rocks at the summit of the great mountain. He was buried in Oyamazaki in Kyoto. Maki appears as a minor character in Kenji Morita's manga Getsumei Seiki and Minamoto Taro's Fuunjitachi Bakumatsuhen, and in the 1986 Asahi TV miniseries Byakkotai.
makkhali-gosala: Gosala is called Gosala Mankhaliputta in Jain Prakrit sources and Maskarin Gośāla in other texts. The Jain Bhagavati Sutra states that he became Mahavira's disciple three years after Mahavira began his asceticism and travelled with him for the next six years. A commentary to the Jain Avasyaka Sutra gives details of those years, many of which reflect poorly on Gosala, a likely sign of sectarian bias, and some incidents may have been adapted from Ajivika sources and recast by Jain chroniclers. Mahavira is later shown rescuing Gosala from an enraged renunciant who attacked him with magical powers gained through austerities, a story said to explain Gosala's own pursuit of such powers.

In several of the Jain stories Mahavira makes predictions that come true despite Gosala's attempts to foil them, incidents probably included to account for Gosala's later belief in the inevitability of fate. The Bhagavati Sutra tells of a roadside plant that Gosala uprooted at night to disprove Mahavira's prediction about it; a sudden shower revived it, and it grew exactly as foretold. Gosala was so impressed that he became convinced all living things were capable of such reanimation, and the story's terms mimic a technical term for the reanimation of the dead found elsewhere in Ajivika doctrine. Mahavira disagreed, and this seems to have caused their separation.

The historian A. L. Basham dated Gosala's death to 484 BCE on the basis of the Mahavamsa. Gosala appears briefly in Gore Vidal's 1981 novel Creation, in which the Persian diplomat Cyrus Spitama meets him at Mathura and hears his views on fate and his disagreements with Mahavira. He is the subject of Khanti Kikatia, a novel in the Magahi language by Ashwini Kumar Pankaj.
maktoum-bin-butti: Dubai is thought to have begun in the early eighteenth century as a fishing village on the Trucial Coast, tributary to the Bani Yas of Abu Dhabi. By 1820 it was ruled for Abu Dhabi by a regent, and by 1822 it had some 700 to 800 residents. In 1833 a coup removed Sheikh Tahnun bin Shakhbut Al Nahyan as ruler of Abu Dhabi. The Al Bu Falasah, a section of the Bani Yas, disagreed with the new ruler, Khalifa bin Shakhbut, and some 800 of them moved north to Dubai under Maktoum bin Butti and Obeid bin Said bin Rashid. Mohammed bin Hazza bin Zaal, then head man, stepped aside.

Obeid bin Said bin Rashid died of old age in 1836, and Maktoum took over entirely. The port near the Al Fahidi Fort grew as a wharfage for trading and pearling vessels. Khalifa bin Shakhbut disliked the secession and in May 1838 raided the town while its pearling fleet was away, destroying a watchtower in fierce fighting. In 1841 about 500 of the Al Bu Muhair left for Sharjah, and fever struck Dubai. Khalifa plundered the nearly empty Bur Dubai, destroying date plantations, food stores and boats. A later advance was beaten back, and Khalifa sued for peace. By 1843 the two were close allies, and Maktoum, who lost an eye fighting the Ghafalah, helped him against the tribes of the interior.

Maktoum also dealt with the Qasimi rulers. In 1840 he encouraged Saqr bin Sultan Al Qasimi to break from his father, Sultan bin Saqr, hoping for a friendly buffer state. When Sultan bin Saqr and Khalifa planned to destroy Dubai, Maktoum offered his submission and 1,000 dollars, and the plan was dropped.

Obeid bin Said had acceded to the first annual maritime truce with the British in 1835, and Maktoum signed those that followed. In 1843 he signed the ten-year Maritime Truce, the model for the Perpetual Maritime Truce of 4 May 1853, which was signed by his successor Saeed bin Butti. He also signed the 1847 engagement to prohibit the export of slaves from Africa. He died of smallpox at sea in 1852 on a journey from Muscat to Qeshm, and he is regarded as the founder of the Al Maktoum dynasty.
mala-strana: Malá Strana means the Little Side, and the district is also called the Lesser Town, the Lesser Quarter or the Lesser Side. It lies on the left bank of the Vltava on the slopes just below Prague Castle, and is joined by the Charles Bridge to the larger districts of the right bank. In the Middle Ages it was a dominant centre of Prague's ethnic German citizens, and from the 16th century also of Italian ones. It housed many noble palaces, while the towns of the right bank were more bourgeois and more Czech.

King Ottokar II of Bohemia founded Malá Strana in 1257 as a royal town with many privileges, joining several settlements beneath the castle into one administrative unit. Its original residents were expelled and mostly German craftsmen and merchants were invited in. It was first called the New Town beneath Prague Castle, but after Charles IV founded the New Town of Prague in 1348 it was renamed the Lesser Town of Prague, and the unofficial name Little Quarter came into use in the 17th century. In the second half of the 14th century Charles IV extended it and built a new defensive wall, the Hunger Wall.

The Hussites burned the Lesser Town down in 1419 and 1420. In 1541 a fire that killed fifty people again damaged it severely, and it was rebuilt in the Renaissance style with many noble palaces. Baroque architecture, brought in after that fire, came to dominate. The market place, now Lesser Town Square, was the centre of the town, divided into an upper and a lower part by the Church of St Nicholas.

The largest Baroque building in the district is the Wallenstein Palace, built for Albrecht von Wallenstein, general-in-chief of Emperor Ferdinand II, with five courtyards and a garden laid out as a French park. St Nicholas, the finest church, is a masterpiece of Christoph Dientzenhofer and his son Kilian Ignaz. The Church of Our Lady Victorious holds the statue of the Holy Infant Jesus of Prague, which has drawn Catholic pilgrims for years. In 1989 thousands of East German refugees gathered at the West German embassy in the Lobkowicz Palace. The novelist Jan Neruda was born and lived in the district and wrote about it, and Nerudova Street is named after him.
malacca: Malacca faces the Strait of Malacca on the south-western coast of the Malay Peninsula, in a low, flat landscape in which 98 percent of the land lies below 150 metres. The Malacca River drains most of its catchment. Its position at a narrow point of the strait gave it a port accessible in all seasons, and it lay on the maritime routes between China, India, the Middle East, Africa and Europe.

Before a sultan arrived, the area was a fishing village. Malay tradition says Parameswara, also called Iskandar Shah, founded the settlement after fleeing a Majapahit invasion of Singapura, and that the name comes from a Malacca tree under which he sheltered when a mouse deer pushed a hunting dog into a river. With the Orang Laut, the "sea people", he required passing ships to call and built warehouses and trading facilities. In 1403 the first official Chinese envoy, Admiral Yin Qing, arrived, and in 1405 Zheng He brought a stone tablet and an imperial order raising the port to the status of a country. Ming protection shielded it from Siam and Majapahit, and China made it a base for its voyages into the Indian Ocean.

On 24 August 1511 the Portuguese under Afonso de Albuquerque, who had sailed from Goa with about 1,200 men, conquered the city. Trade then spread among rival ports such as Aceh and Johor, and the Jesuit Francis Xavier visited in 1545, 1546 and 1549. The Dutch East India Company, allied with the Johor Sultanate, captured Malacca on 14 January 1641 after a long siege and held it until the late 18th century. It passed to the British under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 in exchange for Bencoolen, joined the Straits Settlements with Singapore and Penang, and was occupied by Japan from 1942 to 1945.

Malacca is a state of Malaysia, which it joined on 16 September 1963, after Malayan independence on 31 August 1957. Its capital, Malacca City, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site with George Town in 2008. The state has about one million people, among them Malays, Chinese, Indians, Peranakan Chinese, Kristang, Chitty and Temuan. Surviving buildings from the Dutch period include the Stadthuys.
malaika: The authorship of Malaika is disputed. Most people credit Adam Salim, a little-published Tanzanian songwriter born in 1916, who is said to have composed it while living in Nairobi in 1945 and 1946 for his girlfriend Halima Ramadhani Maruwa. According to this story their parents disapproved of the match, and Halima was forced to marry a wealthy Asian man, a tajir.

The Kenyan singer Fadhili William, who made the first recording with his band The Jambo Boys, always insisted that he wrote the song and described the circumstances in detail, but he is recognised as composer only for royalty purposes. The producer Charles Worrod credited Grant Charo, William's brother-in-law, who is not known to have confirmed the claim, and Lucas Tututu of Mombasa also claimed to be the author.

The song is sung by a poor young man who wishes to marry his beloved, his angel or little bird, but is defeated by the bride price. Its Swahili is probably Tanzanian, possibly Kenyan. Fadhili William's early recording has only two verses; Miriam Makeba's adds a third, the Pesa verse, which also appears on a later record by William. Makeba's and Angélique Kidjo's versions change the song considerably.

Worrod re-recorded the song at Equator Sound Studios and marketed it until it won an international audience, and Miriam Makeba's early recording carried it throughout the continent and eventually the world. Through her performances it reached Harry Belafonte, Pete Seeger, Usha Uthup and others, and it is a staple of many African musicians.

The Swedish group the Hep Stars heard it from a chef at their hotel in Nairobi while filming there and recorded it at Europafilm Studios in April 1967. Their single entered Kvällstoppen at number 4 on 9 May 1967, held number 1 for five weeks and stayed 18 weeks on the chart, the only song wholly in an African language to reach number one on a Swedish chart. Boney M. released it in 1981 from their album Boonoonoonoos; it reached number 13 in Germany and the top ten in Spain, and a Lambada remix followed in 1989.
malaita: Malaita is a thin island about 164 kilometres long and 37 kilometres wide at its widest point. To the south-west the Indispensable Strait separates it from Guadalcanal, and to the north-west lies Santa Isabel. A central ridge runs along its length, rising to about 980 metres in the north and 1,300 metres in the south, and the coastal plain is very narrow. The people of the Langa Langa and Lau lagoons call themselves wane i asi, salt-water people, to distinguish themselves from the wane i tolo, bush people, of the interior. The main languages include To'abaita, Kwara'ae, Kwaio and ꞋAreꞌare, and the traditional religion is ancestor worship.

The first recorded European sighting was by the Spaniard Álvaro de Mendaña on 11 April 1568, and the Solomon Islands were then not found again for two hundred years. From the 1870s to 1903 Malaitan men, and some women, formed the largest number of Solomon Islander workers in the indentured labour trade to Queensland and Fiji, which began with illegal recruiting known as blackbirding. Returning labourers had often learnt to read and become Christian, and the Queensland Kanaka Mission sent its first party to the Solomons in 1904.

There was no central power on the island, and blood feuds were made worse by guns. Britain proclaimed the British Solomon Islands Protectorate in 1893, and Auki became a government station in 1909. District Commissioner William R. Bell was killed by a Kwaio in 1927, with a cadet and 13 Solomon Islanders in his charge. A punitive expedition followed, known as the Malaita massacre, in which at least 60 Kwaio were killed, nearly 200 detained at Tulagi and many sacred sites destroyed or desecrated.

After the Second World War, Malaitans who had served in battalions started Maasina Ruru, or Marching Rule, a movement for self-determination that united people across religious, ethnic and clan lines and refused to cooperate with the British. In September 1947 most of its chiefs were tried in Honiara and convicted. The creation of the Malaita Council, the first local government in the Solomon Islands, eased tensions.

Malaita had a population of 172,740 in 2019. Its largest city and provincial capital is Auki, on the northwest coast. Most Malaitans live by subsistence farming, with taro and sweet potatoes the main crops, and shell money made in the Langa Langa lagoon remains a traditional currency.
malang: Malang, historically known as Tumapel, lies in the south of Java at about 506 metres above sea level, which gives it a mild climate. In the Pleistocene the area was a deep basin ringed by volcanoes, uninhabited because of the lava flows, which filled in the rainy season to form an ancient swamp and lakes. The origin of the name is uncertain. One theory derives it from Malangkuçeçwara, a temple of tradition whose name is read as God has destroyed the false and enforced the right. The name Malang first appears in the Pamotoh or Ukirnegara Inscription of 1198, found in 1975.

The Dinoyo inscription of 760 is the main early document for the area. It was long taken as showing that the Hindu kingdom of King Gajayana, called Kanjuruhan, began government in Malang in the 8th century, and it gives the date as 28 November 760. A newer inscription found in 1986 has not yet been deciphered. The city was later the capital of Singhasari, in 1222.

Under the Dutch, Malang was modernised, and its climate and nearness to the port of Surabaya made it popular with Europeans. The railway reached it in 1879, which encouraged industry, and on 1 April 1914 it became a gemeente, a municipality. The Imperial Japanese Army occupied it on 7 March 1942, and the Dutch troop headquarters on Jalan Semeru became a Japanese security building. Malang joined the Republic of Indonesia on 21 September 1945, and re-entered it on 2 March 1947 after Dutch reoccupation.

Malang is a landlocked city and the second most populous in East Java, with about 3.1 million people in the Malang Valley. Most residents are Javanese, with Madurese and Chinese minorities. Dutch Gothic buildings such as the Kayutangan church and Ijen Cathedral survive, and the Tugu Malang monument stands in the round Alun-alun. Brawijaya University and Malang State University make it known as an educational city, and the Malang Tempo Doeloe Festival preserves its cultural heritage.
malatesta-family: The family's progenitor is said to be Rodolfo of Carpegna, whose fighting spirit earned him the nickname mala testa, bad head, and who from 1004 built a castle on the rock of Pennabilli. In the 11th century the family held lands around Gabicce Mare, Gatteo and Poggio Berni, and Giovanni Malatesta, who died in 1150, was the first to settle in Rimini. His son married into the Traversari, lords of Ravenna and Rimini. The Malatesta became lords of Torriana in 1186 and citizens of Rimini in 1216, and Giovanni's grandsons founded the branches of Sogliano al Rubicone and of Pennabilli and Verucchio.

Malatesta I was podestà of Pistoia in 1228 and of Rimini in 1239 and 1247 and supported Emperor Frederick II, but his son Malatesta da Verucchio went over to the Guelphs after the emperor's defeat near Parma in 1248. In 1295 he made himself sole master of Rimini after expelling the rival Ghibelline Parcitadi. His son Giovanni murdered his wife Francesca da Polenta and his brother Paolo in 1285, a crime recorded in Dante's Inferno and by Giovanni Boccaccio. In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries the family ruled Pesaro, Fano, Cesena, Fossombrone and Cervia, and at its height reached Ascoli Piceno and the territories of Bergamo and Brescia.

Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta fought the papacy over territorial claims and his rival Federico da Montefeltro, and lost almost all his lands except Rimini, which he held with the support of the Republic of Venice. His grandson Pandolfo was driven out of Rimini by Cesare Borgia in 1500, and after a last failed attempt by Pandolfo's son Sigismondo the city was absorbed into the Papal States in 1528.

Many Malatesta served as condottieri for Italian states, and the family remained a source of them in the 16th and 17th centuries. Malatesta Novello built the Malatestiana Library at Cesena between 1447 and 1452, and from 1450 Sigismondo built the Tempio Malatestiano, the cathedral of Rimini. The Sogliano branch died out in 1640, the last of the Rimini branch was the Jesuit Roberto Malatesta, who died in 1708, and the Ghiaggiolo branch ended with Lamberto in 1757.
malatya: Malatya lies in Eastern Anatolia, and its name is thought to come from the Hittite word melid or milit, "honey". Over time it has been called Malidiya in Hittite, Meliddu in Akkadian, Meliṭeia in Urartian and Melitene in Roman times. The ruins of ancient Melitene lie around Arslantepe in the Battalgazi district. The historical city stayed at Battalgazi, once called Old Malatya, until the 19th century, when it gradually moved to its present site.

Arslantepe has been inhabited for nearly 6,000 years, since the development of agriculture. In the Bronze Age it became the administrative centre of a larger region in the kingdom of Isuwa, and it was heavily fortified. The Hittites conquered it in the 14th century BCE. After the end of the Hittite Empire it became the centre of the Neo-Hittite state of Kammanu, which kept Hittite traditions and styles; archaeologists found a palace within the walls with monumental stone lions and a statue of the ruler. Kammanu was a vassal of Urartu between 804 and 743 BCE. The Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser I made the kingdom of Malidiya pay tribute, and Sargon II sacked the city in 712 BCE.

Under Roman rule the settlement was refounded in 72 CE on a different site as Melitene, the base of the Legio XII Fulminata, which controlled access to southern Armenia and the upper Tigris. Trajan probably gave it city status in the early second century.

In 392 Theodosius I made it the capital of Second Armenia, and the emperors Anastasius and Justinian built its walls in the sixth century. The Sassanids sacked it in 575. It was captured by Arab forces, and in the ninth century the emir Umar al-Aqta made it a major opponent of the Byzantine Empire until he was killed at the Battle of Lalakaon in 863. John Kourkouas took it for the Byzantines in May 934. Its merchants grew very wealthy, but the Seljuks attacked and devastated the city in 1058, and many people were killed or sold into slavery. The Danishmends took it in 1101.

Malatya is the capital of Malatya Province in Eastern Anatolia and a regional centre of industry, education and agriculture. It is one of the most prominent apricot-growing areas in the world and is nicknamed the Land of Apricots. The French archaeologist Louis Delaporte began excavating Arslantepe in the 1930s, and an Italian team has worked at the site since 1961.
malavikagnimitram: The title means Mālavikā and Agnimitra. The play draws on events of the reign of Pushyamitra Shunga, Agnimitra's father, and is a drama in five acts set in Vidisa and its neighbourhood, with King Agnimitra as its hero and Mālavikā, a princess in the service of the chief queen Dharini, as its heroine. It opens with an invocation of Siva, after which the stage-manager and his assistant announce the play, and it contains an elaborate exposition of a theory of music and acting.

The king has seen Mālavikā in a group portrait and the queen keeps her from his sight. With the help of his jester, the Vidushaka Gautama, he provokes a quarrel between the dancing-masters Ganadasa and Haradatta, and a contest between their pupils lets him watch Mālavikā dance. Later, sent by Dharini to touch an Asoka tree with her foot to make it blossom, she is overheard confessing her love, and the jealous second queen Iravati breaks in on the lovers.

Dharini then has Mālavikā and her friend Vakulavalika locked in a cellar, to be released only on sight of the queen's snake-seal ring. The jester pretends to be bitten by a serpent, obtains the ring for his cure and frees them. In the last act captive maids brought back from the war against Vidarbha recognise Mālavikā as the lost sister of Madhavasena; news comes that Agnimitra's son Vasumitra has won a victory while guarding his grandfather's sacrificial horse, and the queen gives Mālavikā to the king.

The play ends with the customary Bharatavakya, here a wish for peace and happiness among the king's subjects. In 1929 Dadasaheb Phalke adapted it as an Indian silent film, Malvikagni Mitra, and Kamlesh Pandey retold it as a comic in the 569th issue of the Indian comic book series Amar Chitra Katha.
malawi: Malawi is a landlocked country in Southeast Africa, bordered by Zambia, Tanzania and Mozambique. The Great Rift Valley runs through it from north to south, and Lake Malawi, also called Lake Nyasa, makes up over three-quarters of its eastern boundary. The lake is about 587 kilometres long and 84 kilometres wide, and the Shire River flows from its southern end to join the Zambezi in Mozambique. South of the lake lie the Shire Highlands, where the Zomba and Mulanje peaks rise. The altitude moderates what would otherwise be an equatorial climate, with rains between November and April.

The name Malawi means 'flames' in Chichewa and Chitumbuka and was chosen by the first president, Hastings Banda, after independence in 1964. It comes from the Maravi, a Bantu ethnic group that emigrated from the southern Congo around 1400.

Before the arrival of Bantu peoples from the north around the 10th century CE, the area had a small population of hunter-gatherers, known in oral tradition as Akafula or BaTwa, who were gradually overtaken by agrarian Bantu peoples. By the 16th century the Bantu groups had established kingdoms such as the Maravi Empire, which reached from north of Nkhotakota to the Zambezi River, and the Nkhamanga. In the 17th century, with the area mostly united under one ruler, people began trading and making alliances with Portuguese traders and soldiers. By the 18th century the empire had broken up.

The Indian Ocean slave trade reached its height in the mid-19th century, when about 20,000 people a year are believed to have been enslaved and taken from Nkhotakota to Kilwa. David Livingstone reached Lake Malawi in 1859 and identified the Shire Highlands as suitable for European settlement.

Anglican and Presbyterian missions followed Livingstone's visit in the 1860s and 1870s, the African Lakes Company was established in 1878, and a British consul took up residence at Blantyre in 1883. To prevent Portuguese occupation, the British government sent Harry Johnston as consul to make treaties with local rulers. In 1891 the area became the British Central African Protectorate, renamed Nyasaland in 1907. Nyasaland became independent under Hastings Banda in 1964.

Malawi is the Republic of Malawi, with its capital and largest city at Lilongwe and its commercial centre at Blantyre. English is the official language, and Chichewa, Chitumbuka and Chiyao are major regional languages. Lake Malawi National Park, listed in 1984, and the Chongoni Rock Art Area, listed in 2006, are its two UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
malawi-congress-party: The party was founded by Orton Chirwa, Nyasaland's first African barrister, soon after his release from Gwelo Prison, together with other leaders of the Nyasaland African Congress, among them Aleke Banda and S. Kamwendo, and in agreement with Hastings Kamuzu Banda, who was still in prison. A new name allowed the movement to work freely, since the old congress had been banned. Chirwa served as its first president until Banda, once released, took over the leadership. In later years affiliate groups grew up around the party, among them Kokoliko, Mighty Tambala Graduates, Born Free and the Malawi Congress Party Diaspora Network.

In the Nyasaland elections of 1961 the party won every seat in the legislature. When Malawi became a republic in 1966 it was declared the only legal party, and for the next 27 years the government and the party were effectively one: all adult citizens had to be members and to carry party cards at all times. The party lost its monopoly in a referendum in 1993 and was heavily defeated in the country's first free elections the following year.

After Banda, the party was led by Gwanda Chakuamba from 1994 to 2003, John Tembo from 2003 to 2013 and then Lazarus Chakwera. It remained a major force in opposition, its support strongest in the central region, home of the Chewa and Nyanja peoples. In 2020 it returned to power within the Tonse Alliance, formed with the United Transformation Movement, the People's Party and others, when Chakwera won the presidential election.
