After the alliance broke up, Chakwera conceded defeat in the 2025 general election to Peter Mutharika of the Democratic Progressive Party.
malay-annals: The original title is Sulalatus Salatin, the Genealogy of Kings. The introduction of the oldest version says it derives from a manuscript called the Hikayat Melayu, perhaps dating from the time of the Malacca Sultanate, which the last sultan, Mahmud Shah, took with him when he fled to Kampar in 1511. Portuguese soldiers seized it in their attack on Johor Lama in 1536 and took it to Goa, and a nobleman, Orang Kaya Sogoh, brought it back to Johor; the historian Abdul Samad Ahmad suggests it came from Gowa in Sulawesi instead, and William Linehan from Gua in Pahang.

On 13 May 1612, under Sultan Alauddin Riayat Shah III, the regent Raja Abdullah commissioned the bendahara Tun Sri Lanang to rewrite and compile it. When the Aceh Sultanate sacked Batu Sawar in 1613 and carried the court into exile, Tun Sri Lanang finished the work in captivity in Aceh.

Written in Classical Malay in Jawi script, the work opens in praise of God, the Prophet Muhammad and his companions and traces the sultans of Malacca to Raja Iskandar Zulkarnain. Its stories include Sang Sapurba's oath with Demang Lebar Daun of Palembang, the strongman Badang, the fall of Singapura to Majapahit after Sri Iskandar Shah wrongly punished a concubine, the founding of Malacca, the career of the bendahara Tun Perak, Hang Tuah and the fairy princess of Mount Ophir. Its account of the Portuguese conquest differs from Portuguese records, which say the siege lasted 15 days and that Ahmad Shah died in battle.

The chronicles carried the Malaccan tradition onward and enshrined the sanctity of the ruler, or daulat, legitimising the absolutist governments of Malacca's successor states, and Johor used them to claim to be the centre of Malay culture. Raffles MS no.18, acquired by Sir Stamford Raffles, is considered the oldest and most faithful version; John Leyden's English translation of it appeared in 1821, and Richard Olaf Winstedt's in 1938. More than 30 manuscripts survive, and in 2001 the work was listed on UNESCO's Memory of the World International Register.
malay-language: Historical linguists agree that the Malayic homeland was probably in western Borneo. A form called Proto-Malayic was spoken there by at least 1000 BCE and is argued to be the ancestor of all later Malayic languages. Its own ancestor, Proto-Malayo-Polynesian, began to break up by at least 2000 BCE, possibly through the southward expansion of Austronesian peoples from Taiwan.

Old Malay, believed to be the ancestor of Classical Malay, was influenced by Sanskrit. The earliest known stone inscription in Old Malay, the Kedukan Bukit inscription, was found on Sumatra near Palembang and is dated 1 May 683, written in the Pallava variety of the Grantha alphabet. Srivijaya, a maritime empire based on Sumatra from the 7th to the 11th centuries, spread Old Malay through the Malay Peninsula and Archipelago, where it served as the lingua franca of traders in ports and marketplaces.

The Terengganu Inscription Stone, dated approximately to 1303 CE and written in Jawi script, is considered the earliest evidence of Classical Malay. Its ruler urges his subjects to uphold Islam and sets out ten basic laws. Classical Malay came into wide use as a lingua franca under the Malacca Sultanate (1402 to 1511), a hub of trade and Islamic learning. Islamic literature brought a large infusion of Arabic vocabulary, alongside continued influence from Sanskrit and Tamil.

After the Portuguese captured Malacca in 1511 the court re-established itself as the Johor Sultanate and kept Classical Malay as its literary and administrative language, while literary centres dispersed to Aceh, Java, Makassar, the Moluccas and Champa. In the 19th century the Dutch and British, divided by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824, both used Malay as a tool of centralisation and modernisation.

Before Arabic script arrived, Malay was written in the Pallava, Kawi and Rencong scripts. From the era of the Kingdom of Pasai and the golden age of Malacca, Jawi gradually replaced them. From the 17th century, under Dutch and British influence, the Latin script Rumi gradually replaced Jawi.

Malay is an Austronesian pluricentric macrolanguage, native to several islands of Maritime Southeast Asia and the Malay Peninsula. It is an official language of Brunei, Malaysia and Singapore, where its standard form is Standard Malay, and Indonesian, an autonomous standard, is the official language of Indonesia. It is spoken as a first language by about 80 million people and as a first or second language by close to 300 million. Latin script is official in Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, and Jawi is co-official with it in Brunei and Malaysia.
malay-peninsula: The peninsula runs approximately north to south, and at its end, Tanjung Piai, lies the southernmost point of the Asian continental mainland. It contains Peninsular Malaysia, Southern Thailand and the southernmost tip of Myanmar, at Kawthaung. Singapore, an island country, has historical and cultural ties with the region. The Titiwangsa Mountains, part of the Tenasserim Hills system, form the backbone of the peninsula. The Kra Isthmus is its narrowest point, the Strait of Malacca separates it from the Indonesian island of Sumatra, and the Straits of Johor separate its south coast from Singapore.

Ancient and medieval sources name the peninsula in various ways. Some scholars think that Malayadvipa, mentioned in the ancient Indian text the Vayu Purana, may refer to it. An inscription on the south wall of the Brihadeeswarar Temple records Malaiur, a kingdom with a strong mountain for its rampart. Ptolemy's Geographia names a region of the Golden Chersonese as Maleu-kolon, and the Tabula Rogeriana of Muhammad al-Idrisi shows a long island called Malai. Chinese chronicles of the Yuan dynasty mention Ma-li-yu-er, a nation threatened by the southward expansion of the Sukhothai Kingdom under King Ram Khamhaeng, and Marco Polo refers to Malauir.

The Malay term Tanah Melayu, meaning the Malay land, appears in texts from the early 17th century, notably the Hikayat Hang Tuah, where it refers to the area under the dominion of the Malacca Sultanate. The Negarakertagama, written in 1365, calls the area Hujung Medini. The Portuguese apothecary Tomé Pires, who stayed in Malacca from 1512 to 1515, used the form Terra de Tana Malaio for south-eastern Sumatra, where the deposed sultan Mahmud Shah established his exiled government.

In the early 20th century, during the rise of Malay nationalism, Tanah Melayu was used for the idea of uniting all the Malay states of the peninsula under one nation. The ambition was largely realised in 1948 with the formation of the Federation of Malaya.

The peninsula is covered with tropical moist broadleaf forests, with dipterocarp trees in the lowlands and evergreen trees on the mountains. Its fauna includes the Asian elephant, tiger, sun bear and Malayan tapir. The Kangar-Pattani floristic boundary crosses it in southern Thailand and the far north of Malaysia, marking the boundary between the biogeographic region of Indochina to the north and Sundaland and Malesia to the south. Extensive mangroves line both coasts.
malayalam-language: The origin of Malayalam is disputed. The mainstream view holds that it descends from a western coastal dialect of early Middle Tamil, which began to separate in the 8th century and became distinct between the 9th and 13th centuries. The Western Ghats isolate the Malabar Coast, and Sanskrit and Prakrit influence from the Nambudiri Brahmins helped the dialect to diverge. A second view, generally rejected by historical linguists, holds that Tamil and Malayalam developed separately from a common ancestor. Some scholars treat the Quilon Syrian copper plates of 849 or 850 CE as the oldest inscription in Old Malayalam, though others regard the language of such inscriptions as a variety of Tamil. The Malayalam calendar dates from 825 CE.

Malayalam is the majority language of Kerala and an official language in Kerala, Lakshadweep and Mahé in Puducherry. At the census of 2011 there were 32,413,213 speakers in Kerala. Its word order is subject-object-verb, and verbs are conjugated for tense, mood and aspect but not for person, gender or number. It has borrowed most from Sanskrit and later English, and also from Arabic, Dutch, Persian, Portuguese and Syriac. Besides its own script it has been written in others: Suriyani Malayalam, in a Syriac script, was used by the Saint Thomas Christians until the 20th century, and Arabi Malayalam, in an Arabic script, until the early 20th century.

Folk songs, the oldest literary form, were oral. The Ramacharitam, of the late 12th or early 13th century, is the oldest extant work distinct from the Tamil tradition. Middle Malayalam was shaped by Manipravalam, a blend of Tamil and Sanskrit whose name means ruby-coral. Cherusseri Namboothiri's Krishnagatha, written for the court of Udaya Varman Kolathiri in the 15th century, appears to be the first work in the present-day language. In the 16th century Thunchaththu Ezhuthachan wrote the Adhyathmaramayanam Kilippattu. The first travelogue in any Indian language is the Malayalam Varthamanappusthakam, by Paremmakkal Thoma Kathanar in 1785. Later writers include Thakazhi Sivasankara Pillai, M. T. Vasudevan Nair, Vaikom Muhammed Basheer and Arundhati Roy.
malayan-communist-party: Communist youth leagues had appeared among Chinese students in Pahang towns such as Raub and Bentong in the mid-1920s. In April 1930 the South Seas Communist Party was dissolved and replaced by the Communist Party of Malaya, which also worked in Thailand and the Dutch East Indies. Illegal under British rule, it was nearly destroyed on 29 April 1930, when a police raid on a house at 24 Nassim Road in Singapore took eight of its founders. It still gained ground in the unions, leading a strike at the Batu Arang coal mine in 1935.

After Japan invaded China in 1937 the party drew on anti-Japanese feeling among Malayan Chinese, and by mid-1939 it claimed about 40,000 members. Its Secretary-General from April 1939, Lai Teck, was a British agent. When Japan invaded in December 1941, British instructors trained about 165 cadres in guerrilla warfare, and the party's Malayan People's Anti-Japanese Army grew to over 6,000 fighters. In September 1942 the Japanese, informed by Lai Teck, ambushed its leaders at Batu Caves. Lai Teck fled with party funds in 1947, and Chin Peng took his place.

After the killing of plantation managers in Perak, the government declared an emergency on 16 June 1948 and banned the party on 23 July. Its fighters, renamed the Malayan National Liberation Army in February 1949, reached about 4,000 by 1950, supported by the Min Yuen underground. The resettlement of 500,000 rural Chinese into guarded New Villages under the Briggs Plan cut off their food and shelter, and the Baling Talks of 1955 with Tunku Abdul Rahman failed when the government refused to legalise the party.

From the Thai border the party resumed armed struggle in 1969, helped by the Suara Revolusi Malaya radio service broadcasting from Hunan until 1981, but purges and splits weakened it in the 1970s. On 2 December 1989 it signed separate peace agreements with Malaysia and Thailand at Hat Yai and dissolved the same day. Because of its history, communism has remained a taboo political subject in both Malaysia and Singapore.
malayan-emergency: The economic disruption of the Second World War left British Malaya with unemployment, low wages and rising food prices, and trade unions and the Malayan Communist Party grew. Communists organised a 24-hour general strike on 29 January 1946 and 300 strikes in 1947. The British used police and soldiers as strikebreakers, and on 12 June 1948 they banned the PMFTU, Malaya's largest trade union.

On 17 June 1948, in the Sungai Siput incident, three European plantation managers were killed at the Elphil Estate by three young Chinese men suspected to be communists. The authorities declared a state of emergency; the British used the word Emergency to avoid calling it a war, because London-based insurers would not pay out in cases of civil war.

Chin Peng, the party's leader, and his allies fled into the jungle and formed the Malayan National Liberation Army (MNLA) on 1 February 1949. It was partly a re-formation of the Malayan Peoples' Anti-Japanese Army, which the British had helped form in 1942.

The MNLA attacked military and police outposts and sabotaged rubber plantations and tin mines. 12 million ethnic Chinese in Malaya, who were denied equal voting rights and were usually poor, and its supply network, the Min Yuen, also gathered intelligence. In the first two years British forces conducted a campaign of sweeps, cordons, deportations and capital charges, a campaign marked by heavy coercion of civilians.

The Briggs Plan forcibly relocated civilians into new villages, and food rationing, the killing of livestock and aerial spraying of herbicide were used to starve the guerrillas. British troops killed unarmed villagers at Batang Kali, and a headhunting scandal over decapitated bodies followed in 1952.

In 1951 the MNLA adopted the October Resolution, reducing attacks on economic targets and civilians in favour of political organisation. Australian ground forces joined in 1955, and troops from New Zealand, Fiji, Kenya, Nyasaland and Northern and Southern Rhodesia also served. On 8 September 1955 the Federation's government, under Chief Minister Tunku Abdul Rahman, offered amnesty to the communists but rejected negotiations.

Malaya became independent on 31 August 1957, and the Emergency was declared over in 1960. Security forces killed 6,710 MNLA guerrillas, and 1,346 Malayan troops and police, 1,443 British personnel and 2,478 civilians died; some 11,000 people died in all. The MNLA never numbered more than 8,000 at a time.

After 1960 it withdrew to the Malaysia–Thailand border, and Chin Peng renewed the insurgency against the Malaysian government in 1968, after an ambush at Kroh–Betong on 17 June; it lasted until the party dissolved in 1989. In the late 1960s coverage of the My Lai massacre prompted inquiries in Britain into Batang Kali, and the British government agreed to investigate in 2009.
malayan-peoples-anti-japanese-army: Anti-Japanese feeling among the Chinese of Malaya grew from the invasion of Manchuria in 1931 and Japan's war on China in 1937. The Malayan Communist Party offered the British co-operation in July 1941 and was refused, but after the Japanese invasion of 8 December 1941 the British accepted on 18 December. The party would recruit and the British would train: 165 party members went through rushed ten-day courses in sabotage and guerrilla warfare at the 101 Special Training School in Singapore, run by the Special Operations Executive, from 21 December 1941.

Cut off after the fall of Singapore, the guerrillas fought for bare survival, and an estimated third of the force died within 18 months. The party's secretary-general, Lai Teck, was a double agent of the British Special Branch who after his arrest in March 1942 also worked for the Kempeitai. At his meeting near the Batu Caves, Japanese forces attacked at daybreak on 1 September 1942 and killed 92 members, among them 29 senior party officials. Younger leaders such as Chin Peng and Liao Wei-chung, known as Colonel Itu, took their place, and the force grew to over 7,000 by the end of 1944.

Force 136 landed Colonel John Davis on the Perak coast on 24 May 1943, and on 1 January 1944 the guerrillas agreed at Bukit Bidor to take British orders for arms, money and supplies and to disarm after the war. Air drops began only in December 1944. After the surrender of 15 August 1945 the army seized territory and punished collaborators, many of them Malay policemen, which led to clashes between Chinese and Malays. It was dissolved on 1 December 1945, when 6,800 guerrillas handed in 5,497 weapons, mostly old ones.

The army had eight independent regiments of 400 to 500 members under the Central Military Committee of the party; the 5th Regiment in Perak was the strongest. Members called one another comrade, Mandarin was its common language, and many were not communists but had joined out of anger at the Japanese treatment of civilians. Historians disagree on its aims: Cheah Boon Kheng and the authors of Rehearsal for War argue that the party was preparing to fight the British, while Lee Ting Hui holds that its only wartime target was the Japanese.
malaysia-agreement: Before World War II, British Malaya consisted of the Federated Malay States, five Unfederated Malay States and the crown colony of the Straits Settlements. The Malayan Union of 1946 was replaced by the Federation of Malaya on 1 February 1948, which became independent on 31 August 1957, while Singapore stayed a crown colony. The United Nations had declared in Resolution 1514 of 1960 that colonialism should be brought to a speedy end, and a joint British and Malayan statement of 23 November 1961 held that the views of the peoples of North Borneo and Sarawak must first be found out.

A five-man Commission of Enquiry under Lord Cobbold, two Malayans and three British representatives, was appointed in January 1962 and reported on 1 August 1962 in favour of Malaysia, stressing that all parties should enter as equal partners. In a private letter to Prime Minister Harold Macmillan, Cobbold wrote that a federation without Singapore would have few attractions. In Singapore the People's Action Party, weakened by the split that created the Barisan Sosialis in 1961, held a referendum in 1962 to win a new mandate for merger.

The agreement, formally the Agreement relating to Malaysia, provided for the union of North Borneo (Sabah), Sarawak and Singapore with the states of the Federation of Malaya. Britain undertook to give up its sovereignty over the three territories, which it did through the Malaysia Act 1963. Several provisions were written for Singapore to meet objections that it would have fewer federal seats than its population warranted and would pay 40% of its revenue to the federal government. Brunei sent a delegation but did not sign, over the Sultan's wish to be senior ruler, the sharing of oil revenue and the Brunei revolt.

Kelantan's government sued on 11 September 1963 to have the agreement declared void, but Chief Justice Sir James Thomson dismissed the suit. Singapore left Malaysia on 9 August 1965. Many academics and politicians later argued that the safeguards promised to Sabah and Sarawak had been eroded. A constitutional amendment in force from 11 February 2022 recognised the agreement in the federal constitution, and on 17 October 2025 the High Court at Kota Kinabalu ruled that the federal government had acted unlawfully in failing to honour Sabah's entitlement to 40% of the federal revenue derived from the state.
malaysian-chinese-association: The Malayan Chinese Association was formed on 27 February 1949 with the implicit support of the British colonial administration, chiefly to manage the welfare of people interned in the New Villages created under the Briggs Plan. Its declaration as a political party in 1951 was written by the Straits Chinese businessman Tan Cheng Lock, its first president. Early members were mostly landowners and businessmen, while working people in the New Villages largely joined the Socialist Front. Many leading members, such as Leong Yew Koh and Henry H.S. Lee, were also Kuomintang members opposed to the Malayan Communist Party.

In 1952 the party allied with the United Malays National Organisation for the Kuala Lumpur municipal elections, the start of the Alliance Party, which the Malaysian Indian Congress joined in 1954. In 1955 the Alliance won 51 of 52 seats, the MCA all 15 of its own. Lim Chong Eu, president from 1958, quarrelled with Tunku Abdul Rahman over seat numbers and resigned. Tan Siew Sin, son of Tan Cheng Lock, led the party from 1961. In 1969, challenged by the new Democratic Action Party and Gerakan, it won only 13 of the 33 seats it contested, and the election was followed by the May 13 Riots.

When the Alliance widened into Barisan Nasional, the party lost standing beside UMNO. In 1982 Lee San Choon led it to 24 of its 28 allocated parliamentary seats. The Deposit-Taking Cooperatives begun by Tan Koon Swan ended in a scandal that cost depositors an estimated RM3.6 billion. Ling Liong Sik, president from 1986, rebuilt its finances, founded Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman in 2001 and won 30 of its 34 allocated parliamentary seats in 1995. Factional quarrels between Team A and Team B followed, and the purchase of Nanyang Siang Pau through Huaren Holdings drew public protests.

After its losses in 2008, the party won only 7 of the 37 parliamentary seats it contested in 2013 and for a time had no cabinet minister, for the first time since independence, until Liow Tiong Lai led it back into government. In 2018 it kept one parliamentary seat and went into opposition with Barisan Nasional. It returned to government in March 2020 alongside Perikatan Nasional, and after the 2022 election, in which it won two seats, it sat on the government backbench without cabinet posts.
malaysian-indian-congress: John Thivy, who had met Mahatma Gandhi in London while studying law, founded the party in August 1946 to work for Indian independence, and took the word Congress from the Indian National Congress. After India became independent in 1947 the party turned to the independence of Malaya. Unlike most Indians in the country it opposed the Malayan Union, and it later joined the All-Malaya Council of Joint Action under Tun Tan Cheng Lock against the Federation of Malaya Agreement.

Its early leaders, Thivy, Baba Budh Singh Ji, K. Ramanathan and Kundan Lal Devaser, were of North Indian or Malayalee origin, while most Indians in Malaya were Tamil plantation labourers whose wages, about 50 cents a day, rose and fell with rubber prices. Defeated in the 1952 Kuala Lumpur Municipal Elections alongside the Independence of Malaya Party, the party joined the Alliance in 1954. In March 1955 the Tamil daily Tamil Murasu urged Tamils to boycott it, and Devaser stepped down.

Tun V. T. Sambanthan, elected president in May 1955, recruited plantation workers by touring estates and by promoting the Tamil language, Hinduism in its South Indian form and Tamil culture, and under him the party became in effect a conservative Tamil party. It was the weakest of the three Alliance parties, with the smallest electorate, 7.4% in 1959. Sambanthan took part in the negotiations with the Reid Commission on the constitution, and in 1963, when Malaysia was formed, the party took the name Malaysian Indian Congress.

V. Manickavasagam, president from 1973 to 1978, saw the Alliance become the Barisan Nasional and set up the MIC Education Fund and the Nesa Multipurpose Cooperative. Samy Vellu led the party from 1979 to 2010; in 1984 it founded the Maju Institute of Education Development and in 2001 AIMST University. In the 2008 election Indian voters turned against the party and the Barisan Nasional, Vellu lost his seat, and support shifted to the Democratic Action Party and the People's Justice Party.
malaysian-new-economic-policy: Under British rule the profits of tin mining, which drew Chinese miners from the 1820s, were shared mainly between the British and the Chinese, while rubber estates worked largely by labour from India were dominated by British firms such as Dunlop, Guthrie and Harrisons & Crossfield. Colonial policy kept the indigenous population in subsistence farming. Up to 1970 the poverty rate stood at 49%, and indigenous communities held less than 3% of the economy.
After the riots of 1969 Parliament was suspended and the National Operations Council, chaired by Tun Abdul Razak, governed. The policy was announced in the Second Malaysia Plan of 1971 to 1975.

The policy aimed both to cut absolute poverty for all Malaysians and to end the identification of race with economic function and place. Ownership was to move from a ratio of 2.4:33:63 between Bumiputra, other Malaysians and foreigners to 30:40:30, a target proposed by Ismail Abdul Rahman when the government could not agree on a goal. Growth was meant to let the Bumiputra share rise without shrinking the others in absolute terms, the so-called expanding pie. Initial public offerings had to set aside 30% of shares for Bumiputra investors, public universities admitted them by quota until 2002, and from 1975 the Heavy Industries Corporation of Malaysia promoted heavy industry.

Bumiputra wealth rose from 4% in 1970 to about 20% in 1997, and absolute poverty fell from 50% to 6.8%, though what part the policy played is unclear. Between 1970 and 1990 the Bumiputra share of engineers rose from 7 to 35 per cent and of doctors from 4 to 28 per cent. The share of non-Bumiputra in national wealth also passed 40%, while Malaysian Indians and the Orang Asli remained among the poorest.

Critics have argued that the policy was based on race rather than need, favoured wealthy Bumiputra and encouraged emigration by non-Malays. Tunku Abdul Rahman wrote in the 1980s that the target was pursued without regard to the ability to reach it. After 1990 much of it continued under the National Development Policy, and in 2006 a report by the Asian Strategic and Leadership Institute that put Bumiputra equity at 45% against an official 18.9% set off a public dispute before it was withdrawn.
malbork: Malbork lies on the Nogat river in the region of Powiśle, in the Pomeranian Voivodeship of northern Poland. The river and the flat terrain allowed barges to reach the town a hundred kilometres from the sea. The town grew around the fortress Ordensburg Marienburg, founded in 1274 on the east bank of the Nogat by the Teutonic Knights. Both castle and town were named for their patron saint, the Virgin Mary, and are called Marienburg in German and Malbork in Polish.

Under the Teutonic Order the town collected tolls on river traffic and the Order held a monopoly on the amber trade. The town later joined the Hanseatic League. After the Battle of Grunwald the Order was greatly weakened, and the Teutonic Knights burned the town in 1410 before the Polish and Lithuanian siege of the castle, which failed. In the Thirteen Years' War the Order pawned the castle to its soldiers from Bohemia, who sold it in 1457 to King Casimir IV of Poland. The town resisted for three more years under Mayor Bartholomäus Blume, who was hanged and quartered when it fell.

From 1457 to 1772 the castle was one of the royal residences of Poland, and from 1568 it housed the Polish Admiralty. In 1710, during the Great Northern War, half the population died of cholera. The First Partition of Poland brought the town to Prussia in 1772. Near the end of the Second World War the town was declared a fortress and almost completely destroyed in fighting between German forces and the Red Army, which lasted until 9 March 1945. In June 1945 it was handed to Polish authorities and renamed Malbork, and the remaining German population was expelled.

Malbork Castle was built over nearly 230 years and is in fact three castles combined in one. It is the world's largest brick castle and Europe's largest Gothic fortress. More than half of it was destroyed in the war, and restoration has been ongoing since. The castle and its museum are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Other sights include the Gothic church of St John the Baptist, the Gothic town hall and parts of the medieval town walls.
malbork-castle: The Teutonic Order had been founded in 1191 in Acre, and after that stronghold fell to the Muslims in 1291 it moved its headquarters to Venice before arriving in Prussia. The castle was built after the conquest of Old Prussia, and its main purpose was to strengthen the Order's control after it suppressed the Great Prussian Uprising of the Baltic tribes in 1274. Work lasted until around 1300 under Commander Heinrich von Wilnowe, and it was named Marienburg for Mary, patron saint of the Order. The castle stands on the south-eastern bank of the Nogat.

The castle grew in importance after the conquest of Gdańsk and Eastern Pomerania in 1308, when the Order's administrative centre moved there from Elbing. Grand Master Siegfried von Feuchtwangen, who came from Venice, undertook the next phase of building and in 1309 relocated his headquarters to Marienburg. The complex has three separate castles, the High, Middle and Lower, divided by dry moats and towers, on a site of nearly 21 hectares, and once housed about 3,000 brothers in arms. The Order collected river tolls, held a monopoly on the amber trade, and the town's membership in the Hanseatic League brought Hanseatic meetings there. Most historians accept the years from 1274 to 1406 as the construction period.

After the defeat at Grunwald in the summer of 1410, Heinrich von Plauen led the defence in a siege during which the town outside was razed. By 1456, in the Thirteen Years' War, the Order was in severe financial distress. Its Bohemian mercenaries, long unpaid, agreed to sell the castle, and in 1457 King Casimir IV Jagiellon entered it in triumph. For over 300 years the castle served as a Polish royal residence, home to the Polish Admiralty from 1568, a royal mint from 1584 and the Commonwealth's largest arsenal. Swedish forces occupied it in 1626 and 1629 and again from 1656 to 1660.

After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 the castle became a Prussian barracks and poorhouse, and in 1794 the architect David Gilly surveyed it. His son Friedrich Gilly's engravings, published from 1799 to 1803, led the Prussian public to rediscover it, and after the Napoleonic Wars it became a symbol of Prussian history. Restoration began in 1816 under Theodor von Schön. In the early 1930s the Nazis used it as a pilgrimage destination, and fighting with the Red Army in early 1945 destroyed more than half of it. Restoration has been ongoing since 1962, and UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in December 1997.
malbrough-sen-va-t-en-guerre: The song is a burlesque lament on the death of John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough, written on a false rumour of his death after the Battle of Malplaquet in 1709, the bloodiest battle of the War of the Spanish Succession. Marlborough in fact lived until 1722. It tells how his wife, waiting for his return from the war, receives the news that her husband has died, how he was buried, and how a nightingale sang over his grave. For years it was known only by tradition, and it does not appear among the many anecdotal songs printed in France in the middle of the 18th century.

Pierre Beaumarchais used the tune in his 1778 play The Marriage of Figaro for a despairing love song sung by Cherubino, and in 1780 Carl Stamitz ended a sonata for viola d'amore and viola with it while in Paris. When Prince Louis-Joseph, son of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, was born in 1781, his wet nurse Geneviève Poitrine sang it while rocking his cradle. The queen took it up, the king and the court followed, and it was sung in the state apartments, kitchens and stables of Versailles. Nicolas Dalayrac quoted it in the first act of his opera Renaud d'Ast in 1787.

From the court it passed to the tradespeople of Paris and on from town to town and country to country. It became as popular in England as in France, and Johann Wolfgang von Goethe is said to have come to hate Marlborough because he heard the tune everywhere on his travels in France. In Spain, through the Bourbon nobility, the name became Mambrú and children sang it while playing hopscotch; Fernando Sor wrote variations on it for guitar in 1826, and from Spain it reached Latin America.

The craze faded slowly after the French Revolution, though Napoleon is said to have hummed the tune while crossing the Memel in June 1812. In the United Kingdom the melody was sung by the mid-19th century with the words For He's a Jolly Good Fellow, which were familiar in America by 1862, and it also became the tune of The Bear Went Over the Mountain. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published an English version, and Ludwig van Beethoven used the tune for the French in Wellington's Victory.
malchow: Malchow is a municipality in the Mecklenburgische Seenplatte district of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. It lies on the river Elde, 25,5 kilometres west of Waren and 35 kilometres north of Wittstock. The old town stands on an island between the Plauer See and the Fleesensee, and the surrounding landscape is one of lakes of the Mecklenburgische Seenplatte and the woods of the Müritz National Park.

In the Middle Ages the site was a centre of Slavic paganism. It was sacked by Saxons in 1147, during the Wendish Crusade against the Polabian Slavs, and the same year the German town of Malchow, founded on the island, was first mentioned in writing. It received a town charter under Schwerin Law in 1235. In 1298 Malchow Abbey, a Cistercian nunnery, moved to the south shore of Lake Malchow, opposite the island. Over the following centuries the town expanded to the mainland in the north-west, linked to the original settlement by a succession of bridges, and the mainland settlement gradually came to predominate.

A munitions factory of the Alfred Nobel Co. was established there in 1938, during the Nazi period, and during the World War II hundreds of prisoners of war, as well as women and children, were used there as forced labour. In 1943 the Ravensbrück concentration camp extended to Malchow, and over the next two years many inmates, including numerous Hungarian Jewish women, died there in appalling conditions. After the war the Soviet occupation authorities accused some 30 teenage residents of anti-Soviet activities, and 12 of them eventually lost their lives in Soviet captivity or were executed.

After the reunification of Germany in 1990 the historic town centre was extensively restored. The former Cistercian abbey now houses the Mecklenburg Organ Museum. Among the people connected with the town are Dietrich von Müller, a lieutenant general of the Wehrmacht (1891–1961), and Konrad von Finckenstein, born in 1945, a Canadian judge and public servant.
malcolm-ii-of-scotland: Máel Coluim mac Cinaeda, anglicised Malcolm II, was a son of King Kenneth II and a grandson of Malcolm I. The Prophecy of Berchán says his mother was a woman of Leinster. Succession among Scottish kings of the time often involved murder, and Malcolm killed Kenneth III in 1005 in a battle at Monzievaird in Strathearn. The Irish annals call him ard rí Alban, high king of Scotland, though the geographical area of modern Scotland also held a king of Strathclyde in the south-west, Norse–Gaels kings on the western coast and the Hebrides, and the kings or mormaers of Moray, his nearest and most dangerous rivals.

The first reliable report of the reign is an attack in 1006 on the lands of the Northumbrian rulers of Bamburgh, perhaps the customary raid of a new king, which included a siege of Durham. According to the Annals of Ulster it ended in a heavy defeat by Uhtred of Bamburgh. A second war, probably in 1018, went better. At the Battle of Carham, by the River Tweed, the Scots under Malcolm and the men of Strathclyde under their king, Owain Foel, were victorious. A twelfth-century tract claims that Eadwulf Cudel, Uhtred's brother, then surrendered Lothian to Malcolm.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle reports that Cnut the Great led an army into Scotland on his return from a pilgrimage to Rome. It dates this to 1031, though there are reasons to place it in 1027. The Burgundian chronicler Rodulfus Glaber describes Malcolm as powerful in resources and arms and very Christian, and says the two made peace. Cnut came away with a promise of peace and friendship, and the Chronicle remarks that Malcolm kept to the submission only a little while.

Malcolm had no surviving sons. He arranged marriages for his daughters with the regional dynasties that might otherwise have rivalled him. Bethóc married Crínán of Dunkeld, and a daughter named Donada is said by later writers to have married Finlay of Moray, father of Macbeth.

Marianus Scotus gives the date of Malcolm's death as 25 November 1034, and the king lists place it at Glamis Castle. The Annals of Tigernach call him the honour of all the west of Europe, while later accounts say he was killed fighting bandits. His grandson Duncan I succeeded him as his chosen heir and reigned for five years and nine months. Tradition from the time of John of Fordun, if not earlier, called a Pictish stone at Glamis King Malcolm's grave stone.
malcolm-iii-of-scotland: Malcolm was the son of Duncan I, who became king in late 1034 and was killed in battle in Moray on 15 August 1040 by a force under Macbeth. Malcolm and his brother Donald were probably children. Later tradition says they were sent away for safety, Malcolm to England, but neither the place of exile nor the fact of it is certain; Orkney, Ireland and Strathclyde have also been suggested. Later tradition, attested by the fifteenth century, made his mother the daughter of the miller of Forteviot.

Chroniclers report that Malcolm killed Macbeth at Lumphanan in Aberdeenshire on 15 August 1057. Macbeth's stepson Lulach was crowned at Scone, probably on 8 September 1057, and was killed by Malcolm "by treachery" near Huntly on 23 April 1058.

Malcolm's kingdom did not cover all of modern Scotland: many islands and the land north of the River Oykel were Scandinavian, and south of the Firth of Forth lay independent or semi-independent realms. In 1061 the Scots plundered Lindisfarne. In 1068 Malcolm gave asylum to English exiles fleeing William of Normandy, among them Edgar Ætheling and his sisters Margaret and Cristina. By the end of 1070 he had married Margaret, later Saint Margaret. Their sons were given English royal names, including Edward and Edmund, and also Alexander and David, the later kings Alexander I and David I.

In 1072 William came north, and at Abernethy Malcolm became his man, as the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle puts it, and handed over his eldest son Duncan as a hostage. Raids into Northumbria followed. In 1080 William's son Robert Curthose marched north and Malcolm again made peace. In 1091 Malcolm besieged Newcastle, then withdrew before William Rufus's army and again acknowledged English overlordship. A tradition in the Orkneyinga saga gives him an earlier marriage to Ingibiorg, widow of Thorfinn Sigurdsson.

In August 1093 Malcolm travelled to Gloucester, but William Rufus refused to negotiate and insisted that English barons decide the dispute. Malcolm returned north and invaded Northumbria, a ravaging seen as harsh even by the standards of the time. On 13 November 1093 Robert de Mowbray's forces confronted him on his march north, and Robert's steward Morel of Bamburgh killed him. His son Edward was mortally wounded, and Margaret is said to have died soon after hearing the news.

His brother Donald III succeeded him. His body was buried at Tynemouth Priory and later moved north, probably to Dunfermline Abbey. In 1250, after Margaret was canonised, both were reburied beside the altar there. Malcolm secured the line that ruled Scotland until the late thirteenth century, and he is a major character in Shakespeare's Macbeth.
malcolm-x: Malcolm X was born on 19 May 1925 in Omaha, Nebraska, the fourth of seven children of Louise Little, born in Grenada, and the Reverend Earl Little, a Baptist minister. Both parents admired the Pan-African activist Marcus Garvey and led the local branch of his Universal Negro Improvement Association, and they taught their children self-reliance and black pride. In 1946 he was sentenced to eight to ten years in prison for larceny and burglary. There he met a fellow convict, John Bembry, who gave him a voracious appetite for reading, and joined the Nation of Islam, taking the name Malcolm X in place of what he called the white slavemaster name of Little.

After his parole in August 1952 Malcolm X rose quickly in the Nation. He took charge of Temple Number 7 in Harlem in 1954 and became its public face for twelve years, preaching black empowerment and the separation of Black and white Americans, and criticising Martin Luther King Jr. and the mainstream civil rights movement for its emphasis on non-violence and integration. The Federal Bureau of Investigation began watching him in 1953. He is credited with helping the Nation grow from about 1,200 members in the early 1950s to an estimated 50,000 to 100,000 by the early 1960s.

On 8 March 1964 he announced that he was leaving the Nation. He founded Muslim Mosque, Inc., a religious organisation, and the Organization of Afro-American Unity, a secular group advocating Pan-Africanism. In April 1964 he made the Hajj to Mecca, and he then toured Africa.

Throughout 1964 Malcolm X received death threats as his conflict with the Nation intensified. On 21 February 1965 he was shot as he prepared to address the Organization of Afro-American Unity at the Audubon Ballroom in Manhattan. Three Nation of Islam members were convicted, and in 2021 two of the convictions were vacated. Whether others conceived or aided the killing has been debated since.

Apart from his autobiography, written with Alex Haley and published posthumously in 1965, Malcolm X left no published writings, and his philosophy is known from his speeches and interviews. His ideas were an important influence on the Black power movement.
malebo-pool: Malebo Pool is a broad, lake-like widening of the lower Congo River, about 35 km long and 23 km wide, covering about 500 square kilometres. It is shallow, mostly 3 to 10 metres deep, and seasonal floods can change its level by up to 3 metres. M'Bamou Island, the largest of its islands, lies at its centre.

The pool is the boundary between the Republic of the Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with Brazzaville on its northern shore and Kinshasa on its southern one. Malebo is the plural of lilebo, the Lingala word for the Borassus palm. The pool was renamed Stanley Pool in 1887 after Henry Morton Stanley and took its present name in January 1972. Upstream the pool marks the start of the navigable Congo toward Kisangani, and downstream the river drops about 300 metres through the Livingstone Falls to the port of Matadi.

The older names include Ntamo, Nkuna and Mpumbu. Olfert Dapper described Pombo as a province under the Makoko, ruler of the Téké, and Jan Vansina reads the name as the northern shore of the pool, the political centre of the Téké kingdom. It is also understood to mean large market. From the sixteenth century the pool was a transshipment point on a trade axis along the Congo. The western zone, from the coast to the pool, relied on overland routes, while the eastern zone upriver produced pottery, salt, ivory, rubber and copal.

The Bobangi moved from the Ubangi to the pool between the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, drawn by its trade, and traded ivory and enslaved people for guns and textiles. Slave exports continued until about 1850 to 1860. In the 1870s they brought 5,000 to 6,000 elephant tusks to the pool, and the river-trade language Lingala spread from their commerce. In 1881 Stanley founded the post of Léopoldville and launched the steamboat L'En Avant. By 1894 forty-three steamers worked the basin, and in 1907 the port handled 16,205 tons of traffic and employed 1,462 workers, 112 of them Europeans.

The pool has a dry season of about three months, from June to August. Palm and papyrus swamps fringe its margins, and the water hyacinth Eichhornia crassipes, an invasive plant, forms dense mats that drift along the channel and displace native vegetation.
malerkotla: Malerkotla lies in the fertile heart of the Malwa region of Punjab, about 45-50 km south of Ludhiana and 35 km south of Sangrur. It is a municipality and the administrative headquarters of Malerkotla district, in the Patiala division. The district was carved out of Sangrur district in 2021. The town is known for its food, mosques, badge-making industry, poets and the ornate tombs of its princely rulers.

Sheikh Sadruddin-i-Jahan, an Afghan known popularly as Baba Haider Sheikh, founded the town in the 15th century, and it was ruled by his Sherwani descendants. He married a daughter of Bahlul Khan Lodi of the Delhi Sultanate, who granted him a broad tract of land along the river basin. According to local records, the fortified city of Kotla was established in 1657 by Bayazid Khan, a descendant of Sheikh Sadruddin, with the permission of the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, after Bayazid had defended him from a tiger. The merger of adjacent settlements formed Malerkotla as the capital of the state.

In 1705 the Mughal governor of Sirhind, Wazir Khan, ordered Guru Gobind Singh's younger sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, aged nine and seven, to be bricked up alive, though other records say they were beheaded. Nawab Sher Mohammad Khan of Malerkotla, a Mughal general who had lost his brother and nephew in the fighting at Chamkaur, protested that the act was against Islam and the Quran and walked out. His cry of anguish is remembered as Haa da Naara. Guru Gobind Singh is said to have blessed the Nawab and the people of Malerkotla with peace. Sikhs later built the Gurudwara Sahib Haw Da Naara in his honour.

Under British rule, a Namdhari uprising was suppressed, and on 17 and 18 January 1872 officials ordered 65 captured rebels executed by cannon without trial. During the partition of India in 1947 there were no riots or bloodshed anywhere in Malerkotla State, whose last Nawab, Iftikhar Ali Khan, kept calm. He remained in India and died in 1982. The state joined India in 1947 and was merged into the Patiala and East Punjab States Union.

Malerkotla is the only Muslim-majority city of Indian Punjab, and Urdu is taught alongside Punjabi in its schools. The Nawab Sher Mohammad Khan Institute of Advanced Studies in Urdu, Persian and Arabic, part of Punjabi University in Patiala, is named after one of the state's founders. The town lies on the Delhi-Jakhal-Dhuri-Ludhiana railway line.
malhar-rao-holkar: Malhar Rao was born on 16 March 1693 in Murum village near Phaltan, in Satara district, to Khandu Ji Holkar, a deshgavda of a Dhangar family. His father died in 1696, and he grew up at Taloda in the castle of his maternal uncle Sardar Bhojrajrao Bargal, who held a cavalry under the Maratha noble Sardar Kadam Bande and soon gave him charge of a cavalry detachment. In 1717 he married his uncle's daughter Gautama Bai, and between 1719 and 1726 he took three more wives.

With Ranoji Scindia and Anandrao Pawar he led the Maratha drive into Malwa. When the Mughals made Jai Singh II of Jaipur governor of Malwa again in 1732-1733, forces led by Holkar defeated him near Mandsaur, and Jai Singh agreed to pay six lakh rupees and cede 28 parganas. Malhar Rao fought at Jalesar, Delhi and Bhopal in 1737, helped take Vasai from the Portuguese in 1739, and from 1748 his position in Malwa was secure.

He helped Safdarjung defeat the Rohillas and Bangash in 1751-1752. At the siege of Kumher Fort in 1754 his only son Khanderao was killed by a cannonball, but rivalry with Jayappa Sindhia led him to accept a treaty with the Jat Maharaja Suraj Mal on 18 May 1754. With Raghunathrao he routed the Mughal emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur at the First Battle of Sikandarabad, took Delhi on 11 August 1757 and Lahore on 20 April 1758. The Afghan general Jahan Khan defeated him at the Second Battle of Sikandarabad in 1760. Historians are divided over his failure to aid Dattaji Scindia and his withdrawal from Panipat, which saved thousands of civilians.

After Panipat he defeated Rajput forces at the Battle of Mangrol and helped restore Maratha power in Central India, including that of Mahadji Scindia. After Khanderao's death he had kept his daughter-in-law Ahilya Bai from committing sati. He died at Alampur on 20 May 1766. His grandson Male Rao ruled Indore under Ahilyabai's regency but died within months, and she then ruled herself. She built his samadhi chhatri at the place of his cremation at Alampur, in Bhind district, and he is counted among the architects of Maratha control over India.
mali: Mali is a landlocked country of 1,240,192 square kilometres in West Africa, the eighth largest in Africa. Its northern borders reach deep into the Sahara Desert, and most of the country lies in the southern Sahara, while southern Mali, where the majority of inhabitants live, is in the Sudanian savanna. The Niger and Senegal rivers run through the south. Late April to early October is the rainy season there, and flooding of the Niger is common, creating the Inner Niger Delta. The Adrar des Ifoghas massif lies in the northeast, and gold, uranium, phosphates, salt and limestone are among its natural resources.

Rock art in the Sahara suggests that northern Mali has been inhabited since about 10,000 BCE, when the Sahara was fertile. Early ceramics from Ounjougou, dating to about 9,400 BCE, are believed to show an independent invention of pottery. Farming took place by 5000 BCE and iron was used by around 500 BCE. In the first millennium BCE Mandé peoples related to the Soninke created early towns along the middle Niger, among them Dia, from around 900 BCE, and Djenné-Djenno, which lasted from around 300 BCE to 900 CE.

Mali was part of three successive West African empires that controlled this trade: the Ghana Empire, the Mali Empire and the Songhai Empire. At its peak in 1300 the Mali Empire was the wealthiest country in Africa, and Mansa Musa is believed to have been one of the wealthiest individuals in history. Medieval Mali was a centre of Islam, culture and knowledge, and Timbuktu became a notable place of education.

The Songhai Empire absorbed the Mali Empire in 1468, and a Saadian army defeated the Songhai in 1591. In the late 19th century France seized control during the Scramble for Africa and made it part of French Sudan. It became independent in 1960, first in a brief federation with Senegal, and then as the Republic of Mali.

Bamako is the capital and largest city. The name Mali comes from the Mali Empire and originally meant hippopotamus, the clan symbol of the Keita dynasty. Most people live in the south, and the Bambara are the largest ethnic group, with the Fulani, Senufo, Malinke, Soninke, Dogon, Songhai and Tuareg among others. Malian musical tradition derives from the griots, the Keepers of Memories, and literary tradition is passed mainly by word of mouth, with jalis reciting histories and stories known by heart.
mali-empire: The empire began as a small Mandinka kingdom at the upper reaches of the Niger River, in the Manding region, which developed in the eleventh and twelfth centuries as the Ghana Empire declined. From at least the beginning of the eleventh century Mandinka kings ruled from the city-state of Ka-ba, today Kangaba, in the name of Ghana. When Ghana's control ended in the twelfth century, the province split into twelve kingdoms.

Sundiata Keita, a warrior-prince of the Keita dynasty, led the combined armies of Mema, Wagadou and the Mandinka city-states against the Sosso king Soumaoro Kanté. They defeated the Sosso army at the Battle of Kirina in about 1235, and Sundiata was declared mansa over the twelve kingdoms. The Kouroukan Fouga, an assembly of clan delegates, set out the empire's constitution. History before the thirteenth century is unclear, since Arab chroniclers and oral traditionalists give conflicting accounts.

After Sundiata's death in about 1255, rulers took the title mansa. In 1285 Sakura, a former slave of the imperial family who had become a general, carried out a coup, and the Keita line returned after his death. Mansa Musa took the throne in about 1312 and made his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324-1326, where his gifts and spending of gold caused significant inflation in Egypt. Ibn Battuta visited the empire in 1352, in the reign of Suleyman, who had deposed his nephew Maghan I in 1341. Suleyman's death ended the Golden Age and began a slow decline.

In 1433-1434 Mali lost Timbuktu to the Tuareg, and the Songhai Empire took Mema in 1465 and Timbuktu in 1468. The Mossi conquered Macina in 1477. Mali was still a sizeable state in the fifteenth century and in the early sixteenth, when Leo Africanus described it, but neighbours cut away at its borders from 1507. In 1599 Mansa Mahmud IV tried to take Djenne after the Moroccan conquest of Songhai and was defeated by Moroccan forces with firearms. He died around 1610, after which no single Keita ruled Manden, and the Keitas became provincial chiefs at Kangaba.

The empire was a loose structure of provinces and vassal states, and the farther from the capital, the weaker the mansa's direct power. Its wealth came from taxing the gold, copper and salt that entered its borders, rather than from direct rule of the gold-producing regions. Most people were farmers. Historians disagree about the site of the capital, placing it at Niani in Guinea, elsewhere on the Niger or even on the upper Gambia. Its spread of language, laws and customs, notably through Dyula traders, left political institutions with Malian structures and terms in West Africa into the colonial period and beyond.
mali-federation: After the May 1958 crisis the colonies of French West Africa were offered a choice between immediate independence and membership of a reorganised French Community, and only Guinea chose independence. In late November 1958 French Sudan, Senegal, Upper Volta and Dahomey declared their intention to form a federation. A congress at Bamako from 28 to 30 December, with Modibo Keïta as its president, produced the name Mali Federation, largely through Léopold Sédar Senghor. Pressure from France and the Ivory Coast kept Upper Volta and Dahomey from ratifying the constitution, so only French Sudan and Senegal remained.

The federation was to rest on parity: a federal assembly of 20 members from each colony, six ministers, three from each, and a single party. Until a president was elected, Keïta was premier and Mamadou Dia of Senegal vice-premier in charge of the armed forces. France, which had resisted the federation, supported it once both countries agreed to remain in the French Community and keep French military bases.

Tensions grew over the powers of a federal executive: French Sudan wanted a single strong executive, Senegal wanted to keep parity. Senghor and Keïta also had different visions, Keïta claiming later that he pursued socialism and Senghor a bourgeois agenda. The crisis came in August 1960, as a federal president was to be elected, and on 19 August Keïta dismissed Dia as defence minister, declared a state of emergency and mobilised the army. Senghor and Dia had the army demobilised and called out the gendarmerie, which surrounded Keïta's house and the government offices. Senegal declared its independence from the federation at a midnight session on 20 August. Little violence occurred, and the Sudanese officials were sent back to Bamako on a sealed train.

On 22 September 1960 Keïta's party renamed the Sudanese Republic Mali and broke its ties with the French Community. Both countries were admitted to the United Nations later that month. Senghor was president of Senegal from 1960 to 1980 and Keïta of Mali from 1960 to 1968. Keïta refused diplomatic relations with Senegal for many years, and Senghor became wary of unification efforts. The railway between the two countries reopened on 22 June 1963, when the two leaders embraced at the border.
malietoa-laupepa: Laupepa was born in 1841 at Sapapaliʻi on Savaiʻi, the son of Malietoa Mōli and Faʻalaitaua Fuatino Suʻapaʻia. Raised in Malie and educated at Malua Seminary, he was known as a devout Christian. He led the Sā Mōlī, based mainly in northern Tuamasaga, and tied himself to Palauli on Savaiʻi by marrying Sisavaiʻi Malupo. He was first crowned in 1875 and fought a long struggle against his uncle Talavou, being made joint king and deputy king before the German, American and British consuls crowned him sole King of Samoa in March 1881.

Ātua and Aʻana refused to accept him and set up their own government at Leulumoega under Tupua Tamasese Titimaea. The Lackawanna Agreement of 12 July 1881, mediated by the US Navy captain J. H. Gillis, kept Laupepa as king with Titimaea as vice-king and Mataʻafa Iosefo as premier. Laupepa petitioned Queen Victoria for protection against German interference in 1883 and twice in 1884, and the German consuls answered by banishing him from Apia and placing Tamasese in his office.

In February 1887 he signed a Deed of Federation with the Kingdom of Hawaii, but no help came. Driven into hiding by the German-backed army, he was forced by Captain Eugen Brandeis to recognise Titimaea on 15 September 1887 and was taken by German warships to Kamerun.

Mataʻafa then led the Malietoa side to victory, but the General Act of Berlin of 14 June 1889 declared Laupepa king again. He returned on 8 November 1889 and at first acknowledged Mataʻafa's title, but his supporters proclaimed him king at Lepea on 4 December 1889. In April 1893 Laupepa drove Mataʻafa from Malie, and after the war of that year Mataʻafa and other leaders were deported to Jaluit in the Marshall Islands.

His defeats and exile had cost him much prestige among Samoans, though he kept the backing of the foreign consuls. He died on the morning of 22 August 1898 and was succeeded by his son Malietoa Tanumafili I. His death was followed by the Second Samoan Civil War, and the conflicts of his reign are the subject of A Footnote to History: Eight Years of Trouble in Samoa.
malietoa-tanumafili-i: Tanumafili was the son of Malietoa Laupepa and Sisavai‘i Malupo Niuva‘ai and attended the London Missionary College at Malua. When his father died in 1898 he was declared King of Samoa (Tafaʻifa) by William Lea Chambers and recognised by Germany, Britain and the United States, with Tupua Tamasese Lealofi I as vice-king. Most of Samoa, including the Germans and the leading orator bodies of Ātua-A‘ana, Savai‘i, Manono and Tuamasaga, rejected the claim; the orator Lauaki Namulau‘ulu Mamoe argued that he was too young and that his installation broke Samoan custom. On 12 November 1898 the Pule and Tumua assemblies declared Matā‘afa Iosefo king instead.

With British and American naval support Tanumafili was declared king on 31 December 1898, but his allies were beaten in the One Day War on 1 January 1899, and he and Tamasese lived aboard a British ship for over two months. Rearmed by the Americans and British, he defeated Matā‘afa and was named king again on 23 March. In June 1899 the three powers abolished the kingship, and the convention signed in Washington on 7 November divided the islands without Samoan consent. Tanumafili left to study in Fiji.

Returning in January 1903, he disappointed many followers by refusing the kingly ‘ava and declaring that the honour once held by Malietoa now belonged to the Kaiser. After Matā‘afa's death on 6 February 1912 he regained support as Fautua and sole Malietoa. When New Zealand took Samoa in 1914 he was made joint Fautua with Tupua Tamasese Lealofi I, and after 1915 with Tuimaleali‘ifano Si‘u.

Under the New Zealand mandate Tanumafili appeared loyal, at least in public, while other heads of the royal families backed the Mau independence movement; families and villages allied to the Malietoa opposed it as a challenge to his authority, and in March 1928 his intervention probably prevented a massacre near Apia. A founder of Apia's Toe‘aina Club for high chiefs, he sat on the Legislative Council from 1929, was made an honorary Officer of the Order of the British Empire in 1931 and resigned in 1937. He died on 5 July 1939 after 41 years as Malietoa. He married Momoe Lupeuluiva Meleiseā; their five children included Tanumafili II.
malik-ambar: Malik Ambar was born in 1548 in Harar, in the Adal Sultanate, and was known as Chapu. Early sources say he came from the Maya tribe, while the historian Richard M. Eaton places his origin in the Kambata region of southern Ethiopia. According to the Futuhat-i Adil Shahi, his parents sold him into slavery; he was sold again at al-Mukha in Yemen and in Baghdad, and Mir Qasim al-Baghdadi converted him to Islam, educated him, named him Ambar and took him to the Deccan. There he was bought by Changiz Khan, a former Habshi slave who was peshwa of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate.

Freed by his master's widow, Ambar served the Sultan of Bijapur, where he gained the title Malik, but left in 1595 for the Nizam Shahi army. As regent he strengthened Murtaza Nizam Shah II, and by 1610 his army included 10,000 Habshis and 40,000 Deccanis. Over the next decade he defeated Emperor Jahangir's attempts to take the kingdom, and Jahangir called him the ill-starred and the black fated; in 1615 the court painter Abu'l Hasan showed the emperor shooting arrows at Ambar's severed head. With Maratha chiefs such as Lakhuji Jadhavrao, Maloji Bhosale and Shahaji Bhosale he took Ahmednagar Fort from the Mughals, but later defeats by Shah Jahan forced him to give it up and weakened his power.

Ambar died on 14 May 1626 at the age of 77, and his tomb lies in Khuldabad. His son Fateh Khan succeeded him as regent, but amid struggles among the nobles the sultanate fell to the Mughal Empire within ten years. Ambar moved the capital from Paranda to Junnar and in 1610 founded Khirki, which Fateh Khan renamed Fatehpur and Aurangzeb, after 1653, Aurangabad. Its Neher canal, a tunnel 7 feet deep with 140 manholes, ran for 321 years before it first needed cleaning in 1931. Historians such as Joseph E. Harris praise his patronage of learning and the arts, while Eaton holds that late defeats undermined his authority.
malik-ashraf: Malik Ashraf, whose regnal name was Ghiyāth al-Dīn Shāh Malik Ashraf, was the second son of Timurtash and his wife Daulat Khatun, born some time after his brother Hasan Kuchak. After their father's execution he and his brothers were imprisoned in Karahisar by the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id. Serving under Hasan Kuchak, he defeated an army of Khurasan sent against Hasan by Togha Temur in 1341, and in August 1342, answering a request from the Injuid Abu Ishaq, he defeated Abu Ishaq's cousin Pir Hosayn, so that Abu Ishaq briefly regained Shiraz.

When Hasan Kuchak died in 1343, the Chupanid lands were at first divided between Malik Ashraf and his uncles Yagi Basti and Surgan. The division did not last: Malik defeated Surgan in battle, had Yagi Basti murdered in 1344 and fought Surgan again in Kurdistan in 1345. Accusing the former puppet khan Suleiman Khan of Hasan's murder, he raised another puppet, Anushirwan, as Ilkhan in Arran and rode to Tabriz in 1346, where he made 'Abd al-Hayy Hammami Tabrizi his vizier.

As ruler he grew increasingly suspicious and violent. He executed his younger brother Misr Malek together with Aliki Bahadur, viceroy of Nakhchivan, and later turned on his own vizier, seizing a large sum of money from him by force. A campaign against Baghdad led by his brother Malek Ashtar in 1347 failed with heavy losses, and in 1350 an attempt to take Fars from the Injuids failed before Isfahan, leaving him to settle for tribute.

His cruelty, together with the spread of bubonic plague in the region, drove many people away. In 1357 he raised another obscure puppet, Ghazan II, as Ilkhan, but Jani Beg of the Golden Horde invaded through Shirvan the same year and demanded his submission, which he refused. Trying to flee to Anatolia, Malik Ashraf lost 2,000 to 3,000 men in a battle near Sarab, fled to Marand and was captured near Khoy. He was hanged in Tabriz, to the joy of its people, and Jani Beg took his mother and children with him when he left. His only son, Temürtas, was killed by Shaikh Uvais in 1360.
malik-kafur: Kafur, also known as Taj al-Din Izz al-Dawla, was reportedly of Hindu descent; the 14th-century chronicler Isami calls him a Mahratta. In his youth he was a eunuch slave of a wealthy Khwaja of Khambhat, and his epithet hazar-dinari, the thousand-dinar man, is said to refer to his price, though the figure is probably a metaphorical compliment. Alauddin's general Nusrat Khan captured him at Khambhat during the invasion of Gujarat in 1299, and he was converted to Islam and presented to Alauddin in Delhi. He rose quickly as a counsellor and commander, holding the rank of barbeg by 1306.

In 1306 he routed a Mongol army of the Chagatai Khanate that had advanced to the Ravi River, with the help of commanders including Malik Tughluq. Sent against the Yadava king Ramachandra of Devagiri, who had stopped paying tribute, he brought him to Delhi to acknowledge Alauddin. In January 1310 he reached the Kakatiya capital, Warangal, and after a month-long siege its ruler, Prataparudra, surrendered and agreed to pay tribute; the Koh-i-Noor diamond was said to be among the spoils. On 25 February 1311 he besieged the Hoysala capital, Dwarasamudra, and on 24 April he occupied Madurai. In 1313 he annexed Devagiri, which he governed for two years.

Recalled when Alauddin fell ill in 1315, he held executive power as Na'ib and seems to have driven a purge of rival officers. He had the noble Alp Khan killed and Prince Khizr Khan imprisoned at Gwalior. The chronicler Ziauddin Barani wrote that the sultan had fallen deeply in love with him; some scholars read this as a homosexual relationship, while the historian Banarsi Prasad Saksena holds that it was not sexual.

After Alauddin died on the night of 4 January 1316, Kafur placed the six-year-old Shihabuddin on the throne as his regent, had Khizr Khan and Shadi Khan blinded and imprisoned the prince Mubarak Shah. Alauddin's former bodyguards, led by Mubashshir, killed him within about a month. Barani was severely critical of him, but the historian Abraham Eraly argues that Barani was prejudiced against his non-Turkic, Hindu origins and his status as a eunuch. Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq later restored his tomb, whose site is now unknown.
malik-maqbul-tilangani: Before his conversion he was known as Mala Yugandharudu or Gannama Nayaka. Marana's Telugu Markandeya Puranamu calls him Pedda Mala Devudu and Gannavibhudu and describes him as the commander of Warangal Fort, the Kakatiya capital; the title Mala Devudu, meaning lord, suggests a very high place in the Kakatiya hierarchy. After Ulugh Khan, son and general of Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, took Warangal in 1323, Gannaya was captured, converted to Islam and given the name Malik Maqbul. Ulugh Khan, soon to rule Delhi as Muhammad bin Tughluq, left Warangal in his charge.

The new province of Teling faced rebellion at once: the coast around Rajahmundry broke away as soon as Ulugh Khan left, the land south of the Krishna River in 1325, the Bhadrachalam area in 1330 and western Telangana between 1330 and 1335. The sultan's march south in 1334 was halted by an epidemic in his army, and after the rebels took Warangal, Maqbul fled to Delhi. He then served as governor of Multan and of Cambay, where the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta met him, and accompanied Muhammad bin Tughluq against rebels at Broach, where he put them all to death and seized great wealth.

Under Firuz Shah Tughlaq he became finance minister and then wazir. He defended Delhi while the sultan was away for six months in Sindh and Gujarat without news, and Firuz Shah remarked that Khan-i-Jahan was the real ruler of Delhi. Maqbul kept the sultan informed, entered the governors' presents in the royal treasury and was strict in collecting dues. His powers were checked by the auditor and the Accountant-General; in one dispute with the Accountant-General Ain-i-Mahru he threatened to leave for Mecca, and the sultan dismissed Ain-i-Mahru.

Firuz Shah had promised that the office of wazir would pass to Maqbul's son, and after his death in 1369 Jauna Khan, also called Junan Shah, succeeded him. Jauna Khan built seven large mosques in and around Delhi, among them the Khirki Masjid and Kalan Masjid, but was captured and executed in the succession struggle. Maqbul's tomb in Nizamuddin West, built by his son in 1388, was the first octagonal mausoleum in Delhi and now stands in a very poor state of repair.
malik-muhammad-jayasi: Much of what is told of Jayasi comes from legend, and his date and place of birth are debated. His nisba ties him to Jayas, an important Sufi centre in present-day Uttar Pradesh, but whether he was born there or came for religious education is uncertain. Legend says he lost his father young and his mother some years later, was blinded in one eye and scarred by smallpox, and was raised by Sufi ascetics.

According to the same tradition he married and had seven sons, until he mocked a pir's opium addiction in a work called Posti-nama; the roof of his house then fell and killed all seven, and he turned to a religious life at Jayas. He belonged to the Mehdavia sect and named the lineage of Saiyid Muhammad of Jaunpur among his teachers, his own preceptor being Shaikh Burhanuddin Ansari of Kalpi.

Jayasi wrote 25 works in Awadhi, set down in the Persian Nastaʿlīq script. Akhiri Kalam dates from 1529–30, in the reign of Babur. In Padmavat, Alauddin Khalji attacks Chittor after hearing of the beauty of Queen Padmavati, wife of King Ratansen, and the poem draws on the siege of Chittor in 1303. His other works include Akhrawat and Kanhavat, a poem on Krishna.

Legend has Raja Ram Singh of Amethi invite him to court after hearing a mendicant recite the Padmavat, and has him spend his last years in the forests near Amethi, where he would turn himself into a tiger until the king's hunters killed him. He died in 1542, and his tomb lies 3 km north of Ram Nagar, near Amethi; a Jaisi Smarak, or memorial, stands in Jayas. More than a century later hagiographies began to portray him as a charismatic pir, and Ghulam Muinuddin Abdullah Khweshgi's Maarijul-Wilayat of 1682–83 called him muhaqqiq-i hindi, the knower of the truth of al-Hind.
malik-sarwar: Malik Sarwar was a eunuch of common birth in the Delhi Sultanate, possibly a slave of African descent. The first contemporary record of him, from the reign of Firuz Shah Tughlaq, describes him as custodian of the royal jewellery, and he was later appointed Shahnah-i-Shahr, governor of the city of Delhi.

He played an important part in bringing Muhammad Shah to the throne of Delhi and was made wazir with the title Khwaja-i-Jahan; the same sultan later gave him the governorship of the eastern provinces. He went on to take part in the struggles around the throne, among them the accession of Mahmud Shah.

In May 1394, when news came of a rebellion in Jaunpur, Sultan Mahmud Shah sent him back to his earlier post as governor of the eastern provinces with a large army and twenty elephants. Malik Sarwar defeated the rebels and established himself at Jaunpur. With the Delhi Sultanate in decline he became practically independent of it: he issued coins in his own name, had the Friday sermon read in his name and took the title Atabak-i-Azam, the great lord. He died in 1399.

As a eunuch he had no children of his own and adopted Malik Mubarak Qaranfal and his brothers. Mubarak succeeded him as Mubarak Shah and was followed by his younger brother Ibrahim Shah. The line they founded, the Sharqi dynasty, took its name from the title Malik Sarwar had received as governor of the east, the Sharq.
malik-shah-i: Malik-Shah was born on 16 August 1055 and spent his youth in Isfahan. In 1064 he joined his father Alp Arslan's campaign in the Caucasus with the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, and in 1066 he was named heir at a ceremony near Merv and given Isfahan as a fief. In 1072 Alp Arslan was fatally wounded on a campaign in Transoxiana against the Karakhanids, and Malik-Shah was declared sultan.

His uncle Qavurt claimed the throne as the elder brother. Malik-Shah replied that a brother does not inherit when there is a son. In 1073 they fought the three-day Battle of Kerj Abu Dulaf near Hamadan, where Malik-Shah's army of ghulams and Kurdish and Arab contingents defeated Qavurt's Turkmens, although the Turks in his own army mutinied. Qavurt was captured and later strangled with a bowstring.

Nizam al-Mulk held near absolute power under the nominal sultan. Malik-Shah repelled the Karakhanids in 1073, and campaigns in 1087 and 1089 took Bukhara and Samarkand and brought Transoxiana up to the borders of China under Seljuk rule. In the Caucasus, George II of Georgia submitted as a vassal in Isfahan in 1088 after campaigns in 1075 and 1078 and 1079. In 1086 the army took Aleppo, Antioch, Edessa and Harran in northern Syria. In 1092 Seljuk armies took Yemen and Aden.

Revolts in the family marked the reign. His brother Tekish rebelled in Khorasan in 1081 and again in 1086, when he was captured and blinded, and another brother, Toghan-Shah, rebelled at Herat and was imprisoned. Isfahan became the chief residence, and he built mosques there and the Isfahan Observatory, whose work led to the Jalali Calendar. Omar Khayyam's poetry belongs to his reign.

In 1092 Nizam al-Mulk was assassinated near Sihna by a man disguised as a Sufi. One theory blames the Assassins; another suggests Malik-Shah had tired of his overmighty vizier. Malik-Shah then went to Baghdad and sought to depose the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadi.

He died on 19 November 1092 while hunting, probably poisoned, by the caliph or by supporters of Nizam al-Mulk according to one view. He was buried in a madrasa in Isfahan. The empire then fell into chaos as rival successors and governors divided it and fought one another. The success of the First Crusade is attributed at least in part to the political confusion that followed his death.
maliki-school: The Maliki school was founded in the 8th century by Malik ibn Anas, who lived from about 711 to 795 and was a native of Medina. Malik taught al-Shafi'i, who in turn taught Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and he was himself a student of Ja'far al-Sadiq, as was Abu Hanifah. In the Muslim east the school faced competition from the Shafi'i, Hanbali and Zahiri schools, and it was the Hanafi school that earned official favour from the Abbasids. The Malikis had more success in Africa, and for a time in Spain and Sicily.

Unlike the Ahl al-Hadith and the Ahl al-Ra'y, the Maliki school takes a position known as Ahl al-A'mal: it treats the Sunnah as sourced chiefly from the practice of the people of Medina and the living tradition of the community. Its sources are ranked: the Quran, mass-transmitted traditions of Muhammad, the customs of Medina, single-chain hadith, the consensus and opinions of the Companions, analogy, public benefit and finally common opinion.

The school rests on the Muwatta of Malik, which records the practice of Medina beside the hadith, and on the Mudawwana, compiled from the notes of Malik's student Ibn Qasim and the questions of Sahnun. It is closest to the Hanafi school, but it gives analogy less weight and uses public benefit and common opinion where the Quran and the mass-transmitted traditions give no guidance.

Under the Umayyads and their remnants in al-Andalus, the Maliki school was promoted as the official code of law, and its judges were expected in return to legitimise the rulers. The Almoravids continued this dominance, but they gave way to the predominantly Zahiri Almohads, under whom the Malikis lost official favour. After the loss of the Iberian Peninsula the school kept its hold across North and West Africa. Although it was at first hostile to some mystical practices, many Maliki scholars later learned from Sufi practice. Notable figures include Sahnun, Averroes, Ibn Khaldun and, in the 19th century, Usman dan Fodio, founder of the Sokoto Caliphate.
maliseet: The people call themselves Wəlastəkwewiyik or Wolastoqiyik after the Wolastoq, the Saint John River, whose watershed is their homeland. Their neighbours are the Mi'kmaq to the east, the Penobscot to the west and the Passamaquoddy to the south. The name Maliseet comes from Malesse'jik, a Mi'kmaq word for people of other nations, which the French wrote as Malécite and the English colonists anglicised. When Europeans arrived, the Wolastoqiyik lived in walled villages and grew corn, beans, squash and tobacco.

Samuel de Champlain and Marc Lescarbot described a large village at the mouth of the Saint John River early in the 17th century; later their centre moved upriver to Meductic. The French established a fur trade and Jesuit missions, and many converted to Catholicism, while European diseases caused heavy losses. In the colonial wars the Wolastoqiyik were allies of the French, and for a time their warriors were almost a military organisation. As the beaver trade declined and settlers took the farmland along the river, many were displaced.

In the 19th century they still built wigwams and birchbark canoes, and potato farming in Maine and New Brunswick created demand for their baskets. Officials set up the first reserves, among them Oromocto, Kingsclear, Woodstock, Tobique and Madawaska, after reports of widespread hunger. The Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians, in Maine, have been treaty allies of the United States since 19 July 1776.

Their customs and language are very close to those of the Passamaquoddy, and linguists treat the two as dialects of one language; about 650 native speakers of Wolastoqey remain. Some 7,700 Wolastoqiyik with status live in six First Nations of New Brunswick, 1,700 in the Houlton Band and 1,200 in the Wolastoqiyik Wahsipekuk First Nation of Quebec. Songs recorded on wax cylinders by William H. Mechling were revived by the musician Jeremy Dutcher on his album Wolastoqiyik Lintuwakonawa (2018).
mallorca: Mallorca takes its name from the Latin insula maior, the larger island, which became Maiorca in Medieval Latin in contrast with Menorca, the smaller one. Geologically it extends the fold mountains of the Betic Cordillera of Andalusia. It has two mountain ranges, the Serra de Tramuntana in the north-west and the Serres de Llevant in the east, and the highest peak, Puig Major, rises to about 1,445 metres.

Humans first colonised the Balearic Islands around 2500–2300 BCE, from the Iberian Peninsula or southern France, among people associated with the Bell Beaker culture. Their arrival caused the rapid extinction of the three land mammals native to Mallorca. The islanders built prehistoric settlements called talaiots and raised Bronze Age megaliths as part of their Talaiotic culture. The Phoenicians arrived around the eighth century BCE, and the island came under the control of Carthage; after the Second Punic War the Romans took over.

In 534 the Eastern Roman Empire recaptured the island from the Vandals. From 707 Muslim raiders from North Africa attacked repeatedly, and the islanders asked Charlemagne for help. In 902 Issam al-Khawlani conquered the Balearic Islands, which became part of the Emirate of Córdoba. Palma was reshaped and expanded as Medina Mayurqa, and the Muslims improved agriculture with irrigation.

James I of Aragon took the island in 1229. Barbary corsairs attacked the islands so often that the people built coastal watchtowers and fortified churches. In the Spanish Civil War the island, a Nationalist stronghold, was the target of a Republican landing on 16 August 1936; Nationalist air power, supplied largely by Fascist Italy, forced the Republicans to leave by 12 September.

Mallorca is the largest of Spain's Balearic Islands, with its capital at Palma, which is also the capital of the autonomous community. Catalan and Spanish are the two official languages.
