The Cultural Landscape of the Serra de Tramuntana was registered as a World Heritage Site in 2011. The Majorcan cartographic school, which flourished in the 13th to 15th centuries, developed the normal portolan chart.
malmedy: Malmedy is a city and municipality of Wallonia in the province of Liège. It lies on the Warche river, whose regular floods are said to have given the town its name, from the Latin phrase A malo mundarum, meaning "purifying from evil". The municipality has three districts: Malmedy, Bellevaux-Ligneuville and Bévercé, which includes the hamlets of Baugnez and Xhoffraix. A portion of the Spa-Francorchamps motor-racing circuit lies within it, although most of the circuit is in neighbouring Stavelot.

Saint Remacle, abbot of Solignac Abbey in France, founded the town in 648 with a Benedictine monastery. From then until 1794 its history is that of the Princely Abbey of Stavelot-Malmedy, a clerical microstate ruled by a prince-abbot. The two towns formed one principality for 1,146 years under seventy-seven successive prince-abbots, but a rivalry grew between them, because Remacle chose Stavelot as the main city. From the 16th century cloth, leather and gunpowder industries appeared, and in the 17th century the principality became the most important tannery centre in Europe. Papermaking was the main industry and brought the town considerable wealth.

France annexed the principality in 1795, and Malmedy became a lower prefecture in the département of the Ourthe. In 1815 the Congress of Vienna joined the Romance and Walloon town to Prussia. Its people kept the right to use French, even in the town council, until the German Empire was founded after the Franco-German War of 1870. Under Chancellor Bismarck a policy of Germanisation banned French lessons in schools and forbade priests to preach in French. Malmedy was annexed to Belgium after the First World War under the Treaty of Versailles, after a plebiscite in which pro-German voters had to register their names; it was formally annexed in 1920 and joined the province of Liège in 1925.

Between 1940 and 1945 Malmedy was again part of Germany. In the Battle of the Bulge in 1944 the area saw the Malmedy massacre, in which SS troops under Joachim Peiper killed 84 American prisoners of war. On 21 December 1944 German forces under Otto Skorzeny attacked the town, then held by American troops, and were repelled. On 23, 24 and 25 December United States aircraft bombed it repeatedly in friendly-fire incidents that killed about 200 civilians.

The town has about 12,000 inhabitants, roughly 95 per cent of them French speakers, with a German-speaking minority that has language facilities. Walloon, the historical language, is spoken mostly by older people but survives in the songs of the Cwarmê, the carnival held from Shrove Friday to Shrove Tuesday, in which the Haguète and the Long-Né are among the traditional costumes.
malmesbury-abbey: The site was first chosen by Máel Dub, an Irish monk who kept a hermitage and taught local children before the Saxons conquered the area. The Benedictine monastery, dedicated to Saint Peter and Saint Paul, was founded around 676 by the scholar-poet Aldhelm, a nephew of King Ine of Wessex. The town grew up around it and under Alfred the Great became a burh assessed at 12 hides. It was one of the few English religious houses with a continuous history from the 7th century to the Dissolution.

The choice of Malmesbury rather than the New Minster at Winchester for the burial of King Æthelstan suggests that he remained an outsider to the West Saxon court, and a mint was founded at the abbey around then. Its learning drew on abbots such as John Scotus Eriugena, Alfred of Malmesbury and Aelfric of Eynsham. In the early 11th century the monk Eilmer of Malmesbury flew more than 200 yards from a tower with wings strapped to his body and broke both legs on landing.

The Norman church was substantially complete by 1180, and its south porch keeps fine Romanesque sculpture. Its tower and spire fell in a storm around 1500, destroying much of the east end. The abbey, which owned 23,000 acres in the Malmesbury Hundred, was closed in 1539 and sold to the merchant William Stumpe, who gave the church back to the town and filled the buildings with looms.

In August 1541 Thomas Cranmer licensed the abbey church to replace St Paul's as the town's parish church. The west tower fell around 1550, so less than half of the building now stands, and bullet marks from the English Civil War remain on its walls. It was listed Grade I in 1949 and serves the Diocese of Bristol. Its Anglo-Saxon charters, though extended by forgeries made in its own scriptorium, are a source for the history of Wessex.
malnad: Malenadu covers the western and eastern slopes of the Western Ghats in Karnataka and in part the Eastern Ghats. It is counted today as thirteen districts, though the districts first taken to make up the region were Shivamogga, Chikkamagaluru, Uttara Kannada, Kodagu, Hassan and Belagavi. The origin of the name is unclear: in Kannada male without a retroflex l means mountain, giving mountainous land, while with a retroflex l it means rain, giving rainy land; the first form is the more common.

The Western Ghats, also called the Sahyadri ranges, block the south-west monsoon winds from the Arabian Sea, so the region receives 1,000 to 3,800 millimetres of rain a year, and the village of Agumbe the highest rainfall in Karnataka. Its forests act as sponges that feed the Sharavathi, Tunga, Bhadra, Kaveri, Kabini, Netravathi and other rivers long after the monsoon. Mullayyanagiri, at 1,925 metres the highest peak in Karnataka, rises in the Chandra Drona ranges, and the region's waterfalls include Jog Falls. Organised farming on land cleared from the forest has been practised there for a thousand years.

Villages are scattered and remote, and an Area Development Board was created in 1991 to carry out projects in the region. Its protected areas, among them Kudremukh National Park, the Bhadra Wildlife Sanctuary and Nagarahole, shelter tigers, elephants, lion-tailed macaques, hornbills and king cobras, within a Western Ghats that ranks among the world's biodiversity hotspots. Its cooking, largely non-vegetarian and spicy, includes akki rotti, kadubu, neer dose and the pandi curry of Coorg.
malolos: Malolos lies 45 kilometres north of Manila, in the south-western part of Bulacan in the Central Luzon Region on the island of Luzon. It is bounded by Calumpit, Plaridel, Guiguinto, Paombong and Bulakan, and by Manila Bay on the south. The land is flat, rising to about 6 metres above sea level at its highest, and a network of natural waterways and rivers runs through it to the bay. The city is divided into 51 barangays.

Miguel López de Legazpi conquered eight villages along the Malolos River and united them on 14 November 1571 as the encomienda of Malolos, entrusted to Marcos de Herrera. On 5 April 1572 he merged it with Calumpit. Augustinian friars began the Christianization of Malolos in May 1572, and a mission chapel became a house of the order on 11 June 1580. Because frequent high tides flooded the site, the friars moved the church in 1590 to its present place in the Poblacion. Work on a stone church began in 1599 and was finished in 1673.

In 1898 the Malolos Convention met at the sanctuary of Barasoain Church, and the convent of Malolos Cathedral served as the presidential palace. Malolos was the capital of the First Philippine Republic under Emilio Aguinaldo from 1898 to 1899. The Malolos Constitution was approved by a partially elected congress and called for a representative democracy. The Academia Militar, the first military school in the Philippines, was founded on 25 October 1898, and the Burgos Institute, a law school, and the Universidad Scientifico Literaria de Filipinas were established there.

After the Battle of Malolos in 1899 American forces occupied the town and the seat of power went back to Manila. On 27 February 1901 the Philippine Commission moved the provincial seat of Bulacan from the damaged town of Bulakan to Malolos. Joseph Estrada was inaugurated as president at Barasoain Church on 30 June 1998, and Malolos became a component city under Republic Act No. 8754 of 4 November 1999.

Malolos is a component city and the capital of Bulacan, with a population of 269,809 in the 2024 census. Most residents trace their roots to the Tagalog people, and most are Roman Catholic. Its historic town centre was declared a National Heritage Landmark on 15 August 2001 as Malolos Heritage Town, and the Museo ng Bulacan stands about 500 metres from Barasoain Church. The city is also a centre of education in Central Luzon, with Bulacan State University among its universities.
malolos-constitution: After the Battle of Manila Bay on 1 May 1898, the United States Navy brought Emilio Aguinaldo back to the Philippines. He declared independence on 12 June, and elections held from 23 June to 10 September chose the Malolos Congress, which met on 15 September and named a drafting committee of wealthy, well-educated men.

The text adopted was written by Felipe Calderón y Roca and Felipe Buencamino as an alternative to proposals by Apolinario Mabini and Pedro Paterno. Congress debated Calderón's draft between 25 October and 29 November 1898, adding a guarantee of religious freedom by a single vote on 28 November. Mabini, Aguinaldo's adviser, thought the system unworkable in wartime, and at Aguinaldo's request provisions were added giving him temporary powers to rule by decree.

Written in Spanish, the constitution has 101 articles in fourteen titles, with eight transitory articles and one unnumbered article. Its structure follows the Spanish Constitution of 1812; Calderón also studied the charters of Belgium, Mexico, Brazil, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Guatemala and the French Constitution of 1793. Its central idea was the retroversion of sovereignty to the people. Title IV's twenty-seven articles set out civil liberties, many drawn from the Spanish Constitution of 1869, and Article 5 recognised the freedom of all beliefs and the separation of Church and State.

The government was to be popular, representative, alternative and responsible, with separate legislative, executive and judicial branches. A one-house National Assembly could censure and question officials, and the president governed through secretaries collectively responsible to it, as in a parliamentary system. A Permanent Commission of seven members acted for the Assembly between sessions. Article 99 allowed the executive a free hand in wartime.

No foreign government recognised the republic, and the constitution was never enforced across the whole archipelago. The Philippine–American War began on 4 February 1899, Aguinaldo was captured on 23 March 1901, and General Miguel Malvar surrendered on 13 April 1902. Later Philippine constitutions, from the Philippine Organic Act of 1902 to the 1987 Constitution, followed American models, so the Malolos text had limited influence on them. Isagani Giron, a former president of the Historical Society of Bulacan, called it the best constitution the country ever had. The original is kept in the archives of the Batasang Pambansa Complex, closed to the public, and a marker was placed at Barasoain Church in 1969.
malta: Malta is an archipelago in the central Mediterranean, about 80 kilometres from southern Italy across the Malta Channel. Only Malta, Gozo and Comino have permanent residents, and Comino is practically uninhabited. The islands lie on a shallow shelf that was once part of a land bridge between Sicily and North Africa, and the archipelago sits on the African tectonic plate. The terrain is coarse and hilly, with many harbours along an indented coastline. The highest point, Ta' Dmejrek near Dingli, is 253 metres high, and Malta has no rivers or lakes.

The earliest reliable evidence of habitation dates to 6500 BCE, when Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, probably from Sicily, arrived. Neolithic farmers from Sicily are thought to have followed by around 5400 BCE. Around 3500 BCE the islanders built the Ġgantija temples on Gozo, among the oldest free-standing structures in the world, and other early temples include those at Ħaġar Qim and Mnajdra. After 2500 BCE Malta was depopulated until a new people arrived who cremated their dead and built small dolmens as tombs; they probably differed from the temple builders.

Phoenician traders colonised the islands around 1000 BCE, with their seat of government at Mdina and their main port at Cospicua on the Grand Harbour, which they called Maleth. Carthage controlled the islands after the fall of Phoenicia. It is unsure whether Roman rule began after the first or second Punic War, but Rome held Malta after the second, when it was surrendered by Hamilcar, a son of Gisco, to the consul Titus Sempronius Longus. The Arabs, Normans and Aragonese ruled in the Middle Ages, and the Knights Hospitaller, French and British in the modern era.

Malta became a British crown colony in the early 19th century and served as headquarters of the British Mediterranean Fleet. It was besieged by the Axis powers in the Second World War. Independence came in 1964, and the current parliamentary republic was established in 1974. Malta joined the European Union in 2004 and the eurozone on 1 January 2008.

The two official languages are Maltese, a Semitic language with close ties to Arabic and Sicilian, and English. Catholicism is the state religion, though the constitution guarantees freedom of religion. The 2025 census counted 588,254 people.
maltese-language: Maltese is a Central Semitic language derived from late medieval Sicilian Arabic. The pioneering Maltese linguists Giovanni Pietro Francesco Agius de Soldanis and Mikiel Anton Vassalli both hypothesised that it came from the Punic language, a view that later scholars did not accept. The language is generally traced to the arrival, early in the 11th century, of settlers from neighbouring Sicily, where Siculo-Arabic was spoken.

The Norman conquest of 1091, followed by the expulsion of the Muslims, complete by 1249, permanently isolated the vernacular from its Arabic source and created the conditions for its evolution into a distinct language. In Sicily, Siculo-Arabic became extinct and was replaced by Sicilian, but in Malta the vernacular continued to develop alongside Italian. The first written reference to it is in a will of 1436, where it is called lingua maltensi, and the oldest known document in Maltese is the 15th-century poem Il-Kantilena by Pietru Caxaro.

Maltese is spoken by the Maltese people and is a national language of Malta. It is the only standardised Semitic language written exclusively in the Latin script. The core vocabulary, including the most common words and the function words, is Semitic, and the Arabic base makes up around one third of the vocabulary. About half of the vocabulary comes from standard Italian and Sicilian, and English words make up between 6 and 20 per cent. The rural dialects keep archaic features and use more Semitic roots and broken plurals than Standard Maltese. The modern spelling system was introduced in 1924.

Under the Knights Hospitaller both French and Italian were used for official documents, and in the British colonial period English was encouraged through education, with Italian as the next most important language. Hieronymus Megiser, who visited Malta in 1588 and 1589, included a list of Maltese words in two works, and Agius de Soldanis produced the first systematic lexicon and grammar and proposed a standard orthography. Late in the 18th century and through the 19th, Vassalli and others made a concerted effort to standardise the written language. Maltese was recognised as an official language, alongside English, in 1934. Its use declined under British administration relative to English, and after independence language reforms increased its use.
maluku-islands: The Maluku Islands cover about 850,000 km2, 90 per cent of it sea, and number an estimated 1027 islands. The two largest, Halmahera and Seram, are sparsely populated, while the most developed, Ambon and Ternate, are small. Most of the islands are forested and mountainous, and several, such as Ternate, are volcanoes rising from the sea; there have been over 70 serious eruptions in the last 500 years. All but the Aru group lie in Wallacea, between Weber's Line and Lydekker's Line, so their fauna is more Australasian than Asian.

Australo-Melanesians were the first people on the islands, at least 40,000 years ago, and Austronesian speakers arrived around 2000 BCE. Arab merchants began to arrive in the fourteenth century, bringing Islam, which took hold especially in the trading centres. The earliest recorded word identifiable with Maluku, Maloko, appears in the Old Javanese Nagarakertagama of 1365.

The Portuguese conquered Malacca in August 1511 and soon sent ships to the Spice Islands. Francisco Serrão, shipwrecked at Hitu on Ambon in 1512, allied himself with the ruler of Ternate and built a fortress there. From 1546 Portuguese missionary work under Francis Xavier created large Christian communities. The Dutch arrived in 1599, and in 1605 the Dutch East India Company, allied with the Sultan of Ternate, conquered Ambon and Tidore and expelled the Portuguese. It then monopolised the production and trade of spices by a ruthless policy, including the genocidal conquest of the nutmeg-producing Banda Islands in 1621, the elimination of the English on Ambon in 1623 and the subordination of Ternate and Tidore in the 1650s.

The Nuku Rebellion, led by a Tidore prince, spread across much of Maluku and Papua in 1780-1810. British forces held the islands in 1796-1801 and again in 1810-1817, and uprooted many spice trees for planting elsewhere in the British Empire. After Indonesian independence a Republic of South Maluku was declared in 1950 and was put down by the Indonesian army.

Since 1999 the islands have formed two Indonesian provinces: Maluku, with its capital at Ambon, and North Maluku, with its capital at Sofifi on Halmahera. Their combined population in 2020 was 3,131,860. Over 130 languages were once spoken, and many speakers have moved to the creoles of Ternate and Ambon. Cloves and nutmeg are still grown, alongside cocoa, coffee and fruit, and fishing is a large industry.
malwa: Malwa occupies a plateau of volcanic origin in western Madhya Pradesh and south-eastern Rajasthan, with Gujarat to the west. The Vindhya Range lies to the south and east, and the Bundelkhand upland to the north. The plateau is an extension of the Deccan Traps, and its black soil owes its colour to the high iron content of the basalt and holds moisture well. The Mahi drains the western part, the Chambal the centre and the Betwa the east, and the Shipra River is of historical importance because of the Simhastha mela, held every 12 years. The name derives from the ancient tribe of the Malavas. Its main language is Malvi.

The Malwa culture was a Chalcolithic culture of the region in the 2nd millennium BCE. Ujjain, also called Ujjaiyini and Avanti, emerged as the first major centre in the 7th century BCE, and around 600 BCE an earthen rampart was built around a city of considerable size. It was the capital of the Avanti kingdom, one of the mahajanapadas. The region was conquered by the Nanda Empire in the mid-4th century BCE and then became part of the Maurya Empire, and Ashoka was governor of Ujjain in his youth. Ujjain became a major trading centre in the 1st century CE.

Towards the end of the 13th century the fort of Mandu, originally the capital of the Parmar rulers, came under the Sultans of Malwa, who built palaces such as the Jahaz Mahal and the Hindola Mahal. Dhar was the capital before Mandu took over in 1405. Malwa opium, produced for the western Indian ports and China in the 18th and 19th centuries, challenged the monopoly of the British East India Company, which imposed restrictions on its production and trade. The Malwa Agency of British India was an administrative division until 1947, when it was merged into Madhya Bharat.

Malwa's population was 22,773,993 in 2011. Indore is its largest city and commercial centre, and agriculture is the main occupation. Ujjain is sacred for its Mahakal Temple, one of the twelve jyotirlingas, and several prominent figures of Indian history lived in Malwa, among them the poet Kalidasa and the king Bhoja.
malwa-agency: The Malwa Agency was formed in 1895 from princely states that had been under the authority of the British agent for Indore, together with those of the Western Malwa Agency, a sub-agency of the Central India Agency since 1854, which was abolished. The political agent had his headquarters at Neemuch (Nimach); the other chief towns of the region were Ratlam and Jaora.

The two Dewas States, Dewas Senior and Dewas Junior, were added to the agency in 1907. In 1925 it was joined with the Bhopawar Agency to form the Malwa and Bhopawar Agency, renamed the Malwa and Southern States Agency in 1927. The Dewas States passed to the Bhopal Agency in 1931, and in 1934 the agency was once again named the Malwa Agency. After Indian independence in 1947 the rulers of its states acceded to the Government of India, and the states were joined to the new Indian state of Madhya Bharat, which was merged into Madhya Pradesh on 1 November 1956.

The salute states, in order of precedence, were Ratlam, whose ruler bore the title Maharaja Bahadur and a hereditary salute of 13 guns (15 locally); Jaora, under a Nawab with 13 guns; Sailana, under a Raja Bahadur with 11 guns; and Jhabua and Sitamau, each under a Raja with 11 guns.

The non-salute states were Piploda, whose ruler was styled Rao, originally Thakur, the Panth-Piploda Estate and Barkhera Panth State. The agency also covered portions of the territories of Gwalior State, Indore State, Tonk State and the two Dewas States, Senior and Junior.
maly-trostenets: Maly Trostenets was an extermination site and forced-labour camp operated by Nazi Germany in Belarus during the World War II, twelve kilometres south-east of Minsk. It comprised two sites: a forced-labour camp, established at an uncertain date between November 1941 and January 1942, and a nearby site in the Blagovshchina Forest intended solely for mass murder. In April and May 1942 Eduard Strauch, the commander of the Security Police and SD in Minsk, took over the 250-hectare Karl Marx collective farm for the camp. Soviet, Polish and Western and Central European Jews who had been held in the Minsk Ghetto were imprisoned there, along with local suspected partisans, and the number of inmates mostly stood between 500 and 1,000.

In March and April 1942 Adolf Eichmann, Heinrich Himmler and Reinhard Heydrich came to Minsk and decided to resume deportations of Jews there and to have deportees murdered on arrival. From May to October 1942 transports came from the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Poland. Most deportees were shot soon after arrival and buried in mass graves; gas vans were in use by June 1942 at the latest.

By August 1942 a railway siding had been extended so that trains could go directly to the killing site. The largest massacre, on 28 to 30 July 1942, killed about 10,000 Jews of the Minsk Ghetto who were judged unable to work.

From October 1942 central European Jews were sent instead to the extermination camps in occupied Poland. After the Minsk Ghetto was liquidated in October 1943, prisoners were forced to exhume and burn the bodies in Sonderaktion 1005, and were then murdered. From late 1943 the Shashkovka Forest replaced Blagovshchina as the place where local non-Jewish civilians, suspected partisans and prisoners were killed. On 29 and 30 June 1944, as the Red Army advanced in Operation Bagration, German forces killed the remaining prisoners in a barn and burned the camp.

The death toll is hard to establish because the graves were opened and the bodies burned from October 1943. Soviet postwar estimates, among them Ilya Ehrenburg's figure of 206,500, counted all victims of the surrounding execution sites, and the figure stood on a memorial sign in 2015 without mention of Jewish victims.

Recent research gives lower numbers: Christian Gerlach and Petra Rentrop put the toll at about 60,000, while Stephan Lehnstaedt estimated at least 106,000 Jews. Scholars regard it as the fourth-largest Nazi extermination site. The killings were not mentioned at the Nuremberg Trials and were largely ignored by Soviet and Belarusian officials until the late 1990s. A memorial complex now stands at the site, and Waltraud Barton collected the names of 10,000 Austrian Jews murdered there.
mamai: Mamai belonged to the Turco-Mongol Kiyat clan, which claimed descent from an older brother of Genghis Khan's father Yesugei Baghatur. Because he was not a descendant of Genghis Khan and his son Jochi in the male line, he never took the title of khan. His birth is dated only to the mid-to-late 1320s, and his father is named as Alash Beg, possibly Ali Beg. Members of the clan had served the Golden Horde from the time of Batu Khan, and some governed the Crimea and the eastern lands of the Horde. Mamai became an emir under Jani Beg, who reigned from 1342 to 1357, and under Berdi Beg he was named chief emir and married the khan's daughter.

After Berdi Beg's death in August 1359 Mamai lost his place at court. From 1361 he acted as kingmaker, promoting khans of his own choosing from a base in the Crimea and the western Horde. He installed his first khan, Abdallah, at Sarai in 1362, but rivals from the line of Jochi's son Shiban expelled him within the year. Over the next decade Mamai took the capital and lost it again several times. In 1362 a Lithuanian victory at the Battle of Blue Waters cost him Podolia. He lowered the tribute of the Venetians at Tana, was received with honour in Genoese Caffa in 1374, and restored friendly relations with Mamluk Egypt.

Mamai's dealings with the Russian princes were opportunistic. He played Dmitrij of Moscow against Mihail of Tver' for the grand princedom of Vladimir, and each had to bring gifts. After 1374 Dmitrij refused tribute. Mamai defeated the men of Nižnij Novgorod at the P'jana river and burned their city in 1377. In 1378 a Mongol army he sent against Rjazan' was beaten by Dmitrij at the Voža river on 11 August. Mamai then demanded submission and higher tribute for his new khan, Tūlāk. Dmitrij refused, and on 8 September 1380 the Russian forces attacked Mamai's army at Kulikovo Field, near the Don, and routed it.

Tokhtamysh, a descendant of Jochi's son Tuqa-Timur, had meanwhile taken Sarai and gained the Horde's allegiance. Mamai met him on the Kalka River without a legitimate khan to put forward. Many of his commanders deserted to Tokhtamysh with their troops, and Mamai fled, losing his harem and much of his property. The Genoese of Caffa refused to admit him, as did the governor and people of Solkhat. At the end of 1380 or the beginning of 1381 agents of Tokhtamysh caught up with him outside Solkhat and killed him, though Tokhtamysh ordered an honourable burial. His death opened the way for Tokhtamysh's attempt to reunite the Golden Horde. The Princes Glinski, later prominent in Lithuania, were said to descend from his son Mansur Kiyat.
mamallapuram: Mamallapuram lies on the Coromandel Coast of the Bay of Bengal, about 60 kilometres south of Chennai. Its ancient name was Thirukadalmallai. The earliest mention is in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, by an unknown Greek navigator, and Ptolemy calls the place Malange. Mariners have known it since at least the time of Marco Polo as the Seven Pagodas, after shrines on the shore, of which only the Shore Temple survives.

A Neolithic burial urn, cairn circles and burial jars of the 1st century BCE have been found nearby. Chinese coins and Roman coins of Theodosius I from the 4th century CE show that the port was an active hub of trade in the late classical period. The Pallava kings ruled it from Kanchipuram, their capital from the 3rd to the 9th century CE, and used the port to launch trade and diplomatic missions to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

The town was named after the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I, also known as Mamalla, who reigned from 630 to 670 CE and is said to have founded it in the 7th century. A group of royal monuments, many carved from the living rock, was built largely under him and his successor Rajasimhavarman, and they show the shift from rock-cut to structural architecture. The present town plan was established under the British Raj in 1827.

The Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with some 40 ancient monuments. They include the ratha temples, monolithic processional chariots built between 630 and 668 CE, among them the Pancha Rathas, each carved from a single stone. There are over ten rock-cut cave temples of the 7th century and the giant open-air rock relief known as the Descent of the Ganges or Arjuna's Penance, one of the largest in the world. The Shore Temple, of dressed stone and dedicated to Shiva, was built about half a century after the rock-cut works.
mamankam-festival: The festival can be dated at least to the era before the Cheras of Cranganore (c. 800–1124 CE), and its early nature, wrapped in myth and legend, is disputed. It seems to have begun as a temple festival, comparable to the Kumbha Melas, at a place sacred because the river flows there between the Nava Mukunda temple of Vishnu and temples of Brahma and Siva. Native traditions tell that a Perumal chosen by the Brahmin assembly was crowned there for twelve years, the Great Feast marking each new term. The name has been read as Maha Magha, the great Magha month, or Maha Makham, the great sacrifice.

Held every twelve years, the fair drew pilgrims, traders and travellers and combined trade with martial and intellectual contests, Hindu rituals and folk performances; it was believed that the goddess Ganga then descended into the river. Tradition holds that the last Chera Perumal gave the chief of Valluvanad, the Vellattiri, the right to conduct it as Rakshapurusha, the Great Protector. The Zamorin of Calicut captured Tirunavaya, a conquest dated to 1486, and made the fair a display of his power.

Other chiefs, the ruler of Travancore among them, sent flags in submission, but the Valluvanad chief sent chavers, Nair warriors pledged to die trying to kill the Zamorin, led by men of four leading Nair houses and driven by blood feud.

William Logan, drawing on the Kozhikode Granthavaris, described the Mamankam of 1683, when eighteen warriors led by a man of the Putumanna Panikkar house died charging the Zamorin's spearmen. Alexander Hamilton recorded that in 1695 a youth of fifteen or sixteen reached the Zamorin's tent and nearly killed him before being cut down. According to K. V. Krishna Iyer the last fair was held in 1755; Hyder Ali's conquest of Calicut in 1766 and British rule ended it. Five sites at Tirunavaya, among them the Nilapadu Thara platform and the Manikkinar well, where the fallen were reportedly thrown, are protected monuments of the Kerala State Archaeology Department.
mamia-iii-gurieli: Mamia, also known as the Great Gurieli or the Black Gurieli, was a younger son of George III Gurieli and Princess Tamar Chijavadze. When his father fell in battle at Rokiti against King Alexander IV of Imereti in 1684, Mamia joined his brothers in exile at Akhaltsikhe under the protection of its Ottoman governor, Yusuf-Pasha. In the fighting that followed, his elder brother Kaikhosro II Gurieli lost his life and his uncle Malakia II Gurieli was blinded. In 1689 the nobles of Guria called Mamia home, and he was installed as prince with the pasha's support.

In the power struggles of Imereti Mamia at first supported his father-in-law, George Abashidze, but in 1699 helped Abashidze's estranged son-in-law, King Simon, recover the crown, Simon agreeing to marry Mamia's sister. When Abashidze massed troops on the border and promised to make Mamia king if Simon died, Mamia refused to kill Simon himself but let Abashidze's agents shoot him in 1701. Made king in name only, with Abashidze holding the royal lands and revenues, Mamia had to sell his Gurian subjects into slavery to meet his expenses, and he abdicated later that year.

In 1703 an Ottoman invasion of western Georgia cost Guria the coast around Batumi for good. After George VI, with Ottoman support, defeated Abashidze in 1709 and ravaged Guria, Mamia won over the nobles of Mingrelia, Racha and Lechkhumi and made himself king of Imereti in October 1711, leaving Guria to his son George IV Gurieli. During this reign he banned the slave trade and opened schools in Guria. In June 1712 George VI and Zurab Abashidze defeated him at Chkhari, and he fled to Racha and then to Kartli.

With the support of the government of Kartli, Mamia returned and in November 1713, joined by the Dadiani, the duke of Racha, George Abashidze and the Lechkhumians, defeated King George at Kutaisi and drove him to Akhaltsikhe. He died two months later, on 5 January 1714, and was buried at the Shemokmedi Monastery. His widow Tamar then married his rival, George VI. Of his six children, George IV Gurieli and Kaikhosro III Gurieli later ruled Guria.
mamia-v-gurieli: Mamia was the only son of Simon III Gurieli, Prince of Guria, and Princess Marine Tsereteli. When Simon died in 1792 his younger brother Vakhtang III Gurieli took over the government. The dowager Marine, who felt persecuted by Vakhtang, found protection with the next brother, Kaikhosro, who deposed Vakhtang in 1797, proclaimed the boy Mamia ruler and governed as his regent. Kaikhosro brought Guria a degree of stability and drew closer to Russia, angering the Ottoman government, which claimed suzerainty over all of western Georgia.

Kaikhosro handed all ruling powers to Mamia in 1809. That year Russian forces under General Dimitri Orbeliani besieged the Ottoman stronghold of Poti; after corresponding with the Ottoman commanders, Mamia struck the defenders from the rear at Grigoleti and helped win the victory in November 1809. In March 1810 he and Levan V Dadiani of Mingrelia joined the Russian conquest of the Kingdom of Imereti. He swore fealty to Tsar Alexander I at Guriamta in April 1810 and in 1811 received the imperial diploma, the Order of St. Anna and the rank of major-general.

Mamia worked to reform the administration, economy and education of a state of about 6,000 families; a foreign observer called him very desirous of adopting European customs. Around 1817 he gave land and serfs to the Scotsman James Patrick Montague Marr to introduce indigo, and Marr's son was the linguist Nicholas Marr. When his uncle Kaikhosro and his brother-in-law Ivane Abashidze led a rising against Russian rule in March 1820, Mamia stayed loyal, though he kept out of the fighting, and General Aleksey Yermolov credited that loyalty for containing the revolt.

After the rising Mamia fell into depression, and he died at Ozurgeti on 21 November 1826. He had married the Imeretian princess Sophia Tsulukidze around 1814, and they had four daughters and a son. During the Russo-Ottoman war of 1828 and 1829 Sophia defected from the Russian Empire, which cost Guria its self-rule. After her death in exile the children were amnestied and settled in Saint Petersburg, and David, the last titular prince, died as a Russian officer at Akhulgo in 1839.
mamikonian-dynasty: The origin of the Mamikonians is unknown. Movses Khorenatsi tells that a nobleman named Mamgon fled from the land of Chenk, thought to mean China, to the Persian court and was sent on to Armenia, where King Trdat gave him land; the Primary History attributed to Sebeos names two brothers, Mamik and Konak. Pavstos Buzand also gives them royal Chen descent, equal to that of the Arsacids. Nicholas Adontz, Cyril Toumanoff and Robert Hewsen instead see them as old dynasts of Tayk, connecting Chenk with the Georgian Tzans, while others place it near the Syr Darya.

Besides the office of sparapet, the family held that of dayeak, royal tutor, which let it act as kingmaker, and it ruled Taron, Tayk, Sasun, Bagrevand and other lands. The first lord known with certainty is Vache Mamikonian, active in 330–339. In the 4th century Vasak Mamikonian led the defence against Shapur II until he was lured to Persia and flayed alive, and his son Mushegh I restored King Pap with help from the emperor Valens. Hamazasp Mamikonian's marriage to a daughter of Patriarch Isaac the Great brought much church land to the family.

After Vardan Mamikonian's death at Avarayr, his nephew Vahan Mamikonian kept up the revolt until the Treaty of Nvarsak of 484 restored Armenian autonomy and religious rights, and he became marzpan, Persian governor, in 485. The family often sided with the Eastern Roman Empire, and the failed revolt of Vardan II Mamikonian in the late 6th century began its decline. Under Arab rule the rival Bagratunis gained favour, took the office of sparapet in the 8th century and by 750 held Taron. Grigor Mamikonian's rising ended with his flight to Byzantium around 748.

The final blow came in the mid-770s, when Mushegh Mamikonian fell at the Battle of Bagrevand against the Abbasids. His sons were murdered, and his daughter's marriage to the tribal chief Djahap al-Qais founded the Kaysite emirate of Manzikert on former Mamikonian lands. Lesser lines lasted until the later 9th century. Some Georgian houses and Byzantine families, among them the emperor Philippikos Bardanes, have been claimed as descendants, though Nina Garsoïan judges this cannot be proven. Several princes were buried at the Surb Karapet Monastery near Mush.
mamilia-gens: The Mamilii traced their name and descent to the mythical Mamilia, daughter of Telegonus, held to be the founder of Tusculum and son of Ulysses and the goddess Circe. A coin of the family alludes to this: its obverse shows the head of Mercury, ancestor of Ulysses, and its reverse Ulysses himself in the humble disguise he wore to hide from the suitors of Penelope. At Rome the family was plebeian. Its first member known to history bore the praenomen Octavius, rare at Rome; his descendants used the common names Lucius, Quintus, Gaius and Marcus.

Octavius Mamilius, a prince of Tusculum, commanded the Latin army as dictator at the Battle of Lake Regillus and was killed there by Titus Herminius Aquilinus. Lucius Mamilius, perhaps his grandson, was dictator of Tusculum in 460 BCE and sent an army to help recover the Capitol during the revolt of Appius Herdonius; after the Romans helped him retake Tusculum's citadel from the Aequi, the senate granted him Roman citizenship in 458 BCE.

The family had three branches. The Vituli gave Rome the consuls of 265 and 262 BCE; Quintus Mamilius Vitulus took Agrigentum with Lucius Postumius Megellus in the First Punic War, and Gaius Mamilius Vitulus became the first plebeian curio maximus in 209 BCE. The Turrini gave a consul in 239 BCE and a praetor in 206 BCE. Gaius Mamilius Limetanus, tribune of the plebs in 109 BCE, carried a law to inquire into those who had taken bribes from Jugurtha.

The historian Niebuhr supposed that Vitulus was another form of Italus and Turrinus of Tyrrhenus, an Etruscan, since great houses took surnames from peoples to whom they were bound by blood or hospitality. The ancients instead linked Vitulus with the Latin word for a calf, and Turrinus may come from turris, a tower: the Turris Mamilia in the Subura figured in the ritual fight between two neighbourhoods of Rome for the head of the October Horse.
mamluk: The Arabic word mamluk means one who is owned. Mamluks were non-Arab and ethnically diverse enslaved mercenaries, slave-soldiers and freed slaves given military and administrative duties in the Muslim world. At first they were mostly Turks from the Eurasian Steppe, and the institution later took in Circassians, Mongols, Georgians, Armenians, Russians and Balkan peoples such as Albanians and Greeks. David Ayalon called the creation of this warrior class the Mamluk or Ghulam phenomenon. It lasted nearly a thousand years, from the 9th century to the early 19th. Historians agree that a large slave military class developed in the 9th-century Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad, under the caliph al-Muʿtaṣim.

From the 900s to the 1200s Egypt was controlled by foreign dynasties, among them the Ikhshidids, Fatimids and Ayyubids, who used thousands of mamluk soldiers and some of whom took high office. In 1249 the Seventh Crusade under Louis IX of France landed in Egypt. After the sultan as-Salih Ayyub died, his widow Shajar al-Durr took control with Mamluk support, and the Bahri commander Baibars defeated Louis's troops. Louis was captured in March 1250. After the assassination of Aybak, Shajar al-Durr's husband, Qutuz took power and founded the Mamluk Sultanate and the Bahri dynasty.

In 1260 the Mamluk army under Qutuz ambushed a reduced Ilkhanate force at the Battle of Ain Jalut and routed it. With the capture of Ruad in 1302 the Sultanate formally expelled the last Crusaders from the Levant. In 1382 the Burji dynasty began when Barquq was proclaimed sultan, and by then most Mamluks were Circassians. The Mamluk Sultanate lasted from 1250 to 1517. In 1798 Napoleon Bonaparte's army defeated a Mamluk army at the Battle of the Pyramids.

Under the Mamluk Sultanate of Cairo, Mamluks were bought as young males and raised in the barracks of the Citadel of Cairo. Because they had no social ties or political affiliations and went through austere military training, they were trusted to be loyal to their rulers. After training they were freed but stayed attached to the patron who had bought them, whose reputation in turn depended on his recruits. Their status was above that of ordinary slaves, who could not carry weapons.

Georgian mamluks in Egypt kept their native language and sent gifts to relatives. The practice ended in Egypt after 1 March 1811, when Muhammad Ali invited the leading Mamluks to his palace and his forces killed almost all of the 600 to 700 who came, in the Massacre of the Citadel.
mamluk-dynasty-delhi: Historians use the name for three dynasties of Mamluk origin that ruled the Ghurid territories in India and then the Sultanate of Delhi: the Qutbi dynasty (1206–1211), the first Ilbari or Shamsi dynasty (1211–1266) and the second Ilbari dynasty (1266–1290). Mamluks were soldiers of slave origin who had converted to Islam. They became a powerful military class in several Muslim societies, in Egypt, the Levant, Iraq and India.

Qutb al-Din Aibak served as a Ghurid administrator from 1192 to 1206 and led forays into the Gangetic plain. When Muhammad of Ghor, Sultan of the Ghurid Empire, was assassinated in 1206 without male heirs, the empire split into minor sultanates under his former Mamluk generals: Taj-ud-Din Yildoz held Ghazni, Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khilji took Bengal and Nasir-ud-Din Qabacha became sultan of Multan. Aibak became sultan of Delhi.

Aibak made Lahore his capital and began the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar. He died in 1210 after a fall from his horse while playing polo. Forty nobles known as the Chihalgani then conspired against his successor Aram Shah and invited Shams-ud-din Iltutmish, governor of Badaun, to replace him. Iltutmish defeated Aram in 1211, moved the capital to Delhi, defeated Qabacha and Yildoz, and incorporated Bengal in 1227. He kept India clear of the Mongol invasions that followed Genghis Khan's defeat of the Khwarazmshah Jalal-ud-din Mangabarni at the Battle of the Indus in 1221.

After Iltutmish died in 1236 a series of weak rulers followed. Rukn-ud-din Feroze reigned seven months, with his mother Shah Turkan running the government, and both were killed by the Chihalgani on 9 November 1236. Razia al-Din, the first female Muslim ruler in India, reigned until 1240; nobles resented her, and she was defeated and killed on 14 October 1240. Muiz-ud-din Bahram was put to death in 1242 while the Mongols sacked Lahore. Ala-ud-din Masud was a puppet of the Chihalgani until 1246, when Nasiruddin Mahmud replaced him; his Deputy Sultan, Ghiyath-ud-din Balban, handled state affairs.

Balban ruled from 1266 to 1287. He consolidated royal authority, eliminated rival members of the Chihalgani and used news-writers and spies to curb insubordination. The court chronicler Ziauddin Barani records that his expeditions in Mewat and Katehr involved large-scale executions and the demolition of forts. Balban repelled many Mongol invasions and lost his son Prince Muhammad at the Battle of Beas River. His grandson Muiz-ud-din Qaiqabad ruled from 1287 until his murder in 1290, and the dynasty ended with the rise of the Khalji dynasty. Iltutmish's Hauz-i-Shamsi reservoir and Sultan Ghari, the first Islamic mausoleum in Delhi, survive from the period.
mamluk-sultanate: A mamluk was a freed slave soldier, trained in martial arts, court etiquette and Islamic sciences and expected to stay loyal to his former master. Mamluks had served in Syria and Egypt since at least the 9th century, and under the Ayyubids, beginning with Saladin, they were the backbone of Egypt's army. Most were Kipchak Turks from Central Asia. In 1249 Louis IX of France captured Damietta in the Seventh Crusade, and the Ayyubid sultan al-Salih died. His son Turanshah promoted his own entourage at the expense of his father's mamluks, and on 2 May 1250 disgruntled emirs of that corps assassinated him at Fariskur, which established the sultanate.

Under Sultan Qutuz and Baybars the Mamluks routed the Mongols in 1260, halting their southward expansion, and took the Ayyubids' Syrian principalities. Baybars re-established an Abbasid caliph in Cairo, though with a ceremonial role. By the end of the 13th century Baybars, Qalawun and al-Ashraf Khalil had conquered the Crusader states and expanded into Makuria, Cyrenaica, the Hejaz and southern Anatolia. Historians call the period to 1382 Bahri and that from 1382 to 1517 Burji or Circassian. Stability and prosperity marked the third reign of al-Nasir Muhammad (1310–1341).

Foreign invasions, tribal rebellions and natural disasters then eroded Mamluk authority, and the state fell into financial distress. Sultan Barsbay monopolised trade with Europe and forced Cyprus to submit in 1426. The last effective sultan, Qansuh al-Ghuri, was killed in battle against the Ottoman sultan Selim I in 1516, and Selim conquered Egypt in 1517, ending Mamluk rule.

The sultan was the supreme authority and delegated power to provincial governors, mamluk emirs called nuwwab al-saltana. The Mamluks left the Ayyubid administrative, legal and economic systems largely unchanged, but their state was unitary, with Cairo holding absolute paramountcy over Syria. Entry into the military hierarchy was essentially restricted to mamluks, and revenue came largely from the iqta', a right to collect revenue from a fixed territory, granted to emirs to provision their soldiers.

The economy was mainly agrarian, but Egypt and Syria also stood at the centre of trade between Europe and the Indian Ocean. Cairo reached the peak of its size and wealth before the modern period. Mamluk enamelled glass, inlaid metalwork and illuminated Qur'an manuscripts were prized around the Mediterranean, and Mamluk architecture still makes up much of historic Cairo.
mammad-amin-rasulzade: Mahammad Amin Rasulzade was born on 31 January 1884 in Novkhany, near Baku, and studied at the Russian-Muslim Secondary School and the Technical College in Baku. While a student he created the Muslim Youth Organisation Musavat, the first secret organisation in Azerbaijan's modern history. From 1903 he wrote for opposition newspapers, and in 1904 he founded Hummet, the first Muslim social-democratic organisation, editing its papers Takamul and Yoldash. He took an active part in the First Russian Revolution of 1905 to 1907.

Persecuted by the tsarist authorities, he fled in 1909 to Iran, where he edited the newspaper Iran-e Azad, helped found the Democrat Party of Persia and published Iran-e Now. After Russian troops entered Iran in 1911 he went to Istanbul and founded the journal Türk Yurdu. Under the Amnesty Act of 1913 he returned to Baku and joined the Musavat party, which had been established in 1911 and which he soon led. After the February Revolution it became a leading party of the Caucasian Muslims.

On 28 May 1918 the Azerbaijani National Council, headed by Rasulzade, declared an independent Azerbaijan Republic. His phrase, The flag once raised shall never fall, became the motto of the independence movement. He also initiated the founding of Baku State University in 1919, with funds from the oil magnate Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev, and taught Ottoman literature there. After the republic collapsed in April 1920 he went into hiding in the village of Lahıc to direct resistance to Sovietization. He was arrested in August 1920, but was released, said to be because he had once hidden Joseph Stalin from the police, and was transferred to Russia.

Rasulzade escaped to Finland in 1922 and lived the rest of his life in exile, first in Turkey, where he edited the magazine Yeni Kafkasya from 1923 to 1927. He was expelled from Turkey in 1931 and later went to Poland. In 1942 the leadership of Nazi Germany approached him, and in May 1942 he sought an alliance to restore Azerbaijan's independence, demanding a commitment to the restoration of the Transcaucasian states, which the Reich evaded. He returned to Ankara in 1947. He died in 1955 and was buried in the Cebeci Asri cemetery in Ankara.
Baku State University was named in his honour, and he appeared on the Azerbaijani 1000 manat banknote of 1993 to 2006. A high school in Ankara also bears his name.
mamprusi: Mamprusi tradition traces its monarchy to a warrior named Tohazie, the Red Hunter, so called by his people for his fair complexion. His grandson, Naa Gbewaa, settled at Pusiga, a village 14 kilometres from Bawku, and founded the kingdom of Mamprugu there around the 13th century. The Mamprusi revere Pusiga as their ancestral home, and the founder's tomb stands there. The kingdom is among the oldest in the lands later called the Gold Coast and then Ghana.

Succession to a skin, the seat of a chief, is hereditary, and only male direct descendants of the founder are eligible. The Mamprusi base their claim to seniority on succession through the eldest male child, though Gbewaa himself did not follow this rule: he named a younger son, Kufoɣu, to rule over his eldest child Kachaɣu and his eldest son Zirile.

The kingdom is called Mamprugu, the people Mamprusi and their language Mampruli. Mamprugu spans most of the North East Region and parts of the Northern Region of Ghana, of northern Togo and of Burkina Faso. Of the related peoples, the Mamprusi, Dagomba, Nanumba and Mossi, the Mamprusi count as the eldest, and the Nayiri, king of Mamprugu, still symbolically enskins the Moronaba, king of the Mossi in Burkina Faso.

Estimates of 2013 put about 200,000 Mamprusi in the north of Ghana, living mainly in Nalerigu, Gambaga, Walewale and the towns and villages around them. The majority of the Mamprusi are adherents of Islam, which spread among them through the influence of Dyula merchants. Their traditional occupations are farming and raising livestock.
mampuru-ii: Mampuru was born in 1824. Pedi custom gave the succession to the children of the timamollo, the candle wife or great wife, ahead of other descendants, and Mampuru was the child of the candle wife of Sekwati's elder brother, Malekutu; Sekwati afterwards married his mother. When Sekwati died in 1861, Mampuru claimed to have been named heir and held the royal insignia. Sekhukhune, Sekwati's elder son, answered that Sekwati was not Mampuru's father and that the marriage was not lawful, the customary black bull never having been given. Sekhukhune seized power, killed Mampuru's advisers and drove him from the realm.

After Britain annexed the Transvaal in 1877, a British and Swazi force invaded the Pedi kingdom in 1879 and deposed Sekhukhune, and the High Commissioner, Sir Garnet Wolseley, installed Mampuru in his place. The Transvaal regained some independence after the First Boer War of 1880–81. Claiming that Sekhukhune was plotting to regain the throne, Mampuru ordered his murder, and Sekhukhune was stabbed to death at the Great Place, Manoge, on 13 August 1882.

Mampuru, who also opposed the hut tax that the South African Republic imposed on black people, was arrested and charged with public violence, revolt and the murder of Sekhukhune. On 22 November 1883 he was stripped naked and hanged in public at Pretoria Central Prison; the rope broke and he was hanged a second time.

Sekhukhune's descendants took the kingship after his death, and in 2008 the Commission on Traditional Leadership Disputes and Claims ruled that the Sekhukhune line was the legitimate one. Mampuru has been described as one of South Africa's first liberation icons. Potgieter Street in Pretoria was renamed after him in 2007, an annual Mampuru II day is held in January, and on 10 April 2013 the prison where he died was renamed Kgosi Mampuru II. The location of his remains is unknown; in January 2019 the government committed to search for them.
man-dynasty: Traditional Lebanese histories bring the family to the Chouf in the 12th century, where its founder, said to come from a clan of the Rabi'a confederation, fought the Crusader lords of Beirut and Sidon beside the Tanukhid Buhturids; the historian Kamal Salibi judged these accounts without foundation. They may have belonged to a wider settlement of Arab tribesmen in Mount Lebanon by the rulers of Damascus as a buffer against the Crusader coast. The first member whose existence is certain is Fakhr al-Din I, who died in 1506, was called emir of the Chouf, and founded the Fakhreddine Mosque at the family seat of Deir al-Qamar.

In 1518 three Ma'nid chiefs were arrested by Janbirdi al-Ghazali, governor of Damascus, and released by Sultan Selim I after a heavy fine. The Druze of the Chouf were repeatedly attacked by Ottoman expeditions for evading tax collectors and hoarding firearms, and after the destructive campaign of 1585 the emir Qurqumaz ibn Yunis died in hiding in Kisrawan.

His son Fakhr al-Din II worked with the Ottomans instead, becoming governor of Sidon-Beirut in 1593 and of Safed in 1602. After a campaign against him in 1613 he fled to Italy, returned in 1618, defeated Yusuf Sayfa of Tripoli and extended his rule into Maronite northern Mount Lebanon, but a second Ottoman expedition in 1633 killed most of the family.

His nephew Mulhim, son of Yunus, drove out the rival Druze chief Ali Alam al-Din and in 1642 became tax farmer of the Druze Mountain. Mulhim's son Qurqumaz was killed by the governor of Damascus in 1662, according to Istifan al-Duwayhi, while his brother Ahmad defeated the Alam al-Dins in 1667 and held the Chouf and Kisrawan despite campaigns against him for backing Shia rebels.

After Ahmad died without a son, the Druze chiefs chose Bashir Shihab, whose mother was Mulhim's daughter, and the Shihabs held the region until the expulsion of Bashir II in 1841. Historians see the emirate of the Ma'ns and Shihabs as an early precursor of present-day Lebanon. In Tyre, the ruins of the family's residence, later a khan, stand in the souk; Israeli bombing in 1982 partly destroyed them.
man-singh-i: Man Singh was born on 21 December 1550, the son of Raja Bhagwant Das of Amer and his wife Bhagawati. Known as Kunwar, or prince, he received the title of Raja and a mansab of 5000 from Akbar after his father's death on 10 December 1589, and became the 24th Kachawaha ruler of Amber. On 26 August 1605 he was made a mansabdar of 7,000, the highest command open to anyone but a son of the emperor. He is commonly counted among the Navaratnas, the nine gems of Akbar's court.

Sent to persuade Maharana Pratap to accept Mughal sovereignty, he led the Mughal army when Pratap refused; at Haldighati the Mughals won but failed to capture Pratap, who escaped to the hills. When rebels declared Mirza Hakim emperor in 1581, Man Singh led Akbar's advance force across the Indus to Kabul, and he later governed the province. After the Yusufzai rising of 1585, in which Raja Birbal was killed, he crossed the Khyber Pass and defeated the rebel tribes.

As Subahdar of Bihar from 1587 he brought the local rajas, such as Raja Puranmal of Gidhaur, to submission. In Orissa the Afghans of Qatlu Khan Lohani submitted, rebelled again and were defeated near Jaleswar on 9 April 1592, and the Raja of Khurda surrendered. Made viceroy of Bengal and guardian of Prince Salim in 1594, he founded a new capital, Akbarnagar, on 7 November 1595 and defeated the Afghans under Isa Bhati and, later, Kedar Rai of Bhushna.

He favoured Khusrau Mirza over Salim for the succession but did not oppose Salim once he was crowned as Jahangir, who sent him in 1611 against the revolt led by Malik Ambar. He died at Ellichpur on 6 July 1614 and was succeeded by his son Mirza Raja Bhau Singh. A devotee of Krishna, he built a seven-storied temple for Rupa Goswami in Vrindavan, the temple of Shila Devi at Amber Fort and others at Benaras and Allahabad.
man-singh-tomar: Man Singh was the son of Raja Kalyanmall, the Tomar Rajput ruler of Gwalior, and ruled for more than thirty years. In his time the Tomar were sometimes at war with the sultans of Delhi and sometimes their allies. Newly crowned and unready for an invasion, he avoided war by paying Bahlul Lodi a tribute of 800,000 tankas.

Sikandar Lodi succeeded Bahlul in 1489. In 1500 Man Singh gave asylum to rebels who had plotted against him, and in 1501 the sultan took Dholpur, a dependency of Gwalior. An epidemic halted his march after he crossed the Chambal River, and Man Singh made peace by sending his son Vikramaditya with gifts and promising to expel the rebels if Dholpur was restored. The historian Kishori Saran Lal suggests the loss of Dholpur was invented by Delhi chroniclers to flatter the sultan.

In 1504 Sikandar took the Mandrayal fort, but another epidemic drove him back. From his new base at Agra he called his next campaign a jihad, and from September 1505 to May 1506 he ravaged the country around Gwalior, yet Man Singh's hit-and-run tactics kept the fort out of his hands. Food ran short, and as the sultan withdrew Man Singh ambushed his army near Jatwar with heavy losses. Sikandar then took the smaller forts around Gwalior, Uditnagar in 1507 and Narwar after a year-long siege, but illness stopped a last attempt in 1516.

Man Singh died in 1516. He was a patron of music who sang dhrupad and compiled the book Manakautuhal, and his court musicians included Baiju and Swami Haridasa. He married Mrignayani, a Gurjar woman, and because of friction with his other wives over her lower caste built the Gujari Mahal for her below the fortress, with a constant water supply from the River Rai. Its exterior survives almost intact and its interior is now an archaeological museum. In the Man Mandir, the chambers behind fine stone screens were music halls where the royal women learned from masters.
manabendra-shah: Manabendra Shah was born on 26 May 1921, the son of Maharaja Narendra Shah and Maharani Indu Matt Devi. He studied at Government College, Lahore, and at the ICS Camp in Dehradun. He became the last ruling Maharaja of Tehri Garhwal in 1946, and the princely state acceded to independent India on 1 August 1949. He also held the honorary rank of lieutenant colonel in the Bengal Engineer Group, the old Bengal Sappers and Miners.

Shah represented the Tehri Garhwal constituency in the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 10th, 11th, 12th, 13th and 14th Lok Sabha. He began in the Indian National Congress, moved to the Bharatiya Jan Sangh and later sat for the Bharatiya Janata Party, becoming one of its longest-serving members. He was also India's ambassador to Ireland from 1980 to 1983.

In the Lok Sabha he chaired the Committee on Health and Drinking Water for the Hills and the Committee on Public Undertakings, and sat on the committees on estimates, finance, external affairs, transport and tourism, and home affairs, as well as on the consultative committees of the ministries of surface transport, power and defence. Outside Parliament he was patron of the Badrinath and Kedarnath temples, president of the temple board of Tehri Garhwal and a trustee of the Maharaja Narendra Shah Trust and the Maharaja Kirti Shah Trust.

Shah died in New Delhi on 5 January 2007 after a long illness and was given a state funeral at Narendranagar in Tehri Garhwal on 7 January. His daughter-in-law Mala Rajya Laxmi Shah was elected to the Lok Sabha for the same seat in 2012, and his son-in-law Mahendra Singh Mewar sat for Chittorgarh after the 1989 general election.
manadeva-i: Manadeva was the son of Dharmadeva, the grandson of Shankardeva and the great-grandson of Vrsadeva. His father died while he was still young, and he was crowned at an early age. His mother, Rajyabati, chose not to commit sati on her husband's death but stayed to help her son rule the kingdom. He had at least three queens, Bhogini, Ksemasundari and Gunavati.

Soon after his accession the Thakuri governors of the eastern provinces revolted, seeking independence from Licchavi rule, and Manadeva marched against them with a large army and put down the rebellion by force. With his maternal uncle he then turned west and conquered Mallapuri, Nabalpur and several other small states. His kingdom reached the Himalayas in the north, the far side of the Gandaki River in the west and the Kosi River in the east.

He set up 14 inscriptions during his reign. The one at the Changu Narayan Temple, dated 464 CE, is the earliest inscription of the Licchavi period and of ancient Nepal as a whole. He minted coins called Mananka, and the Managriha palace he built for himself later became a centre of Licchavi administration.

Although he was a devoted worshipper of Vishnu, Manadeva was tolerant of other faiths: his queens and his daughter set up images of Shiva. He ruled for more than 41 years without any challenge to his authority and was succeeded by his son, Mahideva.
manado: Manado lies on the Bay of Manado, surrounded by mountains, with a tropical rainforest climate and no real dry season. The name comes from the Sangir word manaro, meaning on the far coast or in the distance, and first referred to the farther of two islands seen from the mainland. When the settlement there moved to the mainland the name came with it, and the island became Manado Tua. A world map by the French cartographer Nicolas Desliens, which shows the island as Manarow, mentions it first.

Before Europeans arrived, the area was ruled by the Sultan of Ternate, who collected tribute and introduced Islam. The Portuguese made the sultan their vassal and set up a trading post at Wenang. The Spanish took the Portuguese fortress at Amurang in the 1550s with native allies and built a fort at Manado, and one of the first Indo-Eurasian communities of the archipelago developed there in the 16th century. The first King of Manado, Muntu Untu, in 1630, was the son of a Spanish mestizo. Spain later renounced its Minahasa possessions to the Portuguese for 350,000 ducats, and the Minahasa, allied with the Dutch, expelled the last Portuguese.

The Dutch East India Company built Fort Amsterdam in 1658, and missionaries spread Christianity there; the first church, the Oude Kerk, still stands as Gereja Sentrum. HMS Dover captured Manado in June 1810, and in 1830 the Dutch exiled the Javanese prince Diponegoro there. The Japanese captured it in January 1942, and Allied bombing badly damaged it. In 1958 the rebel movement Permesta moved its headquarters to Manado; the central government bombed the city in February and invaded in June. In 1962 it was declared capital of North Sulawesi.

Manado is the second largest city of Sulawesi after Makassar. Most residents belong to the Minahasa people, and the main language is Manado Malay, a Malay-based creole. Christianity is the majority religion, and the city holds a large Christmas celebration each year. The Ban Hin Kiong Temple, founded in 1819, is the oldest temple in the city, and Bunaken National Park lies offshore.
managua: Managua stands on the southern shore of Lake Managua, also called Lake Xolotlán, in western Nicaragua, with a tropical wet and dry climate and two seasons: a rainy season from mid-May to mid-November and a dry one for the rest of the year. The lake has been polluted by the dumping of chemicals and waste water since 1927, and a waste-water treatment plant at Las Mercedes, funded by the German government, was inaugurated in 2009. The name may come from the Nahuatl mana-ahuac, 'adjacent to the water', or from a word in the Mangue language meaning 'place of the big man' or 'chief'.

The area was inhabited by Paleo-Indians as far back as 12,000 BCE. The footprints of Acahualinca, fossilised in volcanic ash along the shore, are 2,100 years old. Founded as a pre-Columbian fishing town, the settlement was incorporated in 1819 as Leal Villa de Santiago de Managua. Efforts to make it the capital began in 1824, after the Central American nations attained independence from Spain, and Nicaragua became an independent nation in 1838. Its position between the rival cities of León and Granada made it a logical compromise, and it was officially selected as the national capital in 1852. Between 1842 and 1930 it expanded and urbanised rapidly.

A disastrous earthquake in 1931 destroyed much of the city and killed between 1,000 and 2,450 people, and a large fire in 1936 destroyed much of what was left. Under the rule of Anastasio Somoza García and his family, from 1936 to 1979, the city was rebuilt and grew rapidly, with new government buildings, industry and universities. The earthquake of 1972 destroyed 90 percent of the city. Among the few buildings to survive were the National Palace, the Rubén Darío National Theatre and, though heavily damaged, the Old Cathedral, built from 1928 to 1938 as the first cathedral in the Western Hemisphere made entirely of concrete on a metal frame. The New Cathedral, designed by Ricardo Legorreta, was inaugurated in 1993 to replace it.

Managua is the capital and largest city of Nicaragua, with an estimated population of 1,063,815 in 2023, and the main economic, political and cultural hub of the country. Most of its universities are there, among them the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua, established in 1812 at León. The Plaza de la Revolución, on the shore of the lake, holds its historic centre, the Old Cathedral, the National Palace of Culture, which houses the National Museum, and the Rubén Darío National Theatre. The Museum of Acahualinca preserves the ancient footprints. The city's patron saint, Santo Domingo de Guzmán, is honoured each August in a festival in which his statue is carried across the city.
manama: Manama lies in the north-eastern corner of Bahrain on a small peninsula along the Persian Gulf. The land is flat and arid, with extremely hot summers and mild winters, and reclaimed land has extended the coastline in recent decades. Its coastal position made it a port and trading point of the Gulf. Historically the city was confined to what is now the Manama Souq and the Manama Fort to its south, and it has since grown to take in suburban developments and older neighbouring villages.

There is evidence of human settlement on Bahrain's northern coastline from the Bronze Age. The Dilmun civilisation inhabited the area in 3000 BCE as a trading hub between Mesopotamia, Magan and the Indus Valley Civilisation, and about 100,000 Dilmun burial mounds have been found across the north and centre of the country. The name Manamah is first recorded around 730 AH, about 1330 CE, during a visit by Turan Shah of Hurmuz to the island. Manama remained a small trading port until the Portuguese took control in the early 1500s, and in 1602 the Safavid Persians expelled them. The Safavids sidelined Manama and made the nearby town of Bilad Al Qadeem the provincial capital, while the islands' pearl exports grew.

The twin towns of Manama and Muharraq appear to have been founded together in the 1800s. Muharraq, with its more defensible position, was the capital of Bahrain until 1923, while Manama became the mercantile capital and the gateway to the main island. After the outbreak of the First World War in 1914 the British Raj used Manama as a base for the Mesopotamian campaign, and a municipal government was established there in 1919. In the 1920s the British pressed administrative reforms, including a reorganised customs office in 1923, civil courts, and in 1926 the appointment of Charles Belgrave as financial adviser. Manama was declared the capital when Bahrain became independent in 1971.

Manama is the capital and largest city of Bahrain, and its population has long been cosmopolitan: in 1904 it was estimated at 25,000, half of them foreigners from Basra, Najd, al-Hasa, Iran, India and Europe. Shia and Sunni Islam have coexisted there for centuries, each represented by distinct ethnic groups. Oil wealth spurred growth in the 20th century, and diversification from the 1990s made the city a financial hub of the Persian Gulf and a centre of Islamic banking. Bab Al Bahrain and the adjacent souq are among its notable cultural sites, and the city centre is the main location of Muharram processions in the country.
manas-river: The Manas, known in Bhutan as the Drangme Chhu, is the largest of Bhutan's four major river systems. It drains 41,350 square kilometres of eastern Bhutan and northeast India through three main branches, the Drangme Chhu, the Mangde Chhu and the Bumthang or Chamkhar Chhu. Part of its main stem rises in southern Tibet at about 4,500 metres and enters India in the Tawang district of Arunachal Pradesh before crossing into Bhutan near Trashigang. The Lhobrak or Kuri Chhu, its main central tributary, is the only one that rises north of the Great Himalayas.

In Bhutan the river runs southwest through V-shaped gorges between two ranges of the Lower Himalayas. In the foothills the valley widens into swamps and marshes. The Aie River joins it in Assam, and it then meanders for about 75 kilometres to the Brahmaputra near Jogighopa. It is the largest tributary on the Brahmaputra's north bank and contributes 5.48 per cent of its average volume. From May to October the southwest monsoon brings more than 4,000 millimetres of rain to the southern part of the basin; the flow in the monsoon is said to be as much as 20 times that of the dry season.

The core of the present Manas Wildlife Sanctuary in Assam was designated a sanctuary in 1928 and declared a tiger reserve in 1978; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in December 1985. A dam proposed in the 1970s would have sent a canal 100 kilometres long through the tiger reserve to the Sankosh River. India's Ministry of Environment and Forests objected, the World Heritage Committee of UNESCO supported the objection, and Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi discontinued the project. Two dams proposed on the Bhutanese side were dropped in 1986. In February 1989 members of the All Bodo Students Union entered the park and killed several wardens and guards.

The lowlands north of the confluence, the Duars, are very fertile and have been made into tea estates and paddy fields. Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan, raised to a national park in 1993, is 92 per cent forested, and five thousand people live in villages inside it. The two reserves shelter the Bengal tiger, Asian elephant, greater one-horned rhinoceros, wild water buffalo, pygmy hog, hispid hare and golden langur, and the Ganges river dolphin lives in the river.
manasseh-of-judah: Manasseh was the fourteenth king of the Kingdom of Judah and the oldest of the sons of Hezekiah and Hephzibah. According to the books of Kings and Chronicles he became king at the age of 12 and reigned for 55 years, the longest reign in the history of Judah. He was the first king of Judah who was not a contemporary of the northern kingdom of Israel, which the Assyrians had destroyed around 720 BCE, deporting much of its population. He married Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz of Jotbah, and their son Amon succeeded him.

Manasseh is named in Assyrian records as a loyal vassal of Sennacherib's son Esarhaddon, among twenty-two kings required to provide materials for his building projects. Esarhaddon's son Ashurbanipal also names him among the vassals who assisted a campaign against Egypt. These records agree with archaeological evidence of demographic trends and settlement patterns that suggest a period of stability in Judah. The archaeologists Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman credit Manasseh with reviving the rural economy, with an export trade in olive oil and forts protecting the trade routes, though they argue that trade also deepened the gap between rich and poor.

The books of Kings condemn his religious policy. They say he reversed his father Hezekiah's centralising reforms, re-established local shrines, restored the worship of Baal and Asherah, sponsored an Assyrian astral cult and took part in the cult of Moloch. They also report a persecution of the prophets, and later tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two on his orders. Chronicles adds that he was taken in chains to the Assyrian king in Babylon, then restored, repented and removed the foreign idols. Arnold J. Toynbee thought him nearer to a pious conservative defending his ancestors' faith.

Manasseh was buried not in the City of David among his ancestors but in the garden of Uzza, the garden of his own house. Jeremiah 15:4 links the coming destruction of Judah to the evil done by Manasseh. Finkelstein and Silberman suggest that the writer or editor of 2 Kings reworked the traditions about him to present his outward-looking involvement in trade as apostasy. The Prayer of Manasseh, a penitential prayer attributed to him, appears in some Christian Bibles but is regarded as apocryphal by Jews, Catholics and Protestants. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's 1 Meqabyan cites him as an example of an ungodly king.
manaw-gododdin: Manaw Gododdin was a coastal district on the Firth of Forth, part of the Brythonic-speaking Kingdom of Gododdin in the post-Roman era, adjacent to and possibly including Eidyn, the region around modern Edinburgh. The lands on both sides of the firth were known as Manaw, but from the post-Roman era only the southern part is called Manaw Gododdin. The Isle of Man is also Manaw in Welsh (Ynys Manaw), and Irish uses Manann for both places, so many early references are ambiguous.

About 150 CE Ptolemy placed the Otadini, or Votadini, along the coasts of south-eastern Scotland and north-eastern England. The Romans built no forts in their homeland, which suggests an understanding with the Romans, though the northern end of Dere Street ran through Manaw. The Historia Brittonum says that Cunedda, ancestor of Maelgwn of Gwynedd, came from Manaw Gododdin 146 years before Maelgwn's reign and expelled the Gaels with great slaughter; his arrival in Wales, about 450, is traditionally taken as the start of the history of modern Wales. Manaw was also the homeland of the warriors of the poem Y Gododdin.

Squeezed between the Picts and the Anglian Bernicians, the district was destroyed in the 7th century and absorbed into Northumbria; the defeat of Penda of Mercia at the Battle of Winwaed in 655 confirmed Bernician control. In 711, according to the Annals of Ulster, the Northumbrians defeated the Picts on the field of Manaw, placed by William Forbes Skene between the rivers Avon and Carron.

South of the Forth the name survives in Slamannan Moor and the village of Slamannan in Falkirk, from Sliabh Manann, and in Dalmeny, about 5 miles north-west of Edinburgh, once Dumanyn. Gaelic later replaced Brythonic in the region, and the old names were kept with a new pronunciation.
manbij: Manbij lies in the north-east of Aleppo Governorate in northern Syria, 30 kilometres west of the Euphrates. Coins struck there before Alexander's conquest give its Aramean name as Manbug, meaning Site of the Spring; the Assyrians knew it as Nappigu or Nanpigi, and the Greeks hellenised it as Bambyce. As the centre of worship of the Syrian goddess Atargatis it became Hieropolis, City of the Sanctuary, and then Hierapolis, the Holy City. The cult was described in De Dea Syria, traditionally attributed to Lucian of Samosata, which tells of a sacred tank of fish, a temple served by some three hundred priests and a lake where votaries swam out to decorate an altar.

The city was part of the kingdom of Bit Adini and was annexed by the Assyrians in 856 BCE; Shalmaneser III renamed it Lita-Ashur and built a palace there, and Tiglath-Pileser III reconquered it in 738 BCE. At the end of the Achaemenid Empire it seems to have been the centre of a dynasty of Aramean priest-kings. Under the Seleucids it was the chief station on their main road between Antioch and Seleucia on the Tigris. Crassus sacked the temple in 53 BCE on his way to meet the Parthians. In the third century it was the capital of the province of Euphratensis, and Khosrau I held it to ransom after Justinian I failed to defend it.

Harun al-Rashid restored Manbij at the end of the 8th century as capital of the frontier province of al-Awasim. Salih ibn Mirdas took it about 1022 and made it a foundation of the Mirdasid emirate. In 1068 the Byzantine emperor Romanos Diogenes captured it, killed its inhabitants and plundered the countryside. The Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah I took it in 1086, and in 1124 Belek Ghazi was killed by an arrow during his siege. The Crusaders never captured it. Nur ad-Din took it by 1152, Saladin conquered it in 1175, and in 1260 the Mongols under Hulagu destroyed Ayyubid Manbij.

Almost all the ancient remains, including the temple of Atargatis, its sacred lake, colonnades, Roman baths and theatres, Byzantine churches and medieval madrasas, have been destroyed, and the sacred lake has become a football field. The Ottoman government resettled the area with Circassian refugees from the Russo-Turkish War in 1878, and in 1915 Armenian refugees were brought to a camp there. The 2004 census gave a population of nearly 100,000, largely Arab with Kurdish, Turkmen, Circassian and Chechen minorities. Manbij changed hands several times in the Syrian civil war, from 2012 onwards.
manchukuo: Manchuria, now Northeast China, was historically the homeland of the Manchu people, but by the twentieth century Han Chinese were by far its largest group. The Qing dynasty fell in the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 and the last emperor Puyi abdicated at the age of six. In the Warlord Era Marshal Zhang Zuolin established himself in Manchuria with Japanese backing, and the Japanese Kwantung Army had him assassinated in 1928, expecting anarchy that would justify seizing the region. The plot failed because his son Zhang Xueliang succeeded him without incident.

Japan invaded and occupied Manchuria in 1931 after the Mukden incident. A puppet government was set up the following year, with Puyi as nominal regent. Manchukuo was proclaimed a monarchy on 1 March 1934, with Puyi as emperor.

The State Council was the centre of power. Each of its ministers was assisted by a Japanese vice-minister, and the commander-in-chief of the Kwantung Army served as Japanese ambassador with the ability to veto the emperor's decisions.
