Chinese advisers gradually resigned or were dismissed. The Legislative Council was largely ceremonial, and the only authorised party was the government-sponsored Concordia Association. Manchukuo received only limited diplomatic recognition, mainly from states aligned with the Axis powers.

More than a million Japanese settled there by 1945, many of them land-poor farmers resettled by Japan. Under the vice-minister Nobusuke Kishi and the Manchurian Industrial Development Company heavy industry expanded, using the forced labour of local people. Manchukuo was the base for Japan's invasion of the rest of China, beginning with the Marco Polo Bridge incident of 1937.

On 8 August 1945 the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded Manchukuo. Its imperial army, on paper 200,000 strong, performed poorly, and whole units surrendered without firing a shot. Puyi abdicated on 17 August. The Soviets captured him and later extradited him to China, where he was imprisoned on war crimes charges after the Communist Party came to power in 1949. The government was formally dissolved after Japan's surrender in September 1945, and the territory was transferred to Chinese administration the following year.
manchuria: Manchuria is most often associated with the three Chinese provinces of Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning. Its extent varies with the definition: the Qing region also included land now in the Russian Far East, and the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo added Chengde and parts of Inner Mongolia. The seasons are extreme, from humid heat in summer to dry Arctic cold in winter.

The name Manchuria is an exonym of Japanese origin, from Manshu, used by Japanese cartographers from the late eighteenth century. In Qing times the region was called the Three Eastern Provinces or Guandong, 'east of the pass'. In China the term is now deprecated because of its association with Japanese imperialism, and the area is called the Northeast.

Many peoples rose to power here, among them the Sushen, Donghu, Xianbei, Wuhuan, Mohe, Khitan and Jurchens, and the Koreanic kingdoms of Gojoseon, Buyeo and Goguryeo held large parts of it. The Qin, Han, Cao Wei, Western Jin and Tang dynasties controlled parts, and the First Turkic Khaganate and Eastern Turkic Khaganate held parts of the north-west. The Khitan Liao dynasty (916-1125) was the first state to control all of Manchuria.

The Qing forbade Han Chinese from settling in the region in 1668, and in 1681 built the Willow Palisade to mark the limit of settlement, but Han farmers kept arriving. The Qianlong Emperor allowed refugees from famine in the north to move in, and by 1800, according to one observer, Han Chinese made up 80 to 90 per cent of the population of garrisons and towns. The Treaty of Aigun in 1858 and the Treaty of Peking in 1860 ceded the lands north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri to Russia, and the Qing lost access to the Sea of Japan.

Russia built the Chinese Eastern Railway from 1896. After the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905, Japan took over its southern branch as the South Manchurian Railway, and in 1915 it forced China to cede economic privileges there. Manchuria supplied Japan with coal and other raw materials. Under the People's Republic it became a centre of heavy industry, with the Daqing oil field developed from the 1960s.

Manchuria is home to Manchus, Mongols, Koreans, Han Chinese, Nanai, Nivkhs and Ulchs, though the Han are now the large majority. Of the old Qing region, the parts north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri remain in Russia; a boundary dispute over islands in the Amur was settled by agreements of 2004 and 2008.
manchus: The Manchus are a Tungusic East Asian ethnic group native to Manchuria, the region that takes its name from them. Their name, manju in Manchu, was adopted as the official name of the people by Emperor Hong Taiji in 1635, replacing the earlier name Jurchen. The Qing dynasty's own record derived it from Mañjuśrī.

The Manchus are said to descend from the Jurchens who founded the Jin dynasty, although historians dispute this. The Jianzhou Jurchens, from whom they came, originated in part from the Huligai, whom the Liao dynasty classed as separate from the Jurchens of the Jin. When Nurhaci reorganised the Jurchens into the Eight Banners, many Manchu clans were artificially created from unrelated people, who took a place name as their clan name.

The Manchus founded the Later Jin dynasty (1616 to 1636) and the Qing dynasty (1636 to 1912). After 1644 the majority of the people living in the inner city of Beijing were Manchu and Mongol bannermen, and Han Chinese were not allowed to enter it until after the Hundred Days' Reform. Manchu and bannermen were declared legally equivalent in the 17th century, so banner membership was never genetically uniform, and Manchu identity was traditionally patrilineal. Many Manchu bannermen in Beijing supported the Boxers in the Boxer Rebellion and sustained heavy casualties.

The Manchus were sedentary agriculturalists who lived in permanent villages and practised hunting and mounted archery. Hong Taiji said that riding and archery were the most important martial arts of the country, and the results of yearly tests could affect Manchu rank in the nobility. Manchu men traditionally shave the front of the head and wear the hair at the back in a single braid, the queue, which the Qing made compulsory for Han men under pain of execution for treason.

Nurhaci ordered the scholars G'ag'ai and Erdeni to make a Manchu script from the Mongolian script, and Dahai later added dots and circles to complete it. Fluency among the bannermen declined from the early 18th century. Manchus were Buddhists with shamanist influences, and after the conquest of China adopted Confucianism, though shamanic traditions persisted. Their most important piece of literature is the Tale of the Nisan Shaman.
manco-capac: Manco Cápac, also known as Manco Inca and Ayar Manco, was according to some historians the first governor and founder of the Inca civilisation in Cusco, possibly in the early 13th century. Although several chronicles mention him, his actual existence remains uncertain. In the account given as history, he was born in Tamputoco, which some locate in the present-day province of Paruro in Peru, the son of Apu Tambo, head of a local tribal ayllu of several dozen families. The family lived a nomadic life, and on his father's death Manco Cápac succeeded him as head of the ayllu. His main wife, his sister Mama Uqllu, bore his son and successor, Sinchi Ruq'a.

On reaching the Cusco valley the ayllu defeated three small tribes, the Sahuares, Huallas and Alcahuisas, and settled in a swampy area between two small streams, where the main plaza of Cusco stands today. The new city was divided into four districts: Chumbicancha, Quinticancha, Sairecancha and Yarambuycancha. His ayllu occupied only a small part of the valley, and larger tribes, among them a confederated lordship of Ayarmacas and Pinaguas to the north, regarded the newcomers as invaders and often attacked them. Manco Cápac and later his son had to defend the city against them. He died a natural death and left Cusco to his son Sinchi Roca.

His body was mummified and remained in Cusco until Pachacuti ordered it moved to the Temple of the Sun on Isla del Sol, leaving a statue in the city. He is the protagonist of the two best-known legends of the origin of the Inca. In the first, he is Ayar Manco, a son of Viracocha of Paqariq Tampu, who with his brothers and sisters set out to conquer the tribes of the Cusco valley, and in some versions got rid of his brothers by trapping them or turning them to stone.

In the second, he is a son of the sun god Inti and the moon goddess Mama Killa, who emerged with his siblings from the cave of Pacaritambo carrying the golden staff tapac-yauri and was told to build a Temple of the Sun where it sank into the earth. No written tradition of this second tale is recorded before Garcilaso de la Vega's Comentarios Reales de los Incas of 1609.
manco-inca: Manco Inca, also called Manco II, was one of more than fifty sons of Huayna Capac and a younger brother of Huáscar. He was born in Cuzco around 1515, and his early history is obscure. He took part in the conquest of the Antisuyu in the years 1532 to 1533. When Atahualpa's troops took Cuzco under General Quizquiz they killed Huayna Capac's descendants, the supporters of Huáscar and anyone who might replace the Inca, so Manco fled and avoided the Atahualpists. On 14 November 1533 he met Francisco Pizarro. That meeting and events such as the killing of Atahualpa led him to believe that the Spaniards were saviours sent by the gods.

After the death of Túpac Huallpa, a puppet ruler crowned by Pizarro, Manco joined Pizarro and Diego de Almagro at Cajamarca. When Pizarro's forces reached Cusco he had the caciques acknowledge Manco as their Inca. Pizarro then left for Jauja in pursuit of Quizquiz, leaving his younger brothers Gonzalo Pizarro and Juan Pizarro as regidores with a garrison of ninety men. The brothers so mistreated Manco that he tried to escape in 1535, failed and was imprisoned. Hernando Pizarro released him to recover a golden statue of Huayna Capac, and he escaped a second time.

Taking advantage of Almagro's absence, Manco gathered an army, put at 200,000 warriors, and besieged Cusco in early 1536, though factions such as Paullu Inca's would not join. A siege of Lima was led by his captain Quiso Yupanqui, and the Incas defeated four relief expeditions sent by Pizarro, in which nearly 500 Spanish soldiers died. After ten months Manco withdrew to the fortress of Ollantaytambo, where in January 1537 he successfully defended against Spanish attacks. He then gave up the highlands, retreating to Vitcos and finally to Vilcabamba, where he founded the Neo-Inca State, which lasted until the death of Túpac Amaru in 1572.

The Spaniards crowned Manco's younger half-brother Paullu Inca as a puppet Sapa Inca. They captured Manco's sister-wife Cura Ocllo, whom Gonzalo Pizarro raped, and had her murdered in 1539. After many guerrilla battles in the mountains of Vilcabamba, Manco was murdered in 1544 at Vitcos by supporters of Diego de Almagro, who had assassinated Francisco Pizarro and were hiding under his protection. Manco's soldiers killed them in turn. His body was preserved at Vilcabamba in a Temple of the Sun, and his son Sayri Tupaq succeeded him. His other sons included Titu Cusi and Túpac Amaru.
mandal-commission: Formally the Second Backward Classes Commission, it was appointed by the Janata Party government of Prime Minister Morarji Desai. Unlike the broad first commission, its five members were drawn from the backward castes: four were from the Other Backward Classes, and L. R. Naik was its only Dalit member. To identify backward classes it used eleven indicators, social, educational and economic, weighted three, two and one points each, and listed as backward every caste scoring at least 11 of a possible 22.

Using data from the 1931 census, the last to record caste, the commission estimated that 52 per cent of the population outside the Scheduled Castes and Tribes, in 3,743 castes and communities, was backward. Since the Supreme Court had capped reservations below 50 per cent, it recommended 27 per cent, bringing the total for these groups to 49.5 per cent. Naik refused to sign, arguing that the intermediate backward classes were relatively powerful while the most backward remained marginalised.

The report was submitted in December 1980, after the Janata government had fallen, and the Congress governments of Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi did not act on it. On 7 August 1990 V. P. Singh's National Front government announced the reservations. Students in northern India protested on a large scale; after Rajiv Goswami of Deshbandhu College attempted self-immolation on 19 September 1990, nearly 200 students set themselves alight, and 62 died. Police firing in six states claimed more than 50 lives. Ramachandra Guha notes that the agitation found less support in the south, where affirmative action was long established.
Indra Sawhney challenged the order in the Supreme Court, which upheld it on 16 November 1992 with a 50 per cent ceiling and the exclusion of a creamy layer of better-off OBC families.

The recommendation for higher education was carried out in 2006 through the Ninety-third Amendment, which provoked the anti-reservation protests of that year until the Supreme Court upheld the measure on 10 April 2008. The commission's population figure remains disputed: the National Sample Survey of 1999 and 2000 put OBCs at about 36 per cent, and the psephologist Yogendra Yadav called the Mandal figure a construct without empirical basis.
mandala-political-model: In a mandala, relations rested on personal ties between an overlord and subordinate rulers rather than on fixed borders. A tributary owed allegiance to the overlord himself, not to his state, so a strong ruler drew in new tributaries and a weak one lost them; this has been offered as one cause of the swift rise of Sukhothai under Ramkhamhaeng and its decline after his death. The system was not territorial: no ruler had authority over unpopulated land.

A tributary usually paid bunga mas, regular gifts including miniature trees of gold and silver, and supplied men and goods in war; the overlord answered with presents often worth more and offered protection, which the historian Thongchai Winichakul calls often mafia-like, against the overlord himself. Tributaries generally kept their own armies and taxes. Ties were not exclusive: a border state might pay tribute to two or three powers and play them off, as the Malay kingdoms of Langkasuka and Tambralinga did between Ayutthaya and Majapahit.

The main overlord states were the Khmer Empire, Srivijaya, the Javanese kingdoms of Mataram, Kediri, Singhasari and Majapahit, Ayutthaya, Champa and early Đại Việt, while post-Angkor Cambodia, Lan Xang and Lanna were tributaries. The Vietnamese emperor Gia Long called 18th-century Cambodia an independent country that is slave of two. After Islam came, the pattern continued, as in the Negeri Sembilan coalition centred on Seri Menanti. European colonisation in the mid-19th century imposed single sovereignty and fixed borders between French Indochina, the Dutch East Indies, British Malaya and Burma.

The name compares the pattern to the mandala of Hindu and Buddhist cosmology. The anthropologist S. J. Tambiah spoke of a galactic polity and Victor Lieberman prefers a solar polity. O. W. Wolters developed the concept, Martin Stuart-Fox applied it to Lan Xang, and Sunait Chutintaranond argued that provincial governors in Ayutthaya were never brought fully under the centre.
mandalay: Mandalay lies on the east bank of the Irrawaddy River, 631 km north of Yangon, in the central Dry Zone, at about 80 metres above sea level. It stands on the Sagaing Fault, the boundary between the India and Sunda plates. An earthquake on 23 March 1839, of an estimated magnitude of 8.2, destroyed the former capital Ava and did great damage in nearby cities, and a quake of magnitude 7 in 1956 did most harm at Sagaing. The city takes its name from Mandalay Hill, probably from a Pali word, perhaps mandala, a circular plain.

King Mindon founded the royal city on 13 February 1857 at the foot of Mandalay Hill, ostensibly to fulfil a prophecy that a great city of Buddhism would be founded on that spot at the 2,400th jubilee of Buddhism. Its official name was Yadanarbon, from the Pali Ratanapura, meaning City of Gems. It was the last royal capital before the British annexation of 1885, after which commercial and political importance moved to Yangon. The British looted the palace, and part of the treasure went on display in the Victoria and Albert Museum until it was returned in 1964. A railway reached Mandalay in 1889, but its first college was founded only in 1925.

The city was extensively destroyed in the Japanese conquest of Burma in the Second World War, and most of the palace was burnt, a replica standing there now. After independence in 1948 Mandalay remained the main cultural, educational and economic centre of Upper Burma. Fires in the 1980s cleared large areas, and from the 1990s a large migration of Han Chinese, mostly from Yunnan, changed the ethnic makeup of the city and its commerce. Its population doubled from about 500,000 in 1980 to one million in 2008.

Mandalay is the second-largest city of Myanmar, with 1,225,553 inhabitants in 2014, and the economic centre of Upper Myanmar. It is regarded as the centre of Burmese culture and Buddhism, with numerous monasteries and more than 700 pagodas. At the Kuthodaw Pagoda at the foot of Mandalay Hill, 729 stone slabs carry the whole Pali Canon, each in its own white stupa. Traditional industries include silk weaving, jade cutting, stone and wood carving, and the making of bronze and marble Buddha images.
mandarin-chinese: The hundreds of modern local varieties of Chinese developed from regional variants of Old Chinese and Middle Chinese. Besides Mandarin, six other major groups are traditionally recognised: Wu, Gan, Xiang, Min, Hakka and Yue. Mandarin originated in North China, and its spread is attributed to the greater ease of travel on the North China Plain compared with the mountainous south.

After the fall of the Northern Song in 1126, and under the Jin and the Yuan dynasties in northern China, a common form of speech developed from the dialects of the North China Plain around the capital, called Old Mandarin. New genres of vernacular literature were written in it. The Zhongyuan Yinyun, a rime dictionary of 1324, records many features of modern Mandarin, such as the disappearance of final plosives.

Mandarin is the largest branch of the Sinitic languages. Mandarin varieties are natively spoken by 71 per cent of all Chinese speakers, over an area stretching from Yunnan in the southwest to Xinjiang in the northwest and Heilongjiang in the northeast. Many varieties are not mutually intelligible with the Beijing dialect. Most have four lexical tones, and many keep retroflex initial consonants, which southern varieties have lost. Chinese languages are strongly analytic, relying on word order and particles rather than inflection.

The English word mandarin originally meant an official of the Ming and Qing empires. These officials, whose native varieties were often mutually unintelligible, ran the empire in a koiné based on northern varieties called Guānhuà, the language of the officials; Jesuit missionaries who learned it in the 16th century called it Mandarin. Until the early 20th century formal writing was in Literary Chinese, but a literature in written vernacular Chinese had grown up from at least the Yuan dynasty, with Water Margin and Dream of the Red Chamber.

After the Republic's founding, intellectuals of the New Culture Movement, among them Hu Shih and Chen Duxiu, campaigned to replace Literary Chinese with it. The National Language Unification Commission settled on the Beijing dialect as the national standard in 1932, and the People's Republic, founded in 1949, kept it as pǔtōnghuà. Singapore's Speak Mandarin Campaign began in 1979.
mandate-of-heaven: In the doctrine, Heaven (Tian) bestows its mandate on a virtuous ruler, the Son of Heaven (Tianzi), who rules all under heaven (Tianxia). It does not require noble birth: the Han and Ming dynasties were founded by men of common origins, who were seen as successful because they had gained the mandate. Keeping it depended on the just and able performance of the ruler and his heirs.

The Zhou were the first to use the concept to explain their right to rule. They held that the Shang came to power because the Xia had lost their mandate, and that the Shang ruling house had become morally corrupt. Early records such as the Da Yu ding inscription speak of 'the great command in the sky'. Heaven's authority was held to pass through the founder, King Wen, to his heirs.

In the Eastern Zhou the kings lost real power but not their divine legitimacy, while inscriptions show that the rulers of the state of Qin held privately that their ancestors had received the mandate. Qin's own surviving material never mentions it. Han writers painted the Qin as tyrannical and so as having lost the mandate, and Liu Bang, who came from outside the aristocracy, was credited with a magical birth and later a divine ancestry.

In 220 CE the last Han emperor abdicated to Cao Pi, and the court prognosticator Xu Zhi listed signs showing that Wei should succeed the Han. To justify their own succession the Song had the scholar Xue Juzheng argue that the mandate had passed through each of the Five Dynasties. The Qing, a Manchu dynasty, argued that peasant rebels led by Li Zicheng had overthrown the Ming and that they themselves had won the mandate by defeating those rebels and restoring stability.

Mencius held that the people are of supreme importance and the ruler last, so the mandate gave no unconditional right to rule. Han Feizi rejected the idea of a just rebellion entirely. The right of rebellion was never written into law, and rebellion was always punished. Because the winner decided who held the mandate, some Chinese scholars regard it as victor's justice, and accounts of a dynasty's fall must be read with caution.

The idea spread to other East Asian countries. The Joseon dynasty made it an enduring state ideology, and in Vietnam it gave the emperor the right to rule on his competence rather than his lineage. Japan's Taihō Code of 703 adapted Tang government but omitted it.
mandla: Mandla is the administrative headquarters of Mandla district in Madhya Pradesh. The city stands in a loop of the Narmada River that surrounds it on three sides, and for 15 miles between Mandla and Ramnagar the river flows in a deep bed unbroken by rocks. The Narmada is worshipped here, and many ghats have been built on its banks. Alexander Cunningham, John Faithfull Fleet and other writers have identified Mandla as the ancient Mahishmati.

According to an inscription in the palace of Ramnagar, the Gond dynasty of the Garha kingdom began in the fifth century with Jadho Rai, though Cunningham placed it in 664. The Garha-Mandla kingdom was a petty local chiefship until Raje Sangram Shah, the forty-seventh king, came to the throne in 1480 and extended it over the Narmada Valley and much of the Satpura hills. In 1564 the Mughal viceroy Asaf Khan invaded. The queen Durgavati, regent for her infant son, was defeated near Singorgarh, and at a defile near Mandla she took her own life rather than withdraw.

The kingdom declined rapidly afterwards, and it ceded the lands later forming Bhopal to the Emperor Akbar to secure recognition of its next raja, Chandra Shah. Mandla was made the kingdom's capital in 1670.

The Peshwa invaded in 1742 and exacted chauth, and in 1781 the last king of the Gondwana line was deposed and Mandla was annexed to the Maratha government of Sagar. The Bhonsles of Nagpur took it in 1799, and the Marathas built a wall on the landward side. Mandla was ceded to the British in 1818 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War, when a force under General Marshall took the fort by assault. It became a municipality in 1867.

The Gond rulers built a palace and a fort at Mandla, which have fallen into ruin for lack of care. The town is represented in the Lok Sabha by the Mandla constituency. At the 2011 census it had 71,579 inhabitants, and scheduled tribes make up much of the population.
mandore: Mandore lies 9 km north of Jodhpur city in the Jodhpur district of Rajasthan, and is now a suburb as well as a historical town. It was the seat of the Pratiharas of Mandavyapura, who ruled the region in the 6th century CE, and a Pratihara family went on ruling there after the Gurjara-Pratihara empire broke up. Local belief holds it to be the native place of Mandodari, wife of Ravan, and a Ravan temple stands there.

To defend its chiefdom against the Tughluq dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, the Pratihara family allied with the Rathore chief Rao Chunda (r. c. 1383–1424), who married a Pratihara princess and received the Mandore Fort as her dowry. Rao Ranmal Rathore took the throne of Mandore in 1427 and also served as administrator of Mewar for Maharana Mokal and then Rana Kumbha. In 1438 Rana Kumbha had Ranmal assassinated in Chittor and seized Mandore.

Ranmal's son Rao Jodha escaped with about 700 horsemen, but after fighting near Chittor and at the Someshwar Pass only seven men were with him when he reached Mandore. He abandoned it and took refuge at Kahuni, near present-day Bikaner. For 15 years he tried to retake it, and in 1453, while Rana Kumbha faced attacks by the Sultans of Malwa and Gujarat, he took it by surprise. Mandore stayed the capital of Marwar until Rao Jodha moved it to his new city of Jodhpur.

Mandore remained the royal cremation ground, with the devals of every king of Marwar up to Maharaja Takht Singh. The ruined fort, built in stages, holds a large ruined temple with carvings of plants, birds, animals and planets. The Mandore gardens contain the chhatris of many rulers of Jodhpur State, among them that of Maharaja Ajit Singh, built in 1793, together with a government museum founded in 1968 in the Janana Mahal and a Hall of Heroes of 16 figures carved from a single rock.
mandsaur: Mandsaur is identified with the city of Daśapura, attested in ancient and medieval texts and inscriptions. According to the 12th-century Jain work Pariśiṣṭaparvan, a group of visiting merchants gave the city that name at the royal fortress of a king named Udayana and his ten sons. The 47th stanza of Kalidas's poem Meghdoot mentions Dashpur and the beauty of its women's eyes.

Inscriptions have revealed two royal houses calling themselves Aulikaras who ruled from Dashapura. The first comprised Jayavarma, Simhavarma, Naravarma, Vishvavarma and Bandhuvarma. The Risthal stone slab inscription, found in 1983, revealed another line: Drumavardhana, Jayavardhana, Ajitavardhana, Vibhishanavardhana, Rajyavardhana and Prakashadharma. Prakashadharma was followed by Yashodharma, identified with Vishnuvardhana, who raised a pillar of victory at Bayana, which was renamed Vijaygarh. At Sondani, a village about 4 kilometres from Mandsaur, a pillar inscription has Yashodharman praising himself for defeating King Mihirakula.

The Gurjara-Pratihara empire extended to Mandasor in the reign of Mahendrapala II. In February 1732 the Marathas surrounded Jai Singh II of Amber at Mandsaur with their cavalry and cut off his supplies. The Marathas attacked the rearguard of the Jaipur army and killed its commander, and Jai Singh was forced to surrender, to pay six lakhs and to let Holkar collect chauth from 28 parganas in Malwa. Kota and Bundi became the next Maratha targets.

In the 19th century, before India's independence in 1947, Mandsaur belonged to the princely state of Gwalior. It gave its name to the treaty with the Holkar Maharaja of Indore that concluded the Third Anglo-Maratha War and the Pindari War in 1818, and at the turn of the 20th century it was a centre of the Malwa opium trade. The city lies on the border of the Mewar and Malwa regions of Madhya Pradesh and is the administrative headquarters of Mandsaur District. The ancient Pashupatinath Temple stands there, and the 2011 census counted 141,468 people.
mandume-ya-ndemufayo: The Oukwanyama kingdom had been divided by the Berlin Conference of 1884 between Portuguese West Africa and German South West Africa. Mandume grew up amid the upheaval brought by European merchants and missionaries, and as third in line to the throne he lived in fear of assassination from an early age.

He came to the throne peacefully by Kwanyama standards and at once moved the royal residence to Ondjiva. He expelled Portuguese traders in protest at rising prices, forbade the picking of unripe fruit as a guard against drought and banned the needless use of firearms, a valued trade good. Under him rape carried harsh penalties and women could own cattle, which had been illegal. His aim was to restore the kingdom's former wealth against a decaying system of local leadership. He was also known for driving out Christians, many of whom fled to the Ondonga kingdom, and he favoured neither the Portuguese Catholic missionaries nor the German Rhenish Missionary Society.

No colonial power challenged the well-armed Ovambo kingdoms until 1915, when the beginning of World War I coincided with a severe drought. At the Battle of Omongwa the Kwanyama held off a Portuguese attack for three days, while South African forces took the part of the kingdom that had been German. After heavy losses Mandume moved his capital into South West Africa. He refused to submit to South African control and died in battle in February 1917. South African records attribute his death to machine-gun fire, while oral and popular history holds that he took his own life.

The Oukwanyama kingship was abolished after his death and revived only in February 1998. Mandume is one of the nine national heroes recognised at Namibia's Heroes' Acre near Windhoek, opened in 2002, where a granite tombstone bears his portrait. A university in Angola founded in 1963 and streets in several cities of Angola and in Windhoek carry his name. In February 2017 thousands attended the centenary of his death at Omhedi, where a bust of him was unveiled.
manduria: Manduria stands in the province of Taranto in Apulia, about 35 kilometres east of the city of Taranto. Its name is thought to derive from a Proto-Indo-European stem meaning foal, which would make it Messapic in origin and related to the Illyrian theonym Iuppiter Menzanas and the Albanian word for foal. Plutarch also refers to it as Mandonion. The ancient town lay close to the modern one, and considerable remains of its defences can still be seen: a double line of walls of rectangular stone blocks laid without mortar, with a broad ditch in front.

In antiquity Manduria was an important stronghold of the Messapii against Taras. Archidamus III, king of Sparta, was killed beneath its walls in 338 BCE while leading the army of Taras. The town revolted to Hannibal but was taken by the Romans in 209 BCE.

Pliny the Elder, in his Natural History, describes a well in which the water level never changed however much was drawn, with an almond tree growing from the middle of the shaft. The Saracens destroyed the town in the 10th century. Its people rebuilt on the site of the present town, which they called Casalnuovo, and in 1700 they took back the ancient name of Manduria. Tombs with gold ornaments were found in 1886.

The well, called the Fonte Pliniano, can still be seen as Pliny described it and is the symbol of the city. Other sights include the medieval Chiesa Madre, renovated in the 16th century, the Church of the Holy Trinity of the 11th or 12th century, with three Renaissance portals and a 15th-century bell tower, the medieval Jewish quarter and a castle that was the seat of the Imperiali princes from 1719. The Church of San Pietro Mandurino was probably a Hellenistic hall tomb adapted as a church in the 8th or 9th century. The local Primitivo di Manduria wine is made from the Primitivo grape alone.
manetho: Little is certain about the life of Manetho. His name is a Greek form of an Egyptian name, and scholars have no agreement on the original: it may invoke Thoth or Neith, or be an occupational name meaning shepherd or groom. He came from Sebennytos and was probably a priest of the sun god Ra at Heliopolis, and an authority on the temple cult of Serapis.

He worked at the beginning of the Hellenistic order in Egypt, when Ptolemy I Soter founded the Ptolemaic Kingdom in 305 BCE. Manetho wrote under Ptolemy I or Ptolemy II Philadelphus to preserve the history of his homeland and, since he wrote in Greek, for its new foreign rulers. Ancient writers grouped him with the Mesopotamian writer Berossus, and both used king-lists as the framework of their histories.

Eight works have been attributed to Manetho, but modern scholars agree only that he wrote the Aegyptiaca. This was a chronological history in three scrolls, perhaps written in answer to Herodotus. It ran from a mythical age of divine rulers through the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt by Menes and thirty or thirty-one dynasties to the establishment of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in 305 BCE, and treated periods of stability against internal strife and foreign rule by the Hyksos, Kushites and Achaemenids.

Manetho coined the word dynasty, but he meant groups of rulers separated by a break, of place or of descent, not simply a line of blood relatives. His division of the rulers into thirty or thirty-one dynasties remains the chronological framework of Egyptology. Because he wrote in Greek, his history stayed readable after the last hieroglyphic text of 394 CE. His own writings are lost, and the fragments survive through later authors including Josephus, Africanus, Eusebius and Syncellus.

In the account preserved by Josephus, Manetho described the departure of the Israelites as the expulsion of a colony of lepers and ritually polluted people, led by the renegade priest Osarseph whom he identified with Moses. Scholars read this as an answer to the anti-Egyptian side of the Exodus story.
manfred-king-of-sicily: Manfred was born in 1232 at Venosa, a natural son of Emperor Frederick II, who seems to have regarded him as legitimate and named him Prince of Taranto in his will. He studied in Paris and Bologna and shared his father's love of poetry and science. After Frederick's death in 1250 he acted as regent of Sicily while his half-brother Conrad IV was in Germany. When Conrad came to southern Italy in 1252 he stripped Manfred of his fiefs except Taranto. Conrad died of malaria in May 1254, and Manfred took the regency for the infant Conradin.

Pope Innocent IV excommunicated him in July 1254. Manfred submitted in September and accepted the title of papal vicar, but he fled to the Saracens at Lucera, and with their help defeated the papal army at Foggia on 2 December 1254. By 1257 he had crushed another papal army and put down the rebellions.

On 10 August 1258, on a rumour that Conradin was dead, Manfred was crowned king of Sicily at Palermo. The pope declared the coronation void, but Manfred named vicars in Tuscany, Spoleto, the Marche, Romagna and Lombardy. After Montaperti he was recognised as protector of Tuscany by the citizens of Florence, and in 1262 his daughter Constance married the future Peter III of Aragon. He also took Helena Angelina Doukaina, daughter of the ruler of Epirus, as his second wife.

Pope Urban IV excommunicated him and in 1263 gave the investiture of Sicily to Charles of Anjou, a brother of Louis IX of France. Charles entered Italy in late 1265 with an army of some 30,000 and was crowned in Rome in January 1266. The armies met at the Battle of Benevento on 26 February 1266. Manfred refused to flee, rushed into the midst of his enemies and was killed.

Manfred was buried on the battlefield under a heap of stones, but with the pope's consent his remains were dug up and interred on the bank of the Garigliano, outside the territory of Naples and the Papal States. Charles imprisoned Helena, who died in 1271, and kept her sons in chains for decades. Peter III eventually became king of Sicily in 1282 after the Sicilian Vespers. Manfred founded the modern city of Manfredonia between 1256 and 1263, and in the Divine Comedy Dante meets him outside the gates of Purgatory.
manfredo-fanti: Manfredo Fanti was born at Carpi on 23 February 1806 and educated at the military college of Modena. Implicated in Ciro Menotti's revolutionary movement of 1831, he was condemned to death and hanged in effigy, but escaped to France and served in the French engineers. In 1833 he joined Giuseppe Mazzini's failed attempt to invade Savoy, and from 1835 he spent thirteen years in Spain in Queen Christina's army against the Carlists, rising to a high staff post.

When war broke out between Piedmont and Austria in 1848 he returned and was given a Lombard brigade, and his courage and tact steadied the situation in the confusion after Charles Albert's retreat to Milan. Elected to the Piedmontese Chamber of Deputies in 1849, he again commanded a Lombard brigade under General Girolamo Ramorino. Distrusted as a Mazzinian and soldier of fortune, he was court-martialled for those operations and acquitted, but not employed again until the Crimean expedition of 1855.

In 1859 he commanded the 2nd Division at Palestro, Magenta and Solferino. After the Armistice of Villafranca he turned the army of the United Provinces of Central Italy into a drilled force of 45,000 men, steering between Bettino Ricasoli's caution and the impetuosity of his second-in-command Giuseppe Garibaldi, who resigned. Leading two army corps into the Papal States, he took Ancona and defeated the Papal army at Castelfidardo, capturing General Lamoricière; in three weeks he conquered the Marche and Umbria and took 28,000 prisoners. In the Neapolitan campaign he served as chief of staff under the king, defeated a Neapolitan force at Mola and organised the siege of Gaeta.

As minister of war and marine under Cavour, Fanti merged the league's army into Piedmont's and reformed the army, clashing with Alfonso La Marmora. He opposed Garibaldi's wish to keep his volunteer army: the Esercito Meridionale was disbanded and only 1,700 of its 7,000 officers entered the new, conscription-based Royal Italian Army, for which the Left criticised him severely. He resigned on Cavour's death on 7 June 1861, and many of his reforms were reversed by later ministers. He died in Florence on 5 April 1865 and is known as the founder of the Royal Italian Army.
mangaia: Mangaia, traditionally A'ua'u Enua, meaning terraced island, is the second largest of the Cook Islands after Rarotonga, 203 kilometres from it, and has an area of 51.8 square kilometres. Geologists estimate that it is at least 18 million years old. A fringing coral reef surrounds a high ring of fossil coral cliffs, 60 metres high, called the makatea. The inner rim of the makatea falls steeply to swamps and a central volcanic plateau. The interior drains through underground channels in the makatea, which lead to extensive caves that have been used as refuges and for burials. The highest point is Rangi-motia, 169 metres above sea level. Tamaeu, who came from Aitutaki in 1775, named the island Mangaia.

Excavation of the Tangatatau Rockshelter shows that Mangaia was first settled around 1000 CE; the site also holds the earliest recorded evidence of sweet potato cultivation in Polynesia. According to oral tradition, the island was not discovered but emerged from the underworld of Avaiki already populated, and it was later settled further from Rarotonga, Aitutaki, Atiu, Tonga and Tahiti. Adze heads and basalt tools show trade with Rarotonga, Samoa and Raiatea. By the sixteenth century settlement had moved inland from the coast and inter-island trade had virtually disappeared, and oral histories tell of chiefs competing for land and status.

Captain James Cook came on 29 March 1777, the first European visitor. John Williams of the London Missionary Society arrived in 1823 but could not land; in 1824 he returned and left two preachers from Taha'a, who began converting the island. Before then the society was marked by violent struggles between war-leaders competing for the title of mangaia, the supreme temporal power, while the ariki served as priests. The last mangaia, Pangemiro, died soon after the missionaries came, and the abolition of war froze the division of land and titles as it was in 1823. In 1888 Mangaia became a British protectorate, and in 1901 New Zealand annexed it.

Mangaia is divided into six districts, with its capital at the village of Oneroa on the west coast, which holds about half the population. John Williams estimated the population at two to three thousand in 1823; it peaked at 2,002 in 1966 and had fallen to 499 by 2016. Unlike other southern Cook Islands, Mangaia has kept its collective land tenure, with land use decided by each district's kavana, and its own dialect of Cook Islands Maori, reo Mangaia. It is an Important Bird Area.
mangalore: Mangaluru lies on the western coast of India in Dakshina Kannada district, between the Laccadive Sea and the Western Ghats. The Gurupura flows around its north and the Netravati around its south, and the two rivers form an estuary in the south-west of the city before reaching the sea. The landscape is one of rolling hills, coconut palms and hard laterite soil. It has a tropical monsoon climate, and about 95 percent of the year's rain falls between May and September. The name comes from the goddess Mangaladevi, whose temple stands at Bolar; local legend tells of a princess from Malabar who became a disciple of Matsyendranath and was renamed Mangaladevi.

Foreign writers mention the coast from early times. In the first century CE Pliny the Elder named a place called Nitrias, where pirates made landing undesirable, and in the second century Ptolemy named Nitra, probably the area of the Netravati River. In the sixth century the Greek monk Cosmas Indicopleustes listed Mangarouth, the port of Mangaluru, among the five pepper markets that exported pepper. The city was ruled by several powers, among them the Mauryan empire, the Kadambas, the Alupas, the Vijayanagara Empire and the Keladi Nayaks.

European influence began in 1498, when Vasco da Gama landed at the nearby St Mary's Islands. The Portuguese were friendly with Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara and sought to destroy the Arab and Mappila coastal trade. In 1524 Vasco da Gama ordered the rivers blockaded after hearing that Muslim merchants of Kozhikode had agents at Mangaluru and Basrur, and in 1526 the Portuguese under the viceroy Lopo Vaz de Sampaio took the city, and the coastal trade passed into their hands. The city was later contested between the British and the Mysore rulers Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, and the British annexed it in 1799. It stayed in the Madras Presidency until 1947 and joined Mysore State, now Karnataka, in 1956.

A municipal council was set up on 23 May 1866 under the Madras Town Improvement Act. Italian Jesuits who arrived in 1878 played an important part in education, health and social welfare. The railway reached the city in 1907, and by the early 20th century it was a major source of educated workers for Bombay, Bengaluru and the Middle East.

Mangaluru is the administrative headquarters of Dakshina Kannada district, and its urban area held 619,664 people at the 2011 census. A new port was built in 1968. Tulu, Konkani, Kannada and Beary are all spoken there, and Tulu is the most widespread first language. Hindus form the largest religious community, with large Christian and Muslim communities; the Masjid Zeenath Baksh is among the oldest mosques in the Indian subcontinent.
mangareva: Mangareva is the central and largest island of the Gambier Islands in French Polynesia, surrounded by smaller islands: Taravai to the south-west, Aukena and Akamaru to the south-east, and others to the north. It is about eight kilometres long and 15.4 square kilometres in area, some 56 percent of the land of the whole group. A high ridge runs its length, and Mount Duff, at 441 metres, is the highest point of the Gambiers. The island lies within a large lagoon 24 kilometres across, whose reefs gave ancient islanders fish and shellfish and helped them survive much more successfully than on nearby islands without reefs. Rikitea is the chief town of the Gambier Islands.

Polynesians first settled Mangareva in the first millennium CE. Carbon dating has so far dated settlements only to 1160 to 1220, but trade with the Pitcairn Islands from 1000 CE and likely settlement around 800 CE are suggested. The island was once heavily forested and supported a large population that traded by canoe, but logging between the 10th and 15th centuries deforested it, with disastrous effects on environment and economy. The first European visitor was the British captain James Wilson, who arrived in 1797 on the ship Duff and named the group for Admiral James Gambier.

The islands were ruled by a line of kings and later regents. King Maputeoa asked for a French protectorate on 16 February 1844, which France never ratified; in 1870 the prince regent Arone Teikatoara withdrew the request, but on 30 November 1871 he signed an agreement with the French authority in Tahiti reaffirming the protectorate. The Gambier Islands were annexed on 21 February 1881 under Prince Regent Bernardo Putairi, and the French president approved this on 30 January 1882. In July 1966 the islanders were exposed to radioactive fallout from French nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa; officials knew the doses and kept them secret until 1998, and the French government acknowledged it in 2006.

Mangareva has a permanent population of 1,239 in 2012 and is reached by boat from the airport across the lagoon. It is the usual link to Pitcairn Island, a 32-hour boat journey away. Islanders developed a binary number system, reported in 2013, that shortened counting: 150 needs four signs in it, VTPK for 80, 40, 20 and 10, against eight digits in modern binary. Later work in 2020 showed it to be an extension of the traditional Polynesian way of counting objects in pairs, fours and eights. Mangarevan mythology shares gods common across Polynesia, among them Tu, the most important god, and the demigod Māui.
manghud: The Manghud belonged to the Urud-Manghud federation of the Mongolian plateau, and ancient sources derive them from the Kiyat Mongols. The Persian historian Rashid-al-Din Hamadani, who chronicled the Mongols, claimed that many old Mongol clans, the Manghud among them, were founded by members of the Borjigin.

Some Manghud warriors supported Genghis Khan, while a body of them resisted his rise to power. As the Mongol Empire expanded, the Manghud were carried westward with many other Mongol tribes. The clan name was also used for Mongol vanguard troops, though sources differ widely on the military units called mangudai.

In the Golden Horde the Manghud supported Nogai, who died in 1299, and formed a horde of their own, semi-independent of the khans at Sarai. After Nogai's death most of their warriors entered the service of Tokhta Khan. Edigu, who lived from 1352 to 1419 and was the son of the noble Kutlukiya, led the eastern begs and by the end of the 14th century dominated the Golden Horde.

The Nogais guarded the northern borders of the Astrakhan and Crimean khanates and by organised raids into the northern steppes prevented Russian and Lithuanian settlement. Many entered the service of the Crimean khan and contributed to the formation of the Crimean Tatars. About 1630 the Kalmyks, migrating from southern Siberia to the lower Volga, drove the Nogais out; they fled to the plains of the northern Caucasus and to the Crimea, and a small part joined the Kazakh Khanate.

Other Manghits had been settled by Genghis Khan around the city of Qarshi, which remained their base under the Khanate of Bukhara. Their power there grew in the early 18th century through the office of ataliq to the khan. After the death of Nader Shah in 1747 the ataliq Muhammad Rahim Bi had the ruling Abu al-Fayz Khan and his young son killed. The family ruled behind the scenes until the 1780s, when the emir Shah Murad declared himself ruler openly. Not being descendants of Genghis Khan, the Manghits took the Islamic title of emir, not khan, and based their legitimacy on Islam.

The last emir, Mohammed Alim Khan, was ousted by the Soviet Red Army in September 1920 and fled to Afghanistan. Whether his dynasty was of Mongol or of plain Uzbek origin is disputed. The Nogai and Karakalpak peoples are counted among the descendants of the Manghud, and Manghits are found among the Tatars of Russia, the Bashkirs and the Kazakhs, as well as among the Khalkha Mongols of Mongolia.
mangkunegara-i: Raden Mas Said was born in Kartasura, the son of Raden Ayu Wulan and Prince Mangkunegara of Kartasura, the eldest son of Amangkurat IV by a concubine and crown prince of Mataram. His mother was a daughter of Prince Blitar, Amangkurat IV's younger brother, so his parents were first cousins. His name Sambernyawa, the life-reaping prince, came from his banner of the same name. He married Raden Ayu Kusumapatahati, daughter of the cleric Kyai Kasan Nur Iman, and later Raden Ajeng Inten, a daughter of Prince Mangkubumi, afterwards Hamengkubuwana I.

His war began with the rebellion at Kartasura Palace on 30 June 1742, led by Raden Mas Garendi, also called Sunan Kuning, which drove King Pakubuwono II to Ponorogo. Said joined his uncle Mangkubumi against the Dutch East India Company and the king, whom they saw as its puppet, built a fortress at Randuwalang north of Surakarta and joined his men to Sunan Kuning's forces. Pakubuwono II paid for the Company's help by ceding the north coast of Java from Rembang to Surabaya and Madura and by submitting court appointments to its approval.

Said later separated from Garendi, set up headquarters at Panambangan and declared himself Prince Mangkunegara I. On Pakubuwono II's death he urged Mangkubumi to proclaim himself king, and Mangkubumi became Sultan Hamengkubuwono, with Said as his warlord. The two then fell out, and Said fought the Company alone. He rejected the Treaty of Giyanti of 13 February 1755, which divided Mataram, as a blow to the unity of its people. Over 16 years he fought 250 battles, and even the Dutch governor Baron van Hohendorff admitted his skill in war.

After the Treaty of Salatiga in 1757 his alliance with Hamengkubuwana I turned to rivalry. It deepened when Gusti Kanjeng Ratu Alit, eldest daughter of Pakubuwana III, married Said's eldest son rather than the crown prince of Yogyakarta, a slight that led Said's wife, Ratu Bendara, to return to Yogyakarta and seek a divorce. Said died on 28 December 1795. The son of that marriage, Pangeran Arya Prangwadana, succeeded his grandfather as Mangkunegara II, and the Babad Panambangan of 1918 lists more than twenty of Mangkunegara I's children.
mangkunegara-iv: He was born on 3 March 1811 as Raden Mas Sudira, the seventh child and third son of Kanjeng Pangeran Arya Hadiwijaya. His mother, Raden Ajeng Kèli, was a younger daughter of Mangkunegara II, who took the boy into his own household. From the age of ten he was raised by his elder cousin, the future Mangkunegara III, who cared for him like his eldest son.

At 22 he married his first cousin Raden Ajeng Semi, who died in 1850 giving birth to their fourteenth child. That year he received the princely title Kanjeng Pangeran Arya Gandakusuma. When Mangkunegara III died in March 1853 he was named heir and succeeded him. A letter of Governor-General Albertus Jacobus Duymaer van Twist dated 16 April 1853 allowed him to marry the late ruler's daughter, Raden Ajeng Dunuk, who became the mother of his successors Mangkunegara V and Mangkunegara VI.

During his reign the foundations of estate agriculture producing coffee and sugar were laid in the principality, and he became the first non-European to own sugar factories, at Tjolomadoe and Tasikmadu. The profits were reinvested in his domains rather than sent abroad, though the inhabitants came to depend on the world price of these cash crops. He abolished the appanage system by which retainers and officials had been rewarded with land and paid them salaries instead.

He still had to deal with the Netherlands and with the other rulers of central Java. In 1857 and again in 1877 he failed to reclaim land that had been leased to European planters. He ruled until his death on 2 September 1881.

His court is known above all for its part in the traditional arts. He was himself a poet and worked with Raden Ngabei Ranggawarsita (1802–1873), who is said to have been the last of the great court poets. His best-known poem, Wedhatama (Exalted Wisdom), praises a morality in keeping with the mystical Islam of Java, in contrast to the more self-consciously orthodox Islamic community.

He is also credited with several ketawang, a form of gamelan music. One of them, Puspawarna, was placed on the Voyager Golden Record sent into space in the 1970s. His daughter Gusti Raden Ajeng Sumarti became the principal consort of Pakubuwana X.
mangkunegara-vii: Mangkunegara VII was born Raden Mas Soerjosoeparto, the seventh child and third son among the 28 children of Mangkunegara V. As a young man he was forbidden by his uncle to enrol in the HBS, so he left the palace to live on his own, working as a Dutch-Javanese translator and as a district official. He then studied for three years at Leiden University before returning to Java to succeed his uncle, Mangkunegara VI, who abdicated in 1916. His principal consort was a princess of Yogyakarta, a daughter of Hamengkubuwana VII. His son Sarosa Notosuparto later reigned as Mangkunegara VIII.

He raised the principality's income through its plantations, above all sugar, and reformed its government by royal decrees of 1917 and 1923, which turned its districts into regencies under a bupati and created new departments for health and village education. From 1917 his administration declared reforestation a public interest, set up a forestry department and regulated teak forests and illegal logging; forest cover grew from 23,567 hectares in 1917 to 26,002 hectares by 1940. In 1936 he commissioned the architect Thomas Karsten to build a public bathhouse and toilets on the Pepe River.

He helped found the Java Instituut for Javanese language, literature and culture, wrote a study of the symbolism of wayang in 1920, opened court arts to the public through wayang wong performances and singing courses, and founded the Javanese Padvinders Organisatie, the first indigenous scouting organisation in the Indies, with a women's wing. He was a leading figure in the Budi Utomo movement and an adviser to Jong Java, and served as a colonel in the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army, commanding the Legion of Mangkunegaran.

Mangkunegara VII died in 1944 and was buried at Astana Girilayu in Karanganyar Regency, Central Java. For his work for Javanese culture the Indonesian government awarded him the Bintang Budaya Parama Dharma after his death, presented to his granddaughter on 15 August 2016.
mangrai: Mangrai was born at Ngoenyang on the Mekong River, the son of the local ruler Lao Meng and of Thep Kham Khai, a daughter of Hung Kaen Chai, Tai Lue ruler of Chiang Hung, now Jinghong in Xishuangbanna, China. On succeeding his father he became the first independent king of the unified Tai city states of the north. Seeing them disunited and in danger, he conquered Muang Lai and Chiang Khong, and Chiang Kham and Thoeng, which had belonged to Phayao, and made alliances with other states.

In 1287 he made peace between King Ngammueang of Phayao and King Ramkhamhaeng of Sukhothai, who had seduced Ngammueang's queen, and the three entered the pact later called the Three Kings Alliance; the historian Chusak Satienpattanodom links it to the Mongol destruction of Pagan that year. Hearing from Mon merchants of the wealth of Haripunchai, Mangrai sent a merchant named Ai Fa to win the confidence of its King Yi Ba. Ai Fa became chief minister and undermined the king, and when the people were discontented Mangrai conquered the kingdom; Yi Ba fled to Lampang.

Mangrai first built a capital at Wiang Kum Kam on the Ping River in 1294, but floods led him to a site at the foot of Doi Suthep, on an older fortified town of the Lua people, where Chiang Mai, the New City, was begun. When Yi Ba's son, King Boek of Lampang, attacked it, Mangrai's second son, Prince Khram, defeated Boek in combat on elephant-back at Khua Mung; Boek was caught and executed, and Mangrai's troops took Lampang.

His eldest son, Prince Khueang, tried to seize the throne and was killed on Mangrai's orders, and Prince Khram was named heir. Tradition holds that Mangrai was struck by lightning in the market of Chiang Mai. Six kings ruled in the eleven years after his death, and only with the accession of his grandson Kham Fu in 1328 did the kingdom regain the stability it had known under its founder. Chiang Mai has been the capital of the north more or less ever since.
manhattan: Manhattan is the geographically smallest of the five boroughs of New York City and is coextensive with New York County. It lies almost entirely on Manhattan Island, bounded by the Hudson River to the west and the East River to the east, while the Harlem River divides it from the Bronx. The island is 13.4 miles long and 2.3 miles wide at its widest point, near 14th Street, and is loosely divided into Lower Manhattan, Midtown and Upper Manhattan. Its bedrock of Inwood marble, Fordham gneiss and Manhattan schist is well suited to the foundations of skyscrapers.

Manhattan was part of Lenapehoking, the territory of the Munsee, Lenape and Wappinger peoples. Their main trail, from what is now Inwood to Battery Park, later became Broadway. Giovanni da Verrazzano, sailing for Francis I of France, became the first documented European to visit the area, in April 1524. Dutch colonists set up a trading post on the island in 1624, named New Amsterdam in 1626. The English took the territory in 1664 and renamed it New York for the Duke of York.

Manhattan was at the centre of the New York Campaign in the American Revolutionary War, and the Continental Army abandoned it after the Battle of Fort Washington on 16 November 1776. British occupation lasted until 25 November 1783. New York was the capital of the United States from 1785 until 1790, and by 1810 it was the most populous city in the country. The Commissioners' Plan of 1811 laid out the grid, and the Erie Canal opened in 1825. The subway opened in 1904, and Manhattan became a borough in the consolidation of 1898.

Manhattan had 1,694,250 residents at the 2020 census, in a land area of about 22.7 square miles. It is the economic and administrative centre of New York City, with City Hall, Wall Street, the New York Stock Exchange and the headquarters of the United Nations in Turtle Bay. Central Park, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux in the 1850s, covers 840 acres. The Statue of Liberty is part of the borough, and its landmarks include the Empire State Building, Grand Central Terminal and Times Square.
manhattan-project: The discovery of nuclear fission by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in 1938, and its theoretical explanation by Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, made a uranium bomb theoretically possible, and there were fears that Germany would build one first. In August 1939 Leo Szilard and Eugene Wigner drafted a letter, signed by Albert Einstein and delivered to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, that warned of "extremely powerful bombs of a new type".

In Britain, Otto Robert Frisch and Rudolf Peierls calculated in 1939 that the critical mass of uranium-235 was within an order of magnitude of 10 kilograms, and their March 1940 memorandum began the British project, Tube Alloys. The United States committee meeting of 18 December 1941 met just after the attack on Pearl Harbor, and work went ahead on several methods of isotope separation and on reactors.

In June 1942 Colonel James C. Marshall began to head the Army's part from a temporary headquarters at 270 Broadway in Manhattan, which gave the Manhattan District its name. Major General Leslie Groves then took over the project, which employed nearly 130,000 people at its peak and cost nearly 2 billion dollars. Enriched uranium was produced at the Clinton Engineer Works at Oak Ridge in Tennessee, on land acquired by eminent domain that affected about 1,000 families. Plutonium came from the world's first industrial-scale reactors at Hanford in Washington. J. Robert Oppenheimer directed the Los Alamos Laboratory in New Mexico, which designed two weapons: the uranium gun-type Little Boy and the plutonium implosion bomb Fat Man.

The key raw material was uranium. In 1940 there were four known major deposits, in Colorado, northern Canada, Joachimsthal and the Belgian Congo, and Kenneth Nichols negotiated the purchase of 1,200 short tons of ore from the Congo stored on Staten Island.

Canada supplied uranium and heavy water. The Fat Man design was at first a low-priority fallback, but in 1944 it was confirmed that Hanford plutonium was unsuitable for a gun-type bomb. The first nuclear device was detonated at the Trinity test in New Mexico on 16 July 1945.

The project delivered the bombs used in the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Through Operation Alsos its personnel also gathered intelligence on the German nuclear programme, and Soviet spies penetrated the project despite its emphasis on secrecy. After the war it tested weapons at Bikini Atoll in Operation Crossroads, helped to create the network of national laboratories and laid the foundations of the nuclear navy. It kept control of American atomic weapons research and production until the United States Atomic Energy Commission was formed in January 1947.
manichaeism: Mani was born in 216 CE in or near Ctesiphon, then in the Parthian Empire. According to the Cologne Mani-Codex, his parents belonged to the Jewish Christian Gnostic sect of the Elcesaites. His writings say he received revelations at the ages of 12 and 24, and that he grew dissatisfied with the Elcesaites. He saw his teaching as completing the partial truths of earlier faiths, among them Zoroastrian, Buddhist, Jewish and Christian traditions, and he wrote seven works, six in Syriac and one, the Shabuhragan, in Middle Persian. He presented that book to the Sasanian emperor Shapur I, who tolerated the spread of the religion but is not known to have followed it.

Manichaeism teaches a dualism in which a spiritual world of light stands against a material world of darkness. In its account the Father of Greatness ruled the World of Light and the King of Darkness the World of Darkness. When Darkness attacked, the Father of Greatness sent Original Man to fight it. Humanity, the world and the soul came from this battle, and light is gradually drawn out of matter and returned to the divine. Followers held that Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus had brought true teachings later corrupted, and that Mani was the final prophet.

Its sacramental rites included prayers, almsgiving, fasting and, most centrally, the daily ritual meal of the elect. Communal life centred on confession and the singing of hymns. As the religion spread east, translators often replaced the names of its deities with those of Zoroastrian figures, so that the Father of Greatness could be rendered as Zurwān.

Manichaeism spread quickly through Aramaic-speaking lands, the Mediterranean and the Middle East. It reached Rome in about 280, and persecution followed. The Sasanian emperor Bahram II had the apostle Mar Sisin killed in 291, and Roman rulers legislated against the religion under Diocletian, later in 372 under Valentinian I and Valens, and in 382 under Theodosius I. It had largely vanished from the Roman West by the end of the sixth century.

In the east it lasted longer. It reached Tang China in the seventh century and was the official religion of the Uyghur Khaganate until the khaganate collapsed in 840. The Tang court then banned it, but it revived under the Yuan dynasty in the 13th and 14th centuries before being absorbed into Buddhism and Taoism. The temple of Cao'an in Jinjiang, Fujian, survives. Most of Mani's writings were lost, and manuscripts found at Turpan and Dunhuang in the early 20th century now supply original texts.
manie-maritz: Maritz was born in Kimberley, then in the British Cape Colony, and christened Salomon Gerhardus Maritz. At 19 he went to Johannesburg to work as a cab driver for his uncle. Volunteering as a guard of the Johannesburg fort during the Jameson Raid made him a citizen of the Zuid-Afrikaansche Republiek, which allowed him to join its police, the ZARP.

In the Second Boer War he served with the Boksburg Commando on the Natal front, then in Daniel Theron's reconnaissance corps and in the invasion of the Cape Colony, ending in the north-western Cape. He claimed that Jan Smuts had made him a fighting general; Deneys Reitz, then on Smuts's staff, called him only a leader of rebel bands. Near the end of the war he ordered the killing of 35 Coloured (Khoikhoi) people in the Leliefontein massacre, in retaliation for an attack on his party. Rather than take the oath of allegiance, he crossed into German South West Africa.

He later worked in Madagascar as a land purchase agent for the French millionaire Jacques Lebaudy and is believed to have helped the Germans during the Herero and Nama genocide. Commissioned in the Active Citizen Force of the Union Defence Force in 1913, he commanded the area bordering German South-West Africa and was already in contact with its German governor. Ordered on 23 September 1914 to advance towards Sandfontein, where part of Lieutenant-Colonel Lukin's force was stranded, he refused. He rebelled on 9 October, occupied Keimoes the next day and was wounded on 22 October.

Returning in 1923, he was convicted of high treason and sentenced to three years' imprisonment, but was released after three months when General Hertzog's National Party won the 1924 election. In the 1930s he became an outspoken Nazi sympathiser. The anti-Semitic statements of his 1939 autobiography, My Lewe en Strewe, brought a conviction for fomenting racial hatred and a fine of £75. He died in a car crash in Pretoria in 1940. In John Buchan's novel Greenmantle (1916) British spies pose as veterans of his rebellion.
manifestis-probatum: The Papacy had not recognised Afonso's adoption of the royal title in 1139 and continued to regard him as a vassal of León. On 13 December 1143 Afonso wrote to Pope Innocent II the letter Claves Regni, declaring that he placed Portugal in fief to the Holy See. On 1 May 1144 Pope Lucius II replied that he recognised Afonso's devotion, but still called Portugal a land rather than a kingdom and Afonso a duke rather than a king. The change in papal policy in 1179 followed Afonso's conquests in the south of the Iberian Peninsula, lands to which no other Christian monarch had a claim.

The bull is addressed by Alexander, servant of the servants of God, to Afonso, illustrious king of the Portuguese, and to his heirs in perpetuity. It praises his services to the Church in fighting the enemies of the Christian name and spreading the faith, takes him under the protection of Saint Peter, and grants the Kingdom of Portugal the full honours and dignity of a kingdom, together with all the places he had won from the Saracens to which neighbouring Christian princes could claim no rights. The pope promises to extend the grant to Afonso's heirs and to defend it.

In token that the kingdom belonged to Saint Peter, Afonso undertook to pay two marks of gold every year, delivered through the Archbishop of Braga. Anyone who challenged the grant and gave no satisfaction after a second or third warning was threatened with the loss of office and exclusion from communion. The bull was given at the Lateran and bears the subscriptions of the pope and of the cardinal bishops, priests and deacons of the curia.

Pope Innocent III confirmed the bull on 16 April 1212, in the reign of King Afonso II, and Pope Honorius III confirmed it again on 11 January 1218 with the bull Manifestis Probatum est, addressed to the same king. It is regarded as the founding document of Portugal and the most important written record of its path to independence from the Kingdom of León.
manifesto-of-the-algerian-people: During World War II, with France under German occupation and Anglo-American forces landed in Algiers in Operation Torch in 1942, Ferhat Abbas set out to unite Algeria's political forces, among them elected members of the Algerian People's Party and the ulama, around a common programme. On 17 January 1943 members of the party and of the ulama met with several Muslim representatives at the house of the lawyer and politician Ahmed Boumendjel in Algiers. Abbas was asked to write the text, which he did in Setif, in a room above his pharmacy.

Published on 10 February 1943 and signed by 28 elected Muslim officials, the manifesto called for a new status for the Algerian nation and asserted the right of the Algerian people to govern themselves. Besides a constitution guaranteeing liberty and equality regardless of race and religion and official status for Arabic beside French, it demanded freedom of religion with the separation of church and state. An addendum called for an Algerian Assembly at the end of the war and proposed that Algeria become an autonomous state federated with France, reached through negotiation with the French authorities. In the words of the historian Benjamin Stora, it established the political majority of the Algerian people, drawing on the followers of both Messali Hadj and Abbas.

The addendum went to the governor-general Peyrouton in May 1943. Charles de Gaulle, on his arrival, called for an end to the project, and on 23 June 1943 General Catroux, the new governor-general of Algeria, rejected the manifesto. In March 1944 its supporters founded the Friends of the Manifesto and Liberty, known by its French initials AML, to defend it.
manikya-dynasty: The Rajmala traces the dynasty to Druhya, a son of Yayati of the Lunar dynasty of Hindu tradition, and lists an unbroken line of 144 Tripura kings, probably mythological, before Ratna Fa, said to have become the first Manikya when the Sultan of Bengal granted him the title. Historians now believe the chronicle mistaken in the genealogy and chronology of the first Manikyas. Coins suggest that the first historical Manikya was Maha Manikya, a Tripuri chief who founded the kingdom in the early 1400s by establishing dominance over neighbouring tribes and took the title Manikya in honour of a victory over Bengal.

His early successors are said to have conquered territory in Bengal, Assam and Burma. Tripura was at its largest in the 16th century under kings such as Dhanya Manikya and Vijaya Manikya II, when its lands ran from the Garo Hills in the north to the Bay of Bengal in the south. As Hindu kings the Manikyas were long rivals of the Muslim rulers of Bengal, fighting sultans, governors and nawabs, before coming under Mughal suzerainty in the early 17th century. When Mughal power waned the conflict with Bengal broke out again, and they turned to the British for aid.
Bir Chandra Manikya, who came to the throne in 1870, reformed his government on the British model, adopted Bengali at court and became a friend of the poet Rabindranath Tagore.

Early in the 20th century Tripura was briefly part of the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam. In 1947 Maharaja Bir Bikram Kishore, the last Manikya monarch, chose to join the Dominion of India. The final accession was signed by his widow, Kanchan Prava Devi, on behalf of the young Kirit Bikram Kishore, ending five centuries of Manikya rule over the north-east of the subcontinent.
manila: Manila lies on the eastern shore of Manila Bay, on the western coast of the island of Luzon, 1,300 kilometres from mainland Asia. The protected harbour is regarded as the finest in Asia. The Pasig River flows through the middle of the city and divides it into northern and southern sections. Almost all of the city sits on prehistoric alluvial deposits built by the Pasig and on land reclaimed from the bay. The name derives from Maynilà, commonly interpreted as the place where indigo plants are abundant, from the Sanskrit nīla; it was probably given for the plants growing around the settlement, since indigo extraction became important in the area only in the 18th century.

The earliest evidence of human life near Manila is the Angono Petroglyphs, dated to around 3000 BCE. By 1258 a fortified Tagalog polity called Maynila existed on the site, and with Tondo it traded with the Song and Yuan dynasties of China. In 1365 both Brunei and Manila were conquered by the Majapahit Empire, which named Manila Selurong in Sanskrit texts.

On 24 June 1571, after Rajah Sulayman, the polity's last indigenous ruler, was defeated at the Battle of Bangkusay, the Spanish conquistador Miguel López de Legazpi began building the walled fortification of Intramuros. Manila became the capital of the captaincy general of the Spanish East Indies, administered for the Spanish crown from Mexico City in the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Its commercial networks were the first to extend across the Pacific Ocean and connect Asia with the Spanish Americas through the galleon trade.

Under American occupation Manila became the first chartered city in the country, by Philippine Commission Act No. 183 of 31 July 1901, and in 1905 Daniel Burnham was commissioned to design the new capital on the principles of the City Beautiful movement. During the Second World War it was razed by Japanese forces and by American shelling. It became autonomous with the Revised Charter of 18 June 1949, and most historical buildings were reconstructed, though many in Intramuros were damaged beyond repair.

Manila is the capital of the Philippines and its second most populous city after Quezon City, with 1,902,590 people in the 2024 census. It has 16 administrative districts, and the name is also used for Metro Manila, the capital region. The National Museum Complex in Rizal Park holds Juan Luna's painting Spoliarium, and the historic Walled City of Intramuros is administered by a national agency, the Intramuros Administration.
manila-galleon: Spain's presence in the Philippines came from a wish to compete with Portugal for the spice trade. Magellan's expedition of 1521 sailed west across the Pacific and claimed the Mariana Islands and the Philippines for Spain. To trade with the islands from the Americas, an eastward return path was needed, and attempts in 1529 and 1543 failed.

The navigator Andrés de Urdaneta persuaded officials in New Spain that a route to Mexico was best. Sailing with the expedition of Miguel López de Legazpi in 1564, he reasoned that Pacific winds might move in a gyre, as the Atlantic winds did, and sailed north to the 38th parallel off Japan to catch the westerlies. His ship reached Acapulco on 8 October 1565 after 129 days, most of its crew having died for lack of provisions.

Galleons left Cavite in Manila Bay at the end of June or the first week of July and reached Acapulco in March or April. Most were built in Cavite from Philippine hardwoods, and were the largest class of European ships built to that date, carrying 300 to 500 passengers. The great majority of crews were Filipino, many press-ganged; less than a third were Spanish, usually in key positions. Mortality was high from starvation, disease and scurvy. A decree of 1593 limited sailings to two ships a year, after Seville merchants petitioned Philip II to protect their monopoly, and contraband became widespread.

Cargoes included Chinese silk and porcelain, Indian ivory and precious stones and cloves from the Moluccas, bought mostly with silver from New Spain and Potosí. Slaves from East Africa, Portuguese India, Southeast Asian sultanates and the Philippines were also sold in New Spain. Goods crossed Mexico by mule train to Veracruz for shipping to Spain.

In 1813 the Cortes of Cádiz decreed the suppression of the route. The trade ended in 1815, and Mexico became independent in 1821. Between 1565 and 1815, 108 ships operated as Manila galleons, of which 26 were captured or sunk by enemies. The route is regarded as an early instance of globalisation, linking all the world's continents in the silver trade, and economic shocks from Spanish-American silver arriving in China were among the factors that led to the end of the Ming dynasty. It also left a Hispanic and Mexican influence on Philippine culture.
maniots: Maniots, historically also called Mainotes, claim descent from the ancient Spartans. In one tradition, followers of the laws of Lycurgus left for Mani after the Romans took Laconia rather than live under the Achaean League or Rome. Mani also became a refuge when Slavs and Avars entered the Peloponnese and people from northern Greece and Macedonia fled south into its mountains. In the 10th century Emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus wrote that the Maniots had not been conquered by the Slavs and descended from the ancient Romaioi.

Genetic studies support a long isolation. A study of 2017 found Maniots genetically distinct from other groups of the Peloponnese, with the lowest levels of Slavic ancestry in the region, and a study of 2026 of the people of Inner Mani found paternal lineages linked to Bronze Age, Iron Age and Roman-period Greek populations, with strong founder effects of about the 4th to 7th centuries. The clan structure itself has been dated by shared paternal lines mainly to the 14th and 15th centuries.

Maniot society was built on clans living in fortified villages and tower houses, raised against Frankish and Ottoman invaders. Piracy was their main source of income into at least the 18th century; most pirates came from Inner Mani, and local Orthodox priests blessed the raiding ships and sometimes sailed with them. Folklore was rich in witches, demons, vampires and ghosts.

Vendettas were decided at family gatherings and aimed at wiping out the rival family, whose members killed each other from their towers for months or years. Feuds ended when a family was destroyed or left the town, or through a settlement or exchange of property, and a truce, the treva, could pause them for harvests or festivals. All feuds stopped whenever the community faced a Turkish threat; the longest known treva was announced by the Mavromichalis clan in March 1821, when war was declared on the Ottoman Empire. Vendettas continued after independence, and one of the last needed police, 1,000 soldiers and 200 sailors to end it.

Maniots speak a variety of Modern Greek that shares old features with Tsakonian and with the speech of Athens before the 19th century. In Outer Mani family names end in -eas, in Inner Mani in -akis or -akos. Two dances, the Palio Maniatiko and the Modern Maniatiko, are performed only in Mani.
manisa: Manisa lies about 40 kilometres north-east of İzmir, with its historic quarter on the forested slopes of Mount Sipylus beside the Çaybaşı Stream. Near it are the rock called Niobe's Weeping Rock and an ancient bridge, the Red Bridge. The Gediz plain, formed by river deposits, stretches out below. Ancient writers called the city Magnesia ad Sipylum to tell it from Magnesia on the Maeander. Pliny the Elder says a notable city called Tantalis, the city of Tantalus, once stood on the same spot, and its ruins were still visible in his time.

The Cybele monument at Akpınar, on the northern flank of Mount Sipylus, is among the evidence of Hittite influence in the region of the Luwian kingdom of Arzawa. Figures of tradition such as Tantalus, Pelops and Niobe are tied to the mountain. In the early seventh century BCE the Lydians under the Mermnad dynasty ruled much of Anatolia from Sardis, 62 kilometres inland.

Under Roman rule the city became important after the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BCE, was nearly destroyed by an earthquake in the reign of Tiberius, and was restored by him. The Seljuks took it in 1076, and the Byzantine Empire recovered it after the Battle of Dorylaeum in 1097. During the Empire of Nicea, from 1204 to 1261, it held the imperial mint and treasury and was in effect the capital.
