Turkish raids in the late 13th and early 14th centuries drove most inhabitants away after a failed campaign in 1302 by Michael IX. In 1313 Manisa fell to the Beylik of Saruhan, whose founder reigned until 1346, and the Ottomans absorbed it in 1410, after an interval following the Battle of Ankara. In a practice begun by Murad II in 1437, fifteen members of the Ottoman dynasty, among them Mehmed II and Süleyman I, governed the Saruhan district in seventeen near-continuous periods until 1595. The princes there gained experience of government, and the city is still known as the city of shahzades. A severe earthquake in 1595 dealt a heavy blow to its prosperity.

Manisa was one of the first Ottoman cities served by a railway, the Smyrna Cassaba line, which reached Kasaba in 1866. The Greek army occupied it on 26 May 1919 and left on 8 September 1922; most of the city was burned as the army retreated. Manisa was rebuilt, and its name replaced Saruhan for the province and the city in 1927.
manishtushu: Manishtushu was the son of Sargon of Akkad, the brother of Enheduanna, Rimush and Shu-Enlil, and the father of Naram-Sin. His name means 'Who is with him?'. Old Babylonian tradition counts him as the third king of the Akkadian Empire, though the Ur III recension of the Sumerian King List lists him second, after Sargon. He became king about 2270 BCE after the death of his brother Rimush, whose reign had been troubled by rebellions.

Freed of those rebellions, Manishtushu led campaigns to distant lands. According to one of his inscriptions, he sent ships across the Lower Sea, the Persian Gulf, where thirty-two cities assembled for battle; he won, plundered their cities as far as the Silver Mines, quarried black stone in the mountains across the sea and moored the ships loaded with it at the quay of Agade.

He also conquered Anshan in Elam and rebuilt the destroyed temple of Inanna at Nineveh about 2260 BCE. He installed governors in Elam and Pashime, Eshpum and Ilshu-rabi. His inscriptions style him king of Kish and king of the world. Only one year name is known, recording the founding of Dūr-Maništusu, a fortress whose site is unknown.

The Manishtushu Obelisk, a diorite kudurru found at Susa in 1897 by Jacques de Morgan and now in the Louvre Museum, records his purchase of eight parcels of land totalling 3,430 hectares. Its text is in Akkadian with Sumerian spelling and gives the price of a field as 3 talents 33 minas of silver, the earliest written use of the talent. The fields lay around four cities, Dur-Sin, Girtab, Marda and Kish.

Manishtushu died about 2255 BCE, possibly assassinated by members of his own court; the claim rests on an Old Babylonian omen text that speaks of Manishtushu 'whom his palace killed'. His son Naram-Sin succeeded him and deified him after death, and texts of the Ur III period record offerings to the deified king and a town and temple named for him. Later ages handled his monuments in different ways.

The cruciform monument found at Sippar in 1881 was long taken as a copy of an Old Akkadian original, but later research showed it to be an Old Babylonian forgery, and more recent scholarship dates it to the Neo-Babylonian period. About a thousand years after his reign the Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte carried a stele and a statue attributed to Manishtushu from Akkadian lands to Susa.
manitoba: Manitoba lies at the longitudinal centre of Canada, bordered by Nunavut and the Northwest Territories to the north, Hudson Bay to the northeast, Ontario to the east, North Dakota and Minnesota to the south and Saskatchewan to the west. Its landscape runs from arctic tundra and the Hudson Bay coast in the north to boreal forest, large freshwater lakes and prairie in the centre and south. It lies at the centre of the Hudson Bay drainage basin, where much of the water drains into Lake Winnipeg and then north down the Nelson River. Most of the inhabited south developed in the bed of the prehistoric Glacial Lake Agassiz, and the Red River Valley is flat and fertile.

First Nations peoples settled the area about 10,000 years ago, shortly after the last ice age glaciers retreated. The Ojibwe, Cree, Dene, Sioux, Mandan and Assiniboine founded settlements, and the first farming was along the Red River, where corn and other seed crops were planted before contact with Europeans. English and French fur traders arrived in the early 17th century. England secured the region in 1670 as Rupert's Land under the Hudson's Bay Company, and the early economy centred on the trade of beaver pelts and other furs. Lord Selkirk brought the first agricultural settlers in 1811, and a Red River Colony of Indigenous and Métis people grew up.

Deep disagreements over self-determination during the transfer of Rupert's Land to Canada in 1869 led to armed resistance under the Métis leader Louis Riel, who established a provisional government. Its assembly sent three delegates to Ottawa, and the negotiations produced the Manitoba Act, introduced by Prime Minister Sir John A. Macdonald, which made Manitoba the fifth province of Canada in 1870. The name was chosen by Thomas Spence, and Riel preferred it to the alternative Assiniboia. Riel fled into exile, and the Canadian government blocked the Métis' attempts to obtain the land promised to them. Facing racism from a flood of settlers from Ontario, many Métis moved to what became Saskatchewan and Alberta.

By 1911 Winnipeg was the third largest city in Canada. Nellie McClung led the campaign for women's votes, and on 28 January 1916 Manitoba became the first province to allow women to vote in provincial elections, two years before Canada did so nationally.

Manitoba is a province of Canada with Winnipeg as its capital and largest city, home to nearly two thirds of the provincial population in its metropolitan region. English and French are both official languages of its legislature and courts under the Manitoba Act, a status the Supreme Court of Canada upheld in 1985. The population was 1,342,153 at the 2021 census. The Winnipeg-based Royal Winnipeg Ballet, granted its royal title in 1953, is Canada's oldest ballet company.
manitoba-act: The Red River Colony lay in Rupert's Land, controlled by the Hudson's Bay Company, which surrendered it to the British Crown under the Rupert's Land Act 1868; Canada paid £300,000 for it, though Indigenous and Métis people lived there. The Métis were not consulted when William McDougall was appointed lieutenant governor and set out for Red River in September 1869. Armed Métis barred his party at the 49th parallel, and on 16 December he gave up for the time being.

Under Louis Riel, chosen for his education and his command of French and English, the Métis formed a provisional government that Ottawa considered illegal and occupied Fort Garry, where they held 45 Ontario settlers. The execution of one prisoner, Thomas Scott, on 4 March 1870 outraged opinion in Canada. The provisional government drew up four successive lists of rights; the last, dated 9 May 1870, asked for entry as a province rather than a territory, a bilingual lieutenant governor and no legal consequences for its members.

The act, which received royal assent on 12 May 1870 and is part of the Constitution of Canada, made Manitoba the fifth province and created its legislature and government. Laws had to be passed and published in French and English, either language could be used in the legislature and the courts, and denominational schools existing by law or practice at the union were protected, though teaching in French was not guaranteed. Ottawa paid subsidies, and the province received four seats in the House of Commons and two in the Senate. Section 31 set aside 1.4 million acres for the children of Métis families, beyond the land they already farmed.

Colonel Garnet Wolseley's Red River Expedition followed, and militiamen seeking to avenge Scott carried out reprisals that newspapers called the Reign of Terror; many Métis fled to Saskatchewan and Riel to the United States. The land promised proved too little for the claims, and money scrip replaced it; historian D. N. Sprague notes that later laws took land from the Métis. In the 1890s Manitoba ended funding for denominational schools, creating the Manitoba Schools Question, and made English its only official language, a law the Supreme Court found unconstitutional in 1985. Section 31 was central to the 2013 case Manitoba Métis Federation v. Canada. The Constitution Act, 1871 confirmed Parliament's power to create provinces.
manius-curius-dentatus: According to Pliny, Manius Curius was born with teeth, which earned him the surname Dentatus, meaning toothed. His praenomen is sometimes given wrongly as Marcus, because the standard abbreviation of Manius, M'., is confused with the M. that stands for Marcus. He first appears as a tribune of the plebs at some point between 298 and 291 BCE, when he foiled the efforts of the interrex Appius Claudius Caecus to keep plebeian candidates out of the consular elections.

In his first consulship, in 290 BCE, his colleague was P. Cornelius Rufinus, an ancestor of the dictator Lucius Cornelius Sulla Felix. Dentatus defeated both the Samnites and the Sabines and was granted two triumphs. On his return he undertook a large public work, partly draining Lake Velinus. In 283 BCE he took the place of Lucius Caecilius Metellus Denter, who had been killed at the Battle of Arretium, as praetor or possibly consul, and Polybius says he drove the Gauls from their territory, opening the way for a Roman colony at Sena.

Consul again in 275 BCE, he fought Pyrrhus at the Battle of Beneventum, after which Pyrrhus left Italy. He held a further consulship the next year, defeated the Lucani and was granted an ovation. He served as censor in 272 BCE.

In 270 BCE Dentatus and Lucius Papirius Cursor were chosen as commissioners for the Anio Vetus, Rome's second aqueduct, which he paid for with his own share of the booty from his campaigns. He died while it was being built, and his fellow commissioner Marcus Fulvius Flaccus completed it.

He was remembered as frugal and incorruptible. In the best-known story, Samnite envoys bringing costly gifts found him by his hearth roasting turnips; he refused the gifts, saying he preferred ruling those who possessed gold to possessing it himself. The story may be an invention of Cato, but it inspired paintings by Jacopo Amigoni, Govert Flinck and others.
manmohan-singh: Manmohan Singh was born on 26 September 1932 in Gah, in Punjab, British India, into a Punjabi Sikh family of dried fruit traders. His mother died when he was very young, and his paternal grandmother, Jamna Devi, raised him. He was first educated at a local gurdwara and a government primary school in Urdu, then at the Khalsa School in Peshawar after the family moved there. After the Partition of India his family migrated to Haldwani and in 1948 to Amritsar. He took his bachelor's and master's degrees in economics at Panjab University in 1952 and 1954, completed the Economics Tripos at the University of Cambridge in 1957 and earned a doctorate at Oxford. He married Gursharan Kaur in 1958, and they had three daughters.

Singh taught economics at Panjab University and the Delhi School of Economics, and worked for the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development from 1966 to 1969. He served the Government of India as chief economic adviser from 1972, as secretary in the Finance Ministry from 1976, as governor of the Reserve Bank of India from 1982 to 1985, and as deputy chairman of the Planning Commission from 1985 to 1987. From 1987 to 1990 he was secretary general of the South Commission in Geneva.

In June 1991 Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao chose him as finance minister. India's foreign reserves then barely covered two weeks of imports. Despite resistance within the party, Singh and Rao removed the licensing system known as the licence raj, reduced state control and import taxes, eased foreign direct investment and began the privatisation of public companies. Singh sat in the Rajya Sabha from 1991 and was leader of the opposition there from 1998 to 2004.

After the 2004 general election Sonia Gandhi, chairperson of the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance, named Singh, a technocrat who had never won a direct popular election, as its candidate for prime minister. He took the oath on 22 May 2004. His first ministry passed laws and launched schemes including the Rural Employment Guarantee scheme and the Right to Information Act. In 2008 the Left Front withdrew its support over a civil nuclear agreement with the United States. After the 2009 election he was sworn in again on 22 May 2009, the first prime minister since Jawaharlal Nehru to win re-election after a full five-year term. His premiership ended on 17 May 2014.

Singh remained a member of the Rajya Sabha until April 2024. He died in New Delhi on 26 December 2024, aged 92, and received a state funeral on 28 December. He was the first Sikh prime minister of India. His colleague P. Chidambaram compared his part in the reforms of 1991 to that of Deng Xiaoping in China.
mannheim: Mannheim stands at the confluence of the Upper Rhine and the Neckar, in the Electoral Palatinate region of north-western Baden-Württemberg, on the Upper Rhine Plain. It forms a continuous urban zone with Ludwigshafen am Rhein across the river. The city centre is unusual for Germany: its streets are laid out in a grid, earning the nickname Quadratestadt, and most of the blocks are named by a letter and a number rather than by street names. The practice is centuries old and comes from the original use of the centre as a fort, whose internal system was kept when the streets became public.

A brick kiln of 74 CE to the early second century shows Roman settlement. The name was first recorded as Mannenheim in 766, in a twelfth-century copy of a Lorsch Abbey codex, and the place remained a village throughout the Middle Ages. In 1606 Frederick IV, Elector Palatine began building the fortress of Friedrichsburg and the adjacent city centre with its grid, and on 24 January 1607 he gave Mannheim the status of a city. Tilly's forces mostly levelled it around 1622 in the Thirty Years' War, and after rebuilding it was badly damaged by the French army in 1689. The National Theatre, founded in 1779, is called the oldest stage in Germany, and Friedrich Schiller's Die Räuber premiered there in 1782.

The city became known for inventions. Karl Drais built the first two-wheeled draisine in 1817, and Karl Benz drove the first automobile on the streets of Mannheim in 1886; in August 1888 his wife Bertha Benz made the first road trip by automobile, to Pforzheim and back. The Lanz Bulldog tractor followed in 1921, and Benz and Cie. built the first compact diesel-powered car in 1923. Mannheim became a Großstadt in 1896, and the Schütte-Lanz company, founded in 1909, built 22 airships. In the Second World War air raids destroyed the city centre and killed thousands of civilians, while 2,262 of the city's Jews were sent to concentration camps. The palace and water tower were rebuilt, and the University of Mannheim was established in 1967.

Mannheim is the second-largest city of Baden-Württemberg after Stuttgart, with a population of over 315,000, and the cultural and economic centre of the Rhine-Neckar region. It is a major railway junction and river port. Mannheim Palace, the former home of the Prince-elector of the Electoral Palatinate, now houses the University of Mannheim, and the Mannheim Water Tower, completed in 1886, is the civic symbol. The city has been a UNESCO City of Music since 2014.
manorialism: Manorialism grew out of the rural economy of the later Roman Empire, in which labour was the key factor of production. Successive administrations tried to stabilise the economy by fixing the social structure in place, and the coloni, the cultivators of the land, were not to leave the land they were attached to. Laws of Constantine I around 325 reinforced their semi-servile status. As Germanic kingdoms replaced Roman authority in the fifth century, Roman landlords were often simply replaced by Germanic ones with little change to the underlying situation. Self-sufficiency in the countryside received a boost in the eighth century, when normal trade in the Mediterranean was disrupted.

A manor was a local jurisdiction held by a lord, the seigneur, usually in return for undertakings to a higher lord. Bishops, abbots and military orders could be lords too. A manor held up to three classes of land: the demesne, directly controlled by the lord; dependent holdings of serfs or villeins, who supplied labour or part of their output; and free peasant land owing a fixed money rent. The lord also took charges for the use of his mill, bakery or wine-press, for hunting and feeding pigs in his woodland, and payments at each change of tenant.

Villeins were not slaves: they had legal rights under local custom and could go to court. Their holdings became in practice hereditary, and from the 13th century labour on the demesne was increasingly commuted into money payments. The demesne usually made up roughly a third of the arable area, and manors varied greatly from place to place.

Manorialism faded away slowly, together with its most vivid feature in the landscape, the open field system. It outlasted serfdom, since it continued with freehold labourers. According to Andrew Jones it also outlasted feudalism because it could maintain a warrior just as well as a capitalist landlord. The last feudal dues in France were abolished in the French Revolution, and in parts of eastern Germany the Rittergut manors of the Junkers remained until World War II.
manrique-perez-de-lara: Manrique was a son of Count Pedro González de Lara, who died in 1130, and of Eva, whose parentage is unknown; her name and her son's suggest a family from north of the Pyrenees. He had three full brothers, Álvaro, Nuño and Rodrigo. Between 1134 and 1137 he served Alfonso VII as alférez, head of the military household, a post for young nobles of promise. He went on to hold the tenencias of Atienza, Ávila, Madrid and Toledo, and on 21 August 1145 the king made him a count at León.

Manrique helped capture Calatrava in January 1147 and took part in the conquest of Almería that August, receiving Baeza, which he governed until 1157; the Poema de Almería praises his generosity and skill in war. In 1149 he became tutor to the heir, the future Sancho III. Before December 1153 he married Ermessinde, daughter of Aimeric II of Narbonne, and he may have been the first Castilian noble to seal his documents. The fuero he and Ermessinde granted Molina on 21 April 1154, known from a 13th-century copy, set out the settlers' privileges, a municipal council, a legal code and the duties of a local militia.

After Sancho III died on 31 August 1158, Manrique became regent and guardian of the child Alfonso VIII. A century later Rodrigo Jiménez de Rada blamed the division of Alfonso VII's realms on the counsel of Manrique and Fernando Pérez de Traba. The dispute over the regency drove the Castro family into exile and started a civil war; in March 1160 the Castro leader Fernando Rodríguez defeated the Laras at the Battle of Lobregal and captured Manrique's brother Nuño. By 1161 Manrique was styled nutritius regis, nurturer of the king.

Fernando Rodríguez killed Manrique at the Battle of Huete in 1164. The day is uncertain: the Anales toledanos primeros give 9 July, while an earlier charter of 21 June places the battle on 3 June. He was buried in the Cistercian abbey of Santa María de Huerta, which the Laras went on to patronise heavily. Ermessinde lived until at least 1175, endowing Huerta, the Order of Calatrava and the Knights Hospitaller. Molina, after passing to the crown through the marriage of María de Molina and Sancho IV, survived as a subsidiary royal title until the time of Isabel II.
mansa-musa: Musa was the ninth mansa of the Mali Empire. His birth date is unknown, but he appears to have been a young man in 1324. Accounts of his parentage differ: Djibril Tamsir Niane names his father as Faga Leye, a descendant of a brother of Sunjata, while Francois-Xavier Fauvelle has proposed that he was a grandson of Sunjata through his daughter.

By his own account, his predecessor led an expedition to explore the Atlantic and appointed Musa deputy, and when the mansa did not return Musa was crowned. Some modern historians suspect he deposed his predecessor and invented the story. Most of what is known comes from Arabic writers, especially Al-Umari and Ibn Khaldun.

Musa's wealth came mainly from taxing the salt trade from the north and from gold mined in Bambuk and Bure to the south. His early reign was spent in conflict with neighbouring non-Muslim societies. The empire reached its territorial peak under him, and Gao and Timbuktu came under Mali.

He made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and 1325, leaving his son Muhammad to rule. Arabic chroniclers give widely varying figures for his caravan and its gold, and modern historians treat them as rhetorical rather than statistical. He stayed about three months in Cairo, where his gifts are said to have lowered the value of gold, although Warren Schultz argues the fall was normal. The return journey cost many lives, and he borrowed from Cairo merchants. He persuaded the Andalusian poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili and Maliki jurists to come to Mali, and Timbuktu became a centre of Islamic learning.

The date of his death is uncertain: Ibn Khaldun's reign lengths suggest 1332, while a later report points to 1337, which Nehemia Levtzion thought most likely. Musa is commonly seen as Mali's golden age, though this may reflect that his reign is the best recorded in Arabic sources. In Mandé oral tradition he is less prominent than earlier rulers, and some jeliw criticise him for wasting Mali's wealth. European maps from the Catalan Atlas of 1375 onward show a wealthy West African ruler inspired by his pilgrimage.
mansa-sakura: Sakura is known chiefly from the account of Ibn Khaldun in his Kitāb al-ʻIbar. He did not belong to the ruling Keita dynasty. He is commonly said to have been a slave of the royal court, but Ibn Khaldun calls him a mawlā, a client, which may mean he had been enslaved and freed by the Keitas. Oral tradition names him jonni, little slave, and he may have belonged to the tontajon taniworo, the sixteen clans of freemen with the right to bear a quiver, who are spoken of metaphorically as slaves. Tradition gives him a daughter, Sogolon Nyuman.

Late in the 13th century the court was divided by a power struggle between the gbara, the Grand Council, and the donson ton, the hunters' guilds. The historian Nehemia Levtzion suggested that Sakura may have taken part in an earlier coup that replaced Mansa Khalifa with Abu Bakr, a grandson or nephew of Sunjata, before seizing the throne himself; Maurice Delafosse put his accession in 1285. According to Ibn Khaldun, Malian rule under Sakura reached west to the ocean and east to Takrur, meaning a land east of Gao and west of Kanem, and trade with the rest of the Muslim world flourished.

Ibn Khaldun credits him with taking Gao, but also gives the conquest to Mansa Musa, as the Tarikh al-Sudan does; Mali's hold on Gao may have come and gone. Sakura made the hajj, the first mansa to do so since Uli, though oral tradition does not record it. Ibn Khaldun says he was killed on the way home at Tajura, 12 miles east of Tripoli; oral tradition says that Kon Mamadi (Qu), a grandson of Sunjata, killed him with the help of Sakura's daughter, and Qu succeeded him.

Ibn Khaldun saw Sakura as a mighty ruler, and Djibril Tamsir Niane held that he saved the empire from political crisis. Oral histories mention him little, mostly as a usurper, which Niane thought a deliberate exclusion; his memory may partly live on in the general Fakoli of tradition. Michael A. Gomez doubts the account of his reign, suggesting that deeds of Musa were assigned to Sakura so that Musa could be criticised indirectly.
mansoor-ali-khan-pataudi: Mansoor Ali Khan was born in Bhopal on 5 January 1941, the son of the cricketer Iftikhar Ali Khan Pataudi, last ruler of the princely state of Pataudi, and of Sajida Sultan, Nawab Begum of Bhopal. His father died playing polo in Delhi on Mansoor's eleventh birthday in 1952, and he succeeded as ninth Nawab. He was educated at Welham Boys' School in Dehradun, Lockers Park in Hertfordshire, where Frank Woolley coached him, and Winchester College, and read Arabic and French at Balliol College, Oxford.

At Winchester he scored 1,068 runs as captain in 1959, beating Douglas Jardine's school record. He made his first-class debut for Sussex at 16 in 1957 and became Oxford's first Indian captain. On 1 July 1961 a car accident in Hove drove a shard of glass into his right eye and left him seeing a doubled image, but he learned to bat with one eye and made his Test debut against England in Delhi that December. His 103 in Madras helped India to its first series win over England.

He took the captaincy in Barbados in March 1962, at 21 years and 77 days, when Nari Contractor was injured. In 46 Tests between 1961 and 1975 he scored 2,793 runs at 34.91 with six centuries; as captain he won 9 matches, lost 19 and drew 19. John Arlott and Ted Dexter called him the best fielder in the world. He also captained Sussex in 1966 and played for Delhi and Hyderabad, and was Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 1968.

He stood unsuccessfully for the Lok Sabha from Gurgaon in 1971 and from Bhopal in 1991. He married the actress Sharmila Tagore on 27 December 1968; their children are Saif, Saba and Soha Ali Khan. He published an autobiography, Tiger's Tale, in 1969, and received the Arjuna Award, the Padma Shri and in 2001 the C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award. He died of respiratory failure in Delhi on 22 September 2011 and is buried at Pataudi.
mansur-shah-of-malacca: Mansur Shah, the sixth Sultan of Malacca, came to the throne on the death of his father, Muzaffar Shah. Under his policy of expansion the sultanate reached its widest territorial extent. Perak, Bernam and Siak became vassals of Malacca, Manjung, Rupat, Singapore and Bintan came under its control, and Pahang, Kampar and Inderagiri tried without success to assert their autonomy; one of his sons was made ruler of Pahang.

He bound conquered states to Malacca by marriage: his daughter Princess Mahadewi married the king of Siak, and he himself married princesses of conquered states such as Princess Wanang Seri of Pahang and Raden Galoh Candra Kirana. Siantan and Indragiri in Sumatra came to Malacca as the dowry of a princess of Majapahit. Such alliances helped Islam spread in maritime Southeast Asia. Princess Hang Li Po remains a figure of legend: no Ming source records a princess of that name, and the emperor of the time was Yingzong, not Yongle.

He lowered taxes on trade to draw merchants, levying 6 percent on traders from west of Malacca such as Arabia and India and 3 percent on those of maritime Southeast Asia, while merchants from China, Japan and Java paid nothing. He studied Sufism under Maulana Abu Bakar, who brought the Ab Darul Manzum to Malacca, had it translated into Malay by Makhdum Patakan, and consulted scholars from Pasai on religious questions.

Two inscribed stones said to come from his tomb, found against the wall of the residency at Malacca and studied by Jean Pierre Moquette and Richard Olaf Winstedt, call him the just and magnanimous sultan, son of Muzaffar Shah, though the two readings differ over the year of his death after the Hijrah. His palace is one of the most fully described buildings in Malay historical sources; nothing of it survived the Portuguese capture of Malacca in 1511. A replica, built of hardwoods with a roof of belian wood and funded under Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, opened on 17 July 1984 and serves as a museum.
mansura-sindh: Mansura, the triumphant city, was known in later centuries as Brahmanabad or Bahmanabad. It stood on the banks of the Indus amid fertile farmland, and historians describe it as a town of mango orchards and date-palm groves. Its site lies 18 kilometres south-east of Shahdadpur and 75 kilometres north-east of Hyderabad. William Vincent identified the place with Patala, the city whose chief, Mæris, submitted to Alexander the Great and then fled into the desert with his people, leaving the Macedonians an empty town.

After Muhammad ibn Qasim took the Brahmanabad territory, the Umayyad governor of Sind, al-Hakam, founded a city called al-Mahfuza at a time when, the sources say, no place in Sind was safe for Muslims, and his deputy al-Thaqafi founded al-Mansura opposite it. The historian Blankinship believes that one was a base for the Yamani troops of the caliphate and the other for the Mudari. By the time of al-Baladhuri the old Brahmanabad was in ruins and the new city carried its name. In the Abbasid era it was developed by Khalid ibn Barmak and grew into a metropolis richer than Multan or Debal.

Ibn Hauqal described wealthy merchants of Sindhi-Arab origin dressed in the fashion of Baghdad, living in houses of clay, baked brick and plaster. The city sent herbs, spices, textiles, ivory, metals and mirrors to Baghdad, and its schools produced the first translation of the Quran into Sindhi. Its people included the hadith compiler Abu Mashar Sindhi. An earthquake struck Mansura and Debal in 893. When the inhabitants refused to open their gates to Mahmud of Ghazni, his forces sacked the city, which never recovered.

The ruins lie on an open sandy plain, a boot-shaped field of brick mounds about 9.25 kilometres round, crossed by the hollows of old streets and ringed by the remains of walls and bastions. Nothing stands above the surface but one tower-like core of brick; there is no stone masonry, and charred wood shows where timber once was. The largest ruin is the courtyard of a Jamia Masjid. In early excavations A. P. Bellasis found a seal inscribed Imam al-Baqir, thought to belong to the fifth Shi'ite imam.
manta-ecuador: Manta, also known as San Pablo de Manta, is the head of the Manta Canton and the largest and most populated city of Manabí Province. It lies on the Pacific coast and has the largest seaport in Ecuador. Despite its position on the equator, the Humboldt Current gives it an arid climate. The city is cloudy and hot most of the year, and rainfall is erratic and largely confined to the months between January and April, occurring mainly during El Niño events, when the Humboldt Current weakens.

Manta has existed since Pre-Columbian times, when it was a trading post for the Manta, also known as the Manteños. The Central Bank Museum in the city holds an important collection of Pre-Columbian craft.

In 1735 Charles Marie de La Condamine, leading the French mission to measure the location of the equator, arrived in Ecuador through the port of Manta, and from there began his journey inland to Quito. Nearby Montecristi, founded in the early 17th century, has colonial architecture and is known for its wickerwork weaving; the original Panama hats were historically produced in Ecuador, and are made at Montecristi.

Between 1999 and 2009 the Manta Air Base, also called the Eloy Alfaro Air Base, was used by U.S. air forces to support anti-narcotics operations and surveillance flights against Colombian drug trafficking cartels. The Ecuadorian government did not renew the lease.

The 2022 census gave the city a population of 258,697. Its main economic activity is tuna fishing and canning, with processed tuna exported abroad, alongside vegetable oil and other chemical products. Manta has an international airport, several universities, including the Universidad Laica Eloy Alfaro, and an international film festival.
mantaro-valley: The Mantaro Valley, also called the Jauja Valley, lies 200 kilometres east of Lima. It runs north to south for about 60 kilometres between Jauja and Huancayo, with the Mantaro River emerging from a steep gorge at its northern end and entering another at its southern end. The floor averages about 10 kilometres wide at 3,150 to 3,500 metres, and mountains of more than 4,500 metres rise on either side, the highest being Huaytapallana at 5,567 metres. Unusually for the Andes, it holds about 65,000 hectares of arable land, cultivable up to 4,200 metres, and it has been a breadbasket since pre-Columbian times.

The valley was home to the Wanka, or Huanca, a self-governing nation known for strong warriors and for rites that honoured the ancestors. Local legend tells of a warrior who drowned following a mermaid into the lake of Laguna de Paca and whose body became a mountain range in the shape of a man. The Huanca were subdued in the reign of the Inca king Pachacutec, and later took the side of the Spanish against their former overlords; the Spanish, suppressing paganism, then destroyed their temple of Wariwillka near Huancayo.

Under the Incas the valley was one of the largest and most fertile parts of the empire. Archaeologists have studied its 2,573 storage silos, or qullqas, more than in any other region of Peru: half stood in the centre of the valley and half among 48 compounds along the river, with a combined capacity of 170,000 cubic metres. During the Spanish conquest of the 1530s they supplied an army of 35,000 soldiers. Jauja served as Peru's provisional capital in 1534. In the 18th and early 19th centuries the Convent of Santa Rosa de Ocopa was the headquarters of Franciscan missions in the Amazon rain forest.

The valley grows potatoes, maize and vegetables, and Huancayo is its largest city. Its towns keep their own crafts: tapestries and blankets at Hualhuas, woodcarving at Molinos, silver filigree at San Jeronimo de Tunan, ceramics at Aco and Quilcas, wooden masks at Mito, and the carved gourds of Cochas Grande and Cochas Chico.
mantsala-rebellion: On 27 February 1932 some 400 armed members of the Civil Guards broke up a meeting of Social Democrats at Mäntsälä with small arms fire. The action began with a regional branch of the Lapua Movement, but the national organisation soon joined it, and in the following days its leaders and hundreds of armed Civil Guards gathered at Mäntsälä. Major General Wallenius, a former Chief of General Staff, joined the leadership. The men refused to disperse and demanded the cabinet's resignation and a change of political course.

Two days later the cabinet ordered the arrest of the movement's leaders under the Protection of the Republic Act, a law the movement itself had urged for a year. The Chief of Defence, Lieutenant General Aarne Sihvo, was ready to use force, and the defence of Helsinki was to be reinforced with tanks and artillery if the situation worsened. As tension grew, so did drinking among the instigators.

On 2 March President Pehr Evind Svinhufvud, having taken command of the armed forces to restore order, spoke on the radio. He ordered the militiamen to go home, warned that the White Guard would suffer if its members forgot their oath, and promised that only the instigators would be punished.

The men dispersed, and the leaders were arrested a few days later. Only a small part of the Civil Guards had joined the rebels, while most stayed loyal to the government. In the spring the Lapua Movement was disbanded. An indictment of 16 July 1932 sought the punishment of 102 rebels, of whom 52 received prison terms and 32 conditional terms.
The rebellion can be seen as the last major incident of the radical right in Finland after the Civil War. In the following years the economy improved and radical movements lost support.
manua-islands: Ofu and Olosega are separated only by the shallow Āsaga Strait, 137 metres wide, and are now joined by a bridge. All three islands are mountainous volcanic remnants rising from the sea 14 degrees south of the equator. Taʻū, the largest, covers 44 square kilometres and reaches 931 metres, and the sea cliffs of its southern coast rise to 3,000 feet. The land is owned communally by the Samoan families of Manuʻa, and the park lands are only leased to the United States.

According to Samoan oral tradition, Manuʻa was once the ruling centre of a large Polynesian empire that took in the whole Samoan archipelago and other islands, among them Tonga and parts of Fiji. Its traditional capital is the village of Taʻū. Many high titles of other parts of Samoa derive from that of the Tui Manuʻa, and Manuʻa was the only part of Samoa never subjected to Tongan rule, because Tongans and Samoans alike regarded it as sacred.

The Tripartite Convention of 1899 gave the United States the eastern Samoan islands. Tutuila's leaders agreed in 1901, and Manuʻa formalised its acceptance in a Deed of Succession signed by the Tui Manuʻa on 16 July 1904. The last holder, Tuimanuʻa Elisara, wished the title to die with him, and he died on 2 July 1909; the title and its estates remain in the custody of the Anoalo clan, though no one holds it.

A hurricane struck overnight on 9 January 1915, uprooting an estimated 75 per cent of the coconut trees, washing away the village of Sili and cutting the islands off. Contact was restored only after 22 days, when Pele Scoles repaired a longboat and rowed from Ofu to Tutuila. It was the first time the United States Congress and the American Red Cross sent aid to American Samoa.

The islands form the Manuʻa District, one of the three administrative divisions of American Samoa, with a combined area of 56 square kilometres and a population of 1,400. Their share of the territory's people fell from some 20 per cent in the 1930s to 6 per cent by the 1980s, as young people left for Tutuila. Part of the National Park of American Samoa lies on Taʻū, including Alei Ridge and its plateau, where a survey in 2006 found star mounds, terraces and house platforms.
manuchihri: In the words of the scholar J. W. Clinton, very little is known of the poet's life, and that little comes only from his poetry; later tadhkira writers, the compilers of biographies of poets, expanded it with speculations that are easily refuted. His epithet Damghani shows that he came from Damghan in Iran. His verse displays a wide knowledge of Arabic and Persian poetry, which he presumably acquired in youth.

His career can be dated only through the people his praise poems address. About a third of his panegyrics are addressed to the sultan, and most of the rest to leading officials of the sultan's court, though some name patrons who cannot be identified or none at all. In 1031–1033 he wrote poems for the sultan's deputies while the ruler was based at Ray.

Some time after the death of the vizier Ahmad ibn Hasan Maymandi in 1033 he made his way to the court at Ghazna. None of his poems seems to date from after his time there; the sultan died in 1041 after his defeat in battle at Dandanaqan. Clinton counts him the third and last, after Unsuri and Farrukhi, of the major panegyrists of the early court of Ghazna.

His divan holds fifty-seven qasidas, a few ruba'is, ghazals and shorter pieces, and eleven musammats, stanza poems of a form he is said to have invented in Persian. Clinton sets him apart from his contemporaries by his enthusiasm for Arabic poetry, which led him to imitate the old Arabic qasida, and by his skill in describing the royal garden at Nawruz and Mihrgan and its festivities. He also gave life to ideas such as the battle of the seasons and wine as the daughter of the vine.

One of his best known musammats, of 35 stanzas, begins by calling on the listener to bring furs because autumn has come and a cold wind blows from Khwarazm, and plays on words of similar sound. His text with a translation and notes was published in Paris in 1886 by A. de Biberstein Kazimirski. From 1939 the British modernist poet Basil Bunting published adaptations of several of his poems, and something of their sound-patterning seems to have passed into Bunting's own verse.
manuel-amador-guerrero: Manuel Amador Guerrero was born on 30 June 1833 at Turbaco, in the Bolívar Department of Colombia, to María Mercedes Guerrero Córdoba and José María Amador Leguina. Little is known of his youth. He trained as a surgeon and graduated in 1854, and the next year he came to Panama, settling at Colón, where he worked as a doctor for the Panama Railroad and held a post as postmaster. He later moved to Santiago de Veraguas and ran an export business, Amador Hermanos, with his brother Juan de Dios while continuing as a doctor and holding local office. He served as a deputy in Bogotá from 1858 to 1859.

In 1866 the Conservative Party named him its first successor for the presidency of the Sovereign State of Panama. When General Fernando Ponce staged a rebellion, Amador was captured and sent into exile at Cartagena. He returned in 1869, moved to Panama City and spent years managing the Hospital Santo Tomás, a charity hospital, largely without pay. He was the last President of the Sovereign State of Panama, from 5 June to 5 August 1886. When the French canal company went bankrupt at the end of 1888, his brothers’ business failed too, and he covered its losses.

In 1903 the Colombian congress was to consider the Hay–Herrán Treaty on the canal. Amador joined a group led by José Agustín Arango that planned Panama’s independence and became the movement’s leader. In September 1903 he travelled to New York to learn how the United States might help. When Colombian troops landed at Colón in early November, his wife María de la Ossa proposed separating the Colombian generals from their troops with the help of railway officials, and the plan succeeded. Independence was proclaimed, and Amador and Federico Boyd went to Washington, where they found Philippe-Jean Bunau-Varilla had already signed a canal treaty.

On 20 February 1904 the constitutional convention unanimously elected Amador the first president of Panama, with a clause added to let him serve although he was not native-born. His administration established the gold balboa as currency at par with the United States gold dollar, adopted the flag and the national anthem, founded the national theatre and museum, disbanded the army in favour of a police force and expanded education. With Secretary of War William Howard Taft and Minister Charles Edward Magoon he settled a dispute over the canal zone in the Taft Memorandum of November 1904. He did not seek re-election in 1908 and died at Panama City on 2 May 1909.
manuel-azana: Manuel Azaña Díaz was born on 10 January 1880 into a wealthy family and was orphaned young. He took a doctorate at the Universidad Complutense in 1900, worked from 1909 in the Directorate of the Registries and practised as a civil law notary. He joined the Reformist Republican Party in 1914, wrote for newspapers and was secretary of the Ateneo de Madrid from 1913 to 1920. He published a manifesto against the dictator Primo de Rivera and Alfonso XIII in 1924, and in 1930 signed the Pact of San Sebastián, which united the republican and regionalist parties.

After the Second Republic was proclaimed on 14 April 1931 Azaña became Minister of War and then, in October, prime minister, leading a coalition of left-wing parties and the Socialists. His government expanded public education, passed labour laws, reduced the size of the army and abolished Church-operated schools and charities. An agrarian law, passed late in 1932, was little carried out: only 12,000 families received land in the first two years. Alcalá-Zamora ordered his resignation on 8 September 1933, and the right won the election that November.

Azaña founded the Republican Left in 1934 and helped build the Popular Front, which won the election of 16 February 1936. He became prime minister again on 19 February and was elected President of the Republic on 7 April 1936. On 17 July a military rising began the Spanish Civil War. From October 1936 he never lived in Madrid again, and on 5 February 1939 he crossed into France on foot.

Azaña resigned as president on 3 March 1939 rather than return to Madrid, a decision that Nationalist and Republican commentators alike condemned as desertion. After the German invasion of France the Mexican government gave him citizenship and the rank of honorary ambassador, so that he could not be arrested. He died at Montauban on 3 November 1940, and the flag of Mexico covered his coffin. His diaries are a main source for the Republican government in the war, and his speech of 18 July 1938 asked for peace, pity and pardon. Piers Brendon calls him a brilliant speaker but a clumsy actor in politics, and he has become a hero of the left in Spain.
manuel-belgrano: Manuel Belgrano was born in Buenos Aires on 3 June 1770, the fourth child of the Italian merchant Domingo Belgrano y Peri. As a criollo he ranked below the peninsulares. He studied at the San Carlos school, then in Spain, where he chose law rather than commerce. A papal dispensation let him read forbidden authors such as Montesquieu and Rousseau. He returned in 1794 as perpetual secretary of the Commerce Consulate of Buenos Aires and held the post until 1810. Unable to change the economic system, he put his effort into education, advocating schools of agriculture and commerce and free primary schools for poor children.

Belgrano first took part in fighting during the first British invasion of the River Plate, when his untrained men scattered after a single cannon shot. After Ferdinand VII was deposed, he led the Carlotist movement, which sought to put the king's sister Carlota Joaquina, then in Rio de Janeiro, in his place.

He took part in the plot against the viceroy Baltasar Hidalgo de Cisneros in May 1810 and was elected to the Primera Junta. As the junta's delegate he led the campaign to Paraguay, where Bernardo de Velasco beat him at Paraguarí and Tacuarí.

He designed the flag while fortifying Rosario. The First Triumvirate did not approve it, and Belgrano learned this only weeks later, at Jujuy. Facing royalist armies from Upper Peru, he ordered the Jujuy Exodus, which moved the province's whole population to San Miguel de Tucumán. His counter-offensive won the Battle of Tucumán and then a full victory over Pío Tristán at Salta.

Defeats at Vilcapugio and Ayohuma ended his incursion into Upper Peru, and José de San Martín replaced him. Belgrano then went to Europe with Bernardino Rivadavia to seek support, and on his return took part in the Congress of Tucumán, which declared independence in 1816. He backed the Inca plan for a constitutional monarchy under an Inca descendant, which delegates from Buenos Aires strongly rejected.

Belgrano took command of the Army of the North again, but his troops mutinied in January 1820. Gravely ill, he was briefly imprisoned in Tucumán during a coup and was released when it ended. He died of dropsy on 20 June 1820, reportedly saying, Oh, my homeland. His flag was approved by the Congress of Tucumán as the national flag. Argentines regard him as one of the main Founding Fathers, and National Flag Day is held on 20 June in memory of his death.

A bronze equestrian statue stands in the Plaza de Mayo, and a mausoleum by Ettore Ximenes, completed in 1903, holds his ashes at the Santo Domingo Convent. He remained a monarchist, favouring a constitutional monarchy on the British pattern, and he translated George Washington's Farewell Address into Spanish.
manuel-bulnes: Manuel Bulnes Prieto was born in Concepción on 25 December 1799. At the age of 16 the Spanish authorities imprisoned him as a revolutionary, but he was soon released, and in 1818 he joined the army of San Martín, under whom he served as colonel throughout the Chilean War of Independence. Three years of continuous warfare 1820–23 ended in the temporary conquest of the Araucanian Indians. He became brigadier general in 1831, and in 1832 he crossed the Cordillera and decisively defeated the Pincheira brothers at the battle of Epulafquén.

In 1838 Bulnes commanded the Chilean army against General Santa Cruz in Peru. After taking Lima and winning the battles of Huaraz and Puente del Buin, he combined his forces with those of Gamarra and defeated Santa Cruz at the Battle of Yungay on 19 January 1839. This ended the confederation between Peru and Bolivia.

Bulnes was President of Chile from 1841 to 1851. His presidencies were marked by educational and cultural expansion, supported by encouraging foreign intellectuals to come to Chile. The National Institute was reformed, several junior schools were established, and the University of Chile was founded in Santiago in 1842, together with a technical training school from which the University of Santiago descends. He presided over a general amnesty to reconcile the groups that had opposed one another in the Civil War of 1829.

In 1843 he founded Fuerte Bulnes to establish sovereignty over the Straits of Magellan; the settlement was moved six years later to Punta Arenas. Germans were targeted to colonise the sparsely inhabited south. During his presidency Spain recognised Chile's independence, and Chile's first railway was built. Bulnes died in Santiago on 18 October 1866.
manuel-chrysoloras: Manuel Chrysoloras was born in Constantinople into a distinguished Greek Orthodox family. In 1390 he led an embassy from the Byzantine emperor Manuel II Palaiologos to the Republic of Venice, asking the aid of the Christian princes of Europe against the invasions of the Ottoman Turks. In Venice he met Roberto de' Rossi of Florence, and in 1395 Rossi's acquaintance Jacopo d'Angelo went to Constantinople to study Greek with him. In 1396 Coluccio Salutati, the Chancellor of Florence, invited him to Florence to teach Greek grammar and literature.

Chrysoloras arrived in the winter of 1397. Leonardo Bruni, one of his most well-known pupils, remembered it as a great opportunity: there were many teachers of law, but no one in northern Italy had studied Greek for 700 years. He taught in Florence from 1397 to 1400, beginning with the rudiments, and then in Bologna, Venice and Rome. A close-knit group of chosen students became among the first humanists of the Renaissance, including Bruni, d'Angelo, Ambrogio Traversari, Guarino da Verona, Niccolò de' Niccoli, Carlo Marsuppini, Pier Paolo Vergerio, Uberto Decembrio and Palla Strozzi.

He later visited Milan and Pavia, lived for several years in Venice, and went to Rome at the invitation of Bruni, then secretary to Pope Gregory XII. In 1408 he went to Paris on a mission for Manuel II, and in 1413 to Germany to the Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund, to fix a place for the church council that later met at Constance. He was chosen to represent the Greek Church there when he died suddenly on 15 April 1415. Guarino da Verona gathered the commemorative essays his death prompted in the Chrysolorina.

Chrysoloras translated Homer, Aristotle and Plato's Republic into Latin. His Erotemata, or Questions, was the first basic Greek grammar in use in Western Europe; it was first published in 1484 and widely reprinted, and Thomas Linacre at Oxford and Desiderius Erasmus at Cambridge studied it at once. His Three Letters on the Comparison of Old and New Rome compared Rome and Constantinople. He was chiefly influential through his teaching, which made men such as Bruni, Salutati and Guarino familiar with the masterpieces of ancient Greek literature and philosophy.
manuel-da-nobrega: Nóbrega was born on 18 October 1517 in Sanfins do Douro, in Trás-os-Montes e Alto Douro, the son of Baltasar da Nóbrega, a prominent judge. He studied humanities at Porto and Salamanca and took his baccalaureate in canon law and philosophy at the University of Coimbra in 1541. He entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1544 and, after ordination, did pastoral work in Entre-Douro-e-Minho and Beira.

Nóbrega arrived in Bahia on 29 March 1549 with five other Jesuits, sent at the request of King John III of Portugal. His defence of the Indians against settlers who mistreated and enslaved them brought clashes with the colonists and with the first two governors-general, and he asked for a bishopric to strengthen his hand; Pero Fernandes Sardinha, the first Bishop of Brazil, took office on 22 June 1552. Nóbrega founded the Jesuit College of Salvador and was the first Provincial of the Society of Jesus in the New World until 1559. By his own report, 500 natives were baptised in the first five months.

Finding adults hard to convert, he turned to teaching children Portuguese, Latin, reading and religion, and he was among the first in Brazil to use music in education. He brought seven orphan children to Brazil to learn Tupi and act as translators. Unable to limit slavery among the settlers, he moved toward separating the natives from the Portuguese in mission villages. When the Tamoio Confederation rose against the colonists, he and José de Anchieta stayed at Iperoig under threat of death until a temporary peace was reached, Anchieta's command of Tupi making up for Nóbrega's lack of it.

After the French settlement at Guanabara Bay drew Indian allies against the Portuguese, Nóbrega supported the punitive expeditions of Mem de Sá in 1560 and Estácio de Sá in 1565. He then founded the College of Saint Vincent in Rio de Janeiro and became its rector. Named Provincial again in 1570, he died before taking office, on his 53rd birthday, 18 October 1570. He wrote the Dialogues on the Conversion of the Gentile (1554) and letters from Brazil.
manuel-de-amat-y-junyent: Amat was born in Vacarisses, in the Province of Barcelona, into an aristocratic Catalan family; his father was José de Amat y de Planella, 1st Marquess of Castellbell. He entered the army young, fought the French in Aragon in 1719, and at 17 joined the Order of Malta and spent four years on the island. After service in northern Africa he commanded a regiment of dragoons, distinguished himself at the Battle of Bitonto on 25 May 1734 and at the siege of Gaeta later that year, and rose to field marshal.

Sent to Chile in 1755 as Royal Governor and president of the Audiencia Real, he built fortifications on the coast and along the frontier with the Mapuche people, founded towns such as Talcamávida, Hualqui and Nacimiento, and negotiated with the Mapuche at Salto del Laja in 1758 and at Santiago de Chile in 1760. In Santiago he improved the bridges over the Río Mapocho, reformed the Royal University of San Felipe and on 12 October 1758 founded Chile's first police force, the Dragones de la Reina.

As Viceroy of Peru, succeeding José Manso de Velasco, he expelled the Jesuit missionaries in September 1767 on the Crown's orders and issued the first Regulation of Commerce, which led to the customshouse in Callao. He built the fortress of Real Felipe in Callao, finished in 1774, founded the Royal College of San Carlos and gave Lima the Alameda de los Descalzos, the Paseo de Aguas and the Plaza de Toros de Acho, opened in 1762. To keep foreign bases away from Peru he sent Domingo de Bonechea to Tahiti and the islands round it.

Tradition holds that the Paseo de Aguas was built for his mistress, the actress Micaela Villegas, La Perricholi, whose story inspired Prosper Mérimée's Le Carrosse du Saint-Sacrement, Jacques Offenbach's La Périchole and Thornton Wilder's The Bridge of San Luis Rey. Amat returned to Barcelona on 22 October 1777, to the Virreina Palace he had built on La Rambla, married María Francisca de Fivaller y de Bru in June 1779 and died there on 14 February 1782, with no legitimate children.
manuel-enrique-araujo: Manuel Enrique Araujo Rodríguez was born on 12 October 1865 at Hacienda Condadillo, Estanzuelas, in the department of Usulután, the youngest of eight children of a Basque father and a Portuguese mother. He studied at the University of El Salvador and then in Paris and Vienna, and practised as a surgeon in the 1890s and 1900s. In 1887 he married María Hortensia Peralta Lagos, daughter of the former acting president José María Peralta. In 1907 he was elected vice president under Fernando Figueroa with 95.47 percent of the vote, and both took office on 1 March 1907.

Chosen by Figueroa as his successor, Araujo won the 1911 election with 182,964 votes; the historian Alastair White remarked that opponents were allowed to take part but not to win. He took office on 1 March 1911, the first civilian president since Rafael Zaldívar was deposed in 1885. Fearing a coup backed by the Guatemalan president Manuel Estrada Cabrera, he cultivated popular support, visiting schools, prisons and hospitals. His Work Accidents Law made the state and employers share compensation for disabled workers, though not rural labourers; he also allowed the direct taxation of property and abolished imprisonment for debt. He began the National Theater in San Salvador.

In June 1912 he created the National Guard, modelled on the Spanish Civil Guard, and rural patrols of retired conscripts. His government used both to repress peasants who criticised it and to defend allied landowners; the Guard remained an instrument of repression until it was abolished in 1992. Araujo denounced the United States' military intervention in Nicaragua as a great scandal and, when President William Howard Taft protested, replied that he obeyed no one's orders.

On 4 February 1913, sitting without an escort in Bolívar Park, he was attacked by three men with machetes and a revolver. He died on 9 February after his wounds became infected. Three farmers were shot on 19 February; the man they named, Major Fernando Carmona, killed himself in prison. The former vice president Prudencio Alfaro was executed in 1915 for an alleged role, and White judged that Araujo was probably killed on Alfaro's orders. Some 15,000 people attended his funeral. He remains the only Salvadoran president assassinated in office.
manuel-esquivel: Manuel Amadeo Esquivel was born on 2 May 1940 in Belize City, then the capital of the British Crown Colony of British Honduras. He attended St John's College, took a degree in physics at Loyola University New Orleans and a postgraduate certificate in physics education at Bristol University in England. In Bristol he met Kathleen Levy, whom he married in 1971; they had three children.

After the 1969 election he became head of the pro-business Liberal Party, which merged with two other parties in 1973 to form the United Democratic Party (UDP). He served two terms on the Belize City Council and was UDP chairman from 1976 to 1982. In 1979 he lost the Freetown constituency to the Premier, George Cadle Price, and was then appointed to the Senate. In January 1983 he defeated Philip Goldson for the party leadership, the only senator ever elected leader of a major Belizean party.

In December 1984 he won the new Caribbean Shores seat in Belize City and became prime minister, the first time an opposition party had won since universal suffrage was introduced in 1954. He moved the economy away from Price's mixed model, encouraging foreign direct investment and tourism. In his second term he imposed austerity, suspending public pay rises from 1995 to 1997, and introduced a 15% value-added tax in 1995, for which the opposition called him VATMAN. He lost his seat to Jose Coye in 1998.

After the UDP returned to power in 2008, Prime Minister Dean Barrow made him senior adviser with the rank of minister, and in 2011 he became Chairman of the Central Bank of Belize, stepping down in 2013 and leaving the Cabinet in 2014. He was appointed to the Privy Council of the United Kingdom in 1986 and a Knight Commander of the Order of St Michael and St George in 2010. He died on 10 February 2022, aged 81. An overpass in Belize City and the coastal road between Belize District and Stann Creek District bear his name.
manuel-estrada-cabrera: Manuel José Estrada Cabrera was born on 21 November 1857. He studied at the Universidad Nacional and practised as a lawyer, with no military background. Under President José María Reina Barrios he was Secretary of the Interior for most of the regime and became First Designated for the Presidency, the first in line of succession, when Reina Barrios began his second term.

After Reina Barrios was assassinated on 8 February 1898, the cabinet met to choose a successor without inviting Estrada Cabrera. Two versions survive of how he took office: in one he entered the meeting with pistol drawn, in the other he simply demanded the post as First Designated. He then held power through controlled elections in 1904, 1910 and 1916, becoming the longest-serving leader of Guatemala.

To finish the railway from Puerto Barrios to Guatemala City, which had stalled sixty miles short, he signed a contract in 1904 with Minor Cooper Keith of the United Fruit Company, without consulting the legislature or judiciary, granting tax exemptions, land and control of the Atlantic railways. The line was completed in 1908. His rule relied on surveillance and repression, including armed strike-breaking. A bomb was set off on his route on 29 April 1907, and in 1908 cadets planned to seize him from a Good Friday procession, a plot his spies uncovered.

Opposition grew after the earthquakes of 1917 and 1918, when he proved unable to lead the recovery. In 1919 the Catholic Church turned against him for the first time, and conservative leaders formed a Unionist party backed by students and labour associations. Deposed and declared mentally incompetent, he was jailed for corruption and sentenced to prison for life. He died in 1924 and was buried in Quetzaltenango. He is also remembered for the Fiestas Minervalias, festivals for students held from 1899 in Temples of Minerva in the Hellenic style, built in all the major cities.
manuel-gamio: Gamio was born in Mexico City and studied engineering at the School of Mining. At 19 he left his studies to work on a family rubber plantation where the states of Oaxaca, Veracruz and Puebla meet; there he learned Nahuatl from the workers and took a lasting interest in Mexico's indigenous cultures. He studied archaeology, ethnology and anthropology under Nicolás León and Jesús Galindo y Villa, and Zélia Nuttall sent him in 1909 to Columbia University, where he earned a Ph.D. under Franz Boas, who counted him among his best students.

He was the first scientific investigator to explore Teotihuacan, and estimated its maximum population at 300,000. He criticised the Mexican census for classing Spanish-speaking Indians as whites and those married by traditional rites as single. In the 1920s he studied pottery styles in the highlands of Guatemala near Quiche, Huehuetenango and Quetzaltenango; from their likeness to central Mexican pottery he held central Mexico to be the original source of Maya civilisation.

In 1925, after denouncing corruption in the Mexican Ministry of Education, he moved to the United States and studied Mexican migration and labour for the Social Science Research Council in Washington, D.C. He returned to Mexico in 1930, held government posts, carried out applied anthropological research, and directed the Inter-American Indian Institute from its foundation in 1942 until his death in 1960.

In Forjando patria: pro nacionalismo (1916) Gamio argued for the cultural assimilation of indigenous Mexicans into the country's racially mixed society, a cause he shared with many, among them President Lázaro Cárdenas in the 1930s. Although he rejected full sovereignty for indigenous communities, he held that their own institutions, such as tribal governments, municipal bodies and elected leaders, should be recognised and respected. Later books include Hacia un México nuevo (1935) and Consideraciones sobre el problema del indigenismo (1948).

His studies of Mexicans in the United States appeared in English as Mexican Immigration to the United States (1930) and The Mexican Immigrant: His Life Story (1931), and were translated into Spanish only much later. He also made documentary films.
manuel-gomes-da-costa: Manuel de Oliveira Gomes da Costa was born on 14 January 1863, the son of Carlos Dias da Costa and Madalena de Oliveira, and grew up with two younger sisters. He entered the Colégio Militar at the age of ten. From 1893 to 1915 he had a distinguished career in Portugal’s colonies, serving in India, Mozambique, Angola and São Tomé under Mouzinho de Albuquerque. Portugal entered the First World War on the Allied side in early 1917, and he commanded a division of the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps. At the Battle of the Lys on 9 April 1918 the corps lost 400 dead and about 6,500 prisoners, a third of its front-line forces, and his division was hit particularly hard.

For his command he was made a general and a Grand Officer of the Military Order of Avis, and he received its Grand Cross on 5 October 1921. After the war he became active in politics, in staunch opposition to the dominant Democratic Party. A convinced monarchist, he had dealings with people of many political convictions, and with his reputation as a soldier this led right-wing conspirators to choose him to lead the coup of 28 May 1926, launched at Braga, after General Alves Roçadas, their first choice, fell fatally ill. The coup overthrew the First Portuguese Republic.

After the coup Gomes da Costa did not at first take power. He left the posts of President of the Republic and President of the Council of Ministers to José Mendes Cabeçadas, the leader of the revolution in Lisbon. The coup leaders soon disliked Mendes Cabeçadas, a choice of the former president Bernardino Machado and still sympathetic to the old republic, and Gomes da Costa replaced him in both posts at a meeting at Sacavém on 17 June 1926. His government was the first to include António de Oliveira Salazar, later prime minister and dictator, as finance minister.

On 9 July a new coup, begun by João José Sinel de Cordes and Óscar Carmona, overthrew him after he tried to remove Carmona as foreign minister. He had no wish to set up a long military regime, which set him against the most authoritarian officers. Carmona took over on the pretext that he was unfit for office. Gomes da Costa was exiled to the Azores but also promoted to Marshal, and he later returned to mainland Portugal, already very ill.
manuel-gonzalez-flores: Manuel González Flores was born at Matamoros, Tamaulipas, on 17 June 1833, though some sources give 20 June. He began his military career in 1847, fighting the United States invaders in the Mexican-American War after they killed his father. From 1853 to 1855 he fought with the Conservative forces and in 1859 took part in Miguel Miramón's attack on Veracruz against Benito Juárez's government. In 1860 he took an amnesty and offered his services to the Liberals.

He fought under Porfirio Díaz against the French, was wounded and captured at the Battle of Puebla on 5 May 1862 but escaped, and lost his right arm at the siege of Puebla in 1867. He supported Díaz in the revolt of the Plan de la Noria and in the successful revolt of the Plan of Tuxtepec in 1876, and became general of division in 1877.

Díaz could not seek re-election in 1880, since his coup against Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada rested on the principle of no re-election, and he promoted González, who had been his secretary of war from 1878 to 1879. González was announced as winner on 24 September 1880 with 11,528 votes and served from 1 December 1880 to 30 November 1884. He continued Díaz's policy of order and progress and of foreign investment. A mining code in 1884 gave landowners rights to the subsoil, and a land law let the government sell vacant lands. He raised military spending by 400 percent, built a loyal rural police, and resolved a dispute with Guatemala over Chiapas and Soconusco in Mexico's favour.

Relations with Britain, France and Germany were renewed after Mexico recognised a British bond debt of 11.5 million pounds, which brought protests in Congress and riots in the capital that were put down forcefully. The Banco Nacional de México was founded, the railway from Mexico City to Paso del Norte was built, and Mexico's first submarine cable opened. Nickel coins issued in 1882 brought inflation and riots on 21 December 1883.

Díaz succeeded him in 1884. Congress charged González with misappropriating public funds in 1885, but the charges were dropped on 30 October 1888. He was elected governor of Guanajuato unanimously in 1884, served three terms, and died of pancreatic cancer on 8 May 1893. The presidency has been judged corrupt, but that view is coloured by the financial difficulties of 1884 and by Díaz's campaign to discredit his successor, according to the account of his presidency. His biographer Don M. Coerver wrote the one full scholarly study of it.
manuel-i-komnenos: Manuel was born on 28 November 1118 in the Purple Chamber of the Great Palace of Constantinople, and was therefore called Porphyrogenitus, born in the purple. He was the eighth child and fourth son of the emperor John II Komnenos and Irene of Hungary. He was trained as a soldier and accompanied his father on campaigns against the Anatolian Turks. In 1143 John lay dying from a hunting accident and chose Manuel over his elder surviving brother Isaac, citing Manuel's courage and readiness to take advice. After John died on 8 April 1143 the armies acclaimed Manuel, and he was crowned in Constantinople in mid-August 1143 after John Axouch had arrested Isaac.

Manuel pursued an energetic foreign policy meant to restore the empire as the great power of the Mediterranean. In 1146 he led a punitive expedition against Masud, Sultan of Rûm. In 1147 the Second Crusade crossed his lands, with clashes between Byzantines and Germans, and Roger II of Sicily captured Corfu. Manuel allied with Conrad III of Germany and the Venetians and recovered Corfu in 1149. After Conrad died in 1152 no agreement could be reached with Frederick Barbarossa, and Manuel turned to the Papacy, the Normans, Hungary and the crusader states.

In 1167 an army under Andronikos Kontostephanos won a decisive victory at Sirmium, and the peace that followed gave the empire Syrmia, Bosnia and Dalmatia, so that by 1168 nearly the whole eastern Adriatic coast was in his hands. He established a protectorate over the crusader states, and in autumn 1169 sent a large fleet and army to join King Amalric I of Jerusalem in an invasion of Egypt.

Manuel's last years were marked by the defeat at Myriokephalon, which resulted largely from his attacking a well-defended Seljuk position. He then made an advantageous peace with Kilij Arslan II, but Myriokephalon proved the empire's last unsuccessful effort to recover the interior of Anatolia. He died on 24 September 1180, and his son Alexios II Komnenos succeeded him.

His secretary John Kinnamos wrote a history that credits him with every virtue. Niketas Choniates criticised him for raising taxes and spending lavishly, some of it on failed expeditions. Some historians hold that the power he wielded belonged to the Komnenos dynasty rather than to him, and others look to his reign for the causes of the empire's steep decline after his death.
manuel-i-of-portugal: Manuel was born at Alcochete on 31 May 1469, the ninth child of Ferdinand, Duke of Viseu, and Beatriz of Portugal. He grew up amid strife between the noble families and King John II: in 1483 Fernando II, Duke of Braganza, was executed for treason, and in 1484 Manuel's older brother Diogo, accused of a conspiracy, was stabbed to death by the king himself. After the death of his son Prince Afonso, John II named his cousin Manuel heir, and Manuel succeeded him in 1495.

Manuel supported Atlantic exploration and commerce. Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498, Pedro Álvares Cabral voyaged to Brazil in 1500, and Francisco de Almeida became the first viceroy of India in 1505. Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa in 1510, Malacca in 1511 and Ormus in 1515, and in Morocco the Portuguese took Safi in 1508 and Azamor in 1513. Manuel founded the Casa da Índia to manage the monopolies, and the trade made him the wealthiest monarch in Europe. Royal absolutism was the method of government, and the Cortes met only four times.

His religious policy was harsh. In 1496, while seeking to marry Isabella of Aragon, he yielded to pressure from her parents and decreed that Jews who refused baptism must leave; then, before the deadline, he converted all Jews by royal decree. In the Lisbon massacre of 1506 thousands of accused Jews were murdered, and Manuel executed the leaders of the riot. He also ordered the expulsion of Muslims from Portugal.

Manuel married three times, each time to a member of the Spanish royal family: Isabella, who died in childbirth in 1498, then her sister Maria, and finally Eleanor of Austria. He died on 13 December 1521, aged 52, after a fever, while Lisbon suffered an outbreak of plague, and was succeeded by his son John III. His remains were moved to the Jerónimos Monastery in 1551. He financed the Monastery of Jerónimos and patronised the playwright Gil Vicente, and the Manueline style of architecture is named for him.
manuel-ii-of-portugal: Manuel was born on 15 November 1889 in the Palace of Belém, Lisbon, the third child and second son of Carlos I and Amélie of Orléans. Before ascending the throne he held the title Duke of Beja. He received the traditional education of a royal family member, without the political preparation of his elder brother, who was expected to be king. He studied history and languages, learning English and French early, loved literature and music, especially Beethoven and Wagner, and played the piano. He entered the naval school in 1907.

On 1 February 1908 the royal family was returning to Lisbon when shots were fired in the Terreiro do Paço by two republican activists, Alfredo Luis da Costa and Manuel Buiça, who were shot dead by the royal bodyguard. King Carlos was killed, Prince Luís Filipe was mortally wounded and Manuel was hit in the arm. Days later, aged eighteen, he was proclaimed king. He asked João Franco to resign and appointed a government of national unity. Judging that his father's interference in politics had contributed to the events, he declared that he would reign but not govern. In 1909 he invited the French sociologist Léon Poinsard to study the social question.

Political stability deteriorated, and seven governments rose and fell in 24 months while the Republican Party gained ground. In elections on 28 August 1910 the republicans won only 14 seats, but the Setúbal Congress of April 1909 had already decided that they would take power by force. The murder of a prominent republican precipitated the coup that ended nearly 800 years of monarchy in 1910.

Manuel and his family fled into exile in the UK, and he lived at Fulwell Park in Twickenham. Attempts to restore him in 1911, 1912 and 1919 failed. He married Augusta Victoria of Hohenzollern on 4 September 1913. He defended Portugal's entry into the First World War. In exile he built a considerable library of Portuguese books and wrote on medieval and Renaissance literature. He died unexpectedly on 2 July 1932 at Twickenham, of suffocation from swelling of the glottis. The Portuguese government authorised a state funeral in Lisbon, and he was buried at the Monastery of São Vicente de Fora.
manuel-ii-palaiologos: Manuel was born on 27 June 1350, the second son of Emperor John V Palaiologos and Helena Kantakouzene. His father gave him the title of despotes, and he travelled west to seek support for the empire in 1365 and 1370, serving as governor in Thessalonica from 1369. After his older brother Andronikos IV attempted a usurpation in 1373, Manuel was proclaimed his father's heir and emperor on 25 September 1373.

Andronikos and then his son John VII displaced Manuel and his father in 1376 to 1379 and again in 1390, but Manuel defeated his nephew in 1390 with help from Venice and the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I. Bayezid then kept him at Prousa as an honorary hostage and made him join the campaign that took Philadelpheia, the last Byzantine enclave in Anatolia.

On hearing in February 1391 of his father's death, Manuel fled the Ottoman court and secured Constantinople against John VII. In 1392 he was married and crowned with Helena Dragaš, daughter of the fellow Ottoman vassal Constantine Dragaš. Bayezid blockaded Constantinople from 1394 to 1402. He wrote to Charles VI of France, who sent Marshal Jean II Le Maingre with six ships and 1,200 men.

After some five years of siege, Manuel left his nephew John VII in charge of the city with a French garrison and sailed on 10 December 1399. He reached Venice in April 1400, met Gian Galeazzo Visconti in Milan and Charles VI at Charenton on 3 June 1400. In December he travelled to England, where Henry IV received him at Blackheath on 21 December, and he stayed at Eltham Palace until mid-February 1401, making him the only Byzantine emperor to visit England.

The defeat of Bayezid by Timur at the Battle of Ankara in 1402 relieved the pressure. In the Treaty of Gallipoli, John VII recovered the European shore of the Sea of Marmara and Thessalonica, and later returned the capital to Manuel.

A stroke paralysed him on 1 October 1422, though his mind was unaffected. He became a monk with the name Matthew and died on 21 July 1425, aged 75, and was buried at the Pantokrator Monastery. His sons John VIII and Constantine XI became emperors.
manuel-iii-of-trebizond: Manuel Megas Komnenos was born on 16 December 1364, the son of Emperor Alexios III of Trebizond and Theodora Kantakouzene, and became heir after the death of his elder brother Basil in 1377. That year he married Gulkhan-Eudokia of Georgia, a daughter of King David IX of Georgia and the widow of his half-brother Andronikos; their sons included Alexios and Theodore. In 1395 he married Anna Philanthropene of the Byzantine Doukas family. He became emperor on 20 March 1390.

In 1398 Sultan Bayezid I led an army along the Black Sea coast to Trebizond's border. Timur returned to Anatolia and took Sivas on 27 August 1400, killing all its defenders. Manuel avoided Timur's demand that he and his army join the war on the Ottomans, though he sent twenty galleys. After Ankara, Timur plundered Ottoman lands for eight months, and the Ottomans were not a threat again until 1413. On leaving in 1403, part of his army ravaged the country around Kerasous, and Timur put his nephew Mirza Halil in charge of Armenia, Trebizond and Georgia.

Ruy Gonzáles de Clavijo, passing through in April 1404 on his embassy to Timur, described Manuel and his son in tall hats crowned with cranes' feathers and wrote that the emperor paid tribute to Timur and to other Turks. Manuel renewed Venice's privileges in 1391 and in 1396 granted the Venetians a church, bank and law court of their own, while his quarrels with Genoa over its castle at Trebizond grew serious by 1416.

His last years were troubled by his son Alexios IV. When nobles angered by the favour shown to a page of humble birth rose with Alexios and besieged Manuel in the upper citadel, he banished the favourite, and father and son were reconciled. Manuel died on 5 March 1417; George Finlay records the rumour that Alexios was suspected of hastening his death. In the year of his accession he had given the Soumela Monastery a reliquary cross believed to hold a piece of the cross on which Jesus was crucified.
manuel-jose-arce: Manuel José Arce y Fagoaga was born on 1 January 1787 in the Intendancy of San Salvador, son of the Spaniard Bernardo José de Arce, its colonial intendant in 1800 and 1801, and Antonia Fagoaga. Sent to Guatemala in 1801, he graduated in philosophy from the Colegio de San Francisco Borja and began medicine at the Universidad de San Carlos de Borromeo, but broke off when his father fell ill.
