In December 1808 he married Felipa de Aranzamendi y Aguiar in San Salvador.

Arce joined the first Cry for Independence in San Salvador on 5 November 1811, led by his uncle José Matías Delgado, the vicar of San Salvador; the rebels held the government for nearly a month. His part in the second rising of 22 January 1814 cost him four years in prison. He opposed the Mexican Empire of Agustín de Iturbide, and as a colonel he was one of the commanders of San Salvador when Manuel Arzú's Guatemalan troops, fighting for Mexico, entered the city on 3 June 1822 after nine hours of fighting. On a journey back from the United States in 1823 he tried in Mexico to raise a force to free Cuba from Spain, without success.

Elected in October 1823 to the executive triumvirate of Central America, he served from 15 March to 20 October 1824, when the government pacified Nicaragua with little violence. In the 1825 elections José Cecilio del Valle won the most votes, but the Liberal Congress ruled that he lacked an absolute majority and chose Arce, who served from 29 April 1825 to 13 April 1829.

He soon lost the support of the Liberals in Congress and leaned on the clergy and the Conservative Party. His removal of the Liberal Guatemalan governor Juan Barrundia led the Salvadoran state to rebel. When he tried to resume the presidency from Vice President Mariano Beltranena y Llano, Beltranena refused and held office until liberal troops took Guatemala City in April 1829.

In 1832 Arce led an expedition from Soconusco against the federal government of Francisco Morazán and was defeated on 24 February 1832. Back in El Salvador in 1842, he soon fled again, and in 1844 he led armed attempts against Francisco Malespín. He left politics in 1846 to write a book on the reorganisation of Central America, and died in poverty in San Salvador on 14 December 1847. His remains were moved to the Military Museum of the Armed Forces of El Salvador in 2003, and the town of El Chilamatal was renamed Ciudad Arce in 1947.
manuel-kantakouzenos: Manuel was the second son of John VI Kantakouzenos and Irene Asanina; the historian Donald Nicol places his birth around 1326 or slightly later. He is first mentioned in March 1342, when he and his brother Matthew Kantakouzenos accompanied their father from Didymoteichos towards Thessalonica as officers in the civil war. In April of the next year his father took Veria with the help of Stephen Dushan and made Manuel its governor, but Dushan seized the city from him in 1347, and he took refuge with his uncle John Angelos in Thessaly.

Once his father held Constantinople in May 1347, Manuel was called to the city, and in 1348 he was entrusted with its government. As its kephalatikeuontes, or headsman, he led its defence against the Genoese in the war of 1348 and 1349. When that war ended he was sent to govern the Morea, arriving on 25 October 1349. He was the first of a line of long-ruling governors there who bore the title despotēs and were close kin of the emperors.

Manuel crushed the opposition of the local notables, the archontes, and was strong enough that when John V Palaiologos forced his father to abdicate, he resisted being replaced and was in time recognised by the new regime. His family, including his brother Matthew, joined him in the province.

He kept peace with his Latin neighbours for most of his rule and, according to the Aragonese Chronicle of the Morea, joined Gautier de Lor, the Venetians and the Hospitallers in a naval victory off Megara that burned 35 Turkish ships. In the mid-1370s an army of 1000 knights and 2000 infantry he led against Francesco Sansverino, bailli of Achaea, at Gardiki was crushed. He encouraged Albanians to settle in the depopulated province. He died on 10 April 1380 and was succeeded by Matthew. His wife, Isabelle de Lusignan, had no children by him.
manuel-l-quezon: Manuel Luis Quezon y Molina was born on 19 August 1878 in Baler, then part of Nueva Écija. His parents, Lucio Quezon Urbina and María Dolores Molina, were both primary-school teachers, and his father was also a retired sergeant of the Guardia Civil. He finished secondary school at the Colegio de San Juan de Letrán in 1894. In 1898 his father and his brother Pedro were killed by road bandits on the way to Baler.

In 1907 Quezon was elected to the first Philippine Assembly for the first district of Tayabas. In 1909 he became one of the Philippines' two resident commissioners in Washington, D.C., and until 1916 he lobbied for the Philippine Autonomy Act, the Jones Law. On 16 October 1916 the new legislature elected him Senate President, and he led the Senate for 19 years. He headed the first independent mission to the United States Congress in 1919 and secured the Tydings–McDuffie Act of 1934. His rivalry with Sergio Osmeña split the Nacionalista Party in 1922 and again over the Hare–Hawes–Cutting bill in 1933.

In 1935 he won the first national presidential election with nearly 68 percent of the vote against Emilio Aguinaldo and Gregorio Aglipay, and was inaugurated on 15 November 1935. His government reorganised the executive departments, appointed the first all-Filipino cabinet and set up a national-defense system under the National Defense Act of 1935. Scholars have described his leadership as a de facto dictatorship after he removed his own term limit.

After the Japanese invasion in the Second World War Quezon was inaugurated for his second term on Corregidor, then moved to Australia and the United States, where he established the Commonwealth government in exile in Washington, D.C. He signed the United Nations declaration against the Axis powers and wrote his autobiography, The Good Fight.

Quezon had tuberculosis and died at Saranac Lake, New York, on 1 August 1944, aged 65. He was first buried at Arlington National Cemetery, and his remains were re-interred in Manila in 1946 and moved to the Quezon Memorial Shrine in Quezon City in 1979. Quezon City and Quezon Province are named after him.
manuel-noriega: Manuel Antonio Noriega Moreno was born in Panama City into a poor pardo family, of Native Panamanian, African and Spanish heritage. His date of birth is generally given as 11 February 1934 but is uncertain: it has been recorded as 1934, 1936 and 1938, and Noriega himself gave differing dates. Both his parents were dead by the time he was five. He graduated from the Chorrillos Military School in Lima in 1962 and joined the Panama National Guard, where his commanding officer, the then Major Omar Torrijos, became his patron.

When Torrijos overthrew President Arnulfo Arias in 1968, Noriega was an important supporter. As chief of military intelligence he exiled 1,300 Panamanians seen as threats and kept files on officials that allowed him to blackmail them.

After Torrijos died in 1981, Noriega consolidated power and became Panama's de facto ruler in 1983. He never held the presidency, preferring to rule behind the scenes. Law 20 of 1983 tripled the size of the military. He had worked with United States intelligence agencies since the 1950s and was a conduit for support to the Contra rebels in Nicaragua, while also profiting from drug trafficking that peaked in 1984.

His relations with Washington worsened after the murder of the critic Hugo Spadafora and reports that he sold intelligence to Cuba. In 1988 federal grand juries in Miami and Tampa indicted him on drug and racketeering charges. After he annulled the 1989 election, the United States invaded on 20 December 1989 with more than 27,000 soldiers, its largest military action since the Vietnam War. On the fifth day Noriega took refuge in the embassy of the Holy See.

Tried in Miami, Noriega was convicted in April 1992 on eight of ten charges and sentenced to 40 years, of which he served 17. Panama convicted him in absentia of the murders of Spadafora and of Giroldi, who had led a coup attempt in 1989, and of the massacre of Albrook. France convicted him of laundering 3 million dollars and extradited him to Panama on 11 December 2011. He died on 29 May 2017 after complications in surgery for a brain tumour.
manuel-pavia-y-rodriguez-de-alburquerque: Pavía was born in Cádiz and entered the Royal Artillery College at Segovia in 1841. He became a lieutenant in 1846 and a captain in 1855, fought in the Hispano-Moroccan War of 1859 to 1860 and took part in the European expedition to Mexico in 1862, the year he was made major. In January 1866 he served under General Juan Prim in an unsuccessful mutiny against the regime of Isabella II, and after a second failed rising at the end of that year he and Prim escaped to Portugal.

Pavía returned from exile to work with Prim in the Revolution of 1868, which removed Isabella II, and fought in Navarra at the beginning of the Third Carlist War. Under the First Spanish Republic he and General Arsenio Martínez Campos put down the cantonalist insurrection that had begun at Cartagena on 12 July 1873, taking almost all the cantons between 26 July and 8 August; only Cartagena held out, until 13 January 1874. By the end of 1873 he was captain general of Castilla la Nueva, with his seat in Madrid.

When President Emilio Castelar lost a vote of confidence and the Cortes moved to elect a new government, Pavía, who favoured a united centralist state, ordered its president, Nicolás Salmerón, to vacate the chamber. The deputies stayed in their seats until a crew of the Civil Guard entered and evicted them. Pavía then called the parties, except the Cantonalists and Carlists, to form a government of national concentration, which gave power to General Francisco Serrano. Supporters of parliamentary rule judged the act harshly, and Castelar published a protest the next day, though rumours persisted that he had connived in it.

Pavía commanded the Central Army for some months until he was replaced on 28 September 1874. Under the restored monarchy of Alfonso XII he was captain general of Catalonia from 1880 to 1881 and again of Castilla la Nueva in 1885, and in 1886 he defeated the anti-dynastic rising of Manuel Villacampa in Madrid. In his last years he presided over the Consejo Supremo de Guerra y Marina and wrote military histories. He died on 4 January 1895.
manuel-piar: Piar was the son of Fernando Alonso Piar y Lottyn, a Spanish merchant seaman of Canarian origin, and María Isabel Gómez, a woman of Willemstad in Curaçao whose father was Afro-Venezuelan and whose mother was Dutch. As a quadroon he grew up under the limits that colonial society placed on people of mixed descent. He came to Venezuela with his mother at the age of ten and settled in La Guaira, where, without formal schooling, he taught himself several languages.

At 23 he took part in the unsuccessful Gual and España Conspiracy of 1797. In 1804 he served in the Curaçao militia that expelled the British occupiers and restored Dutch rule, and in 1807 he was in Haiti, commanding a warship in support of the revolution there.

From 1810 Piar served the Venezuelan rising against Spain, first in the navy at Puerto Cabello, where he fought the Spanish fleet in several engagements, among them the Battle of Sorondo on the Orinoco in 1812. After a spell of refuge in Trinidad he returned in 1813 as an army colonel, defended Maturín and helped free the east of the country. As a brigadier general in 1814 he fought in the provinces of Barcelona, Caracas and Cumaná, and lost an engagement to José Tomás Boves near El Salado.

Promoted to major general, he joined Simón Bolívar in the Los Cayos expedition from Haiti. In 1816 he defeated Francisco Tomás Morales at El Juncal and marched into Guayana, where his victory over Miguel de la Torre at San Félix was followed by his promotion to General-in-Chief.

Piar wanted independence and also greater social and political rights for the mestizos, and he was the only senior commander who was not a white criollo. After his victories he came into conflict with Bolívar, who stripped him of direct command; Piar took leave in June 1817 and stayed in Guayana to win support for his views. Other commanders, among them Santiago Mariño and José Francisco Bermúdez, also opposed Bolívar, but Piar alone was arrested, on 28 September 1817, and it is generally agreed that Bolívar meant to make an example of him.

A court martial found him guilty of desertion, insubordination and conspiracy, and on 16 October 1817 he was shot against the wall of the cathedral of Angostura. Bolívar, who did not attend, is said to have heard the shots from his office and said in tears, "He derramado mi sangre" (I have spilled my blood).
manuel-roxas: Manuel Roxas was born on 1 January 1892 in Capiz, now Roxas City, a posthumous child: his father had been mortally wounded by the Spanish Guardia Civil the year before. His mother and her father raised him. He graduated from Manila High School with honours in 1909, took a law degree at the University of the Philippines in 1913 as class valedictorian and topped the bar examinations that year with 92 per cent.

He served on the municipal council of Capiz from 1917 to 1919 and as its provincial governor from 1919 to 1922, the youngest the province had had. Elected to the Philippine House of Representatives in 1922, he was Speaker for twelve consecutive years. He also sat in the Constitutional Convention of 1934, served as secretary of finance and held a commission as a brigadier general in the United States Army Forces in the Far East.

Elected to the Senate in 1941, Roxas could not serve until 1945. After the fall of Corregidor he was captured by Japanese forces and held at Malaybalay and Davao, where the officer Nobuhiko Jimbo failed to persuade him to join the Philippine Executive Commission and later shielded him from an order to execute him. He became chief adviser to the collaborationist government of José P. Laurel and surrendered to American forces at Baguio in April 1945.

In 1946 he left the Nacionalista Party with Elpidio Quirino to form the Liberal Party. With the support of General Douglas MacArthur he won the presidential election on 23 April 1946 with 54 per cent of the vote. He was last president of the Commonwealth from 28 May to 4 July 1946, then first president of the Third Republic when independence was proclaimed before some 300,000 people at Luneta Park. Congress ratified the Treaty of General Relations on 5 August 1946, which recognised independence and reserved bases for the United States. The country faced near bankruptcy after the war. His administration was marred by graft and by the abuses of the provincial military police, which contributed to the rise of the Huk movement.

On 15 April 1948, after a speech to the Thirteenth Air Force at Clark Air Base, Roxas suffered dizziness and fatigue and died that night of multiple heart attacks at the age of 56. Vice President Quirino took the oath as president on 17 April, and Roxas was buried at the Manila North Cemetery.

Several towns were renamed for him, beginning with Roxas, Oriental Mindoro, in 1948, as was Roxas City, Capiz, in 1951. Dewey Boulevard in Metro Manila was renamed in his memory, and he appeared on the 100 peso bill.
manuha: Manuha, called Makuta in Mon, ruled Thaton from the 1030s until his defeat in 1057. Mon tradition makes him the 59th king of a line that supposedly founded Thaton in the time of the Buddha, in the 6th century BCE. In the traditional Burmese and Mon accounts, King Anawrahta of Pagan, a recent convert to Theravada Buddhism, asked him for the Theravada canon, and Manuha refused, saying that the uncultured Burmans of the north were not worthy of the religion; Anawrahta used the refusal as a pretext for invading. Historians think it more likely that Anawrahta conquered Thaton to check the westward advance of the Khmer Empire along the Tenasserim coast.

According to traditional belief, Manuha and his family were taken to Pagan together with some 30,000 monks and artisans, and between 1050 and about 1085 Mon craftsmen helped to build some two thousand monuments there. A minority of recent scholars hold that this Mon influence on the interior after the conquest is a greatly exaggerated legend of later times and that Lower Burma had no substantial independent state before Pagan expanded; the historian Michael Aung-Thwin argues that the existence of Thaton is not supported by contemporary evidence.

Manuha asked for and was granted leave to build the Manuha Temple at Pagan in 1059. Its three giant Buddha statues, two seated and one reclining, seem too large for their chambers, and their cramped positions are said to represent the discomfort the captive king had to endure.
manuscript: A manuscript is any text written by hand rather than printed or reproduced by mechanical means. The word comes from the Latin manūscriptum, from manus, hand, and scriptum, from scribere, to write, and is first recorded in English in 1597. A manuscript may be a codex, bound as a book, a scroll, or a set of loose pages, and it may combine writing with calculations, maps, music, diagrams or illustrations. Illuminated manuscripts are enriched with pictures, border decorations and elaborate initial letters. The study of the handwriting in surviving manuscripts is called palaeography.

Before printing, in China by woodblock and in Europe by movable type, all written documents were produced by hand. In Europe they took the form of scrolls or codices, written on vellum and other parchment, on papyrus and, later, on paper. In the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia palm leaf manuscripts were used from the 5th century BCE or earlier, and in some cases until the 19th century. In China bamboo and wooden slips preceded paper, and in Russia birch bark documents as old as the 11th century have survived. Paper spread from China through the Islamic world to Europe by the 14th century and had largely replaced parchment by the late 15th.

The oldest manuscripts survive mainly because of the dry climate of the Middle East, in Egyptian tombs, in the rubbish heaps of Oxyrhynchus, and in jars and caves, as with the Nag Hammadi library and the Dead Sea Scrolls. Volcanic ash preserved part of the library of the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum. Woodblock printing was used for books in China from about the 7th century, and the earliest dated example is the Diamond Sutra of 868. In the Islamic world and the West all books were manuscripts until movable type arrived in about 1450.

Because errors crept in each time a manuscript was copied, tracing the relationships between different versions of a text is a fundamental part of textual criticism. In medieval Europe the most common genres were Bibles and their commentaries, with books of hours for private prayer and liturgical books for the Church. Liturgical books were the most elegantly written and finely decorated. The Carolingian minuscule, a calligraphic script used in the Holy Roman Empire between about 800 and 1200, gave Latin writing a standard form.

Manuscript copying continued for at least a century after printing, because printing remained expensive, and private and government documents stayed handwritten until the typewriter of the late 19th century. In the Islamic world paper reached Central Asia and spread to Iran, Iraq, Syria, Egypt and North Africa during the 8th century.
manuscript-illumination: An illuminated manuscript is a formally prepared document whose text is decorated with borders, miniature illustrations and other flourishes. The earliest to survive are a small number from late antiquity, dating from between 400 and 600 CE, among them the Vergilius Romanus, the Vergilius Vaticanus and the Rossano Gospels. Most surviving examples come from the Middle Ages, and many thousands survive. Islamic manuscripts can also be called illuminated and use essentially the same techniques, but comparable works from the Far East and Mesoamerica are described as painted.

The first known decorated Arabic manuscripts are some Qur'ans of the 9th century, with decorated frontispieces and headings but no illustrations. Illustrated Arabic manuscripts grew from the Graeco-Arabic translation movement, and production greatly increased in the 12th and especially the 13th century. The Persian miniature tradition began mostly in whole books, and the Great Mongol Shahnameh, probably from the 1330s, is a very early manuscript of a work that became a favourite for grand illustrated books in Persian courts.

Under the strictest definition a manuscript is not illuminated unless it contains metal, normally gold leaf or shell gold paint, which from the 12th century was usually burnished. Gold exalted a religious text and displayed a patron's wealth, until it became so common that it made up only a tenth of the cost of production.

Most manuscripts were written on parchment, or on vellum from calf skin, and bound into codices. The text was usually written first with space reserved for decoration. A rubricator added titles and initials in red, and then an illuminator drew the design, applied gold and painted the colours. A Gothic page might hold a framed miniature, a historiated initial and a border with drolleries, often by different artists.

Illumination served prayers and liturgical books such as psalters, and from the 13th century also secular texts. Up to the 12th century most manuscripts were produced in monastic scriptoria, and by the 14th century commercial workshops in cities such as Paris, Rome and in the Netherlands did much of the work. Wealthy patrons commissioned books of hours, with calendars of their own saints, and the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry is one of the best known. Printing rapidly led to the decline of illumination, and in the early 16th century books were still made but in much smaller numbers, mostly for the very wealthy.
manusmriti: The Manusmriti, also called the Manava Dharmashastra, is a Sanskrit text in verse, usually placed between 200 BCE and 200 CE. The title Manusmriti is a relatively modern term, probably coined because the text is in verse; the manuscripts never use it and give the title Manava Dharmashastra in the colophons of their chapters.

Early philologists dated the work far too early, William Jones to about 1250 BCE and Karl Wilhelm Friedrich Schlegel to about 1000 BCE, though its language must be later than the late Vedic texts. It presents itself as a dialogue in which Manu teaches and his student Bhrigu speaks most of the verses.

The traditional twelve chapters do not go back to the original text. The work moves from the creation of the world to the sources of dharma, then to the dharma of the four varnas, and ends with the law of karma, rebirth and final liberation. It names as sources of law the whole Veda, then the tradition and conduct of those who know it, the customs of holy men and self-satisfaction.

Its largest portions are on Brahmins, with 1,034 verses, and on Kshatriyas, with 971; rules for Vaishyas and Shudras are brief. A long section on kings covers officials, taxation, war and eighteen grounds for litigation, and the laws of war say that civilians and those who have surrendered must not be harmed. The text imposes many restrictions on women, who it says should never be independent, and it forbids widows to remarry, although other verses allow remarriage in cases of abandonment or abuse.

Over fifty manuscripts are known, and they differ from one another. The Calcutta manuscript with the commentary of Kulluka Bhatta was long presumed authentic, and it was translated by Jones, Burnell, Bühler and Doniger.

Some scholars doubt that it was ever administered as law in ancient or medieval India, and David Buxbaum called it in great part an ideal picture of what a Brahmin held ought to be law. It was nevertheless honoured in Burma, Siam, Cambodia and Java-Bali, where it was copied and built into local codes, and British officials used it to construct a law for Hindus in the East India Company's enclaves.

Critics condemn its rules on Shudras, who it says cannot be released from servitude, and on women. B. R. Ambedkar attended a conference at which copies were burned in 1927 to protest against caste discrimination.
manx-language: Manx, in Manx Gaelg or Gailck, is a Gaelic language of the insular Celtic branch of the Celtic family, and the heritage language of the Manx people. It is one of the three daughter languages of Old Irish, by way of Middle Irish, with Irish and Scottish Gaelic, and is partly mutually intelligible with them: native speakers of one find it easy to gain passive, even spoken, competence in the others. The word Manx means Mannish and comes from Old Norse. The name Manx Gaelic is often used to tell the language from Manx English, the form of English spoken on the island.

A little-documented Brythonic language, related to Welsh, Cornish and Breton, may have been spoken on the Isle of Man before Christian missionaries arrived from Ireland in the early Middle Ages, though little evidence survives. Between 1400 and 1900 Manx diverged considerably from the Gaelic of Scotland and Ireland. The Plantation of Ulster in the 17th century, the decline of Irish in Leinster and the extinction of Galloway Gaelic left it geographically isolated, and the development of a separate orthography increased the difference. Two historical dialects are attested, Northern and Southern Manx, and written Manx may represent a midlands dialect of Douglas and the area around it.

In the 17th century some students left the island to attend school in England, and governor Isaac Barrow required teaching in English in the schools he founded. He also promoted English in churches, which he thought a better language for reading the Bible, but because most ministers spoke only Manx his views had little practical effect. The use of Manx declined during the 19th century, and the Manx Language Society was founded in 1899.

By the middle of the 20th century only a few elderly native speakers remained, and the last of them, Ned Maddrell, died on 27 December 1974. A scholarly revival had begun by then, and a few people were teaching the language in schools. The revival was helped because the language was well recorded: the Bible and the Book of Common Prayer had been translated into Manx. The Manx Language Unit was formed in 1992. Manx has become more visible with signage, radio broadcasts and a Manx-medium primary school, and in 2021 around 2,023 people had some second-language conversational ability. Manx is used in the annual Tynwald ceremony.
manyakheta: Manyakheta rose to prominence when the capital of the Rashtrakutas moved there from Mayurkhandi, in present-day Bidar district, during the reign of Amoghavarsha I. He is said to have built the imperial capital to match that of Lord Indra, with elaborately designed buildings for the royal household. Amoghavarsha I, a Jain ruler who reigned for sixty-four years, wrote the Kavirajamarga, the first classical Kannada work. He patronised Jain scholars including the mathematician Mahaviracharya and the intellectuals Ajitasenacharya, Gunabhadracharya and Jinasenacharya, and his reign is often regarded as a high point of Kannada literary culture.

According to Dhanapala's Pāiyalacchi, the Paramara king Harṣa Sīyaka sacked the city in 972–73, the year he completed that work. Later the area passed under the Southern Kalachuris, Cholas, Yadavas and Kakatiyas, then under the Delhi Sultanate, the Bahmani, Bidar and Bijapur sultanates, the Mughal Empire and the Nizam of Hyderabad, until 1948.

Malkheda lies on the Kagina river in the Sedam taluk of Kalaburagi district, Karnataka, about 40 kilometres from Kalaburagi. It is on State Highway 10 and has a railway station nearby. It was a historical centre of Jainism and has two ancient institutions, the Jain Bhattaraka Math and the temple of Neminath, whose pillars and walls date between the ninth and eleventh centuries. The Neminath temple holds images of tirthankaras and a panchdhatu shrine with 96 images.

Works composed at Manyakheta include the Mahapurana of Acharya Jinasena and his pupil Gunabhadra in the ninth century, and the mathematical text Ganita Saara Sangraha by Mahaviracharya. The Apabhramsha poet Pushapadanta also lived there. A historical fort stands in the town and is being restored.
mao-gong-ding: The Mao Gong ding, Lord Mao's cauldron, is a bronze tripod vessel of the ding type from the Western Zhou dynasty (c. 1045 – c. 771 BCE). It takes its name from the Lord Yin of Mao, who presented it to King Xuan of Zhou after being appointed to help run the affairs of state. The vessel is 53.8 cm high and 47.9 cm wide and weighs 34.7 kilograms. Its inscription, cast in 32 lines, covers the inner surface.

According to the National Palace Museum, the text bears witness to the restoration under King Xuan, the revival of Western Zhou after his accession ended the Gonghe interregnum. It opens with the king's instructions to the Duke of Mao. The middle part recalls how King Wen of Zhou and King Wu of Zhou had held the Mandate of Heaven and founded the kingdom, and expresses the king's vigilance and unease at inheriting the Mandate himself. The last part lists in detail the gifts the king bestowed on the duke, who closes by giving thanks and offering the ding as a record for later generations.

The ding was excavated in Qishan County, Shaanxi, in 1843, in the reign of the Daoguang Emperor. The collector Chen Jieqi (1813–1884) acquired it in 1852, and he and his studio made precise rubbings of the inscription. Between 1909 and 1911 Duanfang (1861–1911) bought it from the Chen family.

It later passed to Ye Gongchuo (1881–1968), whose friends bought it from the Tianjin Dao Sheng Bank, which had held it as security for a loan. During the Second Sino-Japanese War the Ye family sold it to Chen Yon Ren, a Shanghai millionaire, who in April 1946 gave it through an army general to the Kuomintang government in Shanghai. In 1949 Chiang Kai-shek and the Kuomintang took it to Taiwan, where the National Palace Museum counts it among its three treasures, with the Jadeite Cabbage and the Meat-Shaped Stone.
mao-zedong: Mao Zedong was born on 26 December 1893 near Shaoshan village in Hunan, under the Qing dynasty. His father, Mao Yichang, was a formerly impoverished peasant who had become one of the wealthiest farmers in Shaoshan. He preferred classic novels such as Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Water Margin to the Confucian texts he was taught. At 13 he was married by arrangement to Luo Yixiu, whom he refused to recognise as his wife.

In Beijing he worked as assistant to the Peking University librarian Li Dazhao, an early Chinese Communist, whose articles on the October Revolution added Marxism to the doctrines of the Chinese revolutionary movement. Mao joined Li's Study Group and developed rapidly toward Marxism in the winter of 1919. In 1921 he became a founding member of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

After Chiang Kai-shek turned on the Communists in 1927, the CCP lost about 15,000 of its 25,000 members. The party founded the Workers' and Peasants' Red Army, and Mao was made its commander-in-chief. His Autumn Harvest Uprising against Changsha failed, and on 15 September he marched east with 1,000 survivors to the Jinggang Mountains of Jiangxi. In 1935 he became leader of the CCP during the Long March, a retreat to the Yan'an Soviet in Shaanxi. The civil war resumed after Japan's surrender in 1945, and the Nationalist government withdrew to Taiwan in 1949.

Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China from Tiananmen on 1 October 1949. He sent the People's Volunteer Army into the Korean War in October 1950. From 1958 to 1962 he oversaw the Great Leap Forward, which aimed to collectivise agriculture and industrialise the country and was followed by the Great Chinese Famine. In 1966 he launched the Cultural Revolution, marked by violent class struggle, destruction of historical artifacts and a cult of personality.

Mao died shortly after midnight on 9 September 1976, aged 82, after three heart attacks that year. Despite his request to be cremated, his embalmed body was later placed on permanent display in a mausoleum. Historians and others judge his rule in different ways. His policies are held to have caused the deaths of tens of millions of people, mainly through starvation, but also through persecution, prison labour and executions. He is also credited with ending decades of civil war, improving literacy, education and the status of women. On 27 June 1981 the CCP Central Committee adopted a resolution stating that his contributions to the revolution far outweighed his mistakes.
maoism: Maoism, officially Mao Zedong Thought, developed while Mao Zedong tried to realise a socialist revolution in the agricultural, pre-industrial society of the Republic of China and later the People's Republic of China. The English term was coined in 1951 by Benjamin I. Schwartz, who used it for Mao's pragmatic strategy of revolution, with a disciplined and hierarchical Communist Party supported by a mobilised peasant mass base.

After the Long March, Mao and the Chinese Communist Party were headquartered in the Yan'an Soviet in Shaanxi. In these years Mao established himself as a Marxist theoretician and wrote most of the works later canonised as the Thought of Mao Zedong. The period also established his and the party's ideological independence from Moscow.

Maoism differs from conventional European Marxism in looking to the agrarian countryside rather than to urban industrial workers. Its theory of New Democracy held that the long road to socialism could be opened only by a national, popular, democratic, anti-feudal and anti-imperialist revolution run by the communists. Its idea of people's war means mobilising large rural populations for guerrilla warfare and surrounding the cities from the countryside. The mass line is summarised as from the masses, to the masses. In 1974 China announced its Three Worlds Theory at the UN.

From the 1950s until the reform and opening up of Deng Xiaoping in the late 1970s, Maoism was the political and military ideology of the Chinese Communist Party and of Maoist revolutionary movements worldwide. After the Sino-Soviet split of the 1960s, the Chinese and Soviet parties each claimed to be the sole heir of Joseph Stalin. The Albanian Party of Labour sided early with China, and Maoist groups arose in Peru, India, Bangladesh and the Philippines, where the Communist Party of the Philippines was founded on 26 December 1968. In Peru the Shining Path fought an insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s that resulted in tens of thousands of deaths.
Deng Xiaoping described the true spirit of Mao Zedong Thought as seeking truth from facts, and made clear that Mao was fallible, judging him 70 percent right and 30 percent wrong.
maori-language-act-1987: The act, in Māori Te Ture mō te Reo Māori 1987, came after years of campaigning by Māori, particularly the Māori protest movement, and after a shift in thinking about the Treaty of Waitangi, which had gained new relevance by the mid-1980s chiefly through the Waitangi Tribunal. It drew on precedents abroad, above all Ireland's Bord na Gaeilge Act 1978, which it cites several times, and also the United Kingdom's Welsh Language Act 1967, which had allowed Welsh to be used in Welsh courts.

Besides making Māori an official language and giving speakers the right to use it in courts and other legal settings, the act set up the Māori Language Commission, at first called Te Komihana Mo Te Reo Maori, to promote the language and give advice on it. Māori did not gain the same standing in law as English: tax records, for instance, had to be kept in English unless the Commissioner of Internal Revenue agreed otherwise.

The law was enacted as the Maori Language Act 1987, written without macrons. After the Legislation Act 2012 allowed the Chief Parliamentary Counsel to rewrite Māori words in current spelling when reprinting legislation, macrons were added in its reprints.

The Maori Language Amendment Act 1991 renamed the commission Te Taura Whiri I Te Reo Māori and slightly widened the legal settings in which Māori could be used, to include bodies such as the Tenancy Tribunal and any Commission of Inquiry. The Māori Language Act 2016 (Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016), which repealed and replaced it, created Te Mātāwai to act on behalf of Māori for the protection, promotion and revitalisation of the language. It was the first New Zealand act enacted in two official versions, Māori and English, with the Māori version to prevail in any conflict of meaning.
maoz-tzur: The hymn is commonly thought to date from the 13th century, in the age of the Crusades, though Avraham Fränkel suggests it was composed in Germany between 1160 and 1190. The acrostic Mordechai identifies its author, but who he was is uncertain. He may have been Mordecai ben Isaac ha-Levi, author of the Sabbath table-hymn Mah Yafit, or, judging by the appeal in the closing verse, the Mordecai whose father-in-law was killed in the Mainz massacre of 1096 during the First Crusade. It was first sung only at home and has been used in the synagogue since at least the 19th century.

Its six stanzas retell Jewish history and celebrate deliverance from four ancient enemies: Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Haman and Antiochus. The four middle stanzas recall the Exodus from Egypt, the end of the Babylonian captivity, the escape from Haman in Persia remembered at Purim, and the Hasmonean revolt against Greek rule commemorated at Hanukkah. The text is full of allusions to Biblical literature and rabbinic interpretation: Egypt is malchut eglah, after Jeremiah, the Jewish people are shoshanim, after the Song of Songs. The first stanza, in the present tense, hopes for the rebuilding of the Temple. The first letters of the last stanza's opening words spell hazak, be strong.

That final stanza again calls for retribution against the enemies of the Jewish people, and its Admon, the red one, was understood by some as Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. It was not found in print before the 18th century; some hold it was kept only in oral tradition as self-censorship for its anti-Christian hints, others that it was added later. Today often only the first stanza, or the first and fifth, is sung.

Its best-known tune, identified by Cantor Birnbaum of Königsberg as an adaptation of the German folk-song So weiss ich eins, was widespread among German Jews by 1450; Luther used the same melody for a chorale. Isaac Nathan made the earliest transcription of the Jewish form in Byron's Hebrew Melodies of 1815, and Julius Mombach shaped the version favoured by British Jews. The English Rock of Ages, a free translation by Marcus Jastrow and Gustav Gottheil, rests on Leopold Stein's German version. In 1969 the hymn inspired Naomi Shemer's song Shivchei Ma'oz.
mapuche: The Mapuche are a group of Indigenous inhabitants of south-central Chile and south-western Argentina, who share a common social, religious and economic structure and the Mapudungun language. Archaeological finds show that Mapuche culture existed in Chile and Argentina as early as 600 to 500 BCE. At the time of the Spanish arrival the Picunche lived in the valleys between the Choapa and Itata rivers, the Mapuche proper between the Itata and Toltén, and the Huilliche and Cunco as far south as the Chiloé Archipelago.

Troops of the Inca Empire are reported to have reached the Maule River and fought the Mapuche between the Maule and the Itata. Most modern scholars place the southern border of the Inca Empire between Santiago and the Maipo River, or somewhere between Santiago and the Maule, so the bulk of the Mapuche escaped Inca rule.

Spanish expansion into Mapuche territory was an offshoot of the conquest of Peru. In 1536 Diego de Almagro set out to conquer Chile but was met at the Battle of Reynogüelén by a large Mapuche force armed with bows and pikes, and he retreated to Peru the following year. In 1541 Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago. The Picunche leader Michimalonco led resistance to the Spanish between 1541 and 1545, and his best-known achievement is the destruction of Santiago. The Mapuche learned horse riding and cavalry warfare from the Spaniards.

In the 17th to 19th centuries Mapuche groups migrated eastward into the Andes and Pampas, and the Tehuelche adopted the Mapuche language and some of their culture, in a process called Araucanization. Mapuche society in Araucanía and Patagonia remained independent until the late 19th century. Between 1861 and 1879 Chile and Argentina incorporated several Mapuche territories, and in January 1881, after Chile had defeated Peru, the conquest resumed.

The traditional economy is based on agriculture, and the traditional social organisation consists of extended families led by a lonko, or chief. In wartime the Mapuche united in larger groups and elected a toki, meaning axe-bearer, as leader. Mapuche cosmology centres on a creator, ngenechen, who takes the form of an older man, an older woman, a young man and a young woman. The best-known ceremony is the Ngillatun, a communal prayer.

Textiles are among their best-known arts. Women spun and wove, with skills passed on by mothers, grandmothers and aunts, and a man was expected to give a larger dowry for a bride who was an accomplished weaver. From the later 18th century Mapuche silversmiths made large amounts of silver jewellery, working Spanish, Argentine and Chilean coins into headdresses called trarilonko. Mapudungun is spoken in Chile and Argentina, and about 92 per cent of Mapuche live in Chile.
maputo: Maputo stands on the west side of Maputo Bay, an inlet of the Indian Ocean 95 kilometres long and 30 kilometres wide, where the rivers Tembe, Umbeluzi, Matola and Infulene drain into the Espírito Santo Estuary. The island of Inhaca lies at the eastern end of the bay. The city is 120 kilometres from the South African border at Ressano Garcia and 80 kilometres from the border with Eswatini. Its economy has long centred on its port, through which much of the country's imports and exports pass.

The area was first settled as a fishing village by ancestors of the Tsonga people. It was named after the Portuguese navigator Lourenço Marques, who with António Caldeira was sent by the governor of Mozambique to explore the rivers flowing into Delagoa Bay in the mid-16th century. The forts and trading stations that the Portuguese established, abandoned and reoccupied on the north bank were all called Lourenço Marques. The existing town dates from about 1850, the earlier settlement having been entirely destroyed by the local people, and it grew around a Portuguese fortress. It was raised to city status in 1877.

In 1898 the colony of Portuguese Mozambique moved its capital there, and in the late 19th and early 20th centuries the city grew as a port. The main port handled 17 million tons of cargo in 1971, at its peak. Some of its best-known buildings date from this time, including the Central Train Station, built between 1913 and 1916 and sometimes mistaken for the work of Gustav Eiffel, and the Hotel Polana, designed by Herbert Baker.

The People's Republic of Mozambique was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 under the Lusaka Accord of September 1974. The capital had been expected to be renamed Can Phumo, after a Shangaan chief who lived there before the Portuguese arrived, but in February 1976 it became Maputo, a name tied to the Maputo River and to the FRELIMO slogan Hail Mozambique, united from the Rovuma to the Maputo. The civil war devastated its economy, and street names were changed to remove colonial figures and reflect ties with the Eastern Bloc.

Maputo is the capital and largest city of Mozambique, with 1,088,449 inhabitants in 2017 and 2,717,437 in the metropolitan area, which includes Matola. It is administered as a separate province. Its architecture mixes Portuguese colonial Neoclassical and Manueline styles with art deco and modernist buildings, and it is known as the City of Acacias. Eduardo Mondlane University, founded in 1968, is the oldest in the country.
maqoma: Maqoma was born around 1798 in the Right Hand House of the Xhosa Kingdom, the eldest son of Chief Ngqika, an older brother of Sandile kaNgqika and a nephew of Hintsa. In 1818 he commanded his father's forces. Throughout his life he opposed Ngqika's policy of ceding land to the Cape Colony, and he moved into the so-called Neutral Zone to found a chiefdom of his own, from which British troops expelled him.

In the Sixth Frontier War the settlers accused the Xhosa of cattle raids and the Xhosa accused the settlers of killing their chiefs. After a Cape government commando killed a chief of high rank on 11 December 1834, a Xhosa army led by Maqoma swept across the frontier in small raiding parties, burning homesteads, and refugees crowded into Grahamstown. Boer commandos under Piet Retief, burgher and Khoi commandos and British troops under Colonel Sir Harry Smith struck back. Maqoma and Tyali withdrew into the Amatola Mountains, and the land to the Great Kei River was annexed as Queen Adelaide Province. Hostilities died down on 17 September 1836.

In the Eighth Frontier War, which followed Smith's removal of Xhosa from the Kat River region during drought, Maqoma held the forested Waterkloof, with his stronghold on Mount Misery between the Waterkloof and Harry's Kloof. The fighting there lasted two years; his forces killed Lieutenant-colonel John Fordyce and inflicted heavy losses on Smith's troops. George Cathcart replaced Smith in March 1852, and in February 1853 Sandile and the other chiefs surrendered. The war ended in the complete subjugation of the Ciskei Xhosa.

Maqoma was imprisoned twice on Robben Island. During the first term his wife and son were allowed to stay with him, but for the second, at the age of seventy-three, he was sent alone. A visiting Anglican chaplain saw his last moments in 1873, when he cried bitterly before dying of old age and dejection. He died on 9 September 1873 and remains a figure of importance in South African history.
maqsud-shah: Maqsud Shah was the Uyghur Jasagh Prince, or Qinwang, of the Kumul Khanate in China and the last ruler of its Borjigid dynasty. He succeeded his uncle Muhammad Shah in 1882. The khans were officially vassals of the Qing dynasty and every six years had to travel to Beijing to serve the emperor for 40 days; Maqsud Shah also sent melons as tribute. Unlike the rest of Xinjiang, where the state encouraged settlement, Kumul was not opened to Han Chinese settlers.

Twenty-one begs administered Kumul under the khan, who received 1,200 taels of silver from the Xinjiang government after sending his tribute. Maqsud Shah spoke fluent Chinese, spoke Turkic with a Chinese accent and often wore Chinese clothing. He was said to drink heavily and allowed no one to photograph him. After the Xinhai Revolution overthrew the Qing in 1912, the new Republic of China appointed Yang Zengxin governor of Xinjiang. Yang was a monarchist who supported the khanate, so it kept its status as a vassal while Yang governed.

That arrangement ended when Yang Zengxin was assassinated in 1928 and was succeeded as governor by the warlord Jin Shuren, whose rule was marked by strife, corruption and ethnic intolerance. When Maqsud Shah died in 1930, Jin Shuren replaced the khanate with three administrative districts, Hami, Yihe and Yiwu, and did not allow Maqsud Shah's son and designated heir, Nasir, to succeed him to the throne. The events that followed set off the Kumul Rebellion, in which Yulbars Khan, who had served as Maqsud Shah's chancellor at court, took part in support of the rising.
mara-salvatrucha: Mara Salvatrucha was set up in the 1980s in the Pico-Union, Westlake and Rampart neighbourhoods of Los Angeles by Salvadoran immigrants who had left after the Central American civil wars. Through the 1970s and 1980s Salvadoran asylum seekers were refused asylum in the United States and classed as undocumented immigrants, and their claims were largely neglected until the 1991 case American Baptist Churches v.

Thornburgh required them to be reconsidered. The gang was first formed to protect Salvadoran immigrants from other gangs and over time became a more traditional criminal organisation. The origin of the name is disputed: mara is said to mean 'swarm' in Caliche slang, from marabunta, a type of ant, and Salvatrucha may combine Salvadoran with trucha, 'alert'.

Many members were deported to El Salvador after the end of the Salvadoran Civil War in 1992, or on arrest, which spread the gang through Central America, where it is strongest in El Salvador, Honduras and Guatemala. Gang violence in El Salvador peaked in the 1990s. Governments of the ARENA party answered with the Mano Dura and Super Mano Dura policies, which outside observers and gang members themselves believed increased the gangs' power. On 23 December 2004 gunmen attacked an intercity bus at Chamelecón, Honduras, killing 28 passengers and wounding 21; the attack was organised as a protest against a proposal to restore the death penalty.

Under President Mauricio Funes the government and gang representatives negotiated unofficially a truce with MS-13 and its rival, the 18th Street gang: homicides fell in exchange for transfers to lower-security prisons, but the truce was unpopular and controversial. Under President Nayib Bukele a State of Exception crackdown began, and by 2023 the national police database recorded more than 120,000 gang members, aspiring members and collaborators. On 20 January 2025 President Donald Trump signed an executive order starting the process of designating MS-13 and other gangs as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, enacted on 20 February 2025.

Members are mainly Salvadorans and Salvadoran Americans, with Hondurans, Guatemalans and Mexicans, organised in local cliques. In 2018 the American membership of up to 10,000 was under 1 per cent of the 1.4 million gang members in the country. Recruitment is often forced, and aspirants are beaten for 13 seconds in an initiation known as 'jumping-in'. The gang is affiliated with the Sureño coalition, which pays tribute to the Mexican Mafia, and is rival to the 18th Street gang. Its activities include trafficking in narcotics, the extortion of businesses in its territory, alien smuggling and homicide.
maracaibo: Maracaibo is the capital of Zulia, on the western shore of the strait that links Lake Maracaibo to the Gulf of Venezuela. The first settlements of the region were established by Arawak and Carib peoples, and among them the Añu built rows of stilt houses along the northern shore of the lake. The first Europeans arrived in 1499. The origin of the name is uncertain: a popular legend of a cacique called Mara who resisted the Spanish is considered unlikely, and another theory derives it from an indigenous term meaning place where serpents abound.

The city was founded three times. In the period when the Welser banking family of Augsburg controlled Venezuela Province, Ambrosius Ehinger established a settlement on 8 September 1529 and called it Neu-Nürnberg. Nikolaus Federmann moved its people away in 1535. Alonso Pacheco made a second attempt in 1569, abandoned in 1573 under attacks by local peoples. In 1574 Captain Pedro Maldonado, under orders from Governor Diego de Mazariegos, founded it permanently as Nueva Zamora de la Laguna de Maracaibo.

In the 17th century European pirates attacked the city repeatedly. François l'Olonnais sacked it in 1667 with eight ships and 600 men, and Henry Morgan raided it in March 1669, afterwards destroying two Spanish warships and forcing a third to surrender in order to escape the lake. Michel de Grammont attacked in June 1678 with six ships and 700 men. After pirates destroyed Gibraltar, at the head of the lake, in 1669, Maracaibo became the transshipment point for the inland settlements.

In 1810 the Province of Maracaibo stayed loyal to the Spanish Crown and did not join the First Republic of Venezuela. Patriot troops led by Rafael Urdaneta fought royalist forces, and the Battle of Lake Maracaibo on 24 July 1823 ended Spanish control in Venezuela. For nearly 380 years the city was relatively isolated from the rest of the country, trading more with the Caribbean than with eastern Venezuela. The discovery of petroleum in 1917 brought rapid population growth through migration.

Maracaibo is the second-largest city of Venezuela after Caracas, with an estimated 1,752,602 inhabitants. The General Rafael Urdaneta Bridge, opened in 1962 across the narrows of the lake, links it with the eastern shore and the national highway network. It was the longest prestressed concrete bridge in the world at the time. In 1964 a tanker struck one of its piers and a section of the roadway collapsed, killing seven people.
marad: Marad, called Marda in Sumerian, lay on the west bank of what was then the western branch of the Euphrates, roughly 50 km south-east of Kish, on the Arahtu River and on the Abgal canal between Babylon and Isin. The site covers about 50 hectares of small mounds and ridges; its main mound, locally called Bint as-Sheikh, rises 14 metres above the plain and holds the temple. It was identified in 1912 from a Neo-Babylonian cylinder of Nebuchadrezzar recording the temple's restoration, found by locals rather than excavated, and confirmed by four inscribed door sockets reportedly found at the site.

Marad was established about 2700 BCE, in the Early Dynastic II period. It is absent from the Sumerian King List, but one of the Temple Hymns attributed to Enheduanna is devoted to its god, Lugal-Marada, a god of earth and the plough whom some think a manifestation of Ninurta; his temple was the E-igi-kalama. After its capture by Sargon of Akkad, Marad was ruled by governors, among them Lipit-ilē, who built the god's temple. Under the Ur III empire it again had a governor, and Ur-Nammu claimed to have freed it, with Umma and Kazallu, after a brief period under the control of Elam.

After a time under Isin, Marad had a brief independence before Babylon captured it, and in Old Babylonian times it is often named with Kazallu, perhaps as part of the same kingdom. Its known kings include Sumu-numhim, Alumbiumu, who seized Dilbat and whose daughter was made a nadītu at Sippar, and Ašdumlû, who dug the ditch of the Abgal canal. Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt the temple on what he called the platform of Naram-Sin, and there was light occupation in the Kassite and Parthian periods.

Teams from the Iraqi General Directorate of Antiquities and the Qādissiyyah University excavated the site in 1991, led by Na'el Hannoon, and in 2005 and 2007, led by Abbas Al-Hussainy. They uncovered a hall thought to be the E-igi-kalama, much damaged by looters, Old Babylonian houses and about 40 inscribed objects. Work in 2019 and 2023 found further cuneiform tablets, many from the Ilum-bāni archives on the business of date palm cultivation.
maragha: Maragheh stands on the Sufi Chay river, 130 kilometres from Tabriz, in a narrow valley at the eastern end of a well-cultivated plain opening towards Lake Urmia, which lies 30 kilometres to the west. It sits at the southern foot of Mount Sahand. The mild, moist climate and abundant water make the surrounding area very fertile, with extensive vineyards and orchards watered by canals from the river. It has long been suggested that Maragheh is the same as Phraaspa or Phraata, the winter capital of Atropatene.

The town received the name Maragheh during the Islamic conquest, around the time the Umayyad prince Marwan ibn Muhammad stayed there in 740. In 893 the Sajid governor Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj made Maragheh his capital, though he usually resided in Barda'a, and his successor Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj destroyed its walls and moved the capital to Ardabil. The last Sajid ruler, Abu'l-Musafir al-Fath, was killed at Maragheh in 929. Oghuz Turks sacked the town in 1039, destroying its mosque and killing many inhabitants. The last Ahmadili ruler of Maragheh was Sulafa Khatun, who ruled from 1209 to 1225.

The Mongol generals Jebe and Subutai stormed the city on 30 March 1221, burning it and killing its inhabitants. Mongol rule became definite in 1231, and after Hulagu Khan captured Baghdad in 1258 he established his residence at Maragheh. The first Ilkhanate rulers lived a semi-nomadic life, so few buildings of the period survive. In 1312 Öljaitü appointed Qara-Sunqur ruler of Maragheh, and Ibn Battuta reports that it was called Little Damascus. From the 18th to the 20th century it was governed by the Moqaddam family.

On a hill west of the town stand the remains of the observatory, called Rasad Khaneh, built in the thirteenth century under Hulagu Khan for the scholar Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. Construction began in 1259 and took three years. It is said to have housed at least ten astronomers and a library of over 40,000 books. Scholars came from across the Islamic world, and the Tusi-couple, a geometrical device that solved problems of planetary motion in the Ptolemaic system, is associated with it. Tusi died in 1274, his son took over, and the observatory became inactive early in the 14th century. Maragheh is today the capital of Maragheh County in East Azerbaijan province, Iran, and its people are mostly Azerbaijanis.
maragtas: Written in a mixture of the Hiligaynon and Kinaray-a languages, the Maragtas presents itself as based on written and oral sources of which no copy survives, and its author makes no claim to be transcribing particular pre-colonial documents. It has a publisher's introduction by Salvador Laguda, a foreword, six chapters and an epilogue. The first chapter describes the customs of the Ati of Panay and their chief Marikudo, son of Chief Polpulan. The second tells how ten datus fled the tyranny of Raja Makatunaw in Borneo and bartered gold with Marikudo for the plains and valleys, Datu Paiburong receiving Irong-Irong, now the province of Iloilo.

The third chapter tells of Sumakwel, his wife Kapinangan and her lover Gurung-garung; the fourth ends the tale of the datus with their political arrangements and their voyage round the island. The fifth describes language, trade, dress, marriage, funerals, cockfighting and calendars, and the sixth lists Spanish officials from 1637 to 1808.

Philippine historians made little use of the book before the Japanese occupation. The historian H. Otley Beyer later described a document he called the Margitas, dating probably from about 1225 and transliterated into romanised Visayan in early Spanish days, and the idea that the Maragtas copied an ancient text spread among academics. William Henry Scott, writing in 1984, concluded that it was an original work by Monteclaro, while holding that the legend probably preserves the memory of an actual event that cannot be dated. The anthropologist F. Landa Jocano argued in 2000 that Beyer's document was the Maragtas itself, and a 2019 thesis at De La Salle University held that Monteclaro's text is a secondary source for a tradition also recorded by Fr. Tomás Santaren.

The story has inspired many artists. Ricaredo Demetillo's Barter in Panay won the UP Golden Jubilee Award for Poetry in 1958, and his verse tragedy The Heart of Emptiness is Black won the Palanca Award in 1973. Orlando Nadre adapted it as the musical Kapinangan in 1981, with music by Ryan Cayabyab, and Jeremías Elizalde Navarro painted a scene from it in the mural Bulawan nga Saduk. Writers from Panay including Magdalena Jalandoni and Ramón Muzones retold it as novels.
marajo: Marajó is the largest island of the Marajó Archipelago and the second largest in South America, with a land area of 40,100 square kilometres, comparable to Switzerland. It lies just south of the Equator at the mouth of the Amazon River and is separated from the mainland by Marajó Bay, the Pará River, smaller rivers and the Atlantic Ocean. It is almost entirely flat: the eastern side has savanna plains at about 6 metres above sea level and the western side has rainforest around sea level.

During the rainy season much of the island is flooded and looks like one large lake, and many settlements stand on stilts. The island is known for the pororoca, a tidal bore that makes waves up to 4 metres high.

The island was home to an advanced society, the Marajoara culture, before the arrival of Europeans, and has been a centre of archaeological work since the 19th century. Scholars from the 1980s on divide the period before Cabral into five phases: Ananatuba (c. 1100 to c. 200 BCE), Mangueiras (c. 1000 BCE to c. 100 CE), Formiga (c. 100–400 CE), Marajoará (c. 400–1200 CE) and Aruã (1200–1500 CE).

Since the 1990s the origins of this society have been debated. From fieldwork in the 1940s and 1950s Betty Meggers argued that emigrants from the Andes founded the culture and that poor soil caused its steady decline. Anna Curtenius Roosevelt, who re-excavated Marajó in the 1980s, rejects this: in her view the culture developed independently within the Amazon, with intensive agriculture and major public works, and a population of more than 100,000 at its peak. The people organised themselves into matrilineal clans. The arrival of Europeans in the 16th century was catastrophic, since about 90 per cent of the indigenous population died of Eurasian infectious diseases against which they had no immunity.

Sixteen municipalities share the island, and the largest city is Breves. Soure, on the Atlantic coast, is reached by ferry from Belém. Domestic water buffalo, technically invasive, now number about 450,000, more than the human population, and graze on large ranches on the savannas. Lumber and açaí palm are produced in the western forests. The island is also the seat of the Roman Catholic Territorial Prelature of Marajó.
maramures: Maramureș is a valley enclosed by the Oaș, Gutâi, Țibleș and Rodnei mountains to the west and south and by the Maramureș Mountains and the central part of the Outer Eastern Carpathians to the east and north. It is one of the largest depressions in the Carpathians, covering about 10,000 km2, and is drained through a narrow opening, the Khust Gate, at Khust. Its length from Khust to the Prislop Pass is about 150 km. The passes that link it to neighbouring regions are high and in the past were hardly accessible in winter; the Prislop Pass leads to Moldavia and the Frasini Pass to Galicia. The last wisent in what is now Romania, a symbol of the region, was hunted to extinction in 1852.

In ancient times the area was settled by Celts, Dacians, Sarmatians, Germanic peoples and Akatziri. In the first century BCE it belonged to the Dacian kingdom under Burebista, and in the early Middle Ages it was ruled in turn by the Hunnic Empire, the Gepids, the Avars, White Croatia, the Hungarians and even Kievan Rus'. From the eleventh century it was part of the Kingdom of Hungary. At first its Romanian inhabitants were allowed to keep their own political organisation, the Voivodeship of Maramureș, divided into many small autonomous areas, and the king long struggled to persuade the voivodes to accept the title of count, which implied a loss of independence. The region was reorganised as Máramaros County in the fourteenth century.

In the sixteenth century, after the Ottoman invasion of Hungary, the area came under the semi-independent Principality of Transylvania, and later in the seventeenth century under the Habsburg monarchy. In 1732 it was transferred to the Habsburg Kingdom of Hungary, and after 1867 it lay in the Hungarian part of Austria-Hungary. After the First World War it was divided between Romania and the Czechoslovak region of Carpathian Ruthenia. Hungary annexed Carpathian Ruthenia in March 1939 and Northern Transylvania, which included southern Maramureș, in August 1940, and held them until 1944.

Since World War II the southern section has belonged to Romania, as Maramureș County, and the northern section to the Soviet Union and now to Ukraine as part of Zakarpattia Oblast. In the south most people are Romanians, with Hungarians, Rusyns, Ukrainians, Zipser Germans, Jews and Roma; in the north most are Ukrainians. Villages have been cut in two by the state border since the 1940s.
maranao-people: The ancestral group is believed to have called itself Iranaoan. It later diverged: the Maguindanaon and the Iranun people, whose names can also be translated as people of the lake, moved away, while those who stayed at Lake Lanao became the Maranao. The three groups remain related, share similar cultures and speak languages of the Danao family, which also gave its name to the island of Mindanao. Lake Lanao, the largest lake in Mindanao and the second-largest and deepest in the Philippines, is the centre of Maranao life and the subject of many myths and legends.

The Maranao were the last of the Muslims of the southern Philippines to adopt Islam, chiefly under the influence of Arab-Malay missionaries such as Sharif Kabungsuwan and others from Borneo. Before Islam their leaders were tribal chiefs called datu; with its arrival in the 16th century they formed kingdoms ruled by sultans. Through the nominal Spanish occupation of the Philippines, and later the American and Japanese, they kept their own leaders. Amai Pakpak led a resistance against Spanish colonisation of Lanao and is honoured as a national hero, and in the 20th century Rashid Lucman, a journalist and World War II guerrilla, was an early proponent of Moro independence or autonomy.

Traditional society is divided into two strata: the mapiyatao, of pure descent and entitled to ascend to thrones by royal bloodline, and the kasilidan, suspected of mixed descent, who are further divided into categories that include non-Maranao and slaves. These distinctions have begun to decline as economic conditions have improved. The Maranao have long lived by fishing and farming, growing wet rice, corn and sweet potatoes, and their textiles and woodcarvings are sold throughout the country. They numbered about 1,800,000 in 2020, living mainly in Lanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur.

Houses stand on piles in three tiers of rank: the torogan of royalty, the mala a walay of the lesser nobility and the lawig of commoners. The Sarimanok, a bird of Maranao myth holding a fish and decorated with okir scrolls, is a symbol of good fortune found throughout their art. Kulintang gong music, the Singkil dance, based on a scene of the Darangen, and the Maharadia Lawana, a version of the Ramayana, are part of their heritage, and in 2005 UNESCO selected the Darangen as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
maranhao: Maranhão has a coastline of 2,243 km on the Atlantic and borders the states of Piauí, Tocantins and Pará. Its northern part is a heavily forested plain crossed by many rivers, with moist forests in the north-west and forests of the babaçu palm in the north-centre and north-east. The south belongs to the lower terraces of the Brazilian Highlands and is covered by cerrado savanna.

The rivers all flow north to the Atlantic, and the Mearim, like the Amazon, has a pororoca, a tidal bore, in its lower channel. The coast holds the tallest mangrove forests in the world, and the dune fields of the Lençóis Maranhenses lie to the east. The name is uncertain; it probably comes from Portuguese settlers from Maranhão in Avis, Alentejo.

The Spanish explorer Vicente Yáñez Pinzón was the first known European to explore the area, in 1500, but it was granted as a Portuguese hereditary captaincy to João de Barros in 1534. The first European settlement was made in 1594 by a French trading expedition under Jacques Riffault of Dieppe, who lost two of his three ships near the island of São Luís. Daniel de La Touche, commissioned by the French crown, founded a colony there in 1612, called Equinoctial France. The Portuguese expelled the French in 1615, and the Dutch held the island from 1641 to 1644.

In 1621 Ceará, Maranhão and Pará were united as the Estado do Maranhão, separate from the southern captaincies. The Jesuits began successful missions among the Indians, and were temporarily expelled after a civil war in 1684 because they opposed the enslavement of the Indians. Ceará was later detached, and the state remained separate until 1774, when it again came under the colonial administration of Brazil. In the late 18th century, as cotton growing increased, many enslaved people were brought into the region, and by the historian Sven Beckert's account its cotton exports doubled between 1770 and 1780, nearly doubled again by 1790 and nearly tripled once more by 1800.

Maranhão did not join the Brazilian declaration of independence of 1822. In the following year the British admiral Lord Cochrane drove out the Portuguese, and the province joined the Empire of Brazil; he became the 1st Marques of Maranhão and governor.

Maranhão is a state in Brazil's Northeast Region with an area of 332,000 square kilometres and 217 municipalities. Its capital, São Luís, is the Brazilian state capital that most closely resembles a Portuguese city, and its historic centre was declared a World Heritage Site in 1997. The state had 6,776,699 residents in 2022, and Portuguese is the language of its schools.
maranon-river: The Marañón rises about 160 kilometres north-east of Lima and runs north-west across plateaus about 3,650 metres high, through a deeply eroded Andean valley along the eastern base of the Cordillera. At about 5° 36′ south it bends north-east and cuts through the high jungle, where unnavigable rapids and gorges called pongos mark its course.

The last is the Pongo de Manseriche, about 5 kilometres long, which in 1868 Captain Carbajal described as a rent in the Andes about 600 metres deep and in places only 30 metres wide, with a current at times near 20 kilometres an hour. It has wrecked many ships. Below it the river enters the flat Amazon basin, the low jungle of Peruvian Amazonia, home to the Urarina, Candoshi and Cocama-Cocamilla peoples.

The Marañón was considered the source of the Amazon from the 1707 map of Padre Samuel Fritz, who placed its source in a lake called Lauriocha, near Huánuco, and judged that it contributed more water than any other tributary. For most of the 18th and 19th centuries and into the 20th it was generally held to be the source.

Later exploration proposed two headwater rivers, the Lauricocha and the Nupe, which join near the village of Rondos. The Apurímac and Mantaro have also been put forward as the Amazon's source, but the Marañón is still called its mainstem source because of its higher annual discharge. Historically the name was often applied to the whole river to the Atlantic, whereas it is now generally taken to end at the confluence with the Ucayali.

In 1743 the Frenchman Charles Marie de La Condamine travelled from the Chinchipe confluence to the Atlantic, taking to the water at the Chiriaco confluence and running several pongos, including the Pongo de Manseriche. In 1941 and 1942 Bertrand Flornoy, sent by the National Museum of Natural History of France, found the sources of the river.

A 552-kilometre section between Puente Copuma and Corral Quemado, much of it in a canyon up to 3,000 metres deep and in dry country, has been called the Grand Canyon of the Amazon. It flows past the village of Calemar, where Ciro Alegría set his novel La serpiente de oro of 1935. The river has also been the subject of plans for hydroelectric dams, one of which, at Chaglla, was begun in 2012.
maratha-empire: The Marathas were a Marathi-speaking warrior group from the western Deccan Plateau. Shivaji, a Maratha aristocrat of the Bhonsle clan, began resistance to the Sultanate of Bijapur in 1645 by taking the fort of Torna. He established Hindavi Swarajya, meaning the self-rule of Hindus, with Raigad as his capital, and was crowned Chhatrapati, or sovereign, in 1674. At his death his dominion held about 300 forts, about 40,000 cavalry and naval establishments on the west coast. His son Sambhaji succeeded in 1681, and Aurangzeb headed south the same year with his whole court and an army of about 500,000.

After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, Shivaji's grandson Shahu revived Maratha power and gave much authority to the Bhat family, who became hereditary peshwas, or prime ministers. Baji Rao I, Peshwa from 1720, is credited with expanding the kingdom tenfold by 1740. He defeated the Nizam at Palkhed on 28 February 1728 and at Bhopal in 1737. After Shahu died in 1749 the peshwas became the effective rulers.

The leading families, the Scindia, Holkar, Bhonsle and Gaekwad, extended conquests in northern and central India and grew more independent. The expansion was halted by the defeat at Panipat in 1761 at the hands of the Durrani Empire, but the Marathas retook most of their lost territory ten years later under Peshwa Madhavrao I. After the Holkars defeated him in 1802, Peshwa Baji Rao II sought protection from the British East India Company, whose intervention in the Second and Third Anglo-Maratha Wars destroyed the confederacy by 1818.

The state was a confederacy of four rulers under the Peshwa at Poona (Pune): the Scindia, the Gaekwad at Baroda, the Holkar at Indore and the Bhonsle at Nagpur. Historians question both empire and confederacy as names: Barbara Ramusack notes that neither is fully accurate, and Stewart Gordon observes that power within the leadership changed as often as every decade. Many rulers paid chauth, a regular tax, to the Marathas.

Shivaji created the Ashtapradhan, a council of eight ministers headed by the Peshwa. Under the peshwas his homogeneous army gave way to a feudal force provided by the sardars, with soldiers of many backgrounds, among them Arabs, Sikhs, Rajputs and Europeans. The navy under Kanhoji Angre built dockyards along the western coast.
maravarman-sundara-pandya-i: Maravarman Sundara Pandya came to power in 1216 on the death of his elder brother, Jatavarman Kulasekara Pandyan, who had been a vassal of the Chola king Kulottunga III. Kulasekara had opposed his overlord and been defeated in 1205, when the victorious Chola armies burned the ancient Pandya coronation hall at Madurai. Avenging that humiliation became the aim of the new king.

Kulottunga was near the end of a reign of some forty years, and old age left him unready for the speed of the Pandya invasion. Sundara Pandya sacked Thanjavur and Uraiyur and drove the Chola king and his crown prince Rajaraja Chola III into exile. He marked his victory with a virabisheka, an anointment of heroes, in the Chola coronation hall at Ayirattali, then marched to Chidambaram, camped at Pon Amaravathi and performed a Thulabaram, an offering of his own weight, at the Chidambaram temple.

Kulottunga appealed to his son-in-law, the Hoysala king Veera Ballala II, who sent an army under his son Vira Narasimha II. Under this threat Sundara Pandya agreed to restore the Chola kingdom once the Cholas acknowledged his overlordship, and Kulottunga made his formal submission at Pon Amaravathi. In 1225 Sundara Pandya drove out a company of Odda soldiers who had occupied Srirangam. He later allied with the Kadava chieftain Kopperunchinga I, who captured Rajaraja Chola III at Tellaru in 1231, but Vira Narasimha II defeated Sundara Pandya at Mahendramangalam on the Kaveri that year and Rajaraja was restored. Peace among the Chola, Hoysala, Kadava and Pandya kingdoms was sealed by dynastic marriages.

His reign marked the beginning of the second Pandya empire, and from his time the Cholas declined steadily in territory and standing. Inscriptions at Thiruvandipuram give him the titles Kaliyugaraman and Adisayapandiyadevan, and his coins bear the title Sonadugondan, conqueror of the Chola country. He is the hero of Akilan's historical novel Kayalvizhi, serialised in 1964-65, and was played by M. G. Ramachandran in its 1978 film adaptation.
marburg: Marburg lies along the valley of the river Lahn in Hesse. It grew at the crossing of two early medieval highways, the trade route linking Cologne and Prague and the route from the North Sea to the Alps and Italy. The settlement is first mentioned in 822 in the Reinhardsbrunner Chronik. A small castle was built in the ninth or tenth century by the Gisos, and coins show that it was a town by 1140.

The Gisos lost the settlement to the Landgraves of Thuringia, who resided at the Wartburg. In 1222 Marburg received town privileges. In 1228 the widowed Elizabeth of Hungary, landgravine of Thuringia, chose it as her dowager seat after falling out with her brother-in-law. She devoted her life to the sick, died in 1231 aged 24 and was canonised in 1235. In 1264 her daughter Sophie of Brabant won Hesse for her son Henry, and from then until about 1540 Marburg was, with Kassel, one of its capitals. It was the capital of Hessen-Marburg after the first division of the landgraviate and again later in the 16th century.

Philip I of Hesse founded the University of Marburg in 1527, the oldest existing Protestant-founded university in the world. In 1529 he arranged the Marburg Colloquy to reconcile Martin Luther and Huldrych Zwingli. The Thirty Years' War then ravaged the region, which Hesse-Darmstadt and Hesse-Kassel fought over, and the territory around Marburg lost more than two-thirds of its population. After that the town lay neglected for two centuries and survived as a largely intact Gothic town.

Romanticism brought it back to life. Friedrich Carl von Savigny, Achim von Arnim, Clemens Brentano and Bettina von Arnim lived or studied there, and the Brothers Grimm collected many of their fairy tales in the town. After Prussia annexed Hesse in 1866 it made Marburg its main administrative centre in the province of Hessen-Nassau and made the university a regional academic centre. In the Second World War the city was bombed 13 times but largely survived, and from 1942 to 1945 it served as a hospital town.

Marburg is a university town of about 76,000 people and the capital of the Marburg-Biedenkopf district. The Marburg Castle and its medieval churches, among them the Elisabethkirche, still crown the hill. The disease Marburg virus disease takes its name from the town, where the virus was first recognised in the 1967 outbreak among laboratory workers.
marburg-colloquy: After the Diet of Speyer confirmed the Edict of Worms, Philip I of Hesse believed that a divided Protestant movement was vulnerable to Charles V, and that religious harmony was needed for a political alliance of the Protestant states. He therefore brought the leading reformers to Marburg Castle, where the meeting ran from 1 to 4 October 1529. Besides Luther and Zwingli, the participants included Stephan Agricola, Johannes Brenz, Martin Bucer, Caspar Hedio, Justus Jonas, Philip Melanchthon, Johannes Oecolampadius, Andreas Osiander and Bernhard Rothmann.

Both sides rejected transubstantiation and the view of the Eucharist as a sacrifice for the living and the dead, and both insisted on communion in both kinds. They divided over the real presence. Luther held that the words "this is my body" could not be understood otherwise than as written, and that Christ's human body, infused with the attributes of God, was present everywhere and so in the bread and wine. Zwingli, stressing the distinction of Christ's two natures, held that his human body could be in one place only, at the right hand of the Father, and that Christ was present only in the hearts of believers.

Zwingli objected that Luther placed the chief point of salvation in physically eating the body of Christ, and summed up his own view as Credere est edere, to believe is to eat. When it was clear that no agreement would be reached, Philip asked Luther to draft a list of the doctrines both sides accepted.
