The Marburg Articles had fifteen points, and everyone present could agree on the first fourteen. The fifteenth affirmed the sacrament but recorded that they could not agree whether the body and blood were corporally present, and asked each party to show the other Christian love.

The failure stirred strong feeling on both sides. On parting Zwingli is reported to have said in tears that there were no people on earth with whom he would rather be at one than the Wittenbergers. Luther at first refused to acknowledge Zwingli and his followers as Christians, though after the colloquy the two showed more mutual respect in their writings. At the later Diet of Augsburg the Zwinglians and Lutherans again presented separate statements, and the two views of the Supper came to divide the Lutheran and Reformed traditions.
marbury-v-madison: John Adams, a Federalist, lost the presidential election of 1800 narrowly to Thomas Jefferson of the Democratic-Republican Party. On 2 March 1801, two days before his term ended, Adams nominated nearly 60 Federalist supporters to new circuit judge and justice of the peace posts. The Senate approved them the next day, and John Marshall, who had been named chief justice in January but still served as Secretary of State, sealed their commissions. Jefferson's supporters called the nominees the "Midnight Judges".

A few commissions were not delivered before Jefferson's inauguration, among them that of William Marbury, a Maryland businessman and ardent Federalist. Jefferson held them void and told his Secretary of State, James Madison, to withhold them. In December 1801 Marbury sued Madison at the Supreme Court, asking for a writ of mandamus.

On 24 February 1803 the court gave a unanimous 4-0 decision against Marbury, in an opinion by Chief Justice Marshall. It held that Marbury had a right to his commission, since delivery was only a custom, and that the law gave him a remedy, a writ of mandamus. The remaining question was whether the court could issue it.

Marbury argued that section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 allowed the court to issue such writs in cases under its original jurisdiction. The court accepted that reading, but Article III gives original jurisdiction only in cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and those in which a state is a party. Marbury's case was neither, so the court held that Congress cannot enlarge its original jurisdiction and struck down the relevant part of section 13.

A writ for Marbury would probably have been ignored by Jefferson and Madison, while a plain ruling against him would have been a victory for the Democratic-Republicans. Marshall declared the withholding unlawful, which pleased the Federalists, yet denied the writ, which gave Jefferson the result he wanted. Jefferson criticised the decision but accepted it.

The opinion was the Supreme Court's first exercise of judicial review, although the idea was not new: Alexander Hamilton had defended it in Federalist No. 78. Marbury made the practice more routine and prepared the way for McCulloch v. Maryland in 1819. It also covers executive actions where the executive has a legal duty, as in United States v. Nixon in 1974.
marc-antoine-charpentier: Charpentier was born in or near Paris, the son of a master scribe well connected to influential families in the Parlement of Paris. He received a very good education, perhaps with the help of the Jesuits, and registered at the Paris law school at eighteen but left after one semester. A legend that he went to Rome to study painting is undocumented and possibly untrue, since his 28 volumes of manuscripts contain not a single drawing. In Rome he learned contemporary Italian practice, which he brought back to France.

On his return he probably became house composer to Marie de Lorraine, duchesse de Guise, who gave him an apartment in the Hôtel de Guise, which suggests he was a courtier rather than a paid domestic. For seventeen years he wrote psalm settings, hymns, motets, a Magnificat, a mass, a Dies Irae and Italianate oratorios for her. He was not, as is often asserted, director of her ensemble; that was Philippe Goibaut.

Mme de Guise, Louis XIV's first cousin, protected the performance of his chamber operas against the monopoly of Jean Baptiste Lully. After Molière's break with Lully in 1672, Charpentier wrote incidental music for Molière and then for his successors, until the troupe gave up defying Lully's limits by 1685. In 1679 he also began to compose for Louis XIV's son, the Dauphin, and he received a royal pension by early 1683.

From late 1687 to early 1698 he was maître de musique to the Jesuits, at the Collège Louis-le-Grand, where he wrote David et Jonathas, and then at the church of Saint-Louis, where he wrote mostly psalms and liturgical settings. His opera Médée, on a play by Corneille, was a failure, after which he devoted himself to religious music. In 1698 he became maître de musique at the Sainte-Chapelle.

Charpentier died at the Sainte-Chapelle on 24 February 1704 and was buried in the small cemetery behind its choir. Almost none of his music from 1690 to 1704 survives, because on the death of a maître de musique the royal administration routinely confiscated everything he had written for the Chapel. In 1727 his heirs sold his 28 folio volumes of autograph manuscripts, the Mélanges, to the Royal Library, now the Bibliothèque nationale de France; his two series of numbered notebooks allow scholars to date his works. He was also a respected theoretician who wrote a composition manual for Philippe, Duke of Chartres. Bud Greenspan's Olympiad films also used the prelude to his Te Deum as introductory music.
marcabru: Marcabru, who was active from about 1130 to 1150, is one of the earliest troubadours whose poems are known, yet nothing certain is known about him. Two vidas, or short biographies, are attached to his poems and tell different stories, and both appear to be built on hints in the poems rather than independent information. The shorter, in BnF manuscript 12473, makes him a Gascon, the son of a poor woman named Marcabrunela, which seems to come from a reading of one of his own poems. Details of the dialect of his poems support the Gascon origin.

The longer vida says he was abandoned at a rich man’s door, raised by Aldric del Vilar and taught to compose by Cercamon, and first nicknamed Pan-perdut. It adds that the lords of Gascony, about whom he had said many bad things, eventually put him to death. It seems to rest on poems and guesswork, and modern scholars doubt the link with Cercamon.

Among his patrons were William X of Aquitaine and, probably, Alfonso VII of León. He may have travelled to Spain in the 1130s in the entourage of Alfonso Jordan, Count of Toulouse. He may also have originated the tenso, a debate poem, in an exchange with Uc Catola on the nature of love and the decline of courtly behaviour, dated as early as 1133. In the 1140s he was a propagandist for the Reconquista. In his poem beginning with the Latin words Pax in nomine Domini! he called Spain a lavador, a washer, where knights could go to have their souls cleansed by fighting the infidel.

Forty-four poems are attributed to him. They are learned, often difficult, sometimes obscene and relentlessly critical of the morality of lords and ladies. He experimented with the pastorela, a parodic genre that he used to point out the futility of lust. L’autrer jost’una sebissa tells how a shepherdess reviles the speaker’s advances on the basis of class, and it survives with music. Another poem tells how a man’s attempt to seduce a woman whose husband was away on crusade is firmly rebuffed. Four melodies for his poems survive, and three more, for poems that may be contrafacta of his work, may be attributed to him. He was a powerful influence on later poets who adopted the obscure style known as trobar clus.
marcantonio-colonna: Marcantonio Colonna was born in 1535 at Civita Lavinia into the Colonna family of Lazio, then one of the most powerful feudal dynasties of the Papal States and the Kingdom of Sicily. He was the son of Ascanio Colonna, who served Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. His mother, Giovanna d'Aragona, a niece of King Ferdinand I of Naples, divorced Ascanio and took the boy with her when he was one year old, so he grew up as a political enemy of his father. In 1548 he became a page to Prince Philip, and in 1552 he married Felicia Orsini, daughter of Girolamo Orsini, Lord of Bracciano. His father disinherited him that December.

From 1553 Colonna served in the Spanish army under Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, Duke of Alba, and used Spanish force to seize his father's lands. He fought in the cavalry at the Battle of Marciano, which destroyed the Franco-Sienese army. When the pro-French Pope Paul IV was elected, Colonna plotted a rebellion against him; the plot was discovered, and in May 1556 the pope excommunicated him and confiscated his lands. In the war that followed he captured Paliano, Palestrina and Terracina, defeated Giulio Orsini at Acuto in 1557 and entered Rome in triumph. Pope Pius IV lifted the excommunication in 1559.

In the summer of 1570 Pope Pius V made him Captain General of the papal fleet, although he had no direct naval experience. His first campaign, to relieve the siege of Nicosia, broke down in quarrels with Giovanni Andrea Doria, and a storm between Corfu and Ancona sank most of the papal flotilla. In 1571 he persuaded Venice to stop negotiating with the Ottoman Empire, and the Holy League was signed on 25 May, with Colonna as lieutenant to John of Austria. At Lepanto on 7 October 1571 he came to the aid of Don John's flagship, the Real, and was shot twice in the chest. The following year he faced the Ottoman admiral Occhiali in the Cerigo Channel, where Occhiali declined battle.

Colonna died on 1 August 1584, in circumstances that are not recorded. As Lord of Marino he was honoured by its inhabitants with an annual celebration, which survives as the Sagra dell'Uva. His daughter Costanza Colonna was the first patroness of the painter Michelangelo di Caravaggio, and his son Ascanio Colonna became a cardinal and viceroy of Aragon. In November 2022 the Italian Navy launched an offshore patrol ship named after him.
marcelo-caetano: Marcello José das Neves Alves Caetano was born on 17 August 1906, son of José Maria de Almeida Alves Caetano and Josefa Maria das Neves. He took a licentiate and a doctorate in law and became a professor at the Faculty of Law of the University of Lisbon. A self-proclaimed reactionary in his youth, he began his political career in the early days of Salazar's regime.

In 1940 he was made chief of the Portuguese Youth Organisation, and from 1944 to 1947 he was minister of the colonies. He presided over the Corporative Chamber from 1949 to 1955 and was the most powerful man in the regime after Salazar between 1955 and 1958. He became rector of the University of Lisbon in 1959 but resigned after the Academic Crisis of 1962.

In August 1968 Salazar suffered a stroke, and President Américo Tomás appointed Caetano on 27 September 1968. Many hoped he would soften the regime and modernise the economy. In what was called the Marcellist Spring he renamed the National Union the People's National Action and the secret police PIDE the DGS, eased press censorship and allowed the first independent labour unions since the 1920s. He also gave rural workers a monthly pension and backed large investments such as the oil processing centre at Sines.

Yet the elections of 1969 and 1973 differed little from earlier ones, the opposition was harshly repressed, and after 1973 hardliners close to Tomás pressed him to abandon his reforms. Inflation reached double digits in 1970 and the 1973 oil crisis added to the strain. The wars in Africa consumed about 40 per cent of the budget by 1970, and Portugal faced growing arms embargoes and sanctions. In 1973 the priest Adrian Hastings reported that the army had massacred about 400 villagers at Wiriyamu in Mozambique in December 1972.

The Armed Forces Movement, formed within the army, overthrew the regime in the Carnation Revolution on 25 April 1974, after a failed right-wing coup attempt in March. Caetano resigned and was taken into military custody. He was flown to Madeira and then into exile in Brazil, where he directed the Institute of Comparative Law at Gama Filho University in Rio de Janeiro. He published two books of memoirs, Minhas Memórias de Salazar and Depoimento, and works on administrative and constitutional law. He died of a heart attack in Rio de Janeiro in 1980 and was buried in the São João Batista cemetery.
marcelo-t-de-alvear: Máximo Marcelo Torcuato de Alvear y Pacheco was born in Buenos Aires on 4 October 1868, son of Torcuato de Alvear and Elvira Pacheco y Reinoso, of a wealthy patrician family of Basque origin. His grandfather Carlos María de Alvear became supreme director of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, and his father was mayor of Buenos Aires. In 1889 he organised the meeting in the Florida Garden that popularised Leandro N. Alem among the young, and he then worked as Alem's secretary.

In 1898 he met the Portuguese soprano Regina Pacini and pursued her across Europe for eight years. They married in Lisbon on 29 April 1907. He later served as a deputy for the province of Buenos Aires and as ambassador to France.

Hipólito Yrigoyen backed Alvear, then ambassador in France and of the conservative wing of the Radical Civic Union, as his successor. He won the election of 2 April 1922 with 47.5 per cent of the vote and took office on 12 October. Radio broadcast the ceremony, the first time a president's voice was heard on it. His cabinet displeased many radicals, and the distance between him and Yrigoyen began.

His government favoured agricultural exports, especially meat and cereals. Social measures included a Children's Bureau, a law ending night work for bakers and Law 11,357 of 22 September 1926, which gave unmarried, divorced and widowed women of age the civil rights of men. He appointed General Enrique Mosconi to head the state oil company YPF. By 1923 nine radical senators had declared themselves anti-personalists, against Yrigoyen's personal leadership, and the party split. Yrigoyen won the 1928 election with 62 per cent.

After his term Alvear settled in Paris. He returned to Argentina in April 1931 to reunify his party and seek the presidency again, but the military government of José Félix Uriburu barred him, and after a revolt in Corrientes in July 1931 he was forced into exile. Alvear and other radicals were persecuted, imprisoned or exiled repeatedly in the following years, and he spent time in the prison on Martín García island.

By 1936 he led the party with almost no internal resistance, though some leaders called his harsh character dictatorial. He died of a heart attack at his home in Don Torcuato on 23 March 1942, beside his wife. Cartoonists nicknamed him the bald man, as against the hairy Yrigoyen.
march-across-the-belts: In 1655 Charles X Gustav attacked the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, but despite taking Warsaw he could not end the war, while Austria and the Netherlands aided Poland and Brandenburg-Prussia changed sides. When Denmark declared war on Sweden on 5 June 1657, he marched his army of about 17,000 men, only 4,000 of them Swedes, through Pomerania into Jutland and took the fortress of Frederiksodde on 27 October. The Danish Straits and the Danish navy still barred the way to Copenhagen, so in the exceptionally cold winter he waited in Jutland for the ice to thicken.

On 30 January 1658 the army moved out from Brandsø onto the frozen Little Belt, between 6,000 and 7,000 men by one account and up to 12,000 by others, with the cavalry in two wings under Carl Gustaf Wrangel and the king. Dragoons with sleds carried beams and boards to bridge weak ice. The Swedes defeated the Danes at Tybrind Vig and Iversnæs, where the Danish army under Ulrik Christian Gyldenløve was short of food, clothing and experienced officers. Danish resistance on Funen collapsed; Odense fell that evening and Nyborg the next day, and Gyldenløve and much of the Danish government were captured.

From Svendborg, on the night of 6 February, between 2,000 and 3,000 cavalry led their horses across the Great Belt by way of Tåsinge and Langeland, at times through water standing on the ice, then through Lolland and Falster. They reached Zealand on 11 February, and on 15 February, with Swedish troops 22 kilometres from Copenhagen, King Frederick III of Denmark agreed to an unconditional peace.

By the Treaty of Roskilde, signed in Roskilde Cathedral on 26 February 1658, Denmark ceded Scania, Blekinge, Halland, Bohuslän, Bornholm and Trøndelag. Charles X Gustav renewed the war on 5 August 1658, aiming to end Denmark as a sovereign state, but the Netherlands came to its aid, and after his death in 1660 the Treaty of Copenhagen returned Bornholm and Trøndelag to Denmark. Swedish historians long treated the campaign as a success story, and in the age of romantic nationalism Charles X Gustav was hailed as the king who gave Sweden its natural borders, while the part of quartermaster general Erik Dahlbergh in the decision to cross the Great Belt has long been debated.
march-first-movement: In 1910 Japan formally annexed Korea. Japanese rule was at first especially tight: Japan took control of the Korean economy and began a process of forced cultural assimilation, land was confiscated from Koreans and given to Japanese people, and freedom of speech and the press were tightly controlled. The devastation of the First World War led intellectuals in Korea and elsewhere to discuss anti-colonialism and liberal reform. Korean students in Japan, exposed to liberal democracy through Japan’s Taishō Democracy movement and Wilson’s Fourteen Points, issued a declaration of independence on 8 February. In late 1918 leaders of the Korean religion Cheondoism, including Son Byong-hi, concluded that nonviolent resistance would best win international opinion.

Around noon on 1 March 1919, 29 of the 33 signers of the Declaration of Independence gathered in the T’aehwagwan restaurant in Seoul and read it aloud. The owner reported the gathering to the Japanese Government-General, and about 80 military police arrested the signers. Similar protests were held the same day in Pyongyang, Chinnamp’o, Anju and Wonsan, and by 19 March all thirteen provinces had hosted protests. All but seven of Korea’s 218 administrative districts did so. Estimates run to about 1,500 to 1,800 protests. They were decentralised and shaped by local religion: Christians led in some regions and Cheondoists in others. The Government-General brought in more police, military police and army divisions, armed with lethal weapons.

Suppression was often violent. A Korean estimate of 1920 claimed 7,509 deaths and 46,948 arrests, while Japanese authorities reported much lower numbers. Yu Gwan-sun, a sixteen-year-old student, became a symbol of the movement. On 1 April the military police fired on 3,000 protesters at Cheonan and killed 19, among them her parents. Foreign missionaries such as Frank Schofield documented the events for the press abroad.

The movement did not bring Korea’s liberation, but it invigorated the independence movement. Korean exiles who gathered in Shanghai founded the Korean Provisional Government in April 1919, now considered a predecessor of the government of South Korea. The colonial government made limited concessions known as cultural rule, which allowed Korean newspapers such as The Dong-A Ilbo and The Chosun Ilbo to be founded. Chinese writers praised the protests, though historians debate how far the movement influenced other protests. In South Korea 1 March is a national holiday, and the constitution’s first sentence refers to the movement.
march-of-ancona: The March of Ancona, in Italian Marca Anconitana or Anconetana, was a frontier march centred first on the city of Ancona and later on Fermo and then Macerata. Its name survives in the Italian region of the Marche, which it covered almost entirely, not only the Province of Ancona. Along the Adriatic it reached as far north as Urbino and included the cities of Loreto, Camerino, Fermo, Macerata, Osimo, San Severino and Tolentino. Under papal rule it had three towns of more than 10,000 people: Ancona, Ascoli Piceno and Fermo.

Originally part of Imperial Italy, the march was formed around 1100 from the March of Fermo and a southern part of the Byzantine Pentapolis. It first bore the name of its earliest ruler, as the march of Werner, who held it from 1093 to 1109. Empire and Church disputed their rights in it. In 1173 an imperial army under Christian of Mainz invaded against pro-papal resistance led by Countess Boltruda Frangipani, and in 1177 Pope Alexander III described the march as partly belonging to the empire but largely to the Church. Markward von Annweiler held it from 1184.

The Papal States acquired it definitively under Pope Innocent III in 1198. It was governed by a rector named by the pope, who answered to a general rector reporting to the pope himself, and the province was reorganised by the Constitutiones Sanctæ Matris Ecclesiæ in 1357. From the late Middle Ages the actual running of many towns lay with local urban elites organised as hereditary patriciates, on whom the popes relied to keep the peace and collect taxes. According to Paul Sabatier's biography of Francis of Assisi, the march became the home of the Spiritual Franciscans after Francis's death. Francesco I Sforza held it from 1434 to 1443.
march-of-the-volunteers: The Japanese invasion of Manchuria brought a boom of nationalistic arts and literature in China. The playwright Tian Han composed the lyrics in 1934, as two stanzas of his poem The Great Wall, for a play he was working on. Nie Er set them to music in Japan in March and April 1935, and the Russian composer Aaron Avshalomov arranged the orchestral accompaniment. The song was chosen for the climax of the film Children of Troubled Times, in which the protagonists join the masses in taking up arms against the Japanese.

Later legend held that Tian wrote it in prison on cigarette-box paper. In fact he was arrested in Shanghai and held in Nanjing just after completing his draft for the film. The song was first heard in public at the film's screening in Shanghai in May 1935, and a record was released two months later. The English title refers to the volunteer armies that opposed the Japanese in Manchuria; the Chinese name literally means the righteous and brave armies.

Although the film did not do well, the song became wildly popular. The musicologist Feng Zikai heard crowds singing it in rural villages from Zhejiang to Hunan within months. A National Salvation singing campaign promoted it in Shanghai, and it became a military song in the Second Sino-Japanese War among forces beyond the Chinese Communist Party. The Nationalist general Dai Anlan designated it the anthem of the 200th Division, which fought in Burma.

In 1940, in New York, Liu Liangmo taught it to Paul Robeson, who recorded it in Chinese and English as Chee Lai in early 1941, with proceeds going to the Chinese resistance. Allied radio broadcasts used the song to represent China throughout the Second World War.

The song was used as a Chinese national anthem for the first time at the World Peace Conference in April 1949, held in Prague. A committee set up that June received 632 entries. The painter Xu Beihong suggested the march and Zhou Enlai supported it, against objections to a line about the peril facing the Chinese nation. On 27 September 1949 it became the provisional anthem of the People's Republic.

Tian Han was criticised in the Cultural Revolution and died in prison in 1968. The song was played without words from 1969, restored in 1978 with rewritten lyrics, and in 1982 the National People's Congress restored Tian's original verses. It was enshrined in the Constitution in 2004. The anthem was played at the handovers of Hong Kong in 1997 and Macau in 1999.
march-of-verona: The march roughly covered historic Friuli and the Veneto, from the Chiese River in the west to the Tagliamento and the Isonzo in the east, and from the Adriatic, except for the lagoons Venice held, to the Dolomites and the Carnic Alps. Besides Verona and Aquileia it held Udine, Cividale, the port of Grado, Vicenza, Treviso and Padua. After Otto I campaigned against King Berengar II of Italy in 951, the Reichstag at Augsburg in 952 left Berengar his kingdom but took the march from him. The March of Istria was attached to it as a county.

From 952 to 975 Verona and Carinthia were both held by the dukes of Bavaria, relatives of the Ottonian dynasty. In 975 Otto II chartered a commune in Verona and ceded to it the powers of the marquisate, and from then on Verona and other cities of the march slowly became independent city-states, while the title of margrave became an empty hereditary honour. The emperors began to appoint vicars in Verona instead.

The march lost land piece by piece. From 1004 Henry II gave territories around Trento to its bishops, whom Conrad II made imperial prince-bishops in 1027. In 1061 Empress Agnes enfeoffed Berthold of the House of Zähringen with Carinthia and Verona; his descendants of the House of Baden kept the title. Istria became a march of its own again in 1070, and in 1077, during the Investiture Controversy, Friuli around Aquileia went to the Patriarchate of Aquileia. In 1151 Conrad III gave what remained to Margrave Herman III of Baden.

In 1164 Venice, Verona, Padua, Vicenza and Treviso formed the Veronese League against Frederick Barbarossa, and in 1167 the cities joined the Lombard League, the march's end in practice, confirmed by the Lombard victory at Legnano in 1176. From the 13th century the real lords of Verona were the Scaliger, and after the city submitted to Venice in 1405 Venice conquered most of the former march by about 1420.
march-on-rome: Benito Mussolini founded the first Italian Fasces of Combat in March 1919, at the start of the Red Biennium, two years of strikes, factory and land occupations and clashes between socialists and landowners. The government tried to act as a neutral mediator and satisfied neither side. Local elites allied with the small Fascist movement, which contained many veterans of the First World War and had a reputation for violence, hoping its paramilitary squads would destroy socialist organisations.

From 1919 the squadristi, known as Blackshirts, attacked socialist politicians and militants, and in many towns of northern and central Italy they made local government impossible. The police often failed to intervene. The Fascists won 35 seats in the 1921 election, and in November 1921 the movement became the National Fascist Party, with about 320,000 members. In August 1922 squads razed socialist buildings in Ancona, Genoa and Milan.

On 24 October 1922 Mussolini told 60,000 militants at a rally in Naples: "Our program is simple: we want to rule Italy." He named four Quadrumvirs, Emilio De Bono, Italo Balbo, Michele Bianchi and Cesare Maria de Vecchi, to lead the march, while he went to Milan. He did not march himself, though he allowed photographs to be taken of him with the marchers.

As the squads gathered outside Rome, Prime Minister Luigi Facta ordered a state of siege, expecting the King to agree. King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign. His reasons have been explained as concern about the army's loyalty and the ambitions of his pro-Fascist cousin, the Duke of Aosta. The march involved fewer than 30,000 men, but the squadristi already controlled the Po plain and much of the country, and the King feared civil war.

Mussolini took office within the framework of the Statuto Albertino, the Italian constitution, and not by force. Historians therefore describe the March on Rome not as the seizure of power that Fascism later proclaimed, but as the pressure that precipitated a transfer of power, made possible by the surrender of public authorities in the face of intimidation. Many business and financial leaders believed Mussolini could be manipulated.

He went on to install a dictatorship after the assassination of the socialist Giacomo Matteotti on 10 June 1924. At the end of 1923 participants in the march were authorised to wear a Commemorative Medal, and royal decrees between 1926 and 1938 widened eligibility until all Blackshirts and members of the armed forces could wear it.
march-on-washington: After the American Civil War constitutional amendments freed enslaved people, granted citizenship and gave African American men voting rights. Democrats regained power when Reconstruction ended in 1877 and imposed many restrictions on people of colour in the South. Around the turn of the century Southern states passed constitutions and laws that disenfranchised most black people, and the Jim Crow system of legal discrimination lasted into the 1960s.

A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin began planning the march in December 1961, envisioning protest focused on joblessness and a public works programme to employ black people. Walter Reuther, president of the United Auto Workers, persuaded them to hold the rally at the Lincoln Memorial rather than outside the Capitol, on condition that he pay $19,000 for a sound system.

Thousands travelled to Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, 28 August 1963. Some 450 buses left New York City from Harlem. The authorities prepared for disorder: 5,900 police officers were on duty, 2,000 National Guard soldiers were mustered and the Pentagon readied 19,000 troops. Liquor sales were banned for the first time since Prohibition. Estimates of attendance ran from 200,000 to 300,000, and observers thought 75 to 80 per cent of the marchers were black.

Mahalia Jackson and Marian Anderson sang, and representatives of the sponsoring organisations spoke from the Lincoln Memorial. None of the official speeches was by a woman. John Lewis of SNCC softened his speech at the urging of other leaders, who objected to its attacks on the Kennedy administration's civil rights bill. Roy Wilkins announced that W. E. B. Du Bois had died in Ghana the previous night. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke last. When Mahalia Jackson called out, "Tell them about the dream, Martin!", he departed from his prepared text for the improvised passage that gave the speech its name.

The speakers then met President John F. Kennedy at the White House to discuss proposed civil rights legislation. The march is credited with creating political momentum for the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and with preceding the Selma voting rights movement, whose national coverage contributed to the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Its meaning was contested from the start. Malcolm X called it a picnic and a circus and argued that the leaders had diluted its anger by letting white organisations help plan it.

Randolph and Rustin lost faith in marching on Washington, while King concluded that future marchers must draw attention to economic injustice and organised the Poor People's Campaign of 1967 and 1968. At the fiftieth anniversary march in 2013, President Barack Obama conferred a posthumous Presidential Medal of Freedom on Rustin.
marcha-real: The Marcha Real is among the oldest national anthems in the world. It was first printed in a document dated 1761, Manuel de Espinosa's Book of the Ordinance of Newly Played Military Fife and Drum Calls by The Spanish Infantry, where it is called La Marcha Granadera, the Grenadier March, and Manuel de Espinosa de los Monteros is named as composer. In 1861 a periodical claimed that Frederick II of Prussia had composed it, and in 1864 Col. Antonio Vallecillo said he had given it to the Count of Colomera, who was learning Prussian tactics by order of King Charles III. This story, which entered the Enciclopedia Espasa in 1908, is spurious.

In 1770 Charles III declared the Marcha de Granaderos the official Honor March, formalising its use in public on solemn occasions. It became the official Spanish anthem during the reign of Queen Isabella II. After the 1868 Revolution General Juan Prim organised a contest for a new anthem in 1870, and over 400 compositions were submitted, but the jury advised that the Marcha de Granaderos was already regarded as the official anthem, and the contest was suspended. A Royal Circular Order of 27 August 1908 made the score orchestrated by Bartolomé Pérez Casas the official version.

The present version was written by Francisco Grau and has been official since the Royal Decree of 10 October 1997, when Spain bought the author rights from Pérez Casas's heirs for 130 million pesetas. It is sixteen bars long, in two sections of four repeated bars each, in B-flat major, and lasts 52 seconds. The full version is the honours music for the King.

The Marcha Real is one of only three national anthems, with those of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo, with no official lyrics. Words have been written for it, including verses by Eduardo Marquina for the silver wedding anniversary of Alfonso XIII, a Carlist version, and lyrics by José María Pemán adapted to the ideology of General Francisco Franco, but none was made official. During the Second Republic the Himno de Riego was the republic's anthem. The Marcha Real has been played without words since 1978.
marche: Marche is bordered by Emilia-Romagna and San Marino to the north, Tuscany and Umbria to the west, Lazio to the south-west, Abruzzo to the south and the Adriatic Sea to the east. It covers 9,366 square kilometres. Most of it is mountainous or hilly, and only Monte Vettore, at 2,476 metres, rises above 2,400 metres. The coastline is 173 kilometres long and mostly flat and straight. The name is the plural of the medieval word marca, a march or border zone, and first referred to border territories of the Holy Roman Empire such as the March of Ancona.

In ancient times the region was known as Picenum, and in the Iron Age it was almost entirely inhabited by the Picentes. In the fourth century BCE the Senones, a tribe of Gauls, occupied the north. After the Battle of Sentinum in 295 BCE the Romans founded numerous colonies there, linked to Rome by the Via Flaminia and the Via Salaria. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the Goths invaded, and it was later part of the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna, with Ancona, Fano, Pesaro, Rimini and Senigallia forming the Pentapolis. Charlemagne conquered it in the late eighth century, and between the ninth and eleventh centuries the marches of Camerino, Fermo and Ancona were created.

Marche was nominally part of the Papal States, but most of it was held by local lords while the main cities ruled themselves as free communes. In the twelfth century the commune of Ancona resisted both Frederick Barbarossa and the Republic of Venice as a maritime republic. In the Renaissance rival families such as the Malatesta and the house of Montefeltro of Urbino fought over the region, and the Duchy of Urbino, the last independent entity, was dissolved in 1631. After Napoleon's defeat the region returned to papal rule until 4 November 1860, when a plebiscite annexed it to the unified Kingdom of Italy.

Marche is one of the twenty regions of Italy, with Ancona as its capital and largest city and a population of nearly 1.5 million. It is divided into five provinces: Ancona, Ascoli Piceno, Fermo, Macerata, and Pesaro and Urbino. Urbino, a major centre of Renaissance history, was the birthplace of Raphael, and the region is also the birthplace of Donato Bramante, Giacomo Leopardi, Gioachino Rossini and Maria Montessori. Castelfidardo is a centre for making accordions.
marcianopolis: The city was given its name after the Second Dacian War, which ended in 106, in honour of Trajan's sister Ulpia Marciana. An important strategic centre, it belonged to Roman Thrace until 187 to 193 and then to Moesia Inferior. Its prosperity under the Severan dynasty was ended by a Gothic raid in 248 to 249 and by later invasions from the north, and the Romans repulsed another Gothic attack on the town in 267 or 268, in the reign of Gallienus.

Under Diocletian it was rebuilt thoroughly in the late 3rd and early 4th centuries and grew at the expense of neighbouring Odessos, the present Varna. It was an important episcopal centre, and during the war of Emperor Valens with the Goths from 366 to 369 it served as a temporary capital of the empire; a source of the time calls it the largest city of Thrace. The Huns under Attila destroyed it in 447, immediately after the battle of the Utus river. Justinian I restored and fortified it.

The Avars sacked it in 587, though the Byzantines retook it at once, and the Byzantine army was quartered there in 596 before crossing the Danube against them. An Avar raid finally destroyed the city in 614 to 615, though it was still marked on maps long after.

The Slavs who settled in the Balkans in the 7th century called the ruins Devina, and the site lies at modern Devnya in Bulgaria. Partly excavated, it has an amphitheatre, streets and a basilica found in the 20th century. The mosaic floors of the House of Antiope, a villa of the late 3rd or early 4th century, are shown in the Museum of Mosaics, some of them where they were laid.
marco-antonio-bragadin: Bragadin was born in Venice on 21 April 1523. After a short time as a lawyer in 1543 he turned to the navy, held several posts on the Venetian galleys and joined the Fanti da Mar, the marines of the Republic of Venice. Back in Venice he served among the city's magistrates and was made a galley governor in 1560 and again in 1566, though he never actually commanded a ship.

In 1569 he was elected Captain of the Kingdom of Cyprus and moved to Famagusta, then a rich port, taking the civil governorship of the whole island while a clash with the Ottoman fleet was expected. He strengthened the harbour's defences, among them the Martinengo bastion. The Ottomans landed on 3 July 1570 and took Nicosia after a two-month siege, and the severed head of its viceroy, Niccolò Dandolo, was sent to Bragadin.

The siege of Famagusta began on 17 September 1570. Bragadin led the defence with Lorenzo Tiepolo, Captain of Paphos, and General Astorre Baglioni; Venetian chroniclers put the garrison at about 6,000 against some 100,000 Ottoman troops with 1,500 cannons and about 150 ships blockading the port. The besiegers filled the ground before the walls with earth and dug tunnels to undermine them. In July 1571 they broke into the citadel and were driven back only with heavy losses, and on 1 August, with food and ammunition running out and no relief from Venice, Bragadin asked for terms.

The terms promised the Westerners safe passage to Crete, and the evacuation went smoothly for four days. At the surrender ceremony on 5 August the Ottoman commander, Mustafa, accused Bragadin of murdering Turkish prisoners and hiding munitions, cut off his right ear and had his guards cut off the other and his nose, and the Christians still in the city were massacred. After two weeks in prison Bragadin was flayed alive in the main square. In 1580 Girolamo Polidori stole his skin from the arsenal of Constantinople, and it now lies in the Basilica di San Giovanni e Paolo. Historians debate why Venice sent no help from Souda in Crete.
marco-aurelio-soto: Marco Aurelio Soto Martínez was born in Tegucigalpa on 13 November 1846, the son of Máximo Soto and Francisca Martínez. When he was nine years old he moved with his father to Guatemala, where he studied and qualified as a lawyer. As a young man he wrote literary and political articles, the political ones inspired by the principles of the revolution of 1871 in Guatemala, which he supported.

General Justo Rufino Barrios appointed Soto Sub-secretary of State in Guatemala. When the minister was relieved of office, Soto took charge of the Ministry of the Interior, Justice and Ecclesiastical Affairs, and he was soon appointed to it permanently. He later also held the ministries of Foreign Affairs and Public Instruction, and in the latter he organised the first public primary, secondary and vocational schooling founded on modern principles. In 1876 he was sent as Minister Plenipotentiary to secure peace between Guatemala and El Salvador, and on 8 May he signed the Soto-Ulloa Treaty at Santa Ana.

Soto became interim president of Honduras in 1876 and constitutional president in 1877, a term extended by his re-election until 1883. With the help of his cousin Ramón Rosa he launched administrative, political, economic and social reforms. His government improved communications and the mail service, built some railways and a telegraph system, began a large programme of education and founded the Biblioteca Nacional de Honduras in 1880. Honduras nevertheless remained poorly developed, since it lacked export products such as coffee to pay for new infrastructure.

His presidency came under threat from the Guatemalan government of Justo Rufino Barrios, and Soto left the country, handing it to a council of ministers. He died in Paris on 25 February 1908, at the age of 61.
marco-polo: Marco Polo was born around 1254 in Venice, though the exact date and place of birth are not recorded in the archives. A few theories place his birth on the island of Korčula or in Constantinople, but most scholars have not accepted them. His father Niccolò Polo was a merchant who traded with the Near East. Niccolò and his brother Maffeo left on a trading voyage before Marco's birth and, according to The Travels of Marco Polo, passed through much of Asia and met Kublai Khan.

Marco's mother died, and an aunt and uncle raised him. He learned mercantile subjects such as foreign currency, appraising and the handling of cargo ships, and he learned little or no Latin. Around 1269 Niccolò returned to Venice and met his 15-year-old son for the first time.

Marco travelled through Asia along the Silk Road with his father and uncle until they reached Cathay and the court of Kublai Khan. Kublai was impressed by Marco's intelligence and humility and appointed him a foreign emissary, sent on diplomatic missions through the empire and Southeast Asia. He lived in the emperor's lands for 17 years. Around 1291 the Polos offered to accompany the Mongol princess Kököchin to Persia, where they arrived around 1293. They then went overland to Constantinople and Venice, returning home after many years away.

Venice was then at war with Genoa. Marco joined the war effort and was captured by the Genoese. In prison he dictated his stories to a cellmate, Rustichello da Pisa. He was released in 1299, became a wealthy merchant, married and had three children. He died in 1324 and was buried in the church of San Lorenzo in Venice.

The Travels of Marco Polo, also called Il Milione, was written down by Rustichello in Franco-Venetian as Devisement du Monde, probably as a handbook for merchants. There is no authoritative version, because the early manuscripts differ significantly, and about 150 copies in various languages are known. The first English translation, by John Frampton, was published in 1579.

Polo was not the first European in China, but he was the first to leave a detailed chronicle. He gave the first Western record of porcelain, gunpowder and paper money. Sceptics have pointed to omissions, such as the Great Wall, tea and chopsticks, and Frances Wood argued in 1995 that he went no farther than Persia. Supporters reply that the Great Wall known today is a Ming structure built two centuries later. His book inspired Christopher Columbus, who owned a copy with handwritten annotations.
marco-polo-bridge-incident: Tensions between Japan and the Republic of China had been high since the Japanese invasion of Manchuria in 1931 and the creation of the puppet state of Manchukuo in 1932. China agreed to the Tanggu Truce in 1933, and a series of limited armed clashes followed, each ending in uneasy peace. Under the Boxer Protocol of 7 September 1901, foreign powers could station guards at twelve points on the railways between Beijing and Tianjin. By July 1937 Japan had an estimated 7,000 to 15,000 men in China, mostly along the railways, far above those limits, and had already surrounded Beijing and Tianjin.

On the night of 7 July Japanese units from Fengtai held exercises, and at about 23:00 they and Chinese forces outside Wanping, a walled town 16.4 km south-west of Beijing, exchanged fire. The cause remains unknown. A Japanese private, Shimura Kikujiro, had failed to return to his post, and the Japanese demanded to enter Wanping to search for him. The Chinese refused. He had merely lost his way and was found shortly after, but the Japanese now sought the soldiers who had fired the first shots.

Later that night Japanese infantry tried to breach Wanping's walls and were repulsed. At around 04:45 on 8 July a shot was heard and both sides opened fire. Colonel Ji Xingwen held the bridge with about 100 men and reinforcements, at heavy cost. A ceasefire was agreed in Beiping on 11 July, negotiated mainly by General Song Zheyuan, but it did not last.

Both central governments hardened their positions. Tokyo, despite an order of 8 July from Major General Kanji Ishiwara's faction to avoid force, approved reinforcements, and by 20 July Japan had more than 180,000 personnel in the Beiping-Tianjin area. Chiang Kai-shek sent Central Army divisions into Hebei, and in the Lushan Statement of 17 July called for total resistance. Ambushes at Langfang on 25 July and at the Guanganmen gate on 26 July ended the talks. Japan attacked Beiping and Tianjin on 28 July and took Beiping and the Taku Forts on 29 and 30 July. Fighting at Shanghai followed in August.

Historians have debated whether the incident was planned, as the earlier Mukden incident was. Jim Huffman says that notion has been widely rejected, and modern scholarship such as Nobu Iwatani's treats the shooting as a trifling event that grew through mutual distrust. In China the incident raised patriotic feeling and brought a temporary unity among rival groups. The bridge was renovated in 1987, and the People's Anti-Japanese War Museum was built near it.
marcomannic-wars: The war against Parthia of 161 to 166, fought under the joint rule of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, ended successfully, but the returning troops brought the Antonine Plague, which killed an estimated 7 to 8 million people. At the same time the Goths began to move south-east from the mouth of the River Vistula, putting pressure on the Germanic tribes to the north and east, and raids crossed the Danube and the Rhine. Until then the Marcomanni and Quadi had generally enjoyed friendly relations and trade with the Empire. The Marcomanni sought incorporation into the Empire on favourable economic terms, which Marcus was unwilling to accept.

In late 166 thousands of Langobardi and Lacringi crossed into Pannonia and were quickly defeated, and the governor Marcus Iallius Bassus negotiated a truce with eleven tribes. The plague delayed a punitive expedition until 168, when Marcus and Lucius Verus set up headquarters at Aquileia; Verus died of a stroke in January 169. In autumn 169 Marcus resumed the campaign, selling imperial property to pay for it. The Marcomanni under King Ballomar then defeated a Roman force of 20,000 near Carnuntum, destroyed Oderzo and besieged Aquileia, the first hostile incursion into Italy since the Cimbri in 101 BCE.

Command passed to Tiberius Claudius Pompeianus, with the future emperor Pertinax under him, and by late 171 the invaders had been expelled. Rome signed treaties with the Quadi and the Iazyges and in 172 crossed the Danube and subdued the Marcomanni, and Marcus took the title Germanicus.

In 173 the Legio XII Fulminata, surrounded in a campaign against the Quadi, was saved by a storm, the Miracle of the Rain: Cassius Dio credited an Egyptian magician invoking Mercury, and the Christian writer Tertullian credited Christian prayer. The Iazyges surrendered in 175, and their king, Zanticus, returned 100,000 Roman prisoners. The revolt of Avidius Cassius in Syria interrupted plans for new provinces named Marcomannia and Sarmatia.

The Quadi rebelled in 177 and the Marcomanni joined them, and Marcus reached Carnuntum in August 178 for a second campaign. He died at Vindobona on 17 March 180. His son Commodus ignored his generals' advice, negotiated peace with the Marcomanni and Quadi and held a triumph on 22 October 180.

The wars showed the weakness of Rome's northern defences, and afterwards 16 of the Empire's 33 legions were stationed along the Rhine and Danube. Germanic settlement in frontier regions grew; settlers at Ravenna rebelled and briefly seized the city, and Marcus banned further settlement of barbarians in Italy. The wars are said to have foreshadowed the invasions of the fourth and fifth centuries, and Marcus began writing his Meditations during these campaigns.
marcomer: The invasion of 388 is known from Gregory of Tours, who quoted the lost work of Sulpicius Alexander. It came while the usurper Magnus Maximus, master of Roman Gaul, was surrounded by Theodosius I at Aquileia. Marcomer, Sunno and Genobaud broke through the limes into Germania Inferior and Gallia Belgica, killed many people, laid waste the most fruitful lands and threw Cologne into panic. Most of the Franks then went back over the Rhine with their booty, but some stayed in the forest called Silva Carbonaria.

The Roman generals Nanninus and Quintinus attacked those who remained and killed many of them. Quintinus then crossed the Rhine to punish the Franks in their own country, but his army was surrounded and beaten, some soldiers drowning in the marshes, and few returned. After the fall of Magnus Maximus, Marcomer and Sunno met the Frankish general Arbogastes, a magister militum in Roman service, and gave hostages as usual.
A few years later Arbogastes, who had by then seized power in the West, crossed the Rhine with a Roman army. Marcomer appeared as leader of the Chatti and Ampsivarii, but the two sides did not fight.

The poet Claudian records that Marcomer was captured by the Romans and exiled to a villa in Tuscany. His brother Sunno crossed the Rhine to take over his band but was killed by his own people. The later Liber Historiae Francorum made Marcomer a descendant of the Trojans and a son of a king called Priam, and says he urged the Franks to live under one king, proposing his son Pharamond, who is first mentioned in that work and whom scholars do not treat as a historical figure. Modern scholars such as Edward James do not accept this account as historical.
marcos-perez-jimenez: Marcos Evangelista Pérez Jiménez was born on 25 April 1914 in Michelena, Táchira State, the son of a farmer and a schoolteacher from Cúcuta, Colombia. He graduated from the Military Academy of Venezuela in 1934 at the top of his class and studied later at Chorrillos Military School in Peru. In 1945 he took part in a coup that installed Rómulo Betancourt, and elections in 1947 brought Rómulo Gallegos to the presidency.

Fears of cuts in soldiers' pay and a lack of modern equipment led him and Carlos Delgado Chalbaud to stage another coup in 1948, after which a junta suppressed political parties and banished the Communist Party. After Delgado Chalbaud was murdered following a clumsily arranged kidnapping, Pérez Jiménez pulled the strings behind the puppet president Germán Suárez Flamerich.

The junta called an election in 1952 for a Constituent Assembly. When early results showed the opposition ahead, it halted the count and on 2 December 1952 announced a majority for its own front, then dissolved itself and made Pérez provisional president. The Assembly, from which the opposition had withdrawn, elected him president on 19 April 1953 and enacted a constitution giving him virtually unlimited powers. He renamed the country the Republic of Venezuela. Oil revenue paid for roads, bridges, government buildings, large public housing complexes and industries such as hydroelectricity and steel, and the economy grew rapidly.

His secret police, the Seguridad Nacional, pursued, imprisoned and often tortured opponents, who were painted as communists. In 1957 he held a plebiscite on another term, which by all accounts was rigged. On 23 January 1958, after mass demonstrations for democratic reform, a military revolt deposed him.

Pérez Jiménez went to the Dominican Republic and then Miami, and in 1963 was extradited to Venezuela on charges of embezzling $200 million. After five years awaiting trial he was convicted of embezzlement and sentenced to four years, which he had already served, and was exiled to Spain. In 1968 he was elected to the Senate, but was kept from taking office by a law excluding former prisoners. He died near Madrid on 20 September 2001. His supporters formed the Nationalist Civic Crusade, which held seats in Congress from 1968 to 1978, and the documentary Tiempos de dictadura, directed by Carlos Oteyza, treats his period in power.
marcus-aemilius-lepidus-triumvir: Lepidus was the son of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, consul in 78 BCE, who led an unsuccessful rebellion against the optimates in 78 to 77 BCE and died in Sardinia. He joined the College of Pontiffs as a child and began his career as a triumvir monetalis, overseeing coinage, from about 62 to 58 BCE. He married Junia Secunda, half-sister of Marcus Junius Brutus.

He became one of Julius Caesar's strongest supporters. As praetor in 49 BCE he was put in charge of Rome while Caesar fought Pompey in Greece. As propraetor of Hispania Citerior he settled a rebellion by negotiation and limited force, and was granted a triumph. He was consul in 46 BCE and twice served as Caesar's magister equitum, or deputy. After Caesar's assassination on 15 March 44 BCE he succeeded him as pontifex maximus.

Sent to negotiate with Sextus Pompey, Lepidus then governed Hispania and Narbonese Gaul. When Mark Antony was defeated at the Battle of Mutina, Lepidus engaged in talks with him, and large parts of his army joined Antony. Lepidus, Antony and Octavian formed the Second Triumvirate under the Lex Titia of 43 BCE, a legal body with consular power for five years that sidelined the consuls and the Senate. Lepidus gave up seven legions to the others and agreed to the proscriptions that killed Cicero. Cassius Dio hints that he helped his brother Lucius Aemilius Lepidus Paullus, who was also proscribed, to escape.

After Philippi, in which he took no part, he received Africa as proconsul. In 36 BCE he raised fourteen legions against Sextus Pompey in the Sicilian revolt, then disputed with Octavian who held authority in Sicily. His legions defected to Octavian, and on 22 September 36 BCE he lost all his offices except that of pontifex maximus and was confined at Circeii.

His son Marcus Aemilius Lepidus Minor joined a plot against Octavian after 31 BCE and was executed, but Lepidus was left unharmed. He lived on in obscurity, and Augustus is said to have asked for his vote last in the Senate. He died peacefully, in late 13 or early 12 BCE, and Augustus was elected pontifex maximus on 6 March 12 BCE.

Lepidus has usually been portrayed as the weakest triumvir. Cicero and Decimus Brutus, who called him a weathercock, attacked him, and Shakespeare shows him as a slight, unmeritable man. His biographer Richard D. Weigel argues that this evidence is largely politically motivated and that his career was no more inconsistent than those of his colleagues.
marcus-aurelius: Marcus was born in Rome on 26 April 121, the son of the praetor Marcus Annius Verus, whose family came from Ucubi in Baetica, and of his wife. His father probably died in 125 or 126, and Marcus was raised by his grandfather Marcus Annius Verus, who held legal authority over him. In late 136 Hadrian chose Lucius Ceionius Commodus as his heir, apparently with the aim of eventually placing the young Marcus on the throne, but Commodus died in 138. Hadrian then adopted Antoninus Pius, who in turn adopted Marcus and Lucius, the son of Commodus. Marcus studied Greek and Latin under tutors including Herodes Atticus and Marcus Cornelius Fronto, and in 145 he married Antoninus's daughter Faustina.

After Antoninus died in 161 the Senate granted Marcus the name Augustus. He is said to have been compelled to take power, and his Stoic training made it clear that it was his duty. He soon betrothed his daughter Annia Lucilla to Lucius Verus, and the two emperors were popular for their lack of pomp. Marcus spent much of his time on law, giving particular attention to the manumission of slaves, the guardianship of orphans and minors, and the choice of city councillors; jurists called him an emperor most skilled in the law.

In late summer or early autumn of 161 Vologases IV of Parthia entered Armenia, then a Roman client state, and installed his own king. Marcus Sedatius Severianus, governor of Cappadocia, led a legion into Armenia and was trapped at Elegeia by the Parthian general Chosrhoes; he killed himself and his legion was massacred. The Parthian War lasted from 161 to 166. On the northern frontier the situation looked grave, with a frontier post destroyed and peoples of central and northern Europe in turmoil, and Marcus fought the Germanic tribes from 166 to 180. He reduced the silver purity of the denarius.

Persecution of Christians appears to have increased during his reign, though how far the emperor directed or knew of it is unclear and much debated by historians. He mentions Christians once in his Meditations, criticising what he saw as their theatrical approach to martyrdom.

Marcus died on 17 March 180, aged 58, of unknown causes, in his military quarters either at Vindobona or near Sirmium. He was deified at once, and his ashes were returned to Rome. His Meditations, written in Greek on campaign between 170 and 180 for his own guidance, is one of the most important sources for ancient Stoic philosophy. In Rome his bronze equestrian statue, made around 175 and the only Roman equestrian statue to survive, and his column, which celebrates his victory over the Sarmatians and Germanic tribes in 176, still stand.
marcus-aurelius-cotta: Cotta came from a distinguished plebeian family. He was the son of Lucius Aurelius Cotta, consul in 119 BCE; his older brother Gaius Aurelius Cotta was consul in 75 BCE, the year before him, and his younger brother Lucius Aurelius Cotta held the office in 65 BCE. Aurelia Cotta, the mother of Julius Caesar, was his half-sister. He climbed the cursus honorum, the sequence of military and administrative posts held by aspiring politicians, and is assumed to have been praetor in 77 BCE.

His consulship coincided with the crisis brought on by Rome's acquisition of the new province of Bithynia, which King Mithridates VI of Pontus invaded. Cotta received Bithynia as his proconsular command, with a fleet to protect it, and left for the east towards the end of his year in office. The plan was for him to tie down the Pontic fleet from Chalcedon while his colleague Lucius Licinius Lucullus marched through Phrygia to invade Pontus by land.

Mithridates instead marched rapidly westward and attacked Cotta, who lost sixty-four ships, captured or burnt, and three thousand men, and was driven behind the walls of Chalcedon. He remained there under siege until Lucullus trapped the Pontic army before Cyzicus, where famine and disease destroyed it and Mithridates fled by sea. From Nicomedia, Cotta watched the king escape down the Bosporus to Heraclea Pontica, which he reinforced with 4,000 troops.

Joined by Lucullus at Nicomedia in 73 BCE, Cotta was given the task of securing the rear by taking Heraclea. After reducing the Pontic coast he besieged the city for two years before capturing and sacking it. During the campaign he dismissed one of his quaestors, P. Oppius, charging him with bribery and conspiracy. In Rome he was at first widely acclaimed for the victory, but Gaius Papirius Carbo later accused him of appropriating the booty, and his conviction and expulsion from the Senate were a signal mark of disgrace.
marcus-claudius-marcellus: Little is known of Marcellus' early years, since ancient writers were more concerned with his military exploits. The fullest account is Plutarch's Life of Marcellus. Scholars are certain he was born before 268 BCE, because he had to be over 42 when elected consul in 222 BCE and was elected to a fifth consulship in 208 BCE after the age of 60. According to Plutarch he was a skilled fighter in his youth, raised for military service, and he saved the life of his brother Otacilius when they were surrounded by enemy soldiers. He served in the First Punic War and was elected curule aedile in 226 BCE.

In 222 BCE Marcellus was consul, and at Clastidium he killed the Gallic king Viridomarus in single combat, taking his armour as the spolia opima, which he dedicated to Jupiter Feretrius. Plutarch's detailed account may have been exaggerated to glorify him, and Polybius does not mention the spolia opima in relation to Marcellus. In the Second Punic War, after the defeat at Cannae, he held Nola against Hannibal, a victory important as the first check Hannibal had received.

Sent to Sicily in 214 BCE, he stormed Leontini and besieged Syracuse, which had gone over to the Carthaginian side; the siege lasted two years, partly because of the machines of Archimedes. The city fell in the summer of 212 BCE after a night attack at a weak point in its walls. Archimedes was killed, which Marcellus regretted, and Greek art taken as plunder went to Rome. His enemies denied him a triumph, and when he was elected consul for 210 BCE, Sicilian cities complained of his brutality. In Apulia he kept Hannibal in check by attrition, without a decisive battle.

Elected consul for the fifth time for 208 BCE, Marcellus took command at Venusia. On a reconnaissance with his fellow consul Titus Quinctius Crispinus and 220 horsemen, he was ambushed by Numidian cavalry and impaled by a spear. Crispinus died of his wounds. Hannibal is said to have allowed him a proper funeral and sent his ashes to his son in a silver urn, though two ancient writers say they never arrived. The loss of both consuls was a heavy blow to Roman morale. He is known as the Sword of Rome, and the only one of the three men said to have won the spolia opima whose achievement is historically confirmed.
marcus-furius-camillus: The traditional account of Camillus comes from Livy and from Plutarch's Life, both based on an annalistic tradition that made him the dominant figure of his period. Livy organised his fifth and sixth books around his career. Modern scholars are doubtful of his supposed exploits and think many wrongly attributed or wholly fictitious, though most believe that he existed, since the fasti record his importance in public life. Mary Beard wrote that he is probably not much less fictional than the first Romulus. The cognomen Camillus derives from the title of an aristocratic youth who helped in religious duties. He is first firmly recorded in public office in 401 BCE, as consular tribune, and again in 398 BCE against the Falisci and the Capenates.

As dictator, Camillus was supposed to have completed the campaign against Veii that saw the city captured in 396 BCE. Livy's story of the ten-year siege is mostly myth and modelled on the Trojan war, with the Alban Lake rising, a tunnel to drain it and Camillus persuading Veii's goddess Juno Regina to move to Rome. Livy reports that the free population was sold into slavery and the land resettled with Roman citizens.

In 394 BCE he supposedly secured the surrender of Falerii Veteres after refusing to accept pupils from a schoolmaster as hostages. He was then reportedly convicted and exiled, a story that historians think was invented to place him away from Rome during the Gallic sack.

In Livy's account Camillus was recalled from exile at Ardea, appointed dictator again, and returned with an army as a ransom of gold was being weighed out, defeating the Gauls and recovering it. Ogilvie called this one of the most daring fabrications in Roman history. Polybius reports instead that the Gauls occupied the city for about seven months before the Romans bought them off.

Camillus is also said to have opposed a plan to move the city to Veii, to have taken Tusculum in 381 BCE and to have been dictator in 368 BCE when the Licinio-Sextian rogations were passed, and then to have reconciled patricians and plebeians and built a temple to Concordia. Scholars think much of this narrative cannot be accepted as it stands.

According to Roman tradition Camillus died during an epidemic in 365 BCE, though later annalists may simply have assumed it. By the late republic the Romans believed he had held six consular tribunates and been dictator five times, and he was hailed as the second founder of the city. A bronze statue of him stood on the rostra in the Forum. Livy cites him eight times as an example to follow, and his memory became part of the public image of Augustus.
marcus-garvey: Marcus Mosiah Garvey was born on 17 August 1887 in Saint Ann's Bay, in the British colony of Jamaica. His paternal great-grandfather had been born into slavery, and his Irish surname came from the family's former enslavers. He was apprenticed in the printing trade and in 1905 moved to Kingston, where he became the first Afro-Jamaican foreman at the printing division of the P. A. Benjamin Manufacturing Company. In 1910 he went to Costa Rica, where in 1911 he launched a bilingual newspaper criticising the United Fruit Company's treatment of workers.

Garvey returned to Jamaica in July 1914 and founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association. In 1916 he moved to the United States, lodging in Harlem, and toured 38 states as a speaker. In 1918 he launched the weekly Negro World. He argued that black people should be financially independent of white-dominated societies and set up the Negro Factories Corporation and the Black Star Line, a shipping company of which he became president in 1919. He called for a united Africa and for part of the diaspora to migrate there. His readiness to deal with white racists such as the Ku Klux Klan, who shared his separatism, set him against W. E. B. Du Bois, who promoted integration.

In January 1922 he was arrested for mail fraud over the advertised sale of stock in a ship the company did not yet own. He represented himself at his trial in 1923 and was found guilty, while his three co-defendants were acquitted. He served nearly two years in the Atlanta penitentiary, and President Calvin Coolidge commuted his sentence. He was deported to Jamaica in 1927.

In Jamaica Garvey founded the People's Political Party in 1929. He moved to London in 1935, and died there on 10 June 1940, aged 52, after a stroke. His body was returned to Jamaica in 1964, and he was the first person formally recognised there as a National Hero. Critics attacked his collaboration with white supremacists, his violent rhetoric and his prejudice against mixed-race people and Jews, while others praised him for encouraging pride and self-worth amid poverty, discrimination and colonialism. His ideas influenced Rastafari, the Nation of Islam and the Black Power movement.
marcus-julius-cottius: Cottius was the son and successor of King Donnus, who ruled the Celtic and Ligurian inhabitants of the mountains then known as the Alpes Taurinae (Taurine Alps). Coins suggest that Donnus had established friendly relations with Julius Caesar, who needed to cross the kingdom in 58 BCE on his way to Gaul and agreed with Donnus to move his troops along the king's road and to have a new paved road built.

After Caesar's death many Gallic tribes rebelled, and Augustus put the revolts down. The destruction of the Salassi and the subjugation of the Ligurian tribes in 14 BCE appear to have persuaded Cottius to use his control of the Alpine passes as leverage for an alliance that would keep him in power. The historian Ammianus Marcellinus remarked that even after Gaul was subdued, Cottius alone continued to rely on the strategic position of his kingdom.

The alliance was made in 13 or 12 BCE. Cottius became a client ruler of Rome, giving up part of his authority in return for keeping his autonomy and his hereditary position, an arrangement that Millar called a dual sovereignty. He received Roman citizenship, took the name Marcus Julius Cottius, and was made praefectus civitatium, a governor of several tribes. Such posts usually had a fixed term, but his was permanent and hereditary, and the 14 tribes under him joined the Alpine regiments of the Roman army.

Cottius grew rich from the trade between Italy and Gaul, as his pass over the Montgenevre was the main route between them. His capital, Segusium, was adorned with public monuments, and the region later had a Roman amphitheatre and aqueduct. His people adopted Roman customs, laws and language while keeping their own religious cults.

Cottius was remembered as a fair king with foresight, and his mausoleum was still visited in the 4th century CE. His son Gaius Julius Donnus II succeeded him, followed by his grandson Marcus Julius Cottius II, who was given more land by the emperors Claudius and Nero and, according to Cassius Dio, was then called king for the first time. Another son, the centurion Julius Vestalis, retook the Danube post of Aegyssus from the Getae, a deed praised by the poet Ovid in his Epistulae ex Ponto. Strabo called the region the country of Cottius.
marcus-junius-brutus: Marcus Junius Brutus belonged to the plebeian gens Junia, whose founder, Lucius Junius Brutus, was decisive in the overthrow of the last Roman king and was one of the first two consuls of the Republic in 509 BCE. Brutus's father was killed by Pompey in 77 BCE. His mother, Servilia, was the half-sister of Cato the Younger and later Julius Caesar's mistress. Some ancient sources raised the possibility that Caesar was his real father, but modern scholars largely reject this as chronologically improbable, since Caesar was only fifteen when Brutus was born.

In 54 BCE Brutus served as triumvir monetalis and issued denarii with the portraits of two ancestors honoured as defenders of liberty, Lucius Junius Brutus and Gaius Servilius Ahala. In 52 he wrote a pamphlet opposing demands that Pompey be made dictator.

When Caesar's Civil War began in January 49 BCE, Brutus sided with Pompey, his father's killer, perhaps because his closest allies, among them Cato and Cicero, also did. After Pompey's defeat at Pharsalus on 9 August 48 BCE, Brutus wrote to Caesar, who welcomed him into his camp. Caesar later made him governor of Cisalpine Gaul and praetor urbanus for 44.

By autumn 45 BCE public opinion of Caesar was souring, and ancient authors report graffiti recalling Lucius Junius Brutus and taunts that Marcus was failing his ancestors. In February 44 Caesar accepted the title dictator perpetuo. Brutus took a leading part in the assassination on the Ides of March (15 March) 44 BCE. Cicero brokered a settlement with an amnesty for the assassins and ratification of Caesar's acts for two years.

Brutus and Cassius left Rome in April 44 BCE and went east. After Octavian had a law passed retroactively making the conspirators murderers, a second civil war followed. At the two battles of Philippi in October 42 BCE the Caesarians decisively defeated their armies, and Brutus took his own life.

His name has become a byword for betrayal, and Dante placed him in the lowest circle of Hell. Others have praised him as a committed republican who fought for freedom against tyranny. Historians hold no consensus on his actions, and Ronald Syme observed that to judge Brutus because he failed is simply to judge from the results.
marcus-licinius-crassus: Crassus belonged to the gens Licinia, an old and highly respected plebeian family, and was the second of three sons of the senator Publius Licinius Crassus. His father and younger brother were killed, or took their own lives, in Rome in the winter of 87 to 86 BCE when hunted down by supporters of Gaius Marius. Plutarch says his wealth was acquired rather than inherited and that he was raised in modest circumstances. He fled to Hispania, where he raised 2,500 men, and later joined Sulla. At the Battle of the Colline Gate he commanded the right flank, whose success helped Sulla win the battle.

Crassus rebuilt his family's wealth by buying the seized property of Sulla's victims at discounted auctions. Pliny the Elder put his wealth at about 200 million sesterces. Plutarch says that he bought burnt and collapsing houses cheaply and rebuilt them with slave labour.

As praetor in 73 BCE he was sent by the Senate against Spartacus after several legions had been defeated. When part of his army fled, he revived decimation, the execution of one man in ten, chosen by lot. In the battle at the Silarius river he won a decisive victory, and Spartacus is believed to have been killed. Crassus ordered the six thousand captured slaves crucified along the Via Appia. He and Pompey were consuls in 70 BCE and were not friendly in office.

In 65 BCE Crassus was censor and acted as Julius Caesar's patron. Caesar's mediation between Crassus and Pompey led to the First Triumvirate in 60 BCE. After the Luca Conference in 56 BCE, a law assigned Syria to Crassus.

As governor of Syria, Crassus crossed the Euphrates to attack Parthia, seeking riches and a victory to match those of Pompey and Caesar. At the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE, Parthian horse archers defeated his heavy infantry. His son Publius died in the battle, and a fight broke out at a parley with the Parthian general Surena, in which Crassus was killed. A later story says the Parthians poured molten gold into his mouth to mock his greed. His death permanently unravelled the alliance between Caesar and Pompey, and within four years Caesar crossed the Rubicon.
marcus-lollius: Lollius belonged to the plebeian gens Lollia and was probably a new man in politics. He has been identified with the Marcus whom Appian describes as a legate of Marcus Junius Brutus, proscribed after the Battle of Philippi in 42 BCE, who hid as a slave until Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa persuaded Octavian to remove his name from the lists. He fought at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE.

In 25 BCE Augustus made him the first Roman governor of Galatia, formerly a kingdom whose last king, Amyntas, had died. Lollius brought Amyntas's army into the Roman army and founded a Roman colony in the province. He was consul in 21 BCE with his old friend Quintus Aemilius Lepidus, the first of his gens to hold the office, and their names stand on the Pons Fabricius in Rome, whose repairs they approved. As governor of Macedonia in 19/18 BCE he defeated the Thracian Bersi.

As governor of Gaul his legions on the Rhine were defeated by the Sicambri, Tencteri and Usipetes. Suetonius, pairing the clades Lolliana with the disaster of Publius Quinctilius Varus, called it disgraceful rather than dangerous. Tiberius was sent in 15 BCE to recover the standard, and Lollius never again commanded an army, though he stayed on friendly terms with Augustus. In 2/1 BCE Augustus made him tutor to Gaius Caesar on his mission to the East. Lollius was blamed for turning Gaius against Tiberius and accused of taking bribes from the Parthian king Phraates; according to different sources he then poisoned himself, killed himself in some other way, or died of natural causes.

Pliny the Elder called Lollius a hypocrite who cared only for wealth, and Velleius Paterculus, a partisan of Tiberius, described him as greedy and corrupt, while his friend the poet Horace praised him as reliable and above avarice. His fortune passed to his granddaughter Lollia Paulina, who married Caligula. At Sagalassos in Turkey, excavations in 2005 and 2006 found the base of a colossal statue honouring him as the city's patron; its remains are in the Burdur Museum.
marcus-perperna-vento: Both Perperna and Perpenna are attested for his family name, which is of Etruscan origin; Perperna is the more frequent form and the one used in the most reliable inscriptions. Little is known of him before the civil wars. A member of the faction of Cinna and Marius, he governed Sicily as propraetor in the second civil war, but abandoned the island when he heard of the force Sulla sent under Pompey, Sulla's stepson-in-law, to recover Sicily and Africa. Proscribed when Sulla became dictator, he went into exile.

After Sulla's death he was recalled by Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, consul of 78 BCE, and joined his rebellion. When Lepidus was beaten outside Rome by Quintus Lutatius Catulus, the two withdrew through Etruria to Sardinia, where Lepidus died. Perperna took their army to Liguria and, hearing that Pompey was coming with a large army, moved it to Hispania. His soldiers, unhappy with his leadership, threatened to desert to Sertorius unless he led them there, and he yielded, bringing 53 cohorts, though he took it as a humiliation.

Sertorius sent him with 20,000 infantry and 1,500 cavalry to join the legate Gaius Herennius and hold the crossing of the lower Ebro, but Pompey crossed unhindered. Early in 75 BCE Pompey defeated Perperna and Herennius in a bloody battle near Valentia, where Herennius was among 10,000 dead and the city was sacked. Perperna failed to stop Metellus at the time of the Battle of Sucro, and at the Battle of Saguntum, the largest of the war, he lost 6,000 men. In 74 BCE he marched to the western coast and took Portus Cale.

As the war went badly, Perperna fed the jealousy of the Roman nobles around Sertorius and, with them, oppressed the local tribes in his name. He then invited Sertorius to a feast for a supposed victory and gave the signal for his killing there. Sertorius's will named Perperna his chief heir, and the soldiers turned against him. Pompey lured his army into an ambush with ten cohorts as bait and destroyed it. Perperna offered Sertorius's letters, which named contacts at the highest levels in Rome, to save his life; Pompey accepted them, burned them, averting the risk of another civil war, and executed him with all of Sertorius's killers. Plutarch remarked that Perperna was as bad at command as at obeying orders.
marcus-petreius: Petreius came, like Pompey, from Picenum in eastern Italy, and was one of Pompey's clients. He was the first of his family to enter the Senate. The early stages of his career are unclear, but Sallust describes him as a military man who by 62 BCE had thirty years' service as military tribune, prefect and legate behind him. He was praetor no later than 64 BCE, though the year is unknown.

He first served under Pompeius Strabo in the Social War of 91–87 BCE, and from 76 to 71 BCE he was Pompey's legate in Spain against Sertorius. As legate of the consul Gaius Antonius Hybrida he led the Senate's forces against Lucius Sergius Catilina at Pistoria in early 62 BCE, while Hybrida stayed away from the battle with a foot ache. During the consulship of Gaius Julius Caesar in 59 BCE he sided with Marcus Porcius Cato the Younger.

From 55 BCE he and Lucius Afranius governed the Spanish provinces as legates for Pompey, who stayed in Rome. When civil war broke out in 49 BCE they marched against Caesar in Spain and, after early successes, capitulated at Ilerda on 2 August and disbanded their army. Caesar let them go free, and they joined Pompey in Greece. After the Battle of Pharsalus, Petreius and Cato fled from the Peloponnese to North Africa, where he and Titus Labienus again won several successes against Caesar.
