After the Pompeian defeat at Thapsus he fled with King Juba of Numidia. Seeing that their position was hopeless, the two resolved to die on an estate near Zama by fighting a duel. The accounts of their deaths differ. In the version held most likely, one killed the other, and the survivor, failing to stab himself with his sword, had a slave kill him.
marcus-terentius-varro-lucullus: He was born in Rome as Marcus Licinius Lucullus and was later adopted by an otherwise unknown Marcus Terentius Varro, so that inscriptions give his name as M. Terentius M. f. Varro Lucullus; literary texts usually call him simply Lucullus, which has caused confusion with his brother. In the early 90s BCE the two brothers unsuccessfully prosecuted Servilius the Augur, who had earlier prosecuted their father, Lucius Licinius Lucullus, and sent him into exile in Lucania.

When Sulla returned from the East in 83 BCE, Marcus joined him and served as a legatus in northern Italy under his cousin Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius. At Fidentia, with 15 cohorts, he defeated a force of 50 cohorts under a legate of Gnaeus Papirius Carbo. He probably entered the Pontifical College when Sulla enlarged it in 81 BCE. As curule aedile in 79 BCE with his brother he gave games that Cicero long remembered, with revolving stage backdrops and the first fight of an elephant against a steer. As praetor peregrinus in 76 BCE he presided over the trial of Gaius Antonius Hybrida, prosecuted by the young Julius Caesar.

As consul, with Gaius Cassius Longinus, he passed the lex Terentia et Cassia frumentaria, which gave subsidised grain to poor citizens. As governor of Macedonia he campaigned against the Bessi, reached the Danube and took Greek cities that had been bases of Mithridates VI, and he held a triumph in 71 BCE. Recalled to fight Spartacus, he landed at Brundisium, and the news turned Spartacus back to face Crassus in the war's final battle.

In 70 BCE he testified for the prosecution of Verres, and in 66 or 65 BCE he was tried by Gaius Memmius for his acts under Sulla and acquitted. He opposed Catilina in 63 BCE, was the main witness for the defence of the poet Licinius Archias, and in 58 and 57 BCE worked for Cicero's return from exile. When his brother lost his mental powers, Marcus became his guardian, and he buried him at his Tusculan estate in 56 BCE, dying himself not long afterwards.
marcus-vipsanius-agrippa: Agrippa came from a plebeian family of uncertain origin in the Italian countryside, humbler than the great aristocratic houses though wealthy by ordinary standards. Pliny the Elder derived his cognomen from a breech birth and said he was lame as a child. He was the same age as Octavian, the future Augustus, and the two were educated together. In 45 BCE Julius Caesar sent them to study at Apollonia on the Illyrian coast, where news of Caesar's assassination reached them in March 44 BCE. Agrippa and Quintus Salvidienus Rufus advised Octavian to march on Rome with the troops from Macedonia, but Octavian sailed to Italy with a small retinue.

Agrippa helped Octavian raise troops, probably fought at Philippi in 42 BCE and took a major part in the Perusine War. As urban praetor in 40 BCE he defended Italy against Sextus Pompeius and retook Sipontum from Antony. As governor of Transalpine Gaul he put down an Aquitanian rising in 38 BCE and crossed the Rhine. He was consul for 37 BCE, far below the usual minimum age of 43, to prepare the war against Sextus Pompeius, building the harbour of Portus Julius and larger ships with an improved grappling hook. In 36 BCE he won the battles of Mylae and Naulochus and received a naval crown decorated with ships' beaks.

As aedile in 33 BCE he repaired streets and aqueducts, cleaned the Cloaca Maxima and built baths and gardens. At Actium on 2 September 31 BCE the victory is held to have been mainly his, and he built the first Pantheon to mark it. After 23 BCE his powers grew to include proconsular authority and, in 18 BCE, the powers of a tribune; in 21 BCE he married Augustus's daughter Julia the Elder. In 19 BCE he put down a rising of the Cantabrians in Hispania, and from 17 BCE he governed the east a second time.

Agrippa began the conquest of the upper Danube region, which became the province of Pannonia in 13 BCE, and died in Campania in 12 BCE, aged fifty or fifty-one. Augustus gave him a lavish funeral, mourned for over a month and placed his remains in his own mausoleum. Agrippa also wrote on geography; under his supervision Caesar's plan for a survey of the empire was carried out, and a circular chart was set up in the colonnade built by his sister Polla. He was the maternal grandfather of Caligula and the maternal great-grandfather of Nero.
mardavij: Mardavij was born around 890 in Gilan into a Zoroastrian family. His father Ziyar belonged to the Shahanshahvand, a royal clan, and his mother was a sister of the Gilaki ruler Harusindan. His tribe, the Arghich, claimed descent from Arghush Farhadan, a king of Gilan of the time of Kay Khosrow, and he grew up among living memories of the old Iranian empire. Like many Gilaki leaders he entered the service of the Alids who ruled Tabaristan, Gilan and Daylam, and around 913 he joined the army of his kinsman Asfar ibn Shiruya.

In 930 Asfar invaded the lands of the Zaydi ruler Abu Muhammad Hasan ibn Qasim, whom Mardavij badly wounded near Amol, avenging his uncle Harusindan. Asfar made him governor of Zanjan, but during the siege of Tarom, capital of the Sallarid ruler Muhammad bin Musafir, Mardavij turned against him with the help of Muhammad and Makan ibn Kaki, killed Asfar's brother Shirzad and took Asfar's lands, among them Ray, Qazvin, Qom and Karaj. He is said to have worn a crown of Anushirvan at his court.

He defeated and killed Asfar in 931 and took Hamadan, Dinavar, Kashan and Isfahan from the Abbasids, making Isfahan his capital. He hoped to take Baghdad, end the caliphate and be crowned at Ctesiphon. In 933 he made peace with the Samanid ruler Nasr II, giving up Gurgan and paying tribute for Ray, and his troops then advanced as far as Ahvaz and forced Ali ibn Buya in Shiraz to accept his authority again. He had a jewelled golden throne made and a crown said to copy that of Khosrow I.

In January 935, shortly before the Nowruz festival, his Turkic slaves, whom he had treated badly while favouring his Daylamite and Gilaki troops, killed him. His brother Vushmgir succeeded him in northern Iran, while Ali ibn Buya took over his possessions in central and southern Iran. He was buried at Gonbad-e Mardaviz near Rey. Remembered for upholding pre-Islamic Iranian customs, he appeared as a hero in children's magazines in the 1960s, during the Pahlavi era.
mardin: Mardin lies near the Syrian border on a rocky hill near the Tigris River. The old city is built mostly on the southern slope of a long hill topped by a rocky ridge, and the slope descends towards the Mesopotamian plain. The historic citadel occupies the top of the ridge. Houses have several levels and terraces to suit the sloping site, which gives the old city its stepped appearance, and most buildings are of beige limestone quarried locally.

A legal document of the Neo-Assyrian period mentions a road to Mardiānê, commonly identified with Mardin. In the Roman period the city was known as Marida, from a Syriac word meaning fortress. The Byzantine city was captured in 640 by the Muslim commander Iyad ibn Ghanm, and control then passed between the Hamdanids, the Marwanids, the Uqaylids and, from 1085, the Great Seljuks.

From 1103 Mardin was the capital of one of the two main branches of the Artuqid dynasty, an Oghuz Turkish family, under whom many of its mosques and madrasas were built. The last Artuqid ruler, al-Salih, yielded the city to Qara Yusuf of the Qara Qoyunlu in 1408–9. The Aq Qoyunlu held it for the rest of the 15th century, and the Safavid ruler Ismail I captured it in 1507. The Ottomans forced its surrender in late 1516 or early 1517.

Mardin kept large Syriac and Armenian populations and was a centre of several churches. On the eve of the First World War it had over 12,000 Syriacs and over 7,500 Armenians. In the war it was one of the sites of the Syriac and Armenian genocides. In 1923 it became the capital of a province of the same name.

Mardin is known for the Artuqid architecture of its old city. Its landmarks include the Great Mosque of Mardin, the Sultan İsa Medrese of 1385 and Mardin Castle. The Syriac Orthodox Saffron Monastery stands about 5 kilometres to the south-east. In February 2000 the Turkish Ministry of Culture placed the city and its surrounding landscape on the country's Tentative List for UNESCO World Heritage nomination. The population is a mix of Kurds, Arabs, Mhallami and Assyrians.
marduk: Marduk, written in cuneiform dAMAR.UTU, from the Sumerian for calf of the sun, was a god of ancient Mesopotamia and patron deity of Babylon, where he was worshipped in the Esagila temple. He and Babylon were unimportant in the 3rd millennium BCE, and the earliest mention is a fragmentary inscription in which an unnamed ruler of a city probably to be read as Babylon built a temple for him. His original role is unknown; one scholar suggests a minor underworld god.

Under the First Dynasty of Babylon, in the reign of Sumu-la-El, Marduk appears in oaths and year names. Sanctuaries to him began to appear in other cities from the reign of Hammurabi. In the Kassite period names containing his name passed 10 per cent and his temple at Nippur was well established, though Enlil still headed the list of gods with Anu and Ea.

Marduk came to be worshipped as a god of creation, justice, water, agriculture, magic and medicine. His symbol was the spade, he was associated with the dragon-like Mušḫuššu, and by the 1st millennium BCE he was linked with the planet Jupiter. He was the son of Ea and was identified with Asalluhi, who appears with Ea in incantations, and with Enlil, so that he was often called the Enlil of the gods. He was commonly called Bēl, lord. Under Nebuchadnezzar I in the 2nd millennium BCE he was enshrined as leader of the Mesopotamian pantheon.

The Enūma Eliš, the Babylonian epic of creation, tells how Marduk, born to Ea and Damkina, defeats Tiamat, fashions the world from her corpse with Babylon at its centre, becomes king of the gods and receives fifty names, fifty being the number of Enlil. A ritual tablet says the epic was recited, and perhaps reenacted, at the Akitu festival. Other texts show his anger and mercy: in Ludlul bēl nēmeqi, called the Babylonian Job, a sufferer blames Marduk's anger for his illness and praises his mercy once healed.

In the Epic of Erra, by contrast, Marduk leaves his seat in the Esagila and the world falls into instability. In the Assyrian Marduk Ordeal Text he is held captive and subjected to a river ordeal, though the text is not simply hostile to him. In Neo-Assyrian Assyria only Shamash was invoked more often than Marduk in incantation-prayers.
marduk-nadin-ahhe: Marduk-nādin-aḫḫē was the sixth king of the Second Dynasty of Isin and was related to all three kings before him. His father, Ninurta-nādin-šumi, was the third king of the dynasty, his brother Nabu-kudurri-uṣur the fourth, and his nephew Enlil-nādin-apli the fifth. He took the throne by revolt. A reconstructed passage of the Walker Chronicle tells how, while Enlil-nādin-apli was away campaigning in Assyria, Marduk-nādin-aḫḫē and the nobles rebelled, and the returning king was killed with the sword.

Early in his reign he raided Assyria and carried off the cult statues of Adad and Šala from Ekallāte, a town about thirty miles from Assur. The Assyrian king Tukultī-apil-Ešarra answered with raids into Babylonia, claiming in his building inscription to have taken Dūr-Kurigalzu, Sippar of Šamaš, Sippar of Anunitu, Babylon and Upi and to have burned the king's palaces in Babylon. According to the Synchronistic History he defeated Marduk-nādin-aḫḫē twice, by the Lower Zab and at Gurmarritu, but these places lay on the edge of Babylonia, and the statues stayed in Babylon.

An astrologer named Ea-mušallim sent the king a report on a solar eclipse in 1090 BCE, and a later letter quoting that report speaks of rains so scanty that no harvests were reaped. An Assyrian chronicle relates that he lost his throne and disappeared amid the disorder caused by Arameans moving into Mesopotamia under the pressure of famine, when Babylonians are said to have eaten one another's flesh.

Seven kudurrus, or boundary stones, and other inscriptions record his reign. They show ordinary dealings in land in northern Babylonia: one grants land to Adad-zer-iqiša in thanks for fighting the Assyrians, another exempts the people near the mouth of the Ṣalmani Canal from forced labour. He restored the Eganunmaḫ at Ur on the plan of the Kassite king Kurigalzu and built a kitchen complex beside the ziggurat. He may be the third king of the text known as Prophecy A, whose fertile reign of 18 years ends in revolt. The statues of Ekallāte were returned only by Sennacherib of Assyria, 418 years later, after he took Babylon in 689 BCE.
marduk-zakir-shumi-i: Marduk-zâkir-šumi, whose name means Marduk pronounced the name, ruled in the mixed dynastic period known in antiquity as the dynasty of E, and was a contemporary and ally of the Assyrian kings Shalmaneser III and Šamši-Adad V. Few inscriptions of his reign survive. A kudurru of his second year grants land to Ibni-Ištar, a priest of the Eanna temple in Uruk, and names as witnesses the crown prince Marduk-balāssu-iqbi and Nazi-Enlil, governor of Nippur, the first holder of that office since Kassite times. A lapis lazuli seal of his shows Marduk's statue resting on the dragon Mušḫuššu.

His younger brother Marduk-bēl-ušati rebelled and set up a brief regime in the Diyāla region, seizing Daban. In 851 and 850 BCE Shalmaneser III came to the king's aid. In the first campaign the rebel was beaten outside Ganannate but held the city; in the second it fell, and he fled with some of his officers to Arman, which was taken after a siege. Shalmaneser's Black Obelisk says he cut down the rebel and his officers with the sword. The Assyrian king then received tribute from Chaldean leaders, the earliest record of these groups, and made sacrifices in Babylon, Borsippa and Kutha.

The king repaid the favour about 826 BCE, when Shalmaneser's son Aššur-danin-apli rebelled and 27 cities went over to him. A treaty between Šamši-Adad V and Marduk-zâkir-šumi seems to place the Assyrian in an inferior position, and it ends with curses apparently copied from the Code of Hammurabi, leaving out the god Aššur. It may have been sealed by the marriage of the king's daughter Shammuramat, the inspiration for the legend of Semiramis, to Šamši-Adad. Šamši-Adad resented his subordinate place and later took a terrible revenge in the reign of Marduk-balāssu-iqbi.
mare-liberum: Hugo Grotius, the Dutch jurist and philosopher, wrote the treatise while serving as counsel to the Dutch East India Company in the dispute over its seizure of the Portuguese carrack Santa Catarina. The Zeeland Chamber of the company assigned him the work in 1608. It was aimed at the Portuguese policy of a closed sea, mare clausum, and at their claim to a monopoly of the trade of the East Indies. Elzevier published it in the spring of 1609.

In its first chapter Grotius set out to show briefly and clearly that the Dutch had the right to sail to the East Indies and to trade with the people there. He rested his case on what he called the most specific and unimpeachable axiom of the Law of Nations, a first principle self-evident and immutable: that every nation is free to travel to every other nation and to trade with it. From this he argued that the right to travel and trade required a right of innocent passage over land and a similar right at sea.

The sea, he held, was more like the air than the land. The air cannot be occupied and its use is meant for all; for the same reasons the sea is common to all, because it is so limitless that no one can possess it, and because it suits the use of all, whether for navigation or for fisheries. On this ground he formulated the principle that the sea was international territory, free to every nation for seafaring trade.

The book has been translated into English twice. Richard Hakluyt made the first translation at some time between 1609 and his death in 1616, but it was not printed until 2004, when Liberty Fund issued it as The Free Sea in its Natural Law and Enlightenment Classics series. The second, by Ralph Van Deman Magoffin of Johns Hopkins University, belonged to the debate on free shipping during the First World War and was published in 1916 by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and Oxford University Press.
mare-nostrum: Mare Nostrum is Latin for Our Sea. The Romans first used it of the Tyrrhenian Sea after their conquest of Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica in the Punic Wars with Carthage. By 30 BCE Roman dominion extended from the Iberian Peninsula to Egypt, and the phrase came to be used of the whole Mediterranean Sea. Other names were also employed, including Mare Internum, or Internal Sea. Mare Mediterraneum was a Late Latin creation attested only well after the fall of Rome. Rome is the only state in history to have controlled the entire Mediterranean coast.

After the unification of Italy in 1861, Italian nationalists who saw Italy as successor to the Roman Empire tried to revive the term. During the Scramble for Africa in the 1880s, calls for an Italian colonial empire gave it a modern sense, as in the words of Emilio Lupi, who argued that Tripoli had to be taken even if it were a desert, to avoid being suffocated in Mare Nostrum.

Benito Mussolini took up the term in fascist propaganda, in a manner similar to Adolf Hitler's Lebensraum. He wanted to re-establish the greatness of the Roman Empire, built one of the most powerful navies of the world, and spoke of making the Mediterranean an Italian lake. He promoted a project, to be realised after an expected Axis victory, of an enlarged Italian Empire from the Mediterranean shores of Egypt to the Indian Ocean shores of Somalia and eastern Kenya. The invasions of Albania, Greece, Yugoslavia and Egypt and the Siege of Malta sought to extend Axis control over the sea, but Allied armies and navies thwarted the aim before Italy surrendered in September 1943.

Mare Nostrum is the title of a best-selling novel by the Spanish author Vicente Blasco Ibáñez, published in 1918, and a film based on it was released in 1948. In June 2012 the term was the theme of the inaugural conference of the Society for Mediterranean Law and Culture at the University of Cagliari, where it was meant to embrace the diversity of Mediterranean cultures. After the 2013 Lampedusa migrant shipwreck the Italian government authorised Operation Mare Nostrum, a military and humanitarian operation to rescue migrants and arrest traffickers.
mareb-river: The Mereb, known lower down as the Gash, has its headwaters in central Eritrea. It flows first south, along the Ethiopian frontier, and then west through western Eritrea until it reaches the Sudanese plains near Kassala. The Statistical Abstract of Ethiopia for 1967/68 gave its length as 440 kilometres. The Ethiopian Ministry of Water Resources reports a catchment of 5,700 square kilometres on the Ethiopian side, while other sources give the whole basin as between 21,000 and 44,000 square kilometres.

The river is dry for much of the year but, like the Takazze, is subject to sudden floods in the rainy season, when its flow can reach 870 cubic metres per second against an average of 21.6. Its main tributary on the right bank, in Eritrea, is the Obel; on the left bank, in Ethiopia, it receives the Sarana, Balasa, Mai Shawesh and Engweya. Only the left bank of the upper course lies in Ethiopian territory. Unlike the Setit, its waters do not usually reach the Nile but spread out and vanish in the sands of the eastern Sudanese plains.

The river long marked the line between two separately governed lands. To the north lay the realm of the Bahr negash, whose title means kingdom of the sea in Tigrinya; his lands, also called Medri Bahri, reached the Red Sea coast and extended south and west as far as Shire, and his capital was at Debarwa, about 30 kilometres south of Asmara. To the south of the river lay Tigray.

In modern times part of the boundary between Eritrea and Ethiopia follows the Mereb, between the point where the Mai Ambassa enters it and its confluence with the Balasa. Its Eritrean floodplain also gained attention in 2001, when a sizable herd of elephants was sighted there, the first such sighting in Eritrea since 1955.
marfa-boretskaya: Marfa was the daughter of Ivan Loshinsky and married the boyar Isaak Boretsky, who was posadnik, or mayor, of Novgorod until his death in the 1460s; they had two sons, Dmitry and Fyodor. Her name Posadnitsa, the Mayoress, was no formal office: Russians gave the wives of certain officials the feminine form of their husbands' titles, and offices in Novgorod were held only by male landowners. She owned large estates producing flax and fur, and after her husband's death she settled new lands along the Onega River, becoming the third-largest landholder in Novgorod.

By the 1460s she led the boyar faction opposed to Moscow's centralising policy. In 1471 she and her sons tried to negotiate the city's passage to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania with its ancient rights kept, and invited Mikhailo Olelkovich to rule it. Ivan III saw this as a breach of the Treaty of Yazhelbitsy and marched on Novgorod; after the battle her son Dmitry, who had led the Novgorodian army, was executed on 24 July 1471.

During Ivan's visit to Novgorod in the winter of 1475-1476, Fyodor and Marfa's brother Ivan were arrested after residents accused a group of nobles of causing a disturbance, and they were exiled to Murom. When Ivan III subjugated the city, Marfa and her grandsons were taken into custody and escorted to Moscow on 7 February 1478. Tradition holds that she was made to take the veil in Nizhny Novgorod, but the historian Gail Lenhoff argues that her later fate is uncertain.

The 15th-century Sofia Chronicle called her the evil woman behind the Lithuanian alliance, claiming that she meant to marry a Lithuanian noble, and this account shaped her reputation. More recent research argues that Archbishop Feofil of Novgorod made her a scapegoat to hide his own part in the city's failure to meet its treaty obligations. Nikolai Karamzin made her the heroine of his short novel Martha the Mayoress, or the Fall of Novgorod, Pushkin devoted an essay to her in 1830, and her statue stands on the Millennium of Russia monument in Novgorod.
margaret-i-of-denmark: Margaret was born in March 1353 at Søborg Castle, the sixth and youngest child of Valdemar IV of Denmark and Queen Helvig. In 1359, aged six, she was engaged to the 18-year-old Haakon VI, youngest son of King Magnus IV and VII of Sweden and Norway. The match served her father's wish to regain Scania, which had been mortgaged to Sweden since 1332, and it was dissolved and revived amid the wars of those years. The wedding took place in Copenhagen on 9 April 1363, when she was ten.

After her father's death in 1375, Margaret secured the election of the infant Olaf as king of Denmark, over the claims of her sister Ingeborg's husband Henry III, Duke of Mecklenburg, and their son Albert. Olaf succeeded Haakon in Norway and died in 1387, aged 16. Margaret was then chosen regent of Denmark and Norway. She had already recovered Schleswig from the Holstein-Rendsburg counts through the Compact of Nyborg of 1386, which left the Danish crown with most of the advantages.

Swedish nobles in revolt against King Albert of Mecklenburg offered her the regency of Sweden. In March 1388, at Dalaborg Castle, they elected her Sovereign Lady and Ruler. Albert returned with mercenaries, and on 24 February 1389 his forces were beaten near Falköping, at either Aasle or Falan, even though Margaret's Mecklenburger commander Henrik Parow was killed.

Albert was released under the Compact of Lindholm of 1395 on a promise to pay 60,000 marks, and the Hanseatic League handed Stockholm to Margaret in September 1398. She adopted her great-nephew Bogislav, who took the name Erik of Pomerania, and on 17 June 1397 he was crowned in Kalmar as king of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, while she remained the effective ruler.

Margaret took back crown lands from nobles and the church, replaced worthless copper tokens with silver coin and kept out of the war between France and England. She bought Gotland from Albert of Mecklenburg and the Livonian Order and regained much of Schleswig by purchase.

In 1412 she went to war with Holstein to recover the rest, and she fell ill on board her ship in Flensburg Harbour and died on the night of 28 October. Her sarcophagus, made by Johannes Junge in 1423, stands behind the high altar of Roskilde Cathedral. Historians have seen her as an idealist, a nationalist or a calculating pursuer of dynastic power, while few dispute her political skill.
margaret-iii-countess-of-flanders: Margaret was born on 13 April 1350, the only surviving child and heir of Count Louis II of Flanders and Margaret of Brabant. In 1355 she married Philip of Rouvres, grandson and heir of Duke Odo IV of Burgundy, who was Count of Burgundy and Artois and Duke of Burgundy and became Count of Auvergne and Boulogne in 1360.

Philip died after a riding accident in 1361, and Margaret was widowed without children. King John II of France then claimed the Duchy of Burgundy for the Kingdom of France by escheat, and in 1363 he granted it to his youngest son, Philip the Bold, who married Margaret in 1369.

When her father died in 1384, Margaret and Philip inherited the counties of Artois, Burgundy, Flanders, Nevers and Rethel. She ruled as Countess of Flanders and of Artois, Auvergne and Boulogne from 1384 to 1405, and was the last ruler of Flanders of the House of Dampierre. The Dampierres, originally only counts of Flanders, had through marriages inherited Nevers in 1280 and Rethel in 1328, and these lands became the core of the dominions of the House of Valois-Burgundy.

Margaret and Philip had nine children. Their eldest son, John the Fearless, succeeded his father as Duke of Burgundy in 1404 and also became Count of Flanders, and a younger son, Anthony, inherited Brabant and Limburg in 1406. Three daughters married into the houses of Bavaria, Austria and Savoy. The Château de Germolles, given to Margaret by Philip, became a country estate where she planted a large rose garden and sent the petals to Flanders to make rose water; in 1390 she and Philip hosted King Charles VI of France there.

Philip died in 1404, and Margaret died the following year, in March 1405. With her death the House of Dampierre came to an end and Flanders lost its relative independence from Burgundy; it passed to her son John the Fearless, of the House of Valois-Burgundy, and later to the House of Habsburg. Her sons Anthony and Philip II of Nevers both died at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415.
margaret-maid-of-norway: Margaret was born at Tønsberg in Norway between March and 9 April 1283, the only child of King Eric II of Norway and Margaret, daughter of Alexander III of Scotland, who died apparently from complications of childbirth. The infant was kept in Bergen in the custody of Narve, Bishop of Bergen.

Alexander III's last surviving son died on 28 January 1284, and on 5 February the king had his earls, barons and clan chiefs swear at Scone to accept Margaret as his heir. Alexander set out on horseback in stormy weather on the evening of 18 March 1286 and was found dead with a broken neck the next day, and his posthumous child by Yolanda of Dreux was stillborn in November.

After Alexander's death, Scottish magnates chose six guardians to govern the country. Robert Bruce, 5th Lord of Annandale, and John Balliol, Lord of Galloway, were in dispute, and Bruce raised a rebellion with his son, the Earl of Carrick, which was defeated in early 1287. Because the situation was precarious, Eric was reluctant to send his three-year-old daughter to Scotland.

In 1289 he and Edward I of England negotiated her marriage to Edward of Caernarfon, and the Treaty of Salisbury of 6 November 1289 asked Edward to act for his grandniece. The Treaty of Birgham, agreed on 18 July 1290, provided that Scotland would remain fully independent despite the union and that Margaret alone would be inaugurated at Scone.

Margaret sailed from Bergen in late summer 1290 on her father's ship, with Bishop Narve in her entourage. She fell ill, and the ship put in at Orkney about 23 September. She suffered for up to a week, from food poisoning or, less likely, motion sickness, and died between 26 and 29 September 1290 in the arms of Bishop Narve. Her coffin was taken to Bergen, where Eric had it opened to confirm her identity.

Margaret was the last legitimate descendant of William the Lion, and thirteen men claimed the succession, chiefly Bruce and Balliol. In 1301 a German woman impersonated her and was burned at the stake. Historians disagree whether she was a queen. She was never inaugurated, and Scots called her their lady far more often than their queen. Her biographer Archie Duncan argues that she was never queen of Scots, while Norman H. Reid holds that she was accepted as queen, though her reign never started. Modern writers nearly always call her queen, and reference books give 19 March 1286 as the start of her reign.
margaret-maultasch: Margaret was the only surviving daughter of Duke Henry of Carinthia, Count of Tyrol and former King of Bohemia, and his second wife Adelaide of Brunswick. Having no sons, Henry agreed with Emperor Louis IV in 1330 that she would inherit Carinthia and Tyrol. King John of Bohemia had arranged in 1327 for her to marry his younger son John Henry, brother of the future Emperor Charles IV, and the wedding was held at Innsbruck in 1330, when the groom was eight and the bride twelve. Contemporary sources say the children disliked each other from the start.

When Henry died in 1335, the emperor broke his promise, giving Carinthia to the Habsburg Duke Albert II of Austria and claiming Tyrol for the Wittelsbachs, but Charles IV and the local nobles secured Margaret's succession in Tyrol. On 1 November 1341 she shut John Henry out of Tyrol Castle, and on 10 February 1342 at Meran she married the emperor's son, Margrave Louis I of Brandenburg. Pope Clement VI excommunicated the couple, while William of Ockham and Marsilius of Padua defended the match, arguing that the first marriage had never been consummated.

A year after his election as anti-king in 1346, Charles IV besieged Tyrol Castle without success and burned Bozen and Meran. He later had his brother's marriage dissolved under canon law, and Margaret's son Meinhard III married Margaret of Habsburg, a daughter of Albert II. With Habsburg help Pope Innocent VI absolved Margaret and Louis in 1359.

Louis died in 1361 and Meinhard less than two years later, after which Duke Stephen II of Bavaria-Landshut invaded and claimed Tyrol, so Margaret passed the county to Rudolf IV of Austria. She died in exile in Vienna on 3 October 1369 and was buried at the Minoritenkirche. Her nickname Maultasch, roughly bag mouth, came from church propaganda over her divorce and is first recorded in 1366, though the chronicler John of Winterthur called her exceptionally beautiful. Quentin Matsys's portrait The Ugly Duchess of 1513 may refer to her, and Lion Feuchtwanger told her story in a novel of 1923.
margaret-of-anjou: Margaret was born on 23 March 1430 at Pont-à-Mousson in Lorraine, the second daughter of René of Anjou, titular king of Naples, Sicily and Jerusalem, and Isabella, Duchess of Lorraine. Several women of her family exercised power as regents, among them her mother and her grandmother Yolande of Aragon, which may have shaped her later actions.

In 1444 she was betrothed by proxy to Henry VI of England, in a marriage negotiated principally by William de la Pole, Duke of Suffolk, as part of peace efforts near the end of the Hundred Years' War. She married Henry at Titchfield Abbey on 23 April 1445 and was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 30 May. The loss of Maine to Anjou, negotiated soon afterwards, was deeply unpopular.

Henry's mental condition was unstable when they married, and by the birth of their only son, Edward of Westminster, on 13 October 1453, he had suffered a complete breakdown. Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York, was Lord Protector in 1453 and 1454. In May 1455 Margaret and Henry called a Great Council that excluded the Yorkists, and York marched south to meet the Lancastrian army, which was crushed at the First Battle of St Albans on 22 May. Historians differ on when her enmity with York began. Helen Maurer places it in 1455, while Paul Murray Kendall held that it came earlier.

Margaret's commander Henry Beaufort, 3rd Duke of Somerset, won the Battle of Wakefield on 30 December 1460, where York was killed. She won the Second Battle of St Albans on 17 February 1461. The Lancastrians lost at Towton on 29 March 1461, and Edward, York's son, deposed Henry and took the throne as Edward IV. Margaret fled to Scotland and then France, where, at the instigation of her cousin Louis XI, she accepted an alliance with Warwick, sealed by the marriage of her son to Warwick's daughter Anne Neville.

Warwick was defeated and killed at the Battle of Barnet on 14 April 1471. At the Battle of Tewkesbury on 4 May, Margaret led her own army to defeat, and her seventeen-year-old son was killed. It is not known whether he died in the fighting or was executed afterwards by the Duke of Clarence. She was taken captive and in 1475 was ransomed by Louis XI. She lived in France for seven years as a poor relation of the king, and died on 25 August 1482 at the castle of Dampierre-sur-Loire, aged 52.
She obtained a licence on 30 March 1448 to found Queens' College, Cambridge, and many of her letters survive. William Shakespeare made her a major character in his first group of history plays.
margaret-of-austria-duchess-of-savoy: Margaret was born in Brussels on 10 January 1480, the daughter of Maximilian of Austria and Mary of Burgundy. Her mother died in 1482, and the Treaty of Arras that year promised her in marriage to the Dauphin Charles of France, and she was raised at the French court as a future queen. In 1497 she married John, Prince of Asturias, in Burgos Cathedral, but he died of fever six months later, and she gave birth to a stillborn daughter in 1498.

In 1501 she married Philibert II, Duke of Savoy. When she came to Savoy the government was in the hands of his illegitimate brother René, and she fought to strip him of his powers until he was declared a traitor and took refuge in France. She then took hold of the government herself. Philibert died in 1504.

In 1507 her father Maximilian I named her governor of the Low Countries and guardian of her nephew Charles. She governed from Mechelen until 1515 and again from 1519 until her death, for Maximilian and then for Charles V. In 1508 she helped form the League of Cambrai, which turned French attention to northern Italy; she struggled with Charles of Egmont of Guelders and in 1513 had to recognise him as duke. She restored the Intercursus Magnus trade agreement with England, which favoured Flemish textiles, and in 1524 signed a grain agreement with Frederick I of Denmark. Her rule was relatively peaceful apart from the early Reformation: Jan van Essen and Hendrik Vos were burnt in Brussels in 1523.
Her court at Mechelen was visited by Erasmus, Adrian of Utrecht and Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, who dedicated a work on the female sex to her, and from 1513 to 1514 Anne Boleyn was in her household.

Margaret commissioned manuscripts from the Ghent-Bruges school and had the Sforza Hours finished by her court artist Gerard Horenbout. Her collection passed to Charles V and Mary of Hungary and later to Philip II of Spain. On 15 November 1530 she stepped on broken glass, gangrene set in and her leg was amputated. She died soon after midnight on 1 December, having named Charles her heir. She was buried beside Philibert at the Royal Monastery of Brou, under a tomb by Conrat Meit, and Mary of Hungary succeeded her as governor.
margaret-of-parma: Margaret was born on 5 July 1522, the illegitimate daughter of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and Johanna Maria van der Gheynst, a servant of Count Charles de Lalaing. She was brought up at Mechelen under her great-aunt Margaret of Austria and her aunt Mary of Austria, successive governors of the Habsburg Netherlands. Charles used her to secure his plans in Italy: she was engaged in 1527 to Alessandro de' Medici, Duke of Florence, a nephew of Pope Clement VII, and from 1533 she was educated in the courts of Florence, Rome and Parma. Though multilingual, she preferred Italian for the rest of her life.

She married Alessandro on 13 June 1536, and he was assassinated on 6 January 1537. On 4 November 1538 the 15-year-old widow married Ottavio Farnese, Duke of Parma, who was 14. She at first refused. The marriage was unhappy and the couple lived apart for much of their lives, but it produced twin sons, one of whom died in infancy.

In 1555 Margaret left Italy for the Netherlands, leaving her son in the care of her half-brother Philip II, and in 1559, when Philip left for Spain, he appointed her Governor of the Habsburg Netherlands. Her authority was largely nominal. She faced growing discontent against the Inquisition and Spanish rule and had to follow the advice of Cardinal Granvelle, who was much disliked and was exiled in 1564.

In 1565 an opposition party formed among the Dutch nobility, and with no army to put it down she promised to stop religious repression. In 1566 she quelled iconoclastic riots with the help of the stadtholders Philip of Noircarmes and William of Orange. Philip then sent the Duke of Alba with an army, and Margaret, warning that his actions would lead to catastrophe, resigned in 1567 when she learned that Alba's power of attorney superseded her own.

Margaret retired in 1567 to L'Aquila in Italy and was appointed Governor of Abruzzo. In 1578 her son Alexander Farnese became governor-general of the Netherlands, and Philip made her co-regent, but the two could not work together and she retired to Namur in 1582. She returned to Italy with Philip's permission in 1583, died at Ortona on 18 January 1586 and was buried at S. Sisto in Piacenza. Charlie R. Steen describes her as a woman dedicated to compromise and conciliation in public affairs.
margaret-of-york: Margaret of York was born at Fotheringhay Castle on 3 May 1446, the daughter of Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York, and Cecily Neville, and the sister of Edward IV and Richard III. When her father held power in 1453-1454, marriage talks with the Burgundian court proposed her as a wife for Charles the Bold, but they petered out. Her father was killed at the Battle of Wakefield on 30 December 1460, and by 1465 her brother was king, which made her a far more valuable bride. When Charles's wife Isabella of Bourbon died in September 1465, he sent an envoy to London to propose the match.

The marriage took years to arrange. Louis XI of France opposed an alliance between his two main enemies, and in 1466 Margaret was briefly betrothed to Peter, Constable of Portugal, who died on 29 June. Edward IV agreed formally in October 1467, the contract was completed in February 1468, and Margaret crossed from Margate to Sluys on 23 June 1468. She and Charles were married privately at Damme on 3 July. The Bruges celebrations, including the Tournament of the Golden Tree, impressed observers as the marriage of the century. She presented her crown in 1475 to the Church of Our Lady at Aachen, where it survives.

The marriage produced no children, but Margaret became a mother figure to her stepdaughter Mary. After Charles was killed outside Nancy on 5 January 1477, she advised Mary to marry Maximilian of Austria, and they wed on 18 August. Mary died after a riding accident on 27 March 1482. In December 1482 the Treaty of Arras gave Louis XI the Burgundian Lowlands, Picardy and Boulogne. Margaret later governed with the Burgundian Estates and guarded Mary's son Philip, and her residence at Mechelen became a princely court.

After Richard III was killed at Bosworth in 1485, Margaret supported challengers to Henry VII, backing Lambert Simnel and Perkin Warbeck, whom she acknowledged as her nephew and funded with mercenaries in 1495. Warbeck was defeated at Deal and failed to take Waterford. She died on 23 November 1503, aged 57, and was buried at the Church of the Cordeliers in Mechelen.

William Caxton counted her among his patrons, and a presentation copy of his Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye shows him offering it to her. She also commissioned illuminated manuscripts, among them The Visions of Tondal, illustrated by Simon Marmion. Her actions are credited with the survival of the Burgundian state.
margaret-thatcher: Margaret Hilda Roberts was born on 13 October 1925 in Grantham, Lincolnshire. Her father, Alfred Roberts, owned a tobacconist's and a grocery shop, served as an alderman and was a Methodist local preacher; he brought her up as a strict Wesleyan Methodist. She won a scholarship to Kesteven and Grantham Girls' School and entered Somerville College, Oxford, in October 1943 to study chemistry.

In 1950 and 1951 she was the Conservative candidate for the Labour seat of Dartford, losing both times. She married Denis Thatcher in December 1951 and qualified as a barrister in 1953. She was elected Member of Parliament for Finchley in 1959. Edward Heath appointed her Secretary of State for Education and Science in 1970, and in 1975 she defeated him in the Conservative Party leadership election, becoming the first woman to lead a major British political party.

Thatcher became prime minister on 4 May 1979. Her economic policies emphasised individual liberty, the privatisation of state-owned companies and reducing the power of trade unions. Her popularity waned during the recession and rising unemployment, but victory in the Falklands War in 1982 brought a resurgence of support and a landslide victory in 1983. In 1984 she survived the Provisional IRA's bombing of a Brighton hotel, and she achieved a political victory against the National Union of Mineworkers in the strike of 1984–85. In 1986 she oversaw the deregulation of financial markets known as the Big Bang.

She won a third term in 1987. Her support for the Community Charge, also called the poll tax, was widely unpopular, and her increasingly Eurosceptic views were not shared by others in her cabinet. After a challenge to her leadership she resigned in 1990 and was succeeded by John Major.

Thatcher retired from the House of Commons in 1992 and became Baroness Thatcher with a life peerage. She died of a stroke at the Ritz Hotel, London, on 8 April 2013, aged 87. Thatcherism was a systematic overhaul of the post-war consensus on Keynesianism, the welfare state, nationalised industry and high taxes. During her tenure the number of adults owning shares rose from 7 per cent to 25 per cent, and more than a million families bought their council houses. She remains a polarising figure, and the legacy of the shift towards neoliberal policies is still debated.
margaret-tudor: Margaret was born on 29 November 1489 at the Palace of Westminster, the second child and first daughter of Henry VII and Elizabeth of York. Her siblings included Arthur, Prince of Wales, the future Henry VIII, and Mary, who briefly became Queen of France. The Treaty of Perpetual Peace of 24 January 1502 was the first peace between England and Scotland in over 170 years, and the marriage treaty concluded the same day was meant to guarantee it. The marriage was completed by proxy at Richmond Palace on 15 January 1503, and Margaret left for Scotland that summer, crossing the border at Berwick upon Tweed on 1 August.

After James IV died at Flodden in 1513, a parliament at Stirling confirmed Margaret as regent. She was the sister of an enemy king, and a pro-French party urged that John Stewart, Duke of Albany, born and raised in France, replace her. By July 1514 she had reconciled the contending parties, and Scotland and France concluded peace with England. But on 6 August 1514 she secretly married Archibald Douglas, 6th Earl of Angus, which alienated other noble houses, and by the terms of her husband's will she had forfeited the regency. Albany was installed in 1515 and gained custody of her two sons. Pregnant by Angus, she escaped to England, where Henry VIII received her well, and returned in 1517.

Her marriage to Angus declined. In 1524 she took advantage of Albany's absence in France to bring the twelve-year-old James V from Stirling to Edinburgh, and Parliament declared the regency over. She was recognised in November as the king's chief councillor. When Angus arrived in Edinburgh with armed men she had cannon fired on him. In March 1527 Pope Clement VII granted her divorce, and on 3 March 1528 she married Henry Stewart, whom James V made Lord Methven. In June 1528 James freed himself from Angus. Margaret helped bring about the Anglo-Scottish peace agreement of May 1534.

Margaret died at Methven Castle on 18 October 1541, aged 51, after what was reported as palsy, possibly resulting from a stroke. She was buried at the Charterhouse in Perth. Through her first marriage she was the grandmother of Mary, Queen of Scots, and through her second, of Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley. Her descendants brought the House of Stuart to the thrones of England and Ireland, culminating in the Union of the Crowns under her great-grandson James VI and I in 1603.
margarete-steiff: Margarete Steiff was born on 24 July 1847 in Giengen, in the Kingdom of Württemberg, the daughter of the building contractor Friedrich Steiff and his wife Maria Margarete, née Haehnle. At eighteen months a high fever left her legs paralysed and her right arm difficult to raise; doctors diagnosed polio only three years later. Her sisters and other children took her to school in a small hand-pulled cart, and she completed her training as a seamstress in the needlework classes of Frau Schelling at the age of 17. She also taught the zither, and her savings bought a sewing machine, the first in Giengen.

By her mid-twenties she was making fashionable clothes and travelling to other towns to work. In 1877 she opened a felt store and made felt underskirts for the firm of Christian Siegle in Stuttgart, employing other workers. She then came across a pattern for a toy elephant and made it from felt filled with lambswool as a gift for children of the family. In 1879 the American magazine The Delineator published patterns for a cloth mouse, rabbit and elephant, which the German magazine Modenwelt reproduced. By 1880 she was selling small numbers of such animals.

Her brother Fritz took samples to the market in Heidenheim and returned with many orders, and production grew each year. Pull-along and ride-on toys were added, with metal frames inside. By 1889 the firm had a larger building with a corner shop marked "Felt-Toy-Factory", and a printed catalogue followed. In 1892 it applied for a patent for making animals and other figures as playthings, which was later withdrawn when another German toy manufacturer contested it. In 1897 her nephew Richard Steiff, who had studied at the Kunstgewerbeschule in Stuttgart, joined the company.

Between 1897 and 1899 the firm made dancing-bear toys. In 1902 Richard designed Bear 55 PB, the first soft toy with movable joints. It drew little interest in a New York showroom in 1903, but at the Leipzig spring fair in March of that year an American buyer ordered 3,000. Such bears became known as teddy bears, after President Theodore Roosevelt, and one million had been produced by 1907. In 1910 Steiff won the Grand Prix at the Brussels International Exposition. Margarete Steiff is cited in writing on German entrepreneurs as a model of female entrepreneurship, a woman with a lifelong disability who built a business that spread beyond Germany.
margarita-island: Margarita Island lies in the Caribbean Sea off the north-west coast of Venezuela. It is in fact two islands, Paraguachoa in the east and Macanao in the west, joined by La Restinga, a sandy tombolo that encloses a lagoon. Together they are 78 kilometres long and up to 20 kilometres wide. With the islands of Coche and Cubagua the island forms the state of Nueva Esparta, whose capital, La Asunción, lies on it. Macanao has a mountain range along its length, and Paraguachoa one running north to south.

Christopher Columbus was the first European to reach the island, in 1498. Its native people were the Waikeri. The coast was rich in pearls, which accounted for almost a third of all tribute from the Western Hemisphere to the Spanish Crown. The island became the centre of the Spanish colonial Margarita Province, established in 1525, and was fortified against pirate attacks. In 1561 the conquistador Lope de Aguirre seized it and killed the governor Juan Villadrando. After the French buccaneer Marquis de Maintenon attacked in early 1676, the Santa Rosa de la Eminencia castle was built.

The island gained independence from the Spanish in 1814, after the collapse of the First Republic of Venezuela, and became the first permanently free territory in Venezuela. In that year Luisa Cáceres de Arismendi was held in the Fortress of Santa Rosa to put pressure on her husband Juan Bautista Arismendi, who was fighting for independence. In 1815 General Pablo Morillo landed with 18 warships and 42 cargo ships to put down revolts. In 1816 Simón Bolívar was confirmed there as Commander-in-Chief of the Second Republic of Venezuela, and from the island began a nine-year campaign to free Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from the Spanish Crown.

La Asunción, the state capital, is overlooked by the Santa Rosa de la Eminencia castle, and Pampatar holds the San Carlos de Borromeo Fortress, built in the late 17th century. Porlamar is the largest city. The island became a duty-free port in 1974, and tourism has been its main industry. The Tetas de María Guevara, two small hills, lie in the Laguna de La Restinga National Park, declared in 1974.
margaritus-of-brindisi: Margaritus, called the new Neptune, was the last great ammiratus ammiratorum, or grand admiral, of the Kingdom of Sicily, following Christodulus, George of Antioch and Maio of Bari in that office. He probably began as a Greek pirate and rose to be a privateer before becoming a permanent admiral of the navy. He married Marina or Martina, an illegitimate daughter of King Roger II of Sicily. He first appears in the record beside Tancred, then Count of Lecce, as a leader of the fleet that took Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Ithaca and then captured many ships of Emperor Isaac II Angelos at Cyprus.

After Saladin took Jerusalem on 2 October 1187, King William II sent Margaritus to the Holy Land. With 60 ships and 200 knights he patrolled the Palestine coast and kept Saladin from taking the vital seaports of the crusader kingdom; in July 1188 he arrived at Tripoli and forced Saladin to raise the siege of Krak des Chevaliers, and similar episodes followed at Marqab, Latakia and Tyre. His fleet returned after William died on 11 November 1189, and on 4 October 1190 he fled Messina when Richard the Lionheart sacked and burnt the city.

A staunch supporter of Tancred against Henry VI, King of Germany, who claimed the kingdom through his wife Constance, Margaritus defended Naples when Henry besieged it in 1191, harassing the Pisan navy and keeping the harbour open. When the people of Salerno captured Constance, he carried her to Tancred at Messina, and Tancred made him the first Count of Malta in 1192.

A second, larger fleet under Markward von Anweiler reached the bay of Naples on 25 August 1194, and Palermo, where Margaritus held the citadel, surrendered on 20 November. According to Roger of Howden, Henry confirmed him as admiral and gave him the duchy of Durazzo, probably meaning Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Ithaca. Four days after the Christmas coronation he was arrested with Nicholas, Archbishop of Salerno, Tancred's widow Sibylla of Acerra and his brief successor William III on charges of conspiracy. Blinded in Germany, he died there in 1197. Karl Hopf's undocumented conjecture that his daughters married the later rulers of Cephalonia and Corfu has been rejected by modern scholarship.
margiana: Margiana, called Marguš in Old Persian and Marv in Middle Persian, was a historical region centred on the oasis of Merv. It lay in the valley of the Murghab River, which rises in the mountains of Afghanistan, passes through Murghab District in modern Afghanistan and reaches the oasis of Merv in modern Turkmenistan. Margiana bordered Parthia to the south-west, Aria in the south, Bactria in the east and Sogdia in the north. It was a minor satrapy within the Achaemenid satrapy of Bactria and a province under its successors, the Seleucid, Parthian and Sasanian empires. It is considered part of a Bronze Age civilisation, the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex, also called the Oxus civilisation, and historians disagree about its history before the Achaemenid conquest.

Cyrus the Great conquered Margiana between 545 and 539 BCE and is said to have founded Merv. A revolt there led by Frâda (Phraates) after Darius the Great's victory over Gaumata was suppressed in December 521 BCE by Dadarsi, the satrap of Bactria. The Aramaic version of the Behistun Inscription claims that 55,423 Margians were killed and 6,972 taken captive. In 328 BCE Alexander the Great sent Craterus to fortify Margiana, and Merv was re-founded as Alexandria in Margiana. After the Wars of the Diadochi it came under Seleucus I Nicator. Under Antiochus I Soter the oasis was surrounded by a wall over 300 km long and the city re-founded as Antiochia in Margiana, capital of a separate satrapy, to secure the routes east.

Mithridates I of Parthia conquered Margiana about 170 BCE. Saka invaders passed through it about 140 BCE, and the Yuezhi held it until Mithridates II re-established control in 115 BCE. In 53 BCE, 10,000 Roman prisoners taken at the Battle of Carrhae were settled at Antiochia in Margiana. After Ardashir I defeated the last Parthian king in 224 CE, Margiana submitted as a vassal and was annexed by Shapur I about 260. The Hephthalites held it from about 480 to 565. The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, fled to Margiana after the defeat at Nihawand, and was defeated by the Rashidun general Ahnaf ibn Qais at the Battle of Oxus River; he was killed by a Margian miller, ending the Sasanian Empire.

Its place on the Silk Road gave Margiana a varied religious life. Most of the population practised Zoroastrianism, but Buddhist, Christian, Manichaean and Jewish communities also existed. Merv was a major centre of Buddhist learning, a Manichaean community is known from the mid third century CE, and a Nestorian diocese of Merv is known from 424 CE.
maria-beatrice-d-este-duchess-of-massa: Maria Beatrice d'Este was born in Modena on 7 April 1750, the eldest child of Ercole Rinaldo d'Este, heir to the Duchy of Modena and Reggio, and Maria Teresa Cybo-Malaspina, Duchess of Massa and Princess of Carrara. Her parents' marriage was unhappy and they lived apart. Her only brother died aged four months in 1753, leaving her the only surviving child. Modena and Reggio followed Salic law, which barred female succession, whereas Massa and Carrara did not. To keep the duchy from being absorbed by the Empire, her grandfather Francis III concluded two treaties with the House of Austria in 1753, one public and one secret, engaging her to Archduke Leopold, a son of Empress Maria Theresa.

In 1761 Leopold became heir to Tuscany, and in 1763, despite her father's opposition, the families substituted Archduke Ferdinand Karl, four years younger than his betrothed. The Diet of Regensburg ratified his future investiture in January 1771, and the couple married in Milan in October, founding the House of Austria-Este. Mozart's Ascanio in Alba and Hasse's Il Ruggiero were performed at the festivities. They lived in Milan for nearly 25 years and had ten children.

When her mother died in 1790 Maria Beatrice became Duchess of Massa and Carrara. She proved a scrupulous administrator but never moved to the duchy. After the French conquest of northern Italy she lived mostly in Austria, at the court of her nephew-in-law Francis II in Vienna. Her youngest daughter married him in 1808, and she was mother-in-law also of Victor Emmanuel I of Sardinia and of Elector Charles Theodore of Bavaria.

Under the principle of legitimacy advocated by Metternich at the Congress of Vienna, she was restored as sovereign of the Duchy of Massa and Principality of Carrara, and the imperial fiefs in Lunigiana were also granted to her. By an agreement in December she ceded the Lunigiana fiefs to her son Francis IV, who had been installed as Duke of Modena and Reggio.
When she died in 1829, Francis IV succeeded her in Massa and Carrara and in a few years absorbed her domains into the Este States. The House of Austria-Este ruled Modena until 1859.
maria-carolina-of-austria: Maria Carolina was born on 13 August 1752 at Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna, the thirteenth child of Empress Maria Theresa and Holy Roman Emperor Francis I. She was known in the family as Charlotte and was the daughter who most resembled her mother in her strong-willed character. She grew up close to her youngest sister, Maria Antonia, with whom she shared a governess.

Her marriage came about because two elder sisters, each engaged to Ferdinand IV of Naples, died of smallpox. Charles III of Spain, Ferdinand's father, wanted to keep the Austro-Spanish alliance and asked for a replacement. Maria Carolina was married by proxy on 7 April 1768 and entered the kingdom on 12 May. She bore eighteen children between 1772 and 1793, of whom seven reached adulthood.

After the birth of an heir in 1775 she joined the Privy Council. A quarrel over Freemasonry, which she favoured, led to the dismissal of the minister Bernardo Tanucci in October 1776 and ended Spanish influence in Naples. Together with Sir John Acton she enlarged the navy, opening four marine colleges and commissioning 150 ships. She patronised Angelica Kauffman and Jacob Philipp Hackert, and in 1784 founded the San Leucio silk-weaving colony.

The French Revolution changed her course. Alarmed for her sister Marie Antoinette, she abandoned enlightened absolutism, divided Naples into twelve police wards and created a secret police. After Marie Antoinette's execution in October 1793 she banned the works of Gaetano Filangieri and Giuseppe Maria Galanti and allied Naples with Britain against France. A failed attack on the Roman Republic forced the royal family to flee to Sicily in January 1799, and the Parthenopean Republic lasted six months before royal forces retook Naples.

The court returned to Naples in 1802 after Maria Carolina's two years in Vienna. French forces under Napoleon's brother Joseph Bonaparte drove the family back to Sicily in February 1806. In 1813 her husband appointed their son Francis regent, which ended her political influence, and she was made to leave for Vienna.

She reached Vienna in January 1814 and negotiated with Prince Metternich for the restoration of her husband. She died on 8 September 1814 of a stroke, a year before his return, and was buried in the Imperial Crypt. She was the last surviving child of Maria Theresa.
maria-de-molina: María Alfonso Téllez de Meneses, known as María de Molina, was the daughter of the infante Alfonso of Molina and Mayor Alfonso de Meneses, and her paternal grandparents were King Alfonso IX of León and Queen Berengaria of Castile. In 1282 she married her first cousin once removed, Sancho, although the dispensation for their kinship had not been granted beforehand. When Sancho's father, Alfonso X, died, the couple became king and queen of Castile and León and were crowned together in the cathedral of Toledo. Rome and others pressed them to separate, but Sancho chose to honour his wife and delegated many responsibilities to her, including the regency for their son after his death.

Sancho IV died on 25 April 1295, leaving the nine-year-old Ferdinand IV as heir. Although the Crónica de Sancho IV says Sancho named María sole regent, she had to share the regency with Sancho's uncle Henry the Senator, who was often more of an antagonist than a defender of his great-nephew. Ferdinand's rule was challenged by a coalition of his uncle Juan, the infantes de la Cerda, King James II of Aragón and King Denis of Portugal. Because of the doubts over her marriage, María had to overcome many difficulties to keep her son on the throne.

She built her own coalition through marriage alliances, gifts of territory and shrewd politics, relied on the Castilian Cortes to confirm her authority, and played the powerful family of Haro against the Laras, who supported the opposition. In the Courts of Valladolid in 1295 Henry was named guardian of the king, but she obtained custody of her son with the support of the cities. Civil war continued for several years.

Around 1300 the alliance against Ferdinand began to crumble when one of his principal enemies, Juan Núñez de Lara, was captured and reconciled to him, and Portugal returned to his allegiance with the promise of a marriage to the princess Constance. In 1301 María received a papal bull from Boniface VIII legitimising her marriage and her children. Only Aragón was left to support the claim of Alfonso de la Cerda, which was set aside in a later treaty between Castile and Aragón. After Ferdinand died in 1312 she became regent for her grandson Alfonso XI, a minor. She died in Valladolid in 1321. A Spanish Navy screw corvette, Doña María de Molina, in commission from 1869 to 1886, was named for her.
maria-ii-of-portugal: Maria da Glória was born on 4 April 1819 in the Palace of São Cristóvão in Rio de Janeiro, the eldest daughter of Pedro, later Pedro I of Brazil, and of Maria Leopoldina, daughter of Francis II, Holy Roman Emperor. She is the only European monarch to have been born outside Europe. The death of her grandfather João VI in March 1826 caused a succession crisis, since Pedro had proclaimed Brazilian independence in 1822 and his younger brother Miguel had been exiled to Austria after rebellions. Pedro renounced the Portuguese throne in favour of the seven-year-old Maria, who was to marry Miguel, accept the liberal constitution and act as regent until she came of age.

Maria stayed in Brazil during her first reign, with her aunt Isabel Maria as regent until Miguel returned in early 1828. A few months after his arrival he deposed Maria, proclaimed himself king on 11 July 1828 and abrogated the constitution, which began the Liberal Wars. Maria arrived in Gibraltar on 3 September 1828 to learn of the coup. She went to London, where the Wellington and Peel ministry backed Miguel, and returned to Brazil in October 1829.

In 1831 Pedro abdicated the Brazilian crown and came to Europe, taking the title Duke of Braganza and acting as regent in her name. He left Maria in Paris to finish her education, sailed to the Azores in March 1832 and landed at Matosinhos on 8 July. After the Siege of Porto, his forces entered Lisbon on 24 July 1833. Maria reached Lisbon for the first time in September 1833. Miguel abdicated in 1834, and Maria was restored as undisputed queen at fifteen.

Her second reign was marked by turmoil. She married Auguste, Duke of Leuchtenberg, in January 1835, and he died two months later. In April 1836 she married Prince Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, who became King Fernando II. The September Revolution of 1836 led to the Constitution of 1838, Costa Cabral restored the Charter of 1826 in 1842, and the Maria da Fonte revolt of 1846 led to the Patuleia civil war, which ended in June 1847.

Maria faced difficult pregnancies from the age of eighteen, and doctors warned her of the risks. She is said to have replied that if she died she would die at her post. She died on 15 November 1853, aged 34, in labour with the stillborn Infante Eugénio, her eleventh child. Her eldest son succeeded as Pedro V. She is remembered as the Educator, for policies aimed at raising the level of education, and as the Good Mother.
maria-ii-zaccaria: Maria was the daughter of Centurione I Zaccaria, Baron of Damala, Chalandritsa and Estamira, and of his Byzantine wife, probably Helene, a younger sister of the Byzantine Empress Irene Asanina and daughter of Andronikos Asan. Through her mother she descended from the imperial families of the Palaiologoi, Komnenoi, Angeloi and Asenids. Historians sometimes call her Asanina, but she does not seem to have used the name. She had three known brothers, Andronico, Filippo and Martino.

She married Pedro de San Superano, leader of the Navarrese Company from 1386 and de facto ruler of Achaea, whom King Ladislaus of Naples invested as Prince of Achaea in 1396. The names of their children, possibly two or more sons, are not recorded.

After Pedro died in November 1402, Maria ruled the principality for two years as regent for one of her underage sons. Her letters suggest she lived at Patras, where she held discussions with Venice over the appointment of a Venetian prelate. She chose as her bailee her ambitious nephew Centurione II Zaccaria, son of her brother Andronikos, and the choice proved her undoing.

Pedro had promised his suzerain, King Ladislaus, 3,000 ducats for the princely title but had never paid. When Ladislaus demanded the sum from Maria at once, she did not pay. Centurione secretly sent a trusted man to Naples to tell the king that Maria and her children could not pay, but that he would, if recognised as sole ruler. Ladislaus accepted and on 20 April 1404 declared Centurione prince of Achaea, excluding Maria and her son. He justified this by their failure to renew the feudal oath owed by the Princes of Achaea to Naples. After their dispossession Maria and her children disappear from the historical record.
maria-komnene-queen-of-jerusalem: Maria Komnene was the daughter of the Byzantine protosebastos John Doukas Komnenos and a grandniece of Emperor Manuel I Komnenos. Her cousin Theodora Komnene had been queen of Jerusalem as the wife of Baldwin III, in a marriage that sealed his alliance with Manuel. Baldwin died childless in 1163, and his brother Amalric succeeded. To restore the Byzantine alliance, Amalric sent envoys to Manuel in 1165, and after two years of negotiation Maria was chosen.

She landed at Tyre in August 1167 and was crowned before her wedding, as Theodora had been. The Latin patriarch Amalric of Nesle married the couple at the Cathedral of Tyre on 29 August 1167. As queen she had no influence on government. Their only surviving child, Isabella, was born in 1172.

Amalric died on 11 July 1174, having granted Maria the city of Nablus as her dower. His son Baldwin IV, who had a living mother, Agnes of Courtenay, succeeded, so Maria had no role at court and retired to Nablus with Isabella. When Baldwin proved to have leprosy and could not father an heir, Isabella and her half-sister Sibylla became crucial, and Maria became more powerful as Isabella's mother than she had been as Amalric's wife. In late 1177 she married Balian of Ibelin; they had four children, Helvis, John, Margaret and Philip.

From 1180 she belonged to the faction opposing Sibylla and her husband Guy of Lusignan. Historians believe she probably conducted the defence of Nablus when Saladin attacked it in September 1184, taking the whole population into the citadel so that no Franks were killed.

After Baldwin V died in 1186, Maria and her party planned to crown Isabella and Humphrey IV of Toron, but Humphrey submitted to Sibylla and Guy. Saladin won the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187 and took Jerusalem on 2 October. When Sibylla died in 1190, Maria had Isabella's marriage to Humphrey annulled, over Isabella's reluctance, so that she could marry Conrad of Montferrat.

Balian died in 1194 and Maria did not remarry. She supervised the marriage contract of her granddaughter Alice of Champagne in 1210, and died in mid-1217 in the reign of her great-granddaughter Isabella II. All the kings of Jerusalem and Cyprus and much of the thirteenth-century nobility of both kingdoms descended from her. The hostile Itinerarium Regis Ricardi called her steeped in Greek filth from the cradle, while the historian Bernard Hamilton judged her resilient and adaptable, and concluded that there was some truth in her opponents' view of her as ruthless and scheming.
maria-kunigunde-of-saxony: Born in Warsaw on 10 November 1740, Maria Kunigunde was the sixteenth and youngest child of Augustus III and Maria Josepha of Austria. She was taught Polish, Latin, French, English, philosophy, geography, religion, drawing, music and dance, and sang the title role in Johann Adolph Hasse's opera Leucippo at the Dresden court. In 1764 the Saxon court proposed her as a bride for Archduke Joseph of Austria, later Emperor Joseph II. At a secret dinner at Teplice she hardly said a word, Joseph judged her too timid and married her cousin Maria Josepha of Bavaria instead, and the story made a suitable marriage almost impossible to arrange.

Dresden demanded an imperial abbey for her as compensation, which would make her an Imperial Princess. Her admission at Münsterbilsen met fierce resistance from the chapter, but in 1775 she was elected coadjutor of Essen and Thorn, unanimously after Vienna and Dresden paid 45,000 guilders to the voting canons and canonesses, and she succeeded Francisca Christina of Sulzbach on 16 July 1776. She spent most of her time at the court of her brother Wenceslas in Koblenz, where he took almost no decision without consulting her, and governed her abbeys from a distance.

Her adviser Johann Jakob Schmitz pursued an enlightened absolutist programme that clashed with the chapter and estates; a forestry and hunting regulation of 1786 led to a suit before the Reichskammergericht. After Schmitz left in 1792, the compromise of 17 September 1794 gave the principality its first written constitution. She also banned abortion, regulated surgeons and midwives, founded a school for upper-class girls and supported compulsory education. When the estates refused funds, she built a toll road between Wesel and the Mark with a personal loan, later selling it to Prussia for 45,000 thalers, and invested in ironworks such as Gute Hoffnung and St. Antony, a pioneer of heavy industry in the Ruhr.

After the secularisation she kept her rank as a clerical sovereign and an annual stipend of 6,500 thalers from Prussia. She lived with Wenceslas, mostly at Oberdorf in Bavaria, until his death in 1812, then returned to Dresden to stay with her nephew Frederick Augustus. The last of her siblings to die, she was buried in the crypt of the Cathedral of the Holy Trinity. Her will of 1821, rediscovered in the Saxon state archives in 2001, left bequests to her household, from her Hofmeister to the cook.
maria-lekapene: Maria was the daughter of Christopher Lekapenos, son and co-emperor of Romanos I Lekapenos, and of his wife Augusta Sophia. Her marriage grew out of the War of 913–927 between Byzantium and Bulgaria. To prove himself a worthy successor to his father at home and abroad, the new Bulgarian ruler Peter I invaded Byzantine Thrace in May 927, but he showed himself ready to negotiate a lasting peace. Romanos took the occasion to propose a marriage alliance between the two imperial houses.

It was the first time in Byzantine history that a Byzantine princess was to be married to a foreign ruler. In October 927 Peter came to the neighbourhood of Constantinople to meet Romanos and sign the peace treaty, and he married Maria on 8 November. Decades later Constantine VII, Romanos's son-in-law and co-ruler, criticised Romanos for this concession. Besides Boris II, who succeeded as emperor of Bulgaria in 969, and Roman, who succeeded in 977, the couple had a son named Plenimir.

The year of her death is not known exactly. It is mentioned by the Byzantine chroniclers John Skylitzes and John Zonaras, the second of whom relied on the first. Because the account sits in the narrative of the last years of Emperor Romanos II, some scholars place her death in 963, while the historians Brzozowska and Leszka treat that year as the latest possible date.

How she died is also unknown. There is no reliable evidence that she became a nun at the end of her life, and these authors think she most likely died as a laywoman, since medieval Bulgarian writing paid particular attention to female rulers who entered monasteries. Her death is sometimes linked to the worsening of Bulgarian–Byzantine relations, but the sources do not allow a causal link to be established with certainty.
maria-luisa-duchess-of-lucca: Maria Luisa was born on 6 July 1782 at La Granja de San Ildefonso, a daughter of King Charles IV of Spain and Maria Luisa of Parma. In 1795 she married her first cousin Louis of Bourbon-Parma, heir to the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza, who had come to the Spanish court to finish his education. He had been expected to marry her older sister Maria Amalia but preferred her. The marriage was happy, though clouded by his frail health and epileptic seizures. Their son Charles Louis was born in Madrid on 22 December 1799.

Under the Treaty of Aranjuez, Napoleon created the Kingdom of Etruria from the Grand Duchy of Tuscany as compensation for the loss of Parma. Maria Luisa opposed the plan, but she and her husband went to Paris, where Napoleon received them, and arrived in Florence in August 1801. After Louis died in 1803 she acted as regent for her son. With her minister Count Fossombroni she reorganised the tax system, created manufactures such as tobacco and porcelain, enlarged the army and founded a Higher School of Science.

Napoleon distrusted her government and accused her of not enforcing the English blockade. On 23 November 1807 a French minister told her that Spain had ceded Etruria to France, and she left Florence on 10 December with her children. Napoleon annexed the territory. After the Mutiny of Aranjuez and the French occupation of Spain she was reunited with her parents in France. She was the only member of the Spanish royal family to oppose Napoleon directly, and after a planned escape was discovered she was imprisoned in a Roman convent from 1811 with her daughter.

She regained her freedom in 1814. To press her claim she published her Memoirs, but the Congress of Vienna gave her the smaller Duchy of Lucca, not Parma, which went to Napoleon's wife Marie Louise of Austria. She refused the settlement for more than two years and took up the government in December 1817, once her family had been granted the right of reversion to Parma. As duchess she disregarded the constitution the Congress had imposed, renewed the Palazzo Ducale, built an aqueduct and developed the port of Viareggio, and founded seventeen new convents. She died of cancer in Rome on 13 March 1824 and was buried at El Escorial; her son succeeded her.
maria-montessori: Maria Tecla Artemisia Montessori was born on 31 August 1870 in Chiaravalle, in the province of Ancona. Her father, Alessandro Montessori, was an official of the Ministry of Finance working in the local state tobacco factory; her mother, Renilde Stoppani, was well educated for the time and a niece of the geologist Antonio Stoppani. The family moved to Rome in 1875.

She first enrolled at an all-boys technical school, hoping to become an engineer, then entered medical school at the Sapienza University of Rome as one of the first women to study medicine in Italy, and graduated with honours in 1896. From 1896 to 1901 she researched children then described as phrenasthenic, in modern terms children with some form of cognitive delay or disability, and became an advocate for women's rights and for the education of children with learning difficulties.

In 1902 Montessori enrolled in the philosophy course at the University of Rome, which then included much of what is now psychology, and did anthropological research with Italian schoolchildren. She lectured at the university's Pedagogic School until 1908. In 1906 she was invited to oversee the care of children of working parents in a new apartment building for low-income families in the San Lorenzo district of Rome.

The first Casa dei Bambini opened on 6 January 1907 with 50 or 60 children aged between two or three and six or seven. Montessori observed while the building porter's daughter did the daily teaching. By the end of 1911 Montessori education had been adopted in public schools in Italy and Switzerland, and by 1912 schools had opened in Paris and many other Western European cities. In 1916 she moved to Barcelona and for twenty years taught training courses across Europe. In 1946 she returned to Amsterdam, and she died of a cerebral haemorrhage on 6 May 1952 in Noordwijk aan Zee.

Montessori drew on Jean Marc Gaspard Itard, Édouard Séguin, Friedrich Fröbel and Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi. Her method rests on observing children free to act in an environment prepared to meet their needs. She concluded that their spontaneous activity revealed an internal programme of development and that the educator's role was to remove obstacles to it. She described four planes of development, from birth to six, six to twelve, twelve to eighteen and eighteen to twenty-four, and developed methods and materials for the first two. Her major books include The Montessori Method, in English in 1912.

The name Montessori is not trademarked, so a range of practices exists under it. Common elements are mixed-age classrooms, free choice of activity, long uninterrupted work periods and specially trained teachers.
maria-of-mangup: Maria Asanina Palaiologina, also called Maria of Doros, belonged to the ruling class of the Principality of Theodoro, or Gothia. Her parentage is uncertain. On her mother's side she was probably descended from the Palaiologos dynasty of the Byzantine Empire and the Asen dynasty of the Second Bulgarian Empire, and the Gustynskaia Chronicle makes her a cousin of Sophia Palaiologina of Muscovy. Historians variously name her father as Olubei, his predecessor John, or a lesser Byzantine refugee in Venice, Zuan Tzamplakon, whom others see as her uncle; the warring princes Alexios II and Isaac were her close relatives.

The marriage to Stephen the Great, negotiated by Tzamplakon, was probably political. Some scholars think it strengthened Stephen's position on the Black Sea; a theory that he hoped to claim the Byzantine throne has been rejected by others.

At court Maria and her relatives supported the Catholic–Orthodox union and were close to Basilios Bessarion, and with Tzamplakon she drew Stephen nearer the Catholic world. Dan Ioan Mureșan argues that this strained relations with the church hierarchy, which may explain why her place is blank in a miniature of the Humor Monastery Gospel; others think her portrait was erased on Stephen's orders.

Stephen backed an expedition that replaced Isaac with the anti-Ottoman Alexios II, but after Theodoro fell to the Ottomans in December 1475 he appears to have lost interest in her.
