Sources disagree on whether he divorced her for Maria Voichița of Wallachia. She is thought to have had up to five children, of whom only a daughter, Ana, is believed to have reached adulthood.

In her last years Maria returned to Orthodoxy and lived apart from the court; in July 1476, when the Crimean Khanate invaded, she was recorded among the refugees at Khotyn or Costești. Her tombstone at Putna gives the year 6985, read as 1477, and Bishop Teoctist led her funeral.

Her shroud of red silk with gold embroidery, 1.88 by 1.02 metres, shows her in court robes under an arch, with monograms and double-headed eagles in each corner. Art historians see in it Byzantine art with Gothic, Islamic and Ottoman elements. Mihail Sadoveanu told her wedding in his 1935 novel Frații Jderi, filmed in 1974.
maria-temryukovna: Maria was born Kucheney, the daughter of the Eastern Circassian Prince Temryuk of Kabardia. After the death of Ivan the Terrible's first wife, Anastasia Romanovna, she was presented to the tsar in Moscow, and the marriage followed the collapse of his negotiations to marry Catherine Jagiellon of Poland. Ivan was so struck by her beauty that he resolved to marry her at once. She was baptised before the wedding, taking the name Maria, and the marriage took place on 21 August 1561, four days before Ivan's 31st birthday, when she was about 15.

As tsaritsa of all Russia she had a son, Vasili, named after her father-in-law, who was born on 21 March 1563 and died on 3 May the same year. Some contemporaries described her as cruel, illiterate and vindictive, unable to adapt fully to Muscovite life and a poor stepmother to Ivan's sons Ivan and Feodor, and some sources claim that she first urged her husband to create the oprichniki. The historian Isabel de Madariaga, however, notes that most historians reject the idea that she or any of his other wives had influence over Ivan. In the summer of 1564 she went with him on a pilgrimage to Pereslavl-Zalessky, where monks and other observers were impressed by her modest bearing, piety and grasp of affairs.

Maria died on 1 September 1569, in her early twenties. Rumours spread that her husband had poisoned her, but there is no historical evidence for them. She appears as Marie in Georges Bizet's opera Ivan IV, in the Soviet silent film The Wings of a Serf of 1926, in Pavel Lungin's film Tsar of 2009 and in the Russian miniseries The Terrible of 2020, and Heinz Konsalik told her story with Ivan's in his book Der Leibarzt der Zarin.
maria-theresa: Maria Theresa was born in Vienna on 13 May 1717, the eldest surviving child of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI and Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Her father, the only surviving male of the House of Habsburg, had hoped for a son, and her birth was a disappointment to him. He spent his reign securing the Pragmatic Sanction through international diplomacy and, against the advice of Prince Eugene of Savoy, neglected the army and treasury. She married Francis Stephen of Lorraine, whom she had become close to as a girl, and bore sixteen children between 1737 and 1756.

Charles VI died on 20 October 1740, leaving a bankrupt state and an army of about 108,000 instead of the full 160,000. Saxony, Prussia, Bavaria and France repudiated the sanction, and Frederick II of Prussia invaded and took Silesia, beginning the War of the Austrian Succession. She won the support of the Hungarians, defended most of her lands and lost Silesia and a few minor territories in Italy. Her attempt to recover Silesia in the Seven Years' War, which began with Frederick's invasion of Saxony in 1756, failed. Before it, Wenzel Anton of Kaunitz-Rietberg arranged the First Treaty of Versailles of 1 May 1756 with France.

She ruled as an autocratic sovereign, with her husband and her son Joseph as co-rulers in Austria and Bohemia. Friedrich Wilhelm von Haugwitz created a standing army of 108,000 men, taxed the nobility, who had never before paid taxes, and in 1749 headed a new central Directory; Hungary and several other lands were left almost untouched. Gerard van Swieten reformed medicine, a criminal code of 1769 allowed torture, and the Theresianum, founded in 1746, and a military academy of 1751 trained officials and officers. She was a devout Catholic who rejected religious toleration, exiled Protestants to Transylvania, regarded Jews as dangerous to the state and censored books.

Francis died on 18 August 1765, and Maria Theresa dressed in mourning for the rest of her life. She died on 29 November 1780, and Joseph issued a Patent of Toleration soon after. Her reforms made the empire a modern state of international standing, and her reign is seen as the start of enlightened absolutism in Austria, although historians such as Vocelka judge her reforms more absolutist and centralist than enlightened. A bronze monument to her stands at Maria-Theresien-Platz in Vienna, built in 1888.
mariamne-i: Mariamne was the daughter of Alexander of Judaea and Alexandra, who were cousins and both descended from Alexander Jannaeus. Her only sibling was Aristobulus III, and she was known for her great beauty, as he was. Her mother arranged her betrothal to Herod in 41 BCE, and the two were married in Samaria four years later, in 37 BCE. She bore Herod five children: the sons Alexandros and Aristobulus, both executed in 7 BCE, the daughters Salampsio and Cypros, and a third son who drowned young.

Josephus writes that Herod made her brother Aristobulus High Priest because of her vehement insistence. Aristobulus, not yet eighteen, drowned in 36 BCE, and his mother Alexandra blamed Herod. She wrote to Cleopatra, who urged Mark Antony to punish Herod, and Antony summoned him to defend himself. Herod left Mariamne with his uncle Joseph, with orders that she be killed if Antony killed him. Joseph told her of this, and Herod's sister Salome later accused Mariamne of adultery with Joseph.

When Herod visited Augustus in Rhodes in 31 BCE he again left orders that Mariamne and her mother be killed if he died, this time in the care of a man named Sohemus, who also revealed them. On his return Mariamne treated him coldly. Salome insinuated that she planned to give Herod a love potion, and after a favourite eunuch was tortured, Herod had Sohemus executed and put Mariamne on trial. She was sentenced to death, and Salome insisted that the sentence stand. Mariamne was executed in 29 BCE, and Herod grieved for her for many months.

The Mariamne Tower in Jerusalem, built by Herod, was no doubt named after her. Giovanni Boccaccio included her in De Mulieribus Claris, composed in 1361–62. From the Renaissance onward her story and her relationship with Herod were the subject of many works, among them Elizabeth Tanfield Cary's English drama The Tragedy of Mariam, from 1613, Voltaire's Mariamne, of 1723, Christian Friedrich Hebbel's Herodes und Mariamne, of 1850, and John William Waterhouse's painting of 1887.
marian-anderson: Marian Anderson was born in Philadelphia on 27 February 1897 to John Berkley Anderson, who sold ice and coal at the Reading Terminal, and Annie Delilah Rucker. Her mother had worked as a teacher in Virginia but could not teach in Philadelphia, under a law applied only to Black teachers, and earned her living caring for small children. Marian was the eldest of three children, and her sisters Alyse and Ethel also became singers. Ethel's son James Anderson DePreist became a noted conductor.

Anderson's first break came in 1925, when she won a competition sponsored by the New York Philharmonic and sang with the orchestra on 26 August. Racial prejudice kept her career from gaining momentum, though she made her first Carnegie Hall appearance in 1928. A Rosenwald Fellowship of 1,500 dollars paid for study in Berlin, followed by a successful European tour. In Scandinavia in 1930 she met the pianist Kosti Vehanen, who became her accompanist, and the composer Jean Sibelius, who for many years altered and composed songs for her. Sol Hurok became her manager in 1934. She gave about seventy recitals a year in the United States, yet some hotels and restaurants turned her away; Albert Einstein hosted her several times, first in 1937.

In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution refused her Constitution Hall in Washington under a white performers-only policy. With the help of Eleanor Roosevelt and President Franklin D. Roosevelt she sang on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial on Easter Sunday, 9 April 1939, before an integrated crowd of more than 75,000 and a radio audience in the millions. She sang at Constitution Hall in 1943 at the DAR's invitation.

On 7 January 1955 she became the first Black American singer at the Metropolitan Opera, as Ulrica in Verdi's Un ballo in maschera. In 1957 she sang at Dwight D. Eisenhower's inauguration and toured India and the Far East, and she was later a delegate to the United Nations Human Rights Committee. She sang at the March on Washington in 1963 and retired from singing in 1965. Honours included the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1963, the Congressional Gold Medal in 1977 and Kennedy Center Honors in 1978.
mariana-islands: The Mariana Islands form a crescent of fifteen mostly dormant volcanic summits in the north-western Pacific, between the 12th and 21st parallels north and along the 145th meridian east. They lie south-south-east of Japan and east of the Philippines, in the northern part of Micronesia. A northern group of ten volcanic islands, all uninhabited, is separated from a southern group of five coral limestone islands: Rota, Guam, Aguijan, Tinian and Saipan. The islands rise from the Izu–Bonin–Mariana arc, where the Pacific Plate dives under the Mariana plate, and the Mariana Trench just east of them is named after them.

Migrants from the Philippines first settled the Marianas around 1500 to 1400 BCE, in the first ocean-crossing voyage of the Austronesian peoples into Remote Oceania, and the Chamorro language is closest to the Philippine languages. From about 900 to 1700 CE the Latte period brought rapid change. Its mark is the megalithic latte stones, pillars capped with a stone that kept rodents from climbing, which supported wooden houses. Rice agriculture, unique in the pre-contact Pacific, was introduced then.

The first Europeans, on the expedition of Ferdinand Magellan, saw the islands on 6 March 1521. Antonio Pigafetta wrote that the inhabitants stole a skiff from the flagship, and the Spanish burned houses and killed seven men in return, so naming the islands the Islands of the Thieves. Spain claimed them formally in 1667, and in 1668 it began a colony and named them Las Marianas after Queen Mariana of Austria. Settlement began on 14 June 1668, and Guam became a stop for the Manila galleons. The Chamorros were estimated at 50,000 in 1668, but diseases brought by the galleons killed many, and a century later only 1,800 natives remained, most of the population being of mixed Spanish and Chamorro descent.

Spain ceded Guam to the United States in 1898 after the Spanish–American War. It sold the Northern Marianas to Germany in 1899, and Japan seized them in the First World War and held them under a League of Nations mandate. In 1944 the United States captured the chain. Saipan and Tinian then became bases for B-29 bombers, and the Enola Gay and Bockscar flew from Tinian's North Field in August 1945. Afterwards the Northern Marianas came under American trusteeship, separate from Guam.
mariano-arista: José Mariano Martín Buenaventura Ignacio Nepomuceno García de Arista Nuez was born on 26 July 1802. In 1813 he enlisted as a cadet in the regiment of provincials of Puebla, and he first fought as a Royalist in the Mexican War of Independence, becoming an officer in 1818. In 1821 he joined Agustín de Iturbide's Plan of Iguala, presenting himself on 11 June 1821 to the Army of the Three Guarantees with five officers and twenty dragoons. After the capture of Mexico City he was made a captain, and in December 1821 a lieutenant colonel. In February 1823 he joined the proclamation against the First Mexican Empire.

Arista rose to brigadier general in 1831 under President Anastasio Bustamante and fought several uprisings. In 1833 he joined rebels who wanted to proclaim Santa Anna dictator, was banished to the United States, and returned in 1834. During the Pastry War he was taken prisoner at Veracruz on 5 December 1838 and held on a French ship until 28 January 1839. At the end of 1839 he became commander in chief of the armies of the north, where he defeated federalist insurgents.

In 1846 he commanded Mexican forces in the opening battles of the Mexican-American War at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma, both disastrous losses. The government recalled him, and he requested a court-martial and was absolved. He later served as Minister of War under President José Joaquín de Herrera.

Arista won the election of 1851 with thirteen of the nineteen state votes and took office on 15 January 1851, in the first peaceful transfer of power since 1824. Government income stood at 8 million pesos against expenditure of 26 million, and he cut public salaries by up to seventy-five per cent in some cases. Finance Minister Manuel Payno resigned, as did four of his successors within about a month. Revolts followed, among them one led by José María Jesús Carbajal in the northeast and the Plan of Jalisco, begun by José Maria Blancarte on 26 July 1852.

Arista resigned on 5 January 1853, and Juan Bautista Ceballos took over. Santa Anna returned to power and exiled him. After travelling in Europe he died on board the steamer Tagus on 7 August 1855 and was buried in Lisbon.
mariano-galvez: Gálvez was a foundling, left in a basket at the house of Fray Toribio Carvajal, who gave him for adoption to the wealthy family of Gertrudis Gálvez, whose name he took. He studied at the convent school in Guatemala City and then law at the Royal and Pontifical University of San Carlos Borromeo, receiving a doctorate on 16 December 1819. He counselled Gabino Gaínza, favoured the annexation of Guatemala to Mexico after independence, and in 1825 presided over the first federal Congress of Central America. In the civil war of 1826 he sided with the Federalists and joined the forces of Francisco Morazán.

Chief of state from 28 August 1831 to 3 March 1838, Gálvez governed after the expulsion of the conservative Aycinena family and the regular clergy in 1829. Liberal historians such as Ramón Rosa and Lorenzo Montúfar y Rivera credit him with making public instruction independent of the Church, ending religious festivals as holidays, founding the National Library and the National Museum and guaranteeing freedom of the press and thought. He also reformed the courts and municipal government and imposed a general head tax that bore heavily on the native population.

On 6 August 1834 he contracted with Marshall Bennett, Morazán's partner in the fine wood business, to colonise Izabal, las Verapaces, Petén and Belize within twenty years, which proved impossible. Re-elected in February 1835, he faced an epidemic of Asiatic cholera that clergy blamed on the government poisoning the springs, and from 1837 peasant revolts against the heretics spread in the name of the true religion. His scorched-earth repression of rural communities turned former friends such as José Francisco Barrundia and Pedro Molina against him. In February 1838 the forces of Rafael Carrera entered Guatemala City and he gave up power.

Gálvez died in Mexico on 29 March 1862 and was buried in the Cemetery of San Fernando. His remains were brought back to Guatemala in 1925 and placed in the old School of Law in Guatemala City. The Universidad Mariano Gálvez de Guatemala, founded in 1966, is named after him, and in 1836 he had been elected a member of the American Philosophical Society.
mariano-guadalupe-vallejo: Vallejo was born in Monterey, the eighth of thirteen children of Ignacio Vicente Ferrer Vallejo, a sergeant at the Presidio of Monterey, and María Antonia Lugo. As a teenager he, his nephew Juan Bautista Alvarado and José Castro were taught by Governor Pablo Vicente de Solá, and the English merchant William Hartnell taught him English, French and Latin. Governor Luis Argüello made him a cadet in 1824 and appointed him to the diputación, the territorial legislature. In 1829 he led soldiers against the Miwok under Estanislao. On 6 March 1832 he married Francisca Benicia Carrillo at San Diego.

Commander of the Presidio of San Francisco from 1833, Vallejo oversaw the secularisation of Mission San Francisco Solano and took most of its land into his Rancho Petaluma. In 1835 he became Comandante of the Fourth Military District and Director of Colonization of the Northern Frontier, built the Presidio of Sonoma against the Russians at Fort Ross and allied with Sem-Yeto, Chief Solano of the Suisunes. After Alvarado's uprising of 1836 the diputación made him colonel and Comandante General, with Alvarado as governor, until Manuel Micheltorena replaced them in 1842.

Disillusioned with Mexico City, he granted passports to the immigrant party of John Bidwell and John Bartleson in 1841, and came to believe that California's best hope lay with the United States. Seized on 14 June 1846 by Ezekiel Merritt's band, he was held at Sutter's Fort on John C. Frémont's orders, caught malaria and was released on 2 August 1846, weighing 96 pounds. He later wrote that the bear flag made Californios take the rebels for robbers.

He offered 156 acres of Rancho Suscol for a state capitol, and the legislature met in the new city of Vallejo in 1851 before moving to Sacramento. A long legal challenge to his land titles, despite the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, cost him almost all his land. He died on 18 January 1890 at his Lachryma Montis home in Sonoma and lies in the Mountain Cemetery there. The city of Vallejo bears his name, and Benicia his wife's; his Petaluma adobe and Sonoma home are state historic parks.
mariano-iv-of-arborea: Born at Oristano, Marianus was the son of Hugh II and spent most of his youth at Barcelona, educated at the court of Alfonso IV of Aragon. He took part in the coronation of Peter IV in 1336 and in the same year married Timbora, daughter of Dalmatius IV of Rocabertí. In 1339 Peter invested him with the counties of Goceano and Marmilla in Sardinia. He succeeded his childless elder brother Peter III in 1347 and returned to Oristano on 11 September 1349.

Arborea had been allied with Aragon for more than fifty years, but Marianus came to see that Peter IV aimed at nothing less than the annexation of Sardinia, and after the conquest of Alghero in 1353 he joined the Genoese and the Doria. His armies drove the Aragonese from every stronghold of the island except Castel di Castro, and he threatened Sassari in 1354. When Peter IV landed at Nulauro, Marianus waged a guerrilla war of ambushes until a peace signed at Sanluri at the end of 1355, by which he gave up Alghero.

War resumed in full in 1365, and Pope Urban V confirmed Arborea's possession of the whole island except Sassari, Alghero and Cagliari. An Aragonese army under Pere de Luna struck deep into Arborea towards Oristano and was trapped and defeated between the forces of Marianus and his son, the future Hugh III. In 1368 Marianus occupied Sassari. He was preparing another campaign when he died suddenly of bubonic plague in 1376.

During the two years of peace he began to set down in writing the oral laws and customs of Arborea. His chief legislative work, the Codice Rurale, was later taken into the Carta de Logu of his daughter Eleanor, who succeeded her brother Hugh III. He was also a religious man, with connections to Catherine of Siena. His daughter Beatrice married Aimery VI of Narbonne in 1363.
mariano-melgarejo: Melgarejo was born on 13 April 1820 in the town of Tarata, in the present department of Cochabamba, then part of the Viceroyalty of Peru. His mother, Ignacia Melgarejo, was mestiza; his father, the Spaniard José Linares, did not recognise him, so he took his mother's surname and grew up in a humble home in Tarata. He married Rosa Rojas, with whom he had two sons, Federico and Severo.

He entered the army as a private in 1836, fought in the War of the Confederation and was made a sergeant in 1839. For his conduct at the Battle of Ingavi against Peru in 1841, under José Ballivián, he became a second lieutenant. In 1854 he led a revolt at Santa Cruz de la Sierra against President Manuel Isidoro Belzu and was sentenced to death for high treason, but Belzu pardoned him at the plea of ladies of Cochabamba. He then helped José María Linares overthrow Jorge Córdova in 1857 and José María de Achá overthrow Linares in 1861, and Achá made him a general in 1862.

Melgarejo took power on 28 December 1864 in a coup against Achá. In March 1865 Belzu, back from exile in Europe, took La Paz, but when he entered the Palacio Quemado he was shot dead, by Melgarejo or by a soldier behind him. Rebels known as the Constitutionalists fought on until their surrender at Letanias on 24 January 1866.

Melgarejo declared the communal lands of the indigenous communities the property of the state, had the communities evicted in favour of allied landowners and abolished the municipal governments. His treaty of 1866 with Chile recognised Chilean interests in the saltpetre of the Antofagasta coast, and the Treaty of Ayacucho of 1867 sold 102,400 km2 of the Acre region to the Empire of Brazil. His constitution of 1868 gave him almost unlimited powers, and the family of his mistress Juana Sánchez grew rich at the treasury's expense.

A revolt in Potosí, which he crushed with massacres, was followed by a general uprising, and on 15 January 1871 his army under José María Calderón was defeated by General Agustín Morales. Later that year he went to Lima in search of Juana Sánchez, who refused to receive him, and on 23 November 1871 he was shot in front of her house by her brother Aurelio Sánchez, whose life he had once spared. He remains the subject of many popular anecdotes, and a skull set into a wall of the church of Tarata is attributed to him.
mariano-ospina-rodriguez: Ospina was born in Guasca, in the Viceroyalty of New Granada, on 18 October 1805, the son of Santiago Ospina and Urbina Rodríguez. Taught at home by his parents and then by José Félix Restrepo, he studied at the School of San Bartolomé in Bogotá and took a law degree in 1827. In 1828 he joined the intellectuals and officers who opposed Simón Bolívar's assumption of dictatorial power, and on the night of 25 September 1828 he was among those who assaulted the Palacio de San Carlos in the failed coup known as the Noche Septembrina. He escaped to Antioquia, fought in 1829 in the army of General José María Córdova and hid in the mountains after Córdova was killed.

In 1841 Ospina entered the cabinet of President Pedro Alcántara Herrán, first as Secretary of the Interior and then as Secretary of State, and in 1842 he carried out a comprehensive plan to expand the resources and programmes of the universities. He was elected governor of Antioquia in 1845 and again in 1854, and sat in Congress from 1849. With José Eusebio Caro he wrote the ideological platform of the Conservative Party and founded the newspaper La Civilización, and he was one of the Conservative leaders in the civil war of 1851, which they lost. In the election of 1857 he defeated two Liberals, Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera and Manuel Murillo Toro.

Imprisoned by Mosquera after his presidency, Ospina escaped with his brother Pastor in 1862 and in 1863 reached Guatemala, which granted them asylum. On the Pacific piedmont of Costa Cuca the family founded the coffee plantation Las Mercedes, known as one of the best managed in Central America, and ran a Scientific and Industrial College.

He had experimented with coffee at Fredonia, Antioquia, since 1835, and after returning to Colombia in October 1871 he promoted its cultivation among farmers. In 1880 he established the Escuela Nacional de Minas de Medellín and the National Press published his manual Cultivo del Café. He died in Medellín on 11 January 1885 and was buried in the San Pedro Cemetery. His son Pedro Nel Ospina and his grandson Mariano Ospina Pérez both became president.
mariano-paredes: José Mariano Epifanio Paredes y Arrillaga was born on 7 January 1797 and became a cadet on 6 January 1812, during the Mexican War of Independence, at first on the Spanish loyalist side. In March 1821 his regiment joined Agustín de Iturbide's Plan of Iguala. He fought at Arroyo Hondo, for which Iturbide granted him a coat of arms, and after the capture of Querétaro and Mexico City he was made a lieutenant colonel. His superiors thought him quarrelsome, and he was made a general in 1831.

Paredes backed the centralist movement of 1835 and commanded the brigade that took Zacatecas from the federalists. In 1841, when President Anastasio Bustamante could not deal with the country's political and financial crises, he called for a new government and marched on Tacubaya, where Santa Anna joined him; yet he was offered no post, being thought to lack political talent. In 1844 he proclaimed against Santa Anna at Guadalajara, and the north joined him. José Joaquín de Herrera became president on 6 December 1844 and Santa Anna was arrested, so that Paredes had again led a revolution without taking the presidency.

When Herrera was ready to consider recognising Texan independence so long as there was no annexation, Paredes called the government treasonous. From San Luis Potosí he called for its overthrow, and Herrera, who could muster little support, resigned.

Paredes became president on 3 January 1846. On 26 January he summoned an extraordinary congress of 160 deputies representing nine classes, from landowners and merchants to clergy and army, rather than regions. Its unrestricted powers were widely taken as a path to monarchy, and Paredes had expressed monarchist sentiments since 1832. A press war followed between monarchists around Lucas Alamán's newspaper El Tiempo and republican papers. On 24 April, after the American invasion had begun, he declared that he supported the republic until the nation resolved upon a change.

In the first months of the Mexican–American War, Zachary Taylor's troops crossed the Rio Grande and reached Saltillo, while American forces took California. The congress ratified Paredes as president on 12 June, with Nicolás Bravo as vice president. Facing revolution, Paredes gave up the presidency to return to the army. The garrisons of Veracruz and San Juan de Ulúa revolted in August, and he was captured and imprisoned; on 22 August the provisional president José Mariano Salas restored the federal system. Paredes was exiled to France, returned before the war ended, was cleared by an amnesty in April 1849 and died in September of that year.
marias-massacre: Relations between the Niitsitapi Confederacy of the Blackfeet, Blood and Piegan peoples and the settlers of Montana Territory had long been hostile, as settlers encroached on Native land and resources and some Blackfeet stole horses and raided settlements. The immediate cause was the killing of the rancher and former fur trader Malcolm Clarke on 17 August 1869 by Owl Child, a young Piegan warrior whom Clarke and his son Horace had beaten and humiliated in 1867; Blackfeet accounts say Clarke had also raped Owl Child's wife. Owl Child joined Mountain Chief's band, and General Philip Sheridan ordered Baker to strike that band hard.

Baker left Fort Ellis on 6 January 1870 and moved north from Fort Shaw with four companies of the 2nd Cavalry and 55 mounted men of the 13th Infantry. Before dawn on 23 January his men took the high ground above a camp of 32 lodges on the Marias River. The scout Joe Kipp recognised it as Heavy Runner's camp, which was not to be attacked, but Baker answered that they were all Piegans and ordered the attack.

Smallpox had struck the camp, and most of the healthy men were away hunting. Heavy Runner ran towards the soldiers waving a safe-conduct paper and was shot dead. The troops fired into lodges full of sleeping people, then entered the camp, collapsed burning lodges onto those inside and set everything on fire.

Mountain Chief's band escaped into Canada. Baker's men counted 173 dead and lost one soldier; Kipp later put the Blackfeet dead at 217. The Blackfeet agent William B. Pease reported eighteen older men, ninety women and fifty children killed, and only fifteen young men. Published in The New York Times, his findings caused a national outcry, but Baker's reports, which claimed 120 fighting men among the dead, became the official record, and Sheridan prevented an official investigation.

President Ulysses S. Grant adopted his Peace Policy, ended discussion of returning Indian affairs to the army and appointed Quakers and other church nominees as agents. Executive orders in 1872 and 1873 reduced the Blackfeet Reservation, and a memorial was raised at the site in 2010.
marib: Marib lies in the region of the Sarawat Mountains, about 120 kilometres east of Sanaa. It is the capital of Marib Governorate. The ancient city, known as Mirwah, is one of the most important places for Arabian archaeology. In 2023 UNESCO added it to the World Heritage List as one of the Landmarks of the Ancient Kingdom of Saba, Marib. The modern town stands about 3.5 kilometres north of the centre of the ancient city.

The Sabaean kingdom was based around Marib, with territory in northern Yemen, and its kings made the city their capital. Some scholars believe Saba to be the Sheba of biblical fame. The Sabaean kings built great irrigation works such as the Marib Dam, whose ruins are still visible and which supported a flourishing culture for more than a thousand years. They also built castles and temples in the area, most notably the temples of Almaqah at Awwam and Barran. Saba was known for dealing in the frankincense and myrrh trade.

In 25 BCE Aelius Gallus led a Roman expedition to Marib and laid siege to the city. He suffered heavy losses and was forced to retreat to Egypt. The site of the ancient city was largely abandoned during the 20th century. A small village remains, but the multi-storey mud-brick buildings of the historic city are mostly in ruins.

After floods ravaged the country in 1982, the president of the U.A.E., Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, financed the building of the present Marib Dam in 1984. He was reportedly descended from people who migrated from the Marib area to what is now the U.A.E. A refinery opened in Marib in 1986, and an oil pipeline runs from the town to Ra's Isa.
Marib has a hot desert climate. It had 16,794 inhabitants in 2005. Its ancient ruins, above all the dam and the temples at Awwam and Barran, are the chief survivals of the Sabaean past.
marib-dam: The dam stood upstream, to the south-west, of the city of Maʾrib, capital of the Kingdom of Sabaʾ, a trading state that controlled the frankincense and spice routes. The Sabaeans built it to catch the periodic monsoon rains that fall on the nearby mountains. The earliest inscription on the dam records construction or repair under Yatha' Amar Watar I, who reigned in 760–740 BCE, and minor repairs followed under his successors.

In this form the dam was a bank of packed earth, triangular in cross section, 580 metres long and 4 metres high, joined to the rock on either side by stonework, with a spillway and sluices at its northern end. Around 500 BCE it was raised to 7 metres, its water face was covered with stone, and irrigation was extended to the southern side.

After the Himyarites took control around 115 BCE they rebuilt it to a height of 14 metres, with five spillway channels, two masonry-reinforced sluices, a settling pond and a 1,000-metre canal to a distribution tank. These works, finished only in 325, irrigated about 100 square kilometres. The medieval geographer Yāqūt al-Ḥamawī described the water gathering behind the dam like a sea, to be let out through sluice gates as the crops needed it.

Silt building up behind the dam made upkeep ever more onerous. Major breaches are recorded in 449, 450, 542 and 548. Inscriptions on the dam give the costs and the large workforces of the repairs by Sharḥabīl Yaˁfar in 450 and by Abrahah in 543, and the last recorded repairs took place in 557.

The Quran (34:15–17) alludes to its destruction as the Flood of the ʿArim, sent upon Sabaʾ, whose two gardens were replaced with gardens of bitter fruit and tamarisks. Many scholars link that flood to a breach of about 145 BCE, during the war between the people of Raydān and Sabaʾ, but this remains uncertain, as migrations of the 2nd or 3rd centuries CE are also ascribed to the dam's failure. The collapse of the irrigation system provoked the migration of up to 50,000 people to other parts of Arabia and to the Levant.

A new earth dam, 38 metres high and 763 metres long, was opened 3 kilometres upstream on 20 December 1986, built by Doğuş Group at the expense of Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan. In 2023 three locations across the ancient dam were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List with other landmarks of the Kingdom of Saba.
maribor: Maribor is the largest city of the traditional region of Lower Styria and the economic, administrative, educational and cultural centre of eastern Slovenia. The Drava River divides it, and two hills, Calvary Hill and Pyramid Hill, rise among vineyards. Settlement in the area goes back to the fifth millennium BCE, and in Roman times it lay in the province of Noricum on the border with Pannonia.

A castle was built on Pyramid Hill to guard the Frankish Empire against Hungarian raids, and it was first mentioned on 20 October 1164 as Castrum Marchburch. The settlement below it received town privileges in 1254 and grew rapidly after Rudolf I of Habsburg defeated King Otakar II of Bohemia in 1278. Jews are first mentioned in 1277 and had their own quarter and synagogue; Maximilian I ordered them out in 1496. Matthias Corvinus besieged the town in 1480 and 1481 without success, and in 1532 a large Ottoman army under Suleiman attacked it and was repulsed. Fires and plague in the seventeenth century cost the town 35 per cent of its population.

The Southern Railway reached it in 1846, and in 1859 Bishop Anton Martin Slomšek moved the seat of the diocese to Maribor. In 1900 the city was 82.3 per cent German-speaking, though most of the surrounding land was Slovene. In November 1918 Rudolf Maister organised Slovene units that took control of the city from those who wished it to join German Austria. On 27 January 1919 Slovene troops fired on a German crowd, killing nine; who gave the order has never been established. The Treaty of Saint-Germain of 10 September 1919 recognised the city as part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

Nazi Germany annexed Lower Styria in 1941 and expelled many Slovenes, and the Jews of Maribor were deported. Allied bombing in the closing years of the war devastated some 47 per cent of the city area. After the war it became an industrial centre of Slovenia and Yugoslavia, and in 1991 it became part of independent Slovenia.

Maribor Cathedral dates from the thirteenth century and the Maribor Synagogue from the fourteenth, which is described as the second oldest synagogue in Europe. The Lent Festival is held every June, and the house at Lent grows the grapevine Žametovka, over 400 years old, recorded in 2004 as the world's oldest. The University of Maribor was established in 1975. Maribor was a European Capital of Culture in 2012.
marie-adelaide-grand-duchess-of-luxembou: Marie-Adélaïde was born on 14 June 1894 at Berg Castle, the eldest child of Grand Duke William IV and Infanta Marie Anne of Portugal. Her father had six daughters and no sons, and because Luxembourg followed Salic law he proclaimed her heir presumptive on 10 July 1907 to avert a succession crisis. When he died on 25 February 1912 she became the first reigning Grand Duchess of Luxembourg at the age of 17. Her mother served as regent until her eighteenth birthday on 18 June 1912, when the President of the Chamber, Auguste Laval, swore her in.

The constitution gave the monarch extensive political powers, and unlike her father and grandfather she took an active part in politics. A devout Catholic with very conservative views, she refused on the day of her accession to sign a law reducing the role of priests in education, and in 1915 she hesitated before appointing two mayors known for their anticlerical views. In late 1915 she dissolved the Chamber of Deputies to end a deadlock, with elections on 23 December. The act was permitted by the constitution but unconventional, and socialists and liberals resented it as resembling a coup d'état.

When Germany violated Luxembourg's neutrality at the outbreak of the First World War, she and her government protested formally but did not oppose the occupation further, which spared the country fighting and left its state intact. The Grand Duchess and her family worked for the Red Cross and cared for German and French soldiers. Her critics pointed to her German blood, her sister's betrothal to a German prince and her reception of the Kaiser. After the war the French government declared that it considered her government gravely compromised.

In January 1919 voices in parliament demanded her abdication, and Belgium sought to annex Luxembourg. On 9 January a group of Socialist and Liberal deputies proclaimed a republic after losing a vote to abolish the monarchy, and unrest followed in the streets. On 14 January 1919, on the advice of the Prime Minister, she abdicated in favour of her younger sister Charlotte, who saved the monarchy in a national referendum later that year. The constitution was revised and the monarch lost much of the political power the earlier text had given.

Marie-Adélaïde entered a Carmelite convent in Modena in 1920 and later joined the Little Sisters of the Poor in Rome, but poor health forced her to leave. She died of influenza at Schloss Hohenburg in Bavaria on 24 January 1924, aged 29, and in 1947 her body was interred in the Grand Ducal Crypt in Luxembourg City.
marie-antoinette: Maria Antonia Josepha Johanna was born on 2 November 1755 at the Hofburg Palace in Vienna, the fifteenth child and youngest daughter of Empress Maria Theresa and Francis I, Holy Roman Emperor. After the Seven Years' War, Maria Theresa ended her long hostility with Louis XV of France. Both wished to check the ambitions of Prussia and Great Britain, and they sealed the alliance with a marriage: on 7 February 1770 Louis XV formally asked for her hand for his grandson and heir, the Dauphin. When Louis XV died on 10 May 1774, the dauphin became Louis XVI and she became queen consort. Two weeks later the king gave her the Petit Trianon, a small château at Versailles.

As queen she became a target of those who opposed the policies of Louis XVI and of the monarchy in general. Libelles accused her of extravagance, promiscuity and sympathy for Austria. In 1785 members of her court defrauded jewellers in the Affair of the Diamond Necklace; she was falsely accused, but her reputation suffered. She was later called Madame Déficit, as the financial crisis was blamed on her spending and her opposition to reforms proposed by Turgot and Necker. In July 1789 she urged Necker's dismissal, and Paris rose to storm the Bastille.

In June 1791 the royal family tried to flee to Montmédy, the Flight to Varennes, which failed through poor execution. France declared war on Austria on 20 April 1792, and the queen was seen as an enemy. The attack on the Tuileries on 10 August 1792 forced the family to take refuge at the Legislative Assembly, and they were imprisoned in the Temple. The monarchy was abolished on 21 September, and Louis XVI was executed on 21 January 1793.

Marie Antoinette was moved to the Conciergerie, and a plot to free her failed in late August. Her trial before the Revolutionary Tribunal began on 14 October 1793; she and her lawyers had less than a day to prepare. The charges included sending millions of livres to Austria and incest, an accusation made by her son Louis-Charles under pressure from Jacques Hébert. She was convicted of high treason and guillotined on 16 October 1793. Her remains were exhumed in 1815, during the Bourbon Restoration, and buried at the Basilica of Saint-Denis. For many revolutionaries she symbolised the faults of the old regime.
marie-de-france: Almost nothing is known of Marie's life. Her name comes from a line of one of her works, Marie ai num, si sui de France, meaning My name is Marie, and I am from France, and the French scholar Claude Fauchet first called her Marie de France in 1581. Proposed identities include Marie of France, Countess of Champagne, the abbesses of Shaftesbury, Reading and Barking, Marie I of Boulogne and Marie de Meulan.

She was probably born in France but spent much of her adult life in England, where many manuscripts of her works were found. She was highly educated, wrote in an Old French with Anglo-Norman elements, and knew Latin, Middle English and possibly Breton, so she was probably of aristocratic birth or belonged to a religious house.

Scholars date her works between about 1160 and 1215. She was almost certainly known at the court of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine. The English poet Denis Piramus mentions the lais of a Marie, popular in aristocratic circles, in his Life of Saint Edmund the King of about 1180.

The Lais are dedicated to a noble king, usually taken to be Henry II or his eldest son Henry the Young King, and the Fables to a Count William, who may be William of Mandeville, William Marshall or William Longsword. Besides the Lais and the 102 Fables she wrote the Espurgatoire seint Patriz, a retelling of the legend of the Purgatory of St Patrick from a Latin text, and has been tentatively named as author of a saint's life, the Life of Saint Audrey.

The Lais are twelve narrative poems in eight-syllable verse, from 118 lines in Chevrefoil to 1,184 in Eliduc. Marie says she heard their stories from Breton minstrels, and she may have been the first to give the lai a narrative form. Most concern love entangled in triangles of loss and adventure, with intrusions from the fairy world, as in Bisclavret, whose hero is a werewolf, and Lanval, in which a fairy woman takes her lover to Avalon.

Over half involve adultery, and heroines are often shut in by jealous husbands. Only five manuscripts hold some or all of the Lais, but 25 hold the Fables, whose epilogue says they were translated from an English version by Alfred the Great. Fable 51 is an early version of the Reynard tales and inspired Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale, and in the late 14th century Thomas Chestre based his Middle English Sir Launfal on Lanval.
marie-louise-duchess-of-parma: Marie Louise was born at the Hofburg Palace in Vienna on 12 December 1791, the eldest child of Archduke Francis, who became Holy Roman Emperor the next year. She was brought up to detest France and the Revolution, influenced by her grandmother Maria Carolina, whose sister Marie Antoinette had died in it. The imperial family had to leave Vienna in 1805 and again in 1809. She learned English, French, Italian, Latin and Spanish, and her parents allowed her almost no contact with men.

After the Treaty of Schönbrunn in October 1809 Napoleon wanted an heir and a bride from a leading dynasty. His wish to marry a sister of Tsar Alexander I alarmed Austria, and at the urging of Prince Metternich a match with Marie Louise was proposed. Asked for her consent, she answered that she wished only what her duty commanded. They married by proxy on 11 March 1810 and in a civil ceremony on 1 April, and she became Empress of the French. Reserved in public, she never interfered in politics. On 20 March 1811 she bore a son, the King of Rome, later Napoleon II.

She served as regent when Napoleon was away, though he took all decisions. She left Paris on 29 March 1814, and after his abdication returned to Vienna with her son. The Treaty of Fontainebleau and the Congress of Vienna gave her the duchies of Parma, Piacenza and Guastalla for her lifetime only, since the Allies did not want a descendant of Napoleon to hold them by right.

Marie Louise entered Parma on 18 April 1816 with Count Adam Albert von Neipperg, an Austrian officer she had met in 1814, who became her chamberlain and lover and ran daily government on instructions from Metternich. After Napoleon died on 5 May 1821 she married Neipperg, who died in 1829. In 1831 an uprising inspired by the Carbonari forced her out of the city for a time, and Austrian troops crushed it. She then married Charles-René de Bombelles, who reformed the duchy's finances, on 17 February 1834. Her son died of tuberculosis in 1832. She died of pleurisy on 17 December 1847 and was buried in Vienna; Parma then passed to the Bourbons.
marie-of-montpellier: Marie was the daughter of William VIII, Lord of Montpellier, and Eudokia Komnene, a niece of the Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos. A clause in her parents' marriage contract made the firstborn child, boy or girl, heir to Montpellier. In April 1187 William VIII repudiated Eudokia, who entered a Benedictine convent at Aniane, and married Agnes, a relative of the Kings of Aragon. That marriage was declared invalid and its eight children illegitimate, so Marie remained the heiress.

In 1192 or shortly before she married Viscount Raymond Geoffrey II of Marseille, also called Barral, and was widowed at the end of that year. In December 1197 she married Count Bernard IV of Comminges and, at her father's insistence, renounced her rights to Montpellier in favour of her eldest half-brother, William, son of Agnes. She had two daughters by Bernard, Mathilde and Petronille. The marriage was notoriously polygamous, since Bernard had two other living wives, and it was annulled in 1201, by some accounts at Marie's insistence and by others at that of Peter II of Aragon. Her father nonetheless openly acknowledged his son as heir.

After William VIII died in 1202 her half-brother took control of the city, but Marie asserted her right. On 15 June 1204 she married Peter II of Aragon, and a revolt against William IX brought her recognition as Lady of Montpellier. She had two children by Peter: Sancha, born in 1205, who died aged one, and James.

Peter II tried to divorce her, hoping to marry Maria of Montferrat, queen of Jerusalem, and to claim Montpellier for himself. Marie spent her last years resisting these political and matrimonial manoeuvres, and Pope Innocent III at last decided in her favour and refused the divorce. She died in Rome on 21 April 1213, on her way back to Aragon. Peter II was killed a few months later, on 14 September 1213, at the Battle of Muret, and their only surviving child, James, inherited both Aragon and Montpellier.
marie-of-the-incarnation-ursuline: Marie Guyart was born in Tours, the fourth of the eight children of Florent Guyart, a baker, and Jeanne Michelet. At fourteen she asked to enter the Benedictines of Beaumont Abbey, but her parents married her in 1617 to Claude Martin, a master silk worker. Within two years she had a son, Claude, and her husband died six months after the birth, leaving her a widow at nineteen. She lost his failing business and went to live with her family.

She took vows of chastity, obedience and poverty and recorded a series of visions, the first at the age of seven. In 1627 she read the Vida of the Spanish mystic Teresa of Ávila, who became her model. On 25 January 1631 she entered the Ursuline convent in Tours, leaving her son with the Buisson family; the boy, who later became a Benedictine monk, once tried to storm the convent with a band of school friends.

After professing her vows in 1633 she took the name Marie de l'Incarnation. A vision that Christmas, which her priest identified as showing Canada, set her on a mission to New France. The widow Madeleine de la Peltrie funded the venture, and on 4 May 1639 the two women sailed from Dieppe on the Saint Joseph, landing at Quebec City on 1 August. In 1642 the Ursulines moved from a small house in the lower town to a stone building in the upper town.

The school taught the basics of faith, French and Latin literature and civility. French girls paid one hundred and twenty livres for education and pension, while Innu, Huron and Algonquin girls paid nothing and were taught French manners and dress, then encouraged to share these at home. Smallpox outbreaks from the 1630s to the 1650s led many Native people to suspect the nuns' crosses and icons of spreading disease, and Iroquois victories in the 1650s and a fire that destroyed the convent in 1650 brought the community close to despair.

She died of a liver illness on 30 April 1672. Besides two autobiographies, the second lost in a fire while still in manuscript, she wrote between 8,000 and 20,000 letters, most to her son, who published many of them after her death. Pope John Paul II beatified her on 22 June 1980, and Pope Francis granted her equipollent canonisation on 2 April 2014, alongside François de Laval, the first Bishop of Quebec. The Anglican Church of Canada keeps her feast on 30 April.
mariehamn: Mariehamn lies on the main island of Åland and borders Jomala to the north and west and Lemland to the east. It stands on a peninsula with two main harbours, west and east, both ice-free for most of the year and with minimal tidal variation. The Baltic Sea moderates the climate, giving mild winters and cool summers, and summers are cooler than in most of Sweden and Finland.

The town was founded on 21 February 1861 on land that belonged to the village of Övernäs in Jomala, and named after the Russian empress Maria Alexandrovna, so that the name means 'Marie's Port'. It grew from a planned layout that remains largely intact. One of its oldest streets, Södragatan, has preserved nineteenth-century wooden houses.

In the late nineteenth century shipping became central to the local economy, and shipowners and shipyards settled in the town. After the First World War Mariehamn became known for its Grain Fleet. The shipowner Gustaf Erikson (1872-1947) operated sailing ships from the town.

Mariehamn is the capital of Åland, an autonomous region of Finland, and the seat of its government and parliament. It has about 40 per cent of the region's population, and most residents have Swedish as their native language. Several buildings, among them the church of Mariehamn (1927), the Åland Maritime College (1927) and the town hall (1939), were designed by the Finnish architect Lars Sonck. The four-masted barque Pommern, now part of the Åland Maritime Museum, is moored in the Western Harbour, which has ferry connections to Sweden, Estonia and mainland Finland.
mariel-boatlift: The exodus was set off by a sharp downturn in the Cuban economy and followed decades of Cuban emigration to the United States. In the late 1970s President Jimmy Carter had tried to improve relations, lifting travel restrictions, and in September 1977 both countries opened an Interests Section in each other's capital, though Cuba's support for Soviet interventions in Africa and the Middle East kept relations strained. Cubans had already sought asylum in foreign embassies: in 1979 a group crashed a bus into the Venezuelan embassy, and early in 1980 the Peruvian and Venezuelan embassies took in asylum seekers.

After some 10,000 Cubans crowded into the grounds of the Peruvian embassy, the government let them leave. About 7,500 first went by air, at first to Costa Rica. On 20 April Fidel Castro declared the port of Mariel open to anyone with someone to collect them, and Cuban Americans began sending boats; the first reached Key West on 21 April with 48 refugees, and by 25 April as many as 300 boats were in the harbour. Around 1,700 boats made the crossing. The Cuban government treated the exodus as a cleansing of undesirables and organised acts of repudiation against those leaving.

In the United States the refugees were processed in camps around Miami, including the Orange Bowl, then moved to bases such as Fort Chaffee, where riots broke out. Carter's administration classed them with Haitian arrivals as Cuban-Haitian entrants. The two governments ended the boatlift by agreement in late October 1980.

Most of the refugees were ordinary Cubans, tens of thousands of them Seventh-Day Adventists or Jehovah's Witnesses; 2,746, or 2.2 percent, were classed as serious or violent criminals and denied citizenship. They gained permanent legal status in 1984 under a revision of the Cuban Adjustment Act. David Card's study of Miami found that the arrivals, about half of whom settled there, had only a marginal effect on wages. Carter's opponents called the boatlift a failure of his administration, a CBS and New York Times poll of June 1980 found 71% of Americans disapproving, and in November 1980 voters in Miami Dade County removed Spanish as a second official language.
marienberg-fortress: The fortress occupies a spur of the 266-metre Marienberg, which rises about 100 metres above the left bank of the Main, with vineyards on its slopes. Around 1000 BCE people of the Urnfield culture built a refuge castle here, and finds suggest that under the later Hallstatt culture, around 500 BCE, the hill had trade contacts with Ancient Greece and may have been the seat of a prince. A 7th-century document calls the fortification Uburzi, the origin of the name Würzburg; the name Marienberg, Mary's Mount, came from the chapel built under Duke Hedan II.

From around 1200 the prince-bishops fortified the hill, and Bishop Hermann von Lobdeburg moved his court there permanently in 1253 after quarrels with the townspeople, who sided with the Emperor. In 1373 the burghers attacked it with catapults and the garrison answered with gunpowder weapons, the first recorded use of guns in Würzburg. In 1525, during the German Peasants' War, a peasant army of 15,000 besieged it without breaching the walls; the Swabian League then outflanked the besiegers and more than 8,000 peasants were killed. The sculptor Tilman Riemenschneider was imprisoned and tortured there that year.

Bishop Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn completed its transformation into a Renaissance residence. Swedish troops plundered it in 1631 and carried most of its library to Uppsala. It became a Reichsfestung in 1648 and its outer works took their present form in 1711 to 1715. Once the court had moved across the river, it served only as a military post, changing hands in the wars of 1795 to 1815, and lost its status as a fortress in 1867.

Incendiary bombs dropped by the Royal Air Force on 16 March 1945 burned much of the fortress, and rebuilding lasted from 1950 to 1990. The Museum für Franken in the Baroque armoury shows Franconian art including Gothic sculpture by Riemenschneider, and the Fürstenbaumuseum tells 1,200 years of the history of the city and the fortress.
marienstatt-abbey: The abbey stood in a direct line of Cistercian foundations: it was settled from Heisterbach Abbey, which had been founded from Himmerod Abbey, itself a daughter of Clairvaux Abbey in 1134. The community was first established in 1212 at Neunkhausen, made possible by a donation from Eberhard of Arenberg and his wife Adelheid von Molsberg. Climate and soil proved poor there, and in 1222 the monks moved to the present site in the Nister valley. According to legend, the abbot chose it after dreaming of a hawthorn bush that flowered in winter. The first church was consecrated on 27 December 1227 under Conrad, the third abbot.

From 1476 lay people could attend services in the abbey church, and in 1485 the octave of Corpus Christi became its pilgrimage day. The Counts of Sayn introduced the Reformation in their territories from 1561. In the Thirty Years' War Sweden claimed the property as crown land on 3 October 1633, expelling the monks and damaging the buildings; in 1637 abbot Johannes Wittig lived there with only one brother and one novice. After the war the monastery recovered, the church was decorated in Baroque style under abbot Benedikt Bach, and the old buildings were replaced from 1735 to 1751 under Petrus Emons.

During secularisation the abbey was given to Frederick William, Prince of Nassau-Weilburg, and the last monks left in 1803, though Catholic masses continued; from 1831 the church served a new parish, which saved it from demolition. In 1864 Bishop Peter Joseph Blum of Limburg bought the site and opened a home for neglected boys. In 1888 monks of Wettingen-Mehrerau Abbey bought it back and resettled it under Dominikus Willi, later Bishop of Limburg.

Abbot Konrad II Kolb built a library in 1909, and the school he opened in 1910 grew after the Second World War into the Privates Gymnasium Marienstatt; in 2024 the historian Uli Jungbluth published former pupils' accounts of harsh treatment at its boarding school between 1947 and 1954. The church belongs to the state of Rhineland-Palatinate and the other buildings to the abbey, which keeps a brewery, a guest house and a library of about 112,700 books. Its organ, built by Franz Rieger in 1969-1970 and later enlarged, has 67 stops.
marija-gimbutas: Marija Birutė Alseikaitė was born in Vilnius to Veronika Janulaitytė-Alseikienė and Danielius Alseika, members of the Lithuanian intelligentsia. Her mother held a doctorate in ophthalmology from Berlin and her father a medical degree from Dorpat. Her parents were connoisseurs of Lithuanian folk art and received writers and scholars, among them Jonas Basanavičius, whose collected folklore remained important to her. The family settled in Kaunas in 1931, and after her father's sudden death five years later she resolved to become a scholar. From 1936 she joined ethnographic expeditions to record folklore and studied Lithuanian beliefs and rituals of death.

She studied linguistics at Vytautas Magnus University from 1938, then archaeology, ethnology and folklore at the University of Vilnius, where she took her master's degree in 1942. In 1941 she married the architect Jurgis Gimbutas. With a young daughter she fled the advancing Soviet army to areas held by Germany, and in 1946 she received a doctorate from the University of Tübingen for a study of prehistoric burial rites in Lithuania.

In the 1950s the family moved to the United States. She worked at Harvard, becoming a Fellow of the Peabody Museum in 1955, and then moved to UCLA, where she was Professor of European Archaeology and Indo-European Studies and became Curator of Old World Archaeology in 1965.

In 1956 she proposed the Kurgan hypothesis, which joined the archaeology of burial mounds to linguistics to explain the origin and migrations of the Proto-Indo-European speakers. Between 1967 and 1980 she directed excavations of Neolithic sites in southeastern Europe, including Anzabegovo in North Macedonia and Sitagroi and Achilleion in Greece. Her Bronze Age Cultures of Central and Eastern Europe appeared in 1965.

Her last three English-language books, The Goddesses and Gods of Old Europe (1974), The Language of the Goddess (1989) and The Civilization of the Goddess (1991), described a goddess-centred, peaceful Old Europe that she held was overturned by patriarchal Kurgan warriors. Joseph Campbell admired the work, and the ecofeminist Charlene Spretnak later argued that a backlash against it had been organised.

Many archaeologists rejected it: Bernard Wailes judged her knowledgeable but weak in critical analysis, and David W. Anthony, who praised her view of the Indo-European homeland, noted that Europe had hillforts and weapons long before the Kurgan peoples. Three genetic studies of 2015 were taken to support the Kurgan theory. She died in Los Angeles in 1994.
marikana-massacre: The strike took place against rivalry between the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM), the largest affiliate of the Congress of South African Trade Unions, and the Association of Mineworkers and Construction Union (AMCU), founded by Joseph Mathunjwa after he fell out with the NUM in 1998. The NUM's popularity had begun to decline, partly because of its perceived closeness to government and management. The strike was driven by rock drill operators, about 4,100 of whom Lonmin employed, who worked in some of the most dangerous conditions underground. They sought a rise from R4,000 to R12,500 a month, although the collective wage agreement ran until 2013.

After a mass meeting on 8 August 2012 at which NUM leaders refused to support the demand, the rock drillers began an unauthorised strike on 10 August. On 11 August, according to strikers and other witnesses, NUM representatives opened fire on the strikers as they marched on the union's office. The police presence grew from 209 officers on 13 August to 718 on 16 August, and between 12 and 14 August at least ten people were killed, including two police officers and two Lonmin security officers.

On the morning of 16 August the police command referred to the day as "D-Day", and a police spokesman said the gathering on a koppie near the mine would be ended. When police moved in with barbed wire and Nyala vehicles, officers, who said they were under attack, shot strikers at two sites; 17 were fatally wounded at each, and 78 were injured. Afterwards 270 miners were arrested and charged with the murder of their colleagues under the common purpose doctrine, charges later dropped after public outcry.

The strike ended on 18 September with a wage agreement giving increases averaging 11 to 22 per cent; wildcat strikes spread to other mines, and President Jacob Zuma sent the army to the platinum belt. The Farlam Commission, set up in August 2012 and chaired by the retired judge Ian Farlam, found the decisive cause of the deaths to be the decision of 15 August to enter a tactical phase to disarm and disperse the miners; the plan was prepared in haste and could not be carried out without significant bloodshed.

It also found that some shootings at the first scene were in self-defence, but that some of the dead had presented no threat. It criticised the strikers, unions and mine management as well. It made no findings on the second scene, where it said events were a chaotic free for all. Phiyega, named in the report, was suspended with full pay. Farlam lamented in 2022 that no disciplinary proceedings had followed, and only a handful of police officers had been charged, none for the deaths of 16 August.
marimekko: Marimekko was founded in Helsinki in 1951 by Viljo and Armi Ratia after Viljo's oil-cloth factory project failed and was converted to a garment plant. Armi asked artist friends to apply their graphic designs to textiles, and the company designed and sold a line of simple dresses to show how the fabric could be used. Armi Ratia first thought of Armi as the company's name, but it was already registered. Her middle name was Maria, shortened to Mari, and in her home town of Koivisto she heard people talking about dresses (mekko in Finnish), which gave the name Marimekko.

Two designers set the tone. Vuokko Nurmesniemi designed the red and white striped Jokapoika shirt in 1956, and Maija Isola designed the Unikko poppy print in 1964. In 1957 the industrial designer Timo Sarpaneva invited the company to present a fashion show at the Triennale in Milan, which was cancelled at short notice. The architect Benjamin C. Thompson introduced the brand to the United States through his Design Research stores, and Jacqueline Kennedy bought eight Marimekko dresses that she wore during the 1960 presidential campaign. By 1965 the company employed over 400 people and made fabrics, toys and dinnerware.

In 1985 the company was sold to Amer-yhtymä. In the early 1990s it was close to bankruptcy until Kirsti Paakkanen bought it from Amer and introduced new business methods; by 2005 its revenue had quadrupled since her purchase. By 2011 there were 84 stores across the world. Products are made in several countries, including China, India, Thailand, Portugal and Lithuania, while the fabrics are printed in a textile factory in Helsinki. The logo, in use since 1954, was made by the graphic designer Helge Mether-Borgström from modified Olivetti typewriter letters.

The New York Times writer Cindy Babski said that for people who came of age in the 1960s the clothes and fabrics represented more than a brand name, conjuring up an era. In 2007 Heidi Avellan wrote in the Swedish newspaper Sydsvenskan that Marimekko was no longer a statement. In 2013 the company was accused of plagiarism after a design painted on a Finnair plane was found to copy a 1963 painting by the Ukrainian artist Maria Primachenko, and the designer Kristina Isola admitted copying elements of it. Other designs were also questioned, and the chief executive later apologised for misleading consumers about the originality of one of them.
marin-drzic: Marin Držić was born into a large and affluent family of Ragusa, with six sisters and five brothers. He was trained and ordained as a priest in Dubrovnik, and his uncle Džore Držić was also an author. After his ordination in 1526 he was sent in 1538 to Siena in Tuscany to study canon law. His academic results were average, but his extroverted and warm personality is said to have won over his fellow students and professors, and he was elected rector of the university. Losing interest in his studies, he returned to the Dubrovnik Republic in 1543.

At home he became an acquaintance of the Austrian adventurer Christoph Rogendorf, who was at odds with the court of Vienna, and after a brief stay in Vienna he came back to his native city. His later exploits included relations with a group of Dubrovnik outlaws and journeys to Constantinople and Venice. He worked as an interpreter, a scrivener and a church musician.

Držić's works cover lyric poetry, pastorals, political letters and pamphlets, and comedies. His pastorals Tirena, Venera i Adon and Plakir are still highly regarded as examples of the genre, although the pastoral as an art form has virtually disappeared. His comedies are counted among the best of European Renaissance literature. Like those of Lope de Vega, Ben Jonson or Molière, they are full of vitality, celebrating love, liberty and sincerity and mocking avarice, egoism and petty tyrants, in the family and in the state.

Pomet, lost today, is dated to 1548 or 1553, and some historians regard it as his debut. Novela od Stanca belongs to 1550 and Skup to 1554; the latter is thematically similar to the Aulularia of Plautus and Molière's The Miser. Dundo Maroje, arguably his best-known play, has also been staged in theatres abroad.

Convinced that Dubrovnik was governed by a small circle of aristocrats bent on tyranny, Držić wrote five letters, four of which survive, urging the powerful Medici family in Florence to help him overthrow the government of his home town. They did not respond. He died suddenly in Venice on 2 May 1567 and was buried in the Church of St. John and Paul.

Independent Croatia has awarded the Marin Držić Award for dramatic work, and the Croatian Parliament declared 2008, the 500th anniversary of his birth, the Year of Marin Držić. An avenue in Zagreb bears his name, as does a stage in Draškovićeva street, named after his nickname Vidra, a word that can also mean a perfidious and resourceful person.
marine-chronometer: Until the mid-1750s, accurate navigation at sea out of sight of land was an unsolved problem because longitude was hard to calculate. Navigators could find latitude from the angle of the sun at noon or of Polaris, but longitude required a time standard that would work aboard a ship. Gemma Frisius first proposed using a chronometer for the purpose in 1530. Pendulum clocks were useless at sea, since the rolling of a ship and variations in gravity of up to 0.2% disturbed them. Christiaan Huygens made the first attempt at a marine chronometer in 1673 and in 1675 devised one regulated by a balance wheel and spiral spring, but it remained imprecise at sea.

In 1714 the British government offered a longitude prize, with awards from £10,000 to £20,000 depending on accuracy. John Harrison, a Yorkshire carpenter, completed a clock in 1735 with counter-oscillating weighted beams, and his H1 and H2 used that system. H3 of 1759 introduced the bi-metallic strip and caged roller bearings but was still inaccurate. His much smaller H4 solved the precision problems in 1761, with a fast-beating balance wheel and a temperature-compensated spiral spring, and he submitted it for the £20,000 prize.

The chronometer keeps the time of a known place, usually Greenwich. The difference between it and local time found from celestial observations gives the ship's longitude, and every four seconds of error can put the east–west position off by just over one nautical mile. It was kept below decks in a box in gimbals, and a hack watch set from it was carried on deck for observations. Ships often checked chronometers against the time ball at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, before a voyage.

The Royal Observatory began testing chronometers in 1820 in an Admiralty trial, and observatories in Western Europe later certified them in chronometer competitions. Accuracy of mechanical marine chronometers reached about 0.5 second per day.

Pierre Le Roy invented the detent escapement in 1748, and in 1766 produced a chronometer that Rupert Gould considered the foundation of the modern one. Thomas Earnshaw and John Arnold developed simplified spring detent escapements from 1780, which served as the basis of marine chronometers until the electronic era. The instruments were at first so expensive that not all ships carried them, as the wreck of the East Indiaman Arniston with the loss of 372 lives showed, but by 1825 the Royal Navy was supplying its vessels routinely.

It is argued that without them the Royal Navy's ascendancy might not have occurred so overwhelmingly. Mechanical chronometers were mass-produced in the Second World War, notably by Hamilton in the United States and in Germany.
marinid-dynasty: The Marinids were a faction of the Zenata Berber tribal confederation. The Banu Marin were nomads from the Zab, a region around Biskra in present-day Algeria, who were pushed out after Arab Bedouins arrived in North Africa. They entered what is now Morocco in force by the beginning of the 13th century. They first submitted to the Almohads. Their leader Mahyu contributed to the Almohad victory at the Battle of Alarcos in 1195, though he died of his wounds, and his son Abd al-Haqq was the effective founder of the dynasty.

After the Almohad defeat at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa on 16 July 1212, the state was weakened. From 1213 or 1214 the Marinids began to tax farming communities in the north-east of today's Morocco, and from 1215 fighting with the Almohads broke out regularly.

Early rulers governed as emirs, first at Taza, then at Fez from 1244. Abu Yusuf Ya'qub captured Marrakesh in 1269, ending Almohad rule, and the later rulers were sultans of Fez and Morocco. The Marinids supported the Emirate of Granada against Castile, and after Granada ceded Algeciras they tried to control the traffic of the Strait of Gibraltar. By 1294 they had occupied Rota, Tarifa and Gibraltar. In the mid-14th century, under Abu al-Hasan and his son Abu Inan, they briefly held sway over most of the Maghreb, including large parts of modern Algeria and Tunisia. They were defeated at the Battle of Río Salado in 1340, and the Castilian capture of Algeciras in 1344 expelled them for good from the Iberian Peninsula.

After the death of Abu Inan Faris in 1358, real power lay with viziers while sultans succeeded one another quickly. In 1359 Hintata tribesmen from the High Atlas occupied Marrakesh and governed it independently until 1526. From the early 15th century the related Wattasid dynasty competed with the Marinids, whose last sultan, Abd al-Haqq II, reigned until 1465.

The Marinids largely continued Almohad structures, ruling a tribal state with little civil administration beyond the capital and relying on family members as governors. Their army was drawn from loyal tribes, other Zenata tribes, Arab tribes such as the Banu Hilal and Banu Ma'qil, and Christian mercenaries who served as the sultan's bodyguard. They made Fez their capital and restored Maliki Sunni Islam as the official religion. The Marinids built madrasas across the country, and the Qarawiyyin of Fez reached its height of prestige. They were the first to use zellij tilework extensively.
marino-faliero: Marino Faliero was the son of Jacopo Faliero and Beriola of the Loredan family, and had three brothers and a sister. The Faliero family was one of the oldest in the Venetian patriciate, and by the 14th century it was counted among the twelve most prestigious, so-called apostolic noble families. He married twice. His first wife, whose name is unknown, bore him numerous children; in 1335 he married the much younger Alvica Gradenigo, a granddaughter of Doge Pietro Gradenigo, and that marriage was childless.

Because many members of the family shared the same name, his early career is certain only after 1330. His first known post, in October 1315, was as one of the three heads of the Council of Ten, which examined a sympathiser of the failed Tiepolo conspiracy of 1310. In 1323 he became bailo and captain of Negroponte (Euboea).

Faliero served as podestà of Chioggia, Padua, Treviso and Serravalle, and as captain of the galleys for the Black Sea and Constantinople in 1333. At Padua he helped Ubertino I da Carrara overhaul the city's statutes. In 1344 he went as envoy to Pope Clement VI in Avignon and obtained permission to trade with Alexandria. In 1346 he commanded Venetian naval forces against the revolt of Zara. In 1350 he was sent as ambassador to Genoa to avert war, but was recalled, and war came.

He was elected doge in succession to Andrea Dandolo and learned of it while on a mission to the papal court at Avignon. He took office on 11 September 1354. The populace was disenchanted with the ruling aristocrats, who were blamed for the naval defeat by Genoa at Portolungo in 1354.

In April 1355 Faliero attempted a coup. The plot intended to murder the chief patricians on 15 April and proclaim him prince of Venice. It was badly organised and was discovered when some conspirators made revelations. The Council of Ten arrested the ringleaders and posted armed guards across the town. Faliero pleaded guilty and was beheaded on 17 April; ten more ringleaders were hanged from the Doge's Palace.

A later tradition held that he acted to avenge an insult to his wife by the patrician Michele Steno. Modern historians often dismiss this and suggest he thought autocratic rule, the norm abroad, could secure Venice's future. Frederic C. Lane proposed that he served the war party dissatisfied with the peace with Genoa. He was condemned to damnatio memoriae, and his portrait in the Hall of the Great Council was replaced by a black shroud. Byron, Casimir Delavigne and Donizetti treated the story, as did Delacroix's painting of 1826.
marino-sanudo-torsello: Sanudo was born in Venice around 1270 into an aristocratic trading family active in the eastern Mediterranean, a branch of which had founded the Duchy of the Archipelago on Naxos after the Fourth Crusade; his father sat in the Venetian Senate. As a teenager he stayed at Acre, the last stronghold of the Crusader states, before its fall in 1291, and he later travelled to Greece, Romania, Palestine, Egypt, Armenia, Cyprus and Rhodes. He is sometimes called Marino Sanuto the Elder, to tell him from the later Venetian diarist of the same name.

He joined the entourage of Giovanni Dandolo, Doge of Venice, was at the court of Palermo in 1305 and then entered the service of Cardinal Riccardo Petroni at Rome, while also handling business for his family. His correspondents included the Venetian traveller Guglielmo Bernardi de Furvo, Bishop Jerome of Kaffa and Andronikos II Palaiologos, the Emperor of Byzantium. Why he took up the cause of a crusade is unclear: the fall of Acre, or a patron who favoured a new crusade, may have moved him.

His Secreta fidelium crucis, first written in 1306 and 1307 for Pope Clement V, stressed strategy and secure finance: a blockade of Egypt over several years, then the capture of the sultanate as a base for invading the Holy Land, with manoeuvres planned and their daily costs budgeted. He kept expanding it with a history of the Holy Land and a geography of the Levant, presented a new version to Pope John XXII in 1321 and sent a French translation to King Charles IV of France. At least eleven copies survive.

The treatise carries maps of the eastern Mediterranean, Arabia, Egypt, the Black Sea, Italy and western Europe, the earliest surviving medieval maps made for military strategy, and a world map joining the mappamundi with the accuracy of a portolan chart; the Genoese cartographer Pietro Vesconte was their main author. His Latin history of the Frankish principalities and Byzantium, written between 1326 and 1333, survives only in a Venetian translation, the Istoria del regno di Romania, and gives a unique account of the recovery of Constantinople by Michael VIII Palaiologos.
marinus-of-tyre: Marinus came from Tyre in the Roman province of Phoenicia and wrote in Greek. He could draw on a wealth of new geographical information gathered by trade and military expeditions, and his interest in trade routes may point to a background in commerce, though Ptolemy quotes him as saying that merchants cared little for exploration and often magnified distances through love of boasting. He probably worked at the Library of Alexandria, and a young Ptolemy, who calls him the most recent geographer of his time, may have met him there. Little else is known of his life.

His treatise, possibly called A Revision of the Geographical Map, is lost; it may date from between 106 and 114. He collected astronomically determined latitudes, relative positions of cities, lists of cities on the same meridian or parallel, nautical charts, the borders of Roman provinces and the reports of traders and military expeditions, and tried to combine them in one world map. He made a preliminary version but never finished it. Ptolemy praised his improvements yet judged his grasp of mathematics and astronomy limited.

Marinus divided the globe into horizontal strips along parallels and vertical strips between meridians. His zero meridian ran through the Isles of the Blessed, the westernmost land then known, near the present-day Canary or Cape Verde Islands. He used an equirectangular projection with the parallel of Rhodes, at 36 degrees North, as its standard, and reckoned the equator at 180,000 stadia. In his view the inhabited world reached from Thule at 63 degrees North to Agisymba at 24 degrees South, and east as far as Sera, China. His maps were the first in the Roman Empire to show China. He also coined the term Antarctic.

Ptolemy, some forty years later, used the work as a source for his Geography, acknowledged his debt and quoted it directly, but corrected its data. In his judgement Marinus had stretched Asia too far east and Africa too far south, placing central Africa at 24 degrees South where Ptolemy preferred about 16.4. Because Ptolemy describes his corrections in detail, the map can be roughly reconstructed by reversing them, and Ernst Honigmann did so in 1930. In the tenth century an Arab geographer cited Marinus five times in his Book of Admonition and Revision, though all five remarks go back to Ptolemy. A crater on the Moon was named after him in 1935.
