mario-soares: Mário Soares was born in Lisbon on 7 December 1924, the son of João Lopes Soares, founder of the Colégio Moderno and a republican activist who had once been a priest. He studied there, where for a short time Álvaro Cunhal, later the leader of Portuguese Communism and one of his chief rivals, taught him geography.

At university he joined the Portuguese Communist Party and led its youth section, which he left in 1951. The political police, PIDE, first arrested him in 1946. His arrests ended his career as a lecturer in history and philosophy, so he studied law and became a lawyer who defended political prisoners of the dictatorship founded by António de Oliveira Salazar.

In 1958 he supported General Humberto Delgado's presidential campaign and later became his family's lawyer after Delgado's murder in 1965. In April 1964 he helped found the Acção Socialista Portuguesa in Geneva. Arrested again in March 1968, he was banished to São Tomé and Príncipe, but he was released within eight months after Marcello Caetano replaced Salazar. Exiled in 1970, he taught in France, and in 1973 the Portuguese Socialist Action became the Socialist Party, founded in Bad Münstereifel under the umbrella of Willy Brandt's SPD, with Soares as secretary-general.

After the Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 he returned and became minister for overseas negotiations in the provisional government, meeting Samora Machel of Frelimo about Mozambique's independence. He opposed an attempt by the Communist Party and radical officers to extend their control, which ended with the dismissal of Vasco Gonçalves in September 1975 and a failed far-left coup in November.

After the 1976 Constitution the Socialists won a plurality in the Assembly of the Republic and Soares formed a minority government, resigning in 1978 after an unpopular austerity policy. He returned as prime minister after the 1983 elections, and his main achievement was negotiating Portugal's entry into the European Economic Community.

In 1986 Soares was elected president, defeating Diogo Freitas do Amaral by little more than two per cent, and he was re-elected in 1991 with almost 70 per cent of the vote. He devised the Presidência Aberta, tours of the country each addressing a particular issue.

After leaving office in 1996 he sat in the European Parliament from 1999 to 2004. He died on 7 January 2017, aged 92, and was given a state funeral, the first in Portugal since that of President Óscar Carmona in 1951. He is considered the father of Portuguese democracy.
mario-vargas-llosa: Mario Vargas Llosa was born to a middle-class family on 28 March 1936 in the southern Peruvian city of Arequipa. He was the only child of Ernesto Vargas Maldonado, a radio operator in an aviation company, and Dora Llosa Ureta, the daughter of an old criollo family. His parents separated a few months before his birth. His first literary influences were relatively obscure Peruvian writers such as Martín Adán, Carlos Oquendo de Amat and César Moro, from whom he sought new narrative structures to describe urban Peru.

His first novel, The Time of the Hero (1963), is set among cadets in a Lima military school and draws on his own experiences at the Leoncio Prado Military Academy. It won the Premio de la Crítica Española, and its sharp criticism of the Peruvian military led several generals to attack it. The Green House (1965) and Conversation in The Cathedral (1969), a two-volume novel based on the dictatorship of President Manuel A. Odría, followed. In 1971 he published a study of Gabriel García Márquez, his doctoral thesis for the Complutense University of Madrid; the two writers' friendship ended in 1976, when Vargas Llosa struck García Márquez at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City.

The War of the End of the World (1981) was his first historical novel, recreating the 19th-century War of Canudos in Brazil. He initially supported Fidel Castro's Cuban government, but broke with it over the imprisonment of the poet Heberto Padilla in 1971 and afterwards identified as a liberal. In 1983 he served on the commission investigating the Uchuraccay massacre, whose conclusions drew intense criticism from anthropologists. In 1987 he became a leader of the centre-right Movimiento Libertad, and in 1990 he ran for the presidency of Peru for the FREDEMO coalition, losing to Alberto Fujimori.

From the 1990s he lived mainly in Madrid and acquired Spanish citizenship in 1993. He received the Rómulo Gallegos Prize in 1967, the Prince of Asturias Award in 1986, the Miguel de Cervantes Prize in 1994 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2010. King Juan Carlos I made him Marquess of Vargas Llosa in 2011, and in 2021 he was elected to the Académie Française.

Vargas Llosa died in Lima on 13 April 2025, aged 89, surrounded by his family. His main theme was the individual's struggle for freedom within an oppressive reality, and he often challenged the inadequacies of society through his fiction. Scholars read his early novels as modernist and later ones such as Captain Pantoja and the Special Service as postmodernist and comic. He is counted among the major Latin American writers alongside Octavio Paz, Julio Cortázar, Jorge Luis Borges and Gabriel García Márquez.
marion-mahony-griffin: Marion Lucy Mahony was born in Chicago, the daughter of Jeremiah Mahony, a journalist, poet and teacher from Cork, and Clara Hamilton, a schoolteacher. After the Great Chicago Fire the family moved to Winnetka, whose open landscape later shaped her attention to nature. Following her father's suicide in 1882 her mother became a school principal in Chicago and was active in women's groups. Encouraged by her cousin, the architect Dwight Perkins, and funded by Anna Wilmarth, she studied architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, graduating in 1894 as the second woman to do so after Sophia Hayden.

She began in Perkins's office in Steinway Hall and in 1898 became the first licensed female architect in Illinois. Frank Lloyd Wright hired her as his first employee in 1895, and she worked with him until 1909, designing buildings, furniture, stained glass and decorative panels. Her drawings, which combined perspective, plan and section on one sheet and drew on Japanese prints, became a mark of his style; historians now credit her with about half the drawings in his Wasmuth Portfolio, though Wright gave her little credit. When he left for Europe in 1909, she worked under Hermann V. von Holst on his abandoned commissions.

She married Walter Burley Griffin in 1911 and worked in his practice. Thomas S. Hines and other historians hold that her watercolour perspectives were instrumental in winning the Canberra competition. From 1914 she ran the couple's Sydney office and its private commissions, among them Cafe Australia, Newman College and the Capitol Theatre in Melbourne. The Griffins embraced Rudolf Steiner's anthroposophy, developed the Knitlock building method and settled at Castlecrag. In 1936 she joined her husband's practice in Lucknow, managing the office and training draughtsmen.

After Walter's death she returned to the United States in 1939 and largely retired. She spent about twenty years on The Magic of America, a 1,400-page account with 650 illustrations, never formally published but online since 2007. Suffering memory loss, she died in poverty in 1961 aged 90 and was buried in Graceland Cemetery. Long treated as a helper of Wright and her husband, she was later described by Reyner Banham as the first woman architect who needed no apology in a world of men. A Chicago beach was named after her in 2015.
maritsa: The Maritsa rises at the Marichini Lakes in the Rila Mountains of western Bulgaria and flows east-southeast between the Balkan and Rhodope Mountains, past Plovdiv and Dimitrovgrad to Edirne in Turkey. East of Svilengrad it forms the border between Bulgaria and Greece, and below Edirne, where it receives its two chief tributaries, the Tundzha and the Arda, it turns south and divides Greece on the west bank from Turkey on the east.

It enters the Aegean near Enez in a delta. Its basin covers about 53,000 square kilometres, two thirds of it in Bulgaria, and holds most of the historical region of Thrace. The river cannot be navigated; it is used for hydroelectric power and irrigation, and its upper valley is a principal east-west route in Bulgaria.

The earliest recorded name is the Greek Euros, used by the poet Alcman in the 7th or 6th century BCE. In Thracian the name became Ebros, which gave the Greek Hebros and the Latin Hebrus. The modern name Maritsa may derive from the name of a mountain near the river's mouth in antiquity. Proto-Indo-European roots meaning wide have been proposed for the ancient name, as has a Thracian word meaning splasher.

In 1371 the river gave its name to the Battle of Maritsa, also called the battle of Chernomen, in which Ottoman forces defeated the Serbian rulers Vukašin Mrnjavčević and Jovan Uglješa, both of whom died. After 1923 the lower river became the modern border between Greece and Turkey.

The lower course, where the river forms the Greek-Turkish border, floods for about four months in a typical year, and the low lands beside it suffer losses to farming and roads. The river lends its name to the Maritsa motorway in Bulgaria and to Shumi Maritsa, which was the Bulgarian national anthem from 1886 to 1947 and whose words picture the river running bloody after fighting. Since Greece joined the European Union in 1981 the river has been part of the Union's external boundary.
maritz-rebellion: Twelve years after the Second Boer War, many Boers who had fought to the end, the Bittereinders, still hoped to restore the South African Republic in the Transvaal, and some saw a war between Britain and Germany, their old supporter, as their opportunity. When war broke out in August 1914, Prime Minister Louis Botha told London that South Africa could defend itself and agreed to invade German South-West Africa. Troops under General Henry Lukin and Lieutenant Colonel Manie Maritz were mobilised on the border in early September, and another force occupied the port of Lüderitz on 19 September 1914.

Brigadier-General Christiaan Frederick Beyers, Commandant-General of the Union Defence Force, resigned on 15 September in protest. That day he set off with General Koos de la Rey to visit Major Jan Kemp at Potchefstroom, and on the way de la Rey was shot dead by a policeman at a road block set up for the Foster gang; many nationalist Afrikaners believed it a government assassination. Maritz then allied himself with the Germans and proclaimed a provisional government of a free South Africa. General de Wet seized Heilbron, and about 12,000 rebels gathered, against some 32,000 government troops, about 20,000 of them Afrikaners.

Martial law was declared on 12 October 1914. Maritz was defeated on 24 October and took refuge with the Germans, Beyers's commando was dispersed at Commissioners Drift on 28 October, and Beyers drowned in the Vaal River on 8 December. De Wet was captured in Bechuanaland on 1 December. Kemp led his commando across the Kalahari Desert, losing 300 of his 800 men on the 1,100 kilometre trek, and surrendered on 4 February 1915.

At least 124 rebels were killed in battle and at least 229 wounded. The leaders were sentenced to six or seven years in prison and heavy fines, but were released two years later, as Botha valued reconciliation. Jopie Fourie, an officer who had not resigned his commission before joining the rebels and whose men had fired on government troops during a truce, was shot by firing squad at Pretoria Central Prison on 20 December 1914. South African forces went on to conquer German South West Africa by July 1915.
mark-antony: Marcus Antonius was born in Rome on 14 January 83 BCE into the plebeian gens Antonia. His family claimed descent from Anton, a son of Heracles, and he harnessed lions to his chariot and put a lion on many of his coins in memory of it. His father was Marcus Antonius Creticus, and his grandfather, the noted orator Marcus Antonius, was murdered in the purges of Gaius Marius in 87-86 BCE. His mother, Julia, was a third cousin of Julius Caesar. In 57 BCE he joined the staff of Aulus Gabinius, Proconsul of Syria, as cavalry commander, and won his first distinctions in Judea at Alexandrium and Machaerus.

Publius Clodius Pulcher secured Antony a place on Caesar's staff in 54 BCE. After a year in Gaul he was elected quaestor for 52 BCE, and he returned to command Caesar's cavalry at the Battle of Alesia against Vercingetorix. In the winter before the civil war he proposed that Caesar keep only two of his eight legions, a concession that Pompey found satisfactory but Cato and Lentulus refused; Antony then fled Rome for Caesar's camp. Caesar made him master of horse and left him to govern Italy. They were reconciled by 44 BCE, when Antony was elected consul alongside Caesar.

After Caesar's assassination Antony joined Lepidus and Octavian in the Second Triumvirate, and in 42 BCE they defeated Brutus and Cassius at the Battle of Philippi. Antony took the eastern provinces. He spent the winter in Athens, where he presented himself as a friend of Greek culture and was initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries, and at Ephesus he was worshipped as Dionysus born anew. He married Octavia, Octavian's sister, in 40 BCE, but lived with Cleopatra VII, who bore him three children. Lepidus was expelled in 36 BCE, and the two remaining triumvirs split in 33 BCE.

In 31 BCE the Roman republic declared war on Cleopatra and proclaimed Antony a traitor, and Octavian's forces defeated him at Actium. Octavian invaded Egypt with Agrippa in August 30 BCE. Antony stabbed himself, mistakenly believing that Cleopatra had already died, and according to Plutarch he died in her arms at her tomb. She killed herself in mid-August. Octavian had Caesarion and Antony's son Antyllus put to death, but spared Antony's other children. His honours were revoked and his statues removed, though he was not subject to a complete damnatio memoriae. Octavian, known as Augustus from 27 BCE, became the uncontested ruler of Rome. Through his daughters by Octavia, Antony was ancestor of the emperors Caligula, Claudius and Nero.
mark-sittich-von-hohenems-altemps: Mark Sittich was born at Hohenems, the son of Wolf Ludwig von Hohenems and Chiara de' Medici, whose brother Giovanni Angelo Medici became Pope Pius IV. The name Altemps comes from Alt-Ems, from the Latin altus, high, as Hohenems means High Ems. Nothing is known of his education. As a young man he fought in the Italian War of 1551 to 1559 under his uncle Giangiacopo de' Medici, took part in the attempt of Charles V to win Metz back from France in 1552, was at the siege of Siena and helped repulse an Ottoman attack on Piombino. He became a Knight of the Order of Santiago.

After his uncle's election on 26 December 1559, Mark Sittich was made Bishop of Cassano on 29 May 1560 and a cardinal deacon on 26 February 1561, with the church of Santi Apostoli. The chapter of Konstanz Minster elected him bishop, confirmed by the pope on 24 October 1561, and he was also made perpetual legate in Avignon and archpriest of the Lateran Basilica. Before his appointment as legate to the Council of Trent on 10 November 1561, he went as legate to Emperor Maximilian II and to Ferdinand, King of the Romans, to win their help in reopening the council.

He collected the income of many governorships, including Fermo, Ascoli Piceno and Ancona, while others governed for him. In Konstanz he held a diocesan synod in 1566, authorised the Catechism of Pius V in 1577 and sought to bring in the Jesuits. He took part in the conclaves from 1565 to 1592, which elected Pius V, Gregory XIII, Sixtus V, Urban VII, Gregory XIV, Innocent IX and Clement VIII.

In 1568 he began rebuilding the Palazzo Altemps to designs by Martino Longhi the Elder, and he assembled a large collection of Roman antiquities and sculptures. He died in Rome on 15 February 1595 and was buried in Santa Maria in Trastevere. His legitimised son Roberto became Duke of Gallese, and he guided the early career of his nephew, the later Prince-Archbishop of Salzburg.
mark-the-evangelist: Mark the Evangelist is also known as John Mark, and an unbroken tradition, according to William Lane, identifies him with John Mark and with the cousin of Barnabas. Hippolytus of Rome, in On the Seventy Apostles, instead distinguishes three figures: Mark the Evangelist, John Mark and Mark the cousin of Barnabas. All three, he says, were among the Seventy Disciples whom Jesus sent out to Judea.

Coptic tradition holds that Mark was born in Cyrene, in the Pentapolis of North Africa, and that his house hosted the disciples after the death of Jesus. Other denominations do not share the belief that he was a Roman African from ancient Libya.

According to Eusebius of Caesarea, Peter met Mark on his journey through Asia Minor and took him as companion and interpreter. Mark wrote down Peter's sermons, and so composed the Gospel according to Mark. The Acts of the Apostles says that after the Council of Jerusalem Mark went to Cyprus with Barnabas.

Tradition holds that Mark then travelled to Alexandria and founded the church there, from which the Coptic Orthodox Church, the Greek Orthodox Church of Alexandria and the Coptic Catholic Church all trace their origins. He is honoured as its first bishop and as the founder of Christianity in Africa. Eusebius says that Anianus succeeded him as bishop in the eighth year of Nero, probably because Mark's death was near.

Scholars are divided over the gospel's authorship. It does not name its author, as was common among ancient biographies. The earliest evidence for Mark's authorship comes from Papias, c. 60 – c. 130, whose information modern scholars find hard to interpret. Most scholars favour Rome as the place of composition.

Later Coptic tradition says that Mark was martyred in 68. According to this tradition, the pagans of Alexandria resented his efforts to turn the city away from its traditional gods, put a rope around his neck and dragged him through the streets until he died.

His feast is kept on 25 April by the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, and also by the Church of England. The Coptic Orthodox Church keeps it on Parmouti 30, which falls on the same date in the Julian calendar. In art Mark is shown writing or holding his gospel, and his symbol is the winged lion. Major shrines include the Basilica di San Marco in Venice and Saint Mark's Coptic Orthodox Cathedral in Alexandria.
mark-twain: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born on 30 November 1835 in Florida, Missouri, the sixth of seven children of Jane Lampton, a native of Kentucky, and John Marshall Clemens, a lawyer from Virginia. Only three of his siblings lived beyond childhood. When he was four the family moved to Hannibal, Missouri, a port town on the Mississippi River that inspired the fictional St. Petersburg of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn. Slavery was legal in Missouri at the time and became a theme in those books.

Twain became a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi, which gave him the material for Life on the Mississippi (1883). He then went west to join Orion in Nevada, joked about his failure at mining, and turned to journalism for the Virginia City Territorial Enterprise. A humorous story about a jumping frog of Calaveras County, published in 1865 and based on a tale he heard at the Angels Hotel in Angels Camp, California, brought him international attention. He became a much sought-after speaker.

His novels include The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876), Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court (1889) and Pudd'nhead Wilson (1894), and he wrote The Gilded Age (1873) with Charles Dudley Warner. He began with light humorous verse and became a chronicler of the vanities, hypocrisies and murderous acts of mankind. In Huckleberry Finn he combined humor, narrative and social criticism, and he helped create a distinctive American literature built on American themes and language. The book has been repeatedly restricted in American high schools, not least for its frequent use of a racial slur.

His pen name, he said, came from the riverboatman's cry of mark twain, meaning that the water was two fathoms deep. He also said he took it from Captain Isaiah Sellers, who signed river news with it for the New Orleans Picayune. Some have doubted this story. His views became more radical with age, and he supported the labour movement, among others the Knights of Labor. He died of a heart attack on 21 April 1910, the day after Halley's Comet was closest to the Sun, as he had predicted.
marklin: Theodor Friedrich Wilhelm Märklin founded the company in 1859 and died in 1866, early in its life. His wife Caroline Märklin led the business until 1888, when Eugen Märklin and Karl Märklin took it over. In 1891 the firm released its first wind-up train with carriages that ran on standardised track. It reasoned that railway toys could follow the practice of doll's houses, where an initial purchase was expanded with accessories for years afterwards, and it offered extra rolling stock and track to enlarge its boxed sets.

In 1891 Märklin defined gauges 1 to 5 as standards for toy trains and presented them at the Leipzig Toy Fair, and they soon became international standards. O gauge followed, by some accounts as early as 1895 or as late as 1901, then H0 scale in 1935 and the 1:220 Z scale in 1972 under the name Mini-Club, a reply to Arnold Rapido's N gauge. From 1914 to 1999 it made mechanical construction sets like Meccano and Erector, from 1967 to 1982 a slot-car system called Märklin Sprint, and from 1909 into the 1950s alcohol-burning model steam engines.

Until 2006 the company belonged to the Märklin, Friz and Safft families. On 11 May 2006 it was sold to the British investment group Kingsbridge Capital for about 38 million dollars, after years of slumping sales had left debts of about 70.5 million dollars. It bought the assets of Trix in 1997 and those of the bankrupt Lehmann firm, owner of the LGB brand, in 2007. It filed for insolvency on 4 February 2009 and announced a return to profit on 5 February 2010. The Simba Dickie Group acquired it in 2013.

The Märklin system places a third rail in the roadbed, with only small studs showing through the ties, which gives simple wiring for reverse loops while only two rails are visible. For many years Märklin was the only maker to run its H0 trains on alternating current. Its first digital train control, using Motorola microchips, appeared in 1984, and a later system developed with Lenz and Arnold for two-rail direct-current locomotives grew into Digital Command Control. H0, at 1:87, is the largest part of its sales, and in German-speaking countries the company holds about half the market. Older Märklin trains are highly collectible, and in January 2005 more than 100 pieces were stolen from its museum in Göppingen and recovered in March 2005.
markos-botsaris: Botsaris was the fifth child of Kitsos Botsaris and his first wife Chrysoula, of the Botsaris clan, the most powerful fara of Souli. Like other Souliotes he spoke a dialect of Albanian as his first language, in which he was known as Marko Boçari, though he also spoke Greek. From 1800 his grandfather George Botsaris served Ali Pasha as armatolos of Tzoumerka, and the clan's departure weakened Souli before its surrender in 1803. In 1804 Ali Pasha's army besieged the clan in Agrafa, and Kitsos escaped with his family to Parga and the Ionian Islands.

Markos married Eleni Karakitsou in 1806, divorced her around 1810 and later married Chrysoula Kalogerou. He served as an officer in the Albanian Regiment of the French army until 1813. A Greek–Albanian lexicon of 1809, made at the request of François Pouqueville, is known as the Botsaris dictionary, though scholars such as Xhevat Lloshi and Dinos Georgoudis argue that he wrote down what his elders dictated rather than composing it.

In 1820 he returned to Epirus and fought at first against Ali Pasha at the Siege of Ioannina, before the Souliotes changed sides in exchange for a promise that they would regain Souli. In December 1820 he took the fortress of Variades and attacked a convoy of the sultan at Kompsades. In 1821 he led Souliot bands in the War of Independence and joined the siege of Arta. After the defeat at the Battle of Peta, Souli surrendered again in September 1822 and he fled to Missolonghi.

Promoted general of Western Central Greece on 12 October 1822 at the request of Alexandros Mavrokordatos, he drew out surrender talks during the First Siege of Missolonghi until reinforcements arrived from the Morea, and the siege was lifted after a failed Ottoman assault on Christmas Eve. When the prefect Konstantinos Metaxas made all the rival chieftains generals in 1823, Botsaris tore up his own certificate of rank.

Against the advance of Mustafa Pasha of Shkodër, he struck the Ottoman vanguard of about 5,000 men near Karpenisi with 350–450 men shortly after midnight, and was shot in the head. He was buried with full honours in Missolonghi; his grave was desecrated after the Ottomans took the city in 1826. Fitz-Greene Halleck and Dionysios Solomos wrote poems about him, Pavlos Carrer composed the opera Marco Bozzari in 1858, and he appeared on the Greek 50 lepta coin of 1976–2001.
markos-monastery: The monastery stands in the village of Markova Sušica, 18 kilometres from central Skopje, and has been in use since it was founded. It takes its name from the Serbian Prince Marko, who reigned when the building was completed in the 14th century. Its single church, dedicated to Saint Demetrius, is built on a cross plan of brick and stone, with a narthex, a central dome and a smaller dome to the west; the iconostasis is made of stone pillars. Around it stand lodgings, a belfry, a well, warehouses, a bakery and a mill, and the monks still keep a special oven for making rakija.

The frescoes were the work of several painters from the region. Among their subjects are the Holy Mother of God, the twelve great feasts, Jesus Christ and Saint Nicholas, and the founders King Vukašin and his son Prince Marko appear as ktetors, the donors of the church.

Before Ottoman rule the monastery kept a school, and its monks and priests copied manuscripts. Skopje came under Ottoman rule in 1392, and many churches and monasteries of the area were destroyed, but Marko's Monastery suffered almost no damage. An Ottoman record of 1467/8 counts 20 monks there. Kiril Peychinovich was its hegumen, or abbot, from 1801 to 1818, and in 1830 the Ottoman aristocrat Hamzi Paşa added an exonarthex, an outer porch, to the church.

In 1894 the Bulgarian metropolitan of Skopje had frescoes overpainted with a fat-based paint, an act of national fanaticism that most damaged the portraits of Vukašin and Marko. Attempts to restore the damaged paintings were made in the 1920s.
marmaduke-grove: Grove was born in Copiapó, the son of the lawyer José Marmaduke Grove Avalos and Ana Vallejo Burgos. In 1891 his father, a local leader of the Radical Party, was imprisoned for criticising President José Manuel Balmaceda. Grove entered the Chilean Naval Academy in 1892 but was expelled in 1894 for joining a student revolt against its directors. He entered the Military Academy in 1897, where his classmates included Carlos Ibáñez del Campo and Arturo Puga, and graduated as an artillery sub-lieutenant. He trained in Germany from 1906 to 1911 and had become a Freemason by 1912.

Grove was Under-Director of the Military Academy from 1920 to 1924 and Director of the Air Force Academy from 1925. On 3 September 1924 he took part in the saber rattling, a protest by 56 officers over low pay, and carried the military committee's petitions to the president; the crisis ended with the resignation of President Arturo Alessandri. Sent abroad as military attaché once Ibáñez was in power, Grove conspired with the exiled Alessandri and signed the Calais pact on 17 January 1929. In November that year he was retired from the army and deported to Buenos Aires.

On 21 September 1930 he flew to Concepción in a small red plane to raise a revolt. It failed, and he was deported to Easter Island, from which he escaped on a French corvette. He returned after the fall of Ibáñez in 1931, and President Juan Esteban Montero made him Air Force Commander-in-chief in March 1932. During the Socialist Republic he was Defense minister from 5 to 16 June 1932. In that year's presidential election, back from a second exile on Easter Island only two days before the vote, he came second to Alessandri with 17.7 per cent.

With Oscar Schnake, Salvador Allende and Carlos Alberto Martínez he founded the Socialist Party of Chile on 19 April 1933, became its General Secretary in 1938 and presided over the Popular Front, which won that year's presidential election with Pedro Aguirre Cerda. Elected senator in a by-election on 9 May 1934 while held in jail, he proposed Chile's first plan of agrarian reform in 1939 under the slogan "Neither land without men nor men without land". He was re-elected in 1941, left the Senate in 1949 after a defeat by Ibáñez, and died in Santiago on 15 May 1954.
marmara-ereglisi: Marmara Ereğlisi is a municipality and district of Tekirdağ Province with an area of 175 square kilometres. It lies 30 km east of the town of Tekirdağ and 90 km west of Istanbul, near a small pointed headland on the north shore of the Sea of Marmara. The name distinguishes it from two other large towns in Turkey called Ereğli, a name that derives from the Greek Heraclea: Konya Ereğlisi in Konya Province and Karadeniz Ereğli on the Black Sea coast.

The town was founded as Perinthos, usually called Perinthus in English, as a Samian colony. In about 300 CE it was renamed Heraclea. It was built like an amphitheatre on the hillside of a cape extending into the Sea of Marmara, close to where the modern town stands. Its port and its position at the junction of several sea routes made it a town of commercial importance, and it became known for its resistance to Philip II of Macedon in 340 BCE. Many of its coins survive and identify the festivals held there.

Heraclea became a Christian bishopric at an early date, according to tradition in the Apostolic Age. As a provincial capital it was the metropolitan see for all the bishoprics of its province, including Byzantium, which became Constantinople in 330. Justinian I later restored its aqueducts and palace. The see of Constantinople soon gained superiority over Heraclea, which nonetheless had five suffragan sees in the list of Pseudo-Epiphanius, fifteen in an early tenth-century list and seventeen in one of 1022 to 1025. With the Ottoman conquests the number fell sharply. Today it survives as a titular see of the Ecumenical Patriarchate and, for the Catholic Church, as Heraclea in Europa.

In 1815 Edward Daniel Clarke visited the area looking for antiquities. He found scarcely any at the village of Eski Ereğli, now Gümüşyaka in Silivri district, and was told that the coastal village known as Büyük Ereğli, some six miles away, corresponded to ancient Heraclea.

The district had a population of 29,549 in 2022. The town is a mixture of modern blocks and old country houses, with a small harbour, and the coast on either side is lined with holiday compounds used by people from Istanbul. The area has two natural harbours and three small ports, with tanker ports of Botaş and Total, an LNG storage facility and a gas-fired power plant at Sultanköy. A large fault follows the coast.
marmarica: Marmarica was a coastal district of ancient Libya lying between Cyrenaica and Egypt, along what is now the frontier between Libya and Egypt. Its towns included Bomba, the ancient Phthia, Timimi, the ancient Paliurus, Tobruk, the ancient Antipyrgus, Acroma, the ancient Gonia, Bardiya, As-Salum and Sidi Barrani, the ancient Zygra. To the south it reached as far as the Siwa Oasis, known at the time for its sanctuary of the god Amun. Marmarica proper ended in the east at the escarpment of Catabathmus Magnus, now Akabah el-Kebir, at Salum.

The inhabitants were known generally as Marmaridae, with the names Adyrmachidae and Giligammae in the coastal districts and Nasamones and Augilae in the interior. The Adyrmachidae, whom the Periplus of Pseudo-Scylax names as the first people of Libya, are said to have differed from the nomadic tribes and to have closely resembled the Egyptians. South of the Libyan Nomos lived the Ammonii, centred on the fertile oasis of Ammon at Siwa.

The eastern part of the region, between the Catabathmus and the Bay of Plinthine, was called the Libycus Nomus; it had formerly been counted as part of Egypt, and some geographers treated it as a separate district, but under the Roman Empire it was included in Marmarica. Paraetonium, also called Ammonia and now Mersa Matruh, was the westernmost town of Egypt and, with Pelusium, one of the horns of Egypt. Menelaus Portus, which tradition held was founded by Menelaus, was remembered as the place where Agesilaus II died.

In late antiquity Marmarica was also called Libya Inferior, and Cyrenaica Libya Superior. In the 4th century both belonged to the diocese of Egypt, within the Praetorian prefecture of the East. Several bishoprics of the province, among them Ammoniace, Antiphrae, Antipyrgos, Darnis, Zagylis and Zygris, are listed in the Annuario Pontificio as titular sees.
maroboduus: Maroboduus, also known as Marbod, was born into a noble family of the Marcomanni, a Germanic Suebian people. As a young man he lived in Italy and was reportedly well regarded by the Emperor Augustus. The name is a latinised form of the Gaulish Maro-boduos, from maro- meaning great and boduos meaning crow, a word that in Celtic and Germanic languages is linked with battle.

The Marcomanni reportedly suffered a significant defeat at Roman hands in 10 BCE. About 9 BCE Maroboduus returned to Germania and became ruler of his people. To escape Roman expansion into the Rhine–Danube basin, he led them to the area later called Bohemia, took the title of king and organised a confederation of neighbouring Germanic tribes. He was the first documented ruler of Bohemia with a government.

In 6 CE Augustus planned to destroy the kingdom as too dangerous. The future emperor Tiberius commanded 12 legions against the Marcomanni, but a revolt in Illyria forced him to make a treaty with Maroboduus and recognise him as king. His rivalry with Arminius, who destroyed the legions of Publius Quinctilius Varus in 9 CE, prevented a concerted attack on Roman territory from north and south. According to Velleius Paterculus, Arminius sent Varus's head to Maroboduus, who sent it on to Augustus. In 16 CE he stayed neutral in the war of Tiberius and Germanicus against the Cherusci.

War broke out between Arminius and Maroboduus in 17 CE, and after an indecisive battle he withdrew into the forests of Bohemia in 18. The next year Catualda, a young Marcomannic nobleman who had lived in exile among the Gutones, returned, perhaps through Roman intervention, and defeated him. Maroboduus fled to Italy, where Tiberius held him in Ravenna for 18 years. He died there in 37 CE. Catualda was in turn defeated by the Hermunduri Vibilius, and the realm was then ruled by the Quadian Vannius, until Vibilius and his nephews Vangio and Sido deposed him and ruled as Roman client kings.
maronites: The Maronites take their name from Saint Maron, a Syriac monk whose teachings spread through the northern Levant. Christianity spread slowly in the Lebanese highlands, which were still largely pagan in the 5th century. Maron's first disciple, Abraham of Cyrrhus, called the Apostle of Lebanon, set out in 402 to convert the inhabitants of the coast and mountains. In 451 the Maronites followed the Council of Chalcedon, and a massacre of 350 monks of Maron's monastery in 517 is thought to have resulted, though who ordered it, and the event itself, have been debated.

After the Muslim conquest of the Levant in 637, Christians of the lowlands began to settle in Mount Lebanon. In 685 John Maron became the first Patriarch of the Maronite Church, which angered the Byzantine emperor and led to persecution. Maronite monks left the Orontes Valley for Mount Lebanon, and by the 10th century they were the majority of the Christians around Tripoli and Byblos. They welcomed the First Crusade in 1096, and the church returned to communion with Rome in 1180, although the Maronites hold that they were never out of it.

The Ottomans conquered the region in 1516, and France took the role of protector of the Maronites in 1649. In the 1860 conflict thousands of Maronites were massacred by Druze; some estimates put the Christian dead at about 11,000. Many fled to Egypt, and emigration to the Americas began. Famine in the First World War is estimated to have killed one third to one half of the population. After the war the Maronites campaigned successfully for Greater Lebanon, established in 1920 under the French Mandate.

The Maronite Church is an Eastern Catholic church in full communion with the pope, using the Antiochian Rite, with its patriarch traditionally seated at Bkerke north of Beirut. Classical Syriac remains its liturgical language alongside Arabic. Under the unwritten National Pact the president of Lebanon is a Maronite. Maronite communities also live in Syria, Cyprus and Israel, and the diaspora is estimated at between 7 and 12 million. In the 20th century many Maronite intellectuals favoured a distinct Lebanese identity, some promoting Phoenicianism, while others, such as Kahlil Gibran, contributed to modern Arab thought.
maroons: Maroon was an English term for Africans in the Americas and the islands of the Indian Ocean who escaped from slavery, through flight or manumission, and lived in independent settlements. They were called cimarrones in Spanish America. The word entered English around the 1590s, from the French marron and probably the American Spanish cimarrón, first used in Hispaniola of feral cattle, then of Indian slaves who escaped to the hills, and by the early 1530s of enslaved Africans who did the same. As early as 1512 enslaved Africans escaped from Spanish captors and joined Indigenous peoples or lived on their own. The earliest Maroon communities formed in what is now the Dominican Republic after the first slave rebellion on 26 December 1522.

Colonial authorities tried to eradicate the Maroons, who hid in remote bush, caves and mountains and defended themselves by guerrilla warfare, sometimes allying with enemies of a colony. They farmed and hunted, and raided plantations to burn crops, steal livestock and invite others to join them. On small islands Maroons lost ground as planters took more land, and only on larger islands could organised communities thrive.

In Brazil, the quilombo of Palmares, established around 1600 near Recife, had at its height more than 30,000 free people and was ruled by King Zumbi. It withstood Dutch expeditions and on average one Portuguese expedition nearly every year between 1672 and 1694, when the Portuguese conquered it. In Panama, Bayano led a rebellion in 1552, and the Spanish offered his followers freedom on condition that they admit no newcomers and return runaways. After the Second Maroon War in Jamaica, nearly 600 Maroons were deported in 1796 to Nova Scotia and in 1800 to Sierra Leone.

Maroon cultures varied widely with history, geography, the African origins of their members and contact with Indigenous peoples. Some developed creole languages from European and African tongues, such as Saramaccan in Suriname, and some mixed with Indigenous peoples, as with the Garifuna, descended from Maroon communities on Saint Vincent and deported to Honduras in 1797. The Ndyuka treaty remains important in defining the territorial rights of the Maroons of Suriname, and in the Jamaican town of Accompong a festival on 6 January commemorates the peace treaty with the British.
marquesas-islands: The Marquesas Islands, known in Marquesan as Te Henua ʻEnana or Te Fenua ʻEnata, "the land of men", are among the most remote islands in the world. They lie about 1,370 kilometres north-east of Tahiti and about 4,800 kilometres south-west of Mexico. Most are volcanic, created by the Marquesas hotspot, and the highest point is Mount Oave on Ua Pou, at 1,230 metres. A northern group is centred on Nuku Hiva, and a southern group on Hiva ʻOa. Rainfall is greater on the northern and eastern windward coasts, and droughts, which seem to be linked with El Niño, are frequent and sometimes last several years.

The first settlers were Polynesians from West Polynesia, descendants of the Lapita culture. Early radiocarbon dates suggested arrival before 100 CE or about 600 CE, but a 2010 study with higher-precision methods found that eastern Polynesia was settled much later, in two waves. The first reached the Society Islands, and the second, between about 1190 and 1290 CE, spread to the Marquesas. Such rapid settlement is thought to explain the close uniformity of East Polynesian culture, biology and language.

The abundant natural resources long supported a large population, which lived by fishing, collecting shellfish, hunting birds and gardening. Breadfruit was the staple, and at least 32 other introduced crops were grown. Basalt from the quarry island of Eiao was carried by sailing canoe for more than 2,500 kilometres, to supply adze heads to Moʻorea, Mangareva, Tubuai, Rarotonga and Tabuaeran.

The first Europeans to arrive may have been the crew of the Spanish ship San Lesmes, which vanished in a storm in June 1526. Álvaro de Mendaña reached the islands on 21 July 1595 and named them after his patron García Hurtado de Mendoza, Marquis of Cañete, Viceroy of Peru. He visited Fatu Hiva and Tahuata before sailing to the Solomon Islands. The first missionaries, William Pascoe Crook and John Harris of the London Missionary Society, arrived in 1797; Harris left after a few months, and Crook stayed until 1799.

The Marquesas form one of the five administrative divisions of French Polynesia, with its capital at Taioha'e on Nuku Hiva. French and Tahitian are the official languages, and the Marquesan languages remain widely spoken. The islands had 9,346 inhabitants at the 2017 census, and most are Catholic. In 2024 UNESCO listed the islands as a World Heritage Site under the name Te Henua Enata.
marquis-de-bussy: Charles Joseph Patissier de Bussy was the son of N. Patissier de Bussy, a colonel of infantry, and Sophie Ernestine Passaval; he was born on 8 February in either Bucy-le-Long or Ancienville. He became a lieutenant in 1733 and a captain in 1734. After his father died in 1736 he entered the service of the French East India Company and landed that year at Port-Louis on Isle de France (Mauritius), then governed by Bertrand-François Mahé de La Bourdonnais, where he took part in the island's defence. By 1738 he was on Île Bourbon (Réunion).

As one of the main subordinates of Joseph François Dupleix, Bussy helped extend French activity in the Northern Circars and along the Coromandel Coast, and Hyder Ali of Mysore served under his command. By a grant of 23 November 1753, Salabat Jang, Subedar of the Deccan, conceded to him the paraganas of Chicacole, Ellore, Rajahmundry and others for the upkeep of the French troops in his service. The agreement, known as the Treaty of Aurangabad, was signed for Salabat Jang by his prime minister, Lashkar Khan. In 1755 the new Mughal emperor Alamgir II wrote asking for a French contingent of 1,000 men against the Maratha Confederacy, promising payment and support for the French in the Carnatic Wars.

Around Hyderabad in 1750 many of his soldiers died of disease, and Pusapati Peda Vijaya Rama Raju, king of Vizianagaram, helped him out of a financial crisis and to rebuild his battalion. In 1757 Bussy's force aided the raja of Vizianagaram in the Battle of Bobbili, which began on 23 January and ended with the Bobbili fort destroyed and many of its soldiers dead. The Yanam region was given to him in gratitude for this help, and a street there still bears his name.

In March 1754 Bussy married Marie, the youngest stepdaughter of Dupleix; their daughter died in Paris in 1759. For his service under Dupleix he received the Order of Saint Louis. In 1782 he was named to command all French forces beyond the Cape of Good Hope, and he coordinated his operations with Pierre André de Suffren against the British in the Indian campaigns of the American War of Independence. He was Governor General of Pondicherry from 1783 until his death there on 7 January 1785. He appears as an antagonist in the Telugu films Bobbili Yuddham (1964) and Tandra Paparayudu (1986).
marquis-de-lafayette: Lafayette was born on 6 September 1757 at the Château de Chavaniac in the province of Auvergne, into a wealthy land-owning family with a martial tradition, and was commissioned an officer at age 13. After the marriage contract of 1773 he lived with his young wife in his father-in-law's house in Versailles. The Continental Congress lacked funds for his voyage, so he bought the ship Victoire with his own money. The French Crown disapproved, and he landed near Georgetown, South Carolina, on 13 June 1777. He offered to serve without pay, and Congress commissioned him a major general on 31 July 1777.

Lafayette first saw combat at the Battle of Brandywine on 11 September 1777, where he was shot in the leg but rallied troops during the retreat. In May 1778 he escaped a British attempt to trap him at Barren Hill. He returned to France in 1779 to seek more support, and spent eight days under house arrest for disobeying the king. Back in America in 1780, he evaded Lord Cornwallis in Virginia in 1781 with small squads that gave the impression his force was larger than it was.

In France he sat in the Assembly of Notables in 1787 and was elected to the Estates General in 1789. On 15 July 1789 he became commander of the Parisian National Guard and proposed the blue, white and red cockade, which began the French tricolour. He was blamed for the royal family's flight to Varennes in June 1791. On 17 July 1791 his troops fired on a crowd at the Champ de Mars, killing an unknown number of people. Radical factions ordered his arrest in August 1792.

Napoleon restored his citizenship in 1800, and Lafayette refused the offices he offered. After the Bourbon Restoration he opposed the narrow franchise and sat in the Chamber of Deputies from 1827. He broke with Louis-Philippe when the king backtracked on reforms. He died on 20 May 1834 and is buried in Picpus Cemetery in Paris, under soil from Bunker Hill.

Lafayette believed in a constitutional monarchy and opposed slavery, proposing that enslaved people work as free tenants. In the United States his image rested on his fighting without pay for a country not his own, and Samuel Adams praised him for it.
marquis-wen-of-wei: Wei Si succeeded his father Viscount Huan as head of the Wei clan, one of the noble houses that dominated Jin, and in 424 BCE took the title of marquess on his own initiative. He sought out worthy men: the Confucian scholar Zixia came to Xihe at his invitation and trained students there, and he also consulted Tian Zifang and Duangan Mu. He appointed Li Kui to reform government on the principles that food requires labour and salary requires meritorious service, and Wei's laws were later codified as the Canon of Laws.

When Han and Zhao, at war with each other, each asked Wei for troops, he refused both, calling each ruler his brother, then mediated, and both came to pay tribute to Wei. The general Wu Qi held Qin territory east of the Luo River from 409 to 406 BCE, and its five captured cities became the Xihe Commandery. Ximen Bao, as magistrate of Ye, ended the yearly sacrifice of a maiden to the river god Hebo and cut twelve canals from the Zhang River, which turned its floods into irrigation.

Given passage through Zhao, Wei's army under Yue Yang besieged the capital of Zhongshan for three years and ended that state in 406 BCE. In 405 BCE an allied army of the three Jin houses under Zhai Jue attacked the Great Wall of Qi and captured Duke Kang of Qi. In 403 BCE King Weilie of Zhou recognised the leaders of Wei, Han and Zhao as rulers in their own right, an event often taken as the start of the Warring States period.

On his deathbed in 396 BCE he entrusted his son, who succeeded as Marquess Wu of Wei, to Wu Qi, Ximen Bao and Beimen Ke. Sima Qian praised his eagerness to learn, and Sima Guang judged that Wei became the strongest of the Jin states. His appointment of Li Kui, often regarded as the first Legalist, and of Zhai Huang, Yue Yang, Wu Qi and Ximen Bao arguably made Wei one of the first states to adopt measures later called Legalist.
marquis-yi-of-zeng: Zeng was a state of the Spring and Autumn period, and the Marquis, sometimes called Duke Yi, died at the end of that period or the start of the Warring States period. A date written on an astronomical diagram on a lacquered clothing chest from his tomb is thought to mark his death or another key day of his life, and has been worked out as the evening of the third day of the third lunar month of 433 BCE. A bell sent by King Hui of Chu records the king's hurried journey to attend his funeral in the 56th year of his reign.
Bamboo slips from the tomb list the officials and royalty of Chu and Zeng who came to the funeral, with details of their transport such as the number of horses drawing their chariots.

The People's Liberation Army found the tomb by accident in 1977 while levelling a hill to build a factory. Built of large wooden timbers over 220 square metres, it is one of a handful of ancient Chinese royal tombs found intact and excavated by modern methods. Its four chambers resemble the plan of a palace. The Marquis lay in the eastern chamber in a lacquer coffin nested inside a larger one, with eight coffins of women; the western chamber held thirteen more women. In 1981 a smaller tomb about 100 metres away held a woman related to him, with 36 bronze bells.

The central chamber held a set of bianzhong bells on an elaborate frame, which needed five players. Each bell gives two tones, struck at the centre or the side, thanks to its almond-shaped cross-section, and the set spans five octaves; inscriptions relate the pitch standards of Zeng, Chu and Zhou. Stone chimes, the string instruments se, qin and zhu, pan flutes and gourd-moulded sheng lay with them.

There were 88 ritual bronze vessels and implements, among them sets of ding and li cauldrons and a unique two-piece pan wine vessel 33 cm high, as well as weapons, 173 glass eye beads in a western Asian style, and the earliest Chinese ink writings on bamboo.
marquisate-of-bodonitsa: Bodonitsa, also written Vodonitsa or Boudonitza, lay at present-day Mendenitsa in Phthiotis, about 180 km northwest of Athens. In 1204 Boniface, the first king of Thessalonica, granted it to Guy Pallavicini as a margravial holding, a march meant to hold the pass of Thermopylae. Guy ruled until 1237 and was followed by Ubertino, who held it until 1278. The marquisate survived the fall of Thessalonica after Boniface's death, and in 1248 it was made subordinate to the Principality of Achaea.

Ubertino's successor Isabella ruled from 1278 to 1286, possibly with a husband, Antoine le Flamenc, though his rule is only a conjecture. After a dispute with her widower the title passed to Thomas, a grandson of Guy's brother Rubino, and then about 1300 to Albert, who held it until 1311.

The state survived the arrival of the Catalan Company in 1311, but it then passed in quick succession to two Venetian families, the Cornaro and the Zorzi. Albert's wife Maria dalle Carceri held a share until 1323, with her husband Andrea Cornaro from 1312, while Guglielma ruled from 1311 to 1358, with her husbands Bartolommeo Zaccaria from 1327 to 1334 and then Nicholas I Zorzi, the first of the Zorzi margraves. In the list of eighteen Catalan vassals of the area for 1380-1, the margrave of Bodonitsa ranks third, after Count Demitre and the Count of Salona.

The Zorzi, Francis from 1345 and Jacob from 1388, held the marquisate until the Ottoman Turks took it in 1414. Nicholas II went on using the margravial title afterwards, but the territory was never recovered.
marriage-of-the-sea-ceremony: Rites of propitiation linked to the sea go back to antiquity. The French archaeologist and historian of religion Salomon Reinach recalled Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, throwing a precious ring into the sea to appease the gods, and Empress Helena casting a nail of the True Cross into the Adriatic to make it gentler to sailors, and he held that the Venetian ceremony came from a pagan ritual taken over by the Catholic Church. Pope Alexander III confirmed its principle in 1176, during the truce in Venice, giving Doge Sebastiano Ziani a gold ring as the wedding ring of his marriage to the sea and asking that he and his successors marry her every year.

The doge boarded the bucentaur at the Môle before the Doge's Palace in a mantle of gold and silver brocade with ermine, wearing the corno ducale and holding a command rod. He sat at the stern with the papal legate on his right and the French ambassador on his left, while the Senate filled four rows of seats. Off the Lido the Patriarch came aboard from another ship, and after his blessing the doge threw the ring with the words Desponsamus te, mare, in signum veri perpetuique dominii: we espouse thee, O sea, as a sign of true and perpetual dominion.

The galley's return opened the Festa della Sensa, a feast known across Europe for its splendour and wealth, with a large fair in Saint Mark's Square. A Grand Admiral answered for the passengers' safety, since the flat-bottomed, shallow bucentaur was hard to handle and could capsize. Giacomo Casanova remarked that the slightest headwind could drown the doge with the whole government, and that Europe would then laugh that the doge had at last gone to consummate his marriage.

The art historian Sergio Bettini saw the ceremony, like the great Roman and Byzantine ceremonies, as the periodic representation and incarnation of the myth of Venice in real life, and UNESCO describes it as a fundamental rite of ancient Venice. In the modern re-enactment the mayor travels with the patriarch and other dignitaries on a replica of the bucentaur to San Nicolò Church, where a ring is thrown into the sea. The only surviving ring, that of an unidentified doge found by chance in the sea, is kept in the collection of Saint Mark's Basilica.
mars-mythology: In ancient Roman religion Mars was the god of war and also an agricultural guardian, a combination characteristic of early Rome. He was usually held to be the son of Jupiter and Juno, though in Ovid's version Juno bore him alone, after the goddess Flora touched her belly with a magic flower. His consort was Nerio, whose name means valour, and Venus was joined to him as a complementary pair in the public banquet of 217 BCE. The Latin name gave English "martial" and names such as Marcus.

Unlike the Greek Ares, who is often treated with contempt in Greek literature, Mars represented military power as a way to secure peace. Roman writers took over the myths of Ares and retold them under his name. His sacred animals were the wolf and the woodpecker. Mars may have begun as a god of the wild, and the Arval Brothers invoked him as ferus, "savage". By the third century CE soldiers of the legions worshipped him above all.

His main priest was the Flamen Martialis, and twelve patrician youths, the Salii, danced in armour through the city in March. Most festivals fell in March, the month named after him, and in October, which began and ended the seasons of campaigning and farming. They included the Equirria horse races on 27 February and 14 March, his birthday on 1 March, and the Mamuralia, a new year rite in which Mamurius Veturius was driven out. On 15 October the October Horse was sacrificed, Rome's only known horse sacrifice. The usual offering was a bull, and the suovetaurilia of pig, ram and bull was offered to Mars Pater.

His earliest centre was the Altar of Mars in the Campus Martius, which Romans thought Numa Pompilius had set up. Newly elected censors placed their chairs beside it, and after the census the citizens were purified there. A spear kept in the Regia was said to tremble before danger to the state, as it did before the assassination of Julius Caesar.

Mars took many titles. Mars Gradivus, "the Strider", was invoked by soldiers swearing oaths, and Mars Quirinus protected the citizens. Augustus created the cult of Mars Ultor, "the Avenger", after the defeat of Caesar's assassins at Philippi in 42 BCE and the return of the standards lost at Carrhae, and built a temple to him in his new forum. The 4th-century historian Ammianus Marcellinus treats Mars as still a living cult in his day. In 363 the emperor Julian sacrificed ten bulls to Mars Ultor before the siege of Ctesiphon; the tenth broke free, and the omens were bad.
mars-orbiter-mission: The first public acknowledgement of an uncrewed Mars mission came in November 2008, from the then ISRO chairman G. Madhavan Nair. The concept grew from a feasibility study made in 2010 by the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, after the launch of the lunar satellite Chandrayaan-1 in 2008. Prime Minister Manmohan Singh approved the project on 3 August 2012. The mission was meant as a technology demonstrator, to develop the means of designing, planning, managing and operating an interplanetary mission, and its secondary aim was to study Mars's surface features, mineralogy and atmosphere with five indigenous instruments. ISRO chose its Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle after the larger rocket failed twice in 2010.

The probe lifted off from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota on 5 November 2013. Because the rocket could not send it directly to Mars, the spacecraft spent about a month in Earth orbit and used its own thrusters in a series of perigee burns. On 30 November 2013 a 23-minute engine firing sent it on a trajectory toward Mars, and it travelled some 780,000,000 kilometres in a 298-day transit. On 24 September 2014 it entered a highly elliptical Martian orbit, with a period of about 73 hours, as planned.

The orbiter returned the first global view of Mars on 28 September 2014. On 7 October 2014 ISRO moved it behind Mars for the passage of comet Siding Spring on 19 October. Its instruments reported argon in the Martian exosphere and mapped surface reflectance, and in 2015 its radio signals, passing through the solar corona, helped scientists study the Sun. It also provided the first views of the far side of Deimos.

The mission made India the first Asian nation to reach Martian orbit and ISRO the fourth space agency to do so, after the Soviet programme, NASA and the European Space Agency. The mission team won the National Space Society's 2015 Space Pioneer Award, and an illustration of the spacecraft appears on the reverse of India's 2,000 rupee note. In April 2022 the orbiter entered a seven-hour eclipse it was not designed to survive. On 2 October 2022 it was reported to have lost communications irrecoverably, and the next day ISRO declared it dead. A follow-up mission, Mangalyaan-2, is planned with a larger scientific payload.
marshall-islands: The Marshall Islands lie west of the International Date Line and north of the equator, about halfway between Hawaii and Australia, on the tops of ancient submerged volcanoes. The country consists of 29 atolls and five individual islands, and the atolls and islands form two roughly parallel chains running northwest to southeast, Ratak (sunrise) and Ralik (sunset). They cover about 1,900,000 square kilometres of ocean but only about 180 square kilometres of land, at an average height of 2.1 metres above sea level. The largest atoll by land area is Kwajalein, which surrounds a lagoon of about 1,700 square kilometres. Twenty-four of the atolls and islands are inhabited.

Austronesian settlers, possibly from the Solomon Islands, brought coconuts, giant swamp taro, breadfruit and domesticated chickens. Radiocarbon dates suggest Bikini Atoll may have been inhabited by 1200 BCE, though the samples are doubtful, and excavations on Majuro and Kwajalein show habitation around the 1st century CE. The wetter southern atolls probably held denser populations.

The first Europeans were the Spanish crew of Alonso de Salazar, who reached Taongi in 1526, and European charts later named the group for the British captain John Marshall, who explored the region in 1788. American Protestant missionaries and Western traders arrived from the 1850s, and German copra traders dominated the economy in the 1870s and 1880s. After the First World War the islands became the Japanese South Seas Mandate. Under United States administration, 67 nuclear tests were conducted at Bikini and Enewetak between 1946 and 1958. In 1979 the United States recognised the Marshallese constitution and its president, Amata Kabua.

The capital and largest city is Majuro, where about half of the population lives; the 2021 census counted 42,418 residents. Marshallese and English are the official languages. The country is a presidential parliamentary republic in free association with the United States, with a legislature called the Nitijela and an advisory Council of Iroij of twelve paramount chiefs. Land is the main measure of a family's wealth and is inherited through the maternal line. Some 96.2 per cent of people identified with a Christian denomination at the 2021 census, the largest being the United Church of Christ - Congregational in the Marshall Islands.
marshall-mcluhan: Herbert Marshall McLuhan was born on 21 July 1911 in Edmonton, Alberta. His mother, Elsie Naomi Hall, was a Baptist school teacher who later became an actress, and his father, Herbert Ernest McLuhan, a Methodist, ran a real-estate business. The family moved to Winnipeg in 1915. McLuhan studied at the University of Manitoba, where he took a Bachelor of Arts in 1933 and a Master of Arts in English in 1934, and then went to Trinity Hall, Cambridge. His reading of G. K. Chesterton led him to convert to Catholicism in 1937.

McLuhan took a teaching post at the University of Wisconsin–Madison for the academic year 1936–1937 and then taught English at Saint Louis University from 1937 to 1944, with a return to Cambridge in 1939–1940. There he befriended and tutored Walter J. Ong. He moved to the University of Toronto in 1946 and stayed there for the rest of his life. In the early 1950s he began the Communication and Culture seminars, funded by the Ford Foundation, and with Edmund Carpenter he produced the journal Explorations. To keep him from moving elsewhere, the university created the Centre for Culture and Technology in 1963. McLuhan suffered a stroke in September 1979 that affected his speech, and he died in his sleep on 31 December 1980.

His first book, The Mechanical Bride (1951), studied advertising and popular culture. The Gutenberg Galaxy (1962) examined how alphabetic writing, the printing press and electronic media affect cognitive organisation and, through it, social organisation. In Understanding Media (1964) he put forward the aphorism the medium is the message, which calls attention to the effects that communications media have apart from their content, and he used the term global village. The Medium Is the Massage (1967), designed with Quentin Fiore, sold nearly a million copies.

In the posthumous Laws of Media (1988) he summarised his ideas in a tetrad of four questions: what a medium enhances, what it makes obsolete, what it retrieves that had been obsolete earlier, and what it flips into when pushed to extremes. His reputation was at its height in the late 1960s and declined in the early 1970s.
marshall-plan: By the end of the Second World War much of Europe was devastated. Bombing had damaged most major cities and industrial plants, trade flows were disrupted, and millions of refugees lived in temporary camps on aid from the United States. Food shortages were severe, especially in the harsh winter of 1946 to 1947. In 1947 agricultural production stood at 83% of the 1938 level, industrial production at 88% and exports at 59%, although the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and France had by the end of that year restored production to pre-war levels.

In 1947 the Moscow conference of the foreign ministers failed after six weeks of talks with the Soviets on rebuilding Germany, and the United States concluded that a solution could not wait. Secretary of State George C. Marshall gave an address at Harvard University on 5 June 1947 offering American aid to promote European recovery. The plan was largely the creation of State Department officials, especially William L. Clayton and George F. Kennan, and had bipartisan support in Washington, where Republicans controlled Congress and Harry S. Truman was president.

After Marshall's speech, British Foreign Secretary Ernest Bevin and French Foreign Minister Georges Bidault quickly arranged a European response, which led to the Committee of European Economic Co-operation. The offer included the Soviet Union, but Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov left Paris rejecting the plan, and the Soviet Union also blocked its Eastern Bloc neighbours, including Romania and Poland, from taking part. The USSR devised its own programme, the Molotov Plan.

The plan was enacted in 1948 and operated for four years from 3 April 1948. The United States transferred 13.3 billion dollars to participating countries, roughly on a per capita basis, with more for the major industrial powers. The United Kingdom received about 26% of the total, France 18% and West Germany 11%. Allied countries received somewhat more per person than former Axis or neutral ones.

The goals of the United States were to rebuild war-torn regions, remove trade barriers, modernise industry, improve prosperity and prevent the spread of communism. The plan encouraged the economic integration of Europe and the adoption of modern business procedures. How far it caused the rapid recovery is debated: aid amounted to about 3% of the recipients' combined national income between 1948 and 1951. Yugoslavia, after breaking with Stalin in 1948, later received American aid that was not part of the plan. The phrase "a Marshall Plan" is still used for any large rescue programme.
marsilio-ficino: Marsilio Ficino was born at Figline Valdarno on 19 October 1433. His father, Diotifeci d'Agnolo, was a physician under the patronage of Cosimo de' Medici, who took the young man into his household and remained his lifelong patron. Ficino became tutor to Cosimo's grandson Lorenzo de' Medici, and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola was another of his students. In 1459 he became a pupil of John Argyropoulos, who was lecturing on Greek language and literature at Florence. Trained as a physician, he became a priest in 1473. A later account by the historian Cesare Baronio says that he and his friend Michele Mercati were first Epicureans before turning to Platonism.

The sessions of the Council of Ferrara-Florence in 1438–1445 had brought Cosimo's circle into contact with the Neoplatonist George Gemistos Plethon. When Cosimo decided to refound Plato's Academy at Florence, he chose Ficino as its head, and in 1462 supplied him with Greek manuscripts of Plato. Ficino translated the whole corpus into Latin, finishing a draft of the dialogues in 1468–69 and publishing it in 1484. He also translated the collection later called the Hermetica and writings of Neoplatonists including Porphyry, Iamblichus and Plotinus. His students included Niccolò Valori and Francesco Cattani da Diacceto, whom he regarded as his successor as head of the Academy.

In 1474 he completed the Platonic Theology, a treatise on the immortality of the soul, and On the Christian Religion, a history of religions and defence of Christianity. In 1489 he was accused of heresy before Pope Innocent VIII, partly because of his interest in astrology, and was acquitted. His letters from 1474 to 1494 survive.

Ficino wrote Of Love, a commentary on Plato's Symposium, in 1484, and coined the term Platonic love, which first appears in a letter of 1476. His letters to his friend Giovanni Cavalcanti and the treatise helped spread the notion in western Europe. His Three Books on Life of 1489 gives medical and astrological advice for health and vigour and presents the world as ensouled and linked to the human soul. He also wrote treatises on medicine, among them advice on treating plague, and they influenced Renaissance physicians such as Paracelsus.

Behind his work lay a tendency to seek concord between Platonism and Christianity. In his commentary on Plotinus he reinterpreted the more pagan Neoplatonic doctrines, such as the transmigration of the soul, as moral allegories. In 1494 he revised his position on astrology as allegorical rather than dogmatic. Ficino died on 1 October 1499 at Careggi, and in 1521 a bust by Andrea Ferrucci was set up in his memory in the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore.
marsilius-of-padua: Marsilius was born in Padua, near Venice, around 1275, with the family name Mainardi or Mainardini. He was trained in medicine, probably at the University of Padua, and practised a variety of professions. He later went to the University of Paris, where he became a devoted admirer of Aristotle, whom he called the divine philosopher. He served as rector of the University of Paris approximately in 1312 and 1313, and probably taught there before and after his term.

Marsilius wrote Defensor pacis in 1324, during a power struggle between Pope John XXII and Louis of Bavaria, the elected candidate for Holy Roman Emperor. In 1323 Louis had sent an army to Italy to protect Milan against the Kingdom of Naples, a strong ally of the pope; John excommunicated him and demanded that he give up his claim to the imperial crown. Marsilius argued from reason and from authority that the empire was independent of the papacy and that the powers claimed by the popes were empty. Much of the work is theology: relying on Scripture, he sought to show that Jesus claimed no temporal power and that the church should be subordinate to the state in both secular and spiritual matters.

Its political philosophy is what it is remembered for. Marsilius agreed with Aristotle that government serves the natural human desire for a sufficient life, but went beyond him in embracing a republicanism in which the people are the only legitimate source of authority. The people should elect, correct and if necessary depose their rulers, and democracy, he argued, tends to produce the wisest laws. He held that scripture stands above the church and that the papacy was created by human arrangement. Pope John XXII declared a number of his views heretical in 1327. In the later Defensor minor he took up ecclesiastical jurisdiction, indulgences, excommunication and marriage.

Marsilius and John of Jandun, sometimes credited as a co-author, left France for Louis's court in Bavaria, where Louis protected them together with Michael of Cesena and William of Ockham. In 1326 Marsilius went with Louis to Italy. Louis was crowned King of Italy in Milan in 1327 and entered Rome in January 1328, where he was crowned emperor and declared John XXII deposed for heresy. Marsilius was appointed archbishop of Milan as recompense for his services. He died in Munich around 1342, still unreconciled to the Church. Some scholars see Defensor pacis as the most revolutionary political treatise of the later Middle Ages, and he is sometimes seen as a forerunner of the Reformation.
martand-singh: Martand Singh was born on 15 March 1923 at the Fort of Govindgarh, the son of Maharaja Gulab Singh of Rewa. He studied at Daly College in Indore and then at Mayo College in Ajmer, from which he graduated in 1941. In 1946 the British authorities imprisoned his father for his part in the freedom struggle, and Martand Singh became Maharaja of Rewa. He kept the title, though not its powers, until the government of India abolished royal titles in 1970. He married Princess Pravina of Cutch, and the couple had one son.

After the abolition of royalty Singh represented Rewa in the 5th Lok Sabha, elected in 1971, and in the 7th and 8th Lok Sabha of 1980 and 1984. Much of his life was given to conservation and to the fight against poaching. The founding of the Bandhavgarh National Park in the Vindhya Mountains was his initiative.

In 1951 he found a rare white cub, a mutant form of the Bengal tiger, in the forests of the former Rewa state, in what is now Madhya Pradesh, and captured and reared him. The tiger, named Mohan, was the first white tiger to be bred in captivity, and all the white Bengal tigers living today trace their descent from him.

The Government of India awarded him the Padma Bhushan, its third-highest civilian honour, in 1986 for wildlife conservation. He died on 20 November 1995 at the age of 72. His property is held by the Maharaja Martand Singh Charitable Trust. The white tiger safari and zoo at Mukundpur in Satna, described as the first white tiger safari in the world, is named after him.
martand-sun-temple: The temple stands at Mattan, in the Anantnag district of the Kashmir Valley. It was dedicated to Surya, the Hindu sun god, who is also known by the Sanskrit name Martand, Mārtaṇḍa. According to the chronicler Kalhana, it was commissioned by Lalitaditya Muktapida in the 8th century CE. It was built on a plateau from which the whole of the Kashmir Valley can be seen.

The ruins and finds show it as a fine example of Kashmiri architecture, which blended Gandharan, Gupta, Chinese and possibly Syrian-Byzantine forms. A colonnaded courtyard 220 feet long and 142 feet broad holds the main shrine at its centre, surrounded by 84 smaller shrines, and takes in a smaller temple built earlier. It is the largest example of a peristyle in Kashmir. The main entrance, on the western side of the quadrangle, is as wide as the temple itself and richly decorated. The central temple proper is thought to have had a pyramidal roof, a common feature of Kashmiri temples, and carvings in its antechamber show Vishnu and the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna as well as Surya.

According to Jonaraja, who flourished about 1430, and to Hasan Ali, the temple was destroyed by Sikandar Shah Miri (1389–1413) in a drive to Islamise society on the advice of the Sufi preacher Mir Muhammad Hamadani; Jonaraja blamed his chief counsellor Suhabhatta, a Brahman convert. Scholars caution against taking these sources at face value, since Jonaraja wrote for Sikandar's son and later Muslim chroniclers had motives of their own. Chitralekha Zutshi and Richard G. Salomon see Sikandar's policy as realpolitik aimed at Brahminical wealth and power, while Slaje holds that religious motives were present.

Earthquakes later damaged the ruins further. The Archaeological Survey of India lists the temple as a centrally protected monument of national importance, under the name Martanda (Sun Temple), and in March 2024 the government of Jammu and Kashmir began efforts to restore it. Its ruins have served as the setting of songs in Hindi films, among them Aandhi in 1975 and Haider in 2014.
marthanda-varma: Marthanda Varma was born in 1706 to Karthika Thirunal Umadevi, senior queen of Attingal, and Raghava Varma of Kilimanoor Palace, who died when the boy was one year old. He was the nephew of the Venadu king Rama Varma, whom he was to succeed under the matrilineal inheritance of Kerala. When Rama Varma died in 1729, his sons Valiya Thampi and Kunju Thampi claimed the throne, backed by the Nair aristocracy of the Ettuveettil Pillamar and their associates the Yogakkar, who held more power than the kings. Many of Marthanda Varma's relatives were killed.

He killed the Thampis, used spies against the Pillamar, executed most of their families and destroyed the power of more than 70 nobles, expelling the Yogakkar and the Brahmins who had supported them. He built a standing army of about 50,000 Nair men, used Marava and Pathan cavalry, and fortified the north with the Travancore Lines. Between 1743, when he declared a state monopoly on pepper, and 1752 he annexed Quilon, Kayamkulam, Thekkumkur, Vadakkumkur and Purakkad, aiming at the spice lands that supplied the Dutch at Kochi.

After the victory over the Dutch at Colachel on 10 August 1741 he took Eustachius de Lannoy, one of the prisoners, into his service; de Lannoy drilled a regiment and rose to general. The Treaty of Mavelikkara with the Dutch East India Company followed on 15 August 1753. A Dalava headed military, fiscal and commercial administration over a new hierarchy of officials, black pepper and other goods became royal monopolies, and Syrian Christian traders received his patronage as a check on European trade.

He rebuilt the Padmanabhaswamy Temple at Thiruvananthapuram on its present scale, introduced state ceremonies such as Murajapam and Bhadra Deepam, and patronised Kathakali, Koodiyattam and Thullal; Kunchan Nambiar was among his court poets. He died in 1758, two years after his friend and minister Ramayyan Dalawa. His nephew Rama Varma, Dharma Raja, continued his policies and defended Travancore against the Kingdom of Mysore.
marthas-vineyard: Martha's Vineyard lies just south of Cape Cod and has a land area of about 96 square miles (250 km2). It includes the peninsula of Chappaquiddick Island and forms the bulk of Dukes County, Massachusetts, together with the Elizabeth Islands and Nomans Land. In the Massachusett language its Wampanoag name Noepe means land amid the streams. Another native name, Capawock, appears in the 1691 Massachusetts Charter as Cappawock.

The English name probably honours Martha Golding, the mother-in-law of the explorer Bartholomew Gosnold, who partly funded his 1602 expedition to Cape Cod. The name first belonged to a smaller island to the south and later moved to this one. For a time the island was also called Martin's Vineyard, possibly after John Martin, a captain in the party.

About 3,000 Wampanoag lived on the island in 1642; by 1764 the number had fallen to 313. English settlement began when Thomas Mayhew of Watertown bought Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket and the Elizabeth Islands. His son, also Thomas Mayhew, founded the first settlement in 1642 at Great Harbor, later Edgartown, and built a relationship with the Wampanoag neighbour Hiacoomes, whose family converted to Christianity. The Mayhews respected Wampanoag land rights, and the island's band did not join the uprising of King Philip's War.

In 1665 the Mayhew lands were included in a grant to the Duke of York, and a settlement of 1671 placed them under the Province of New York. Enslaved people were bought, sold and probated on the island, though Samuel Sewall publicly opposed slavery in 1700. Whaling brought prosperity in the nineteenth century and had almost collapsed by 1870, when petroleum offered cheaper lamp oil. After the Old Colony railroad reached Woods Hole in 1872, summer residences began to appear.

The island was the last refuge of the heath hen, whose last known bird died in 1932. It also had an unusually high rate of hereditary deafness, and by the late nineteenth century about one person in 155 was born deaf. Sign language was widely used among hearing and deaf residents alike. The linguist William Labov studied the island's dialect in 1963.
