The island is divided into six towns, each governed by selectmen and town meetings, and all belong to the Martha's Vineyard Commission, which regulates island-wide building and environmental matters. A substantial Wampanoag population remains, mainly in the town of Aquinnah. The island is reached by ferry, chiefly from Woods Hole, and is a summer resort.
marthinus-wessel-pretorius: Marthinus Wessel Pretorius was born in the Cape Colony on 17 September 1819. He accompanied his father, the Voortrekker leader Andries Pretorius, in the migration to the interior. After his father died in 1853 he was appointed to succeed him as Commandant-General of the Boer settlers around Potchefstroom and moved there from his farm, Kalkheuwel, near Broederstroom. He held that post from 1853 through 1856. An Afrikaner, or Boer, he helped establish the South African Republic, which was also called Transvaal, and became its first president.

In 1857 the nascent South African Republic (Zuid-Afrikaansche Republiek, also called the Transvaal) elected Pretorius as its first president. In 1859, in an effort to create closer bonds with the Orange Free State, he also became its State President. This created tension in the Transvaal, and in 1860 he resigned as its president. He served in the Free State until 1863, was re-elected president of the South African Republic in 1864, and served a second term until 1871. He also compiled the republic's constitution. Between 1880 and 1883 he was joint head of state in the triumvirate.

Between 1854 and 1855 Pretorius bought two farms, Elandspoort and Daspoort, on which he founded the city of Pretoria in 1855. Ds. van der Hoff had first named the local church congregation Pretoria Philadelphia, in honour of Pretorius's father, and the town later took the shortened name Pretoria. Five years later the capital of the republic was moved from Potchefstroom to Pretoria. He was also an important South African Freemason, and he died at Potchefstroom on 19 May 1901.
martim-afonso-de-sousa: Martim Afonso was born in Vila Viçosa and raised in the household of the Duke of Bragança; he was a cousin of King John III of Portugal and his friend from childhood. On leaving the duke's service for the royal court in 1516 he studied mathematics, cosmography and geography with the chief cosmographer Pedro Nunes. After the death of Manuel I he accompanied the widowed Queen Leonor of Austria to Castile, where around June 1523 he married Ana Pimentel, a match that linked him to some of the main lineages of Spain. In four years there he fought for Emperor Charles V against the French and played a prominent part in the capture of Fuenterrabía in the winter of 1525.

Threatened by French ships along the Brazilian coast, the crown sent him in December 1530 with a fleet of 400 people to establish control and explore, placing Portuguese markers as far south as the River Plate, where he was shipwrecked. In 1532, guided by native inhabitants and by earlier settlers such as João Ramalho, he led troops up the Serra do Mar and founded the town of Santo André on the plateau near the future São Paulo. He also set up a sugar mill near São Vicente with cane from the Cape Verde islands, setting the pattern of raids into the interior and export sugar on the coast that Portuguese colonists long followed.

Back in Portugal in 1533, he was sent on 19 December that year to India as Captain-Major of the Indian Sea with five ships, a posting the chronicler Gaspar Correia says he resented as the work of his cousin António de Ataíde, Count of Castanheira. In the East he defended Diu against its enemies, defeated the Zamorin of Calicut, fought the corsairs who plundered Portuguese shipping and negotiated the building of the Fortress of Diu at Chaul in 1535.

The end of his career is disputed. Some historians hold that he returned to Portugal and joined the Council of State; others that he was recalled on charges of embezzling crown money and illicit enrichment and stayed away from public life thereafter. He was Lord of Alcoentre, donatary captain of São Vicente and Rio de Janeiro and a commendator in the Order of Christ, and late in life he regained the lordship of Prado, which he had sold as a young man. He was buried in the Convent of São Francisco da Cidade in Lisbon.
martin-behaim: Martin Behaim was born in Nuremberg on 6 October 1459, the oldest son of the merchant Martin Behaim, a senator of the city from 1461, and Agnes Schopper. He probably received a good education at one of the city's best grammar schools, but it is unlikely that he was ever a student of the mathematician and astronomer Regiomontanus. When his father died in 1474, his uncle Leonhard sent him at 15 to Mechelen in Flanders to train as a textile merchant. He then moved to Antwerp and joined the cloth dye house of Fritz Heberlein.

In 1484 Behaim moved to Lisbon, probably seeking trading opportunities in a city that was the hub of a network in spices, slaves and gold from Africa. He found favour as a counsellor at the court of King John II, and on 18 February 1485 John II knighted him, though no record gives the reasons. He appears to have taken part in a voyage to West Africa around 1485, more likely a trading voyage to Guinea led by João Afonso de Aveiro than the second expedition of Diogo Cão, as is sometimes claimed.

After his marriage to Joana de Macedo in 1486 he lived on the Portuguese island of Faial in the Azores, where his father-in-law, Josse van Huerter, was Captain-donatário and leader of the Flemish community. In 1490 he returned to Nuremberg to settle a will case and remained for three years, and in 1493 he went back to Faial by way of Flanders and Lisbon, staying there until 1506. He died in the hospice of Saint Bartholomew in Lisbon on 29 July 1507, while visiting on business.

Leading members of the Nuremberg council financed a terrestrial globe built under Behaim's direction, with Georg Glockendon drawing the maps. It is about 51 centimetres in diameter, made of papier-mâché coated with gypsum, with map drawings on parchment strips pasted around it. It carries more than 2,000 place names, 100 pictorial illustrations and more than 50 long legends, and its map rests mainly on Ptolemy, combined with Marco Polo, John Mandeville and Diogo Gomes. It lacks current Portuguese data that Behaim should have had, and it contains many errors. Townspeople called it the Erdapfel, earth apple, and it is the oldest extant globe, now in the German National Museum in Nuremberg.

Many claims about Behaim are unsupported by documents. Johann Christoph Wagenseil claimed in 1682 that he discovered America before Columbus, but there is no evidence that he sailed west, and no evidence of any scientific education or writings. His supposed contribution to Portuguese navigation is also doubtful, since the instruments and methods were already in use there.
martin-bucer: Martin Bucer was born on 11 November 1491 in Sélestat, a free imperial city of Alsace. His father and grandfather, both called Claus Butzer, were coopers. After the Latin school of Sélestat he joined the Dominican Order as a novice in 1507, and he later claimed that his grandfather had forced him into it. He was ordained deacon in 1510 and by 1515 was studying theology at the Dominican monastery in Heidelberg. In January 1517 he enrolled at the University of Heidelberg, where humanism influenced him. In 1518 he was influenced by Martin Luther and had his monastic vows annulled, and he then worked for the Reformation with the support of Franz von Sickingen.

His efforts at Wissembourg led to his excommunication, and he arrived in Strasbourg without means in 1523. The council was under the influence of Matthew Zell. On 24 August 1523 the largest guild appointed Bucer pastor of St Aurelia's Church, and the council accepted his application for citizenship a month later. He joined Zell, Wolfgang Capito and Caspar Hedio. From 1524 he tried to mediate between Luther and Huldrych Zwingli on the Eucharist. In 1530 he wrote the Tetrapolitan Confession, adopted by Strasbourg, Konstanz, Memmingen and Lindau. Strasbourg suspended the mass on 20 February 1529.

By 1534 he was a leading figure in the German Reformation and sought agreement between Wittenberg, the south German cities and Switzerland, with talks with Philipp Melanchthon at Kassel in December 1534. In 1538 Philip of Hesse commissioned him to draw up a policy on the Jews, and Bucer recommended stricter limits than Philip's draft; the ordinance of 1539 was a compromise, and many Jews left Hesse. From 1542 he led church reform at Bonn for the archbishop-elector Hermann von Wied of Cologne.

After the Schmalkaldic War Strasbourg surrendered to the imperial army on 21 March 1547, and the Protestants retreated within the Empire. Charles V sought the endorsement of a leading reformer for the Augsburg Interim, which imposed Catholic rites throughout the Empire, and chose Bucer. In 1549 he accepted Thomas Cranmer's invitation to England, arriving in London on 25 April, and became Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge. He influenced the Edwardine Ordinals and the second revision of the Book of Common Prayer. He died in Cambridge on 28 February 1551, aged 59. His ministry did not lead to a new denomination, but many Protestant denominations claim him, and he is remembered as an early pioneer of ecumenism.
martin-de-goiti: Goiti was one of the soldiers of the Spanish voyage of exploration to the East Indies and the Pacific in 1565, which sought gold, spice and places to settle. Its aim was a route to the islands where the earlier Spanish expeditions of Ferdinand Magellan in 1521 and Ruy López de Villalobos in 1543 had landed. On the orders of the general Miguel López de Legazpi he later led the expedition to Manila.

The Spaniards reached Luzon on 8 May 1570 and camped on the shores of Manila Bay for several weeks while making alliances with the local peoples. On 24 May hostility broke out. The Spaniards defeated most of the forces of Rajah Sulayman, marched to the Pasig River and on 6 June 1570 occupied the settlements of Manila and burned them. Goiti also fought the chieftains Rajah Matanda and Rajah Lakandula.

Guerrilla fighting followed for about ten months. The Spaniards fortified themselves and built the barracks of Fort Santiago, which became their outpost for trade with Mexico, and gained control of the settlements on 24 June 1571, after López de Legazpi arrived in Manila, which became the permanent capital of the Spanish East Indies. Between 1571 and 1573 Goiti explored Pampanga and Pangasinan and founded several Spanish settlements in Luzon. He and other soldiers were granted haciendas by King Philip II of Spain for the lands they had conquered.

In 1574 about 6,500 Chinese pirates under Limahong sailed from the South China Sea and laid siege to the Spanish settlements in Manila, and Goiti was killed by them. His second in command, Juan de Salcedo, hurried from Ilocos Sur, drove the pirates out of Manila and in 1575 besieged them for three months in Pangasinan, where they surrendered. Goiti's remains lie in a knight's tomb inside the San Agustin Church in Intramuros.
martin-de-porres: Martín de Porras Velázquez was born in Lima, in the Viceroyalty of Peru, on 9 December 1579. He was the illegitimate son of a Spanish nobleman, Don Juan de Porras y de la Peña, and Ana Velázquez, a freed slave of African and Native descent. After the birth of his sister Juana in 1581 the father abandoned the family, and Ana supported her children by taking in laundry.

Martin was sent to a primary school for two years and then apprenticed to a barber surgeon. Under Peruvian law, descendants of Africans and Native Americans could not become full members of religious orders, so at 15 he asked the Dominicans of the Convent of the Rosary in Lima to accept him as a donado, a volunteer who did menial tasks in return for the habit and a place in the community.

Martin kept up his trades of barbering and healing and took on kitchen work, laundry and cleaning. After eight years the prior, Juan de Lorenzana, chose to overlook the law and let him take vows in the Third Order of Saint Dominic. Not all of the 300 men at the priory accepted this: one novice called him a mulatto dog, and a priest mocked his illegitimacy and descent from slaves.
In 1603, at 24, he professed vows as a Dominican lay brother; he never became a priest. At 34 he was put in charge of the infirmary, where he served until his death.

He cared for the sick inside and outside the convent, without distinction between Spanish nobles and slaves lately brought from Africa. When an epidemic struck Lima, 60 friars were ill, and he is said to have passed through locked doors to reach them. He begged for alms that, in normal times, fed 160 poor people a day, and founded a residence for orphans and abandoned children. He did not eat meat. Many miracles were attributed to him, among them cures, levitation, bilocation and a rapport with animals.

Martin died on 3 November 1639, aged 59, and was a friend of Saint Juan Macías and Saint Rose of Lima. As his body lay on display, each visitor snipped a piece of his habit as a relic. Pope Gregory XVI beatified him on 29 October 1837, and Pope John XXIII canonised him in Rome on 6 May 1962. His feast day is 3 November.

He is the patron saint of people of mixed race, barbers, innkeepers and public health workers, and is often shown as a young friar with a broom, since he held all work sacred, sometimes with a dog, a cat and a mouse eating from one dish. Schools, churches and a programme at the Las Casas Institute at Blackfriars Hall, Oxford, bear his name.
martin-i-of-sicily: Martin the Younger was born about 1374 or 1376, the son of the future King Martin I of Aragon. His grandparents were King Peter IV of Aragon and Eleanor of Sicily. In February 1390 he married Maria of Sicily, born in 1362 or 1363, and became King of Sicily through the marriage. In 1392 he returned with Maria to Sicily with a military force and defeated a group of opposing barons.

Martin ruled Sicily jointly with Maria until her death at Lentini on 25 May 1401. Their only son, Peter, born in 1398 and crown prince of Sicily, had died in 1400. After Maria's death Martin repudiated the Treaty of Villeneuve of 1372 and ruled alone. He married Blanche of Navarre, heiress of the Evreux family and future queen of Navarre, by proxy at Catania on 21 May 1402 and in person on 26 December 1402. Their only son, Martin, was born in 1403 and died at Valencia in 1407. Martin the Younger also left two illegitimate children: Fadrique, born in 1400 or 1403 to the Sicilian Tarsia Rizzari, and Violante, born to the Sicilian Agathe de Pesce, who died about 1428.

In 1409 Martin led the troops in the conquest of Sardinia and decisively defeated the ruler of Arborea at the Battle of Sanluri just before his own death. He died at Cagliari on 25 July 1409. None of the children of his two marriages survived childhood, so his father, by then King of Aragon, ruled Sicily as Martin II. Martin II tried to make Fadrique his successor in the Aragonese realms, but Fadrique was denied the succession by the Pact of Caspe. Fadrique married Yolande Louise de Mur and died at Urena in 1438 without issue.
martin-luther: Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 to Hans Luder and his wife Margarethe in Eisleben. In 1484 the family moved to Mansfeld, where his father leased copper mines and smelters and later became a town councillor. Hans was determined that his eldest son should become a lawyer, and Luther entered the University of Erfurt in 1501 and received his master's degree in 1505, but dropped out of law almost at once. According to one story, a lightning bolt struck near him during a thunderstorm on 2 July 1505, and he cried out, "Help! Saint Anna, I will become a monk!" He entered St Augustine's Monastery in Erfurt on 17 July 1505, to his father's fury.

As an Augustinian friar Luther devoted himself to fasting, prayer and confession, and described this period as one of deep spiritual despair. He was ordained on 3 April 1507, began teaching theology at the University of Wittenberg in 1508 and received his Doctor of Theology on 19 October 1512, succeeding Johann von Staupitz as chair of theology.

From 1510 to 1520 he lectured on the Psalms, Hebrews, Romans and Galatians, and became convinced that the Church was corrupt. The most important doctrine for him was justification by faith alone through God's grace, which he held to be entirely God's work. He taught that the Bible is the only source of divinely revealed knowledge of the Gospel, which challenged the authority of the pope and bishops. Pope Leo X excommunicated him in January 1521, and that year Emperor Charles V condemned him as an outlaw at the Diet of Worms.

At Luther's death in 1546 his excommunication was still in effect. He made effective use of the printing press and wrote in German to reach a broader audience; between 1500 and 1530 his works made up one fifth of all materials printed in Germany. His German Bible of 1534 helped to establish a standard version of the German language, and his marriage to Katharina von Bora, a former nun, set a model for clerical marriage.

Luther expressed staunchly antisemitic views, calling for the expulsion of Jews and the burning of synagogues. According to the prevailing opinion among historians, his anti-Jewish rhetoric contributed significantly to the development of antisemitism in Germany, and Nazi propaganda cited it.
martin-luther-king-jr: Martin Luther King Jr. was born Michael King Jr. on 15 January 1929 in Atlanta, the second of three children of Michael King and Alberta King. His maternal grandfather, Adam Daniel Williams, was a minister who became pastor of the Ebenezer Baptist Church. King enrolled at Crozer Theological Seminary in Pennsylvania, where he was elected president of the student body, and later studied at Boston University. He married Coretta Scott on 18 June 1953.

King oversaw the 1955 Montgomery bus boycott, was the first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, helped organise the 1963 protests in Birmingham, Alabama, and was one of the leaders of the 1963 March on Washington, where he gave the I Have a Dream speech. On 14 October 1964 he became the youngest winner of the Nobel Peace Prize. The FBI director J. Edgar Hoover ordered surveillance of him, and a 1975 congressional investigation found that from December 1963 until his death he was the target of an intensive campaign to neutralise him.

In March 1968 King went to Memphis, Tennessee, to support striking black sanitation workers, and on 3 April gave the address I've Been to the Mountaintop. He was assassinated on 4 April 1968. James Earl Ray was convicted of the killing, though conspiracy theories persist, and King's death led to riots in American cities. Martin Luther King Jr. Day was first observed as a federal holiday in 1986.
martin-miguel-de-guemes: Güemes was born in Salta on 8 February 1785 into a wealthy family. His father, Gabriel de Güemes Montero, a learned man from Santander in Cantabria, was royal treasurer of the Spanish crown, and his mother, María Magdalena de Goyechea y la Corte, was a criolla of Salta. Educated by private teachers and then at the Royal College of San Carlos in Buenos Aires, he fought in the defence of the city during the British invasions of the Río de la Plata, when he and his cavalrymen charged and seized the armed British merchantman Justine, moored in shallow water.

After the May Revolution of 1810 he joined the army sent against the Spanish in Upper Peru, which won the Battle of Suipacha, and then served at the siege of Montevideo. Returning to Salta in 1815, he organised local gauchos trained in guerrilla tactics. When General José Rondeau, defeated in Upper Peru, tried to take their weapons, Güemes refused; an agreement left him in command, and the Supreme Director Juan Martín de Pueyrredón, after visiting Salta, promoted him colonel major. The royalist general Joaquín de la Pezuela wrote that his army waged, almost with impunity, a slow but tiring and harmful war.

Early in 1817 Marshal José de la Serna invaded with 5,400 experienced soldiers. Güemes retook Humahuaca on 1 March and met the advance with a scorched-earth retreat and constant raids; de la Serna reached Salta City on 16 April, but after the news of San Martín's victory at the Battle of Chacabuco his troops withdrew north. Further invasions in March 1819 and February 1820 were repelled, though without reinforcements Güemes extorted money by force from Salta's landowners.

The civil war that followed the Battle of Cepeda in 1820 left him between the royalists and Bernabé Aráoz, governor of Tucumán, who allied with Salta's landowners and defeated him on 3 April 1821. The cabildo deposed him, his gauchos restored him in May, and on 7 June the royalist colonel José María Valdés occupied the city with the landowners' support. Shot in the back as he fled, Güemes reached his camp at La Chamical and died on 17 June in the Quebrada de La Horqueta. His men retook Salta for good on 22 July. The 1942 film La Guerra Gaucha is set in his wars.
martin-mutschmann: Mutschmann was born on 9 March 1879 in Hirschberg on the Saale, in the Principality of Reuss-Gera, and grew up in Plauen in Saxony. Trained as an embroiderer, he worked in lace and linen factories in Plauen, Herford and Köln, did military service from 1901 to 1903 and in October 1907 founded his own lace factory, Mutschmann & Eisentraut, in Plauen. In World War I he served on the Western Front with Reserve Infantry Regiment 133 until he was severely wounded in April 1916, received the Iron Cross, 2nd class, and was discharged as unfit for field service.

After the war he joined the nationalist and antisemitic Deutschvölkischer Schutz und Trutzbund, and in April 1922 the Nazi Party, founding its Plauen branch and giving it money of his own. Though he lost his business in the Great Depression, he went on raising donations from other firms, which won him favour with Adolf Hitler, whom he visited in Landsberg prison. While the party was banned after the Beer Hall Putsch he led its front organisation, the National Socialist Freedom Movement, in Saxony from August 1924, and on 27 March 1925 he became its Landesleiter, later Gauleiter.

Elected to the Reichstag for Chemnitz-Zwickau in September 1930, he also edited the Nazi daily Der Freiheitskampf. Appointed Reichsstatthalter on 5 May 1933, he became Minister-President of Saxony as well on 28 February 1935, displacing his rival Manfred Freiherr von Killinger, and was one of only a few Gauleiters to hold both posts. A passionate hunter, he was often accused of caring more for the hunt than for Saxony.

From 1939 he was Reich Defense Commissioner, responsible for air and civil defence, and was blamed for the poor preparation of Dresden for the bombing of 13–15 February 1945. He declared Dresden a fortress city on 14 April, ordered public mourning after Hitler's suicide and on 5 May falsely announced a great German offensive in the east. He fled as the Red Army occupied the city on 8 May, was arrested at Tellerhäuser on 17 May and handed over to the NKVD. Held in the Lubyanka, he was sentenced to death by the Military Collegium of the Supreme Court of the Soviet Union on 30 January 1947 and shot on 14 February.
martin-of-aragon: Martin was born in 1356, in either Girona or Perpignan, both then in the Principality of Catalonia. He was the second son of King Peter IV of Aragon and Eleanor of Sicily, a princess of the Sicilian branch of the House of Aragon. As a younger prince he received the County of Besalú, and on 13 June 1372 he married María López de Luna, daughter and heiress of the Count of Luna.

In 1380 his father appointed him lord and regent of Sicily, whose queen, Maria of Sicily, was still a minor. His son Martin the Younger married her in 1391 and was crowned king of Sicily beside her. The Sicilians, led by the Alagona family, rebelled in 1392, partly because the marriage had been conducted by the Antipope Clement VII. Martin led an expedition that took Trapani and Palermo, but the opposition held out until 1398.

In 1396 Martin succeeded his elder brother John I, who had died without a son. Unrest in Sicily kept him there, and his wife claimed the throne on his behalf until he arrived in 1397. His right was contested by Count Matthew of Foix on behalf of his wife Joanna, John's elder daughter, and Martin defeated an invasion by the count's troops. After Joanna's death her sister Yolande of Aragon continued the claim. Martin launched crusades against the Moors of North Africa in 1398 and 1399.

In Sardinia the principality of Arborea had driven the Aragonese back under Eleanor of Arborea. Martin sent his son to reconquer the island, and Martin the Younger won the Battle of Sanluri in 1409 and subdued many Sardinian nobles, though he died soon afterwards of malaria. The father then became king of Sicily as Martin II. He supported the Avignon line of popes, and in 1403 his troops freed the Aragonese Pope Benedict XIII from his rivals.

Martin died on 31 May 1410 in the monastery of Valldonzella outside Barcelona. The cause is unclear: plague, uremic coma linked to his severe obesity, or poison, a claim supported only by one Renaissance chronicler. A story that he died laughing at a jester's joke lacks historical evidence. Asked whether the throne should go to the most legitimate claimant, he is said to have answered only "Hoc" (Yes), and he named no heir.

His second marriage, to Margaret of Prades in September 1409, produced no children. His illegitimate grandson Frederick, Count of Luna, could not be confirmed as heir in time. The two-year interregnum brought forward at least five contenders, among them Frederick and James II of Urgell. The Compromise of Caspe, on 28 June 1412, chose Martin's nephew Ferdinand, infante of Castile, and so began the House of Trastámara.
martin-of-braga: Martin was born in Pannonia, in Central Europe, and made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, where he became a monk. Around 550 he travelled by sea to Hispania and settled in Gallaecia. His intentions in going to so remote a place are unknown, in the words of Roger Collins. Some scholars have suggested that he was an agent of Byzantine diplomacy, since his journey coincided with the beginning of the Byzantine reconquest of parts of Visigothic south-eastern Hispania; others suggest he was sent to the Suevic court as a missionary. Neither hypothesis is certain.

His arrival was historically significant, for he did much to convert the Suevi from Arian belief to Chalcedonian Christianity. He founded several monasteries, the best known at Dumium, near the Suevic capital at Braga, and became bishop of that monastic see. He attended the First Council of Braga in 561. At some point before the Second Council of Braga, over which he presided in 572, he was raised to metropolitan bishop of Braga, and he led the reorganising of the church in the Suevic kingdom. Gregory of Tours called him full of virtue and second to none in learning of his time. The Catholic Church canonised him, with the title Apostle to the Suevi; his feast day is 20 March.

He was a prolific author. He translated from Greek into Latin a collection of 109 sayings of the Desert Fathers, the Sententiae patrum Aegyptiorum, and assembled a large collection of church canons, mostly translated from Greek, which were presented at the Second Council of Braga.

In his last decade he wrote the short treatises De ira and Formula vitae honestae, which drew heavily on Seneca the Younger, and three essays on vices that reflect John Cassian. Formula vitae honestae, addressed to the Suevic king Miro, treats the four cardinal virtues; by the twelfth century it circulated without his preface and was mistaken for a genuine work of Seneca.

His best-known work is De correctione rusticorum, a model sermon in the form of a letter to Bishop Polemius of Astorga, who had asked how to convert rural pagans. It catalogues sixth-century Iberian pagan practices in an unusually tolerant tone, and is written in deliberately rustic Latin. Roger Collins argues it does not reflect the actual pre-Christian cults of rural Galicia. Martin objects there to naming the days of the week after gods; Portuguese and Galician, alone among the Romance languages, took their weekday names from numbers and Catholic liturgy.
martin-of-tours: Martin was born in Savaria in the Diocese of Pannonia, now Szombathely in Hungary. His father was a tribune in the Roman army, who was given veteran status and land at Ticinum, now Pavia, in northern Italy, where Martin grew up. At the age of ten he attended a Christian church against his parents' wishes and became a catechumen. He served in the Roman cavalry in Gaul, and his contemporary biographer Sulpicius Severus tells how at the gates of Amiens he cut his military cloak in half to share it with a beggar. That night he dreamed of Jesus wearing the half he had given, and he was baptised at 18.

Martin left military service before 361 and became a disciple of Hilary of Poitiers, whose Nicene orthodoxy he shared in opposition to the Arianism of the imperial court. In Illyricum he took the Nicene side with so much zeal that he was publicly whipped and made to leave. He established the monastery at Ligugé.

In 371 he succeeded Litorius as the third bishop of Tours. According to one tradition he hid in a barn full of geese to avoid it, but their cackling gave him away. He ordered the destruction of pagan temples, altars and sculptures. In 385 Magnus Maximus ordered the beheading of the ascetic Priscillian and his followers. Martin, though strongly opposed to their teaching, had travelled to the imperial court at Trier to reject Bishop Ithacius's principle of putting heretics to death and the emperor's intrusion into such matters, as Ambrose of Milan also did. Maximus granted him a promise to spare Priscillian, then broke it.

Martin died at Candes-Saint-Martin in 397. People of Poitou and of Tours quarrelled over his burial, and residents of Tours carried the body by boat down the Loire to their city. His shrine became one of the most prominent establishments in medieval France. Charlemagne made his adviser Alcuin abbot, and the scriptorium at Tours developed Carolingian minuscule. The abbey was ransacked by Vikings in 853 and 903.

The half of the cloak he kept became a relic of the Merovingian kings, first attested in the royal treasury in 679, and was carried into battle and used for oaths. He is the patron of beggars, tailors, vintners and geese, and of cities such as Szombathely and Utrecht, and is usually shown on horseback dividing his cloak.
martin-schongauer: Schongauer was born at Colmar in Alsace, the third of four or five sons of Caspar Schongauer, a goldsmith and patrician from Augsburg. He presumably learned engraving from his father, since goldsmiths had long engraved metal vessels. Unusually for an artist of his time he was sent to university, matriculating at Leipzig in 1465, but seems to have left after a year. Caspar Isenmann, who was influenced by Early Netherlandish painting, is thought to have trained him as a painter. A drawing dated 1469 copies the figure of Christ in Rogier van der Weyden's Beaune Altarpiece, and by 1471 he had a workshop in Colmar. His Madonna of the Rose Bower of 1473 is his only dated painting.

Schongauer was the first German painter to be a significant engraver. One hundred and sixteen engravings are generally recognised as his, signed with the monogram M†S, though none is dated. They were well known in Germany, Italy and even England and Spain, and Vasari says Michelangelo copied one, the Temptation of Saint Anthony. The great majority of his subjects are religious, but a handful show comic scenes of ordinary life. His style shows no trace of Italian influence but a clear, organised Gothic.

He went beyond Master E. S. in using cross-hatching to show volume, and was the first engraver to curve parallel lines. His early prints are crowded, as in the Passion series, perhaps of about 1480, and his later ones simpler. The demons in his Temptation of Saint Anthony set the hybrids of fish, bird and insect that Hieronymus Bosch and others followed.

Schongauer died in Breisach on 2 February 1491, perhaps before the age of forty. Since 1488 he had been painting a large Last Judgment in the cathedral there, the largest mural painting north of the Alps, which was incomplete at his death. The next year Albrecht Dürer travelled to Colmar to meet him, only to find he had died. Dürer collected his drawings and prints, and his own Flight into Egypt includes the same two exotic trees as Schongauer's, as an homage. In Germany Dürer was seen as the next leader of the tradition Schongauer had dominated for twenty years.
martin-slovakia: Martin lies in northern Slovakia on the Turiec river, in the Turiec Basin just south of the confluence of the Turiec with the Váh, between the Malá Fatra and Veľká Fatra mountains. It stands at an altitude of 402 metres. The nearest major cities are Žilina, 30 kilometres to the north-west, and Banská Bystrica, 60 kilometres to the south-east, and it is the centre of the Turiec region. Its older names were Turčiansky Svätý Martin in Slovak, Turócszentmárton in Hungarian and Turz-Sankt Martin in German.

From the second half of the 10th century until 1918 the area belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary. The first written reference to Martin dates from 1284, under the name Vila Sancti Martini. The 15th century was turbulent: the Hussites attacked in 1433 and burned the town, and ten years later an earthquake destroyed it again. Martin slowly declined from a royal town to a privileged one under the direct influence of the Révay family. In the 18th century it became the centre of Turóc county.

In the 19th century Martin became the foremost Slovak cultural centre. Several cultural institutions, among them the Slovak Matica and the Slovak National Museum, were founded there, and most of the political activity that led to Slovak national emancipation in the 19th and early 20th centuries was organised in or from the town. It was also industrialised then: its first printing works opened in 1869 and the furniture factory Tatra nábytok in 1890. The town lost some of its importance after Pressburg, today's Bratislava, became the capital of Slovakia in 1919.

Martin is the seat of the Slovak National Library and of Matica slovenská, and on 24 August 1994 the National Council of the Slovak Republic declared it the centre of national culture of the Slovaks. Its oldest building is a Romanesque church of Saint Martin of Tours, dating from the 13th century. The Slovak National Museum keeps its ethnographic collection there, and an open-air museum in the suburbs shows the traditional rural architecture of the Turiec region. The Slovak National Cemetery serves as the Slovak hall of fame and was inspired by the Panthéon in Paris. The Slovak Chamber Theatre, founded in 1944, was the second professional theatre company in Slovakia, and the Jessenius Faculty of Medicine is one of the country's three medical schools.
martino-zaccaria: Martino came of the Genoese Zaccaria family; modern sources disagree whether his father was Paleologo or Nicolino Zaccaria, so he was either grandson or nephew of Benedetto I Zaccaria, who had taken Chios from the Byzantine Empire in 1304. The emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos acknowledged the occupation, first for ten years and then in five-year renewals. When Paleologo died childless in 1314, Chios passed to Martino and his brother Benedetto II. It was small but wealthy, yielding 120,000 gold hyperpyra a year.

Martino built a small realm of islands off Asia Minor, including Samos and Kos, and with the Knights Hospitaller of Rhodes became the chief Latin opponent of the Turkish pirates, above all the Emirate of Aydin. In 1319 he joined a Hospitaller fleet with seven ships that crushed an Aydinid fleet from Ephesus. He was said to have taken or killed more than 10,000 Turks, and Pope John XXII praised him for stopping the slave trade of the Genoese of Alexandria. Marriage to Jacqueline de la Roche brought him the Barony of Veligosti–Damala, and in 1325 the titular Latin emperor Philip II named him King and Despot of Asia Minor.

About 1325 he ousted his brother and minted coins in his own name. The new emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos, urged by the Chian noble Leo Kalothetos, sailed against Chios in autumn 1329 with 105 vessels. Martino sank his three galleys and shut himself in his citadel with 800 men, but when Benedetto surrendered his fort and the islanders welcomed the Byzantines, he gave in. The emperor spared his life, though the islanders demanded his execution, and took him to Constantinople.

Released in 1337 at the intercession of the Pope and Philip VI of France, Martino became Genoa's ambassador to the Holy See. In September 1343 he took command of the four papal galleys in the crusade against Umur Bey under Henry of Asti, the Pope warning against any attempt to recover Chios. The crusaders took the lower town of Smyrna on 28 October 1344, and on 17 January 1345 the Turks attacked a mass held between the lines, killing Martino and Henry. His son Centurione I Zaccaria founded the line that later held Achaea.
martinus-theunis-steyn: Steyn was born on 2 October 1857 on the farm Rietfontein near Winburg, where his mother Cecilia was staying with her sister Gertruida and her husband Theunis Wessels while his father Marthinus was away in the Cape Colony; he was named after both men. During the Free State–Basotho War of 1858 the family was driven from its farm and lost almost everything, and he grew up on the farm Zuurfontein on the Modder River near Bloemfontein.

After Grey College and four years of farming, he was persuaded by Judge James Buchanan of the High Court to study law. He sailed for Europe in May 1877, studied at the Gymnasium in Deventer, then entered the Inner Temple in London and was called to the English bar in November 1882. Back in Bloemfontein he practised as a barrister, became state attorney in 1889 and first puisne judge of the high court in 1893.

When President Francis William Reitz resigned in 1895, Steyn stood as the candidate of the pan-Dutch party and won the election of February 1896 decisively. At the outbreak of the Second Boer War in 1899 he tied his state to the Transvaal against the British Empire, and once the British occupied the Orange Free State he ran his government from the field, helping to coordinate the guerrilla warfare that made up most of the war from 1900.

Counted among the most irreconcilable Boer leaders, he took part in the preliminary peace talks at Klerksdorp in April 1902, but illness kept him from signing the Treaty of Vereeniging at Pretoria on 31 May 1902. The treaty ended the independence of the Orange Free State, and with it his term as president.

Suffering from myasthenia gravis, he stayed in Europe from July 1902 to the autumn of 1904, then took the oath of allegiance to the British crown and returned to politics. He was vice-president of the National Convention of 1908–1909, and in 1914 left the South African Party with James Barry Munnik Hertzog and Christiaan Rudolf de Wet to found the National Party. He died of a heart attack while addressing a meeting in Bloemfontein in November 1916.

He initiated the C&N Oranje Meisieskool, a girls' school opened in 1907, and with Emily Hobhouse inspired the National Women's Monument, unveiled on 16 December 1913. The University of the Free State, established in 1904, answered the hope for a university at Bloemfontein that he voiced at his inauguration in 1896.
martos: Martos is a city and municipality in the province of Jaén in Andalusia. The housing lies at the foot of the Peña de Martos, a rock of 1,003 metres on the western side of the Sierra Sur de Jaén, a subrange of the Baetic System in the south of the Iberian Peninsula. Its economy has long rested on agriculture, above all the cultivation of the olive tree, and olive groves cover some 22,000 hectares, about 85 percent of the municipal area. The town has been nicknamed the Cradle of the Olive Grove.

The city has been linked to the Roman settlement of Colonia Augusta Gemella. Around 250 CE a bishopric was established in what is now Martos under the name Tucci, on territory taken from the suppressed Diocese of Iliturgi, as a suffragan of the archdiocese of Sevilla. In 350 it lost territory to the new Diocese of Cástulo and regained it when that see was suppressed about 400. In 715 the see was itself suppressed to found the Diocese of Beaza. The recorded bishops include Rogato, in office from about 675 to 688, and Teudisclo from about 693.

From the 8th century the Moors ruled the city under various Islamic states for over 500 years. In 1225 Ferdinand III of Castile and León received it from al-Bayyasi, in exchange for helping al-Bayyasi in his war against the Almohads in Andalusia, and incorporated it into his kingdom. During the Middle Ages it became a strategic place, and numerous fortifications were built to strengthen its defences.

At the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th, Martos went through a period of economic and urban growth, reflected in its architecture, thanks largely to the industrial production of olive oil. It became one of the most prosperous cities of eastern Andalusia. The population grew strongly in the first half of the 20th century, peaking at over 30,000 in the 1950s, and then fell as work was scarce and many people left for Madrid, Barcelona and the Spanish Levante.

Martos has a population of about 24,000, the fifth largest municipality of its province. It is also an industrial centre of inland Andalusia. The population rises unofficially in winter, when migrant workers come for the olive harvest.
martti-ahtisaari: Martti Ahtisaari was born in Viipuri (now Vyborg, Russia) on 23 June 1937. His father, Oiva, a non-commissioned officer in the supply troops, was at the front during the Continuation War, and his mother, Tyyne, took him to Kuopio in 1940, where he spent most of his childhood. The family moved to Oulu in 1952, and he graduated from high school in 1956 and qualified as a primary-school teacher in 1959. In 1960 he became director of a physical education boarding school in Karachi, Pakistan. In 1965 he joined the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, where he helped set up its International Development Assistance Office.

His diplomatic career began in 1973 as Finland's ambassador to Tanzania, Zambia, Somalia and Mozambique. In 1977 the United Nations recalled him to succeed Seán MacBride as Commissioner for Namibia. In April 1989 he went to Namibia as UN Special Representative to head the United Nations Transition Assistance Group. When SWAPO fighters crossed from Angola, he approved the deployment of South African troops to restore order, and in the fighting that followed at least 375 SWAPO insurgents were killed; some observers thought he had made too many concessions to the South Africans. After the independence elections he and his wife were made honorary Namibian citizens in 1992.

He was a UN under-secretary-general from 1987 to 1991, Secretary of State at Finland's Ministry for Foreign Affairs from 1991, and in 1992-1993 chaired the working group on Bosnia and Herzegovina at the Conference on Yugoslavia. Elected in the first direct presidential election, he beat Elisabeth Rehn in the second round and was sworn in on 1 March 1994. He supported Finland's entry into the European Union, approved by 57 per cent in a 1994 referendum, and in 1999 negotiated with Viktor Chernomyrdin to end the fighting in Kosovo with Slobodan Milošević. He did not stand for re-election, and Tarja Halonen succeeded him on 1 March 2000. He was the last strong president before the 2000 constitution reduced the office's powers.

He became chairman of the International Crisis Group in 2000 and founded the Crisis Management Initiative. In November 2005 UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed him Special Envoy for the Kosovo status process, which ended in 2007 and was followed by Kosovo's declaration of independence in February 2008. On 10 October 2008 he was announced as winner of the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to resolve international conflicts over more than three decades. He died in Helsinki on 16 October 2023, aged 86, after an illness announced in 2021, and was buried at Hietaniemi Cemetery after a state funeral.
martti-rautanen: Rautanen was born on 10 November 1845 into a poor Finnish family in Tikopis, in the parish of Novasolkka in Ingria, in the Saint Petersburg Governorate. The family came from Joroinen in the Savo region of Eastern Finland, and Rautanen thought of himself as Russian, having been born and raised in Russia. Encouraged by his pastor and his mother, he left Ingria in 1863 for Helsinki to attend the preparatory school for missionaries run by the Finnish Missionary Society. He came to speak Finnish, English, German, Dutch, Russian, Latin and Greek, and later Otjiherero and Oshindonga.

Rautanen left Finland with four colleagues on 24 June 1868. They first worked with Carl Hugo Hahn of the Rhenish Mission Society, spent more than a year in Hereroland from April 1869, and reached Ovamboland in July 1870, where they began work among the Ondonga. Their first station, founded that year at Omandongo, moved to Olukonda the following year. In 1872 Rautanen married Frieda Kleinschmidt, daughter of the German missionary Franz Heinrich Kleinschmidt; several of their nine children died young of malaria. The first local people became pastors in 1925.

He published a hymnal in Ndonga in 1892 and wrote poems used as new hymns. He began translating the Bible in 1885: the New Testament appeared in 1903, the Old Testament was finished in 1920 but not printed until 1954. After the Swiss botanist Hans Schinz visited in 1885-86, Rautanen collected plants and ethnographic material for museums in Finland, Germany and South Africa, and Schinz named the genus Neorautanenia and the mongongo tree Ricinodendron rautanenii after him.

Shortly before his death the University of Helsinki gave him an honorary doctorate in theology. He died at Olukonda on 19 October 1926. His nickname Nakambale, from the skullcap that reminded people of a small basket, was written on his tombstone. A selection of his texts appeared in 1934 as Travel Rod. His ethnographic collection is in the National Museum of Finland, his diaries at the University of Turku, and the family home at Olukonda is now the Nakambale Museum.
martynas-mazvydas: Mažvydas was of Samogitian origin, born near Žemaičių Naumiestis in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; his parents were said to be poor townspeople. He spent his youth in Vilnius, where he worked with other early Lithuanian authors such as Abraomas Kulvietis, Jurgis Zablockis and possibly Stanislovas Rapolionis, some of whose works he later published. Persecuted in Roman Catholic Lithuania for his Protestant leanings, he accepted an invitation from Duke Albrecht of Prussia to come to Königsberg.

He entered Albertina University in 1546 and graduated with a bachelor's degree in 1548. That he finished in a year and a half suggests he had studied elsewhere before, possibly in Kraków or at the school Kulvietis had founded in Vilnius.

In 1549 he was appointed priest in Ragainė, the present-day town of Neman, and in 1554 he became its archdeacon. He oversaw the education of his parishioners and regulated agricultural matters while he went on writing in Lithuanian. He translated The Form of Baptism from German and published it in Königsberg in 1559. His Christian Songs appeared in two parts in 1566 and 1570, printed by his cousin Baltramiejus Vilentas, and became the basis for later Protestant songbooks of Lithuania Minor. He died in Königsberg on 21 May 1563.

Duke Albrecht commissioned Lutheran texts in Old Prussian and Lithuanian to spread the new faith, and the catechism of 1547, Catechismusa Prasty Szadei (The Simple Words of Catechism), was printed at the Hans Weinreich printing works. It was based on the Polish version of Martin Luther's Kleiner Katechismus and shows the Samogitian dialect with clear Aukštaitian traits. It opens with a Latin dedication to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and two prefaces, one in Latin prose and one in Lithuanian verse.

The verse preface, The Appeal of the Small Book Itself unto Lithuanians and Samogitians, is the first authentic verse in Lithuanian, and the first letters of its lines 3 to 19 spell Martinus Masvidius, confirming his authorship. The prefaces state his aims: to educate the people and spread culture, to fight the remains of heathen beliefs and to consolidate the Protestant religion. Only two copies survive, one at the Vilnius University Library and one at the library of Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń. Mažvydas set the pattern for several genres of Lithuanian writing, among them the primer, the prayer book and the book of songs with notes.
martyrdom-of-the-holy-queen-shushanik: The work tells the martyrdom of Saint Shushanik, consort of Varsken, the bidaxshe or high prince who ruled Gogarene and had renounced Christianity for Zoroastrianism. Shushanik was the daughter of Vardan Mamikonyan, the sparapet or military leader of the Christians in Armenia. She refused to follow her husband and died a martyr after years of imprisonment and torture. Its author, Iakob Tsurtaveli, was a contemporary of the events he describes and a participant in them, and the work is sometimes called a hagiographic novel.

The text is held to have been written between 476 and 483 and survives in eleven manuscripts. The oldest, the Parkhali Mravaltavi, is presumably a 10th-century codex copied at Parkhali Monastery; it holds only the first 12 chapters, because its 16th quire of eight folios was lost at an unknown date, taking the final third of the narrative with it. A short recension survives in the 10th-century manuscript Ivir. georg. 57 on Mount Athos, and a concise liturgical version entered the Georgian Synaxarion.

Mikhail Sabinin first printed the long text in 1882. Sargis Gorgadze published a critical edition from four manuscripts in 1917 and Ilia Abuladze one from eight in 1938, followed in 1963 by an edition using all eleven. Aleksandre Khakhanashvili edited the Athos version in 1910 with so many transcription errors that Abuladze republished it in 1938 from photographs of the codex. A new scholarly edition with commentary and facsimiles of the main manuscripts appeared in 2025.

The work has been translated into Russian, French, English, German, Spanish, Hungarian and Icelandic, and in 1979 UNESCO marked the 1,500th anniversary of the Martyrdom. A passage of The Conversion of Kartli, the narrative of the Cross of Saint Nino, also recounts Shushanik's death.
martyrs-of-cordoba: After the Umayyad caliphs were deposed in Damascus in 750, the dynasty ruled an emirate from Córdoba, which grew in wealth and importance as a centre of Iberian Muslim culture. Under Islamic law as applied there, blasphemy, which included insulting Muhammad, and apostasy from Islam were capital offences, and anyone with a Muslim father was a Muslim from birth. Christians, as People of the Book, held the inferior status of dhimmi: they kept their churches and property on payment of the jizya and kharaj taxes and had to avoid public displays of their faith. Many fled north, withdrew to monasteries in the sierras or converted, and the Christian population of al-Andalus shrank.

The first to die was the priest Perfectus, beheaded on 18 April 850 after declaring before the authorities that Muhammad had committed fornication. On 3 June 851 Isaac, a former official of the emir who had become a monk at Tábanos, proclaimed his faith before the court and was executed, and others followed, mostly monks, priests and nuns from Córdoba and the monasteries around it. Some, like the sisters Flora and Maria, executed on 24 November 851, were children of mixed marriages, so that their Christianity counted in law as apostasy. A few, such as the priest Abundius, were denounced by others rather than coming forward themselves.

Emir Abd al-Rahman II first detained the Christian clergy, releasing them in November 851, and later ordered the bishops to hold a council in Córdoba to stop the public dissent. Bishop Reccafred of Córdoba urged compromise. After 852 Muhammad I removed Christians from palace offices, and the monastery of Tábanos was closed. The last to die were Eulogius, executed on 11 March 859 for hiding the convert Leocritia, and Leocritia herself four days later.

Eulogius's martyrologies, among them the three books of the Memoriale sanctorum, survive in a single manuscript preserved at Oviedo in the Kingdom of Asturias, to which his relics were moved in 884. Historians caution that the lack of any source after his death may give the false impression that such cases ended there. Jessica A. Coope sees the movement as a protest against assimilation, while Kenneth Wolf distinguishes the martyrs' own motives from those of their chroniclers and reads them through the penitential piety of 9th-century Iberian Christianity.
marvdasht: Marvdasht is the capital of both Marvdasht County and its Central District in Fars province. The city lies about 45 kilometres north of Shiraz, at an altitude of 1620 metres. The county covers 3687 square kilometres and borders Arsenjan, Pasargad, Khorambid, Eghlid, Sepidan and Shiraz. It has three cities, Marvdasht, Seydan and Kamfirouz, and four districts: Central, Kamfirouz, Doroudzan and Seydan. The climate is cold in the hilly areas and moderate elsewhere.

Historians disagree about the origin of the name. Some hold that Marvdasht was originally the name of a neighbourhood of the ancient city of Estakhr, until the whole area came to be called by it. Others argue that marv was the name of a plant that grew there and that dasht, the Persian word for plain, was added to make a descriptive placename.

Excavations show that settled people had lived on the Marvdasht plain for millennia before Darius chose the plain below Mount Rahmat for his royal residence. The Tokyo University Iraq-Iran Archaeological Expedition, headed by Namio Egami, worked there for three seasons between 1956 and 1965. It dug the prehistoric mounds of Tall-i Bakun A and B, Tall-i Gap A, Tall-i Jari A and B, and Tall-i Mushki. At Tall-e Gap many ceramic items were found, and the site was identified as an important settlement of the Bakun culture, in its Middle Bakun sub-phase of the Chalcolithic of the 5th millennium BCE.

The modern city was built in the 20th century. After the Pahlavi government opened a sugar factory in 1935, the city grew around it, as people left nearby villages or gave up a nomadic life to settle there. Before the Iranian Revolution of 1979 it became the most important industrial city of Fars province, with a petrochemical complex, the Azmayesh appliance works, the Charmineh leather factory, the Fars meat complex and the Dadli biscuit company, and it grew to be the second most populated city of the province.

The fertile land around the city is a major centre of Iranian farming, producing wheat, maize, tomatoes, cucumbers and other crops. The census of 2006 counted 123,858 people in the city, that of 2011 counted 138,649 and that of 2016 counted 148,858. The city has several universities and colleges, among them a branch of Islamic Azad University and a branch of Payame Noor University.
marwan-ii: Marwan ibn Muhammad belonged to the Marwanid house of the Umayyad Caliphate. He was the son of Muhammad ibn Marwan, a grandson of the caliph Marwan I and a nephew of the caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. Historical tradition places his birth around 695. Political opponents used his mother's lineage against him during the civil wars of the Third Fitna: hostile accounts claimed she was a non-Arab concubine of Kurdish origin who was already pregnant when Muhammad acquired her.

In 732-733 Caliph Hisham appointed Marwan governor of Armenia. In 735-736 he invaded Georgia, devastated it, took three fortresses of the Alans and made peace with Tumanshah; further raids in 739-740 brought tribute. For several years he supervised campaigns against the Byzantines and the Khazars on the northwestern frontiers. When a plot against al-Walid II took shape, he wrote from Armenia urging his relatives to preserve the unity of the Umayyad house, but he was ignored, and Yazid III deposed al-Walid. Yazid then made him governor of Upper Mesopotamia, where he lived at Harran.

Marwan at first opposed Yazid III and then gave him allegiance. When Yazid died early, Marwan ignored the successor Yazid had named, Ibrahim ibn al-Walid, and became caliph. Ibrahim received assurances of personal safety and accompanied him to Hisham's residence at Rusafah. Marwan named his sons Ubaydallah and Abdullah as heirs. Anti-Umayyad feeling was strong, especially in Iran and Iraq, and his reign was almost entirely devoted to holding the empire together.

He took Emesa (Homs) after a ten-month siege and fought a Kharijite rebellion led by al-Dahhak ibn Qays al-Shaybani, which took Kufa; Marwan besieged the rebels at Mosul for six months before driving them out. In Khurasan the governor Nasr ibn Sayyar faced rivals while Abbasid envoys arrived, and during Ramadan of 747 the Abbasids unfurled the standards of their revolt. Nasr died at Rayy on 9 November 748. Marwan's campaign in Egypt in 749 against the Bashmuric Revolt failed.

Marwan suffered a decisive defeat by Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah on the Great Zab, at the Battle of the Zab, where over 300 members of the Umayyad family died. He fled through Damascus, Jordan and Palestine to Egypt, where he was caught and killed on 6 August 750. His sons escaped to what is now Eritrea, and Abdallah died fighting there.

His death ended Umayyad fortunes in the East and was followed by a mass killing of Umayyads by the Abbasids. Almost the entire dynasty was killed, except the prince Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya, who escaped to Spain and founded an Umayyad dynasty there.
marxism-leninism: Marxism–Leninism drew on Bolshevism, Leninism and classical Marxism. It began as the practical politics of the Bolshevik faction of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, which Vladimir Lenin turned into a vanguard of professional revolutionaries who chose leaders and policy by democratic centralism. The Bolsheviks seized power in the October Revolution of 1917 and fought the White Movement in the Russian Civil War. In the 1917 election to the Constituent Assembly they won 23.3 percent of the vote against 37.6 for the Socialist Revolutionary Party, and the assembly was dissolved in January 1918.

After Lenin's death on 21 January 1924, Joseph Stalin and his supporters gained control of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, and Marxism–Leninism became a distinct movement. It rejected the view of Western Marxists that world revolution was needed first, in favour of socialism in one country. By the late 1920s Stalin had established ideological orthodoxy in the party and the Communist International.

Marxism–Leninism holds that a two-stage communist revolution must replace capitalism. A vanguard party, organised through democratic centralism, seizes power on behalf of the proletariat and establishes a one-party state, which controls the means of production and suppresses opposition to pave the way for a classless and stateless society. Its worldview is atheist, and it supports universal welfare, with healthcare and education provided by the state. Its approach to international relations rests on Lenin's essay Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism of 1917.

From 1928 Stalin's five-year plans brought rapid industrialisation, concentrated on heavy industry, and the collectivisation of agriculture, which stood at 23.6 percent in 1930 and 98.0 percent in 1941. After Stalin's death it was revised into Titoism, Guevarism, Ho Chi Minh Thought, Hoxhaism and Maoism.

Marxism–Leninism was the state ideology of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc during the Cold War, and of the Communist International. The union Solidarity, formed in Poland in 1980, was the first trade union in the Warsaw Pact not controlled by a Marxist–Leninist party, and the Eastern European governments and the Soviet Union fell by 1991.

Critics from across the political spectrum have attacked it, above all in its Stalinist and Maoist forms. Historians such as Silvio Pons and David Martin Walker connect killings and repression of dissidents and social classes, as in the Red Terror and the Great Purge in the Soviet Union, partly to the ideology, while others offer different explanations. Rosa Luxemburg rejected the vanguard idea, and some left-wing critics see it as state capitalism.
mary-i-of-england: Mary was born on 18 February 1516 at the Palace of Placentia in Greenwich, the only child of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon to survive infancy. She could read and write Latin by the age of nine. In 1525 Henry sent her to preside over the Council of Wales and the Marches from Ludlow Castle. The annulment of her parents' marriage in 1533 declared her illegitimate and barred her from the succession, and after Anne Boleyn's fall in 1536 she was bullied into signing a document accepting Henry as head of the Church, her parents' marriage as unlawful and her own illegitimacy. The Third Succession Act of 1543 restored her place in the line.

Edward VI died on 6 July 1553, having excluded Mary and Elizabeth from the succession in favour of Lady Jane Grey at the urging of John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland. Mary fled to East Anglia, where Catholic supporters and Northumberland's enemies lived, and wrote to the privy council from Kenninghall on 9 July to order her own proclamation. Lady Jane was deposed, and Mary was crowned by Stephen Gardiner at Westminster Abbey on 1 October 1553. Northumberland was the only conspirator of rank executed at once.

A parliamentary delegation asked her to choose an English husband, but she chose Philip, son of her cousin Charles V, and they married in July 1554. Her first Parliament declared her parents' marriage valid and abolished Edward's religious laws, and the church returned to Roman jurisdiction. The Heresy Acts were revived in January 1555, and more than 280 religious dissenters were burned at the stake, among them Protestant churchmen such as Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer, John Hooper and John Rogers. Queen's and King's Counties were founded in Ireland. In 1554 and again in 1557 she believed herself pregnant, but no child was born.

Weak and ill from May 1558, Mary died on 17 November 1558, aged 42, at St James's Palace, during an influenza epidemic, and was succeeded by Elizabeth I. She was buried in Westminster Abbey on 14 December in a tomb she later shared with Elizabeth. She was the first woman to successfully claim the throne of England. Protestant writers have often condemned her reign, and John Foxe's Actes and Monuments (1563) helped shape the picture of a bloodthirsty tyrant. By the seventeenth century the persecutions had given her the name Bloody Mary.
mary-ii-of-england: Mary was born on 30 April 1662 at St James's Palace in London, the daughter of James, Duke of York, and his first wife, Anne Hyde. Her uncle Charles II had no legitimate children, so for most of her childhood she was second in line to the throne. Although her father converted to Roman Catholicism, she and her sister Anne were brought up as Anglicans on the command of Charles II.

At the age of 15 she was betrothed to her first cousin William of Orange, the Protestant Stadtholder of Holland, and they married at St James's Palace on 4 November 1677. When her father told her of the match, she wept all that afternoon and all the following day. She had no surviving children, and her childlessness caused her deep unhappiness.

James II's attempt to grant religious freedom by royal decree, and the birth of his Catholic son in June 1688, led seven English nobles to invite William to England. Mary stayed in the Netherlands while William landed on 5 November 1688. On 13 February 1689 Parliament offered the crown to William and Mary as joint sovereigns, with the exercise of royal power to rest with William. They were crowned at Westminster Abbey on 11 April 1689.

While William was campaigning abroad, usually from spring to autumn, Mary governed with the advice of a nine-member Cabinet Council. When he was in England she kept out of politics. She nevertheless proved firm, ordering the arrest of her uncle Henry Hyde, 2nd Earl of Clarendon, for plotting to restore James. In January 1692 John Churchill, 1st Earl of Marlborough, was dismissed on similar charges, and the affair ended with her final quarrel with Anne. Mary was devout, and the composer Henry Purcell wrote birthday odes for her.

Mary contracted smallpox in late 1694 and died at Kensington Palace shortly after midnight on 28 December, aged 32. She was buried at Westminster Abbey on 5 March, in the first royal funeral attended by all the members of both Houses of Parliament. William was devastated.

Mary endowed the College of William and Mary in Virginia in 1693 and helped to found the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich. Jacobites portrayed her as a daughter who had destroyed her father for gain, while the assessment that came down to posterity was of a dutiful wife who took power reluctantly, used it ably when needed and deferred it to her husband.
mary-mother-of-jesus: Mary was a first-century Jewish woman of Nazareth, the wife of Joseph and the mother of Jesus. The canonical Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles are the primary sources, and they give limited information because they focus on the teaching of Jesus and his apostles. They are generally dated to about 66–110 CE, and their historical reliability is debated. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke describe Mary as a virgin chosen by God to conceive Jesus through the Holy Spirit. After the birth in Bethlehem, she and Joseph raised him in Nazareth in Galilee, and she was in Jerusalem at his crucifixion.

Apocryphal texts add details, such as the Gospel of James, which names her parents as Joachim and Anne and says she was given to the Temple in Jerusalem at the age of three. Scholars generally consider such texts mainly unreliable. In the 2nd century the pagan philosopher Celsus claimed that Jesus was the illegitimate son of a Roman soldier named Panthera, and the Church Father Origen dismissed this as a fabrication.

The Bible does not describe the end of Mary's life. Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and some Oriental Orthodox and Protestant traditions hold that her body was raised into heaven at its close, which Western Christianity calls the Assumption and Eastern Christianity the Dormition of the Mother of God. The Catholic Church also holds the dogma of her Immaculate Conception.

Mary has been venerated since early Christianity. Eastern and Oriental Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches hold that she is the Mother of God, while many Protestants pay far less attention to her. Devotion takes the form of prayers and hymns, feast days, the veneration of images and relics, churches and pilgrimages. In Islam, where she is called Maryam, she has the highest position among women, and a chapter of the Quran is named for her. She is also revered in the Druze and Bahá'í faiths. In Western art she is traditionally painted in blue, a custom that goes back to the Byzantine Empire.
mary-of-burgundy: Mary was born on 13 February 1457 in Brussels, at the ducal Palace of Coudenberg, to Charles the Bold, then Count of Charolais, and Isabella of Bourbon. When her grandfather Philip the Good died in 1467 and her father took control of the Burgundian State, Mary became his heir presumptive. He held the Duchy of Burgundy, the Free County of Burgundy and most of the Low Countries, so many princes sought her hand. Louis XI wanted her for his son Charles VIII, who was thirteen years younger, and Edward IV of England prevented a match with George Plantagenet, Duke of Clarence.

Charles was killed at the Battle of Nancy on 5 January 1477, and Mary, aged 19, claimed the whole inheritance, which included Limburg, Brabant, Luxembourg, Namur, Holland and Hainaut. Louis XI seized the Duchy of Burgundy, Franche-Comté, Picardy and Artois. When he took Arras, the people refused to submit without her approval, and he had eighteen burgesses beheaded for trying to see her. The dispute led to the War of the Burgundian Succession.

At Ghent on 10 February 1477 she signed the Great Privilege, a charter by which Flanders, Brabant, Hainaut and Holland recovered the local rights the dukes had abolished, and she undertook not to declare war, make peace or raise taxes without consent. On 19 August 1477 she married Archduke Maximilian of Austria, son of the emperor Frederick III. He came without money or army, but his prestige and military competence strengthened her position. The state had lost a quarter of its tax revenue, and Mary pawned heirlooms to pay for the armies. Her marriage began the long rivalry between France and the Habsburgs.

In 1482 Mary was hunting with falcons near Wijnendale Castle when her horse tripped and fell on her, breaking her back. She died on 27 March from internal injuries, after making a detailed will, and was buried in the Church of Our Lady in Bruges. She was pregnant. Her children were Philip the Handsome, Margaret of Austria and Franz, who died in infancy.

By the Treaty of Arras of 1482 Franche-Comté and Artois passed for a time to France, and the Treaty of Senlis of 1493 recovered them. Her son Philip I the Handsome inherited her domains and claims under the guardianship of his father. In the 19th century she became a national symbol of Belgium.
mary-of-guise: Mary of Guise was born on 22 November 1515 at Bar-le-Duc, Lorraine, the eldest of twelve children of Claude, Duke of Guise, and Antoinette of Bourbon. Her siblings included François, Duke of Guise, and Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine. She grew up partly in the convent of the Poor Clares at Pont-à-Mousson and reached a height of 5 feet 11 inches (1.80 metres). On 4 August 1534 she married Louis II d'Orléans, Duke of Longueville, Grand Chamberlain of France, and had two sons, of whom Francis survived. Louis died on 9 June 1537, leaving her a widow at 21.

Both Henry VIII of England and James V of Scotland sought her hand. After persuasion from Francis I of France she agreed to marry James, and they wed in person on 18 June 1538 at St Andrews Cathedral. She was crowned at Holyrood Abbey on 22 February 1540. Both her sons by James died in April 1541, and when James V died in December 1542 their daughter Mary became Queen of Scots at six days old. James Hamilton, 2nd Earl of Arran, became regent, and Henry VIII's wish to marry the infant to his son Edward led to the Rough Wooing and an English invasion.

With the Treaty of Haddington in 1548 the child queen was betrothed to the Dauphin Francis and sent to France. Mary of Guise stayed in Scotland, and in July 1548 she came to watch the siege of Haddington and came within range of the English guns, which killed sixteen of her entourage. She replaced Arran as regent on 12 April 1554. Her regency aimed to protect her daughter's dynastic interests, maintain the Franco-Scottish alliance and restore the power of the Scottish crown. She was tolerant of the reform movement and sought accommodation with Protestants.

The marriage of Mary, Queen of Scots, to the dauphin on 24 April 1558 and the accession of Elizabeth I in England in November 1558 raised the stakes. Henry II of France died in July 1559. French troops were stationed at Leith, and the Lords of the Congregation complained of Frenchmen holding Scottish posts. After an English assault on Leith was repulsed, Mary fell seriously ill in Edinburgh Castle, made her will on 8 June and died of dropsy on 11 June 1560.

Apart from John Knox, historians have generally judged her favourably. Rosalind K. Marshall describes her as charming, highly intelligent and hard-working, and says she fought a long and in the end hopeless struggle to keep Scotland a pro-French, Roman Catholic nation for her daughter, never merely a pawn of the French king.
mary-of-hungary-queen-of-naples: Mary of Hungary, of the Árpád dynasty, was the daughter of Stephen V of Hungary and Elizabeth the Cuman. She was the second of six children; her sisters Elizabeth and Catherine both became queens of Serbia, her sister Anna married Andronikos II Palaiologos, and her only brother was Ladislaus IV of Hungary. At twelve she married Charles II of Naples at Naples on 6 August 1270. The marriage was meant as a double alliance between Naples and Hungary for a planned conquest of Byzantium, but it failed when her brother allied with Byzantium in 1272. She spent four years from 1278 in Provence with her husband and in 1284 freed the Aragonese prisoner Beatrice of Hohenstaufen when Charles was captured by Aragon.

Charles became monarch in 1285 while still in an Aragonese prison. Mary stayed in Provence and helped administer it, took part in the negotiations for his release and made a peace treaty with Aragon in 1288. She was regent in Provence from 1290 to 1294 and in Naples in 1295 to 1296, 1296 to 1298 and 1302.

When Ladislaus IV was murdered by three Cuman assassins on 10 July 1290, leaving no child, Mary and her sisters claimed the succession. Andrew the Venetian was crowned Andrew III on 23 July, but Mary denied his right, holding that his father Stephen the Posthumous was illegitimate. In April 1291 she declared her own claim, and in January 1292 transferred it to her eighteen-year-old son Charles Martel, whom Pope Nicholas IV and the church party made titular king.

Charles Martel died of the plague in Naples on 12 August 1295, and the Pope confirmed Mary's sole rights on 30 August. In 1300 her grandson Charles Robert landed at Split. After Andrew III died on 14 January 1301 he was crowned with a provisional crown, which most Hungarians thought unlawful. He was proclaimed king on 27 November 1308 and crowned on 27 August 1310 in Székesfehérvár.

After 1302 Mary lost influence over state affairs and devoted herself to pious works, financing convents and churches. Her husband died in May 1309. There is no evidence that she became a nun, though she spent much time in convents. She lived in Naples until her death on 25 March 1323 and was buried at Santa Maria Donna Regina. She had fourteen children, among them Charles Martel, Louis, Bishop of Toulouse, later canonised, and Robert I of Naples. The Hungarian claims of Mary and Catherine were united in their great-great-granddaughter Mary of Hungary, who took the throne in 1382.
mary-shelley: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in Somers Town, London, on 30 August 1797, the child of the philosopher William Godwin and the women's rights advocate Mary Wollstonecraft, who died of puerperal fever eleven days after the birth. Godwin brought her up with her older half-sister, Fanny Imlay, gave her a rich informal education and encouraged her in his own anarchist political theories. When she was four, he married a neighbour, Mary Jane Clairmont, with whom Mary had a troubled relationship.

In 1814 she began a romance with Percy Bysshe Shelley, a follower of her father who was already married. With her stepsister Claire Clairmont they left for France and travelled through Europe. After their return they faced ostracism, constant debt and the death of their daughter. Percy's wife Harriet was found drowned in December 1816, and Mary and Percy married on 30 December.

In May 1816 the couple and Claire Clairmont went to Geneva to spend the summer with Lord Byron, who rented the Villa Diodati with his physician John William Polidori. There Mary conceived the idea for Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, published in 1818. How far Percy contributed to it is argued: James Rieger saw him as editor or minor collaborator, while Anne K. Mellor held that he only made technical corrections.

The Shelleys left Britain for Italy in 1818. Two of their children died there, and Percy Florence was born on 12 November 1819. In 1822 Percy drowned when his boat sank in a storm near Viareggio, and a year later she returned to England as a professional author. Her novels include Valperga, The Last Man (1826), Lodore and Falkner, and she wrote biographies for Dionysius Lardner's Cabinet Cyclopaedia between 1832 and 1839. She published Percy's Posthumous Poems in 1824 and a new edition of his poetry in 1839.

The last decade of her life was dogged by illness, most likely caused by the brain tumour that killed her at the age of 53, on 1 February 1851. Until the 1970s she was known mainly for Frankenstein and her efforts to publish her husband's works. Recent scholarship finds in her other writing a political radical who argued that cooperation and sympathy, as practised by women in the family, were the ways to reform society.
mary-wollstonecraft: Mary Wollstonecraft was born on 27 April 1759 in Spitalfields, London, the second of the seven children of Elizabeth Dixon and Edward John Wollstonecraft. The family had a comfortable income in her childhood, but her father gradually squandered it on speculative projects, and the family moved often. He was apparently a violent man who beat his wife in drunken rages, and as a teenager Wollstonecraft lay outside her mother's bedroom door to protect her. She played a similar maternal role for her sisters Everina and Eliza. In 1784 she arranged for Eliza, probably suffering from postpartum depression, to leave her husband and infant, a decision that brought her sister social condemnation and poverty.

After Blood's death in 1785, Wollstonecraft's friends helped her to a post as governess to the daughters of the Anglo-Irish Kingsborough family in Ireland. Her early writings concern education, among them Thoughts on the Education of Daughters (1787), the children's book Original Stories from Real Life (1788) and the anthology The Female Reader. She also translated children's works. Her first novel, Mary: A Fiction, appeared in 1788, and her unfinished Maria: or, The Wrongs of Woman was published after her death in 1798. Both novels criticise marriage and its effects on women.

A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790) answered Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, attacking aristocracy and advocating republicanism, and it was the first reply in what became known as the Revolution Controversy. Wollstonecraft left for Paris in December 1792, shortly before Louis XVI was guillotined, and associated mostly with the moderate Girondins. There she fell in love with the American adventurer Gilbert Imlay, and their daughter Fanny was born. She was disillusioned by what she saw, writing that the new government remained venal and brutal, and wrote An Historical and Moral View of the French Revolution (1794).

Imlay rejected her when she returned to London in April 1795, and she attempted suicide twice. She travelled to Scandinavia on his business and recounted the journey in Letters Written in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark (1796). She later married the philosopher William Godwin.
