Wollstonecraft gave birth to her second daughter, Mary, on 30 August 1797 and died of septicaemia on 10 September, at the age of 38. The daughter became the author of Frankenstein. Godwin's Memoirs of 1798 revealed her love affairs, illegitimate children and suicide attempts, and the Romantic poet Robert Southey accused him of stripping his dead wife naked. Her reputation lay in tatters for nearly a century, and novelists such as Maria Edgeworth pilloried her in their characters. With the feminist movement at the turn of the twentieth century her advocacy of women's equality was increasingly recognised.
maryland: Maryland borders Virginia to the south, West Virginia to the west, Pennsylvania to the north and Delaware to the east, as well as the Atlantic Ocean to the east and Washington, D.C. to the southwest. With an area of 12,407 square miles (32,130 km2) it is the ninth-smallest state by land area. The western portion contains stretches of the Appalachian Mountains, the centre is mainly Piedmont, and the east takes in a large part of the Chesapeake Bay, which nearly bisects the state.

The variety of its landscape, from sandy dunes in the east to marshes near the bay, oak forests in the Piedmont and pine groves in the mountains, has earned it the nickname America in Miniature. Its history as a border state has left it with traits of both North and South.

Present-day Maryland was inhabited by Native peoples, mostly Algonquian, including the Piscataway, the Nanticoke and the Susquehannock. George Calvert, 1st Baron Baltimore, sought a charter from King Charles I for the territory between Massachusetts and Virginia. After he died in April 1632, the charter was granted to his son Cecilius Calvert, 2nd Baron Baltimore, on 20 June 1632. The colony was named in honour of Henrietta Maria of France, wife of Charles I.

The land was first settled in 1634, primarily to provide a religious haven for Catholics persecuted in England. Religious strife was common in the early years, and Catholics remained a minority, though in greater numbers than in any other English colony. The original capital was St. Mary's City on the north shore of the Potomac River. The economy was plantation-based and centred on tobacco, and demand for cheap labour led to the importation of many indentured servants and enslaved Africans.

Maryland's current boundaries took form in 1760, after the settlement of a long-running border dispute with Pennsylvania. Georgetown, Maryland, and other land from Montgomery and Prince George's counties was ceded to the federal government in 1790 to form Washington, D.C. Although Maryland was a slave state, it remained in the Union during the American Civil War, in part because Abraham Lincoln left the National Guard there.

The capital is Annapolis and the most populous city is Baltimore. The 2020 census counted 6,185,278 residents. Its nearness to Washington, D.C. shapes its economy, which includes defence, biotechnology and higher education, and the state hosts some of the highest numbers of historic landmarks per capita.
maryland-county: Maryland was first established in 1834 as a colony of the Maryland State Colonization Society, which had played an important part in the formation of the larger American Colonization Society. After a referendum in 1853 the colony declared its independence from the society and formed the Republic of Maryland in 1854. It held the land along the south coast between the Grand Cess and San Pedro Rivers.

In 1856 the Republic of Maryland asked Liberia for military aid in a war with the Grebo and Kru peoples, who were resisting the settlers' efforts to control their trade in slaves. Liberian President Joseph Jenkins Roberts helped, and a joint campaign won the war. After a referendum in February 1857, the republic joined Liberia as Maryland County on 6 April 1857.

In the 1970s the county was terrorised by ritual killings, regarded as Liberia's most notorious ritual killing case because of the number of murders, the involvement of high-ranking government officials and their later public executions. In 1984 the Kru Coast Territory, which had been administered as part of the county, was detached under People's Redemption Council Decree No. 87 and merged with the Sasstown Territory of Sinoe County to form Grand Kru County.

Maryland County is one of the 15 counties of Liberia, named after the State of Maryland, and has an area of 887 square miles. Its population was 172,202 at the 2022 census, and its largest city is Pleebo. Grand Kru County lies to the west and River Gee County to the north, and the Cavalla River separates the eastern part from Côte d'Ivoire. William V. S. Tubman University in Harper traces its origins to a college of technology founded in 1978 and became a university in 2009. Farming, mainly rice and cassava, employs about 60 per cent of residents. After a documentary on the region, Africa's Maryland, was made in 2007, the American state signed a sister state agreement with Bong and Maryland counties.
maryland-state-colonization-society: The society was the Maryland branch of the American Colonization Society, founded in 1816 to send free African Americans to Africa. A Maryland Colonization Society was founded in 1827 with the wealthy planter Charles Carroll of Carrollton, a substantial slaveholder, as its first president; he supported the gradual abolition of slavery and introduced a bill for it in the Maryland senate, which did not pass, but he kept his own slaves. Many planters belonged, among them the Steuart family, including George H. Steuart, a major general of the Maryland Militia. The society presented itself as a remedy for slavery, and it was founded in part as a response to the threat of slave rebellion, such as that of Nat Turner in Virginia in 1831.

In December 1831 the Maryland legislature voted funds, up to a total of $260,000 over 26 years, to transport free Black people and former slaves to Africa, and empowered the society to carry out the plan. Settlers were offered free passage, rent, 5 acres of land and loans. At the same time freed slaves were required to leave the state unless a court allowed them to stay, and in 1832 free Black people were barred from voting, serving on juries and holding office, to encourage them to emigrate. John Latrobe, the society's president for two decades, declared that sooner or later every free person of colour would be persuaded to leave Maryland.

The settlement at Cape Palmas, a small rocky peninsula south of the rest of Liberia, was named Maryland in Africa on 12 February 1834. In 1836 John Brown Russwurm became its first Black governor and held the post until his death in 1851. The colony stayed out of the Commonwealth of Liberia, as the society wished to keep its trade monopoly, and became the State of Maryland on 2 February 1841. It declared independence on 29 May 1854, with its capital at Harper. Attacked by the Grebo and the Kru, it called on Liberia for help, and on 18 March 1857 it was annexed as Maryland County.

By the 1850s few Marylanders still believed that colonisation would solve the problem of slavery, which ended in Maryland only with the Union's victory in the American Civil War in 1865. The society did not become the remedy it had promised, but it contributed to the making of the modern state of Liberia. The American Colonization Society, of which it was a branch, was formally dissolved in 1964.
maryland-toleration-act: The Province of Maryland was founded in 1634 by Cecil Calvert, 2nd Baron Baltimore, who, like his father George Calvert, 1st Baron Baltimore, was a Catholic in a kingdom dominated by the Church of England. The Calverts meant the colony as a haven for English Catholics and a source of income for their family, but Anglican and Puritan newcomers soon outnumbered the first Catholic settlers. Calvert urged the colonists to leave religious rivalries behind and asked Catholics to practise their faith as privately as possible.

The English Civil War opened religious rifts in the colony. In 1647, after the death of Governor Leonard Calvert, Protestants seized control. Cecil Calvert soon regained power but saw that toleration not written into law was vulnerable, and he had also promised freedom of worship to a group of Puritans he induced to settle Providence, now Annapolis. He wrote the act himself, and the assembly, by then dominated by Protestants, passed it on 21 April 1649 at St. Mary's City.

The act, also called the Act Concerning Religion, provided that no one professing to believe in Jesus Christ should be troubled or molested for their religion or in its free exercise. Insulting the Virgin Mary, the apostles or the evangelists could bring whipping, prison or a fine, and calling others heretics was forbidden. Denying the Trinity or the divinity of Jesus could be punished by death or the seizure of land. In 1658 a Jew, Jacob Lumbrozo, was accused of blasphemy under it, but the case was dismissed.

Some Puritans and Anglicans opposed the law. In 1652 the parliamentary commissioners William Claiborne and Richard Bennett took over the colonial government, and in 1654 they repealed the act and barred Catholics from openly practising their religion. Calvert regained control by a deal with the colony's Protestants, and the act was passed again in 1657. After the Glorious Revolution, Protestant rebels overthrew Calvert rule and rescinded it in 1692; the colony made the Church of England its official church in 1702 and barred Catholics from voting in 1718.

The act is regarded as the first legal guarantee of religious tolerance in British North America, and its example may have influenced later measures such as the British Act of Toleration of 1689 and the Holy Experiment in Pennsylvania. The First Amendment to the United States Constitution echoes its phrase "free exercise thereof". Rhode Island, however, had passed laws against religious persecution from 1636.
marzuban-ibn-muhammad: Marzuban was a son of Muhammad bin Musafir, ruler of Tarum. In 941 he and his brother Wahsudan ibn Muhammad, with their mother's tacit approval, deposed and imprisoned their father, whose harsh rule had alienated many of his subjects, and Wahsudan took Tarum. Abu'l-Qasim Ja'far b. 'Ali, who had fled his post as vizier to Daisam, ruler of Azerbaijan, then offered Marzuban the chance to overthrow his master. All three were Isma'ilis, which may explain why Ja'far turned to them.

Daisam's Dailamite troops went over to Marzuban, who occupied Ardebil and Tabriz. Ja'far, fearing for his position, invited Daisam back to Tabriz and killed the Dailamite leaders there, and Daisam won over the Kurds, but Marzuban defeated them and besieged Daisam in Ardebil until he surrendered in 942 or 943. The town paid a heavy tribute and had to pull down its wall. Marzuban then pushed north and west: the Shirvanshah became his tributary vassal, and by 945 he held Dvin.

When the Rus came up the Kura River and held Barda, his larger army was defeated several times, and only after disease had weakened them did he ambush and kill 700. While he besieged Barda, the Hamdanid Nasir al-Daula of Mosul sent his nephew al-Husain b. Sa'id to claim Azerbaijan; leaving a small force to watch the Rus, Marzuban defeated him in a winter campaign. The Rus then left with their loot and prisoners.

Around 948, angered by an insult to his envoy, he marched against Ray, held by the Buwayhid Rukn al-Daula, but was defeated at Qazvin and captured. In his absence Daisam returned to power, and the Rawadids and Shaddadids seized lands near Tabriz and Dvin.

Marzuban escaped from prison in 953, and his army drove Daisam to Armenia. In 954/5 he made peace with Rukn al-Daula, who married his daughter; he expelled the Shaddadids from Dvin and made the Rawadids pay tribute. When Daisam took Salmas in 955 or 956 with the help of Saif al-Daula of Aleppo, Marzuban defeated him, and the king of Vaspurakan handed Daisam over to be blinded and imprisoned. Marzuban died in 957. His first will named his sons Justan, Ibrahim and Nasir; a later one named Wahsudan, but he never cancelled the first, and war followed his death.
masaccio: Masaccio was born Tommaso di Ser Giovanni di Simone Cassai on 21 December 1401 at Castel San Giovanni di Altura, now San Giovanni Valdarno in Tuscany. His father was a notary, who died in 1406, and his mother the daughter of an innkeeper. The name Masaccio is a humorous form of Maso, short for Tommaso, meaning clumsy or messy Tom, and may have been coined to tell him apart from his collaborator Masolino.

There is no evidence of his training. He is first documented in Florence on 7 January 1422, when he joined the painters' guild as an independent master. His first attributed works are the San Giovenale Triptych of 1422 and the Virgin and Child with Saint Anne of about 1424, painted with the older Masolino da Panicale.

In 1424 Felice Brancacci commissioned Masaccio and Masolino to paint frescoes in the Brancacci Chapel in Santa Maria del Carmine, Florence, and work began around 1425. Most scenes show the life of Saint Peter, with the temptation and expulsion of Adam and Eve at the entrance. Masolino left for Hungary in September 1425, and Masaccio left the cycle unfinished in 1426 and returned in 1427. Filippino Lippi completed it in the 1480s. The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden influenced Michelangelo, and in The Tribute Money the shadows of the figures fall away from the chapel window as if it lit them.

Around 1427 he painted the Holy Trinity for Santa Maria Novella in Florence, considered by many his masterwork and the earliest surviving painting to use systematic linear perspective, possibly devised with the help of Brunelleschi. A skeleton below the figures bears the inscription: I once was what now you are, and what I am you shall yet be.

Masaccio died in 1428 at the age of 26, and little is known of the circumstances. A legend says a jealous rival painter poisoned him. Filippo Brunelleschi said on hearing the news: We have suffered a great loss. Only four frescoes undoubtedly by his hand survive. He is considered to have begun the Early Italian Renaissance in painting by moving away from the ornament of International Gothic towards naturalism, perspective and chiaroscuro. Vasari wrote that the most distinguished painters from his time on studied the Brancacci Chapel, among them Michelangelo.
masada: Masada, Hebrew for fortress, is a mountain-top fortress complex in the Judaean Desert, overlooking the western shore of the Dead Sea in southeastern Israel, 20 km east of modern Arad. It stands on a natural plateau rising over 400 metres above the surrounding terrain. The flat top measures about 550 by 270 metres and ends in cliffs, so the natural approaches are very difficult. Herod built a casemate wall 4 metres high and 1,300 metres long around it, with towers, and three narrow, winding paths led up to fortified gates.

Almost all historical information about Masada comes from the Jewish Roman historian Josephus. The most significant remains date to the reign of Herod the Great, king of Judaea under Roman administration from about 37 to 4 BCE, who made it a fortified desert refuge. He built storerooms, an advanced water system, bathhouses and two elaborate palaces, among the finest examples of Herodian architecture.

In 66 CE the Sicarii, a Jewish rebel group, took the fortress from its Roman garrison by a ruse. After the fall of Jerusalem it was the last stronghold. The Roman governor Lucius Flavius Silva laid siege with the Tenth Legion, building a circumvallation wall and a massive ramp against the western face. According to Josephus, when the Romans entered in 73 or 74 CE, the defenders, 960 men, women and children, had killed themselves after speeches by their leader Eleazar ben Ya'ir; two women and five children survived. Archaeology does not match him exactly: he mentions one palace where excavation found two, and counts 960 dead where the remains of at most 28 people have been found. Some scholars reject the mass suicide altogether.

Excavations led by Yigael Yadin in 1963–1965 found the palaces, storerooms, ritual baths, a synagogue and scroll fragments of Deuteronomy and Ezekiel, and a Byzantine church. The Roman ramp, circumvallation wall and eight siege camps are among the best preserved Roman siege works, and for them Masada was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. In the 20th century the siege became a central symbol of heroism in Israeli national identity. The site lies in the Masada National Park, reached by a steep trail or a cable car, and a museum in memory of Yadin opened there in 2007.
masalit-people: The Masalit are an ethnic group of western Sudan and eastern Chad. Their own tradition traces their origins to Tunisia, and holds that they migrated through Chad before settling in what is now Sudan. Most live in and around Geneina, the capital of West Darfur, though a few thousand live in Al Qadarif State in eastern Sudan and in South Darfur. Ethnologue counted 462,000 Masalit speakers in 2011, of whom 350,000 lived in Sudan.

Before 1874 the Masalit were divided between several polities of the region, among them the Wadai Sultanate and the Sultanate of Darfur. After the Ottomans and Egyptians conquered the Sultanate of Darfur in 1874, Hajjam Hasab Allah united the Masalit into a sultanate. His rule was seen as oppressive, and Ismail Abdel Nebi ousted him in 1883. In 1895 the Mahdist State invaded, and the sultan escaped capture by placing himself under the protection of the sultan of Wadai.

The fall of the Mahdist state in 1898 did not bring peace. The restored Darfur Sultanate under 'Ali Dinar claimed sovereignty over all the small frontier states, and in 1903 he defeated the Masalit and captured and executed their sultan. The sultan's brother, Taj al-Din Isma'il, then rallied the Masalit and drove out the Darfuri army. The peace treaty of 1908 left 'Ali Dinar in de jure control, but in practice it placed Taj al-Din at the head of a small Masalit state under the vassalage of Darfur.

Masalit groups were among the rebels who fought the Sudanese government and the pro-government Janjaweed militia in the War in Darfur from 2003. Reprisals and ethnic cleansing led to an estimated 170,000 deaths over two years. In the civil war of 2023 the Rapid Support Forces, a successor to the Janjaweed, began a new campaign of ethnic cleansing in Darfur.

The Masalit speak the Masalit language, of the Maban group of the Nilo-Saharan family. It is most closely related to Marfa, Maba and Karanga, and is written in the Latin script. Most Masalit are also bilingual in Arabic, except in the central area, where the vernacular is mainly spoken.

They are chiefly subsistence farmers, growing peanuts and millet, and sorghum and other crops further south. A typical dwelling is conical, built of wood and thatch. The Masalit are Muslim, and their religious practice incorporates traditional beliefs and customs; Islam first appeared in the area around the 17th century with wandering Muslim mystics.
masaniello: Tommaso Aniello was born in Vico Rotto al Mercato, one of the lanes around the market square of Naples, and was baptised on the day of his birth in the Church of Santa Caterina. He was long thought to be a native of Amalfi because his father was called Francesco, or Cicco, d'Amalfi. His family was humble but not poor: his father was a fisherman and shopkeeper, and Masaniello too worked as a fisherman and fishmonger. In 1641 he married the sixteen-year-old Bernardina Pisa.

Habsburg Spain, burdened by several wars, laid a heavy tax burden on the Viceroy of Naples. Masaniello smuggled goods, chiefly for feudal nobles, and was imprisoned for evading taxes. According to tradition, his wife's eight days in prison for carrying flour into the city, and the ransom of one hundred crowns he paid, made him want to avenge the people. In prison he met the lawyer Marco Vitale, and he became a pupil of the elderly priest Giulio Genoino, who had once defended the people against the nobility.

The occasion of the revolt was a new tax on fruit. It began on 7 July 1647 with a riot at the city gates between fruit vendors and customs officers, and the customs office was burnt. The rioters forced their way into the palace of the viceroy, Rodrigo Ponce de León, Duke of Arcos, who took refuge in Castel Nuovo. Masaniello gave audiences and administered justice from a wooden scaffold outside his house, and the crowd elected him captain-general.

On 13 July 1647, through the mediation of Cardinal Ascanio Filomarino, the Duke of Arcos and Masaniello signed a convention that pardoned the rebels and removed the more oppressive taxes. After that he behaved erratically, which contemporaries put down to strain, sudden fortune or poison. On 16 July he denounced his fellow citizens in the Church of the Carmine and was taken to a monastery, where grain merchants assassinated him. The next day the populace dug up his body and gave it a splendid funeral.

The revolt outlived him. A second revolution in August ended with Genoino's exile and the proclamation of a Neapolitan Republic under French protection, and the Spanish recovered Naples in April 1648. John Locke used Masaniello's government against Robert Filmer, and Thomas Paine named him as a warning in Common Sense. Daniel Auber's opera La Muette de Portici of 1828 is said to have sent its Brussels audience into the streets to begin the Belgian Revolution of 1830.
mascara-algeria: Mascara lies in north-western Algeria. Relizane is 65 kilometres to the north-east, Sidi Bel Abbès 90 kilometres to the south-west, Oran 105 kilometres to the north-west and Saïda 80 kilometres to the south. The name is said to derive from an older form, either Oum El Asker, meaning the mother of soldiers, or Mo'asker, meaning the place where soldiers gather. Locally it is pronounced Mʿaskar. The town has an older Muslim part and a newer French one, and large parts of it lie inside the ruins of its ancient ramparts.

Mascara is said to have been founded in the 10th century by the Banu Ifran. In 1701, under the Regency of Algiers, a military garrison was built in the town, and the Ottomans and the Algerians settled many Muslims with Andalucian origins there. In 1708 the tribes of Mascara, led by the bey Mustapha Ben Youcef, captured Oran and expelled the Spaniards while Spain was occupied with the War of the Spanish Succession. Spain regained Oran in 1732.

In 1790 famine and sickness had worsened the Spanish position in Oran, and the bey of Mascara appeared before the town with 30,000 men. The Spanish commander held out until the Spanish government, having made terms with the bey of Algiers, was allowed to withdraw with its guns and ammunition. The bey Mohammed took possession of Oran in March 1792 and made it his residence in place of Mascara.

In 1832 Abd al-Qadir made Mascara his headquarters, and he is the best-known figure of the town. The French destroyed it in 1835 and established full control over it in 1841. An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 on 18 August 1994 killed 171 people there.

Mascara is the capital of Mascara Province and an administrative, commercial and market centre. Its trade has centred on leather goods, grain and olive oil, and the region is especially known for its wine. The 2008 estimate gave it 150,000 inhabitants. It has road and rail links with other Algerian towns.
maselekwane-modjadji-i: Lobedu tradition traces the royal line to the house of Monomotapa, which ruled the Kalanga people of present-day Zimbabwe in the 1400s and 1500s. In the late 1500s, the story goes, a princess of that house bore a child to her brother and was banished, fleeing south to what is now Limpopo, where over the next two centuries a kingdom grew up in the area now called Bolobedu.

In the late 18th century, according to the tradition, the ruler Mambo Mokoto was warned by ancestral spirits that his sons were plotting against him, and was told to kill them and take his daughter, Princess Dzungundini, as wife, so that the heir would be a queen with power over the rain. Their first child, a son named Tladi, was strangled as an infant. The second, a daughter born in 1782, was named Maselekwane and also Modjadji, because she was born when the sun was very hot; every later Rain Queen has borne that title.

Maselekwane took the throne in 1800, at the age of eighteen. She lived in complete seclusion deep in the forest, where she carried out secret rituals to make rain, and was seen as an intermediary between her people, the royal ancestors and the rain goddess. Her kingdom was small, but she was revered far beyond it. King Moshoeshoe I of Lesotho, the Swati kings and many other rulers of southern Africa sent tribute to her for rain. A legend holds that King Shaka spared her in return for rain and sent her black cattle, though Shaka never in fact went beyond northern Zululand.

She had at least two children, Masalanabo Modjadji II and Princess Leakhali. In 1854 she took her own life by poison, a ritual suicide meant to pass her spirit into the next Rain Queen, to increase that queen's power over the rain and, it was believed, to make her immortal. Masalanabo Modjadji II succeeded her, continuing the line of queens.
maseru: Maseru lies in north-western Lesotho, directly on the border with South Africa, which is marked by the Mohokare, or Caledon, River. A border post at the Maseru Bridge connects the two countries, and the nearest town on the South African side is Ladybrand. The city sits in a shallow valley at the foot of the Hlabeng-Sa-Likhama, foothills of the Maloti Mountains, at about 1,600 metres above sea level. It has a subtropical highland climate with warm, rainy summers and cool to chilly, dry winters. The name is a Sesotho word meaning red sandstones.

The British founded Maseru as a small police camp in 1869, after the end of the Free State–Basotho Wars, when Basutoland became a British protectorate. It stands at the edge of the conquered territories relinquished to the Orange Free State under the peace terms, 24 kilometres west of King Moshoeshoe I's stronghold of Thaba Bosiu, the previous de facto capital. A busy market town soon grew around the camp.

Maseru served as the administrative capital from 1869 to 1871, before administration passed to the Cape Colony. During Cape rule from 1871 to 1884 Basutoland was treated like forcibly annexed territory, which led to the Gun War of 1881 and the burning of many buildings in Maseru. In 1884 Basutoland was restored to the status of a Crown colony and Maseru became the capital again. It stayed small under British rule, which took little interest in developing it. After independence in 1966 its area grew about sevenfold, from around 20 to 138 square kilometres, as nearby villages were incorporated, and its population grew by around 7% a year for several decades. Riots after the 1998 parliamentary elections damaged much of the city.

Maseru is the capital and largest city of Lesotho and of Maseru District, and the 2016 census counted 330,760 people, about one seventh of the country's population. Traditional thatched mud-brick rondavels have largely given way to modern buildings. Colonial-era buildings include the Roman Catholic Cathedral of Our Lady of Victories and the Anglican St. John's Church, and the city also has the Royal Palace, the Parliament building and the State House. Kingsway, which joins the Royal Palace and the airport, was the first paved road in Lesotho. The national stadium, Setsoto Stadium, is in the city.
masfut: The village forms part of the exclave of Masfout, which is surrounded by Ras Al Khaimah, the Dubai exclave of Hatta and the Omani wilayat of Mahdha in Al Buraimi Governorate. It can be reached from Ajman itself only by crossing the territory of Sharjah, Ras Al Khaimah and Oman. Masfout Fort stands on the craggy mountains above the village, built to guard against bandits heading to Oman, and the other densely inhabited part of the exclave is the village of Sayh Mudayrah.

Masfout was traditionally home to the Na'im tribe, most of whom had settled at Buraimi. In 1905 the Bedouin Bani Qitab built a fort at Wadi Hatta and began to harass caravans using the pass to the Omani Batina coast. After a meeting of the Trucial Sheikhs in Dubai in April that year, the Na'im won the support of Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi against Sheikh Rashid bin Ahmad Al Mualla of Umm Al Quwain, who backed the Bani Qitab, and kept the village. They remained in almost constant conflict with the people of Hajarain, later the Dubai dependency of Hatta.

In 1948, after a period of decline for the Na'im, Sheikh Rashid bin Humaid Al Nuaimi III of Ajman seized Masfout from its Na'im sheikh, Saqr bin Sultan Al Hamouda, who could not raise a force to oppose him. The rulers and tribes of the interior then jostled for influence in order to sign petroleum concessions, the Sultan in Muscat and the Saudis paying for loyalties that often proved short-lived, a contest that led to the Buraimi Dispute. Masfout has belonged to Ajman ever since.

The census of 2017 counted 8,988 people on 86.59 km2. Its public buildings include a courthouse built in 2017, and Waraqa Park surrounds the former house of Sheikh Rashid bin Humaid Al Nuaimi, founder of Ajman. Masfout Fort, restored in the 1940s, and the Bin Sultan Mosque of 1815 survive. The Ajman government banned the digging of wells after more than 80 unregulated wells depleted the aquifers.
mashhad: Mashhad lies in north-eastern Iran, about 740 kilometres east of Tehran and about 250 km from Ashgabat in Turkmenistan. It stands in the valley of the Kashafrud River, between the Binalood and Hezar Masjed mountain ranges, with hot summers, cold winters and about 250 millimetres of precipitation a year.

By the 9th century Mashhad was a small village known as Sanabad, lying with Tus on the ancient Silk Road towards Merv. It outgrew the surrounding villages and took its present name, meaning place of martyrdom, from the shrine of the eighth Shia Imam, Ali al-Rida, who is buried there; the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid is buried in the same shrine. In 1389 Miran Shah, a son of Timur, stormed Tus after a siege of several months and massacred 10,000 of its inhabitants; those who escaped settled near the shrine, Tus was abandoned, and Mashhad became the capital of the district.

In the 16th century the town suffered from the raids of the Uzbeks, who took it in 1507 and again entered it in 1544, plundering and killing. Shah Abbas I did not retake it until 1598. He is said to have walked from Isfahan to Mashhad, and in the Safavid period the city gained further religious recognition. Between 1736 and 1796 it was the capital of Afsharid Iran, founded by Nader Shah, whose tomb is in the city. In 1796 Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar conquered Khorasan.

Mashhad is the capital of Razavi Khorasan province. The Imam Reza shrine draws millions of pilgrims each year, and several theological schools are associated with it. The shrine's administration, the Astan Quds Razavi, owns much of the city's real estate. The poet Ferdowsi, author of the Shahnameh, was born in nearby Tus, and many institutions in Mashhad bear his name.
mashobra: Mashobra is a town in Shimla district of Himachal Pradesh, at an average elevation of 2,146 metres, linked to Shimla by the Hindustan–Tibet Road, built in 1850 under Lord Dalhousie. It lies within the Shimla Water Catchment and Wildlife Sanctuary, where pine, oak, Himalayan deodar, rhododendron, maple and horse chestnut grow, and where monkeys, langurs, jackals, barking deer, the occasional leopard and birds such as the Himalayan eagle, pheasants, chikor and partridges live.

In the colonial period Mashobra belonged to the princely state of Koti. Towards the end of the 19th century it became a popular weekend resort for the elite of Shimla, the summer capital of the British Raj. Wildflower Hall at nearby Chharabra was a residence of Lord Kitchener and of Lord Ripon. About 3 km from Mashobra, the Italian photographer Federico Peliti built a villa he named Carignano after his native town near Turin; it became a weekend resort in 1920.

In May 1948, before returning to London at the end of his mission as viceroy and then governor general of India, Lord Mountbatten spent a few weeks at the retreat with his wife, Lady Edwina, and Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru visited them there.

The retreat, a wooden building first constructed in 1850, is one of the two presidential retreats of India, the other being Rashtrapati Nilayam in Secunderabad, and the president visits it at least once a year. Wildflower Hall is a property of Oberoi Hotels, and the Himalayan International School at Chharabra is a large residential school.
mashonaland: Mashonaland is a region in northeastern Zimbabwe, home to nearly half of the country's population. Most of its people belong to the Shona nation, and the Zezuru and Korekore dialects are the most common. Harare, the capital and largest city, lies entirely within it and forms a province of its own; Chitungwiza is the next largest city. The territory is a broad plateau sloping gradually to the north and north-west. Its northern border is formed by the Zambezi River, with Zambia beyond.

About half the land lies above 1,200 metres, and the central watershed in the south and centre is at 1,500 to 1,650 metres. Much of the landscape is rolling low hills divided by river valleys. The highest point is in the Wedza Mountains in the south-east, at 1,789 metres. Most of the region drains into the Zambezi basin, while a small part at the south-eastern edge drains to the Save River.

Mashonaland was originally one of the regions into which the country was divided after occupation by the Pioneer Column in 1890. It was the territory under the administration of the British South Africa Company, distinct from the land directly controlled by the Matabele king, Lobengula, which was named Matabeleland when it was occupied in 1893. The two had separate administrations for part of the company's colonial period.

A revolt against the company broke out in 1896, led by priests of the Mwari religion. The British prevailed, executed some leaders and tried to reform the system. In 1923 the territory became part of the self-governing colony of Southern Rhodesia, and Mashonaland became one of its five provinces. An administrative reform in 1970 divided it into a northern and a southern half, and in 1983 it was divided into the present three provinces, with Harare given its own status. Since the constitutional amendments that took effect in 1988, each province is run by a governor appointed by the president.

Mashonaland is divided into the provinces of Mashonaland West, Mashonaland Central and Mashonaland East, together with Harare. About 7.4 million people live there, around half of the population of Zimbabwe. The region has mineral resources including gold, platinum, nickel, chrome, copper and lithium, and its main agricultural products include maize, tobacco, cotton, citrus and beef. Manufacturing is concentrated in and around Harare and Kadoma, and electricity comes from the Kariba South power station.
masindi: Masindi lies in the Western Region of Uganda, on the road between Kampala and the Murchison Falls National Park. It is about 211 kilometres north-west of Kampala by an all-weather highway and 57 kilometres north-east of Hoima, the largest city in the Bunyoro sub-region, at an average elevation of 1,227 metres above sea level.

As the capital of Bunyoro, Masindi received the British explorers and anti-slavery campaigners Samuel and Florence Baker, who stayed from 25 April 1872 to 14 June 1873, until the hostility of the Omukama Kabaléga forced their expedition to withdraw. The town grew as a commercial centre through the cotton trade of the second half of the 19th century, and the White Fathers founded a mission there in the 1910s. The Masindi Hotel, built in 1923, is the oldest hotel in the country; Ernest Hemingway, Katharine Hepburn and Humphrey Bogart stayed there.

During World War II Masindi held the second-largest camp in East Africa for Poles who had escaped from Soviet-occupied Poland: 3,635 people, 1,759 of them children. The camp had a Polish preschool, three primary schools, a general education liceum and a vocational school for girls, and two Polish newspapers, Czuj Duch and Brzask, were published there.

Masindi is the headquarters of Masindi District, and the national census of August 2014 counted 94,622 people in the town. It has a 200-bed public hospital and a public airport, and Kinyara Sugar Works, one of the three major manufacturers of refined sugar in Uganda, lies 15 kilometres to the west. The main campus of the Kigumba Petroleum Institute is 44 kilometres to the north-east.
masinissa: Masinissa, whose name appears on his tomb as MSNSN, was the son of Gaia, chieftain of the Numidian Massylii, and was brought up in Carthage, his father's ally. Much of what is known of him comes from Livy and, to a lesser extent, Cicero's Scipio's Dream. At the start of the Second Punic War he fought for Carthage against Syphax, king of the western Masaesyli, who had allied with Rome, and won a decisive victory. He was betrothed to the daughter of the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Gisco, then commanded Numidian cavalry in Spain, where he was placed in charge of all Carthaginian horse and fought a guerrilla campaign against Scipio Africanus in 208 and 207.

When Gaia died in 206 BCE, Masinissa quarrelled with Oezalces, his father's brother, over the inheritance, and Syphax took much of eastern Numidia. Concluding that Rome was winning the war, Masinissa defected and promised to help Scipio invade Africa. Hasdrubal turned to Syphax, who married his daughter Sophonisba. Masinissa fought at the Battle of the Great Plains and Bagbrades in 203, and with Gaius Laelius pursued Syphax to Cirta, where he was captured. Masinissa married Sophonisba, but Scipio demanded that she be shown in a Roman triumph, and Masinissa sent her poison, with which she killed herself.

At the Battle of Zama he commanded the cavalry on Scipio's right wing, 6,000 Numidian and 3,000 Roman, and his return against the rear of the Carthaginian lines decided the battle. He received Syphax's kingdom and ruled both the Massylii and the Masaesyli. With Cirta as his capital he sought to build a unified state from semi-nomadic tribes, introduced Carthaginian farming methods and settled many Numidians as peasants. Major towns included Capsa, Thugga, Bulla Regia and Hippo Regius.

The peace treaty of 201 forbade Carthage to make war without Roman permission, which let Masinissa encroach on its territory. He defeated the Carthaginians at the Battle of Oroscopa in 151 BCE. Carthage's retaliation against Numidian raids, in defiance of the treaty, led to the Third Punic War. He died early in 148 BCE, aged over 90, apparently still leading his armies, without a breach in his alliance with Rome.

Polybius called him the best man of all the kings of his time and credited him with showing that Numidia could produce cultivated fruits; it later became known as the breadbasket of Rome. Delos honoured him in 179 BCE with a golden crown and a statue after a gift of grain. Micipsa succeeded him, and his descendants included Juba I and Juba II. Many Berbers regard him as an icon and forefather.
masjed-soleyman: Masjed Soleyman is the capital of Masjed Soleyman County in Khuzestan province. It is home to a large population of the Haft-lang branch of the Bakhtiari, a semi-nomadic people whose livelihood depended on herds of sheep, cattle and horses. The four main divisions of the Haft Lang are the Duraki, Babadi, Bakhtiarwand and Dinaruni. The city is counted among the ancient cities of the Elam civilisation, said to have been called Assak and renamed Parsomash by the early Achaemenids, and in 1955 Roman Ghirshman, who thought Parsomash might have been the oldest capital of the Achaemenid Empire, found evidence of human habitation some 10,000 years old in a nearby cave.

Ruins in the area include an ancient fire-temple known locally as Sar-masjid and the remains of an Achaemenid palace. The city stayed important under the Seleucids and Parthians, and in the Sasanian era canals and weir-bridges allowed tobacco and cereals to be grown. After the Muslim conquest many ancient structures were demolished and the region remained relatively obscure until the Qajar period, when it became a centre of the tar trade.

The Bakhtiari played a large part in Iran's Constitutional Revolution of 1905 to 1907. A Bakhtiari tribal coalition led by Ali-Gholi Khan, Sardar Asaad II, and his brother Najaf Qoli Khan marched up to the gates of Tehran in 1909 and deposed Mohammad Ali Shah Qajar. Reza Shah, who ruled from 1925 to 1941, later made the destruction of Bakhtiari influence his mission, and the oil on their territory gave him a further motive to curb the tribe's autonomy.

In 1901 Mozaffar al-Din Shah signed a sixty-year concession giving the millionaire William Knox D'Arcy exclusive rights to prospect for petroleum over about three quarters of Persia. A drilling team under George B. Reynolds struck oil near the present Iran-Iraq border in 1904, but the venture strained D'Arcy's funds, and in 1905 the British Admiralty steered him to the Burmah Oil Company, which financed a Concession Syndicate. Drilling moved to Masjed Soleyman, where Reynolds met hostile tribes and paid them fees and promised them a share of profits to protect the concession.

At 4 a.m. on 26 May 1908 a fifty-foot gusher of petroleum shot up from the first rig. The syndicate was renamed the Anglo-Persian Oil Company in 1909, later British Petroleum, and by 1911 a pipeline ran from the field to a refinery at Abadan.
masjid-al-haram: The Masjid al-Haram, 'the Sacred Mosque', encloses the Kaaba in Mecca and is among the pilgrimage sites of the hajj. It is also the main site of the umrah, the lesser pilgrimage that can be made at any time of the year, and the rites of both include circling the Kaaba. Within the mosque stand the Black Stone, the Zamzam Well, the Maqam Ibrahim and the hills of Safa and Marwa, where pilgrims perform the sa'i in memory of Hajar's search for water for her son Ismail.

Islamic tradition holds that Abraham and his son Ismail raised the foundations of the Kaaba, and that the Black Stone was brought to Abraham by an angel. After Muhammad's return to Mecca in 630 CE he and a number of his companions broke the idols in and around the Kaaba. The caliph Umar enlarged the mosque in 637 CE, and Uthman added covered porticoes. In 682 Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr enlarged it again, and after the Umayyads retook Mecca in 692 Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan ordered the first major renovation, which raised the outer walls. Before then the mosque was a small open area with the Kaaba at its centre.

The Abbasid caliphs al-Mansur, al-Mahdi and al-Hadi enlarged it between 754 and 786 to 28,000 m2, and it kept this form until Ottoman times. A fire in 1400 damaged its colonnades and wooden roofs, and Mamluk sultans paid for rebuilding. In 1570 Sultan Selim II commissioned the architect Mimar Sinan to replace the flat roof with domes, and the columns of that work are among the oldest surviving parts of the building. Murad IV had it renovated in 1629 after floods.

The first Saudi renovation ran from 1955 to 1976, added four minarets, brought the Mas'a gallery inside the mosque and demolished many Ottoman features. On 20 November 1979 insurgents who called for the overthrow of the Saudi dynasty seized the mosque and took hostages. Hundreds were killed in the siege that followed, and the events shocked the Islamic world, in which violence is strictly forbidden within the mosque. King Fahd's expansion between 1986 and 1994 added a new wing and an outdoor prayer area.

The mosque is under the control of the King of Saudi Arabia, who holds the title Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques. The Kaaba is the qibla, the direction of prayer for Muslims worldwide, and its fabric covering, the kiswah, is replaced every year in a formal ceremony. The hajj is one of the Pillars of Islam, required of every Muslim who is able to make it.
mask-of-agamemnon: Heinrich Schliemann found the gold funerary mask in 1876 in a shaft tomb designated Grave V in Grave Circle A at Mycenae. Eight men were found in Grave Circle A, all with weapons in their graves, but only five had masks, and those lay in Grave IV and Grave V. The quantities of gold and the carefully worked objects indicate honour, wealth and status. The historian Cathy Gere has called the mask the Mona Lisa of prehistory.

Schliemann named it after the mythical Greek king Agamemnon of Homer's Iliad and took it as evidence that the Trojan War was a real event. After finding it he notified King George I, and is supposed to have telegraphed that he had gazed upon the face of Agamemnon. Near the end of his life he accepted doubts about the mask's owner, and is quoted as saying: "So this is not Agamemnon... these are not his ornaments? All right, let's call him Schulze." Modern research dates the mask to around the 16th century BCE, 300 to 400 years before the period of the mythical Trojan War.

The mask was made from a single thick sheet of gold, heated and hammered against a wooden background, with the details chased on later with a sharp tool. It is displayed in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens. It differs from three of the other masks found: it is three-dimensional rather than flat, the ears are cut out, the eyes are shown both open and shut, the mouth is well defined and the brows form two arches. Alone among depictions of faces in Mycenaean art it has a full pointed beard with a handlebar moustache.

In the latter half of the 20th century and the early 21st, the mask's authenticity was formally questioned, chiefly by William Calder III and David Traill, and Archaeology magazine ran articles presenting both sides. Those who argued fraud pointed to Schliemann's reputation for salting digs with objects from elsewhere and held that he could have had the mask made on the model of the other Mycenaean masks.

Defenders replied that after the Troy controversy the Greek Archaeological Society had sent Panagiotis Stamatakis to supervise the excavation. The dig was closed on 26 and 27 November for a Sunday holiday and rain, and Stamatakis arranged credible witnesses before it reopened. The three other masks were found on the 28th and the Mask of Agamemnon on the 30th. They also argued that the lip, the triangular beard and the beard's detail closely resemble the mane of the gold lion-head rhyton from Shaft Grave IV, and that Schliemann's duplicity has been exaggerated, claiming that his attackers conducted a vendetta. Modern archaeological research suggests the mask is genuine.
mask-of-warka: The carved white marble face probably depicts a goddess, and Inanna has been suggested, though it is only a presumption that a deity is shown. It was most likely part of a life-sized statue, probably of wood, in which only the exposed skin of the head, arms, hands and feet was of the much rarer marble. The flat back of the head, drilled for attachment, would have been covered with bitumen and coloured metal, probably gold leaf or copper, forming hair that waved over the forehead and was fixed with metal studs.

The hollowed eyes and eyebrows keep traces of an ancient inlay, perhaps shell for the whites and lapis lazuli for the pupils, and perforations at the ears show that the image once wore jewellery. Earlier attempts at the human face, such as the Tell Brak Head, had exaggerated noses and ears, and the mask has no parallels in its period.

The expedition of the German Archaeological Institute led by A. Nöldeke found the mask on 22 February 1939 in the Eanna district of Uruk, named after the goddess Inanna, to whom its temples were dedicated. The name Warka comes from the modern village close to the ancient city, south of modern Baghdad.

When the United States invaded Iraq in 2003, the National Museum of Iraq was looted, and the mask is thought to have been taken between 10 and 12 April with forty other pieces, among them the Warka Vase and the Bassetki Statue. Marine Reserve Colonel Matthew Bogdanos began an investigation with his team on 21 April.

An Iraqi informant came to the museum with a tip that he knew where antiquities were hidden, and investigators raided a farm in northern Baghdad. The mask was not found at first, but the farmer admitted to having an antiquity buried behind the farm, where it was dug up intact. The 812th Military Police Company recovered it just before October, and it is again in the National Museum of Iraq.
maslama-al-majriti: His full name was Abu al-Qasim Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Faradi al-Hasib al-Majriti al-Qurtubi al-Andalusi, and Latin writers in Europe knew him as Methilem. He was born around 950 and was active in al-Andalus during the reign of Al-Hakam II. Besides astronomy and mathematics he was counted an alchemist and a scholar of economics, and he wrote a book on taxation and the economy of al-Andalus.

Al-Majriti took part in the translation of the Planisphaerium of Ptolemy and improved the existing translations of the Almagest. Beyond revising the tables of Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, he worked out tables for converting Persian dates into years of the Hijri calendar, which aided historians. With his colleague Ibn al-Saffar he introduced new methods of surveying and triangulation. When the Encyclopedia of the Brethren of Purity reached al-Andalus he edited parts of it and made changes.

The historian Said al-Andalusi judged him the leading mathematician and astronomer of his time in al-Andalus. The school of astronomy and mathematics he built marked the beginning of organised scientific research there, and his pupils included Ibn al-Saffar, Abu al-Salt and al-Turtushi.

Two influential works of alchemy and magic came to bear his name: the Rutbat al-hakim, or Rank of the Wise, and the Picatrix. Their dates do not fit his lifetime, and the general view today is that they were written by someone else who claimed his reputation; the Arabic original of the Picatrix probably dates from the middle of the eleventh century. Both were translated into Latin in 1252 on the orders of King Alfonso X of Castile, in a version adjusted to Christian doctrine.

The Rutbat gives alchemical recipes and instructions for purifying precious metals, and describes heating mercury for forty days until it turned into a red powder of unchanged weight, an early statement of the conservation of mass. The Picatrix deals with astrology, talismanic magic and prophecy. Several modern writers also credit him with a daughter, the astronomer Fatima of Madrid, but she is first mentioned only in an encyclopedia published in the 1920s.
masnavi: Rumi began dictating the Masnavi in the final years of his life, at around the age of 54, about the year 1258, and kept composing verses until his death in 1273. It is documented that he began at the request of his favourite disciple, Husam al-Din Chalabi, who observed that many of Rumi's followers dutifully read the works of Sana'i and 'Attar. Rumi therefore created a work in their didactic style to complement his other poetry. The inconclusive ending of the sixth book has led some to suggest that the work was unfinished at Rumi's death, and others to claim that another volume exists.

The title Masnavi-ye Ma'navi means The Spiritual Couplets. The work is a series of six books amounting to around 25,000 verses, or 50,000 lines, each book of about 4,000 verses with its own prose introduction and prologue. It collects anecdotes and stories drawn from the Quran, hadith and everyday tales, and each story illustrates a point whose moral is then discussed in detail. It has no framed plot, and its scenes range from the local bazaar to fables and tales of Rumi's time. In contrast to Rumi's Divan-i Shams-i Tabrizi, it is a relatively sober text that explains the dimensions of spiritual life and practice to Sufi disciples.

The books fall into three pairs. Books 1 and 2 are chiefly concerned with the nafs, the lower carnal self, and its self-deception. The themes of Books 3 and 4 are Reason and Knowledge, which Rumi personifies in the figure of Moses. Books 5 and 6 are joined by the ideal that a person must deny physical earthly existence to understand God's existence. Rumi speaks in several voices, among them the authority of a teacher, the storyteller, the analogist and the characters of dialogue, and he sometimes questions his own verses.

The Masnavi is one of the most influential works in the history of Sufism. It has sometimes been described as a Quran in Persian, and some Muslims regard it as among the most important works of Islamic literature, behind only the Quran. Many commentators have viewed it as the finest mystical poem in world literature. R. A. Nicholson edited it from the oldest manuscripts, with the first complete English translation, in eight volumes. Jawid Mojaddedi's translation for Oxford World's Classics is the first complete one in English verse, its sixth book published in 2025.
mason-dixon-line: The Mason–Dixon line is made up of four segments that follow the terms of the settlement of 1767: the tangent line, the north line, the arc line and the parallel at 39°43′ N. The east–west Maryland–Pennsylvania boundary lies 15 miles south of what was then the southernmost point of Philadelphia, and the surveyors also fixed the arc that bounds Delaware around New Castle and the boundary between Delaware and Maryland. The line was marked by stones every mile and by crownstones every five miles, shipped from England, with an M on the Maryland side and a P on the Pennsylvania side.

Maryland's charter of 1632 granted land north of the Potomac up to the 40th parallel. Pennsylvania's charter of 1681 defined its southern border as the same line but described it differently, because Charles II relied on an inaccurate map. The 40th parallel lies north of the site Penn had chosen for Philadelphia, so the Maryland claim would have put the city in Maryland. A provisional agreement of 1732 between Lord Baltimore and Penn's sons was never carried out, and from the mid-1730s settlers loyal to each colony fought in what became known as Cresap's War. The dispute ended when Frederick Calvert, 6th Baron Baltimore, accepted the earlier agreements.

The Penns and the Calverts then commissioned the English astronomer Charles Mason and the surveyor Jeremiah Dixon, who worked between 1763 and 1767 and began the Maryland–Pennsylvania line in April 1765. It cost £3,512 and covered 244 miles. In 1767 their Iroquois guides refused to go further, having reached the edge of their lands, where they were at war with the Lenape, and in 1784 David Rittenhouse and Andrew Ellicott carried the line to the southwest corner of Pennsylvania. A small wedge of land between Delaware and Pennsylvania stayed in dispute until 1921.

The 1768 official report of the survey did not mention Mason and Dixon by name. The phrase 'Mason and Dixon's line' came into wide use in the congressional debates on the Missouri Compromise of 1820, because after Pennsylvania abolished slavery in 1781 the line and the Ohio River formed a border between slave and free states. Delaware kept slavery until the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865. The Confederate States of America claimed the Virginia portion of the line as part of its northern border. The name is still used for the line dividing the Northeast from the South.
masovia: Masovia lies on the North European Plain, roughly between Łódź and Białystok, on both sides of the Vistula and its confluence with the Narew and the Bug. The landscape is flat, in contrast to Lesser Poland, with no lakes, in contrast to Greater Poland, and forests, mainly coniferous, cover about a fifth of the region, among them the Kampinos Forest. The region developed a distinct sub-culture of folk songs, architecture, dress and traditions.

The region at first covered only the right bank of the Vistula near Płock, which was one of the seats of the first Piast rulers and in 1037 to 1047 the capital of an independent Mazovian state under Masław. Between 1079 and 1138 Płock was in practice the capital of Poland. Masovia was incorporated into the Polish state in the second half of the tenth century under Mieszko I. After the death of Bolesław III Wrymouth the Duchy of Mazovia was established in 1138, governed by a separate branch of the Piast dynasty. To protect its northern part, Conrad I of Mazovia called in the Teutonic Knights in 1226 and gave them the Chełmno Land as a fief.

Masovia became a fief of the Polish crown in 1351, and western Masovia, and in 1526 to 1529 the main part, with its capital at Warsaw, were incorporated into the Polish state. During the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth over 20 per cent of the population were petty nobility. The Union of Lublin of 1569 made Masovia the central region of the Commonwealth, with Warsaw as the seat of the sejm, and in 1596 King Sigismund III Vasa moved the capital from Kraków to Warsaw.

Prussia annexed western Masovia in 1793 and the rest two years later, and the region joined the Congress Kingdom of Poland in 1815, where it saw the November and January uprisings against Russian rule. Poland won the Battle of Warsaw against Soviet Russia in 1920. During the Second World War the region suffered massacres, the Warsaw Ghetto, and the deaths of some 200,000 inhabitants in the Warsaw Uprising of 1944. Warsaw's Old Town, almost entirely demolished in the war, was restored and designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1980. The present Mazovian Voivodeship was created in 1999, and its borders do not exactly follow historical Masovia.
massachusetts-government-act: After the Boston Tea Party the British Parliament passed a series of measures, the Intolerable Acts, also called the Coercive or Repressive Acts, meant to suppress dissent and restore order in Massachusetts. British officials believed that their failure to control the colony lay partly in the independent nature of its local government. On 2 May 1774 Lord North, as head of the ministry, asked Parliament to adopt the act, describing the whole colony as "in a distempered state of disturbance and opposition to the laws of the mother country". It received royal assent on 20 May 1774.

The act effectively set aside the 1691 charter of the Province of Massachusetts Bay. Massachusetts had been the only colony whose executive council was elected; now the king alone would appoint and dismiss its members. Lord North said the purpose was "to take the executive power from the hands of the democratic part of government". The royal governor could appoint and remove, without the council's consent, the judges of the inferior courts of common pleas, the attorney general, justices of the peace, marshals and other officers, and could name the sheriffs.

The provision on town meetings, the main instrument of local rule, was the most important. Complaining that inhabitants had been misled into passing "many dangerous and unwarrantable resolves", the act forbade any meeting without the governor's leave, apart from one annual meeting for elections. Colonists declared that it changed the basic structure of their government by parliamentary fiat and vowed to block it.

In October 1774 Governor Thomas Gage used the act to dissolve the provincial assembly. Its Patriot leaders replied that the act had nullified the contract between the king and the people. The inhabitants ignored Gage's call for new elections and set up the Massachusetts Provincial Congress, an alternative government that controlled everything outside Boston, where the governor's soldiers were based. The congress governed the province, and from 1776 the state, until the Massachusetts State Constitution was adopted in 1780. The act was a major step towards the American Revolution. Parliament later repealed it in its attempts to end the American Revolutionary War by diplomacy.
massasoit: Massasoit means Great Sachem. It was his title, but the English colonists took it for his name and it stuck. When the Pilgrims arrived, the realm of the Wampanoag, also called the Pokanokets, took in parts of Rhode Island and much of south-eastern Massachusetts, and lesser Pokanoket sachems owed him allegiance. Outbreaks of an unidentified disease had devastated his people and left them exposed to the Narragansetts, who held the land west of Narragansett Bay.

Seeking allies against the Narragansetts, Massasoit sent Samoset, a minor Abenaki sachem from Maine who had learned English from fishermen, to find out whether the colonists meant peace, and in 1621 he sent Squanto to live among them. The peace treaty of 22 March 1621 bound him to William Bradford, Edward Winslow, Stephen Hopkins, John Carver and Myles Standish. According to English sources, his help saved Plymouth Colony from failure and starvation in its first years, and the alliance kept the Pokanokets neutral in the Pequot War in 1636.

Tension rose when the colonists refused to give up Squanto, whom Massasoit believed had betrayed him, but it was resolved in March 1623 when Winslow nursed the gravely ill sachem back to health. Massasoit then warned the English of a plan by Massachusett warriors to destroy the Wessagusset and Plymouth colonies. He sheltered Roger Williams in the winter of 1635-36 and gave him land on the Seekonk River. As settlement spread, he sold a tract 14 miles square to Myles Standish and others of Duxbury in 1649, at Sachem Rock in East Bridgewater.

Massasoit had five children: Wamsutta, Metacom, Sonkanuchoo, Amie and Sarah. After his death Wamsutta and Metacom asked Plymouth for English names and were called Alexander and Philip. Wamsutta, who succeeded his father and turned to an alliance with Connecticut Colony, died within a year; Metacom, who followed him in 1662, believed the colonists had murdered him, one cause of King Philip's War, which only Amie of the five children survived. Statues of Massasoit by Cyrus E. Dallin stand near Plymouth Rock and in Utah and Missouri.
massawa: Massawa lies on the Red Sea at the northern end of the Gulf of Zula, beside the Dahlak Archipelago. The historical city stands on the islands of Basé, with the old centre, and Taulud, joined to each other and to the mainland by causeways. It seems to have emerged as a port between the 8th and 10th centuries, after the decline of Adulis, about 50 kilometres to the south.

With the rise of the Sultanate of Dahlak in the 11th century, Massawa became the main link between the Muslim-dominated coast and the Christian highlands. From the 14th century highland rulers took more interest in it. Emperor Zara Yaqob appears to have reached it in the mid-15th century, and both Massawa and Dahlak were pillaged by the Abyssinians in 1464/65. The Portuguese gained a foothold at Massawa and Arkiko in 1513 as a port from which to reach allied Ethiopia against the Ottomans.

The Ottomans captured Massawa in 1557 and tried to make it the capital of Habesh Eyalet, though they did not conquer the rest of Eritrea. In May 1865 the port passed to the Khedive of Egypt with Ottoman consent, and the governor Werner Munzinger rebuilt it, with a customs house, a school, a hospital and causeways.

The Italians took the port in February 1885, with British agreement, and it was their colonial capital until Governor Ferdinando Martini moved to Asmara in 1897. They built a railway to Asmara and an Asmara-Massawa cableway, 75 kilometres long, which was the longest ropeway conveyor in the world at the time. A great earthquake in 1921 destroyed most of the city, and later buildings were of reinforced concrete.

Massawa was besieged unsuccessfully by the Eritrean Liberation Front in 1977–78 and was captured by the Eritrean People's Liberation Front in February 1990, in an attack by land and sea known as Operation Fenkil. Most of the city was destroyed in the shelling and bombing that followed. Eritrea's independence in 1991 left Ethiopia landlocked.

The old town keeps coral-stone houses, the Sheikh Hanafi Mosque of the 15th century, and the Imperial Palace built in 1872 to 1874 for Munzinger. A naval base, dhow docks, a railway station and an airport serve the city, and ferries run to the Dahlak Islands.
massif-central: The Massif Central is an old massif formed during the Variscan orogeny and made up mostly of granitic and metamorphic rocks. It covers about 15 per cent of mainland France and is separated from the Alps by the deep cleft of the Rhône.

Uplift in the Paleogene, as the Alps and the Pyrenees rose, lifted its eastern and southern parts, so that the highlands of the south and east, including the Cévennes, look down on the Rhône valley and the plains of Languedoc, while Limousin in the north-west is lower. Mont Lozère, at 1,699 metres, is the highest non-volcanic summit. The region was a barrier to transport within France until the A75 motorway opened it.

The massif is volcanic, though activity has subsided in the last 10,000 years. It holds about 450 extinct volcanoes, among them the stratovolcanoes of Cantal and the Monts Dore, where the Puy de Sancy reaches 1,886 metres, and the volcanic plateaus of Aubrac and Cézallier. The Chaîne des Puys near Clermont-Ferrand, less than 160 square kilometres, has 115 small monogenic cones, with the Puy de Dôme at 1,464 metres. In the south the Causses are raised limestone plateaus cut by deep canyons, of which the Gorges du Tarn are the best known.

Twenty departments are generally counted as part of the massif, in the regions of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, Nouvelle-Aquitaine and Occitania. Its largest cities are Clermont-Ferrand, Limoges and Saint-Étienne. Industry is little developed except locally, with metallurgy at Saint-Étienne, tyres at Clermont-Ferrand, where Michelin has its headquarters, and aeronautics at Figeac. Cattle are raised in the west for meat and milk, including Cantal cheese, and sheep on the southern limestone plateaus for Roquefort cheese, while the Limagne plain grows cereals. The volcanoes of the Chaîne des Puys and the region of the Causses and Cévennes have UNESCO heritage status, and the Millau Viaduct stands on the A75.
mastanabal: Mastanabal was a son of Masinissa, king of Numidia, a Berber kingdom in present-day Algeria. His name is written MSTNB in Numidian and mstnʿbʾ in Punic; the linguist Salem Chaker has suggested it may be reconstructed as Amastan (a)B(a), perhaps meaning defender or protector of (a)b(a).

He was well versed in Greek literature and studied law. From his youth he was a keen horseman and athlete, kept a stud of purebred horses and drove in chariot races. Around 168 or 164 BCE he won the chariot race at the hippodrome of Athens during the Panathenaic Games.

After Masinissa's death in 148 BCE the three legitimate sons ruled Numidia together under their father's will, with the help of the Roman general Scipio Aemilianus. By Scipio's own account, Mastanabal was then given authority over the administration of Numidia. According to the Greek historian Appian, in his Roman History, Mastanabal shared power with his brothers Micipsa and Gulussa and took charge of judicial affairs. While his elder brother Gulussa led a cavalry force to join the Roman forces fighting Carthage in the Third Punic War, Mastanabal stayed in Numidia with Micipsa.

The Roman historian Sallust, in his War of Jugurtha, says that Mastanabal died of an illness. His son Jugurtha was later adopted by his uncle Micipsa and made co-heir with Micipsa's own sons, Adherbal and Hiempsal. Jugurtha afterwards had both of them put to death in a coup d'état in order to remain sole ruler. Mastanabal's other son, Gauda, born of a second marriage, was named as a subsidiary heir to the kingdom.
masties: Masties ruled a Romano-Berber polity sometimes called the Kingdom of the Aures, in the former Roman province of Numidia. His rise is linked to the revolt of the Aurès described by Procopius, which in 484 took the mountains permanently out of Vandal control. That revolt may have drawn strength from the persecution of Nicene Christians begun that year by the Arian Vandal king Huneric, recorded by Victor of Vita, and Masties is believed to have taken the title imperator as he moved towards autonomy in the 480s.

He appealed openly to Christians, using the cross as a symbol and claiming divine favour. The historian Modéran argues that the villages, churches and countryside of the Aurès gave him a rural power base and encouraged an emerging Romano-Berber identity. Greg Fisher and Alexander Drost attribute his rise to a strong military personality, a link to Roman power and tolerance towards those fleeing Vandal persecution. He was later succeeded by Iaudas.

The epitaph from Arris, found in 1941 by Pierre Morizot and published in detail by Carcopino in 1944, is mostly a self-eulogy spoken by Masties; in its penultimate line a certain Vartaia records that he and his brothers raised the monument for one hundred solidi. Its stress on keeping faith may answer the literary stereotype of the Moors as faithless, but its opening formula, D.S.M., sacred to the spirits of the departed, has also been read as pagan or Donatist, suggesting political opportunism.

Carcopino suggested that Valentinian III appointed Masties dux, which cannot be verified; it seems more likely that the title was used by hereditary Berber leaders under the Vandals. One recent suggestion has him dux from about 426 and dead in 494. Morizot instead identified him with Mastigas, a Mauro-Roman king active in the 530s and 540s, which would change his dates.
mastino-i-della-scala: Born Leonardo or Leonardino, Mastino was the son of Jacopino della Scala. Like the rest of his family he supported the Ghibelline leader Ezzelino III da Romano, who made him podestà of Cerea in 1258 and of Verona itself from January 1259. When Ezzelino died that year, the Veronese guilds elected Mastino podestà del popolo, the people's podestà.

Mastino never held a single title that made him master of Verona. He ruled instead through a set of high offices: from 1261 to 1269 he was podestà of the Casa dei Mercanti, which gave him control over all production and trade in the city, and from 1262 he combined it with the office of capitano del popolo, the people's captain. His policy continued Ezzelino's, keeping the Guelph faction and other exiles out and securing political and economic stability.

In 1264 he led the Veronese army to take Lonigo and Montebello, threatening Vicenza, and for a short time he annexed the lands of the bishop of Trent. He won from the Republic of Venice free access for Veronese trade on the Adige and made peace with the Guelph city of Mantua.

In 1267 he allied with Conradin, the last of the Hohenstaufen, who had come into Italy to reconquer the Kingdom of Sicily. Pope Clement IV, an ally of Charles I of Anjou, excommunicated Conradin and his Ghibelline supporters, Mastino and Verona among them. The ban was lifted only some years later, after 166 Cathars captured at Sirmione were burnt alive in the Arena. While Mastino was away, the counts of San Bonifacio raised a civil war and took most of his garrisons, and his brother Bocca died in the fighting, but Mastino soon defeated the rebels and had his brother Alberto made podestà of Mantua.

Mastino was murdered in Verona on 26 October 1277 by a member of the local aristocracy opposed to Scaliger rule; Alberto's alleged part in the plot is unproven. Alberto, his chosen successor as head of the merchants since 1269, was at once voted captain and rector of the city for life, turning Verona into a signoria. The della Scala held it until 1387.
mastino-ii-della-scala: Mastino II was the son of Alboino I della Scala and Beatrice da Correggio, and a member of the Scaliger family that ruled Verona. When Cangrande I died, Mastino and his brother Alberto II were both associated with the rule of the city, but Mastino's independent manner soon overshadowed his brother. In 1328 he married Taddea da Carrara, a daughter of Jacopo I of Padua.

Abandoning the careful policy of balance kept by his predecessors, Mastino turned to conquest in the first part of his rule. He took Brescia in 1332, and in 1335 Parma in Lombardy and Lucca in Tuscany. The growth of his power drew the other local powers into a league against him: Florence, Siena, Bologna, Perugia and Venice. Mastino held out in the first year of the war, but in 1337 the league was joined by Azzone Visconti of Milan, the Este of Ferrara, the Gonzaga of Mantua and the Papal States.

Surrounded on every side, he could only seek peace through the mediation of Emperor Louis IV of Bavaria, which he obtained in 1339. His lands were reduced to Verona and Vicenza, and the rest was divided among the victors. A later attempt to recover part of what he had lost, using the German mercenaries who had stayed in Vicenza after the war under Lodrisio Visconti, failed.

Mastino died in Verona on 3 June 1351. He was buried in a Gothic mausoleum near the church of Santa Maria Antica, one of the Scaliger Tombs. His sons Cangrande, Alboino and Cansignorio survived him; Cangrande married Elisabeth of Bavaria, a daughter of Louis IV, and Cansignorio married Agnes of Durazzo. His daughter Verde married Niccolò II d'Este, Marquis of Ferrara, and his daughter Beatrice Regina married Bernabò Visconti on 27 September 1350, ties that joined the Scaliger family to two of the houses that had fought him. Among his illegitimate children, Pietro became Bishop of Lodi.
mastoureh-ardalan: Mah Sharaf Khanom Mastoureh Ardalan, also written Mastura Ardalan, was born in Sanandaj in Qajar Iran in 1805. A member of the aristocracy of the court of the Principality of Ardalan, she studied Kurdish, Arabic and Persian under the supervision of her father, Abolhasan Beig Qadiri. Her husband, Khasraw Khan Ardalan, was the ruler of the principality. After his death the principality was vulnerable to outside interference, and when the Qajar state conquered Ardalan territory in the nineteenth century she and her family left for the Baban principality, centred on Sulaymaniyah. Her son Reza Qulikhan, who succeeded Khasraw Khan, was imprisoned by the Qajars. She died in Sulaymaniyah in 1848, in the Ottoman Empire.

She wrote several books of poetry, history and literature. Most of her poetry is in Hawrami, or Gorani, a Kurdish dialect, and in Persian, with a few poems in Central Kurdish. She also wrote a history of the Kurdish Ardalan dynasty, and she is described as a historiographer of the Middle East. Most of her Kurdish poetry was forgotten during the twentieth century and was rediscovered and published at the end of that century and the beginning of the twenty-first. A collection of her poems has been republished in recent years.

Her two-hundredth birthday was marked by a festival in Erbil in the Iraqi Kurdistan region, where a statue of her was unveiled. A conference on her works was held in Erbil from 11 to 15 December 2005. More than one hundred scientific and cultural figures attended, and thirty articles in Kurdish, Persian, English and Arabic were presented about her life and works. The organisers also published several of her works in Persian and Kurdish during the congress. A statue of her by the Iranian sculptor Hadi Zia-dini stands in Sanandaj.
masud-i-of-ghazni: Mas'ud was born in 998 at Ghazni, the Ghaznavid capital, together with his younger twin brother Mohammad. In 1015 his father, Mahmud of Ghazni, named him heir and made him governor of Herat. He led an expedition into Ghur, then still a pagan enclave, and took part in his father's campaigns in Jibal, which annexed the Buyid amirate of Ray. He then directed the Ghaznavid wars in western Iran and forced the Kakuyid ruler Muhammad ibn Rustam Dushmanziyar to recognise Ghaznavid authority.

Relations with his father were poor, and Mahmud changed his mind and named Mohammad, far less experienced, as heir. When Mahmud died, Mohammad succeeded him, but Mas'ud had the backing of his uncle Yusuf ibn Sabuktigin and of the army, including the officer Ali Daya. He marched on Ghazni, defeated and imprisoned his brother, who was blinded, and crowned himself sultan.

Mas'ud brought the former statesman Ahmad Maymandi out of prison to serve as his vizier, while his old assistant Abu Sahl Zawzani grew powerful at court. Suspicious of his father's officers, he imprisoned his uncle Yusuf and the statesman Ali ibn Il-Arslan. His reign was spent in constant war: against the Kara-Khanids, who killed his governor of Khwarazm, Altun Tash, at Dabusiyya; against the Buyids in Kerman, which he took and lost again; against the rebel Ahmad Inaltigin; and in India, where he won the Siege of Hansi in 1037. In 1034 he sacked Amul for four days and then burned it.

Meanwhile the Seljuq Turks under Tughril, who had asked him for asylum, defeated the army he sent against them and won the cession of Nasa, Farava and Dihistan. They went on to take the cities of Khorasan, and Tughril proclaimed himself its ruler at Nishapur. Mas'ud drove them from Herat and Nishapur, then marched on Merv with an army of 50,000 men.

After the defeat at Dandanaqan, near Merv, Mas'ud left Ghazni to set up his capital in India and imprisoned Ali Daya and other generals at Lahore. His army revolted and restored Mohammad, who confined Mas'ud at Giri, where he was killed on the orders of Mohammad or of Mohammad's son Ahmed. Mas'ud's son Maw'dud later avenged him by killing Mohammad and took the throne; three other sons, Ibrahim, Ali and Farrukh-Zad, also ruled the empire in later years. He is remembered by the title Amir-i Shahid, the martyr king.
masuna: Masuna is the earliest recorded ruler of the Mauro-Roman Kingdom, a Berber kingdom that arose in the former province of Mauretania Caesariensis after the collapse of the Western Roman Empire. Unlike many other successor kingdoms, it reached beyond the old Roman frontier into Berber lands that had never been under Roman control. Masuna is attested as a Christian, and he kept his kingdom independent by resisting occupation by the Vandals; the tribes of Mauretania are said to have obeyed him.

He is known only from an inscription on a fortification at Altava, the modern Ouled Mimoun in the region of Oran, in which he styles himself Rex gentium Maurorum et Romanorum, king of the Moorish and Roman peoples. The text names officials he appointed at Castra Severiana and Safar, so he held at least those two towns besides Altava, which is assumed to have been his capital because of its prominence under later kings. Castra Severiana was the seat of a diocese, which may have made its control particularly important.

The Eastern Roman historian Procopius mentions a Berber king called Massonas who allied with the forces of the Eastern Roman Empire against the Vandal Kingdom in the Vandalic War of the 530s. He is assumed to have been among the Berber rulers who submitted willingly to Belisarius, asking in return for the symbols of their office: a silver crown, a staff of silver gilt, a tunic and gilded boots.

Once the Vandals were defeated, Berber raids troubled the restored Roman provinces, above all Byzacena. The praetorian prefect Solomon defeated the raiders twice, and the survivors joined Iaudas, King of the Aurès, in Numidia.
