Massonas, the son of the chieftain Mephanias, whom his brother-in-law Iaudas had assassinated, joined Ortaias, a king in the former province of Mauretania Sitifensis, in urging Solomon to pursue them. Solomon paid his Berber allies large sums and advanced cautiously into the Aurès with the two as guides.

The armies watched each other for three days before Iaudas withdrew. Short of supplies and distrusting the loyalty of his allies, Solomon ended the campaign, built a fortified camp on the plains and secured the roads between Byzacena and Numidia with a line of fortified posts. Massonas disappears from the sources after this campaign. He is often identified with Masuna, but some historians believe they were different men.
masuria: Masuria occupies much of the Masurian Lake District, known for its 2,000 lakes, and covers some 10,000 square kilometres with about 500,000 inhabitants. It is bordered by Warmia, Powiśle and Chełmno Land in the west, Mazovia in the south, Podlachia and the Suwałki Region in the east, and Lithuania Minor in the north. Its biggest city, Ełk, is often regarded as its capital.

The lakes were ground out of the land by glaciers during the Pleistocene ice age, and the terrain is hilly, with connecting lakes, rivers and streams. Forests account for about 30 per cent of the area: broadleaved in the north, pine and mixed in the south. The two largest lakes of Poland, Śniardwy and Mamry, lie here.

Before the 13th century the region was inhabited by Old Prussians, a Baltic people, and part of it was known as Galindia, probably a deeply forested and lightly populated area. The Teutonic Order, invited to Poland by Konrad I of Masovia in 1226, conquered it over more than 50 years; the original population was partly exterminated, particularly during the Prussian rebellion of 1261–1283. Poles from Mazovia then began to settle in the south-east, followed by German, Dutch, Flemish and Danish colonists from the north-west. The Battle of Grunwald was fought in western Masuria in 1410.

After the Order was secularised and Albert of Prussia turned Lutheran in 1525, the area became Protestant under the Duchy of Prussia, a vassal of Poland. Polish-speaking settlers from Mazovia filled the south, and Ełk and Węgorzewo became Polish printing centres. The region passed to the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701, and the name Masuria came into official use after the Prussian reforms after 1818. After the unification of Germany in 1871 Polish lessons were removed from schools in 1872 and Germanisation policies spread.

Under the Yalta and Potsdam decisions the region passed to Poland in 1945. Most of the remaining Germans were expelled, and Masurians who stayed faced a nationality verification by the new authorities. Poles from central Poland and the areas annexed by the Soviet Union, and Ukrainians resettled under Operation Vistula, moved in. Since 1999 Masuria and Warmia have formed the Warmian–Masurian Voivodeship, and the region hosts summer music festivals in Ostróda, Mrągowo, Giżycko and Ełk.
masyaf: Masyaf lies on the foothills of the eastern slopes of the Jabal Ansariyah coastal range, just west of the al-Ghab Plain, at an elevation of about 485 metres. Hama is 45 kilometres to the east and Baniyas 54 kilometres to the west. The surrounding land is marked by gardens, orchards and fields of wheat and barley. The name comes from the Assyrian Manṣuate, which one scholar takes to mean a raised platform, a description of the promontory on which the fortress stands.

Masyaf is the most probable site of the Aramean city of Mansuate of the 8th century BCE, later the centre of an Assyrian province of that name, and probably of the Marsyas of Roman and Byzantine writers. Crusader chroniclers first mention the fortress in 1099. In the autumn of 999 the Byzantine emperor Basil II destroyed its fortifications, and in 1127 the Mirdasids sold it to the Banu Munqidh of Shaizar.

In 1140 the Nizari Ismailis captured it by ambushing and killing its defender, a Banu Munqidh mamluk named Sunqur. Persecuted in Aleppo, Damascus and Banias, they had chosen to settle in the fortresses of the Jabal Ansariyah, and with al-Kahf, Khawabi, al-Qadmus and al-Rusafa, Masyaf let them keep an autonomous territory among the Crusader states and local Muslim dynasties.

Rashid ad-Din Sinan's men made two unsuccessful attempts on the life of Saladin, who in 1176 marched against Masyaf but withdrew within days to face Crusader attacks in the Beqaa; a truce was mediated by his uncle Shihab al-Din Mahmud al-Harimi. In 1249 the Ismaili leader Taj al-Din Abu'l Futuh built a wall around the town. The Mongols under Hulagu briefly occupied Masyaf in 1260 and withdrew after the Battle of Ain Jalut.

The Mamluk sultan Baibars demanded tribute in 1262, and in 1270 Masyaf was fully incorporated into the sultanate, though Ismailis continued to live there. It passed to the Ottomans in 1516–17. In 1808 the Raslan clan captured the fortress and killed about 300 Ismailis, and Ismaili control was restored in 1810 after an Ottoman force recaptured it.

Masyaf had a population of 22,508 at the 2004 census and is the administrative centre of the Masyaf District. It is a religiously mixed city of Ismailis and Alawites, with a Christian minority. The fortress was largely abandoned by its residents after the Allied capture of Syria in 1917 and is now a national monument under the Syrian Directorate of Antiquities. Within the walls stands a mosque dating from the 12th century, which local residents associate with Saladin.
mat-kilau: Muhammad Kilau bin Rasu, known as Mat Kilau, was born in 1866 or 1867 in Kampung Masjid, Pulau Tawar, in the Jerantut District of Pahang. He was the eldest son of Tok Gajah, a high-ranking noble of the Pahang court, by his third wife, Teh Mahda binti Tok Kaut. He was said to excel in Quranic recitation and the Dikir Pahang, to be a master of Silat and to possess magical powers. At about twenty he married Yang Chik binti Imam Daud, daughter of a religious teacher, and they had four children. Hugh Clifford, the British agent, befriended him in 1888 and found him easier to deal with than his father.

The uprising began in 1891 in Semantan under its chief, Dato' Bahaman, and spread as other chiefs joined. On 10 April 1892 Mat Kilau and a hundred followers armed with swords, spears and muskets sacked Kuala Lipis and then threatened the gold mines at Raub. On 21 May a force of Perak Sikhs under Lieutenant Colonel Robert Sandilands Frowd Walker, with Clifford as political advisor, burned his stronghold at Budu, and he escaped with sixty men and their families to join Bahaman at Ulu Cheka.

Sultan Ahmad prevented the arrest of Tok Gajah and let him slip away to the Kelantan-Terengganu border, where Mat Kilau joined him. An amnesty of 16 October 1892 excluded only Tok Gajah and Bahaman. The rebels took a British stockade at Kuala Tembeling on 14 June 1894 but were defeated at Jeram Ampai on 29 June. With Siam, the overlord of Kelantan and Terengganu, pledging not to shelter them, the leaders were hunted down, and several were captured in late 1895 and deported to Chiang Mai.

British reports placed his death in 1895, without a burial place. Mat Kilau later said he had been badly beaten by Siamese soldiers and left for dead, and that the Sultan of Kelantan freed him and had the bark of a banana tree buried in his place. He lived under several names as a rubber collector, labourer and Silat teacher. On 26 December 1969 he announced at the mosque in Pulau Tawar that he was Mat Kilau. A committee reported in July 1970, the state confirmed him on 6 August, and he died on 16 August 1970, receiving a state funeral. A 2022 Malaysian film tells his story.
mataafa-iosefo: Mata'afa is one of the highest matai, or chiefly, titles of Samoa; Iosefo was his personal name, and he was also styled Tupua Malietoa To'oa Mata'afa Iosefo. He succeeded his father, Mata'afa Tafagamanu, in the title. He lived through the years when Germany, Great Britain and the United States competed for control of the Samoa Islands, each backing its own chiefly candidate for the kingship.

He first came to prominence in September 1888, when his followers rose against Tamasese, whom the Germans backed as Tafa'ifa, or king. In the First Samoan Civil War his warriors drove Tamasese's forces back to Mulinuʻu Point, where a German gunship protected them. After the Germans bombarded his villages, his men wiped out an invading German contingent and plundered German plantations at the First Battle of Vailele. The three powers eventually agreed to restore Malietoa Laupepa. Mata'afa was later exiled to the Marshall Islands, and during his exile German opinion of him improved; he was allowed to return in 1898 and was crowned king on 15 November that year.

In the Second Samoan Civil War his German-backed faction fought Malietoa Tanumafili I, who was supported by American and British forces. Mata'afa occupied Apia on 1 January 1899 and ignored an ultimatum from the American admiral Albert Kautz in March to leave the town. At the Second Battle of Vailele his men defeated Samoan loyalists and British and American warships, though at a cost in dead far heavier than their opponents'. In May 1899 he agreed to disarm as a condition of the ceasefire talks, and his claim was backed by the early Mau movement of the orator Lauaki Namulauulu Mamoe.

Because neither side could capture or kill him, the powers settled on dividing Samoa: Germany took the western islands as German Samoa, the United States annexed the eastern islands, and Britain withdrew in exchange for concessions in the Solomon Islands. In 1900 the German colonial authorities declared him Ali'i Sili, or highest chief. He died at Mulinuʻu in 1912 and was succeeded by Mata'afa Tupuola Iose.
matadi: Matadi lies on the left bank of the Congo River, 148 kilometres from its mouth and about 8 kilometres below the last navigable point before the rapids that make the river impassable for a long stretch upstream. It is close to the border with Angola. Its name means stone in the Kikongo language, and the town is built on steep hills; a local saying holds that to live in Matadi one must know the verbs to go up, to go down and to sweat.

Upstream is a series of caves called the rock of Diogo Cão, after graffiti the Portuguese explorer carved there in 1485 to mark the limit of his travels up the river. The climate is a relatively dry tropical savanna, with a long dry season from June to September.

Matadi stands near the site of the state of Vungu, first mentioned in 1535 and said to have been destroyed in 1624. The town was founded by Sir Henry Morton Stanley in 1879. It was strategically important as the last navigable port going upstream and became the furthest inland port in the Congo Free State. The Matadi–Kinshasa Railway, built between 1890 and 1898, made it possible to carry goods from deeper within the Congo to the port, which grew into an important trading centre. Portuguese and French West African commercial interests influenced its architecture and urban design, which borrowed from neighbouring Angola and Congo-Brazzaville.

Matadi is the chief seaport of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and capital of the province of Kongo Central. It is divided into three communes, Matadi, Mvuzi and Nzanza. The railway to Kinshasa is 366 kilometres long, and a monument to its builders stands on a nearby hill. The Matadi Bridge, a suspension bridge 722 metres long built in 1983, carries the road from Kinshasa to the coast and is the only bridge over the main stem of the Congo River. The chief exports are coffee and timber.
matadi-kinshasa-railway: In the 1880s the Congo Free State relied on the Congo River to reach the interior, but between Matadi and Léopoldville the river is barred for 300 km by the Livingstone Falls. Goods were carried by human bearers, a slow and often fatal system. On 31 July 1887 the Compagnie du Congo pour le Commerce et l'Industrie was incorporated together with its subsidiary, the Compagnie du Chemin de Fer du Congo, and Albert Thys directed the work; the station of Thysville, now Mbanza-Ngungu, was named after him.

The hardest stretch led the line out of the river's gorges, through the canyon of the M'pozo River and along the Monts de Cristal. Conditions were miserable and medical care lacking: in 1892 an average of one hundred and fifty workers a month died of smallpox, dysentery, beriberi and exhaustion, and of 7,000 recruited by the end of that year 3,500 had died or fled. Thys then brought workers from Barbados and China; the Barbadians were forced off their ships at Matadi at gunpoint, and seven people were killed. The official toll was 1,932 dead, 1,800 Africans and 132 Europeans, and the real figure was likely higher.

The 366 km line, a portage railway, soon proved profitable, chiefly through the transport of ivory and rubber. It was laid to a gauge of 765 mm and worked by tank engines and later Garratts. From 1923 to 1931 it was rebuilt to a gauge of 1,067 mm on a new alignment by tens of thousands of convicts and forced workers, of whom seven thousand died, and in 1928 Belgium and Portugal exchanged land between the Congo and Angola for the new route.

With the port of Matadi the railway became Kinshasa's main link to the outside world. After a derailment killed 11 people in 2003 it went unused for more than a decade, reopening in September 2015; traffic stopped again in 2020 and resumed in September 2025, with railcars bought from JR Hokkaido. The hard labour of its building is remembered in Heart of Darkness by Joseph Conrad, who saw it while working in the Congo Free State.
matagalpa: Matagalpa lies on the continental divide between the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, more than 700 metres above sea level, beside the Grand River of Matagalpa and surrounded by mountains. Its climate is tropical savanna, with spring-like weather all year, which gives it the names Land of Eternal Spring and Pearl of the North. The name has been explained in several ways: the historian Jeronimo Perez, who visited the area in 1855–1856, took it to mean Main Head or Big Town from indigenous words, while the linguist Guillermo Kiene derived it from the Sumo language, meaning let us go where the rocks are.

Matagalpa was an indigenous village, home to a people called the Cacaopera or Matagalpa, whose language has been extinct since 1875. They made ceramics in styles known as Ceramica Negra and Naranja Segovia and built stone statues of their chieftain and warriors. They were feared by the Spanish as brave and skilful with bows, and the account given says it took the Spanish 300 years to subdue them. Spaniards first reached the town by 1528, in search of a water passage to the Caribbean.

Gold was discovered around Matagalpa by 1840 and drew Spaniards, mestizos and German, American and British immigrants. Ludwig Elster and his wife Katharina Braun planted the first coffee trees in the area, and coffee agriculture attracted more than 120 European immigrants, many of whom married Matagalpan women. In 1856 Nicaraguans fleeing the filibuster William Walker took refuge in the city and organised the Ejército del Septentrión, the Army of the North. With help from 60 Matagalpa archers it won the Battle of San Jacinto on 14 September 1856, which helped to end Walker's rule. In 1923 some Danish immigrants settled in the highlands, and three families, the Gröns, the Möllers and the Petersens, stayed.

Matagalpa is the capital of the department of Matagalpa and had a population of 112,697 in a 2022 estimate, the largest city in the interior of Nicaragua. The region is known for coffee, cattle, dairy products, vegetables, flowers and eco-tourism, with mountain resorts such as Selva Negra, whose wildlife refuge covers over 120 hectares. A panoramic highway runs 30 kilometres from Matagalpa to Jinotega. The department was the birthplace of the poet Rubén Darío (1867–1916), of President Bartolomé Martínez, who held office in 1923–24, and of Carlos Fonseca Amador, founder of the Sandinista Front in 1961.
matagorda-bay: The bay lies in Calhoun and Matagorda counties, about 130 km northeast of Corpus Christi, and is one of seven major estuaries on the Texas Gulf coast and the state's third largest estuarine system, after Galveston Bay and Laguna Madre. It averages 2 metres deep and covers about 1,093 square kilometres, with arms reaching into Lavaca Bay, Tres Palacios Bay and East Matagorda Bay. The Colorado and Lavaca Rivers flow into it, and it meets the Gulf of Mexico at Pass Cavallo and other channels, so its water is only about half as salty as the sea.

Early European records call the area Espíritu Santo and the Costa y Bahía de San Bernardo, and a map of the late 1510s by Alonso Álvarez de Pineda seems to be the first to show it. La Salle reached it in 1685 after missing the mouth of the Mississippi. Disease killed half of his colonists at Fort St. Louis and the Karankawa killed nearly all the rest, sparing five children whom the expeditions of Alonso De León and Domingo Terán de los Ríos later rescued. In 1722 the Spanish built Presidio La Bahia and a mission on the fort's site.

Linnville, founded on the bay in 1831, was a main port of the Republic of Texas until the Great Comanche Raid of 1840 destroyed it; Lavaca, founded in 1841, took its place. Indianola, founded in 1846 as a landing for German immigrants, became the second port of Texas by the 1860s. During the Civil War the bay changed hands several times, and on 17 April 1861 Earl Van Dorn captured the Union supply ship Star of the West there without bloodshed. Hurricanes in 1875 and 1886 ruined Indianola, which was abandoned the next year. In 1934 the Colorado River was turned straight into the Gulf, cutting off East Matagorda Bay; it was diverted back in 1992.

Port Lavaca is the largest port on the bay, with Palacios and Port O'Connor on its other shores. Fishing for shrimp, blue crab and oysters, seafood processing, farming of rice and other crops, and industry at Point Comfort support the towns, and the Mad Island-Oyster Lake area on the eastern shore shelters over 300 species of birds.
matanzas: Matanzas lies on all three sides of the Bay of Matanzas on the north shore of Cuba, 102 kilometres east of Havana. Three rivers, the Yumurí, the San Juan and the Canimar, flow into the bay within the city limits. Seventeen bridges cross them, which gave the city the name City of Bridges and the comparison with Venice. It was also called the Athens of Cuba for its poets.

A royal decree of 25 September 1690 ordered the bay and port to be settled by 30 families from the Canary Islands, and the city was founded on 12 October 1693 as San Carlos y San Severino de Matanzas. The name means massacre and is said to refer to a slaughter in 1510, when 30 Spanish soldiers crossing a river in boats handled by native fishermen drowned in their armour after the fishermen capsized the boats.

Matanzas was one of the regions where sugar plantations developed most intensively, and enslaved people were imported in large numbers, especially in the first half of the nineteenth century. There were 1,900 enslaved people in 1792, about 30 per cent of the population; 10,773 in 1817, nearly half; and 53,331 in 1841, or 62.7 per cent. The area saw several slave insurrections and plots, among them the Escalera conspiracy, discovered in late 1843. On 25 April 1898 American warships bombarded the city in the first action of the Spanish–American War.

Matanzas is the capital of the province of Matanzas. It is known as the birthplace of the music and dance traditions danzón and rumba. Its landmarks include the Sauto Theatre, opened in 1863 and a National Monument of Cuba, the cathedral of San Carlos de Borromeo, the aqueduct of 1870 and the nearby Bellamar caves.
matanzas-inlet: The inlet runs between two barrier islands and the mainland at the south end of the Matanzas River, in the southern part of St. Johns County. It is not stabilised by jetties and so is subject to shifting: maps made by Spanish military engineers in the 18th century show that it has moved many hundreds of yards south of where it lay in the time of the Spanish Empire. It is the last remaining natural, undredged inlet on the Atlantic coast of Florida.

The name goes back to the contest between the French and the Spanish over Florida. René Goulaine de Laudonnière founded Fort Caroline, in what is now Jacksonville, in 1564 as a haven for Huguenot settlers. In response to this encroachment on what Spain regarded as its territory, Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine in 1565 and soon set out overland to attack Fort Caroline, while the French sailed from the fort intending to attack St. Augustine from the sea.

The Spanish overwhelmed the lightly defended Fort Caroline, sparing only the women and children, although some 25 men escaped. A storm drove the French fleet off course, and many of its ships were wrecked on the coast south of St. Augustine. When the Spanish found the main group of shipwreck survivors, Menéndez de Avilés ordered all of the Huguenots executed, and the place became known as Matanzas.

The inlet was the southernmost access for boat travel between St. Augustine and Havana. In 1740 a British invasion force from Fort Frederica in Georgia blockaded it, and shortly afterwards the Spanish authorities in Florida built a coquina stone tower, 50 feet square and 30 feet high, to safeguard the inlet. The tower is now called Fort Matanzas.
matchlock: A matchlock, or firelock, is a firearm in which gunpowder is ignited by a burning piece of flammable cord or twine, brought into contact with the powder by a mechanism worked with a lever or trigger. It improved on the hand cannon, which had no trigger and needed the musketeer or an assistant to apply a match to the powder by hand. The earliest matchlock arquebus appeared in Europe by 1411 and in the Ottoman Empire by 1425, but these early guns did not have the mechanism later associated with the weapon, and the exact dating of the matchlock is disputed.

References to Janissary tüfek date from 1394 to 1465, and Godfrey Goodwin dates their matchlock arquebuses to no earlier than 1465. The first dated illustration of the mechanism is from 1475, and by the sixteenth century matchlocks were in universal use.

The classic matchlock held a slow match in a clamp at the end of a curved lever called the serpentine. Pulling a lever or, in later models, a trigger dropped the match into the flash pan, and the flash passed through the touch hole to the main charge in the barrel. Both ends of the match were usually kept alight.

Its weakness was the need to keep the match lit: damp cord was hard to light in wet weather, a glowing match gave away the carrier's position at night, and burning matches were dangerous near gunpowder. Keeping both ends lit every night for a year needed a mile of match. Soldiers guarding ammunition were among the first to receive self-igniting guns such as the wheellock and snaphance.

Babur brought improved versions of the Ottoman arquebus to India in 1526. The Chinese obtained matchlock arquebus technology from the Portuguese in the sixteenth century, though Turkish muskets may have reached China earlier, and used matchlocks into the nineteenth century. In Japan the matchlock, known as the tanegashima, was first documented in 1543, when the lord of Tanegashima island, Tanegashima Tokitaka, bought two from the Portuguese and had a swordsmith copy them. Its low cost and simplicity kept it in European armies until about 1750, when the flintlock replaced it. In Japan and China matchlocks saw military use to the mid-nineteenth century, and Arabian Bedouin and Tibetans kept using them into the twentieth.
mateo-de-toro-zambrano: Mateo de Toro Zambrano was born in Santiago on 20 September 1727, the legitimate son of Carlos José de Toro-Zambrano y Escobar and Jerónima de Ureta y Prado, a family of high standing in the city. Through his mother he was related to the grandfather of José Miguel Carrera, and the Prado family of his maternal grandmother traced their origins to the Inca emperor Manco Cápac. On 3 May 1751 he married María Nicolasa de Valdés y de la Carrera in Santiago; they had ten children.

Toro Zambrano served on the council of Santiago, as water magistrate in 1750 and as ordinary mayor of the city in 1761. In 1761 Manuel de Amat y Juniet appointed him magistrate of Santiago, mayor of mines and lieutenant of the captain general, posts he held again in 1768. In 1762 José Perfecto de Salas described him as an honour to the Creole spirit, a man of few words, great judgement and significant wealth.

He had a reputation for strict observance of the rules and a strong sense of duty. When the council lacked funds for dikes on the Mapocho River, he paid for the work himself. During a rising of the Pehuenche people in the Biobío region in 1769, he funded a cavalry company, the Prince of Asturias, led by his son José Gregorio, which guarded the Piuquenes Pass. A royal decree of 6 March 1770 made him Count of La Conquista, a title recalling the conquest of the Canary Islands, in which his ancestor Juan de Toro had taken part.

On 16 July 1810, after Governor Francisco Antonio García Carrasco resigned, Toro Zambrano became interim president-governor and captain general of Chile. He faced constant pressure to set up a governing junta, which he opposed, but on 18 September 1810 he took the presidency of the First National Government Junta, Chile's first autonomous government, and so became the first leader of the movement that led to independence. His death in the following year kept him from a larger part in that history. His son José Gregorio inherited the title and estate.
mathilde-abbess-of-essen: Mathilde was the daughter of Duke Liudolf of Swabia and Ida, a daughter of Duke Hermann I of Swabia, and through her grandmother Eadgyth she was descended from the kings of Wessex. She was probably educated at Essen Abbey from 953 or 957, by Abbess Hathwig and Abbess Ida, and is first attested on 1 March 966, when her grandfather granted the canonesses land at her request. The abbey's books included Prudentius, Boethius, Alcuin and Terence, and the inscription on the Marsus Shrine was reported to say she wrote Latin and knew some Greek.

At about 24, below the usual age, Mathilde obtained from Emperor Otto II at Aachen on 23 July 973 the confirmation of the abbey's free election, property and immunity. The deaths of her brother Otto of Swabia in 982 and of Otto II a year later made her the last of the Swabian branch of the Liudolfings and the manager of its wealth, at a time when Henry the Wrangler claimed the regency for the child Otto III. Her part in that crisis is not documented, but in 993 Otto III gave Essen the crown of his coronation and a ceremonial sword, gifts some historians read as thanks for her help.

With her family's fortune she commissioned jewelled crosses with enamel portraits of herself, among them the Cross of Otto and Mathilde, a seven-armed candelabrum over seven feet high and the Shrine of Marsus, the oldest reliquary chasse in the Empire, melted down after 1794. The Anglo-Saxon Earl Æthelweard translated his chronicle into Latin at her request. Art historians since Georg Humann have ascribed the westwerk of Essen Minster to her, though some credit Abbess Theophanu.

After Henry II succeeded Otto III, no gifts of hers can be dated, and building on the westwerk stopped, which suggests that her Ottonian income was cut and that she sided with the opposition to his succession. Mathilde died at Essen on 5 November 1011 and was probably buried in the crypt of Essen Minster. A manuscript of about 1300 calls her mother of our church, and an exhibition in Essen marked the 1000th anniversary of her death in 2011.
mathura: Mathura is the administrative headquarters of Mathura district in Uttar Pradesh, about 15 kilometres from the town of Vrindavan. In ancient times it was an economic hub at the junction of important caravan routes, where the northern trade route of the Indo-Gangetic Plain met the routes to Malwa and the west coast. It lies at the centre of the cultural region of Braj. It is one of the Sapta Puri, the seven cities Hindus consider holy, and part of the Krishna circuit.

Tradition holds that Mathura was founded by Shatrughna after he killed Lavanasura, son of Madhu of the Yadu tribe. The forested place was called Madhuvan, then Madhupura, and later Mathura. Hindus believe that Krishna, of the Yadu dynasty, was born there, and that the Kesava Deo Temple was built on the site of his birthplace, a prison. The city was the capital of the kingdom of Surasena, ruled by Kamsa, Krishna's maternal uncle.

Excavations show a village growing into an important city during the Vedic age, beginning with the Painted Grey Ware culture of 1100 to 500 BCE. The Krishna Janmasthan site yielded pottery of the sixth century BCE and the remains of a large Buddhist complex, including a monastery called Yasha Vihara of the Gupta period, as well as Jain sculptures of the same era. Mathura was later ruled by the Maurya empire, and Megasthenes in the early third century BCE mentions it as a great city.

Mahmud of Ghazni sacked it in 1018, and the historian al-Utbi describes its stone wall and the thousand houses with attached temples. In 1724 Raja Jai Singh visited Mathura and married his daughter there on Janmashtami.

Mathura is regarded as the heart of Braj Bhoomi, the land of Krishna. The Krishna Janmasthan Temple Complex stands around what is considered his birthplace, and Vishram Ghat on the Yamuna is said to be where Krishna rested after killing Kamsa. Krishna Janmashtami is observed there every year, and the city shares Braj cuisine with Vrindavan.
mathura-lion-capital: The capital, once the top of a pillar, was unearthed at the Saptarishi mound of Mathura by Bhagwan Lal Indraji in 1869. It is dated to the first decade of the 1st century CE and was consecrated under the rule of Rajuvula, one of the Northern Satraps of the Mathura region. It is on display in the South Asia section of the Sir Joseph Hotung Gallery for China and South Asia at the British Museum.

The stone is covered with inscriptions in Prakrit, written in the Kharoshthi script of north-western India. They say that the capital was made for the funeral of "the illustrious king Muki and his horse"; Muki has been conjectured to be Maues. Among other donations they record the gift of a stupa holding a relic of the Buddha by the chief queen of Rajuvula, and they set out the genealogy of several Indo-Scythian satraps of Mathura, among them Sodasa, the son of Rajuvula, who succeeded him and also ruled from Mathura.

A Buddhist triratana symbol is carved at the centre of the capital, further evidence of the Indo-Scythian rulers' involvement with Buddhism, and the inscription shows support for the Sarvastivadin school against the Mahasamghikas.

Sten Konow, who compiled a standard listing of Indian Buddhist inscriptions, read the queen's mother's clan name Kamuia as a form of the Sanskrit Kambojika and suggested that Kharoshtha, his father Arta and perhaps Moga were Kambojas, which would explain why the Kambojas are sometimes named with the Sakas and Yavanas. Aurel Stein proposed on phonetic grounds that Kamuia represents a Gandhari Prakrit form of Kamboja, the name of an ancient Indo-Iranian people. Later scholars treat the equation with caution, since the inscription does not give the name in a form that matches the Sanskrit, and it remains a hypothesis. Many of Konow's readings, including the link with Maues, have been revised in the light of a new reading by H. Falk.
mathurin-leonard-duphot: Duphot was born on 21 September 1769 at la Guillotière, a suburb of Lyon, the son of a stonemason. He joined the Vermandois regiment on 25 July 1785, aged 15, and became a sergeant on 25 March 1792. He took part in the French expedition to Savoy and was sent on to Nice, and he served in one of the national volunteer battalions raised after the outbreak of the French Revolution. He was also a poet: his Ode aux mânes des héros morts pour la liberté was highly fashionable in its day.

He was made chef de bataillon adjudant-général in November 1794, but on 13 June 1795 he was taken off the list of active officers. Recalled in February 1796 for home service, he rejoined General Augereau in Italy in August 1796 and fought at Mantua, Rivoli and La Favorita, and Augereau often mentioned him in dispatches. Bonaparte then put him in charge of organising the troops of the Cisalpine Republic, and on 30 March 1797 he was promoted général de brigade in the armée d'Italie.

Duphot went to Rome with the French ambassador Joseph Bonaparte, and the two tried to stir up a republican rising there, above all by holding a republican festival at Joseph's palace. The festival led to a riot in which Duphot was shot by troops of the Papal States on 28 December 1797. The next day Pope Pius VI sent a formal apology to the French Directory, which refused it, and the killing served as the pretext for the occupation of Rome, the end of the Papal States and the creation of the Roman Republic.

Duphot had been due to marry Désirée Clary, the sister-in-law of Joseph Bonaparte, on the day after his death. She later married Jean-Baptiste Jules Bernadotte and became Queen of Sweden when he became King Charles XIV John in 1818. In Le Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène Napoleon praised Duphot as a general of much promise and called him "virtue itself".
matilda-i-countess-of-boulogne: Matilda was born between 1102 and 1110, the only known child of Count Eustace III of Boulogne and Mary of Scotland, and was heir to the counties of Boulogne and Lens and to estates in England. Her aunt Matilda of Scotland was queen of England, and through her mother she descended from the Anglo-Saxon kings. Around 1125 Count Eustace and King Henry I arranged her marriage to Henry's nephew Stephen of Blois. Eustace then gave up his titles and died as a monk, and Matilda became countess of Boulogne in her own right. Her inheritance included Boulogne and Wissant, the main ports on the shortest crossing to England, and the couple governed their lands together, though she took charge of the daily administration.

Henry I died on 1 December 1135, and Stephen was crowned king on 22 December, with Matilda crowned queen in Westminster Abbey on 22 March 1136. The civil war known as the Anarchy began in 1138, when Earl Robert of Gloucester rebelled for his half-sister Empress Matilda. The queen laid siege to Dover with a large army by land and her Boulogne allies by sea, and took the surrender of the rebel Walkelin Maminot. With a papal legate she brokered the Treaty of Durham with her uncle David I of Scotland, signed on 9 April 1139, and she arranged the marriage of her son Eustace to Constance, sister of King Louis VII of France.

After Stephen was captured at the Battle of Lincoln on 2 February 1141, Matilda led the royalist cause from Kent. On 24 June 1141 the citizens of London, pressed by her and angered by the empress's harsh rule, drove the empress out and opened the gates to the queen's troops. In September the queen and William of Ypres besieged the empress's army at Winchester and routed it on 14 September, capturing Robert of Gloucester. She then exchanged him for her husband.

Matilda patronised the reformed religious orders. She founded the abbeys of Coggeshall, Faversham and Lillechurch, Cressing Temple, Temple Cowley and the hospital of St Katharine's by the Tower. She and Stephen worked to secure the succession of their son Eustace. She died on 3 May 1152, and after her death Stephen recognised the empress's son Henry as his heir, which ended the Anarchy. Historians credit her courage and determination with Stephen's continued hold on the throne.
matilda-of-england-duchess-of-saxony: Matilda was born in or around June 1156, probably in London, the third child and eldest daughter of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, and was named after her paternal grandmother, Empress Matilda. In 1165 the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I sent an embassy under Rainald of Dassel, Archbishop of Cologne, to arrange a double marriage of Henry II's daughters Matilda and Eleanor to the emperor's son Frederick V of Swabia and to Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony. Only the Saxon match was agreed.

Matilda returned from Normandy to England in the autumn of 1166, and in 1167 she travelled to Germany with her mother. She married Henry the Lion in Minden Cathedral on 1 February 1168. He was 27 years older than she and had divorced his first wife, Clementia of Zähringen, in 1162.

The duke's residence was at Brunswick. There Matilda bore her first child, Richenza, in 1172 while her husband was on pilgrimage to the Holy Land, and James Panton writes that in the early years she ruled his estates in his absence. The couple held a large court at Dankwarderode Castle, had Brunswick Cathedral built from 1173, and initiated the Lucidarius, the first original German prose work, and the Gospels of Henry the Lion, a masterpiece of Romanesque illumination.

In 1180 Henry was tried in absentia at Würzburg and stripped of his lands, after refusing in 1174 to join Frederick on an expedition against Normandy, which belonged to Matilda's father. When the emperor besieged Brunswick, where Matilda had just given birth to her son Lothair, she addressed him as a knight, but he sent only a keg of wine.

Henry obeyed in November 1181 and went into exile, and Matilda chose to join him at her father's court, with all the children except Lothair, who remained a hostage. In Normandy she met the troubadour Bertran de Born, who addressed two poems of courtly love to her. In 1185, at Henry II's request, the family was restored to Brunswick.

In spring 1189 the emperor ordered Henry the Lion to join the Third Crusade or go into exile, and he went again to his father-in-law, while Matilda stayed in Brunswick with her children to defend his interests. She died there in June or July 1189, sources giving various days, and was buried in Brunswick Cathedral. Henry, who died in 1195, wished to lie at her right hand. Five children are certainly documented, among them Henry, who made peace between the Welf and Hohenstaufen houses by his marriage, Otto, who became Otto IV, King of Germany and Holy Roman Emperor, and William, from whom the dukes of Brunswick and Luneburg descend.
matilda-of-flanders: Matilda was born into the House of Flanders, the daughter of Baldwin V of Flanders and Adela of France. She was descended from Charlemagne and from Alfred the Great, and her uncle was King Henry I of France, William's suzerain. She was of grander birth than William, who was illegitimate.

William began to negotiate with Baldwin as early as 1047. Both had reasons to want the match: Baldwin was in conflict with the Holy Roman Emperor Henry III and needed support, and the marriage would settle border disputes between Flanders and Normandy. Pope Leo IX banned it in 1049 at the Council of Reims on grounds of consanguinity, since the two were fourth cousins. The couple nevertheless married in about 1051 or 1052. Lanfranc, prior of Bec Abbey, went to Rome for William, and Pope Nicholas II granted a dispensation in 1059.

The marriage was by all accounts happy and fruitful. Matilda bore William at least nine children, four sons and at least five daughters, among them the future kings William II and Henry I of England. The daughters learned to read Latin at the Abbey of Sainte-Trinité in Caen, and the sons were tutored by Lanfranc.

When William set out to conquer England, Matilda was appointed regent of Normandy and guided the duchy without major unrest. She served as regent six times between 1066 and 1076. She first travelled to England in April 1068 and was crowned queen on 11 May 1068 in Westminster Abbey, at Pentecost, in a ceremony presided over by the archbishop of York. Three new phrases in the rite declared that she was placed by God, shared in royal power and blessed her people. Historians no longer believe that she had a hand in the Bayeux Tapestry, which seems to have been commissioned by William's half-brother Odo, Bishop of Bayeux.

Matilda fell ill in the summer of 1083 and died on 2 November 1083, with William present at her final confession. He swore to give up hunting in his grief and died four years later. She was buried at the Abbaye aux Dames in Caen, where a black slab with her epitaph marks the grave. Her skeleton was examined in 1959, and her height was found to be about 152 centimetres, a normal height for the time.
matilda-of-hainaut: Matilda was born in November 1293, the only child of Isabella of Villehardouin and Florent of Hainaut, who held Achaea as vassals of King Charles II of Naples on condition that Isabella or any daughter would not remarry without royal consent. After Florent's death in 1297 the three-year-old was married to Guy II de la Roche, Duke of Athens; Charles objected, but consented on 20 April 1300 after Pope Boniface VIII had sanctioned the match.

In 1307 Charles revoked the rights of Isabella and her second husband, Philip of Savoy. Matilda, about fourteen, claimed the principality, but the bailiff Nicholas III of Saint Omer refused her and Charles gave it to his son Philip of Taranto. Guy died on 8 October 1308, and Philip betrothed the widow to his eldest son, Charles of Taranto, until in 1313 she was married instead to Louis of Burgundy, to whom and to Matilda Philip renounced his rights.

Before they arrived, Ferdinand of Majorca, who had received the claim of Matilda's aunt Margaret of Villehardouin, landed near Glarentza in 1315 and took most of the principality. Matilda came to Navarino with 1,000 Burgundians, and Louis defeated Ferdinand at the Battle of Manolada on 5 July 1316, where Ferdinand was killed. Less than a month later Louis died, some contemporaries suspecting poison by John I Orsini, Count of Cephalonia.

King Robert of Naples then proposed that she marry his brother, John of Gravina. She refused, and in 1318 Robert's emissaries carried her to Naples by force, where she was made to go through a marriage ceremony and John took the title of Prince of Achaea. Brought before Pope John XXII at Avignon, she still refused, declaring that she had secretly married the Burgundian knight Hugh de la Palisse. Robert used that marriage to deprive her of the principality and falsely accused her of a plot against his life.

She was held in the Castel dell'Ovo at Naples and from 1328 at Aversa. Her cousin William I, Count of Hainaut, offered 100,000 livres for her release in 1324, and King Charles IV of France pleaded for her, both in vain. She died a prisoner in 1331, the last descendant of Geoffrey I of Villehardouin to rule Achaea, and on her deathbed named as heir James, son of her old rival Ferdinand of Majorca.
matilda-of-ringelheim: Matilda was born around 892, a daughter of Dietrich and Reinhild. Her father was a count in the Duchy of Saxony, and he was descended from the Saxon duke Widukind, who had fought against Charlemagne. She was raised in Herford Abbey by her grandmother, who was also called Matilda. In 909, when she was seventeen, Matilda married Henry, then duke of Saxony and later king of East Francia. His first marriage, to Hatheburg of Merseburg, had been annulled. About twenty years later, in 929, Henry gave her a dower in the so-called Hausordnung, including land at Quedlinburg and Nordhausen.

Matilda bore Henry five children. Otto was crowned emperor in 962, Henry became duke of Bavaria in 948, and Bruno was elected archbishop of Cologne in 953 and made duke of Lorraine in 954. As queen, Matilda took an interest in women's monasteries, and her influence on the king's reign is said to have lain in her strong sense of justice.

Henry died in 936 at Memleben and was buried in Quedlinburg, where Matilda founded a convent in the same year. She lived there for the following years and looked after the family's legacy. Quedlinburg became a centre of prayer for the kingdom and a place to commemorate its dead, and, like other convents, it educated the daughters of noble families. In 966, after thirty years of leadership, she passed the convent to her granddaughter Matilda, daughter of Otto I and Adelheid of Burgundy, who became its first abbess. Matilda also founded a convent at Enger in 947 and, in 961, her last foundation, at Nordhausen.
Between 936 and 946 her son Otto disputed her handling of her dower and claimed her possessions, and she fled into exile. Otto's wife, Queen Eadgyth, is said to have brought about a reconciliation.

Shortly before her death Matilda acquired papal privileges for all the monasteries of eastern Saxony, to protect her legacy. These were overridden after her death, when her dower passed to Theophanu, wife of her grandson Otto II. She died in the convent at Quedlinburg on 14 March 968 after a long illness and was buried beside her husband. Two hagiographies and The Deeds of the Saxons are the main sources for her life. A plaque to her stands in the Walhalla memorial near Regensburg, and her feast day is 14 March.
matilda-of-tuscany: Matilda of Canossa, called la Gran Contessa, was born around 1046, the youngest of three children of Boniface and Beatrice of Lorraine, who had married in June 1037. Beatrice was the niece and foster daughter of Empress Gisela of Swabia. Around 1055 Matilda was betrothed to her stepbrother Godfrey the Hunchback, and by 1069 she is clearly recorded as his wife. She bore a daughter in 1071 who died within weeks. She then repudiated her husband, a decision that ensured her independence. Her mother Beatrice trained her for rule by holding court with her and encouraging her to issue charters as countess and duchess.

After her mother's death Matilda took over her inheritance, though under Salic and Lombard law Emperor Henry IV would have been the legal heir. She made Canossa Castle, in the Apennines south-west of Reggio Emilia, the centre of domains that included present-day Lombardy, Emilia, Romagna and Tuscany. Pope Gregory VII excommunicated Henry IV in 1076, and in January 1077 Henry made his penitential walk before Canossa Castle and was received back into the Church. From 1080, when conflict with Henry resumed, Matilda put all her military and material resources at the service of the papacy. Her court sheltered many refugees and became a cultural centre.

Between 1081 and 1098 the disputes with Henry put her rule in crisis. A coalition with the southern German dukes brought a turning point, and when Henry withdrew north of the Alps in 1097 she regained many lost domains from autumn 1098. Childless, she adopted Guido Guerra of the Guidi family around 1099 and, in November 1102, renewed a donation of her property to the Apostolic See. She directed her last gifts to Polirone Abbey, where she chose to be buried. According to Donizo, Henry V crowned her Imperial Vicar and Vice-Queen of Italy at Bianello Castle in May 1111.

Matilda died on 24 July 1115, and the House of Canossa became extinct; popes and emperors fought over the Terre Matildiche, as her domains were called, well into the thirteenth century. The struggle between regnum and sacerdotium changed the Italian cities permanently, giving them room to escape foreign rule and develop as communes. Donizo's chronicle, called the Vita Mathildis, written between 1111 and 1115, is the main source for her life. In 1630 Pope Urban VIII had her body moved to Rome, where she was the first woman buried in Saint Peter's Basilica. The Istituto Superiore di Studi Matildici, founded in Italy in 1977, studies the Canossa family.
matins-of-bruges: After Count Guy of Dampierre renounced his fealty and allied with the English King Edward I, the Franco-Flemish War broke out in 1297; Guy surrendered in 1300 and Jacques de Châtillon became governor of Flanders. Bruges had at first favoured the French, surrendering to Philip IV in 1297 and letting the French army build a second city wall seven kilometres long. Opinion turned during the joyous entry of the king and Queen Joan between 29 May and 4 June 1301, when the craft guilds were made to pay for the tournament, gifts and clothes laid on by the town's merchant governors.

Pieter de Coninck emerged as the leader of the discontented and was imprisoned with twenty-five companions in Het Steen until the guild militia freed them. Châtillon then exiled the rebels, sent 500 hostages to Tournai, ordered the new walls partly demolished and revoked the town's charter of 1297, which turned anger against the French. When the Parlement of Paris rejected the town's appeal in March 1302, a new rebellion installed a government of the guilds under William of Jülich, a grandson of Guy.

Ghent did not join the revolt, and on 14 May Châtillon and the chancellor Pierre Flotte appeared before Bruges with an army. Under the surrender about 5,000 rebels left for Damme, Aardenburg and Oostburg, but on 17 May Châtillon entered with the bulk of his army instead of the agreed 300 unarmed horsemen. Fearing revenge, the townspeople called the rebels back. They came in before dawn through the gaps in the walls, searched the houses and used the shibboleth schild en vriend, shield and friend, to tell the French from the natives. Around 120 were killed and 85 nobles and knights, nineteen of them Flemish, were captured and later ransomed.

Châtillon and Flotte escaped, the governor reaching the castle of Kortrijk with most of the survivors. On 23 May Pieter de Coninck and William of Jülich returned to Bruges in triumph, and William was made Ruwaard of Flanders while the count remained a prisoner in France. Philip IV sent Robert II of Artois to crush the revolt. Modern historians named the rising after the Sicilian Vespers of 1282.
matrilineal-descent: Matrilineality, also called matriliny, is the tracing of kinship through the female line. In a matrilineal system individuals belong to the same descent group as their mothers, and property and titles may pass through that line. The matriline of historical nobility was also called their enatic or uterine ancestry, in contrast to the patrilineal or agnatic line. Matrilineal groups are often made up of clans, each with a separate female ancestor. In some matrilineal cultures, particularly matrilocal ones, an uncle termed a social father looks after his sisters' children, while the biological father plays little part in raising them.

Among the Akan, who include the Ashanti, political, economic and social organisation rests on maternal lineages, the basis of inheritance and succession. Public offices, land and other property belong to the lineage and pass only to matrilineal kin, men before women and seniors before juniors. Among the Haudenosaunee, women kept matrilineal rights and took part in deciding such matters as war. The Lenape of present-day New Jersey inherited male leadership through the maternal line, and women elders could remove leaders they disapproved of. The Minangkabau of Indonesia are one of the world's largest matrilineal societies.

In Europe there is evidence of matrilineal royal descent from maternal uncle to nephew among Celts of about 500 BCE, and Pictish leaders were succeeded by a brother or perhaps a nephew rather than a son. In the United States the children of enslaved women inherited their mothers' status.

Scholars disagree about early human kinship. In the late 19th century most, influenced by Lewis H. Morgan's Ancient Society, believed early kinship was matrilineal, and Friedrich Engels took this up, making it communist orthodoxy. By the 20th century most social anthropologists disagreed, though feminist scholars often revived the thesis in the 1970s and 1980s. In Judaism descent is traced through the mother, a practice followed from at least early Tannaitic times, c. 10 to 70 CE. Orthodox Judaism holds it to be Oral Law from the time of Sinai, while some modern academics date it to the time of Ezra or the early Tannaitic period.
matsu-islands: The Matsu Islands lie in the East China Sea alongside the southeastern coast of mainland China. They form Lienchiang County, the smallest county in the Taiwan Area by area and population. The five major islands are Nangan, Dongju, Xiju, Beigan and Dongyin; Dongyin is the northernmost and Dongju the southernmost. Dongyin is slightly over 10 nautical miles (19 kilometres) from the mainland. The islands are mainly granite and diabase, the soil is not ideal for farming, and the highest point, on Beigan, is 298 metres. The climate is subtropical maritime, foggy in spring and summer.

Chinese from Fukien and Chekiang began migrating to the islands during the Yuan dynasty; most of the people of Matsu came from Houguan, today Changle in Fujian. Net fishing laid the base for the settlement at Fuao. Some crewmen of Zheng He stayed on the islands for a time during the Ming dynasty. In the early Qing dynasty pirates gathered there and the residents left temporarily. Unlike Taiwan and Penghu, the islands were not ceded to Japan by the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895. In 1912 the British established the Dongyong Lighthouse on Dongyin Island.

The historical Lienchiang County lay partly on the mainland. After the Chinese Civil War it was effectively divided in 1949: the mainland portion came under the People's Republic of China, while the offshore islands stayed under the Republic of China, so that the county is the only former geographical unit of its name now divided between two administrations. Large numbers of soldiers were stationed there after 1949 and during the First and Second Taiwan Strait Crisis in 1954 and 1958 respectively, and the population reached a peak of 17,088 in 1971. It then fell as young people left for lack of work. County magistrates were appointed until 1993.

The islands are administered as Lienchiang County with Nangan Township as the county seat; it has no city or urban township. The native speech is the Matsu dialect, a subdialect of the Fuzhou dialect. The islands are named after the sea goddess Mazu, and the Matsu Nangan Tianhou Temple holds the sarcophagus of Lin Moniang. Tourism, military sites such as the granite tunnels, and the Matsu Distillery are central to the economy. Since 1990 a bird sanctuary has protected the Chinese crested tern, found nesting there in 2000.
matsudaira-harusato: Harusato was born in 1751 at the Matsudaira residence in Edo, present-day Tokyo, the second son of Matsudaira Munenobu, who then ruled the Matsue domain. When Munenobu, the sixth lord, retired in 1769, the sixth year of the Meiwa era, Harusato succeeded him. By then the domain had been reduced to poverty, largely by the contributions the shogunate had ordered for the repair of the temple of Enryaku-ji.

With the support of his chief retainer, Asahi Tamba, Harusato set out to reverse the domain's decline quickly. He raised the production of its main products and made its rice paddies more secure by promoting flood control. These efforts succeeded, and Matsue was among the fastest of the domains to complete its reforms. The relationship was not without friction: Asahi criticised him for spending domain funds on the tea ceremony.

After the Tokugawa shogunate was established, the practice of chanoyu by samurai had lost its appeal and its role as a focus of political ties among them. From about the middle of the 18th century the older samurai who had scorned it as a pastime of idle men had died, and a new generation of daimyo were leading the development of urban culture. Harusato stood out among them.

In 1770, early in his reform of the domain, he wrote a treatise called Mudagoto, Useless Words, apparently in answer to Asahi's criticism. In it he wrote that making chanoyu a luxury and exhausting beauty to make it splendid was a distressing thing, and that it could instead be an aid to governing the country well. His tradition of tea descended through Isa Kotaku, a disciple of the Rinzai Zen monk Ikei Soetsu, abbot of the Daitokuji temple in Kyoto, who had learned from the daimyo and tea master Katagiri Sadamasa Sekishu. From Arai Itsusho, an Edo devotee in the tradition of Hosokawa Tadaoki, he also obtained a copy of the Nanporoku, a record of the teachings of Sen no Rikyu.
matsudaira-katamori: Matsudaira Katamori was born on 15 February 1836 in the Yotsuya district of Edo, at the residence of the Takasu Domain, the seventh son of its daimyō Matsudaira Yoshitatsu by a concubine. Takasu was small but prestigious as a branch of the Tokugawa clan, and the boy, first called Keinosuke, was adopted by his uncle Matsudaira Katataka, 8th daimyō of Aizu. He took the name Katamori, was educated at the domain academy, Nisshinkan, and married Katataka's daughter Toshihime. As 9th daimyō he held the title Higo-no-kami and a seat in the tamari-no-ma chamber of Edo Castle. When the Perry Expedition entered Edo Bay, Aizu provided patrol boats and coastal security.

In 1862 the shogunate created the post of Kyoto Shugoshoku, or Military Commissioner of Kyoto, to restore order in a city swayed by sonnō-jōi militants. Katamori and his councillors tried to decline it; Saigō Tanomo and Tanaka Tosa warned that Aizu, already burdened with the defence of Edo Bay and eastern Ezo, faced financial ruin. Under pressure from Matsudaira Yoshinaga and Tokugawa Yoshinobu he accepted, telling his men to be prepared to meet their grave in Kyoto. He left Edo on 27 January 1863 at the head of a thousand-strong Aizu force and entered Kyoto on 11 February.

The court received him warmly as an agent of the Kōbu gattai movement for cooperation between court and shogunate. He used city patrols, among them the Shinsengumi, which he established in 1863 as the Mibu Roshigumi. He took part in the coup d'état of 30 September and the Kinmon incident, both clashes with Chōshū Domain, and urged a hard line in the Chōshū expeditions, which earned Aizu Chōshū's enmity. He also hired the Prussian John Henry Schnell, who later led Aizu settlers to found the short-lived Wakamatsu Tea and Silk Farm Colony in California in 1869.

After the Battle of Toba–Fushimi Katamori apologised to the court many times and sent a letter of submission, but the new government, led by men of Chōshū and Satsuma, ignored him. After Aizu's defeat he spent some years under house arrest in Tokyo. He died on 5 December 1893, was buried with Shinto rites and received the posthumous name Masane-reishin.
matsudaira-sadaaki: Born Matsudaira Tetsunosuke on 18 January 1847 at Ichigaya in Edo, he was the eighth son of Matsudaira Yoshitatsu, daimyō of the Takasu Domain; his elder brothers included Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu and Tokugawa Yoshikatsu and Tokugawa Mochinaga of the Owari Domain. In 1859 he was adopted posthumously as heir to Matsudaira Sadamichi of Kuwana, of the Hisamatsu Matsudaira clan descended from Tokugawa Ieyasu's brother Hisamatsu Sadakatsu, and was betrothed to Sadamichi's three-year-old daughter Matsudaira Hatsu. In 1863 he accompanied Shogun Tokugawa Iemochi to Kyoto, the first shogunal visit there in 230 years.

He served as Kyoto Shoshidai from 16 May 1864 to 3 January 1868, the last holder of the post, which oversaw relations with the imperial court and the administration of Kyoto and eight provinces. The appointment was unusual, as the office normally went to an older fudai daimyō. He supported his brother Katamori, the Kyoto Shugoshoku, deployed Kuwana troops in the Kinmon incident and against the Tengu-tō uprising, and under Tokugawa Yoshinobu held the authority of a rōjū. He was known as a keen horseman who rode the streets in western military dress.

After Yoshinobu resigned in November 1867, Sadaaki withdrew with him to Osaka Castle. Following the Battle of Toba–Fushimi he sailed to Kashiwazaki in Echigo Province, an exclave of his domain, then fought on at Aizu, went to the Yonezawa Domain for reinforcements, and joined Enomoto Takeaki's fleet to the Ezo Republic. Before Hakodate fell he fled to Shanghai, but lacking funds he returned to Yokohama and surrendered. Kuwana Castle had already yielded without resistance.

Pardoned and released in 1872, he married Hatsu, studied English at a school founded by the missionary Samuel Robbins Brown, and in 1874 accompanied his son Matsudaira Sadanori to Rutgers University in the United States. In the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 he led former Kuwana samurai for the Imperial Japanese Army. From 1894 he was one of the kannushi of the Nikkō Tōshō-gū with Katamori and Saigō Tanomo. The diarist Clara Whitney recorded that he was a skilled organ player. He died on 12 July 1908 and is buried in the Somei Cemetery in Tokyo.
matsudaira-tadanao: Tadanao was born in Settsu Province on 16 July 1595, the eldest son of Yūki Hideyasu; his childhood name was Senchiyomaru. In 1603 he travelled to Edo with his father and was received by his uncle, Shōgun Tokugawa Hidetada, who took a great liking to him. He was given the courtesy title Mikawa-no-kami and court rank in 1605. On his father's death in 1607 he became daimyō of the 670,000 koku Fukui Domain, and in 1611 he married Katsuhime, a daughter of Hidetada, taking a character of Hidetada's name as Matsudaira Tadanao.

His rule began badly. In 1612 and 1613 armed conflict broke out among his senior retainers, and the shogunate settled it only with difficulty, blaming Tadanao's youth and inexperience. He led the Fukui troops in the Osaka Winter Campaign but lost control of his mercenaries and was severely scolded by his grandfather, the retired shōgun Tokugawa Ieyasu. In the Summer Campaign that followed he took the head of Sanada Yukimura and led his men at the very tip of the Tokugawa advance into Osaka Castle.

He received no reward for this. His court rank stayed at senior third rank and councillor, below the Middle Councillor his father had held, though he was given further courtesy titles in 1615. Taking this as an insult, he feigned illness in 1621 and skipped his required sankin kōtai journey to Edo. He was also said to have tried to poison his wife, who was saved when one of her maids took her place, and to have led his soldiers on rampages through his retainers' homes.

Hidetada banished him to Funai Domain in Bungo Province with an allowance of 10,000 koku. He became a Buddhist priest under the name Ippaku and lived at first at Ogiwara village on the coast, until local authorities, fearing he might escape, made him move inland. He died on 5 October 1650, aged 56. His son Matsudaira Mitsunaga was moved from Fukui to Takada Domain in Echigo Province, while his brother Tadamasa received Fukui, which the family then held until the end of the Edo period.
matsudaira-yoshinaga: Yoshinaga was born in Edo Castle, the eighth son of Tokugawa Narimasa, head of the Tayasu-Tokugawa, one of the gosankyō cadet branches of the Tokugawa clan. Intended for adoption into the Iyo-Matsuyama Domain, he was instead chosen as daimyō of Fukui when its young lord, Matsudaira Narisawa, died without an heir on 27 July 1838. He took a character of his name from Shōgun Tokugawa Ieyoshi, and in 1839 married Yu-hime, a daughter of Hosokawa Narimori of Kumamoto Domain.

In Fukui he cut the stipends of his retainers by half for three years and his own expenses for five, set up a translation bureau for Western learning, an armaments factory and the Meidōkan school, and joined the domain with wealthy merchants in a trading venture. After the Perry Expedition of 1853 he first sided with the anti-foreign party of Tokugawa Nariaki, then came round to opening the country. He backed Tokugawa Yoshinobu in the shogunal succession, protested at Ii Naosuke's signing of the Treaty of Amity and Commerce without the emperor's assent, and on 5 July 1858 was forced to resign in the Ansei purge, taking the name Shungaku.

After Ii's assassination he returned in April 1862 and, as Seiji sōsaishoku, supported the kōbu gattai union of court and shogunate. He formed the Rōshigumi, which became the Shinsengumi, and invited Yokoi Shōnan as an adviser, in what was called the Bunkyū Renovation. Pressed by the Sonnō jōi movement, he resigned and in 1863 planned a march on Kyoto that never took place. In 1864 he sat in the short-lived Sanyo Kaigi council of great lords, and in the Boshin War he acted as an intermediary until 1869.

In the Meiji government he held several high posts, including Chief Executive of Internal Affairs, but resigned in protest at the dominance of men from Chōshū and Satsuma. In 1870 he invited William Elliot Griffis to teach in Fukui, and in 1881 he helped compile the Tokugawa reiten roku, a record of shogunal ritual. He is counted among the Four Wise Lords of the Bakumatsu period and is credited with naming the Meiji era. He died in 1890 and is buried at Kaian-ji in Shinagawa, Tokyo.
matsue: Matsue lies at the northernmost point of Shimane Prefecture, on the banks of the Ohashi River, which connects Lake Shinji and Lake Nakaumi. It stands in the ancient province of Izumo, and archaeological sites of the Yayoi, Kofun and Nara periods lie within its borders. In the Sengoku period the area was the stronghold of the Amago clan.

The castle town was established by Horio Yoshiharu, who built Matsue Castle and planned the town around it over five years, from 1607 to 1611. After the Horio line ended with a childless heir, Izumo passed to the Kyōgoku, and Kyōgoku Tadataka received it in 1634. He too died childless.

The domain then went to the Matsudaira clan. Matsudaira Naomasa, a grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu, had made a name at the Battle of Osaka at the age of 14, and he became ruler of Izumo in 1638. His heirs held Izumo for ten generations until the end of the Edo period. The best known after Naomasa is the seventh daimyō, Matsudaira Harusato, known as Fumai, who set the clan's finances in order, planted mulberry bushes and promoted foods such as shijimi clams. He was an enthusiast of the tea ceremony, and the sweets for which Matsue is known, especially wakakusa, are credited to his influence. The city itself was founded on 1 April 1889.

Matsue is the capital of Shimane Prefecture. Its castle is one of the twelve original castles that survive in Japan. Lafcadio Hearn taught in the city from 1890 to 1891, and a memorial museum is dedicated to him. At the Sada Shrine the Sada Shin Noh, a sacred dance of purification, was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2011.
matsumae-yoshihiro: Yoshihiro was the third son of Kakizaki Suehiro. In his youth the Kakizaki clan held suzerainty over the lords of the fortified residences on the Oshima Peninsula, but it was itself subordinate to the Andō clan of Tōhoku. Its authority, moreover, reached only the Japanese inhabitants of the Wajinchi, the Land of the Wajin, and not the Ainu with whom the clan traded.

After Toyotomi Hideyoshi defeated the Hōjō at Odawara in 1590 and moved to check the great clans of the north, Yoshihiro travelled to Kyōto and in the twelfth month of that year was received by Hideyoshi at the Jurakudai palace. He reported on Ezo and declined a grant of five thousand koku, but received Junior Fifth Court Rank, Lower Grade and the office of Minbu Taifu, which freed him from the Andō. He reached the Oshima Peninsula again in the third month of 1591.

Later in 1591 Yoshihiro sent troops, among them Ainu archers, to help suppress the Kunohe Rebellion. In the eleventh month of 1592 he travelled to Ōsaka and then to Hideyoshi's camp at Hizen Nagoya in Kyūshū, the base for the invasion of Korea, where the two discussed Ezo and the war. Three days after that audience he was given a red-seal letter confirming his right to trade with the Ainu.

The charter that Tokugawa Ieyasu granted in 1604 made those trading rights exclusive. Neither document gave specific territorial rights or a fictive rice income, but the Matsumae Domain came to be treated as the equal of a tozama daimyō with an income of ten thousand koku. Yoshihiro built Matsumae Castle, also known as Fukuyama Castle.
matsunaga-hisahide: Matsunaga Danjō Hisahide, head of the Yamato Matsunaga clan, served Miyoshi Nagayoshi as a retainer from the 1540s. In the 1560s he directed the conquest of Yamato Province, and by 1564 his power base there made him effectively independent. On 4 January 1561 he was granted the court title of Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade.

Hisahide is believed to have been plotting against his lord in these years. Between 1561 and 1563 three of Nagayoshi's brothers and his son Yoshiaki died, so that when Nagayoshi himself died in 1564 his adopted heir, Miyoshi Yoshitsugu, was too young to rule; his guardianship was shared by Miyoshi Nagayuki, Miyoshi Masayasu and Iwanari Tomomichi. After the attack on the palace of the shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiteru in 1565, the shōgun's brother Ashikaga Yoshiaki fled and Yoshiteru was replaced by his younger cousin, Yoshihide.

Fighting broke out between Hisahide and the Miyoshi in 1566. At first it went badly for him, and his apparent destruction of the Buddhist temple of Tōdai-ji in Nara was held to be an act of infamy. In 1568 Oda Nobunaga, with Yoshiaki as his figurehead, attacked him and took Kyoto in November, and Hisahide submitted. He kept Yamato and for a time fought for Nobunaga against the Miyoshi and others, but in 1573 he briefly joined the Miyoshi before returning to Nobunaga's side.

In 1577 Nobunaga besieged him at Shigisan Castle. Defeated, Hisahide killed himself. He was a noted tea master and broke his tea bowl so that his enemies would not have it, and he ordered that his head be destroyed rather than taken as a trophy. His son Hisamichi also died by suicide in the siege. Tradition counts him among Japan's Three Great Villains, with Ukita Naoie and Saitō Dōsan, for his ambition, treachery and use of assassination.
matsuo-basho: Matsuo Bashō was born Matsuo Kinsaku in 1644 near Ueno, in Iga Province. The Matsuo family was of samurai descent, and his father was probably a musokunin, one of a class of landowning peasants with certain samurai privileges. In his late teens he became a servant, in a humble capacity, to Tōdō Yoshitada, with whom he shared a love of haikai no renga, a form of collaborative poetry. A sequence opened with a verse of 5-7-5 mora called a hokku, later renamed haiku when it stood alone.

Yoshitada's sudden death in 1666 ended Bashō's peaceful life, and he is believed to have given up any chance of samurai status. By 1680 he taught twenty disciples in Edo, and that winter he moved to Fukagawa, where his disciples built him a hut and planted a banana tree, bashō in Japanese, which gave him his pen name.

In 1684 he left Edo on the first of four major journeys, travelling alone on routes regarded as dangerous. His poems grew less introspective, and in early 1686 he composed the hokku about an ancient pond and a frog jumping in, which was at once widely praised.

On 16 May 1689 he left Edo with his student Kawai Sora for the Northern Provinces of Honshū, a journey of 600 ri, about 2,400 km, that became his masterwork Oku no Hosomichi, The Narrow Road to the Deep North. He edited it for three years, and the first edition appeared posthumously in 1702. It was an immediate commercial success and other itinerant poets followed his route. Bashō himself believed his best work lay in leading and joining renku.

In 1693 he adopted karumi, or lightness, a semi-Buddhist philosophy of greeting the mundane world instead of separating from it. In the summer of 1694 he left Edo for the last time and in Osaka fell ill with a stomach complaint, dying peacefully on 28 November 1694 among his disciples. In 1793 the Shinto bureaucracy deified him, so that for a time criticising his poetry was blasphemous. Masaoka Shiki challenged this orthodoxy in the late 19th century, yet also made Bashō accessible in English and coined the term haiku.
mattathias: Mattathias ben Johanan was a Kohen, a Jewish priest, who lived in the rural village of Modi'in. All surviving accounts from the Second Temple period place him there, though it is not clear whether he was a native: 1 Maccabees says he moved away from Jerusalem and settled in Modi'in, while Josephus in his Wars calls him a priest of a village called Modi'in, which implies it was his origin.

1 Maccabees names him a son of John and grandson of Simeon, a priest of the order of Joarib. Josephus adds the name Asamonaius, probably a family title, which is why Mattathias and his descendants are known as the Hasmoneans. He had five sons: Judas Maccabeus, Eleazar Avaran, Simon Thassi, John Gaddi and Jonathan Apphus. Like many priests he probably served in the Temple in Jerusalem, though sources that call him a High Priest are late and anachronistic.

Seleucid persecutions of traditional Judaism began in 168–167 BCE, led by King Antiochus IV Epiphanes and possibly the High Priest Menelaus. In 167 BCE Greek soldiers came to Modi'in with orders to enforce sacrifice to the Greek gods. Mattathias, as an esteemed member of the community, was asked to lead the village in the sacrifice and was promised riches and the title Friend of the King. He refused, and when another Jew stepped forward he killed him and the official supervising, calling out, according to 1 Maccabees 2:27, for everyone zealous for the law and supporting the covenant to follow him.

He and his sons fled to the wilderness of Judea, to the Gophna Hills, and began to build a guerrilla force. He led the revolt for a year and, before his death, named Simon counsellor and Judah military commander. According to 1 Maccabees he died in the 146th year of the Macedonian calendar, between spring 166 and spring 165 BCE, and was buried in the tomb of his ancestors at Modiin.

After an incident in which Jewish fighters had let themselves be killed rather than fight on the Sabbath, Mattathias is said to have ruled that they should fight anyone who attacked them on that day. This is the earliest known rejection of the common prohibition of fighting on the Sabbath. The revolt he began led to a Jewish independence not enjoyed for more than 400 years, and its events form the basis of Hanukkah, kept on 25 Kislev. He is named in the Al HaNissim prayer added to the Amidah and the Birkat Hamazon during the festival, and appears in Talmudic references and in 1 Meqabyan, canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.
mattavilasa-prahasana: The play opens with two drunken Kapalikas, the mendicant Satyasoma and his partner Devasoma, stumbling from tavern to tavern in search of more liquor. The Kapalikas are presented as followers of a heretical Saivite sect whose rites included drinking, wild dancing and singing, and ritual intercourse. Asking for alms, Satyasoma finds that his skull-bowl is gone. It is not at the tavern they last visited, and he suspects that either a dog or a Buddhist monk has taken it.

A Buddhist monk named Nagasena then enters, and Satyasoma accuses him of the theft. He charges the monk with stealing, lying and desiring liquor, meat and women although his religion forbids them, and accuses Buddhism itself of stealing ideas from the Mahabharata and the Vedanta. The monk denies everything and the quarrel becomes a brawl, which a Pasupata acquaintance of Satyasoma tries to mediate. In despair the monk hands over his own begging bowl. At last a Madman comes on stage carrying the real skull-bowl, which he has recovered from a dog; it is returned to its owner and all leave on friendly terms.

The play was written during a strong revival of Hinduism in southern India, which Mahendravarman I supported; he had temples cut into the rock, most of them dedicated to Siva. It is widely held to be a satire on sects that seemed degenerate or peculiar in his day. The Kapalikas stood for Tantrism, in which enlightenment was sought through unorthodox rituals involving liquor and ritual intercourse; the monk, in turn, wonders why Buddhism forbids liquor and women, and both Kapalikas call the Jains heretics.

The text also gives a view of life in seventh-century Kanchipuram, with references to the sound of drums, flower shops, festive taverns, temple towers and courts whose officials were sometimes bribed. English translations include those of Michael Lockwood and A. Vishnu Bhat, of 1981, and David Lorenzen, of 2001. A dance-theatre adaptation directed by Stella Uppal-Subbiah, which gave prominence to bharatanatyam, toured the United Kingdom in 2003 and 2004.
matteo-i-visconti: Matteo was the son of Teobaldo Visconti and Anastasia Pirovano. In August 1269 he married Bonacossa Borri, with whom he had many children, among them Galeazzo I, Luchino, Marco, Stefano and Giovanni, later archbishop of Milan. His great-uncle Ottone Visconti, archbishop and first lord of Milan, appointed him Captain of the People, and the citizens re-elected him to the office in 1289 and 1294.

After the death of William VII, Marquess of Montferrat, in 1292, Matteo took Casale and the lordships of Novara and Vercelli, though John of Monferrat soon drove the Ghibellines out again. Ottone's death in 1295 reopened the struggle between the Ghibellines and the Guelphs, led by the Della Torre family. In June 1302 a league of the Torriani and hostile cities, led by Alberto Scotti and Ghiberto da Correggio, gave the lordship of Milan to Guido della Torre; Matteo's house was looted and he spent several years in exile as a guest of the Scaliger family.

In 1311 he met King Henry VII at Asti. After Henry's soldiers defeated Guido della Torre in February, Henry sold Matteo the title of imperial vicar for Milan on 13 July 1311, and a league of Ghibelline cities followed, among them Como, Bergamo, Brescia, Cremona and Piacenza. Matteo had little military talent, but in October 1315 his sons Marco and Luchino defeated the Tuscan Guelphs on the Scrivia River near Voghera and took Pavia.

In 1317 Pope John XXII, in the bull Si fratrum, threatened with excommunication anyone who used the title of imperial vicar without papal consent, and Matteo took instead the title of General Lord of the Milanese People. The papal legate, Cardinal Bertrand du Poujet, proclaimed a crusade against the Visconti. In 1322 the pope charged Matteo with necromancy, and he was convicted in absentia after refusing to come to Avignon; the archbishop Aicardo da Camodeia condemned him and Galeazzo as heretics. At the end of May 1322 Matteo handed power to Galeazzo and retired to Crescenzago. He died on 24 June 1322.
matteo-maria-boiardo: Boiardo was born at or near Scandiano, in the present province of Reggio Emilia, the son of Giovanni di Feltrino and Lucia Strozzi. His mother was the sister of the humanist poet Tito Vespasiano Strozzi, and his grandfather Feltrino had been made Count of Scandiano by Niccolò III d'Este. The family moved to Ferrara, where he grew up until his father died in 1451. He entered the University of Ferrara early, learned Greek and Latin and was admitted doctor in philosophy and in law.

When his grandfather died in 1460, Matteo Maria and his cousin Giovanni inherited the fief of Scandiano. Joint administration led to family feuds, and in 1474 he narrowly escaped poisoning, instigated by his aunt Taddea Pio, Giovanni's mother. The lands were then divided and Boiardo became Lord of Scandiano.

Boiardo enjoyed the favour of Borso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara, who sent him to meet Frederick III in 1469 and took him in his train to visit Pope Paul II in 1471. In 1473 he joined the escort that brought Eleonora of Aragon to Ferrara to meet her husband Ercole.
