In 1476 he returned to Ferrara as Duke Ercole's companion, and in 1478 he married Taddea dei Gonzaga of Novellara, with whom he had six children.

In 1481 he became governor of Reggio, an office he held with success until his death, except for a brief interval when he was governor of Modena. The war between Ferrara and Venice and his concern for Scandiano made him give up the post for a time. In 1487 Ercole appointed him ducal emissary for Reggio. His administrative letters from that office form the largest part of his surviving correspondence.

Boiardo wrote Latin works for the Este, the Carmina de laudibus Estensium and the Pastoralia, dating from 1463–4, and his Amorum libri tres, 180 sonnets, canzoni and madrigals in the Petrarchan manner, followed the course of his love for Antonia Caprara. Around 1476 he began Orlando Innamorato. It is the first chivalric poem to fuse the Carolingian and Arthurian cycles deliberately, and it makes Orlando, hero of the Song of Roland, a lover. Love is its main theme, beside arms, magic, honour and adventure. The poem was left unfinished and drew sequels, above all Ludovico Ariosto's Orlando Furioso.

Taste later turned against it, and Francesco Berni's recasting in Tuscan of 1542 replaced the original for centuries. Anthony Panizzi's edition of 1830 restored the text. Boiardo died at Reggio in December 1494, the same year as Poliziano and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.
matteo-ricci: Matteo Ricci was born on 6 October 1552 in Macerata. He studied law in Rome for two years and entered the Society of Jesus at the Roman College in April 1571, where he also studied mathematics, cosmology and astronomy under Christopher Clavius. He sailed from Lisbon in March 1578 and reached Goa that September, and in 1582 he was summoned to Macau.

In 1583 Ricci and Michele Ruggieri settled at Zhaoqing at the invitation of the governor Wang Pan. He stayed until 1589, when a new viceroy expelled him. In 1584 he composed a first European-style world map in Chinese, and the two men are thought to have compiled the first Portuguese-Chinese dictionary. He reached Nanjing and Nanchang in 1595, and in August 1597 his superior Alessandro Valignano appointed him head of the China mission. He first reached Beijing on 7 September 1598 but could not enter the palace.

In 1601 the Wanli Emperor invited him to the court in recognition of his scientific skill, chiefly his predictions of solar eclipses. He had free access to the Forbidden City but never met the emperor, who gave him a stipend. He founded the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, the oldest Catholic church in Beijing, and converted a number of officials, the most prominent being the agronomist Xu Guangqi.

Ricci adopted the dress of the Confucian literati and argued that Chinese people had always believed in God and that Christianity completed their faith. He used the term Tiānzhǔ, Lord of Heaven, for God, and took an accommodating view of rites such as ancestor worship, which Dominican and Franciscan missionaries later challenged in the Chinese rites controversy. His book The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven argued that Confucianism and Christianity were not opposed, and his Chinese Euclid appeared in 1607.

Ricci died in Beijing on 11 May 1610. Ming law required foreigners who died in China to be buried in Macau, but Diego de Pantoja pleaded for a plot, and the Wanli Emperor granted one at a Buddhist temple. His journals were edited by Nicolas Trigault and published in 1615.
matter-of-britain: The Matter of Britain was one of the three great Western story cycles recalled repeatedly in medieval literature, with the Matter of France, concerning Charlemagne and his companions, and the Matter of Rome, drawn from classical mythology and history. The poet Jean Bodel named the three in his Chanson des Saisnes, writing that there are only three subject matters: that of France, that of Britain and that of great Rome. Its chronicles and chivalric romances, in prose and verse, flourished from the 12th to the 16th century.

Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th-century Historia Regum Britanniae is a central component. Geoffrey drew on earlier British texts, including the 9th-century Historia Brittonum, the earliest known source of the story of Brutus of Troy, which linked Britain to the heroes scattered after the Trojan War. He listed Coel Hen as a king of the Britons whose daughter Helena bore the future Emperor Constantine the Great, and he told how the post-Roman Britons under Arthur briefly conquered much of Europe. This pseudo-history gave the new Norman England a body of national myth, portraying the Norman Conquest as a restoration of the Britain of the Celtic Britons.

The Arthurian legend is the best-known part. Geoffrey and his successor Wace, together with Welsh and Breton tales such as the Mabinogion, became the foundation for the Arthurian romances that first emerged in northern France in the second half of the 12th century. Chrétien de Troyes and Robert de Boron introduced or popularised many of its motifs, among them the Grail, Camelot, Excalibur, Merlin and the love of Lancelot and Guinevere. The Vulgate Cycle of the early 13th century set out Arthur's kingdom and the quest for the Grail, in which Galahad, Perceval and Bors succeed.

Thomas Malory's 15th-century Le Morte d'Arthur established an English-language quasi-canon based on the French prose cycles. Interest largely waned by the end of the Middle Ages and survived mainly in England and, to some degree, France into the 17th century. The 19th-century Romantic revival brought the legend back, chiefly in Malory's telling.

Since the Celtic Revival, scholars have tried to link the Arthurian tales to Celtic mythology, identifying Morgan le Fay with the Welsh goddess Modron or the Irish Morrígan. Other schools read the Grail tradition as an allegory of spiritual growth, as Joseph Campbell did, or traced it to ritual, as Jessie L. Weston did in From Ritual to Romance in 1920, an interpretation no longer fashionable. Whether Arthur existed as a historical figure remains a long-running debate.
matterhorn: The Matterhorn is a large, near-symmetrical pyramid in the Pennine Alps, whose summit is 4,478 metres above sea level. It has four faces, roughly facing the four cardinal points, separated by the Hörnli, Furggen, Zmutt and Leone ridges. Three faces are on the Swiss side and one on the Italian side. It overlooks the town of Zermatt to the northeast and Breuil-Cervinia to the south. The nearby Theodul Pass has been a trade route since Roman times. The name comes from the German Matte, meadow, and Horn. Early maps of 1545 and 1548 labelled the mountain Mons Silvius. In August 1792 Horace-Bénédict de Saussure made the first measurement of its height, using a sextant and a chain spread on the Theodul glacier.

The Matterhorn was one of the last main Alpine peaks to be climbed, less because of its technical difficulty than because of the fear it inspired in early mountaineers. The first serious attempts were from the Italian side, led by Jean-Antoine Carrel and his uncle Jean-Jacques Carrel, who tried in 1857 and 1858. Edward Whymper, an English artist and engraver hired to sketch the mountains around Zermatt, first saw it in the summer of 1860 and made his first attempt in August 1861.

Whymper and his party left Zermatt on 13 July 1865, and made the first ascent by the Hörnli ridge. Whymper found it much easier than the Italian ridge. During the descent a sudden fall killed four of the seven climbers, a disaster that marked the end of the golden age of alpinism. Two days after the first ascent Jean-Antoine Carrel set out to prove that the Italian side could be climbed, with Amé Gorret, Jean-Baptiste Bich and Jean-Augustin Meynet.

Lucy Walker became the first woman to reach the summit on 22 August 1871. A party of three English mountaineers made the first ascent without guides on 23 July 1876. The north face was not climbed until 1931, and the west face, the highest of the four, was completely climbed only in 1962.

Mountaineers try to climb the Matterhorn every year, most of them from the Hörnli Hut by the northeast Hörnli ridge. It is estimated that over 500 people had died on it by the late 1980s. The mountain is mainly composed of gneiss, which belonged to the African plate before the Alpine orogeny. It has become an emblem of Switzerland and of the Alps, and has been part of the Swiss Federal Inventory of Natural Monuments since 1983.
matthaus-schiner: Schiner was born at Mühlebach, in what is now the Swiss canton of Valais, the son of Peter Schiner, a farmer and carpenter, and Anna Welschen. His uncle Nicholas Schiner, later Bishop of Sion, gave him his early instruction. The year of his birth is disputed, the statements differing by nearly twenty years, but as he was a priest by 1492 it cannot have been later than 1470. He became parish priest of Aernen in 1496 and canon and dean of the cathedral of Sion, and succeeded his uncle as bishop on 20 September 1499.

His diplomatic skill and influence on the Swiss Confederacy made him the right hand of Pope Julius II and Pope Leo X in their efforts to expel the French from Italy. For the alliance he arranged in 1511 he was made Bishop of Novara and cardinal. In 1512, as papal legate for Italy and Germany, he commanded a Swiss and Venetian army that drove the French from Milan and installed Maximilian Sforza as duke. When Louis XII retook Milan, Schiner led the Swiss to victory at the Battle of Novara in 1513 and received the margraviate of Vigevano.

He led the Swiss troops at the Battle of Marignano in 1515 against Francis I of France. In 1516 he raised another army with the aid of England but could not regain Milan, and went to London to build an alliance of the pope, the emperor, England and Spain, which came to nothing when the Swiss and the emperor made peace with France.

During his absence the French party at home, led by his enemy George Supersax, rose and drove him from Sion. He lived at Zürich from 1517 to 1519 and then mostly at the imperial court, supported the election of Emperor Charles V in 1519, was made bishop of Catania in November 1520, and in 1521 led Swiss troops in the imperial campaign for Milan. Pope Adrian VI called him to Rome as administrator of the States of the Church, and he died there of the plague on 1 October 1522 without seeing his diocese again. His widely scattered correspondence is the only writing he left.
matthew-baillie-begbie: Begbie was the son of an army colonel and spent his first seven years on the island of Mauritius before his parents brought him back to Great Britain. From the age of eleven to seventeen he attended Elizabeth College, Guernsey, with his brother Thomas Stirling Begbie. He took his first degree at Peterhouse, Cambridge, in mathematics and the classics, and was busy outside his studies with singing and amateur acting, dining societies, chess, rowing and tennis. He then read law at Lincoln's Inn and built a successful practice in London.

He reached Fort Victoria on 16 November 1858 with a commission dated 2 September 1858 and was sworn in at Fort Langley on 19 November by David Cameron, Chief Justice of Vancouver Island, as the new Colony of British Columbia was proclaimed. The Fraser Canyon Gold Rush and the Cariboo Gold Rush of 1861 brought prospectors in large numbers, and his court was central to establishing order. In his early years he also drafted legislation, among it the Aliens Act and the Gold Fields Act of 1859 and the Pre-emption Act of 1860.

In 1860 he found a Californian, William Marshall, guilty of assaulting a First Nations man on the testimony of First Nations witnesses alone, the first such verdict. He learned several Indigenous languages, held some trials in them without an interpreter, recognised Aboriginal marriage and let witnesses swear on objects sacred to them instead of the Bible.

In 1864 he presided at the trial of five Tsilhqot'in men of the Chilcotin War; juries found them guilty and he pronounced the mandatory death sentence. The British Columbia government exonerated the Chilcotin leaders in 2014. He was made a Knight Bachelor in 1875 and denied wrongdoing in land dealings at Cottonwood, known as the Cottonwood Scandal.

He kept sitting into his last illness and died in Victoria on 11 June 1894; he was buried in Ross Bay Cemetery after a funeral procession of unusual size. The name "the Hanging Judge" was attached to him only after his death. In 1886 he ruled that a law imposing very high licence fees discriminated against Chinese residents, since laundries were then overwhelmingly run by Chinese people, and a similar ruling two years later made Victoria renew the licences of Chinese pawnbrokers. Mount Begbie near Revelstoke bears his name; his statues at the Law Society of British Columbia and at New Westminster were removed in 2017 and 2019.
matthew-c-perry: Matthew Calbraith Perry was born on 10 April 1794 in Newport, Rhode Island, a son of Navy Captain Christopher Raymond Perry and Sarah Wallace Perry. His brother was Oliver Hazard Perry. He received a midshipman's warrant in 1809, at about fifteen, and served aboard USS President during the War of 1812, where a bursting cannon killed and wounded several men, Perry among the wounded.

After the war he served in the Mediterranean, in the Second Barbary War under Commodore William Bainbridge, and off West Africa and in the West Indies against piracy and the slave trade. On 25 March 1822 he sailed the schooner USS Shark to Key West and planted the American flag there.

Perry took a close interest in naval education and in the steam engine. He oversaw the building of the Navy's second steam frigate, USS Fulton, organised America's first corps of naval engineers and ran the first U.S. naval gunnery school from 1839 to 1841. He was called the Father of the Steam Navy. In 1841 he received the title of commodore, which, as the Navy had no rank above captain until 1857, carried considerable weight. In the Mexican–American War he captured Frontera and Tuxpan and led a landing force of 1,173 men against San Juan Bautista in June 1847.

In 1852 President Millard Fillmore sent him to open Japanese ports to American trade, by gunboat diplomacy if necessary. Whaling, trade with China, the search for coaling stations and the return of shipwrecked sailors were among the motives. Perry reached Uraga on 8 July 1853, refused to go to Nagasaki and delivered a letter for the Japanese ruler at Kurihama on 14 July. He returned on 13 February 1854 with ten ships and 1,600 men, landed at Kanagawa on 8 March, and signed the Convention of Kanagawa on 31 March. Afterwards he visited Hakodate and Shimoda, the two ports it opened.

Back in the United States, Congress voted him a reward of $20,000, and he published an account of the expedition in three volumes. His health failed in his last years, with arthritis, gout and cirrhosis of the liver, and he is known to have been an alcoholic. He died in New York City on 4 March 1858 of rheumatic fever that had spread to the heart, and was later reburied in Newport.

Japanese woodblock portraits showed him with blue eyeballs, a sign of the threatening in Japanese culture, and sometimes as a tengu. Over 90 per cent of Japanese schoolchildren can identify him. A monument at Yokosuka marks his landing place, and his diplomatic gifts from Japan are in the Smithsonian Institution.
matthew-iii-csak: Matthew was a son of the Palatine Peter I Csák, of the Csák kindred, which medieval chroniclers traced to Szabolcs, the second captain of the Hungarians. Around 1283 he and his brother Csák inherited their father's lands at Komárom and Szenic, and their uncles' estates around Nagytapolcsány, Hrussó and Tata. A diploma records that he was lame, either from birth or from a war wound. In 1291 he joined King Andrew III of Hungary's campaign against Austria, and the next year he recovered Pozsony and Detrekő for the king from the rebel Nicholas I Kőszegi.

Andrew made him master of the horse and ispán of Pozsony County, and in 1296 Palatine, but their relations soured and Matthew lost that office in 1297, though he went on styling himself Palatine. He enlarged his lands by purchase, pressure on neighbouring landowners and outright seizure, acquired Trencsén around the end of 1296 and set up a court of his own around 1297, usurping royal prerogatives. After the death of Andrew, the last male Árpád, on 14 January 1301, he backed in turn the Neapolitan claimant Charles and Wenceslaus of Bohemia, who granted him Trencsén and Nyitra counties.

In 1308 the papal legate Cardinal Gentile Portino da Montefiore persuaded him to accept Charles, who named him Palatine and then master of the treasury, yet Matthew kept away from the coronations and went on taking castles. He was excommunicated in 1311 after pillaging the lands around Buda. By then his domain held 14 counties and about 50 castles. On 15 June 1312 the king's armies defeated him and the sons of Amade Aba at the Battle of Rozgony.

Royal and Bohemian invasions in 1314 and 1315 failed to take his domain, and he held it until his death on 18 March 1321. His son had died before him, and his cousin Stephen Sternberg lost the lands to the king within months. The region was still called Matthew's Land, terra Matthei, into the 15th century. In the 19th-century Slovak national revival, writers such as Ľudovít Štúr made him a national hero, a view Slovak historiography rejected by 1923.
matthew-orsini: Matthew's origin is obscure. Older historiography, following a largely conjectured genealogy by the 19th-century scholar Karl Hopf, made him a member of the Roman House of Orsini and a grandson or son-in-law of Admiral Margaritus of Brindisi, who had conquered Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Ithaca in 1185, and held that he succeeded Margaritus after the admiral's disgrace in 1194. More recent research finds him most likely a native of Monopoli in Apulia, unrelated to Margaritus; the surname Orsini is attested in no primary source for him or his descendants.

The Aragonese version of the Chronicle of the Morea makes him a respected swine herder expelled from Monopoli who fled to Cephalonia with his followers and married the daughter of the Byzantine governor. The historian Andreas Kiesewetter thinks this may be close to the truth, and the Breve Chronicon de Rebus Siculis calls him a man of Monopoli. Brendan Oswald notes that such humble origins could explain why the family appears in the sources only as de Cefalonia.

The partition of the Byzantine Empire after the Fourth Crusade in 1204 assigned the Ionian Islands to Venice, which occupied Corfu in 1205. Matthew placed himself under Pope Innocent III in 1207 and, according to Venetian chroniclers of later centuries, accepted Venetian suzerainty two years later. He also turned to the Latin Empire of Constantinople, and after the death of Emperor Henry of Flanders in 1216 he sought papal protection while drawing close to Theodore Komnenos Doukas, the Greek ruler of the Epirote mainland, whose sister he married in 1227.

After Theodore's defeat at Klokotnitsa in 1230, Matthew became a vassal of the Principality of Achaea in 1236. He last appears in January 1238, when Pope Gregory IX urged him to defend Constantinople against the Empire of Nicaea. Count Richard Orsini is often taken for his son and successor, but the chronology makes this doubtful, and another ruler, possibly named Theodore, may have come between them as Richard's father.
matthias-corvinus: Matthias was born in Kolozsvár, now Cluj-Napoca in Romania, on 23 February 1443, the second son of John Hunyadi and Elizabeth Szilágyi. Scholars such as Gregory of Sanok and John Vitéz frequented the Hunyadi court, and under their influence he became an enthusiastic supporter of Renaissance humanism. In 1457 King Ladislaus the Posthumous had him imprisoned with his older brother Ladislaus Hunyadi, who was executed. The king then died unexpectedly, and Matthias's uncle Michael Szilágyi arrived at the Diet with 15,000 troops. The nobles, gathered on the frozen Danube, proclaimed the 14-year-old Matthias king on 24 January 1458.

Matthias took effective control of government within two weeks. He fought the Czech mercenaries who dominated Upper Hungary and Emperor Frederick III, who claimed Hungary for himself; a treaty of 1463 returned the Holy Crown, and Matthias was crowned on 29 March 1464. In 1468 he declared war on the Hussite King George of Bohemia and conquered Moravia, Silesia and Lusatia. The Catholic Estates proclaimed him King of Bohemia on 3 May 1469, but the Hussite lords elected Vladislaus Jagiellon. A treaty of 1478 confirmed the division of the Bohemian lands between them, and between 1482 and 1487 Matthias occupied Lower Austria.

He kept taxes very high, which provoked a rebellion in Transylvania in 1467. He maintained one of the earliest professional standing armies in medieval Europe, the Black Army, united the highest courts into one supreme court and promoted men for their abilities rather than their rank.

Matthias was the first non-Italian monarch to promote the Renaissance style in his realm, and his marriage to Beatrice of Naples strengthened Italian influence. From about 1479 his builders enlarged the castle of Buda and rebuilt the palace at Visegrád, and artists such as Andrea Mantegna and Filippino Lippi worked for him. His royal library, the Bibliotheca Corviniana, begun around 1465 under the librarian Martius Galeotti, was one of the largest collections of books in Europe. His nickname comes from the Latin corvus, raven, an emblem on the family coat of arms.

After his death on 6 April 1490 his conquests were lost within months, and Vladislaus Jagiellon was elected king on condition that he abolish Matthias's innovations, above all the extraordinary tax. Matthias remains a popular hero of Hungarian and Slovak folk tales as Matthias the Just.
matthias-holy-roman-emperor: Matthias was born in Vienna on 24 February 1557, the third son of Maximilian II, Holy Roman Emperor, and Maria of Spain. His brothers included Rudolf, later Emperor Rudolf II, Ernest, Maximilian, Albert and Wenceslaus. Almost nothing is known of his upbringing, though one of his teachers was the writer and historian Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq. When their father died the family's estates passed to Rudolf as the eldest, and the other sons received cash pensions and church or state appointments. Matthias married Archduchess Anna of Tyrol, and the marriage produced no surviving children.

In 1578 the States-General of the rebellious Netherlands provinces invited Matthias to be Governor-General, an arrangement made with Philippe III de Croÿ, Duke of Aarschot, and other moderates against the will of Philip II of Spain. Philip never recognised it. Matthias set down rules for religious peace in most of the United Provinces, and his work is noted in Article 13 of the 1579 Union of Utrecht, which made freedom of religion a local matter. He stayed as titular governor until 1581, when the rebels deposed Philip II.

Back in Austria from 1583, he failed in several attempts to become a bishop, and only after his brother Ernest took the Netherlands governorship in 1593 did he secure the government of Austria. There he faced Protestant estates defending their religious rights, heavy taxes and troops raised for the Long Turkish War. Peasants rose in Lower and Upper Austria in 1595 and 1597, and he forced them to submit with mercenary troops. He then followed a strict Counter-Reformation course, with Melchior Klesl as his chancellor.

From 1599 Matthias urged the childless Rudolf II in vain to arrange his succession. In 1606 the archdukes declared Rudolf insane and named Matthias head of the family. That year Matthias ended the conflict in Hungary by granting religious freedom there and guaranteeing Transylvania the right to elect its own princes. In April 1608 he marched on Prague, and the treaty of June 1608 left Rudolf Bohemia, Silesia and Lusatia while Matthias received Hungary, Austria and Moravia.

Matthias was crowned King of Bohemia on 23 May 1611 and, after Rudolf's death on 20 January 1612, was elected emperor. His rule was dominated by Klesl, who sought a compromise between Catholic and Protestant states. More intransigent Habsburgs, led by Archduke Maximilian, wanted the succession for Archduke Ferdinand, later Emperor Ferdinand II, who was elected King of Bohemia in June 1617. The Bohemian Protestant revolt led Matthias to imprison Klesl, but old and ailing he could not stop Maximilian's faction. He died of natural causes on 20 March 1619.
matthias-von-jagow: Matthias von Jagow came from the old noble von Jagow family of the Altmark and was born at Aulosen. He studied theology and law and for a time was dean of the nunnery at Spandau. He was elected Bishop of Brandenburg as successor to Hieronymus Schulz and Dietrich V of Hardenberg, both determined opponents of Martin Luther. The pope confirmed his election in 1532 on condition that he first be ordained, but Jagow, who had been ordained only as a subdeacon, never met that condition.

Although convinced of the need for church reform, he limited himself during the lifetime of the anti-reform Elector Joachim I to correcting abuses and improving the clergy. As the most influential advisor of Joachim's successor, Joachim II, he persuaded the elector to adopt Lutheranism, and on 1 November 1539 he gave him communion under both kinds, and the magistrates of Berlin on the following day. In 1541 he led the first church visitation in the Mark Brandenburg, through which the Reformation was carried out, and in the same year he married. Around 1535 he had a bishop's cap built on top of the keep of his residence, Ziesar Castle, as a sign of its church use.

Jagow died at Ziesar in 1544. Centuries later the sculptor Harro Magnussen made a bust of him as a secondary figure beside Joachim II in group 20 of the Siegesallee in Berlin, whose theme was the Reformation. As no portrait of the bishop survived, Magnussen asked Emperor William II to sit as the model, citing the bust of Johann Sebastian Bach beside Frederick the Great as a precedent; the emperor refused, and the bishop was shown as a bearded elderly man with a raised collar.
mattium: Its exact location is unknown. Tacitus places Mattium north of the river Adrana, the Eder, and following his description it is generally assumed to lie somewhere in the wider neighbourhood of Fritzlar in northern Hesse. Some linguistic analysis suggests that the names of the villages Maden and Metze and of the brook Matzoff may derive from Mattium, which would place it near them, but no archaeological find has yet given an exact location or confirmed either Tacitus or the linguistic argument.

The Altenburg, an ancient fortified site in the same neighbourhood, was often equated with Mattium in older literature. More recent research, in particular the dating of artefacts from the site, has concluded that it was abandoned decades before the Roman troops destroyed Mattium, and it is no longer considered a suitable candidate.

Tacitus mentions Mattium in Book I, chapter 56 of his Annals, describing the Roman campaign against the Chatti under Germanicus in 15 CE: the Roman army destroyed the caput gentis Mattium directly after crossing the Eder. The term caput gentis may denote a capital in the sense of a single large fortified settlement, but it could also refer to a central place of worship. In that case Mattium may have been a larger area of ritual sites and the settlements connected to them rather than one central settlement.

Mattium is not to be confused with Mattiacum, the modern Wiesbaden, also called Aquae Mattiacorum, the principal settlement of the Mattiaci. They were a separate tribe living between the Rhine and the Taunus range, and unlike the Chatti they were incorporated into the Roman Empire when the Limes Germanicus was built. Because Mattiaci could be understood as people from Mattium, some scholars believe they were related to the Chatti and had split off from them at an earlier time.
matvei-platov: Matvei Ivanovich Platov was born on 19 August 1753 (8 August by the old calendar) at Pribilyanskoe, into a family of Greek descent. He entered the service of the Don Cossacks in 1766 and became a yesaul in 1769. He distinguished himself in the Crimean campaign of 1771 and was given command of a Cossack regiment in 1772. Between 1774 and 1784 he fought the Crimean Tatars, twice serving under Alexander Suvorov in the Kuban Valley, Chechnya and Dagestan.

He received the Order of St George in 1790 for the capture of Ochakov and again for the storming of Izmail, and he became a major-general on 12 January 1793. Disgraced by Emperor Paul I through rumours spread by courtiers, he was exiled to Kostroma and held in the Peter and Paul Fortress before he was cleared and sent on the abortive Russian expedition to India of 1800, which reached only Orenburg. Under Alexander I he became ataman and moved the Cossack capital from Starocherkassk to Novocherkassk.

He commanded a Cossack corps at Eylau, Guttstadt and Friedland in 1806–1807, fought the Turks in the Danube valley in 1808–1809 and became General of Cavalry on 11 October 1809. In 1812 he covered the retreat of General Bagration's 2nd Western Army. At Borodino he and Fyodor Uvarov struck at the French left flank; the raid was judged a failure at the time, but it later emerged that it led Napoleon to hold back the Imperial Guard. For harrying the French retreat from Moscow he was made a Count of the Russian Empire.

Platov accompanied Alexander I to London, where he received a golden sword, and Sir Thomas Lawrence painted his full-length portrait for the Waterloo Chamber at Windsor Castle. He then settled in Novocherkassk, founded a school there and headed the local administration. He died on 15 January 1818 at Epanchitskoe, near Taganrog, and was buried in Novocherkassk Cathedral. Gavrila Derzhavin dedicated his last ode to him, and he appears in Leskov's folk-styled tale Levsha of 1881. The international airport of Rostov-on-Don, opened in 2017, bears his name.
matyas-rakosi: Mátyás Rákosi, born Rosenfeld on 9 March 1892 in Ada, then in the Kingdom of Hungary, was the fourth son of a grocer, József Rosenfeld, and Cecília Léderer. His father, a supporter of the Party of Independence and '48, changed the family name to Rákosi in 1903. A diligent student, Rákosi finished school in Szeged in 1910, studied external trade, and won scholarships to Hamburg in 1912 and London in 1913. He joined the Hungarian Social Democratic Party in 1910.

After the First World War he joined the communist movement of Béla Kun. During the 133-day Hungarian Soviet Republic of 1919 he was a people's commissar and took part in its military campaigns against Czechoslovakia and Romania. He fled on 2 August 1919 and worked in the Soviet Union for the Communist International. Arrested in 1924 after trying to return to Hungary, he spent more than fifteen years in prison before being allowed to leave for the Soviet Union in 1940.

Returning in 1945 as the Red Army drove the German forces out, Rákosi became General Secretary of the Hungarian Communist Party and deputy prime minister. The party was beaten in the free election by the Independent Smallholders' Party, but Moscow insisted that the Communists hold key posts. From 1947 they pressed the other parties to exclude those unwilling to cooperate, on grounds that they were fascists or sympathisers. The phrase salami tactics was later attached to Rákosi, though no verified source for it has been found. In 1948 the Social Democrats were forced to merge into the Hungarian Working People's Party, and in 1949 Hungary was proclaimed a people's republic.

His government was loyal to the Soviet Union and built a personality cult modelled on Stalin's. Hundreds of thousands were imprisoned and thousands died. Show trials claimed victims including his former lieutenant László Rajk. After Stalin's death in 1953 Imre Nagy became prime minister at Moscow's wish, but Rákosi used his post as First Secretary to block reform and secured Nagy's removal in 1955. Khrushchev's secret speech of February 1956 fatally weakened him, and he resigned in July 1956.

Rákosi left for the Soviet Union, and the Hungarian Revolution broke out about three months later. János Kádár, who came to power after its suppression, refused to let him return. He lived in Tokmok, Arzamas and finally Gorky. Offered return in 1970 on condition that he stay out of politics, he refused, and he died in Gorky on 5 February 1971. His ashes were secretly returned to Budapest, where the gravestone bears only his initials. He is generally seen in Hungary as a symbol of tyranny and oppression.
mau-mau-rebellion: Land was the first British interest in Kenya, which had some of the richest agricultural soils in the world, in districts where Europeans could live permanently. Kenya was claimed as a protectorate by a proclamation of 1 July 1895 and declared a colony in 1920. Kikuyu squatters formed most of the labour on settler farms, and from 1918 a series of Resident Native Labourers Ordinances curtailed their rights. The Ordinance of 1939 removed their remaining tenancy rights and let settlers demand 270 days' labour a year.

Political organisation grew in step. The Kenya African Study Union was founded on 1 October 1944 and became the Kenya African Union in 1946. Many organisers were ex-soldiers who had fought for Britain in Ceylon, Somalia and Burma, and who returned to find that they were unpaid and unrecognised, while British counterparts received medals and land.

The Kenya Land and Freedom Army, called Mau Mau by others, was made up mainly of Kikuyu, Meru and Embu fighters. The origin of the name is uncertain. The British and much international opinion saw it as a savage tribal cult. On 20 October 1952 Governor Evelyn Baring declared a State of Emergency, and Operation Jock Scott arrested Jomo Kenyatta and about 180 other identified leaders. Hundreds, then thousands, of adherents fled to the forests of the Aberdares and around Mount Kenya, where they formed platoons. In May 1953 General George Erskine was sent to restore order.

The British screened suspects in camps, the system known as the Pipeline, which developed into what has been described as a British gulag. Villagisation concentrated rural people in fortified villages, and the Swynnerton Plan created larger family holdings. The capture of Field Marshal Dedan Kimathi on 21 October 1956 signalled the defeat of Mau Mau and essentially ended the military campaign. Suppression cost Britain £55 million and at least 11,000 deaths, including 1,090 executions by hanging, with some estimates far higher. The war also set rebels against African loyalists within the Kikuyu community.

In June 1956 a land reform enlarged Kikuyu holdings and the ban on Africans growing coffee was relaxed. Direct election of African members to the Legislative Assembly followed, and a conference at Lancaster House in January 1960 accepted majority rule. Historians disagree on how far the rebellion hastened independence: a common view holds that continued colonial rule would have needed more force than the British public would tolerate, while others stress the growth of nationalism.

Mau Mau remained banned until September 2003. On 6 June 2013 the British government announced a settlement with 5,228 claimants, worth £19.9 million, and support for a memorial in Nairobi, while denying liability. Its place in Kenyan memory has been contested since independence.
mau-movement: Mau means resolute or firm in Samoan, and the movement's motto was Samoa mo Samoa, Samoa for the Samoans. Its first form arose from a dispute in 1908 between the German administration and the Samoan Council of Chiefs over a copra business owned by Samoans. Lauaki Namulau'ulu Mamoe, deposed by Governor Wilhelm Solf, formed the Mau a Pule on Savai'i; after a peace meeting aboard a German ship he and other leaders were exiled in 1909 to the Marianas, and Lauaki died on the way home in 1915.

New Zealand forces took Western Samoa in 1914. In 1919 some 7,500 Samoans, about 22 per cent of the population, died of influenza after an infected ship was allowed to dock at Apia, and the epidemic deepened distrust of an administration many Samoans already saw as incompetent and dishonest.

The revived movement drew its strength from the matai, the heads of families, and from Samoans of mixed parentage such as the merchant Olaf Frederick Nelson, who formed the Samoan League, O le Mau, in Apia in 1926. Village committees of chiefs and talking men formed an alternative government, and by the late 1920s around 85 per cent of Samoans were in open resistance. Members boycotted imports, refused taxes and ignored officials; when 400 were arrested, so many others gave themselves up that the jails could not hold them. Nelson was exiled with Alfred Smyth and Edwin Gurr.

In December 1929 New Zealand police fired on a peaceful procession welcoming Smyth home. Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III was shot in the back while calling for calm; eleven Samoans died and about 50 were wounded, and a policeman was clubbed to death. Dying, he told his followers not to avenge his blood, as it was spilt in peace. As the men hid from arrests and from marines sent in January 1930, the Women's Mau carried on its work, and a truce was declared on 12 March 1930.

Repression eased after Labour won the New Zealand election of 1935, and an elected Samoan Fono was opened in 1936. When Western Samoa became independent in 1962, Tupua Tamasese Meaole, younger brother of the Mau leader, became its first co-head of state. In 2002 Prime Minister Helen Clark apologised to Samoa for the influenza epidemic, the shooting of the Mau protesters and the banishing of chiefs. In American Samoa the Navy barred the Mau leader Samuel Sailele Ripley from returning, and the movement there was suppressed.
maubeuge: Maubeuge is a commune in the Nord department of northern France. It lies on both banks of the Sambre, which is canalised at this point, 36 km east of Valenciennes and about 9 km from the Belgian border. Its Latin name was Malbodium, from the Old Frankish Malboden, meaning assizes of Boden. Because of its position near the border, the railway station has lines towards Mons and Charleroi in Belgium.

The town owes its origin to Maubeuge Abbey, a double monastery for men and women founded in the 7th century, whose founder's relics are kept in the church. The area later belonged to the territory of Hainaut. As part of the Spanish Netherlands the town changed hands several times before it was ceded to France in the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1678. Louis XIV had it extensively fortified as part of Vauban's pré carré, a plan that protected the northern border of France with a double line of fortresses.

In 1793 Prince Josias of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld besieged Maubeuge, and the siege was lifted by the victory of Wattignies, which a monument in the town commemorates. An attempt on the town in 1814 failed, but it capitulated after vigorous resistance during the Hundred Days. After the War of 1870 a new fortress was built, later modernised and enlarged, with an entrenched camp of 18 miles in perimeter. Its forts were besieged by the German Empire in World War I. In World War II bombardments in May 1940 destroyed 90 per cent of the town centre, and fighting occurred again around its outskirts in early September 1944, involving units of the U.S. 1st Infantry Division.

The town was rebuilt after the war, and the new Hôtel de Ville was completed in 1970. Maubeuge has foundries, forges and blast furnaces, together with manufacture of machine tools and porcelain. It was the early home of the cyclist Maurice Garin, winner of the first Tour de France in 1903, who began his career with the local cycling club in 1892.
maues: Maues's name is known mainly from his coins, in the Gandhari form Moa and the Greek form Maúēs, both variants of the Saka name *Mava, meaning tiger and hero. The Taxila copper plate gives it as Moga, from the Saka *Mauka with the same meaning, and the Mathura lion capital inscription calls him Mevaki Miyika. The Sakas were nomadic Eastern Iranian peoples, closely associated with the Pahlavas. Some scholars, following Sten Konow's edition of the Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum (1929), have suggested that Maues was of Kamboja lineage; others see him as an Iranian from the east, Parthian, Sistani Persian or Saka.

How and when Maues reached India is uncertain. The Han Shu records that when the Ta Yüeh-chih turned west and expelled the king of the Sai, the Sai moved south and crossed the Suspended Crossing. Inscriptions bearing Maues's name in the Chilas and Gilgit area suggest that this route, from the Pamirs into the Gilgit valley, was used in his time.

Maues, the first recorded ruler of the Sakas in the Indus region, took the title Great King of Kings, an enlarged form of a traditional Persian royal title. He seized key cities along the Indus from the Indo-Greek kingdoms, among them Taxila in Punjab and Pushkalavati, the capital of Gandhara; at Taxila he overstruck coins of Archebius and Apollodotus II. Saka power reached as far as Mathura during his reign. The Moga inscription is dated in the seventy-eighth year of the Great King, the Great Moga, and an inscription at Maira in the Salt Range may name him as Moasa.

Some of his coins were issued jointly with a queen, Machene, who may have been a daughter of one of the Indo-Greek houses, and the Indo-Greek king Artemidoros called himself son of Maues on his own coins. A few square coins show a seated figure holding a sword, more probably the king himself than an early image of the Buddha. Others carry the lion, a Buddhist symbol since the Mauryan king Ashoka, and the bull of Shiva, which suggests wide religious tolerance; whether his support for Buddhism was sincere or political is unclear.
maui: Maui is the second-largest island in the Hawaiian archipelago, with an area of 1,883 square kilometres. Once part of Maui Nui, it is dominated by two volcanic features, Haleakalā in the southeast and the West Maui Mountains in the northwest, joined by an isthmus about six miles wide that gives the island its nickname, the Valley Isle. Like the other Hawaiian Islands it was formed by volcanism associated with the Hawaii hotspot, and is a volcanic doublet, made of two shield volcanoes that overlapped. In Native Hawaiian tradition the navigator Hawaiʻiloa named the island after his son, who was himself named for the demigod Māui; its earlier name was ʻIhikapalaumaewa.

Polynesians from Tahiti were the original inhabitants, and they introduced the kapu system, a strict social order that affected all aspects of life and became the core of Hawaiian culture. The island's central position gave it a decisive place in Hawaiian history. In 1790 Kamehameha I, king of Hawaiʻi island, invaded Maui and fought the inconclusive Battle of Kepaniwai. He returned to Hawaiʻi to fight a rival and subdued Maui a few years later.

James Cook sighted Maui on 26 November 1778 but found no suitable landing, and the first European ashore was the Comte de Lapérouse, on 29 May 1786 at what became La Perouse Bay. Traders, whalers, loggers of sandalwood and missionaries followed. The missionaries, who began arriving from New England in 1823, settled at Lahaina, then the Hawaiian capital. They devised the Hawaiian alphabet to translate a Bible, ran a printing press in Lahaina and began recording history that had been passed down orally. They opened the Lahainaluna Mission School in 1831, which still exists.

During the height of the whaling era, from 1843 to 1860, Lahaina was a major centre: in one season over 400 ships visited, with up to 100 anchored at once. Whaling declined steeply at the end of the 19th century as petroleum replaced whale oil. Maui was part of the Hawaiian Kingdom, the Republic of Hawaii, the Hawaiian territory and then the state of Hawaii, and during the Second World War, in 1943–1944, over 100,000 soldiers were based there.

Tourism is the island's major industry, and agriculture has long included sugar and pineapple. Sugar production ended in 2016. Haleakalā National Park, Hāna and the Hāna Highway, and ʻĪao Valley are among its principal sights. The summit of Haleakalā has an observatory, the first astronomical facility in Hawaii. In August 2023 wildfires destroyed much of the town of Lahaina.
maule-river: The Maule, called Río Maule and named from a Mapudungun word meaning rainy, is about 240 kilometres long, and its basin covers around 20,600 square kilometres, of which thirty per cent lies in the Andean range. It rises in Laguna del Maule in Talca Province at an altitude of 2,200 metres, near the border with Argentina. It flows westward and is soon joined by the Melado River, and further on by the Colorado, Claro, Puelche and Cipreses rivers.

Before it reaches the central valley the river is dammed into the Colbún dam lake, which feeds the hydroelectric power station of the same name. Further on it is joined by another river named Claro and by the Loncomilla, which receives the Putagán, the Perquilauquén, the Purapel and the Cauquenes among its tributaries. In its lower reaches it receives one modest tributary, the Estero de los Puercos, and ends at the Pacific Ocean north of the city of Constitución.

The river is linked to Chile's pre-Hispanic times, its conquest, its colonial period, its wars of Independence and its agriculture, including wine and traditional crops. It marked the southern limit of the Inca Empire. The Maule Region takes its name from the river, and many people notable in Chilean history were born there. The Valley of Maule is a viticultural region, a subregion of the Central Valley.

The Maule has been called Chile's literary river par excellence, and "the river of the fogs" has given its name to the region. Many poets, writers, historians, journalists, composers and folk musicians were born or settled in the Maule Region, and many Latin American stories have the river as their setting or protagonist. The Chilean wine palm, Jubaea chilensis, was once present in the basin, but the growth of the human population has restricted this endangered tree to a smaller range that still includes some of the northern part of the Maule Region.
mauretania-sitifensis: The province was formed from the eastern part of Mauretania Caesariensis, the stretch from Saldae on the coast to the river Ampsaga, and took its name from the inland town of Setifis. It covered about 17,800 square miles at first. Its farmland was good, above all for cereals, and the grain was shipped out through the port of Saldae, the province's outlet to the Mediterranean.

In the time of Constantine the Great, Mauretania Sitifensis belonged to the administrative Diocese of Africa, under the Praetorian prefecture of Italy. The fourth century brought it great economic growth, which lasted until the Vandal conquest. It was also a place of religious contest: the Christian denomination known as Donatism challenged the Roman Church, which had become the main local faith after Constantine, while Setifis was a centre of Mithraism.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire some areas of the province came under Vandal and later Byzantine control, but most of it was ruled by Berber kingdoms such as the Kingdom of Altava. Only the coast around Saldae and Setifis remained fully Romanized. Under Byzantine rule the province shrank to its coastal section, about a third of its original area. In 578 the Patricius Gennadius, appointed magister militum Africae and later the first exarch of Africa, defeated the Romano-Moorish kingdom of Garmul and enlarged the territory again.

Setifis is the modern city of Setif in Algeria. The province's many ancient bishoprics, among them the metropolitan see of Sitifis and the sees of Saldae, Assava at Hammam-Guergour, Arae in Mauretania at Ksar-Tarmounth and Zabi at Bechilga, are listed in the Annuario Pontificio as titular sees.
mauri: Mauri was the Latin name for the Berber population of the Kingdom of Mauretania in the western Maghreb. Strabo, writing in the early 1st century, gives Mauri as the people's own name, adopted into Latin, and Maurusii as the Greek one. The name first meant the Berber population of present-day Morocco, but as the kingdom grew it was also applied to those of Algeria, who belonged to the Numidian tribal groups. Both names probably cover the first Berber-speaking peoples; the oldest Libyco-Berber inscriptions date to around the 3rd century BCE.

Under Rome the region was later divided into Mauretania Caesariensis and Mauretania Tingitana. Mauri from beyond the frontier crossed the Strait of Gibraltar to raid Baetica in southern Spain in the early 170s and again under Commodus, when they besieged Singilia Barba. Mauri cavalry served in Aurelian's army against Zenobia in 272, and units of Equites Mauri were later stationed along the Persian and Danube frontiers. Others resisted Rome: Maximian campaigned against them for two years in 296–297, and in 372 the chieftain Firmus revolted. His brother Gildo helped Theodosius the Elder defeat him, rose to command in Africa and rebelled in turn in 397.

Under the Vandals the Mauri took much of the interior and all the land west of Caesarea. After Belisarius conquered the Vandal kingdom in 533–534 they raided again, and in 544 the massacre of chiefs of the Levathi at a parley set off a rising in which the general Solomon was killed. John Troglita defeated the revolt in 546–547, but further risings followed in 563 and 569 and under the Emperor Maurice.

Mauri resistance seems to have continued for about 50 years after the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb ended Byzantine rule in the late 600s. The Chronicle of 754 still names the Mauri, but by the High Middle Ages the name had largely dropped out of Western documents, and Christian writers applied its descendant, Moors, to the Muslim populations of the Maghreb and the Iberian Peninsula. In 1903 French officials named the colony of Mauritania after the ancient kingdom, though it lies far to the south of it.
maurice-bishop: Maurice Rupert Bishop was born on 29 May 1944 on Aruba, where his father Rupert, from north-east Grenada, worked in the oil refinery. The family returned to Grenada in 1950 and opened a small shop in St. George's. Bishop won a government scholarship to the Presentation Brothers' College, edited the newspaper Student Voice, and admired the Cuban Revolution of 1959. In 1962 he and Bernard Coard created the Grenada Assembly of Youth Fighting for Truth.

In December 1963 he went to the University of London to study law, and in England he read Marx, Lenin and Mao Zedong. He returned to Grenada in December 1970 and defended striking nurses. In January 1973 the movement he had helped organise merged with two others to form the New JEWEL Movement, and he and Unison Whiteman became its joint coordinating secretaries.

On 18 November 1973, known as Bloody Sunday, police and the paramilitary Mongoose Gang beat Bishop and other leaders of the movement. On 21 January 1974, Bloody Monday, his father was shot dead during a demonstration against Prime Minister Eric Gairy. In 1976 Bishop was elected to Parliament and served as Leader of the Opposition until 1979. On 13 March 1979 the movement deposed Gairy while he was addressing the United Nations, and Bishop became prime minister and suspended the constitution.

His government formed a partnership with Cuba and began a new international airport financed with Cuban money and labour. It created the National Women's Organization, gave women equal pay and paid maternity leave, and made sex discrimination illegal. It held no elections and restricted the press and the opposition. US President Ronald Reagan accused Grenada of planning to use the airport's runway for Soviet military aircraft.

In September 1983 a faction led by Deputy Prime Minister Bernard Coard tried to make Bishop step down or share power. He refused, and was placed under house arrest on 13 October. On 19 October crowds freed him and he seized Fort Rupert, but Coard sent troops, who captured him and seven others, including his partner Jacqueline Creft. A firing squad of the People's Revolutionary Army shot them in the fort's courtyard, and their bodies were partly burned at Calivigny. After an appeal from regional states and Governor-General Sir Paul Scoon, Reagan launched an invasion within days. In 2009 Grenada's international airport was renamed Maurice Bishop International Airport.
maurice-bishop-international-airport: The airport stands on Point Salines, the south-western point of Grenada, in the parish of St. George; the capital, St. George's, lies about 8 kilometres to the north. It was designed to replace the obsolete Pearls Airport on the north side of the island and was championed from 1979 by Prime Minister Maurice Bishop. The Grenadian government said that long-range jets carrying tourists could not land on the short, geographically difficult runway at Pearls, so visitors had to change to smaller regional planes. It hoped direct flights from Europe and North America would raise tourism. A Canadian firm designed the airport, specialised contracts went to European contractors, and two private American firms took part.
President Ronald Reagan cited the project as evidence that Grenada meant to let Soviet military aircraft use it as a way point to Cuba, pointing in part to the Cuban workers building it.

The unfinished airport was the jump-off point for the United States invasion of Grenada in October 1983. The event that precipitated the invasion was not the airport but a violent coup in which Bishop was killed. The American justification was the perceived threat to American medical students at St. George's University, whose campus is a short distance from the airfield.

At dawn on 25 October 1983 more than 500 Rangers of the 1st and 2nd Battalions of the 75th Ranger Regiment made a low-altitude parachute assault onto the airport. Despite resistance from the People's Revolutionary Army and armed Cuban construction workers, they secured their objectives quickly. From 2:05 p.m. United States Air Force C-141 transports landed and unloaded six battalions of paratroopers of the 82nd Airborne Division.

After the invasion the airport was completed with 19 million dollars of American assistance, and it received its first commercial passenger plane on 28 October 1984. In 2009 the National Democratic Congress government renamed it after Bishop, in the presence of his mother Alimenta Bishop. It lies 12 metres above sea level and has one asphalt runway, 10/28, measuring 2,744 by 45 metres. It houses the Grenada outstation of the Eastern Caribbean Civil Aviation Authority.
maurice-duke-of-saxe-zeitz: Maurice was born in Dresden on 28 March 1619, the youngest surviving son of John George I, Elector of Saxony, and his second wife, Magdalene Sibylle of Prussia, and a member of the House of Wettin. He was educated with his brothers at the electoral court in Dresden, where Field Marshal Kurt of Einsiedel took a leading part among his teachers. From August 1642 to September 1645 he and his brother Christian made a Grand Tour through northern Germany and the Netherlands, and soon after his return Prince Ludwig I of Anhalt-Köthen chose him as a member of the Fruitbearing Society.

In 1650 the Teutonic Knights appointed him to their Bailiwick of Thuringia. On 19 November 1650 in Dresden he married Sophie Hedwig of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Glücksburg, while his brother Christian married her sister Christiana; Heinrich Schütz composed the opera Paris und Helena for the occasion. Both sons of this marriage died as infants. On 3 July 1656 in Weimar he married Dorothea Maria of Saxe-Weimar, a daughter of Duke Wilhelm, and they had ten children.

John George I's will of 20 July 1652 ordered a division of the Albertine lands, which was carried out in Dresden on 22 April 1657, and Maurice became the first duke at Zeitz. He chose the state scientist and theologian Veit Ludwig von Seckendorff as his chancellor and president of his consistory, and the dramatist Johann Sebastian Mitternacht as court preacher. To give himself a fitting residence he had the old bishop's castle removed and a new baroque palace, Schloss Moritzburg, built in its place between 1657 and 1678. On 14 June 1676 in Wiesenburg he married for a third time, Sophie Elisabeth of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Wiesenburg; the marriage was childless.

Maurice died in Dresden on 4 December 1681. Several of his children died in infancy. His son Maurice Wilhelm became Duke of Saxe-Zeitz, Christian August rose to be a cardinal, Archbishop of Gran and Primate of Hungary, and Frederick Heinrich inherited Pegau and Neustadt. His daughter Erdmuthe Dorothea married Duke Christian II of Saxe-Merseburg in 1679.
maurice-elector-of-saxony: Maurice was the fourth child but first son of the future Henry IV, Duke of Saxony, and his Protestant wife, Catherine of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. His uncle Duke George had him educated as a Catholic, but in 1536 his father became a Protestant and, on succeeding George in 1539, made the duchy Protestant. In 1539 Maurice went to live at Torgau with his cousin John Frederick I, Elector of Saxony, whom he despised. With another cousin, Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse, he formed a lifelong friendship. On 9 January 1541 he married Philip's eldest daughter, Agnes, at Marburg.

Maurice succeeded his father on 18 August 1541. He joined the imperial army in campaigns in 1542, 1543 and 1544, while confiscating Church property at home. From the wealth of dissolved monasteries he founded the princes' schools at Schulpforta, Meissen and Grimma. He refused to join the Protestant Schmalkaldic League, largely, it is generally held, from hatred of John Frederick and the emperor's promise of the Saxon electorate.

When Charles V placed John Frederick under the Imperial Ban in 1546, Maurice undertook to enforce it. He occupied the electorate almost without a fight, and at the Battle of Mühlberg on 24 April 1547 the imperial forces captured both John Frederick and Philip of Hesse. By the Capitulation of Wittenberg John Frederick ceded the electorate and large lands, and on 4 June 1547 Maurice was raised to elector in a brief ceremony in the field camp. Philip, to whom he had promised that he would not be imprisoned, was taken prisoner, and Maurice was called a Judas by his compatriots. He was formally invested at the Diet of Augsburg on 25 February 1548.

Angered by Charles's plans to restore Catholicism and by Philip's continued imprisonment, Maurice used a commission to subdue Magdeburg in 1550 to raise an army. In January 1552 he agreed the Treaty of Chambord with Henry II of France, who then took Metz, Toul, Verdun and Cambrai. In March the rebels overran southern Germany and forced Charles to flee over the Alps and free Philip. Maurice then negotiated with Ferdinand I, and the Peace of Passau of August 1552 provisionally guaranteed the Lutheran position.

Maurice then sided again with Ferdinand and other princes against Albert Alcibiades of Brandenburg-Kulmbach, who had rejected the Passau armistice. At the Battle of Sievershausen on 9 July 1553 Maurice won, but was shot in the stomach from behind and died two days later in the field camp, aged 32. With no surviving male heir, he was succeeded as elector by his brother Augustus.
maurice-emperor: Maurice was born in Arabissus in Cappadocia in 539, the son of a man named Paul, and contemporary sources call him a native Greek speaker. He came to Constantinople as a notary and served the commander of the imperial bodyguard, Tiberius, and when Tiberius was named Caesar in 574 Maurice succeeded him in that command. In late 577, with no military experience, he was made commander-in-chief in the east and fought the war against Sasanian Persia. He failed to reach Ctesiphon in 581 and quarrelled with the Ghassanid ruler al-Mundhir III, whom he accused of treason, a charge modern historians dismiss.

The dying Tiberius II named Maurice his heir and son-in-law, and Maurice was crowned on 13 August 582. He inherited a bankrupt empire at war with Persia, paying the Avars 80,000 gold solidi a year, while the Slavs ravaged the Balkans. In 590 the Persian king Hormizd IV was overthrown and his son Khosrow II fled to Constantinople. Although the Senate advised against it, Maurice helped him regain his throne, and in 591 the combined forces defeated the rebel Bahram Chobin. Khosrow ceded western Armenia, and the empire no longer paid tribute to Persia.

From 591 Maurice turned to the Balkans, retaking Singidunum in 592 and crossing the Danube, the first Roman emperor to do so in over two centuries. In the west he created the Exarchate of Italy in 584, against the Lombards, and the Exarchate of Africa in 591. His fiscal measures were unpopular: in 588 he cut army pay by a quarter, and the troops on the Persian front mutinied, and about 599 he refused to pay a small ransom for 12,000 soldiers held by the Avars, who killed them.

In autumn 602 Maurice ordered the army to winter beyond the Danube, and the exhausted troops mutinied and proclaimed an officer named Phocas. Maurice left Constantinople by ship on 22 November, Phocas was crowned on 23 November, and Maurice was captured and murdered at Chalcedon on 27 November 602 after watching five of his sons executed. Khosrow II used the murder as a pretext for a war of twenty-six years that devastated both empires before the Arab conquests. The Strategikon, a manual of war, is traditionally attributed to Maurice, though some historians now think it the work of his brother or another general.
maurice-fitzgerald-lord-of-lanstephan: Maurice was the second-eldest son of Gerald FitzWalter, known as Gerald de Windsor, Constable of Pembroke, and of Nest ferch Rhys, a princess of Deheubarth of the Welsh royal House of Dinefwr. He was born around 1105 and became a Welsh Marcher lord, one of the Cambro-Norman barons of the borderlands. He later held the lordships of Maynooth and Naas in Ireland as well as Llanstephan in Wales.

In 1136 he fought beside his elder brother William FitzGerald and his half-brother Robert FitzStephen, constable of Cardigan, under Robert FitzMartin at the Battle of Crug Mawr. Llansteffan Castle, above the estuary of the River Tywi where it enters Carmarthen Bay, was taken from Maurice and William, Lord of Emlyn, the leading Norman settlers of the district, by Maredudd ap Gruffydd in 1146; the Normans recovered it in 1158.

When Diarmait Mac Murchada, the deposed King of Leinster exiled by the High King of Ireland, sought Cambro-Norman help to win back his throne, Maurice joined the invasion of 1169. He helped Robert FitzStephen at the Siege of Wexford. His nephew Raymond, second-in-command to Strongbow, took the leading part in the capture of Waterford and the assault on Dublin in 1171, and Maurice and his sons fought at Dublin too. He died around September 1176.

Older authorities name his wife as Alice, daughter of Arnulf de Montgomery, said to have been with him and their sons in Ireland in 1171, but the historian Curtis could find no source for her, and her existence is doubted. Seven children are listed, among them Thomas, Gerald, William, Maurice, Alexander and Robert FitzMaurice and a daughter, Nesta, who married Hervey de Montmorenci.

His son Gerald FitzMaurice, 1st Lord of Offaly, was the forebear of the FitzGerald and FitzMaurice Earls of Kildare and Dukes of Leinster. The first Earldom of Desmond in Munster grew from the lands of his eldest son Thomas, whose son John FitzMaurice FitzThomas, killed at the Battle of Callann, was the first Baron Desmond; the Knights of Glin and of Kerry descend from the same line.
maurice-fitzthomas-fitzgerald-1st-earl-o: Maurice was the second son of Thomas FitzMaurice FitzGerald, 2nd Baron Desmond, and his wife Margaret, who belonged either to the family of Barry or to that of de Burgh, a point still disputed. His father died in 1298, while Maurice was a child, and in 1307 he succeeded his elder brother Thomas FitzGerald, 3rd Baron Desmond, as 4th Baron, inheriting great wealth and large estates. Called Maurice the Great, he was also captain of Desmond Castle in Kinsale. In 1312 he married Lady Katherine, a daughter of Richard de Burgh, 2nd Earl of Ulster.

By 1326 there were rumours of a plot to make him King of Ireland, which modern historians tend to dismiss. On 27 August 1329, by letters patent dated at Gloucester, he was created Earl of Desmond and confirmed in the county palatine of Kerry, part of a Crown policy of winning the magnates over with earldoms. Summoned in 1330 by the Lord Justice, John Darcy, 1st Baron Darcy de Knayth, he campaigned against Irish rebels, routing the O'Nolans and O'Murroughs in Wicklow.

He introduced coigne and livery, the quartering of troops on the people they were sent to protect. Fresh rumours in 1331 led the Crown to imprison him for over 18 months, during which it took the lordship of Dunamark at the head of Bantry Bay.

In 1345 he presided over an assembly of Anglo-Irish magnates at Callan, ignored a summons to the Irish Parliament and attacked Nenagh. For two years his defeat was the Crown's main concern. He surrendered on a promise that his life would be spared, while other rebels, Sir Eustace le Poer among them, were hanged.

Deciding it could not govern Ireland without the magnates, the Crown released him in 1348 and pardoned him in 1349, and his loyalty was not questioned again. In July 1355 he was appointed Lord Justice of Ireland for life, but he died in Dublin Castle on 25 January 1356 and was buried in the Church of the Friars-preachers in Tralee. He married three times; his sons included Maurice FitzGerald, 2nd Earl of Desmond, by his first wife, and Gerald FitzGerald, 3rd Earl of Desmond, known as Gerald the Poet, by his third.
maurice-frydman: Maurice Frydman, Maurycy Frydman or Frydman-Mor in Polish, was a Polish Jew born in Warsaw, then in the Russian Empire, who later converted to Hinduism. He came to India in the late 1930s as a Jewish refugee. An engineer and a successful capitalist, he was managing director of the Mysore State Government Electrical Factory in Bangalore before Hindu philosophy won him over and he became a sannyasi.

Frydman became close to the Raja of Aundh, Bhawanrao Shriniwasrao Pant Pratinidhi, and his son Apa Pant. According to Apa Pant, Frydman urged the Raja to declare to Gandhi that he was giving all power to his people, as a help to the freedom struggle. Frydman wrote a draft declaration, the Raja and his son took it to Gandhi at Wardha, and the new constitution of Aundh, giving the people full responsible government, was adopted on 21 January 1939.

The Aundh Experiment lasted until the princely states merged into India in 1948. Frydman also took charge of the state's prisoners in an open prison, an episode that inspired V. Shantaram's film Do Aankhen Barah Haath; he refused to be credited in it.

He lived in Gandhi's ashram, made the spinning wheel Gandhi himself used and designed several new types in search of the most efficient and economical wheel for India. He was close to Nehru and associated with Ramana Maharshi and Jiddu Krishnamurti. He helped the Polish theosophist Wanda Dynowska found a Polish-Indian Library of translations, helped move Polish orphans from Siberia through Iran to India during the war, and after 1959 worked with Dynowska for Tibetan refugees.

Frydman was a longtime friend of the Advaita teacher Nisargadatta Maharaj, who considered him a jnani. He edited and translated Nisargadatta's tape-recorded conversations into the English book I Am That, published in 1973, with an appendix of his own, Nisarga Yoga. He died in India with Nisargadatta at his bedside.
maurice-landgrave-of-hesse-kassel: Maurice was born in Kassel on 25 May 1572, the son of William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, and Sabine of Württemberg. He was raised a Lutheran and succeeded as landgrave in the Holy Roman Empire in 1592. On 23 September 1593 he married Agnes of Solms-Laubach, who died in 1602 after bearing six children, two of them stillborn. On 22 May 1603 he married Countess Juliane of Nassau-Siegen, and they had fourteen children.

In 1605 Maurice converted to Calvinism, and under the principle cuius regio eius religio his subjects were required to convert. This was controversial because the Peace of Augsburg had settled religion only between Roman Catholics and Lutherans and had not considered Calvinists. He tried to introduce Calvinism in the lands he had inherited from the extinct Hesse-Marburg branch of his family. This was contrary to the inheritance rules and led to conflict with the Hesse-Darmstadt branch and with the Holy Roman Emperor Matthias. In 1609, with the support of King Henry IV of France, he led the mediation of the Treaty of Dortmund, which aimed to settle the succession of Julich-Cleves-Berg.

Maurice was a great supporter of the performing arts. English strolling players, known as Die Englische Comoedianten, visited towns and cities in Germany, including Kassel, during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and in 1605 he built the Ottoneum, the first permanent theatre in Germany. The building survives as a natural history museum.

Maurice's actions, though not necessarily the Ottoneum, ruined Hesse-Kassel financially. In 1627 he abdicated in favour of his son William V, and he died five years later, on 15 March 1632, in Eschwege. He was a serious musician and an expert composer; a pavane of his for the lute has been recorded several times by lutenists and guitarists. The musicians he supported included Heinrich Schütz and John Dowland. Several of his sons inherited lands of their own: Herman received Rotenburg, Frederick Eschwege and Ernest Rheinfels.
maurice-prince-of-orange: Maurice was born on 14 November 1567 at the castle of Dillenburg, the son of William the Silent and Anna of Saxony, and was named after his maternal grandfather, the Elector Maurice of Saxony. He was raised in Dillenburg by his uncle Johan of Nassau and studied with his cousin Willem Lodewijk at Heidelberg and then at Leiden, where he met Simon Stevin. The States of Holland and Zeeland paid for his studies. When his father was murdered in Delft in 1584 he was sixteen. The monarchs of England and France had refused sovereignty over the Dutch provinces, which left him the only acceptable candidate for his father's office.

Maurice became stadtholder of Holland and Zeeland in 1585, of Guelders, Overijssel and Utrecht in 1590 and of Groningen and Drenthe in 1620. In 1587 he was appointed captain-general of the army, bypassing the Earl of Leicester. With Willem Lodewijk he reorganised the Dutch States Army, and paid close attention to Stevin's siege theories. In the period known as the Ten Glory Years, 1588 to 1598, he took Breda in 1590, Zutphen and Knodsenburg in 1591, Steenwijk and Coevorden in 1592, Geertruidenberg in 1593 and Groningen in 1594, and in 1597 a further series of towns. These victories rounded out the borders of the Dutch Republic.

At Turnhout in 1597 and Nieuwpoort in 1600 he won pitched battles through cooperation between the arms, with cavalry playing a major part. Drill and exercise, for him, were the fundamental postulates of tactics; volley fire was first used in European combat at Nieuwpoort. Historians note his preference for sieges, and Spanish forces under Ambrogio Spinola defeated him at Mülheim in October 1605.

Maurice began as the protégé of Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, but they quarrelled over the Twelve Years' Truce of 1609 to 1621, which Oldenbarnevelt signed against his advice, and over religion, Maurice backing the Gomarists and Oldenbarnevelt the Remonstrants. Maurice had him arrested and tried, and he was beheaded in 1619 for high treason despite requests for mercy. In 1618 Maurice succeeded his half-brother Philip William as Prince of Orange.

War with Spain resumed in 1621. Maurice died at The Hague on 23 April 1625, with the Spanish siege of Breda still under way, and Justin of Nassau surrendered the town in June. He had no legitimate children and was succeeded by his half-brother Frederick Henry. His reforms were applied later by pupils such as Marshal Turenne and Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden. The island of Mauritius was named in his honour by Wybrant Warwijck in 1598.
maurice-william-duke-of-saxe-zeitz: Maurice William was born on 12 March 1664 at Moritzburg Castle in Zeitz, the eldest son of Duke Maurice of Saxe-Zeitz and his second wife Dorothea Maria, a daughter of Duke Wilhelm of Saxe-Weimar. His father had received Saxe-Zeitz as a secundogeniture from Elector John George I of Saxony in 1652. The prince was educated mainly in ancient languages and theology, met Philipp Spener at Frankfurt on his Grand Tour in 1681, and later corresponded with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.

He succeeded his father on 4 December 1681 at the age of sixteen, under the guardianship of his cousin Elector John George III until 1684. Relations with the electors stayed tense, and he sought support at the Imperial court in Vienna and in Brandenburg, marrying Marie Amalie, a daughter of the Great Elector Frederick William, in Potsdam on 25 June 1689. Christian Thomasius had to leave strongly Lutheran Leipzig for Halle after publishing a defence of the marriage.

He tried to have his lands recognised as a sovereign Imperial State, citing the rights of the former bishops of Naumburg-Zeitz, but the electors vetoed it, and when he sought Swedish support in the Great Northern War, Saxon troops occupied his country in 1709. After his son and heir Frederick Augustus died in 1710 at the age of nine, he reconciled with the electors and gave up all claims to Imperial immediacy.

His youngest brother Frederick Henry, chosen as heir, died in 1713. Late in life the duke converted to Catholicism to please his brother Christian August, Archbishop of Esztergom and Primate of Hungary; forced out of Zeitz, he moved his government to Weida and retired to Osterburg Castle. Urged by his wife and the Halle pietist August Hermann Francke, he revoked his conversion a few weeks before he died at Weida on 15 November 1718. As Christian August and his nephew Maurice Adolf were both priests, Zeitz passed back to the Electorate of Saxony. His daughter Dorothea Wilhelmine had married Landgrave William VIII of Hesse-Kassel in 1717.
maurice-yameogo: According to his official biography, Maurice Nawalagmba Yaméogo was born on 31 December 1921 in Koudougou, west of Ouagadougou, with a twin sister, to Mossi peasants. He became interested in Christianity as a child and was baptised in 1929, taking the name Maurice, and in 1934 he entered the Minor Seminary of Pabré, which produced most of the country's priests and many of its administrators. There he befriended future figures such as Joseph Ki-Zerbo and Joseph Ouédraogo. He left in 1939 without graduating and became a shipping clerk for the French Colonial Administration, later heading the local branch of the French Confederation of Christian Workers.

Yaméogo was elected general councillor for Koudougou in the territorial assembly of Côte d'Ivoire on 15 December 1946, when Upper Volta, divided up in 1932, did not exist as a unit. It was restored on 4 September 1947. He joined the Voltaic Union and was elected grand counsellor of French West Africa on 28 July 1948, aged barely twenty-six. After electoral defeats in 1952 and 1956 he was sent back to clerical work. In March 1957 the Voltaic Democratic Movement list he led at Koudougou won all six seats at stake, and he became minister of agriculture in the coalition government of Ouezzin Coulibaly.

On 20 October 1958 the assembly elected him president of the council. The Republic of Upper Volta was proclaimed on 11 December 1958, and after receiving special powers in January 1959 he dissolved the assembly and won a large majority in the elections of 19 April, with turnout of 47 per cent. He proclaimed independence on 5 August 1960. His regime, described as dictatorial, lost the support of the Catholic church in 1964 and 1965, and his decrees against customary chieftainship were welcomed in the west but angered the east.

Unions formed an inter-union front against his austerity plans in December 1965 and called a general strike for 3 January 1966; Yaméogo declared a state of emergency on 1 January, but religious authorities and the traditional elite supported the movement. He left the presidency on 3 January 1966, was placed under house arrest on 6 January, and was sentenced in 1969 to five years of forced labour and loss of civil rights. Sangoulé Lamizana pardoned him, and he was freed on 5 August 1970.

In 1977 he founded the National Union for the Defense of Democracy, based on nostalgia for the first republic, which became the second-largest party in the legislative elections that year. He was brought to be shot after Thomas Sankara's revolution on 9 November 1983 but survived through the intervention of Blaise Compaoré, and was released in 1984. He died on 15 September 1993.
mauricio-funes: Carlos Mauricio Funes Cartagena was born in San Salvador on 18 October 1959. He finished secondary school at the Jesuit-run Externado San José and took a degree in mass media at the Central American University. He began as a news reporter for Channel 10 in February 1986 and moved to Channel 12 the next year, where he became news director and hosted The Daily Interview. In 1991 he interviewed the FMLN guerrilla leader Schafik Hándal, and Channel 12 lost advertisers as a result. In 1994 he was one of four winners of the Maria Moors Cabot Prize from Columbia University. He worked as a CNN en Español correspondent from 1997 to 2005.

Funes sought the FMLN's nomination for the 2004 election but senior leaders opposed him as not a historic member, and Hándal vetoed his candidacy. For 2009 the party's reformist wing proposed him, on condition that the former guerrilla leader Salvador Sánchez Cerén be his running mate. He became the first non-guerrilla to be the FMLN's presidential candidate. He campaigned on combating tax evasion and creating jobs, modelled his campaign on Barack Obama's, and promised to keep the dollar as currency. He won with 1,354,000 votes, 51.32 per cent, against Rodrigo Ávila of ARENA, and was inaugurated on 1 June 2009 in the first peaceful transfer of power since the civil war ended. His first act was to restore diplomatic relations with Cuba.

His government abolished public health care fees, gave schoolchildren free shoes, meals and uniforms, introduced cash transfers and pensions for the elderly, and raised teachers' salaries. In November 2009 Hurricane Ida buried the community of Verapaz in San Vicente. He was criticised for lacking a plan against rising crime and ordered the army to cooperate with the police. On 16 January 2010 he apologised in the name of the state for atrocities of the civil war, including the 1981 El Mozote massacre, and on 24 March 2010 for the assassination of Archbishop Óscar Romero. In October 2010 he apologised to Indigenous Salvadorans, calling La Matanza of 1932 a genocide.

After leaving office in 2014 Funes faced allegations of criminal conduct, and from 2016 he lived in exile in Nicaragua, which granted him asylum and later citizenship. He died in a hospital in Managua on 21 January 2025, aged 65, and was buried in Nicaragua.
