mauricio-hochschild: Hochschild was born on 17 February 1881 in Biblis into a Jewish family that had been active in mining for more than a generation. He was the eldest son of Louis Hochschild Altschul, a general trader whose cousins Berthold Hochschild and Zachary Hochschild were in the metal industry, the first as founder of the American Metal Company and the second as a partner in Metallgesellschaft. After school he studied mining and engineering at the Freiberg University of Mining and Technology.

In 1905 Hochschild joined the industrial conglomerate Metallgesellschaft, which made him its agent in Spain and Australia. He then worked independently in South America, spending several years in Chile with his brother Sali Hochschild, and returned to Germany until the end of the First World War. In 1918 he married Käthe Rosenbaum, who died in 1924, and in 1920 he moved to Bolivia. Known there as Don Mauricio, he built over the next two decades a business in the mining and trade of tin ore that stretched from Peru to Chile, and the Moritz Hochschild Group reached the height of its economic and political influence in the 1930s.

In 1938 he used his influence with German Busch, Bolivia's military president from 1937 to 1939, to have the country admit Jewish refugees from Nazi Germany, and he paid for their transport and housing. About 9,000 were admitted by one estimate; others put the number he helped escape between 9,000 and 22,000, and he has since been called the Bolivian Schindler. The Bolivian government arrested him and sentenced him to death in 1939 and again in 1944, and two weeks after his release in 1944 he was held by kidnappers for two weeks. Once freed he left Bolivia for good.

In 1951 the Hochschilds gave most of their fortune to the Hochschild Trust and Foundation. When the group was nationalised the following year during the Bolivian National Revolution, they were compensated with 30 per cent of its former assets, and the company grew into Hochschild Mining. In 1961 he opened the Mantos Blancos copper mine at Antofagasta in Chile, his most successful operation. He died in Paris on 12 June 1965 and was buried in Père Lachaise Cemetery.
maurienne: The Maurienne is one of the great transverse valleys of the Alps, shaped by the Arc since the last glaciation. It begins at the village of Écot, in the commune of Bonneval-sur-Arc at the foot of the Col de l'Iseran, and ends where the Arc meets the Isère at Aiton. The Dauphiné and Cottian Alps rise to the south and the Vanoise, part of the Graian Alps, to the north. Geographers divide it into a lower, middle and upper valley, and its old capital, Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne, stands where the Arvan joins the Arc.

The valley shows traces of human settlement since the Paleolithic. In 1032 Humbert the White-Handed received the Maurienne, his native land, from Conrad II the Salian, whom he had helped in his Italian campaigns against Aribert, Archbishop of Milan. His descendants of the House of Savoy kept their independence as counts and then dukes until Savoy was joined to the Kingdom of Sardinia, which included Piedmont.

In the early 19th century the Sardinians built a line of five forts in the valley, the Barrière de l'Esseillon, to protect Piedmont against a French invasion. The Maurienne became part of France only in 1860, under the agreement with Napoleon III that opened the way to the unification of Italy. Besides the Col du Mont-Cenis towards Italy, passes such as the Col du Galibier, the Col de la Croix-de-Fer and the Col de la Madeleine lead out of the valley.

The Maurienne corresponds to the arrondissement of Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne, and the main road and rail route between Lyon and Turin runs through it, leaving France by the Fréjus tunnels at Modane. Twenty-four hydroelectric stations once fed electrochemical and aluminium plants, but tourism and winter sports now lead the economy. Much of the upper valley lies in Vanoise National Park, the first national park in France, created in 1963, which borders Italy's Gran Paradiso National Park.
mauritania: Mauritania lies in the western region of Africa and is generally flat, its 1,030,000 square kilometres forming vast, arid plains broken by occasional ridges and clifflike outcroppings. It borders the Atlantic Ocean, Senegal, Mali, Algeria and Western Sahara, and is considered part of both the Sahel and the Maghreb. Approximately three-quarters of the country is desert or semidesert, and the desert has been expanding since the mid-1960s after extended, severe drought. The highest of its sandstone plateaus, the Adrar Plateau, reaches 500 metres, and the concentric Guelb er Richat is a prominent feature of the north-central region.

The name comes from Mauretania, the Latin name of an ancient Berber kingdom and later Roman province that lay considerably farther north, along the western Mediterranean coast of Africa. The territories do not overlap. Arab geographers more commonly called the land Bilad Chinqit, the land of Chinguetti. The French officially used the term Mauritanie occidentale in 1899, on a proposal by the colonial administrator Xavier Coppolani.

The ancient tribes of Mauritania were the Niger-Congo and Bafour peoples. The Bafour were among the first Saharan peoples to abandon a nomadic lifestyle for agriculture, and migrated southward as the Sahara dried. They were displaced by Berbers who arrived between the 3rd and 7th centuries. The Umayyads were the first Arab Muslims to enter the region, establishing themselves by the end of the 7th century. In the 11th century several Berber confederations in the desert joined to form the Almoravid movement, which built an empire stretching from the Sahara to the Iberian Peninsula.

From 1644 to 1674 the indigenous peoples made a final, unsuccessful effort to repel the Maqil Arabs, led by the Beni Hassan tribe, in the Char Bouba War. The descendants of the Beni Hassan warriors became the upper stratum of Moorish society, and Hassaniya, a bedouin Arabic dialect named for them, became the dominant language of the largely nomadic population. In the early 20th century France colonised the country as part of French West Africa. It became independent in 1960.

Mauritania is the Islamic Republic of Mauritania. Its capital and largest city is Nouakchott, on the Atlantic coast, and its population is about 5 million. Arabic is the official language, with Pulaar, Soninke and Wolof as national languages, and Islam is the state religion. Its manuscript libraries at Chinguetti hold thousands of medieval manuscripts, and it has a long oral tradition of poetry.
mauritius: The main island lies 1,100 nautical miles (2,000 km) off the southeast coast of Africa, between latitudes 19°58.8'S and 20°31.7'S. It is 65 km long and 45 km wide. It is geologically young, created by volcanic activity some 8 million years ago, and with Réunion, Rodrigues and Saint Brandon it forms part of the Mascarene Islands, which are no longer volcanically active. White sandy beaches surround it, and lagoons are protected by a coral reef. The country also includes Rodrigues, Agaléga and St. Brandon. The main island was the only known home of the dodo, which became extinct soon after human settlement.

The island was uninhabited when first visited. Some historians have speculated from the Cantino planisphere of 1502, where it appears as Dina Arobi, that Arab sailors reached it around 975. Portuguese sailors visited in 1507, and Diogo Fernandes Pereira is the first European known to have landed; the Portuguese did not stay. A Dutch squadron under Admiral Wybrand Van Warwyck landed at Grand Port in 1598 and named the island after Prince Maurice of Nassau. The Dutch inhabited it from 1638, exploiting ebony trees and introducing sugar cane, domestic animals and deer.

French colonisation began in 1715, and the island was renamed Isle de France. In 1810 the United Kingdom seized it, and France ceded Mauritius and its dependencies in the Treaty of Paris. The British colony included Rodrigues, Agaléga, St. Brandon, the Chagos Archipelago and, until 1906, the Seychelles. Mauritius became the British Empire's main sugar-producing colony and stayed a plantation colony dominated by sugar until independence in 1968. The country became a republic in 1992.

In 1965, three years before independence, the United Kingdom split the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius to form the British Indian Ocean Territory, established on 8 November 1965. The local population was forcibly expelled, and the main island, Diego Garcia, was leased to the United States for a military base.

Mauritius is a parliamentary republic with a unicameral National Assembly, and its capital and largest city is Port Louis. Its people are diverse in ethnicity, culture, language and faith, drawn from Indian, African, Chinese and European, mostly French, origins. It is the only country in Africa where Hinduism is the most practised religion. Its architecture combines Dutch, French and British styles with influences from India and East Africa.
maurya-empire: The Maurya Empire had its power base in Magadha. Its origins are shrouded in legend. Greek sources refer to confrontations between the Greeks and Chandragupta Maurya, whom they call Sandrokottos, but say almost nothing of his conquest of the Nanda Empire, while Indian sources narrate only that conquest. Buddhist texts place him in the Moriya clan, and Jain texts call him the son of an imperial superintendent of peacocks.

Through military conquests and diplomatic treaties Chandragupta extended his rule as far west as Afghanistan below the Hindu Kush and as far south as the northern Deccan. Beyond the Magadha core, the technology and infrastructure of the time limited how deeply his rule could penetrate society.

Chandragupta was succeeded by Bindusara, and then by Ashoka, his grandson. Ashoka crushed revolts in Ujjain and Taxila as a prince. His conquest of Kalinga in 262–261 BCE became the turning point of his life: an estimated 100,000 soldiers and civilians were killed, and many more were affected by the destruction. Ashoka felt remorse, embraced Buddhism and renounced war. He sent missionaries to Sri Lanka, north-western India and Central Asia and propagated his own dhamma in edicts, most commonly set up along well-travelled roads.

Ashoka was followed for fifty years by weaker emperors. None of his sons took the throne: Mahinda became a Buddhist monk and Kunala was blinded. Dasharatha, Ashoka's grandson, lost many territories, some later retaken by Samprati. The last Mauryan ruler, Brihadratha, was killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga during a military parade, and the Shunga Empire arose.

Ashoka's empire consisted of five parts. Magadha, with the capital at Pataliputra, was ruled directly. Four provinces, with capitals at Tosali, Ujjain, Suvarnagiri and Taxila, were governed by princes. Historians now often see the empire as a network of core regions and trade routes rather than a solid territory. The major rock edicts are found in the frontier provinces and are absent in large parts of the supposed territory, including Tamil Nadu and Kerala.

Megasthenes credited the empire with an army of 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry, 8,000 chariots and 9,000 war elephants. Roads such as the winter road Uttarapath, linking eastern Afghanistan to Pataliputra, promoted trade, and silver and copper coins were widely used. The population is estimated at between 15 and 30 million. The empire favoured Jainism, Buddhism and Ajivikism over Brahmanism.
mauryas-of-konkan: The dynasty is known only from a few records, and there is little clarity on its genealogy, chronology, territory, administration or political standing. The historian D.C. Sircar suggested in 1942 that the Mauryas of Konkana and those of Rajasthan claimed descent from the imperial Maurya prince-viceroys of Ujjayini and Suvarnagiri; later writers repeated the theory, although no concrete evidence of imperial Maurya rule has been found in the Goa region. A stone inscription from Vada of the Maurya king Suketu-varman, recording the building of temples there, places the family in the northern Konkan, and historians have seen them variously as a Traikutaka vassal family, as a branch of the Traikutaka family, or as Kalachuri vassals.

The capital, Puri, has been identified with Gharapuri on Elephanta Island, with Salsette or with Rajapuri. European visitors from as early as 1322 mention a Porus or Pori there, and two small villages on Elephanta, Morbandar and Raj-bandar, may preserve the memory of Maurya rule; other scholars argue that the island is too small and uneven for a capital and that its remains are mainly religious. Chalukya records call Puri the goddess of the fortune of the western ocean, which suggests a local maritime power.

In the sixth and seventh centuries the Mauryas seem to have extended their rule to southern Konkan, the north of present-day Goa, where the Bhojas may have been their feudatories. The Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II calls his father Kirtivarman I the night of doom for the Mauryas, who appear to have been defeated and given a Chalukya governor. They probably held power as vassals under his brother Mangalesha and declared independence during the war of succession between Mangalesha and Pulakeshin II, who then besieged Puri with hundreds of ships and ended their rule.

The economy seems to have combined sea and inland trade, with some evidence of customs posts at Tana near Ponda, Curdi and Cortalim. Agriculture was probably the main source of revenue: inscriptions of the period refer to the khajjana system, later known as khazan, of embankments that kept sea water out of coastal paddy fields, and to the clearing of forest for fields. Kings granted land to Brahmins, who in return legitimised their royal status.
mausolus: Mausolus was the eldest son of Hecatomnus, a native Carian who became satrap of Caria around 395 to 392 BCE, shortly after Tissaphernes died. The two may have shared rule in the early 370s BCE. Mausolus ruled alongside his wife and sister Artemisia, known as Artemisia II. Because they had no children, and incest of this kind was otherwise unknown in Caria, their marriage is thought to have been entirely symbolic. Only Mausolus was ever called satrap, but Artemisia clearly held some political authority as joint dynast.

Mausolus took part in the Revolt of the Satraps, in which many western satraps rebelled against Artaxerxes II, mostly in the 360s BCE. He mainly acted on the king's side: with Autophradates of Lydia he led the siege of Adramyttium in 366 BCE at the king's request, though Greek sources say he briefly rebelled. He was not punished and was rewarded with the governance of Lycia, where independent Lycian coinage ceased and his own coins circulated. He also supported the rebels against Athens in the Social War of 357 to 355 BCE, extending his authority among the neighbouring Greek islands. Rhodes came to be ruled by an oligarchy backed by a Carian garrison.

Greek writers portray him as a despot. The Economics attributed to Aristotle tells of schemes to raise money, such as telling the people of Mylasa that the Persian king was about to attack their unwalled city and then keeping the funds they gave for walls. Inscriptions record that he punished nobles who conspired against him, and he survived an assassination attempt at the festival at Labraunda in 355/4 BCE. Early in his reign he moved the capital from Mylasa to Halicarnassus, which he rebuilt on a new grid and enlarged by moving people from nearby Carian villages. It gained a theatre, an agora and harbour fortifications. He also rebuilt the sanctuaries at Amyzon, Labraunda and Sinuri.

Mausolus died shortly after the attempt at Labraunda. His remains were placed in the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, which tradition says Artemisia ordered built and which was finished only after her death; construction probably began in his lifetime. Its designers included the architects Satyrus and Pythis and the sculptors Scopas of Paros, Leochares, Bryaxis and Timotheus. Antipater of Sidon listed it among the Seven Wonders, and the word mausoleum came to mean any grand tomb. Artemisia held a funeral with games at which Theodectes of Phaselis won the verse contest with a tragedy called Mausolus. Most of the surviving sculpture is in the British Museum. His brother Idrieus probably succeeded him as satrap.
mawanda-of-buganda: Mawanda was the third son of Kabaka Ndawula Nsobya, the 19th kabaka of Buganda. His mother was Nakidde Luyiga of the Ngo clan, the fourth of his father's seven wives. He seized the throne by killing his brother, Kabaka Kikulwe Mawuba, and became the 22nd kabaka of Buganda.

His reign was noted for the expansion of the kingdom. He set up his capital at Katakala, west of present-day Mityana, as a base from which to attack Bunyoro, and annexed the whole region around Lake Wamala, including Bukuya and Kasanda, reaching northwards to Bwanja and Kiboga. He then turned to Kyaggwe, on the eastern side of Buganda, in alliance with Nkutu, a warrior from Lwaje island, who provided a fleet for the campaigns in Kyaggwe and Busoga.

The historian Semakula Kiwanuka wrote that the victories in Busoga were sullied by atrocities and marked by slaughter and arson, and that although later kings such as Kyabaggu did as much there, it was Mawanda's name that struck horror among the Basoga of old; a saying remembered him as the Muganda who slaughtered all our mothers and fathers. Kiwanuka also judged him brave and fearless, with qualities that endeared him to the people.

The historian Samwiri Lwanga-Lunyiigo credits him with administrative reforms that made the monarchy the overriding centre of power in Buganda. He created a parallel system of administration, the Bitongole, whose officials were directly responsible to the kabaka and reached down to the villages.

A group of princes at the royal court conspired to murder Mawanda. Among them was Prince Mwanga Sebanakitta, who took the throne after his death. Mawanda was first buried at Meerera, but his remains were exhumed in 1864 and buried again at Serinnya. Two of his sons, Mulere and Bbengo, later rebelled against Kabaka Kyabaggu; both were defeated, captured and burned alive.
mawdud-of-ghazni: Shahab-ud-Dawla Mawdud was declared heir by his father, Mas'ud I of Ghazni, in 1038, and helped him in his campaigns against the Seljuks and the Kara-Khanid Khanate. After the Seljuks defeated Mas'ud at the Battle of Dandanaqan in 1040, he set out to leave Greater Khorasan for India but was seized by his own soldiers and replaced by his brother Muhammad of Ghazni, who had him killed. Mawdud was then at Balkh with his father's vizier Ahmad Shirazi.

Mawdud invaded his uncle's domains and defeated and killed him at Jalalabad in 1041. He named Ahmad Shirazi his vizier and Abu Sahl Zawzani his chief secretary; in 1043 Shirazi fell from favour and was replaced by Abd al-Razzaq Maymandi. In 1042 Mawdud briefly occupied Balkh and Herat, which led the Karakhanid ruler Böritigin to acknowledge him as suzerain, but in 1043/4 the Seljuq prince Alp Arslan repelled him from Tukharistan, and his efforts to bring the Nasrid ruler of Sistan, Abu'l-Fadl Nasr, under his authority failed. Sistan became a Seljuq vassal, and the Ghaznavid border was pushed back to Bost.

His brother Majdud, who held Lahore and refused to recognise him, died on 11 August 1043, and Mawdud took the city. He then drove the Ismailis out of Multan, where the khutbah was afterwards read for the Abbasid Caliphate instead of the Fatimids. Indian rulers took the offensive: Sandanpal, grandson of the Kabul Shah, was defeated and killed before Lahore, and in 1043-4 a coalition of three Hindu princes under Mahipal of the Tomara dynasty took Hansi, Nagarkot and Thanesar before it too was defeated at Lahore.

Around 1050 Mawdud prepared a new invasion of Khorasan with Böritigin and an army sent by the former Kakuyid ruler Garshasp I, while Böritigin's commander Qashgha attacked Khwarezm and Termez. Mawdud died in 1050 and the invasion failed; the Seljuqs extended their rule as far as Vakhsh, and Böritigin seems to have ceased to recognise Ghaznavid suzerainty. Mawdud was succeeded by his son Mas'ud II. Keikavus, author of the Qabus nama, spent seven or eight years as a guest at his court.
mawlid: The term Mawlid comes from the Arabic root walad, meaning to give birth. It is a generic word for any birthday, but usually refers to the observance of the birthday of Muhammad, also called Mawlid al-Nabi and, in some regions, Milad. It also names the text composed for and recited at the celebration. Most Sunni Muslims hold that Muhammad was born on 12 Rabi I, while many Twelver Shia assert 17 Rabi I, although prominent Shia scholars such as al-Kulayni and Ibn Babawayh have affirmed the 12th. Others contend that the date of his birth is not definitively recorded. Ibn Khallikan records the date as the first proven disagreement about the celebration.

Early observance of Muhammad's birth as a holy day was usually arranged privately, and some of the Tabi'un held sessions in which poetry and songs in his honour were recited. The early celebrations included Sufi elements, with animal sacrifices, torchlight processions, public sermons and a feast, and the ruler was central to them. In 1207 the Turkic general Muzaffar al-Din Gökböri, brother-in-law of Saladin, held a public festival of the Mawlid in Erbil, which included the slaughter of thousands of animals for a banquet said to have cost 300,000 dirhams. The festival then spread across the Muslim world, and the Ottomans declared the day an official holiday in 1588, known as Mevlid Kandil.

Celebrants hold gatherings called mahfils, in which religious poetry in praise of Muhammad is recited, followed by a feast. Other customs are voluntary fasting, prayer and dhikr. Sufi orders often organise large street processions, decorate homes and mosques and distribute food and charity, and scholars and poets recite the Qaṣīda al-Burda by the 13th-century poet Busiri. In Turkey the best known of the many mawlid poems is the Mawlid of Süleyman Çelebi. The word is also used in places such as Egypt for the birthday celebrations of Sufi saints.

The Hanafi, Maliki and Shafi'i schools of Sunni Islam generally approve of the Mawlid, as do the Shia. Jurists justified it as a way of giving thanks for the gift of Muhammad, and the scholars Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali and Ibn Hajar al-Asqalini wrote in this vein, Ibn Hajar allowing any form of celebration that is neutral under Shari'a. Early fatwas criticised hosts for taking contributions from guests. Salafism regards the celebration as a reprehensible innovation, bid'a, and prohibits it, while Deobandi jurists treat it as a matter of scholarly disagreement. It is a national holiday in most Muslim-majority countries.
mawtini: "Mawṭinī", Arabic for 'My Homeland', is an Arabic national poem by the Palestinian poet Ibrahim Tuqan, written around 1934 and composed as a song by the Lebanese musician Mohammed Flayfel. It became a popular patriotic song among Arab people. For much of the 20th century it served as an unofficial anthem of Palestinians and of other peoples of the Middle East, and it was Palestine's de facto national anthem from its beginning until 1996, when "Fidā'ī" officially replaced it. Many Arab artists have re-sung the anthem with new arrangements, among them Elissa, Christina Sawaya and Faia Younan, in a video clip that depicted the Syrian civil war.

The song has been described as a reflection of the shared experiences and struggles of Arab peoples. Its lyrics express a deep love for the homeland, a commitment to its liberation and a vision of a united and free nation. It is regarded as a symbol of resistance and of the collective longing for liberation in periods of occupation and oppression, conveying sorrow, anger and hope and a sense of renewal and solidarity among those who have endured similar adversities. This message resonates widely across the Arab world, reflecting shared struggles for independence, identity and sovereignty.

Many Palestinians still identify strongly with the song alongside "Fidā'ī" and consider it a sort of unofficial second national anthem of their country. In 2004 it was adopted as the national anthem of Iraq on the order of the Coalition Provisional Authority chief Paul Bremer. It replaced an earlier anthem also called "Mawṭinī", an unrelated instrumental piece without lyrics composed by Lewis Zanbaka, which Iraq had used in the late 1950s and early 1960s and had brought back temporarily after the fall of the Ba'athist regime in 2003. That piece had itself replaced "Arḍulfurātayni", in use since 1981 and associated with Saddam Hussein's regime.
max-frisch: Max Rudolf Frisch was born in Zurich on 15 May 1911, the second son of the architect Franz Bruno Frisch and Karolina Bettina Frisch, née Wildermuth. The family lived modestly, and their finances worsened after the father lost his job during the First World War. At school Frisch began writing drama but failed to get it performed and destroyed his early works. His father died in March 1932, and he took up journalism for the Neue Zürcher Zeitung to support his mother. A journey through eastern and southeastern Europe in 1933 led to his first novel, Jürg Reinhart, in 1934.

In 1936 Frisch enrolled at the ETH Zurich to study architecture, supported by a stipend from his friend Werner Coninx. His second novel, An Answer from the Silence (1937), won the 1938 Conrad Ferdinand Meyer Prize, though he burned the manuscript and later refused to include it in a collected edition. In 1942 he came first among 65 entrants in a competition to design the Freibad Letzigraben.

From 1944 Kurt Hirschfeld, director of the Zürich Playhouse, encouraged him to write for the theatre, and his first play, Santa Cruz, was performed in 1946. The Fire Raisers, about a man who shelters vagrants who then burn down his house, made him a dramatist of international standing; Swiss audiences took it as a warning against Communism, and Frisch felt misunderstood. His novels Stiller (1954) and Homo Faber (1957) brought a wider readership.

Frisch's work centres on identity, individuality, responsibility, morality and political commitment, and his post-war writing makes frequent use of irony. A recurring idea, set out in the Diary 1946–1949, applies the biblical ban on graven images to human relations: people reduce one another to fixed images, a sin against both self and other unless love lets each change. The diary became one of his characteristic forms, and the narrator of Stiller cries out that he has no language for his reality.

He received the Georg Büchner Prize in 1958, the Jerusalem Prize in 1965 and the Neustadt International Prize for Literature in 1986. Stiller and Gantenbein were widely taken up as models for treating identity through narrative structure. Frisch died on 4 April 1991; his estate is administered by the Max Frisch Foundation, whose archive is kept at the ETH Zurich.
max-gluckman: Herman Max Gluckman was born in Johannesburg on 26 January 1911 into a Jewish family. He took a BA at the University of the Witwatersrand in 1930, meaning to study law, but turned to anthropology under Winifred Hoernle and earned the equivalent of an MA there in 1934. A Rhodes Scholarship then took him to Exeter College, Oxford, where R. R. Marett supervised him, though his main influences were Radcliffe-Brown and Edward Evan Evans-Pritchard, leading figures of structural functionalism. He did his doctoral fieldwork among the Lozi of Barotseland.

Gluckman joined the Rhodes-Livingstone Institute in 1939 and directed it from 1941 to 1947, making it a major centre of anthropological research, and he kept close ties with it after moving to a lectureship at Oxford in 1947. In 1949 he became the first professor of social anthropology at the University of Manchester and founded its department. His colleagues from the institute and his students there, among them Victor Turner, J. Clyde Mitchell, Ronald Frankenberg and Bruce Kapferer, came to be known as the Manchester School. Its stress on case studies of social interaction, from which rules and assumptions were inferred, owed much to his early legal training.

Gluckman was openly and forcefully anti-colonial and wrote on racism, urbanisation and labour migration under colonial rule. He joined British structural functionalism to a Marxist attention to inequality and oppression. In his work on Zululand he argued that African and European communities formed a single social system, whose division into two racial groups was the basis of its structural unity. His radio lectures, published as Custom and Conflict in Africa, made him widely known. His books include Rituals of Rebellion in South-East Africa (1954), Order and Rebellion in Tribal Africa (1963), Politics, Law and Ritual in Tribal Society (1965) and The Allocation of Responsibility (1972).

He died on 13 April 1975, after which Richard Werbner and his wife Pnina, Gluckman's niece, carried on his legacy at Manchester. Bruce Kapferer, giving the first Max Gluckman Memorial lecture, described him as perhaps the anthropologist whose own life and consciousness embodied some of the critical crises of the modern world and who demanded that anthropology confront them.
max-havelaar: By the middle of the nineteenth century the Dutch government governed the Dutch East Indies. To raise revenue it applied the Cultivation System, which required Indonesian farmers to grow a quota of commercial crops such as sugar and coffee instead of staple foods such as rice, and a tax system in which collecting agents were paid by commission. Together these caused widespread abuse, especially on Java and Sumatra, and brought poverty and starvation.

Multatuli wrote the book in protest against these policies, and also sought rehabilitation after his resignation from government service. J. de Ruyter published the first edition of 1,300 copies in Amsterdam on 17 May 1860.

The protagonist, Max Havelaar, is a Dutch colonial administrator who tries to fight a corrupt government system in Java. His story is told by two opposed narrators: the hypocritical coffee merchant Batavus Droogstoppel, who means to use Havelaar's manuscripts to write about the coffee trade, and the romantic German apprentice Stern, who takes over when Droogstoppel loses interest. At the very end Multatuli himself takes the pen, denounces Dutch colonial policy and appeals to King William III of the Netherlands to intervene on behalf of his Indonesian subjects.

The novel made Europeans aware that their wealth was the result of suffering elsewhere, and that awareness eventually motivated the Ethical Policy, by which the colonial government tried to repay its debt to its subjects by giving education to some classes of native people. The Indonesian novelist Pramoedya Ananta Toer argued that these reforms led to the nationalist movement that ended Dutch colonialism after 1945, and called the book the book that killed colonialism.

It has been translated into thirty-four languages, first into English in 1868. Sukarno and other early Indonesian nationalists cited it as an inspiration, but it was not translated into Indonesian until 1972. A film by Fons Rademakers appeared in 1976 and could not be shown in Indonesia until 1987.
max-mallowan: Max Edgar Lucien Mallowan was born Edgar Mallowan on 6 May 1904 in Wandsworth, London. His father, Frederick Mallowan, was a businessman of Austrian family who had served with the Austrian horse artillery, and his mother, Marguerite, was a daughter of the mezzo-soprano Marthe Duvivier. He was educated at Rokeby School and Lancing College, left school at 17 and studied classics (literae humaniores) at New College, Oxford, where his teachers included H. A. L. Fisher, Percy Gardner and Gilbert Murray. He took a fourth-class honours in Mods in 1923 and third-class honours in Greats in 1925.

Through Fisher, the warden of his college, Mallowan was introduced to D. G. Hogarth and then to Leonard Woolley, and he worked as Woolley's apprentice at Ur from 1925 to 1930. There in 1930 he met the novelist Agatha Christie, whom he married the same year. In 1932 he spent a short time at Nineveh with Reginald Campbell Thompson, where he sank a shaft 21 metres deep to natural level in the Kuyunjiq tell.

He then became field director of expeditions managed jointly by the British Museum and the British School of Archaeology in Iraq. They included the prehistoric village at Tell Arpachiyah and the sites of Chagar Bazar and Tell Brak in the upper Khabur area of Syria. He was also the first to excavate sites in the valley of the river Balikh. In December 1933 he was elected a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries. During the Second World War he served in the Royal Air Force Volunteer Reserve in North Africa.

In 1947 Mallowan became Professor of Western Asiatic Archaeology at the University of London and director of the British School of Archaeology in Iraq, posts he held until 1962 and 1961 respectively. He directed the resumption of work at Nimrud, earlier excavated by A. H. Layard, and published it in Nimrud and its Remains (1966). With Leri Glynne Davies he published Ivories in Assyrian Style (1970).

He became a Fellow of the British Academy in 1954 and a fellow of All Souls College, Oxford, in 1962, a research post without teaching duties that let him write up Nimrud. He was made a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1960 and knighted in 1968. Christie died in 1976, and the next year he married Barbara Hastings Parker, his epigraphist at Nimrud. He died on 19 August 1978 and was buried beside Christie at Cholsey.
max-uhle: Uhle was born in Dresden, in the Kingdom of Saxony, on 25 March 1856. His interest in Peru began while he was a curator at the Dresden Museum, and in 1888 his close friend Alphons Stübel, who had recently published an article on the history of Peruvian archaeology, urged him to concentrate on the region. His first journey to South America, in 1892, took him to Argentina and Bolivia on behalf of the Konigliches Museum fur Völkerkunde in Berlin. His partner on the Tiwanaku study was the photographer and engineer B. von Grumbkow. Uhle married Charlotte Grosse of Philadelphia, where he worked for several years at the University of Pennsylvania.

His second expedition, from 1896, was sponsored by the American Exploration Society in Philadelphia and the University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, with the patronage of Phoebe Hearst, mother of William Randolph Hearst. His report on Pachacamac was highly praised and is still used as a basic text of South American archaeology. At the coastal sites he recognised versions of Tiwanaku sculptural imagery on ceramics and textiles, and the finds he recovered, spanning more than 3,000 years, included Nazca pottery, shells, textiles, metals and objects of wood, feathers, bone and leather. He dated them chiefly by textile design, and those of the Mocha Valley by the sequence of Inca ceramic styles.

He went on to work in the highlands of Bolivia, Ecuador and Chile and excavated the Emeryville shell-mound on San Francisco Bay in California. He also took part in palaeontological digs: in 1926, with the palaeontologist Franz Spillmann, he excavated an almost complete mastodon skeleton about 12 km east of Quito, together with obsidian and bone tools and about 150 potsherds. He died on 11 May 1944. The German-Peruvian Max Uhle School in Arequipa bears his name.
max-von-oppenheim: Oppenheim was born in Cologne, the son of Albert Oppenheim, of the Jewish family of bankers, and Pauline Engels, of a Cologne merchant family. His grandfather Simon was made a baron in Austria-Hungary in 1867, and the family took the name von Oppenheim. Max studied law at Strasbourg and Berlin, passed his examinations in Cologne in 1883 and learned Arabic while training as a lawyer. In 1892 he spent seven months in Cairo, and in 1893–94 he crossed the Syrian desert and Mesopotamia to Basra, the journey of his travelogue Vom Mittelmeer zum Persischen Golf.

Rejected at first by the Foreign Office because of his father's Jewish background, he became an attaché at the German consulate-general in Cairo in 1896; the British press called him a master spy of the Kaiser. Surveying a route for the Baghdad Railway for Deutsche Bank, he found Tell Halaf on 19 November 1899 from villagers' tales of stone idols under the sand, and reburied the statues, as he had no permit to dig.

His campaign of 1911, with five archaeologists, more than 500 local workers and a small steam train, cost about 750,000 marks, paid by his father. Besides the basalt statues and reliefs of King Kapara's Western Palace, it found Neolithic painted pottery of about 6,000 to 5,000 BCE, which gave its name to the Halaf culture. In October 1914 he wrote a memorandum urging that the Ottoman sultan be enlisted to call the world's Muslims to holy war against France and Great Britain, and he headed the Intelligence Bureau for the East in Berlin.

He lost most of his wealth in the inflation of 1923. In 1927 he won a division of his finds with the authorities of the French Mandate: his share went to Berlin and the rest to Aleppo, where the museum he installed became the nucleus of the National Museum. Under Nazi rule, according to the historian Sean McMeekin, he ascribed his statues to Aryan culture. Bombing in 1943 destroyed his apartment and much of his library; he lived through the firebombing of Dresden in February 1945 and died in Landshut, where his grave is a basalt replica of the seated woman statue he admired.

The broken basalt pieces lay untouched in the cellars of the Pergamon Museum under the GDR. After reunification the Vorderasiatisches Museum rebuilt from 2001 to 2010 more than 30 sculptures from around 27,000 fragments, shown in Berlin in 2011 and at the Bundeskunsthalle Bonn in 2014.
max-weber: Maximilian Carl Emil Weber was born on 21 April 1864 in Erfurt and raised in Charlottenburg, the oldest of eight children. His father, Max Weber Sr., was a lawyer, civil servant and National Liberal parliamentarian, and the family's salon welcomed scholars such as the historian Theodor Mommsen. His mother, Helene Fallenstein, was a devout Calvinist and philanthropist. He studied law and history in Berlin, Göttingen and Heidelberg, took his doctorate in law in 1889 and his habilitation in 1891, and in 1893 married his second cousin Marianne Schnitger, a feminist activist and author.

Weber taught in Berlin, Freiburg and Heidelberg. In 1897 he suffered a breakdown after his father died following an argument, and he ceased teaching and travelled for several years. From 1904 he was an associate editor of the Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, in which he published The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism.

He first supported Germany's war effort in 1914 but became a prominent critic of expansionism and of the Kaiser's war policies, and he called for democratisation. After the war he co-founded the German Democratic Party, advised on the drafting of the Weimar Constitution, and taught in Vienna and Munich, where he gave the lectures Science as a Vocation and Politics as a Vocation. He died of pneumonia on 14 June 1920, possibly as a result of the Spanish flu.

A central concern was rationalisation and disenchantment. In The Protestant Ethic he argued that Protestantism, particularly Calvinism, tied piety to a worldly calling and so encouraged rational economic gain. He later studied the religions of China, India and ancient Judaism. He defined the state by its monopoly on the legitimate use of force within a given area, and divided legitimate authority into traditional, charismatic and rational-legal forms.

Methodologically he placed social action at the centre of sociology, sought to understand it through interpretation, and used ideal types as models to compare with reality. Economy and Society was left unfinished. He is now regarded alongside Karl Marx and Émile Durkheim as a founding figure of sociology.
maxim-gun: Hiram Maxim's first British patents for the gun were granted in June and July 1883, and a prototype was shown to invited guests in October 1884. That November he founded the Maxim Gun Company in London with financing from Albert Vickers. The company later joined the Swedish firm Nordenfelt as Maxim Nordenfelt Guns and Ammunition Company, and was finally absorbed into Vickers, leading to the Vickers machine gun.

The gun was recoil-operated: energy from the recoil acting on the breech block ejected each spent cartridge and loaded the next. Maxim's earliest designs used a rotating cam to reverse the block, later simplified to a toggle lock. This made it far more efficient than earlier hand-cranked rapid-firing guns such as the Gatling gun of 1861. Trials showed that it could fire 600 rounds a minute, equal to 60 riflemen of the time.

The Maxim was water cooled, which let it keep up its rate of fire far longer than air-cooled guns but made it heavier and less flexible. A lone soldier could fire it, but it was usually worked by a team of four to six, who reloaded, spotted targets and carried ammunition and water. Moving or mounting it took several men. An air-cooled Extra Light version of 1895 was the lightest machine gun in the world, but it overheated quickly and only 135 were built.

A prototype went with Henry Morton Stanley's Emin Pasha Relief Expedition of 1886 to 1890, more as a publicity stunt than a military contribution, and it was used mainly to frighten off attackers. The first unit in the world to receive the gun was Hermann Wissmann's force, sent in 1888 to suppress the Abushiri revolt. At the Battle of the Shangani on 25 October 1893, in the First Matabele War, 700 soldiers with five Maxims fought off 5,000 Matabele warriors. Historian Martin Gilbert called it the weapon most associated with imperial conquest.

Governments were at first reluctant to adopt it, as soldiers distrusted machine guns that jammed. The British Army ordered 120 in October 1888 under Sir Garnet Wolseley, and Russia, Switzerland, the United States and many others followed. Popular myth has embellished its destructive power in colonial warfare; modern accounts suggest that it was effective in pitched battles such as Omdurman, but that much of its significance lay in its psychological impact. Its descendants include the Vickers, the German MG 08 and the Russian Pulemyot Maxim, which served in both world wars.
maxima-caesariensis: After the Roman conquest Britain was governed as a single province, first from Camulodunum and then from Londinium, until the Severan reforms that followed the revolt of the governor Clodius Albinus divided it into Upper and Lower Britain, with capitals at Londinium and Eboracum. During the first phases of the Diocletian reforms Britain was held by the Britannic Empire of Allectus in the Carausian Revolt.

The province was probably created after Constantius Chlorus defeated Allectus in 296, when the Diocese of the Britains, with its vicar at Londinium, was formed as part of the Prefecture of Gaul. It is named in the Verona List of Roman provinces of about 312. The Britains were divided among three, four or five provinces: Prima, Secunda, Maxima Caesariensis and possibly Flavia Caesariensis and Valentia. The governor of Maxima was at first an equestrian praeses before his elevation to consular rank.

Also known as Britannia Maxima, the province takes its name from an emperor Maximian, and scholars are unsure whether it honoured the western senior emperor Valerius Maximian or the eastern junior emperor Galerius Maximian. Birley has argued that Maxima and Flavia began as a single province, Britannia Caesariensis, so named as a mark of favour for support against Allectus, and that Upper Britain was divided first in two and then in three, repeating an earlier theory of William Camden.

Medieval and early modern writers placed it in the north. Gerald of Wales, describing the sees of the early British church founded by SS Fagan and Duvian, put Maximia at Eboracum and named it after the emperor Maximus. Camden followed him, and Charles Bertram's influential forgery of the 1740s, The Description of Britain, gave Maxima borders from the Humber and Mersey to Hadrian's Wall; the forgery was exposed over the course of the mid-19th century.
maximian: Marcus Aurelius Valerius Maximianus was born around 250 near Sirmium in the province of Pannonia, into a family of shopkeepers. He joined the army and served with Diocletian under the emperors Aurelian and Probus. Probably in July 285, at Mediolanum, Diocletian appointed him Caesar. Historians suggest that Diocletian, who thought himself a mediocre general, wanted a lieutenant to do most of his fighting.

Maximian made his residence at Trier but spent most of his time on campaign. In late 285 he suppressed the Bagaudae, rebels in Gaul. He took the title of Augustus on 1 April 286, in the traditional dating, when the crisis with Carausius had broken out. Carausius, whom he had set to clear the Channel of pirates, rebelled in 286 and took Britain and part of Gaul with him. Maximian campaigned instead against the tribes of the Rhine, and in 288 he and Diocletian laid waste to Alamannic territory, burning crops. His own invasion fleet against Carausius failed in 289 or 290, perhaps lost to storms.

The rebel regime was ended in 296 by his subordinate Constantius. Maximian meanwhile held the Rhine frontier and then led an army through Spain to fight Berber raiders in Mauretania. At Diocletian's insistence he abdicated on 1 May 305 and retired to southern Italy.

Late in 306 Maximian took the title of Augustus again to support his son Maxentius, who had been declared emperor in Rome. In April 307 he tried to depose his son and fled to Constantine at Trier. At the Conference of Carnuntum in November 308 Diocletian and Galerius forced him to renounce his claim once more. In 310, while Constantine was campaigning against the Franks, Maximian announced at Arles that Constantine was dead and took the purple. Most of the army stayed loyal, and Constantine captured him at Marseille. Maximian hanged himself in July 310, on Constantine's urging. His image was first purged and, after Maxentius's defeat, restored, and he was deified.
maximilian-henry-of-bavaria: Maximilian Henry was the third son and fourth child of Albert VI, Duke of Bavaria, and his wife Mechthilde von Leuchtenberg. Around 1640, at the Gymnasium Tricoronatum, he met the brothers Franz Egon of Fürstenberg and Wilhelm Egon von Fürstenberg, a friendship that would guide all three careers. Elected coadjutor in Cologne before 1650, he was the clear successor of his uncle Ferdinand of Bavaria, and when he succeeded him he made Franz his prime minister.

When Ferdinand III, Holy Roman Emperor, died in 1657, Maximilian Henry and the Electors of Mainz and Trier sent Wilhelm to sound out Ferdinand Maria, Elector of Bavaria, as a candidate against his Habsburg cousins, but he declined. The electors then bound Leopold I to restrictions, among them a promise not to support Spain in any way, and Maximilian Henry crowned him on 31 July 1658. In 1659 Cardinal Mazarin asked him and the Elector of Mainz to oversee the negotiations that ended the Franco-Spanish War with the Treaty of the Pyrenees.

In 1665 French funds let him raise an army to support French interests in the coming War of Devolution, in the hope of gaining territory for himself. Before the Franco-Dutch War his subjects grew uneasy: in 1670 the city of Cologne took in a Dutch garrison of 5,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry against an expected French army, and in 1671 he let the French pass freely through his lands and build warehouses there. When the Emperor joined the war on the Dutch side in 1672, his lands were attacked and he sought more French help.

After Wilhelm was arrested on 14 February 1674 for his work against the Habsburgs, Maximilian Henry quickly negotiated an end to Cologne's part in the war. In December he signed a treaty with Austria never to employ the Fürstenbergs again, kept secret until 1677 for fear of French reprisal. Named Bishop of Münster in 1683, he was refused confirmation by Pope Innocent XI. He died in 1688 and was succeeded by Joseph Clemens of Bavaria.
maximilian-i-elector-of-bavaria: Maximilian was born in Munich on 17 April 1573, the eldest son of William V, Duke of Bavaria, and Renata of Lorraine to survive infancy. He was educated by the Jesuits and began to take part in government by about 1591 to 1594, as his father's difficulties in ruling grew. In 1595 he married his cousin Elisabeth Renata, daughter of Charles III, Duke of Lorraine, and he became Duke of Bavaria on his father's abdication in 1597. Frail in health, he had high ambitions for himself and his duchy. Although a rigid adherent of the Catholic faith, he was not always subservient to the church.

Maximilian took no part in German politics until 1607, when he was charged with executing the imperial ban against the Protestant free city of Donauwörth. His troops occupied it in December 1607 and restored Catholic supremacy. Alarmed Protestant princes formed the Protestant Union, which was answered in 1609 by the Catholic League, in whose formation he took an important part. His policy was defensive, and he refused to let the League become a tool of the Habsburgs.

In October 1619 he agreed a treaty with Emperor Ferdinand II, and on 8 November 1620 his troops under Count Tilly defeated Frederick, King of Bohemia, at the Battle of White Mountain. In February 1623 he was invested with the electoral dignity, and the Upper Palatinate came to him.

The war later turned against Bavaria. Early in 1632 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden marched into the electorate and occupied Munich, and the Swedes and their French allies ravaged it. In March 1647 Maximilian concluded the Truce of Ulm with France and Sweden but then disregarded it at the entreaty of Ferdinand III. His forces were defeated at Zusmarshausen in May 1648. By the Peace of Westphalia he kept the electoral dignity, now hereditary, and the Upper Palatinate, but gave up the Lower Palatinate to Charles Louis, Frederick V's son.

At home he restored the state finances, reorganised the administration and army, introduced mercantilist measures and issued a new body of law, the Codex Maximilianeus. He enlarged the Munich Residenz and commissioned four hunt paintings from Peter Paul Rubens.

After the death of Elisabeth Renata, who left no children, Maximilian married his niece Maria Anna of Austria on 15 July 1635, hoping for an heir. Two sons followed, and Ferdinand Maria succeeded him. He died at Ingolstadt on 27 September 1651 and was buried in St Michael's Church, Munich. In 1839 King Ludwig I of Bavaria erected a statue in his memory in Munich.
maximilian-i-holy-roman-emperor: Maximilian was born at Wiener Neustadt on 22 March 1459, the only surviving son of Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor, and Eleanor of Portugal. In his infancy he and his parents were besieged in Vienna by Albert of Austria. Charles the Bold of Burgundy died at the Battle of Nancy on 5 January 1477, and his daughter Mary of Burgundy claimed his lands while Louis XI of France seized the Duchy of Burgundy by force. Mary agreed to marry Maximilian on 19 August 1477, and he took over the defence of her lands without help from the Empire. He defeated the French at the Battle of Guinegate on 7 August 1479.

Maximilian was elected King of the Romans at Frankfurt on 16 February 1486 and crowned at Aachen on 9 April, and he ruled jointly with his father until Frederick's death in 1493. He was never crowned by the Pope because the Venetians blocked the way to Rome, so in 1508 he proclaimed himself elected emperor at Trento, and Pope Julius II later recognised it. This broke the tradition of papal coronation.

He was open to reform. At the Reichstag of 1495 at Worms the Reichskammergericht was introduced as a court largely independent of the emperor, with a new tax, the Gemeine Pfennig. His campaigns in Italy against the French went badly, since the forces he could pay for were too small. He depended on loans from Upper German banking families, notably the Fugger and Welser families, and about 70 percent of his income went to war. His son Philip the Handsome married the future queen Joanna of Castile in 1496, which prepared the Habsburg succession in Spain. Maximilian lost family lands in Switzerland to the Swiss Confederacy.

Maximilian fell from his horse in 1501 and injured his leg, which pained him for the rest of his life, and from 1514 he travelled everywhere with his coffin. He died on 12 January 1519. In German tradition he is the last knight, a title from a poem by Anastasius Grün, and scholars still debate whether he was the last knight or the first Renaissance prince. Through a programme of images unlike any before, with the help of scholars and artists, he built a royal image of himself that historians call unmatched. Historians of the late nineteenth century such as Leopold von Ranke blamed him for putting his dynasty before Germany, while the work of Hermann Wiesflecker has led to a more favourable view.
maximilian-i-joseph-of-bavaria: Maximilian was born on 27 May 1756 at Schwetzingen, the son of Count Palatine Frederick Michael of Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld. After his father's death in 1767 he was educated under the supervision of his uncle, Duke Christian IV of Zweibrücken. He became Count of Rappoltstein in 1776 and in 1777 took service as a colonel in the French Royal Army, rising rapidly to major-general and serving at Strasbourg from 1782 to 1789. At the outbreak of the French Revolution he moved to the Austrian service and fought in the opening campaigns of the French Revolutionary War. He succeeded his brother Charles II as Duke of Zweibrücken on 1 April 1795, though France had entirely occupied the duchy.

On 16 February 1799 Maximilian became Elector of Bavaria, as Maximilian IV Joseph, on the extinction of the Palatinate-Sulzbach line. He found the army in abject condition and made rebuilding it a priority. In his new ministry the most powerful influence was Count Max Josef von Montgelas, whose policies were enlightened and French. Agriculture and commerce were encouraged, a new criminal code was drawn up, taxes were equalised without regard to traditional privileges, and a number of religious houses were suppressed and their revenues used for education. He moved the University of Ingolstadt to Landshut in 1800. Secularisation of 1802 and 1803 nationalised cultural assets of the Church, and Protestants were emancipated.

His foreign policy was dictated by dynastic and Bavarian considerations. Until 1813 he was the most faithful of Napoleon's German allies, a tie strengthened by the marriage of his eldest daughter to Eugène de Beauharnais. The Treaty of Pressburg of 26 December 1805 gave him the royal title and territory in Swabia and Franconia, and he took the title of king on 1 January 1806. After 1809 he received Tyrol and Innviertel from Austria. By the Treaty of Ried on 8 October 1813 he joined the Allies on condition that his kingdom's integrity was guaranteed, and declared war on France on 14 October.

In 1814 Bavaria returned Tyrol to Austria in exchange for Würzburg, and at the Congress of Vienna Maximilian ceded Salzburg and other districts in return for the western Palatinate. He opposed any reorganisation of Germany that endangered Bavarian independence, which contributed to the loose structure of the German Confederation. After Montgelas fell in 1817, he granted a constitution on 26 May 1818, partly to give unity to his varied territories. He founded the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich in 1808 and ordered the National Theatre built in 1810. Maximilian died at Nymphenburg Palace on 13 October 1825 and was succeeded by his son Ludwig I.
maximilian-i-of-mexico: Maximilian was born on 6 July 1832 at the Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna, the son of Archduke Franz Karl and Princess Sophie of Bavaria. Not destined to rule, he trained in the small Imperial Austrian Navy, which his brother Franz Joseph helped to fund, and in 1856 he met and then married Charlotte of Belgium. On 28 February 1857 Franz Joseph named him viceroy of Lombardy-Venetia. His authority did not fully extend over the Austrian garrison, which opposed liberal reforms, and when Franz Joseph refused his request for wider powers, he was left with a limited role while tensions with Piedmont rose. He was dismissed in 1859.

Mexican conservatives, beaten in the civil war of 1858 to 1861, sought outside allies. After the government of Benito Juárez suspended payment of foreign debts in 1861, France began military operations in 1862, was repulsed at Puebla on 5 May 1862, and took the capital in June 1863. Maximilian, approached by Mexican monarchists, accepted the crown on 10 April 1864 after a referendum in Mexico that was not genuine, with a pledge of French military support.

His hold was shaky from the start. Instead of reversing the liberal reforms of the Constitution of 1857, as his conservative backers expected, he supported them and declared an amnesty for liberals. The United States, which saw the French intervention as a breach of the Monroe Doctrine, never recognised the empire, and after its Civil War ended in 1865 it aided Juárez with loans and volunteers. French armies withdrew in 1866 on the orders of Napoleon III.

Maximilian was captured at Querétaro. His trial opened on 13 June 1867, and after one day he was found guilty of conspiracy and sentenced to death. Victor Hugo and Giuseppe Garibaldi were among those who asked for mercy, but Juárez refused, to show that Mexico would not tolerate further foreign invasions. Maximilian was shot on 19 June 1867 with his generals Miguel Miramón and Tomás Mejía. His death ended monarchism as a major force in Mexico. Édouard Manet painted the execution three times, and recent writing treats Maximilian less as a villain and more as a liberal in the line of Juárez and Porfirio Díaz.
maximilian-ii-emanuel-elector-of-bavaria: Maximilian II Emanuel was born in Munich on 11 July 1662, the son of Ferdinand Maria, Elector of Bavaria, and Princess Henriette Adelaide of Savoy. He inherited the electorate while still a minor in 1679 and remained under the regency of his uncle Maximilian Philipp until 1680. By 1683 he had begun a military career, fighting in the defence of Vienna against the Ottoman attempt to push further into Europe. On 15 July 1685 he married Maria Antonia, daughter of Emperor Leopold I, an unhappy marriage that nonetheless produced an heir for both Bavaria and the Spanish monarchy.

His fame was assured in 1688 when he led the capture of Belgrade from the Turks, with the support of Serbian insurgents under Jovan Monasterlija. In the War of the Grand Alliance he fought on the Habsburgs' side on the Rhine frontier and was made governor of the Spanish Netherlands in late 1691. His son Joseph Ferdinand, born in October 1692, was named heir to the Spanish crown but died in 1699. In 1695 French troops besieged and bombarded Brussels, and the resulting fire was the most destructive event in the city's history.

In the War of the Spanish Succession he sided with France. After the defeat at Blenheim in 1704 the Bavarian court went to the Spanish Netherlands, his sons were held for years in Austria, and Bavaria was partitioned between Austria and the Elector Palatine, whose harsh administration provoked a serious peasant uprising. After the Battle of Ramillies on 23 May 1706 he found refuge at Versailles. The Treaty of Rastatt in 1714 compelled Austria to restore him fully, including the Upper Palatinate.

Back in Bavaria Max Emanuel turned to building to make up for the failure of his political ambitions, and was bitter that others were raised to royal rank. In 1717 he sent troops against the Turks again, and in 1724 he united the Wittelsbach lines, which with his son Clemens August of Cologne and the electors Palatine and of Trier commanded four votes in an imperial election. He died of a stroke in 1726 and is buried in the crypt of the Theatinerkirche in Munich.

A patron of the arts, he bought Dutch and Flemish paintings as governor, and his return in 1715 marked the beginning of Bavarian Rococo. The Nymphenburg Palace was enlarged, the new Schleissheim Palace was completed in 1726, and Joseph Effner built the hunting lodge of Fürstenried. His son Charles Albert later became Holy Roman Emperor.
maximilian-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Maximilian was born in Vienna on 31 July 1527, the eldest son of the Habsburg king Ferdinand I and nephew of Emperor Charles V. He was educated mainly in Italy by humanist scholars, learned something of Lutheran teaching in his youth and corresponded early with the Protestant prince Augustus of Saxony. On 13 September 1548 he married his cousin Maria of Spain, and the marriage produced sixteen children, of whom nine lived to adulthood.

In Vienna he grew close to the court preacher Sebastian Pfauser, which alarmed his father. After several refusals he agreed in 1560 to Pfauser's banishment and attended Catholic Mass again, though his views were tinged with Lutheranism to the end of his life.

Maximilian was crowned King of Bohemia in 1562, elected King of the Romans on 24 November 1562 and crowned King of Hungary and Croatia in 1563. He succeeded Ferdinand as emperor on 25 July 1564. He granted religious liberty to the Lutheran nobles and knights in Austria and refused to publish the decrees of the Council of Trent, but he would not meet the demands of the Lutheran princes at the Diet of Augsburg in 1566. His reign saw the high point of Protestantism in Austria and Bohemia, which he did not try to suppress.

War with the Ottomans resumed in 1566, and they took Szigetvár while their sultan died during the siege. The Treaty of Adrianople of 1568 required Maximilian to recognise Ottoman suzerainty over Transylvania, Wallachia and Moldavia. In 1576 part of the Polish and Lithuanian magnates elected him king of Poland against Stephen Báthory, but he was not widely accepted there.

Maximilian died at Regensburg on 12 October 1576 while preparing to invade Poland, and on his deathbed he refused the last sacraments. He is buried in St Vitus Cathedral in Prague. His eldest surviving son Rudolf succeeded him. His court was a centre of humanist scholarship where Catholic and Protestant scholars worked together, including the botanist Carolus Clusius, and his library under Hugo Blotius became the nucleus of the Austrian National Library. Paula Sutter Fichtner holds that he failed in his three main aims, while Peter Marshall argues that his tolerance and patronage kept a precarious peace.
maximilian-ii-of-bavaria: Maximilian was born in Munich on 28 November 1811, the eldest child of Crown Prince Ludwig, later King Ludwig I, and Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen, and was named after his grandfather, King Maximilian I. He studied at Göttingen and Berlin and travelled in Germany, Italy and Greece. His father brought him into the council of state in 1836. He showed a studious disposition and once said that, had he not been born a prince, he would have chosen to be a professor. At the chateau of Hohenschwangau near Füssen, which he had rebuilt, he gathered artists and scholars around him. In 1842 he married the Prussian princess Marie Friederike Franziska Hedwig, and they had two sons, Ludwig II and Otto.

Ludwig I's abdication on 20 March 1848 called him suddenly to the throne, and his choice of ministers promised a liberal regime. An uprising in the Bavarian Palatinate in 1849 was put down with the help of the Prussian army. From 1850 his government leaned towards absolute monarchy, though he steered between classical liberalism, Prussian-inspired Pan-Germanism and the Ultramontanes. He attended the Frankfurt Assembly but opposed its plans, refused to recognise its imperial constitution and helped Austria restore the federal diet.

In 1850 Austria, Bavaria and their allies moved troops towards Hesse-Kassel, and Prussia backed down in the Punctation of Olmütz, which strengthened the alliance of Bavaria with Austria. He nonetheless tried to keep Bavaria independent by playing the two powers against each other. In 1863 he supported Austria's reform plan at the Frankfurt Fürstentag.

He invited scholars such as Geibel, Liebig, Heyse and Sybel to Munich whatever their religion, which angered conservative Catholics and Protestants. He also financed studies of the art, costumes, dialects and customs of the Bavarian peasantry, with the help of his secretary Franz Xaver von Schönwerth, to support a separate Bavarian identity against Pan-Germanism. He consulted ministers and experts before deciding, which caused delays, as did his frequent journeys to Italy and Greece.

Constant ill health often kept him abroad or in the countryside. After a brief illness he died in Munich on 10 March 1864 and was buried in the Theatinerkirche. His son Ludwig II succeeded him. He commissioned Maximilianstrasse and the Bavarian National Museum in Munich and founded the Maximilian Order for Science and Art in 1853. Hans Christian Andersen, who visited him, described him as young and highly amiable.
maximilian-von-montgelas: Montgelas came of a noble family of the Duchy of Savoy. His father, Janus Sigmund Garnerin, Baron Montgelas, served Maximilian III, Elector of Bavaria, and married Countess Ursula von Trauner; Maximilian was their eldest son, born in Munich. He was educated at Nancy, Strasbourg and Ingolstadt and all his life wrote French more easily than German, though he wished to be counted a Bavarian. He entered the censorship of books in 1779, but the Elector Charles Theodore turned against him on learning that he belonged to the Illuminati, the anti-clerical secret society.

He moved to Zweibrücken and became private secretary to Maximilian Joseph, the Duke's brother, who made him a minister on succeeding to the duchy; Montgelas attended the Second Congress of Rastatt in 1798. As early as 1796, while his master was a landless exile in Ansbach, he had drawn up a plan for modernising Bavaria, the Ansbacher mémoire, rediscovered in the 1960s and published in 1970 by his biographer Eberhard Weis. He concluded the Treaty of Bogenhausen with France in August 1805, holding that Bavaria could stand against Austria and Prussia only with French help. German opponents of French supremacy saw him as the type of the unpatriotic politician.

At home he taxed the nobility and clergy, built a full cadastral survey, issued the constitution of 1808, which ended the remains of serfdom, and abolished torture with a new penal code in 1812. He introduced compulsory schooling, military service and vaccination, replaced the old chambers with modern ministries, removed internal tolls and, through the Dienstpragmatik, opened the civil service to the educated regardless of birth or faith. Protestants gained civil rights and the Jewish communities a secure, though still discriminatory, legal status. He kept the parliament promised in 1808 from ever meeting.

The decision to turn against Napoleon in 1814 was taken under the influence of the king's son and Marshal Wrede rather than Montgelas, and his enemies persuaded the king to dismiss him in 1817. He married Countess von Arco in 1803, had eight children and was made a count in 1809. He sat in the Bavarian House of Lords until his death in 1838. In 2005 Bavaria and Munich raised a monument to him at the Promenadenplatz.
maximiliano-hernandez-martinez: Maximiliano Hernández Martínez was born on 21 October 1882 in San Matías, El Salvador. He attended the Polytechnic School of Guatemala, a military academy, and abandoned law studies at the University of El Salvador for a military career, reaching the rank of brigadier general by 1919. In 1931 he withdrew from the presidential race and endorsed Arturo Araujo, who made him vice president and later minister of war. Araujo removed him as minister of war on 1 December 1931, and on 2 December junior officers, angry at unpaid wages, overthrew Araujo. The junta known as the Civic Directory named Martínez provisional president.

In January 1932 Martínez crushed a communist and indigenous rebellion. The killings by the military and police that followed are known as La Matanza, the Massacre, and caused the deaths of between 10,000 and 40,000 peasants. The United States and the other Central American states did not recognise his government until January 1934. In 1933 he founded the National Pro Patria Party, the only legal party, and in 1935, 1939 and 1944 he was the only candidate and received every vote cast. A network of informants known as orejas, or ears, watched for dissent. He founded the Central Reserve Bank, and laws discriminating against Arab, Chinese and indigenous minorities were passed in 1934, 1939 and 1943.

Martínez admired European fascist movements and was described by some as a fascist, yet El Salvador declared war on Germany, Italy and Japan in December 1941, and from 1940 he suppressed Nazi activity.

On Palm Sunday, 2 April 1944, army units launched a coup that failed because the National Police, the National Guard and the rest of the army stayed loyal. Twenty leaders were executed, and on 28 April students and doctors went on strike in protest. Soldiers killed over 100 students, and workers, bankers and professors joined a general strike. Martínez resigned on 9 May 1944 and fled to Guatemala and then Honduras. On 15 May 1966 his taxi driver stabbed him to death in Honduras after a labour dispute. He was the longest-serving Salvadoran president, and his rule is called the Martinato.
maximilien-de-bethune-duke-of-sully: Maximilien de Béthune was born on 13 December 1560 at the Château de Rosny near Mantes-la-Jolie and raised a Huguenot. In 1571, aged eleven, he was presented to Henry of Navarre and remained attached to the future king. He was studying in Paris at the time of the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre and escaped by carrying a Catholic book of hours under his arm. As Baron of Rosny he joined the Protestant army in 1575, and he was seriously wounded at the battle of Ivry in 1590. He advised Henry IV to become Catholic but refused to convert himself.

Rosny took charge of the royal finances as Superintendent of Finances. He allowed the free export of grain and wine, lowered legal interest, set up a court for speculation and abolished several offices. By his rigorous conduct of the finances he saved an average of a million livres a year between 1600 and 1610. In 1606 he was made first Duke of Sully and a peer of France, and he declined the office of constable of France because he would not become a Catholic.

Sully encouraged agriculture, drained swamps, built roads and bridges, began the Canal de Briare and started a great line of frontier defences. He opposed the king's colonial policy, against men such as Samuel Champlain. He negotiated the peace of 1602 after fighting beside Henry in Savoy, and he arranged Henry's marriage to Marie de' Medici. He was unpopular, seen as selfish, obstinate and rude, and he amassed a large personal fortune.

His political role effectively ended with the assassination of Henry IV on 14 May 1610. He resigned as superintendent of finances on 26 January 1611 after a stormy debate in the regency council. He was made a marshal of France in 1634 and died at Villebon on 22 December 1641, aged 81.

His memoirs, the Économies royales, printed in 1638, are valuable sources for the period although they contain fictions. They set out a Grand Design, published in the dead king's name, for a Europe of fifteen roughly equal states under a council with a common army, intended to end the religious wars. Historians stress his part in building a centralised administration, though later monarchs repealed most of his measures. The Pavillon Sully of the Louvre is named for him.
maximilien-robespierre: Robespierre was baptised on 6 May 1758 in Arras, in Artois, the eldest of four children of François Maximilien Barthélémy de Robespierre, a lawyer, and Jacqueline Marguerite Carrault, the daughter of a brewer. After three years of law studies he graduated in July 1780 with a special prize for academic achievement and conduct. Admitted to the bar, he was appointed one of the five judges of the local criminal court in March 1782, but soon resigned, uncomfortable at passing capital sentences because he opposed the death penalty.

In the Estates General he gave his first speech on 6 June 1789, attacking the hierarchy of the church. In 1790 he demanded that all Frenchmen be admissible to public positions without distinction other than virtue and talent, and on 31 March was elected president of the Jacobin Club. In 1791 he gave 328 speeches and argued that all citizens, not only those with the vote, should be allowed to serve in the National Guard. He warned the Jacobins against war with Austria, saying on 2 January 1792 that no one loves armed missionaries.

He was elected to the National Convention in September 1792, where the Jacobins sat on the high benches known as the Mountain, and he worked to bring about the execution of Louis XVI, who was guillotined on 21 January 1793.

On 27 July 1793 Robespierre joined the Committee of Public Safety, at a time when France faced rebellion in the Vendée and in Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux and hostility across Europe. In a report of 5 February 1794 he argued that in revolution the springs of popular government were virtue and terror together. Danton and Desmoulins were tried in April 1794. The Law of 22 Prairial, passed on 10 June, denied accused persons counsel and left the revolutionary tribunals only two verdicts, acquittal or death; within three days 156 people were sent to the guillotine. On 6 and 7 May 1794 he had announced the recognition of God and the immortality of the soul and the festivals of the Supreme Being.

On 9 Thermidor, almost thirty-five deputies, most of them from the Mountain, spoke against Robespierre, and his voice was shouted down. He was arrested with around 90 others, among them Louis Antoine de Saint-Just, Georges Couthon and his brother Augustin. On 28 July 1794 he and twenty-one others were condemned under the Law of 22 Prairial without a hearing and guillotined. The Thermidorians held him the most culpable for the bloodshed, and Lazare Carnot called him a hypocrite. His views and policies remain controversial: he is remembered for his campaigns for the voting rights of all men and against the Atlantic slave trade, and for his part in the repression of the Revolution's opponents.
maximin-of-trier: Maximin was born at Silly near Poitiers and became the sixth bishop of Trier. He stood close to the courts of the emperors Constantine II and Constans, and twice received the exiled Athanasius of Alexandria as an honoured guest, in 336–37 and again in 343.

In the Arian controversy he had first belonged to the party of Paul I of Constantinople, but he took part in the synod of Sardica called by Pope Julius I around 342. When four Arian bishops then came from Antioch to Trier to win Constans to their cause, Maximin refused to receive them and persuaded the emperor to reject their proposals. He died at Poitiers on 12 September 346, and his feast is kept on 29 May.

He was buried in the cemetery outside the northern gate of Trier, in the many-chambered crypt of a church of John the Evangelist, where later bishops were laid beside him; the church later became St. Maximin's Abbey. Gregory of Tours attests to his cult in that church and at his grave. The abbey, one of the oldest in western Europe, was destroyed by the Normans in 882, rebuilt, rebuilt again entirely in the 1680s, secularised in 1802 and bombed in World War II, and has since been largely demolished.

Art shows him as a bishop with a book, a model of a church and a bear carrying his travelling pack, a detail borrowed from the legend of Saint Corbinian. He was invoked against perjury, loss at sea and destructive rains, and his cult was strongest around Trier and in Alsace. Medieval legend confused him with Maximinus of Aix, said to have brought Mary Magdalene to Provence in a boat without rudder or mast; that story was told in Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend.
maximinus-thrax: Maximinus, whose Latin name was Gaius Julius Verus Maximinus, was born in about 173, a date inferred from later sources that give his age at death as 65. Herodian, the only contemporary source, calls him Thraco-Roman. The Historia Augusta, a notoriously unreliable work, says he was born in Thrace or Moesia to a Gothic father and an Alanic mother, a claim many scholars reject as anachronistic; his ancestry remains an open question. He was a provincial of low birth whom the Senate regarded as a barbarian. He joined the army under Septimius Severus and rose to command the Legio IV Italica, whose Pannonian recruits were angered by Severus Alexander's payments to the Alemanni and his avoidance of war.

In 235 the army killed Severus Alexander and his mother at Moguntiacum, modern Mainz, and elected Maximinus emperor. The Praetorian Guard acclaimed him and the Senate grudgingly confirmed the choice. He was the first emperor from neither the senatorial nor the equestrian class. Once in power he removed Alexander's close advisers, put down two plots, and defeated the Alemanni in a swamp in the Agri Decumates, taking the title Germanicus Maximus. He wintered at Sirmium and fought the Dacians and Sarmatians in 235–236, and he doubled the soldiers' pay. This and almost continuous warfare required higher taxes, and tax collectors resorted to violent methods and illegal confiscations, which alienated the governing class.

In early 238 landowners in the province of Africa revolted and proclaimed the governor, Gordian I, and his son Gordian II co-emperors, and the Senate backed them. Capelianus, governor of Numidia, defeated them; Gordian II died in the fighting and Gordian I hanged himself. The Senate then chose Pupienus and Balbinus as co-emperors, and under pressure from the Roman crowd made Gordian I's grandson, Gordian III, caesar.

Maximinus marched on Rome, but Aquileia closed its gates against him. His troops starved and grew disaffected during the siege, and in about May or June 238 soldiers of the Legio II Parthica assassinated him and his son. He never visited Rome as emperor. His accession is commonly seen as the beginning of the Crisis of the Third Century, a period of instability and civil war that lasted until 284.
maximo-gomez: Gómez was born in Baní, in what is now the province of Peravia, while the Dominican Republic was under Haitian rule. As a teenager in the 1850s he fought against the incursions of Faustin Soulouque in the Dominican War of Independence. After the Dominican general Pedro Florentino burned Baní, he fought on the Spanish side in the Dominican Restoration War, a choice he later admitted regretting, and rose from sergeant to commander. When Spain was defeated in 1865 he left with its troops for Cuba, where he started a farm and married Bernarda Toro.

Retiring from the Spanish Army, he joined the Cuban rebels in 1868 and gave the mambises their most feared tactic, the machete charge, first used at the Battle of Pino de Baire on 25 October 1868, where a Spanish column suffered 233 casualties.
