He took command of the Camaguey district after the death of Ignacio Agramonte in May 1873, won at El Naranjo in February 1874 and fought at Las Guasimas, where a battalion of 500 Chinese served under him. In early 1875 he crossed the Trocha, burned 83 plantations around Sancti Spíritus and freed their slaves, until conservative leaders diverted his troops.

Between the wars he worked in Jamaica and Panama, where he supervised a labourers' brigade on the canal, and in 1887 he offered Ramón Emeterio Betances to lead a revolt in Puerto Rico. In the later war he made the torching of cane haciendas a weapon against Spain's economy, though he wrote that he abhorred it, ending with the cry ¡Bendita sea la tea! (Blessed be the torch!). His son Francisco Gómez y Toro was killed on 7 December 1896 trying to recover the body of Antonio Maceo. On 5 March 1898 he refused the offer of Captain-General Ramón Blanco y Erenas to join the Spanish against the United States.

The Asamblea del Cerro dismissed him as general-in-chief in 1899 and abolished the post. In 1901 he refused a presidential nomination he was expected to win unopposed, feeling that as a Dominican he should not be Cuba's civil leader and admitting that he had helped Cuba to make up for fighting his own countrymen. He died at his villa and was buried in the Colón Cemetery in Havana. His portrait appears on the Cuban 10 peso bill, and a major avenue in Santo Domingo bears his name.
may-coup-poland: Józef Piłsudski had largely controlled the politics of the re-established Polish state but lost that advantage after the failed Kiev offensive of spring 1920, while keeping the esteem of parts of the armed forces. In November 1925 the cabinet of Władysław Grabski gave way to that of Aleksander Skrzyński, backed by the National Democrats and the Polish Socialist Party; when the socialists withdrew, it fell in turn and was replaced by a government under Wincenty Witos, formed by the Polish People's Party "Piast" and the Christian Union of National Unity. It had even less popular support than its predecessors.

Piłsudski regarded the constant shifts of power in the Sejm, the Polish parliament, as chaotic and damaging. He also saw threats to Poland's independence in the Locarno Treaties of 1925, by which the western but not the eastern borders of Germany were guaranteed, and in the Treaty of Berlin concluded by Germany and the Soviet Union in 1926.

On 10 May 1926, the day the Witos government was formed, Piłsudski told the newspaper Kurier Poranny that he was ready to fight the evil of sejmocracy, a contemptuous word for rule by parliament, and promised a sanation, or restoration to health, of political life. The edition was confiscated. In the night of 11–12 May units of the Warsaw garrison marched to Rembertów and pledged him their support; on 12 May they moved on Warsaw and took the bridges over the Vistula River.

At about 17:00 Piłsudski met President Stanisław Wojciechowski on the Poniatowski Bridge. He demanded the resignation of the cabinet; the president demanded that his forces capitulate. Fighting began at about 19:00. On 14 May the Polish Socialist Party declared for the rebels and called a general strike, and striking railwaymen kept government reinforcements from reaching Warsaw. To prevent a nationwide civil war, Wojciechowski and Witos resigned. In all 215 soldiers and 164 civilians were killed and some 900 people wounded.

Kazimierz Bartel formed a new government with Piłsudski as minister of military affairs. On 31 May the National Assembly nominated Piłsudski as president, but he declined, and Ignacy Mościcki took the office. Piłsudski held the posts of defence minister and inspector general of the armed forces in every government until his death, and headed two of them himself, in 1926–1928 and 1930. In 1935 his supporters replaced the democratic March Constitution with the April Constitution, which provided for a strong presidency but came too late for him to assume it.
may-coup-serbia: Serbia's rival dynasties had foreign sponsors: the Obrenović family was mostly pro-Austrian, the Karađorđević family mostly pro-Russian. King Milan Obrenović abdicated in 1889 in favour of his son, and Alexander, who declared himself of age in 1893 by imprisoning his regents and ministers in the palace, ruled through a series of coups. His marriage on 23 July 1900 to Draga Mašin, a widow nine years his senior and his mother's former lady-in-waiting, was opposed by both his parents, and the whole Đorđević government resigned in protest.

The queen's false pregnancy cost the king the favour of the Russian court, and her brother Nikola Lunjevica angered the junior officers. In August 1901 officers among them Dragutin Dimitrijević Apis began plotting to kill the royal couple. Peter Karađorđević, living in Geneva, would not commit himself to regicide, but Dimitrijević argued that a living Alexander might trigger a civil war.

The plotters acted on a night when Lieutenant Colonel Mihailo Naumović, one of them, commanded at the palace. Guard lieutenant Petar Živković opened the gate at 2:00 a.m., the electric lighting went out, and for nearly two hours the conspirators searched in vain, killing Naumović, unknown to them, and Captain Jovan Miljković, while Apis was wounded by three bullets in the chest. The king and queen were found hiding in a wardrobe. Accounts of the end differ, but both were killed, and their bodies were mutilated and thrown from a second-floor window.

That night the queen's brothers Nikola and Nikodije were shot by a firing squad under Lieutenant Vojislav Tankosić, and the prime minister Dimitrije Cincar-Marković and the army minister Milovan Pavlović were killed in their homes.

On 4 June 1903 the National Assembly voted Peter Karađorđević king, and a mission brought him from Geneva. Russia and Austria-Hungary condemned the killings; Great Britain and the Netherlands withdrew their ambassadors and imposed sanctions, and by January 1904 only the ambassadors of the Kingdom of Greece and the Ottoman Empire remained. Army units loyal to the fallen king mutinied in Niš in 1904.

Under King Peter the conspirators kept great power, and Dimitrijević became their leader at the head of the Black Hand, which in 1914 ordered the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo. Worsening relations with Austria-Hungary led to the Pig War of 1906–08. After the Salonika Trial, Dimitrijević was found guilty of treason on 23 May 1917 and executed by firing squad.
may-there-always-be-sunshine: The song was first performed by Maya Kristalinskaya on the radio show Good Morning! in July 1962. Tamara Miansarova sang it at the Sopot International Song Festival in 1963 and won first prize there, after which it became popular throughout the Soviet Union and abroad. Young Pioneers sang it at their camps and school meetings, as did Little Octobrists in primary schools and even children below school age.

The words speak of a longing for lasting peace among millions of people, young and old. In war, the song holds, there are no winners, and for the sake of the people and above all their children peace must be won and the dark clouds that cover the sun removed. In the Soviet Union it was widely regarded as expressing the people's desire for peace.

In 1964 the Swedish band Hootenanny Singers, led by the future ABBA member Björn Ulvaeus, released Gabrielle, based on the song, and had a success in Scandinavia that gave the band its first international exposure. Pete Seeger sang it in English, and it appears on Together in Concert, recorded with Arlo Guthrie in 1975. Ilse and Hans Naumilkat and Manfred Streubel made a German version, Immer lebe die Sonne, sung by the Ernst Thälmann Pioneers; Finnish Pioneers sang it as Paistaa aurinko aina, and Estonian Pioneers in a translation by Heljo Mänd, best known in the recording by Georg Ots. Gidi Koren wrote Hebrew words for his group The Brothers & the Sisters.

The Canadian children's musicians Charlotte Diamond, on her album 10 Carrot Diamond of 1985, and Raffi sang the chorus in several languages. The song was part of a medley at the opening ceremony of the 2014 Olympic Winter Games in Sochi, and its title is inscribed on the pedestal of a bronze monument to Samantha Smith at Artek in Crimea.
may-thirtieth-movement: The treaty ports created by the unequal treaties had produced a largely colonial society within China. In Shanghai the British, about 9,000 people, held the largest foreign investment and controlled the administration of the International Settlement, alongside some 14,000 Japanese and growing American interests. The British journalist Arthur Ransome later blamed the shootings on the ethnocentrism, arrogance and racism of British Shanghai, which he called the Shanghai Mind. The American journalist Milly Bennet recalled that acceptance in the city's business circles meant echoing the view that the Chinese should be grateful for British rule.

On 30 May 1925 thousands of workers, students and citizens, mobilised by students, the Chinese Communist Party and the trade unions, marched on Nanjing Road. The Shanghai Municipal Police arrested 15 leaders of a student protest and held them at the Louza police station, where a large crowd gathered to demand their release. Inspector Edward William Everson shouted a warning in English and in Wu and at 3:37 pm, with the crowd within six feet of the entrance, fired his revolver. His Sikh and Chinese officers fired some 40 rounds. At least 11 demonstrators died at the scene and five more later.

On 31 May protesters met at the Chinese Chamber of Commerce and demanded punishment of the officers, an end to extraterritoriality and the closing of the International Settlement. The Municipal Council declared martial law on 1 June, called up the Shanghai Volunteer Corps and raided Shanghai University. By 10 June about 130,000 workers were on strike at 107 foreign establishments.

The strikes and boycotts spread across the country and brought foreign economic interests to a near standstill. Public anger moved from the Japanese to the British, and Hong Kong was hit hardest by what became the Canton–Hong Kong strike; foreigners fired on Chinese protesters at Canton, Mukden and elsewhere. The warlord Feng Yuxiang threatened British interests, while Zhang Zuolin had protesters and CCP members arrested. The movement linked workplace exploitation with the struggle against foreign imperialism in the minds of many Chinese workers, and the Communist Party grew from 994 members early in 1925 to about 10,000 by the end of the year. In 1927 Mao Tse-tung compared it to the fall of the Bastille.
maya-blue: Maya blue is a composite of organic and inorganic matter: indigo from the leaves of the anil plant, Indigofera suffruticosa, called ch'oj in Mayan, bound to palygorskite, a clay of the fuller's earth type, with small traces of other minerals. Palygorskite is most common in the southern United States and is not known in large deposits in Mesoamerica. The pigment withstands nitric acid and other acids, alkalis, solvents and biodegradation, and can be destroyed only by very intense acid treatment under reflux. Its structure has inspired chemists to make new pigments such as Maya Violet.

Mesoamerican peoples used it on artworks, sculptures, murals and probably textiles, and to illuminate codices. Many illustrations of the Florentine Codex of Bernardino de Sahagún contain it, and its presence in the Grolier Codex helped to show that the manuscript, now called the Codex Maya of Mexico, is genuine. Blue was associated with the centre of a flame, the hottest part and so the richest in tonalli, and was held precious.

In 2008 researchers from Wheaton College concluded that the pigment was made in rituals at Chichén Itzá: near the sacred sinkhole, indigo and palygorskite were heated by burning them with copal incense, and the victims were painted blue before being thrown into the pit to please the rain god Chaak. After the conquest the Nahua painter Juan Gerson used it in his paintings at Tecamachalco, an example of the blend of native and European methods called Arte Indocristiano. Its making was later forgotten in Mexico, though examples in Cuba survive from the 19th century.

Powder diffraction in the 1950s showed that the pigment combines palygorskite and indigo. The Mexican historian and chemist Constantino Reyes-Valerio worked out how it was made by rereading early texts by Sahagún, Hernandez, Jimenez and others, examining murals under the microscope and using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy; his recipe, using palygorskite and montmorillonite clays with añil leaves, appeared in his book De Bonampak al Templo Mayor: Historia del Azul Maya en Mesoamerica. Later work with European scientists applied diffraction, Raman and other spectroscopies, voltammetry, nuclear magnetic resonance and computer modelling, gathered in a study in the journal Developments in Clay Science.
maya-script: The script was used mainly in the Classic period to write Classic Maya, a literary form of the extinct Chʼoltiʼ language, on stelae and monuments. After the Classic Maya collapse its use declined and disappeared in the central and southern lowlands. In the Postclassic period it continued in northern Yucatán to write Yucatec Maya, in the surviving codices such as the Dresde, Madrid and Paris. Not every Mayan language used it: the Quichean languages, such as Kʼicheʼ and Kaqchikel, used the Mixteca-Puebla style of central Mexico.

It was a logosyllabic system. A glyph could stand for a word or morpheme or for a syllable. Syllabic glyphs often came from logograms for one-syllable words, so that the sign for a fish fin, read kah, came to stand for the syllable ka. The word bʼalam, jaguar, could be written with one logogram, with syllabic additions, or wholly in syllables as bʼa-la-ma. Texts were arranged in blocks, usually in columns two blocks wide.

The earliest inscriptions identifiably Maya date to the 3rd century BCE, at late Preclassic sites such as Chakjobon and San Bartolo. It was once thought that the Maya took writing from the Olmec or Epi-Olmec culture, but murals excavated in 2005 pushed the origin back by several centuries, and it now seems possible that the Maya invented writing in Mesoamerica. Knowledge of the script was kept to the elite.

Bishop Diego de Landa ordered Maya books collected and destroyed, and many codices were lost. He also recorded a so-called alphabet of Maya signs, which was long dismissed as nonsense but eventually became a key resource in decipherment. Knowledge of the script was lost, probably by the end of the 16th century.

Nineteenth-century and early twentieth-century scholars decoded the numbers and passages on astronomy and the calendar. In 1952 Yuri Knorozov argued that Landa's signs were syllabic, and J. Eric S. Thompson was among the last major opponents of this approach. In 1959 Tatiana Proskouriakoff showed that the dates on the monuments at Piedras Negras recorded the lives of individuals, so that the inscriptions were dynastic histories. In December 1973 a working group at Palenque, including Linda Schele, Floyd Lounsbury and Peter Mathews, reconstructed most of the dynastic list of Palenque in one afternoon.
Since the early 1980s scholars have shown that most of the remaining signs form a syllabary, and the exhibition The Blood of Kings in 1986 brought the results to a wide audience.
mayadunne: Mayadunne was born in 1501 in Kotte, the youngest child of Vijayabahu VII, king of Kotte from 1509 to 1521, and his main queen. His full brothers were Bhuvanekabahu and Raigama Bandara. In 1521 the three revolted against their father, suspecting that he meant to leave the throne to Devaraja, a son of another queen. Mayadunne, though the youngest, is held to have been the mastermind. The revolt, remembered as the Wijayaba Kollaya, the Spoiling of Vijayabahu, ended with the king's assassination by a hired foreigner.

The brothers divided the kingdom. Bhuvanekabahu VII held Kotte with the area around present-day Colombo and Gampaha and the coasts of the North Western and Southern provinces; Raigama Bandara held Raigama, roughly the Kalutara District and the inland Southern Province; and Mayadunne took Sitawaka, present-day Avissawella, with roughly the modern Sabaragamuwa Province.

Bhuvanekabahu VII distrusted him from the start and drew close to the Portuguese, who had built a fort at Colombo in 1517. Local chiefs and people who resented that alliance backed Mayadunne, and in his first campaigns he had help from the anti-Portuguese kingdom of Calicut in India, but Kotte drove his forces back with Portuguese aid. The Portuguese wanted to kill him, but Bhuvanekabahu would not allow a full invasion of Sitawaka. Portuguese reports say that in 1550 their king sent 600 troops to Kotte, who fought Mayadunne at Nawagamuwa, where he had made a vow at the Pattini Devalaya before going to war.

After Raigama was annexed, the monks of Kotte who kept the Sacred Tooth Relic, seeing the Portuguese as hostile to Buddhism, secretly carried it to Sitawaka. By local tradition its holder could claim the throne of every kingdom of the island. As Mayadunne took more of Kotte's lands, Bhuvanekabahu and later Dharmapala of Kotte relied ever more on the Portuguese, and the rivalry became one between Sitawaka and the Portuguese.

Mayadunne's wars formed part of the Sinhalese–Portuguese War. He and his son defeated the Portuguese at the Battle of Mulleriyawa, after which Sitawaka was strong enough to challenge them and they lost the chance to control the whole island. In 1576 the Portuguese destroyed the Nawagamuwa Devale and set up a camp there. Mayadunne died in 1581, aged 80. His resistance, which kept the Portuguese from conquering the whole island, has led to his being counted among the great kings of Sri Lanka.
mayenne: The department lies in the Pays de la Loire region and has no sea coast, though Mont Saint-Michel Bay is about thirty kilometres to the north-west. It is roughly rectangular, 90 km long and 77 km wide, with an area of about 5,175 km2. The Manche, Orne, Sarthe, Maine-et-Loire and Ille-et-Vilaine departments surround it. The river Mayenne flows through its centre from north to south, passing the towns of Mayenne, Laval and Château-Gontier, and then joins the Sarthe to form the Maine, which flows into the Loire.

Mayenne is one of the original 83 departments, created on 4 March 1790 by the National Constituent Assembly during the early stages of the French Revolution. The new departments were meant to be uniform in administration and roughly equal in size and population. The old province of Maine was divided in two: Upper Maine, centred on Le Mans, became Sarthe, and Lower Maine, centred on Laval, became Mayenne. Anjou was too large for a single department and was cut down to form Maine-et-Loire, with Mayenne receiving Château-Gontier and Craon.

The border between Mayenne and Maine-et-Loire followed the southern limit of flax cultivation, since flax was a feature of the local economy. The northern two thirds of the department therefore correspond to western Maine, and the southern third to the northern part of Anjou. The department is also coextensive with the Roman Catholic Diocese of Laval.

The north of the department lies on the Armorican Massif, where the Mont des Avaloirs, at 417 m, is the highest point. The rest is largely flat, with some hilly areas and steep-sided valleys. Laval is the prefecture and largest town, and the department is divided into three arrondissements: Mayenne, Laval and Château-Gontier. It had 305,468 inhabitants in 2023, who are called Mayennais.

About 80 per cent of the land is farmed, and livestock rearing, above all of cattle, horses and pigs, predominates. Apple orchards supply a traditional cider industry. Iron and coal have been mined, and quarries yield marble, slate, limestone and flint. Industries include linen, paper and hemp, office furniture at Château-Gontier, and dairy products and electronics at Laval.
mayflower: The Mayflower was an English square-rigged merchant ship of about 180 tons, roughly 110 feet long and 25 feet in the beam, active from before 1609 until 1622. Her passengers included Separatists from a congregation of about 400 English Protestants who had gone to Leiden in 1608 to worship outside the Church of England, which they judged beyond reform. Others on board were hired hands, servants and farmers recruited by London merchants. The congregation's leader John Robinson stayed in Leiden with those who could not go.

The plan was for the small Speedwell to carry the Leiden group to England and for the Mayflower to take most passengers and supplies across the Atlantic. The Mayflower left London in mid-July 1620 with about 65 passengers and waited at Southampton. Speedwell sprang leaks three times, forcing the ships back to Dartmouth and then to Plymouth in England, and was abandoned, with 20 of her passengers crowded onto the Mayflower.

The ship sailed on 26 September 1620 with 102 passengers and a crew of about 30. The living area was about 20 by 80 feet with a ceiling of about five feet. Western gales slowed the crossing to more than two months. The ship sighted Cape Cod on 19 November 1620, in the old-style calendar, and anchored in what is now Provincetown Harbor on 21 November.

Before landing, the male Pilgrims and the other passengers, whom the Pilgrims called strangers, signed the Mayflower Compact, which set up a rudimentary government. The first winter at Plymouth was severe, with frozen ground, no shelter prepared and illness, and about half the crew died. William Bradford wrote that some who died took the origin of their death on an early exploring trip. The ship sailed for London on 15 April 1621, in the old-style calendar.

No record of the ship survives after 1624, when she was appraised at Rotherhithe at 128 pounds, eight shillings and fourpence. Charles Edward Banks held that she was broken up, and timbers bought from a Rotherhithe shipbreaker's yard in 1624 were used by Thomas Russell to build the Mayflower Barn at Jordans in Buckinghamshire, though this is not certain.

Bradford's journal and letters are the main source for the voyage and for Plymouth Colony. The harvest feast of 1621, attended by 90 Wampanoag people, is regarded as the origin of the American Thanksgiving. Richard Bevan calls the crossing the most culturally important of the voyages to the American colonies between 1620 and 1640.
mayflower-compact: The Pilgrims had hoped to reach America in early October with two ships, but delays meant that only the Mayflower sailed. Their intended destination was the Colony of Virginia, and the voyage was financed by the Company of Merchant Adventurers of London. Storms forced them to anchor at the hook of Cape Cod in Massachusetts, since provisions were running short. Some of the non-Puritan passengers, whom the Puritans called Strangers, then declared that they would use their own liberty, because none had power to command them outside the agreed territory of Virginia.

To prevent this, the Pilgrims determined to establish their own government while affirming allegiance to the Crown. A similar argument had been made earlier by passengers of the Sea Venture, and Stephen Hopkins, thought to be the man of that name aboard the Mayflower, had been convicted of mutiny and pardoned. The Pilgrims had lived for some years in Leiden in the Dutch Republic. Nathaniel Philbrick says that, just as a spiritual covenant had marked the start of their congregation there, a civil covenant would provide the basis for a secular government in America.

The compact is a short text in which the signers, as loyal subjects of King James, state that they have undertaken a voyage to plant the first colony in the northern parts of Virginia for the glory of God, the advancement of the Christian faith and the honour of their king and country. They covenant and combine themselves into a civil body politic and promise to enact just and equal laws, ordinances and offices for the general good of the colony, to which they promise due submission and obedience.

The original document is lost. Three versions survive from the 17th century: in Mourt's Relation of 1622, in William Bradford's journal Of Plimoth Plantation of 1646, and in Nathaniel Morton's New-Englands Memorial of 1669. They differ slightly in wording and significantly in spelling and punctuation. Bradford's manuscript is kept in a vault at the State Library of Massachusetts.

Forty-one of the ship's 101 passengers signed. The list of signers, which includes John Carver, William Bradford, Myles Standish and John Alden, comes from Morton alone, and Thomas Prince first numbered the names in 1736. At a ceremony marking the 300th anniversary of the landing, on 23 November 1920, Massachusetts governor Calvin Coolidge called the compact the foundation of liberty based on law and order and the first real constitution of modern times.
mayo-college: Colonel Sir Oliver St John was the college's first principal. Speaking on the campus in 1879, the Viceroy, the 2nd Baron Lytton, recalled that Colonel Walter's report had argued that India's young rulers and nobles most needed an Indian Eton, and that the report may have influenced Lord Mayo when he founded the college. "Mayo is India's Eton and you are India's Eton boys," he told the students. Its pupils came also from beyond India: Said bin Taimur, later the 13th Sultan of Muscat and Oman, studied there from 1922 to 1927.

The coat of arms combines the Mayo arms, a lion rampant and an open hand, with the sun and moon of the Suryavanshi and Chandravanshi Rajputs, the Panch Rang or five sacred colours of the Rajputs, and a Rajput fort. A Bhil archer and an armoured Rajput support the shield. The motto, "Let there be Light", comes from the Bible, and the badge is a peacock standing on a khanda, a two-handed Rajput sword.

The boys live in twelve houses: eight senior houses, among them Ajmer, Bharatpur, Jaipur, Jodhpur and Colvin, a holding house called Oman for the seventh class, and three junior houses. A council of monitors and prefects drawn from the senior houses shares school and house duties. The Annual Prizegiving is one of the school's oldest ceremonies; its chief guests have included Lord Irwin, Rajendra Prasad, Indira Gandhi and Sam Manekshaw. It is believed that M.N. Kapur ended the use of a rope to divide English and Indian guests at the tea that follows it.

Horse riding, dropped after Independence, was revived in 1993, and the school plays polo, including matches between old boys and pupils. Its cricket ground hosted 19 first-class matches between 1926 and 1986. The Danmal Mathur Museum in Jhalawar House holds antiques and an armoury, and pupils produce several publications, among them the newsletter Mayoor, founded in the late 1960s by the principal Jack Gibson.

On 12 April 1986 the Indian Postal Service issued a stamp showing the college's main building. Its former pupils, known as Old Boys or Mayoites, include members of the royal families of Bikaner, Alwar, Jammu and Kashmir, Jaipur, Udaipur, Jodhpur and Kutch, rulers such as Sawai Man Singh II of Jaipur and Hari Singh of Jammu and Kashmir, and two sultans of Oman. Later alumni include the minister Jaswant Singh, the diplomat K. Natwar Singh, the general Nathu Singh Rathore and the writers Vikram Chandra and Indra Sinha.
mayombe: The low mountains of Mayombe, also written Mayumbe, run from the mouth of the Congo River in the south to the Kouilou-Niari River in the north, and reach into Gabon as well. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo the area lies on the right bank of the Congo just before the river enters the Atlantic at Banana, extending north from Boma. Its highest point is Mount Foungouti at 930 metres, and it is watered by swift rivers, the largest being the Shiloango and its tributaries the Lukula and the Lubuzi.

The Yombe, a branch of the Kongo people, are the most numerous of the groups living in the region. Under French colonial rule Mayombe was a place of exile for Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba, the founder of Mouridism, who spent five years there, and it is well known in Senegal for that reason. A railway, the Mayombe Railway, linked Boma to Tshela, and an extension to the Republic of the Congo was planned; it was dismantled under President Mobutu Sese Seko and its tracks were reused near Gbadolite. In the Republic of the Congo the area is crossed by the Congo-Ocean Railway.

The climate is equatorial with an oceanic influence: a dry season from June to September, milder here than elsewhere in the Lower Congo, and a hot, humid rainy season from October to May. The old forests include valuable trees such as limba, and oil palms are a main resource for the inhabitants. The forests were estimated at 500,000 hectares in 1950 and have since shrunk to about 80,000 hectares. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo Mayombe forms part of Kongo Central province and includes the towns of Lukula, Seke Banza, Kangu and Tshela.
mayor-of-the-palace: The mayor of the palace, in Latin maior palatii or maior domus, was in origin the manager of the Frankish king's household. He directed the operation of the whole court and stood at the head of the Merovingian administrative ladder. The king appointed him from among the magnates, the most powerful families. Austrasia, Neustria and Burgundy each had their own mayor.

Burgundy lost its separate mayor in 626. Chlothar II, who ruled the whole Frankish kingdom, had ordered the execution of Warnachar, the mayor of Burgundy, and the Burgundian magnates then declared that they wanted no mayor of their own. This marks the effective end of the Burgundian court and the start of a Neustrian-Burgundian political alliance against Austrasian influence.

In the second half of the seventh century the office became the power behind the throne. The mayor made the decisions that affected the kingdom, while the kings were reduced to ceremonial duties and became little more than figureheads, known as rois fainéants, the do-nothing kings.

The Austrasian magnates revolted, and at the Battle of Tertry in 687 their leader Pepin of Herstal defeated Neustria and became its mayor of the palace. He took the title Duke of the Franks to mark his wider rule. His son Charles Martel, mayor in both Austrasia and Neustria, ruled without any king during the last four years of his life, from 737 to 741. Charles's sons Carloman and Pepin the Short raised another Merovingian king, Childeric III, but Pepin deposed him in 751 and was crowned king in his place.

The office shows how real power passed from a royal house to its chief servants. Neustria's mayors included Erchinoald, Ebroin and Grimoald II; Charles Martel held the post there from 718 and Pepin the Short from 741 or 742 until he became king.
mayurasharma: Mayurasharma, also called Mayuravarma, was a native of Talagunda, in the modern Shimoga district, and is dated by modern scholars to a reign of 345–365 CE. The Talagunda inscription of 450, held to be the most reliable source on his family and the most free of legend, makes him the son of Bandhushena and grandson of his teacher Veerasharma, and a student at the agrahara, or place of learning, at Talagunda. It says the family took its name from the Kadamba tree that grew near its home. The Gudnapur inscription confirms his parentage.

Later legends gave the founder a divine birth: one tells of a three-eyed, four-armed being, Trilochana Kadamba, sprung from drops of Shiva's sweat at the roots of a Kadamba tree, another that he was born of Rudra and the earth with a third eye on his forehead.

He first established himself in the forests of Shriparvata, possibly modern Srisailam, defeating the Pallava frontier guards and subduing the Banas of Kolar. The Pallavas under Skandavarman recognised him as sovereign from the western ocean to the Malaprabha River. Some scholars see his rise as a successful revolt of Brahmins against Kshatriya rule; others think he timed it to follow the defeat of the Pallava Vishnugopa by Samudragupta of northern India. Some historians also hold that he first served as a commander in the Pallava army, since the inscription calls him Senani.

He went on to defeat the Traikutas, Abhiras, Sendrakas, Maukharis and Punnatas, among others. To mark his successes he performed horse sacrifices and granted 144 villages to the Brahmins of Talagunda, and he invited learned Vedic Brahmins from Ahichatra to conduct the royal rituals.

Before the Kadambas, the powers ruling the region lay outside Karnataka, so their rise as an independent state with Kannada as a major regional language is counted a landmark in the history of modern Karnataka, and the earliest Kannada inscriptions are attributed to the Kadambas of Banavasi. The Havyaka Brahmins claim descent from the Ahichatra Brahmins he brought in, and the Kadambas of Goa, founded by Kadamba Shasthadeva around 960 CE, traced their line to him. His story is told in the Kannada film Mayura (1975), starring Rajkumar, and in Visawanatha Satyanarayana's Telugu novel Kadimi Chettu.
mazandaran: Mazandaran lies on the southern coast of the Caspian Sea, in the Central Alborz mountains and the Hyrcanian forests. Its landscape runs from sandy beaches and plains to the snowcapped Alborz, which includes Mount Damavand. The name is Avestan and is understood as "the gate of the giants" or "the valley of the giants". In the 10th-century Persian epic the Shahnameh it names a land of daevas and sorcerers that is difficult to conquer, and the epic also places the capital of the king Fereydun at Tamishe near Amol, in the land known as Tabarestan.

Human habitation in the area goes back at least 75,000 years. Caves at Belt and Hotu near Behshahr show people there about 9,000 years ago, and excavations at Gohar Tape in Rostamkola show that the area was urbanised more than 5,000 years ago. Before Iranian-speakers arrived, the native people were subsistence hunters and cattle herders. The Amard lived in the mountains bordering the Caspian, including the area of present-day Amol, and the Tapuri, a tribe among the Medes, are mentioned by Ptolemy and Arrian.

After the Umayyad Caliphate replaced the Sasanian Empire in the early seventh century, Tabaristan stayed independent of it. Zoroastrian houses such as the Bavand and the Karen fought an effective guerrilla war against the Umayyads. A short-lived Alid Shiite state collapsed before the Ziyarid princes took over. Later local dynasties fell into three groups: families of pre-Islamic origin, the Alid sayyids, and families of secondary importance.

After the Safavid period the Qajar leader Agha Mohammad Khan campaigned south from Mazandaran and had incorporated it into his realm by 1782. On 21 March 1782 he proclaimed Sari his imperial capital. Local wars in the following years led Fath Ali Shah to move the capital from Sari to Tehran.

Mazandaran is one of the 31 provinces of Iran, with its capital at Sari, and covers 24,842 square kilometres. The population is overwhelmingly Mazandarani, with minorities that include Gilaks, Azerbaijanis, Kurds and Georgians. Rice is present in almost every meal, and the coast is rich in seafood. The Trans-Iranian Railway, built between 1927 and 1938 under Reza Shah, links Tehran to the Caspian Sea. The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands was concluded in 1971 in the city of Ramsar in the province.
mazyar: Mazyar belonged to the Qarinvand dynasty, descended from Sukhra of the House of Karen, de facto ruler of the Sasanian Empire from 484 to 493; Sukhra's son Karin received land south of Amol in Tabaristan from Khosrow I. Mazyar succeeded his father Qarin ibn Vindadhhurmuzd around 817, but the Bavandid ruler Shahriyar I drove him out, and his cousin Vinda-Umid handed him over to Shahriyar. He escaped to the court of the caliph al-Ma'mun, where he met the astrologer Yahya ibn al-Munajjim, embraced Islam and took the name Abu'l-Hasan Muhammad.

Al-Ma'mun gave him Ruyan and Damavand as a fief and made him co-governor of Tabaristan with Musa ibn Hafs. Returning with Abbasid troops in 822/3, he exiled his brother Quhyar and his nephew Qarin I, and in 825/6 he invaded the Bavandid lands and captured Shahriyar's son Shapur, whom he later had beheaded. With Vinda-Umid killed, he united the highlands and took the titles of the Dabuyid king Farrukhan the Great: Gil-Gilan, Ispahbadh and Padishkhwargarshah. He built mosques, but the Muslims of Tabaristan regarded his rule as oppressive.

When the Tahirid Abdallah ibn Tahir demanded the land tax and the release of Muhammad ibn Musa, whom Mazyar had imprisoned, he refused, and Abdallah accused him before al-Mu'tasim of infidelity and tyranny. Mazyar rebelled, with wide support among the native Zoroastrians. Five armies entered Tabaristan; Qarin I went over to the Abbasids, the people of Sari revolted, and Quhyar captured his brother and handed him over.

He was executed at Samarra, and his body was gibbeted beside that of Babak Khorramdin. Quhyar was soon killed by his own Daylamite soldiers, ending the dynasty, and the Tahirids ruled Tabaristan with Qarin I as their vassal. In the Tarikh-e-Tabaristan of the medieval historian Ibn Isfandiyar, Mazyar claims an oath with Afshin and Babak to take the country back from the Arabs, and twentieth-century Iranian nationalist historiography counts him among the national heroes of Iran.
mbabane: Mbabane lies on the Mbabane River and its tributary the Polinjane River in the Mdzimba Mountains, at an average elevation of 1,243 metres. It is in the Hhohho Region, of which it is also the capital. Because of its altitude it has a moderate subtropical highland climate: snow is rare, having fallen only three times since 1900, and the city averages only four days of frost a year. Most of the rain falls in summer. The city takes its name from a chief, Mbabane Kunene, who lived in the area when British settlers arrived.

The town stands at the spot where the route from the Transvaal to Mozambique crossed the Mbabane River. It grew after the administrative centre of the country was moved from Bremersdorp, now called Manzini, in January 1902, and Great Britain declared it the capital of the new Protectorate of Swaziland that year. At that time it consisted of a few shops, churches and schools founded by white settlers, and Swazi Africans were not allowed to live in the town but had to reside in nearby rural districts. By the 1930s it had electricity, running water, a telephone connection and a hospital.

Before World War II most Swazis lived in rural districts and worked outside the country, so there was little growth in the town. After the war, the creation of trade schools in the city, the arrival of the Goba railway connecting Maputo to the mines in South Africa and Lesotho, and foreign investment, particularly in the sugar industry, contributed to its growth. In the years following independence government buildings were built in Mbabane, among them the British Consulate.

Mbabane is the most populous city of Eswatini, previously called Swaziland, with an estimated population of 94,874 in 2010. It is one of the two capitals, the executive capital, alongside Lobamba. The main language is siSwati, and English is widely spoken. Tin and iron were mined nearby, and the city is a commercial and financial hub for the surrounding region and a centre of the country's tourism. It is home to Waterford-Kamhlaba United World College of Southern Africa and one of the three campuses of the University of Eswatini.
mbandzeni: Mbandzeni was a son of King Mswati II and Nandzi Nkambule, who died when he was very young. After Mswati's death in July 1868 the Queen Mother Tsandzile Ndwandwe acted as regent, and Ludvonga II, the son of Mswati and Inkhosikati LaMgangeni Khumalo, was chosen as king. Ludvonga died of poisoning in 1874 before he could take the throne. The council of elders asked LaKhumalo to choose another child to become her son, and she chose the motherless Mbandzeni, making him king and herself queen mother. A rival claimant, Prince Mbilini waMswati, allied with the Zulu kings Mpande and Cetshwayo, never won the throne.

Mbandzeni ruled from his royal capital at Mbekelweni, where many concessionaires came seeking land, mining rights and trade. He and his officials granted overlapping concessions to British and Dutch interests, paid in gold, cattle or other goods, often on the advice of 'Offy' Shepstone, nephew of Sir Theophilus Shepstone of Natal. He could not read or write and signed with a cross, and he was told that the land grants were not permanent, though the papers said otherwise. The discovery of gold in the Transvaal sharpened the settlers' interest.

In the Zulu war of 1879 Mbandzeni refused Cetshwayo's request for help, since Zulu forces often raided southern Swaziland, and Swazi troops helped stop Zulu raids into the Transvaal. That year a large Swazi force backed the British under Sir Garnet Wolseley against the Pedi king Sekhukhune, who was captured and his kingdom destroyed. Britain in return recognised Swazi independence and promised protection against Zulu and Boer encroachment, but the concessions were later used against that independence in the Swaziland conventions of 1884 and 1894.

Mbandzeni died after an illness during the border talks, in which he had little say, and is quoted as saying on his deathbed that "the Swazi kingship dies with me". He was buried at the royal cemetery of Mbilaneni beside Mswati II and Sobhuza I. After a regency under Queen Tibati Nkambule his young son Mahlokohla, later Ngwane V, became king. The conventions fixed a border that left many Swazi, including royal villages such as Mjindini, in what is now South Africa. Some have said that he sold his country; others that he did what he could at a difficult time.
mbanza-kongo: Mbanza Kongo lies close to Angola's border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on top of a flat-topped mountain sometimes called Mongo a Kaila, the mountain of division, because recent legends hold that the king created the clans of the kingdom there and sent them out. The Luezi River runs in the valley to the south. The city stood at a junction of major trade routes, and the Portuguese who first reached it in 1491 travelled ten days to get there from the mouth of the Congo River.

The city, formerly called Nkumba a Ngudi, Mongo wa Kaila and Kongo dia Ngunga, was founded by the first manikongo, Lukeni. It was the capital of the Kingdom of Kongo from before the Portuguese arrived in 1483 until the kingdom's abolition in 1915, apart from a period of abandonment during the civil wars of the seventeenth century. When the Portuguese came it was already a large town, perhaps the largest in sub-equatorial Africa, and a Portuguese ambassador's letter to Lisbon compared the area within its inner walls with the town of Évora. The earliest documented kings called it the city of Congo; the name São Salvador first appears in the letters of Álvaro I of Kongo, who reigned from 1568 to 1587.

By the 1550s a community of Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries lived there, and they plotted with others to overthrow the manikongo Diogo I Nkumbi a Mpudi. In 1568 Jagas invaded and sacked the city, driving out Álvaro I, who regained it with Portuguese military help but had to yield Luanda, source of the nzimbu currency. Under Afonso II stone buildings, including a palace and churches, were added. An ecclesiastical statement of the 1620s reporting 4,500 baptisms is consistent with a population of around 130,000 in the city and its parish, of whom perhaps 30,000 to 45,000 lived in the city on the mountain. It had some twelve churches and a two-storey royal palace.

Several sackings during the civil wars that followed the Battle of Mbwila in 1665 ended with its abandonment in 1678. Followers of Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita reoccupied it in 1705, and King Pedro IV of Kongo restored it as capital in 1709. It was never depopulated again.

Mbanza Kongo is the capital of Zaire Province in north-western Angola. Its ruins of the Cathedral of the Holy Saviour of Congo, said to date from 1491, are claimed by many Angolans as the oldest church in sub-Saharan Africa. Other sites include the Jalankuwo, the manikongo's judgement tree, and the sunguilu, where tradition says the king's body was washed before burial. The Royal Museum holds artefacts of the old kingdom. The city was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017.
mbarara: Mbarara is a city in the Western Region of Uganda, about 270 km by road south-west of Kampala, at an average elevation of about 1,147 metres. It is a transport hub on the road west from Masaka to Kabale, near Lake Mburo National Park. The name comes from a colonial mispronunciation of Emburara, a tall grass that once covered the whole area. The climate is tropical savanna, with the most rainy days in October and the fewest in July.

The census of 2002 put the population of the town at 69,400, and the census of August 2014 at 195,013. From about 2000 modern buildings, including malls, hotels and new hospitals, went up, and the town became the main commercial centre of most of the south-western districts of Uganda and the site of the district headquarters. Mbarara hosted the annual general meeting of the Uganda Local Governments Association in 2004. The cabinet granted it city status in May 2019, which began on 1 July 2020, and the city is divided into six divisions.

Mbarara University of Science and Technology was founded in 1989, and the city also has the regional referral hospital, which is also the teaching hospital of the university's school of medicine, and several other universities and schools. Its water has come from the River Rwizi, which cannot meet the needs of a growing population, and plans were made to draw water from the Kagera River. A northern bypass of 14 kilometres takes long-distance trucks bound for Rwanda, Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo off the city streets.
mbegan-ndour: Mbegan Ndour was born to a Serer father from Saloum and a Serer princess of Sine, and through his mother belonged to the Guelowar maternal dynasty that ruled Sine and Saloum for over six hundred years. In the tradition of Sine his father was Maari Nduur of Mboudaye, nicknamed Marga Tiatj, a hunter and healer still remembered in Sine, Saloum and the Gambia, and his mother was the princess Nyillane Faye, sister of the Maad a Sinig Diessanou Faye. A legend of Saloum makes him a nephew of Maad a Sinig Maissa Wali instead, probably a later invention to legitimate him, since the timelines do not match.

Tradition tells that the king of Sine at first refused to let his sister marry Maari, a man of low status, and would not host the naming ceremony of her son. In the story Maari drew an animal to the ceremony for the sacrifice by his powers and kept the guests dry inside a circle during heavy rain, after which the king accepted the marriage and the child.

His early career is the subject of numerous, sometimes contradictory oral traditions. Most likely he fought in wars in Cayor and Baol, won a reputation as a general and may have ruled for a time as Teigne of Baol. He allied himself with the Buurba Jolof Biram Njeme Kumba, and the support of the Ndiaye dynasty was important in the founding of Saloum. As a potential rival for power he was not welcome at the court of Sine, and was sent to his father's homeland to carve out a kingdom.

The chiefdom of Mbey was under the influence of Eli Bana, a Toucouleur marabout whose attempts to convert the local Serer to Islam had caused friction, so that many joined Mbegan Ndour, whose forces were also strengthened with horses and guns bought from European merchants on the coast. In the legend he became a snake and bit the marabout outside his mosque. He then defeated Diattara Tambedou, a Muslim Soninke and probably a salt merchant: control of salt underpinned the conflict as much as religion. Ruling as Maad Saloum, he allied with Serer lamanes, marabouts and village chiefs, though he directly controlled only Mbey, and later he may have served as regent in Sine for an underage king.
mbunda-people: The Mbunda, or Vambunda, speak Mbunda and comprise several subgroups with dialects of their own, among them the Mbunda Mathzi, Yauma, Nkangala, Mbalango, Sango, Shamuka and Ndundu; they are often counted among the Ganguela peoples. Their oral tradition names Mwene Nkuungu as the first monarch of the Mbunda Kingdom and tells of a settlement on the Mithimoyi, a tributary of the Luena, followed by expansion south into what became known as Mbundaland, with its capital at Lumbala Nguimbo.

Tradition also recounts wars with the Chokwe, set off when the 20th monarch, Mwene Katavola II Musangu, sought to marry a Chokwe slave and was killed, and with the Luvale, whose leader Masambo was shot by King Mwene Mbandu I Lyondthzi Kapova in the Lunjweva area.

Some Mbunda reached Barotseland at the end of the 18th century. The Litunga Mulambwa prized them as fighters, and after they turned back a Luvale invasion he made a treaty with their leader Mwene Chitengi Chiyengele and confirmed him as Senior Chief of the Mbunda, who gained a place on the Barotse National Council. They fought beside the Aluyi against the Makololo in 1830, the Tonga in the 1880s and the Kaonde. In Angola, the Portuguese abducted Mbandu I early in the 20th century; lacking gunpowder, the Mbunda were defeated and a second migration followed. The Angolan War of Independence and the civil war of 1975 to 2002 drove further waves of refugees into western Zambia and northern Namibia.

Rule in the kingdom passed through the central matrilineal line, and the king's decisions were not questioned, though local rule was decentralised. Tradition holds that a prince consort, Mukwetunga Kamenga, brought back the Mukanda circumcision rite from the Mbwela, and that because it was for men only, Queen Vamwene Mukenge was the last woman to reign. In Mukanda, boys spend three to six months at a bush camp, and the Makishi masquerade is performed. The Mbunda work iron and copper, fish, carve wood, weave baskets, make bark-cloth and grow cassava as their staple. Most follow Christianity, Catholic or Protestant; some honour Njambi as creator through the ancestors. The Mbunda Bible was launched in 2008 in Angola and 2009 in Zambia.
mccarthyism: Anti-communist measures in the United States predated Senator Joseph McCarthy. The Smith Act of 1940 made it an offence to advocate overthrowing the government by force. The House Committee on Un-American Activities, formed in 1938 and first known as the Dies Committee, turned to communism early, and its investigation of the espionage charges against Alger Hiss in 1948 convinced many of the usefulness of congressional committees. Truman's Executive Order 9835 of 21 March 1947 required loyalty screening of federal employees, probably in part a response to the Republican sweep of the 1946 elections.

McCarthy's own part began publicly on 9 February 1950, when he told a Republican women's club in Wheeling, West Virginia, that he held a list of known communists working in the State Department. The speech brought a flood of press attention.

Loyalty review boards and committees operated in federal, state and local governments and in private agencies. Between 1949 and 1954 Congress carried out 109 investigations through HUAC, the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee and the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. After Eisenhower took office in 1953 he strengthened the loyalty programme and narrowed the avenues of appeal. In 1954 J. Robert Oppenheimer lost his security clearance after a four-week hearing.

On 25 November 1947 the heads of the major film studios issued the Waldorf Statement, announcing the dismissal of the Hollywood Ten and marking the start of the Hollywood blacklist, which employers never publicly admitted. By 1952 several states had banned communists from public employment and required loyalty oaths. The number imprisoned is in the hundreds, and some ten or twelve thousand lost their jobs. Suspected homosexuality was also a common ground for targeting, and over 5,000 federal workers were fired in what many call the lavender scare.

Support came from the American Legion, militantly anti-communist women's groups and a wider coalition opposed to internationalism and New Deal welfare programmes. Critics included Truman, who in vetoing the McCarran Internal Security Act of 1950 wrote that in a free country men are punished for crimes, never for opinions. On 2 December 1954 the Senate voted 67 to 22 to condemn McCarthy. John Henry Faulk, dismissed by CBS Radio after being marked unfit by the private firm AWARE, won his suit against it in 1962.

Under Chief Justice Earl Warren the Supreme Court issued rulings that helped end the era. Declassified Soviet archives and the Venona decryptions later showed substantial Soviet espionage in the 1940s and that Moscow funded and influenced the Communist Party USA. Some historians, including Ellen Schrecker, hold that Hooverism, after FBI head J. Edgar Hoover, describes the phenomenon better than McCarthyism.
mcmahon-hussein-correspondence: The first documented talks between Britain and the Hashemites took place in February 1914, between the Consul-General in Egypt, Lord Kitchener, and Abdullah bin al-Hussein, second son of Hussein bin Ali, Sharif of Mecca. Hussein was uneasy about the Ottoman governor of the Hejaz, Wehib Pasha, and about the Hejaz railway, which threatened to increase Ottoman centralisation. On 1 November 1914 Kitchener offered to guarantee the independence of the Sharifate against external aggression. After the Ottomans entered the war on Germany's side, British interest in an Arab revolt grew.

Ten letters, five from each side, were exchanged between 14 July 1915 and 10 March 1916 by Hussein and Sir Henry McMahon, British High Commissioner in Egypt, who kept in contact with the Foreign Secretary, Edward Grey. Britain's main aims were to counter the Ottoman declaration of jihad against the Allies and to keep the support of the 70 million Muslims of British India. In his letter of 24 October 1915 McMahon accepted Hussein's proposed limits for Arab independence, except for the districts of Mersina and Alexandretta and portions of Syria west of the districts of Damascus, Homs, Hama and Aleppo, and except where Britain could not act without detriment to France.
On this understanding the Arabs, under Hussein's son Faisal and with the advice of T. E. Lawrence, fought the Ottomans in the Arab Revolt from June 1916 to October 1918.

Palestine is not named in the letters but lies within Hussein's proposed boundaries. The Arab view was that it could not belong to the excluded districts, which lay well to the north. British government documents suggested until 1920 that Palestine was meant to be in the Arab area, and its interpretation then changed, leading to a public dispute that each side argued from fine details of the wording.

Arab leaders regarded the agreement as violated after the Balfour Declaration of November 1917 and the publication of the secret Sykes-Picot Agreement in December 1917. In 1921 Hussein said he could not be expected to "affix his name to a document assigning Palestine to the Zionists and Syria to foreigners". Negotiations were suspended in March 1924, and within six months Britain withdrew its support in favour of Ibn Saud, who conquered Hussein's kingdom.
mcmahon-line: The McMahon Line is the boundary between Tibet and British India as agreed in maps and notes exchanged by their plenipotentiaries on 24 and 25 March 1914 at Delhi, as part of the 1914 Simla Convention. It is named after Henry McMahon, foreign secretary of British India, who signed for Britain, while Lonchen Shatra signed for Tibet. It spans 890 kilometres from the corner of Bhutan to the Isu Razi Pass on the Burma border, largely along the crest of the Himalayas. It delimited the spheres of influence of the two countries along north-east India and northern Burma, which had not been fixed. The Republic of China was not a party to the line.

British India reached east of Bhutan after the First Anglo-Burmese War, and in 1873 the British drew an Inner Line separating directly administered Assam from the tribal hill tracts. After the British expedition to Tibet of 1904, Qing China took control of south-eastern Kham, where the amban Zhao Erfeng pursued brutal policies of subjugation in 1908 to 1911, and his campaigns reached districts next to the Assam Himalaya. British officials grew alarmed, and by 1912 the Army General Staff had proposed a boundary along the Himalayan crest.

At the Simla conference of 1913 and 1914 the final accord of 3 July 1914 lacked any textual boundary description and was never signed by the Chinese plenipotentiary Ivan Chen. The detailed map of March 1914 was signed only by Tibet and Britain. The Government of India first rejected Simla as incompatible with the 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention, and the line was forgotten until 1935, when Olaf Caroe revived it.

The Survey of India published a map showing it as the boundary in 1937, and in 1938 the Simla Accord was published in Aitchison's Treaties, in a replacement volume carrying a false 1929 date. That April a British force under Captain G. S. Lightfoot arrived at Tawang, but the Tibetan government protested, and the district stayed in Tibetan hands until 1951.

India inherited the line in 1947. In 1962 Chinese forces crossed it on 20 October in the Sino-Indian War, advanced as far as Rupa and Walong, then withdrew to it and returned the Indian prisoners in 1963. In 1986 Chinese and Indian troops confronted each other at Sumdorong Chu, and a 1996 agreement set out confidence-building measures.

China rejects the Simla Convention, arguing that Tibet was not sovereign and could not conclude treaties, though a 1959 note by Zhou Enlai treated the line as part of the Line of Actual Control. Chinese maps show some 65,000 square kilometres south of it as South Tibet. In 2008 the 14th Dalai Lama said that Arunachal Pradesh was part of India under the agreement signed by Tibetan and British representatives.
me-agtsom: Tridé Tsuktsen was the son of Tridu Songtsen and Tsenma Toktokteng; his nickname Mé Aktsom, Bearded Grandfather, was given to him later in life because he was so hirsute. According to the Tibetan Annals he was born in the spring of 704, a few months before his father died in battle in the Mywa territory of Nanzhao. The sources on what followed are unclear. The historian Beckwith states that another son, Lha Balpo, took the throne in the winter of 704–705, but that the empress dowager Thrimalö deposed him in favour of the infant, amid revolts and executions.

He was crowned in 705 but not formally enthroned until Thrimalö's death in 712. Princess Jincheng, an adoptive daughter of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang and a devout Buddhist, came to Tibet in 710. Five Buddhist temples were built, and about 737 the princess gave refuge to monks fleeing an anti-Buddhist king of Khotan. After she died of smallpox between 739 and 741, anti-Buddhist factions blamed the epidemic on the royal support for Buddhism, and the monks fled again.

Tibetan armies fought far beyond the kingdom's borders. With the Türgish they attacked Kashgar in 717, and they struck Gilgit in 722 and 736. In 727 the king seized the Chinese fortress of Guazhou, whose stores fell to the Tibetans, but the Chinese drove them out in 728. A treaty of 730 fixed the border at the Chiling Pass east of Kokonor. The Chinese later retook the Nine Loops of the Huang Ho in 738, Anrong in 740 and Shipu in 742, and in 747 forces under Gao Xianzhi drove the Tibetans from the region.

In 751 Tibetan troops helped the Arabs and Qarluq Turks defeat the Chinese at Talas, and the same year Kag-la-bon, ruler of Nanzhao, came to pay his respects; Tibetan armies were sent to help Nanzhao against the Chinese in 754.

According to the pillar later erected at Zhol in front of the Potala, Mé Aktsom was murdered in 755 in a palace revolt sponsored by two ministers. He was followed by his pro-Buddhist son Trisong Detsen, who was given the epithet Dharma King. Edicts of Trisong Detsen and his son Sadnalegs point to dissension and suppression of Buddhism in the latter part of Mé Aktsom's reign.
measles: Measles is a vaccine-preventable infectious disease caused by the measles virus, an RNA virus closely related to rinderpest, which affects cattle, and to canine distemper. Symptoms usually appear 10 to 12 days after exposure and last 7 to 10 days. They begin with fever, often above 40 °C (104 °F), cough, a runny nose and inflamed eyes, followed by a rash that starts on the face and spreads to the rest of the body.

The disease spreads through the air in the coughs and sneezes of infected people. Common complications include diarrhoea in 8 per cent of cases, middle ear infection in 7 per cent and pneumonia in 6 per cent, in part because measles weakens the immune system. Immunity is lifelong once acquired, through vaccination or after recovery.

Measles is of zoonotic origin: it evolved from rinderpest. Genomic analysis indicates that it arose as a human disease between 900 and 2,400 years ago. The Antonine Plague of 165 to 180 CE has been suggested as measles, but its cause is unknown and smallpox is thought more likely.

The first systematic description of measles as distinct from smallpox and chickenpox is credited to the Persian physician Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (860 to 932), who wrote The Book of Smallpox and Measles. Between 1100 and 1200 CE the virus is thought to have diverged completely from rinderpest. This fits the observation that measles needs a susceptible population of over 500,000 to sustain an epidemic, a size reached in historic times with the growth of medieval European cities.

Before vaccination, measles was endemic in every part of the world. In 1954 John Enders and Thomas C. Peebles isolated the virus from a 13-year-old boy in the United States, David Edmonston. Enders grew the Edmonston strain in human kidney tissue, then in amniotic membrane and finally in chick embryo culture, producing over three years a virus that gave immunity without causing disease, a process called attenuation.

At Merck, Maurice Hilleman attenuated the strain further, and the first successful measles vaccine became widely available in the United States in 1963. Measles vaccine was later combined with those for mumps and rubella as the MMR vaccine, licensed in the United States in 1971.
meaux: Meaux is a commune on the river Marne in the Seine-et-Marne department of Île-de-France, about 41 kilometres east-northeast of the centre of Paris. Its inhabitants are called Meldois. Both names come from the Meldi, the Latin name of the Gaulish tribe that occupied this part of the Marne valley.

The historic buildings stand mainly in the old city inside its old defensive walls, of which a segment from the Gallo-Roman period survives. A meander of the Marne divides the old city into the Cathedral Quarter and the Market Quarter. The Cathedral Quarter holds Meaux Cathedral, the episcopal palace and its gardens, which outline the shape of a bishop's mitre, and the archaeological remains of the sanctuary of La Bauve.

The Siege of Meaux took place from October 1421 to May 1422 during the Hundred Years' War, when the English under Henry V besieged the town. Its defence was led by the Bastard of Vaurus, who was known for his savagery. Mining and bombardment brought down the walls, and it is estimated that one sixteenth of the besiegers died of dysentery and smallpox. The town surrendered on 9 March 1422 and the garrison the next day.

The house of Etienne Mangin at 73 Rue du Marché is described on a plaque as the site of the first Reformed Church of France. Fourteen members of the congregation were burned there on 8 October 1546 by decree of the Parliament in Paris. Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet was bishop of Meaux from 1681 to 1704 and is called the eagle of Meaux. Philippe de Vitry, composer and author of the Ars Nova Notandi treatise, was bishop from 1351. In the First Battle of the Marne in September 1914 the German advance was halted at the gates of Meaux.

Meaux is a subprefecture of Seine-et-Marne. It is known for Brie de Meaux, a variety of Brie cheese, and for Meaux mustard, whose recipe has been a label owned by the Pommery company since the 18th century. Its museums include the Musée Bossuet in the episcopal palace and the Musée de la Grande Guerre du pays de Meaux, which stands beside the American monument La Liberté éplorée, erected in 1932.
mecca: Mecca, officially Makkah al-Mukarramah, lies in the Hejaz region of western Arabia, about 70 kilometres inland from Jeddah, in a narrow valley 277 metres above sea level. The city centres on the Masjid al-Haram, the Great Mosque, which contains the Kaaba. Muslims believe the Kaaba was built by Abraham and Ishmael. It is the direction of prayer (qibla) for all Muslims. The mosque is also the site of the Zamzam Well and of two rites of the Hajj and the Umrah, the circumambulation of the Kaaba (tawaf) and the walk between Safa and Marwa.

The early history of Mecca is poorly documented. The city lies in the interior of western Arabia, where few textual or archaeological sources survive, in contrast to Yemen and the Syro-Palestinian frontier. One study, by Majied Robinson, based on early Islamic genealogical records, estimates the population at the time of Muhammad at about 550, while Muslim scholars using traditional sources may place it as high as 10,000. One proposed etymology links the name to an Old South Arabian root meaning temple.

Muslim rulers from in and around the region long tried to control the city. The first printing press came to Mecca in 1885 with the Ottoman governor Osman Nuri Pasha. The city was last conquered in 1925, in the Saudi conquest of the Hejaz by Ibn Saud and his allies. Non-Muslims are forbidden to enter. The first recorded outsider to do so was Ludovico di Varthema of Bologna in 1503; Guru Nanak is said to have visited in December 1518, and Richard Francis Burton entered in 1853 disguised as a Qadiriyya Sufi from Afghanistan.

Mecca is the capital of Mecca Province in Saudi Arabia, and its metropolitan population was 2.4 million in 2022. Pilgrims on the Hajj, observed in the twelfth Hijri month of Dhū al-Ḥijjah as an obligation on Muslims once in their lives, more than triple that number each year. Mecca's economy depends heavily on pilgrimage. In the 20th century it expanded greatly, and several historical structures, among them the Ajyad Fortress, were demolished, in part for the enlargement of the Masjid al-Haram.
mecklenburg-vorpommern: The state covers 23,300 km2, the sixth largest German state by area. Its Baltic coastline of about 2,000 km has peninsulas, lagoons and islands, among them Germany's two biggest, Rügen and Usedom. In the south lies the Mecklenburg Lake District, where Lake Müritz is the largest lake in Germany. The name Vorpommern comes from West Slavic po more, land at the sea, with the German prefix vor- meaning the nearer part of Pomerania.

Human settlement began after the Ice Age, about 10,000 BCE. Germanic peoples recorded there about two thousand years ago mostly left during the Migration Period, and from the sixth century Polabian Slavs settled the area: the Obotrites in Mecklenburg, the Veleti and Rani in Pomerania. Vikings and Slavs set up trading posts along the coast, such as Reric, Ralswiek and Menzlin. In the late 12th century Henry the Lion, Duke of the Saxons, conquered the Obotrites and Christianized them, and German settlers followed in the Ostsiedlung. Mecklenburg became a duchy of the Holy Roman Empire in 1348 and its two grand duchies of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz were created in 1815.

The Duchy of Pomerania was a vassal state of Poland from 1121 to 1138, and its dukes were later vassals of Saxony, the Holy Roman Empire and Denmark before staying with the Empire from 1227. Western Pomerania was under Swedish rule from the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 until 1815 and then became part of the Prussian Province of Pomerania, remaining so until 1945.

The Soviet military administration created the Province of Mecklenburg and West Pomerania on 9 July 1945, by order of Marshal Georgy Zhukov. Expellees from the former eastern territories of Germany raised the population by 40%, and in 1949 they made up 43.3% of it. The state's name was shortened to Land Mecklenburg in 1947, and it became a constituent state of the German Democratic Republic in 1949. In 1952 it was divided into the districts of Rostock, Schwerin and Neubrandenburg. At reunification in 1990 the state was re-established along its postwar boundaries under the name Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

Schwerin is the state capital, and Rostock, with about 205,000 inhabitants, is the largest city. The University of Rostock, founded in 1419, and the University of Greifswald, founded in 1456, are among the oldest in Europe. The old Hanseatic towns of Stralsund and Wismar are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and red Brick Gothic churches and houses are a feature of many towns.
medang-kingdom: The earliest account of the kingdom is the Canggal inscription of 732, found at the Gunung Wukir temple southwest of Magelang. Written in Sanskrit, it records the erection of a lingga, a symbol of Shiva, on the order of King Sanjaya, Rakai of Mataram. It says that Java, rich in rice and gold, was ruled by King Sanna, and that after his death the kingdom fell into disunity until Sanjaya, his sister's son, took the throne and conquered the surrounding areas. The kingdom relied heavily on rice farming, using the fertile volcanic soil of Central Java, and later also benefited from maritime trade.

The period from King Panangkaran to King Balitung, roughly 760 to 910, marked the high point of classical Javanese civilisation, with great temples rising on the Kedu and Kewu plains, among them Sewu, Borobudur and Prambanan. Sanjaya was a Shaivite, but Panangkaran was a Mahayana Buddhist, and Buddhism enjoyed court patronage until the end of Samaratungga's reign. Shaivite Hinduism regained favour under Pikatan. Scholars disagree whether two dynasties, the Shaivite Sanjaya and the Buddhist Shailendra, ruled Central Java, or only one.

Around 929 Mpu Sindok shifted the centre of the kingdom to East Java and founded the Isyana dynasty. One theory blames an eruption of Mount Merapi during the reign of King Wawa, and several temples were found buried under volcanic debris. In 990 Dharmawangsa launched a naval invasion to capture Palembang, and Chinese accounts record that a Srivijayan envoy learned that his country had been attacked by Java. In 1017 the vassal king of Wurawari attacked Dharmawangsa Teguh, breaking up the Mataram state, and Airlangga's kingdom of Kahuripan became its leading successor in East Java.

The bas-reliefs and statues of Mataram's temples, often called Javanese or Shailendra art, are considered among the finest works of the Hindu-Buddhist world, with Prambanan and Borobudur the pinnacle. The Borobudur reliefs hold the most complete rendering of Buddhist sacred texts. The era is hailed as the classical period of Javanese civilisation, when Hindu-Buddhist elements mixed with indigenous ones. Javanese art influenced Srivijayan art in Sumatra and southern Thailand, and the similarity of the Bakong temple in Cambodia to Borobudur suggests a Javanese influence on early Khmer architecture.
medea: Médéa, in Arabic al-Madiya, is the capital of Médéa Province. The hills around it are covered with vineyards, orchards and farms that yield abundant grain. The town has a French character, with a rectangular plan, red tile-roofed buildings and public gardens. Its chief products have been wines, irrigation equipment and handicrafts.

The name goes back to a Roman city called ad Medix or Media, Latin for halfway. It stood equidistant from two rest houses on the road linking Caesarea, now Cherchell, to the colony of Auzia in Mauretania Caesariensis.

In Roman times a settlement called Lamdia stood at Médéa and was the seat of a Christian bishopric of Mauretania Caesariensis. Only one bishop is known, the Donatist Felix, who attended the Conference of Carthage in 411; the town then had no Catholic bishop. Lamdia survives as a titular bishopric. After the defeat of the Berbers in the 11th century, Arab tribes of Hilal and Sulaym descent were settled in the region and mixed with the local Berbers, Arabicizing them.

The Beylik of Titteri was established in 1548, with Médéa as its capital and a bey, a deputy of the Dey of Algiers, in residence. The last bey, Mostefa Boumezrag, ran it from 1819 to 1830, when the French arrived. After the Treaty of Tafna in 1837 Médéa became one of the capitals of the part of Algeria ruled by Abdelkader El Djezairi, but the French occupied it when they took possession of the whole country. Until 1962 it was a garrison town of the French army.

In the nearby village of Tibhirine stands the Abbey of Our Lady of Atlas, home from 1935 to 1996 to a Trappist community. Most of its monks were abducted by the Armed Islamic Group on 27 March 1997; the group announced their deaths two months later. The monastery buildings were afterwards given to the Chemin Neuf Community, a Catholic community from Lyon.
medellin: Medellín lies in the Aburrá Valley, a central region of the Andes in northwestern South America, at an elevation of about 1,500 m. The Medellín River, also called the Porce, flows northward through the valley. Because of its altitude the climate is milder than at other places at the same latitude, with an average temperature of 22 °C that varies little through the year, and the city is known as the City of the Eternal Spring.

In August 1541 Marshal Jorge Robledo saw what he took to be a valley, and Jerónimo Luis Tejelo reached the plain of the Aburrá Valley on the night of 23 August. The Spaniards called it the Valley of Saint Bartholomew, but the name soon gave way to the native name Aburrá, Painters, for the textile decorations of the local rulers. The valley lay between the gold mines northeast of Antioquia and the first provincial capital, Santa Fe de Antioquia, and supplied food to the mines.

In 1616 Francisco de Herrera Campuzano set up a small indigenous village, San Lorenzo de Aburrá, in what is now El Poblado. On 2 November 1675 the queen consort Mariana of Austria founded the Town of Our Lady of Candelaria of Medellín in the Aná region, now the city centre. In 1826 Gran Colombia's National Congress named the city capital of the Department of Antioquia. During the 19th century it was a commercial centre, first exporting gold, then coffee.

In the first half of the 20th century the population grew sixfold, from 59,815 in 1905 to 358,189 in 1951. The Coltejer textile company was founded in 1907 by Alejandro Echavarría. After the murder of the presidential candidate Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in 1948, political violence spread in the countryside, farmers fled to the cities and the valley slopes filled with slums. The city later built the Medellín Metro.

Medellín is the capital of Antioquia and the second-largest city in Colombia after Bogotá, with 2,427,129 people at the 2018 census. The University of Antioquia, the National University of Colombia's Medellín branch and the Pontifical Bolivarian University have long been its academic centres. Little colonial architecture remains; the Candelaria Church and the Church of the Veracruz survive, much altered. The Museum of Antioquia holds works of Fernando Botero.
medellin-cartel: Scholars describe the Medellín Cartel less as a single hierarchy than as a confederation of semi-autonomous traffickers who cooperated in production, transport, finance and enforcement while each kept control of his own operations. Besides Pablo Escobar it included Carlos Lehder, Gonzalo Rodríguez Gacha and the brothers Jorge Luis, Fabio and Juan David Ochoa Vásquez.

The network emerged in the early 1970s from Colombia's long-standing contraband economy, as cocaine replaced marijuana and other goods as the main illicit export. Its traffickers drew on growing demand in the United States, coca grown in Peru and Bolivia, and weak state presence in rural Colombia to build processing laboratories and routes through the Caribbean and Central America.

In the 1980s the network moved large volumes of cocaine to North American and European markets, with revenues counted in billions of US dollars a year. United States and Colombian authorities attributed a substantial share of the cocaine entering the United States to Medellín, though they stressed that the estimates varied and that no single organisation controlled the trade.

The cartel at first had an arrangement with the Cali Cartel, under which Medellín controlled the trade in Los Angeles, Cali that in New York, and the two shared Miami and Houston. A dispute between Escobar and the Cali leader Pacho Herrera, and by 1988 the Monaco Apartment bombing, made the two organisations lasting enemies.

Its chief fear was the extradition treaty between the United States and Colombia, which let Colombians suspected of trafficking be tried in the United States. Against its supporters the cartel used bribery, extortion and violence, and Escobar's group, the Extraditables, began a campaign of kidnappings, murders and bombings. The killing of the Justice Minister Rodrigo Lara on 30 April 1984 and of the Supreme Court Justice Hernando Baquero Borda on 31 July 1986 were among its most notorious acts. Some estimates put the dead at around 3,500, including over 500 police officers in Medellín, though no full list can be made.

The cartel fell apart in 1993. A vigilante group called Los Pepes, formed in January 1993, largely financed by the Cali Cartel and led by the brothers Carlos and Fidel Castaño, turned Escobar's own methods against him, while his enemies inside his own organisation multiplied. On 2 December 1993 Colombian special forces found him hiding in a house in Medellín.

He was shot dead on a rooftop while trying to flee. Its fall shifted the cocaine trade towards more decentralised structures and to other Colombian and Mexican organisations. La Oficina de Envigado is believed to be a partial successor, inheriting the Medellín turf and its criminal links abroad.
media-atropatene: Atropatene, also called Atropatia or Atropatian Media, was an ancient Iranian kingdom, established about 323 BCE by the Persian satrap Atropates and centred mostly on the region of Azerbaijan in north-western Iran. Its Old Persian name, Ātṛpātakāna, is the direct ancestor of the name of the historic Azerbaijan region. According to Strabo, Media was divided into two parts: Greater Media, with Ecbatana as its metropolis, and Atropatian Media, which took its name from the commander Atropates, who prevented this part from becoming subject to the Macedonians. Medieval Arab geographers instead derived the name from Adorbador, a priest whose name means guardian of the fire. Its main hub was Ganzak, near Lake Urmia, which presumably served as the capital of Atropates and his successors.

Atropates fought alongside the Achaemenid army at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE, then declared loyalty to Alexander the Great, who appointed him governor of Media in 328 to 327 BCE.
