After Alexander's death in 323 BCE the satrapy was divided: Media Magna went to Peithon, one of Alexander's bodyguards, and the smaller northern region became Media Atropatene under Atropates, who had by then become father-in-law of the regent Perdiccas. It became an independent kingdom. In 223 BCE Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire attacked it and won, and its king Artabazanes accepted Seleucid ascendancy while keeping internal independence.

Later, Atropatene allied with Parthia against Rome. In 36 BCE the Roman general Antony besieged the city of Fraaspa and withdrew after a long blockade, losing about thirty-five thousand soldiers. The dynasty Atropates founded ruled for several centuries, first independently and then as vassals of the Arsacids, until it was supplanted by a line of the Arsacids in the early 1st century CE. After Pharasmanes II of Iberia devastated the region in 134 to 135 CE, the people of Atropatene allied themselves with the Persian Sasanian prince Ardashir I against the Parthian Artabanus IV. In 226 the region submitted with little resistance to Ardashir I and became a province governed by a marzban.

Atropatene was the only Iranian region to remain under Zoroastrian authority from the Achaemenids to the Arab conquest without interruption, apart from Alexander's brief rule. Under the Atropatids the region gained a dominant place in Zoroastrianism, which continued into the Sasanian period, and it served as a stronghold of Iranian culture. Local claims also placed the birthplace of Zoroaster in Atropatene rather than in the east.
media-region: Media was an Iron Age region of north-western Iran, best known as the political and cultural base of the Medes. In the Achaemenid period it comprised present-day Iranian Azerbaijan, Iranian Kurdistan and western Tabaristan, and as a satrapy it came to stretch as far north as southern Dagestan. Assyrian records of the late 9th to early 7th century BCE place it between the Zagros Mountains in the west and north-west and the Dasht-e Kavir desert in the east, bordered to the north by the non-Iranian states of Gizilbunda and Mannea and to the south by Ellipi and Elam.

Its capital in Achaemenid sources, including the Behistun Inscription, was Ecbatana, modern Hamadan. Other cities were Laodicea (modern Nahavand), Rhages (present-day Rey), the largest city of the Medes, and Apamea, near Ecbatana, whose location is unknown.

In 678 BCE Deioces united the Median tribes and made the first Iranian empire. His grandson Cyaxares united all the Iranian tribes and made the empire a major power, and was succeeded by his son Astyages, the last Median king. In 553 BCE Cyrus the Great of Persia rebelled against his grandfather Astyages and won a decisive victory in 550 BCE, when dissatisfied nobles handed Astyages over to him.

The Medes were subjected to their close kin the Persians but kept a prominent position: they stood next to the Persians in honour and war, their court ceremony was adopted, the kings spent the summer months at Ecbatana, and Medes served as officials, satraps and generals. Greek historians at first called the Achaemenid Empire a Median Empire. Media proper formed the eleventh satrapy under Darius I. A Mede, Fravartish, tried to restore the Median kingdom and was executed at Ecbatana, according to the Behistun inscription of Darius I.

After Alexander the Great entered Media in the summer of 330 BCE he made Atropates satrap of the north in 328 BCE. When Alexander's empire was partitioned, southern Media passed to Antigonus and about 310 BCE to Seleucus I, while Atropates founded an independent kingdom, Atropatene, whose name is said to survive in Azerbaijan. Southern Media remained Seleucid for about a century and a half and Greek towns were founded there. About 150 BCE the Parthian king Mithradates I conquered it, and in 226 CE it passed with Atropatene to the Sassanids.
medieval-inquisition: The Cathars were first noted in southern France in the 1140s and the Waldensians in northern Italy around 1170. Mobs sometimes seized and burned suspected heretics, as at Cambrai, where Pope Gregory VII excommunicated the residents in 1076. Pope Lucius III's bull Ad abolendam of 1184 set up an episcopal inquisition, which obliged bishops to search their dioceses for heretics twice a year and relied first on persuasion through preaching and debate. Under Innocent III papal legates were sent against the Cathar and Waldensian heresies, and procedures were formalised under Gregory IX.

The tribunals were decentralised: each worked on its own under guidelines from the Holy See, with no central authority of the kind later inquisitions had. The Papal Inquisition met strong resistance in the Crown of Aragon and was almost forgotten there by the middle of the 15th century, and Castile never had a tribunal of it during the Middle Ages.

Inquisitors gathered the townspeople in a public place and offered leniency to anyone who came forward to denounce themselves. At least two witnesses were required. Defendants could name those who bore them mortal hatred, and if their accusers were among them the charges were dismissed; there was no confrontation or cross-examination of witnesses, and the accused could appeal to Rome. Innocent IV's bull Ad extirpanda of 15 May 1252 allowed the limited use of torture, once and for a limited time, without bloodshed or mutilation. Those who renounced their heresy received a penance; the unrepentant and relapsed were excommunicated and relaxed to the secular arm, which could burn them, since clerics were forbidden to kill.

Records show how rarely the tribunals ended in death. Of 5,400 people interrogated in Toulouse in 1245 and 1246, 184 received the yellow crosses that marked repentant Cathars, 23 were imprisoned for life and none was sent to the stake; of the 900 guilty verdicts given by Bernard Gui, no more than 45 led to execution. The historian Thomas F. Madden argues that the Inquisition was an attempt to stop unjust executions by lords and mobs. By the 14th century the Waldensians had been driven underground, and Guillaume Belibaste, one of the last known Cathar bons hommes, is believed to have been burned in 1321.
medina: Medina lies in the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia. Its built-up area is surrounded by the Hejaz Mountains, empty valleys, agricultural land and old dormant volcanoes. Before Islam it was called Yathrib, a name attested in an inscription of the Babylonian king Nabonidus of the 6th century BCE and used in the Qur'an. According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad later renamed it Taybah or Tabah, and it came to be called Madinat an-Nabi, "City of the Prophet", and al-Madinah al-Munawwarah, "the Enlightened City", shortened to Madinah.

The city has been inhabited for about 1,500 years before the Hijrah, or about the 9th century BCE. By the fourth century Arab tribes were encroaching from Yemen, and around the time of Muhammad three prominent Jewish tribes lived there: the Banu Qaynuqa, the Banu Qurayza and the Banu Nadir.

Toward the end of the 5th century the Jewish rulers lost control of the city to the two Arab tribes, the 'Aws and Khazraj. In 622 Muhammad and an estimated 70 Meccan Muhajirun left Mecca over a few months for sanctuary in Yathrib. The longstanding enmity between the 'Aws and Khazraj was dampened as many of them and some local Jews embraced Islam, and Muhammad was agreed on as leader of the city. It served as the base of the early Muslim community, and a larger part of the Qur'an was revealed in Medina than in Mecca.

Later the city passed to the Umayyads, whose governors dug the spring called 'Ayn az-Zarqa'a and built irrigation ducts and dams, leading to an agricultural boom. It was held by the Mamluks of Egypt from 1254 to 1517 and then by the Ottomans, after Selim I conquered Mamluk Egypt.

In 1532 Suleiman built a fortress around it, and the Ottoman sultans repeatedly redesigned the Prophet's Mosque. The Sharif of Mecca, Husayn ibn Ali, attacked Medina on 6 June 1916, during the First World War, and the siege that followed brought food shortages, disease and mass emigration. The governor Fakhri Pasha held out until his own men arrested him and the Sharifate took the city on 10 January 1919. The Saudi forces conquered it on 5 December 1925.

Medina is the second holiest city in Islam after Mecca and the capital of Medina Province, with 1,477,023 inhabitants. Al-Masjid al-Nabawi, the Prophet's Mosque, was built by Muhammad in 622 and is the burial site of the prophet. The Quba Mosque is the oldest in Islam. The city also holds Masjid al-Qiblatayn, the Baqi' cemetery, Mount Uhud, site of the Battle of Uhud, and the King Fahd Glorious Qur'an Printing Complex.
medina-del-campo: Medina del Campo lies on the banks of the Zapardiel river, in the central part of the Douro basin. Initially a Berber settlement, it was repopulated after 1085. It was founded on the hill called La Mota in the 11th century, on the site of the castle, and in the Middle Ages that hill was the town centre. The hill holds remains of a stronghold, a medieval village and a Celtic walled settlement of the 4th century BCE. The walls date from the 11th century and were enlarged three times as the population grew.

By the 12th century the walled town was a major population centre of the Kingdom of Castile and drew large trading operations. Its free fairs flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries and supported banking and the trade in wool, textiles and books. In the 16th century the fair became the most important of the great Castilian fairs, with Villalón and Medina de Rioseco, and drew merchants chiefly Castilian, Portuguese, Italian and Flemish.

In 1489 the Treaty of Medina del Campo united Spain and England in a trade agreement meant to last 96 years, with reduced tariffs, the recognition of France as a common enemy and the marriage of Catherine of Aragon to Prince Arthur. During the Revolt of the Comuneros the town housed the royal artillery, and a royalist attempt to seize the guns ended in the burning of the town. Its Jewish community ended with the expulsion of 1492. From the 17th to the 19th century the town declined, and it grew again after the first railway train arrived on 3 September 1860.

The Castle of La Mota, built between the 12th and 15th centuries, served as a royal prison, and Cesare Borgia was among its prisoners. The Royal Palace, begun in the 14th century, is where Isabel la Católica, Queen of Castile, made her will and died on 26 November 1504. The Hospital of Simón Ruiz and the Palacio de Dueñas date from the 16th century, built by merchant bankers who prospered by the fair, and a Museum of the Fairs records the market.
medinaceli: Medinaceli stands on a hilltop at about 1210 metres above sea level, at the confluence of the rivers Jalón and Arbujuelo, and looks over the Jalón valley. The municipality includes other villages, among them Torralba del Moral, and two motorways, the A-15 and the A-2, meet within its bounds. Its name comes from the Arabic madinat Salim, City of Salim, which goes back to the Banu Salim, a lineage of the Berber Masmuda.

Before the Islamic period the site was a Celtiberian town known as Occilis or Okilis. Under Islamic rule it held the status of a madina, a city. The Berber Banu Salim settled in the area, and although they lost favour and were routed in 920, the town kept its strategic importance for the Cordobese authorities. It served as a powerbase for military operations in the north, including the campaign against the Christian settlements of the upper Duero and the suppression of the revolt of the Banu Tujib. In 946 Medinaceli became the head of the Middle March, the frontier district in this region.

The town has a Roman arch built between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE, the only three-gated Roman arch in Spain, which is used as a symbol of Spain's historic sites across the country. The castle was the residence of the Dukes of Medinaceli until the Ducal Palace took over that purpose. Other buildings include the Colegiata de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, whose abbots disputed with the bishops of Sigüenza to defend the city's rights, and the 16th-century Convent of Saint Elizabeth beside the church of San Martín. The beaterio of San Román is in ruins and may once have been a synagogue. A stone gate is one of the few remains of the old city walls dating from the Islamic period.
medinet-habu: Medinet Habu lies near the foot of the Theban Hills on the west bank of the Nile, opposite the modern city of Luxor. It is associated above all with the mortuary temple of Ramesses III, but the locality also holds the poorly preserved temple of Ay and Horemheb. A settlement stood there from pharaonic times until the ninth century, by then a Coptic centre called Jeme. The origin of the name Medinet Habu is unknown. Vivant Denon was the first European to describe the temple in modern literature, visiting between 1799 and 1801.

The mortuary temple is about 150 metres long and closely resembles the Ramesseum of Ramesses II. Its precinct holds more than 7,000 square metres of decorated wall reliefs and 48 rooms, eight of which form the king's mortuary suite. A mudbrick wall surrounded it, and a mudbrick palace stood to the south. Materials came from earlier monuments, including the destroyed mortuary temple of Tausret.

Four long inscriptions describe the battles of Ramesses III, among them a first Libyan war in his fifth year and the Northern War of his eighth year, which tells of an invasion by the Peleset, Theker, Shekelesh, Denye and Weshesh. Thirteen scenes on the north wall are read as one campaign, beginning with the Libyans and ending with the so-called sea peoples. Gaston Maspero proposed over a century ago that two panels showed an invasion of Egypt from Anatolia.

The walls of the mortuary temple are relatively well preserved. Clearance of the main temple between 1859 and 1899, to prepare it for tourism, destroyed many Greco-Roman buildings, including a Byzantine church in the second court, without records. Theodore M. Davis excavated the palace in 1913, and the University of Chicago's Oriental Institute, now the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, published the site. Chapels for the God's Wife of Amun were built in the outer court between the eighth and sixth centuries BCE, and a Coptic town with several churches later filled the temple.
medinet-madi: The Ptolemaic town was laid out on a grid of about 1000 by 600 metres, with its main temples in the west and a long processional way running north to south; it never had walls. The inner part of the temple of Renenutet, temple A, is of dark sandstone: a small hall with papyrus columns leads to three chapels with statues of deities, the central one holding a large statue of Renenutet flanked by Amenemhat III and Amenemhat IV. Reliefs show a king with the goddess Seshat founding the temple, and Amenemhat III before Renenutet with his daughter Neferuptah.

Behind it, temple B was dedicated to Isis-Thermouthis, Thermouthis being the Greek name of Renenutet, and its decoration was never finished. Temple C, of the Ptolemaic period, held two crocodile mummies in its chapel, and a vaulted chamber nearby, where more than thirty crocodile eggs were found in a basin, may have been a nursery for crocodiles.

The temple still functioned in the New Kingdom, when King Merenptah placed a statue of himself in it, but the town was abandoned afterwards and settled again in Ptolemaic times. Under Emperor Diocletian a square fortress of 50 by 50 metres was built north-east of the town, garrisoned by the Cohors IV Numidarum. In Byzantine times the people moved to the south of the town and built several churches, and the town was abandoned after the ninth century.

Thousands of ostraca found in a house of the temple district in 1938, mostly from the late second and early third centuries, are written in Demotic, Greek and a mixed script, and record the priests' horoscopes, school texts and disputes; one drafts a petition asking for priests from Soknopaiou Nesos to help with the cult. Coptic texts found nearby in 1929 include the Manichaean Psalm-book.

The temple complex was excavated by archaeologists of the University of Milan in the 1930s, and its good state may be owed to its seclusion. Temple C was excavated from 1995 to 1999, and in early 2006 an Egyptian expedition uncovered the temple's foundations, administrative buildings, granaries and residences. Zahi Hawass called it the only intact temple surviving from the Middle Kingdom.
mediterranean: The Mediterranean Sea is an intercontinental sea between Europe, Asia and Africa, almost completely enclosed by land. It connects to the Atlantic Ocean by the Strait of Gibraltar, only 14 km wide, to the Black Sea by the Bosporus, and to the Red Sea by the Suez Canal. It covers about 2,500,000 km2 and has fifteen marginal seas, among them the Aegean, Adriatic, Tyrrhenian and Marmara. Its average depth is 1,500 m, and the deepest point, 5,109 m, lies in the Calypso Deep in the Ionian Sea. The Nile is the longest river to end in it. Sicily and Sardinia are its two largest islands.

Geological evidence indicates that around 5.9 million years ago the sea was cut off from the Atlantic and was partly or completely dried up over some 600,000 years, in the Messinian salinity crisis. It was refilled about 5.3 million years ago by the Zanclean flood, in less than two years according to scientists' estimates.

The Levant, in the eastern Mediterranean, was among the first regions in the world with permanent human habitation, as early as 12,000 BCE. The earliest advanced civilisations on the sea were the Egyptians and the Minoans, who traded extensively with each other. Around 1200 BCE the Bronze Age Collapse destroyed many cities and trade routes in the east. The Greek city-states and the Phoenicians later colonised its coastlines extensively. Darius I of Persia, who conquered Egypt, built a canal linking the Red Sea to the Nile and so to the Mediterranean, wide enough for two triremes to pass and needing four days to traverse.

After the Punic Wars of the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE the Roman Republic defeated the Carthaginians and became the preeminent power in the western Mediterranean. Once Augustus founded the Roman Empire, the Romans called it Mare Nostrum, Our Sea. For the next 400 years the empire controlled the sea and virtually all its coasts from Gibraltar to the Levant, which earned it the nickname Roman Lake. Rome is the only state to have ever controlled all of its coasts.

The Romans also called the sea Mare Magnum and Mare Internum. The name Mare Mediterraneum, meaning in the middle of land, is first attested in the 6th century in the work of Isidore of Seville. Arabic writers called it the Sea of the Romans, and the Ancient Egyptians called it Wadj-wr, great green. The countries on its shores include Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt and Morocco, and Cyprus and Malta are island countries within it. Its mild winters and warm summers give their name to the Mediterranean climate type.
medjay: The earliest mention of the Medjay is in the autobiography of Weni, a general under Pepi I Meryre, which lists them among other Nubian peoples. The name then referred to people from the land of Medja, a district thought to lie just east of the Second Cataract of the Nile. The Egyptians called Nubia Ta-Seti, the Land of the bow, and its peoples, the Medjay among them, were known for their military skills, particularly as archers. A decree of Pepi I naming an Overseer of the Medja suggests that the district was at least partly subject to Egyptian government.

Since Alan Gardiner, a common account has held that the term passed through three meanings: a place name in the Old Kingdom, an ethnic group of pastoral nomads in the Eastern Desert around the First and Second Cataracts until the end of the Second Intermediate Period, and an occupational title in the New Kingdom. More recent work suggests that Medjay began as an Egyptian name for others and that those so called were neither one ethnicity nor a unified polity. Kate Liszka has proposed that the distinction drawn under Senusret III, who barred Nubian movement north of Semna, may have led people to take Medjay as an identity.

Middle Kingdom documents such as the Semna Despatches describe them as nomadic desert people, and they served as soldiers, as the stelae of Res and Ptahwer record. In the Second Intermediate Period they fought in Kamose's campaign against the Hyksos. The Pan-Grave culture of about 1800-1550 BCE, named for its circular graves in Lower Nubia and Upper Egypt, with Nerita shells and painted skulls of horned animals, is generally taken to represent them.

By the Eighteenth Dynasty the Medjay were an elite paramilitary police guarding capitals, royal cemeteries and borders, best known for protecting the palaces and tombs of Thebes; more and more Egyptians joined their ranks. The name disappears from the records after the 20th Dynasty. Linguistic evidence indicates that they spoke an ancient Cushitic language related to Beja, and the linguist Rilly regards the Blemmyes as one of their tribes.
medjerda: The Medjerda, the classical Bagradas, is also known as the Wadi Majardah or Mejerda. It originates in the Tell Atlas, part of the Atlas Mountains, in north-eastern Algeria, then flows east into Tunisia and enters the Gulf of Utica of the Mediterranean. The river is dammed in several places and is a major supplier of water to the country's wheat crops. Its water has been used for irrigation and has served the towns and farms along its banks.
The Gulf of Utica was formed by the postglacial rise of the sea about 6,000 years ago. Over time, deposits from the river gradually filled up the northern part of the gulf.

The Medjerda has long been Tunisia's crucial waterway, supplying fresh water to its population centres and agriculture along its banks. As a strategic resource it was fought over and settled many times by the Carthaginians, Romans, Vandals, Byzantines, Arabs and Ottomans. Several major cities were founded on or near it, among them Utica, Carthage and eventually Tunis.

The sequence of changes in historical times has been inferred from ancient documents and archaeological evidence, with aerial and satellite photographs used to study how the landscape evolved over the past 3,000 years. The southern part of the gulf was filled up in late ancient times, and the sea withdrew gradually from the northern part during the Middle Ages and modern times. The ports of Utica and Ghar el-Melh, once called Rusucmona or Porto Farina, were eventually closed by the silting of their harbours. The Ghar el Melh lagoon is the last vestige of the old gulf.

With a length of about 450 km, the Medjerda is the longest river of Tunisia. After the last great flood, in 1973, it shifted its course once more, and it now flows through a canal originally dug to carry off flood overflow.
medo-babylonian-conquest-of-the-assyrian: In the first half of the 7th century BCE the Neo-Assyrian Empire controlled the whole Fertile Crescent. After Assurbanipal died in 631 BCE, his son Ashur-etil-ilani faced unrest, and some vassals took the chance to free themselves. In the middle of 627 BCE Sinsharishkun took the throne, and on the death of Kandalanu, the vassal king of Babylon, he ruled Babylon as well. The empire was also in the midst of a long megadrought, which further weakened it.

The general Sin-shumu-lishir at once rebelled and held Nippur and Babylon for three months before he was defeated. Nabopolassar, using this instability, attacked both cities, and after a failed Assyrian counterattack he was crowned King of Babylon in November 626 BCE. Sinsharishkun took Sippar in 625 BCE and Uruk in 623 BCE, but a revolt by an unnamed general who seized Nineveh in 622 BCE drew him away for about a hundred days, and by 620 BCE Nabopolassar held all of Babylonia.

By 616 BCE the Babylonians had reached the Balikh River and defeated the Assyrians at Arrapha, despite the help of Pharaoh Psamtik I of Egypt. In 615 BCE the Medes under Cyaxares invaded and defeated Sinsharishkun at the Battle of Tarbiṣu, and after they plundered Assur in 614 BCE, killing many of its people, Nabopolassar and Cyaxares made an alliance, sealed by the marriage of Nebuchadnezzar to a Median princess. Their joint armies took Nineveh after a long and brutal siege in 612 BCE; Sinsharishkun is commonly thought to have died defending it.

Ashur-uballit II was crowned at Harran, which he made his capital, and relied on Egypt and Mannea. When the Medo-Babylonian army marched on Harran in November 610 BCE he fled into the Syrian desert with Egyptian troops, and the city fell early in 609 BCE. His attempt to retake it with a large Egyptian force in the summer of 609 BCE was driven off by Nabopolassar.

Ashur-uballit is not mentioned again after 609 BCE, and his fate is unknown. In 608 BCE Pharaoh Necho II led an army into former Assyrian territory, but no great battle is recorded, and Egypt's campaigns in the Levant ended with its defeat at the Battle of Carchemish in 605 BCE. The fall of Assyria brought Egypt and Babylon into direct contact, and through the next century they often fought for control of the Fertile Crescent.
meena: The Meenas were originally a nomadic people and are sometimes considered a sub-group of the Bhil community. They claim mythological descent from the Matsya avatar, the fish incarnation of Vishnu, and from the people of the Matsya Kingdom of the 6th century BCE. The historian Pramod Kumar thinks it likely that tribes of ancient Matsya were called Meena, but finds no certain link with the modern Meenas. Nandini Sinha Kapur argues that their oral traditions were developed from the early 19th century to reconstruct an identity, in answer to medieval Persian and colonial records that portrayed them as violent plunderers.

The Meenas ruled places in Rajasthan until invading Rajputs overpowered them. They then took to the forests and hills and fought to regain their lands. Bundi was taken from them by Rao Dewa in 1342 and Dhundhar by the Kachhwaha Rajputs, and Kota, Jhalawar, Karauli and Jalore were other areas of earlier Meena influence. In the 1840s Lakshminarayan Jharwal led a Meena rebellion against British rule in Jaipur. Under the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871 the Meenas were placed in its first list in 1872, and they remained an officially designated criminal tribe until 1952. They received Scheduled Tribe status in 1954.

The Meenas are divided into clans and sub-clans called adakhs, named after ancestors. The Zamindar Meena descend from those who submitted to the Rajputs and settled on lands granted by them, the Chaukidar Meena from those who kept up guerrilla warfare. Some groups, such as the Ujwal Meena, claim Rajput status and keep a vegetarian diet. Meenas perform Pitra Tarpan after a collective bath on Diwali, worship trees and plants at weddings and festivals under the Dharadi tradition and celebrate Meenesh Jayanti in the month of Chaitra. Their women practise Mandana painting, and the 2011 census counted about 5 million Meenas.
meenakshi-temple: Tamil texts imply that a temple existed in Madurai by the mid-6th century, and the town of Koodal, as Madurai was called, is described as a temple town from which every street radiated. The temple is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams, Shiva temples praised in the Tevaram hymns composed by the Nayanars between the 6th and 11th centuries. Most surviving inscriptions are dated after the 12th century, so the early structures are known chiefly from the Pandya period of the 12th to 13th centuries.

After the death of Maravarman Kulasekhara I in 1310, his sons fought over the Pandya throne while the Khalji dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate raided the south. Records say that Malik Kafur looted and destroyed Hindu temples, the Meenakshi temple among them, and carried gold and jewellery to Delhi in 1311. The Vijayanagara Empire took Madurai in 1378, and Kumara Kampana is said to have rebuilt the temple, fortified it with walls and restored the hidden idols.

The temple stands on the southern bank of the Vaigai River and is dedicated to Meenakshi, a form of Parvati, and her consort Sundareswarar, a form of Shiva. Meenakshi means fish-eyed in Tamil. According to the Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam, she appeared from a sacrificial fire as the daughter of King Malayadhwaja Pandya, ruled as his successor and took her true form when she met Shiva. Her shrine stands at the centre of the inner enclosure, to the right of Sundareswarar's, and pilgrims visit it first.

The complex covers 5.7 hectares inside concentric walled enclosures. It has 14 gopurams, the towers over its gateways, of which the tallest, the southern tower built in the 16th century, rises to 52 metres. The thousand-pillared hall holds 985 carved pillars, and the sacred tank is called the Golden Lotus Pond. The streets around the temple are named after months of the Tamil calendar, because processions began from the spots matching each month.

The temple has long been a centre of Tamil literature. The poet Kumaraguruparar wrote the Meenakshi Pillaitamil in praise of the goddess in the 17th century, and Shyama Shastri composed nine Telugu songs for her, the Navaratnamalika. Its yearly wedding festival, the Meenakshi thirukalyanam, lasts 15 days in the month of Chithirai and is the most attended of the temple's monthly festivals.

Dalits were barred from entering the temple until the early 20th century. On 8 July 1939 a group led by A. Vaidyanatha Iyer and Kakkan entered it, an event that preceded legislation of the Madras Presidency later that year. The Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department of the Government of Tamil Nadu manages the temple, and the state's emblem is based on its west gopuram.
meersburg: Meersburg stands on the northern shore of Lake Constance in Baden-Württemberg. It is known for its medieval town, which is divided into a lower town, the Unterstadt, and an upper town, the Oberstadt. Two stairways and a steep street, the Steigstrasse, link them. Half-timbered houses survive, together with two medieval town gates that are the remains of the fortification. The vineyards on the northern bank of the lake are well known in Germany, and the rosé Weissherbst is a local specialty.

The name means castle on the sea, and refers to a castle that, according to a tradition recorded in 1548, was built here in 630 by the Merovingian king Dagobert I. The Old Castle is held to be one of the oldest surviving castles in Germany. The town gained the status of a free city in 1299, although it nominally remained under the Bishop of Constance. In 1803 it was annexed to the Electorate of Baden. After World War II it lay in the French military occupation area of Germany.
The New Castle was built in the 18th century as the residence of the bishop of Constance. After the Secularization of 1803 it was put to various uses, and it is now a museum.

The poet Annette von Droste-Hülshoff lived her last years at the Old Castle, from 1841 to 1848, and also owned the small vine-covered villa known as the Fürstenhäusle. Franz Anton Mesmer, the 18th-century physician from whose name the verb to mesmerise derives, died in Meersburg in 1815 and is buried by the old wall of the graveyard. Other residents were the Austro-Hungarian novelist Fritz Mauthner, who died there in 1923, and the antiquary Joseph Maria Christoph von Lassberg, who lived at the Old Castle from 1838.
meerut: Meerut lies in the Doab, the fertile land between the Ganges and the Yamuna, and is the administrative headquarters of the Meerut district, which covers 2,522 square kilometres, more than Delhi. The climate is monsoon-influenced and humid subtropical, with very hot summers.

The name is believed to have evolved from Mayarashtra, the capital of a mythological kingdom ruled by Mayasura, an architect and the father of Mandodari, wife of Ravana. Another tradition says King Yudhishthira granted the land to Mayasura in recognition of his skill as a builder.

Excavations of 1950 to 1952 at Vidura-ka-Tila, a group of mounds about 37 kilometres north-east of the city, concluded that the district holds the remains of Hastinapur, the capital of the Kauravas and Pandavas of the Mahabharata. In the eleventh century Har Dat, the Dor Raja of Bulandshahr, built a fort south-west of the city, and Mahmud of Ghazni defeated him in 1018. The local Hindu raja soon regained the city, and Qutb-ud-din Aybak captured it in 1193.

In 1803 Daulat Rao Scindia of the Marathas ceded the territory to the British East India Company. Its cantonment, near Delhi in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, became one of the largest in India, and Meerut was made the district headquarters in 1818. The rebellion of 1857 began in the Kali Paltan in the cantonment. The railway from Delhi was built in 1864. Meerut was one of the first places in northern India where publishing was established, and a major centre of commercial publishing in the 1860s and 1870s.

Meerut is known for sports goods, musical instruments, handloom work and its scissors, and is an education centre of western Uttar Pradesh. The Nauchandi Mela, a fair that began in 1672, is held each year two weeks after Holi. Nearby Hastinapur holds Jain temples and is regarded by Jains as one of their holiest places.
mefitis: Mefitis was worshipped by the Samnites and Osci from the 7th century BCE to the 2nd century CE, mostly in the southwest of central Italy. She was probably first a goddess of underground sources such as springs, and because many of them were sulphurous she came to be linked with noxious gases; the 5th-century writer Servius held that any foul scent belonged to her. Modern scholars mostly reject the idea that she was a goddess of intoxication, noting that sulphurous water is found at Ampsanctus but not at her sanctuaries of Saepinum and Rossano.

Ingrid Edlund-Berry argues that she had a healing role, since Romans held sulphur to purify, while Allison Griffith finds no evidence that her sites served for healing or bathing. Others give her an agricultural role through her title Aravinna, perhaps from arva, soil, or see her as a mediator between the heavens and the underworld.

Her chief shrine stood at Lake Ampsanctus in Samnium, near the present village of Rocca San Felice. Cicero and Pliny the Elder called the lake deadly, and Pliny wrote that anyone entering her temple soon died; Servius called it the navel of Italy. Many clay votive figures from the Ansanto valley show wild boars. The site still gives off large amounts of carbon dioxide, which keeps most plants from growing there.

A temple was built at Rossano di Vaglio in the 4th century BCE. Its 58 inscriptions are mostly in Oscan from the 4th to the 2nd century BCE and later in Latin, perhaps after the Social War. Varro mentions a grove of Mefitis by the Esquiline Hill in Rome, Tacitus a temple at Cremona that survived the city's destruction after the Second Battle of Bedriacum, and a wall inscription in Pompeii a festival in her honour organised by the gens Mamia.

In the Aeneid, Virgil linked the lake of Ampsanctus with the underworld, calling it a breathing place of savage Dis, and used the word mephitim for the deadly vapour of the grove of Albunea. Her name has been explained in many ways: from Greek words for intoxication or honey, from a Proto-Indo-European root for middle, or, as the grammarian Priscian held, from a Greek word for mediator. Finds of Artemis statues at Rossano and shared epithets suggest links with Diana, Juno and Venus.
mefo-bills: The German government needed large sums to rebuild its heavy industry during the Depression and to rearm, but rearmament was illegal under the Treaty of Versailles, a legal limit held interest rates at 4.5%, and a large, visible deficit would have drawn attention. The Reichsbank could lend the government no more than 100 million Reichsmarks. Adolf Hitler, recently come to power, demanded of Hjalmar Schacht that any solution avoid inflation. The scheme Schacht devised followed the earlier Öffa bills as its blueprint.

The limited company Metallurgische Forschungsgesellschaft m.b.H. had no product, service or operation and existed only as a balance sheet. Its bills were six-month promissory notes that any German bank could discount at any time and rediscount at the Reichsbank within the last three months of their earliest maturity, so they served as a highly liquid means of payment that companies could trade among themselves. They paid 4% a year, more than other trade bills of the time, and could be extended by 90 days indefinitely at the government's wish.

So that the bills would never be exchanged for Reichsmarks, which would have caused inflation, their maturity was extended again and again, and by 1939 it had become five years. The total issued was kept secret and the records are not precise. By 1938 there were 12 billion Reichsmarks of Mefo bills, against 19 billion of standard government bonds.

The bills let the Reich run a far larger deficit than it otherwise could, raising billions for military and public works and increasing war production while delaying the strain on government funds. In effect Germany had begun printing money, yet inflation did not rise, because the government rarely redeemed the bills and their interest and supposed security kept most of them in circulation rather than cashed. The continued reliance on debt nonetheless left a large financial deficit.
megabazus: Megabazus, in Old Persian Bagavazdā or Bagabāzu, was the son of Megabates and a first cousin of King Darius I, under whom he became a highly regarded general. Most of what is known of him comes from The Histories of Herodotus.

Megabazus led Darius's army in his European Scythian campaign of 513 BCE. When that campaign was broken off without result, he stayed in Europe in command of an army of 80,000 men, charged with subduing the Greek cities on the Hellespont. His troops took the coastal Greek cities and gold-rich Thrace, then defeated the powerful Paeonians, many of whom he deported to Phrygia.

He then sent envoys to Amyntas I, king of Macedon, demanding his submission. Amyntas gave earth and water, the token of submission to the Achaemenid king, and afterwards acted as Darius's hyparch. A quarrel followed when members of the Persian delegation insulted the Macedonians by taking liberties with their wives, and the Macedonian prince Alexander I had several of the envoys and their followers killed. The conflict was settled by the marriage of Megabazus's son Bubares to Gygaia, a daughter of Amyntas.

Back in Asia Minor, Megabazus was made governor of the satrapy of Hellespontine Phrygia, with its seat at Daskyleion. Suspicious of Histiaeus, tyrant of Miletus, he advised Darius to bring him to Susa where he could be watched; Histiaeus later stirred a revolt in his own city and sided with the Greeks against Persia. Otanes, son of Sisamnes, succeeded Megabazus in his command.

Several of Megabazus's sons held high office. Oebares became satrap of Daskyleion around 493 BCE. Bubares was the managing engineer of Xerxes I's canal through Athos. Megabates commanded the Achaemenid fleet that sailed against Naxos in 500 or 499 BCE and was satrap of Daskyleion in the early 470s, and Pherendates died around 485 BCE while satrap of Egypt.
megali-idea: The expression first appeared in the debates between Prime Minister Ioannis Kolettis and King Otto that preceded the constitution of 1844, but the hope behind it was older. Greeks had long looked for liberation from Ottoman rule and a restoration of the Byzantine Empire; folklore told that the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, had been turned to marble and lay beneath the Golden Gate of Constantinople awaiting the call to reconquer the city. The state created in 1830 was designed by the Great Powers, and most ethnic Greeks still lived outside it, within the Ottoman Empire.

The new state was imagined as the Greece of Two Continents and Five Seas, reaching from the Ionian Sea to Anatolia and the Black Sea and from Thrace, Macedonia and Epirus to Crete and Cyprus. When the Danish prince Wilhelm Georg was elected king in 1863 he was styled King of the Hellenes rather than King of Greece, implying a king of all Greeks wherever they lived.

The Ionian Islands were acquired in 1864. In 1897, with violence growing in Crete, a Greek force of 1,500 men under Colonel Timoleon Vassos landed at Kolymbari on 1 February and proclaimed the island's union with Greece. Irregulars then raided Turkish outposts in Thessaly without orders, and the Ottoman Empire declared war. The Greek army fell back, an armistice was signed in May, and Greece lost small border territories and paid reparations; Crete became an autonomous state with Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner.

Eleftherios Venizelos, a Cretan who became prime minister after the Goudi coup of 1909, was a major proponent of the idea, and under him Greek territory doubled in the Balkan Wars of 1912–13. Greece joined the Allies in 1917 and afterwards gained a protectorate over Smyrna and its hinterland, where a referendum was to follow five years of Greek administration, and a frontier in Thrace a few miles from the walls of Constantinople.

Turkish revolutionaries defeated the Greek army and expelled the Greeks from Anatolia. By the Treaty of Lausanne, Greece ceded Eastern Thrace, Imbros, Tenedos and Smyrna. During the conflict 151,892 Greeks had already fled Asia Minor; the treaty moved 1,104,216 Greeks from Turkey, while 380,000 Turks left Greece. The League of Nations arranged a loan of 150 million francs to help settle the refugees. In 1930 Venizelos paid an official visit to Turkey, where he proposed Mustafa Kemal for the Nobel Peace Prize. The Dodecanese were acquired after the Second World War, in 1947.
megasthenes: Little is known about Megasthenes as a person. He spent time at the court of Sibyrtius, satrap of Arachosia under Antigonus I and then Seleucus I. Arrian writes that Megasthenes lived with Sibyrtius and often spoke of visiting Sandracottus, the king of the Indians, that is Chandragupta Maurya. He served as ambassador of the Seleucid king Seleucus I Nicator at Chandragupta's court in Pataliputra, modern Patna.

The date of the journey is uncertain. Seleucus reigned from 305 to 281 BCE, which gives the loose range within which the mission might have begun. Scholars dispute when he visited India and how long he stayed: A. B. Bosworth argued for a date before Seleucus, while Stoneman and others argue for a date after the Mauryan-Seleucid settlement of about 303 BCE. He appears to have passed through the Punjab, since he gives a detailed account of its rivers, and then travelled to Pataliputra along the Yamuna and the Ganga. It is not certain which other parts of India he saw. Later Greek envoys are known: Deimachus went to Bindusara and Dionysius to Ashoka.
Megasthenes described India in his book Indica, the first written description of India by a person from the Western world. The work is lost and survives in part through quotations by later authors.

Ancient opinion was divided. Arrian was the only ancient writer to speak favourably of him, and Diodorus quotes him while omitting some parts. Eratosthenes accused him of falsehood, though he borrowed much of his content on India from him.

Strabo called him a liar for fabulous stories and wrote that no faith whatever could be placed in Deimachus and Megasthenes. Pliny the Elder criticised his description of the fabulous races of India and his account of Herakles and Dionysus. Modern scholars such as E. A. Schwanbeck and B. C. J. Timmer have found him a generally reliable source of Indian history. Truesdell Sparhawk Brown is more critical, noting that he saw only a small part of India and relied on others, but his work remained the principal source for later writers.
meghalaya: Meghalaya is one of the Seven Sister States of north-eastern India. It covers about 22,429 square kilometres and borders Bangladesh to the south and west and Assam to the north and east. The state is mountainous, with valleys and highland plateaus, and rests mainly on Archean rock that holds deposits of coal, limestone, uranium and sillimanite. Its name means the abode of clouds, from the Sanskrit megha and alaya, and was given by Shiba P. Chatterjee, a geography professor at the University of Calcutta.

The southern Khasi Hills record an average of 12,000 mm of rain a year, and about 70 per cent of the state is forested. Some of the forest survives as sacred groves, small pockets of ancient forest kept by communities for centuries for religious reasons and reserved for ritual. British authorities nicknamed the region the Scotland of the East.

People have lived in Meghalaya since the Neolithic period. Neolithic sites have been found in the high Khasi Hills and the Garo Hills, where shifting cultivation known as jhum is still practised. The limited archaeology suggests ancient settlement, and Ian Glover has proposed that north-eastern India was the most favourable single area for the origin of domesticated rice. Folk tradition ties jhum to rice: one legend has the god of wind shake seeds from a celestial tree, which a bird sowed.

Khasis, Jaintias and Garos each kept traditional political institutions that, according to the account, have existed for hundreds of years and worked at village, clan and state level. Meghalaya itself was formed on 21 January 1972 by carving the united Khasi Hills and Jaintia Hills and the Garo Hills out of Assam. Its Autonomous District Councils exist under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India, which was added on the recommendation of a subcommittee led by Gopinath Bordoloi.

Shillong is the capital. The Khasis are the largest group in the population, followed by the Garos and the Jaintias, who follow a matrilineal system in which descent and inheritance pass through women, and the youngest daughter inherits the property and cares for aged parents. About 75 per cent of people are Christian. Meghalaya has 12 districts and a Legislative Assembly of 60 members.

Living root bridges, made by training the aerial roots of the rubber tree Ficus elastica, are found in the south, built by both Khasis and Jaintias. In July 2018 the International Commission on Stratigraphy named the Meghalayan age, the latest stage of the Holocene, after a stalagmite in Mawmluh cave that records a climate event around 2250 BCE.
mehdi-frasheri: Frashëri was born on 28 February 1872 in Frashër, in the Janina Vilayet of the Ottoman Empire, the son of Ragip bey, kaymakam of Metsovo. He studied in Konica and Monastir and graduated from the Mekteb-i Mülkiye in Istanbul in 1897. In 1901 he was charged in Istanbul with setting up, with a small group of Albanians, a press in a cellar to print Albanian nationalist material.

He served as kaymakam of Peqin from 1901 to 1903 and then joined the Secret Committee for the Liberation of Albania in Ohrid. Under the Ottomans he was governor of the Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem. As a member of the International Commission of Control he signed the Protocol of Corfu on 17 May 1914, and he was mayor of Durrës under Prince Wied, a minister in 1918 and minister of the interior in 1920. He took part in the Congress of Durrës in December 1918, represented Albania at the League of Nations in 1923 and in the early 1930s sat on the committees reforming the civil code.

Frashëri opposed Benito Mussolini's invasion of Albania, broadcast attacks on it and refused to sign a declaration in support of the Italians, taking refuge in the Turkish Legation. He was later arrested and interned in Italy. In 1942 he was honorary chairman of the Conference of Pezë, which gathered Albanian anti-fascists.

After the capitulation of Italy the Germans sought him out, and on 16 September he agreed to come to Tirana for talks with Hermann Neubacher, Major Franz von Scheiger and Martin Schliep. It was agreed that Albania would have its own sovereignty under Nazi Germany, on the model of the Independent State of Croatia, and Frashëri became regent and head of the council. Its chair was meant to rotate, but Lef Nosi declined for health reasons and Anton Harapi refused, as a Catholic monk, any post in which he would have to sanction the death penalty. When the Germans withdrew they took Frashëri with them; he moved to Vienna and then settled in Rome.
mehdya: The town was formerly called al-Ma'mura, the well-populated. An ancient account says the Carthaginians founded a colony on the site in the 5th century BCE, calling it Thymiaterium. The Portuguese captured it in 1515 and named it São João da Mamora, one of several short-lived fortresses they built on the Moroccan Atlantic coast. After the first Anglo-Spanish War ended in 1604, pirates, among them English former privateers, made it their haven; it was the only port of the coast held by neither the Spanish nor the Moroccans, and under Henry Mainwaring it served for selling plunder and careening ships.

Spain blockaded the harbour in 1611, and in August 1614 a fleet under Admiral Luis Fajardo took the town, left a garrison of 1,500 men and began the Fortress of La Mamora with the San Felipe bastion. The warlord Sidi al-Ayachi captured it for a time about 1627 and added it to his Republic of Salé. When Moulay Ismail stormed it, he renamed it al-Mahdiya, and by tradition the statue of Christ taken from its church was later ransomed by Spain and is venerated in Madrid as the Cristo de Medinaceli.

The restored Spanish fortress became the Kasbah Mahdiyya. The port was closed by Mulay Slimane in 1795 and abandoned, and the French occupied the town in 1911; about 9,000 Allied troops landed there from 19 warships during Operation Torch in 1942. Mehdya lies in Kénitra Province and serves mainly as the coastal district of Kenitra, with 58,558 people at the census of 2024.
mehmed-ii: Mehmed II was born on 30 March 1432 in Edirne, then the Ottoman capital, the son of Sultan Murad II and Hüma Hatun, a slave of uncertain origin. At eleven he was sent to Amasya with two advisers to govern and gain experience, as Ottoman princes did, and Murad sent teachers to instruct him. Akshamsaddin stressed to him the duty of overthrowing the Byzantine Empire by taking Constantinople. He was sultan from August 1444 to September 1446 and again from February 1451.

After his return in 1451 Mehmed strengthened the navy and built the fortress of Rumelihisarı on the European shore of the Bosphorus, which gave him control of the strait. When a Venetian vessel ignored the signals to stop, it was sunk, the surviving sailors were beheaded and its captain impaled. He took Constantinople in 1453, aged 21, and claimed the title caesar of Rome, which the Patriarchate of Constantinople soon recognised but most European monarchs rejected. He ordered Hagia Sophia protected and turned it into a mosque.

His later campaigns brought Serbia under Ottoman rule by 1459 or 1460, the Morea in 1460, Trebizond in 1461 and Bosnia in 1463. The Ottoman-Venetian War lasted from 1463 to 1479. In 1475 an Ottoman army was defeated by Stephen the Great at the Battle of Vaslui. Mehmed did not subdue Albania until 1478, ten years after Skanderbeg's death. At home he centralised government, drawing officials largely from the devşirme, and legalised fratricide, so that a sultan who took the throne might execute his brothers. He brought Italian artists and Greek scholars to his court, and wrote poetry under the name Avni.

Mehmed fell ill at Maltepe, near Istanbul, in 1481 and died on 3 May 1481 aged forty-nine. He was buried near the Fatih Mosque complex. The historian Colin Heywood finds substantial circumstantial evidence that he was poisoned, possibly at the behest of his son and successor Bayezid. News of his death was greeted with rejoicing in Europe. He is regarded as a hero in modern Turkey, and Istanbul's Fatih district and the Fatih Mosque bear his name.
mehmed-iii: Mehmed was born at Manisa Palace on 26 May 1566 and was the great-grandson of Suleiman I. His mother, Safiye, was an Albanian from the Dukagjin Highlands. When he heard of the birth, Suleiman named him Mehmed in honour of his own great-grandfather, Mehmed the Conqueror. Suleiman died in September 1566 during the Siege of Szigetvár, and in December 1574 Mehmed's father became Murad III. Mehmed spent most of his childhood and youth in Manisa, and his circumcision ceremony was held on 29 May 1582. Murad III died in January 1595, when Mehmed was 28.

Mehmed III was an idle ruler who left government to his mother. His first major problem was the rivalry between two viziers, Serdar Ferhad Pasha and Koca Sinan Pasha, which led to disturbances by janissaries. On 7 July 1595 he dismissed Ferhad Pasha as Grand Vizier for his failure in Wallachia and replaced him with Sinan. Safiye controlled appointments and dismissals, and her personal purse was three times that of the sultan. In 1600 Mehmed insisted she leave the palace, but after five weeks pressure from the court forced him to cancel her exile.

The Long Turkish War brought a defeat at Nikopol in 1599 by Wallachian forces under Michael the Brave. In 1600 Tiryaki Hasan Pasha captured Nagykanizsa after a 40-day siege. In Anatolia, Karayazıcı Abdülhalim, a former Ottoman official, captured Urfa in 1600 and declared himself sultan, beginning the Jelali revolts. In 1599 Elizabeth I of England sent gifts that included a jewel-studded clockwork organ and a ceremonial coach. England sought an alliance against the Spanish, but it was never concluded.

Safiye helped bring about the execution of Mehmed's son Mahmud in 1603, after she intercepted a message in which a religious seer predicted that Mehmed would die within six months and be succeeded by his son. Mehmed died on 22 December 1603, aged 37. One source gives the cause as distress at Mahmud's death, and another a plague or a stroke. He was buried in the Hagia Sophia. Safiye lost all her power and was exiled to the Old Palace by his successor, Ahmed I.
mehmed-iv: Mehmed IV was born at Topkapı Palace in Constantinople on 2 January 1642, the son of Sultan Ibrahim and Turhan Sultan, a concubine of Russian origin. Soon after his birth his parents quarrelled, and Ibrahim, enraged, flung the infant into a cistern; harem servants rescued him, but he kept a scar on his head for life. He came to the throne in 1648 at the age of six after his father was overthrown in a coup. His grandmother Kösem Sultan, the regent, was suspected of plotting to replace him with his half-brother Suleiman, and in September 1651 Mehmed signed her death warrant.

The early years brought palace intrigues, uprisings in Anatolia, the defeat of the Ottoman navy by the Venetians outside the Dardanelles and food riots. His mother then gave Köprülü Mehmed Pasha full executive powers as Grand Vizier, and he took office on 14 September 1656. The Köprülü era was an exceptionally stable period. Köprülü Mehmed and his son Fazıl Ahmed regained the Aegean islands from Venice, and Crete in the Cretan War of 1645–1669, and campaigned in Transylvania and Poland. When Mehmed accepted the vassalage of Petro Doroshenko, Ottoman rule extended into Podolia. Mehmed loved hunting from a young age, and it earned him the name Avcı, the Hunter. Contemporaries called him pious and gazi, a holy warrior.

The grand vizier Merzifonlu Kara Mustafa supported the Hungarian uprising of Imre Thököly in 1683 and besieged Vienna. On 12 September 1683 the Ottomans suffered a rout at the Battle of Vienna, in a flank attack by Polish cavalry under King John III Sobieski and the Imperial army. This began the Great Turkish War, in which the Holy League drove the Ottomans back toward the Balkans.

After the Second Battle of Mohács in 1687 the army mutinied. On 8 November 1687 it was decided to depose Mehmed and enthrone his brother Suleiman II. Mehmed was imprisoned in Topkapı Palace but allowed to leave it from time to time, and he died at Edirne Palace in 1693.
mehmed-iv-giray: Mehmed, called the Sufi, was a son of Khan Selâmet I Giray and had some reputation as a poet. From 1632 to 1635 he served as nureddin or kalga during the second reign of his cousin Canibek Giray, and he then went to Ottoman territory, probably with the deposed Canibek. Nothing seems to be recorded of his life under the khans İnayet Giray and his brother Bahadır I Giray.

Mehmed came to the throne in 1641 on the death of Bahadır. In 1642 Crimean and Turkish troops, accompanied by the traveller Evliya Çelebi, drove the Don Cossacks out of Azov, which Bahadır had tried and failed to do. His brother Islyam complained to the sultan that he had the better claim, and when the Turkish governor of Kaffa reported that Mehmed had ravaged Circassia without authority, the khan was deposed and replaced by Islyam. Mehmed was living at Rhodes when Islyam died, and he returned to the throne in 1654.

Russia had just allied with the rebellious Cossacks, and Crimea switched sides to support Poland in the Russo-Polish War of 1654 to 1667, though the alliance was loose and Poland paid the Crimeans to invade Ukraine. In 1657 the Crimeans attacked George II Rákóczi of Transylvania, and the next year they sacked his capital, Gyulafehérvár, and returned with about 17,000 slaves. In 1660 Poles and Crimeans defeated Russia at the Battle of Chudnov, and in 1661 the Tatars defeated John Kemény in Transylvania.

In 1666 Mehmed was deposed for sending his son instead of going himself to fight in Hungary and for attacking the Nogais of Bessarabia. He retired to the Shamkhalate of Tarki, where he was granted an estate and lived as a dervish, and his ashes were returned to Bakhchisarai for burial. None of his sons or grandsons became khan. His wife Emine Sultan Biyim is one of only three women known to have had a political role in the Crimean Khanate.
mehrangarh: Mehrangarh is a fort on a hilltop at Jodhpur in Rajasthan. Its name comes from the Sanskrit words mihir, the sun, and garh, fort: it was first called Mihirgarh, a reference to the Rathore clan’s mythical descent from the sun god Surya. Rao Jodha, the fifteenth Rathore ruler, moved his capital from Mandore, whose thousand-year-old fort no longer seemed secure enough, and decided the foundation of the new fort on 12 May 1459. It stands on a rocky hill nine kilometres south of Mandore, known as Bhakurcheeria, the mountain of birds.

According to legend, Rao Jodha had to displace a hermit, Cheeria Nathji, who cursed the citadel to suffer a scarcity of water, and the saint Karni Mata of Deshnoke laid the foundation stone. A further tradition says a man called Raja Ram Meghwal volunteered to be buried alive in the foundations, and his family was granted land.

The hill rises about 122 metres above the plains, and the complex spans 1,200 acres. Though the fort was begun in 1459, most of what stands dates from the time of Maharaja Jaswant Singh (1638–78). Its walls are up to 36 metres high and 21 metres wide. Entry is through seven gates. Jai Pol was built by Maharaja Man Singh in 1806 to celebrate victories over Jaipur and Bikaner, and Fateh Pol commemorates a victory over the Mughals. Dedh Kangra Pol still bears the scars of cannonballs. Inside are palaces including the Moti Mahal, Phool Mahal and Sheesha Mahal, and the Chamunda Mataji temple, where Rao Jodha installed his favourite goddess in 1460.

The museum holds palanquins, howdahs, miniatures, musical instruments, costumes and a collection of arms, among them the sword of Akbar, and a gallery of turbans. The ramparts keep old cannons, including the Kilkila cannon, and give a view of much of the city. Other galleries show the paintings of Marwar-Jodhpur and a royal red tent.

Rudyard Kipling described the fort as “a palace that might have been built by Titans and colored by the morning sun.” The rock on which it stands has been declared a National Geological Monument by the Geological Survey of India. Beside it, the Rao Jodha Desert Rock Park, created in 2006 and opened in February 2011, restores desert vegetation over 72 hectares. A crowd stampede at the Chamunda Devi temple on 30 September 2008 killed 224 people and injured more than 400. The fort has served as a film location and hosts festivals, including the World Sacred Spirit Festival.
mehri-language: Mehri, which its speakers call Mahrīyyt, is the most widely spoken of the Modern South Arabian languages, a group within the Semitic branch of the Afroasiatic family. The group has six distinct languages: Mehri, Shehri, Harsusi, Hobyot, Bathari and Soqotri. Mehri is spoken mainly by the Mehri tribes of the Mahra Governorate of Yemen and the Dhofar Governorate of Oman, and by smaller communities in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Kuwait. Mahris observe 2 October as Mehri Language Day.

Its emphatic consonants are not simply ejectives; they may also be pharyngealised, as in Arabic, so Mehri may preserve evidence of a transition from the ejective consonants of proto-Semitic to the pharyngealised emphatics found in many Semitic languages.

Mehri and its sister languages were spoken in the southern Arabian Peninsula before Arabic spread with Islam in the 7th century CE. The writer Abu Muhammad al-Hasan al-Hamdani, who showed wide knowledge of Arabian dialects and rated each by its distance from classical Arabic, noted that the Mahri speak a barbarous tongue like foreigners. Up to the 19th century speakers lived as far north as central Oman. Arabic has dominated the region for some 1,400 years and Mehri speakers are often bilingual in it, so Mehri is at some risk of extinction.

Mehri exists in two main dialects. Yemeni Mehri, also called Southern Mehri, divides into western and eastern forms. Omani Mehri, also called Dhofari or Nagd Mehri, is spoken by a smaller population and shows no significant variation. The language has a rich oral tradition but little vernacular literature, and almost no native speaker is literate in it. The most common way of writing it uses the unmodified Arabic alphabet, which represents several Mehri sounds with the same letters. Modified Arabic alphabets with extra letters exist, among them sets proposed by the Modern South Arabian Languages Centre at the University of Leeds, but none is standardised.
mehsana-district: Mehsana district, also spelled Mahesana, is one of the 34 districts of Gujarat in western India, with its headquarters at the city of Mehsana. It covers over 4,400 square kilometres and has over 2 million people, about three quarters of them living in rural areas. It has 614 villages and ten talukas: Becharaji, Kadi, Kheralu, Mahesana, Vadnagar, Vijapur, Visnagar, Satlasana, Jotana and Unjha. Banaskantha district lies to the north, Patan and Surendranagar to the west, Gandhinagar and Ahmedabad to the south and Sabarkantha to the east. Its main towns include Mehsana, Vijapur, Unjha, Vadnagar, Kalol, Kadi, Visnagar and Kheralu.

Mehsaji Chavda, a Rajput and an heir of the Chavda dynasty, established Mehsana. He built the city's Toran, an arc gate, and a temple to the Goddess Toran in Vikram Samvat 1414, which is 1358 CE, and a temple dedicated to Chamunda, according to the authors cited for the story. Another legend says he founded it in Vikram Samvat 1375, 1319 CE. The sources show only inconclusively that the town was founded in the Rajput period.

The Gaekwads conquered Baroda and established Baroda State. They expanded their rule into north Gujarat and made Patan their administrative headquarters there, which was later moved to Kadi and, in 1902, to Mehsana. The northern area was divided into eight mahals. The Baroda State railway reached the city on 21 March 1887. Sayajirao Gaekwad III built a palace known as Rajmahal for his son Fatehsinhrao, which is now a district court.

Gujarati is the first language of 97.58 per cent of the district's people and Hindi of 1.76 per cent, according to the 2011 census, which counted 2,035,064 residents. The district sends members to seven Vidhan Sabha constituencies: Kheralu, Unjha, Visnagar, Bechraji, Kadi, Mahesana and Vijapur. Its higher education includes Ganpat University, Indrashil University and Sankalchand Patel University.
meidum: Meidum, also written Maydum or Maidum, is an archaeological site in Lower Egypt. Its ancient Egyptian name, Mr(y)-Jtmw, means beloved of Atum. The site holds a large pyramid and several mudbrick mastabas. Because of its unusual appearance the pyramid is called el-heram el-kaddaab, the false pyramid, in Egyptian Arabic. In its ruined state it stands 65 metres high. Its entrance, on the north side, is about 20 metres above the present ground, and a descending passage 17 metres long leads to a horizontal passage, a vertical shaft and a corbelled burial chamber that was unlikely to have been used for a burial.

The pyramid is thought to be the first of three main pyramids built by Sneferu, although it has been argued that construction began under Huni, the last pharaoh of the Third Dynasty. It was built in three phases, numbered E1 to E3 by the archaeologist Ludwig Borchardt. E1 was a step pyramid like the Djoser Pyramid; E2 added a layer about 5 metres wide and raised the steps from five to seven. In E3 the steps were filled with limestone casing to make a true pyramid, the first in Egypt with smooth sides.

The work had flaws. The outer layer was founded on sand rather than rock, and the platforms of the inner steps sloped outward, which weakened the structure, and the pyramid partly collapsed in antiquity. Franck Monnier and others believe the collapse came only in the New Kingdom. The mortuary temple was found intact under the rubble, and the complex appears never to have been finished: there is no valley temple, the burial chamber has raw walls and the mastabas were never used. The instability is a likely reason for the change of slope from 54 to 43 degrees at Sneferu's Bent Pyramid at Dahshur.

Napoleon's Expedition investigated the pyramid in 1799, when it already had its present three steps. John Shae Perring excavated it in 1837 and Lepsius in 1843. Flinders Petrie later found the mortuary temple, which faces east, and worked out the original proportions: 1100 cubits round and 175 cubits high, the same ratio as the Great Pyramid at Giza. Borchardt studied the area in 1920, Alan Rowe in 1928 and Ali el-Kholi in the 1970s.
meifod: Meifod, formerly also written Meivod, lies seven miles (11 km) north-west of Welshpool on the A495 road, in the valley of the River Vyrnwy, which the River Banwy joins about two miles to the west. The village sits on the river's floodplain and was flooded in 1955. It has never had a railway, although the Llanfyllin branch line ran a few miles to the north-east. Meifod is sometimes identified with the Mediolanum of the Ordovices in Ptolemy's Geography, though others argue for Llanfyllin or Caersws.

About two miles north-east of the princes' residence at Mathrafal, Meifod was an early Christian centre known as Caer Meguaidd or Meguaid, linked with St Gwyddfarch in the 6th century and St Tysilio in the 7th. Tysilio's father, Brochwel Ysgithrog, a prince of Powys, made it his summer residence. The first foundation was probably a clas, a community of clergy, and a monastery. Madog ap Maredudd, the last prince of the whole Kingdom of Powys, built a church dedicated to St Fair, consecrated in 1156, and the churchyard once held three churches, Eglwys Gwydafarch, Eglwys Fair and Eglwys Tysilio.

Madog and his son Gruffydd Maelor, prince of Powys Fadog, who died in 1191, are said to lie in the churchyard, and a weathered slab of the late 9th or early 10th century, carved with a large cross and a smaller cross in a circle, is thought to have covered a tomb. The Barony of Main-yn-Meifod was held by the House of Mathrafal through Iorwerth Goch, his son Iorwerth Vychan and his grandson Madoc Vychan.

The Church of St Tysilio and St Mary occupies a very large site, with parts dating from the 12th century, beside several Nonconformist chapels. Nearby stand Bryngwyn Hall, a late 18th-century house by Robert Mylne listed Grade II*, and Dyffryn Hall, a Georgian manor that was home to Clement Davies, leader of the Liberal Party from 1945 to 1956. The National Eisteddfod of Wales was held at Meifod in 2015.
meiji-constitution: Before 1889 Japan had in practice no written constitution. The old ritsuryo system, whose last code, the Yoro Code of 752, was in theory still in force, had become an empty formality by the Heian period. The Charter Oath of 6 April 1868 called for deliberative assemblies without giving details. The conservative Meiji oligarchy favoured a gradual approach, while the Freedom and People's Rights Movement demanded an elected assembly and a constitution at once.

On 21 October 1881 Itō Hirobumi was appointed to chair a bureau studying constitutional government, and in 1882 he led a mission abroad. The United States Constitution was rejected as too liberal and the French and Spanish models as tending to despotism. The German Empire, above all Prussia, interested the mission most. The draft committee, advised by the German legal scholars Rudolf von Gneist and Lorenz von Stein, worked in secret from 1886 to 1888. Emperor Meiji promulgated the text on 11 February 1889, and it came into force on 29 November 1890, the day the first Imperial Diet convened.

The constitution had 76 articles in seven chapters, about 2,500 words. Sovereignty lay in the emperor through his divine ancestry. Article 1 spoke of a line of emperors unbroken for ages eternal, and Article 3 called the emperor sacred and inviolable. He commanded the army and navy, declared war and made treaties, and Ministers of State answered to him, not to the Diet.

The Diet had two houses: a House of Peers of imperial family members, hereditary peers and appointees, and an elected House of Representatives. Only men paying at least 15 yen in property taxes could vote, about 1.1 percent of the population. The Diet could initiate laws and had to approve the budget. Subjects had rights such as freedom of movement, religion and speech, but each was limited by law. The army and navy ministers had to be serving officers, which gave the military a veto over any cabinet.

The document set up the first parliamentary government in Asia. Its provisions were contradictory about whether the constitution or the emperor was supreme, and leaders and parties argued over whether it could serve authoritarian or liberal ends. Universal male suffrage came with the General Election Law of 1925. The constitution was never amended. After Japan's surrender the postwar constitution was enacted as an amendment under Article 73, to preserve legal continuity, and it took effect on 3 May 1947.
meiji-era: Prince Mutsuhito succeeded his father, Emperor Kōmei, on 3 February 1867 at the age of fourteen, as the 122nd emperor. The shogunate was under pressure to modernise, and a call arose for the restoration of governing power to the emperor. On 9 November 1867 the shōgun Tokugawa Yoshinobu offered his resignation, and the new government was formed on 3 January 1868. The fall of Edo in the summer of 1868 ended the Tokugawa shogunate and brought the Meiji era. Its first reform was the Charter Oath of 1868, which called among other things for a deliberative assembly and for all classes to unite in carrying out the affairs of state.

The leaders set out to catch up with the West through state-led industrialisation. The government built railways, began land reform and set up a Western-based education system, sending thousands of students abroad and hiring more than 3,000 foreign experts. The Iwakura Mission toured Europe and the United States in 1871. Land and tax laws of 1871 to 1873 legalised private ownership and replaced taxes in kind with cash. Military reform brought a small standing army, a large reserve and compulsory militia service for all men.

A new peerage, the Kazoku, with five ranks from prince to baron, was created for about five hundred court nobles, former daimyo and loyal samurai. Itagaki Taisuke led the Freedom and People's Rights Movement for representative government, and helped found the Liberal Party in 1881. In 1885 the essayist Fukuzawa Yukichi argued that Japan should orient itself on the civilised countries of the West.

Rapid change had opponents. Disaffected former samurai rebelled in the 1870s, the best known being Saigō Takamori in the Satsuma Rebellion, although other former samurai, such as Itō Hirobumi and Itagaki Taisuke, served the government. Fukuzawa's essay may also have laid intellectual foundations for later Japanese colonialism in the region.

The government promoted Japanese art abroad at world's fairs, beginning with Vienna in 1873. The years 1890 to 1910 are called the golden age of Japanese cloisonné enamel, and Shibata Zeshin renewed lacquerwork. The emperor promoted Western dress, which became common in public, while the kimono returned in bolder styles in the 1890s. The era ended on 30 July 1912, and the Taishō era followed.
meiji-restoration: In the Edo period Japan was ruled through a hierarchy of inherited rank, with the emperor and court at the top, then the shōgun and the daimyō, then the samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. Since 1633 the shogunate had enforced a policy of national isolation, sakoku, with limited trade through the Dutch at Dejima. Famine and unrest in the 1830s and 1840s, and the failure of the Tenpō Reforms, exposed a deep divide between shogunate and daimyō. The arrival of the Perry Expedition and the unequal treaties that followed brought the shōgun's ability to protect Japanese sovereignty into question, and many lower-ranking samurai became shishi, men of spirit, committed to the slogan sonnō jōi, revere the emperor and expel the barbarian.

After setbacks in 1863 and 1864 the domains organised into an anti-Tokugawa alliance led by Satsuma and Chōshū. On 8 November 1867 the fifteenth shōgun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, returned power to the Imperial Court, and he resigned the title on 19 November. Iwakura Tomomi, Saigō Takamori and Ōkubo Toshimichi then planned a coup within the divided court to strip the Tokugawa house of its lands.

In the early hours of 3 January 1868 domain troops seized the Imperial Palace, and Emperor Meiji announced the restoration of the Imperial House's political functions. Tokugawa forces were beaten at the Battle of Toba–Fushimi on 27 January. Resistance continued in the Boshin War and the short-lived Republic of Ezo. The Charter Oath of 6 April 1868 set out the new government's aims, among them the adoption of Western technology.

The lands of the shōgun became prefectures, and the abolition of the domains followed between 1868 and 1873. In 1876 the conversion of samurai stipends into government bonds became compulsory. A standard language based on Tokyo speech was promoted in schools and government. Industrialisation under the slogan Enrich the country, strengthen the military made Japan a military power by 1895. The changes provoked the Saga Rebellion and the Satsuma Rebellion, and the Meiji Constitution of 1889 remained in force until the Allied occupation after World War II.
meiningen: Meiningen lies in the valley of the Werra between the Thuringian Forest and the Rhön Mountains, 80 kilometres south of Erfurt and 104 kilometres north of Würzburg. It grew from a settlement of the Frankish period, at an intersection of two trade routes and a ford near the Werra.

Meiningen was first mentioned in 982. Emperor Henry II gave it in 1008 to the Roman Catholic Diocese of Würzburg, to which it belonged for 534 years, and the bishops built a moated castle there in the 11th century. It was first called a town in 1230 and was granted wide autonomy in 1344. A fire in 1380 destroyed about a quarter of the town, and two fires at the end of the 15th century destroyed almost all of it. In 1542 it passed to the House of Henneberg in an exchange with the Prince-Bishop of Würzburg, and in 1583 to the Wettin family.

Fustian and linen weaving brought an economic boom that raised the population to about 5,000. The Thirty Years' War ended it: Croatian troops plundered the town in 1634 and Swedish troops besieged it in 1641, and thousands of inhabitants died or were expelled. From 1680 to 1918 Meiningen was the capital of the Duchy of Saxe-Meiningen. Schloss Elisabethenburg was built in 1682–92, and a court orchestra existed by 1690. A fire in September 1874 destroyed a third of the town, which was rebuilt in the Neoclassical style.

Georg II, Duke of Saxe-Meiningen, born in 1826, was a great patron of theatre, and his company, the Meininger, toured Germany and Europe and won international celebrity. In October 1880 the court orchestra began its most successful period under Hans von Bülow, with Johannes Brahms collaborating.

Meiningen is the capital of the district of Schmalkalden-Meiningen and the cultural, judicial and financial centre of southern Thuringia. It has a state theatre, and Schloss Elisabethenburg houses museums and the state archives.
meisenheim: Meisenheim lies in the valley of the River Glan at the northern edge of the North Palatine Uplands, in the Bad Kreuznach district of Rhineland-Palatinate. Its municipal area measures 1,324 hectares. The outlying homesteads of Hof Wieseck, Keddarterhof and Röther Hof belong to it. In 1896 it was joined to the railway network by the Lauter Valley Railway, which was absorbed in 1904 into the Glantalbahn.

Meisenheim is believed to have arisen in the 7th century, and its name is often derived from a hypothetical founder, Meiso. Its first documentary mention is of 1154. A document of 891 that is sometimes cited as the earliest is a forgery. In the 12th century it became the main seat of the Counts of Veldenz, and King Ludwig IV granted it town rights in 1315.

The counts built a castle on what is now Schlossplatz. Of it only two later buildings survive: the Magdalenenbau, today called the Herzog-Wolfgang-Haus, and the Schlosskirche, begun in 1479. Both were built after the Counts of Veldenz died out in 1444 and the county passed to the Dukes of Palatinate-Zweibrücken, who at first kept their seat at Meisenheim but soon moved it to Zweibrücken.

From 1538 to 1571 Duke Wolfgang of Zweibrücken kept a mint in the town, with one interruption, before it moved to Bergzabern. Its double thalers, thalers and half thalers are among the finest coins of Palatinate-Zweibrücken. A Jewish community may have existed from the Middle Ages, but the first Jew named in the records, a Jud Moses, appears in 1551. The Jews were expelled in 1569, and after the Thirty Years' War two families were allowed to settle. The outlaw Schinderhannes, Johannes Bückler, committed one of his early burglaries in the town in early 1797.

The Old Town is the only one in the area with continuous development since the 14th century, uninterrupted by war, fire or other destruction. It keeps parts of its town wall, the Untertor gate, the town hall of 1517 and many noble houses, among them the Boos von Waldeckscher Hof, built about 1400. The late Gothic Schlosskirche was built from 1479 to 1504 to the designs of Philipp von Gmünd, and the Catholic parish church of Saint Anthony of Padua is a Baroque building of 1685 to 1688. The town is a state-recognized recreational resort.
meissen: Meissen, in German Meißen, lies on both banks of the River Elbe in the Free State of Saxony, about 25 kilometres north-west of Dresden, and has about 30,000 inhabitants.
