Its Upper Sorbian name is Mišno. In Germany the spelling Meissen is the registered trademark of the State Porcelain Manufactory, while Meißen refers to the city itself.

The town grew out of the Polabian Slavic settlement of Meisa, inhabited by the Glomacze, a Sorbian tribe. King Henry the Fowler destroyed their fortress of Gana, and later founded the fortress of Misnia, around which the German town developed. Emperor Otto I founded the Margraviate of Meissen in 965 as a frontier march, and the bishopric dates from 968. It was suppressed in 1581, after accepting the Reformation in 1559, and re-created in 1921.

Bolesław I the Brave of Poland briefly seized Meissen in 1002, and the House of Wettin received the margraviate in 1089. A small force under Orda Khan attacked the town in the Mongol raid of 1241, and much of it was destroyed. It received town rights in 1332, and construction of the cathedral began in 1260 on the hill of the Albrechtsburg castle. Meissen became the capital of the Electorate of Saxony in 1423, and the seat moved to Dresden in 1464.

Meissen porcelain was the first high-quality porcelain made outside the Orient, using local deposits of kaolin. By decree of King Augustus II the Strong the factory was established in the Albrechtsburg, and in 1861 production moved to the Triebisch valley, where it remains. The Albrechtsburg, built between 1472 and 1525, is regarded as the first castle used as a royal residence in the German language area. The Gothic cathedral holds a chapel among the notable burial places of the Wettin family, and wine is grown on the slopes of the Elbe valley.
meknes: Meknes is one of the four imperial cities of Morocco. It takes its name from the Miknasa, a Berber tribe whose name derives from a root meaning to fight. The Miknasa settled the region around the 10th century and founded small unfortified villages. After conquering the area in the 11th century the Almoravids built a fortified settlement just south of them, called Tagrart, which formed the beginnings of the old medina. The Nejjarine Mosque and the Grand Mosque date from the Almoravid period.

Under the Alaouite sultan Moulay Rashid, Fes was the capital, and his brother Moulay Isma'il governed Meknes. When Rashid died in 1672, Isma'il became sultan and chose Meknes as his capital. He had had to fight to reconquer Fes and Marrakesh from his nephew Ahmad al-Mahriz, and the ulema of Fes disapproved of his ways, including his use of slaves. Meknes, further west, also seemed more defensible than Fes against Ottoman attacks from Algeria.

His palace complex was built over his entire reign, from 1672 to 1727, on the site of the medieval kasbah, and covers an area about four times larger than the old city. It had several autonomous palaces, gardens, a water system of wells, norias, canals and underground pipes, and monumental granaries said to hold supplies for a siege of ten years. After his death Morocco fell into relative anarchy as his sons competed for power, and Meknes lost its status as capital and was damaged by the earthquake of 1755.

The main monuments stand in the old medina and in the vast former kasbah of Moulay Isma'il to the south. Bab Mansur al-'Alj, the ceremonial entrance to the kasbah, was finished in 1732 by his son Moulay Abdallah. It is named after its designer, Mansour al-'Alj, a former Christian slave who converted to Islam, and is decorated with carved brick and coloured zellij tilework. In front of it lies Place el-Hedim, whose name means rubble and recalls the demolitions Isma'il carried out while building his palaces.

After French rule began in 1912 a new city was built on the plateau opposite the old one, and the capital moved from Fes to Rabat. The Dar Jamaï Museum, in a palace of 1882, is the best-known museum, and the Roman ruins of Volubilis lie about half an hour to the north.
mekong-delta: The Mekong Delta, also called the South-western Region, lies in southwestern Vietnam, where the Mekong River empties into the sea through a network of distributaries. It covers over 40,500 square kilometres, and the area under water varies with the season. The region lies immediately west of Ho Chi Minh City and stretches roughly in a triangle from Mỹ Tho in the east to Châu Đốc and Hà Tiên in the northwest and down to Cà Mau at the southern tip of Vietnam, including the island of Phú Quốc.

It is dominated by flat flood plains. The soil of the lower delta is sediment deposited by the Mekong and its tributaries over thousands of years, and over the last six thousand years the delta has pushed about 200 kilometres seaward.

The delta was probably inhabited long before history, and settlement may reach back to the 4th century BCE. Archaeological finds at Óc Eo and other sites show that it was an important part of the Funan civilisation, with trading ports and canals from the first century CE. Angkor Borei, occupied between 400 BCE and 500 CE, had maritime trade networks across Southeast Asia and with India and may have been Funan's capital. Khmer inscriptions appear in the Chenla period. In the early 15th century Champa made several incursions, and the declining Kingdom of Cambodia asked Ming China for intervention in 1408 and 1414.

Vietnamese acquisition came in two phases. In 1621 Lord Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên married his daughter to the Cambodian king Chey Chettha II in exchange for a Vietnamese trade port at Prei Nokor, now Ho Chi Minh City, and tax exemptions for Vietnamese settlers. The Nguyễn lords later intervened repeatedly in Cambodia, invited Chinese refugees to settle at Mỹ Tho and Biên Hoà, and after fully subduing Champa in 1697 annexed Prei Nokor, renaming it Gia Định.

After a war with Cambodia in 1754 and a ceasefire in 1756 Cambodia ceded Gò Công and Tân An. By 1757 the whole delta, including Cape Cà Mau, was under Vietnamese control. In the 1860s the French established the colony of Cochinchina there.

The inhabitants are mostly ethnic Vietnamese; the delta has the largest Khmer population outside Cambodia, along with Hoa (ethnic Chinese) and Cham communities. It is Vietnam's most productive region for agriculture and aquaculture, with rice grown on much of the land, and Cần Thơ is its economic centre. The delta is rich in wildlife, and its low-lying coast is vulnerable to rising seas and to coastal erosion.
mekong-river: The Mekong is about 4,909 kilometres long and drains some 795,000 square kilometres. It rises as the Za Qu on the Tibetan Plateau and soon becomes the Lancang River, named in Chinese from the Lao kingdom Lan Xang. It flows through Tibet and Yunnan, then along the borders of Myanmar and Laos to the Golden Triangle, where the Ruak River joins it. Downstream it crosses Laos, Thailand and Cambodia and reaches the South China Sea through a complex delta in Vietnam.

Thai and Lao speakers called it Mae Nam Khong, from an old word for river borrowed from Austroasiatic languages. The historian William Dalrymple suggests that the name Mekong derives from the Khmer phrase Me Kongkia, in its Indic values Ma Ganga, meaning mother river, in reference to the Ganges.

Rapids, waterfalls and extreme seasonal variation in flow make the river hard to navigate, so it has divided the peoples near it rather than united them. The earliest recorded civilisation was the Indianised Khmer culture of Funan in the Mekong delta, in the 1st century CE. Excavations at Oc Eo, near modern An Giang, have found coins from as far away as the Roman Empire. Funan was succeeded around the 5th century by the Khmer state of Chenla, and the Khmer Empire of Angkor was the last great Indianised state of the region. From about the time of its fall the Mekong was the front line between the emerging states of Siam and Tonkin, with Laos and Cambodia torn between their influence.

The first European to reach the river was the Portuguese António de Faria in 1540, and a European map of 1563 depicts it, though little was known upstream of the delta. Gerrit van Wuysthoff led an expedition up the river as far as Vientiane in 1641-42. The French captured Saigon in 1861 and established a protectorate over Cambodia in 1863.

The river remains a trade route between Tibet and Southeast Asia, and traditional trade in small boats between riverside communities continues. Its basin holds one of the richest concentrations of plant and animal life in the world, including the Mekong giant catfish. The section of the river in the deep gorges of Yunnan lies within the Three Parallel Rivers of Yunnan Protected Areas, a World Heritage Site, and the Tonle Sap lake in Cambodia is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.
melayu-islam-beraja: The idea goes back to the Kesultanan Melayu Islam, the Islamic Malay Sultanate, a term first used in 1957 and supported by Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III on the initial recommendations of the Jawatankuasa Tujuh Serangkai. The declaration of 1984 rested on discussions held in London on 30 September 1957. After Brunei and the United Kingdom signed their agreement of 1979 on five years of preparation for independence, the Information Department of Brunei spread the concept, and it was named Melayu Islam Beraja in the Declaration of Independence proclaimed by Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah on 1 January 1984.

It is described as "a blend of Malay language, culture, and Malay customs, the teaching of Islamic laws and values and the monarchy system which must be esteemed and practiced by all." Its Malay element presents Brunei as a Malay nation that keeps traditional values and culture handed down through the generations, with the Malay language used in all official business and as a shared language between the country's groups. The seven indigenous peoples named in the 1959 Brunei Constitution, the Brunei Malay, Kedayan, Belait Malay, Tutong Malay, Bisaya, Dusun and Murut, are counted together as Brunei Malay.

Its Islamic element draws on the Quran and Hadith. The 1959 Constitution made Islam the official religion of the state, which it had long been in practice as the guiding principle of the sultanate's administration. The monarchy element places the sultan at the head of the royal institution and of the state, with the authority that the 1959 Constitution set out.

The concept is presented as the foundation of national life and of the conduct of government in all matters. The sultan has called on citizens to practise and carry out the teachings of Islam as part of it, and Radio Television Brunei, the state broadcaster and the country's main media outlet, planned to put the idea into practice.
melbourne: Melbourne occupies much of the northern and eastern coastlines of Port Phillip Bay, in the southeastern part of mainland Australia. The Boonwurrung and Woiwurrung languages call the area Narrm or Naarm; in Boonwurrung, Naarm means the Bay. The city is named after William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne, who was Prime Minister of the United Kingdom when it was founded in 1835. At its centre is the Hoddle Grid, a grid of streets measuring about 1.61 by 0.80 kilometres, whose southern edge fronts onto the Yarra River.

Aboriginal Australians have lived in the Melbourne area for at least 40,000 years. When British colonists arrived in the 19th century, up to 20,000 Kulin people from three language groups, the Wurundjeri, Bunurong and Wathaurong, lived there. The area was an important meeting place for the clans of the Kulin nation alliance and a vital source of food and water. A short-lived British penal settlement was founded at Port Phillip in 1803, then part of the Colony of New South Wales. Melbourne itself was founded in 1835 with the arrival of free settlers from Van Diemen's Land, now Tasmania, and was incorporated as a Crown settlement in 1837.

Queen Victoria declared it a city in 1847, and in 1851 it became the capital of the newly separated Colony of Victoria. The Victorian gold rush of the 1850s began a long boom which, by the late 1880s, had made it one of the largest and wealthiest cities in Australia and the world. After the federation of Australia in 1901 it was the interim seat of government until Canberra became the permanent capital in 1927. In 1956 it hosted the Summer Olympics, the first Olympic Games held outside Europe and the United States.

Melbourne is the capital of the state of Victoria and the second most populous city in Australia, with more than five million people. It is known for the Victorian architecture left by the gold rush and the land boom of the 1880s; the Royal Exhibition Building, completed in 1880, is World Heritage listed. Little survives from before the gold rush, St James Old Cathedral (1839) and St Francis' Church (1845) being among the few examples in the city centre.

The city gave rise to Australian rules football, Australian impressionism and Australian cinema. The Melbourne Cup horse race, first held in 1861, was declared a public holiday for all Melburnians in 1873. The University of Melbourne is the second-oldest university in Australia.
melchior-ndadaye: Melchior Ndadaye was born on 28 March 1953 in the commune of Nyabihanga, Ruanda-Urundi, the first of ten children in a Hutu family. After the Ikiza of 1972, in which the Burundian government targeted and massacred educated Hutus, he fled to Rwanda and finished his schooling at Butare. He earned a degree at the National University of Rwanda in 1980 and taught at Save until 1983.

In exile he founded a movement for Burundian Hutu students in 1976 and, in 1979, helped found the Marxist Burundi Workers' Party. He left it in 1983 over its split between armed revolution and democracy, and returned to Burundi, where he worked in banking and gained a diploma in higher banking studies in Paris in 1992.

In June 1986 Ndadaye and other former members of the Workers' Party founded the underground Front for Democracy in Burundi (FRODEBU), and he became its president. In 1988 he criticised the government of President Pierre Buyoya and was imprisoned for two months. In 1991 he was the only opposition member of Buyoya's Constitution Commission and resigned from it in August, citing its lack of diversity.

FRODEBU was recognised on 23 July 1992 and nominated him for the presidency on 18 April 1993. He campaigned for a 'new Burundi', and proposed rebuilding the Tutsi-dominated army on more equitable recruitment. 20 per cent, in an election certified as free and fair.

Ndadaye was sworn in on 10 July 1993. His government of 23 ministers included nine Tutsi, among them the Prime Minister Sylvie Kinigi of UPRONA, and he named a Council of National Unity of 15 Hutus and 15 Tutsis. Yet he questioned contracts approved under earlier Tutsi governments and began to change the recruitment rules of the army and police, which threatened the army and the Tutsi elite. A plot by a few officers on 3 July had already failed.

On the night of 20 to 21 October 1993, armoured cars of the 11th Armoured Car Battalion surrounded the Presidential Palace, and soldiers captured the president. He was taken to the camp of the 1st Parachute Battalion and killed by junior officers. The coup soon failed, and Kinigi became acting president. The killings that followed claimed many thousands of lives, estimated at over 100,000, and grew into the decade-long Burundi Civil War. Ndadaye is remembered in Burundi as a martyr for democracy, and Ndadaye Day is observed on 21 October.
melendez-quinonez-dynasty: President Manuel Enrique Araujo died on 9 February 1913 of wounds from an assassination attempt five days earlier. As the vice president had resigned, Carlos Meléndez, president of the Legislative Assembly and first presidential designate, became provisional president and had the assassins executed by firing squad. Active in politics since the Revolution of the 44 in 1894, he had lost several earlier contests. To run in 1915 he resigned on 29 August 1914, since the constitution barred anyone who had held the presidency in the six months before an election, and handed office to his brother-in-law Alfonso Quiñónez Molina. He won and took office on 1 March 1915.

In 1918 Jorge Meléndez and Quiñónez founded the National Democratic Party, outside which political activity was soon outlawed; its paramilitary wing, the Red League, intimidated opponents. Rival supporters clashed at the December 1918 municipal elections, killing around 100 people. Carlos resigned through illness on 21 December 1918 and died in New York on 8 October 1919, while Jorge won the 1919 election with 97 percent of the vote. Under Jorge, Arturo Araujo invaded from Honduras in 1920, and cadets and soldiers attempted coups in February and May 1922. On 25 December 1922 security forces and the Red League fired on a rally for Miguel Tomás Molina, killing around a dozen people, and Quiñónez won the 1923 election unanimously.

In 1927 Quiñónez chose his friend Pío Romero Bosque as successor, expecting to rule through him. Romero instead removed Quiñónez's appointees, lifted press censorship and allowed demonstrations, and Quiñónez left for exile in France in June. A coup organised by Jorge failed on 6 December 1927; its two leaders were executed and Jorge fled to Honduras and Costa Rica.

The family ruled for 14 years and 20 days, from 9 February 1913 to 1 March 1927. They were pragmatic liberals, backed by wealthy landowners and by indigenous Salvadorans promised the return of land. Coffee production doubled from its level before the First World War, and by 1926 El Salvador was the leading coffee producer in Central America, while corruption and extortion were common. Urban workers formed unions and held the first recorded strike in the country's history in 1920. Carlos's Meléndez Doctrine declared the Gulf of Fonseca a condominium of El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua.
meles-zenawi: Meles Zenawi was born Legesse Zenawi Asres on 9 May 1955 in Adwa, in northern Ethiopia, the third of six children of Zenawi Asres, a Tigrayan from Adwa, and Alemash Ghebreluel, an Eritrean from Adi Quala. He won a full scholarship to General Wingate High School in Addis Ababa and finished in 1972 with honours. He took the name Meles in honour of Meles Tekle, a fellow Tigrayan university student executed by the Derg government in 1975. In that year he left Haile Selassie I University to join the Tigray People's Liberation Front, or TPLF.

The TPLF was one of the armed groups fighting the Derg, the military junta that governed Ethiopia from 1974 to 1991. Meles was elected to the leadership committee in 1979 and became chairman of the TPLF's executive committee in 1983. He also led the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front, the EPRDF, formed in 1988. After the EPRDF won the civil war in 1991 he became president of the Transitional Government. Eritreans voted for independence in a referendum on 24 May 1993.

A new constitution approved in 1994 provided for a parliamentary system. The EPRDF won the 1995 elections, and Meles was sworn in as prime minister when the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia was inaugurated on 21 August 1995. His governments introduced ethnic federalism and encouraged privatisation, reversing the Derg's communist policy. Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a war over a territorial dispute from 1998 to 2000, and the EPRDF won the elections of 2000, 2005 and 2010.

Meles married Azeb Mesfin, a former TPLF fighter, and had three children. He chaired the Organization of African Unity from June 1995 to June 1996. In July 2012 his absence from African Union meetings raised questions about his health, and he died on 20 August 2012 of an infection in Belgium.

Views of his rule differ. Supporters point to school expansion, in which enrolment rose from 27 per cent of children in 1991, and to years of rapid economic growth. Many human rights groups and analysts describe his government as authoritarian. His principles and policies of ethnic federalism are called Zenawism and are studied by scholars. The Meles Zenawi Foundation was established in 2013 to honour his legacy.
melfi: Melfi stands on a hill at the foot of Mount Vulture in the province of Potenza in Basilicata, roughly midway between Naples and Bari, next to the borders of Campania and Apulia. Daunians and Lucanians lived there, and under the Romans it fell within the territory of the colony of Venusia, founded in 291 BCE.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Melfi was a strategic point between lands held by the Byzantines and by the Lombards. It was assigned to the Norman leader William I of Hauteville, and the Hauteville family began from here their conquest of southern Italy, which led in the early 12th century to the Kingdom of Sicily. In 1059 Melfi became the capital of the Duchy of Apulia, and papal councils met there in that year and in 1089 and 1109. In 1231 Emperor Frederick II promulgated the Constitutions of Melfi, creating a bureaucracy of paid officials who imposed a tax system on resentful feudal lords.

Later Melfi shared the decline of the Kingdom of Naples. In March 1528 the French army under Odet de Foix besieged it and killed about 3.000 people, women and children included, and Charles V then gave Andrea Doria the title of Prince of Melfi. In 1799 Cardinal Fabrizio Ruffo's forces arrived on 29 May, and he prevented a sack. After unification the peasant army of Carmine Crocco occupied the town on 15 April 1861. Antifascists such as Manlio Rossi-Doria were exiled there, and the 1930 earthquake devastated it.

The castle was probably built new by the Normans in the 11th century. Since 1976 it has housed the Museo Nazionale Archeologico Melfese, whose best-known piece is the sarcophagus of Rapolla, an imperial sculpture of the 2nd century CE found in 1856. The cathedral dates from the 11th century and keeps its Norman bell tower, and the town runs along the Norman walls, whose Venosina gate dates from the early 13th century. The rock church of Santa Margherita is dug out of volcanic tufa.
melik-shahnazar-ii: Shahnazar was the son of Melik Hussein of Varanda and Zohra Khanum, a daughter of the Khan of Nakhichevan whom Hussein had captured and married. His year of birth is uncertain: the historian Pavel Chobanyan, who records that he was twelve years old in 1743, places it in 1731, while Artak Maghalyan suggests 1725 or 1726. He had a full brother, Ghahraman Bek, and a half-brother and half-sister, Hovsep and Gayane.

Two accounts of his accession survive. In the one most often repeated, Shahnazar killed his half-brother Melik Hovsep in the disorder after the death of Nader Shah in 1747, took Varanda, and later killed Hovsep's son Sayi Bek, who had fled to Melik Allahverdi of Khachen. Chobanyan held that this story was invented by Muslim historians such as Mirza Jamal Javanshir and Mirza Adigozal Bey to support the claims of the khans of Karabakh before the Russian authorities, and documents suggest that Hovsep outlived Shahnazar.

In the other account, his uncle Mirzabek governed Varanda after Melik Hussein died in 1736, until Nader Shah of Iran removed him in 1743 and raised the boy Shahnazar in his place; the shah's decree survives in the Matenadaran. As ruler, Shahnazar accepted the overlordship of Panah Ali, chief of the Sarijali branch of the Javanshir clan. He drove the meliks of Jraberd and Gulistan to flight and weakened the melik of Dizak. Under a truce of 1760 the meliks kept their lands in return for recognising Panah as khan, and Shahnazar married his daughter Hurizad Khanum to Panah's son Ibrahim Khalil Khan. He died in 1792.

Armenian memory judged him harshly. The Armenian author Raffi, in The Five Melikdoms of Karabagh (1888), called him a traitor and villain, and the traveller Joseph Emin recorded a contemporary's view of him as a true friend of Panah Ali Khan and unworthy of the name of a Christian. Folk tales mocked him through his jester Pele Pughi. In the late 1780s he restored Amaras Monastery, which some authors see as an attempt at atonement. His son Melik Jumshud later played a part in bringing Karabakh under Russian rule in 1805.
melilla: Melilla lies in northwest Africa on the shores of the Alboran Sea, on the eastern side of the peninsula of Cape Tres Forcas, at the foot of Mount Gurugú and around the mouth of the intermittent stream called the Río de Oro. The city is arranged in a wide semicircle around the beach and the port. Its urban nucleus was originally a fortress, Melilla la Vieja, built on a peninsular mound about 30 m high. The Moroccan settlement of Beni Ansar lies immediately to the south.

Melilla was a Phoenician and later Punic trading establishment under the name Rusadir, taken from the Phoenician name of the nearby Cape Three Forks. After Carthage's defeat in the Punic Wars it fell under the Roman client state of Mauretania, and it was later part of the province of Mauretania Tingitana. It was made a Roman colony in 46 CE.

In the 15th century the city declined, like most Mediterranean cities of the Kingdom of Fez, as Atlantic ports eclipsed them. After the Catholic Monarchs conquered the Kingdom of Granada in 1492, their secretary Hernando de Zafra gathered information on the North African coast, and he reported that in 1494 the locals had expelled the authority of the Sultan of Fez and offered to pledge loyalty. The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 placed Melilla within the sphere of Castile, but the conquest waited. It was seized by Christians in 1497 and was a condominium of the House of Medina Sidonia and the Crown of Castile until 1556.

For much of the early modern period the fortress of Melilla la Vieja remained a military garrison with a small civilian population. The current limits of Spanish territory around it were fixed by treaties with Morocco in 1859, 1860, 1861 and 1894, and the area between the old fortress and the outer forts was settled by mainland Spaniards, Sephardi Jews and Riffians.

Melilla became an autonomous city in 1995, having until then been a municipality of Málaga. Spanish is the official language and Tarifit, the Berber language of the Rif, is also spoken. The Chapel of Santiago, with a dome of the mid-16th century, is a rare example of Gothic architecture in Africa, and the architect Enrique Nieto left the city the second largest concentration of Modernista works in Spain after Barcelona.
melingoi: In the early decades of the 7th century Slavic tribes, the Sclaveni, settled across the Balkans after the Byzantine defence of the Danube frontier collapsed, some reaching as far south as the Peloponnese in small groups of families and clans. Two groups are known by name from later sources, the Melingoi and the Ezeritai; the Melingoi lived on the western slopes of Mount Taygetos. The origin of their name is uncertain: it probably derives from the Slavic adjective *milъ, sweet, and some scholars relate it to the early Slavic tribe of the Milceni.

They are first mentioned in the De administrando imperio of Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos (r. 913–959), who records that they paid a tribute of 60 gold nomismata until they revolted in the reign of Romanos I Lekapenos (r. 920–945); defeated by the strategos Krinites Arotras, they then had to pay 600. Under Byzantine rule they kept an autonomous existence but adopted Christianity and became Hellenized in language and culture.

In the 13th and 14th centuries both the Frankish lords of the Principality of Achaea and the Byzantine Greeks of the Despotate of the Morea employed them as soldiers. According to the Chronicle of the Morea, Prince William II of Villehardouin (r. 1246–1278) granted the great droungos of the Melingoi exemption from all duties except military service.

Founder's inscriptions in churches of Laconia still name the Melingoi in the 1330s. One calls Constantine Spanes, of the notable Spanes family, tzaousios of the droungos of the Melingoi, which implies that they still lived as a separate community. N. Nicoloudis identifies the late medieval thema of Kinsterna or Giserna with their area in the north-western Mani peninsula.

Their elite was rich and open to Byzantine and Frankish influence, while the ordinary pastoralist hillmen remained more conservative and secluded. Their Slavic language was still spoken in the 15th century, when the traveller Laskaris Kananos claimed that it resembled the tongue of the Wends, and many Slavic place names in the region survive to this day.
melisende-psalter: The manuscript, Egerton MS 1139, measures 21.6 by 14 centimetres and was the work of seven scribes and illuminators. Its first twenty-four pictures show scenes of the New Testament, from the Annunciation to the Deesis, a choice closer to the Eastern Orthodox liturgy. They were painted by Basilius, who signed the last one Basilius me fecit and is the only named artist of the book; he may have been a Byzantine, a westerner trained in the Greek style, or an Armenian Catholic.

A calendar follows, close to English psalter calendars and apparently based on one of St Swithun's in Winchester. Besides the capture of Jerusalem on 15 July, it marks only the deaths of King Baldwin II and his wife Morphia. The Latin psalms are in a northern French script, with initials in gold on purple by a third artist, and prayers to nine saints are illustrated by a fourth. The ivory covers show King David and the Psychomachia of Prudentius on the front and a king performing the six works of mercy on the back, under a carved falcon that may pun on the name of King Fulk.

The date and recipient are not recorded, but the Byzantine styles, the kings and the feminine word endings of the Latin prayers point to a noblewoman, and circumstantial evidence makes Queen Melisende the likely owner. The English elements probably came through Fulk, who was related to the English royal family by marriage, and the mixed Catholic and Orthodox elements may reflect Melisende's parentage: Baldwin II was Catholic, her mother Morphia an Armenian of the Greek Orthodox faith. If it was hers, Fulk most likely commissioned it after he and Melisende, who had sided with rebels against him, were reconciled.

The manuscript was perhaps at the Grande Chartreuse near Grenoble in the early 19th century. By about 1840 it belonged to Ambroise Comarmond, director of the Museum of Fine Arts of Lyon, and then to Guglielmo Libri, known for stealing manuscripts from French public libraries. He sold it to the London booksellers Payne and Foss, from whom the British Museum bought it in November 1845.
melisende-queen-of-jerusalem: Melisende was the eldest daughter of Baldwin II, then Frankish count of Edessa, and Morphia of Melitene, an Armenian noblewoman of the Greek Orthodox faith. She and her sisters grew up speaking Armenian and probably Greek, and became proficient in French. When Baldwin I of Jerusalem died in 1118, her father was elected to succeed him, and the family joined him in Jerusalem in late 1119. Melisende remained unmarried for an unusually long time, since her father may still have hoped for a son. After Morphia died, probably in 1126 or 1127, Baldwin named Melisende his heir, and in 1129 she married Fulk V of Anjou.

Baldwin II died on 21 August 1131, having commended the kingdom to Melisende, Fulk and their infant son Baldwin, and the patriarch crowned Fulk and Melisende on 14 September. For the first five years Fulk did not associate her with his public acts, against both their marriage contract and her father's will. In 1134 noblemen led by Count Hugh II of Jaffa revolted against Fulk. After their reconciliation, Fulk never again issued a charter for the kingdom without her consent. The Melisende Psalter, a luxurious prayer book, is believed to have been commissioned by Fulk for her around 1135.

Fulk died on 10 November 1143 after a fall from his horse. Melisende took full charge of the government and was crowned again on Christmas 1143 together with her son Baldwin III, then thirteen. She appointed her cousin Manasses of Hierges constable, to command the army in her name. After the fall of Edessa in 1144 she urged intervention from Europe, which led to the Second Crusade. Her relations with Baldwin broke down as she refused to give him real authority. Baldwin invaded her share of the divided kingdom and besieged her in the Tower of David, and she agreed to retire to Nablus.

After her fall Melisende still advised her son and in 1157 took a military initiative while he was in Antioch, when the cave-fortress of el-Hablis was recovered from the Muslims at her insistence. She died in 1161 after an illness, possibly a stroke. William of Tyre, who took her side, praised her wisdom, but two disasters, the fall of Edessa and the failure to take Damascus in 1148, came in her reign, though her personal blame is arguable. The historian Folda calls her the foremost patron of art in the twelfth-century Kingdom of Jerusalem.
melissus-of-samos: Melissus was the third and last member of the Eleatic school, after Parmenides and Zeno. Little is known of his life. He may have been born around 500 BCE, and the date of his death is unknown. What is known comes mostly from a short passage in Plutarch's Life of Pericles, which describes him as commander of the Samian fleet in the Samian War, who defeated the Athenian fleet in 440 BCE. Plutarch also reports that Aristotle said Melissus had beaten Pericles in an earlier battle. He was reputed to be a pupil of Parmenides and the teacher of Leucippus, claims that should be treated with scepticism.

Melissus wrote a treatise, later titled On Nature, in prose rather than in verse like Parmenides. Much of it survives through Simplicius, who quoted it in his commentaries on Aristotle's Physics and On the Heavens, and most fragments are collected in Diels and Kranz. Like Parmenides, he held that what exists is one, ungenerated, indestructible, indivisible, changeless and motionless. He differed in two respects. Parmenides held that Being is limited, while Melissus held it to be wholly unlimited, and where Parmenides placed Being in a timeless present, Melissus made it eternal.

His argument for eternity runs that whatever comes to be must have a beginning, and whatever has a beginning must end. Since the One did not come to be, it has neither beginning nor end. Modern commentators find this reasoning faulty.

His case for the oneness of what exists is regarded as his best: if what exists were more than one, the boundaries between things would limit it, but it is unlimited. He also argued that it cannot change, since change would make it different and so no longer whole, and that it is full and therefore cannot move, because to be empty would be to be nothing. He claimed too that the One has no body, since a body has limits and the One has none.

His version of Eleatic philosophy was the chief source for its presentation in Plato and Aristotle. Aristotle called it a bit crude and said it made invalid arguments from false assumptions. Aristocles of Messene thought several arguments absurd. Modern scholars judge him more kindly, as an inventive philosopher who offered clear, direct arguments and made original contributions to Eleaticism.
melk: Melk lies in Lower Austria next to the Wachau valley on the Danube. The town is first mentioned as Medilica in 831 in a donation of Louis the German, its name coming from a Slavic word for border. In 976 the area was given to Leopold I, Margrave of Austria, to serve as a buffer between the Magyars to the east and Bavaria to the west. A mention in 996 of an area known as Ostarrîchi is the origin of the German word Österreich.

The bluff that carries the abbey held a Babenberg castle until Leopold II gave the site to Benedictine monks from nearby Lambach in 1089. Melk received market rights in 1227 and became a municipality in 1898. The Danube reached 15.8 metres above its usual level in 1501, and the Schiffsmeisterhaus bears marks of high water on its facade. During the Holocaust a subcamp of Mauthausen concentration camp operated at Melk. Its former crematorium is now a museum, and the rest of the camp became part of the Birago barracks of the Austrian Army.

Melk is best known for its massive baroque Benedictine monastery, Melk Abbey, but the town itself holds architecture of many centuries in a small area. The Rathaus on the Rathausplatz was built in 1575, and the Kolomanbrunnen fountain in the square is a gift from the abbey. The Lebzelterhaus dates from 1657, and the Haus am Stein, built in the 15th century, is the oldest building in town. The Old Post Office was built in 1792. The Gothic parish church holds a Kalvarienberg sculpture group, and the Wiener Tor stood until 1874. About five kilometres to the south stands the Renaissance castle Schallaburg. Melk appears in fiction as the home of Adso, the co-protagonist of Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose.
melkote: Melukote lies in Pandavapura taluk of Mandya district, built on a rocky range called Yadugiri, Yaadavagiri or Yadushaila that rises to 1,094 metres above sea level and overlooks the Cauvery valley. It is about 36 km north-west of Mandya and 51 km north of Mysore, and it is the only settlement of the district above 1,000 metres. The name comes from the temple of Narayanaswamy, built on the hillock and surrounded by a fort; mythological accounts also call the place Narayanadri, Vedadri, Yadavadri, Yathishaila and Tirunarayanapuram.

After Ramanuja's stay, large numbers of Iyengar Brahmins settled in the region, forming the Mandyam Iyengar community. Epigraphic evidence shows that the deity of the main temple was already a well-known object of worship before Ramanuja came. The temple enjoyed the patronage of the Vijayanagara and Mysore kings; in 1614 Raja Wodeyar I of Mysore granted it a large estate, and a bas relief of him standing with folded hands is carved on a pillar of its nava-aranga. The fort on the hill was perhaps built in the Hoysala and Vijayanagara period.

The town remembers a massacre of Hindus, among them Mandyam Iyengars, by soldiers of Tipu Sultan, who attacked the temple on a Diwali morning in the 1790s while the puja was going on. The people of Melukote stopped celebrating Diwali after it, and the day has remained one of mourning.

The Cheluvanarayana Swamy temple owns three jewelled crowns: the Raja-mudi, the Krishnaraja-mudi given by Krishnaraja Wodeyar III, and the older Vairamudi of unknown origin. They are kept in the state treasury at Mandya and brought to the temple only for the Vairamudi festival, which has drawn up to 400,000 people. The temple is under the control of the Yadugiri Yathiraja Mutt.

Melukote is also home to the Academy of Sanskrit Research, whose library holds 11,000 manuscripts and 35,000 books, a Sanskrit college founded in 1854, and the Melkote Temple Wildlife Sanctuary, created on 17 June 1974 chiefly to protect wolves. The town is known for its handlooms, especially dhoties and sarees.
mellifont-abbey: Mellifont, known in Irish as An Mhainistir Mhór, the big monastery, takes its English name from the Latin Melli-fons, font of honey. It stands on the banks of the River Mattock, some 10 km north-west of Drogheda, and was founded on the orders of Saint Malachy, Archbishop of Armagh. By 1170 it had one hundred monks and three hundred lay brothers. Its formal style of architecture was imported from the order's abbeys in France, and it became the model for later Cistercian houses in Ireland, which were often called the daughters of Mellifont.

Kings gave gifts to the foundation: Muirchertach Ua Lochlainn, king of Ulster, gave cattle, gold and a townland, Donnchad Ua Cearbhall, king of Airgialla, who had given the land, added gold, and Derbforgaill, wife of Tigernan Ua Ruairc, gave gold, a chalice and altar cloths.

In 1152 Mellifont hosted the Synod of Kells-Mellifont, attended according to the Annals of the Four Masters by bishops and kings with the papal legate Giovanni Cardinal Paparoni. Its church was consecrated in 1157, an occasion on which the Church asserted its authority by banishing the King of Meath, Donnchadh Ua Maeleachlainn.

After the dissolution of 1539 Edward Moore built a fortified house there in 1556 with stone from the abbey. In 1603 the Treaty of Mellifont between the English Crown and Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, was agreed in its grounds; the 1st Viscount Moore, the owner and a close friend of Tyrone, helped persuade him to sign. The Moore family, later Earls of Drogheda, kept Mellifont until 1727. The house was attacked and looted during the Irish Rebellion of 1641, and William of Orange made it his headquarters during the Battle of the Boyne in 1690.

The ruined abbey is a national monument of Ireland and open to the public; little survives beyond a 13th-century lavabo, where the monks washed their hands before eating, some Romanesque arches and a 14th-century chapter house. In 1938 monks from Mount Melleray Abbey re-established a community, New Mellifont, at Collon in County Louth, on land that had once belonged to the old abbey; it became an abbey in 1945.
mellitus: Bede described Mellitus as being of noble birth. Pope Gregory I called him an abbot in his letters, but it is unclear whether he had been abbot of a Roman monastery or was given the rank to make him leader of the expedition. Nothing else of his background is known, though he was probably a native of Italy, like the other bishops consecrated by Augustine, the first Archbishop of Canterbury.

Gregory sent him to England in June 601 in answer to Augustine's appeal for more clergy. The party carried books and objects needed for worship, and a letter urging King Æthelberht of Kent to act like the Emperor Constantine I and to destroy pagan shrines. While Mellitus was on the road, Gregory sent a further letter allowing pagan temples to be converted into churches and animal sacrifices into Christian feasts. It is known as the Epistola ad Mellitum and was preserved by Bede.

Augustine consecrated Mellitus as bishop of the East Saxons in 604, making him the first Bishop of London after the Roman departure. Mellitus had first baptised Sæberht, Æthelberht's nephew, who allowed the bishopric to be established. In February 610 Mellitus attended a council of bishops in Italy called by Pope Boniface IV, and brought papal letters back to England. He also joined Justus, the Bishop of Rochester, in signing a letter from Archbishop Laurence urging the Celtic bishops to adopt the Roman method of calculating Easter.

After the deaths of Sæberht and Æthelberht, Sæberht's three pagan sons drove Mellitus from London. Bede says he was exiled for refusing them a taste of the sacramental bread. He took refuge in Gaul with Justus, and Laurence recalled him after converting Æthelberht's successor Eadbald. He could not return to London, whose people remained pagan.

Mellitus succeeded Laurence as the third Archbishop of Canterbury in 619. He was said to have diverted a fire that threatened the church at Canterbury in 623, when he was carried into the flames and the wind changed direction. Bede praised his sane mind and noted that he suffered from gout. Mellitus died on 24 April 624 and was buried at St Augustine's Abbey that day.

He was revered as a saint, with 24 April as his feast day, and his shrine stood beside those of Augustine and Laurence at St Augustine's. After the Norman Conquest Goscelin wrote a life of him, and those with gout were urged to pray at his tomb.
melqart: The name Melqart is written MLQRT in the Phoenician abjad. Edward Lipinski theorises that it derives from MLK QRT, meaning 'King of the City'; in Akkadian it appears as Milqartu. The earliest occurrence of the name is in the 9th-century BCE Ben-Hadad inscription, found in 1939 north of Aleppo, erected by the son of the king of Aram 'for his lord Melqart'. Archaeological evidence for the cult is earliest in Tyre, and it seems to have spread westward with the colonies Tyre founded, eventually overshadowing the worship of Eshmun in Sidon.

Josephus, following Menander of Ephesus, says that King Hiram I of Tyre (c. 965-935 BCE) built the temple of Heracles and was the first to celebrate the awakening (egersis) of Heracles in the month Peritius. This annual awakening may identify Melqart as a dying-and-rising god, and he was central to the Phoenician spring festival during which he died and was resurrected.

According to María Eugenia Aubet, the name of Melqart was invoked in oaths sanctioning contracts, and it was customary to build a temple to him, as protector of Tyrian traders, in each new colony. At Cádiz the temple is as early as the earliest vestiges of Phoenician occupation. Carthage sent a yearly tribute of 10% of its public treasury to the god in Tyre until the Hellenistic period, and in Tyre the high priest of Melqart ranked second only to the king. Temples are known in Spain at Cádiz, Ibiza and Cartagena, and at Lixus on the Atlantic coast of Morocco.

The Roman historian Livy records that Hannibal, just before setting off for Italy, made a pilgrimage to Gades, the most ancient seat of Phoenician worship in the west, and prayed and sacrificed at the Altar of Melqart. On his return to New Carthage he saw a vision that he believed Melqart had sent.

The Greeks and Romans identified Melqart with Heracles and Hercules, distinguishing him as the Tyrian Hercules. In Cyprus he was syncretised with Eshmun and Asclepius, and from the sixth century BCE he was often shown with the lion skin and club of Heracles. Herodotus, who visited Tyre, describes a richly adorned temple with two pillars, one of pure gold and the other of smaragdos, and reports the priests' claim that it was as old as the city.

Because evidence is sparse, the nature of his cult is debated. William F. Albright suggested he was an underworld god, partly through the god Milku, who may be Melqart and is sometimes equated with Nergal; others regard this as coincidence. It has also been proposed that he began as a sea god who gained solar attributes, or the reverse.
melrose-abbey: An earlier monastery, Old Melrose, stood about 2.5 miles east in a bend of the River Tweed, founded by Saint Aidan of Lindisfarne shortly before his death in 651. Saint Cuthbert trained there and was its prior from 662 before moving to Lindisfarne, and Kenneth I of Scotland raided the site in 839. David I wanted the new Cistercian house on the same spot, but the monks judged the land too poor for farming and chose the present site. Its first community came from Rievaulx Abbey, and its church was dedicated to the Virgin Mary on 28 July 1146.

Melrose became the mother church of the order in Scotland, with 100 monks, wide lands from its founder and fishing rights on the Tweed. Its granges in the Lammermuirs led to grazing disputes with the tenants of the Earl of Dunbar and with the Morville lords of Lauderdale. Waltheof, David's stepson and abbot from 1148 to 1159, gave it a name for holiness and learning, and his tomb drew pilgrims. The Chronicle of Melrose holds one of the earliest accounts of Magna Carta.

Lying on a main road south from Edinburgh, the abbey was largely destroyed by the army of Edward II of England in 1322 and rebuilt on the orders of Robert the Bruce, with Sir James Douglas overseeing its finances, then burned by the army of Richard II of England in 1385 and rebuilt once more. English armies damaged it again in 1544, during the effort to force the marriage of the infant Mary, Queen of Scots, to Henry VIII's son, and it was never fully repaired. From 1541 commendators held the abbacy, and the last monk died in 1590.

Oliver Cromwell's troops later bombarded the walls, and part of the church served as the parish church from 1618 to 1810. Sir Walter Scott, as Sheriff-Depute of Roxburghshire, supervised repairs paid for by the Duke of Buccleuch, who gave the ruins to the state in 1918. The abbey keeps carved saints, dragons and gargoyles and is the only Scottish abbey with some original floor tiles. A lead casket holding a heart, found under the Chapter House in 1921 and presumed to be the Bruce's, was reburied there on 22 June 1998. Alexander II of Scotland is among those buried at Melrose.
meluhha: Meluhha (Sumerian Me-luh-ha) was the name Sumerian texts gave to a prominent trading partner of Sumer in the Middle Bronze Age. Its identification is an open question, but most scholars associate it with the Indus Valley Civilisation. Sumerian texts repeatedly name three trading centres: Magan, now accepted as the area of the United Arab Emirates and Oman, Dilmun, taken to cover Bahrain, Failaka Island and the adjacent coast of Eastern Arabia, and Meluhha. Early texts such as the inscription of the Akkadian king Rimush suggest it lay to the east. A much later text, the Rassam cylinder of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, seems to place it in Africa, near Egypt.

Sargon of Akkad referred to ships coming from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun, and his grandson Naram-Sin named a man of Meluhha among rebel kings. Gudea of Lagash recorded that people of Meluhha came to Sumer to sell gold dust and carnelian, and that he obtained blocks of lapis lazuli and carnelian from Meluhha. Meluhha is named in the myth Enki and Ninhursag as a land that would load carnelian and fine woods into large ships. A king of Ur, Ibbi-Sin, received a speckled or red Meluhha dog as tribute, perhaps a dhole.

A settlement of Meluhhans stood in southern Sumer near Girsu, probably at Gu'abba, and most references to it date from the Akkadian Empire and the Ur III period. Direct trade seems to have faded in the Ur III period and to have been replaced by trade with Dilmun, possibly in step with the end of the cities of the Indus Valley. Rimush claimed to have defeated Meluhha troops in the area of Elam, and Gudea claimed victory over Magan, Meluhha, Elam and Amurru.

Several Indus seals have been found in Mesopotamia, at Ur, Babylon and Kish, and a carnelian monkey figurine from Susa in the Louvre may have come from the Indus region. The archaeological record of the trade is thin, however: Andrew Robinson counts about twenty Indus seals in Mesopotamia, nine dated to the Akkadian period, and a single Indus weight from Ur. Trade goods included timber, ebony and lapis lazuli, mined at the Harappan colony of Shortugai in northern Afghanistan. Asko Parpola derives the name from Dravidian words for a high place and links it to the Sanskrit word mleccha, meaning foreigner.
melus-of-bari: Melus, also called Milus or Meles, came from the Apulian town of Bari and sought to carve an autonomous territory for himself out of the Byzantine catapanate of Italy. In 1009 he and his brother-in-law Dattus rebelled and quickly took Bari, and in 1010 they captured Ascoli and Troia. The new catapan, Basil Mesardonites, raised a large army, and Bari fell on 11 June 1011. Melus fled to Prince Guaimar III of Salerno, while Dattus found refuge at the abbey of Montecassino, which at the urging of Pope Benedict VIII gave him a fortified tower on the Garigliano. Melus' family was captured and taken to Constantinople.

According to the Norman chronicler William of Apulia, Melus went in 1016 to the shrine of Saint Michael at Monte Gargano and there asked Rainulf Drengot and a band of Norman exiles to join his rebellion, promising easy victory and rich spoils. In 1017 the Normans joined his Lombard forces at Capua and marched into Apulia. In May they won an encounter on the Fortore against troops of the catapan Kontoleon Tornikios, and by September they held all the land between the Fortore and Trani.

The new catapan, Basil Boioannes, gathered a large force that included a contingent of the Varangian Guard sent by Emperor Basil II. He met the rebels on the Ofanto at Cannae, where Hannibal had defeated the Romans in 216 BCE. The Normans lost their leader Gilbert, Melus fled to the lands of the Papal States and Dattus returned to his tower.

Melus wandered through southern and central Italy before reaching the court of Emperor Henry II at Bamberg. Henry honoured him with the empty title of Duke of Apulia, but Melus died soon after Pope Benedict came to Bamberg at Eastertide to discuss a response to the Byzantine victories. The emperor gave him a lavish funeral and an ornate tomb in the new Bamberg Cathedral. His son Argyrus, after returning from imprisonment in Constantinople, continued the struggle for Lombard independence in Apulia. Melus' own ambition had inadvertently begun the Norman presence in southern Italy.
melville-herskovits: Herskovits was born to Jewish immigrants in Bellefontaine, Ohio, on 10 September 1895, and served in the United States Army Medical Corps in France during the First World War. After a Bachelor of Philosophy at the University of Chicago in 1920, he took his M.A. and Ph.D. in anthropology at Columbia University under Franz Boas, with a dissertation, The Cattle Complex in East Africa, on power and authority as expressed in the keeping of cattle. In 1924 he married his fellow student Frances Shapiro in Paris; an anthropologist herself, she shared his fieldwork and several of his books.

Herskovits joined Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, in 1927 and founded its Department of Anthropology in 1938. With Frances he worked among the Saramaka of Suriname in 1928 and 1929, spent more than three months in 1934 in the Haitian village of Mirebalais, the basis of Life in a Haitian Valley (1937), and did fieldwork in Benin, Brazil, Ghana, Nigeria and Trinidad. His Program of African Studies began with a $30,000 grant from the Carnegie Foundation, followed in 1951 by $100,000 from the Ford Foundation. In 1957 he founded the African Studies Association and became its first president.

The Myth of the Negro Past rejected the notion that enslaved Africans lost all traces of their past in America, and its emphasis on continuity set Herskovits against the sociologist E. Franklin Frazier, who stressed how Africans had adapted to their new surroundings. Herskovits treated race as a sociological rather than a biological concept and helped forge the idea of cultural relativism, above all in Man and His Works (1948). He advised Stanley J. Stein and Barbara Hadley Stein on recording Jongo songs in Brazil and influenced the song collector Alan Lomax.

After World War II he argued publicly for the independence of African nations and criticised American politicians who treated them as objects of Cold War strategy; he served on the Mayor's Committee on Race Relations in Chicago in 1945 and advised the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in 1959-60. He died on 25 February 1963. Northwestern's Melville J. Herskovits Library of African Studies, established in 1954 from his collection, and the African Studies Association's annual Herskovits Prize bear his name.
melvin-evans: Melvin Herbert Evans was born in Christiansted on 7 August 1917 and was raised by his mother and grandparents after his father moved to New York City. He graduated from Charlotte Amalie High School in 1935 as valedictorian, then from Howard University, magna cum laude in 1940 and as a Doctor of Medicine in 1944, and studied cardiology under Helen B. Taussig at Johns Hopkins Hospital. He served in the United States Army Medical Corps and worked for years at Frederiksted Municipal Hospital on St. Croix.

As health commissioner of the Virgin Islands from 1959 to 1967 he saw infant mortality fall to the national average and Anopheles mosquitoes eliminated. He took a Master of Public Health at the University of California, Berkeley in 1967 and became the first chair of the trustees of the University of the Virgin Islands.

Evans, a Democrat who had become a Republican in 1968, was appointed governor by President Richard Nixon on 13 June 1969, after Nixon's first nominee, Peter Bove, was withdrawn. Under the Elective Governor Acts of 1968 the office became elective, and in 1970, though registered Democrats far outnumbered Republicans, Evans placed first in the opening round and beat Cyril King of the Independent Citizens Movement in the run-off. Thurgood Marshall swore him in on 4 January 1971.

In his first year 25.3 miles of road were built, more than in the previous ten years, a Consumer Protection Council was formed and the police force grew from 105 to 445 officers between 1969 and 1974. He chaired the Southern Governors' Association from 1973 to 1974, the first black person to do so. He lost reelection in 1974.

A liberal Republican, Evans sat on the Republican National Committee from 1976 to 1980. Elected delegate to the United States House of Representatives in 1978, when Ron de Lugo ran for governor, he lost the seat to de Lugo in 1980; he was the only black member of the Republican caucus and the first Republican in the Congressional Black Caucus. President Ronald Reagan made him ambassador to Trinidad and Tobago in 1981. He died of a heart attack in Christiansted in November 1984, and in 1985 the islands' legislature made his birthday Melvin H. Evans Day.
mem-and-zin: Mem and Zin is the most important work of the Kurdish writer and poet Ahmad Khani (1651–1707). He drew on a story handed down from generation to generation through oral tradition, of which his work is the best known of many versions. The oral narrative, known as Memê Alan, probably originated in the 14th century and was carried by the Dengbêj, the Kurdish singers of tales. In the 1930s the Kurdish prince Celadet Ali Bedirxan and the French orientalist Roger Lescot recorded the Memê Alan narrative with the help of several Dengbêj from Adiyaman and Afrin in Syria, and the full legend is now part of Kurdish literature.

Mem, a young man of the Alan clan and heir to the City of the West, falls in love with Zin of the Botan clan. Bakr of the Bakran clan, jealous of the lovers, blocks their union and in the end brings about Mem's death through a complicated conspiracy. Zin collapses and dies while mourning at his grave and is buried beside him in Cizre.

When Bakr's part is revealed, Tacdîn, Mem's best friend, kills him, and Bakr is buried beside the lovers, as Mem had asked so that his enemy might witness their love. A thorn bush fed by Bakr's blood grows from his grave, and its roots divide the two even in death. Alongside the love story the poem carries Sufi themes and a Kurdish national theme.

In 1992 Ümit Elçi directed a film of Mem u Zin; because the Kurdish language was banned in Turkey from 1980 until the late 1990s or early 2000s, it had to be released in Turkish. In 2002 Kurdistan TV produced a dramatised mini-series, Memi Alan, directed by Nasir Hassan. The Mem-u Zin Mausoleum at Cizre has become a place that visitors seek out.
mem-de-sa: Mem de Sá was born in Coimbra, in the Kingdom of Portugal, around 1500, the year a fleet commanded by Pedro Álvares Cabral reached Brazil. In his time Brazil was not yet a major area of Portuguese settlement: Jesuits had set up aldeias, villages for the evangelising of the indigenous peoples, while Portuguese settlers enslaved them. He was nominated in 1556 as the third governor-general, succeeding Duarte da Costa, and governed from Salvador, in the present-day state of Bahia.

He gained the support of two Jesuits, Manuel da Nóbrega and José de Anchieta, who had founded São Paulo on 25 January 1554. The Jesuits had quarrelled with Duarte da Costa, who sided with the plantation owners in their attempts to enslave the Indians. Mem de Sá opposed the planters' usury in the trade in Indian slaves and helped the Jesuits increase the number of their aldeias, and their missions among the warrior societies of the indigenous peoples were counted among the chief results of his government.

In 1560 the crown sent him with a naval expedition of 26 ships and 2,000 soldiers and sailors against France Antarctique, the colony founded by the French vice-admiral Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon on the site of present-day Rio de Janeiro. He destroyed Fort Coligny, which the French had built on a small island in Guanabara Bay, and with the help of the Jesuits persuaded the Tamoyo Confederation to withdraw its support from the French. Their final expulsion came only in 1567, with his nephew Estácio de Sá, who had founded Rio de Janeiro on 1 March 1565. Mem de Sá died in Salvador on 2 March 1572.
memnon-of-heraclea: Memnon was probably a native of Heraclea Pontica, the city whose history he wrote, and his large work is known only through the Excerpta of Photius I of Constantinople. His date is uncertain. The last event in the sixteenth book is the death of Brithagoras, whom the Heracleians sent as ambassador to Julius Caesar after Caesar had won supreme power in 48 BCE. From this Gerardus Vossius placed the work around the time of Augustus, Orelli no later than Hadrian or the Antonines, and the Oxford Classical Dictionary in the 2nd century. Since no one knows how far the whole work ran, the date cannot be fixed.

The history ran to an unknown number of books. Photius read only the ninth to the sixteenth and made a fairly full abstract of them in his Excerpta; he had not read the first eight and mentions others after the sixteenth. The ninth book opens with the tyrant Clearchus, a pupil of Plato and Isocrates, and the work dwells on the tyrants who at times ruled Heraclea. The thirteenth book holds a long account of the rise of Rome. Photius judged the style clear and simple and the words well chosen, though his excerpts contain rare and poetic expressions and a few that show the decline of the Greek language.

Henry Estienne first published the excerpts of Photius separately in Paris in 1557, together with the remains of Ctesias and Agatharchides. The best edition is that of Johann Conrad Orelli, published at Leipzig in 1816 with fragments of other writers on Heraclea. Though compressed and seen from one city, the work is valued as a continuous account of nearly the whole Hellenistic period and as the only reasonably complete example of Greek local history.
memory-of-the-world-programme: UNESCO began the programme in 1992 to preserve and promote documentary heritage, among them manuscripts, maps, rock inscriptions, court documents and diplomatic exchanges, judged to be of such global significance that they transcend the boundaries of time and culture. The programme seeks to safeguard documentary heritage against collective amnesia, neglect, decay and deliberate destruction. Its International Advisory Committee met in an interim capacity from 1993 and created the International Register at its second meeting in 1995. The first inscriptions followed in 1997, after the statutes that made the committee permanent took effect.

Any organisation or individual may propose an item through a UNESCO Member State's National Commission, and two proposals per state are considered in each nomination cycle, with no limit on joint proposals. Items are recommended by the International Advisory Committee, whose 14 members are appointed by UNESCO's Director-General, and endorsed by the Director-General, using the criteria of world significance and outstanding universal value. The register includes manuscripts, oral traditions, audio-visual materials and library and archive holdings, among them recordings of folk music, landmark films and the lifetime works of writers and composers. The committee has subsidiary bodies for the register, preservation, and education and research. National and regional committees are autonomous and made up of local heritage professionals.

National and regional committees keep their own registers for heritage of national or regional importance, such as those of Australia, Canada, Ghana, Mexico and New Zealand, and there are regional registers for Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Africa. The Jikji Prize, established in 2004 with the South Korean government to mark the 2001 inscription of Korea's Jikji, honours institutions that preserve and open documentary heritage; its first recipient, in 2005, was the Czech National Library. The audiovisual concern goes back to UNESCO's 1980 Recommendation for the Safeguarding and Preservation of Moving Images. In 1995 UNESCO published its first Memory of the World list, on national cinematic heritage.
memphis-egypt: Memphis stood on the west bank of the Nile, about 20 kilometres south of Cairo, at the mouth of the Delta, where it marked the boundary between Upper and Lower Egypt. It was the capital of the first nome of Lower Egypt, and its Egyptian name was Inebu-hedj, "the white walls". The principal port, Peru-nefer, held many workshops and warehouses that distributed food and goods through the kingdom. The great temple of Ptah, Hut-ka-Ptah, "Enclosure of the ka of Ptah", gave its name, in Manetho's Greek rendering, to Egypt itself.

According to Manetho, writing in the early third century BCE, King Menes, the first to unite the Two Lands, founded the city by diverting the Nile with dikes. Herodotus tells a similar story and says the Persians later kept the dams in repair. Some Egyptologists identified Menes with Narmer, shown on the Narmer Palette, but a 2012 inscription showing the predynastic king Iry-Hor visiting Memphis suggests that Narmer cannot have been its founder.

The city was capital through the Early Dynastic Period and the Old Kingdom, for more than six consecutive dynasties, and its prestige peaked under the Sixth Dynasty. Its main worship focused on the Memphis triad of Ptah, his consort Sekhmet and their son Nefertem. Djoser's complex at Saqqara, of the Third Dynasty, served as the royal necropolis.

At the start of the Middle Kingdom the court moved to Thebes, but Memphis remained perhaps the most important commercial and artistic centre. Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV of the Eighteenth Dynasty favoured it, and its port became the gateway for trade with Byblos and the Levant. In the Late Period it was often the scene of struggles against Kushite, Assyrian and Persian occupiers, and the Kushite ruler Piankhi captured it and restored its temples. In 332 BCE Alexander the Great was crowned king in the Temple of Ptah. After his death in 323 BCE, Ptolemy I brought his body to Memphis, and Ptolemy II later moved the sarcophagus to Alexandria.

The decline came with the rise of coastal Alexandria, which took away Memphis's economic importance. Its religious role faded after the Edict of Thessalonica of 380 CE made Nicene Christianity the sole religion of the Roman Empire. By the Middle Ages nearby Cairo had become the major political and economic centre.

The footprint of the ancient city is uninhabited, and the nearest settlement is the village of Mit Rahina. Memphis and its necropolis, together with the pyramid fields stretching more than 30 kilometres along the desert plateau to the west, including the Pyramids of Giza, are a World Heritage Site. The ruins are open to the public as an open-air museum, and an alabaster sphinx stands beside the Temple of Ptah.
men-deity: Mēn, whose Greek name means month and Moon, was probably a Phrygian god, linked with the local descendant of the Hitto-Luwian moon god Arma, and he may also have been shaped by the Zoroastrian lunar divinity Mah. Strabo calls him a local god of the Phrygians. He is often found with Persianate elements, above all the goddess Anahita. Lunar symbols dominate his images, and he was held to preside over the lunar months. He was worshipped under local names, such as Mēn Askaenos at Antioch in Pisidia.

The temple estate of Mēn Pharnakou and Selene at Ameria in Pontus was probably founded by Pharnakes I in the 2nd century BCE, apparently to counterbalance the moon goddess Ma of Comana, and the star and crescent on Pontic coins of the time has been traced to this cult.

A similar estate of Mēn Askaenos in Pisidia was centred first on Anabura and then moved to Pisidian Antioch, founded by the Seleucids around 280 BCE. It was a theocratic monarchy ruled by a hereditary Priest of Priests, and according to Strabo this temple state lasted until the Romans refounded the city in 25 BCE as Colonia Caesarea Augusta, settled mainly by veterans of Legio V Alaudae and Legio VII Gemina. Bucrania cut into the rock where the Augusteum was built are thought to be traces of the older cult.

In imperial Rome Mēn was received as a Phrygian god and shown in a Phrygian cap and belted tunic, sometimes with bulls and lions, in a way that partly recalls Mithras. The Augustan History has the emperor Caracalla venerate Lunus, a masculine Moon taken to be a Latin name for Mēn, at Carrhae, and records the local belief that a man who thinks the Moon female will always be ruled by women; David Magie suggests Caracalla in fact visited the temple of the Mesopotamian moon god Sin. In later times Mēn may also have been identified with Attis of Phrygia and Sabazius of Thrace.
men-of-harlech: The siege the song is said to recall was held by a garrison under Constable Dafydd ap Ieuan, son of the Baron of Hendwr, and was the longest known siege in the history of the British Isles; "Through Seven Years" is another name for the song. It has also been linked with the earlier and briefer siege of Harlech about 1407-09, between the forces of Owain Glyndŵr and the future Henry V of England.

The tune first appeared without words in 1794 as "Gorhoffedd Gwŷr Harlech" in the second edition of The Musical and Poetical Relicks of the Welsh Bards, though it is said to be a much older folk song. Welsh words were first printed with it in Y Canigydd, edited by John Owen (Owain Alaw) at Wrexham in 1860. The 1862 collection Welsh Melodies set it with Welsh words by John Jones (Talhaiarn) and English words by Thomas Oliphant, tying it to Glyndŵr's siege, and John Ceiriog Hughes's Welsh words appear in Brinley Richards's The Songs of Wales of 1873. There is no single accepted English text.

The tune is a regimental march of British Army and Commonwealth regiments linked with Wales: the slow march of the Welsh Guards and the quick march of the Royal Welsh, and also a march of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Royal Canadian Hussars (Montreal), The Governor General's Horse Guards and The Ontario Regiment. Welsh football supporters sing adapted versions, and many schools and colleges use it as their song. Bryn Terfel recorded it in 2000.

Franz Joseph Haydn arranged it, Edward German used it in the last movement of his Welsh Rhapsody of 1904, and William Thomas Best wrote an organ fantasia on it. It was part of the startup music of the television station Teledu Cymru in the early 1960s, and appeared in Fritz Spiegl's BBC Radio 4 UK Theme until April 2006.

The song is important to Welsh national culture. It was first heard in the cinema under the titles of How Green Was My Valley in 1941, but is best known from the 1964 film Zulu, which sang lyrics written for the film against the Zulu war chants. During the September 11 attacks Rick Rescorla, chief of security for Morgan Stanley's office at the World Trade Center, sang a Cornish adaptation through a bullhorn to keep up the spirits of the staff as they evacuated, then went back to evacuate others and died when the towers collapsed.
menabe: Menabe was the southern part of the Sakalava territory in western Madagascar. Tradition holds that it was founded by Adriamandazoala, and its territory was enlarged under Andriandahifotsy, who is dated c. 1610 to 1685. It became the strongest kingdom in Madagascar until the middle of the 18th century. One of its best-known rulers was Ranaimo, also called Andriandrainarivo, who ruled from 1718 to 1727 and is known through the memoirs of Europeans such as Robert Drury, James Cook, the crew of the Dutch East Indiaman Barneveld in 1719, and François Valentijn in 1726. Though handsome and imposing, he was a paralytic.

Radama I of the Merina conducted three ravaging campaigns in the kingdom, in 1820, 1821 and 1822. Ramitraho, king of Menabe at the time, sued for peace by giving his daughter Rasalimo to Radama as his wife, but peace did not follow until Rasalimo offered another peace treaty in 1827. Radama died before negotiations could finish. The Merina conquered the southern Menabe territories in 1834, just after Ramitraho's death. Constant war followed, ending in a Merina victory in 1846, after which Queen Ranavalona I garrisoned the major towns and sent farmers to colonise the area. Menabe rulers kept their authority under the local Merina governor, while northern Menabe largely escaped Merina authority and stayed independent.

During the French invasion of Madagascar the Menabe kings united their forces. On 14 August 1897 and 30 August 1897 about a hundred Menabe chiefs with 10,000 warriors armed with rifles met French troops at Anosimena and Ambiky. King Itoera was killed along with his generals and many nobles, but Menabe was not pacified until 1900.

Menabe is now a region of western Madagascar with its capital at Morondava. It covers 46,121 square kilometres and had a population of 700,577 in 2018, mostly Sakalava. Its name means big red, after the laterite rock that dominates the landscape. It lies between the Mangoky and Manambolo rivers and is divided into five districts and 51 communes. Under French colonial rule it was incorporated into the province of Toliara, and it became a region in 2004. The Avenue of the Baobabs, one of the most visited places in the region, lies within a protected area, and Kirindy Mitea National Park is also in Menabe.
menahem: Menahem was the son of Gadi and the sixteenth king of the northern Kingdom of Israel, and the founder of a short dynasty known as the House of Gadi or House of Menahem. His reign is told in 2 Kings 15:14–22. Like Shallum, he had served as a captain in the army of King Zechariah. When Shallum conspired against Zechariah, assassinated him in Samaria and took the throne, Menahem refused to recognise him. According to Josephus he was a general of the army of Israel.

Menahem marched from Tirzah to Samaria, about six miles to the west, besieged and took the city and killed Shallum a month into his reign. The Books of Kings tell that he then put down a revolt at Tiphsah by destroying the city and killing all its inhabitants, ripping open the pregnant women. Their author describes his rule as one of cruelty and oppression, calls him a commander rather than a legitimate heir to the throne and avoids giving him the title of king. The author drew on an older source, the annals of the kings of Israel, and gives few details.

The Assyrians first entered Israel in his reign. Tiglath-Pileser III, called Pul in the Bible, 'came into the land', and Menahem paid him a tribute of a thousand talents of silver, about 34 metric tons, to maintain his independence. To raise it he took fifty shekels of silver from each of the wealthy men of the kingdom, which implies some 60,000 such men.

Tiglath-Pileser records this tribute in one of his inscriptions. After he had been paid he returned to Assyria. The Bible dates the accession to year 39 of Azariah, king of Judah, and gives a reign of ten years; modern scholars date it variously, from 752 BCE in the chronology of E. R. Thiele to 745 BCE in those of Schrader and Albright.

Menahem seems to have died a natural death and was succeeded by his son Pekahiah. From his payment onward the kingdom of Israel was a tributary of Assyria. When Pekah, some ten years later, refused to pay further tribute, the sequence of events began that led to the destruction of the kingdom and the deportation of its population. The Books of Kings were finalised some time after the Babylonian Exile and favour Judah, so the Assyrian sources that name Menahem are a check on the biblical account.
menai-strait: The Menai Strait (Afon Menai in Welsh) separates the island of Anglesey from Gwynedd on the mainland of Wales. It lies between Caernarfon Bay in the south-west and Conwy Bay in the north-east, both inlets of the Irish Sea, and is about 25 km long. Its width varies from 400 metres between Fort Belan and Abermenai Point to 7.5 km between Puffin Island and Penmaenmawr. The present channel is the result of glacial erosion of the bedrock along a line of weakness, the Menai Strait fault system, and was flooded by the sea as ocean levels rose at the end of the last ice age, around 10,000 BCE.

The name Menai comes from Welsh main-aw or main-wy, meaning narrow water. According to Heimskringla, the 11th-century Norse-Gael ruler Echmarcach mac Ragnaill and the Viking Guttorm Gunnhildsson plundered in Wales, quarrelled over the spoil and fought a battle at the strait, which Guttorm won by praying to Saint Olaf, while Echmarcach was killed. In the 12th century a later Viking raid and battle in the strait play a part in the Orkneyinga Saga in the life of Magnus Erlendsson, Earl of Orkney, the future Saint Magnus. He refused to fight in the raid on Anglesey and stayed on his ship singing psalms.

The tides carry large quantities of fish, and fish weirs built on both banks and on several islands made the strait an important source of fish for many centuries. Eight of its weirs are now scheduled monuments. From the 1890s until 1963 the pleasure steamers of the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company sailed from Liverpool and Llandudno along the strait and around Anglesey.

Thomas Telford's Menai Suspension Bridge, completed in 1826, carries the A5 road, and Robert Stephenson's Britannia Bridge, completed in 1850 and severely damaged by fire in 1970, carries the North Wales Main Line and the A55. Tides at the two ends of the strait produce strong currents, and the Swellies, between the bridges, has rocks near the surface, overfalls and whirlpools. The training ship HMS Conway was lost there in 1953.

The strait's sheltered waters hold a diverse seabed life, rich in sponges, which led to the founding of Bangor University's School of Ocean Sciences at Menai Bridge. Its banks are home to the Menai Whitebeam, a very rare tree found only in this part of North Wales. On 14 February 2023 the Welsh Government announced that a proposed third crossing, planned since 2007, would not go ahead.
menalamba-rebellion: French claims over Madagascar had grown for more than four decades under Queen Ranavalona II and Queen Ranavalona III. After a campaign under General Jacques Duchesne the queen surrendered on 14 September 1895, and on 1 October the Merina Kingdom signed a treaty making it a French protectorate. The prime minister and commander-in-chief Rainilaiarivony was deposed and exiled to French Algeria; the queen and much of her administration stayed in place without real power, under a civil governor, Hippolyte Laroche.

The rising was mainly the work of peasants, many of them outlaws called fahavalo, and was rooted in outlying regions already home to brigands, runaway slaves and deserters. Its leaders included Rabozaka and Rabezavana around Anjozorobe and Rainibetsimisaraka in Vakinankaratra. It had no united command and drew in both religious traditionalists and popular Christian preachers. It did not seek to restore the queen, since the rebels blamed the conversion of the royal family for cosmic chaos; its aims included reviving ancestor veneration and ending fanompoana, the forced labour on which the church relied.

The French at first saw only isolated violence, but in March 1896 coordinated attacks on royal government posts announced a full uprising. At its height it may have controlled territory with as many as 300,000 people, and it blockaded Antananarivo from July to September 1896, when a state of siege was declared. On 15 October 1896 General Joseph Gallieni had the queen's uncle Ratsimamanga and her Minister of War, Rainandriamampandry, executed. Some Protestant rebels hoped in vain for British help, and by 1897 hunger was driving groups to surrender; Rabezavana surrendered to Hubert Lyautey in May 1897.
