France replaced its civil governor with Gallieni as military governor, deposed Ranavalona III in 1897 and exiled her to Réunion and later to Algeria, where she died in 1917. The rebels destroyed hundreds of churches and killed five foreign missionaries, among them the Jesuit Jacques Berthieu, canonised in 2012. Malagasy deaths may have reached 100,000; French deaths, from disease and violence, were in the hundreds.
menander-i: Menander was born into a Greek family. One source gives his birthplace as a village called Kalasi near Alexandria of the Caucasus, present-day Bagram in Afghanistan, and another places it near Sagala, modern Sialkot. He might first have been a prince or king of Bactria. Pompeius Trogus and Justin call him a king of India, while Plutarch calls him a king of Bactria. His silver coinage begins with a rare series whose weight and monograms match those of the earlier king Antimachus II, which indicates that he succeeded him.

After conquering the Punjab as far as Taxila and Sagala, Menander ruled an empire stretching from the Kabul River in the west to the Ravi in the east, and from the Swat valley in the north to Arachosia. Strabo wrote that he conquered more tribes than Alexander the Great in India. Ancient Indian writers suggest he may have led expeditions as far east along the Ganges as Pataliputra. He left more silver and bronze coins than any other Indo-Greek king, which points to a long reign and flourishing trade. He was the first to put his own portrait on his coins, a custom unknown among Indian rulers.

According to tradition, Menander embraced Buddhism after his conversations with the sage Nagasena, recorded in the Milinda Panha, whose style may have been influenced by Plato's Dialogues. A Buddhist reliquary found at Bajaur, the Shinkot casket, is dated to the reign of Maharaja Minadra.

Buddhist tradition says Menander handed his kingdom to his son and retired from the world. Plutarch says instead that he died in camp on campaign, and that the cities of his realm shared his ashes equally and erected monuments, probably stupas, to him; modern scholars doubt this, since Plutarch may have confused his death with the Buddha's. The traditional view is that his wife Agathoclea acted as regent for their infant son Strato I, though some numismatists argue that Strato ruled decades later.

After Menander, several Indo-Greek rulers put Buddhist symbols on their coins, and some adopted the title Dharmikasa, follower of the Dharma. The conversion described in the Milinda Panha seems to have prompted Buddhist symbolism on the coinage of nearly half the kings who followed.
menashi-kunashir-rebellion: In 1604 the Tokugawa shogunate gave the Matsumae Domain the sole right to trade with the people of Ezo. From the 1630s the trade ran through a system of trading posts, each assigned to a senior vassal of the Matsumae clan with exclusive rights to deal with the local Ainu. After Shakushain's revolt, and through the eighteenth century, Japanese merchants were increasingly contracted to run the posts for the vassals in return for commission. The Ainu lost their economic independence and became in effect labourers in fisheries and other businesses run by Wajin merchants.

In 1788 the merchant Hidaya Kyūbei began commercial fishing in the Menashi and Kunashiri area, employing Ainu to catch salmon and trout for use as fertiliser. They were worked so hard that they had too little time to lay in food for winter. Hunger, the overbearing conduct of the fishery supervisors, who took Ainu wives as mistresses, and suspicions of poisoning, among them a rumour of poisoned sake given at a loyalty ceremony, led to the rising of May 1789.

It broke out while the local leader Tsukinoe was away hunting sea otters on Uruppu. The Ainu struck on Kunashir, in the Menashi area and at sea. Of the Wajin killed, twenty-two died on Kunashiri and the rest in Menashi, and all but one, a Matsumae soldier, worked for Hidaya. When the news reached Matsumae in early June, the daimyō Matsumae Michihiro sent 260 soldiers east, who recruited local Ainu chieftains on the way.

The force reached the Nemuro area in July, and more than three hundred of those involved surrendered. Of the thirty-eight held directly responsible for the killings, among them Tsukinoe's son Seppayabu, all but one, who had fled, were beheaded and their heads stored in salt; many others were arrested. Matsumae Michihiro then commissioned the Ishūretsuzō, a series of portraits of twelve Ainu elders who had helped put down the revolt. The rising is the subject of Majin no Umi, a children's novel by Maekawa Yasuo that won the prize of the Japanese Association of Writers for Children in 1970.
mencius: Mencius was born Meng Ke in the state of Zou, in what is now Zoucheng, Shandong. His father, Meng Ji, died when he was very young, and his mother, Meng Mu, is often held up as an exemplary woman in Chinese culture. Liu Xiang's Biographies of Exemplary Women gives four stories about her. In the best known she moved house three times, from beside a cemetery to beside a market and finally to beside a school, because her son imitated what he saw around him. He is supposed to have been a pupil of Zisi, the grandson of Confucius.

Mencius lived in the Warring States period. According to legend he travelled throughout China for forty years, as Confucius had, offering advice to rulers on reform. He served as an official and scholar at the Jixia Academy in the state of Qi from 319 to 312 BCE, and took three years' leave from his duties for Qi to mourn his mother. Ying Shao's Fengsu Tongyi records that King Hui of Liang appointed him a high official after the capital of Wei was moved to Daliang. Disappointed that he could not bring about change, he retired from public life. He was buried in the Cemetery of Mencius, 12 km north-east of Zoucheng, where a stele carried by a stone tortoise stands before his grave.

His conversations with rulers form the Mencius, later canonised as a Confucian classic and grouped by Zhu Xi (1130-1200) among the Four Books at the core of orthodox Neo-Confucian thought. Mencius held that human nature is righteous and humane and that society causes bad character. He gave the example of onlookers who feel alarm at a child falling into a well, and argued that feelings of compassion, shame, deference and right and wrong are the beginnings of humanity, righteousness, propriety and wisdom. These can grow or fail, so education in a favourable environment matters. In this he differed from Xunzi, who thought human nature evil.

In politics he stressed the importance of ordinary people. A ruler who ignores their needs and rules harshly is no longer a true ruler, and Mencius said of the overthrow of King Zhou of Shang, 'I have merely heard of killing a villain Zhou, but I have not heard of murdering him as the ruler.' He favoured low taxes and free trade. Neo-Confucians of the Song dynasty took his reading of Confucianism as the orthodox one. François Noël published a full edition in Latin at Prague in 1711.
mendelian-inheritance: Gregor Johann Mendel, a nineteenth-century Moravian monk, formulated his ideas from simple hybridisation experiments with pea plants in the garden of his monastery. Between 1856 and 1863 he cultivated and tested some 28,000 plants. He presented a two-part paper, Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden, to the Brünn Natural History Society on 8 February and 8 March 1865, and it was published in 1866. His method contributed to his success: he started only with plants shown to be true-breeding, measured discrete characters such as the colour, shape and position of seeds, expressed his results numerically and analysed them statistically, followed several successive generations, and used test crosses to reveal recessive characters.

Mendel found that when he crossed purebred white-flowered and purple-flowered peas, every plant of the first generation was purple, so he called purple dominant. Allowing those plants to self-fertilise gave both colours in the next generation in a ratio of 3 to 1. He conceived of heredity units he called factors, now called genes, which exist in alternative forms now called alleles; an organism inherits two, one from each parent.

Three principles became known as laws. Dominance and uniformity: the offspring of two purebred parents differing in one character all show the dominant trait. Segregation: the two alleles separate when gametes are formed, giving a 1:2:1 ratio of genotypes. Independent assortment: alleles for separate traits pass independently, and in dihybrid crosses Mendel found 9:3:3:1 ratios.

Mendel himself warned that care was needed in extending his patterns to other organisms or traits. Many traits are non-Mendelian: many genes have more than two alleles, and some traits, such as height, depend on many genes. Incomplete dominance, in which hybrids look intermediate, appears in four o'clock plants, studied first by Carl Correns.

Mendel's results were at first largely ignored, and even he thought they applied only to some species or traits. Nineteenth-century biologists attached importance to the apparent blending of inherited traits. In 1900 Carl Correns, Erich von Tschermak and Hugo de Vries are credited with rediscovering his work, though the order and nature of the rediscovery is debated. William Bateson promoted it vigorously in Europe and coined the terms genetics and allele. Critics objected that it implied discontinuous heredity. Work by Ronald Fisher showed that several Mendelian factors could produce the continuous variation seen, making the theory compatible with natural selection. Thomas Hunt Morgan integrated it with the chromosome theory in 1915 to create classical genetics.
mendes: Mendes is the Greek name of the ancient Egyptian city of Djedet, also called Per-Banebdjedet, the Domain of the Ram Lord of Djedet, and Anpet. It lay in the eastern Nile Delta on the Mendesian branch of the Nile, now silted up, about 35 kilometres east of al-Mansurah. The city was the capital of the 16th Lower Egyptian nome of Kha until it was replaced by Thmuis in Greco-Roman Egypt, and the two cities stood only several hundred metres apart. During the 29th Dynasty Mendes was also the capital of Egypt.

Archaeological evidence shows a town at Mendes at least as far back as the Naqada II period in the 4th millennium BCE. Under the first pharaohs it became a strong seat of provincial government and remained so throughout the Egyptian period. Ancient geographers and historians, among them Herodotus and Strabo, noticed it, and in Classical times it was known for a perfume called the Mendesium unguentum.

The city declined early and disappears in the first century CE, when Thmuis is the only town of note in the nome. Its position at the junction of the river and a lake probably exposed it to encroaching water after the canals fell into neglect under the Macedonian kings.

The chief deities were the ram Banebdjedet, the Ba of Osiris, and his consort, the fish goddess Hatmehit, who with their child Har-pa-khered, Horus the Child, formed the triad of Mendes. Herodotus described the god as shown with the head and fleece of a goat. In 1855 the occultist Eliphas Levi drew the fictitious medieval idol Baphomet as a figure conflated with the goat of Mendes, an image later repeated by various occultists.

The site is the largest surviving tell in the Nile Delta, made up of Tell El-Ruba, the site of the main temple enclosure, and Tell El-Timai, the settlement site of Thmuis. It is about 3 kilometres long from north to south. An Old Kingdom necropolis is estimated to hold over 9,000 interments, and a cemetery of sacred rams was found in the northwest corner of Tell El-Ruba. Monuments bearing the names of Ramesses II, Merneptah and Ramesses III were found, and a temple built by Amasis II is attested by its foundation deposits.

A joint team from the University of Washington and the University of Toronto discovered the tomb of Nepherites I in 1992–1993, which Donald Redford concluded the Persians had destroyed. A sondage has revealed uninterrupted stratification from the Middle Kingdom down to the First Dynasty, possibly the longest in Egypt.
mendip-hills: The hills run from Weston-super-Mare and the Bristol Channel in the west to the Frome valley in the east, overlooking the Somerset Levels to the south and the Chew Valley to the north. The highest point is Beacon Batch, the summit of Black Down, at 325 metres. They are formed largely of Carboniferous Limestone laid down about 320–350 million years ago and folded in the Variscan orogeny. Erosion and the dissolving of the limestone have left gorges such as Burrington Combe, swallets, limestone pavement and the largest underground river system in Britain.

Twenty Palaeolithic sites have been identified, eleven of them in caves, and the caves of Cheddar Gorge have yielded many remains, among them the Cheddar Man, Britain's oldest complete skeleton, found in Gough's Cave. The more than 200 scheduled ancient monuments include the Priddy Nine Barrows and Ashen Hill barrow cemeteries and the forts at Dolebury Warren. Mining dates back to the late Bronze Age and increased after the Roman invasion, and a branch of the Fosse Way served the lead mines at Charterhouse.

In 1789 William Wilberforce noted the hard conditions of the area, which led Hannah More to begin her work for the Mendip miners and agricultural workers. In the 18th and early 19th centuries 7,300 hectares of common heathland on the hills were enclosed. In World War II a bombing decoy on Black Down was built to confuse bombers aiming at Bristol, and in the 1960s the 293-metre Mendip television mast went up on Pen Hill near Wells. According to legend, Augustus Montague Toplady wrote the words of Rock of Ages while sheltering under a rock in Burrington Combe in 1763.

The higher western part, covering 198 square kilometres, has been an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty since 1972. Nine active quarries supply road stone to southern England. The hills are a national centre for caving and cave diving: after an attempt at Swildon's Hole in 1934, the first successful British cave dive was made at Wookey Hole Caves, whose sump is the deepest in Britain.
mendoza-argentina: Mendoza lies in the northern-central part of its province, in a region of foothills and high plains on the eastern side of the Andes. The road between Buenos Aires and Santiago, Ruta Nacional 7, runs through it, and the city is a frequent stopover for climbers on their way to Aconcagua. Before the 1560s the area was populated by the Huarpes and Puelches. The Huarpes devised a system of irrigation that the Spanish later developed, and its trenches, the acequias, still run along the city's streets.

On 2 March 1561 Pedro del Castillo founded the city and named it Ciudad de Mendoza del Nuevo Valle de La Rioja, after the governor of Chile, García Hurtado de Mendoza. Fewer than 80 Spanish settlers are estimated to have lived in the area before 1600. Prosperity later increased through the use of indigenous and slave labour and the Jesuit presence in the region. In 1776 the city was transferred from the Captaincy General of Chile, and agricultural production grew, with more trade with Buenos Aires, after nearby rivers were tapped for irrigation in 1788.

The state of Cuyo was created in 1813 with José de San Martín as governor. From Mendoza, San Martín and other Argentine and Chilean patriots organised the army with which they won the independence of Chile and Peru.

A severe earthquake in 1861 killed at least 5,000 people. The city was rebuilt with large squares and with wider streets and sidewalks than any other city in Argentina, so as to better withstand seismic activity. The layout of the modern city was established in 1863, with a central main square surrounded by four smaller plazas.

Mendoza is the capital of Mendoza Province. The surrounding region is the largest wine-producing area in South America, and olive oil is the other main local industry. Suburbs such as Godoy Cruz, Guaymallén, Las Heras and Luján de Cuyo have grown far faster than the city proper, and together they make up most of a metropolitan area of over a million people. The Museo del Área Fundacional on Pedro del Castillo Square and the Museo Nacional del Vino, in nearby Maipú, record its history.
mendut: Mendut stands in Mendut village, in the Mungkid sub-district of Magelang Regency. Built around the early ninth century, it is the oldest of the three temples it forms a line with. The Karangtengah inscription, dated 824, records that King Indra of the Shailendra dynasty built a sacred building named Venuvana, meaning bamboo forest, and the Dutch archaeologist J. G. de Casparis connected this with Mendut. The temple was found in 1836 as a ruin overgrown with bushes; restoration began in 1897 and was finished in 1925.

The temple stands on a square base 13.7 metres on each side, raised 3.7 metres above the ground, and rises 26.4 metres. It faces north-west, where stairs flanked by makara statues climb to a terrace meant for pradakshina, the ritual of walking clockwise around a shrine. The side of the stairway carries reliefs of Jataka fables, animal stories of Buddhist teaching, and the outer walls show bodhisattvas, among them Maitreya, Kṣitigarbha, Samantabhadra, Manjushri and Prajnaparamita.

There were originally two chambers, a small one in front and the main one at the centre; the roof, with what was probably a stupa pinnacle like that of Sojiwan temple, and parts of the front chamber are lost. The front chamber has reliefs of Hariti surrounded by children, Atavaka, the wish-granting tree Kalpataru and flying divinities. In the main room the three-metre Vairocana was meant to free devotees from the karma of the body, Avalokiteśvara on the left from that of speech, and Vajrapani on the right from that of thought.

Mendut, Pawon and Borobudur are related in religious terms, though the exact ritual that linked them is unknown. Each year at the full moon of May or June, Buddhists in Indonesia mark Vesak with a procession from Mendut through Pawon to Borobudur, with mass prayer and circumambulation. Followers of Kejawen, Javanese mysticism, have also worshipped at the temple, believed to grant wishes such as healing; childless couples pray before the relief of Hariti, whom Javanese tradition holds to be a patroness of motherhood and protector of children.
menedemus-of-eretria: Menedemus belonged to the noble Theopropidai family of Eretria, which held religious authority but had grown poor by his time, and like his father Cleisthenes he worked as a builder and tent maker. Sent with a military expedition to Megara, probably in 323 or 322 BCE during the Lamian War, he went on to the Platonic Academy in Athens and resolved to give himself to philosophy. At Megara he formed a lifelong friendship with Asclepiades of Phlius; the two are said to have worked by night so that they could study by day.

With Asclepiades he went to Elis and studied under Anchipylus and Moschus, followers of Phaedo of Elis, and he was also a pupil of Stilpo. He then moved the school to Eretria, after which it took that city's name. Around 310 BCE the two friends stayed at the court of King Nikocreon at Salamis in Cyprus. Diogenes Laertius tells that Menedemus married the mother of Asclepiades's wife, and on that wife's death left his own wife to his friend and married a richer woman, with whom he had three daughters.

From about 300 BCE he held a leading place in the politics of Eretria, which had lost much of its old importance. He is said to have worked for its independence and went on many embassies to other Greek cities. He grew close to Antigonus II Gonatas, the king of Macedonia who dominated Euboea, and this friendship seems to have raised doubts about his loyalty. He took refuge first at the temple of Amphiaraus at Oropus and then with Antigonus, at whose court he is said to have died of grief; other accounts say he starved himself after failing to persuade the king to free his city.

His views survive only in remarks by later writers. Athenaeus quotes Epicrates calling him a Platonist, while other accounts say he preferred Stilpo to Plato. Diogenes Laertius reports that he refused to identify the good with the useful and denied the value of negative propositions, holding that only affirmation can express truth. Plutarch and Cicero say he regarded virtue as one, under whatever name, and as intellectual. He counted the poets Aratos of Soloi, Lycophron of Chalcis and Antagoras of Rhodes among his friends.
menelaus: Menelaus was a descendant of Pelops, son of Tantalus, and the younger brother of Agamemnon. In the usual version, followed by Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, the two were sons of Atreus, king of Mycenae, and Aerope. Later sources say that Atreus feuded with his brother Thyestes over the throne of Mycenae, and that Thyestes took it after his son Aegisthus murdered Atreus. Menelaus and Agamemnon went into exile and returned with the help of King Tyndareus of Sparta to drive Thyestes away. Agamemnon took the throne of Mycenae.

When Tyndareus's stepdaughter Helen came to be married, many kings and princes sought her hand. On the advice of Odysseus, all the suitors swore to defend the chosen husband in any quarrel, and straws were drawn. Menelaus won and became ruler of Sparta with Helen. A supposed palace has been found at Pellana in Laconia, though other archaeologists think it too far from other Mycenaean centres to have been his capital.

Paris, the Trojan prince, ran off to Troy with Helen. Invoking the oath, Menelaus and Agamemnon raised a fleet of a thousand ships. In Book 3 of the Iliad Menelaus beats Paris in a duel, but Aphrodite carries Paris away. In Book 4 Pandarus wounds Menelaus with an arrow, though Athena protects him from death, and in Book 17 he recovers the corpse of Patroclus. According to Hyginus he was one of the Greeks hidden in the Trojan Horse, and at the sack he killed Deiphobus. Ancient versions tell how he raised his sword against Helen and then spared her.

According to Book 4 of the Odyssey Menelaus's fleet was blown by storms to Crete and Egypt, where he forced Proteus to reveal the way home, and he reached Sparta eight years after leaving Troy. In Herodotus's account Helen never went to Troy but spent the war in Egypt. In the Odyssey the couple live in harmony at Sparta, though some scholars detect underlying conflict.

Menelaus and Helen were worshipped at the Menelaion in Therapne, and only Pausanias says they were buried there. In the Odyssey it was ordained that Menelaus would not die but go to Elysium, and in Euripides's Helen he spends his afterlife on the Isle of the Blessed. He appears in Greek vase painting from the 6th to the 4th century BCE and in 5th-century tragedies by Sophocles and Euripides.
menelik-ii: Menelik was born in 1844 at Ankober in the Kingdom of Shewa and baptised Sahle Maryam. He was the son of Haile Melekot, Negus of Shewa, of the Shewan branch of the Solomonic dynasty. His grandfather Sahle Selassie named him after Menelik I, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba in tradition. After his father's death in 1855 Emperor Tewodros II imprisoned him at the fortress of Magdala, though he later said Tewodros had treated him like a son. In 1865, as the emperor's power declined, he escaped and returned to Shewa, and in August 1866 he proclaimed himself Negus there.

As king of Shewa he submitted to Emperor Yohannes IV in 1878. Confined to Shewa, he turned south and conquered lands inhabited by Oromo, Wolayta and Gurage peoples, drawing revenue from ivory, coffee, gold and the slave trade. He bought arms through direct European diplomacy with advisers such as the Swiss engineer Alfred Ilg, defeated Negus Tekle Haimanot of Gojjam at the Battle of Embabo in 1882 and took Harar in 1887. When Yohannes was killed fighting the Mahdists in March 1889, Menelik proclaimed himself emperor, and he was crowned on Mount Entoto on 3 November 1889.

The Treaty of Wuchale, signed with Italy in 1889, read in the Italian version as a protectorate, while the Amharic text allowed only optional use of Italian diplomatic help. Menelik rejected it in 1891, and Italy invaded in 1895. With an army of over 100,000 he defeated the Italians at the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896, which secured Ethiopia's independence and full European recognition. Conquests continued until 1900, and he fixed borders by treaty with Britain, France and Italy, began the Addis Ababa–Djibouti Railway and centralised government through ministries, schools and a state bank.

Menelik suffered strokes in 1906, 1908 and 1909, the last leaving him paralysed and barely able to speak. Empress Taytu Betul and later Ras Tessema Nadew acted as regents. He died on 12 December 1913. His grandson Iyasu was nominally his successor but was deposed in 1916, and his daughter Zewditu and then Ras Tafari Makonnen, later Haile Selassie, followed.

He is praised as a symbol of African resistance to colonialism and is widely regarded as the founder of modern Ethiopia. Critics among the groups incorporated into his empire accuse him of forced assimilation, land expropriation and cultural suppression, and historians describe the atrocities of his southern conquests, particularly against the Oromo, in severe terms; some regard them as genocide.
menes: The name Menes first appears in the work of Manetho, a priest and historian of the Ptolemaic period, who wrote it in Greek as Menes. The Egyptian form mnj, meaning He who endures, comes from the Turin and Abydos king lists of the Nineteenth Dynasty.

I. E. S. Edwards suggested it may have been a descriptive epithet for a hero of whom little was known, and others have proposed that it conceals the collective identity of the Naqada III rulers Ka, Scorpion II and Narmer, or a leadership role rather than a person.

Menes is almost absent from the archaeological record, whereas Narmer is firmly credited with the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. An ivory label from Naqada, found in the tomb of Queen Neithhotep, shows the serekh of Hor-Aha beside a building holding the sign mn, usually taken as Menes. A seal impression from Abydos alternates the serekh of Narmer with the gameboard sign mn.

Flinders Petrie matched Menes with Narmer, and Josep Cervelló-Autuori states the identification categorically, while Stephan Seidlmayer judged it a fairly safe inference that Menes was Hor-Aha. Some scholars read the seal as naming a prince of Narmer called Menes, who would then be his successor Hor-Aha. Opinions still vary, and neither document settles the question.

Menes is missing from the Palermo Stone and the Cairo Stone, but later king lists always place him first among human pharaohs, and some sources have him inherit the throne from Horus. He was regarded as a founding figure through much of Egyptian history, as Romulus was in Rome.

Classical writers gave him many deeds. Herodotus said he founded Memphis as his capital after diverting the Nile with a levee, but a relief found in Sinai in 2012 mentions a visit to Memphis by the earlier ruler Iry-Hor, which suggests the city already existed. Manetho called Menes a native of Thinis and said he led the army across the frontier and won great glory. Diodorus Siculus credited him with the worship of the gods, sacrifice and a more luxurious way of living, and Plutarch mentions a pillar at Thebes inscribed with a curse on Menes for introducing luxury.

Diodorus also records a story of the priests of Sobek that Menes, attacked by his own dogs, fled across Lake Moeris on a crocodile and founded Crocodilopolis. Edwards called the legend devoid of historical value. Manetho says that Menes reigned for 30, 60 or 62 years and was killed by a hippopotamus.
meng-chang: Born Meng Renzan in Taiyuan in 919, he was the fifth son of Meng Zhixiang, an officer of Li Cunxu, Prince of Jin, by a Lady Li who had been Li Cunxu's concubine. After Li Cunxu, as emperor of Later Tang, destroyed Former Shu in 925, Meng Zhixiang became military governor of Xichuan Circuit at Chengdu. When his father executed the monitor Li Yan in 927, the boy, his mother and his father's wife were detained for a time at Fengxiang on their way to join him.

Meng Zhixiang declared himself emperor of Later Shu in 934 and, mortally ill that autumn, made Renzan crown prince and regent. Three days after his father's death he took the throne at 15, changing his name to Meng Chang as the will directed. He soon had the general Li Renhan, accused of plotting treason, arrested and put to death with his son, and forced the senior general Li Zhao into retirement.

His long reign was largely peaceful. The court supported the arts, and the Amidst the Flowers Anthology of lyric poetry was compiled in 940, but the state stagnated militarily and politically. Around the new year 947, as the Khitan Liao took the Later Jin capital, He Chongjian surrendered Qin, Jie and Cheng Prefectures to Later Shu, and Feng Prefecture followed. When Later Zhou attacked in 955 to recover them, Meng put to death his attendant Zhao Jizha, who had fled back to Chengdu in panic.

In 964 he sent secret letters in wax pills to Liu Jun of Northern Han proposing joint strikes on Song; one messenger defected, and the Song emperor took the letters as his justification and sent 60,000 men on two fronts. After his surrender Meng travelled with his family down the Yangtze to Kaifeng in spring 965, where he was received with ceremony and made Duke of Qin, but he died a few days later. Emperor Taizu of Song named him Prince of Chu; his mother, Empress Dowager Li, stopped eating and died soon after.
meng-tian: Meng Tian came from a line of military officials and architects. His grandfather Meng Ao was a general from the era of King Zhao, his father Meng Wu served as deputy to Wang Jian, and he was the elder brother of Meng Yi.

In 224 BCE, after Qin had conquered Wei, the Qin king Ying Zheng appointed Li Xin commander-in-chief and Meng Tian vice-general of a 200,000-strong army to attack Chu. The invasion was at first successful and Meng Tian's army took Qigui, but Chu troops under Xiang Yan and Lord Changping then effectively annihilated both armies. Ying Zheng afterwards gave Wang Jian and Meng Wu command of a 600,000-strong army to complete the conquest of Chu.

By the time Qin conquered the other six states and began its rule over a unified China in 221 BCE, the nomadic Xiongnu had grown into a powerful force in the north and were expanding both east and west. Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor, sent a 300,000-strong army under Meng Tian to drive the Xiongnu northward for 1,000 li (about 416 km) and began work on what became known as the Great Wall.

The defensive works were said to extend over 10,000 li (4,158 km) from Lintao to Liaodong, across the Yellow River and through Yangshan and Beijia. The wall ran along the Yellow River and included all of the Ordos Loop. Meng Tian is credited with an efficient, though inhumane, building policy that took account of topography and natural barriers. He also supervised a road system linking the former Yan, Qi, Wu and Chu areas, with roads for imperial use, which became important for transport and economic exchange.

When Fusu, Qin Shi Huang's eldest son and the crown prince, was exiled to the northern border for disputing his father's policies, Meng Tian was ordered to assist him, a task he carried out loyally. After Qin Shi Huang died, Zhao Gao forged a letter in the emperor's name. Meng Tian was forced to commit suicide in prison and his family was killed. Three years later the Qin dynasty collapsed.

Tradition, though erroneously, credits him with inventing the ink brush, and the Huzhou Pen Festival, which developed from festivities at his ancestor temple, remembers him. He is also credited with the guzheng, a bridge zither of twelve or thirteen strings, and appears as a door god in Chinese and Taoist temples, usually paired with Fusu.
meng-zhixiang: Meng Zhixiang was born on 10 May 874 into a family of Xing Prefecture whose men had served for generations as army officers there; his uncles Meng Fangli and Meng Qian both governed Zhaoyi Circuit late in the Tang dynasty. When Meng Qian surrendered Zhaoyi to Zhu Quanzhong in 901, Meng Zhixiang's father stayed with the warlord Li Keyong of Hedong, who was impressed with the young man's talent, gave him his eldest daughter in marriage and made him a training officer.

Under Li Keyong's son Li Cunxu, Prince of Jin, he saved the official Li Yan from execution around 912, and around 919 declined the dangerous post of chief of staff of Tianxiong, recommending Guo Chongtao, who remained grateful. When Li Cunxu proclaimed the Later Tang in 923 as Emperor Zhuangzong, he made Meng mayor of the western capital, Taiyuan. In 925 Guo, leading the campaign against Former Shu, recommended him to govern Xichuan, and after Chengdu fell the emperor appointed him military governor.

Under Emperor Mingzong, Meng prepared to hold the region himself, raising 36 more corps of some 32,000 soldiers beside the 27,000 Guo had left. When the chancellor Ren Huan sent Zhao Jiliang to Chengdu in winter 926, Meng let the stored wealth of Former Shu go to Luoyang but refused to hand over further taxes. Fearing the accusations of Mingzong's chief adviser An Chonghui, he rebelled in alliance with Dong Zhang of Dongchuan Circuit; they repelled attempts to subdue them, and Meng later overpowered Dong and held both domains as a nominal vassal.

After Mingzong's reign, Meng declared himself emperor of Later Shu. Soon afterwards, when Li Congke rebelled and seized the Later Tang throne, the military governors Zhang Qianzhao of Shannan West and Sun Hanshao of Wuding Circuit surrendered their circuits to him, giving Later Shu the region south of the Qinling Mountains. Meng had reportedly suffered a stroke for over a year; in autumn 934 he made his son Meng Renzan crown prince and died the same day, and the son, renamed Meng Chang, took the throne.
mengu-timur: Mengu-Timur, or Möngke Temür, was a son of Toqoqan Khan, himself a son of Batu, and of Köchu Khatun of Oirat. His name means Eternal Iron in Mongolian. He was one of three candidates for the throne after the death of Berke, the others being Berke's son and his own younger brother, Tode Mongke. Some sources say Berke had designated him as heir to secure the support of Batu's followers. The succession caused tension within the Golden Horde, which Russian sources reflect, and after several months the Jochid elites chose him as khan.

At the start of his reign Mengu-Timur reformed the monetary system with new silver coins that bore his name and seal, with no reference to the great khan. He refused to visit Kublai Khan on his enthronement and instead required an ambassador of Kublai to come to him. He increased the number of mints and made coins of one region valid across the Horde, which protected local trade.

His first decree, in 1267, exempted the Russian Church from tax, and Russian Orthodox clergy were also freed from military service. This followed the policy of Genghis Khan and Ögedei Khan of granting priests tarkhan status in exchange for prayers for the khan and his family. He did not convert to Islam, but he exchanged embassies with the Mamluk Sultanate, and the alliance continued after the war with the Ilkhanate ended. Around 1275-1280 he allowed the Genoese to rent Caffa, welcoming the traders as long as they paid taxes and respected the law.

He tried to restore peaceful tributary relations with the Byzantine Empire. Michael VIII Palaiologos sent a large tribute of textiles and offered his daughter Euphrosyne, who was married to Nogai Khan. The agreement that let ships pass through the Bosporus and the Dardanelles from the Black Sea was maintained. In the wider Mongol world he sided with Kaidu, a rival of Kublai.

In 1280 Mengu-Timur launched a campaign against Poland that ended in defeat, and he died soon afterwards. His alliance with the Byzantines strengthened the Golden Horde's control of access to the Black Sea, while the alliance with the Mamluks gave the Jochids access to the Nile and the Red Sea.
menkaure: Menkaure is known in Greek as Mykerinos, Latinized Mycerinus, and to Manetho as Menkheres. Manetho names Bikheris as his predecessor, but the archaeological evidence points almost certainly to Khafre. A flint knife from his mortuary temple mentions a king's mother, Khamerernebty I, which suggests that she and Khafre were his parents. His brothers Nebemakhet, Duaenre, Nikaure and Iunmin served as viziers during his reign. Queen Khamerernebty II was the mother of a king's son, Khuenre, who probably died before his father, and the throne passed to Shepseskaf, a younger son.

The length of the reign is uncertain. Manetho gives 63 years, which is surely an exaggeration. The Turin King List is damaged where the total should stand, and Egyptologists generally accept that 18 years was meant. A workmen's graffito mentions the year after the 11th cattle count; if the count was held every second year, he might have ruled for 22 years. In 2013 a fragment of a sphinx of Menkaure was found at Tel Hazor.

His pyramid at Giza, called Netjer-er-Menkaure, meaning Menkaure is Divine, measures 103.4 metres at the base and 65.5 metres in height, the smallest of the three main pyramids there. Three subsidiary pyramids stand beside it. His valley temple, mainly of brick, yielded the statues for which he is best known: greywacke triads showing the king with the goddess Hathor and the deities of different nomes, and a double statue of the king with a queen, probably Khamerernebty II.

In 1837 Richard William Howard Vyse and John Shae Perring entered the pyramid and found a basalt sarcophagus in the burial chamber, undecorated by hieroglyphs, beside wooden coffin fragments bearing the king's name and a partial skeleton. The ship carrying the sarcophagus to London was lost after leaving Malta in October 1838. The coffin is now thought to be a replacement made during the Saite period, and radiocarbon dating placed the bones in the Coptic period.

Herodotus, writing long afterwards, made Menkaure a pious son of Khufu whose only daughter died before him and whom an oracle at Buto doomed to a short life. He is said to have turned night into day by revelling, to double his remaining six years. This is a late tradition, not contemporary evidence.
menli-i-giray: Meñli I Giray was the sixth son of Hacı I Giray. When Hacı Giray died, power passed to his eldest son Nur Devlet, who was supported by the Great Horde, and Meñli revolted with the backing of the Crimean nobility. In 1467 he occupied the capital, Kyrk-Er, but Nur Devlet soon drove him out and he fled to the Genoese at Kaffa.

In June 1468 a delegation of nobles elected him khan at Kaffa. He marched on the capital with the nobles and a Genoese detachment, and after six months Nur Devlet was expelled; he fled to the North Caucasus but was captured and imprisoned in the Genoese fortress at Sudak. Meñli was khan three times in all, and it took him twelve years to establish himself.

In his second reign Meñli made an anti-Turkish alliance with the Principality of Theodoro, and in the summer of 1469 a Turkish fleet burned villages near Kaffa. In March 1475 the nobles replaced him with his elder brother Hayder, and in May a large Turkish fleet took Kaffa, other Genoese forts and Theodoro. Meñli, who had supported the Genoese, was captured and taken to Constantinople. In the spring of 1478 he was released and returned to Crimea with a Turkish fleet and troops, and became khan as a Turkish vassal.

In 1480 he allied with Ivan III, the grand prince of Moscow, against Poland-Lithuania, the Great Horde and the Khanate of Astrakhan, an alliance that counted in the great stand on the Ugra River. In September 1482 he ravaged Kiev and took Ivan Chodkiewicz and his family hostage, and from 1489 to 1500 the Crimean Tatars repeatedly devastated Podolia and Volyn. In 1502 he defeated the last khan of the Golden Horde, took its capital, Saray, and proclaimed himself Khagan. Genoese mercenaries formed a significant part of his army, and he founded the fortress of Özü.

Meñli was buried in the dürbe of Salaçıq in Bakhchysarai. In that city he commissioned the Zıncırlı Medrese in 1500, the dürbe in 1501 and the Demir Qapı, or Iron Gate, of the Bakhchysarai Palace in 1503, the last by Aloisio the New. Two of his sons, Mehmed I Giray and Sahib I Giray, also became khans. His daughter Ayşe Hatun married first Şehzade Mehmed, a son of Sultan Bayezid II, and after him his half-brother Sultan Selim I. One of his wives, Nur Sultan, was one of only three women known to have had a political role in the Crimean Khanate.
mennonites: The Mennonites trace their roots to the Radical Reformation in the German and Dutch-speaking regions of central Europe. Their persecutors called the forerunners of the movement Täufer or Wiedertäufer, re-baptizers. Their most distinguishing feature was the rejection of infant baptism, an act with political as well as religious meaning, since almost every infant born in western Europe was baptised in the Roman Catholic Church. Their views also developed in opposition to those of Protestant reformers such as Martin Luther and Huldrych Zwingli.

Menno Simons, a Frisian cleric who lived from 1496 to 1561, became a prominent leader of the wider movement and formalised the teachings of earlier Swiss Anabaptist founders. Anabaptists of Dutch and North German background took their name from him, and the Swiss and South German group later adopted it too. A third group, organised by Jakob Hutter, became the Hutterites.

In the 16th century the Mennonites and other Anabaptists were relentlessly persecuted. Martyrs Mirror, published in 1660, records much of it, including accounts of over 4,000 burnings, and numerous stonings, imprisonments and live burials. Persecution continued in parts of Switzerland until 1710. Rather than resist by arms, most early followers survived by fleeing to neighbouring states whose ruling families tolerated believer's baptism.

Beliefs were set out in the Schleitheim Confession of 24 February 1527, which covered the ban, communion, separation from the world, believer's baptism, pastors, renunciation of the sword and renunciation of the oath. The Dordrecht Confession of Faith, adopted by Dutch Mennonites on 21 April 1632, was later taken up by Alsatian and North American Mennonites.

Persecution and the search for employment drove Mennonites from the Netherlands eastward to Germany in the 17th century. Others settled around Danzig and in West Prussia from about 1530, and from 1791 they founded colonies in the south-west of the Russian Empire. In 1683 families from Krefeld settled at Germantown, Pennsylvania, the first permanent Mennonite settlement in the American colonies, and in 1688 four of them signed the first formal protest against slavery in the United States.

Mennonites are known as one of the historic peace churches because of their pacifism. Congregations range from Old Order Mennonites, who live without certain elements of modern technology, to mainline Mennonites who dress like the general population. There is no single world authority, and the Mennonite World Conference, founded at Basel in 1925, coordinates shared causes without making binding decisions. The Mennonite Central Committee, founded in Chicago on 27 September 1920, provides disaster relief and development work around the world.
menorca: Menorca takes its name from the Latin Insula Minor, the smaller island, in contrast to nearby Mallorca. Its capital is Mahón, at the eastern end of the island, and Ciutadella de Menorca and Mahón are the main ports and largest towns. Its highest point, El Toro, rises to 358 metres. The island is known for its megalithic monuments, including navetes, taules and talaiots, which indicate very early prehistoric human activity.

The end of the Punic Wars brought an increase in piracy in the western Mediterranean, and the pirates used Menorca and Mallorca as bases. The Romans invaded in response, and by 123 BCE both islands were fully under Roman control. The Vandals conquered Menorca in the 5th century and the Byzantine Empire recovered it in 534. In 903 it was annexed to the Caliphate of Córdoba and many Muslims emigrated there. The Arabic name Manûrqa was used until the rule of the last Muslim ra'îs, Abû 'Umar ibn Sa'îd, ended in 1287.

After Christian forces took Mallorca in 1231, Menorca chose to become an independent Islamic state that paid tribute to King James I of Aragon. A Catalan-Aragonese invasion under Alfonso III landed on 17 January 1287, and its anniversary is now Menorca's national day. Most of the Muslim inhabitants were enslaved and sold in the markets of Eivissa, Valencia and Barcelona, while others became Christians. The island was part of the Crown of Aragon, was briefly ceded to the Kingdom of Mallorca, and was retaken by Aragon in 1343.

Anglo-Dutch forces captured Menorca in 1708 during the War of the Spanish Succession, and Spain ceded it to Great Britain in the Peace of Utrecht of 1713. Under British rule the capital moved to Mahón and a Royal Navy base was established in its harbour. French forces captured the island in 1756, Britain regained it in 1763, and Franco-Spanish forces took it in 1782. The British captured it once more in 1798 and ceded it to Spain in the Treaty of Amiens of 1802.

Menorca belongs to Spain and forms a political union with the other Balearic Islands, though it is not a province. It had 102,477 inhabitants in 2025. During the Spanish Civil War it stayed loyal to the Second Spanish Republic, and after the Nationalist victory in February 1939 the Royal Navy assisted in a peaceful transfer of power. UNESCO designated the island a biosphere reserve in October 1993.
mensheviks: The Mensheviks were a faction of the Marxist Russian Social Democratic Labour Party that split with Vladimir Lenin's Bolsheviks at the Second Party Congress in August 1903. Julius Martov and Lenin disagreed over the editorial committee of the party newspaper Iskra and over the definition of a party member. Lenin's formulation required membership of one of the party's organisations, while Martov's required only work under the guidance of one. Lenin argued for a small party of professional revolutionaries, Martov for a large party of activists with broad representation.

Martov's definition was accepted by 28 votes to 23. But seven delegates then left, five of them representatives of the Jewish Bund who protested the defeat of their own federalist proposal, and Lenin's supporters gained a slight majority, which decided the names of the factions.

The 4th Congress of 1906 formally reunited the party, with the Mensheviks in the majority, yet Lenin's definition of a party member replaced Martov's. The two factions kept separate structures. Both held that Russia was too undeveloped for socialism, so that the revolution against the tsarist regime would be bourgeois-democratic. After 1905 the Mensheviks were more inclined to work with liberal parties such as the Constitutional Democrats, and argued for legal methods and trade union work, while the Bolsheviks favoured armed violence and alliances with peasant representatives.

Georgi Plekhanov's position that a period of capitalism had to come before a socialist revolution was associated with the Mensheviks. Alexander Potresov called for the party to suspend illegal work, and in 1908 Lenin called Mensheviks who left for legal organisations liquidationists. Leaders included Martov and Pavel Axelrod. The party split formally in 1912. The Menshevik faction split further in 1917: most opposed the war, but a vocal minority supported it as national defence.
menton: Menton lies on the Mediterranean at the Franco-Italian border, just across from the Ligurian town of Ventimiglia. It has always been a frontier town: since the end of the 14th century it has stood on the border between the County of Nice, held by the Duke of Savoy, and the Republic of Genoa. The mild climate favours groves of lemons, oranges, mandarins and clementines, and the lemon is one of the town's symbols.

The first major settlement came in the 11th century, when the count of Ventimiglia built the Château de Puypin. In the 13th century the Vento family of Genoa built a new castle along the Roman road, around which the present town grew. The first mention of Menton is in the peace treaty between Charles of Anjou and Genoa, dated 21 July 1262. In 1346 Charles Grimaldi, Lord of Monaco, acquired it, and the princes of Monaco ruled it until the French Revolution.

In 1848, partly because of a tax on lemon exports, Menton and its neighbour Roquebrune seceded from Monaco and proclaimed the Free Cities of Menton and Roquebrune, hoping to join the Kingdom of Sardinia. Two years later they placed themselves under its protection and were administered by the House of Savoy for ten years.

The Treaty of Turin of 24 March 1860 provided for the annexation of the County of Nice to France, subject to a plebiscite. It was held on 15 and 16 April 1860, and Menton and Roquebrune voted 833 to 54 in favour. Napoleon III paid 4 million francs in compensation to the prince of Monaco, who renounced his rights on 2 February 1861.

James Henry Bennett's book Winter and Spring on the Shores of the Mediterranean (1861) made Menton a destination for sufferers of tuberculosis, and by the end of the 19th century tourism was an important part of its growth. British and Russian aristocrats built many of the hotels, villas and palaces that remain. In June 1940 Menton was the only sizable settlement captured by Italy in its invasion of France, and Italy annexed two thirds of the commune until 8 September 1943. American and Canadian troops of the First Special Service Force liberated it on 8 September 1944. It is nicknamed the Pearl of France and is known for its gardens.
mentuhotep-i: Mentuhotep I, also called Mentuhotep-aa, meaning the Great, may have been a nomarch of Thebes and an independent ruler of Upper Egypt in the early First Intermediate Period, about 2135 BCE. Some Egyptologists instead propose that he is a fictional ancestor, invented during the later Eleventh Dynasty, which rose to prominence under Intef II and Mentuhotep II, to serve as a founding father; no contemporary monument can safely be attributed to him.

The Karnak king list in the Festival Hall of Thutmose III preserves at position 12 the partial name Men- in a royal cartouche, with the Horus name Tepia, 'the ancestor', and it is distinct from those of Mentuhotep II and Mentuhotep III. The list does not seem to present past kings in chronological order, so it cannot show whether or when he lived.

As nomarch of Thebes his dominion perhaps extended south to the first cataract. He may have formed an alliance with the nomarch of Coptos, which would then have brought his successor Intef I to war with the Herakleopolitan kings of the 10th Dynasty and their powerful allies among the nomarchs of Middle Egypt, in particular Ankhtifi. This is hypothesis. His throne name is unknown, and since he may not have been a king, and no later Eleventh Dynasty king bore a throne name until Mentuhotep II, he probably never had one. His Horus name was certainly given to him after his death.

On the base of a statue from the sanctuary of Heqaib on Elephantine, a Mentuhotep is called 'Father of the gods'. The title probably refers to his immediate successors Intef I and Intef II, who reigned as kings over Upper Egypt. Many Egyptologists have concluded from it that he was their father and was never a pharaoh, since the title was usually reserved for the non-royal ancestors of pharaohs.

His wife may have been Neferu I. The Karnak list also names at position 13 a person without a cartouche called Intef, who may be Intef the elder, son of Iku, a Theban nomarch loyal to the Herakleopolitan kings, though the order of the list makes this uncertain.
mentuhotep-ii: Mentuhotep II succeeded his father Intef III on the throne at Thebes and ruled for 51 years according to the Turin Canon. He inherited the lands his predecessors had conquered from the first cataract in the south to Abydos in the north. The rival 10th Dynasty ruled Lower Egypt from Herakleopolis. His first fourteen years seem peaceful. In his fourteenth year, named the Year of the crime of Thinis, the Herakleopolitan kings apparently desecrated the ancient royal necropolis at Abydos, and he sent his armies north. At Deir el-Bahari a tomb held the linen-wrapped bodies of 60 soldiers killed in battle, their shrouds bearing his cartouche, and it is believed to be that of men who died in this conflict.

Reunification probably came shortly before his 39th regnal year, when he changed his titulary to Sematawy, 'He who unifies the two lands'. The process took time: commoners were buried with weapons, and an expedition to Punt sent by his successor some twenty years later still had to clear the Wadi Hammamat of rebels loyal to the fallen Herakleopolitan rulers. In his 29th and 31st years his vizier Khety led campaigns into Nubia, the first attested appearance of the term Kush in Egyptian records, and a garrison was posted at Elephantine.

After unification he reversed the decentralisation that had marked the First Intermediate Period. Nomarchs, whose offices had become hereditary in the 6th Dynasty, lost some of their power. He created the posts of Governor of Upper Egypt and Governor of Lower Egypt over them and sent officials from the capital to travel the country and supervise regional leaders. Nomarchs who had supported the 10th Dynasty, such as the governor of Asyut, certainly lost their power. His viziers were Bebi and Dagi, and the treasurer Meketre is among his officials.

His titularies show a return to Old Kingdom tradition and a programme of self-deification. His subjects regarded him as divine or half divine, and stelae of Senusret III and Amenemhat III, some 200 years later, record ceremonies performed on his statues.

Mentuhotep II was buried at Deir el-Bahari. His terraced mortuary temple, Akh-sut Nebhepetre, broke with the Old Kingdom pyramid complex and was the earliest mortuary temple where the king himself enacts ceremonies for the gods and is identified with Osiris. It inspired the temples of Hatshepsut and Thutmose III, built about 550 years later. Lord Dufferin began excavating it in 1859, Howard Carter found the black seated Ka statue of the king in 1898, and Naville, Winlock and Dieter Arnold followed.
mentuhotep-iii: Sankhkare Mentuhotep III belonged to the 11th Dynasty and ruled Egypt in the Middle Kingdom. He was the son and successor of Mentuhotep II, and his mother was Tem, one of that king's wives, who bore the title Mother of the Dual King. His father had reigned for 51 years, so Mentuhotep III is believed to have been relatively old when he came to the throne.

His family is mostly a mystery. It is currently believed that he fathered his successor Mentuhotep IV with one of his probable harem wives, Imi, though Egyptologists still debate this. His titulary is very similar to the third and final one of his father, and he is known to have had at least two praenomina, the best known being Sankhkare.

The Turin Canon assigns him a reign of 12 years. In the eighth year he sent an expedition to the Land of Punt, something not done since the Old Kingdom. An inscription in the Wadi Hammamat describes it as 3,000 men strong and under the command of the steward Henenu. Leaving Coptos for the Red Sea, perhaps for the port now known as Mersa Gawasis, they dug 12 wells for future expeditions and cleared the region of rebels. They returned from Punt with incense, gum and perfumes, and quarried stone in the Wadi Hammamat.
He also undertook several building projects. He extended the temple of Monthu at Medamud, from which a monumental decorated doorway bearing his likeness and royal titles is now in the Louvre.

He had a mudbrick temple dedicated to the god Montu-Ra built at Thoth Hill in western Thebes, on the site of an older temple; it may have been destroyed by an earthquake towards the end of the dynasty.

It was long presumed that his tomb and mortuary temple were begun at Deir el-Bahari, in a valley a short distance from his father's mortuary temple, but never completed. A burial chamber lined with limestone slabs was finished and sealed but apparently never held a burial. The link to Mentuhotep III rested on the monument's position beside the tomb of the High Steward Meketre, one of the chief officials of the reign. Dorothea Arnold has since offered evidence that it is the unfinished Theban tomb of Amenemhat I, though that attribution is also unproven, so the burial place of Mentuhotep III remains unknown.
mentuhotep-iv: Mentuhotep IV, whose throne name was Nebtawyre, is thought to fit a period in the Turin Canon for which no king is recorded. His parentage is uncertain. A rock inscription in the Wadi Hammamat carries his royal name and mentions a King's Mother named Imi, presumably his mother; some have speculated that she was a concubine. Most scholars suggest that his father was Mentuhotep III, though he could have been a son of Mentuhotep II. His omission from several king lists, and the poor documentation of his reign, have been taken to indicate a crisis of succession at the end of the dynasty.

He is known from inscriptions mainly in the Eastern Desert and on the Red Sea coast, although the Abydos King List omits him. Four inscriptions at Wadi el-Hudi are dated to his first year. At the Red Sea port of Ain Sukhna an inscription records the arrival of the king's men with a workforce of 3,000, sent to bring back turquoise, copper and other products of the desert. Such goods were taken some 120 km across the Eastern Desert to Memphis, or perhaps along the coast to Mersa Gawasis.

Inscriptions in the Wadi Hammamat record expeditions to the Red Sea coast and to quarry stone for the royal monuments. In his second year the expedition was led by his vizier Amenemhat, assumed to be the future Amenemhat I, founder of the 12th Dynasty and his successor. Some Egyptologists suppose that Amenemhat usurped the throne or took power after the king died childless, but no evidence shows how Amenemhat rose to the throne.
menua: Menua was the fifth known king of Urartu, ruling from around 810 BCE to 786 BCE. He was a younger son of the preceding king, Ishpuini, and married Tariria. Ishpuini adopted him as co-ruler in the last years of his reign. An inscription refers to both Ishpuini and Menua, and another mentions his father, himself and his son Inušpua, which suggests that Menua was of some age when he became coregent. His name may be connected etymologically to the Greek names Minos and Minyas.

As sole ruler Menua enlarged the kingdom through numerous wars against neighbouring countries and left many inscriptions across the region, by far the most of any Urartian ruler. He organised a centralised administrative structure, fortified a number of towns and built fortresses, among them Menuakhinili near Mount Ararat, whose exact location is uncertain. It is believed that he founded the city of Manazkert, now Malazgirt.

In the north-west, in what is now Georgia, he defeated Uṭuburšini, King of the Diauehi, who became a vassal paying tribute. An inscription at Alazlı, east of Muş, records his capture of the city of Trtimi in the land of Urme. He ruled briefly with his son Inushpua but was succeeded by another son, Argishti I. A daughter named Tariria gave her name to a vineyard, Taririakhinli.

Menua developed a canal and irrigation system that stretched across the kingdom. The most important was a long canal from the Hoşap valley to Van, named the Menua Canal, which flowed at 1,500 to 3,000 litres of water a second depending on the season. It passed along slopes and in its lower parts was built of huge stones on a wide wall, and several of these canals are still in use. Menua is said to have been the first Urartian king to design and build irrigation networks, which contributed to farming and to the vineyards of Urartu. The Assyrian king Sennacherib is said to have used the skill of Urartian technicians in building his own water works.
menumorut: In the Gesta Hungarorum, written by an unidentified author known as Anonymus, Menumorut's duchy lay between the rivers Tisza, Mureș and Someș and the Igyfon Wood, with Biharia as his main fortress, and was inhabited by Khazars and Székelys. Anonymus makes him the grandson of a Prince Marót who ruled the region in the time of Attila the Hun, calls him a polygamist with many concubines, and links his name to the Hungarian word for stallion. He has him declare that the emperor of Constantinople was his lord.

According to the Gesta, Grand Prince Árpád sent the envoys Ősbő and Velek to demand his land from the Someș to the Meseș Gates, and Menumorut refused. The commanders Tas, Szabolcs and Tétény crossed the Tisza, received the surrender of most of the inhabitants, built an earthen fortress named after Szabolcs and took Satu Mare, but Menumorut's warriors stopped them at the Criș at Szeghalom.

After the birth of Árpád's son Zoltán, Ősbő and Velek came again, joined by the Székelys. Menumorut withdrew with his wife and daughter into the Igyfon Wood, and Biharia surrendered after a siege of twelve days in which, by Anonymus's count, twenty Magyars, fifteen Székelys and 125 defenders died. Menumorut then gave his daughter to Zoltán and kept Biharia for life; he died without a son not long before 907, leaving his kingdom to Zoltán.

Historians question these reports. Gyula Kristó held that Anonymus drew on his own imagination, and György Györffy that Menumorut was invented and named after a place; Carlile Aylmer Macartney saw the episode as a repetition of the story of Salan. Two 13th-century villages called Marótlaka and a clan Morut in Bihar County show that at least one Morut settled there, and Ryszard Grzesik concludes that Menumorut never ruled Bihar but was not an invented person. An early medieval fortress at Biharia has been taken for his capital, though Florin Curta argues that nothing dates it before the 10th century.
meppen: Meppen lies in the central part of the Emsland, at the mouth of the Hase where it meets the Ems, between Lingen and Papenburg and about 20 kilometres from the Dutch border. The Nordradde and the Dortmund–Ems Canal also meet there. The name is said to stem from the word Mappe, meaning delta. Since the district reforms of 1977 it has been the administrative seat of the Emsland district.

The first documented mention dates from 834, in a deed of donation by the Frankish emperor Louis the Pious that transferred a missionary establishment of that name to the abbey of Corvey. Otto the Great granted the settlement coin minting and toll rights in 945 and market rights in 946. In 1252 Countess Jutta von Vechta-Ravensberg sold her possessions to the Bishop of Münster, which brought Meppen into the Lower Prince-Bishopric of Münster. Bishop Adolf granted town rights and permission to build fortifications in 1360. They were extended until 1660 and demolished during the Seven Years War.

After the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss of 1803 Meppen became the capital of the Duchy of Arenberg under Louis Engelbert. It was incorporated into the First French Empire in 1811 and occupied by Prussia in 1813 and 1814, and the Congress of Vienna awarded it with the Duchy of Arenberg to the Kingdom of Hanover. When Hanover was annexed by Prussia in 1866 Meppen followed, and in 1871 it became part of the German Empire.

In November 1938 local Nazi police and SA members destroyed the town synagogue and plundered Jewish property. In 1939 Stalag VI-B was set up at Meppen-Versen for Polish, French, Belgian, Soviet and Italian prisoners of war. In 1944 it became a subcamp of the Neuengamme concentration camp, where over 1,700 forced labourers were held under severe conditions and over 20 percent died. Canadian forces liberated the town on 8 April 1945.

The centre has few historic buildings. The town hall was built in 1408 from glacial erratics and enlarged between 1601 and 1605. The Priory Church of St. Vitus, a late Gothic hall church, dates from about 1461–62, on the site of a stone building of the 9th century. The Koppelschleuse locks of 1826 to 1830 survive from the old Ems–Hase Canal.
merano: Merano, in German Meran, is a municipality in South Tyrol, northern Italy, and the second-largest city of South Tyrol after Bolzano. It lies in a basin at the entrance to the Passeier Valley and the Vinschgau, surrounded by mountains that rise to 3,335 metres. Both the Italian and German names are official, and an early form, Mairania, is recorded from 857.

The area has been inhabited since the third millennium BCE, and the history of the town proper begins in 15 BCE, when the Romans founded a road station there, Statio Maiensis. In the 13th century the Counts at Castle Tyrol raised it to the status of a city and made it capital of their County of Tyrol. The county passed to the Habsburg dynasty in 1363, and in 1420 Duke Friedrich IV of Austria moved the court to Innsbruck. Merano stayed the official capital until 1848 but lost almost all its importance as a trading point on the roads between Italy and Germany.

In 1809 a peasants' army won a victory over French and Bavarian forces on the Küchelberg above the city. In the 19th century its mild Alpine climate made Meran a spa town within Austria-Hungary, visited by Franz Kafka and Empress Elisabeth. After the First World War, under the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye, it became part of Italy.

Merano combines Austrian and Italian cultural heritage. Its medieval city gates survive, as do the Gothic St Nicholas' Church and the Princely Castle, which was a residence of Archduke Sigismund of Austria. The spa years left the Kurhaus, the Stadttheater, the Empress Elisabeth Park and arched promenades along the Passer. Tirol Castle stands close by, and vineyards extend into the city.
mercantilism: Mercantilism became the dominant school of economic thought in Europe through the late Renaissance and the early modern period, before the rise of classical liberalism. Mercantilist practices appeared early in Venice, Genoa and Pisa, in their control of the Mediterranean trade in bullion. The Italian economist Antonio Serra wrote one of the first treatises on political economy in 1613. The term was first used only by critics such as Mirabeau and Adam Smith, and the older English term was the mercantile system. Smith saw the English merchant Thomas Mun as a major creator of the system through Treasure by Foreign Trade, published after his death in 1664.

In its simplest form mercantilism is bullionism, the view that a nation's wealth is measured by the gold and silver it holds. Its writers were concerned with the movement of money more than with hoarding. The aim was to maximise exports and minimise imports and to build state power at the expense of rivals. Policies included high tariffs, banning the export of gold and silver, and the Navigation Acts, which forbade trade to be carried in foreign ships.

In France it is closely tied to Jean-Baptiste Colbert, finance minister for 22 years in the 17th century, so that French mercantilism is sometimes called Colbertism. Under him industries were organised into guilds and monopolies, foreign artisans were brought in, and roads and canals were built. French industrial output grew considerably, but Britain and the Dutch Republic stayed supreme in trade.

Mercantilism fed imperial expansion, as European states conquered colonies as sources of gold or sugar and as exclusive markets, often through chartered monopolies such as the Dutch East India Company. If trade is seen as fixed, one state can increase its trade only by taking it from another, and the Anglo-Dutch Wars can be linked to such theories.

In the 18th century critics undermined it. In 1690 John Locke argued that prices vary in proportion to the quantity of money, and David Hume showed that a constant surplus of trade cannot last. Smith criticised the doctrine as a system serving traders, though he praised the Navigation Acts for their effect on British shipping.
mercator-projection: The Mercator projection is a conformal cylindrical map projection first presented by the Flemish geographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569. Earlier charts did not use it. The 13th-century portolan charts of the Mediterranean, the earliest to survive, are generally not believed to rest on any deliberate projection. They carried networks of windrose lines that helped set a ship's bearing, and over so small a region a course of constant bearing was approximately straight on the chart. Joseph Needham suggested that some Song dynasty star charts used the Mercator projection, but he gave no evidence, and the historian Kazuhiko Miyajima concluded from measurement that they used an equirectangular projection.

The projection can be pictured as wrapping a cylinder around a sphere, touching it along the equator, and unfolding the sphere onto the cylinder so that angles between intersecting curves are kept. Scale is exact along the equator and grows with distance from it, as the secant of the latitude: about 1.15 at 30 degrees, 2 at 60 degrees and over 11 at 85 degrees. Areas therefore swell towards the poles. Greenland appears about the size of Africa, though Africa is 14 times as large.

Its purpose was navigation. Any course of constant bearing, called a rhumb or loxodrome, appears as a straight segment, so a ship can keep one compass direction rather than making error-prone corrections. Mercator observed that on such a course a ship would not arrive by the shortest route but would surely arrive. He understood the difference between rhumb distance and great-circle distance, and advised that rhumb measurements suit short or moderate courses, especially at low latitudes.

In the 18th century it became the standard projection for navigation, and practically every printed marine chart is based on it. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries it was perhaps the commonest projection for world maps, until atlases largely abandoned it for such maps in the 1940s. Critics such as George Kellaway and Irving Fisher judged it unsuitable for general world maps. It has been conjectured that it made people think of countries near the equator as less important, but later perception studies have failed to find such an effect. Mercator himself used the equal-area sinusoidal projection to show relative areas. Variants remain in use, including Web Mercator for online maps and the transverse Mercator behind most national grid systems.
mercedes-sosa: Haydée Mercedes Sosa was born on 9 July 1935 in San Miguel de Tucumán, in the north-western Argentine province of Tucumán, of mestizo ancestry: French, Spanish and Diaguita. Her nickname la Negra, common in Argentina for people with a darker complexion, refers to her indigenous heritage. She began her career singing for the Peronist Party in Tucumán under the name Gladys Osorio. In 1950, at fifteen, she won a singing competition run by a local radio station. She recorded her first album, La voz de la zafra, in 1959.

A performance at the Cosquín National Folklore Festival in 1965, where fellow singer Jorge Cafrune brought her on stage from the audience, drew her to the attention of the Argentine public. She toured the United States and Europe in 1967 and widened her repertoire to include material from across Latin America. In the early 1970s she made two concept albums with the composer Ariel Ramírez and the lyricist Félix Luna, Cantata sudamericana and Mujeres argentinas, and in 1971 a tribute to the Chilean musician Violeta Parra that included Gracias a la vida, one of her signature songs. She also popularised songs by Milton Nascimento of Brazil and by Pablo Milanés and Silvio Rodríguez of Cuba.

After the military junta of Jorge Videla came to power in 1976, Sosa faced death threats against herself and her family but for many years refused to leave. At a concert in La Plata in 1979 she was searched and arrested on stage together with those attending, and they were released through international intervention. She was officially barred from performing and moved to Paris and then Madrid. She returned to Argentina in February 1982, several months before the military regime collapsed, and gave concerts at the Teatro Ópera in Buenos Aires, recorded as Mercedes Sosa en Argentina.

She played the Sistine Chapel in 1994 and in 2002 sold out both Carnegie Hall in New York and the Colosseum in Rome. Sosa disliked being called a protest singer; she held that an artist's constituency is the public and that it is the poetry that matters most. She served as a UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador for Latin America and the Caribbean. She won Latin Grammy awards, including a lifetime achievement award in 2004.

Sosa was hospitalised in Buenos Aires on 18 September 2009 and died on 4 October 2009 of multiple organ failure, aged 74. Her body lay in the National Congress building, and three days of national mourning were ordered.
mercenary: A mercenary, also called a soldier of fortune, is a private individual who joins an armed conflict for personal profit, is otherwise an outsider to the conflict and is not a member of any other official military. Mercenaries fight for money or other forms of payment rather than for political interests. Whether a person counts as a mercenary may be a matter of degree, since financial and political interests can overlap.

Article 47 of the 1977 Protocol Additional to the Geneva Conventions gives the most widely accepted international definition. It lists conditions such as being specially recruited to fight, taking a direct part in hostilities, being motivated essentially by private gain, and being neither a national of a party to the conflict nor a member of its armed forces. A mercenary has no right to be a combatant or a prisoner of war.

Hired soldiers appear in the earliest records. Ramesses II of Egypt is said to have used 11,000 mercenaries in his battles in the thirteenth century BCE, and Egypt long recruited foreign corps such as the Medjay from Nubia. In 401 BCE Cyrus the Younger hired a large army of Greek mercenaries, the Ten Thousand, to seize the Persian throne from his brother Artaxerxes II. After Cyrus died at the Battle of Cunaxa, Xenophon helped lead the survivors north to the Black Sea, as he recounts in the Anabasis. Carthage was unusual in relying primarily on mercenaries.

Kingdoms of the Warring States period in China regularly employed them, and the Tang dynasty hired Tibetan and Uyghur soldiers against the Göktürks. In Japan the Saika group of Kii Province impeded the forces of Oda Nobunaga during the Siege of Ishiyama Hongan-ji between 1570 and 1580. In Nicaragua in 1855 the American William Walker, hired by the Liberals, defeated the Conservatives at the Battle of La Virgen and became the country's de facto ruler. By 1807 Muhammad Ali of Egypt had imported about 400 French mercenaries to train his army.

From the twentieth century mercenaries came to be seen as less entitled to protection under the rules of war. Foreign nationals who serve in a state's regular forces, such as the Gurkha units of the British and Indian armies and the French Foreign Legion, are not classed as mercenaries under Article 47, because they belong to its armed forces.
mercenary-war: The First Punic War ended with the Treaty of Lutatius, by which Carthage evacuated Sicily and paid an indemnity of 3,200 talents. Carthaginian armies were nearly always composed of foreigners, most of them North Africans, whom Roman sources call mercenaries. The 20,000 soldiers of the army in Sicily were sent back to Carthage in small detachments by Gisco, in the expectation that they would be paid their years of back pay. The authorities instead hoped to settle at a lower rate. When the Senate refused to pay in full the men marched to Tunis. Gisco brought money, but discipline broke down, Gisco was taken prisoner, and Spendius and Matho were declared generals.

African towns resentful of Carthaginian taxation rose in revolt, and Polybius says 70,000 men joined the rebels. Hanno won the Battle of Utica in early 240 BCE but lost the counter-attack. Hamilcar Barca, given command of a smaller force, defeated the rebels at the Battle of the Bagradas River, and the Numidian leader Naravas then changed sides with 2,000 cavalry.

Hamilcar treated captured rebels leniently. Spendius and the Gaul Autaritus had 700 Carthaginian prisoners, Gisco among them, tortured to death, and from then on neither side gave mercy: Polybius called it the Truceless War. Utica and Hippo joined the rebels, who besieged Carthage until supplies failed. Hamilcar trapped Spendius's army in a pass called the Saw, where it was massacred, and the leaders he had taken were crucified. Hanno and Hamilcar together later destroyed the remaining 30,000 rebels, and Matho was tortured to death in Carthage.

Rome had declined an appeal from the mutinous garrisons on Sardinia, but when the islanders drove them out, probably in 237 BCE, it agreed to intervene. When Carthage prepared its own expedition, the Roman Senate called this an act of war and required the cession of Sardinia and Corsica and an extra indemnity of 1,200 talents. Polybius considered this bad faith the main cause of the Second Punic War. Hamilcar's victory raised the standing of the Barcid family, and Carthage's generals were afterwards chosen by their armies.
merck-group: The roots of Merck lie in the Landgraviate of Hesse-Darmstadt. In 1668 an apothecary, Friedrich Jacob Merck, took over the Engel-Apotheke, the Angel Pharmacy, in Darmstadt. In 1816 Emanuel Merck, a descendant of the founder, took over the pharmacy. With a scientific education, he isolated and characterised several alkaloids in its laboratory and so invented a number of drugs. In 1827 he began to make these substances in bulk, offering them as a Cabinet of Pharmaceutical and Chemical Innovations. He and his successors gradually built a chemical and pharmaceutical factory that made raw materials for pharmaceutical preparations, many other chemicals and, from 1890, medicines.

After Wilhelm Adam Sertürner isolated morphine from opium in 1805, Merck pioneered its commercial manufacture from 1827 for an expanding world market. From 1884 it also produced and marketed cocaine, and Sigmund Freud, author of Über Coca (1884), collaborated enthusiastically in its cocaine research, though the method of his self-experiments has been challenged.

Vitamins became a new product line, with Vigantol introduced in 1927 and Cebion in 1934. In 1891 Georg Merck set up Merck & Co. in New York with Theodore Weicker; it was later confiscated in the United States, and George W. Merck, a member of an American branch of the family, repurchased its stock in 1919.

Under Nazi rule the firm was led by Karl Emanuel Merck, who joined the Nazi Party in 1933. In the war years it made narcotics, vitamins, biocides and other chemicals. By the company's own account 265 forced labourers worked in the Darmstadt plant, most of them women from Russia and Poland, besides several hundred foreign workers from France and Belgium. An air raid on 12 December 1944 destroyed nearly 70 per cent of the plant and killed 55 employees.
