After the war the military government let Merck resume making drugs, pesticides, food preservatives and laboratory chemicals.

The firm was legally E. Merck oHG until 1995, when it was listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange and became Merck KGaA, with the family still holding a majority of the shares. The Darmstadt company is the legal successor of the original Merck and holds the rights to the name in all countries except the United States and Canada, where Merck & Co. holds them, and the two have contested the name in the courts. It marked its 350th anniversary in 2018 and calls itself the world's oldest operating chemical and pharmaceutical company.
mercosur: Mercosur, called Mercosul in Portuguese, has roots in discussions of a Latin American regional market that go back to the treaty of 1960 establishing the Latin American Free Trade Association. In December 1985 the Brazilian president José Sarney and the Argentine president Raúl Alfonsín signed the Iguaçu Declaration, the basis for economic integration of the Southern Cone. Both countries had just come out of dictatorships and needed to turn their economies outwards. The Integration, Cooperation and Development Treaty of 1988 set the goal of a common market that others could join.

On 6 July 1990 Fernando Collor of Brazil and Carlos Menem of Argentina signed the Buenos Aires Act, aiming at full customs integration by 31 December 1994. Paraguay and Uruguay then showed strong interest in the process.

The four countries signed the Treaty of Asunción in 1991, setting the rules for a free trade zone, and the Protocol of Ouro Preto of 1994 completed its institutions. In 2001, on the tenth anniversary, the Mercosur flag was hoisted for the first time at its headquarters in Montevideo. Trade among the members, excluding Venezuela, grew from 10 billion US dollars in 1991 to 88 billion in 2010, though in 2010 this was only 16 percent of the four countries' total trade, comparable in importance to trade with the European Union.

Membership changed over time. Venezuela became an associate in 2004 and was admitted as a full member on 31 July 2012, after Paraguay was suspended following the removal of Fernando Lugo. Bolivia signed the protocol of accession in 2015 and became a full member in July 2024.

The Common Market Council is the highest body. It is made up of the ministers of foreign affairs and the economy of the members, who preside over it in rotating alphabetical order for six-month periods, and it decides by consensus. The Common Market Group is the executive body, coordinated by the foreign ministries, and work subgroups study matters such as customs, technical standards, transport and agricultural policy.

Mercosur promotes free trade within the zone and the movement of goods, people and currency, and now confines itself to a customs union with free internal trade and a common trade policy. Portuguese and Spanish are its working languages, and Guaraní is a recognised language.
merewalh: Merewalh was a sub-king of the Magonsæte, a western cadet kingdom of Mercia thought to have lain in Herefordshire and Shropshire. He is thought to have lived in the mid to late seventh century and to have come to the throne in the time of Penda of Mercia, who the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle implies was his father. His name signifies a foreigner or a Welshman, and it may show that he, and perhaps even Penda's dynasty, was of Celtic origin.

It is possible that he was a British leader rewarded by Penda for help in war, perhaps at the Battle of Maserfelth. Nothing is known of the origins of his first wife, who could have been a relative of Penda. A British origin might explain his control of lands around Leominster, where no evidence of early settlement by pagan Anglo-Saxons has been found.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle names Merewalh under the year 656, where Wulfhere of Mercia, in making the abbey of Medhamsted wealthy, takes the counsel of his brothers Ethelred and Merwal. Merewalh became a Christian about 660 and founded Leominster Priory. He died between 670 and 685 and was succeeded by his son Merchelm.

The Kentish royal legend makes Merewalh a son of Penda and gives him as wife the Kentish princess Domne Eafe. Their offspring were the saints Mildburh, Mildrið and Mildgið, and a son, Merefin, described as the holy child, who died young. Florence of Worcester called him a youth of eminent piety.
merfyn-frych: Merfyn was also known as Merfyn ap Gwriad, son of Gwriad, and as Merfyn Camwri, the Oppressor. He was the first king of Gwynedd known not to descend in the male line from King Cunedda; his link to the earlier dynasty ran through his mother, Ethyllt ferch Cynan, daughter of King Cynan Dindaethwy. Of his father, Gwriad ap Elidyr, extremely little is known. Merfyn claimed descent from Llywarch Hen through him, as the royal pedigree in Jesus College MS. 20 records.

A cross inscribed Crux Guriat, dated to the 8th or 9th century, was found on the Isle of Man. John Rhys suggested that Gwriad might have taken refuge there during the struggle between Cynan and Hywel and that the cross may refer to him, though Ireland, Galloway and Powys have also been proposed for the Manaw of Gwriad's origins.

Merfyn came to power after years of trouble. A cattle plague struck Wales in 810, war for control of Gwynedd raged from 812 to 816, and Coenwulf of Mercia occupied Rhufoniog in 817 and laid waste to Snowdonia; in 823 Mercia burned Deganwy to the ground. Gwynedd gained a respite when Mercia declined after the death of King Beornwulf in 826 and its conquest by Ecgberht of Wessex in 829. Merfyn allied his house with that of Powys by marrying Nest, daughter or sister of King Cadell ap Brochfael.

Little is known of his reign. The historian Thornton suggests he was probably among the Welsh kings defeated by Ecgberht in 830. He is called a king of the Britons in a copyist's addition to the Historia Brittonum and in the Bamberg Cryptogram, but both were written by men at his own court.

The Annales Cambriae record his death in the same year as a battle at Cetyll, and it is unclear whether he fell in it. He is chiefly remembered as the father of Rhodri Mawr and founder of a dynasty sometimes called the Merfynion after him. His son Gwriad was killed on Anglesey by the Saxons. The prophecy of future kings in the Dialogue between Myrddin and his sister Gwenddydd, in the Red Book of Hergest, names him as Merfyn Frych of the land of Manau.
merida-spain: Mérida lies 217 metres above sea level in the western-central part of the Iberian Peninsula, crossed by the Guadiana and Albarregas rivers, in the Province of Badajoz. The name comes from the Latin Emerita, 'retired' or 'veteran', and is part of the name Augusta Emerita given to the Roman colony. A hoard of gold jewellery excavated from a girl's grave in 1870, now in the British Museum, shows that the site was inhabited in prehistory.

Augustus ordered the town founded in 25 BCE to settle discharged soldiers of the V Alaudae and X Gemina. It guarded a strategic pass and the bridge over the Guadiana, and quickly became one of the most important cities of Roman Hispania. It was the capital of Lusitania and in the fourth century of the Diocese of Hispania, and a terminus of the Vía de la Plata, the Roman road linking the gold mines near Asturica Augusta with the south. In 409 it became capital of the short-lived Kingdom of the Alans under Attaces, who died in battle against the Visigoths in 418; the city was absorbed into the neighbouring Vandal kingdom and taken by the Visigoths in 469.

The Umayyad commander Musa ibn Nusayr conquered Mérida in 713, and it became capital of the Cora of Mérida. The Arabs reused and expanded Roman buildings, and the emir Abd ar-Rahman II built the Alcazaba in 835 on the Roman walls.

In the ninth century the Mozarabs of Mérida rebelled often against the caliphate, which contributed to the city's gradual decline, and during the Fitna of al-Andalus it became part of the Taifa of Badajoz. Its metropolitan seat passed to Santiago de Compostela in 1119. Alfonso IX of León reconquered the city in 1230 and gave it to the Order of Santiago. Recovery began in the fifteenth century. Monuments were damaged in the Napoleonic Wars, and Nationalist forces took the city on 10 August 1936 during the Spanish Civil War.

Mérida is the capital of the autonomous community of Extremadura, a status it received in 1983, and had 60,119 inhabitants in 2017. It preserves more major Roman monuments than any other city in Spain, among them the Roman theatre and amphitheatre, the remains of a circus and the Puente Romano, the longest surviving Roman bridge. Its archaeological site was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993, and the National Museum of Roman Art was designed by Rafael Moneo.
merida-yucatan: Mérida lies slightly inland from the north-west corner of the Yucatán Peninsula, about 35 kilometres from the Gulf of Mexico. The land is very flat, only 9 metres above sea level, and almost no surface water exists, though several cenotes give access to underground water. Many Maya sites lie in the area, among them Chichen Itza, Uxmal, Oxkintok, Sayil and Kabah. The historic centre follows the colonial Spanish pattern, with odd-numbered streets running east to west and even-numbered ones north to south, and with Calles 60 and 61 bounding the Plaza Grande.

The Spanish conquistadors, among them Francisco de Montejo the Younger and Juan de la Cámara, founded Mérida in 1542 and named it after Mérida in Extremadura, whose Roman ruins the Maya ruins reminded them of. The city stands on the Maya city of Ti'ho, also called Ichkanzihóo, "City of Five Hills", for its pyramids. Carved stones from the ruins went into the early Spanish buildings, and are visible in the cathedral, built in the late 16th century.

From colonial times to the middle of the 19th century Mérida was a walled city, intended to protect the peninsulares and criollos from periodic revolts by the Maya. Nahua troops who had accompanied Montejo settled in the districts of San Cristóbal, Santiago and San Román and were exempt from taxes for their military help.

The city is called La Ciudad Blanca, the White City, perhaps for the white limestone of its colonial façades. A folk story says it was named because only white Europeans were allowed to live inside it, but the first arches at its entrances were commissioned only in 1690, almost 150 years after its foundation.

In the late 19th century the surrounding area prospered by growing henequen, whose fibre was made into rope and twine and also into a traditional drink. By the early 20th century factories made tobacco, molasses, rum, soap and leather goods. Korean immigration to Mexico began in 1905, when more than a thousand people arrived in Yucatán from Jemulpo and settled around Mérida to work on henequen plantations.

Mérida is the capital and largest city of the Mexican state of Yucatán, with 921,770 people in 2020, and the cultural and financial centre of the peninsula. The Cathedral of Mérida is said to be the oldest cathedral on the mainland of the Americas. The city's heritage is a blend of Maya and Spanish culture formed in the colonial era.
merionethshire: Merionethshire was a maritime county bounded by Caernarfonshire to the north, Denbighshire to the east, Montgomeryshire and Cardiganshire to the south and Cardigan Bay to the west. With an area of 1,731 km2 it was one of the more sparsely populated counties of Great Britain. It was the most mountainous part of Wales: its highest point, Aran Fawddwy near Dinas Mawddwy, reaches 905 m, and Cader Idris south of Dolgellau is better known. Its chief rivers were the Dwyryd, the Mawddach, the Dyfi and the Dee, and its largest lake Llyn Tegid, 4 miles long.

The county was formed from the cantrefs of Meirionydd and Penllyn and the commote of Ardudwy. Before the 10th century Ardudwy belonged to Dunoding and the other two to Powys. The sons of Gruffudd ap Cynan took Meirionydd from Powys for Gwynedd in 1123, and after the death of Madog ap Maredudd his son Owain Brogyntyn, who held Penllyn, was forced to become a vassal of Owain Gwynedd. In the early 13th century Llywelyn Fawr joined Ardudwy and Meirionydd as an appanage for his son Gruffydd, who was stripped of it in 1221 for ruling too oppressively. After Edward I's invasion and the death of Llywelyn in 1282, the Statute of Rhuddlan ended Gwynedd as a state.

In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Merioneth was an important centre of the Welsh slate industry, with major quarries at Blaenau Ffestiniog and Corris and others at Abergynolwyn, Aberllefenni and Arthog. In 1947, before his marriage to Princess Elizabeth, Lieutenant Philip Mountbatten was created Earl of Merioneth by King George VI. An administrative county came into being on 1 April 1889, with its council at Dolgellau, and under the Local Government Act 1972 the bulk of it became the Meirionnydd district of Gwynedd.

The area remains one of the most strongly Welsh-speaking parts of Wales, though Barmouth and Tywyn are much anglicised. A large part of Snowdonia National Park lies within it, as do Harlech Castle, Castell y Bere, Cymer Abbey, the Roman fort of Tomen-y-mur and the Italianate village of Portmeirion.
merneptah: Merneptah was probably the fourth child of Ramesses II and Isetnofret and his thirteenth son. He came to power only because all his older brothers had died, and he was the first royal-born king since Tutankhamun. He appears as a prince on family stelae from Aswan and Silsila, dated to the thirtieth and thirty-third or thirty-fourth years of Ramesses II, alongside his parents, his sister Bintanath and his brothers Ramesses and Khaemwaset.

Little else is known of him before the fortieth year of his father's reign, when he became Overseer of the Army. After the death of his brother Khaemwaset in the fifty-fifth year, he was proclaimed crown prince and served as prince regent for the last twelve years of the old king's life. Mummy studies suggest that he was over fifty when he took the throne. His Great Royal Wife was Isetnofret II, probably his full sister or his niece.

Merneptah moved the administrative centre from Pi-Ramesses, his father's capital, back to Memphis, where he built a palace beside the temple of Ptah. He ruled for almost ten years, from 13 August 1213 BCE until his death on 2 May 1203 BCE.

In his fifth year Libyans threatened Egypt from the west, helped by the Sea Peoples, whom the texts name as the Ekwesh, Teresh, Lukka, Sherden and Shekelesh. The Libyan chief Meryre, son of Ded, had reached the fields of Perire, probably on the western edge of the Delta. Merneptah's account, inscribed beside the sixth pylon at Karnak and on the Athribis Stele, tells of a victorious battle of six hours in which the invaders threw down their weapons and fled. He claims to have killed 6,000 soldiers and taken 9,000 prisoners.

The same events appear in a poem on the Merneptah Stele, also called the Israel Stele. It also mentions the suppression of revolts in Canaan and says that 'Israel has been wiped out... its seed is no more', the first known ancient Egyptian record of Israel, named as a people rather than a country or city.

Merneptah died on 2 May 1203 BCE after a reign of almost ten years. He was buried in tomb KV8 in the Valley of the Kings, but his mummy was moved in ancient times and was found in 1898 among those in the tomb of Amenhotep II. It showed that he had suffered from arthritis and atherosclerosis and was about 1.71 metres tall. His son Seti II succeeded him, though not without challenge from a rival king, Amenmesse, who seized Upper Egypt and Kush during Seti's reign.
merneptah-stele: The stele is a black granite slab, over 3 metres high, carved in the fifth year of Merneptah of the 19th Dynasty. Its text is engraved on the rough back of a stele of Amenhotep III, which had been set against the wall in the forecourt of Merneptah's own temple. Flinders Petrie found it at Thebes in 1896, and Wilhelm Spiegelberg of his team made the first translation. At the top, the scene keeps its original colouring and shows Amun giving a sword to the king, with Mut and Khonsu on either side. A fragmentary copy was found at Karnak.

Egypt had been the dominant power in the region under Ramesses II. In Merneptah's fifth year a Libu king invaded from the west in alliance with northern peoples, and Merneptah won a great victory that summer. Most of the 28 lines glorify this victory over the Libyans and their Sea People allies.

The last three lines turn to Canaan, then part of Egypt's imperial possessions, where some cities had revolted. They say that Asqaluni was carried off, Gezer seized, Yanoam made non-existent, and Israel laid waste, its seed no more. The phrase about the seed is formulaic and was often used of defeated nations. The three cities are written with the determinative for a city, while Israel carries the signs for a foreign people, which Egyptians typically used for groups without a fixed city-state home.

When Spiegelberg was puzzled by one group of signs, Petrie quickly proposed that it read Israel, and Spiegelberg agreed. A majority of scholars accept the reading, and mainstream scholarship sees a connection with biblical Israel, although minority readings such as Jezreel have been proposed. It is the earliest textual reference to Israel and the only one from ancient Egypt. Most scholars place Merneptah's Israel in the hill country of central Canaan.

In the 1970s Frank J. Yurco argued that reliefs at Karnak long assigned to Ramesses II belong to Merneptah and show the campaign; not all Egyptologists accept this, and Dan'el Kahn has argued that Israelites appear as Shasu nomads in other scenes.
merobaudes-poet: Merobaudes was a Roman of Frankish origin who was raised in Spain, and he was probably a descendant of the general of the same name who flourished in the fourth century. He was the official laureate of Valentinian III and of the general Aetius, and he served in the army of Aetius that campaigned in the Alps. His contemporary Hydatius, in his Chronicle under the year 443, praised him as a poet and orator and recorded the statues set up in his honour.

Until the beginning of the 19th century Merobaudes was known only from that notice in Hydatius. In 1813 the base of a statue was found at Rome, with a long inscription of the year 435 (CIL VI 1724) that honoured Flavius Merobaudes for his merits as warrior and poet. Ten years later B. G. Niebuhr found Latin verses on a palimpsest in the monastery of St Gall. They were traced to Merobaudes because the language of their prose preface closely resembled that of the inscription, and they included a panegyric and minor poems.

Before these finds the only piece known under his name was De Christo, a short poem of 30 hexameters that one manuscript gives to Merobaudes and another to Claudian. A. Ebert disputed his claim to be either its author or a Christian, while T. Birt upheld his authorship in his edition of Claudian (1892). Niebuhr edited the panegyric and minor poems in 1824 and Immanuel Bekker in 1836; F. Bücheler and A. Riese later printed the De Christo in the Anthologia latina, and Frank M. Clover published an English translation with a historical commentary in 1971.
meroe: Meroë stood on the east bank of the Nile, about 35 kilometres north-east of Shendi and about 200 kilometres north-east of Khartoum. It lay on the edge of Butana, the region the ancients called the Island of Meroë. The Kushite rulers are said to have chosen the site, between the Fifth and Sixth Cataracts, because it lay on the fringe of the summer rainfall belt, was rich in iron ore and hardwood for ironworking, and gave access to trade routes to the Red Sea.

The Kingdom of Kush spanned about 800 BCE to about 350 CE, and its main capital was at first farther north at Napata. King Aspelta moved the capital to Meroë, possibly about 591 BCE, just after the pharaoh Psamtik II sacked Napata. From the reign of Arakamani, around 280 BCE, the royal burial ground also moved to Meroë. Herodotus described it as a great city said to be the mother city of the other Ethiopians.

In 23 BCE the Roman governor Publius Petronius invaded Nubia in answer to raids on southern Egypt and sacked Napata the next year. A peace treaty of 22 BCE was signed between Augustus and the Kushite queen Amanirenas. Meroë faded as a power from the 1st or 2nd century CE, weakened by the war with Roman Egypt and the decline of traditional industries. A Greek inscription of an Aksumite king, thought to be Ezana, was found at the site. Some authorities read it as proof that Aksum destroyed Kush, while others point to archaeological evidence of decline around 300.

The site is marked by more than two hundred pyramids in three groups, many in ruins, with the proportions of Nubian pyramids. Frédéric Cailliaud brought the ruins to European notice in 1821, and excavations followed under C. R. Lepsius in 1844, E. A. Wallis Budge in 1902 and 1905 and Garstang from 1910. The Archeological Sites of Meroë were listed by UNESCO as World Heritage Sites in 2011.
meroitic-script: The Meroitic script consists of two alphasyllabic scripts developed to write the Meroitic language at the beginning of the Meroitic Period of the Kingdom of Kush. Meroitic Cursive was derived from Demotic Egyptian, and Meroitic Hieroglyphs from Egyptian hieroglyphs. The cursive is the most widely attested, making up about 90 per cent of inscriptions, and it predates the earliest surviving hieroglyphic inscription by a century or more. Before the Meroitic Period, Egyptian hieroglyphs were used to write Kushite names and words. The Greek historian Diodorus Siculus described the two scripts in his Bibliotheca historica.

There were 23 letters, including four vowels. The consonants were understood to carry an inherent vowel a, so that a single letter m was read ma. The other vowels were written in full, so that mi stood for the syllable mi. The four signs ne, se, te and to stood for consonants with other vowels. The cursive was written from right to left and from top to bottom, while the monumental form ran in columns from top to bottom, right to left, with the signs facing the beginning of the text. The only punctuation mark was a divider of two to three dots. Some scholars, such as Harald Haarmann, believe that the vowel letters show an influence of the Greek alphabet.

The script was deciphered by the British Egyptologist Francis Llewellyn Griffith from the Meroitic spellings of Egyptian names, but the Meroitic language itself remains poorly understood. Later scholars, among them Millet and Rowan, proposed other readings of the sign e and the signs ne, se and te. In late 2008 the first complete royal dedication was found. Both scripts were added to Unicode in 2012.

The last known inscription is the Meroitic Cursive text of the Blemmye king Kharamadoye on a column in the Temple of Kalabsha. After the fall of Meroë the script continued in use for a time, and during the 6th century Christianization of Nubia it was replaced by Byzantine Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian. Old Nubian added three Meroitic Cursive letters to the Greek alphabet.
merovech: Merovech is the ancestor of the Merovingian dynasty and the grandfather of its founder Clovis I, reportedly a king of the Salian Franks, but records of his existence are mixed with legend and myth. Gregory of Tours names him only once, as the father of Childeric I, and remains vague about his relationship to Chlodio, a roughly contemporary Frankish warlord who pushed from the Silva Carbonaria as far south as the Somme. The Chronicle of Fredegar recounts that Merovech was born after Chlodio's wife met a sea creature while bathing, and leaves unclear whether the creature or Chlodio was his father. Another theory takes this legend as a mythological past created to support the rising Frankish rule in Western Europe.

Chlodio is said to have been defeated by Flavius Aëtius at Vicus Helena in Artois in 448, and Ian S. Wood would therefore place Merovech, his apparent son, in the second half of the fifth century. Merovech may have been one of several barbarian kings who joined the Roman general Aëtius against the Huns under Attila at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451. The Salian Franks, bound by a treaty with Rome, probably fought there, but the sources do not say who led them.

The Roman historian Priscus described a fair-haired youth in Rome whom Aëtius had adopted, and said Attila's pretext for war on the Franks was the death of their king and a quarrel among his sons over the succession. Historians are divided on whether Merovech figures in this account. Erich Zöllner thinks the prince was a Ripuarian Frank, Émilienne Demougeot sees Merovech as the king who died, and Christian Settipani takes Merovech to be the son allied with Rome.

Some historians, such as Georg Waitz, suggest Merovech may be a mythological figure, a son of the sea revered before the Franks conversion. Étienne Renard suggests he may be an eponymous founder of the lineage, whose name is linked to no act of war or event. An Austrasian genealogy made between 629 and 639 lists Chloio, Glodobode, Mereveo, Hilbricco and Childeric among the Salian kings, and its order is debated. The legend of his conception was taken up in the 1982 book The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail, whose claim of descent from Jesus has no evidence behind it.
merovingian-dynasty: The Merovingians first appear as kings of the Franks in the Roman army of northern Gaul. The dynastic name means sons of Merovech, a Salian king who was the father of Childeric I, the first well-known Merovingian king. The Chronicle of Fredegar, written in the 7th century, implies that the family descended from a sea-beast like a quinotaur. Today the tale is usually seen as an attempt to explain the name Merovech, meaning sea-bull. Unlike the Anglo-Saxon royal genealogies, the Merovingians never claimed descent from a god.

Their long hair distinguished them from other Franks, who commonly cut theirs short. A Merovingian whose hair was cut could not rule, and a rival could be removed from the succession by being tonsured and sent to a monastery.

In 486 Clovis I defeated Syagrius, a Roman military leader who competed with the Merovingians for power in northern Gaul. According to Gregory of Tours, he adopted his wife Clotilda's Nicene Christian faith when other Germanic tribes were largely Arian. In 507 he defeated the Visigoths at the Battle of Vouillé. The kingdom was treated as a single yet divisible patrimony, so Clovis's four sons divided it, and it stayed divided, with brief exceptions, until 679. The main divisions were Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy and Aquitaine. The Franks conquered Burgundy in 534. In 613 Clotaire II reunited the entire realm.

His son Dagobert I, who died in 639, is commonly seen as the last powerful Merovingian king. Later kings are called rois fainéants, do-nothing kings, and real power passed to the mayors of the palace. Pepin the Middle triumphed at the Battle of Tertry in 687, and his son Charles Martel defeated the Moors at the Battle of Tours in 732. Charles's son Pepin the Short deposed the last king, Childeric III, in 751, with the blessing of Pope Zachary.

On a king's death his property was divided among his heirs as if private. Kings appointed counts to defend, administer and judge, and the counts raised armies, which acclaimed a new king by raising him on their shields. Law depended on a man's origin: the Salian Franks had the Lex Salica, first tentatively codified in 511. Theudebert I was the first to issue distinctly Merovingian coinage. Kings and queens used the church to their advantage, awarding monasteries and bishoprics to supporters, and the most characteristic Merovingian literature is the lives of saints. The main sources are Gregory of Tours, the Chronicle of Fredegar and the Liber Historiae Francorum.
merrimack-river: The Merrimack River rises at the confluence of the Pemigewasset and Winnipesaukee rivers in Franklin, New Hampshire. It flows south through Concord, Manchester and Nashua, enters Massachusetts at Tyngsborough and turns north-east past Lowell, Lawrence and Haverhill to the Gulf of Maine at Newburyport. Its watershed covers 5,010 square miles in southern New Hampshire and north-eastern Massachusetts and is the fourth largest river basin in New England. From Pawtucket Falls in Lowell onward, the Massachusetts and New Hampshire border is roughly the line three miles north of the river.

The name is of uncertain origin. In 1604 native people told Pierre Dugua, Sieur de Monts, of a river to the south, whose native name the French pronounced as Merremack, and Samuel de Champlain found it in 1605 and called it the Riviere du Gas.

Before glaciation the river ran on south to enter the Gulf of Maine near Boston. When the glacier retreated about 14,000 years ago, debris filled the lower valley and turned the river into its present north-eastern bend at Lowell. At the time of European exploration the peoples along it included the Agawam and Naumkeag on the lower reaches, the Pawtucket at Lowell, the Nashua, Souhegan and Namoskeag around Manchester, and the Pennacook northward from Bow.

In the 19th century, when textile mills dominated the New England economy, cities grew along it to use its water power: Concord, Manchester and Nashua in New Hampshire, and Lowell, Lawrence and Haverhill in Massachusetts. Before the Middlesex Canal was built, Newburyport was an important shipbuilding city that received New Hampshire timber floated downriver. The river was dammed and canalled and used for industrial waste, and by the 1960s it was one of the ten most polluted waterways in the United States. The Clean Water Act of 1972 required sewage treatment, and fish such as American shad, striped bass and Atlantic salmon returned.

The most severe recorded flood came in March 1936, when rain and melting snow raised the river at Lowell to 68.4 feet. The Francis Gate, built in 1850 under James B. Francis to seal Lowell's canal system from the river, was called Francis' Folly when it was built but saved the city in 1852 and 1936. In May 2006 rain raised the river more than 8 feet above flood stage, and about 1,500 people evacuated their homes. Henry David Thoreau wrote A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers, and Jack Kerouac set part of Doctor Sax during the flood of 1936.
mers-el-kebir: The name is Arabic, al-Marsā al-Kabīr, meaning the Great Harbor. The port was originally Phoenician, and under the Roman presence it was called Portus Divinus. In the 12th century it became an Almohad naval arsenal, in the 13th century it fell under the rulers of the Kingdom of Tlemcen, and around 1492 it became a centre of pirate activity. Ottoman Turks, Portuguese and Spanish fought over it. The Portuguese were defeated there by Abu Abdallah IV in 1501, and the Spanish by Abu Abd Allah V in 1507.

The Spanish, who called it Mazalquivir, captured it in 1505 under Cardinal Cisneros and used it as a base to take neighbouring Oran in 1509. They were driven out in 1708 by Bey Mustapha Ben Youssef. Their return in 1732 followed the victory of the armada of the Duke of Montemar at the Battle of Aïn-el-Turk. In 1792 King Carlos IV sold both cities to the Dey of Algiers after a siege by the Dey's forces. The French occupied the port in 1830 and renamed it Saint André de Mers-el-Kébir, improving it in 1868 with a lighthouse that was destroyed in the Second World War.

After the fall of France in 1940 a French fleet took shelter in the port. On 3 July 1940 Force H of the Royal Navy, led by Vice-admiral Sir James Somerville, attacked it after the French commanders refused all of Somerville's demands, which were designed to ensure that the ships would not join forces with Nazi Germany, as Vichy France had. Force H destroyed or damaged several French warships. The attack led Vichy France to sever relations with Britain, and it showed the world that the British would fight on against the Axis powers.

After the war France used its naval base at Mers-el-Kébir to assist in atomic tests, and developed the base substantially in 1953. The Évian Accords of 18 March 1962, which recognised Algerian independence, allowed France to keep the base for 15 years, but France withdrew five years later, in 1967. The Algerian navy uses the base.
mersa-gawasis: The harbour, known in ancient Egyptian as Saww, lies at the mouth of Wadi Gawasis, 2 km south of the mouth of Wadi Gasus, with Safaga 25 km to the north and al-Qusair 50 km to the south. Its name joins mersa, port, to gawasis, a medieval term for a scout boat. It appears to have been used as a port from the reign of Senusret I to that of Amenemhat IV of the 12th Dynasty, as a loading point for voyages to Punt and as a starting point for journeys to the mines of Sinai.

The search began when a 12th Dynasty stele naming a nearby port called Saww was found at a Graeco-Roman watering station in Wadi Gasus. The University of Alexandria, under Abdel Monem A.H. Sayed, dug there and then at the mouth of Mersa Gasus without finding pharaonic remains, and concluded that the stele had been carried from Saww in Roman times. Near Mersa Gawasis a small stele bore the cartouche of Senusret I and the place name Bia-n-punt, and a shrine of Ankhu, valet of Senusret I, built on a limestone anchor, again named Sww.

A further stele on an anchor base recorded an order of Senusret I to the vizier Intefiqer for a ship to sail to Bia-Punt. In 1977 potsherds with hieratic inscriptions listing the contents, origin and destination of their cargoes were found, naming a temple of Senusret II, Punt and an official of the time of Senusret III. These finds identified Saww with Mersa Gawasis and showed that Middle Kingdom ships sailed from here to Punt and back, and that on their return they were taken apart and carried to the Nile Valley in pieces. The anchors, of about 110 kg, were made on the spot and left behind, some reused as bases for shrines and stelae.

In 2005 an expedition led by the archaeologist Kathryn Bard found the remains of seagoing vessels and stelae with hieroglyphic texts on royal expeditions to Punt, some 1200 km to the south, among them cedar planks from Queen Hatshepsut's expedition of the 15th century BCE.
merseburg: Merseburg stands on the river Saale in southern Saxony-Anhalt, about 14 kilometres south of Halle and 30 kilometres west of Leipzig. It is the capital of the Saalekreis district. The town was first mentioned in 850.

King Henry the Fowler built a royal palace at Merseburg, and in the vicinity in 933 he won his great victory over the Hungarians at the Battle of Riade. From 968 until the Protestant Reformation the town was the seat of the Bishop of Merseburg, and it was a favourite residence of the German kings in the 10th, 11th and 12th centuries. Fifteen diets were held there during the Middle Ages, and its fairs had an importance that later passed to those of Leipzig. After the death of Ekkehard on 3 April 1002, Bolesław I Chrobry took Merseburg and Meissen with the help of the local Slavic population.

From 1657 to 1738 it was the residence of the Dukes of Saxe-Merseburg, and in 1815, after the Napoleonic Wars, it became part of the Prussian Province of Saxony. The Merseburg Incantations were rediscovered there in 1841. Written in Old High German, they are the only preserved German documents with a heathen theme: one is a charm to release warriors caught in battle, the other a charm to heal a horse's sprained foot. From 1909 to 1913 Carl Bosch and Friedrich Bergius laid the scientific foundations of high-pressure ammonia synthesis, and Merseburg became an industrial town. In 23 air raids of World War II the historic centre was almost destroyed.

The Merseburg Cathedral of St John the Baptist, founded in 1015 and rebuilt in the 13th and 16th centuries, stands beside the episcopal palace of the 15th century. The town also has the German Museum of Chemistry. Among its natives are the chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg and the biologist Ernst Haeckel.
merseburg-charms: The Merseburg charms are two medieval spells in Old High German, the only known examples of Germanic pagan belief preserved in that language. Georg Waitz discovered them in 1841 in a manuscript kept in the library of the cathedral chapter of Merseburg, which gave them their name. They stand on a blank page of a Latin liturgical book, in Caroline minuscule; the manuscript is from Fulda and is dated to the 9th century, and one account has a cleric, possibly at Fulda, recording the charms in the 10th century. There is some speculation about the date of the charms themselves.
Jacob Grimm published them in 1842 and praised the codex as a treasure no library could match. The manuscript was shown at Merseburg cathedral until November 2004, and earlier in 1939.

Each charm has two parts: a preamble that tells a mythological event, and the spell proper, a magic analogy of the form, as it was then, so may it be now. The verse is of a transitional type, with traditional alliteration and also the end-rhymes introduced in Christian verse of the 9th century.

The first is a release charm. It describes women, called idisi, who sat here and there; some fastened bonds, some hindered an army, and some unravelled fetters. The closing words command the captive to escape the bonds and flee the enemy.

In the second, Phol and Wodan ride into the woods, and the foot of Balder's foal is sprained. Sinthgunt, sister of Sunna, Frija, sister of Volla, and Wodan each speak the charm, and Wodan, as well he could, speaks the formula: bone to bone, blood to blood, joint to joint, as if they were glued. Wodan and Frija correspond to the Norse Odin and Frigg. Grimm took Phol to be another name for Balder, but this is not conclusive, and modern scholarship suggests Freyr may be meant.

Charms of the second type are widespread. Parallels from Scandinavia, many from the 18th and 19th centuries, replace Wodan with Jesus, Saint Peter or Saint Olav, as in a Norwegian charm in which Saint Olav rode in the green wood and his horse hurt its foot. Bishop Anton Christian Bang gathered 34 Norwegian horse spells under the heading Odin og Folebenet, though none invokes Odin. A Swedish spell recorded in the 19th century does name Odin.

Similar charms are noted in Gaelic, Lettish and Finnish, and a Shetland charm for a sprained leg of a person, using a thread of black wool with nine knots. Adalbert Kuhn compared the formula with a hymn of the Atharvaveda, and most scholars accept a common Indo-European origin, though some regard the likeness as accidental.
mersin: The coast has been inhabited since the 9th millennium BCE. John Garstang's excavations of the hill of Yumuktepe revealed 23 levels of occupation, with fortifications put up around 4500 BCE. In ancient times the place was ruled by many states, including the Hittites, Assyrians, Persians, Seleucids and Lagids. Under the Greeks it was called Zephyrion, and it profited from its natural harbour, its position on the trade routes of southern Anatolia and trade in molybdenum, or white lead, from nearby mines. It also minted its own coins.

In the Wars of the Diadochi, Ptolemy I Soter established himself there with a fleet. In Roman times the area was part of the province of Cilicia, whose capital was Tarsus, and Mersin was the major port. It was renamed Hadrianopolis in honour of the emperor Hadrian. It was also an episcopal see, and its bishops attended councils from the First Council of Constantinople in 381 to the Council in Trullo in 692.

The Arabs conquered Cilicia in the early 7th century, when Mersin appears to have been a deserted site. The Byzantines held the region between 965 and about 1080, followed by the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia. From 1362 to 1513 the Ramadanid Emirate governed it, first under the Mamluk Sultanate and later under the Ottoman Empire. Sultan Selim I defeated the Mamluks in 1517 and annexed Cilicia.

Mersin remained a modest coastal village for much of the Ottoman period. Only towards the middle of the 19th century did it begin to flourish as the port of the Çukurova region. During the American Civil War the region became a major supplier of cotton, and in 1866 railways were extended to link the cotton-growing areas with Mersin. In 1909 its port received 645 steamships and 797,433 tons of goods. French and British troops occupied the city in 1918, and the Turkish army recovered it in 1921 at the end of the Franco-Turkish War.

Mersin is the capital of Mersin Province, formerly İçel, and is made up of four district municipalities: Akdeniz, Mezitli, Toroslar and Yenişehir. Its name comes from the myrtle plant Myrsine, which grows abundantly there. The city has a Mediterranean climate and the longest seashore in Turkey. Its port is an international hub, and the Mersin Free Zone, set up in 1986, was the first in Turkey. Nearby are the ruins of Soli Pompeiiopolis, where two colonnades of the 2nd or 3rd century remain.
mertola: Mértola stands on a hill above the Guadiana in the south-east of the Alentejo, near the Spanish border, at the northernmost navigable part of the river. Its municipality had 6,206 inhabitants in 2021, and the town itself around 2,500. The site made it a river port: farm produce and silver, gold and tin from the lower Alentejo went down the Guadiana to southern Hispania and the Mediterranean.

The place was inhabited from the Iron Age at least, and the Romans renamed Myrtilis, its pre-Roman name, Myrtilis Iulia. In the 1st and 2nd centuries it was a commercial centre of the Pacensis region and minted its own coin, and it became a municipium in the time of Augustus. In the Migration Period Sueves and Visigoths invaded; trade shrank but continued, as Greek tombstones of the 6th and 7th centuries and Byzantine merchants suggest.

From about 711 Mértola belonged to Al-Andalus for over four hundred years. After the fall of the Caliphate of Córdoba in 1031 it became an independent taifa, until the taifa of Seville took it in 1044-1045. Between 1144 and 1150 it was again the seat of an independent state under Ibn Qasi, a mystic and military leader who united southern Portugal and fought the Almoravides; an Almohad army ended it.

King Sancho II of Portugal took the town in 1238 and gave it to the Order of St James, whose seat was there until 1316. Its economic weight faded, revived briefly in the 15th and 16th centuries when it supplied Portuguese troops in North Africa with cereals, and revived again with copper mined at São Domingos from about 1850 until 1965.

The castle has a 30-metre keep, finished around 1292, with an inner hall covered with Gothic vaulting. The main church was built as a mosque in the 12th and 13th centuries and converted after 1238; it keeps four naves, a mihrab niche and horseshoe-arched portals, and is the only medieval mosque to survive in Portugal. The museum holds the most important nucleus of Islamic art in Portugal. In 2017 the town began the process of seeking UNESCO World Heritage status.
merv: Merv, also called the Merv Oasis, lay on the Murghab River, whose canals irrigate cereals, melons, rice and cotton. Archaeological surveys show village life on the site from the 3rd millennium BCE. Under the Achaemenid Empire the city, named Margu in the Behistun inscriptions of about 515 BCE, belonged to a satrapy of Darius the Great. The Seleucid ruler Antiochus I Soter renamed it Antiochia Margiana and rebuilt it at the site now known as Gyaur Gala.

After the Sasanian king Ardashir I took the city, its coins document almost four centuries of direct Sasanian rule. Zoroastrians, Buddhists, Manichaeans and Christians of the Church of the East lived there, and from the 5th to the 11th century it was the seat of an East Syrian metropolitan province. After the Arab conquest it became the capital of the Umayyad province of Khorasan. In 671 Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan sent 50,000 Arab troops there as a garrison, and Qutayba ibn Muslim used it as a base from 705 to 715 to subdue Balkh, Bukhara and Fergana.

The Seljuk leader Tughril took Merv peacefully in 1037, and from 1118 it was the capital of the whole Seljuk empire. Geographers called it the capital of the eastern Islamic world, and Omar Khayyam spent years working at its observatory. In 1221 it opened its gates to Tolui, a son of Genghis Khan; Ibn al-Athir's account of the massacre that followed gives about 700,000 dead. Merv never regained its prosperity. In 1788 and 1789 Shah Murad of Bukhara razed it and broke its dams, and by the late 19th century the oasis was abandoned.

The ruins stand near Baýramaly in Turkmenistan, about 30 kilometres east of the city of Mary, and are preserved as the State Historical and Cultural Park Ancient Merv, established in 1987. UNESCO lists the site as a World Heritage Site. Merv is several walled cities built beside one another in different eras: Erk Gala of the Achaemenid period, Gyaur Gala of the Hellenistic and Sasanian city, the large city of the Abbasid and Seljuk periods, and the small Timurid city. The Tomb of Ahmad Sanjar still stands. Turkmen and British archaeologists have worked there since 1992.
meryey: Meryey, whose name is also written Meghiey or Meghyey, was a Great Chief of the Libu in the late 13th century BCE and a contemporary of the pharaoh Merneptah, who reigned from 1213 to 1203 BCE. His father had also been Great Chief of the Libu. Meryey had two brothers, Meshken and Kepper, and many wives, who went with him on campaign. He had six sons, all of whom were killed in the war against Egypt.

Meryey built a military alliance of his own people with the Meshwesh, the Lukka and the Sea Peoples known as the Ekwesh, Teresh, Shekelesh and Sherden, and led it against Egypt in the western Nile Delta in Merneptah's 5th and 6th regnal years. His army is said to have numbered 40,000 men, and it had some success at first. The Great Karnak Inscription records that he fell upon the country of Tehenu with his bowmen, bringing his wife and children, and reached the western boundary in the fields of Perire.

The same inscription describes Merneptah as enraged by the report. He addressed his court and dreamed that the god Ptah handed him a sword. After six hours of fighting, the invaders threw down their weapons, abandoned their baggage and dependants, and fled. Merneptah claimed to have killed 6,000 soldiers and taken 9,000 prisoners. The Egyptian list of spoils names Meryey's silver, gold and bronze vessels, his wife's furniture, his throne, his bows and arrows, and his oxen, goats and donkeys.

Merneptah's records give a full account of Meryey's collapse on the battlefield as defeat drew near. They say that he fled alone by night with no plume upon his head, a reference to the ostrich feathers that Libyans wore, while his women were taken, his grain plundered and his camp burned. His brothers turned against him, and on his return his own people spoke against him. The records present his fall as the curse of the gods of Memphis. After his defeat Meryey was replaced as chief by one of his brothers.
mesa-verde: Mesa Verde, Spanish for green table, lies near the Four Corners region of the American Southwest. Streams eroded the hard sandstone to cut its canyons, and elevations range from about 1,829 to 2,613 metres. The land slants to the south, which contributed to the formation of the alcoves that have preserved its cliff dwellings. Domínguez and Escalante, seeking a route from Santa Fe to California, named the region in 1776 for its tree-covered heights, but never got close enough to see the stone villages.

Nomadic Paleo-Indians were in the wider region by about 9500 BCE and used the mesa in increasing numbers from about 7500 BCE. Archaic people followed, and by 1000 BCE corn had arrived and the Basketmaker culture emerged. The Ancestral Puebloans developed from it by 750 CE, living by hunting, gathering and farming corn, beans and squash. In the Pueblo I period they built interconnected year-round houses and used the old pit-houses mainly for community ceremonies.

By the end of the 12th century they were building the large cliff dwellings. Cliff Palace, in the largest alcove, has about 150 rooms and 23 kivas and housed some 125 people, probably as part of a community of sixty nearby pueblos. Long House was built around 1200 and occupied until 1280, and Spruce Tree House, with 130 rooms, was built between 1211 and 1278. A log at Balcony House was dated to 1278. Severe and prolonged droughts brought social and environmental instability, and by 1285 the people had moved south to Arizona and New Mexico, including the Rio Chama, the Albuquerque Basin and the Pajarito Plateau.

The Wetherill family, ranchers who were friendly with the Ute, learned of the cliff dwellings from a Ute man named Acowitz, who called the largest a sacred place. In 1891 the mineralogist Gustaf Nordenskiöld, a guest of the Wetherills, recorded and photographed the sites and sent many artefacts to Sweden; his 1893 book, The Cliff Dwellers of the Mesa Verde, and the shipment raised concern for protection. Congress and President Theodore Roosevelt established the national park in 1906, and in 1911 the Ute reluctantly traded 10,000 acres on Chapin Mesa for land on Ute Mountain. The park, in Montezuma County, Colorado, preserves more than 600 cliff dwellings and became a World Heritage Site in 1978, the only one in Colorado.
mesannepadda: Mesannepada, whose name means "Youngling chosen by An", is the first king listed for the First Dynasty of Ur on the Sumerian King List. The list credits him with a reign of 80 years and says that he overthrew Lugal-kitun of Uruk, so that kingship was carried to Ur. Its next entries are his son Meskiagnun, who reigned 36 years, then Elulu and Balulu. A reign of 80 years is thought unlikely, and the length of his son's reign was probably added to his. An inscribed bead found at Mari names him as son of Meskalamdug, king of Kish.

Mesannepada appears on objects from his own time. A lapis lazuli bead naming Mesannepada, king of Ur, was found at Mari in the so-called Treasure of Ur, a jar of offerings that marked the foundation of a temple there. It was dedicated to the god Lugalkalam. It is unclear how the bead reached Mari, but it suggests some relation between Ur and Mari. Seals from the Royal Cemetery at Ur name Mesannepada, his predecessors Meskalamdug and Akalamdug, and Queen Puabi, and one seal impression calls him king of Kish, a title taken to show his hegemony.

The Old Babylonian Tummal Inscription lists Mesannepada and his son Meskiagnun among rulers who maintained the main temple at Nippur, alongside Gilgamesh of Uruk and his son Ur-Nungal. This supports their status as overlords of Sumer. Another son, A'annepada, is known from tablets recording that he built a temple of Ninhursag, at modern Ubaid, and he is not named on the king list. A small ziggurat beneath the later structure of Ur-Nammu at Ur may date from his time.

In the 1950s Edmund I. Gordon conjectured that Mesannepada and an early king of Kish named Mesilim were the same man, since their names are interchanged in some proverbs, but this was not conclusive. More recent scholars generally treat them as distinct and place Mesilim at Kish before Mesannepada. His tomb may lie in the Royal Cemetery at Ur, and it has been suggested that the tomb PG 1232 or PG 1237, known as the Great Death-Pit, is his.
mesha: The two main sources for Mesha are the Mesha Stele, which he had inscribed and erected at Dibon, and the Hebrew Bible. In the stele he calls himself the son of a king of Moab and the Dibonite. Only the first element of his father's name, Chemosh, survives on the stone; among the reconstructions scholars have proposed, Chemosh-yat(ti) has found some acceptance, since a Moabite king named Chemosh-yat is known from the Kerak Inscription.

According to the Books of Samuel, Moab had been conquered by David and kept by his son Solomon. After the split of Israel into two kingdoms, King Omri of the northern kingdom reconquered it. The stele says nothing of the earlier history and mentions only Omri's conquest of the land.

The Second Book of Kings records that Mesha used to deliver to the king of Israel one hundred thousand lambs and the wool of one hundred thousand rams, and that when Ahab was dead he rebelled against the king of Israel, whom it names as Jehoram. The stele, which does not name the king, records the liberation of Moab from Israelite suzerainty in about 850 BCE.

The two accounts explain the success of the revolt differently. Mesha claims a decisive victory and states that Israel has been defeated. In 2 Kings, Mesha is besieged in his capital, and the Israelites withdraw after he sacrifices to his god Chemosh, on the walls of the city, the eldest son either of himself or of the Edomite king; the text is not explicit. If it was the Edomite prince, the deed may have made Edom leave the coalition, but it is at least as plausible that he offered his own son for deliverance. The Bible says Israel suffered no losses, yet that great wrath came against Israel and they returned to their own land.
mesha-stele: The stele is a smoothed block of basalt about a metre tall, with a surviving inscription of 34 lines. Frederick Augustus Klein, an Anglican missionary, found it intact in August 1868 among the ruins of ancient Dibon, now Dhiban in Jordan. News of the find set off a race among France, Britain and Germany to acquire it. Charles Simon Clermont-Ganneau, at the French consulate in Jerusalem, had a papier-mâché impression, or squeeze, taken of the full stone.

In November 1869 the Bani Hamida broke the stele after the Ottoman government demanded that it be given to the German consulate. Fragments carrying 613 of about a thousand letters were later recovered, and Clermont-Ganneau reconstructed the rest from the squeeze. The stele has been in the Louvre since 1873, and Jordan has asked for its return since 2014.

Mesha, king of Moab and a Dibonite, records that he built a sanctuary for the god Chemosh at Qarho, the citadel of Dibon, in thanks for deliverance from his enemies. He says that Omri, king of Israel, oppressed Moab for many days because Chemosh was angry with his land, and that Omri's son continued this. Mesha describes taking Ataroth from the men of Gad and killing its warriors, and taking Nebo. He lists his building works, including walls, gates, a palace, reservoirs for water and a road across the Arnon, and ends with the capture of Horonaim, where the text breaks off.

The account parallels, with differences, an episode in 2 Kings 3 in which Jehoram of Israel campaigned against his rebellious vassal Mesha. This is the basis of the usual dating of about 840 BCE, though André Lemaire cautions that the identification is not certain and the stele may be as late as 810 BCE. In 1994 Lemaire read a phrase in line 31 as House of David, a reading that others dispute; Matthieu Richelle holds it remains uncertain.

Some scholars questioned the stele's authenticity after its discovery, but the great majority of biblical archaeologists regard it as genuine, and the Khirbat Ataruz inscribed altar, found in 2010, gave further support. Thomas L. Thompson regards the text as allegory, a view John Emerton and Lemaire have criticised. The stele is the major evidence for the Moabite language.
meshan: The province took in the former Parthian vassal kingdom of Characene and reached north along the Shatt al-Arab and then the lower Tigris as far as Madhar, and possibly further. The land was very fertile: Strabo called it the best place for barley, and date palms grew in great numbers. The port of Obolla, also known as Apologos, lay within it, and the province was an important stage of the trade of the Persian Gulf.

Like Asoristan and the other western Sasanian provinces, Meshan was home to many peoples. Assyrians, Mesenian Arabs and nomadic Arabs formed its Semitic population, joined by Nabataean and Palmyrene merchants. Iranians had begun to settle there, as had the Zutt, who had been deported from India, and other Indian groups and Malays may also have been brought in, either as captives or as recruited sailors.

Ardashir I, the first Sasanian ruler, invaded Meshan after taking his home province of Pars and killed its ruler, Bandu. He had the city of Karkh Meshan rebuilt under the name Astarabad-Ardashir, and built or rebuilt the town of Vahman-Ardashir, also called Forat Meshan. A fragmentary Manichean account found at Turfan says that Mihr-šāh, a brother of Shapur I, ruled as vassal king of Meshan and was converted by Mani himself, though some scholars doubt the source. A son of Shapur I, Shapur Mishanshah, is confirmed as ruler of the province until his death in 260, and was probably followed by his wife Denag.

The Paikuli inscription of King Narseh names an Iranian aristocrat, Adurfarrobay, as ruler of Meshan; he later rebelled against Narseh in support of a rival claimant to the throne, Bahram III. By the 5th century Syriac sources name Vahman-Ardashir as the chief city of the province, so it had seemingly taken the place of Karkh Meshan as its capital.
meshchera: The Meshchera lived between the Oka and the Klyazma rivers. The first Russian text to name them is the Tolkovaya Paleya of the 13th century, and later chronicles before the 16th century mention them too, whereas the related Merya and Muroma seem to have been absorbed by the East Slavs by the 10th and 11th centuries. Archaeologists identify the Oka-Ryazan culture with them. Burials found at Zhabki in 1870 held women's bronze ornaments of the 5th to 8th centuries, and twelve such sites run from the Moskva River along the Oka to Kasimov.

Slavic tribes reached Meshchera lands in the 10th to 12th centuries. In the Oka valley the Meshchera culture seems to have vanished by the 11th century, without sign of genocide but with some people pushed away, while in the marshy north, which held less interest for the Slavs, they stayed and became Orthodox. In his will of 1358 Ivan II of Moscow mentions the village of Meshcherka, bought from the native chieftain Alexander Ukovich.

The nobility was converted and assimilated by the 13th century, but hunters and fishermen may have kept their language and beliefs longer: in the 16th century the St Nicholas monastery at Radovitsy was founded to convert the remaining pagans. Documents on Ivan the Terrible's Kazan campaign mention a Meshchera state, Temnikov Meshchera, absorbed by Mordvins and Tatars.

The Meshchera were mainly fishermen, beekeepers, hunters and bronze workers who farmed only a little, and they held animistic beliefs before their assimilation. Women's graves contain rings, jingling pendants, buckles, torcs and round breast plates with distinctive ornament. Their language is unattested: Prince A. M. Kurbsky wrote that a Mordvin language was spoken there, and Pauli Rahkonen has suggested from place names that it was Permic, a view Vladimir Napolskikh has criticised. Ethnographers treat the modern Meshchera as a local group of Russians in the forests where the Moscow, Ryazan and Vladimir Oblasts meet, and the Mishar Tatars may have inherited the name.
meskalamdug: His name means hero of the good land. He does not appear in the Sumerian King List and is known from a few objects. A cylinder seal of shell with a lapis-lazuli core, found in the tomb of a queen, PG 1054, bears the title King Meskalamdug; it shows two crossed lions attacking bulls, with Enkidu and a naked man joining the fight, and is now in the British Museum. A lapis-lazuli bead found at Mari records a dedication to the god Lugalkalam by Mesannepada, king of Ur, son of Meskalamdug, king of Kish.

How the bead came to Mari, about 700 kilometres north-west of Ur, is unclear, but it points to some kind of relation between the two cities at the time. It was found in a jar with other objects from Ur or Kish, probably a dedication to a local temple. His queen was named Ninbanda, and it has been suggested that Puabi may have been his second queen.

Sir Leonard Woolley found grave PG 755 in the Royal Cemetery of Ur in 1924. Its many gold objects include a helmet inscribed with the name Meskalamdug, but without the title king, and because the grave had no attendants Woolley assumed its owner was not royal. The question was reopened ten years later, when André Parrot found the bead at Mari naming Meskalamdug as king and as the father of Mesannepada, who appears in the king list and many other inscriptions.

Since PG 755 lacks the scale and splendour of the other royal tombs, it has been suggested that it belonged to a young prince of the same name, perhaps a son of the king and Ninbanda. The Assyriologist Julian Reade has proposed that the king's own tomb was PG 789, the King's grave, with its many royal attendants, next to the tomb of Queen Puabi. Others think the man of the grave and the king of the seal are simply one person, who took the royal title lugal late in life.
meskhetian-turks: The Meskhetian Turks, also called Ahiska Turks, speak the Kars dialect of Turkish and belong to the Hanafi school of Sunni Islam. They historically lived in Meskheti, the region of Georgia along the Turkish border. Turkic tribes settled there as early as the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and the Turkish presence began with the Ottoman expedition of 1578. By the Peace of Amasya in 1555 Meskheti had been divided between the Safavids and the Ottomans, and by the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 all of it fell under Ottoman control. Most Meskhetian Turks see themselves as descended from Ottoman settlers.

Pro-Georgian historiography has argued that they are Turkified Meskhetians, a Georgian ethnographic subgroup converted to Islam under Ottoman rule. The anthropologist Anatoly Khazanov has argued that this oversimplifies the matter, because their traditional culture, though it held some Georgian elements, was close to the Turkish one. Soviet documents of 1944 called them simply Turks, and the term Meskhetian came into use only in the late 1950s. Most call themselves Turks or Ahiskan Turks.

On 15 November 1944 the Soviet government under Joseph Stalin ordered the deportation of the Meskhetian Turks from Georgia. They were secretly driven from their homes and loaded onto rail cars, and as many as 30,000 to 50,000 died of hunger, thirst and cold. They had been accused of smuggling, banditry and espionage with their kin across the border. The Soviet Union was preparing a pressure campaign against Turkey, and in June 1945 Vyacheslav Molotov demanded the cession of Kars, Ardahan and Artvin. Stalin wanted the strategic border region cleared of people likely to be hostile to Soviet intentions. The deportation was officially acknowledged only in 1968.

Unlike other deported Muslim groups, the Meskhetians were not rehabilitated or permitted to return. In 1970 the leaders of their national movement asked the Turkish embassy in Moscow to let them emigrate to Turkey, and the Soviet government answered by arresting them. In 1989 riots broke out in the Fergana Valley between Meskhetian Turks and Uzbeks. Hundreds were killed or injured and nearly 1,000 properties were destroyed. About 70,000 went to Azerbaijan, and others to Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Ukraine.

The Soviet census of 1989 counted 207,502 Turks in the Soviet Union, but many Meskhetian Turks had been recorded as Azeri, Kazakh, Kyrgyz or Uzbek, so the official figures understate them. They remain dispersed across the former Soviet Union and live also in Turkey and the United States. Only a few hundred have been able to return to Georgia.
meskwaki: The Meskwaki are of Algonquian origin and belong to the prehistoric Woodland period culture area. Their language is a dialect of the Sauk-Fox-Kickapoo language and belongs to the Algic language family. In their own language they call themselves Meshkwahkihaki, "the Red-Earths", a name drawn from a creation story in which the culture hero Wisaka made the first humans from red clay. The name Fox came from a French mistake: hearing people identify as Fox, which was a clan name, the French applied it to the whole tribe as les Renards, and the English and later the United States government adopted it. The Meskwaki and Sauk are two distinct tribal groups, though United States officials treated them as a single political unit.

The Meskwaki controlled the Fox River system in what is now Wisconsin, part of a waterway vital to the French fur trade. The French estimated their number at about 6,500 in 1698, and by 1712 it had fallen to 3,500. They fought the French in the Fox Wars for more than three decades, from 1701 to 1742. The first Fox War lasted from 1712 to 1714, and in 1728 the King of France signed a decree commanding their complete extermination. After the Second Fox War of 1728 they numbered some 1,500. On 9 September 1730 most Meskwaki warriors were killed in Illinois as about 900 people tried to break out, and many women and children were enslaved or killed.

The Sauk and Meskwaki allied in 1735 and later settled along the Mississippi in what is now Iowa. By about 1800 the Meskwaki had recovered from only 200 survivors to around 1,600. After the Black Hawk War of 1832 the United States combined the two peoples for treaty purposes as the Sac and Fox, and a treaty of October 1842 led to their removal, with a reservation in Kansas from 1845.

Some Meskwaki stayed hidden in Iowa and others returned within a few years. In 1851 the Iowa legislature passed an unusual act allowing the Meskwaki to buy land and stay in the state, and in 1857 they bought the first 80 acres of their settlement in Tama County for US$1,000. In 1896 Iowa ceded jurisdiction over them to the federal government. In January 1941 twenty-seven Meskwaki men enlisted together in the United States Army, and some served as code talkers using their own language. Three federally recognised Sac and Fox tribes exist today, in Oklahoma, Iowa and Kansas and Nebraska.
mesoamerica: Mesoamerica lies on the isthmus joining North and South America, between about 10° and 22° north. It covers central and southern Mexico, all of Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador, western Honduras and the Greater Nicoya region of Nicaragua and Costa Rica, although its extent varied through time. Its lowlands, below 1,000 metres, are mostly tropical, while the highlands between 1,000 and 2,000 metres are generally temperate. The northern Yucatán Peninsula has almost no rivers and no lakes, and its water comes from aquifers reached through natural openings called cenotes.

Cultivation began as early as 7000 BCE with squash and chili, and maize, beans, tomato and avocado followed. By 2000 BCE maize was the staple crop. No single society was self-sufficient, so regions specialised in local resources and traded them, long-distance trade being mostly in luxuries such as obsidian, jade, cacao and Spondylus shells. The Olmec of the Gulf Coast built the first complex civilisation, at San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán, La Venta and Tres Zapotes, occupied from roughly 1200 to 400 BCE.

In the Preclassic period Maya centres such as El Mirador and Tikal arose, and the Zapotec founded Monte Albán. The first true Mesoamerican writing systems appeared among the Epi-Olmec and Zapotec, and the tradition reached its height in the Classic Maya logosyllabic script. Counting was vigesimal, with bars worth five and dots worth one. In the Classic period Teotihuacan and Tikal were the dominant cities, and Teotihuacan took part in a far-reaching network of exchange, its talud-tablero architecture being copied at distant sites.

After Teotihuacan collapsed around 600 CE, Xochicalco and Cholula competed in central Mexico, and Nahua peoples moved south into the region. In the Postclassic period the Toltec dominated central Mexico and the Mixtec Oaxaca, while Chichén Itzá and later Mayapán led the Maya north. The Aztecs built a tributary empire over most of central Mesoamerica. The Spanish conquest of the 16th century ended the tradition, and Eurasian diseases such as smallpox and measles killed upwards of 90% of the indigenous people. Many descendants still speak their ancestral languages.
mesoamerican-codices: The name covers manuscripts in the indigenous pictorial tradition of Mesoamerica, whether in content, style or symbolic conventions. Some use Mesoamerican writing systems, but others are pure pictures, native maps without glyphs, or colonial alphabetic texts with indigenous illustrations. Besides the best-known Aztec, Maya and Mixtec codices, important manuscripts were made by the Tlaxcaltec, Purépecha, Otomi, Zapotecs and Cuicatecs. Only about twenty pre-Columbian codices are known to survive.

Strictly, pre-Columbian manuscripts are not codices, a word popularised in the 19th century. They took native forms: the tira, a long strip of hide or paper such as the Codex Boturini; the screenfold, a tira folded into a book, such as the Codex Borgia; the roll, such as the Selden Roll; and the lienzo, a sheet of cloth, such as the Lienzo de Quauhquechollan.

Donald Robertson and John B. Glass, who made the first comprehensive census, sorted the documents into traditional pictorials, the paintings and maps of the Relaciones Geográficas made for the King of Spain in 1579–1585, the Techialoyan manuscripts drawn up as legal documents for indigenous communities, pictorial catechisms, and forgeries. By origin they range from pre-Columbian works such as the Borgia group to codices made under Spanish patronage, such as the Codex Mendoza, and native colonial ones such as the Codex Xolotl. Their subjects include ritual and the calendar, history, genealogy, maps and tribute. Traditional pictorials numbered 434 in the original census, and more are still found in Mexican villages.

Scholars agree that Maya writing is logo-syllabic, but there is no consensus on how picture and writing relate in the non-Maya manuscripts, which are the great majority. Some specialists see a mixture of iconography and true writing, others a system of graphic communication that represents language only in part. Some documents, such as the Codex Borgia, cannot yet be assigned to any language. Because the manuscripts are fragile, conservators now favour non-invasive methods, and digitisation has made them available to a wider public.
mesoamerican-long-count-calendar: The Long Count served where the Calendar Round could not. A day named by both the 260-day tzolkʼin and the 365-day haabʼ recurs only after 18,980 days, about 52 years, so longer spans needed a running tally. The Long Count is a modified base-20 scheme in which only the second place from the right rolls over at 18, so that 0.0.1.0.0 stands for 360 days rather than 400. Dates were written with a dot for one, a bar for five and a shell glyph for zero, one of the earliest uses of the zero concept in history.

On Maya monuments a date is given once, at the head of an inscription, opening with the Introductory Series Initial Glyph and followed by the five digits, the Calendar Round and an optional supplementary series with lunar data such as the age of the Moon. The Maya held that the completion of 13 bʼakʼtuns marked the creation of the world of human beings, when three stones were set at First-Three-Stone-Place and the sky could be raised.

The earliest contemporaneous Long Count inscription yet found is Stela 2 at Chiapa de Corzo in Chiapas, Mexico, with a date of 36 BCE that is not certain; the battered Stela 2 of Takalik Abaj in Guatemala may be earlier. Several of the oldest inscriptions are in an Epi-Olmec rather than Maya style, and three of the sites lie several hundred kilometres west of the Maya homeland, which leads some researchers to believe that the calendar predates the Maya. The first unequivocally Maya example is Stela 29 at Tikal, with a date of 292 CE.

By the time the Spanish reached the Yucatán Peninsula the numbered Long Count was no longer in use; the Maya kept unnumbered kʼatuns and tuns in an abbreviated Short Count. Scholars match it to Western calendars through the Goodman–Martinez–Thompson correlation of 584,283 days, which places the starting date on 11 August 3114 BCE in the proleptic Gregorian calendar. Colonial records such as Diego de Landa's Relación de las cosas de Yucatán, lunar data in the inscriptions and carbon dates from wooden lintels at Tikal support it.

The end of the 13th bʼakʼtun on 21 December 2012 drew wide publicity, but Susan Milbrath of the Florida Museum of Natural History stated that there was no record that the Maya thought the world would end then, and inscriptions at Palenque project dates far beyond it.
mesopotamia: Mesopotamia lies within the Tigris–Euphrates river system, in the northern part of the Fertile Crescent, and corresponds roughly to the territory of modern Iraq. In the broader sense it also includes parts of present-day southwestern Iran, southeastern Turkey, northeastern Syria and Kuwait. The climate is semi-arid, with a vast desert expanse in the north that gives way in the south to a region of marshes, lagoons, mudflats and reed banks of about 15,000 square kilometres. In the south the two rivers unite and empty into the Persian Gulf. The name comes from the Greek for land between rivers.

Mesopotamia is the site of the earliest developments of the Neolithic Revolution, from around 10,000 BCE. Writing emerged there in a pictographic script, proto-cuneiform, in the Uruk IV period, in the late 4th millennium BCE, and the documented record of events begins in the early third millennium BCE with cuneiform records of early dynastic kings. The Sumerians and Akkadians dominated the region from the beginning of recorded history, around 3100 BCE, to the fall of Babylon in 539 BCE. The rise of empires began with Sargon of Akkad around 2350 BCE.

In the early second millennium BCE Mesopotamian society divided into Assyria in the north and Babylonia in the south. From 900 to 612 BCE the Neo-Assyrian Empire controlled much of the ancient Near East. The Babylonians, long overshadowed by Assyria, then seized power and dominated the region for a century as the final independent Mesopotamian realm until the modern era. In 539 BCE Cyrus the Great conquered Mesopotamia for the Achaemenid Empire, and Alexander the Great took it in 332 BCE; among his successors the Seleucids emerged victorious.

Around 150 BCE the region was under the Parthian Empire and became a battleground between Romans and Parthians. In 226 CE the eastern regions fell to the Sassanid Persians under Ardashir I, and the division of the region between the Roman and Sassanid empires lasted until the Muslim conquest of the 7th century CE, after which it came to be known as Iraq.

The earliest language written in Mesopotamia was Sumerian. Akkadian became dominant under the Akkadian and Assyrian empires, but Sumerian was kept for administrative, religious, literary and scientific purposes. Mesopotamian mathematics used a base-60 numeral system, the source of the 60-minute hour and the 360-degree circle, and Babylonian astronomers could predict eclipses and solstices.

Mesopotamia corresponds roughly to modern Iraq. Modern Assyrians remain descendants of the native Mesopotamians, and the Marsh Iraqis are genetically and culturally the closest modern people to the ancient Sumerians.
mesrop-mashtots: Mesrop Mashtots was born in the village of Hatsekats in the canton of Taron. His father was named Vardan; scholars have taken him for a priest, a nobleman, a member of the Mamikonian clan or a peasant. His pupil and biographer Koriun says he received a Greek education, and he also knew Middle Persian and Syriac. In the late 380s he moved to the Armenian capital, Vagharshapat, and worked at the royal court, where sources give him posts including royal chancellor. Around 394 he became a monk and a hermit, then gathered 40 disciples and, with the blessing of the Catholicos Sahak Partev, began missionary work among Armenians, many of whom were still pagan.

Armenia had lost its independence in 387 and was divided between the Byzantine Empire and Persia. Armenians read Christian texts in Greek, Persian and Syriac, which suited the sounds of their language poorly, so scripture and liturgy were largely unintelligible to the faithful. Mashtots, helped by Sahak and King Vramshapuh, and after consulting the bishop Daniel and the monk Rufinus, created an alphabet of thirty-six letters around 405; two more were added in the twelfth century. He founded schools to teach it and sent pupils to Edessa, Constantinople and other centres to study Greek and bring back texts.

The Bible was translated, the version in use being completed about 434, and the decrees of the first three ecumenical councils and many works of the Greek Fathers followed. Medieval Armenian sources also credit him with the Georgian and Caucasian Albanian alphabets; this is disputed, and most scholars link the Georgian script to the conversion of Iberia.

Mashtots survived Sahak by about six months and died on 17 February 440. He is buried at a chapel in Oshakan. The Armenian Apostolic Church keeps two feasts for him, and pilgrims visit his grave. Armenian writers treat him as the founder of Armenian literature and education and a symbol of the language, church and school system; Koriun compared his return after inventing the alphabet to Moses descending from Mount Sinai. Soviet historians presented him as a secular figure, and the Catholicos Karekin I objected in 1991 that his work was described in purely political terms.
messali-hadj: Ahmed Ben Messali Hadj was born in Tlemcen, the son of Hadj Ahmed Messali, who was of Turkish origin, and of Ftéma Sari Ali Hadj-Eddine, daughter of a qadi of the Darqawiyya brotherhood. He went to a local French primary school and received a religious education shaped by the Darqawiyya Sufi order. He served in the French army from 1918 to 1921, becoming a sergeant in 1919, and in October 1923 went to Paris, where he sold Tlemceni handicrafts, took Arabic courses and met his wife, Émilie Busquant.

Abdelkader Hadj Ali recruited him to the colonial commission of the French Communist Party in 1925. Messali founded the Étoile Nord-Africaine in 1926 and in Brussels in 1927 set out its demands: the abolition of the Indigénat, trade union rights, education for all and social welfare. The party was banned in 1929, and Messali was often jailed or exiled. In exile in Geneva he met Shakib Arslan and turned from Marxism to Pan-Arabism and Islamism, founding the Parti du Peuple Algérien in March 1937. A Vichy court sentenced him in March 1941 to 16 years of hard labour.

Amnestied after World War II, he was deported again to Brazzaville in 1945, which helped set off the riots at Sétif in May 1945, after which the army and police killed approximately 10,000 Muslims. In 1946 he founded the Mouvement pour le triomphe des libertés démocratiques, and in 1947 the party approved the creation of the Organisation spéciale. His insistence on Arabism alienated the Kabyles and contributed to the Berberist crisis of 1949.

The war of independence began in 1954 against his wishes. The FLN's armed wing destroyed his movement's guerrillas in Algeria early in the war, and the fighting moved to France in the so-called café wars; the author Remy Mauduit puts the dead at 10,000. Messali supported the proposals of President Charles de Gaulle in 1958. After independence in 1962 he failed to turn his movement into a legal party. He died in exile in France and was buried in Tlemcen. He is often called the father of Algerian nationalism.
