messapic-language: Messapic, also called Messapian or Iapygian, was spoken by the Iapygian peoples: the Calabri and Salentini, known together as the Messapians, the Peucetians and the Daunians. They lived in an area that roughly coincided with modern Apulia, and Messapic was the pre-Roman, non-Italic language of that region. The name is traditionally applied to the whole group of languages of these tribes, though some scholars prefer Iapygian for the group and reserve Messapic for the inscriptions of the Salento peninsula.

Modern archaeological and linguistic research, and some ancient sources, hold that the ancestors of the Iapygians crossed the Adriatic from the western Balkans. Recent archaeological evidence points to a proto-Messapic migration between 1700 BCE and 1400 BCE, and the Iapygians most likely left the eastern Adriatic coast from the 11th century BCE onwards, merging with existing cultures. Contact with Greeks intensified in the second half of the 8th century BCE, especially after Spartan colonists founded Taras. In the 6th century BCE Messapia took the Laconian-Tarantine alphabet and adapted it to the language.

Messapic is grouped with the Paleo-Balkan languages. It is generally regarded as related to, but distinct from, the Illyrian languages, a view supported by similar personal and place names on both sides of the Adriatic, such as Teuta and Teutā or Platōr and Plator-. Eric Hamp grouped Messapic and Illyrian as Messapo-Illyrian, and further with Albanian as Adriatic Indo-European. Hyllested and Joseph in 2022 identified it as the closest language to Albanian. Proposed cognates include Messapic aran and Albanian arë, field, and biliā and bijë, daughter.

A characteristic feature is the absence of the Indo-European opposition between the vowels u and o, so that the alphabet did not keep the letter upsilon. Proto-Indo-European s generally became h at the start of words and between vowels, as in hipa. The Messapic alphabet is an adaptation of the Laconian-Tarantine version of the Western Greek alphabet, and the northern Apulian script is sometimes treated as a distinct system.

Messapic is a fragmentary language, preserved in about 600 inscriptions from the mid-6th century BCE. Many are the names of the dead engraved in burial sites, about 36 per cent of the total, and only a few have been definitely deciphered. Longer texts, including those found in the Grotta della Poesia at Roca Vecchia, have not yet been fully used by scholars. Most inscriptions are published in the Monumenta Linguae Messapicae of 2002.

Greek, Oscan and Messapic were all written in Apulia under Roman influence, and bilingualism in Greek and Messapic was probably common in the south. A few Messapic words passed into Latin, among them gandeia, sword, and deda, nurse. Messapic went extinct following the Roman conquest of the region, and Latin replaced it.
messenians: Greeks of the Classical period thought the earliest inhabitants of Messenia were Pelasgians, followed by Aeolian Greeks. Excavations at Pylos, identified with the site of Ano Englianos, and at Nichoria show a bureaucratic, agricultural kingdom ruled by a wanax at Pylos in the 14th century BCE, whose people spoke Mycenaean Greek and worshipped the Greek gods at shrines such as Sphagianes. In the traditional account of a Dorian invasion, Dorians under Cresphontes are said to have come from Arcadia, made Stenyclarus in the northern plain their capital and extended their rule over the district.

Messenia's fertile soil and favourable climate drew the neighbouring Spartans. The First Messenian War, said to have begun with the murder of the Spartan king Teleclus, ended despite the resistance of King Euphaes and his successor Aristodemus with the subjugation of Messenia around 720 BCE. Two generations later the Messenians rose under Aristomenes and held off Sparta for some seventeen years, until the stronghold of Ira fell after a siege of eleven years. Many of those who did not leave were made helots, bearing half the fruits of their land to their masters, as the Spartan poet Tyrtaeus described.

After an earthquake struck Sparta in 464 BCE, the Messenians revolted again and held the citadel of Ithome for some years, until a truce mediated by the Athenians let their leaders leave the Peloponnese for Naupactus. After Thebes defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BCE, Epaminondas invited the exiled Messenians scattered in Italy, Sicily, Africa and elsewhere to return.

Though independent, Messenia never became strong enough to stand without outside support. It allied with Philip II of Macedon, then joined the Achaean League, and its troops fought at the Battle of Sellasia in 222 BCE. In a later war with the League the Messenians put Philopoemen to death in 183 BCE, and Lycortas took Messene the next year. In 146 BCE they came under Roman rule, and in 25 CE Tiberius and the Senate settled their long dispute with Sparta over the Ager Dentheliales in their favour.
messiah-handel: George Frideric Handel had lived in London since 1712 and was known chiefly for Italian opera. He turned to English oratorio in the 1730s in response to changes in public taste, and Messiah was his sixth work in the genre. Its text was compiled by Charles Jennens from the King James Bible and the Psalms of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer. Jennens was a wealthy landowner who had helped to finance the publication of Handel's scores since 1725 and who received Handel at his estate at Gopsall.

Handel received the text some time after 10 July 1741 and began work on 22 August. He finished Part I in outline by 28 August, Part II by 6 September and Part III by 12 September, and completed the work on 14 September, 24 days in all. Jennens regarded this speed as careless negligence, and the two men remained on strained terms because Handel refused the improvements Jennens urged.

The work is not in dramatic form: its singers play no characters and there is almost no direct speech. Jennens meant it as a reflection on Jesus as the Messiah, not a dramatisation of his life. Part I moves from the prophecies of Isaiah and others to the annunciation to the shepherds. The Passion is treated in Part II, which ends with the Hallelujah chorus. Part III covers Paul's teaching on the resurrection of the dead and the glorification of Christ in heaven.

Handel scored it for two trumpets, timpani, two oboes, two violins, viola and basso continuo. The musicologist Percy M. Young notes its orchestral restraint. The trumpets, introduced in Part I in the chorus Glory to God, are heard afterwards only in The trumpet shall sound, in Hallelujah and in the final chorus, Worthy is the Lamb. Several movements borrow from Handel's Italian cantatas, among them For unto us a child is born.

Handel was invited to Dublin by the Duke of Devonshire, the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, and gave subscription concerts there in the winter of 1741 to 1742. The Dublin reception was warm, but the London premiere at Covent Garden on 23 March 1743 was not. Critics argued that so exalted a subject did not belong in a theatre or with secular singer-actresses, and Handel billed it as a New Sacred Oratorio.

During the 1750s it was performed increasingly at festivals and cathedrals. A fashion for large forces began in 1784, when the Westminster Abbey concerts used 525 performers, and a Great Handel Festival at the Crystal Palace in 1857 used a chorus of 2,000. Mozart's reorchestration, Der Messias, began efforts to update the scoring. From the late 20th century performance has moved towards Handel's original intentions, though large productions continue. The autograph manuscript is in the British Library.
messina: Messina stands in the north-eastern corner of Sicily, on the western shore of the Strait of Messina, and is an important access point to Calabria on the mainland, at Villa San Giovanni and Reggio Calabria. Its municipal area of about 213.75 square kilometres stretches along 56 kilometres of coast, which makes it the longest and most maritime city in Italy. The climate is subtropical Mediterranean, with long hot summers and a wet, mild winter.

The early name of the city was Zancle, which Thucydides derived from a Siculian word meaning scythe, because of the shape of its natural harbour. At the beginning of the 5th century BCE Anaxilas of Rhegium settled refugees from Messenia there and renamed it Messene. It was Messana in the Roman age and became Messina in the Byzantine period. It was a major Roman city, contracted under Byzantine and Arab rule, and rose sharply in importance in the Norman era. Between the late Middle Ages and the mid-17th century it competed with Palermo to be the capital of the Kingdom of Sicily.

After an anti-Spanish revolt Messina was put to fire and sword in 1678, and its ruling class was annihilated. An earthquake seriously damaged it in 1783, and in 1908 another destroyed it almost entirely and killed about half the population. Rebuilding began in 1912, largely in the Liberty style. Allied bombers heavily attacked the city in 1943 during the landing in Sicily, in some 2,800 air raids, and it received the Gold Medal of Military Valor.

Messina is the capital of its metropolitan city and the third largest city on Sicily. Its port, for thousands of years one of the main commercial crossroads of the Mediterranean, is the first in Italy by number of passengers in transit, with ferries to Villa San Giovanni. The University of Messina was founded in 1548 by Pope Paul III, and the city has been an archdiocese since the same year. The Museo Regionale holds paintings by Caravaggio and by the Renaissance painter Antonello da Messina. The Good Friday procession of the Barette goes back to 1610.
mesta: Large-scale sheep transhumance in Castile grew after the Castilian conquest of the Taifa of Toledo in 1085. Much of the Muslim population of the new lands, renamed New Castile, left for North Africa or the Emirate of Granada, and the dry, thinly settled country suited livestock better than crops. Royal charters granting winter pasture in the Tagus valley went first to monasteries with summer pastures in the Sierra de Guadarrama, then to military orders such as those of Santiago and Calatrava, and later to the urban elites of Old Castile and León.

Alfonso X saw that granting similar rights to the towns would bring the crown a large new income, and the conquest of the Guadalquivir valley in the 13th century let northern flocks winter further south. His charter of 1273, the earliest to survive, claimed to replace four older documents, and it assumed the Mesta's existence rather than creating it, protecting its members from local taxes and restrictions.

The Mesta resembled a merchant guild but was a protective association: it owned no sheep or pastures and did not buy or sell wool. Its animals were under royal protection as the Cabaña Real, and the cañadas, the long-distance sheep-walks, were protected in perpetuity from being built on, cultivated or blocked. Ordinances of 1492 and a code of 1511 governed it for most of its existence. It was divided into four quadrillas based on Soria, Segovia, Cuenca and León, under a council whose president was, after 1500, always a member of the Royal Council.

A sales tax exemption for members in the late 15th century stimulated the export of merino wool, sold above all at Burgos, and the trade enriched members who were more and more often great nobles with flocks of over 20,000 sheep. The historian Klein saw the age before Charles V as the golden age of the Mesta and a decline from the 1560s under heavier taxes; others see fluctuating fortunes, with a crisis in the early-to-mid 17th century followed by recovery.

Under the first Bourbon kings the number of transhumant sheep doubled between 1708 and 1780 to its historical peak. Enlightenment reformers backed by Charles III then attacked the Mesta as harmful to agriculture, and Pedro Rodríguez, Count of Campomanes, appointed its president in 1779, went far towards dismantling it. Some Madrid streets are still part of the cañada system.
mestizo: The Spanish word mestizo comes from the Latin mixticius, meaning mixed. It is documented as early as 1275, when it referred to the offspring of an Egyptian and a Canaanite Jew, and was first recorded in English in 1582. In the Spanish colonial period it became one of the labels of the castas, the mixed groups of the colonies. It was a formal label in censuses, parish registers and Inquisition trials, and priests and royal officials could classify persons as mestizos, though individuals also used the word of themselves.

The Spanish colonies developed a complex set of racial terms, often called the sistema de castas. Archival research shows that the labels were not fixed through a person's life, and that in colonial Mexico the category was used flexibly to register births in parishes, without a strict genealogical pattern. The casta paintings made mainly in eighteenth-century Mexico, showing racial types in hierarchical groups, have shaped how modern scholars picture the system.

The term is used chiefly for people whose identity derives mostly from mixing between Spanish and Native heritage. It can also refer to other mixed peoples of partial Spanish descent, such as Filipino Mestizos, and in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands it meant people of mixed Chamorro or Filipino and Spanish ancestry. In Central America, Ladino is a colonial-era term for Spanish speakers who were neither colonial elites nor Indigenous.

With the Bourbon reforms and the independence of the Americas the caste system disappeared and the term lost popularity. The noun mestizaje, for racial mixing, came into use only in the twentieth century. In Mexico the figure of the mestizo became central to a new independent identity, neither wholly Spanish nor wholly Indigenous, and after the Mexican Revolution the government promoted the mestizaje ideology to build a unified identity without racial distinctions. The 1930 census used the word for all Mexicans who did not speak an Indigenous language.

In modern Latin America mestizo is more a cultural term, and indio is kept for those who maintain a separate Indigenous identity. The 1940 census of Peru, the last to use racial categories, grouped mestizos with whites, and together they were more than 53 percent of the population.
mestwin-ii: Mestwin was the son of Swietopelk II and the Přemyslid princess Eufrozyna. In 1243 he was handed to the Teutonic Order as a hostage under a ceasefire between his father and the Order, which failed to return him as agreed and held him until 1248, for a time in an Order castle in Austria. His father most likely made him duke of the Świecie province around 1250.

After his father's death he challenged his younger brother Wratislaw II for Gdańsk in 1266, opening the Pomerelian Civil War against his brother and his uncles Sambor II and Racibor. In the Treaty of Arnswalde on 1 April 1269 he took his lands as a fief from the Ascanian margraves of Brandenburg. A rebellion of his own knights and a short captivity in 1270 led him to hand Gdańsk to the Brandenburg duke Conrad, whom he later forced out with the help of his cousin Bolesław Pobożny of Greater Poland.

Wratislaw died in Wyszogród in 1271 and both uncles in the 1270s, leaving Mestwin sole ruler of a united Pomerelia. Under pressure from the Teutonic Order he gave up his castles and villages on the right bank of the Vistula and recognised, under duress and papal mediation in 1282, the Order's claim to Gniew, which Sambor II had willed to it. Further succession treaties with Przemysł II followed at Słupsk in 1287, including Bogusław IV of Szczecin, and were made public at Nakło in 1291.

He married three times: Judith, daughter of Ditrich I, Euphrosyne of Opole, whom he divorced in 1288, and Sulisława, who died in 1292. He had two daughters, Katarzyna and Eufemia. He died in Gdańsk and was buried in the Cistercian abbey of Oliwa. His sarcophagus was most likely destroyed when the army of Gdańsk burned the abbey in its war against King Stephen Báthory in 1577, but the joint sepulchre of the Samborides, founded in 1615 by Abbot Dawid Konarski, survives.
mesud-i: Mesud was the son of Kilij Arslan I, who died fighting Ridwan of Aleppo at the Battle of the Khabur River in 1107. He was passed over for the throne in favour of his brother Malik Shah. After Malik Shah was defeated by the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos at the Battle of Philomelion in 1116, Mesud rebelled. With the help of his father-in-law, the Danishmend ruler Gümüshtigin, he captured Konya later that year and defeated Malik Shah, who was blinded and eventually murdered.

Mesud later turned on the Danishmends and conquered some of their lands. In 1130 he began building the Alâeddin Mosque in Konya, which was completed in 1221. In 1146 he fended off a Byzantine attack on his capital. Near the end of his reign he fought the armies of the Second Crusade, one led by Emperor Conrad III of Germany and the other by King Louis VII of France. He defeated the first at Dorylaeum, near modern Eskişehir, in 1147, and the second at Laodicea, near modern Denizli, in 1148. In September 1149 he invaded the Principality of Antioch and captured Marash.

Emperor Manuel I Komnenos persuaded him to attack Thoros II and demand his submission. An attack in 1154, provoked by an Armenian raid into Seljuk lands in Cappadocia, was routed by Thoros with a contingent of the Knights Templar. The Armenian chronicler Smbat Sparapet describes the sultan's army fleeing with its horses dying. Mesud died in 1156 and was succeeded by his son Kilij Arslan II. His daughter Kamero married John Tzelepes Komnenos, a Komnenos who had converted to Islam.
mesud-ii: Ghiyath al-Din Mesud was the eldest son of Sultan Kaykaus II. He spent part of his youth in exile in the Crimea and lived for a time in Constantinople, the Byzantine capital. He first appears in Anatolia in 1280 as a pretender to the throne. In 1284 the Ilkhanid ruler Ahmed Tekuder deposed and executed the Seljuq sultan Kaykhusraw III and put Mesud in his place.

Ahmed's successor, Arghun, divided the Seljuq lands and gave Konya and the western half of the kingdom to the two young sons of the deposed sultan. Mesud invaded with a small force, had both boys killed and established himself in Konya in 1286. He then led several campaigns against the rising Turkmen beyliks, always on behalf of the Mongols and usually with Mongol troops.

The best known began late in 1286 against the Germiyanids, a warlike band of Turkmen whom the Seljuqs had settled in south-western Anatolia a generation earlier to hold the more unruly nomads in check. Mesud fought under the guidance of the elder statesman and vizier Fakhr al-Din Ali, and though there were some successes in the field, the mobile Germiyanids remained a strong force. Expeditions with his Mongol allies against the Karamanids, the Eshrefids and the Ottomans proved just as fruitless.

In 1297, amid intrigue and almost constant revolt against the distant Ilkhanate by Mongol officers and local Turkmen lords, Mesud was implicated in a plot against it. He was pardoned, but lost his throne and was held at Tabriz. His replacement, Kayqubad III, was soon caught up in a similar plot and executed by Mahmud Ghazan. Mesud, by then impoverished, returned to the throne in 1303 and held the title until his death, the last of the Seljuks of Rum. Findings made in 2015 suggest that his grave lies in Samsun.
metacom: Metacom was the second son of the sachem Massasoit, after his older brother Wamsutta. In 1660 the two brothers appeared before the Plymouth Court, where the English colonists of Plymouth Colony gave them the names Philip and Alexander; the historian Jill Lepore links the names to the Macedonians of Acts 16:9. Wamsutta briefly became sachem on their father's death in 1661 but soon died too, and Metacom, who believed their father had been poisoned, became sachem in 1662. He married Wootonekanuske, younger sister of Wamsutta's widow Weetamoo, the female sachem of the Pocasset, who became his ally.

His first aim was to live in peace with the colonists, and trade with them was his main charge. Conflicts over land use and the loss of game to spreading settlement turned many peoples of the region against the colonists, while the Iroquois Confederation pressed from the west in the Beaver Wars. In 1671 the leaders of Plymouth Colony forced him to surrender much of his people's arms and ammunition and to accept English law. Hostilities broke out in 1675, and in King Philip's War he led the Wampanoags, Pocomtucs, Nipmucs and Narragansetts against the Puritan settlers and their allies, the Mohegans, Pequots and Christian Indians.

As the colonists' numbers told, he took refuge in the Assowampset Swamp in southern Massachusetts. Hunted by rangers under Captain Benjamin Church, he was shot by John Alderman, a praying Indian, on 12 August 1676 in the Miery Swamp near Mount Hope. His head was set on a pike at the entrance to Plymouth for more than two decades and his body was cut into quarters; his wife and nine-year-old son were sold into slavery. Some scholars hold that his death marked the end of the war.

Later writers made him a figure of literature. Mary Rowlandson described meeting him in her memoir of captivity, Washington Irving wrote a sympathetic sketch, Philip of Pokanoket, in 1820, and John Augustus Stone's tragedy Metamora; or, the Last of the Wampanoags (1829) was popular in the 1830s and 1840s. Many places bear his name, among them the Metacomet Ridge and several towns called Metamora.
metapolitefsi: The name had first been given to an attempt at liberalisation by Georgios Papadopoulos, head of the junta that had taken power in 1967. After the constitution of 1973 made him president, he began in September 1973 what was called the Markezinis Experiment: he dismissed the military men from his cabinet, dissolved the revolutionary council and made Spyros Markezinis prime minister, while abolishing martial law, easing censorship and freeing political prisoners.

In November 1973 the Athens Polytechnic uprising broke out, and on 25 November the hardliner Dimitrios Ioannides used it as a pretext for a counter coup planned months before. Ioannides arrested Papadopoulos and Markezinis, cancelled the elections planned for 1974, restored martial law and installed General Phaedon Gizikis as president and Adamantios Androutsopoulos as prime minister.

On 15 July 1974 the junta's coup deposed Makarios III, archbishop and president of Cyprus, and put Nikos Sampson in his place. Turkey answered on 20 July with Operation Atilla, the invasion of Cyprus. With war with Turkey threatening, the military leaders abandoned Ioannides. On 23 July Gizikis met old guard politicians, among them Panagiotis Kanellopoulos, Markezinis, Stephanos Stephanopoulos and Evangelos Averoff, with the heads of the armed forces. When the others left without agreement, Averoff persuaded Gizikis that only Konstantinos Karamanlis, prime minister from 1955 to 1963, could lead the transition, and Gizikis telephoned him in Paris, pledging that the military would stay out of politics.

Karamanlis flew back on a jet lent by President Valéry Giscard d'Estaing and was sworn in by Archbishop Seraphim of Athens at 4 a.m. on 24 July 1974. For weeks he slept aboard a yacht guarded by a naval destroyer.

Karamanlis legalised the Communist Party of Greece, freed political prisoners and pardoned political offences against the junta, removed its appointees with caution, and put its leaders on trial. He withdrew Greece from NATO's military structure in protest at the allies' inaction over Cyprus. His New Democracy party won 220 of the 300 seats in the first free elections, with 60 for the Centre Union, 12 for Andreas Papandreou's PASOK and 8 for the United Left. Its margin fell in 1977, and Karamanlis became president on 10 May 1980. Some analysts, among them Ino Afentouli, see PASOK's victory in 1981 as the culmination of the metapolitefsi, since 1974 had returned the old political class to power.
methodism: Methodism began as a revival movement within the Church of England, led by John Wesley (1703–1791), his younger brother Charles Wesley (1707–1788) and George Whitefield. The brothers founded the Holy Club at the University of Oxford, whose members took Communion weekly, fasted, avoided most amusements and visited the sick, the poor and prisoners. Fellow students branded them Methodists for the way they used rule and method in their religious affairs. In 1735 both brothers went to North America at the invitation of General James Oglethorpe, founder of the Georgia Colony, as ministers to the colonists and missionaries to the Native Americans, but they were unsuccessful and returned conscious of their lack of genuine faith.

Wesleyan theology centres on sanctification and the transforming effect of the Holy Spirit on a Christian's character. Methodists hold the Arminian view that Christ died for all people and that salvation is open to all, against Calvinist predestination, although Whitefield and several other early leaders were Calvinistic Methodists. Scripture is the primary authority, read with Christian tradition and the historic creeds, and most Methodists recognise two sacraments, baptism and Holy Communion.

Worship combines the liturgy of the Book of Common Prayer with the preaching service, extempore prayer, hymns, many written by Charles Wesley, the quarterly lovefeast and the watchnight service. Members joined class meetings for encouragement. Early Methodists dressed plainly, fasted weekly and condemned gambling, theatre and dancing.

Early Methodism drew followers from all levels of society, and its preachers took the message to outcasts such as criminals. It gave women authority in church leadership, but their role diminished sharply after 1790 as the churches became more structured and male-dominated. In the United States it became the religion of many enslaved people, who later formed black churches in the Methodist tradition.

Methodism became a separate denomination after Wesley's death and spread through the British Empire and the United States by missionary work: to the Caribbean from 1760, to Newfoundland in 1763 and to China in 1847. It is widespread in Fiji, Samoa and Tonga. There is no single Methodist church with universal authority; Methodists belong to many independent denominations, called connexions.
metic: Foreign migration to Athens goes back to the archaic period, and Solon was said to have offered citizenship to foreigners who would settle and practise a craft, but metic status did not yet exist in his time. Scholars have dated its development to the reforms of Cleisthenes in 508 BCE, but the growth of the Athenian population after 480 BCE suggests that immigrants could still become citizens then.

Rebecca Futo Kennedy places the origin of the status in the 460s BCE, and James Watson in 451 BCE, the year in which Pericles introduced his citizenship law. The first known use of the word metoikos is in Aeschylus' Persians of 472 BCE, though Watson argues that there it means only 'immigrant'. The word is formed from the Greek for 'change' and 'dwelling'.

One estimate puts the male metic population of Attica at about 25,000 when the Peloponnesian War began in 431 BCE, roughly a third of the total. Most metics probably came from nearby cities to seek economic opportunities or to flee persecution, though some came from Thrace and Lydia. Citizenship was a matter of inheritance, so a metic could be the descendant of an immigrant many generations back. Metics had no part in political life but might be fully integrated in the city's social and economic life.

Metics were barred from the assembly and exempt from jury service, but they had the same access to the courts as citizens and could prosecute and be prosecuted. Unlike citizens, they could be made to undergo judicial torture, and the penalties for killing them were lighter. A metic could be enslaved for failing to pay the metoikion or to name a sponsor, or for marrying a citizen or claiming to be one. Citizenship was rarely granted; more common was isoteleia, 'equal rights', which freed a metic from the usual liabilities.

The status lost its distinctive legal force in the 4th century BCE, when metics were allowed to act in court without a sponsor, and ended in Hellenistic Athens, when the purchase of citizenship became frequent. The census of Demetrius Phalereus of about 317 BCE counted 21,000 citizens, 10,000 metics and 400,000 slaves. Aristotle, Aspasia and Lysias are among the metics named. In modern French the word métèque was revived as a xenophobic term for immigrants, popularised in the late 19th century by the nationalist writer Charles Maurras.
metis: The Métis are an Indigenous people whose historical homelands include Canada's three Prairie Provinces and extend into parts of Ontario, British Columbia, the Northwest Territories and the northwest United States. They descend from mixed European and Indigenous ancestry, and their distinct identity took shape by the mid-18th century in the early years of the fur trade.

From 1650 onward many French and British fur traders, mostly French and Scottish, married Cree, Ojibwe and Saulteaux women in what was called marriage according to the custom of the country. The Métis Nation originated largely in the Red River Valley and organised politically in the 19th century around the Red River Settlement, now Winnipeg. Their descendants are known as the Red River Métis.

In 1870 the Métis Provisional Government of Louis Riel brought the Red River Settlement into Confederation as the province of Manitoba, which makes Manitoba the only province founded by an Indigenous person. In 1885, during the North-West Rebellion, Riel declared the Provisional Government of Saskatchewan. Its council, the Exovedate, met at Batoche and held real authority only over the Southbranch Settlement; it collapsed after the Battle of Batoche that year.

The Métis sold most of the 600,000 acres they received in the first settlement. In the late 19th century the border along the 49th parallel, which Métis had crossed in either direction in times of conflict, so that it was known as the Medicine Line, came to be enforced by the Canadian government, which split some of the Métis population and restricted their access to buffalo. In the 1930s activists in Alberta and Saskatchewan pressed land claims, and in 1934 the Alberta government formed the Ewing Commission, which led to the Métis Population Betterment Act of 1938.

The Constitution Act, 1982 recognises the Métis as one of three Indigenous peoples of Canada, with the First Nations and Inuit, and in 2014 the Supreme Court of Canada held in Daniels v Canada that Métis and non-status Indians are 'Indians' under section 91(24). The 2021 census counted 624,220 Métis. 25 million acres. The Manitoba Métis Federation, founded in 1967, signed a self-government agreement with the Government of Canada on 6 July 2021.

Many Métis once spoke, and some still speak, Métis French or an Indigenous language; a few spoke Michif, a mixed language of Plains Cree verbs and French nouns, which is most used at the Turtle Mountain Indian Reservation in North Dakota and which Métis councils now encourage.
metohija: Metohija covers 35 per cent of Kosovo, 3,891 square kilometres, and is about 23 kilometres wide at its broadest and about 60 kilometres long, at an average altitude of 450 metres. The Mokra Gora, the Accursed Mountains, Pashtrik, the Šar Mountains and Drenica enclose it. It takes in the districts of Gjakova, Peja and Prizren. Its fertile land is watered by many small rivers and has a Mediterranean influence; it is known for vineyards, fruit orchards and chestnut and almond trees.

The name comes from the Greek metochia, 'monastic estates', a reference to the many villages and estates owned by Serbian Orthodox monasteries and Mount Athos in the Middle Ages. The Albanian name Rrafshi i Dukagjinit takes its name from the Dukagjini family, who ruled much of the area in the 14th and 15th centuries. Jahja Drançolli argues that Metohija did not appear as a geographic term in the medieval and Ottoman periods, only for ecclesiastical property, and that Serbian scholars first used it so in the 19th and 20th centuries.

After the Roman conquests the area was divided between Dardania and Praevalitana. The Slavs settled the Balkans in the 6th and 7th centuries, and in 1019 the region became part of the Eparchy of Prizren. Stefan Nemanja was recognised as independent in 1190 and kept the north, Hvosno, while the south joined the Kingdom of Serbia by the early 13th century. After 1371 the Balšić family and from 1378 the Branković family controlled it, and it remained in the Serbian Despotate until the Ottoman Empire conquered it in 1455.

Ottoman registers of the 16th century suggest that the plains had a majority Albanian population, mostly Christian farmers. In 1912 the Kingdom of Montenegro took most of the region in the First Balkan War, and the Kingdom of Serbia took the Prizren area. In 1944 Yugoslav Partisans liberated it from occupation, and in 1946 it became part of Serbia's Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija.

The 2024 census recorded 570,147 people in Metohija. The term 'Metohija' was official in the names of the Autonomous Region and Province of Kosovo and Metohija from 1945 to 1968, was dropped in 1968, and was restored by the Serbian constitution of September 1990. On 17 February 2008 representatives of Kosovo Albanians declared independence, and Serbia continued to treat Metohija as part of its territory.
metsuke: The metsuke were officials of the bakufu ranking somewhat below the bugyō. Their duty was to detect and investigate maladministration, corruption or disaffection anywhere in Japan, above all among people below the rank of daimyō, and in effect they served as the shogun's intelligence service, reporting to Edo on events across the country. At any one time there were as many as twenty-four of them. They reported to the wakadoshiyori, who ranked just below the rōjū.

Their counterparts, the ōmetsuke, watched over officials and the daimyō themselves and reported directly to the four or five rōjū at the head of the shogunate's bureaucracy. The two groups had no official reporting relationship, but their work was designed to complement each other. The ōmetsuke were chosen from among the bannermen and held the highest rank open to them.

The first four ōmetsuke, Akiyama Masashige, Mizuno Morinobu, Yagyu Munenori and Inoue Masashige, were appointed on 17 December 1632. In the middle of the Edo period the post became more ceremonial, an honorary position often given to bannermen late in their careers.

The shogunate's bureaucracy grew piecemeal, and metsuke or ōmetsuke were sometimes chosen to deal with a particular problem. After 1845 the prefix kaibō-gakari, in charge of maritime defence, was added to the titles of some officials who oversaw coastal waters and, by implication, dealings with foreigners; Arao Norimasa served as kaibō-gakari-metsuke from 1852 to 1854. The term later gave way to gaikoku-gakari, and these posts preceded the gaikoku-bugyō, first appointed in August 1858 to advise on foreign affairs and negotiate with foreign diplomats.

The post was not immune to corruption, and metsuke could be swayed by bribes. In later popular culture they appear in the television jidaigeki Abarenbō Shōgun, as persecutors of Japanese Christians in the film Silence (2016), and as secret policemen in the video game Total War: Shogun 2.
metz: Metz lies on the banks of the Moselle and the Seille, 43 km from the Schengen tripoint where the borders of France, Germany and Luxembourg meet. Several branches of the Moselle form islands there, which the urban plan has taken in. In ancient times the town was known as the city of the Mediomatrici, then as Divodurum Mediomatricum, meaning Holy Village or Holy Fortress of the Mediomatrici. During the 5th century the name evolved to Mettis, from which the present spelling comes.

Before the conquest of Gaul in 52 BCE Metz was the oppidum of the Celtic Mediomatrici. Under Roman rule it quickly became one of the principal towns of Gaul, with a population of 40,000, until its transfer to the Franks about the end of the 5th century. Between the 6th and 8th centuries it was the residence of the Merovingian kings of Austrasia. After the Treaty of Verdun in 843 it became the capital of the Kingdom of Lotharingia, and was in the end integrated into the Holy Roman Empire with semi-independent status. In the 12th century it became a republic, which stood until the 15th century.

Gregorian chant was created in Metz in the 8th century as a fusion of Gallican and ancient Roman repertory, and was then called Messin chant. The bishops of Metz, notably Saint Chrodegang, promoted its use for the Roman liturgy in Gallic lands. The city was also a centre of Carolingian manuscript illumination, producing the Drogo Sacramentary.

Metz is the prefecture of the Moselle department. Its Gothic Saint Stephen's Cathedral, built during the 13th century, has the largest expanse of stained-glass windows in the world, and the Germans' Gate of the 13th century is the last medieval bridge castle in France. The Basilica of Saint-Pierre-aux-Nonnains is described as the oldest church in France. The city is on France's UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List. Since 1919 a local law, running parallel to French law, has preserved rules applied before 1870 and enacted by Germany between 1871 and 1918.
meurthe-et-moselle: The department is part of the Grand Est region and of the traditional region of Lorraine, and takes its name from two rivers, the Meurthe and the Moselle. It borders the departments of Meuse to the west, Vosges to the south, and Moselle and Bas-Rhin to the east. To the north it reaches the Belgian province of Luxembourg and the country of Luxembourg, by a salient formed by the arrondissement of Val-de-Briey. It is one of two French departments that border Luxembourg.

It extends for 130 km from north to south and is between 7 and 103 km wide. Its chief rivers are the Moselle, the Meurthe, the Chiers and the Vezouze, and part of it lies within the Lorraine Regional Natural Park.

The department was created in 1871, at the end of the Franco-Prussian War, from the parts of the former departments of Moselle and Meurthe that remained French territory. Its boundary with Moselle was the frontier between France and Germany from 1871 to 1919 and again between 1940 and 1944. Only one change has been made since. In 1997 the small commune of Han-devant-Pierrepont, previously in the Meuse department, was incorporated into Meurthe-et-Moselle for administrative reasons.

Nancy is the prefecture and the largest city. The department had 732,236 inhabitants in 2023, and its people are known as Meurthe-et-Mosellans. The area around Nancy is highly urbanised, whereas the Saintois in the south remains rural.

The economy depended heavily on mining until the 1960s, with iron, salt and lime extraction sites. Around Nancy it now rests largely on services, research and higher education. Air services are provided by Metz–Nancy–Lorraine Airport, and residents also use the airports of Luxembourg and Strasbourg.
meuse: The Meuse rises at Pouilly-en-Bassigny, in the commune of Le Châtelet-sur-Meuse on the Langres plateau, and flows north past Sedan, the head of navigation, and Charleville-Mézières into Belgium. At Namur it is joined by the Sambre. Beyond Namur it winds east, passes Liège and turns north, forming part of the Belgian-Dutch border. In the Netherlands it passes Venlo and turns west to join the delta it shares with the Rhine and the Scheldt.
The name comes from the Latin Mosa, which derives from a Celtic or Proto-Celtic name probably related to the English word maze, a reference to the river's twists and turns.

From 1301 the upper Meuse roughly marked the western border of the Holy Roman Empire with the Kingdom of France, after Count Henry III of Bar had to receive the western part of the County of Bar as a French fief from King Philip IV. In 1408 a Burgundian army led by John the Fearless helped John III against the citizens of Liège, who were in revolt. After defeating them, John ordered the drowning in the Meuse of burghers and nobles whose loyalties he suspected.

The border stayed relatively stable until King Henry II annexed the Three Bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun in 1552, and until the occupation of the Duchy of Lorraine by the forces of King Louis XIII in 1633. The lower Belgian, Walloon, stretch of the valley, part of the sillon industriel, was the first fully industrialised area on the European continent.

In the Netherlands, a flood in the late Middle Ages connected the Maas with the Merwede at Woudrichem. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries the connection with the Rhine was closed off and the Maas was given a new artificial mouth, the Bergse Maas, which reduced the risk of flooding. This was regarded as the main achievement of Dutch hydraulic engineering before the Zuiderzee Works and Delta Works. The Meuse and its crossings were a key objective in the Battle of France and the Battle of Sedan, and again in the Battle of the Bulge in December 1944 and January 1945.

The river is about 925 km long and is navigable over a substantial part of its length, linking the ports of Rotterdam, Amsterdam and Antwerp with industrial areas upstream as far as Liège and Namur. The river's basin of about 36,000 km2 lies mostly in Wallonia, France and the Netherlands. As a major communication route the Meuse gave its name to Mosan art, and Joachim Patinir painted its landscape.
meuse-inferieure: Meuse-Inférieure, Beneden-Maas in Dutch, the Lower Meuse, was named after the river Meuse and lay in parts of present-day Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany. Before the French annexation its lands had belonged to the County of Loon, Austrian Upper Guelders, Staats-Oppergelre, the County of Horne, the Abbacy of Thorn, Maastricht and part of the Lands of Overmaas. The medieval Duchy of Limburg itself, long governed together with the Lands of Overmaas, was not part of the department.

Its chef-lieu was Maastricht. It was divided into three arrondissements: Maastricht, with cantons including Bilzen, Heerlen, Meerssen, Rolduc and Tongres; Hasselt, with Looz, Peer and Saint-Trond; and Roermond, with Achel, Brée, Maaseik, Ruremonde, Venlo, Weert and Niederkrüchten. A prefect headed it, assisted by a secretary-general, and subprefects governed the arrondissements, though the prefect himself held the subprefecture of Maastricht until 1811.

The department was created on 1 October 1795, when the French Republic formally annexed the Austrian Netherlands and the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. After Napoleon's defeat in 1814, Niederkrüchten and Herzogenrath went to the Kingdom of Prussia, in what is now North Rhine-Westphalia, and the rest became the Province of Limburg of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, together with part of the Roer department.

When Belgium broke away from the kingdom from 1830, the province was divided. By 1839 it was settled that Hasselt and large parts of the other two arrondissements would go to Belgium and the rest stay in the Netherlands. Both parts kept the name Limburg, and the lands of the department now lie mostly in the Belgian and Dutch provinces of that name.
mexica: After the decline of the Toltecs around 1200 CE, Nahua-speaking nomadic peoples entered the Valley of Mexico, possibly all from Aztlan, a homeland whose location is unknown; the Mexica were the last to arrive. According to legend they were seeking a sign from their god Huitzilopochtli, an eagle with a snake in its beak perched on a prickly pear cactus, and found it on an island in Lake Texcoco, where they founded Tenochtitlan in 1325, though some researchers prefer 1345. In 1337 a dissident group built Tlatelolco on an island to the north, which became Tenochtitlan's persistent rival.

The Mexica gave their name to Mexico. They were also called Culhua-Mexica, for their kinship alliance with the Culhua, descendants of the Toltecs, and the people of Tenochtitlan Tenochca, after the city and its founding leader, Tenoch. The name Aztec was coined by Alexander von Humboldt from Aztlán.

Within the Triple Alliance the Tenochca held a dominant position over their allies Texcoco and Tlacopan. In the centre of Tenochtitlan stood the Templo Mayor, a double pyramid-temple dedicated to Tlaloc, the ancient rain god of Central Mexico, and to Huitzilopochtli, the Mexica's own god, associated with the sun. Its buildings expressed a cosmology linking rain and fertility, warfare, sacrifice and empire with the sacred mission of preserving the sun and the cosmic order, and it was the site of large-scale sacrifices of enemy warriors. Nahuatl, their language, became a lingua franca as the empire grew.

After the Tlaxcaltec-Spanish alliance overthrew them in 1521, Tenochtitlan was destroyed and looted and rebuilt as Mexico City, where the Mexica were forbidden to resettle. Many Mexica women were kidnapped and raped, the people were made to submit to the King of Spain and accept baptism, their rituals were suppressed and their children taken to Christian schools, and survivors were sent to work on haciendas, in mines and on canals. Through defeat, overwork and epidemics their numbers fell by perhaps as much as 90% by 1600. Mexica names revived after Mexican independence, and descendants of the Mexica are today among the Nahua people of Mexico.
mexican-american-war: Mexico became independent from Spain with the Treaty of Córdoba in 1821 and a republic in 1824. Its governments were unstable, and the north was poorly controlled and open to raids by Comanche, Apache and Navajo. The secession of Texas in 1836 was followed by the Treaties of Velasco, which Mexico refused to recognise. The United States annexed Texas in 1845, and the border was disputed: the United States and Texas claimed the Rio Grande, while Mexico claimed the more northerly Nueces River.

James K. Polk was elected in 1844 on a platform of expanding to Oregon, California and Texas. His mission to Mexico offered $25 million for the disputed land, California and everything in between, and was refused. Mexican forces repelled a group of US soldiers on 25 April 1846, and Polk used the clash to persuade Congress to declare war.

Stephen W. Kearny's Army of the West occupied New Mexico, while the Pacific Squadron blockaded the Pacific coast. Zachary Taylor won at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma and then took Monterrey after hard fighting. Polk then sent a second army under General Winfield Scott, who carried out the first major amphibious landing in US history at Veracruz on 9 March 1847 with about 12,000 men.

Scott took Puebla on 1 May and advanced on Mexico City on 7 August. After an armistice failed on 6 September 1847, the battles of Molino del Rey and Chapultepec and the storming of the city gates delivered the capital. Guerrilla warfare followed, and desertion was a major problem for both armies.

Nicholas Trist, though recalled by Polk, concluded the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on 2 February 1848. Mexico accepted the Rio Grande as the border and ceded California, Nevada, Utah, most of New Mexico, Arizona and Colorado, and parts of other present-day states. The United States paid $15 million and assumed $3.25 million of Mexican debts to its citizens. A further 30,000 square miles went to the United States in the Gadsden Purchase of 1853.

In the United States most Whigs opposed the war and most Democrats supported it, and the question of slavery in the new territories sharpened sectional division. Some scholars see the war as leading to the American Civil War, in which many officers who had served in Mexico held command. In Mexico the war deepened political turmoil and undermined public finances.
mexican-revolution: Porfirio Díaz came to the presidency in 1876 and, but for the term of his ally Manuel González from 1880 to 1884, stayed in power until 1911 in the era called the Porfiriato. The constitution was amended in 1887 and 1890 to allow unlimited re-election, and regular elections were widely seen as shams.

By 1910 the ageing Díaz had found no orderly way to settle the succession, which set elites and the middle classes against each other during a period of labour unrest, shown in the strikes at Cananea and Río Blanco. The northern landowner Francisco I. Madero challenged him in the 1910 election, and Díaz had him jailed. On 5 October 1910 Madero issued the Plan of San Luis Potosí, calling for a rising from 20 November.

Rebellions broke out first in Morelos and then in northern Mexico. The Federal Army could not put them down, and Díaz resigned in May 1911 and went into exile. Madero became president in November 1911 but, an inexperienced democrat, he dismissed the forces that had brought him to power and faced a revolt by Emiliano Zapata in Morelos, where peasants demanded agrarian reform. In February 1913 generals of the old regime staged a coup in Mexico City, and Madero and Vice President Pino Suárez were assassinated on the orders of the new president, Victoriano Huerta.

Venustiano Carranza, governor of Coahuila, led the Constitutionalist Army against Huerta, while Zapata continued his rising. Huerta's regime fell in July 1914 and the Federal Army was dissolved. The victors then fought one another, and by the summer of 1915 Carranza's faction had defeated Pancho Villa's army. Zapata was killed in 1919 by an agent of Carranza.

A new constitution was promulgated in February 1917. It established universal male suffrage and promoted secularism, workers' rights, economic nationalism and land reform, and strengthened the federal government. Carranza served as president until 1920, when northern generals rose against his attempt to impose a civilian successor; he fled Mexico City and was killed.

Revolutionary generals held the presidency from 1920 to 1940, and the army came under civilian control. The party they founded in 1929 became the Institutional Revolutionary Party and ruled Mexico until the election of 2000. Foreign powers, above all the United States, influenced the outcome, and most of the dead were non-combatants.
mexican-war-of-independence: Mexican independence was not an inevitable outcome of the relationship between the Spanish Empire and its American-born Spaniards, the criollos. The Bourbon Reforms of the mid-eighteenth century aimed to strengthen the Spanish state, weaken the Catholic Church and place peninsular-born officials in office, and many historians see them as hastening the breakdown of imperial unity. An unofficial racial hierarchy kept criollos out of the highest offices, though most did not wish to overturn the social order entirely.

The immediate trigger was Napoleon Bonaparte's invasion of Spain in 1808, which deposed Charles IV and put Joseph Bonaparte on the throne. In Mexico City the city council promoted autonomy for New Spain, but on the night of 15 September 1808 a group led by the landowner Gabriel de Yermo overthrew the viceroy José de Iturrigaray, fearing he might make himself head of a new state.

The first phase began on 16 September 1810, when the priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla issued the Cry of Dolores. He drew tens of thousands of ordinary men, but did not organise them into a disciplined force. Hidalgo was captured, defrocked and executed in July 1811. The insurgency had already spread south, where the priest José María Morelos led a second phase, organising his forces, using guerrilla tactics and producing a written statement of aims, the Sentimientos de la Nación of 1813. Morelos was captured and executed in December 1815.

After that, Vicente Guerrero became the most important leader, and from 1815 to 1821 most of the fighting was guerrilla warfare in the hot country of the south. From 1816 to 1820 the war was a stalemate: the royal army held the major cities, but whole stretches of countryside were not pacified.

The decisive change came from Spain. In 1820 a military coup there forced Ferdinand VII to restore the liberal Constitution of 1812. Conservative royalists in New Spain, seeing it as a threat, came to regard independence as a way of keeping their position. The royalist officer Agustín de Iturbide allied with Guerrero under the Plan of Iguala, and many royalist commanders and soldiers changed sides. On 24 August 1821 Iturbide and the new viceroy Juan O'Donojú signed the Treaty of Córdoba, which the Spanish government refused to accept.

The Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City on 27 September 1821, and independence was proclaimed the next day. A First Mexican Empire under Iturbide gave way in 1823 to a federal republic. Spain recognised Mexican independence on 28 December 1836, making Mexico the first former colony it recognised. Mexicans later marked both 16 September, for Hidalgo's call, and 27 September, for actual independence.
mexico: Mexico covers 1,972,550 square kilometres, the thirteenth-largest country in the world, with coastlines on the Pacific Ocean, the Gulf of California, the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea. The central and northern territories lie at high altitudes. The highest elevations are in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, which includes Pico de Orizaba at 5,700 metres and Popocatépetl at 5,462 metres, and the Sierra Madre Oriental and Sierra Madre Occidental cross the country from north to south. The Chicxulub crater lies on the Yucatán peninsula, and much of the land mass is unsuited to agriculture because of aridity, soil or terrain.

Human presence dates back to at least 11,500 BCE, although dates as old as 28,000 BCE have been proposed for less securely dated sites. Mexico is the site of the domestication of maize, tomato and beans, which allowed sedentary agricultural villages to begin around 5000 BCE.

The Olmec culture, the earliest complex civilisation, flourished on the Gulf Coast from around 1500 BCE, and the Maya and Zapotec civilizations later developed complex centres. Teotihuacán, with a population of more than 150,000, formed a military and commercial empire, and after its collapse around 600 CE other centres competed. Toward the end of the post-Classic period the Aztecs established an empire based in Tenochtitlan.

Spanish colonisation began in 1521 with an indigenous alliance that defeated the Aztec Empire, establishing the colony of New Spain. The Mexican War of Independence of 1810 to 1821 ended Peninsular rule. In 1848 Mexico lost nearly half its territory in the Mexican–American War. Liberal reforms in the Constitution of 1857 led to civil war and French intervention, and the Second Mexican Empire under Emperor Maximilian I of Habsburg was overthrown by Republican forces led by Benito Juárez. The long rule of Porfirio Díaz ended with the Mexican Revolution of 1910 to 1920, which brought the Constitution of 1917, the current one.

Mexico has about 131 million inhabitants, and Mexico City is the capital and largest city. It is a federal republic with a presidential system and 32 states, with a bicameral Congress of the Union of 500 deputies and 128 senators. The Constitution gives Spanish legal equality with 68 indigenous languages.
mexico-city: Mexico City lies in the Valley of Mexico, also called the Basin of Mexico, in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt on the high plateaus of south-central Mexico. Its lowest point is about 2,200 metres above sea level, and mountains and volcanoes of over 5,000 metres surround it. The valley has no natural drainage outlet for the water that runs down from the slopes, so the city has long been open to flooding.

The Mexica founded Mexico-Tenochtitlan in 1325 or 1327 on an island in the lake system, which it shared with a smaller city-state, Tlatelolco. According to legend, the god Huitzilopochtli showed them the site by presenting a golden eagle perched on a prickly pear and devouring a rattlesnake. Between 1325 and 1521 the city came to dominate the other city-states round Lake Texcoco, and the Aztec Empire reached both the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific.

Hernán Cortés, with the aid of many other native peoples, reached Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519 and was greeted by the ruler Moctezuma II, whom he then placed under house arrest. After the siege of 1521 the city was nearly destroyed and was rebuilt to Spanish urban standards. The municipality of México Tenochtitlán was established in 1524, and from 1585 the city was officially Ciudad de México. It was a major political, administrative and financial centre of the colonial period.

After independence, the Federal Constitution of 4 October 1824 let Congress choose the seat of the federal government. Mexico City was preferred to Querétaro, largely through the persuasion of Servando Teresa de Mier, as the centre of the country's population and history. The choice was made official on 18 November 1824, and a surface of two leagues square centred on the Zocalo was separated from the State of Mexico as the Federal District. Residents won the right to elect their head of government in 1997, and on 29 January 2016 the district was renamed Ciudad de México.

Mexico City is the capital and largest city of Mexico, divided into 16 boroughs, or alcaldías. The 2020 census gave the city proper 9,209,944 people, and Greater Mexico City 21,804,515. Its historic centre and the muralist works of José Clemente Orozco, David Alfaro Siqueiros and Diego Rivera, at the National Palace and the Palacio de Bellas Artes among other buildings, belong to the heritage of the Mexican capital.
mfecane: The Mfecane was a period of heightened military conflict and migration in southern Africa, tied to state formation and expansion. It resulted from pre-existing political centralisation interacting with the effects of international trade, environmental instability and European colonisation. State formation had been intensifying since at least the late 1700s and accelerated once the international ivory trade opened, since the trade let leaders amass wealth to build instruments of control.

Deep drought struck south-eastern Africa in the early 19th century, aggravated by the atmospheric effects of volcanic eruptions in 1809 and 1815. Unequal distribution of land and food stores meant ordinary people suffered famine, while leaders facing falling production and scarcer ivory turned to raiding and conquest. A second stage in the 1820s and 1830s was driven largely by slave and cattle raiding by Griqua, Basters and other groups armed and mounted by European settlers.

In the east the Ndwandwe and Mthethwa paramountcies expanded in the 1810s. The Ndwandwe defeated and killed the Mthethwa leader Dingiswayo, and their king Zwide kaLanga then fought Shaka kaSenzangakhona's amaZulu. In 1826 Shaka put the Ndwandwe under Sikhunyana to flight at the Izindololwane Hills, and the Ndwandwe state collapsed. Soshangane founded the Gaza Kingdom, and Zwangendaba led his followers, called Ngoni, north of the Zambezi River. Shaka was assassinated in September 1828 by his brothers Dingane and Mhlangana.

In the interior, amaHlubi under Mpangazita attacked Queen MmaNthatisi's Batlôkwa in 1822, and in 1824 the Sotho polities began coalescing under Moshoeshoe. Mzilikazi's Ndebele raided widely and, after the arrival of Boer settlers and the battles of Vegtkop and Mosega in 1837 and 1838, were driven north of the Limpopo to Matabeleland, where Mzilikazi set up his capital at Bulawayo.

Traditional estimates put the death toll at 1 million to 2 million, but these figures are controversial, and some recent scholars revise them significantly downwards. The period saw the formation of new states, institutions and ethnic identities, among them the kingdom that became Lesotho under Moshoeshoe. The label first emerged in the 1830s and blamed Shaka, who was alleged to have waged near-genocidal wars; since the latter half of the 20th century scholars have largely rejected this for lack of evidence.

In 1988 Julian Cobbing argued that the roots lay in the labour needs of Portuguese slave traders at Delagoa Bay and of settlers in the Cape Colony. Elizabeth Eldredge challenged him, and by the early 2000s a consensus recognised many causes before and after Shaka came to power.
miami-people: The Miami call themselves Myaamiaki, a name that appears to derive from an older term meaning "downstream people". Their language belongs to the Algonquian family. Early Miami people are considered part of the Fisher tradition of Mississippian culture. When French missionaries first met them in the mid-seventeenth century they were living around the western shore of Lake Michigan, and Miami oral tradition says they had moved there to escape Iroquois war parties seeking to control the fur trade of the Ohio Valley. Historically the Miami included several bands, among them the Piankeshaw, Wea, Pepikokia, Kilatika, Mengakonkia and Atchakangouen.

Around the beginning of the eighteenth century, with French support, the Miami returned to their homeland. Their capital Kekionga stood at the junction of the Saint Joseph, Saint Marys and Maumee rivers, where Jean Baptiste Bissot, Sieur de Vincennes, set up a trading post and fort in 1704. The site controlled a portage between the Maumee and the Wabash. After the Revolutionary War, Britain transferred its claim to the Northwest Territory to the United States, and the Miami invited the Delaware and Shawnee, displaced by settlers, to settle at Kekionga. Together they formed the nucleus of the Western Confederacy and fought the Northwest Indian War.

Little Turtle's warriors repulsed an American attack on Kekionga in 1790, and in 1791 the Western Confederacy destroyed the army of General Arthur St. Clair. Anthony Wayne's forces defeated it at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in August 1794 and built Fort Wayne, and in 1795 tribal leaders signed the Treaty of Greenville. Later treaties ceded more land, and the government used debts to traders to press leaders to sign them. In 1846 the tribe's rank and file were forced to leave, first for Kansas and then Oklahoma, while several major families with private property were allowed to stay in Indiana.

The Miami Tribe of Oklahoma has been recognised by the United States government as the official tribal government since 1846, and has about 5,600 enrolled members. The Miami Nation of Indiana, which unsuccessfully sought separate federal recognition, lost the recognition it had under an 1854 treaty in 1897, and the Indiana legislature recognised the Eastern Miami in 1980 as a matter of state law. Daryl Baldwin, who received a MacArthur Foundation award in 2016, founded the Myaamia Center at Miami University in Oxford, Ohio, which works on language and cultural revitalisation. The Florida city of Miami is not named for them.
miao-people: Miao is a Chinese term for many groups with their own names for themselves, such as Hmong, Hmu, Xong and A-Hmao. Most speak Hmongic languages, a subfamily of the Hmong–Mien family, but the languages of the four main groups are mutually unintelligible. Historically the term was applied inconsistently to various non-Han peoples. It reappeared under the Ming dynasty with the sense of barbarian, and Ming writers distinguished raw and cooked Miao by their assimilation and political cooperation. Some scholars hold that Miao existed only as an outsiders' name until the Qing, and others that Miao identity emerged during the rebellions of the 18th and 19th centuries. The term gained official status in 1949 as the name of a nationality.

According to a Tang dynasty legend, the Miao descended from the Jiuli tribe led by Chiyou, who were defeated at the Battle of Zhuolu by Huang Di and Yan Di. Chinese records mention a San Miao kingdom around Dongting Lake, said to have been defeated by Yu the Great.

The Miao are not mentioned again until the Tang dynasty. In the following centuries they migrated across southern China and Southeast Asia, generally living in mountainous or marginal lands and farming by slash-and-burn cultivation. During the Miao rebellions of the Ming dynasty thousands were killed by imperial forces, and mass castrations of Miao boys took place.

Under the Qing the Miao fought three wars against the empire. A rebellion at Weining in Guizhou was suppressed in 1725, and the Yongzheng emperor sent Ortai as Viceroy to the provinces with large Miao populations. In 1735 the Miao of Guizhou rose against forced assimilation, and eight counties with 1,224 villages fought until 1738. A second war, in Guizhou and Hunan, lasted from 1795 to 1806. The largest, from 1854 to 1873, was led in Guizhou by Zhang Xiu-mei until his capture and death at Changsha. It affected over a million people, and by its end, according to Professor Wu of Xiangtan University, only 30 percent of the Miao remained in their home regions. It drove many Hmong to migrate into Laos and Vietnam.

Chinese tradition classes the Miao by the colour of women's clothing: Red Miao (Xong) in west Hunan, Black Miao (Hmu) in south-east Guizhou, Big Flowery Miao (A-Hmao) in west Guizhou and north-east Yunnan, and the Hmong in Yunnan, Sichuan and west Guizhou. Miao women are known for embroidery, weaving, batik and silver jewellery, which symbolises family wealth and is worn at weddings, funerals and spring celebrations. Marriage within one clan name is taboo, and inheritance descends to the youngest son, who stays with and cares for the aging parents.
micaela-bastidas: Micaela Bastidas was born on 23 June 1744, the natural daughter of Josefa Puyucahua Sisa and Manuel Bastidas, who died in 1746. Virtually nothing is known of her father, who was perhaps a priest or of African descent; some documents call her a zamba, the colonial term for a person of mixed African and indigenous ancestry, while her marriage certificate lists both parents as Spaniards, a label that may have been a sign of respectability. As an illegitimate child she was marginalised in the overwhelmingly indigenous highlands. She spoke Quechua better than Spanish, was a devout Catholic and had little formal schooling.

She married on 25 May 1760, before her sixteenth birthday, in the church of Our Lady of Purification in Surimana. Her husband, a descendant of the Inca Túpac Amaru I, was named cacique of Pampamarca, Tungasuca and Surimana in 1764 and traded across a wide network with 350 mules. They lived in Tinta and had three sons, Hipólito, Mariano and Fernando. Letters exchanged early in the rebellion show endearments and concern for each other's safety.

The rebellion opened on 4 November 1780, when the local Spanish commander Antonio de Arriaga was taken prisoner; he was later hanged. The rebels made their headquarters at Tungasuca and defeated the Spanish at Sangarará on 18 November. Because indigenous people were forbidden firearms, obtaining weapons was among the hardest of her tasks. She also issued safe-conducts, took charge of the rearguard, guarded against espionage and organised a service of mounted chasquis that carried messages across rebel territory.

Local rulers called her Señora Gobernadora, La Coya or La Reina, and one description calls her a superior strategist to her husband and certainly more daring. He held off from Cuzco, which allowed the Spaniards to bring in reinforcements. By March 1781 the rebel army numbered seven thousand men and women.

On 18 May 1781 the prisoners were taken to be executed. Hipólito had his tongue cut out and was hanged. Micaela Bastidas fought her executioners until they subdued her and cut off her tongue. A hand-cranked garrote made for the occasion could not be used because her neck was so slender, and she was strangled with a rope, beaten with a club and kicked to death, in front of her husband, who was then killed. Their bodies were dismembered and the parts sent to towns of the region for display. The involvement of women in such risings shocked the Spanish authorities, who gave them the same penalties as men.
micah-prophet: According to the Hebrew Bible, Micah, called the Morashtite, was a prophet of Yahweh, traditionally regarded as the author of the Book of Micah and one of the Twelve Minor Prophets. He is shown as a contemporary of Isaiah, Amos and Hosea. He came from Moresheth, also called Moresheth-Gath, a small town in southwest Judah, and the text gives him no father's name. This has led to the view that he was of common descent, since his message was aimed at the privileged classes. He lived in a rural area and often rebuked the corruption of city life.

He prophesied under the kings Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah, from about 740 to 698 BCE by one reckoning. He was active before the fall of Israel in 722 BCE and lived through Sennacherib's invasion of Judah in 701 BCE. The name means 'Who is like Yah(weh)?', a rhetorical question implying that no one is like God. Jeremiah, who prophesied about thirty years later, recalls Micah of Moresheth as a prophet in the reign of Hezekiah.

Micah's messages were directed chiefly at Jerusalem and mix denunciation with promise. In his early prophecies he foretold the destruction of both Samaria and Jerusalem. Samaria was rebuked for idol worship, and Jerusalem was doomed because its beautification was financed by dishonest business that impoverished its citizens. He also accused the prophets of his day of accepting money for their oracles. He anticipated the destruction of the Judean state and promised its restoration, with an era of universal peace. He is described as the first prophet to predict the downfall of Jerusalem, and Jeremiah 26 repeats his words that Zion will be plowed like a field.

He told the people what God requires of them: 'to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God' (Micah 6:8). The Talmud praises him for distilling the Torah into three principles, justice, loving-kindness and humility. The formation of the Book of Micah is debated, with a consensus that its final stage came in the Persian or Hellenistic period. Christians read Micah 5:2 as a prophecy that Bethlehem would be the birthplace of the Messiah, a passage recalled in Matthew 2:6. Several churches commemorate him as a saint, the Roman Catholic Church on 31 July, and the Eastern Orthodox Church on 14 August.
micanopy: Micanopy was born near present-day St. Augustine, Florida, around 1780; little else is known of his early years. Before he was chosen as chief he was called Sint-chakkee, "pond frequenter", and he was also known as Hulbutta Hajo, "Crazy Alligator". His name comes from the Hitchiti words miko, chief, and naba, above, and means something like "high chief". He succeeded Bolek as hereditary principal chief on the latter's death in 1819, when he was nearly forty. Position passed through the maternal line among the Seminole.

As chief he acquired large holdings of land and cattle and, as was common among the Seminole elite, had more than 100 fugitive slaves working his estates. He encouraged intermarriage between Seminole and black people, and some of their descendants rose to influence in the tribal councils. After the United States bought Florida from Spain through the Adams–Onís Treaty and Andrew Jackson became territorial governor in 1821, settlers poured into northern Florida. Micanopy opposed their advance; by the Treaty of Moultrie Creek in 1823 the Americans took 24 million acres of Seminole land, and the Seminole moved south.

After the Indian Removal Act of 1830, some chiefs signed the Treaty of Payne's Landing on 9 May 1832, giving up more land for a reservation in Indian Territory. Micanopy refused to sign and joined younger leaders such as Osceola, Alligator and his nephew Wild Cat in organising resistance.

After Osceola killed the Indian agent Wiley Thompson in December 1835, Micanopy and Osceola attacked the troops of Major Francis Langhorne Dade and General Duncan Lamont Clinch; only three soldiers survived what Americans called Dade's Massacre. Convinced in time that the war could not be won, he surrendered in June 1837 and began to negotiate removal, but Osceola carried him off. He was later seized by the forces of General Thomas S. Jesup under a flag of truce, a breach that turned much public feeling toward the Seminole.

After imprisonment in South Carolina he was sent west with about 200 other Seminoles, who were at first placed under the authority of the Creek Nation. He never regained his former power, but in 1845 he signed a treaty giving the Seminole partial independence from the Creek Nation, with full independence promised for 1855. He died at Fort Gibson on 2 January 1849 and was succeeded by his sister's son, Jim Jumper. The town of Micanopy, Florida, stands on the site of his capital, Cuscowilla, and is named after him.
michael-faraday: Michael Faraday was born on 22 September 1791 in Newington Butts, Surrey, now part of the London Borough of Southwark, the third of four children. His family was not well off, and his father, James, was a member of the Glasite sect of Christianity. He had only the most basic schooling and had to educate himself.

At 14 he became an apprentice to George Riebau, a bookbinder and bookseller, and during the seven years read widely, including Jane Marcet's Conversations on Chemistry. In 1812 he heard lectures by Humphry Davy at the Royal Institution and sent Davy a 300-page book based on his notes. When Davy damaged his eyesight in an accident with nitrogen trichloride, he hired Faraday, who was appointed Chemical Assistant on 1 March 1813.

Faraday was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1824 and in 1825 became Director of the Laboratory of the Royal Institution. In 1833 he became its first Fullerian Professor of Chemistry, for life and without the obligation to lecture. He founded the Friday Evening Discourses and was the main populariser of the Christmas Lecture Series. He also did public work: with Charles Lyell he wrote a report on a colliery explosion at Haswell in 1846 that killed 95 miners, which indicated for the first time that coal dust worsened explosions. He refused to advise on chemical weapons for the Crimean War, declined a knighthood on religious grounds, and twice refused the presidency of the Royal Society.

In chemistry Faraday discovered benzene and tetrachloroethylene, liquefied several gases and found the laws of electrolysis. He popularised the terms anode, cathode, electrode and ion, which William Whewell largely proposed. In 1821 he built two devices producing what he called electromagnetic rotation, one of them the homopolar motor, a foundation of electric motor technology.

In 1845 he discovered diamagnetism and found that a magnetic field can rotate the plane of polarised light, now called the Faraday effect. His ice pail experiment showed that charge sits on the outside of a conductor, the principle of the Faraday cage. His mathematics went no further than simple algebra, and James Clerk Maxwell, who took up his work, wrote that Faraday's lines of force showed him to have been a mathematician of a very high order.
michael-i-komnenos-doukas: Michael was the illegitimate son of the sebastokrator John Doukas and a descendant of Alexios I Komnenos, and a first cousin of the emperors Isaac II Angelos and Alexios III Angelos. He never used the surname Angelos, which modern scholars have applied to him, and his seals show Michael Doukas or Michael Komnenos Doukas, stressing his link to the Doukas and Komnenos families. His birth date is unknown, and the Greek scholar Konstantinos Varzos places it about 1170. He first appears on 14 February 1190 as a hostage to Frederick I Barbarossa during the passage of the Third Crusade, and later governed Mylasa and Melanoudion. In early 1201 he rebelled against Alexios III, was defeated, and fled to the Seljuk Sultan of Rum.

After the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204, Michael entered the service of Boniface of Montferrat but soon left him for Epirus, where he made himself the leader of the local Greeks against the Latin Crusaders, apparently marrying the daughter or widow of a local magnate. From Arta he ruled the lands between Dyrrhachium and Naupactus. Epirus became, with the Empire of Nicaea, a centre of Greek resistance to Latin rule. To avoid attack he negotiated with Pope Innocent III, made a marriage alliance with the Latin Emperor Henry of Flanders, and in 1210 accepted vassalage to Venice. He also ransomed the deposed Alexios III, which added to his legitimacy.

Michael attacked the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica with the Bulgarians but was defeated by Henry. In 1212 he overran most of Thessaly, taking Larissa, and then took Dyrrhachium from Venice, probably in 1213, and Corfu in 1214. He pushed north into Albania and took Kruja, but was stopped by the Serbs at Skadar.

Michael was assassinated in his sleep at Berat by a servant named Rhomaios, and John V. A. Fine writes that it is unknown whether he was hired and by whom. His half-brother Theodore Komnenos Doukas succeeded him, and the dynasty he founded ruled Epirus until 1318. The metropolitan John Apokaukos praised him as a new Noah, and the archbishop Demetrios Chomatianos estimated that half or more of those who fled Constantinople found refuge in Epirus. The title despotes was first borne in the 1230s by his son Michael II, and the term Despotate of Epirus appeared in Western sources in the fourteenth century.
michael-i-of-romania: Michael was born on 25 October 1921 at Foișor Castle in Sinaia, the son of Crown Prince Carol and the grandson of King Ferdinand I of Romania. In December 1925 Carol eloped with his mistress Elena Magda Lupescu and renounced his rights to the throne, and Michael became heir apparent. When Ferdinand died in July 1927 Michael became king before his sixth birthday, with a regency of his uncle Prince Nicolae, Patriarch Miron Cristea and the Chief Justice. In 1930 politicians dissatisfied with the regency invited Carol back, and parliament proclaimed him Carol II.

Carol II was forced to abdicate in 1940 and Michael returned to the throne on 6 September 1940, while Romania was aligned with Nazi Germany under Ion Antonescu. On 23 August 1944 Michael joined pro-Allies politicians and army officers in a coup, and ordered Antonescu's arrest. He appointed Constantin Sănătescu prime minister, announced a ceasefire, accepted the armistice and declared war on Germany. This did not prevent a rapid Soviet occupation, and about 130,000 Romanian soldiers were captured and taken to the Soviet Union, where many died in camps.

In March 1945 political pressure forced him to appoint a pro-Soviet government under Petru Groza. From August 1945 to January 1946 he refused to sign its decrees in the royal strike, but it failed. On 30 December 1947 Groza compelled him to abdicate and the monarchy was abolished.

Michael married Princess Anne of Bourbon-Parma in June 1948, and the couple had five daughters. The communist authorities stripped him of citizenship that year, and from 1956 the couple lived near Versoix in Switzerland. After the fall of Nicolae Ceaușescu he landed in Romania on 25 December 1990 but was made to leave; in 1992 a speech from a hotel window in Bucharest drew an estimated one million people. His citizenship was restored in 1997, and properties such as Peleș Castle were later returned to his family. He died in Switzerland on 5 December 2017, aged 96.
