michael-ii-asen: Michael was the son of Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria and Irene Komnene Doukaina, and was most probably born in 1239. His father died in the first half of 1241 and was succeeded by Michael's seven-year-old half-brother Kaliman, who died unexpectedly, possibly of poisoning according to contemporaneous rumours, in August or September 1246.

Michael was only seven or eight when he succeeded. According to one scholarly theory his mother ruled during his minority, but she stayed in Thessaloniki just three months after his coronation. According to another, his brother-in-law, the Sevastokrator Peter, assumed the regency.

Soon after Kaliman's death John III Doukas Vatatzes, Emperor of Nicaea, invaded Bulgaria. He captured Serres and Melnik, the latter with local support, and occupied the fortresses of the Vardar valley, while Michael II Komnenos Doukas of Epirus occupied western Macedonia. The Bulgarians acknowledged the conquests in a treaty of late 1246 or early 1247 that also bound them to support Vatatzes against the Latin Empire of Constantinople, and Bulgarian troops helped him in Thrace in August 1247. William of Rubruck listed Michael's realms among the countries paying tribute to the Mongols.

In 1254 Michael allied with the Republic of Ragusa against Stefan Uroš I of Serbia and, after Radoslav of Hum joined, campaigned as far as Bijelo Polje. When Vatatzes died on 4 November 1254, Michael broke into Macedonia and reconquered the lands lost to him. The historian George Akropolites recorded that the Bulgarian-speaking inhabitants supported him because they wanted to shake off the 'yoke of those who spoke another language'. To secure peace with Hungary Michael married Anna of Macsó, a granddaughter of Béla IV.

Vatatzes's son and successor, Theodore II Laskaris, counter-invaded in early 1255 and captured Stara Zagora, then occupied most fortresses in the Rhodope Mountains in the spring. In spring 1256 Michael pillaged Thrace near Constantinople, but the Nicene army defeated his Cuman troops. In June he asked his father-in-law to mediate, and Theodore agreed to peace only after Michael accepted the loss of the lands he had claimed, with the upper Maritsa as the border.

The treaty outraged many boyars, who decided to replace Michael with his cousin Kaliman Asen. Kaliman and his allies attacked the tsar, who died of his wounds. Akropolites says he was mortally wounded by his first cousin Kaliman outside Tarnovo.
michael-ii-komnenos-doukas: Michael II was an illegitimate son of Michael I Komnenos Doukas, the founder of the state of Epirus, and was probably born around 1206. His family descended from the Angelos family, but he preferred the surname Doukas or Komnenos Doukas, and contemporary Byzantine historians also call him Angelos. After his father's murder in 1215 and the succession of his uncle Theodore Komnenos Doukas, he went into exile, according to the hagiography of his later wife, St Theodora of Arta, in the Peloponnese.

After Theodore was defeated and captured by Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria at the Battle of Klokotnitsa, Theodore's brother Manuel Komnenos Doukas held Thessalonica as a client of the Bulgarian tsar. Michael returned to Epirus and, apparently with local support, took control. Manuel gave him the title of Despot, but in reality Michael was independent and by 1236 had seized Corfu. He married Theodora Petraliphaina, which secured the support of local notables, and he cultivated the Empire of Nicaea.

When Manuel died in 1241, Michael occupied Thessaly before his remaining uncles could react. In 1246 he took advantage of Emperor John III Doukas Vatatzes's attack on Bulgaria to expand into Albania and north-western Macedonia. Vatatzes then captured Thessalonica and offered a marriage alliance between Michael's eldest son Nikephoros and his own granddaughter Maria. Michael remained ambivalent. In spring 1251 he and Theodore attacked Thessalonica without success. After defections among his generals, a treaty concluded at Larissa required him to cede his holdings in Macedonia. He received the title of Despot anew and Nikephoros went to Nicaea as a hostage.

In 1256 Michael lost Dyrrhachium and Servia to Nicaea and resolved to expand again. He allied with King Manfred of Sicily, to whom he sent his daughter as wife, and with Prince William II Villehardouin of Achaea. Their coalition was weakened by mutual suspicion at Pelagonia in 1259: Michael's illegitimate son John Doukas deserted to the enemy, Michael abandoned his allies, and William was captured.

Michael fled to the Ionian Islands, and the Nicaeans occupied Epirus but met such resistance that they withdrew. He recovered his domains with further help from Manfred. Another Byzantine victory in 1264 forced him to accept the nominal suzerainty of Michael VIII Palaiologos and to strengthen the bond by dynastic marriages. He died in or shortly before 1268, and his domains were split between his sons Nikephoros I Komnenos Doukas of Epirus and John I Doukas of Thessaly.
michael-joseph-savage: Savage was born in Tatong, Victoria, the youngest of eight children of Irish immigrant parents, and after his mother's death was brought up a Roman Catholic by his sister Rose. From 1886 to 1893 he worked at a wine and spirits shop in Benalla. In 1891 Rose and his brother Joe died, and he took Joe's name. He then worked for seven years as a labourer at Narrandera in New South Wales, where he joined the General Labourers' Union and read the American radicals Henry George and Edward Bellamy.

He reached Wellington on 9 October 1907 and moved to Auckland in 1908, where he worked at a brewery, led its workers' union and in 1910 became president of the Auckland Trades Council. He stood unsuccessfully as the Socialist candidate for Auckland Central in 1911 and 1914, opposed conscription during the First World War, and supported the founding of the New Zealand Labour Party in July 1916. Elected for Auckland West in 1919, he became deputy leader in 1922 and party leader after Harry Holland's death in October 1933. He was credited with the Family Allowances Act 1926 and helped forge Labour's alliance with the Rātana Church.

After Labour won the 1935 election the government gave a Christmas bonus to the unemployed, restored wage cuts and revalued the currency. In 1936 it set up the National Broadcasting Service, made secondary education free up to the age of 19 and passed the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act, with a statutory minimum wage and a 40-hour week. Savage called the social security scheme applied Christianity: the Social Security Act brought unemployment benefits, a free health system and pensions, and came into force on 1 April 1939.

At the Imperial Conference of 1937 he criticised British appeasement, and New Zealand declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939. He had delayed treatment for colon cancer to campaign in 1938, and he died on 27 March 1940. He lies in the Savage Memorial at Bastion Point in Auckland.
michael-manley: Michael Manley was the second son of Norman Washington Manley, later premier of Jamaica, and the artist Edna Manley. He studied at the London School of Economics from 1945, where Fabian socialism and the writings of Harold Laski influenced him. After graduating in 1949 he edited and wrote for the newspaper Public Opinion and became a negotiator for the National Workers Union. He entered the Senate in 1962 and the House of Representatives in 1967, and in 1969, after his father retired, he was elected leader of the People's National Party.

The party won the 1972 general election in a landslide, taking 37 of 53 seats from the Jamaica Labour Party of Hugh Shearer. Manley's government introduced a minimum wage covering domestic workers, equal pay for women, maternity leave, wider free education and the National Housing Trust, under which more than 40,000 houses were built between 1974 and 1980. Abroad he befriended Fidel Castro, Julius Nyerere and Olof Palme, and his support for Cuba's sending of troops to Angola, criticised by Henry Kissinger and others, strained relations with the US.

Political violence between supporters of the two parties reached levels not seen before. After a wave of killings in 1974 his government passed the Gun Court Act and the Suppression of Crime Act, and a state of emergency declared in June 1976 saw about 500 people detained without charge. The party won the December 1976 election with 47 seats to 13, but in 1980, an election year in which over 800 Jamaicans were killed, Edward Seaga's Jamaica Labour Party won 51 of 60 seats.

Manley led the opposition through the 1980s and returned as prime minister after the 1989 election, in which the party won 45 seats to 15. His second term focused on liberalising the economy, with a Social Support Programme to cushion the effects of austerity. In 1992, citing health reasons, he stepped down as prime minister and party leader, and P. J. Patterson succeeded him in both offices.

Manley wrote seven books, including A History of West Indies Cricket, which discussed the links between cricket and West Indian nationalism. He died of prostate cancer on 6 March 1997 and was given a state funeral on 16 March, attended by Fidel Castro among others. He is interred at National Heroes Park, where his father is also buried.
michael-of-russia: Michael, in Russian Mikhail Fyodorovich Romanov, was born on 22 July 1596 (O.S. 12 July), the son of Feodor Nikitich Romanov, later Patriarch Filaret, and Xenia Shestova. He was a first cousin once removed of Feodor I, the last tsar of the Rurik dynasty. In 1600 Tsar Boris Godunov falsely accused his father of treason, and Michael and his mother were exiled to Beloozero.

After the Poles were expelled during the Time of Troubles, a patriotic mood swept the Russian elite. Michael was chosen partly because of his father's martyr-like captivity in Poland and partly because his youth made him seem easily manipulated. On 21 February 1613 some 700 delegates of the Zemsky Sobor agreed on him as a compromise candidate. They did not find him and his mother at the Ipatiev Monastery near Kostroma until 24 March, and he was crowned on 21 July 1613, his seventeenth birthday.

The Treaty of Stolbovo of 17 February 1617 ended the war with Sweden: Russia gave up Ingria and parts of Karelia, and Sweden recognised Michael as its ruler. The Truce of Deulino of 1 December 1618 ended the war with Poland and cost Smolensk, but brought back Filaret, who became Patriarch of Moscow and the effective ruler of Russia until his death in 1633. In the Treaty of Polyanovka in 1634 Władysław IV Vasa gave up his claim to the Russian throne. Meanwhile Cossacks, financed by the Stroganov merchant family, continued the conquest of Siberia, and Russian explorers reached the Pacific before the reign ended.

Michael married three times. His first betrothed, Maria Khlopova, was deported to Siberia after falling ill, and his second wife died four months after the wedding in 1625. His third wife, Eudoxia Streshneva, whom he married in 1626, bore ten children, four of whom reached adulthood, including his successor Alexis. A horse accident early in his life left him with a leg injury that kept him from walking toward the end. He fell ill in April 1645 and died on 23 July 1645. He was a gentle and pious prince who effaced himself behind his counsellors, and the first tsar of the House of Romanov.
michael-panaretos: All that is known of Panaretos comes from his chronicle. He held the titles of protosebastos and protonotarios under Alexios III Komnenos. He first appears in 1351, accompanying the emperor's mother, Irene of Trebizond, to Limnia against the rebel Constantine Doranites, and after the civil war he joined Alexios III in a disastrous attack on Cheriana, from which he barely escaped alive. In April 1363 he names himself as a member of an embassy with the megas logothetes George Scholaris to Constantinople, to arrange a marriage between a daughter of Alexios and a son of John V Palaiologos; they also met John VI Kantakuzenos.
The only personal events he records are the deaths of two sons in 1368, while he was away in Constantinople: Constantine drowned at fifteen and Romanos died of disease at seventeen.

The chronicle fills only about twenty printed pages. About half covers the years 1349 to 1390, within his adult life. He names no sources; Jakob Philipp Fallmerayer suggested that he copied the inscriptions of a frescoed hall of imperial portraits described by Bessarion, and reign dates that do not always agree with reign lengths point to at least two written sources. Panaretos wrote not in learned Attic Greek but in the Pontic Greek of Trebizond, and called his people Romaioi or Christians, never Greeks. Later hands added entries up to 1426, and Anthony Bryer thought a gap near the end once told of the murder of Alexios IV Megas Komnenos.

The text survives in one manuscript, Marcianus graecus 608, dated by Peter Schreiner to the 1440s, which reached the Biblioteca Marciana in Venice through the bequest of Giambattisti Recanti. Fallmerayer found it there in the 19th century. Gottlieb Tafel printed the first edition in 1832, Fallmerayer added a German translation in 1844, and critical editions followed by the Greek scholar Lambros in 1907 and Odysseus Lampsides in 1958; Scott Kennedy published an English translation in 2019. Alexander Vasiliev wrote that this drab but truthful chronicle made it possible to restore the order of events in Trebizond's history, and it also holds valuable material on the early history of the Ottoman Turks.
michael-psellos: Psellos's family came from Nicomedia and, by his own testimony, counted members of the consular and patrician elite among its ancestors. His baptismal name was Constantine; Michael was the monastic name he took on entering a monastery later. Psellos, meaning the stammerer, was probably a personal by-name referring to a speech defect. At about ten he was sent to work outside the capital as secretary to a provincial judge, to help raise a dowry for his sister. When she died he returned to Constantinople to study under John Mauropus, where he met the later patriarchs Constantine Leichoudes and John Xiphilinos and the later emperor Constantine X Doukas.

After a further spell as a provincial judge, he returned to Constantinople before 1042 as a junior secretary in the imperial chancellery and rose quickly. He became an influential adviser to Constantine IX Monomachos, who reigned from 1042 to 1055, and the leading professor at the University of Constantinople, with the title Chief of the Philosophers. Under political pressure he entered the Olympus monastery in Bithynia in 1054, and Empress Theodora recalled him to court after Monomachos died.

He remained an adviser to successive emperors and played a decisive part in the transfers of power from Michael VI to Isaac I Komnenos in 1057, from Isaac to Constantine X Doukas in 1059 and from Romanos IV Diogenes to Michael VII Doukas in 1071. He had taught Michael, but after the mid-1070s nothing is recorded of his role at court, and some scholars think he withdrew again to a monastery.

The Chronographia, his best-known work, is a series of biographies of fourteen emperors and empresses. It stresses character over political and military detail, gives most weight to the periods when Psellos was himself in politics and has the character of a political memoir. The second part is more apologetic and largely praises the Doukas emperors. He also wrote a shorter world chronicle, the Historia syntomos, treatises on philosophy, theology, astronomy, medicine, music and law, a treatise on demons, didactic poems, funeral orations, speeches and several hundred letters.

He prided himself on reviving serious study of Plato and ancient philosophy in Byzantium, and he read Homer and Plato as precursors of Christian doctrine. His fondness for pagan and Neoplatonic thinkers led some contemporaries to doubt his orthodoxy: in 1054 John Xiphilinos accused him of forsaking Christ to follow Plato, and he made a public profession of faith. Modern commentators have called him vain and opportunistic, while others find in his work an ironic undercurrent critical of the emperors he describes.
michael-row-the-boat-ashore: Charles Pickard Ware, an abolitionist and Harvard graduate who supervised plantations on St. Helena Island from 1862 to 1865, wrote the song down in music notation as he heard the freedmen sing it. His cousin William Francis Allen reported in 1863 that the rowers sang it as they took him by boat across Station Creek. Allen, Ware and Lucy McKim Garrison printed it in Slave Songs of the United States in 1867. According to Allen, the Michael of the song is the Archangel Michael, in Catholic tradition a guide of the souls of the dead.

One of the oldest printed versions runs as a series of unrhymed couplets answered by "Hallelujah!", and the same source gives a second, rhymed version about the sounding of the trumpet. Its many oral versions tell of crossing the River Jordan, where Jesus was baptised: a figure of deliverance and salvation, but also of the boundary of the Promised Land and of death and the passage to Heaven. Guy and Candie Carawan recorded a traditional "Row, Michael, Row" on Johns Island in the 1960s; the singer Janie Hunter remembered her father, the son of former slaves, singing it as he rowed home after fishing.

The Boston folksinger and teacher Tony Saletan found the song in a library copy of the 1867 book in 1954, added a guitar accompaniment and replaced the repeated single lines with rhyming traditional couplets for the teenagers of Shaker Village Work Camp. He taught it to Pete Seeger, and the Weavers sang it at their reunion concert on Christmas Eve 1955. The Highwaymen's recording, released in 1960 as "Michael", reached number one on Billboard's Hot 100 for two weeks in September 1961 and also topped the chart in the United Kingdom; it changed "meet my mother on the other side" to "milk and honey on the other side".

The same month, civil rights activists jailed in Amite County, Mississippi, after the murder of Herbert Lee sang a version led by Hollis Watkins, ending "Mississippi's next to go". Harry Belafonte, Lonnie Donegan, Trini Lopez and many others recorded it.
michael-shishman: Michael Shishman, who took the name Michael Asen III after his coronation to stress his link with the Asen dynasty, was born between 1280 and 1292. He was the son of Shishman, despot of Vidin, and a grandson of Ivan Asen II through his mother. After a peace between his father and the Serbian king Stefan Milutin, he was engaged to Milutin’s daughter Ana, and they married in 1298 or 1299. Vidin had been autonomous under weak Bulgarian overlordship since the mid-13th century, and Michael held the title of despot there. On the childless death of George Terter II in 1323 the nobility elected him emperor of Bulgaria.

The death of George Terter II was followed by confusion that the Byzantine emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos exploited, taking cities in northeastern Thrace. Michael marched south, retook the lost cities while the Byzantines besieged Plovdiv, and by 1324 had recovered northern and northeastern Thrace. When Andronikos offered a duel, he reportedly answered that a blacksmith would be foolish to take hot iron in his hands rather than with pincers. A peace followed in autumn 1324; Michael divorced Ana and married Theodora Palaiologina, the widow of Theodore Svetoslav, and the border was set on a line from Plovdiv to Sozopol.

In 1327 he sided with Andronikos III in the Byzantine civil war, while Serbia backed Andronikos II, and in 1329 the two signed a lasting peace and alliance against Serbia. Relations with Serbia had worsened since the divorce, as Ana returned to her brother Stephen Dečanski.

In 1330 Michael marched on Serbia with about 15,000 men. Near Velbazhd, now Kyustendil, the rulers agreed a one-day truce, and he let his army disperse for provisions. On 28 July Serbian reinforcements arrived, including about 1,000 Catalan mercenary horsemen under Stephen Dušan, and the Serbs attacked and won. Accounts of his death differ: Kantakouzenos says he was mortally wounded and died soon after, Serbian chronicles that his horse fell on him, and Gregory Tsamblak that Dušan captured and killed him. He was buried at Staro Nagoričane. Historians describe him as ambitious and opportunistic but forceful; he was the last medieval Bulgarian ruler to try to take Constantinople.
michael-somare: Michael Thomas Somare was born on 9 April 1936 at Rabaul, in a village called Rapikid, where his father Ludwig Somare Sana, a policeman who rose to sergeant, was stationed. He was the eldest of his father's six children. He grew up in the family village of Karau in the Murik Lakes district of East Sepik Province, and his first schooling was at a Japanese-run primary school there during the Second World War. From 1946 he attended Boram Primary School, the Dregerhafen Education Centre and Sogeri High School, and in 1957 he gained a Leaving Certificate that served as a teaching qualification.

Somare stressed his Sepik identity, wearing a lap-lap rather than trousers, and held the title of Sana in his father's line, which marks descent from the clan's founder and the role of peacemaker. He married Veronica in 1965, and they had five children.

Somare entered politics in 1968, sitting in the House of Assembly and then in the national parliament for the East Sepik seat. He was a founding member of the Pangu Party, which led Papua New Guinea to independence in 1975. He was the first chief minister at the end of colonial rule and the first prime minister after independence. He held the office from 1975 to 1980, from 1982 to 1985 and from 2002 to 2011, seventeen years in all.

He was also minister of foreign affairs, leader of the opposition on several occasions and governor of East Sepik Province. As prime minister he declared friends with everybody and enemies of none as the principle of his foreign relations, and he opened relations with China soon after independence. In March 2011, while he was in hospital in Singapore, parliament declared the post vacant and Peter O'Neill became prime minister, a change that led to a constitutional crisis.

Somare died of pancreatic cancer at Port Moresby on 25 February 2021, aged 84. He is widely called the father of the nation. He received honorary doctorates, beginning with one from the University of the Philippines in 1976, and was appointed to the Privy Council in 1977. He was made a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George in 1990.
michael-the-brave: Michael was born in 1558 as Mihai Pătrașcu. He claimed to be the illegitimate son of the Wallachian prince Pătrașcu cel Bun, though some historians think he invented this descent and that his real father was most likely a Greek merchant. His mother was Theodora Kantakouzene. He rose quickly, becoming Ban of Craiova in 1593, but a conflict with Prince Alexandru cel Rău forced him to flee that year. In Constantinople he secured Ottoman support, helped by a loan of 200,000 florins, and Sultan Murad III invested him as prince in September 1593.

Michael soon turned against the Ottomans. In 1594 he joined the Christian alliance formed by Pope Clement VIII and took several citadels near the Danube. In August 1595 an Ottoman army under Sinan Pasha crossed the Danube. Outnumbered, Michael gave battle on marshy ground near Călugăreni and defeated it, but had too few troops to follow up and withdrew. The war went on until he made peace on 26 June 1599, lacking support from his allies. His rule rested on the Oltenian lords, and he passed a law binding serfs to aristocrats' land.

When Andrew Báthory demanded that Michael give up his throne, Michael marched into Transylvania and defeated him at Șelimbăr on 18 October 1599, then entered Gyulafehérvár as imperial governor under Emperor Rudolf II. In April 1600 his troops entered Moldavia and reached Iași on 6 May, and he had a seal showing the three principalities. The Transylvanian Hungarian nobility rose against him with the help of General Giorgio Basta, while Polish forces drove his troops from Moldavia and Wallachia.

Michael visited Prague in 1601 and received 100,000 florins from Rudolf II. Allied with Basta, he defeated the Hungarian army at Guruslău. A few days later, on 9 August 1601, Basta, who wished to control Transylvania himself, had him killed near Câmpia Turzii, on the emperor's order. From the middle of the nineteenth century he was seen as a unifier and precursor of a modern Romania, though the historian A. D. Xenopol held that there was no national element in his politics.
michael-ventris: Michael Ventris was born on 12 July 1922 into an army family, the only child of a lieutenant-colonel in the Indian Army and a mother from a wealthy Jewish and Polish family. The family spent eight years in Switzerland, where he started school at Gstaad with classes in French and German, and he was fluent in Polish by the age of eight. He later learned Swedish and Russian.

At Stowe School he spent much of his spare time learning about Linear B. In 1936, aged 14, he heard Arthur Evans lecture at an exhibition of Cretan archaeology in London and spoke up to confirm that Linear B was undeciphered; he determined to decipher it. In 1940, aged 18, he published an article in the American Journal of Archaeology, Introducing the Minoan Language, which supposed a relation between Etruscan and Linear B.

Ventris studied architecture, was conscripted in 1942 into the Royal Air Force, qualified as a navigator in 1944 and flew in the bombing of Germany with No. 76 Squadron. After the war he completed his architectural education with honours in 1948 and designed schools for the Ministry of Education. His work on Linear B built on Alice Kober's observation that some words had changing endings, like declensions.

He constructed grids that linked the symbols to consonants and vowels, and used photographs by Alison Frantz of some 600 tablets that Carl Blegen had found at Pylos. Noticing that some groups of symbols appeared only in the Cretan texts, he guessed that they were place names, and this proved correct.

On 1 July 1952 he announced preliminary findings on the BBC, showing that the language of Linear B was Greek. John Chadwick, a Cambridge classicist, heard the broadcast and began to collaborate with him. In 1953 a tablet from Pylos showing a tripod cauldron beside symbols that Ventris and Chadwick read as ti-ri-po-de confirmed the reading. Their work showed that Cretan civilisation, at least in the periods of the Linear B tablets, had been part of Mycenaean Greece, which overturned Evans's theories.

Ventris was awarded an OBE in 1955 for services to Mycenaean palaeography. On 6 September 1956 he died at Hatfield, Hertfordshire, when his car struck a parked lorry, a few weeks before the publication of Documents in Mycenaean Greek; the coroner's verdict was accidental death. The British Academy gave him the Kenyon Medal posthumously in 1959. Some scholars remained sceptical of the decipherment into the 1960s. An English Heritage blue plaque marks his home in Hampstead, a street in Heraklion is named after him, and the IAU named the Ventris crater on the far side of the Moon after him in 1970.
michael-vickery: Michael Theodore Vickery was born on 1 April 1931 in Billings, Montana. He took a Bachelor of Arts in Russian studies at the University of Washington in 1952, spent 1953 to 1955 in Finland as a Fulbright scholar and served in the United States Army in Germany from 1956 to 1958. He then taught English in Istanbul from 1958 to 1960, in Cambodia from 1960 to 1964 and in Laos from 1964 to 1967.

He did his thesis research in Cambodia and Thailand from 1970 to 1972 and in 1973 became a lecturer in Southeast Asian history at the Universiti Sains Malaysia in Penang. In 1977 he received his doctorate in history from Yale University for Cambodia After Angkor: The Chronicular Evidence for the Fourteenth to Sixteenth Centuries.

He was then a research fellow at the Australian National University from 1979 to 1982 and at the University of Adelaide from 1982 to 1988, a senior lecturer again at the Universiti Sains Malaysia from 1988 to 1998, and taught Cambodian history at the Royal University of Fine Arts in Phnom Penh from 1998 to 2002. After working as an independent scholar in Chiang Mai Province from 2002 to 2008, he became a visiting professor at the University of Sydney.

He also wrote columns for the Phnom Penh Post from 1992 to 2007, and in 2008 it was announced that he had worked as an analyst and historical expert for the defence team of Ieng Sary, the former Khmer Rouge foreign minister, at the Khmer Rouge Tribunal. He died of a heart attack in Battambang Province, Cambodia, on 29 June 2017, at the age of 86.

His work on pre-Angkorian, Angkorian and post-Angkor Cambodia drew on newly deciphered inscriptions and brought in the views of the Cambodian scholars Khin Sok and Mak Phoen. He argued that much earlier scholarship could be overturned by a single new inscription, and remarked that studying Cambodian history with Georges Coédès was like doing geography with Ptolemy. His books include Cambodia 1975–1982 (1984), on the Pol Pot era and its aftermath, and Society, Economics and Politics in Pre-Angkor Cambodia (1998). Some scholars placed his work in Marxist schools of thought, though he was not a communist, and he wrote for the Bulletin of Concerned Asian Scholars.
michael-viii-palaiologos: Michael VIII Palaiologos was the son of the megas domestikos Andronikos Doukas Komnenos Palaiologos and Theodora Angelina Palaiologina, whose ancestry, according to Deno John Geanakoplos, went back to all three imperial houses that ruled before the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204. He governed the Thracian towns of Melnik and Serres under his father. In 1253 he was accused of plotting against Emperor John III Vatatzes and escaped trial by ordeal with a clever reply, though he remained mistrusted. He served the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum from late 1256 to 1258 before Theodore II Laskaris recalled him. After Theodore's death in 1258 Michael seized the guardianship of the eight-year-old John IV Laskaris from George Mouzalon and was proclaimed emperor at Nymphaion on 1 January 1259.

In 1259 Michael defeated William of Villehardouin and Michael II Komnenos Doukas of Epirus at the Battle of Pelagonia. A treaty with Genoa followed in 1261, though Genoese help proved unneeded when his general Alexios Strategopoulos captured Constantinople from Baldwin II through treachery on 25 July 1261. Michael entered the city on 15 August. He abolished Latin customs, restored Byzantine ceremonies and repopulated the capital, which grew from about 35,000 people to 70,000 by the end of his reign. In December 1261 he had John IV blinded and sent to a monastery, and Patriarch Arsenios excommunicated him for it until 1268.

From 1266 Michael's main opponent was Charles of Anjou, who in 1267 concluded the Treaty of Viterbo to restore the Latin Empire. To restrain him Michael negotiated union of the churches, which was formally proclaimed at the Second Council of Lyon in 1274. Many Greeks bitterly opposed it, and Michael punished anti-unionists, some by blinding or exile. On 30 March 1282 the Sicilian Vespers rebellion broke out before Charles could sail against Constantinople. Pope Martin IV excommunicated Michael, whom many saw as instigator, though Geanakoplos holds that he had nothing to do with the incident at the church of Santo Spirito.

Michael died at Pachomios village in Thrace on 11 December 1282. He was denied burial in Constantinople because of his persecution of the Church in support of union with Rome. In restoring the empire he kept the old administration without correcting its failures. His focus on Constantinople and the Balkans left the Anatolian frontier stripped of troops, which led to its gradual collapse as Turkish bands infiltrated. The Palaiologan dynasty he founded ruled for almost two centuries, longer than any other in Roman history.
michel-aflaq: Michel Aflaq was born on 9 January 1910 to an Orthodox Christian family in Damascus, where his father Joseph worked as a grain merchant. He was educated in the Westernised schools of the French Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon. In 1929 he went to the Sorbonne to study philosophy, where Henri Bergson's works influenced him and he met his long-term collaborator Salah al-Din al-Bitar. He founded an Arab Student Union there and discovered the writings of Karl Marx. Back in Syria in 1932 he became active in communist politics, but he left the movement when France's Popular Front government under Léon Blum kept up the old colonial policies and the Syrian-Lebanese Communist Party backed it.

Aflaq and al-Bitar taught at the Tajhiz secondary school in Damascus, Aflaq history and al-Bitar mathematics and physics. In 1940 they founded the Arab Ihya Movement, renamed the Arab Ba'ath Movement in 1942. The name led Zaki al-Arsuzi, leader of a group with the same name, to accuse them of taking it, and the two men became bitter rivals. At the first congress of the Arab Ba'ath Party at Damascus in 1947, which merged the two groups, Aflaq became Amid, the party's leader, with responsibility for ideology.

The party merged with Akram al-Hawrani's Arab Socialist Party in 1952, and Aflaq was elected its Secretary General in 1954. When Nasser pressed for the union of Egypt and Syria, Aflaq dissolved the party without consulting its members. He was forced to resign as leader in 1965 in a struggle with the party's Military Committee. A coup on 23 February 1966, led by Salah Jadid and Hafez al-Assad, overthrew the Syrian government and the party leadership and exiled him. He escaped to Beirut and later to Brazil. In 1968 he was elected Secretary General of the Iraqi-led Ba'ath Party, but he held no de facto power. The Syrian-led party sentenced him to death in absentia in 1971.

Aflaq's books include The Road to Renaissance, The Battle for One Destiny and The Struggle Against Distorting the Movement of Arab Revolution. He held that the Arab world must be unified into one Arab nation to achieve development, and that freedom would come to the Arabs through unity. He criticised capitalism and communism alike, and held that Arab socialism was not part of the international socialist movement. Aflaq favoured separating state and religion, and opposed atheism. He argued that Islam was the most sublime expression of Arabism, a view that drew criticism from devout Muslims and from some Christians. He died in Paris on 23 June 1989 and was given a state funeral.
michel-le-tellier: Michel Le Tellier was born in Paris on 19 April 1603, the son of the Parisian magistrate Michel III Le Tellier and his wife Claude Chauvelin. He entered royal service under Louis XIII and became a maître des requêtes in 1631. In 1640 he was appointed Intendant of Justice for the French army stationed in Piedmont. He later held the titles of marquis de Barbezieux and seigneur de Chaville et de Viroflay.

He owed his appointment as Secretary of State for War in 1643 to his friendship with Cardinal Jules Mazarin, the chief minister, and he earned a name as an efficient administrator. During the aristocratic uprising of the Fronde he stayed loyal to Mazarin and to the state. The larger and more professional royal army that he helped to build supported the absolute rule of Louis XIV and France's dominance in Europe.

As Chancellor of France from 1677 he restored the teaching of civil law at the University of Paris in April 1679; Pope Honorius III had prohibited it there on 11 May 1219. Le Tellier despised Protestantism. He was among those who persuaded Louis XIV to revoke the Edict of Nantes, which had granted religious freedoms to the Huguenots, and he encouraged their persecution. He signed the revocation together with the king.

Le Tellier died at Versailles on 30 October 1685, fifteen days after the revocation was signed. He had amassed great wealth. His son François Michel Le Tellier, marquis de Louvois, also became Secretary of State for War and, trained by his father, one of the most powerful officials of the reign; his other son, Charles Maurice Le Tellier, became Archbishop of Reims and was one of the leading book collectors of Europe. His correspondence is held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris.
michel-micombero: Michel Micombero was born on 26 August 1940 at Rutovu in Bururi Province, in Belgian-ruled Ruanda-Urundi. His parents were peasants of Hima ethnicity, part of the wider Tutsi group. He studied at Catholic mission schools and in 1960 joined the military then being formed ahead of independence, training at the Royal Military Academy in Brussels. He was a captain at independence in July 1962 and by November was assistant commander-in-chief of the national army. In 1963 he joined the ruling party, UPRONA, and in June was named State Secretary for Defense, making him head of the military at the age of 23.

In October 1965 Hutu soldiers, largely from the National Gendarmerie, attempted a coup against the monarchy of Mwambutsa IV, who fled into exile. Micombero led the repression of the attempt. In July 1966 a second coup brought the king's son Ntare V to power, and Micombero became prime minister and minister of defence. After Ntare tried on 7 November to broadcast a decree dismissing the government, Micombero, by then a colonel, led a coup on 28 November while the king was on a state visit to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. He abolished the monarchy and proclaimed himself first president of the republic.

He made UPRONA the only legal party, abolished parliament in favour of a National Revolutionary Council and placed institutions and media under what was effectively a military dictatorship, combining ideas from Tanzania's socialism and Mobutu's Congo. The regime marginalised Hutus, for instance by introducing height and girth standards for military recruits that usually only Tutsi met. Plots against him were prevented in 1969 and 1971. In April 1972 a Hutu rebellion broke out at Rumonge, in which as many as 1,000 Tutsi were killed. The regime responded with genocidal violence against Hutus in which at least 100,000 people are thought to have been killed, and the deposed King Ntare was murdered. Micombero eventually ordered the massacres to cease.

A coup led by Colonel Jean-Baptiste Bagaza overthrew Micombero in November 1976, and he was arrested. He was exiled in 1977 to Somalia, ruled by his friend Siad Barre, where he gained an economics degree from the Somali National University in 1982. He died of a heart attack at Madina Hospital in Mogadishu in 1983. The researcher Nigel Watt assessed him as the first, and worst, of the three Tutsi military presidents of Burundi, because the violence of 1972 caused lasting hatred that plagued the country for decades.
michel-ney: Michel Ney was born on 10 January 1769 in Sarrelouis, in Lorraine on the French-German border, the second son of a master cooper, Pierre Ney, a veteran of the Seven Years' War. The town was a French enclave in a predominantly German region and Ney grew up bilingual. After schooling until 1782 he worked as a notary's clerk and then in mines and forges. Civil life did not suit him, and in 1787 he enlisted in the Colonel-General Hussar Regiment. Under the Bourbons the officer corps was closed to those without noble ancestry, but he rose quickly through the non-commissioned ranks.

Ney fought at Valmy in 1792 and was commissioned that October. He was wounded at the Siege of Mainz in 1793, and as a cavalry commander was captured at Neuwied on 17 April 1797 and exchanged on 8 May. He became a general of division in March 1799 and fought at Hohenlinden in December 1800. On 19 May 1804 he received his marshal's baton. He commanded VI Corps in 1805, took Innsbruck, fought at Jena and Eylau, and was made Duke of Elchingen on 6 June 1808. In 1810 he invaded Portugal with Marshal André Masséna, and after bitter complaints about the campaign he was removed for insubordination.

In Russia in 1812 Ney led III Corps, was wounded at Smolensk, fought at Borodino and commanded the rearguard on the retreat from Moscow. Cut off at Krasnoi, he escaped across the Dnieper over fragile ice with heavy losses and rejoined the army at Orsha. Napoleon called him the bravest of the brave, and he was made Prince de la Moskowa on 25 March 1813. At Fontainebleau on 4 April 1814 he spoke for the marshals demanding Napoleon's abdication, then served Louis XVIII, who made him a Peer of France.

When Napoleon returned, Ney set out to stop him but joined him at Lons-le-Saulnier on 14 March 1815 with about 6,000 men. At Quatre Bras on 16 June he was criticised for attacking slowly, and at Waterloo on 18 June he ordered a mass cavalry charge that failed to break the infantry squares; five horses were killed under him. Arrested on 3 August, he was tried before the Chamber of Peers after the court-martial declared itself not competent. The Peers voted 137 for death, and he was shot near the Luxembourg Gardens on 7 December 1815. Accounts of his last words differ. He is buried at Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris.
michelangelo: Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni was born on 6 March 1475 in Caprese, near Arezzo in Tuscany, where his father Ludovico was the town's judicial administrator. The family had for generations been small-scale bankers in Florence, but the bank failed. Several months after his birth they returned to Florence. After his mother's death in 1481 he lived with a nanny and her husband, a stonecutter, in Settignano, where his father owned a marble quarry and a small farm. He later said he received the knack of handling chisel and hammer with the milk of his nurse.

Michelangelo achieved fame early, and two of his best-known works, the Pietà and David, were sculpted before he was 30. Born in the Republic of Florence, he was mostly active in Rome from his thirties onward. Although he did not consider himself a painter, he created the scenes from Genesis on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and The Last Judgment on its altar wall, two of the most influential frescoes in Western art.

His design of the Laurentian Library pioneered Mannerist architecture. At 71 he succeeded Antonio da Sangallo the Younger as architect of St. Peter's Basilica, and he changed the plan so that the western end was finished to his design, as was the dome, with some modification after his death on 18 February 1564. He was the first Western artist whose biography was published in his lifetime: Giorgio Vasari's Lives of 1550 called him divino, and Ascanio Condivi's Life of 1553 was prepared with his participation.

The Madonna of the Stairs is his earliest known work in marble, carved in shallow relief. His Bacchus, a commission with a set subject, has the traditional wine cup, vine wreath and fawn, but shows the god with bleary eyes and an unsteady stance. In the Madonna of Bruges the Christ Child, held by his mother's hand, is about to step off into the world. His contemporaries admired his terribilità, the ability to instil awe in those who saw his art.

He wrote more than three hundred sonnets and madrigals. He was a devout Catholic whose faith deepened at the end of his life. Attempts by later artists to imitate the expressive physicality of his style helped bring about Mannerism. The dome of St. Peter's influenced church building for centuries, including St Paul's Cathedral in London, and his unfinished giants for the tomb of Pope Julius II had a deep effect on sculptors such as Rodin and Henry Moore.
michelin: In 1889 the brothers Édouard and André Michelin took over Barbier-Daubrée, a struggling farm implement business of Clermont-Ferrand founded in 1832, which made rubber parts such as valves, gaskets, balls and brake pads. According to the company's story, a cyclist came in with a pneumatic tyre glued to its rim, which took over three hours to remove and repair and then had to dry overnight. When Édouard tested the repaired tyre the next day it failed after a few hundred metres. He and his brother set out to make a tyre that did not need to be glued. The firm was reincorporated and renamed Michelin on 28 May 1889.

In 1891 Michelin took out its first patent for a removable pneumatic tyre, and it was used by Charles Terront to win the first Paris–Brest–Paris cycle race. Four years later the company made pneumatic tyres for an automobile, a car called L'Eclair that raced in the Paris–Bordeaux–Paris of 1895. In the 1920s and 1930s it operated large rubber plantations in Vietnam, where conditions led to the labour movement known as Phú Riềng Đỏ. In the 1930s Michelin bought the bankrupt Citroën.

In 1934 it introduced a tyre that ran on a foam lining if punctured, the ancestor of the run-flat tyre, and in 1946 it patented the radial tyre, first sold as the X and developed with the Citroën Traction Avant and 2CV in mind. Radials spread through Europe and Asia, while in the United States bias-ply tyres still had 87 per cent of the market in 1967. Michelin opened its first North American sales office in 1968, the year Consumer Reports acknowledged the radial's superiority, and in 1989 it bought the tyre businesses of B.F. Goodrich and Uniroyal.

Michelin's inventions include the removable tyre, the automobile pneumatic tyre, twin truck tyres, the asymmetric XAS of 1964 and the green low-resistance tyre unveiled in 1992. It published the Red Guides to hotels and restaurants and the Green Guides for tourists, along with road maps. Its roadmaps were reproduced in England for the Allied invasion in the Second World War, and in 1940 the Germans reproduced the 1938 edition for theirs.

The company supplied tyres for the winner of the first 24 Hours of Le Mans in 1923, and it competed in Formula One from 1977 to 1984 and again from 2001 to 2006. Its Red Guide's stars for restaurants and its mascot Bibendum, the Michelin Man, are widely known.
micheon-of-goguryeo: Micheon was a grandson of the 13th king, Seocheon, and the son of the gochuga Go Dol-go, who was killed by his own brother, the 14th king Bongsang. Korean historical records say that Micheon fled and hid as a servant, doing menial work such as throwing stones into a pond through the night so that his master would not be woken. A year later he left that house to become a salt peddler, without much success. Meanwhile Bongsang grew increasingly unpopular, and court officials led by the Prime Minister Ch'ang Chori overthrew him in a coup and placed Micheon on the throne.

Micheon built the army of Goguryeo into a powerful force and used the disintegration of China's Jin dynasty to push Goguryeo's borders into the Liaodong Peninsula and the Chinese commanderies. His first campaign, in 302, was against the Xuantu Commandery and brought the Daedong River basin around present-day Pyongyang under his control. After an attack on Seoanpyeong, near modern Dandong, Goguryeo annexed the Lelang commandery in 313 and the Daifang commandery in 314.

In the west Goguryeo faced the growing power of the Xianbei, above all the Murong tribe in Liaodong. Micheon allied with the Duan and Yuwen tribes of the Xianbei against the Murong, but their attack failed. In 319 the Goguryeo general Yeo Noja was captured by the Murong, and around January 320 the Jin official Cui Bi took refuge at Micheon's court. Neither side could secure mastery of Liaodong, and in 330 Micheon sent an envoy to the Later Zhao dynasty in the hope of a diversion against the Murong.

Micheon died in 331 and was buried at Micheon-won, whose name means the garden with beautiful stream. In 342, in the reign of King Gogugwon, Former Yan invaders under Mo Yong-hwang dug up his remains and held them for ransom. His queen, of the Ju clan, was taken as a hostage together with the body and was able to return only in 355.
michiel-de-ruyter: Michiel de Ruyter was born on 24 March 1607 in Vlissingen in Zeeland, the son of a seaman who became a member of the guild of beer porters. He worked for a time at a ropewalk and was sent to sea as a boatswain's apprentice at eleven, the usual age for Zeeland boys. In 1622 he fought as a cannoneer under Maurice of Nassau at the relief of Bergen-op-Zoom. He then rose through the merchant fleet to become a ship's master at thirty. He had little formal education but spoke fluent English and tolerable French. The name De Ruyter was probably a nickname, perhaps from the verb ruyten, 'to raid', in reference to his privateering.

In the First Anglo-Dutch War he joined the fleet as a commandeur under Maarten Tromp, after first refusing the post as others were better qualified, and commanded a Zeelandic squadron that convoyed merchant ships through the English Channel. In 1655 he sailed to the Mediterranean with 55 merchantmen to protect Dutch trade and ransom enslaved Christians in Algiers. He took part in the Second Northern War on the Danish side, and was knighted by Frederick III of Denmark after liberating Nyborg in 1659.

As lieutenant admiral in the Second Anglo-Dutch War he retook the Dutch West African posts in 1664, but his raid on Barbados in 1665 had less success. In 1672 an Anglo-French fleet under James, Duke of York, and the Comte d'Estrées faced his fleet of 75 ships. At Solebay he aimed to damage the English ships so heavily they needed long repairs, and later he used the shoals as shelter and detached small squadrons to keep the reluctant French out of the main action. He thus prevented a landing. In 1674 his expedition to Martinique failed with 143 killed and 318 wounded.

In 1676 a cannonball struck him in the leg during the Battle of Augusta, and he died a week later at Syracuse. His embalmed body went to Amsterdam, and on 18 March 1677 he received a state funeral and was buried in the Nieuwe Kerk, where a monument by Rombout Verhulst was completed in 1681. His sailors called him bestevaêr, 'grandfather', for his disregard for hierarchy and bold undertakings. He is credited with a part in founding the Netherlands Marine Corps, established on 10 December 1665, and six ships of the Royal Netherlands Navy have borne his name.
michigamea: The name derives from Algonquian words, michi, great or much, and guma, water, and is also spelled Mitchigamea or Michigamie. The people were said to have come originally from Lake Michigan, perhaps the Chicago area, and at one time they lived near the Sangamon River in Illinois. Historical accounts describe them as not fluent in the Illinois language: in 1673 Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet used a Mitchigamea man who spoke Illinois poorly as their translator with the Dhegiha-speaking Quapaw. Little is known of them today.

At first contact their village stood on the Mississippi and St. Francis rivers, the southernmost of the Illinois Confederation. Archaeological evidence, historical accounts and maps suggest that they wintered in Illinois near the Tamaroa and summered in Arkansas near the Quapaw, combining summer hunting and trade in hides and meat with winter trade with the French. The Jesuit Relations record the Tamaroa awaiting the Mitchigamea, who were to come more than 60 leagues to winter with them and form one village.

The Quapaw drove them north out of Arkansas by 1700, and with the Chepoussa, with whom they later merged, they settled near the mouth of the Kaskaskia River. Their best-known chief was Agapit Chicagou. Writing in 1848, Benjamin Drake described a long war in which a confederation of the Sauk, Meskwaki, Sioux, Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi, joined by the Cherokee and Choctaw, attacked the Illinois peoples. The Sauk overran the main Michigamea settlement in 1752, and accounts of the time say some survivors joined the Kaskaskia and most the Quapaw.

By 1803 the Michigamea had merged into the Kaskaskia, who in turn merged into the Peoria; these were removed to Kansas in the 1830s and in 1867 to a reservation in present-day Ottawa County, Oklahoma. Mitchie Precinct in Monroe County, Illinois, is named after them. One of their villages in the American Bottom, occupied from 1730 to 1752 and known as the Kolmer site, is one of the region's leading archaeological sites.
michoacan: Michoacán lies in west-central Mexico, in the extreme south-west of the central highlands, with a coastline of 217 km on the Pacific Ocean. It borders Colima and Jalisco, Guanajuato, Querétaro, the State of México and Guerrero. Its name comes from Nahuatl Michhuahcan, 'place of the fishermen', which refers to those who fish on Lake Pátzcuaro. Vegetation changes with altitude, from conifer forests above 2,600 metres to tropical forests lower down, and the state holds the main wintering ground of the monarch butterflies, which the Purépecha take to be the spirits of the dead.

The first settlers were hunter-gatherers of the Palaeoindian period, known from fluted projectile points found with the bones of mammoths and bison. The Preclassic population lived in agricultural villages at El Opeño in the west and in the Balsas basin in the south, and for a long time the region held various local cultures. By about 900 CE populations had moved to defensible places in the Cuitzeo and Zacapu basins and along the Lerma and Balsas rivers.

The Purépecha, said to descend from late Chichimeca arrivals from the north, began their state in the thirteenth century at Uayameo, today Santa Fé de la Laguna, and by the fifteenth century dominated the Lake Pátzcuaro area. Between 1401 and 1450 they conquered neighbouring peoples, and by the late fifteenth century their state rivalled that of the Aztecs and reached into parts of Colima, Nayarit, Querétaro, Guanajuato, Guerrero and Jalisco. The Aztecs attacked and were repelled, and the Purépecha later refused them aid against the Spanish. They were also skilled in metallurgy, especially in copper.

The ruler Zuanga died of smallpox before any Spaniard arrived, and Tanganxoan II succeeded him. The first Spaniard to reach the area was Cristóbal de Olid. After the Spanish destroyed Tenochtitlan, Tanganxoan agreed to submit, on a promise that he would remain ruler, but Nuño de Guzmán went back on the agreement and killed him in 1530. The empire became a separate province that grew smaller over the colonial period. The state and its people played a major part in the Mexican War of Independence.

Michoacán is one of the 31 states of Mexico, divided into 113 municipalities, with its capital at Morelia, formerly Valladolid, named after the independence hero José María Morelos, who was born there. Morelia's colonial centre, pink stone cathedral and aqueduct were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991. Many Purépecha still live in the state, and its Day of the Dead celebrations at Janitzio and Pátzcuaro are among the best known in Mexico.
michu-of-silla: Michu was the son of Gudo, a leading general of Silla, and of Lady Sullye of the Park clan, and he married Lady Gwangmyeong of the Seok clan, a daughter of King Jobun. When King Cheomhae died without an heir, the throne passed to Michu as Jobun's son-in-law. His accession shows that the Kim clan had grown strong enough to take power from the Seok, and the Silla custom that gave sons and sons-in-law equal standing may also have played a part. On taking the throne he gave his father the posthumous title galmunwang.

The Samguk sagi reports numerous attacks from Baekje during his reign. Records of his time are few, but they suggest a strong interest in farming: in 264 he visited the peasants to encourage them during a severe famine, and in 268 he sent officials to hear the people's concerns. He also refused to have the palaces rebuilt, so that the people would not have to labour too much. After his death the Seok clan took the throne again with Yurye, a son of Jobun. His daughters married the later kings Naemul and Silseong.

Michu's tomb survives in central Gyeongju and is known as the Jukjangneung, the tomb of the bamboo generals. A legend tells that in the reign of King Yurye, when people from Iseoguk, in present-day Cheongdo County, attacked Gyeongju and Silla was powerless, soldiers with bamboo leaves in their ears appeared and turned the battle. After the enemy withdrew, bamboo leaves were found piled before Michu's tomb. Another legend holds that his spirit protected Silla by appeasing the spirit of Kim Yu-sin.
micipsa: Micipsa was the eldest legitimate son of Masinissa, king of Numidia, a Berber kingdom in North Africa. In 151 BCE Masinissa sent him and his brother Gulussa to Carthage to demand that exiled pro-Numidian politicians be allowed to return, but they were refused entry at the city gates. As the party turned to leave, Hamilcar the Samnite and his supporters attacked Micipsa's convoy and killed some of his attendants. The incident led to a retaliatory strike on the Carthaginian town of Oroscopa, which began the Carthaginian-Numidian War and eventually precipitated the Third Punic War.

Masinissa died in the spring of 148 BCE, and Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus, to whom he had given authority to administer his estate, divided the kingdom among Micipsa, Gulussa and Mastanabal. Micipsa received the Numidian capital of Cirta with its royal palace and treasury, Gulussa the charge of war and Mastanabal the administration of justice. The brothers continued their father's support of Rome against Carthage, though Micipsa is reported to have wavered, always promising arms and money but delaying. After Carthage was destroyed in 146 BCE, Gulussa and then Mastanabal died, leaving Micipsa the whole kingdom. Thousands of Carthaginians fled to Numidia, which aided its cultural and commercial progress.

Micipsa remained a loyal ally of Rome. In 142 BCE Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus asked him for war elephants against the Lusitanian rebel Viriathus, and in 134 BCE he sent archers, slingers and elephants to Scipio Aemilianus at the siege of Numantia, with Jugurtha, the illegitimate son of Mastanabal, in command of the Numidian units.

Micipsa had two sons, Hiempsal and Adherbal, and had brought Jugurtha into his household, treating him as his son and giving him military training. After the fall of Numantia, Scipio wrote praising Jugurtha, and Micipsa formally adopted him as co-heir with his own children. Micipsa died in about 118 BCE, and Numidia was divided into three parts, ruled by Adherbal, Hiempsal and Jugurtha.
micronesia: Micronesia is a subregion of Oceania in the north-western Pacific, with about 2,100 islands and a total land area of only 2,700 square kilometres spread over some 7,400,000 square kilometres of ocean. The largest island is Guam, at 582 square kilometres. There are four main island groups: the Caroline Islands, the Gilbert Islands, the Mariana Islands and the Marshall Islands, with Nauru and a few other islands separate. Most of the islands are coral atolls, formed as coral grew on the slopes of a central volcano that later sank.

The shared name is a modern grouping. Louis Domeny de Rienzi used it a year before Jules Dumont d'Urville, who is usually credited. The set does not correspond to any geological, archaeological, linguistic or cultural unity.

The Northern Mariana Islands were the first islands in Oceania settled by Austronesian peoples, voyagers who sailed east from the Philippines around 1500 BCE. Later groups moved south and east and became the ancestors of the Polynesian people. The earliest known European contact came in 1521, when Ferdinand Magellan's Spanish expedition reached the Marianas, as Antonio Pigafetta recorded. The Chamorro people he met seem to have had no knowledge of people beyond their own islands.

In the early 17th century Spain colonised Guam, the Northern Marianas and the Caroline Islands, governing them from the Philippines. After the Spanish–American War the United States took Guam in 1898 and Wake Island on 17 January 1899, and Spain sold its remaining islands to Germany in 1899. Germany also held Nauru and the British Empire took the Gilbert Islands. Germany lost its colonies in World War I, and the Northern Mariana Islands became a League of Nations Mandate with Japan as mandatory. After World War II they were placed in the United Nations Trust Territory system under the United States.

Micronesia is divided among six sovereign nations and some territories: Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, Kiribati, Nauru and the Marshall Islands, with Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands affiliated with the United States. The Northern Mariana Islands entered a covenant with the United States in 1976 under which they became a commonwealth and their residents received United States citizenship. Wake Island is under United States administration, though the Marshall Islands also claim it. Fishing rights sold to foreign fleets, and grants, mostly from the United States, are the chief sources of income.
microscope: Objects resembling lenses date back 4,000 years, and the earliest known use of simple microscopes, or magnifying glasses, dates to the widespread use of lenses in eyeglasses in the thirteenth century. Several claims for the compound microscope revolve around the spectacle-making centres of the Netherlands, naming Hans Lippershey, who applied for the first telescope patent in 1608, and the expatriate Cornelis Drebbel, who was noted to have a version in London in 1619.

Galileo Galilei seems to have found after 1610 that he could focus his telescope closely to view small objects. After seeing a compound microscope built by Drebbel exhibited in Rome in 1624, he built his own improved version. Giovanni Faber coined the name microscopio in 1625 for the instrument Galileo submitted to the Accademia dei Lincei.

The first detailed account of the microscopic anatomy of organic tissue, Giambattista Odierna's The Fly's Eye, appeared in 1644. Marcello Malpighi began his analysis of biological structures with the lungs. Robert Hooke's Micrographia, published in 1665, had a large impact, largely because of its illustrations. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek achieved up to 300 times magnification with a simple single-lens instrument, rediscovered red blood cells and spermatozoa, and helped popularise the use of microscopes for biological microstructure.

In 1893 August Köhler developed Köhler illumination, which is central to reaching the theoretical limits of resolution. Phase contrast, discovered by Frits Zernike in 1953, and differential interference contrast, by Georges Nomarski in 1955, allowed unstained, transparent samples to be imaged.

In 1931 Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll developed the first prototype electron microscope, which uses electrons in place of light, giving much higher resolution. Knoll developed the scanning electron microscope in 1935, and the first commercial one, the Stereoscan, was marketed in 1965. From 1981 to 1983 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at IBM in Zürich created the scanning probe microscope, and in 1986 the atomic force microscope was invented. Stefan Hell shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the STED technique.
midas: Several kings named Midas ruled Phrygia, and later tradition merged them. The oldest, who belongs to myth, was said to be the son of Gordias and the goddess Cybele, or in Arrian's account the son of Gordios, a poor peasant. Arrian tells that the Phrygians, torn by civil discord, were told by an oracle that a wagon would bring them a king.

Midas arrived in a wagon with his parents, was made king and dedicated the wagon in the citadel to Zeus, giving rise to the saying that whoever loosened its knot would rule Asia. Legends place this Midas before the Trojan War, though Homer does not mention him. A second Midas of the late 8th century BCE is the historical figure, and Herodotus names a third, of the 6th century BCE, grandfather of Adrastus.

The Midas of the late 8th century BCE ruled Phrygia until the sack of Gordium by the Cimmerians. Most historians identify him with Mita, king of the Mushki, who according to Assyrian tablets of the reign of Sargon II attacked Assyria's eastern Anatolian provinces. Some historians think he was called king of the Mushki because he had subjected that people and taken them into his army.

Greek sources say that he married Damodice, daughter of Agamemnon of Cyme, and traded extensively with the Greeks. Herodotus records that a Midas son of Gordias gave a royal throne to the oracle at Delphi and was the only foreigner to give an offering there before Gyges of Lydia. Some historians believe that this was the 8th-century king.

Greek writers, among them Strabo, say that Midas killed himself by drinking bull's blood during the Cimmerian attack, which Eusebius dated to about 695 BCE and Julius Africanus to about 676 BCE. Excavation has confirmed that Gordium was destroyed and burned at about that time. In 1957 Rodney Young opened a royal burial in the Great Tumulus at Gordion, with timbers cut around 740 BCE, a collection of Iron Age drinking vessels and inlaid tables. It was named Tumulus MM, for Midas Mound, and is now generally thought to cover his father.

Myth gave Midas the golden touch, granted by Dionysus in thanks for his kindness to Silenus and lifted when he washed in the river Pactolus, whose sands turned to gold. In another story Apollo gave him donkey's ears when he preferred Pan's music, and his barber's whispered secret grew into reeds that repeated it.
middle-ages: The term Middle Ages first appears in Latin in 1469 as media tempestas, middle season. Other early variants were medium aevum, first recorded in 1604, and media saecula, first recorded in 1625. Medieval writers divided history into periods such as the Six Ages or the Four Empires and considered their own time the last before the end of the world. In the 1330s the Italian humanist Petrarch called the post-Roman centuries dark compared with the light of classical antiquity. Leonardo Bruni was the first historian to use a tripartite periodisation, in 1442, and it became standard after the 17th-century German historian Christoph Cellarius divided history into ancient, medieval and modern.

In the history of Europe the Middle Ages lasted approximately from the 5th to the late 15th centuries and are divided into the Early, High and Late Middle Ages. They began with the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Between the 5th and 8th centuries peoples such as the Ostrogoths under Theoderic the Great, the Burgundians and the Franks filled the political void. The break with classical antiquity was incomplete: the new kingdoms kept Roman institutions, and the Byzantine Empire survived in the Eastern Mediterranean.

In the High Middle Ages, which began after 1000, the population of Europe grew from an estimated 35 to 80 million between 1000 and 1347. Manorialism and feudalism organised society, the East–West Schism came in 1054, and the Crusades were first preached in 1095. The Late Middle Ages brought the Great Famine of 1315–1317 and, from 1347 to 1350, the Black Death, which killed probably about 35 million people, around one-third of Europeans.

The medieval period is often caricatured as a time of ignorance and superstition. The caricature descends from the Renaissance, whose scholars saw the Middle Ages as a decline from the Classical world, and from the Enlightenment, whose scholars saw reason as superior to faith. Others argue that reason was held in high regard in the period.

It is untrue that everyone in the Middle Ages believed the Earth was flat. Lecturers in medieval universities commonly argued that the evidence showed the Earth to be a sphere, and Lindberg and Numbers state that scarcely a Christian scholar of the period failed to acknowledge its sphericity.
middle-angles: Angles probably broke into the Midlands from East Anglia and the Wash early in the 6th century, and those who first established their control came to be called the Middil Engli. Their lands commanded the great land routes of Watling Street and the Fosse Way and the river route of the Trent with its tributaries, the Tame and the Soar. They were incorporated into Mercia apparently well before the reign of Penda, who felt safe enough to keep his base in their territory.

Bede names the Middle Angles as the people to whom the four priests of the mission accepted by Peada were sent; Peada converted partly so that he could marry Alchflaed, daughter of King Oswiu of Northumbria, and the mission, which included St Cedd, arrived in 653. That Peada took a course so different from his father's at the centre of the kingdom suggests local support among the Middle Angles and a continuing local identity within Mercia.

After Penda's defeat and death in 655 and the murder of Peada in 656 at the instigation of his wife, Oswiu dominated Mercia and made the Irish priest Diuma bishop of the Middle Angles and the Mercians. Bede's remark that a shortage of priests forced one bishop on two peoples shows that the Middle Angles were still distinguished from the Mercians proper of the north and west. Diuma was followed by Ceollach, Trumhere and Jaruman. Wulfhere, another son of Penda, ruled Mercia from Tamworth in their territory, and in 669 Chad was sent as bishop of the Mercians and Lindsey people, with a monastery at Lichfield on land Wulfhere gave.

In Bede's account of Chad the Middle Angles are counted simply among the Mercians, as the distinctions between the peoples of Mercia faded; it is unclear whether this reflects Chad's day or Bede's own, in the early 8th century. Their political history is little known, and the name does not appear in the Tribal Hidage. Their church history is better recorded: the early see was at Leicester, it moved to Dorchester-on-Thames when the Danelaw was established, and it was later joined with Lindsey to form the diocese of Lincoln.
middle-assyrian-empire: Through most of the preceding Old Assyrian period, Assur had been a city-state ruled by a governor, the iššiak, together with a city assembly of leading families. The change into a territorial kingdom began in the last decades of Mitanni suzerainty, but historians date the Middle Assyrian period from the independence won under Ashur-uballit I around 1363 BCE and his conquest of the fertile land between the Tigris, the foothills of the Taurus Mountains and the Upper Zab. Ashur-uballit was the first ruler to call himself king of the land of Ashur.

Under Adad-nirari I, Shalmaneser I and Tukulti-Ninurta I, Assyria took the place of Mitanni among the great powers alongside Egypt, the Hittites and Babylonia. Tukulti-Ninurta subjugated Babylonia and founded a new capital, Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta, but growing discontent among the nobility ended in his assassination around 1207 BCE. Conflict within the dynasty followed, and Assyria shrank largely to its heartland, at roughly the time of the Late Bronze Age collapse. Tiglath-Pileser I, who reigned from 1114 to 1076 BCE, led a revival, defeating the Mushki and sending his armies as far as the Mediterranean.

After the death of his son Ashur-bel-kala in 1056 BCE a second, deeper decline set in, and most lands beyond the heartland were lost, partly to Aramean tribes. Recovery began under Ashur-dan II, who reigned from 934 to 912 BCE, and his successes mark for historians the start of the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

The Middle Assyrian kings were autocrats, served by viziers and, from Shalmaneser I onwards, by grand viziers, usually royal kinsmen who also ruled the former Mitanni lands as vassal kings. There was no standing army: levies were raised when needed, beside a more experienced class of soldiers and hired mercenaries. Waxed tablets recorded manpower and rations, and the empire built the earliest known road system of the Ancient Near East. The god Ashur, once a god tied to agriculture, became a god of war who commanded the kings to enlarge his land by conquest.
middle-atlas: The Middle Atlas is the northernmost and second highest of the three main Atlas chains of Morocco. To the south, the Moulouya and Oum Er-Rbia rivers separate it from the High Atlas. To the north, across the Sebou River, lie the Rif mountains, an extension of the Baetic System, which includes the Sierra Nevada in the south of Spain. The range forms the westernmost end of a large plateaued basin that reaches east into Algeria, bounded by the Tell Atlas to the north and the Saharan Atlas to the south.

It is a solid mountain mass about 350 km long, made primarily of limestone. Tabled rock in the west runs to elevations of 800 to 1,000 metres, while folded rock toward the north-east exceeds 3,000 metres. The highest point is Jbel Bou Naceur at 3,340 metres, and the summits of Moussa ou Sabel (3,172 metres) and Jbel Bou Iblane (3,081 metres) also stand high. Volcanic plateaus lie among the limestone, and Jbel Hebri is a cone volcano.

Extensive forests of cedar, holm oak and cork oak cover the slopes, cut by deep valleys, and small lakes rich in fish lie among the volcanic plateaus. The range borders the Plaine du Saïs and the cities of Fes, Meknes and Beni Mellal. Its upper reaches are the stronghold of Berber tribes who speak Tamazight and live at very low population densities. The Barbary macaque, an endangered primate that once ranged more widely across northern Morocco, is native here, and wild boar and polecat also live in the range.

Snow lies in winter and can fall from 600 metres above sea level, and the town of Ifrane has enough of it to serve as a ski resort. The range feeds four major river basins: the Sebou, the Oum Er-Rbia and the Bou Regreg, which drain to the Atlantic, and the Moulouya, which drains to the Mediterranean. One of the principal roads to the south of Morocco crosses it, linking Fes with Tafilalet. Tazekka National Park lies at its eastern end and Ifrane National Park between Khenifra and Ifrane.
middle-east: The Middle East is a geopolitical region generally defined as all of Egypt and all of West Asia except the Caucasus. It roughly corresponds with what Western Europe historically called the Near East, set against the Far East. Its main features are the Arabian Peninsula, Anatolia, the Levant and Mesopotamia, which together make up the Fertile Crescent, and the Iranian plateau. Most of it is hot and arid, but rivers such as the Nile, the Tigris, the Euphrates and the Jordan irrigate farmland.

The term may have originated with the India Office of the United Kingdom in the 1850s. It became widely known after the American naval strategist Alfred Thayer Mahan used it in 1902 for the area between Arabia and India, in an article on the Persian Gulf. Until the Second World War the area centred on Turkey and the eastern Mediterranean was usually called the Near East.

The Middle East was the first region outside Africa to be settled by modern humans and the first in which writing systems developed. Agriculture was independently developed there and spread during the Neolithic to Europe, the Indus Valley and eastern Africa. The earliest civilisations, Sumer, Akkad, Assyria and Babylonia in Mesopotamia and ancient Egypt, arose in the Fertile Crescent and the Nile Valley. They were followed by the Hittite, Greek, Hurrian and Urartian civilisations of Asia Minor, Elam, Persia and Media in Iran, and the Levantine civilisations of Ebla, Mari, Ugarit, Canaan, Phoenicia and Israel.

The Near East was first largely unified under the Neo Assyrian Empire, then under the Achaemenid Empire, followed by the Macedonian Empire and, to some degree, by the Parthian and Sasanian Empires, the Roman Empire and the Byzantine Empire. The Romans stationed five or six legions in the region to defend it from Sasanian and Bedouin raids and invasions. Judaism, Christianity and Islam all originated in the region and have their holiest sites there, as do Manichaeism, Yezidi, the Druze faith and Mandeanism.

Arabs are the largest ethnic group, followed by Iranian and Turkic peoples, with Kurds, Jews, Assyrians and many others. The six languages with most speakers are Arabic, Persian, Turkish, Kurdish, Modern Hebrew and Greek. The Gulf Arab states hold vast reserves of petroleum.
middle-egypt: Middle Egypt is the section of the Nile valley between Lower Egypt, the Delta, and Upper Egypt, stretching upstream from Memphis in the north to Asyut in the south. In ancient times Egypt was divided into Lower and Upper Egypt, and Middle Egypt was technically a subdivision of Upper Egypt. Only in the 19th century did archaeologists feel the need to divide Upper Egypt in two, and they coined the term Middle Egypt for the stretch of river between Cairo and the Qena Bend.

It corresponds to the region the Greeks called Heptanomis, meaning Seven Nomes, a nome being a subdivision of ancient Egypt. In the 19th century it was described as the district that separates the Thebaid from the Delta, though because the name is political rather than territorial its boundaries are hard to define. Its northern part belonged to the kingdom of Lower Egypt, which contained the capital Memphis, and its southern part to the older kingdom of Thebes.

According to Ptolemy and Agatharchides, who wrote long after the original divisions had been modified, the seven nomes were the Memphites, Heracleopolites, Crocodilopolites (renamed Arsinoites), Aphroditopolites, Oxyrhynchites, Cynopolites and Hermopolites. Their capitals were collectively called the Heptapolis, or Seven Cities: Memphis, Heracleopolis, Crocodilopolis (later Arsinoe), Aphroditopolis, Oxyrhynchos, Cynopolis and Hermopolis. The seven principal nomes probably varied over time with local prosperity, war, commerce and migration.

The district contained the Pyramids, the Labyrinth and the Fayyum, the artificial district watered by the canal Bahr Yusif. It was known for its quarries and rock grottoes, among them the grottoes of Beni Hasan and the Speos Artemidos, and the limestone used to case the pyramids came from the quarries of Tourah and Massarah in the Gebel el-Mokattam east of Memphis. Under the Ptolemies the Heptanomis was governed by an epistrategos, and under the Roman emperors by a procurator. In the 3rd century the five northern nomes, with the Nomos Leptopolites, formed the province of Arcadia Ægypti, which later became a metropolitan episcopal see.

Middle Egypt is the part of the Nile valley that, though geographically part of Upper Egypt, is culturally closer to Lower Egypt. The Egyptian Arabic of people from Beni Suef northwards shares features with Cairene and rural Delta Arabic rather than with the Sa'idi Arabic spoken further south, and they are often not considered Sa'idis. Its major cities include Beni Suef, Minya, Giza, Faiyum and the 6th of October City.
middle-francia: Middle Francia was created in 843 by the Treaty of Verdun, which ended nearly three years of civil war among the surviving sons of Louis the Pious and divided the Carolingian Empire into three kingdoms. It was allotted to the eldest son, Lothair I. It lay between East and West Francia and took in the Frankish lands between the Rhine and the Scheldt, the Frisian coast, the former Kingdom of Burgundy except a western portion, Provence and northern Italy as far as the Veneto, an area of about 300,000 to 350,000 square kilometres. Its long borders were hard to defend, and it shared frontiers with few other states, which limited its trade.

In 855, on his deathbed at Prüm Abbey, Lothair I divided the kingdom among his three sons by the Treaty of Prüm.
