Louis II received northern Italy and the imperial title, Charles received Burgundy and Provence, and Lothair II received the northern lands, which became known as Lotharingia. Charles died without sons in 863, and his brothers divided his realm, Lothair II taking the western Lower Burgundian parts and Louis II Provence.

When Lothair II died in 869 his only son, Hugh, born to his mistress Waldrada, was declared illegitimate. His heir was Louis II, who was campaigning against the Emirate of Bari, and by the Treaty of Meerssen in 870 Charles the Bald and Louis the German divided Lotharingia between them. When Louis II died in 875 Charles the Bald took his realm in Italy with the backing of Pope John VIII. Charles the Fat was crowned emperor in 881 and reunited the whole Carolingian Empire in 884, which lasted only until his overthrow in 887.

None of Lothair I's three sons left a legitimate male heir, so the territories of Middle Francia were redistributed step by step, which allowed West Francia and East Francia to claim them. Its eventual disappearance should not be taken to mean that it lacked geographical or cultural cohesion.
middle-kingdom-of-egypt: The Middle Kingdom, also called the Period of Reunification, followed the First Intermediate Period, when Old Kingdom power had collapsed and the country was decentralised. Towards the end of that period two rival dynasties, the Tenth at Herakleopolis ruling Lower Egypt and the Theban Eleventh ruling the south from the First Cataract to the Tenth Nome of Upper Egypt, fought for control.

Mentuhotep II took the Theban throne in 2055 BCE and in his fourteenth regnal year used a revolt in the Thinite Nome to attack Herakleopolis, which put up little resistance. He finished consolidating the country by his 39th year, and is regarded as the founder of the period.

Mentuhotep II campaigned as far south as the Second Cataract, in Nubia, restored Egyptian hegemony over Sinai and depicted himself as a god in his lifetime, wearing the headdresses of Amun and Min. He reigned 51 years. The Eleventh Dynasty ruled from Thebes. The Twelfth, whose kings ruled from el-Lisht, began with Amenemhat I, who had to campaign in the Delta, built the Walls of the Ruler in the east Delta and founded a new northern capital, Amenemhet It Tawy.

The Prophecy of Neferty, dating from about this time, presents a king arising from the far south to restore the kingdom. From the Twelfth Dynasty pharaohs kept standing armies with Nubian contingents, but the kingdom's strategy was defensive, with fortresses at the First Cataract, in the Delta and across the Sinai Isthmus.

After the death of Sobekneferu came a series of short-lived kings, the first of the Thirteenth Dynasty, whose members were mostly unrelated and are attested on few monuments. The period was followed by the Second Intermediate Period, in which the Hyksos of West Asia ruled Lower Egypt.

The Eleventh Dynasty rebuilt a centralised administration under a vizier, sometimes divided between north and south, with the Overseer of Sealed Goods as treasurer and the Overseer of the Estate as chief steward. Provinces stayed in the hands of nomarchs from powerful families. High Nile floods, averaging 19 metres above non-flood levels, accompanied the most prosperous years, under Amenemhat III.

Royal pyramids were built of mud brick with a casing of Tura limestone, and statuary and sarcophagi reached a peak of quality. Literature written for entertainment and reflection appeared in the early Twelfth Dynasty, among it the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor, the Story of Sinuhe and the Dispute between a man and his Ba, which later Egyptians counted as classic.
middle-persian: Middle Persian, whose own name for it was Pārsīg, is a Western Middle Iranian language. The Middle period of the Iranian languages runs from the fall of the Achaemenid Empire in the fourth century BCE to the fall of the Sasanian Empire in the seventh century CE. Middle Persian descended from Old Persian and became the literary language of the Sasanian Empire. During the Sassanid period (224 to 651 CE) it was also called Ērānīg, belonging to Iran, and its use in official inscriptions shows that the Sassanids defined themselves as ethnically and culturally Iranian.

The most important change was from the synthetic structure of Old Persian and Avestan to an analytic one: nouns, pronouns and adjectives lost almost all their case endings, and prepositions marked the roles of words. Stress fell on the last syllable, because the syllables after the stress in Old Persian had been dropped: Old Persian pati became Middle Persian pad.

Middle Persian was written in several scripts. The Pahlavi script is notable for its many Aramaeograms, Aramaic words written but pronounced as Iranian ones. The word for father, pidar, was written with a form that was originally the Aramaic for my father. Few words were actually borrowed from Aramaic. The Manichaean script was more straightforward. Early inscriptions of the 3rd and 4th centuries still had a minimal case system, a direct case and an oblique case, and the usual word order was subject, object, verb.

Texts survive in Sasanian inscriptions, Egyptian papyri, coins and seals, fragments of Manichaean writings and Zoroastrian literature. Zoroastrianism was the state religion of Sasanian Iran until the Muslim conquest, and Pahlavi Middle Persian carries a large body of literature on its traditions. The earliest Zoroastrian texts were probably written down in the 6th and 7th centuries, though they codify earlier oral tradition. Most date from the 9th to the 11th century, when Middle Persian had long ceased to be spoken, and the surviving manuscripts are usually 14th-century copies.

Manichaean Middle Persian was used for religious writings, and the Middle Persian of the Church of the East is attested in the Pahlavi Psalter of the 7th century. Both were used across Central Asia, including Turpan, until the beginning of the second millennium. Middle Persian texts were still intelligible to speakers of Early New Persian in the 10th and 11th centuries, and New Persian, Achomi and Luri are its descendants.
middlesex: The boundary of Middlesex follows the Thames in the south, the Lea to the east and the Colne to the west, with a line of hills marking its northern edge with Hertfordshire. The county lay in the London Basin and was largely low-lying, with clay in the north and alluvium on gravel in the south. In the north, a hedge about 20 kilometres long, of great antiquity, marks the boundary between the Colne and Barnet Gate Wood. It is the second smallest of the historic counties of England, after Rutland.

The county grew from the homeland of the Middle Saxons. Their province occupied at least the area of the later county and much of Hertfordshire, and it is recorded only as part of the Kingdom of Essex, though charters show it was not part of the East Saxon core and it was probably independent at some point. The Diocese of London, re-established in 604 as the East Saxon see, kept boundaries based on Essex until the nineteenth century. It is not known exactly when Middlesex became a county, possibly in the early tenth century. The Domesday Book of 1086 records six hundreds: Edmonton, Elthorne, Gore, Hounslow, Ossulstone and Spelthorne.

The City of London became a self-governing county corporate, while Westminster, dominated by Westminster Abbey until the Dissolution of the Monasteries, was separate from it. In the south-east the Tower Division, or Tower Hamlets, was a county within a county with its own Lord Lieutenant. As London grew, the East End reached the Essex boundary and the Tower Division passed a population of one million, while railways spread the north-western suburbs. The Metropolitan Police served areas near London from 1829 and the whole county from 1840.

In 1889 about twenty per cent of the area and a third of the population became part of the new administrative County of London, and the remainder came under Middlesex County Council. The county never had a single established county town; assizes met at the Old Bailey and quarter sessions at Clerkenwell. Suburban growth after the interwar years led to the creation of Greater London in 1965, which took in almost all of the county.

Middlesex lies almost entirely within the ceremonial county of Greater London, with smaller parts in Hertfordshire and Surrey. Middlesex Day is observed on 16 May, recalling the 57th (West Middlesex) Regiment at the Battle of Albuera in 1811, whose commander, Lieutenant-Colonel William Inglis, urged his men to Die hard. The county's coat of arms shows three seaxes, attributed to the Kingdom of Essex. Middlesex County Cricket Club, founded in 1864, remains active.
midhat-pasha: Midhat Pasha was born in Istanbul in 1822 into a family of Muslim scholars; his father, Rusçuklu Mehmed Eşref, held judicial office. He entered the grand vizier's secretariat in 1836, and in 1854–1856 he put down banditry in the Balkans. In 1858 he spent six months studying in western Europe. Appointed governor of Niš in 1861, he was then the first governor of the model Danube province, where Fuad Pasha tested the Vilayet Law of 1864.

There he built schools, hospitals, granaries, roads and bridges, provided agricultural credit through the first agricultural cooperatives and founded a newspaper, and raised the province's revenue from 26,000 to 300,000 purses. His clash with the grand vizier Mehmed Emin Ali Pasha led to his posting to Baghdad in 1869, which was meant as a punishment.

In Baghdad he opened the city's first state schools and military schools, founded the bilingual newspaper al-Zawra, applied the vilayet system and the land decree of 1858 and re-established Ottoman rule in al-Hasa. Sir Henry Dobbs later called his three years there the most stable and secure period of Ottoman rule in the region.

Abdulaziz appointed him grand vizier in 1872, but they clashed over financial matters and he was dismissed after a short tenure. In 1876 he took a leading part in the coup that began the First Constitutional Era and chaired the constitutional committee. On 15 June 1876 an officer, Çerkez Hasan, attacked a meeting at his mansion and killed the foreign minister and others. He became grand vizier again on 19 December 1876 and announced on 23 December that a constitution would be promulgated.

It guaranteed equal rights for all citizens without distinction of race or creed, abolished slavery, set up an independent judiciary based on civil law, provided universal elementary education and created a parliament with an appointed Senate and an elected Chamber of Deputies. Abdul Hamid II accepted it but added article 113, which let him banish anyone without trial, and on 5 February 1877 he exiled Midhat. After British pressure Midhat returned in 1878 and was governor of Syria from November 1878.

In 1881 Midhat was arrested and charged with the murder of Abdulaziz, and he was sentenced to death, a sentence commuted to life imprisonment at Taif in the Hejaz. Some historians say that the charges were trumped up, with confessions extracted by torture, forged evidence and paid witnesses. He was strangled in his cell, reportedly on the Sultan's orders. In 1951 his remains were brought from Taif and buried at the Monument of Liberty. Bernard Lewis called him one of the ablest administrators in the Ottoman service, and the Midhat Pasha Souq in Damascus still bears his name.
midlands: There is no single definition of the Midlands. Taken as the statistical regions of the East Midlands and West Midlands, it includes Derbyshire, Herefordshire, Leicestershire, most of Lincolnshire, Northamptonshire, Nottinghamshire, Rutland, Shropshire, Staffordshire, Warwickshire, Worcestershire and the West Midlands metropolitan boroughs. Other definitions are wider: the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica described Gloucestershire as a West Midland county, Bedfordshire as South Midland and Huntingdonshire as East Midland, and parts of what was once southern Mercia are often labelled Central England.

The land is mostly low-lying and flat, with isolated hills such as the Wrekin near Telford, which rises to 407 metres. Upland lies in the west and north: the Shropshire Hills, reaching 540 metres at Brown Clee Hill, and the Peak District, whose highest point is Kinder Scout at 636 metres. The Malverns, among the oldest rock in England at around 680 million years, rise to 425 metres at the Worcestershire Beacon. Lincolnshire is the only coastal county.

The region corresponds broadly to the early medieval kingdom of Mercia. A saltire may have been used as a symbol of Mercia as early as the reign of Offa, and by the 13th century it had become the attributed arms of the kingdom, a gold saltire on a blue field. It is flown from Tamworth Castle, the ancient seat of the Mercian kings, and was flown at Birmingham Council House in 2009 while the Staffordshire Hoard was on display. The Flag Institute recognised it as the Mercian flag in 2014.

Nottingham played a notable part in the English Civil War, which is commemorated in place names such as Parliament Street and Standard Hill. In the Industrial Revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries the region became important, and the Black Country, broadly the boroughs of Dudley, Sandwell, Wolverhampton and Walsall, took its name from that industry. Derbyshire's Amber Valley and Erewash keep historic canals and sites of the mining industry.

The Midlands is neither Northern nor Southern England and has elements of both, with the Watford Gap in Northamptonshire often named as the dividing point between north and south. Its largest city is Birmingham. Other cities include Coventry, Derby, Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham, Stoke-on-Trent, Wolverhampton and Worcester. The area is also known for the West Midlands and East Midlands groups of dialects, including Brummie and the Black Country speech, and William Shakespeare came from Warwickshire.
midwestern-united-states: The Midwestern United States, also called the Heartland or the Middle West, is one of the four census regions defined by the United States Census Bureau, which called it the North Central Region until 1984. It lies between the Northeastern and Western United States, with Canada to the north and the Southern United States to the south. The region generally lies on the broad Interior Plain between the Appalachian and Rocky Mountains. Its major rivers include the Ohio River, the upper Mississippi River and the Missouri River.

The earliest Native American cultures in the Great Plains and Great Lakes areas date from about 12,000 to about 8,000 BCE. They were followed by the Archaic period, the Woodland Tradition and, from 900 to 1500 CE, the Mississippian period, whose traits probably began in the area of St. Louis, Missouri. During the colonial period the French settled the upper Mississippi watershed and called it the Illinois Country. French control ended in 1763, and Napoleon sold Louisiana to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.

The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 created the Northwest Territory, bounded by the Great Lakes and the Ohio and Mississippi rivers, and was the first large region of the United States to prohibit slavery. Large-scale settlement became possible only after the defeat of Native American tribes at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794. By the time of the Civil War European immigrants were settling directly in the interior: German immigrants in Ohio, Wisconsin, Minnesota and other states, and Irish immigrants in Great Lakes ports such as Cleveland and Chicago. The Republican Party originated in the Midwest in the 1850s.

The Census Bureau's definition covers 12 states: Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota and Wisconsin. Chicago is the most populous city and the largest economic and financial centre. The economy mixes heavy industry and agriculture, with extensive areas forming part of the Corn Belt.
mie-prefecture: Mie forms the eastern part of the Kii Peninsula, about 170 km from north to south and 80 km from east to west, with a coastline of 1,094.9 km. Bordering Aichi, Gifu, Shiga, Kyoto, Nara and Wakayama prefectures, it is counted as part of both the Kansai and Tokai regions, and Kansai dialect is spoken there. It has five geographical areas: the Suzuka Mountains in the north-west, the Ise Plain along the coast of Ise Bay, where most of the population lives, the Shima Peninsula, the Iga Basin on the border with Nara, and the Nunobiki Mountainous Region in the south. Forest covers about 65 per cent of the land.

Evidence of human habitation in Mie goes back more than 10,000 years, and agricultural communities formed along the rivers and coasts in the Jomon and Yayoi periods. In the seventh century the Saiku Imperial Residence was built in what is now Meiwa to serve as the home and administrative centre of the Saio, an imperial princess who was high priestess of Ise Shrine.

In the Edo period the area was divided among several feudal domains. Port towns such as Ohminato, Kuwana and Anotsu and castle towns flourished along the Tokaido and Ise Roads, and pilgrimages to Ise Shrine became very popular. After the Meiji Restoration the old provinces were reorganised repeatedly: in 1871 the area from the Kiso Three Rivers to Tsu became Anotsu Prefecture and the area south of it Watarai Prefecture. In 1872 the Anotsu seat moved to Yokkaichi and the prefecture was renamed Mie, but the seat returned to Tsu in 1873, and Mie took its present form in 1876, when it merged with Watarai. In 1959 the Ise-wan Typhoon devastated parts of the prefecture and killed many people.

Tsu is the capital and Yokkaichi the largest city. The prefecture contains some of the oldest and holiest sites of Shinto, among them the Ise Grand Shrine and the Tsubaki Grand Shrine, and the Kumano Kodo, an old pilgrimage road in the south that is a World Heritage Site. Northern Mie has manufacturing, mainly of vehicles, ships and heavy chemicals, and Honda has run a factory at Suzuka since 1960. The poet Matsuo Basho was born in Mie, and so were the scholar Norinaga Motoori and the writer Edogawa Ranpo.
mieszko-i: Nothing certain is known of Mieszko's life before he took control of his lands. Only the Lesser Poland Chronicle gives a birth date, which modern researchers do not treat as reliable, and historians propose dates between 922 and 945. He took power after his father's death, probably about 960, and inherited the lands of the Polans and Goplans, the Sieradz-Łęczyca region and Kuyavia, and perhaps Masovia and Gdańsk Pomerania. The territory was mixed and joined chiefly by tribal structures. Around 966 the traveller Abraham ben Jacob, at the court of Boleslaus I the Cruel in Prague, described Mieszko as one of four Slavic kings, with a large and highly regarded army.

In 965 Mieszko married Dobrawa, daughter of Boleslaus I, Duke of Bohemia, in an alliance he probably sought himself, and he was baptised in 966. Most historians see this as a political decision that brought him closer to the Czechs and lowered the risk of attack by German margraves, and it may have helped him to remove a pagan priestly class that blocked centralised rule. On 21 September 967 Polish and Bohemian troops defeated the Wolinians under Wichmann the Younger, giving him control of the mouth of the Oder. In 972 Margrave Odo I of the Saxon Ostmark attacked Poland.

Mieszko allied with Sweden against Denmark, probably in the early 980s, and the Danes were defeated about 991. A war with Bohemia in 990 left Poland holding Silesia, and Lesser Poland came under his rule at about this time. Around 991 to 992 he issued with his wife Oda and their sons the document called Dagome iudex, placing his lands under the protection of the pope and describing their borders. Only a later summary survives.

Mieszko died on 25 May 992 of a fever in old age, according to Thietmar of Merseburg. He was probably buried in Poznań Cathedral, but his remains have never been found. Thietmar says he divided his state among several princes, probably his sons. He is credited with uniting the Polish lands in the first state that can be called Poland, and his acceptance of Western Christianity brought Poland into the structures of Catholic Europe. Gniezno Cathedral was built during his rule. He left his sons a territory at least twice the size of his inheritance, with Silesia, Western Pomerania and probably Lesser Poland added.
mieszko-ii-lambert: Mieszko II was the second son of Bolesław I the Brave but the eldest born to his third wife, Emnilda of Lusatia. He could read and write and knew Greek and Latin, which was unusual for the period. His father named him successor and used him in dealings with Germany. About 1013 he married Richeza, daughter of Count Palatine Ezzo of Lotharingia and niece of Emperor Otto III, and received Kraków to rule, with Wawel as his residence.

In 1014 he was sent as an envoy to Duke Oldřich of Bohemia and was imprisoned there. He then led Polish troops in the war against Emperor Henry II that ended in the Peace of Bautzen of 30 January 1018, on terms very favourable to Poland.

Bolesław died on 17 June 1025, and Mieszko was crowned king on Christmas Day by Archbishop Hipolit in Gniezno Cathedral. He inherited Greater Poland, Lesser Poland, Silesia, Gdańsk Pomerania, Lusatia, Red Ruthenia and the territory of present-day Slovakia. His half-brother Bezprym and his full brother Otto received nothing, since Bolesław did not wish to divide the kingdom, and according to some chroniclers Mieszko expelled them.

Opponents of Emperor Conrad II sought his help, and in 1028 Polish troops invaded Saxony and devastated it. With Hungary as an ally he invaded again in 1030, while the Hungarians briefly occupied Vienna. Yaroslav I the Wise conquered Red Ruthenia, and in 1031 Conrad besieged Milsko, forcing Mieszko to give up lands. That year a Kievan army installed Bezprym, and Mieszko fled to Bohemia, where Oldřich imprisoned him again.

Bezprym lost his authority amid unrest and was murdered in 1032. At Merseburg on 7 July 1032 Conrad II divided Poland between Mieszko, Otto and a cousin named Dytryk. Otto was killed in 1033, Dytryk was probably expelled, and Mieszko reunited the country, though he still faced the nobility. He died suddenly on 10 or 11 May 1034, probably in Poznań, and was buried in the cathedral of St Peter and St Paul.

After his death peasants revolted in what is called the pagan reaction, and his son Casimir I the Restorer was expelled or driven out. Some modern historians think economic grievances, such as new taxes for the Church, counted for more than religion. The Czechs invaded Silesia and Greater Poland in 1039, and the capital moved to Kraków. He is called Mieszko II Gnuśny, the Lazy, which the sources attached to the way his reign ended.
mieszko-ii-the-fat: Mieszko was the eldest son of Duke Casimir I of Opole and his wife Viola, probably a Bulgarian princess. When his father died in 1230 he and his younger brother Władysław were minors, and their mother ruled with Henry I the Bearded, Duke of Wrocław, as regent. In 1233 a bull of Pope Gregory IX, probably issued with Henry's consent, took the boys' guardianship from Viola and gave it to the Archbishop of Gniezno and the Bishops of Wrocław and Olomouc. To calm the rebellion this caused, Henry gave Kalisz and Wieluń to the brothers in 1234 and took full control of Opole-Racibórz, without denying their rights to it.

After Henry I died in 1238, his son Henry II the Pious took over the regency, and Mieszko soon claimed his inheritance, probably taking power in late 1238 or early 1239. He married Judith, daughter of Duke Konrad I of Masovia, a match that strengthened his hand. When the Mongols invaded early in 1241 he did not abandon his duchy, unlike Bolesław V the Chaste of Sandomierz: in March he caught part of their force on the Odra River at Racibórz, giving Henry II time to prepare. At Legnica on 9 April 1241 the Mongols tricked him into retreating at the decisive moment, one of the main reasons for the Christian defeat.

From May 1241 he rebuilt the devastated land. Władysław came of age that year but was content with Kalisz, so Opole-Racibórz was not divided; he lost Kalisz in 1244. In 1243 Mieszko backed Konrad of Masovia's bid for Kraków, which failed partly through the two rulers' mistrust, though in 1246 he took the fortress of Lelów. He encouraged settlement under German law, with little success, and favoured the Teutonic Order, which gained valuable estates in Upper Silesia.

Mieszko had poor health, as his nickname reflects, and died on 22 October 1246 at the age of twenty-six, leaving no children. His sudden death meant that Lelów was never joined to his duchy for good. By his will all his lands went to Władysław except the district of Cieszyn, which he left to their mother Viola as her dower.
mieszko-iii-the-old: Mieszko was the fourth and second surviving son of Duke Bolesław III Wrymouth by his second wife Salomea, daughter of the German count Henry of Berg-Schelklingen. Under his father's testament of 1138, which set up a seniorate system, he received the newly established Duchy of Greater Poland. He had been duke of Poznań, where he had his main residence. His elder half-brother Władysław II was proclaimed high duke and overlord of the Seniorate Province at Kraków.

With his brother Bolesław IV the Curly, Mieszko opposed Władysław II in a series of conflicts from 1140. In 1146 the former high duke was excommunicated by Archbishop Jacob of Gniezno and faced rebellion from his own subjects. By May 1146 all Poland was in the hands of the junior dukes, and Władysław fled to Bohemia and then to Germany. Bolesław became high duke, while Mieszko kept Greater Poland and acted as his brother's ally.

After Bolesław IV died on 3 April 1173, Mieszko became high duke by agnatic seniority. He remained in Greater Poland and left Lesser Poland to a governor, Henryk Kietlicz. His harsh taxes displeased the Lesser Polish magnates, and his efforts to strengthen ducal authority and limit the nobility and clergy brought wide opposition. In 1177 his eldest son Odon rebelled, fearing for his inheritance. He was supported by Bishop Gedko of Kraków, Bolesław the Tall and Casimir II the Just, and Casimir took Kraków as high duke. Mieszko fled to Racibórz and then left Poland.

Refused help by his son-in-law in Bohemia, and unable to pay the 10,000 pieces of silver Barbarossa asked, he was aided by another son-in-law, Duke Bogislaw I of Pomerania. In 1181 he conquered Gniezno and Kalisz and soon recovered all Greater Poland, reconciling with Odon in 1182. In 1191 he briefly retook Kraków, but Casimir regained it. After Casimir's death in 1194 Mieszko tried again, but at the Battle of Mozgawa on 13 September 1195 he was badly wounded and his son Bolesław of Kuyavia was killed.

In 1198 Mieszko negotiated his return to Lesser Poland with Casimir's widow, Helen of Znojmo, giving up Kuyavia. He was deposed again in 1199 and restored in a new settlement three years later, keeping the title of high duke with reduced powers. He died on 13 March 1202, having outlived all his siblings and all his sons but Władysław III Spindleshanks, who succeeded him in Greater Poland.

Medieval chroniclers often portrayed him as harsh and avaricious, while modern historians see a ruler who tried to impose stronger central government in a period that resisted it. His reign and repeated bids for supremacy illustrate the weaknesses of the Piast seniorate system and its part in prolonging Poland's political division.
mieszko-iv-tanglefoot: Mieszko was the second son of Władysław II the Exile and Agnes of Babenberg, and was born about 1130. After his father's deposition in 1146 the family lived mainly in Altenburg in Saxony, and Mieszko studied at Michaelsberg and Bamberg. Władysław died in exile in 1159. His sons continued to fight for their inheritance, and in 1163, with the help of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, Mieszko and his older brother Bolesław I the Tall returned to Silesia. His nickname Tanglefoot appears only in chronicles of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries; a mid-fifteenth century annal records him as Mieszko the bandy-legged, called Platonogy.

The brothers ruled the Duchy of Wrocław together from 1163 to 1173 and regained the major Silesian cities in 1165. Mieszko wanted a duchy of his own, and in 1172 he rebelled against Bolesław, who fled to Erfurt but returned with the emperor's help. He gave Mieszko the towns of Racibórz and Cieszyn. In 1177 Mieszko supported his uncle Mieszko III the Old, and Casimir II the Just, who took Kraków, later gave him Oświęcim and Bytom. In 1195 he and his nephew Jarosław backed Mieszko III again, and the Silesian troops arrived late at the Battle of Mozgawa on 13 September 1195.

Jarosław died on 22 March 1201, and Bolesław died on 7 or 8 December that year, leaving his lands to his son Henry the Bearded. Mieszko attacked suddenly at the start of 1202 and obtained Opole, which was joined to his lands. The Church, which supported Henry, stopped him from taking more.

On 9 June 1210 Pope Innocent III deposed and excommunicated the seniorate rulers, including the high duke Leszek the White, and demanded that the Piast princes follow the will of Bolesław III Wrymouth, under which the most senior Piast duke ruled. While the Synod of Borzykowa met without him, Mieszko marched on Kraków with the support of the Gryfici family and took the capital without a fight. It was the high point of his career. He died on 16 May 1211 and, according to Jan Długosz, was probably buried in Wawel Cathedral. By about 1178 he had married Ludmila, and they had five children, among them a son, Casimir I.
miguel-angel-asturias: Miguel Ángel Asturias was born in Guatemala City on 19 October 1899, the first child of Ernesto Asturias Girón, a lawyer and judge, and María Rosales de Asturias, a schoolteacher. In 1905 the family moved to the house of his grandparents. He lived in Paris in the 1920s, where he studied ethnology at the Sorbonne with Georges Raynaud, an expert on the Quiché Maya, and finished a translation of the Popol Vuh in 1926. He also associated with the Surrealists, and some scholars credit him with bringing features of modernist style, such as magical realism, into Latin American writing.

Asturias was involved in politics throughout his career, opposed the dictatorship of Manuel Estrada Cabrera and served as ambassador in several Latin American countries. He supported the government of Jacobo Árbenz, whose policies ran against the interests of the United Fruit Company. When Árbenz fell in 1954, Carlos Castillo Armas expelled Asturias and stripped him of his citizenship. He spent eight years in Buenos Aires and Chile and then moved to Europe, where he lived in Genoa. In 1966 he won the Soviet Union's Lenin Peace Prize, and in 1967 the Nobel Prize in Literature, which some critics thought was awarded to a writer little known outside Latin America. He spent his last years in Madrid and died there on 9 June 1974.

His first book, Leyendas de Guatemala (1930), retells Maya myths. El Señor Presidente, completed in 1933 and privately published in Mexico in 1946, denounces the dictator Estrada Cabrera, and has been called a study of fear. Hombres de maíz (Men of Maize, 1949) tells of an indigenous community whose land is threatened by planters and sets the Maya belief that the first humans were made of maize against the modernising society around them. The banana trilogy, Viento fuerte (1950), El Papa Verde (1954) and Los ojos de los enterrados (1960), is a fictional account of foreign control of the banana industry and the exploitation of native workers, and it earned him the Lenin Peace Prize. Mulata de tal followed in 1963.

Asturias, himself a mestizo, proposed a hybrid national identity for Guatemala, ladino in language and Maya in mythology. His prose, rhythmic and rich in repetition and onomatopoeia, has been called tropical baroque. The Miguel Ángel Asturias National Prize in Literature, the country's most distinguished literary prize, is named after him.
miguel-cabello-de-balboa: Cabello de Balboa was a great-nephew of Vasco Núñez de Balboa, who in 1513 led the first European expedition from the New World to reach the Pacific Ocean. He was born at Archidona, near Málaga; the exact date is not known. As a young man he chose a military career and fought in the wars of France and the Netherlands under Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy, and Lamoral, Count of Egmont, and with Rodrigo de Basan. He was among the victors of the Battle of Gravelines in 1558 over the French army of Marshal Paul de Thermes.

Back in Málaga in 1565 or 1566, he became a churchman and in 1566 sailed for Peru. From there he went to Quito, where he began the Miscelánea antártica, and he later lived in Lima, where he also wrote verse and prose, apparently including two comedies. A letter of 1602–1603 gives detailed information on the regions of Pelechuco and Apolobamba in eastern Bolivia, between the Andes and the Beni River, in terms that suggest he had been there.

He is also an important source on the northern Andes, especially the Pacific shore and the forests reaching inland to the cordilleras of present-day northern Ecuador and southern Colombia, and his writings on the lowland peoples were gathered in 1945 as Verdadera descripción y relación de la provincia y tierra de las Esmeraldas. He died in 1608 at Camata, in Larecaja Province, Bolivia.

Besides its long account of the Inca past as tradition told it, which gives their origin somewhat differently from other Spanish authors, the Miscelánea antártica records alleged Amerindian traditions of white men who came to South America and preached the gospel, and puts forward the theory that the peoples of Patagonia and Chile descended from pirates of Macassar. In 1853 the original was owned by the historiographer Joaquin Garcia Ycazbalceta in Mexico, and a complete copy is held by the New York Public Library. San Marcos University published the whole work in 1951. Several of his other writings, among them La Volcánea and La Comedia del Cuzco, are lost.
miguel-de-cervantes: Many details of Cervantes's life remain uncertain, including his name, background and appearance. He signed his name as Cerbantes, but his printers used Cervantes, which became the common form. In later life he used Saavedra, the name of a distant relative, rather than Cortinas, after his mother. It is generally accepted that he was born around 29 September 1547 in Alcalá de Henares, the second son of the barber-surgeon Rodrigo de Cervantes and Leonor de Cortinas.

Rodrigo was often in debt or looking for work, and the family moved constantly. When he was imprisoned for debt from October 1553 to April 1554, Leonor supported the family alone. They lived in Córdoba until 1556, when his grandfather died. It has been suggested that one or both parents were New Christians, Catholics of Jewish ancestry, but the view has no wide following. No authenticated portrait of Cervantes is known to exist.

In 1569 Cervantes was forced to leave Spain and went to Rome, where he worked in a cardinal's household. In 1570 he enlisted in a Spanish Navy infantry regiment. He was badly wounded at the Battle of Lepanto in October 1571. Captured by Barbary pirates in 1575 while serving as a soldier, he was ransomed after five years and returned to Madrid.

He claimed to have written more than 20 plays, such as El trato de Argel, based on his captivity, but such works were short-lived. His first significant novel, the pastoral romance La Galatea, appeared in 1585 and received little notice. He worked as a purchasing agent and later as a government tax collector. By 1605 he had not been published for 20 years.

Don Quixote, first published in January 1605, set out explicitly to undermine vain and empty chivalric romances. Its portrayal of real life and its everyday speech were considered innovative, and it was instantly popular: Don Quixote and Sancho Panza appeared in masquerades celebrating the birth of Philip IV on 8 April 1605. An unauthorised sequel under the name Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda came out in 1614, and Cervantes published his own second part in 1615. The first part is more comic, the second more sophisticated, with greater depth of characterisation.

His other works include the twelve Novelas ejemplares of 1613, the allegorical poem Viaje del Parnaso, eight short farces, and Los trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda, published after his death in 1617. English writers rediscovered him in the mid-18th century, and John Bowle published an annotated edition of Don Quixote in 1781. It has been translated into all major languages.
miguel-garcia-granados: García Granados was born on 29 September 1809 in El Puerto de Santa María, Spain, into a wealthy military family, and was brought to Central America as a young adolescent. At twenty-three he travelled in South America and Europe and visited New York and Philadelphia, and he completed his schooling in London. His sister was the Guatemalan writer María Josefa García Granados. He became known as a moderate liberal who compromised with Rafael Carrera and tried to get along with his successor, Vicente Cerna.

Sympathising with the revolt against the government, he went into exile with the support of Guatemalan liberals, and on his return he became the leader of the revolution against Cerna and came to be known as its philosopher. As provisional president after the liberal victory at Guatemala City he sought to regularise the government by building a lawful regime, decreed freedom of the press and supported liberal revolts elsewhere.

He created the Guatemalan flag by decree, and today's flag is almost identical to his version of 1871. He also supported education and the arts, inviting the Italian conductor Pietro Visoni in 1871 to direct the main military band; Visoni went on to found the Martial Symphony Band and the first formal music conservatory in Central America.

After stepping down he wrote for Guatemalan magazines and newspapers, producing accounts of his years as liberal leader and president, an essay on monetary policy and two volumes of memoirs. In 1877 the Cuban writer José Martí, teaching in Guatemala City, often played chess with him and paid his respects to his daughter María García Granados y Saborío, who fell in love with him; Martí returned from Mexico in 1878 already married, and María died a few weeks after he left. Her father died soon after, on 8 September 1878, and was buried in the old San Juan de Dios Cemetery. In 1894 his remains were moved to a monument at the new General Cemetery, and his portrait appears on the 10 quetzal note.
miguel-grau-seminario: Grau was born in Paita, the son of Juan Manuel Grau y Berrío, a Colombian who had come to Peru with Bolivar in the fight for independence from Spain, and María Luisa Seminario y del Castillo, who was married to another man. He entered the Paita Nautical School and first went to sea at nine aboard a merchant schooner bound for Colombia, which sank off Gorgona Island. Undeterred, he sailed again the next year and later served on merchant ships to ports in Oceania, Asia, America and Europe.

He joined the Peruvian Navy as an officer candidate in 1853, at 19. In 1862 he left it for private business and took part in brutal raiding expeditions across Polynesia, in which islanders were coerced, abducted and trafficked into slavery. Back in the navy in 1864, he was sent to Europe to oversee the building of ships for the Peruvian fleet, among them the ironclad Huáscar, launched by Laird at Birkenhead in 1865. In 1868 he was named commander of the Huáscar, and in 1876 he was elected to Congress for Paita, where his seat is still kept and his name called at each session.

When the War of the Pacific began on 5 April 1879, Grau commanded the Huáscar and the navy. Striking by surprise and then vanishing, he cut Chilean lines of communication and supply and put off a Chilean invasion by sea for six months, for which he was promoted to rear admiral. After Iquique he wrote to Carmela Carvajal de Prat, widow of Captain Arturo Prat, returning her husband's belongings, and at Antofagasta he asked the crew of the Matias Cousiño to abandon ship before opening fire. His Chilean opponents called him El Caballero de los Mares, the Gentleman of the Seas.

Intercepted by the Chilean ironclads Cochrane and Blanco Encalada, he turned to face the Cochrane, and a shot from it destroyed the Huáscar's turret and killed him. Most of his body was not recovered; his remains, buried with military honours in Chile, were returned to Peru in 1958 and lie in an underground mausoleum at the Escuela Militar Naval del Peru in El Callao. The Peruvian Congress made him Gran Almirante del Perú in 1967, and in 2000 a popular vote named him Peruvian of the Millennium.
miguel-hidalgo-y-costilla: Hidalgo was born on 8 May 1753, the second child of criollo parents; his father managed a hacienda near Valladolid in Michoacán. He studied with the Jesuits and then at the Colegio de San Nicolás, and took his degree in philosophy and theology at the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico in 1773. He learned Nahuatl, Otomi and Purépecha as well as French, which let him read Enlightenment works forbidden by the Church. He was ordained in 1778 and taught at the Colegio de San Nicolás in Valladolid, becoming its dean in 1790. Authorities ousted him in 1792 for revising traditional teaching and for irregular handling of funds.

He later became parish priest at Dolores, Guanajuato, where he set up brick and pottery works, trained indigenous people in leatherwork and promoted beekeeping, until Spanish mercantile policy ordered him to stop.

After the discovery of the Conspiracy of Querétaro, Hidalgo rang the parish bells on the night of 15 to 16 September 1810 and called the people to arms. His exact words are unknown, and accounts differ on whether they invoked King Ferdinand VII. Hidalgo and Ignacio Allende left Dolores with about 800 men and took San Miguel and Celaya with little resistance. At Guanajuato the insurgents overwhelmed the fortified Alhóndiga de Granaditas and killed an estimated 400 to 600 people. The Inquisition condemned Hidalgo as a seditionist and heretic, and Bishop Manuel Abad y Queipo excommunicated him.

After the Battle of Monte de las Cruces on 30 October 1810 his forces stood close to Mexico City, but Hidalgo turned back, a decision historians still debate. At Guadalajara he formed a government and on 6 December 1810 decreed the abolition of slavery and of tribute. Royalist forces under Félix Calleja defeated his army at the Calderón Bridge in January 1811, and the other leaders took military command from him on 25 January. Ignacio Elizondo betrayed and captured the leaders at the Wells of Baján on 21 March 1811.

Hidalgo was defrocked at Durango on 27 July 1811 and executed, most probably by firing squad, on 30 July at Chihuahua. His head and those of Allende, Aldama and Mariano Jiménez were displayed at the Alhóndiga de Granaditas for ten years. His movement passed to José María Morelos, his former student. Though Agustín de Iturbide became first head of state in 1821, later liberal movements favoured Hidalgo, and 16 September 1810 became recognised as the day of independence. The town of Dolores was renamed Dolores Hidalgo, and the state of Hidalgo was created in 1869. His remains lie in the Angel of Independence in Mexico City.
miguel-lopez-de-legazpi: Miguel López de Legazpi was born in Zumarraga in the Basque province of Guipúzcoa. His family was wealthy and held military and municipal offices, and his father, Juan de Legazpi, was a soldier who had served in the Italian Wars. His education is unknown, but his later posts suggest legal training. After his father's death in 1527 his older brother inherited the family wealth.

Around 1528 he settled in New Spain. He served as clerk of the mint, secretary of the municipal council and, in 1559, alcalde mayor of Mexico City, and he took part in several inquisitorial processes between 1536 and 1543. In 1532 he married Isabel Garcés, with whom he had nine children. Two grandsons, Felipe and Juan de Salcedo, later sailed with him.

In 1564 the viceroy Luís de Velasco commissioned him, on the order of King Philip II, to lead an expedition across the Pacific. Five ships and about 500 soldiers sailed from Barra de Navidad in November 1564, with the friar Andrés de Urdaneta as navigator and spiritual adviser. After 93 days they reached the Mariana Islands, where they fought the Chamorro. In the Philippines Legazpi made blood compacts with local chiefs, including Datu Sikatuna on 16 March 1565, and landed at Cebu on 27 April 1565, where he overcame Rajah Tupas and founded a settlement.

A Portuguese blockade of Cebu in 1568 failed. In 1569 food shortages led him to move to Panay. In 1570 he sent Martín de Goiti to Luzon, and Goiti's force defeated a fleet led by Bambalito at the Bangkusay Channel. Legazpi followed, made a pact with the local rulers Rajah Sulayman and Lakan Dula, and established a settlement at Manila on 24 June 1571. He ordered the walled city of Intramuros built and proclaimed Manila the capital.

Legazpi governed the islands for about a year. He died of a stroke in Manila on 20 August 1572, bankrupt after spending most of his fortune on the conquest, and was buried in San Agustin Church in Intramuros. His letters to Philip II on the expedition are kept in the General Archive of the Indies in Seville.

His expedition with Urdaneta effectively created the Manila galleon trade, in which silver mined in Mexico and Potosí was exchanged for Chinese silk, porcelain, spices and other goods. The Philippines remained a Spanish possession until the Treaty of Paris of 10 December 1898, apart from the British occupation of Manila and Cavite in 1762 to 1764. The capital of Albay province bears his name.
miguel-malvar: Malvar was born on 27 September 1865 in San Miguel, a barrio of Santo Tomas, Batangas, to Máximo Malvar and Tiburcia Carpio, a family known for its wealth. He studied at a school run by Father Valerio Malabanan in Tanauan, where Apolinario Mabini was his classmate, but chose to farm rather than study in Manila, and was elected capitán municipal of his town. In 1891 he married Paula Maloles; eleven of their thirteen children survived, and he often took his family with him on campaign.

An original member of the Katipunan, he rose after August 1896 from leading 70 men to military commander of Batangas, and fought at the Battle of Zapote Bridge on 17 February 1897, where General Edilberto Evangelista fell. After the Tejeros Convention he sided with Andrés Bonifacio against Emilio Aguinaldo. He opposed the Pact of Biak-na-Bato as a Spanish ruse and kept fighting until Aguinaldo ordered the generals to stop, ceasing his offensives on 6 January 1898.

When war with the Americans began in February 1899 he became second-in-command to General Mariano Trías in southern Luzon, and besieged Calamba without success from August to December 1899. After Trías surrendered on 15 March 1901 and Aguinaldo was captured on 23 March, Malvar succeeded under Aguinaldo's line of succession and reorganised the forces as the Army of Liberation. From January 1902 General J. Franklin Bell's scorched earth tactics in Batangas took a heavy toll on fighters and civilians, and Malvar surrendered to Bell at Rosario on 16 April 1902.

He refused every position offered by the American colonial government and died in Manila on 13 October 1911. Some hold that he should be counted as the second president of the Philippines; Representative Rodolfo Valencia filed a bill to that effect in 2007, but the Philippine government does not recognise him as such. The town of Malvar, Batangas, and two ships of the Philippine Navy bear his name.
miguel-miramon: Miguel Gregorio de la Luz Atenógenes Miramón y Tarelo was born in Mexico City on 29 September 1831, into a traditional family of partial French heritage. He entered the military college in February 1846. During the American invasion he fought at the Battle of Molino del Rey and the Battle of Chapultepec, where he was wounded and taken prisoner.

After the liberal Plan of Ayutla triumphed in 1855, Miramón took part in conservative revolts. In October 1856 he was second in command of a revolt at Puebla and, with a thousand soldiers, defended the city for 43 days against an army of 6,000. He joined the forces of Félix María Zuloaga when the Plan of Tacubaya began the Reform War in January 1858.

Miramón's victories in 1858, among them the Battle of Salamanca on 10 March, earned him the press name Young Maccabee. After a moderate conservative faction overthrew Zuloaga in December 1858, a junta elected Miramón president, and Zuloaga formally passed the presidency to him on 31 January 1859. He led two sieges of Veracruz, where Benito Juárez had his liberal government. The first was abandoned by 29 March 1859, and the second failed when the United States Navy captured his naval squadron at the Battle of Antón Lizardo on 6 March 1860.

At the Battle of Calpulalpan on 22 December 1860, his 8,000 troops met 16,000 liberals under Jesús González Ortega, and Miramón lost. The liberals entered Mexico City on 1 January 1861. Miramón fled to Europe and was received at the Spanish court on 2 December 1861.

He returned during the Tripartite Expedition and was exiled to Cuba, then re-entered Mexico in July 1863 and offered his services to the regency of the Second Mexican Empire. Emperor Maximilian sent him to Berlin to study the Prussian army. Miramón came back on 9 November 1866 and took command of the western military district. He was routed at San Jacinto on 1 February 1867 and took refuge at Querétaro, where he became the leading general during the siege.

Colonel Miguel López opened the gates of Querétaro to the Republicans on the night of 14 May, in exchange for gold, and Miramón was shot in the face. Maximilian, Miramón and Tomás Mejía were tried for violating an 1862 decree against traitors and invaders and sentenced to death. On 19 June 1867, at the Cerro de las Campanas, Maximilian yielded Miramón the place of honour in the centre. Before the shooting Miramón read a brief statement disavowing the charge of traitor.
miguel-primo-de-rivera: Miguel Primo de Rivera was born on 8 January 1870 into a landowning military family of Jerez de la Frontera, the son of a retired colonel. His uncle Fernando was Captain General in Madrid. He graduated from the General Military Academy in Toledo in 1884 and served as a junior officer in the colonial wars in Morocco, Cuba and the Philippines. He watched Spain's defeat in the Spanish-American War in 1898. After fighting the Berbers of the Rif he became convinced that Spain probably could not hold its North African colony and should withdraw if it could not dominate it. He was promoted to brigadier general in 1911 and later commanded the military regions of Valencia, Madrid and Barcelona.

Spain's army suffered a heavy defeat at the Battle of Annual in 1921, and by 1923 deputies of the Cortes were calling for an investigation into the responsibility of King Alfonso XIII and the army. On 13 September 1923 Primo de Rivera, as Captain General in Barcelona, led a military coup. The king named him prime minister. He suspended the constitution, dissolved the Cortes and set up a directorate of eight military men, and on 3 December 1925 replaced it with a civilian directory. His Patriotic Union, meant to be an apolitical party, failed to attract many members.

He withdrew Spanish forces in Morocco, and when Moroccans attacked the French sector, French and Spanish united to crush the rebellion in 1925, with victory in 1927. His regime built dams and railways, and the Barcelona Metro opened in 1924. It organised 27 committees to mediate between employers and workers, and unemployment largely disappeared. It also censored the press, closed the Ateneo club and banned the CNT trade union. To suppress Catalan separatism it made the use of Catalan in church services illegal.

The economic boom ended; the peseta fell and inflation rose. He lost the support of the armed forces after he began to inject politics into promotions in the artillery corps, and the king drew away. On 26 January 1930 he asked the military leaders whether he still had their backing. Their cool answers persuaded him to resign two days later, and he died in Paris on 16 March 1930.

The king, discredited by his support for the dictatorship, went into exile on 14 April 1931 after republican candidates won in 41 provincial capitals, and the Second Republic followed. Primo de Rivera's son José Antonio later founded the Falange.
mihail-gerdzhikov: Mihail Gerdzhikov was born in Plovdiv, then in the Ottoman Empire, and studied at the French College there, where he was nicknamed Michel. In 1893, still a pupil, he began his revolutionary work as leader of a Macedonian Secret Revolutionary Committee. As a student in Lausanne and Geneva he took part in the so-called Geneva Group. In 1899 he moved to Ottoman Macedonia, taught at the Bulgarian Men's High School in Bitola and joined the Internal Macedonian Adrianople Revolutionary Organization, where he grew close to Gotse Delchev.

He was a delegate to the Seventh Congress of the Supreme Macedonian-Adrianople Committee in 1900 and to its Eighth Congress in April 1901. After the defeat of the Strandzha Commune in the Preobrazhenie Uprising he saw to the settling of the rebels who withdrew from Ottoman Thrace into Bulgaria, and wrote in the Bulgarian and foreign press calling for international intervention to settle the Eastern question. With Varban Kilifarski he also published newspapers of their own.

When the Balkan War broke out in 1912 he led the Lozengrad guerrilla unit of the Macedonian-Adrianopolitan Volunteer Corps. He was then mobilised into the Bulgarian Army and served in World War I with the Forty-third Infantry Regiment. After the war he joined IMRO (United) and in 1930 attended its conference in Constantinople, where he became a member of its Central Committee, but he returned to Bulgaria in 1931 instead of going to Berlin.

In his later years Gerdzhikov worked as a journalist and translator and wrote for a number of periodicals. During the Second World War he kept apart from the resistance movement, though some of his associates took part in it and he kept up ties with them. After the coup of 9 September he signed an appeal to the Macedonians in Bulgaria. He died in 1947, disappointed with the new communist authorities.
mihailo-i-of-duklja: On the death of Stefan Vojislav his lands were divided among his five sons, according to the Chronicle of the Priest of Duklja. Fighting followed in Travunia, where Mihailo's brother Gojislav was killed by local nobles who set up Domanek in his place. Faced with a Byzantine offensive, the four surviving brothers made peace and signed an alliance, held to be the oldest treaty in Serbian history, after which Radoslav killed Domanek. Mihailo then became knez of Duklja; the Byzantine writer Cedrenus called his realm a principality of the Triballi and Serbs.

In 1050 he received the Byzantine title of protospatharios and married a niece of Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, an arrangement that brought some 20 years of peace. Matters changed after 1071, the year of the Battle of Manzikert. In 1072 the Bulgarian nobles of Skopje, planning a revolt under Georgi Voiteh, offered the Bulgarian throne to one of his sons, and in the autumn Mihailo sent Constantine Bodin with 300 men. At Prizren Bodin was crowned Emperor of the Bulgarians under the name Peter III, but he was later captured, and Langobardopoulos, a captive Byzantine general married to Mihailo's daughter, who was sent to rescue him, went over to the Byzantines.

Estranged from Constantinople, Mihailo turned to the papacy, seeking an archbishopric of his own and a royal title. After the schism of 1054 Pope Gregory VII was willing to crown rulers in the border lands, and he sent Mihailo royal insignia in 1077; a letter of 9 January 1078 addresses him as king of the Slavs. Whether his brothers accepted him as supreme ruler is not known.

Mihailo sealed an alliance with the Normans by marrying Bodin to Jaquinta of Bari, and died in 1081. He left St. Michael's Church in Ston, north of Dubrovnik, a small church mainly in an early Byzantine style that holds one of the oldest known fresco portraits of a South Slavic ruler. Of his seven sons four are known: Vladimir, Constantine Bodin, Dobroslav II and Petrislav, who ruled Rascia.
mihaly-karolyi: Mihály Károlyi was born on 4 March 1875 in the Károlyi Palace in Pest, into one of Hungary's wealthiest Catholic aristocratic families. He was born with a cleft lip and cleft palate, and a successful operation at the age of 14 let him speak normally.

Elected to parliament in 1910 for the opposition Party of Independence, he became one of its foremost progressive voices and an implacable enemy of Prime Minister István Tisza. In 1914 he was lecturing in the United States when the war began, and he warned in the press that the ultimatum to Serbia suggested the Monarchy wanted war.

Károlyi, an opponent of the war and a supporter of the Entente, formed the Hungarian National Council on 25 October 1918 and took power in the Aster Revolution on 31 October. King Charles IV was all but forced to appoint him prime minister, an office he held from 1 to 16 November. He ended the personal union with Austria and on 2 November ordered the unilateral disarmament of the Hungarian army, which still had more than 1,400,000 soldiers, leaving the country open to occupation by Serbian, Czechoslovak and Romanian forces. After Charles withdrew, Károlyi proclaimed the Hungarian Democratic Republic on 16 November, with himself as provisional president.

His government pursued enfranchisement and redistribution, but it shared power with revolutionary councils dominated by the Social Democrats, and it printed money, causing inflation. On 20 March 1919 the French presented the Vix Note, ordering Hungarian troops back. Prime Minister Dénes Berinkey resigned the next day, and the merged Socialist Party announced Károlyi's removal and the Hungarian Soviet Republic.

The Communist government arrested him on its first day, but he escaped and fled to Paris in July 1919. Between 1921 and 1923 the Horthy regime tried him for high treason over the army's disarmament and confiscated his assets, a verdict criticised in the British and French parliaments. He returned to Hungary in 1946, served as ambassador to France from 1947 to 1949 and resigned in protest at the execution of László Rajk. He died in Vence, France, on 19 March 1955.

Hungarians remember him differently. Under the communist government he was praised as founder of the first republic, and Imre Varga's statue of him was installed in Kossuth Lajos tér in 1975. After the fall of communism many blamed him for the territorial losses fixed by the Treaty of Trianon, and the statue was removed on 29 March 2012.
mihira-bhoja: Bhoja inherited a weakened realm from his father, Ramabhadra, and turned it into a large and prosperous empire. A devotee of Vishnu, he took the title Ādivarāha, the primeval boar incarnation of the god, and his capital was Kannauj in present-day Uttar Pradesh. At its height his empire stretched from the foot of the Himalayas to the Narmada River in the south, to the Sutlej in the northwest and up to Bengal in the east. He was succeeded by his son Mahendrapala I.

Bhoja first crushed rebellious feudatories in Rajasthan, then turned on the Palas and Rastrakutas. In a succession war for the throne of Gujarat he backed the younger brother of Dhruva II of the Gujarat Rashtrakuta dynasty with a cavalry raid; Dhruva repulsed it, but Bhoja kept parts of Gujarat and Malwa. Late in his reign the Rashtrakuta king Krishna II defeated him in a large battle at Ujjain, yet by the end of his reign the Gujarat Rashtrakuta line had been destroyed. After the death of the Pala ruler Devapala, Bhoja defeated his successor Narayanapala and pushed east into Pala lands near Gorakhpur.

His Daulatpura-Dausa inscription of 843 confirms his rule around Dausa, and Kalhana's Rajatarangini says his lands reached Kashmir and that he took Punjab from the Thakkiyaka dynasty. He drove the Arabs of Sindh, under its governor Imran ibn-Musa, from the fort of Sindan and out of Kutch between 833 and 842. The Arab chronicler Sulaiman called him a bitter enemy of the Arabs, and the 10th-century Persian geography Hudud-ul-Alam credits the Rai of Qinnauj with 150,000 cavalry and 800 war elephants.

Scholars broadly agree in giving him the Adivaraha dramma coins of billon, which show the boar god with a spoked solar wheel, a mace, a lotus and a conch, and probably a two-headed serpent under his feet. Alexander Cunningham found such coins only in silver and copper, and the copper ones may first have been coated with silver. In the 13th century Thakkar Pheru, mint master under Alauddin Khilji, still noted them in his Dravya-Pariksha.
mihirakula: Mihirakula, also written Mihiragula or Mahiragula, was the son and successor of Toramana and the second and last king of the Alchon Huns in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent. His name is probably Iranian: Janos Harmatta rendered it as Mithra's Begotten, while the Sanskritized form can be read as mihira, sun, and kula, clan. The 6th-century Alexandrian traveller Cosmas Indicopleustes described a lord of India called Gollas, thought to be Mihirakula, who went to war with no fewer than two thousand elephants and a great force of cavalry.

Around 520 the Chinese Buddhist monk Song Yun met Mihirakula, by then master of Sindh, and wrote that he did not believe in any religion, that the Brahmins of his kingdom disliked him and that his people were exhausted by his wars. The Gwalior inscription of his 15th regnal year shows that his rule reached Gwalior. His coins show Oesho or Shiva, and some copper coins carry a bull with the words "The bull should be victorious", which may point to Shaivism.

The 7th-century pilgrim Xuanzang tells, as hearsay, that Mihirakula ruled from Sagala, now Sialkot, and turned against Buddhism when the monks sent him a servant instead of a learned teacher. In this account he was defeated and captured by the Gupta king Narasimhagupta Baladitya of Magadha, spared at the plea of Baladitya's mother, and then seized Kashmir and Gandhara, demolishing 1600 stupas and monasteries. His campaigns ended with his defeat by the Aulikara king Yashodharman in the Battle of Sondani, partly the subject of the Mandsaur Pillar inscriptions.

According to Xuanzang, Mihirakula died a sudden death. The 12th-century Rajatarangini calls him a man of violent acts resembling kala, death, and Buddhist and later Jaina texts remember him as a tyrant. Modern scholars are more cautious. Jason Neelis and Shōshin Kuwayama find no evidence that he destroyed Buddhism in Gandhara, where monasteries went on growing for centuries, and the monastery at Harwan near Srinagar was built in this period. Upinder Singh asks whether his reputation reflects real persecution, or the fact that his rival Baladitya was an ardent patron of the Buddhist sangha.
mihna: In 827 the caliph al-Ma'mun proclaimed the doctrine that the Quran was created, a view held by the Mu'tazilite school, which taught that good and evil were rational categories that unaided reason could establish. Six years later, about four months before his sudden death, he began testing the beliefs of his officials. Scholars explain the step in different ways. Some point to his Mu'tazilite circle, above all Ahmad ibn Abi Du'ad, who became chief qadi and pressed the policy under the next two caliphs. Others stress his closeness to the Alids, shown in his choice of Ali al-Rida as heir, though that link is disputed. Most modern scholars see the Mihna as an attempt to reassert the caliph's religious authority against the ulama.

In his letters to his governors al-Ma'mun presented the caliph as guardian of God's religion and likened scholars who disagreed to an ignorant mob. Under al-Mu'tasim the traditionist Ahmad ibn Hanbal declared the Quran uncreated and was removed from his post, but when the people of Baghdad threatened to riot, the caliph released him. Busy with building Samarra and with his campaigns, al-Mu'tasim let the test become a courtroom formality, in which the testimony of anyone who answered wrongly was inadmissible. Al-Wathiq, also influenced by Ibn Abi Du'ad, revived it in the third year of his reign and sent officials to question jurists.

Al-Mutawakkil turned away from his predecessors' policy, dismissed several of Ibn Abi Du'ad's judges, took hostile steps against the Mu'tazilites and ordered an end to debate on the nature of the Quran. The Mihna is one of the few cases of religious persecution among Muslims in medieval Islam. Law in classical Islam was developed by private scholars, often in conscious opposition to the state, and the Mihna reflects the caliphs' frustration with that juristic culture. After it the domains of political and religious authority became more clearly defined, and in the longer run the caliph's role narrowed to politics and then to a symbol. Literal reading of the Quran and the authority of the Sunnah gained ground in theology.
mikael-sehul: Born Blatta Mikael in the district of Na'eder, he was the son of Abeto Hezeqeyas Wolde Hawaryot and Woizero Ishate Mariam, daughter of Azzaz Yakub; both parents claimed descent from the Solomonic dynasty. He first appears in the record in 1745, when a delegation sent to Cairo for a new Abuna was held up at Massawa and the returning bishop, Abuna Yohannes, was held for ransom at Arqiqo. Emperor Iyasu II sent a punitive campaign against him, but Mikael was too powerful and was soon forgiven.

Offended by his superior, Ras Anda Haymanot of Midre Bahri, he fortified Adwa and rebelled, and in 1759 he captured and executed him. Adwa lay on the trade route between Massawa and Gondar, and its fees and duties paid for an army of 8000 men armed with muskets. Marriage tied him to the imperial house: Empress Mentewab gave him her daughter Aster, and his son Wolde Hawaryat married another daughter, Altash.

Under Emperor Iyoas I a quarrel between Mentewab and the emperor's mother, Welete Bersabe, filled Gondar with rival armies from Qwara and Yejju. Mentewab called on her son-in-law, who arrived with 26,000 men, offered to mediate and took control of the capital. On 22 January 1768 he was made Ras Bitwodad and Enderase of the empire. When Iyoas secretly turned to Fasil and ordered him back to Tigray, Mikael defeated Fasil's army and laid before an assembly of nobles his proof that the emperor had plotted his death. Because the law forbade killing a monarch, the assembly only confined Iyoas, and Mikael then had him strangled with a length of red silk.

He made Yohannes II emperor, soon got rid of him, and replaced him with Tekle Haymanot II. A rising in Gondar met a reign of terror in 1770, but Fasil, Goshu of Amhara and Wand Bewossen of Begemder allied against him, and after the three battles of Sarbakusa he surrendered to Wand Bewossen on 4 June 1771.

After a year in prison he returned to Tigray as its governor, either sent by Wand Bewossen or of his own choice. The explorer James Bruce, who met him, described a lean, lame old man who spoke little. In church affairs he championed the Karva Haymanot doctrine. His son Wolde Samuel, his grandson Wolde Gabriel and his nephew Gabre Maskal followed him in Tigray, each briefly. Some historians date the Zemene Mesafint, the age of regional lords and a weakened monarchy, from the murder of Iyoas.
mikawa-province: Mikawa Province was an old province in the area that is today the eastern half of Aichi Prefecture. It bordered Owari, Mino, Shinano and Tōtōmi Provinces. Its abbreviated name was Sanshū, and it was one of the provinces of the Tōkaidō. The area had been settled since at least the Japanese Paleolithic period, and Mikawa is mentioned in records of the Taika Reform dated 645 and in Nara period chronicles including the Kujiki.

The exact site of the provincial capital is not known. It was traditionally placed in the Ko-machi area of Toyokawa, but excavations at Hakuho-machi in Toyota from 1991 to 1997 revealed extensive ruins and ceramic shards suggesting it may have stood there, and the ruins of the provincial temple were found nearby in 1999. During the Heian period the province was divided into many estates controlled by local samurai clans. In the Kamakura period it came under Adachi Morinaga and then the Ashikaga clan, and for much of the Muromachi period under the Isshiki clan.

By the Sengoku period the province had split into small territories largely dominated by the Matsudaira clan and contested by the Imagawa to the east and the Oda to the west. It was united under Tokugawa Ieyasu after the Imagawa were defeated at the Battle of Okehazama. Under the Tokugawa shogunate parts of the province were assigned as domains to trusted hereditary retainers, with large portions administered directly by the shogunate through hatamoto. Mikawa was the only area the shogunate permitted to produce gunpowder, which led to its modern fireworks industry.

The han system was abolished in 1871, and in January 1872 the whole of former Mikawa Province became part of the new Aichi Prefecture. After World War II the territory prospered as the capital of the Japanese automobile industry.
mikhail-artemyevich-muravyov: Muravyov was born on 25 September 1880 into a peasant family in Burdukovo, a village near Vetluga in the Kostroma Governorate, and studied at the Kostroma seminary. He enlisted as a volunteer in 1898 and in 1901 graduated from the Kazan infantry cadet school. In the Russo-Japanese War he commanded a company of the 122nd Tambov Regiment and was seriously wounded in the head in February 1905. He then spent about five years abroad, mainly in France, and in 1907 joined Boris Savinkov's Socialist Revolutionary group.

After the February Revolution he led the formation of volunteer shock units to continue the war, raising up to one hundred death battalions and several women's battalions, and Alexander Kerensky appointed him chief of security of the Provisional Government. After the defeat of the Kornilov coup he broke with the government and joined the Left Socialist Revolutionaries. Following the October Revolution he became a member of the Revolutionary Military Committee and commanded the troops sent against the forces of Kerensky and Krasnov, but resigned on 8 November when the Left Socialist Revolutionaries withdrew from government posts.

In Ukraine he served first as chief of staff to Vladimir Antonov-Ovseyenko and then directed the campaign against the Central Council of Ukraine. At Poltava he ordered the execution of 98 cadets and officers. In Kyiv a regime of Red Terror followed: according to the Ukrainian Red Cross, up to five thousand people were killed in the first days, up to three thousand of them officers, and he imposed an indemnity of five million rubles on the city's bourgeoisie. The People's Secretariat of Ukraine demanded his removal from the city.

From 14 February he commanded against the Romanian forces seeking Bessarabia and Transnistria, and he led the troops of the Odessa Soviet Republic until March, when he could not hold the city. In mid-April he was arrested in Moscow on charges of abuse of power and links with anarchists, but the case was dismissed. Appointed commander of the Eastern Front on 13 June, he rebelled during the Left Socialist Revolutionary uprising, left Kazan with two loyal regiments on the night of 9 to 10 July and declared war on Germany. On 11 July he occupied Simbirsk and arrested Mikhail Tukhachevsky, but Latvian Riflemen and a Cheka detachment surrounded the meeting of the provincial executive committee, and he was killed resisting arrest.
mikhail-bakunin: Mikhail Alexandrovich Bakunin was born on 30 May 1814 (18 May in the old style) into the Russian nobility. His family's Priamukhino estate in the Tver region had over 500 serfs. His father, Alexander Mikhailovich Bakunin, a diplomat who had served in Italy, raised ten children on the Rousseauan model, and Mikhail was the third child and eldest son.

He trained as a military officer, deserted in 1835 and was discharged. In Moscow he joined the circle of Nikolai Stankevich, read German philosophy and produced the first Russian translation of Hegel. Alexander Herzen funded his studies at the University of Berlin from 1840, where he drew towards the Young Hegelians. His first original publication, The Reaction in Germany, appeared in 1842 and marked his shift from philosophy to revolutionary rhetoric.

Bakunin left for Zürich in 1843, and when he defied Russian orders to return, the Russian Senate stripped him of his noble rights and sentenced him in absentia to penal labour in Siberia. In Paris he befriended Pierre-Joseph Proudhon and met Karl Marx. A speech to Polish emigrants in 1847 led to his deportation from France. He took part in the Prague Slavic Congress and its insurrection in 1848, and in the Dresden uprising of 1849.

Imprisoned, sentenced to death and extradited several times, he was held in solitary confinement in the Peter and Paul Fortress in 1851. Exiled to Siberia in 1857, he escaped in 1861 via Japan and the United States and reached London, where he worked with Herzen on the journal Kolokol.

He joined the International Workingmen's Association in 1868. At the 1872 Hague Congress, which he could not reach, Marx's side prevailed and Bakunin was expelled, after which he founded the Anti-Authoritarian International. He took part in the Lyon insurrection of 1870, wrote Statism and Anarchy in 1873, and planned an unsuccessful insurrection at Bologna in 1874. He died in Bern on 1 July 1876.

Bakunin wrote prolifically but fragmentarily, and was not a systematic thinker; much of his work was published after his death. He first called himself an anarchist in 1867. He wished to replace the state and hierarchical religious, social and economic institutions with free federations of communes and voluntary associations of producers, organised from below upward. God and the State, published in 1882 from a fragment, became his most widely translated work.

He rejected Marx's idea of a dictatorship of the proletariat, warning that a Marxist state would rule over the workers rather than be ruled by them. His split with Marx divided the socialist movement from the anarchist one.
mikhail-frunze: Mikhail Vasilyevich Frunze was born on 2 February 1885 in Pishpek, now Bishkek, then a small Russian garrison town in Russian Turkestan. His father was a Bessarabian Romanian paramedic and his mother was Russian. He began higher studies at Verniy, now Almaty, and in 1904 entered the Saint Petersburg Polytechnical University. In the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party he sided at eighteen with Lenin's Bolsheviks. In the 1905 Revolution he led striking textile workers in Shuya and Ivanovo. Arrested in 1907, he was sentenced to death, spent months on death row, and had the sentence commuted to life at hard labour. After ten years in Siberian prisons he escaped to Chita and edited a Bolshevik weekly.

In 1917 Frunze headed the Minsk civilian militia and was elected president of the Byelorussian Soviet, then led an armed force of workers in Moscow. In March 1919 he took command of the Southern Army Group of the Eastern Front. After his troops defeated Admiral Alexander Kolchak at Omsk, Leon Trotsky gave him overall command of the Eastern Front on 19 July 1919. He drove Basmachi insurgents and White troops from Turkestan and captured Khiva in February 1920 and Bukhara in September 1920. In November 1920 his army took the Crimea and pushed Pyotr Wrangel out of Russia, and he also led the destruction of Nestor Makhno's anarchist movement in Ukraine.

In December 1921 Frunze visited Ankara as an ambassador of the Ukrainian SSR and established Turkish-Soviet relations. His diary of the visit records massacres of Greeks and Armenians that he saw in the Pontus region. He was elected to the Central Committee in 1921, became a candidate member of the Politburo on 2 June 1924 and in January 1925 was named chairman of the Revolutionary Military Council.

Frunze had a chronic ulcer and favoured conservative treatment, but Stalin and Anastas Mikoyan urged an operation. He died during surgery on 31 October 1925, and a number of historians attribute his death to chloroform poisoning. Rumours have held that Stalin arranged it; the claim rests on the accounts of authors such as Roman Brackman and Vadim Rogovin. He was buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis. Pishpek was renamed Frunze in 1926 and took back its name Bishkek in 1991. The Frunze Military Academy in Moscow and many streets and Metro stations were named after him, and some remember him for his military doctrine.
mikhail-gorbachev: Mikhail Sergeyevich Gorbachev was born on 2 March 1931 in Privolnoye, in North Caucasus Krai, into a poor peasant family of Russian and Ukrainian heritage. His parents named him Viktor, but at his mother's insistence he was secretly baptised Mikhail. At three he moved to the collective farm that his maternal grandfather, a Communist Party member since 1928, chaired. He studied at Moscow State University, married fellow student Raisa Titarenko in 1953 and took his law degree in 1955. In Stavropol he worked for the Komsomol and supported Khrushchev's de-Stalinization. He became first party secretary of the Stavropol Regional Committee in 1970, and in 1978 returned to Moscow as a secretary of the Central Committee.

On 11 March 1985 the Politburo elected Gorbachev general secretary after the death of Konstantin Chernenko. He wished to preserve the Soviet state and its Marxist-Leninist principles but held that significant reform was needed. His glasnost, or openness, widened freedom of speech and the press, and perestroika, restructuring, sought to decentralise economic decision-making. He withdrew troops from the Soviet-Afghan War and met United States president Ronald Reagan at the Reykjavik Summit to discuss limiting nuclear weapons and ending the Cold War.

The elected Congress of People's Deputies that he formed undermined the party's supremacy. When Warsaw Pact countries abandoned Marxist-Leninist rule in 1989 he declined to intervene militarily, and in November East Germany opened the Berlin Wall, a decision he praised. German reunification followed in 1990, and many observers then declared the Cold War over. He received the Nobel Peace Prize that year.

Growing nationalism in the republics threatened to break up the Soviet Union, and in August 1991 hardliners launched an unsuccessful coup against him. In its wake the union dissolved, against his wishes. Out of office he launched the Gorbachev Foundation in 1992 and Green Cross International in 1993. He died in Moscow on 30 August 2022, aged 91. Many, particularly in Western countries, praise his role in ending the Cold War and tolerating the fall of Marxist-Leninist governments in central and eastern Europe, while critics hold that he weakened Russia's global influence and precipitated an economic collapse.
