mikhail-kalinin: Kalinin was born on 19 November 1875 into a peasant family in the village of Verkhnyaya Troitsa in Tver Governorate. He worked on the land with his father until he was 13, and a local landowning family later took him to Saint Petersburg as a footman. At 18 he became a lathe operator at the Putilov works.

He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1898. He was arrested the following year, imprisoned for ten months and exiled to the Caucasus, where in Tbilisi he met Sergei Alliluyev and came to know Stalin through the Alliluyev family. Further arrests followed, and in 1906 he joined the Bolshevik faction and married Ekaterina Lorberg, an ethnic Estonian.

At the 1912 Bolshevik conference in Prague Kalinin was elected an alternate member of the Central Committee but not a full member, because he was suspected of being an agent of the Okhrana; the real agent was Roman Malinovsky. In April 1917 he favoured conditional support for the Provisional Government, a position at odds with Lenin's. He was chosen mayor of Petrograd in the autumn city elections and administered it during and after the revolution of 7 November.

When Yakov Sverdlov died in March 1919, Kalinin replaced him as head of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee, the titular head of state. The post was renamed in 1922 and again in 1938, and he held it without a break until 1946. He became a full member of the Politburo in January 1926 and remained one until his death.

The official press called Kalinin the All-Union Elder, a title that stressed his peasant origins, but by the 1930s his part in decisions was nominal. Khrushchev later said that under Stalin Kalinin was the nominal signatory of all decrees. On 5 March 1940 he was one of six Politburo members who signed the order to execute 25,700 Polish prisoners, which led to the Katyn massacre. His wife Ekaterina, arrested on 25 October 1938 as a Trotskyist, was sentenced in 1939 to fifteen years in a labour camp; she was released shortly before he died.

He retired in 1946 and died of cancer in Moscow on 3 June that year. He was buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis after a state funeral. The city of Königsberg, annexed by the Soviet Union in 1945, was renamed Kaliningrad after him in 1946, and Tver was called Kalinin until its historic name was restored in 1990.
mikhail-of-chernigov: Mikhail Vsevolodovich was a son of Prince Vsevolod the Red, of the Olgovichi clan. Over his life he held many thrones: Pereyaslavl in 1206, Novgorod-Seversk from 1219 to 1226, Novgorod twice, Chernigov from 1223 to 1235 and again from 1242, Galicia in 1235 and 1236, and Kiev as grand prince from 1236 to 1239 and from 1241 to 1243. He married Elena, or Maria, a daughter of Prince Roman Mstislavich of Halych, in 1210 or 1211.

In 1223 Mikhail fought the Tatars at the Battle of Kalka. After the death of Mstislav the Brave in 1228 he claimed the throne of Galicia-Volhynia, which brought him into conflict with Daniel and Vasylko, the sons of Roman the Great, and their ally Vladimir Rurikovich. Archaeology shows that the towns of Chernigov prospered as never before under his rule, which suggests that he made trade a priority; commerce partly drew him to Halych and Kiev, through which goods from the Rhine valley and Hungary reached Chernigov. He made trade treaties and alliances with the Poles and Hungarians, and in Novgorod he lightened taxes and gave the boyars more freedom from the prince.

When the Mongols invaded Kievan Rus' he fled to Hungary in 1239. On his return he briefly held Kiev and later sought a yarlyk, a patent from the khan, to confirm his rule over Chernigov. Another explanation of his execution in 1246 points to his pro-Western policy rather than his refusal of the court rituals.

Tradition holds that he was killed with his loyal boyar Theodore, and both were canonised as martyrs. Their remains lay in the Transfiguration Cathedral of Chernigov until around 1580, when Tsar Ivan the Terrible had them moved to the Cathedral of the Archangel in Moscow. The papal legate Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, who travelled through the region in the late 1240s, wrote that Mikhail refused to bow to an image of Chingis Khan and was trampled and beheaded. The fuller vita of his martyrdom appears only in later chronicles, and its reliability is uncertain. The princes of the Upper Oka principalities of the 14th and 15th centuries all descended from him, as did later families such as the Dolgorukie, Obolenskie and Gorchakovy.
mikhail-of-tver: Mikhail Yaroslavich was the second son of Yaroslav III Yaroslavich of Tver, a younger brother of Aleksandr Nevsky. His mother Xenia is venerated as Xenia of Tarusa. He succeeded his elder brother as prince of Tver in 1285, and on the death of Andrei Aleksandrovich, Aleksandr Nevsky's son, became grand prince of Vladimir, in keeping with traditional succession, confirmed by Tokhta, khan of the Golden Horde. In 1294 he married Princess Anna of Rostov, and they had five children.

Mikhail met a series of setbacks. He was accepted as prince of Novgorod in 1309 but quarrelled with the city and in 1312 withdrew his lieutenants and cut off its grain. He paid homage to Uzbeg Khan on his accession in 1313 and stayed in Sarai until 1315, while Yury of Moscow gained influence in Novgorod, which in 1314 called on Yury to replace him. Mikhail retook the city in 1316 with Mongol aid, but in 1317 Uzbeg gave the yarlik, the patent of office, to Yury, who married the khan's sister.

The church also turned against him. When Metropolitan Maksim died in 1305, Mikhail nominated another candidate, but the Patriarch of Constantinople consecrated Petr, who sided with Moscow and in 1309 appointed David as archbishop of Novgorod.

The khan sent an army under the general Kavgadii to help Yury. On 22 December 1317 Mikhail defeated Yury at Bortenevo, 40 kilometres from Tver, and captured Yury's wife, the khan's sister. She died in his custody and he was blamed, though it seems unlikely he would have killed her at such political cost. Kavgadii accused him in Sarai of murder, withholding tribute and warring against his overlord. Summoned to the Horde, Mikhail was executed on 22 November 1318.

The Russian Orthodox Church later canonised him for his piety when summoned to a death he foresaw, and because his relics were found incorrupt. After 1317 Moscow's Danilovich princes held the grand princely title for all but two years.
mikhail-skobelev: Mikhail Dmitriyevich Skobelev was born in Saint Petersburg on 29 September 1843, at the Peter and Paul Fortress, where his grandfather was commandant. His mother was the philanthropist Olga Skobeleva and his father the general Dmitry Ivanovich Skobelev. After graduating from the General Staff Academy as a staff officer, he was sent to Turkestan in 1868. Apart from two years on the staff of the Grand Duke Michael in the Caucasus, he stayed in Central Asia until 1877.

In the Khivan campaign of 1873 he commanded the advance guard of General Lomakin's column from Kinderly Bay on the Caspian Sea and, after great suffering on the desert march, took a prominent part in the capture of the Khivan capital. In 1875 he held an important command in the expedition against the Khanate of Kokand under General Konstantin Petrovich von Kaufmann. At Makram he outmanoeuvred a much larger force and captured 58 guns. He was promoted to major general and made the first governor of the Fergana Oblast.

In the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 he crossed the Danube with the 8th Corps and fought at Plevna. After promotion to lieutenant general and command of the 16th Division, he took part in the investment of Pleven and in the fight of 9 December, when Osman Pasha surrendered with his army.

In January 1878 he crossed the Balkans in a severe snowstorm and defeated the Turks at Sheynovo, near Shipka, capturing 36,000 men and 90 guns. His men called him the White General, and the Turks the White Pasha, after the white uniform and horse he used. In 1880 and 1881 he returned to Turkestan to avenge the defeats the Tekke Turkmen had inflicted on Russian forces.

When the fortress of Geok Tepe was stormed, around 8,000 Turkmen soldiers and civilians, women and children among them, were killed in flight, along with another 6,500 who died inside. The Russians spared some 5,000 women and children and freed 600 Persian slaves. The slaughter broke Turkmen resistance and Transcaspia was annexed. Skobelev was recalled, officially to appease European opinion.

In his last years he supported Russian nationalism and Pan-Slavism, and speeches in Paris and Moscow in 1882, predicting strife between Slavs and Germans, led to his recall to Saint Petersburg. He died in Moscow on 7 July 1882, by the official account of a heart attack. A monument was raised to him in Moscow, and the town of Fergana was renamed Skobelev. Bulgarians built Skobelev Park in Pleven, and a boulevard in Sofia bears his name.
mikhail-speransky: Mikhail Mikhailovich Speransky was born on 12 January 1772 at Cherkutino, in Vladimir Province, the son of a village priest, Mikhail Tretyakov. He studied at the religious seminaries in Vladimir and St Petersburg, where he took the surname Speransky from the Latin verb sperare, to hope. At the seminary in St Petersburg he became a professor of mathematics and physics. His skills led him to become secretary to Prince Kurakin and a capable imperial official. He is believed to have married an Englishwoman, Elizabeth Jane Stephens, in 1798; she died the next year, after giving birth to a daughter.

In 1808 Emperor Alexander I took him to the Congress of Erfurt and introduced him to Napoleon. His reform projects envisaged a constitutional system of dumas, from the cantonal assembly to a Duma of the empire, with a nominated council of state between the autocrat and the Duma. From this plan the Council of the Empire came into existence in January 1810.

From 1809 to 1812 he held great power as de facto sole minister. His plan to reorganise the masonic order in Russia to educate the Orthodox clergy added the clergy to his enemies, and critics reported his sharp remarks about the emperor. Alexander dismissed him on 17/29 March 1812 and held him responsible for the unpopularity of the reforms and of the French policy.

He was appointed governor of Penza in 1816 and governor-general of Siberia in 1819, and in 1821 he returned to St Petersburg as a member of the State Council. After the Decembrist Revolt of 1825 he sat on the court of investigation. In 1826 Nicholas I made him head of the Second Section of the imperial chancellery, the committee that codified Russian law.

Under his leadership the committee published the complete collection of the laws of the Russian Empire, containing 35,993 enactments, which formed the basis for the Svod Zakonov, the positive law of the empire. He received the Order of St Andrew and, in January 1839, the title of count. He died at St Petersburg on 23 February 1839 and was buried at the Tikhvin Cemetery of the Alexander Nevsky Monastery. His plans were later seen to have foreshadowed the Duma of 1905 and the zemstvo of 1864, and he is called the father of Russian liberalism. Konstantin Kavelin and Boris Chicherin later developed his liberal ideas.
mikhail-tukhachevsky: Mikhail Nikolayevich Tukhachevsky was born on 16 February 1893 (4 February in the old style) at Alexandrovskoye, near Smolensk, into a family of impoverished hereditary nobles. He attended the Cadet Corps and graduated from the Aleksandrovskoye Military School in 1914, joining the Semyenovsky Guards Regiment as a second lieutenant. Captured by the German forces in February 1915, he escaped four times from prison camps and was held as an incorrigible escapee in the fortress of Ingolstadt, where he shared a cell with Captain Charles de Gaulle. His fifth escape succeeded and he returned to Russia in September 1917, after which he joined the Bolsheviks despite his noble birth.

In the Russian Civil War he was made responsible for defending Moscow, and in 1919 Leon Trotsky gave him command of the Fifth Army, which retook Siberia from Aleksandr Kolchak's forces. In 1920 he completed the defeat of Anton Denikin, and in March 1921 he commanded the 7th Army in the suppression of the Kronstadt rebellion.

In 1920 he commanded the Western Front in the Polish–Soviet War and pushed back the Polish and Ukrainian forces that had taken Kiev in May, but he was beaten by Piłsudski at the Battle of Warsaw. He and Joseph Stalin blamed each other for the failure.

He served as Chief of Staff of the Red Army from 1925 to 1928, became First Deputy Commissar for defence under Kliment Voroshilov, who disliked him. After Stalin accepted the need for an industrialised military in 1931, Tukhachevsky was a leader of reform and pressed for tanks, aircraft and airborne forces. He was made a Marshal of the Soviet Union on 20 November 1935. He is often credited with the theory of deep operations, though his exact role is disputed for want of firsthand sources.

He was arrested on 22 May 1937. The NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov supervised his interrogation and torture, and he confessed to treason. A military tribunal tried him and eight generals on 11 June 1937, found them guilty that night, and he was shot within the hour.

His wife and two brothers were shot, three sisters were sent to the Gulag, and his daughter Svetlana was raised in an orphanage and the Gulag. In 1956 Nikita Khrushchev's Secret Speech ended the official view of him as a fascist, and on 31 January 1957 he and his co-defendants were rehabilitated.
miklos-horthy: Miklós Horthy de Nagybánya was born on 18 June 1868 at Kenderes, the fourth of eight children of an untitled Hungarian noble family raised in the Reformed Church. His father, István Horthy de Nagybánya, sat in the House of Magnates and held an estate of 610 hectares. At 14 Horthy entered the Imperial and Royal Naval Academy in Fiume, where teaching was in German, so that he spoke Hungarian with a slight Austro-German accent for the rest of his life.

He became a sub-lieutenant in 1896, served as aide-de-camp to Emperor Franz Josef from November 1909, and fought in the Battle of the Strait of Otranto. In February 1918 Emperor Karl I made him rear admiral and the last commander in chief of the fleet, ahead of eleven other admirals.

Hungary lost two thirds of its territory and a third of its Hungarian speakers in the settlement ratified as the Treaty of Trianon in 1920, and the Communist leader Béla Kun seized power in Budapest in March 1919. Horthy returned to the capital with the National Army. On 1 March 1920 the National Assembly re-established the kingdom, and with National Army officers controlling the parliament building it voted him regent over Count Albert Apponyi by 131 votes to 7. Former king Charles IV tried twice to return and was escorted into exile in 1921.

His first decade was spent stabilising the economy and the political system with his prime minister, István Bethlen, with British support. Historians describe the regime as national conservative and aimed at revising Trianon; some critics point to anti-Jewish laws passed from 1920.

Hungary became in effect a member of the Axis in April 1941 and declared war on the Soviet Union on 27 June 1941. In 1944 Horthy's government made approaches to the Allies, and Hitler summoned him to Klessheim, where he allowed the deportation of a large number of Jews, generally put at 100,000, but refused to go further. In August he installed a new government under Géza Lakatos and halted the mass deportations. After his arrest by the Germans he was held until the end of the war, interviewed at Nuremberg and lived in Portugal until his death on 9 February 1957. His memoirs appeared in 1953.

His body was returned to Kenderes in 1993. Hungarians still dispute whether he was a conservative who allied with Germany to recover lost land or a ruler whose policies led to collaboration in the Holocaust.
mikmaq: Miꞌkmaq, singular Miꞌkmaw, comes from a word meaning my friends, and they also call themselves Lꞌnuk, the people. Their territory, Miꞌkmaꞌki, is one of the five confederated Wabanaki countries and was traditionally divided into seven districts, eight if Ktaqmkuk in Newfoundland is counted. Each had its own government, with a district chief and a council of band chiefs, elders and other leaders, which made laws, administered justice, apportioned hunting and fishing grounds and made war and peace. The Grand Council, Santeꞌ Mawioꞌmi, was the senior body. The 1876 Indian Act disrupted its authority by requiring elected governments on the Canadian model.

The Miꞌkmaq speak Miꞌkmawi'simk, an Eastern Algonquian language. A hieroglyphic writing was created in 1677 by the French missionary Chrestien Le Clerq, who noted that children memorised prayers by counting marks, and the language is now written mainly in Latin letters. Traditions were passed down orally in religious narratives, legends and folklore, the best known being those of Glooscap, a creator and culture hero. Some Miꞌkmaq follow the Catholic faith, some only traditional beliefs, and many both. Chapel Island in Bras d'Or Lake, the gathering place of the Grand Council, is a pilgrimage site.

Archaeological evidence in south-western Nova Scotia traces land use to at least 4,000 years ago. The pre-contact population is estimated at 3,000 to 30,000. In 1616 Father Biard believed it to exceed 3,000, but he remarked that European diseases had caused large losses during the 16th century. Smallpox, other infectious diseases, wars and alcoholism brought a further decline to a low point in the middle of the 17th century. After King Philip's War in southern New England the Miꞌkmaq joined the Wabanaki Confederacy, with the Abenaki, Penobscot, Passamaquoddy and Maliseet, which was allied with the Acadian people.

The Miꞌkmaq, Maliseet and Passamaquoddy signed a series of Peace and Friendship Treaties with the British Crown through the 18th century, the first in 1725 and the last in 1779. The Miꞌkmaq maintain that they did not cede their land title through them. The Shubenacadie Indian Residential School was the only such school in the region and operated from 1930 to 1967.

On 17 September 1999 the Supreme Court of Canada, in R v Marshall, upheld a treaty right of the Miꞌkmaq to hunt, fish and gather in pursuit of a moderate livelihood, a right already set out in the Peace and Friendship Treaty of 1752. The case began with fishing charges laid in 1993 against Donald Marshall Jr. In 2005 the Miꞌkmaw Nora Bernard led a class action for survivors of the residential schools, which the Government of Canada settled. The first school run by the Miꞌkmaq in Nova Scotia, Miꞌkmaq Kina' matnewey, was established in 1982.
mikulcice: Mikulčice is a municipality and village in Hodonín District in the South Moravian Region, with about 2,000 inhabitants. It lies on the Kyjovka River in the flat Lower Morava Valley, about 6 kilometres southwest of Hodonín and 52 kilometres southeast of Brno, on the border with Slovakia. The Czech-Slovak border is formed here by the Morava River. The municipality has two parts, Mikulčice and Těšice, with 974 and 921 inhabitants in the 2021 census.

From the 6th until the 10th century a Slavic fortified settlement existed 3 kilometres southeast of the modern village, at the site called Mikulčice-Valy. It was one of the main centres of the Great Moravian Empire and plausibly its capital city. Excavations unearthed the remnants of twelve churches, a palace and more than 2,500 graves, including a horse burial.

The first written mention of the village is from 1141, and its Church of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary was first mentioned in 1353. At the beginning of the 15th century a fortress stood here, probably destroyed during the Hussite Wars.

The main landmark is the Church of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary. The original Gothic building of the mid-14th century was replaced by the present structure around 1500, burned down in 1605 and 1683 and was reconstructed, and was rebuilt in the Baroque style in the 1730s, with its Gothic core preserved.

Mikulčice-Valy is the main tourist attraction and is freely accessible. An exhibition of archaeological finds from the area is administered by the Masaryk Museum in Hodonín, and the site has been a national cultural monument since 1962. The local economy rests mainly on agriculture and tourism. The village was heavily damaged by the 2021 South Moravia tornado.
mikulov: Mikulov is a town of about 7,600 inhabitants in Břeclav District, South Moravia, on the border with Austria, about 18 km north-west of Břeclav and 42 km south of Brno. Most of its territory lies in the Pálava Protected Landscape Area. The name comes from Mikul, a short form of Mikuláš, the Czech form of Nicholas; the German name Nikolsburg prevailed in the earliest times, and Mikulov has been used since the 19th century.

A deed mentioning Mikulov in 1173 is a hoax of the 14th century. The first trustworthy mention is from 1249, when the Přemyslid margrave Ottokar II granted a castle and its surroundings to the Austrian noble Henry I of Liechtenstein. In 1572 Emperor Maximilian II granted the fief to Adam of Dietrichstein, and from 1575 until the 20th century the town belonged to the Dietrichstein family and its Mensdorff-Pouilly successors. Under Cardinal Franz von Dietrichstein it became one of the most important towns in Moravia, and in 1621 he signed the Treaty of Nikolsburg with the Transylvanian prince Gabriel Bethlen at the castle. After a fire in 1719 the family rebuilt the castle to its present appearance.

Jewish settlement began in 1421, when Albert II of Austria expelled Jews from Vienna and Lower Austria, and more came after 1454. In the first half of the 16th century Nikolsburg became the seat of the regional rabbi of Moravia. Between 1553 and 1573 Judah Loew ben Bezalel officiated there for twenty years. A census of 1754 counted some 620 Jewish families, about 3,000 people and half the town. In 1938 there were 472 Jewish residents. Only 110 emigrated in time, and 327 did not survive the Holocaust. The German population, 98 per cent in 1890 and 82 per cent in 1930, was expelled after the Second World War.

Mikulov Castle, built in the Romanesque style and rebuilt in the Renaissance and Baroque styles, houses the Regional Museum. The synagogue, originally of the 16th century, is the only preserved synagogue of the Polish type in Moravia. The Jewish cemetery, founded in the mid-15th century, has around 4,000 tombs, the oldest readable one from 1605. The town is the centre of the Mikulovská wine region.
milan: Milan lies in the north-western part of the Po Valley, roughly halfway between the river Po to the south and the foothills of the Alps, with the lakes Como, Maggiore and Lugano to the north, the Ticino to the west and the Adda to the east. The land is flat, and the highest point is 122 m above sea level. The Celtic name Medhelanon, later Latinized as Mediolanum, is usually explained as a settlement in the midst of the plain, or between watercourses, given the Olona, Lambro and Seveso rivers.

According to the account of Livy, the Gaulish king Ambicatus sent his nephew Bellovesus into northern Italy, and Bellovesus is said to have founded the settlement in the reign of Tarquinius Priscus. Around 590 BCE a Celtic tribe of the Insubres, belonging to the Golasecca culture, settled the site as Medhelanon, around a sanctuary in the shape of an ellipse with axes of 443 m and 323 m, near the present Piazza della Scala. The Romans conquered the city in 222 BCE. From 284 to 402 CE it was capital of the western part of the Roman Empire.

In the late fourth century Saint Ambrose, as bishop of Milan, reshaped the centre and built the great basilicas at the city gates: Sant'Ambrogio, San Nazaro in Brolo, San Simpliciano and Sant'Eustorgio, which still stand. In the Late Middle Ages the wealthy Duchy of Milan was one of the great forces behind the Renaissance, and the Visconti family, major patrons of the arts, made the city a centre of Gothic art. Work on the cathedral began in 1386 and ended in 1877. Leonardo da Vinci worked in Milan from 1482 until 1499 and painted the Virgin of the Rocks and The Last Supper there.

In the early modern period Milan was a major centre of the Italian Enlightenment, and its cultural and political struggle against Austrian domination was crucial in the reunification of the Kingdom of Italy. From the 19th century the city led the industrial and financial development of Italy. After the Second World War its population grew with migration, first from poorer and rural parts of Italy and later from abroad, and it peaked at 1,743,427 in 1973.

Milan is the capital of Lombardy and the second-largest city in Italy after Rome, with a population of 1,362,863. It is regarded as the country's industrial and financial centre and is a world centre of fashion. The Cathedral, the largest church in Italy, the Pinacoteca di Brera and the Castello Sforzesco, which holds Michelangelo's last sculpture, the Rondanini Pietà, are among its principal monuments. Of the Roman city, few remains survive, notably the Colonne di San Lorenzo.
milan-acimovic: Aćimović was born on 31 May 1898 in Pinosava, in the Belgrade municipality of Voždovac. He finished gymnasium in Belgrade and took a law degree at the University of Belgrade in 1923. On 2 September 1935 he and Velibor Jonić won from the Ministry of the Interior the legalisation of the Yugoslav National Movement, Zbor. He became chief of police in Belgrade in 1938, and Milan Stojadinović made him Minister of the Interior on 21 December 1938, an office he held until 5 February 1939. In April 1939 he was arrested with Stojadinović and held until August 1940.

In April 1941 Reinhard Heydrich came to Belgrade and told the occupiers to rely on the senior police officers Aćimović and Dragi Jovanović, with whom he had already worked. The Germans preferred Aćimović to Dimitrije Ljotić, the leader of Zbor, as a security expert without Ljotić's ideological burden. At the end of April Harald Turner and Helmuth Förster formed the Commissioner Government with Aćimović as its head and commissioner of the interior, an auxiliary body of the German military administration rather than even a puppet government. He replaced officials who were not Serbs or were thought anti-German, and on 13 July 1941 ordered the arrest of family members of communists in hiding.

Divided between Ljotić's supporters and Stojadinović's old allies, the government collapsed in August 1941 when Ljotić withdrew two ministers, and Milan Nedić took over. Aćimović stayed on as Nedić's interior minister. He kept contact with Draža Mihailović's movement and in December 1941 warned Mihailović of an operation against him; when the Germans learned of it, Nedić barred him from the matter, and on 10 November 1942 Tanasije Dinić replaced him because of his Chetnik ties.

After the Germans were driven from Serbia in October 1944, Aćimović served as a link between the German envoy for the Balkans, Hermann Neubacher, and Mihailović, travelling to Mihailović's headquarters in Bosnia. He died on 25 May 1945 in the Battle of Zelengora while retreating with the Chetniks before the Partisans.
milan-cathedral: The cathedral stands on what was the most central site in Roman Mediolanum, that of the public basilica facing the forum. The first cathedral, the new basilica dedicated to St Thecla, was completed by 355, and the old octagonal baptistery, dating to 335, can be visited under the present building. A fire damaged the cathedral and its adjoining basilica in 1075, and they were rebuilt as the Duomo.

In 1386 Archbishop Antonio da Saluzzo began construction of the present cathedral, at the time Gian Galeazzo Visconti took power in Milan. The work was regulated by the Fabbrica del Duomo, which had 300 employees. In 1389 the French engineer Nicolas de Bonaventure was appointed and added Rayonnant Gothic, and Gian Galeazzo gave the Fabbrica exclusive use of the marble of the Candoglia quarry.

The plan is a nave with four side aisles, crossed by a transept and followed by a choir and apse. The nave is about 45 metres high, with the highest Gothic vaults in a completed church. The building is of brick faced with marble, and the roof is known for its forest of openwork pinnacles and spires. In 1762 the spire bearing the Madonnina statue was erected at a height of 108.5 metres. The best-known statue inside is Saint Bartholomew Flayed, of 1562, by Marco d'Agrate.

Construction stalled almost completely after 1402, when about half of the cathedral was complete, and resumed in earnest only after 1480. In 1488 Leonardo da Vinci and Donato Bramante made models for the central cupola. Carlo Borromeo consecrated the whole building in 1577. On 20 May 1805 Napoleon Bonaparte ordered the façade to be finished, and it was completed within seven years. The last portal was inaugurated on 6 January 1965.

Opinions have been divided. John Ruskin called the cathedral a theft from every style, while Henry James found it grandly curious and superbly rich. Mark Twain gave a chapter of The Innocents Abroad to it.
milan-i-of-serbia: Milan Obrenović was born on 22 August 1854 in Mărășești in Moldavia, where his family had lived in exile since the House of Karađorđević returned to the Serbian throne in 1842. His father, Miloš Obrenović, was a grandnephew of Prince Miloš Obrenović I, and died in 1860 or 1861 fighting as a mercenary in the Romanian Army. His mother lived a lavish life and showed little interest in her children, so the boy was adopted by his cousin Prince Mihailo Obrenović III, who brought him to Kragujevac and sent him to the Lycée Louis-le-Grand in Paris.

Prince Mihailo was assassinated on 10 June 1868, when Milan was fourteen. The cabinet minister Milivoje Petrović Blaznavac, who controlled the army, proposed him as successor, and a three-man regency headed by Blaznavac, with Jovan Ristić and Jovan Gavrilović, ruled in his name. Milan was declared of age on 22 August 1872 and took the government into his own hands, manoeuvring between Austrian and Russian interests with a lean towards Austria. He married Natalie Keshko on 17 October 1875, and their son Alexander was born in 1876.

When the Serbian–Ottoman War of 1876 broke out, it was against his own preference and out of deference to public opinion. The Serbs were defeated at Aleksinac, and a Russian ultimatum won an armistice on 1 November 1876. A peace of 1 March 1877 restored the situation before the war. In the Second Serbian–Ottoman War of 1876–78 Serbia was victorious, and Europe's powers induced the Ottomans to acknowledge Serbian independence at the Treaty of Berlin. The principality was declared a kingdom on 6 March 1882 and Milan became king.

As king he worked under Austro-Hungarian influence to improve communications and develop resources, but the cost, increased by extravagance, brought heavy taxation. The union of Eastern Rumelia and Bulgaria in September 1885 led him to declare war on Bulgaria on 15 November; the Serbs were routed at Slivnitsa and Pirot, and Austria-Hungary's intervention saved his throne. He separated from Queen Natalija in 1886. On 3 January 1889 he adopted a more liberal constitution and, on 6 March, abdicated in favour of his twelve-year-old son.

Milan settled in Paris, renounced his rights and Serbian nationality in 1892, and was reinstated into the royal family in 1894 after his son's coup. In 1897 he was appointed commander-in-chief of the Royal Serbian Army, and he improved its system markedly. He opposed Alexander's marriage to Draga Mašin in July 1900, resigned and was banished. He died unexpectedly in Vienna on 11 February 1901 and was buried at Krušedol monastery.
milan-kundera: Milan Kundera was born on 1 April 1929 in Královo Pole, a district of Brno, Czechoslovakia, to a middle-class family. His father, Ludvík Kundera, was a Czech musicologist and pianist who headed the Janáček Music Academy in Brno from 1948 to 1961. He learned the piano from his father and studied musicology and composition, and musical references appear throughout his work. In 1947, at eighteen, he joined the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia. He studied film at the Film and TV School of the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague, and in 1952 became a lecturer in world literature there.

Kundera was expelled from the party in 1950, readmitted in 1956 and expelled again in 1970. His first expulsion inspired the main theme of his first novel, The Joke (1967), a satire of the ruling party. He was peripherally involved in the Prague Spring, which the Warsaw Pact invasion crushed in August 1968. He lost his teaching post, and his books were banned.

On a first visit to Paris in 1968 he befriended the publisher Claude Gallimard, who later smuggled the manuscript of Life Is Elsewhere out of Czechoslovakia and encouraged him to emigrate. Kundera moved to France in 1975. His Czechoslovak citizenship was revoked in 1979, and he became a French citizen in 1981. From 1985 he made a conscious transition from Czech to French, and his first work written in French, Slowness, appeared in 1995.

His early poetry was staunchly pro-communist, but his novels escape ideological classification, and he insisted that he was a novelist rather than a politically motivated writer. The Book of Laughter and Forgetting appeared in 1979 and mixed novel, stories and the author's reflections. The Unbearable Lightness of Being, published in 1984, is his best-known work. It deals with the fragility of an individual fate and the idea of eternal return, and follows a Czech surgeon from Prague to Zurich and back. A film of it appeared in 1988. A Czech edition by an expatriate in Canada was published in 1985, and an official one in Czechoslovakia only in 2006.

His fiction mingles philosophical digression with narrative and drew on Robert Musil. Recurring themes include exile, identity and history as a continual return. He lived quietly and rarely spoke to the media. He received the Jerusalem Prize in 1985 and the Herder Prize in 2000, and died on 11 July 2023.
milan-nedic: Milan Nedić was born on 2 September 1878 in Grocka, a suburb of Belgrade, the son of a local district chief and a teacher. He was commissioned into the Serbian Army in 1904, fought in the Balkan Wars and the First World War, and at 38 was the youngest colonel on the Serbian General Staff. In the Royal Yugoslav Army he became Chief of the General Staff in June 1934, and on 13 August 1939 Minister of the Army and Navy. Prince Paul dismissed him on 6 November 1940, because Nedić had pressed Yugoslavia to sign the Tripartite Pact. He commanded the 3rd Army Group in April 1941 and was released to his home in Belgrade.

The German military administration, wanting local forces to fight guerrillas while troops went east for Operation Barbarossa, entrusted Nedić with administering occupied Serbia. Edmund Veesenmayer chose him as a respected Serb who was fanatically anti-Communist. He became prime minister of the Government of National Salvation on 29 August 1941, and declared that his aim was to save the core of the Serbian people by accepting occupation. Germany controlled the economy, finances, police and military. He imposed censorship and purged the education system, and his propaganda was antisemitic and anti-Communist.

His government implemented the occupiers' regulations against Jews and Roma, and Serbia was declared free of Jews in August 1942. The Serbian State Guard, founded in March 1942, passed under SS control. Nedić met Hitler in September 1943 and asked for territorial additions to Serbia. The government was disbanded on 4 October 1944.

Nedić fled to Austria, where British forces took him in and handed him to the Partisans on 1 January 1946. He died on 4 February 1946 in a Belgrade prison; official records call it suicide by jumping from a window, while others hold that he was pushed. Since the 1990s some Serbian writers and churchmen have presented his collaboration as a way of saving Serbs, but the High Court in Belgrade rejected an application to rehabilitate him on 11 July 2018. About 15,000 Jews lived in occupied Serbia in 1941, according to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and estimates of those killed differ.
milan-rastislav-stefanik: Milan Rastislav Štefánik was born on 21 July 1880 at Košariská, then in the Kingdom of Hungary, one of twelve children of a Lutheran pastor, Pavol Štefánik, and Albertína Jurenková. He studied engineering in Prague from 1898 and then astronomy, physics and philosophy at Charles University, where Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk's lectures inspired him with the idea of cooperation between Czechs and Slovaks. He took part in the Slovak student association Detvan. He graduated in 1904 with a doctorate, writing on the supernova of 1572 in the constellation Cassiopeia.

In 1904 Štefánik went to Paris, where Pierre Janssen gave him work at the Paris-Meudon Observatory. He observed from Mont Blanc and joined a French expedition to observe a solar eclipse in Spain, and in 1907 he received the Prix Jules Janssen of the Société astronomique de France. From 1908 he undertook scientific and political missions for the French authorities on several continents, building an observatory in Tahiti, and in 1912 he led a Bureau des Longitudes eclipse mission to Brazil. He became a French citizen in 1912 and patented a design for colour photography in 1911.

In the First World War he joined the French army and trained as an aviator, flying missions over the Serbian Front in 1915. In 1916 he, Masaryk and Edvard Beneš founded the Czechoslovak National Council, and he organised Czechoslovak legions in France and Italy and travelled to Russia in 1917 and Siberia in 1918. His diplomacy helped lead the Entente to recognise the Council as a de facto government. He became Czechoslovakia's Minister of War.

On 4 May 1919 Štefánik was flying home from Italy in a Caproni Ca.3 when the plane crashed near Ivanka pri Dunaji, close to Bratislava, and he died with its three crew. Rumours held that it was shot down, but an Italian eyewitness said an engine exploded during a second landing attempt. His tomb, designed by Dušan Jurkovič, was built on Bradlo Hill in 1927 and 1928. Bratislava Airport, the Slovak armed forces academy and the minor planet 3571 Milanštefánik bear his name.
milan-stojadinovic: Milan Stojadinović was born on 4 August 1888 in Čačak. His father, Mihailo, was a municipal judge who moved to Belgrade in 1904. The young Stojadinović sympathised with the Serbian Social Democratic Party, but came to believe that the liberation of Serbs in the Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires mattered more, and joined the People's Radical Party of Nikola Pašić. A stay in Austria in 1906 made him a supporter of Yugoslav unity.

He studied law at the University of Belgrade, specialising in economics and finance, and spent three years abroad in Munich and Potsdam, Paris and London. His doctoral dissertation on Germany's budget reflected the influence of the German historical school of economics. During World War I he helped stabilise the Serbian dinar while the government was in exile on Corfu, and he was Finance Minister three times between 1922 and 1935.

In 1935 Stojadinović became leader of the Serbian Radical Party, which formed the Yugoslav Radical Union with the Slovene People's Party of Anton Korošec and the Yugoslav Muslim Organization of Mehmed Spaho. He called this a 'three-legged chair' lacking the support of the Croats. On 24 June 1935 he became prime minister and foreign minister. Prince Regent Paul chose him partly as a financial expert and partly in the hope of a deal with Croat politicians. He loosened press censorship and freed 10,000 political prisoners. Richard Crampton wrote that his power rested on political jobbery and corruption.

Stojadinović tied Yugoslavia's economy closer to Germany, which took 60% of its trade by 1938. After the remilitarisation of the Rhineland on 7 March 1936 he broke with the traditional pro-French policy. He signed a friendship pact with Bulgaria on 24 January 1937 and a treaty with Italy on 25 March 1937, and met Adolf Hitler in January 1938. His concordat with the Holy See was withdrawn after protests by the Serbian Orthodox Church in 1937.

After the elections of 11 December 1938, in which he was re-elected with a smaller margin, Paul replaced him on 5 February 1939 with Dragiša Cvetković, having come to see him and his uniformed 'Green Shirts' as a threat. On 17 March 1941 he was exiled to Mauritius.

In 1946 Stojadinović went to Rio de Janeiro and then Buenos Aires, where he advised Argentine governments on economic affairs and founded the financial newspaper El Economista. In 1954 he agreed to cooperate with Ante Pavelić on independent Croatian and Serbian states, which largely discredited him in Yugoslavia and among Serbs abroad. He died in 1961. His memoirs, Neither War, Nor Pact, were published in Buenos Aires in 1963.
milas: Milas lies on a fertile plain at the foot of Mount Sodra in south-western Turkey, about 20 kilometres from the coast, and has a hot-summer Mediterranean climate. Large quarries of white marble on and around the mountain have been used since very ancient times. The district has 150 kilometres of coastline on the Gulf of Güllük and the Gulf of Gökova. The ancient name, Mylasa, with its old Anatolian ending in -asa, points to a very early foundation.

The earliest historical mention is from the beginning of the 7th century BCE, when Arselis, a Carian leader from Mylasa, helped Gyges of Lydia in his contest for the Lydian throne. Under Achaemenid rule Mylasa was the chief city of Caria. The Lygdamid dynasty ruled it in the 5th century BCE, and between 460 and 450 BCE it belonged to the Delian League. The Hecatomnids, satraps of the Persian Empire who were Greek in language and culture, made it their capital. Under Mausolus, who ruled from 377 to 352 BCE, the capital moved to Halicarnassus, but Mylasa kept its importance.

In 40 BCE it suffered great damage when Labienus took it in the Roman Civil War. An inscription from Mylasa gives one of the few certain facts about the life of Tacitus, showing that he governed Asia in 112-13.

Saint Ephrem, in the fifth century, was one of its bishops. Turks under Menteşe Bey took the region in the late thirteenth century, and his beylik made the city its capital. Its rulers' administrative centre was the more defensible castle of Beçin, 5 kilometres away. The Ottomans took the beylik in 1390. Timur restored it to the Menteşe beys after the Battle of Ankara, and Sultan Mehmed I brought it back under Ottoman rule in 1420. One of the first acts of the Ottomans was to move the regional seat to Muğla. In 1923 the Greeks of Milas, some 2,900 of 9,000 inhabitants in 1912, were exchanged with Turks from Greece.

Milas is a district of Muğla Province, with twenty-seven archaeological sites of note. Among the sights are the Mausoleum of Hecatomnus, the Roman Baltalıkapı gate, the tomb called Gümüşkesen, and the Orhan Bey Mosque of 1330 and the Great Mosque of 1378, both from the Menteşe period. The ancient cult centre of Labranda lies 14 kilometres away. Milas carpets and rugs of wool have been known internationally for centuries.
milceni: The Milceni were a Sorbian tribe belonging to the wider group of Polabian Slavs. Their land, Milzavia, spread over the upper basins of the Neisse, Spree and Black Elster rivers. Its settled core, on fertile loess soil, measured about 50 km from east to west and 20 km from north to south, bordered by swamps to the north, the Lausitzer Bergland to the south, the hills of Burkau near Kamenz to the west and the Besunzane to the east. The origin of the name is disputed: scholars have derived it from personal names, from a river, from the Latin milites or from the Slavic word for sweet.

The Bavarian Geographer first mentioned them as the Milzane in the middle of the 9th century, with 30 civitates. The German king Henry the Fowler defeated them in 932 and demanded their conversion, with partial success. Margrave Ekkehard I of Meissen subjugated them around 990 and joined their land to the Holy Roman Empire, but in 1002 the Polish duke Bolesław I the Brave seized Bautzen and the lands up to the Elbe.

The Germans recaptured the region in 1031 and returned it to the March of Meissen. In 1076 it was enfeoffed to Duke Vratislaus II of Bohemia and later became the Land of Budissin, known from the 15th century as Upper Lusatia. The Milceni were still named in the 12th century, and the Song of Roland mentions men from Misnes with bristles down their backs like hogs.

Archaeology has found large fortifications and castles in the Milceni's land, some with outlying castles, which point to a central authority; such a seat is missing among the neighbouring Lusici of Lower Lusatia. The castle network was probably built in defence before Henry's campaign. Little is known of the Milceni's princes, though one may have been Dobremirus, a venerable elder mentioned by Thietmar of Merseburg, whose daughter Emnilda married Bolesław I. Their descendants are the Upper Sorbian-speaking Sorbs of Saxony.
milcom: In the Masoretic Text of the Hebrew Bible the name Milcom occurs three times, each in a list of foreign gods whose worship offends Yahweh: 1 Kings 11:5 calls him the detestation of the Ammonites, 1 Kings 11:33 the god of the children of Ammon, and 2 Kings 23:13 their abomination. The Bible presents him as the Ammonites' state god, in the role Yahweh held in Israel and Chemosh in Moab, and since he was worshipped in Jerusalem by royal sanction, he may also have been honoured there as a native god.

Written without vowels, mlkm can also be read as their king. The Septuagint renders the name as Melchom in several places where the Hebrew reads their king, such as 2 Samuel 12:30 and Zephaniah 1:5, and the Hebrew probably once read Milcom in at least some of them; conversely it translates 1 Kings 11:5 and 33 as their king.

Three Ammonite seals of unknown origin link Milcom with bull imagery and present him as benevolent, exalted and strong, with ties to the stars. The Amman Citadel Inscription of the 9th or 8th century BCE contains an oracle from him, with the first letter of his name reconstructed, and the name appears on the Tell el-Mazar ostracon and in five Ammonite personal names. Stone statues from Ammon that may show him wear the atef crown of the Egyptian god Osiris. A bilingual inscription from Qasr Bayir names an MLKM beside gods identified with Qaws and Chemosh.

The name seems to come from the root mlk, to rule, and its relation to similar names, such as MLKM at Ugarit, Malkum at Drehem and Malik at Nineveh, is unclear. Moloch is once called the god of the Ammonites, perhaps by a scribal error, but E. Puech notes that the Bible gives the two separate places of worship in Jerusalem. Because names with El are commoner in Ammon, some scholars suggest Milcom was an epithet of El or grew to be associated with him; Collin Cornell argues that this lacks evidence.
mildburh: Mildburh, also written Milburga or Milburgh, was a daughter of Merewalh, king of the Mercian sub-kingdom of the Magonsaete, and of Domne Eafe, and the older sister of Mildrith and Mildgytha; the three have been likened to the theological virtues, Mildburh standing for faith. She was educated in France. A story tells that a neighbouring prince resolved to marry her even by force, and that when she fled across a river it rose so high that he could not follow.

The nunnery at Wenlock, now Much Wenlock in Shropshire, was endowed by her father and her uncle, Wulfhere of Mercia, and Theodore installed her as its abbess. She organised the evangelisation and pastoral care of south Shropshire and was noted for her humility. Popular stories credit her with healing and restoring sight to the blind, with a power over birds, which spared the crops when she asked, and with making a spring and causing barley to grow. In one tale her veil, slipping as she woke, hung on a sunbeam until she took it. The medievalist Pamela Berger argues that she took over the role of an older pagan protectress of the grain.

Her feast day, 23 February, is now also kept as Shropshire Day. Her tomb was venerated until invading Danes destroyed the abbey. After the Norman Conquest, Cluniac monks from France built a new house on the site and promoted the bones they found as hers as a place of pilgrimage for lepers, which drew visitors from France and Wales. Accounts of her life followed, among them the Miracula Inventionis Beatae Mylburge Virginis and the Vita of the hagiographer Goscelin. She is named in the Kentish Royal Legend and in the Secgan, the Old English list of saints' resting-places.
miles-macdonell: Miles Macdonell was born in Inverness around 1767. In 1773 his father, Colonel John MacDonell of Scothouse, known as Spanish John, chartered the Pearl with three of his cousins and brought over five hundred of their families and friends to settle at Caughnawaga on the Mohawk River, in the Province of New York, at the invitation of Sir William Johnson. Miles showed military tendencies early: he was appointed ensign in the King's Royal Regiment of New York in 1792, lieutenant in the Royal Canadian volunteers in 1794 and captain in the same corps in 1796.

At the request of Lord Selkirk he came to London in 1803 and agreed to govern the colony Selkirk planned on the Red River. Selkirk, a shareholder in the Hudson's Bay Company, had bought 300,000 square kilometres of the Red River Valley from the company, to give destitute Scots a home in the New World and to deny the land to its rival, the North West Company. Macdonell gathered the first colonists, mainly Highlanders evicted from the Sutherland estates, sailed with them from Stornoway, wintered at York Factory and reached the Red River the following August.

From his arrival he faced the opposition of the agents of the North West Company, whose headquarters were at Montreal. On 11 June 1815 the company's men fired on the colonists and demanded his surrender, and he gave himself up to avoid bloodshed. He was taken to Montreal as a prisoner; charges were laid against him, but his case was never tried. He later returned to his farm at Osnabruck in Upper Canada.

Historians have generally agreed that, despite the difficulties of founding a colony amid the rivalry of the fur-trading companies, Macdonell bears some of the responsibility for its first failure. They point to his obstinacy, arrogance and lack of diplomatic skill and to his failure to win the trust of his own people, and above all to the Pemmican Proclamation, issued when the colony was too weak to defend itself, which gave the North West Company ready propaganda against the Hudson's Bay Company and Selkirk. He died in 1828 at the home of his brother John at Pointe-Fortune on the Ottawa River. Miles Macdonell Collegiate in Winnipeg, opened in 1952, is named after him.
mileseva-monastery: King Stefan Vladislav founded Mileševa between 1234 and 1236 in the valley of the Mileševa River, near Prijepolje, and the narthex was added in 1236. He brought there the relics of his uncle Saint Sava, who had died at Trnovo in Bulgaria. Some historians believe that Tvrtko I was crowned King of the Serbs and Bosnia at Mileševa in 1377, and in the 15th century the monastery was the seat of the Metropolitanate of Dabar-Bosnia.

The Ottomans set it on fire in 1459, but it was soon restored. In the first half of the 16th century service books were illuminated in its printing house, and it also kept one of the oldest schools. It was thoroughly renovated in the time of Patriarch Makarije, after the Serbian Patriarchate was restored in 1557, when its outer narthex was built and painted. A restoration of 1863, after several Ottoman military engagements, changed the church's appearance considerably.

The church, dedicated to the Ascension of Our Lord, belongs to the Raška school and has a unique ground plan: its single nave widens from west to east, so that the three altar apses lean directly on the domed east wall, and inside the dome rises on arches arranged like a stairway.

The first frescoes date from the 1230s, and those of the narthex and the adjacent chapel were probably painted in the 1230s and 1240s. They show bishops, warrior saints, martyrs and monks, Christ's earthly life and the Last Judgment. In the narthex the Nemanjić family appears: Stefan Nemanja as the monk Simeon, Sava as the first archbishop, Stefan the First-Crowned as king, and his sons Radoslav and Vladislav. A layer painted in the second half of the 16th century, of which fragments survive, protected the earlier work when fire damaged the church.

Mileševa drew pilgrims and travellers, among them Cornelis de Schepper, and received gifts from Ivan IV Vasilyevich of Russia and from rulers of Wallachia and Moldavia. In 1594 the Ottomans took Saint Sava's relics and burned them publicly on Vračar hill in Belgrade, making him a posthumous martyr. On 27 October 1941 Communist forces broke into the monastery and killed its hegumen, Nestor Trkulja. It was declared a Monument of Culture of Exceptional Importance in 1979.
milford-connecticut: Milford lies on the coast between New Haven and Bridgeport, and includes the village of Devon and the borough of Woodmont. When the English first came, the Paugussett, an Algonquian-speaking people, predominated in the territory. The small river that runs through the town gave the area its early English name, Wepawaug.

English colonists affiliated with the New Haven Colony bought the land of present-day Milford, Orange and West Haven on 1 February 1639 from Ansantawae, chief of the local Paugusset. They built a grist mill by the Wepawaug River in 1640. During the Revolutionary War the Milford section of the Boston Post Road, a vital route linking Boston, New York and other coastal cities, was blockaded by Continental forces, and Fort Trumbull was built to protect the town. The Liberty Rock monument marks the site of the blockade.

Milford gave rise to several towns. Woodbridge was formed in 1784, partly from New Haven, and Orange, originally North Milford, was chartered in 1822 by residents of the northern and eastern sections. West Haven was created from Orange in 1921. The remaining town was known for shipbuilding, farming and oystering, and in the later 19th century it became a beach resort for people from New Haven and Bridgeport. The Memorial Bridge, a stone bridge and tower commemorating the founders, replaced the last mill over the Wepawaug in 1899. Woodmont was incorporated as a borough in 1903, and in 1959 the town, with Woodmont, became the City of Milford.

One curiosity dates from 1902, when boxes of Quaker Oats held a coupon for the legal deed to a tiny lot, sometimes ten feet by ten, in a subdivision called Liberty Park that was never built. The lots caused paperwork for tax collectors, who often could not find the owners, until the town ended them in the mid-1970s by a general foreclosure.

The 2020 census counted 50,558 people. In the post-World War II period Milford suburbanised, and the Milford section of Interstate 95 was completed in 1958. The Connecticut Post Mall was built in the 1960s and 1970s, and a firm called SCELBI Computer Consulting, which many credit as the world's first personal-computer maker, was on the Boston Post Road in the 1970s. The Milford Oyster Festival has been held each August since 1975. The shoreline includes Silver Sands State Park, where a sandbar at low tide leads to Charles Island, a protected bird nesting ground.
milindapanha: The Milindapañhā, whose title means Questions of Milinda, dates from sometime between 100 BCE and 200 CE. It purports to record a dialogue between the Buddhist sage Nāgasena and the 2nd-century BCE Indo-Greek king Menander I, called Milinda in Pali. Scholars generally accept that the work is composite, with additions made over time, and note that the Chinese versions are substantially shorter. The text may first have been written in Sanskrit, and Oskar von Hinüber suggests, from a Chinese translation and some unique concepts in the text, that the original language might have been Gandhari.

Apart from the Sri Lankan Pali edition and its derivatives no other copies are known. The oldest Pali manuscript was copied in 1495, and significant sections are lost, making it the only Pali text known to have been passed down incomplete.

The work begins with a background history, then turns to questions on distinguishing characteristics, such as attention, wisdom, feeling and perception, and questions for the cutting off of perplexity, which take up transmigration and rebirth and the soul. It goes on to eighty-two dilemmas, a question solved by inference, the special qualities of asceticism, and questions on similes.

In the text Menander is the king of the city of Sāgala, learned, eloquent and wise, accompanied by a guard of 500 Greek soldiers, with counsellors named Demetrius and Antiochus. Buddhist tradition relates that after his discussions with Nāgasena he adopted the Buddhist faith for as long as life should last, gave his kingdom to his son and later attained enlightenment. Von Hinüber observes that Menander is a historical figure but Nāgasena is otherwise unknown, that the text includes anachronisms, and that the dialogue shows no sign of Greek influence and can be traced to the Upanisads.

The Milindapañhā is regarded as canonical in Burmese Buddhism, as part of the Khuddaka Nikāya, but not in Thai or Sri Lankan Buddhism. An abridged version appears in Chinese translations, and the Monk Nāgasena Sutra, translated in the Eastern Jin dynasty, corresponds to its first three chapters. The Grande Inscription d'Angkor, engraved in 1701 on the walls of Angkor Wat, mentions it. Thomas Rhys Davids called it the masterpiece of Indian prose, though Moriz Winternitz held that this is true only of the earlier parts. It has been translated into English by Rhys Davids in 1890, Isaline Blew Horner in 1969 and Maria Heim in 2025.
military-industrial-complex: The expression military–industrial complex describes the relationship between a country's military and the defence industry that supplies it, seen together as a vested interest that influences public policy. Both sides benefit, one by obtaining weapons and the other by being paid to supply them. The concept is generally treated as unique to the United States, and its use for other countries is ambiguous. President Dwight D. Eisenhower used the term in his Farewell Address to the Nation on 17 January 1961, saying that the conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry was new in American experience, and that government must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence by the complex.

The speech was written by Ralph E. Williams and Malcolm Moos, and how far Eisenhower and his brother Milton shaped it is unclear from the surviving documents. Eisenhower was neither the first to use the phrase nor the first to warn of the danger. The first known use was by Winfield W. Riefler in 1947, who used it of the economic potentials of the states at war. C. Wright Mills's 1956 book The Power Elite, which described a powerful elite of military and corporate chiefs set against a powerless mass society, served as a framework for the debate of the 1960s and 1970s.

In its later meanings the phrase moved from Eisenhower's warning of a future danger to a claim that the complex already shaped policy. During the Vietnam War, opponents used it, partly because Eisenhower's conservative reputation protected them from charges of disloyalty, as John Kenneth Galbraith said. The Port Huron Statement used it closer to Mills's sense of a power elite. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke in a 1963 sermon of millions of citizens disturbed that the military-industrial complex too often shaped national policy. Dow Chemical became linked with the war after 1966 through its contract to make napalm, and protesters picketed its offices and disrupted shareholder meetings, among them Honeywell's in 1970.

Congress passed the Mansfield Amendment of 1969 to restrict military-sponsored university research, and Stanford and MIT spun off such work into SRI International and Draper Laboratory. Senator William Proxmire became the chief advocate of the view of the complex as an unaccountable bureaucracy, and in 1968 he named 23 defence contractors in a press conference. The economist Seymour Melman argued for converting arms industries to civilian work, while Murray Weidenbaum held that dependence on government contracts harms the contractors themselves. The phrase is often used as a pejorative, and some scholars say it suggests a conspiracy.
military-revolution: The historian Michael Roberts first set out the idea in 1955, in a lecture at the Queen's University of Belfast later published as The Military Revolution, 1560–1660. Studying Sweden, he argued that Dutch and Swedish innovations in tactics, drill and doctrine, made to get the most out of portable firearms, called for more trained soldiers and so for standing armies. Armies grew larger and costlier, and the money, men and supplies they needed produced new financial demands and new institutions of government. In his view the modern art of war made the modern state both possible and necessary.

In the 1990s Geoffrey Parker moved the cause from tactics to fortification. He asked why the supposedly outdated Spanish tercios beat the Swedish lines at Nördlingen in 1634, and argued that the trace italienne, the bastioned fortress, turned war into a series of long sieges and demanded larger armies to besiege and garrison the new works. He placed the revolution's start in the early 16th century, later stretched it from 1450 to 1800, and saw it, with a naval revolution, as the main reason relatively small European powers could conquer the Americas and much of Africa and Asia.

Others moved the dates. Ayton and Price stressed an infantry revolution of the early 14th century, David Eltis put the decisive shift to gunpowder in the early 16th century, and Jeremy Black chose 1660–1710, when European armies grew fastest. Clifford J. Rogers proposed five successive revolutions, of infantry, artillery, fortification, firearms and army size, between the 14th century and 1715, in bursts like the punctuated equilibrium of biology.

Michael Duffy and Black called the theory misleading, exaggerated and simplistic, and Black argued that state growth allowed larger armies rather than the reverse. David Parrott found no significant growth in French armies in the age of the trace italienne, and the political scientist Jason Sharman has criticised Parker's case for European advantage. A 2013 study explained why the changes failed in the Ottoman Empire, whose early and cohesive standing army could block reform. Many historians now prefer a slow evolution in which organisation, command and logistics mattered more than technology, and some reject the idea entirely after comparing Europe with Japan, Korea, the Mughal Empire and the Ottoman Empire.
military-settlement: Settlements were organised on a large scale from 1816. The settled troops were formed from married soldiers with at least six years of service and local men, mostly peasants, aged 18 to 45, both called master settlers; other fit men of that age served as their assistants and in reserve units. Children under 18 were enrolled as cantonists, with military schooling from the age of 7, later 10, and joined the units at 18. Settlers retired at 45 and went on serving in hospitals and other establishments.

Each settlement had 60 linked houses with a regiment of 228 men, four masters to a house. These model houses were largely for show to inspecting officials, while the settlers lived in small side buildings; Arakcheyev's rules punished anyone found inside the living quarters or moving a pot from its place. His instructions fixed farm work by date with little regard for weather or distance, hay might be cut 7–10 miles away, and near Saint Petersburg peasants used to hunting, fishing, crafts and trade were ordered to grow wheat, which brought poverty and hunger.

Because the settlements were set up on state lands, they provoked riots among the state peasants, in the Novgorod guberniya in 1817 and among the Bug Cossacks in 1817–1818. Alexander I declared that the settlements would be created even if the road from Saint Petersburg to Chudovo had to be paved with corpses. By 1825 they existed in the Petersburg, Novgorod, Mogilev, Kherson and Ekaterinoslav guberniyas and in Sloboda Ukraine, had saved some 32 million rubles, and still could not meet the army's need for recruits.

After the Chuguyev rising of 1819, which spread to the Taganrog regiment, Arakcheyev led the punitive expedition: more than 2,000 men were arrested, 313 tried, and hundreds sentenced to 12,000 blows with metal rods, under which 25 are known to have died. The Staraya Russa rising of 1831 began amid cholera riots, spread across most of the Novgorod settlements and won over a battalion sent against it; participants were made to run the gauntlet and exiled to Siberia, and many were sent to katorga at Kronstadt.

From 1831 many settlements were renamed districts of ploughing soldiers, which in effect ended most of them, and all were abolished in 1857. The system is generally judged a failure, its settlers effective neither as soldiers nor as farmers. The exception was the Caucasus, where settlers helped defend against raids by local peoples and later joined the Cossack hosts.
millau: Millau stands at the confluence of the Tarn and Dourbie rivers, in a large depression at about 340 metres, on the southern edge of the Massif Central. Its territory lies in the Grands Causses, limestone plateaus known for sheep farming and for cheese, including Roquefort, and is cut by gorges and ravines. The town is a subprefecture of the Aveyron department, in the former province of Rouergue, where people spoke Rouergat, a dialect of Occitan.

The town dates back nearly 3,000 years, when it stood on the Granède hills above the present town. In the second or first century BCE it moved to the plain on the left bank of the Tarn, and took its Gallic name, Condatomagus, from words for confluence and market. Close by was La Graufesenque, one of the major earthenware centres of the Roman Empire, where luxury ceramics such as red terra sigillata were made. By the second century CE trade had collapsed under competition, and barbarian invasions of the 4th and 5th centuries sent the town to the other bank, where it was called Amiliavum.

By the 9th century Millau was a seat of viguerie and a centre of lambskin glove production, with ramparts around it. In 1112 it passed to Béranger III, father of the future king of Aragon, and in 1187 a consular charter gave it communal freedom and consuls to raise taxes and apply justice. In 1271 it passed to the crown of France.

It came under English rule in 1361, during the Hundred Years War, and Louis XI attached it to the crown in 1476. The medieval bridge over the Tarn had 17 arches, and after one collapsed in the 18th century only a single arch remained. Gloves became a major industry in the 19th century, and in the first half of the 20th more than half the townspeople lived from leather. A six-month general strike in the winter of 1934 to 1935 followed a wage cut of 25 to 30 per cent, and the glove industry began to decline in the 1960s.

Millau has 11 listed historical monuments, among them the archaeological site of La Graufesenque, the church of Notre-Dame de l'Espinasse, a 12th-century belfry and the Pégayrolles mansion of 1738, which holds the town museum with its pottery, tannery and glove collections. A few workshops still make gloves for fashion and luxury brands. The Millau Viaduct, a cable-stayed road bridge carrying the A75 motorway across the Tarn valley, opened in 2004 and took traffic out of the town centre. The surrounding Causses and Cévennes have been a World Heritage Site since 2011.
millet: Millets are a varied group of small-seeded grasses grown as a staple cereal and used as fodder for livestock and as food for humans. Most belong to the tribe Paniceae, but the species are not all closely related. Common kinds include pearl millet, the most widely grown, proso, foxtail and finger millet, and fonio. Sorghum is sometimes called great millet. Millets tolerate drought and extreme weather and give a crop in a short season under hot, dry conditions, and their nutrition is comparable to wheat and rice.

Millets may have been eaten for about 7,000 years. In China proso and foxtail millet were important from the Early Neolithic, and the earliest evidence is at Cishan, where proso millet remains in storage pits date to roughly 10,300 to 8,700 years ago. Millet was farmed in Korea from about 3500 BCE. Little millet and kodo millet were domesticated in the Indian subcontinent by about 3000 and 3700 BCE.

Finger millet is native to the highlands of East Africa, and pearl millet was domesticated in the Sahel of West Africa, with early finds at Dhar Tichitt in Mauritania and in the Tilemsi valley in Mali. Proso millet reached Italy around 1500 BCE and northern Germany from 1200 BCE. Hesiod and Theophrastus mention it in Greece.

Millet is a staple of the Sahel, making up much of the cereal eaten in Burkina Faso, Chad and the Gambia, and it can be ground and mixed with milk to make fura and brukina. In Namibia pearl millet, there called mahangu, is the dominant food staple. In Ukraine it was a common food of the Zaporozhian Cossacks, as a porridge called kulish.
In India it is usually eaten as a flour, and in the Himalayas it is fermented into drinks such as tongba and raksi. It is also a forage crop, on which lambs gain weight faster than on forage sorghum.
millicent-garrett-fawcett: Millicent Garrett was born on 11 June 1847 in Aldeburgh, the eighth of ten children of Newson Garrett, a businessman from nearby Leiston, and his wife Louisa. The family encouraged children to read widely and to share their father's political interests. Her elder sister Elizabeth Garrett Anderson, who became Britain's first female doctor, introduced her to the suffragist Emily Davies, who told her that she was the younger and must attend to the vote.

In 1865 she heard a lecture by John Stuart Mill. Through Mill she met Henry Fawcett, a Liberal Member of Parliament who had been blinded in a shooting accident in 1858. They married on 23 April 1867, and she acted as his secretary while building a writing career. Their only child, Philippa, was born in 1868.

Fawcett joined the London Suffrage Committee in 1868 and spoke at the first public pro-suffrage meeting in London in 1869. Her Political Economy for Beginners (1870) ran to ten editions in forty-one years. With Anne Clough she helped found Newnham Hall in 1871. After Henry died on 6 November 1884 she withdrew briefly from public life, then returned in 1885. She joined the Liberal Unionist Party in 1886 to oppose Irish Home Rule, and resigned from the Unionists in 1904 over free trade.

After the death of Lydia Becker she led the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, as its president by 1897. She kept to argument and legal change and distanced herself from the militant Women's Social and Political Union, which she believed would sour public opinion and alienate members of Parliament. By 1905 the NUWSS had 305 constituent societies and almost 50,000 members. It held its first large open-air procession, the Mud March, on 9 February 1907.

In July 1901 she sailed to South Africa to lead a commission of women investigating conditions in the camps where Boer families were interned. She also campaigned to raise the age of consent and to repeal the Contagious Diseases Acts, which she saw as built on a sexual double standard.

The NUWSS kept campaigning during the First World War, and Fawcett held her post until 1919, a year after women first received the vote under the Representation of the People Act 1918. She was appointed Dame Grand Cross of the Order of the British Empire in 1925 and died at her London home in Gower Street on 5 August 1929. A memorial in Westminster Abbey, unveiled in 1932, reads: A wise constant and courageous Englishwoman. She won citizenship for women. In 2018 a statue by Gillian Wearing was unveiled in Parliament Square, after a campaign led by Caroline Criado Perez that gathered over 84,000 signatures.
milners-kindergarten: Alfred Milner had been chosen as High Commissioner by the Colonial Secretary Joseph Chamberlain in 1897, after the Jameson Raid. When the reconstruction of the conquered Boer republics fell to him during the Second Boer War, he gathered young men from Oxford University and the Colonial Office, preferring, as he put it, brains and character to experience. The group began with twelve men, most of them Oxford graduates, who went to South Africa from 1901. The name was first used derisively by Sir William Thackeray Marriott, and the members adopted it for themselves.

Most of the recruits worked in the Transvaal, where reconstruction was needed most. Peter Perry became Assistant Imperial Secretary for the African territories and negotiated with the Portuguese for mine labour; Lionel Curtis became Town Clerk of Johannesburg under its new municipal charter; Patrick Duncan became Treasurer and then Colonial Secretary of the Transvaal; Geoffrey Robinson became Secretary for Municipal Affairs and later editor of the Johannesburg Star. After Milner left for England on 2 April 1905 they served under his successor, Lord Selborne, until responsible government was formed in 1907.

The Liberal government of Henry Campbell-Bannerman set aside the Lyttelton Constitution and gave the former republics self-government. An effort led by Curtis, Philip Kerr and Robinson in 1906 and 1907 to keep South Africa British failed, and after the elections of 1907 400 British civil servants were dismissed. The group had wanted an American-style federation of the four colonies, but a unitary union was chosen in 1909.

In July 1909 Selborne and most of the members returned to England, where they renamed themselves the Round Table and drew in Waldorf Astor and F. S. Oliver. Their quarterly, The Round Table, funded mainly by the mining magnate Abe Bailey and the Rhodes Trust, first appeared in November 1910 to promote imperial federation. Several members rose high: Robinson, as Geoffrey Dawson, edited The Times; Kerr became British Ambassador to the United States; Curtis founded the Royal Institute of International Affairs; Duncan was Governor General of South Africa from 1937 to 1943. Richard Feetham, the last survivor, died in 1965.
milo-of-croton: Milo came from Croton, in what is now southern Italy. He won the boys' wrestling at the 60th Olympics and the men's wrestling at five Olympics from the 62nd to the 66th. He kept competing long after an athlete's usual prime and would have been over 40 by the 67th Olympiad. He also took part in many Pythian Games. His existence is attested by many classical authors, among them Aristotle, Pausanias, Cicero, Herodotus, Vitruvius and Epictetus, and by the author of the Suda, although many stories of doubtful truth surround him.

Diodorus Siculus wrote that Milo was a follower of Pythagoras and commanded the army of Croton that defeated the Sybarites, going into battle wearing his Olympic wreaths and, like Heracles, a lion's skin and carrying a club. Ancient sources report that he liked to show off his strength: he challenged others to bend his little finger, to push him off a greased disk or to take a pomegranate from his grip, and nobody succeeded. In his best-known feat he carried a newborn calf on his back daily until it was a four-year-old cow, then carried it the length of the stadium and ate it.

Pausanias records that the statue of Milo was made by Dameas, also of Croton, and that Milo carried his own statue into the Altis. He adds that when Milo came to wrestle at Olympia for a seventh time he could not master the young Timasitheus, a fellow citizen who refused to come to close quarters. According to legend, Milo's showing off ended his life: he tried to split a tree stump with his bare hands, the wedges fell out, and trapped by the fingers he was killed by wolves or a lion. The scene became a popular subject of late Italian Renaissance sculpture and continued to about 1900.
milos-obrenovic: Miloš Obrenović was born Miloš Teodorović, the son of Teodor Mihailović from Dobrinja and of Višnja, whose first husband was Obren Martinović. His family descended from the Bratonožići tribe. He fought in the First Serbian Uprising until it ended in 1813 and was wounded in the battle for Užice.

After the death of his half-brother Milan, a voivode of the Rudnik district, he took the surname Obrenović, derived from the name of his stepfather Obren. When the rising collapsed, he was among the few leaders who stayed in Serbia to face the returning Ottomans, and the Ottoman commander Serčesma left him in charge of his area; Grand Vizier Hurshid Pasha recognised him as governor of the Rudnik nahiya.

Ottoman rule under Sulejman Pasha Skopljak turned harsh, with disarming and extortion, and a rebellion broke out under Hadži-Prodan. In April 1815 Miloš organised and led the Second Serbian Uprising, and the Ottomans agreed to terms the same year. After the killing of Karađorđe Petrović in 1817 he became leader of the Serbs. Serbia gained some autonomy but stayed under Ottoman sovereignty, with Miloš as absolute ruler.

A legislative commission he set up between late 1828 and autumn 1830 first set out to translate the Code Napoléon into Serbian; he then invited two legal specialists from Hungary, Vasilije Lazarević and Jovan Hadžić, to prepare civil and criminal codes. In January 1831 he told a great national assembly that the Sultan had ended the direct obligations of Serbian peasants to their former Turkish lords. The Sultan's decrees of 1830 and 1833 made Serbia a sovereign principality with Miloš as hereditary prince, and a Metropolitanate of Serbia was set up in Belgrade.

Miloš was an autocrat who consistently refused to decentralise power, which provoked strong opposition. After one rebellion he agreed to the Sretenje Constitution of 1835, which Austria, the Ottoman Empire and Russia opposed; he abolished it at the demand of Russia and the Ottomans, and the Constitution of 1838 replaced it.

He abdicated in 1839 in favour of his sons, Milan, who died a few weeks later, and Mihailo. Mihailo was deposed in 1842, and the family was out of power until 1858, when Miloš was restored for the last two years of his life. He died on 26 September 1860. The National Assembly proclaimed him Father of the Fatherland, and he is also known as Miloš the Great.
milovan-djilas: Milovan Djilas was born on 12 June 1911 at Podbišće near Mojkovac in the Kingdom of Montenegro, the fourth of nine children in a peasant family. His father Nikola had served in the Montenegrin Army and opposed the incorporation of Montenegro into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Djilas began studying literature at the University of Belgrade in 1929, already a committed communist. In March 1932 he was jailed for eight days for an anti-government demonstration.
