Arrested again eleven months later, he was tortured and sentenced to three years in Sremska Mitrovica Prison, where he met senior party members and became a committed Stalinist.

After his release in 1936 he gave up study for the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, sided with Josip Broz Tito against Stalin's attempts to control it, and entered the Central Committee in 1938 and the politburo the next year.

After the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia in April 1941, Djilas helped Tito establish the Partisan resistance. The party resolved to begin an uprising on 4 July, and he was sent to Montenegro to organise it. In November 1941 Tito dismissed him from command there for his errors, including what were called leftist errors, and made him editor of the party paper Borba. In March 1944 he went on a mission to the Soviet Union and met Stalin. After the war he became vice-president in Tito's government, and in 1948 he was sent to Moscow in an attempt to bridge the gap between Moscow and Belgrade. As the break came, he became one of the leading critics of Stalin's efforts to control Yugoslavia.

Djilas was widely seen as Tito's possible successor, and he held the post of President of the Federal People's Assembly from 25 December 1953 to 28 January 1954. In his Borba articles of that winter he criticised bureaucratic Stalinism and went on to argue against the one-party state itself. He was expelled from the Central Committee in January 1954 and resigned from the League of Communists in March.

He was sentenced in 1956 for backing the Hungarian Revolution, and in 1957 for The New Class, published abroad, which argued that communism was creating a new class of privileged party bureaucrats. It was translated into more than 40 languages. Conversations with Stalin brought a further sentence in 1962. In prison he wrote a biography of Njegoš and translated Paradise Lost into Serbo-Croatian. He was freed by amnesty on 31 December 1966.

Djilas stayed in Belgrade as a dissident. He opposed the breakup of Yugoslavia, though he predicted in the 1980s that it would come on lines of bureaucratic nationalism after Tito. He died on 20 April 1995.
miltiades: Miltiades was a well-born Athenian of the prominent Philaid clan, son of Cimon Coalemos, who won the Olympic chariot race three times in succession. He came of age under the tyranny of the Peisistratids and was named after his father's maternal half-brother, Miltiades the Elder, who had founded a semi-autonomous tyranny on the Thracian Chersonese around 555 BCE. Miltiades the Younger held the eponymous archonship under the tyrant Hippias in 524/23 BCE. When Stesagoras, who had inherited the Chersonese, was killed by an axe in 516 BCE, Hippias sent him to claim the lands. He feigned mourning and imprisoned the men of rank who came to console him, kept 500 troops and made an alliance with King Olorus of Thrace by marrying his daughter Hegesipyle.

Around 513 BCE Darius I of Persia forced the Chersonese into submission and made Miltiades his vassal. Miltiades joined the Scythian expedition and was left with other Greek officers to guard the bridge over the Danube. He later claimed that he urged them to destroy it; some historians doubt the claim. He took part in the Ionian Revolt of 499 BCE and captured Lemnos and Imbros, which he ceded to Athens. When the revolt collapsed in 494 BCE, he and his family fled to Athens in five ships in 493 BCE. He was put on trial as a former tyrant. He presented himself as a defender of Greek freedom against Persian despotism and was acquitted.

Elected one of the ten generals for 490 BCE, he insisted, as the general with most experience of the Persians, that they be fought at once at Marathon, and the polemarch Callimachus gave the deciding vote for attack when the generals were split five to five. He is often credited with the tactics that won the battle, among them a thinner centre of four ranks against eight on the flanks, and a run at the Persian line across the range of their archers.

In 489 BCE Miltiades led seventy ships against Paros, which he held a grudge against, and failed to take it. A grievous leg wound left him incapacitated. His rivals exploited the failure, he was charged with treason and sentenced to death, and the sentence was converted to a fine of fifty talents. He died in prison, probably of gangrene from the wound, and his son Cimon paid the debt. The Athenians refused to let him write his name on the Stoa Poikile but had him painted in the front rank of a battle painting there. Pheidias later made a statue of Nemesis at Rhamnus in his honour, said to have been cut from marble Datis had brought for a memorial to Persian victory.
milton-cato: Robert Milton Cato was born on 3 June 1915 in Saint Vincent, then part of the British Windward Islands, and attended the St. Vincent Grammar School from 1928 to 1933. He was articled to a barrister in Kingstown. In 1945 he joined the First Canadian Army, rose to sergeant and saw active service in France, Belgium, Holland and Germany. He was called to the Bar at the Middle Temple in 1948 and later married Lucy-Ann Alexandra Cato.

Cato became Chief Minister on 19 May 1967 as head of the Saint Vincent Labour Party, and when the island became an associated state on 27 October 1969 he was its first Premier, also holding the finance portfolio. His party lost the elections of 1972, when James Fitz-Allen Mitchell became Premier, and Cato led the opposition until his party and its coalition partners won in 1974 and he returned as premier and minister of finance. He represented the West St. George constituency for many years. At independence from Britain on 27 October 1979 he took the offices of Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, and he is known as the Father of Independence.

After his party's defeat in the general election of 1984, Cato was leader of the opposition from August to November 1984 and then retired from politics. He died on 10 February 1997 at the age of 81. In October 2000 the Kingstown General Hospital was renamed the Milton Cato Memorial Hospital in his honour, and in July 2026 the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank announced that he would appear on a new 5 dollar banknote with the Grenadian athlete Sir Kirani James.
milton-friedman: Milton Friedman was born on 31 July 1912, the youngest of four children and the only son of Jewish working-class immigrants from Beregszász in the Kingdom of Hungary, now Berehove in Ukraine. His parents worked as dry goods merchants, and the family moved soon after his birth to Rahway, New Jersey. Unable to find academic work, he followed his friend W. Allen Wallis to Washington, D.C., in 1935, where the New Deal gave many young economists employment. From 1937 he worked for the National Bureau of Economic Research, where he assisted Simon Kuznets.

From 1943 Friedman worked at the Division of War Research at Columbia University as a mathematical statistician, on weapons design and tactics. His work there produced sequential sampling, later described as the standard analysis of quality control inspection. In 1946 he began teaching economic theory at the University of Chicago, where he stayed for thirty years and helped build the Chicago school. He wrote a weekly column for Newsweek from 1966 to 1984. After retiring in 1977 he was affiliated with the Hoover Institution at Stanford University, and from 1981 he served on President Ronald Reagan's Economic Policy Advisory Board.

Friedman revived interest in the money supply as a determinant of the nominal value of output and is largely responsible for the modern form of monetarism. In 1968 he argued that a government producing greater inflation cannot permanently lower unemployment, which in the long run is set by frictions in the labour market. His book A Theory of the Consumption Function (1957) set out consumption smoothing and the permanent income hypothesis. In Capitalism and Freedom he argued for a volunteer military, freely floating exchange rates, a negative income tax and school vouchers.

His 1976 Nobel prize was controversial, mainly because of his association with the Chilean military ruler Augusto Pinochet; in 1975 Friedman had spent seven days in Chile giving lectures. He died in San Francisco on 16 November 2006, aged 94.
milton-margai: Margai was born on 7 December 1895 in Gbangbatoke, Moyamba District, in the British protectorate of Sierra Leone, the eldest of eighteen children of Mende parents; his father was an affluent trader and his grandfather a Mende warrior chief. After the Albert Academy in Freetown and a degree in history from Fourah Bay College in 1921, he qualified as a doctor at the Durham University College of Medicine in 1926 and also attended the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, becoming the first doctor from the protectorate.

Returning in 1928, he served in 11 of the protectorate's 12 districts in the Colonial Medical Service and campaigned on hygiene and social welfare. Working with the Sande, the Mende women's society that handed down knowledge of midwifery, he set up camps teaching hygiene to its initiates, wrote a manual on midwifery in Mende and trained the midwives who became known as Mamma Nurses; he described the work in his 1948 article Welfare Work in a Secret Society. He entered the Protectorate assembly in the 1930s, and in 1951 he founded the Sierra Leone People's Party with Siaka Stevens, which won that year's election to the Legislative Council.

After heading the departments of health, agriculture and forestry, Margai became chief minister. In 1958 his brother Albert narrowly won a party challenge to his leadership but declined it and founded the opposition People's National Party, rejoining him in coalition in 1960, the year Margai led the delegation to the constitutional talks in London with the Colonial Secretary Iain Macleod. Pro-British and conservative, he sought good relations with the British government after independence. His party won the general election of 27 May 1962, and he appointed northern leaders to key ministries to ease the grievances of northern groups.

He concentrated on education, health and agriculture but was criticised for suppressing the opposition All People's Congress and sometimes withholding funds from councils it controlled. He gradually brought Sierra Leoneans into command of the army, whose officers were ethnically mixed by 1964. He died in office on 28 April 1964, aged 68, and was succeeded by Albert. The Milton Margai School for the Blind in Freetown, whose foundation stone he laid in 1962, and the Milton Margai College of Education and Technology carry his name.
milton-obote: Apollo Milton Obote was born on 28 December 1925 in the village of Akokoro in northern Uganda, the third of nine children of a chief of the Oyima clan of the Lango people. He studied at Busoga College Mwiri and Makerere University, where he took a general arts course because law was not taught, and left without a degree. He worked in Buganda and then in Kenya, where he was involved in the independence movement. After returning to Uganda in 1956 he joined the Uganda National Congress and was elected to the colonial legislative council in 1957. In 1959 he led a faction into the Uganda People's Congress.

Before independence Obote formed a coalition with the Buganda royalist party Kabaka Yekka, and he became prime minister on 25 April 1962; Mutesa II, the Kabaka of Buganda, became ceremonial president. In January 1964 the army mutinied at Jinja, and a settlement gave soldiers large pay rises and rapid promotions, among them Idi Amin. Obote was later implicated in a gold-smuggling plot with Amin. When Parliament demanded an investigation, he suspended the constitution in March 1966 and declared himself president, and an attack on Mutesa's palace sent Mutesa into exile. A new constitution in 1967 abolished the federal structure and created an executive presidency.

After an assassination attempt on 19 December 1969 all opposition parties were banned. His Common Man's Charter set out his Move to the Left, and in 1970 the state took a 60 percent share in major companies and banks. His secret police, the General Service Unit, was held responsible for many cruelties. The army under Amin overthrew him in January 1971 while he attended a Commonwealth conference in Singapore.

Obote went into exile in Tanzania, where President Julius Nyerere supported him, and a rebel invasion of Uganda in 1972 failed. After Tanzanian forces and Ugandan exiles ousted Amin in 1979, his party won the elections of 1980, which its opponents believed were rigged, and a guerrilla war began under Yoweri Museveni. In 1983 Operation Bonanza killed tens of thousands of people. Estimates of the deaths in the fighting range from 100,000 to 500,000. Army commanders deposed Obote on 27 July 1985, and he lived in Kenya and Zambia. He died of kidney failure in Johannesburg on 10 October 2005, aged 79, and was given a state funeral in Kampala.
mimar-sinan: Sinan was born in Ağırnas, a small town near Kayseri in Anatolia. His origins are disputed. He is often thought to have been of Armenian or Cappadocian Greek origin, and less popular theories make him Albanian, Jewish, Bulgarian or Christian Turkish. In 1512 he was conscripted under the devshirme system, sent to Constantinople to train as an officer of the Janissary Corps, and converted to Islam. He learned carpentry and mathematics and assisted leading architects. He served on campaigns under Suleiman I, including the Battle of Mohács, and on campaign he built fortifications, roads and bridges.

At about the age of fifty Sinan was appointed chief royal architect, a post he held for almost fifty years, overseeing all construction for the empire with a large team of architects and master builders. His army training gave him an empirical rather than theoretical approach. Sources disagree on how many buildings he built or supervised, with counts from more than 300 to 476, and he relied on his office rather than designing every one. They included mosques, schools, mausoleums, hospitals, aqueducts, bridges and baths. Suleiman ordered the Süleymaniye Mosque with its complex of colleges, soup kitchen, hospital and caravanserai, and Sinan finished it in seven years.

Sinan described the Şehzade Mosque as the work of his apprenticeship, the Süleymaniye as that of his qualification and the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne as that of his mastery. In his autobiography he named the Selimiye his masterpiece. Its octagonal central dome is 31.28 metres wide and rests on eight piers, and its four minarets are 83 metres high. He claimed its dome surpassed that of the Hagia Sophia, though the diameter is only about half a metre greater. He sought the largest volume under a single dome and a unified interior. His assistants included Sedefkar Mehmed Agha, architect of the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, and Mimar Hayruddin, architect of the Stari Most at Mostar.
mimnermus: Almost no reliable biographical details of Mimnermus have been recorded. The Byzantine encyclopaedia Suda calls him the son of Ligyrtyades, from Colophon, Smyrna or Astypalaea, and says he flourished in the 37th Olympiad, 632 to 629 BCE. Smyrna seems the most likely home, and the Astypalaea suggestion is unsupported. Smyrna's disappearance for three hundred years after its last siege by Alyattes of Lydia may be why Colophon was able to claim him. He may have been alive at that siege and possibly died with the town.

Elegy was accompanied by the aulos, a wind instrument, so its performance needed a singer and a player. Ancient accounts associate Mimnermus with an aulos player named Nanno, and one makes her his lover. Strabo describes him as both a pipe-player and an elegiac poet.

His work was collected by Alexandrian scholars in two books, of which only small fragments survive. Modern scholars think they were the Nanno, a collection of short poems on varied themes, and the Smyrneis, a quasi-epic on Smyrna's conflict with the Lydians. Fragment 1 asks what life is without golden Aphrodite and wishes for death when love and its gifts no longer matter. It goes on to a bleak picture of old age. He also wrote in a patriotic vein: a quotation in Strabo is the earliest surviving account of the Ionian migration from Pylos, and another describes a Greek warrior's deeds against the cavalry of the Lydian king Gyges.

Mimnermus reworked myth to his own needs. Aelian records that he gave Niobe twenty children, where Homer gave her twelve. He was strongly influenced by Homer, whose vocabulary, formulas and similes recur in his verse. The scholar David A. Campbell describes the result as distinctive poetry of easy grace and pleasing rhythm.

Solon, addressing him as Ligyaistades, objected to a couplet in which Mimnermus wished to die at sixty, and urged him to change it to eighty. Plutarch also criticised his self-indulgence. Callimachus praised the sweetness of one of his books, and Hellenistic poets such as Callimachus drew on his work. Propertius preferred his verses to Homer's on love, and Horace cited him as holding that nothing is pleasant without love and jests. Later poets regarded him chiefly as a love poet, though the fragments suggest a sturdier character than that.
min-bin: Min Bin was born Min Pa in 1493, the son of Crown Prince Raza of Mrauk-U and Princess Saw Nandi, who were first cousins. His father became king in 1502 and later made him a general. When Raza was overthrown in 1513, Min Pa kept out of sight through eight years of court struggles under three kings. In 1521 King Minkhaung made him governor of Thandwe (Sandoway), the second city of the kingdom, where he built a loyal following and gathered arms. Ten years later he marched on Mrauk-U by land and water, defeated the royal army and had Minkhaung executed.

Min Bin took the throne on 27 May 1531 and was crowned on 16 September. Claiming that all of Bengal had belonged to his forebears, he invaded on 7 October 1532 with about 12,000 men, took Chittagong and entered Dhaka on 11 December without a fight. There he received the tribute of local lords and made a sixteen-year-old Bengali princess his queen, before a pilgrimage to Bodh Gaya. Beyond Chittagong his rule was largely nominal, and raids by Tripuri forces continued throughout his reign.

In 1535 a small Portuguese force came up the Kaladan River and attacked Mrauk-U itself; the king led the defence and drove it to the sea by 7 March. Afterwards he hired Portuguese mercenaries for his army and fleet. In 1542 he sent troops and a flotilla to relieve Prome against Toungoo, but his army was destroyed by Gen. Kyawhtin Nawrahta as it came out of the Padaung Pass. During the Toungoo siege of his capital in 1547 he flooded the attackers by opening the sluices of the city's reservoirs, and Tabinshwehti agreed to a truce on 30 January.

Min Bin died on 11 January 1554 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Min Dikkha. The defences he built across the kingdom are credited with deterring another Toungoo invasion until 1580, and his fleet laid the basis for the later Arakanese control of the coast from the Sundarbans to the Gulf of Martaban. Burmese chronicles say his brother Min Aung Hla, displaced as governor of Thandwe, invited the Toungoo invasion; Arakanese chronicles deny it.
min-saw-mon: Saw Mon was born in 1380/81 to Prince Razathu II and Princess Saw Nyet Htwa of the Launggyet kingdom, in present-day northern Rakhine State. The kingdom had been unstable for three decades, its throne fought over by court factions often backed by its stronger eastern neighbours, the Ava and Hanthawaddy kingdoms. His father Razathu was deposed and the family exiled to Kyeintali, but he regained the throne in 1397 and ruled until his death in 1401. His successor, Saw Mon's uncle Theinkhathu, was assassinated in 1404 by an abbot of the royal monastery, and Saw Mon took the throne in April 1404.

The Arakanese chronicles say that the young king forced Saw Pu Nyo, sister of the Viceroy of Dalet, to divorce her husband, who was then killed, and that her brother turned to Ava for help. Arakan was soon drawn into the Forty Years' War between Ava and Pegu: in November 1406 King Minkhaung I of Ava sent his crown prince Minye Kyawswa, whose troops overran Launggyet on 29 November 1406, and Saw Mon fled to Chittagong with a few followers.

In Bengal he served Sultan Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah as a commander. In February or March 1429 he invaded Arakan with Bengali troops; a first attempt failed when he quarrelled with the Bengal general Wali Khan, who imprisoned him, but the second succeeded, and he was proclaimed king at Launggyet on 18 April 1429.

For some time he ruled as a vassal of the sultanate, and his authority reached only northern Arakan, since Sandoway in the south was still independent. Launggyet had been ruined by decades of war, so he founded Mrauk-U nearby on a site much harder for invaders to attack, on 16 November 1430 by one reckoning, 20 August 1430 by another. He moved there when the city was finished in 1432/33 and died soon after, on 9 May 1433; his younger half-brother Khayi succeeded him.

The chronicles tell that court astrologers warned him he would die within a year of founding the new capital, and that he answered he would rather die and leave a safer kingdom than live long and leave a weak one. He built the Le-myet-hna Temple north of the palace, the twin Myatazaung pagodas on the hill beyond it, finished in 1431, and the nine small Koe-tan stupas above the royal palace. His chief queen was Saw Sit II.
minab: Minab is a city in the Central District of Minab County in Hormozgan province, Iran, and the capital of both the county and the district. It was historically part of the province of Kerman. Its climate is a hot desert one: summer daytime averages reach 37 degrees from May to September, and annual rainfall is around 124 millimetres. Most of its people speak a Bandari dialect of Persian and are Shia Muslims. The census counted 54,623 people in 2006, 63,229 in 2011 and 73,170 in 2016.

Human presence around Minab reaches into remote prehistory: Middle Palaeolithic stone tools 200,000 to 250,000 years old were found there in the 1970s, and pottery from the 3rd millennium BCE in a nearby village. Painted pottery from the Parthian and Sasanian periods has also been found. In the early medieval period the area was well populated, as large quantities of East Asian ceramics show, reflecting maritime trade with China and Southeast Asia. A fortress at Minab is documented in 1318, when it sheltered the king of Hormuz. Minab, Manujan and Vashkerd were governed each by a vizier as the outer territories of the original Kingdom of Hormuz.

In 1515 Hormuz became a vassal of the Portuguese Empire, which Safavid Iran disputed, since it counted Hormuz as its own vassal. When the Ottoman commander Piri Reis attacked Hormuz in 1552, Iranian and Portuguese families took refuge in Minab. On 17 October 1602 Iranian forces under Allahverdi Khan, governor of Fars, attacked Minab and Shamil to stop Portuguese attempts to retake Bahrain. After a three-month siege of Shamil the army took Minab quickly, with heavy casualties on both sides. In 1621 Maani, the wife of the Italian composer Pietro Della Valle, died there. Later the governor Emamqoli Khan made an alliance at Minab with British East India Company representatives, who agreed to help Abbas the Great expel the Portuguese from Hormuz and Qeshm Island.

After the Safavids fell in 1722 the mayor, Mir Abdollah, asked the Dutch for help in defending the fort, without success. Afghan troops captured Minab in 1727, and in 1744 Mohammad Baqer Beg Lari plundered the region. Nader Shah placed Minab and Bandar Abbas under temporary Dutch administration that year. About 1794 the Omani Empire captured Minab and held it through much of the 19th century. A Dutch record of 1756 said its people lived from agriculture, not navigation.

In the 21st century the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy's Asef Missile Brigade was based at Minab by 2019. On 28 February 2026, during Israeli and United States strikes on Iran, an elementary girls' school in the city was struck, and Iranian officials said at least 180 people, mostly schoolgirls, were killed and 95 injured.
minamoto-clan: The name removed its holders from the royal class altogether, a reduction in rank even for princes of the ō rank who were not in the line of succession. There were 21 branches of the clan, each named after the emperor from whom it descended, and some were populous while a few left no descendants. Among the Saga Genji, descended from Emperor Saga, three sons became Minister of the Left and were among the most powerful figures at court in the early Heian period, and some descendants of Minamoto no Tōru settled in the provinces as warrior houses, among them the Watanabe and Matsuura. The Kazan Genji became the Shirakawa family, which headed the Jingi-kan, the office for Shinto.

The Seiwa Genji descended from Minamoto no Tsunemoto (897–961), a grandson of Emperor Seiwa, who went to the provinces and founded a major warrior dynasty. Minamoto no Mitsunaka (912–997) allied with the Fujiwara, who afterwards often called on the Minamoto to restore order in Heian-Kyō. His son Yorinobu suppressed the rebellion of Taira no Tadatsune in 1032, and Yorinobu's son Yoriyoshi and grandson Yoshiie pacified most of northeastern Japan between 1051 and 1087.

The Taira executed most of the line, including Minamoto no Tameyoshi, in the Hōgen Rebellion of 1156, and Minamoto no Yoshitomo died in the Heiji Disturbance of 1160. Taira no Kiyomori then exiled Minamoto no Yoritomo (1147–1199), who in 1180 mounted the rebellion that destroyed the Taira within five years.

Three eras of Japanese history trace to Minamoto lines. Yoritomo founded the Kamakura period, Ashikaga Takauji the Muromachi period, and Tokugawa Ieyasu, who claimed descent from the Seiwa Genji through the Nitta clan, the Edo period. The Nitta, Takeda, Matsudaira, Shimazu, Sasaki and many other clans also formed from Minamoto lines. Evidence suggested in the late 19th century that Tsunemoto was a grandson of Emperor Yōzei rather than Seiwa is not widely accepted. The Tale of Genji takes its title from the surname, which its hero Hikaru Genji received from his father the emperor, and the Tale of the Heike tells of the struggle with the Taira.
minamoto-no-yoritomo: Yoritomo was the third son of Minamoto no Yoshitomo and Yura Gozen, daughter of Fujiwara no Suenori, High Priest of Atsuta Shrine. He was born at the family villa beside Atsuta Shrine in Owari Province, and was a descendant of Emperor Seiwa. His childhood name was Onitakemaru. In the Hōgen Rebellion of 1156 his father sided with the winning party of Emperor Go-Shirakawa and Taira no Kiyomori and had his own father executed.

In December 1159 Yoshitomo joined Fujiwara no Nobuyori in the Heiji rebellion, attacked Sanjō Palace and seized the emperor and the retired emperor while Kiyomori was away. Kiyomori returned and defeated the Minamoto at Rokuhara, and Yoshitomo was betrayed and executed. Yoritomo and his younger brothers were spared because of their age and sent to temples as monks. He grew up in exile and married Hōjō Masako, daughter of Hōjō Tokimasa.

In 1180 Prince Mochihito called the Minamoto clan throughout Japan to arms against the Taira, and Yoritomo took part. He set up his base at Kamakura in the east. His uncle Minamoto no Yukiie and his cousin Minamoto no Yoshinaka plotted against him. He lost his first major battle, at Ishibashiyama in September 1180, and spent the next six months raising a new army. His brothers Minamoto no Yoshitsune and Minamoto no Noriyori defeated the Taira in several battles, though Yoshinaka entered Kyoto in 1183. From 1181 to 1184 a truce with the Taira-dominated court gave Yoritomo time to build an administration of his own at Kamakura.

In the summer of 1189 he invaded the northern provinces of Mutsu and Dewa and razed Hiraizumi, the capital of the northern Fujiwara. Go-Shirakawa died in spring 1192, and Yoritomo took the title of Sei-i Tai Shōgun, which formally placed the feudal lords, the jitō and the shugo under his control. Kyoto was left with national ceremony and ritual.

During the great hunt at Fuji in May 1193 the brothers Soga Sukenari and Soga Tokimune killed Kudō Suketsune, the killer of their father, and Tokimune then raided Yoritomo's mansion before being stopped. Yoritomo was ordained a Buddhist monk in 1199 and died two days later, aged 51.

After his death his wife's family, the Hōjō, held power at Kamakura as regents, under the title of shikken, until 1333. The historian George Bailey Sansom wrote that Yoritomo was a truly great man, with foresight and practical good sense in building machinery to match his growing power. A stone pagoda beside Shirahata Shrine is traditionally believed to be his grave.
minamoto-no-yoshitsune: Yoshitsune was the ninth son of Minamoto no Yoshitomo and the third child he fathered with Tokiwa Gozen. His childhood name was Ushiwakamaru. Yoshitomo and his two eldest sons were killed in the Heiji Rebellion of 1160, and the infant survived by fleeing the capital with his mother. At ten he was placed with the monks of Kurama temple near Kyoto. Not wanting to become a monk, he left and in 1174 followed a gold merchant to Hiraizumi in Mutsu Province, where Fujiwara no Hidehira, head of the Northern Fujiwara, protected him. Legend adds that he defeated the warrior monk Benkei in a duel, after which Benkei became his retainer.

In 1180 Yoshitsune heard that his brother Yoritomo had raised an army against the Taira, and he joined him in the Genpei War. On Yoritomo's orders he attacked and killed his cousin Minamoto no Yoshinaka at the Battle of Awazu in early 1184. He then defeated the Taira at Ichi-no-Tani in March 1184 and at Yashima in March 1185, and destroyed them a month later at Dan-no-ura.

The cloistered emperor Go-Shirakawa appointed him Governor of Iyo, but Yoritomo, suspicious of him, nullified the titles. Yoshitsune obtained imperial authorisation to ally with his uncle Minamoto no Yukiie against Yoritomo, and fled Kyoto in 1185. His Koshigoe Letter of June 1185 was a final appeal of loyalty. He returned to Hiraizumi, where Hidehira's son Fujiwara no Yasuhira, under pressure from Yoritomo, surrounded his residence and forced him to commit seppuku in 1189.

Legends of Yoshitsune began to appear in the fourteenth century, and the Gikeiki tells of his life after the defeat of the Taira. His popularity gave Japanese the term hōgan-biiki, sympathy for the underdog, from his title Hōgan. According to some Ainu accounts he escaped to Hokkaido, and a later theory, popularised by Suematsu Kenchō, made him Genghis Khan; it waned after 1945. The Noh play Ataka and the kabuki play Kanjinchō draw on his story.
minangkabau-people: The Minangkabau language belongs to the Malayic subgroup of the Austronesian family and is closest to Malay, though when the two split from a common ancestor is not known. The highlands suit settlement, with fresh water, fertile soil and a cool climate, and until the twentieth century most of Sumatra's population lived there. Wet rice cultivation probably developed there long before it appeared elsewhere on the island.

Minangkabau tradition, passed down orally, says that the first Minangkabau arrived by ship and landed on Mount Marapi when it was no bigger than an egg. They then spread over the slopes and valleys of the region called the darek, made up of three luhak: Tanah Datar, Agam and Limapuluh Koto. Before Islam spread into the area in the sixteenth century, Buddhism was popular; the Padang Roco Inscription of 1286 records that an image of Avalokiteśvara was brought from Java to Dharmasraya.

The Minangkabau are regarded as the largest matrilineal society in the world. Property, family name and land pass from mother to daughter, while religious and political affairs are the responsibility of men, though some women also play important roles. The ideal is that married sisters stay in the parental home, their husbands having a visiting status, although in the 1990s the anthropologist Evelyn Blackwood found that only about 22 per cent of households in a conservative village were of this kind.

The traditional home is the rumah gadang, or big house, owned by the women of the family. Its roof curves upward in multi-tiered gables, said to imitate the horns of the water buffalo. Clan chiefs, the panghulu, give ceremonial speeches at weddings and funerals, and storytellers recite folktales called kaba to the rebab. Randai, a folk theatre combining music, dance, drama and the martial art silat, took shape early in the twentieth century.

The highlands were the seat of the Pagaruyung Kingdom and the scene of the Padri War of 1821 to 1837. Wandering abroad, called rantau, is seen by many Minangkabau as the way to maturity and success, and over half of them can be counted as living outside the homeland. They form the majority of the population of Negeri Sembilan in Malaysia and have a reputation as merchants. Overseas Minangkabau shaped language, food, music and martial arts in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. Mohammad Hatta, a co-founder of the Republic of Indonesia, Yusof Ishak, the first President of Singapore, and Tuanku Abdul Rahman, the first Yang di-Pertuan Agong of Malaysia, were all Minangkabau.
minaret-of-jam: The Ghurids controlled what is now Afghanistan in the 12th and 13th centuries, together with parts of eastern Iran, Central Asia, northern India and Pakistan. The Minaret of Jam probably stands at the site of their capital, Firozkoh. Its Arabic dating inscription is unclear, but a Kufic inscription on the north face gives the year five hundred ninety, equivalent to 27 December 1193 to 16 December 1194. The British archaeologist Ralph Pinder-Wilson believed it commemorated the victory of Mu'izz ad-Din, Ghiyath ud-Din's brother, over Prithviraj Chauhan, which opened the northern Indian subcontinent to Islam.

The minaret belongs to a group of about 60 minarets and towers built between the 11th and 13th centuries in Central Asia, Iran and Afghanistan. Some are thought to have been symbols of Islam's victory. Its architect, Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Naysaburi, is named in an inscription.

The circular tower rests on an octagonal base. It had two wooden balconies and was topped by a lantern. It is built of baked brick, stucco, terracotta and turquoise glazed tiles, and its outer face is decorated with floral and geometric designs, with bands of Kufic and Naskhi calligraphy and intersecting rhomboidal knots. Inside, a central pillar carries double spiral staircases of 159 steps each, leading up to the balconies, and above them six vaulted brick platforms.

The inscriptions include the Muslim confession of faith in the uppermost band, a verse from the surah al-Saff promising help from God and present victory, the names and titles of the Ghurid sultan Ghiyath ad-Din Muhammad bin Sam, and interlaced bands of the surah Maryam. Its form resembles the Ghazni minarets built by Masud III, and it is thought to have inspired the Qutub Minar in Delhi.

The minaret was assumed to be attached to the Friday Mosque of Firozkoh, which the chronicler Minhaj-i Siraj Juzjani says was washed away in a flash flood before the Mongol sieges of the early 13th century. Juzjani says the Mongols destroyed Firuzkuh in 1222. Sir Thomas Holdich reported the minaret in 1886 while working for the Afghan Boundary Commission, but it did not come to wide attention until 1957, through the work of the French archaeologists André Maricq and Gaston Wiet. The landscape around it holds the ruins of a palace, fortifications, a pottery kiln and a Jewish cemetery. The site was nominated in 2002 as Afghanistan's first World Heritage site.
minas-gerais: Minas Gerais, literally General Mines, lies in Brazil's Southeast Region and takes its name from the mines found across the territory. Its terrain is rugged: more than 90 per cent lies above 300 metres, and the highest point, Pico da Bandeira, reaches 2,891 metres. The state is the source of several of Brazil's main rivers, among them the São Francisco, Grande, Doce and Jequitinhonha.

The region was inhabited by Indigenous peoples as long as 11,400 to 12,000 years ago. The first European expedition crossed the north between 1553 and 1555. From the late 16th century bandeirantes from São Paulo travelled through the territory in search of gold, precious stones and Indigenous people to enslave. The discovery of gold in the late 17th century brought a large migration and wealth to the captaincy, but gold soon became scarce and many people left. Beginning in the early 1700s along the Jequitinhonha River, Minas Gerais was for about 150 years the world's major supplier of gem diamonds.

The republic was proclaimed in 1889 and Minas Gerais became a state, passing through 14 administrative periods in its first 19 months; coffee growers rose to considerable influence in state politics. Benedito Valadares governed the state from 1933 to 1945, and the Manifesto dos Mineiros of 24 October 1943 called for the democratisation of the country.

Minas Gerais is one of Brazil's 27 federative units, with Belo Horizonte as capital and largest city. Its heritage of colonial architecture and art is preserved in towns such as Ouro Preto, Diamantina, São João del-Rei, Mariana, Tiradentes and Congonhas. The Estrada Real, a tourist circuit, follows the old roads used to carry gold from the mines to Rio de Janeiro and Parati.
mincio: The Mincio is a river in the Lombardy region of northern Italy and the main outlet of Lake Garda, part of the Sarca-Mincio river system that also includes the river Sarca. It starts at the south-eastern tip of the lake at Peschiera del Garda and flows for about 65 kilometres past Mantua into the Po. From Lake Garda until it reaches Pozzolo it forms the boundary between the regions of Veneto and Lombardy.

In the Etruscan period the Mincio probably joined the river Tartaro and flowed into the Adriatic. In the Roman Republic Quintus Curius Hostilius made it flow into the Po in three branches from Mantua. These were reunited in a single embanked channel in 1198 on a project by Alberto Pitentino, and dams such as those at Ponte dei Mulini in Mantua and at Governolo were built to make the river navigable, to protect Mantua from the flooding of the Po and to improve the air. Its former lower course ran to the Adriatic near Adria until a breach at Cucca in 589, roughly along the line of the Canal Bianco.

At Mantua the river was widened in the late 12th century to form a series of three lakes, originally four, that skirt the old city. The first settlement there, from about 2000 BCE, stood on an island in the Mincio. In 452 CE Attila the Hun received near the river an embassy sent by the Western Roman Emperor Valentinian III and led by Pope Leo I, after which he withdrew from Italy. The last act of Verdi's opera Rigoletto is set at an inn on the banks of the Mincio just outside Mantua.
mindanao: Mindanao covers 97,530 square kilometres and is mountainous; Mount Apo is its highest peak and the highest in the Philippines. Four seas surround it: the Sulu Sea to the west, the Philippine Sea to the east, the Celebes Sea to the south and the Mindanao Sea to the north. The upland plateaus of Bukidnon and Lanao del Sur hold Lake Lanao, the largest lake on the island, and two large lowlands lie in the valleys of the Agusan River and the Rio Grande de Mindanao. The name comes from the Maguindanao language: min, a past-tense prefix, and danao, 'lake'.

Archaeological finds show human activity about ten thousand years ago, and Austronesian peoples spread through the Philippines around 1500 BCE. Caves in the Zamboanga Peninsula held burial jars, celadons of the Yuan and Ming periods and gold ornaments, which point to long trade between the Subanon and the Chinese. From about 900 CE the people of Mindanao were strongly influenced by Hindu and Buddhist belief from Indonesia and Malaysia, and the island has yielded a golden kinnara and a Ganesha pendant.

Islam spread in the Philippines from the 14th century through merchants from the western Malay Archipelago, and the first mosque in the country was built in the mid-14th century at Simunul. About the 16th century the sultanates of Sulu, Lanao and Maguindanao grew out of earlier Hindu-Buddhist rajahnates. In 1521 Antonio Pigafetta, who sailed with Magellan, wrote of reaching the island. In 1898 Spain sold the archipelago to the United States for 20 million dollars. Settlers from Luzon and the Visayas were encouraged to move to Mindanao in the early 1900s, and settlement displaced the Blaan and Tboli. Japanese forces invaded in April 1942 and burned many towns.

Mindanao is divided into six administrative regions, and its largest cities include Davao City, Zamboanga City, Cagayan de Oro and General Santos. Dozens of languages are spoken, of which Cebuano has the most speakers. Most residents are Christian, and Muslims form the largest minority. The island is a major supplier of pineapples and bananas.
mindaugas: Little is known of Mindaugas's origins or rise to power. Contemporary sources are scarce, and the main ones, the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle and the Hypatian Codex, were produced by enemies of Lithuania and lack dates and places even for major events. A treaty with Galicia-Volhynia in 1219 lists Mindaugas and his brother Dausprungas among the elder dukes of Lithuania, and the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle describes him as ruler of all Lithuania in 1236.

Ruthenian chronicles say he murdered or expelled several dukes, including relatives. The historian S. C. Rowell described his rise as taking place through marriage, murder and military conquest. During the 1230s and 1240s he extended his power over Black Ruthenia and the Principality of Polotsk and made his seat at Navahrudak.

In 1249 war broke out when Mindaugas tried to seize the lands of his nephews Tautvilas and Edivydas and of Duke Vykintas of Samogitia, who allied with the Livonian Order and Daniel of Galicia. Mindaugas bribed the Order's Master, Andreas von Stierland, and agreed to be baptised as a Catholic and to give up some western lands, in return for Pope Innocent IV's recognition as king. He and his wife Morta were crowned in the summer of 1253.

About eight years of relative peace followed. Mindaugas made peace with Galicia-Volhynia, began a court, an administration and a diplomatic service, issued silver coins and sponsored a cathedral in Vilnius. Lithuanian rule in the west stayed weak, and the Livonian Order's government of Samogitian lands was seen as oppressive. In 1261 Mindaugas broke the peace with the Order and may have returned to paganism, though the accounts of this come from enemies.

After Morta died, Mindaugas took her sister, who was already married to Duke Daumantas of Pskov. In retaliation Daumantas and Mindaugas's nephew Treniota killed him and two of his sons in the autumn of 1263. Lithuania fell into disorder, and three of his successors were assassinated within seven years. Stability returned under Traidenis, grand duke from about 1270.

Mindaugas's standing was uncertain until the Lithuanian national revival of the 19th century. He is now generally considered the founder of the Lithuanian state. In the 1990s Edvardas Gudavičius argued for an exact coronation date, 6 July 1253. It is disputed, but it is now Statehood Day, a national holiday.
mindelheim: Mindelheim lies on the river Mindel, about 90 kilometres (56 miles) west of Munich, and is the capital of the Unterallgäu district. Memmingen and the spa towns of Bad Grönenbach, Ottobeuren and Bad Wörishofen are nearby. At various points in its history it was the chief settlement of a state of its own.

In 1365 the Dukes of Teck-Owen came into possession of Mindelheim. The last of that line, Louis of Teck, Patriarch of Aquileia from 1412, died in 1439. An Elector of Bavaria bought the town in the sixteenth century, and in 1704 it was confiscated from Elector Maximilian II Emanuel for his treachery and effectively occupied after the Battle of Blenheim.

On 18 November 1705 Emperor Joseph I made John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough, Prince of Mindelheim, and Marlborough was invested at an Imperial Diet in Innsbruck on 24 May 1706. The principality lay south of the Danube, 45 km south-west of Augsburg, and covered about 15 square miles (39 km2), with an income of £2,000. Marlborough's investiture cost was reduced to £4,500 from the usual £12–15,000, and he avoided the wartime imperial tax of £6,000.

The King of Prussia, through the prince of Anhalt-Dessau, proposed that the title pass to all of Marlborough's heirs, but the princes opposed it, and no special remainder was provided. Marlborough visited in late May 1713 and received princely honours. The principality's fate depended on the peace, and under the Treaty of Utrecht Mindelheim was lost in 1714 to the Elector of Bavaria.

The town centre keeps the plan of a medieval settlement, with the town hall and churches around a central market square and parts of the old wall and gates still standing. The castle Mindelburg, with its donjon, is used for festivals and markets. The town has a museum of historic tower clocks and a museum of ethnic art.
minden: The town centre lies on a plateau on the western side of the Weser, 5 kilometres north of the Porta Westfalica gap between the Weser Hills and the Wiehen Hills, where the river leaves the Weser Uplands and flows into the North German Plain. The small Bastau stream joins the Weser from the west near the centre, and the edge of the plateau divides the upper town from the lower town. Routes from the south converged at the gap and met a west to east way and a ford across the river.

The name Minda first appears in the Royal Frankish Annals, in a record of an army assembly held by Charlemagne in 798. A permanent Frankish camp and a royal estate are supposed to have stood close by. The bishopric, founded around 800, was one of seven diocesan foundations of Charlemagne's rule. After the dissolution of the Duchy of Saxony in 1180 the bishop became sovereign of the Prince-Bishopric of Minden, which remained a territory of the Holy Roman Empire until 1648.

The Lutheran Reformation was introduced in 1529, during a vacancy after the death of Bishop Francis of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, and the buildings of the dissolved Dominican convent became the first Protestant Gymnasium in Westphalia. Minden kept fortifications from the 15th century to the late 19th, and the fortress was dissolved in 1873. French troops occupied the town on 13 November 1806, and when they left on 3 November 1813 they blew up some arches of the Weser bridge. A Jewish community has existed since 1270. Between 1603 and 1684 there were 128 prosecutions for witchcraft, almost all of the accused women.

Minden is the capital of the district of Minden-Lübbecke in North Rhine-Westphalia. Its cathedral dates to the 11th century, with a Romanesque westwerk and an early Gothic nave of the 13th century; it was badly damaged by bombing in the Second World War and rebuilt by 1957. The town has been the terminus of one of the oldest German railway trunks since 1847, and the Mittelland Canal crosses the Weser here on an aqueduct.
mindon-min: Mindon was born Maung Lwin, a son of Tharrawaddy Min and Chandra Mata Mahay, and studied at the Maha Zawtika monastic college in Amarapura until the age of 23. By 1853 Burma had lost Arakan and the Irrawaddy Delta to the British, who blockaded it, cutting its trade through ports. Under his half-brother Pagan Min, Mindon presided over the Council of State when the Second Anglo-Burmese War began. He opposed continuing the war, and his closest ally was his brother Kanaung Mintha.

In November 1852 a plot to implicate Mindon and Kanaung in a series of robberies sent them and their followers fleeing to Shwebo, the seat of their ancestor Alaungpaya. The court of Pagan Min collapsed, and the brothers entered the capital, Ava, unopposed. Mindon was enthroned on 18 February 1853, and a ceasefire with the British took effect on 30 June 1853.

Mindon ruled jointly with Kanaung, whom he named heir and put in charge of technology, modernisation and the arts. A revolt at Kanpyin and attacks from Siam troubled his first months; in the end he sent 3,000 cavalry supported by artillery, which stopped the Siamese encroachment. Scholars were sent to France, Italy, the United States and Great Britain to learn from the Industrial Revolution. His reforms centralised the administration, paid officials salaries, fixed judicial fees, reorganised finances, removed customs duties and modernised the army and police.

The marble slabs of the Pali canon were each housed in a small stupa at the Kuthodaw Pagoda at the foot of Mandalay Hill. In 1871 he donated a new hti to the Shwedagon Pagoda, though he was not allowed to visit it, and in 1873 he enacted the Seventeen Articles, one of the first indigenous press freedom laws in Southeast Asia. He supported Buddhist monasteries but was also tolerant: he sent his son Thibaw Min to a missionary school.

In 1866 two of his sons, Prince Myingun and Prince Myingundaing, attempted a palace coup in which Kanaung was killed. Mindon escaped, and Myingun fled by steamer to British Burma. The revolt made Mindon reluctant to name a new heir for fear of civil war.

In his last days his queen Hsinbyumashin dominated the court. By her edict nearly all possible heirs were put to death, so that her daughter Supayalat and son-in-law Thibaw could rule. Thibaw, a son of a lesser queen, succeeded in 1878 and was defeated by the British in the Third Anglo-Burmese War in November 1885, which ended in the total annexation of Burma.
mindoro: Mindoro has a land area of 10,571 square kilometres and lies off the south-western coast of Luzon and north-east of Palawan. It is divided into the provinces of Occidental Mindoro and Oriental Mindoro, and Calapan is its only city. The Mindoro Mountain Range runs 200 km north to south, and Mount Halcon in Oriental Mindoro is the highest point. During the Pleistocene, when lower sea levels joined most Philippine islands, the deeper channels around Mindoro kept it isolated, and the island has a large number of species found nowhere else in the archipelago, including the Mindoro dwarf buffalo, the tamaraw.

The name probably comes from Minolo, the native name recorded by Domingo Navarette in 1676, though the Spaniards also called the island Mina de Oro, gold mine. Han Chinese traders knew it as Ma-i or Mait. According to the historian William Henry Scott, the official history of the Song dynasty for the year 972 mentions Ma-i as a state that traded with China, and later Chinese records refer to it. Its traders exchanged beeswax, cotton, true pearls, tortoiseshell and betel nuts for Chinese porcelain, gold, iron pots, lead, copper, glass beads and iron needles. The Mangyans are the indigenous peoples.

The Sultanate of Brunei conquered the island and there were Moro settlements before the Spanish arrived and converted the population to Christianity. Wars between the Spaniards and Moros from Mindanao, who sought to enslave the converted people, then depopulated the island. Most of the population fled to nearby Batangas, and the once-rich towns fell into ruin. Mindoro joined the Philippine Revolution in 1898 and was the site of a battle in the Second World War. It was a single province from 1920 to 1950, when a referendum split it into its present two.

About 1.4 million people live on the island. Tagalog is the principal language, and indigenous Mangyan languages such as Iraya, Buhid, Tawbuid and Hanuno'o are also spoken. Christianity is the main religion, while the Mangyans are animists. The economy rests chiefly on farming, and only about 5 per cent of the original forest remains. Puerto Galera is its best-known tourist destination.
minerva: Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom, justice, law, victory and the sponsor of arts, trade and strategy. Her Etruscan form is Menrva, and it is disputed whether the Romans borrowed her from the Etruscans or the reverse. Varro attributed Sabine origins to her. She may have taken her place in the Capitoline Triad, with Jupiter and Juno, under Etruscan influence, since the Etruscans had a similar group of Tinia, Uni and Menrva. From the second century BCE the Romans equated her with Athena.

Excavations at a sanctuary in Lavinium found terracotta statues of Minerva from the 4th century BCE, with votive figures of girls and veiled women, swaddled infants and anatomical offerings. The archaeologist Fritz Graf concludes that she guarded young women in the passage to marriage and motherhood.

Minerva is a virgin goddess whose domain includes medicine, wisdom, commerce, weaving and the crafts. She is also a goddess of war, but of strategy rather than the violence of Mars. She is usually shown tall and armed, with a spear, and her sacred creature is the owl. Roman myth gives her the stories of Athena. She was born fully armed from the head of Jupiter, whom Vulcan split with a hammer. She made the olive tree in her contest with Neptune over the naming of Athens, and she turned the weaver Arachne into a spider after a contest. She is thought to have invented the flute, which she threw away because it puffed out her cheeks.

Her festival, the Quinquatria, ran from 19 to 23 March and was a holiday for artisans. According to Ovid the first day was her birthday, with no blood shed, and the next four days had games with drawn swords. A smaller festival of the flute-players was held on the Ides of June. According to Livy the annual nail marking the year was driven into her temple because she was thought to have invented numbers.

In Roman Britain carpenters owned tools decorated with her image for protection. At Bath she was equated with the Celtic goddess Sulis, and the two names were used together or interchangeably for the deity of the hot springs, whose healing was thought to cure ailments such as rheumatism.
mines-and-works-act-1911: The Mines and Works Act, 1911, Act No. 12 of 1911, was enacted to set out the duties and responsibilities of workers in mines and works. It did not specify that Black South Africans should be discriminated against in any way; indeed it made no mention of race or colour, nor did it clearly give the government Mining Engineer powers to introduce a legal colour bar. Under section 4(n), however, it gave the Governor-General powers to grant, cancel and suspend certificates of competency for mine managers, overseers, surveyors, mechanical engineers, engine-drivers and miners entitled to blast, and to decide which other occupations required such certificates.

The colour bar came through the regulations. A commission that had criticised mine managements for employing large numbers of unskilled whites nonetheless submitted, when it reported in 1910, draft regulations heavy with colour bars. The words white person were written into the definitions of banksman, onsetter, ganger and mine manager; only whites were to be employed in blasting, running elevators, driving engines and supervising boilers and other machinery, or as shift boss and mine overseer; and only whites could obtain the certificates of competence required of engine drivers and boiler attendants. With some changes these drafts became the Mines and Works Regulations, 1912.

The Mines and Works Amendment Act, 1926, Act No. 25 of 1926, placed Coloured workers beside whites in a position of privilege. Its key section required the minister, before announcing regulations for certificates of competency, including the blasting certificate, to seek through advisory committees the advice of the owners and of the organisations whose members held most of the certificates, that is, the white unions.

The act, with or without its amendments, is sometimes called the Colour Bar or the Colour Bar Act, though the term colour bar usually refers to a wider group of labour practices, informal trade union practices, government regulations and laws, developed over time to keep Black workers from competing for jobs monopolised by whites. Further amending acts followed in 1931 and 1934. The Mines and Works Act, 1956 then repealed the earlier acts and their amendments; it still empowered the Governor-General to make regulations on certificates of competency for persons other than Black workers.
ming-empire: The Mongol-led Yuan dynasty ruled before the Ming. Explanations for its decline include discrimination against the Han people, overtaxation of areas hit by inflation, and massive flooding of the Yellow River after irrigation projects were abandoned. Rebellion broke out among the peasants called up to repair the levees, and a number of Han groups revolted, among them the Red Turbans in 1351. Zhu Yuanzhang, a penniless peasant and Buddhist monk, joined the Red Turbans in 1352, and in 1356 his force captured Nanjing, which he later made the capital. As the Hongwu Emperor (r. 1368–1398) he kept a standing army of over one million troops.

The Jianwen Emperor (r. 1398–1402) came to the throne after the Hongwu Emperor's death, and when he moved against his uncle Zhu Di a three-year civil war followed. The palace at Nanjing was burned, and Zhu Di took the throne as the Yongle Emperor (r. 1402–1424). He made Beijing a capital, built the Forbidden City, and sent the eunuch Zheng He on seven voyages into the Indian Ocean as far as Arabia and eastern Africa.

In July 1449 the Oirat leader Esen Tayisi invaded and captured the Zhengtong Emperor on 8 September, an event known as the Tumu Crisis. The navy was then allowed to fall into disrepair, while forced labour fortified the Great Wall into its modern form. In the 16th century European trade, restricted to islands near Guangzhou such as Macau, brought maize, potatoes and chili peppers and a large influx of South American silver, which re-monetised an economy whose paper money was no longer trusted.

A slowdown in agriculture during the Little Ice Age, a rise in the value of silver, crop failure, floods and an epidemic undermined the dynasty. Meanwhile Nurhaci, a Ming vassal, united the Jurchen clans into a Manchu identity and in 1618 renounced Ming overlordship. The dynasty collapsed in 1644 when the rebel Li Zicheng entered Beijing. His Shun dynasty was defeated shortly afterwards by the Manchu-led armies of the Qing dynasty, with the help of the defecting Ming general Wu Sangui, and remnant regimes called the Southern Ming lasted until 1662.
ming-rui: Mingrui, courtesy name Yunting, was born in 1730 into the Fuca clan of the Manchu Bordered Yellow Banner. His father was Fuwen, Duke Cheng'en, his grandfather Lirongbao, a high official under the Kangxi Emperor, and his uncles included Fuheng. His aunt was Empress Xiaoxianchun, the consort of the Qianlong Emperor.

In 1756 the Qianlong Emperor gave him a command, with the rank of vice commander-in-chief, in the campaign against Amursana. For his part in it he was made vice minister of the Ministry of Revenue and a military advisor, and the honorific Yiyong was added to his ducal title. In 1759 he campaigned against Khoja Kalan; on his return the emperor had his portrait displayed in the Ziguang Hall, and he was made commander-in-chief of the Han Bordered White Banner.

From October 1762 to March 1767 he was the first General of Ili. When the Uyghurs of Uqturpan rebelled in 1765 under the minor beg Laiheimutula, Mingrui directed the campaign from the rear while his deputy Guanyinbao led the troops, and together they encircled and defeated the rebels.

The border war with the Konbaung dynasty of Burma had by then cost the lives of two Qing commanders: Liu Zao killed himself after repeated defeats, and his successor Yang Yingju was ordered to take his own life. In March 1767 Mingrui became Viceroy of Yun-Gui and Minister of War. He planned for his main force to advance through Wanting and Mobang while Deputy Commander E'erdeng'e took a northern route from Mengmi, the two to converge on Ava.

In December 1767 he reached Wanting and took Mobang, then led more than 10,000 troops against Manjie, where 20,000 Burmese held 16 stockades behind trenches, palisades and war elephants. He was wounded in the eye but went on commanding, and the stockades fell when the elephants stampeded into the Burmese ranks. His army was destroyed at the Battle of Maymyo in March 1768, and he killed himself on 27 March, sending his queue to the emperor as a token of loyalty. The Qianlong Emperor had E'erdeng'e put to death by slicing for failing to reach the rendezvous, and wrote a poem in Mingrui's honour.
ming-sheng: Ming Sheng was the son of Ming Yuzhen, a leader of the Red Turban Rebellions and founder of Ming Xia in Sichuan. Ming Yuzhen died in 1366, possibly killed by his younger brother, who was in turn killed by Ming Sheng's mother, née Peng. She then acted as regent for her son, who was proclaimed the Lesser Lord of Radiance, a title with Manichean associations close to the Lesser Prince of Radiance used by the rebel leader Han Lin'er.

His father had held the government together, but after his death the court split and regional generals acted on their own; Wu Youren of Baoning invaded Chongqing and executed the men who had killed his fellow general Wan Sheng. The court still kept to Ming Yuzhen's defensive foreign policy, and Ming Sheng stressed his father's precedent to secure his legitimacy. An edict issued on his accession prayed for a long-lasting Mandate of Heaven and alluded to the Duke of Zhou, regent for King Cheng of Zhou, as his mother was for him.

In 1365 Zhu Yuanzhang, the future founder of the Ming dynasty, had sent the governor of Huguang, Yang Jing, with a favourable offer of surrender, and received no reply. In 1367 Zhu had a Xia envoy watch the army of general Xu Da, hoping to frighten Ming Xia into submission, but the Xia only strengthened their defences.

During the Ming conquest of Sichuan in 1371, Ming Sheng fell into the hands of a force under Tang He and Liao Yongzhong and was brought to Nanjing in August. Made Marquis Returned to Righteousness, he lived in comfort alongside Chen Li, son of the rebel Chen Youliang, until both became rallying points for those discontented with the Ming. The Hongwu Emperor then asked King Gongmin of Goryeo to take them, and they were sent to Korea, where he was known as Myŏng Sŭng.

In March 1373 he married the daughter of the Goryeo official Yun Hŭi-chong, and at Hongwu's request his family was given farmland and freed from taxes and corvée labour. King Taejo, founder of Joseon, confirmed these privileges. His descendants in Pyongyang and Yeonju lost them after the Qing invasion of 1636, regained them later that year, and lost them for good in 1655.
ming-treasure-voyages: The Yongle Emperor, Zhu Di, who took the throne on 17 July 1402, inherited a powerful navy from his father, the Hongwu Emperor, and developed it as an instrument of an expansive overseas policy. In 1403 the provincial governments of Fujian, Jiangxi, Zhejiang and Huguang and the garrisons of Nanjing, Suzhou and other cities were ordered to begin building ships. The Taizong Shilu records orders pointing to at least 2,868 ships between 1403 and 1419. The fleet sailed from the Longjiang shipyard down the Yangtze, and waited at Changle in Fujian for the winter monsoon before putting to sea.

Six of the seven voyages fell in the Yongle Emperor's reign and the seventh in the reign of the Xuande Emperor. The order for the first was issued in 1405, addressed to Zheng He, Wang Jinghong and others, to lead 27,000 troops. The first three voyages reached Calicut on India's Malabar Coast, the fourth went as far as Hormuz in the Persian Gulf, and the last three reached the Arabian Peninsula and East Africa. The port of Qui Nhon in Champa was always the first foreign destination.

The fleet was heavily militarised and carried great treasures, including gifts for rulers, goods for exchange and Chinese monopolies such as silk, ceramics and musk. Along the way it destroyed the pirate fleet of Chen Zuyi at Palembang, captured the Sinhalese king Alakeshvara of Kotte, and defeated the Semudera pretender Sekandar in northern Sumatra. It brought home ambassadors whose rulers agreed to be tributaries of China, and goods that included spices, ivory, pepper and animals such as giraffes and ostriches. On 14 May 1421 the emperor suspended the voyages for his campaigns against the Mongols.

The voyages ended in 1433. Why is not exactly known. Duyvendak suggested heavy costs played a part, but Ray, Finlay and Dreyer note that the costs did not overburden the treasury, and Ray held that the voyages were profitable. The eunuch establishment that led the fleet depended on imperial favour, while civil officials, who disliked the expense and the trade in foreign goods, gained the upper hand.

Ming China had become the pre-eminent naval power of the early 15th century. Historians still debate the purpose of the voyages, the size of the ships and fleet, the routes and the cargo. First-hand accounts survive from Ma Huan, Fei Xin and Gong Zhen, who sailed on the voyages.
ming-yuzhen: Ming Yuzhen came from a family of landowners in the village of Meiqiu in Sui County, in present-day Hubei. He served as an officer of the local militia, commanding patrolling archers, and when the Red Turban Rebellion broke out the village council entrusted him with the defence of the town. Around 1352 he joined the rebels and rose quickly in the Red Army of the Song state, known to historians as Tianwan, serving under Ni Wenjun.

Sent to find food for the army in 1357, he led the Song fleet up the Yangtze from Yiling and took Chongqing, whose defence was weakened by a feud between the Yuan garrison commander Yang Han and the provincial governor Öljeitu. Xu Shouhui made him governor of Sichuan, where he fought Yuan forces based at Jiading and Chengdu until 1360 and turned back an invasion by the Green Turban Army of Li Xixi in 1358. When Chen Youliang seized power, Ming warned Xu of him, and after learning of Xu's murder he recalled the troops he had sent to help Chen against Zhu Yuanzhang and cut all ties with Chen.

In 1360 he declared himself King of Longshu, and in 1362, urged by his chief minister Liu Zhen, emperor of the Great Xia. He held Jiezhou in southern Gansu but failed against Hanzhong, and in 1363 his minister Wan Sheng took Zhongqing, present-day Kunming, before the Yuan armies drove the Xia back from Yunnan. He then built a government on the Rites of Zhou and, from 1363, on Yuan offices such as the Central Secretariat, calling himself the Lord of Light while supporting Confucianism, which won him the trust of the people and the gentry.

He died of illness in 1366 and was succeeded by his nine-year-old son, Ming Sheng. The ministers Wan Sheng and Dai Shou fought for control of the young emperor, and Wan was killed; in 1367 the official Wu Youren rose against Dai, and the two came to terms. Without firm leadership the Xia waited on events, and the Ming dynasty, founded by Zhu Yuanzhang in 1368, conquered Sichuan in 1371 without facing any major obstacles.
mingun-pahtodawgyi: King Bodawpaya supervised the work himself from an observation post on an island off Mingun, and the project is often seen as an expression of his eccentricities. The labour came from thousands of prisoners of war from Arakan: some 20,000 people were deported to central Burma as slaves to build the stupa. The work weighed heavily on the population and the state, and it is said that a prophecy was spread to play on the king's superstition, warning that the country would be gone as soon as the pagoda was finished.

In another version of the story the king himself would die once the work was done, so building was slowed, and when Bodawpaya died the project stopped altogether. The ruin was left deliberately unfinished at about 50 metres. A small model nearby, the Pon Daw Pagoda, shows the 150-metre temple that was planned, following the practice of other great projects such as the Shwedagon Pagoda and the Thatbyinnyu Temple.

An earthquake on 23 March 1839 opened large cracks across the face of the brickwork. The monument now draws visitors more than worshippers, though a small shrine with an image of the Buddha is still used for prayer and meditation. Bodawpaya also had the Mingun Bell cast to go with the stupa. It weighs 90 tons, given in Burmese measure as 55,555 viss, a figure remembered by the phrase Min Hpyu Hman Hman Pyaw, whose consonants stand for the number five in Burmese numerology. Mingun is reached by ferry across the Irrawaddy from Mandalay.
mingyi-nyo: Mingyi Nyo was born in 1459 to Maha Thinkhaya, a descendant of Kyawswa I of Pinya, and Min Hla Nyet, daughter of Sithu Kyawhtin, most likely at Ava, where his grandfather served at the court of Thihathura I until he became viceroy of Toungoo in 1470. After Sithu Kyawhtin's death in 1481 the viceroyship passed to his son Min Sithu, who repeatedly refused Nyo's requests to marry his cousin Soe Min Hteik-Tin. Nyo murdered his uncle, married his cousin and seized power around April 1485.

King Minkhaung II of Ava, facing his brother Minye Kyawswa's rebellion at Yamethin, accepted a gift of two young elephants and recognised Nyo as governor, and Toungoo fought for Ava for the rest of the 1490s. Nyo built the fortified city of Dwayawaddy on 11 November 1491. A raid into Hanthawaddy without Ava's leave, in which he killed the Shan governor of Kaungbya in single combat, brought a Hanthawaddy force of 16,000 that besieged Dwayawaddy in late 1495; Toungoo barely survived, and Nyo never again fought his southern neighbour.

After Minkhaung II died in April 1501, Nyo sheltered those who had tried to kill the new king, Shwenankyawshin, who sought his loyalty in 1502 with a royal bride and the Kyaukse granary. Nyo took Kyaukse, moved many of its people to his capital and joined the rebel princes of Nyaungyan and Prome. In 1510 he founded Ketumati, the present Toungoo, and he was crowned king on 11 April 1511. Ava besieged Toungoo for a month in 1525 without success. When the Confederation of Shan States took Ava in March 1527, he laid waste the land between them to make it impassable.

He died on 24 November 1530 and was succeeded by his son Tabinshwehti. Cut off from the Irrawaddy valley between the Bago Yoma and the Karen hill country, Toungoo had been one of the few stable states of Upper Burma, and the refugees it drew gave Tabinshwehti and his deputy Bayinnaung the manpower to imagine offensive war against larger kingdoms.
mingyi-swa: Mingyi Swa was born in Pegu (Bago) in 1558, the first son of Crown Prince Nanda and his chief consort Hanthawaddy Mibaya, and grew up while his grandfather King Bayinnaung built the largest empire in Southeast Asia. Bayinnaung died on 10 October 1581, and five days later the new king made Swa heir apparent. The empire had been held together by the vassals' personal loyalty to Bayinnaung, and within three years both Ava (Inwa) and Siam revolted.

Swa was guarding Pegu in 1584 when Crown Prince Naresuan refused his orders and declared Ayutthaya's independence. The expedition sent after the Siamese was caught in the flooded country by the Chao Phraya and nearly destroyed. In 1586 Swa led an army from Lan Na into northern Siam but could not pass the fortified town of Lampang. He invaded again from Lan Na in November 1590; this time his army of some 20,000 was routed outside Lampang in March 1591, and his father rebuked him and executed several of his generals.

His personal life also strained the court. He spent much time pursuing his half-aunt, Princess Yaza Datu Kalaya, and in 1583 his first wife, his double cousin Natshin Medaw, complained bitterly to her parents, a quarrel that led to the Ava rebellion of 1584. While Nanda was away in 1586, Swa forcibly made Yaza Datu Kalaya his wife and divorced Natshin Medaw.

In November 1592 Swa led a fifth invasion with 24,000 men and reached the neighbourhood of Ayutthaya. The accounts of his death differ. The Burmese chronicles say an elephant in musth drove his own mount into the open, where he was felled by a mortar round, and that his mahout hid his death until the battle ended. The Ayutthaya chronicle tells of single combat in which Naresuan struck him down. The historian B. J. Terwiel, comparing ten accounts, judged the formal duel a legend. All agree the Burmese then retreated, and Siam's independence was secured. Swa's body was cremated with high honours at Pegu.
minh-huong: The Minh Hương were among the first ethnic Han to settle in southern Vietnam. Some 3,000 Ming refugees, fiercely loyal to the fallen dynasty and opposed to the Qing, came to Vietnam at the end of the Ming. Most were soldiers and single men, and they married Vietnamese women. Their descendants identified strongly as Han despite their Vietnamese mothers, and unlike later Han migrants of the Qing period they did not wear the Manchu hairstyle.

After the Qing conquest of China proper, Han leaders who refused to submit, among them Mạc Cửu, Trần Thượng Xuyên and Dương Ngạn Địch, reached the Mekong Delta and set up polities of their own at Hà Tiên, Biên Hòa and Mỹ Tho. They later submitted to the Nguyễn lords, who gave them noble titles and protection against threats from the Khmer and Siam. Many Minh Hương, such as Trịnh Hoài Đức and Ngô Nhân Tịnh, became ministers of the Nguyễn and took an important part in the exploration and settlement of the Mekong Delta.

Their name was first written with characters meaning those who worship Ming ancestors, and in 1827 the Minh Mạng Emperor ordered it written with characters meaning of Ming origin. In the records of the Nguyễn dynasty they were called Minh nhân or Minh Hương, to set them apart from the Thanh nhân, Han people from Qing China. From 1829 they were treated as Vietnamese rather than Han, and they were not allowed to travel to China or to wear the Manchu queue.

The Minh Hương often married Viet people, and most have adopted Vietnamese culture. Unlike later waves of Han immigrants, they are counted by the Vietnamese government as Kinh rather than Hoa, and they overwhelmingly identify themselves as Kinh. Among those of Minh Hương descent were the rulers of the Principality of Hà Tiên, Mạc Cửu and Mạc Thiên Tứ, the 18th-century scholar Võ Trường Toản, and Phan Thanh Giản and Trần Tiễn Thành, mandarins in the reign of Tự Đức.
minh-mang: Minh Mạng was born Nguyễn Phúc Đảm on 25 May 1791 at Gia Định, during the Second Tây Sơn–Nguyễn War. He was the fourth son of Nguyễn Phúc Ánh, the future Emperor Gia Long, and his second wife Trần Thị Đang. At the age of three he was taken in and raised by Gia Long's first wife, the Empress Thừa Thiên, under a written agreement between her and Gia Long. After her death in 1814 Gia Long insisted that Đảm, as her son, perform the funeral duties instead of her grandson, despite opposition from mandarins. In 1816 he appointed Đảm his heir apparent, and the prince began assisting him with documents and affairs of state.

He became emperor on 14 February 1820. A cholera epidemic reached Vietnam that summer and removed 206,835 taxpayers from the registers. He continued his father's reorganisation of the administration, with highways, a postal service, public food storehouses and monetary and agrarian reforms. He further centralised government, and in 1839 introduced salaries and pensions for princes and mandarins in place of fief estates. About 200 rebellions were recorded in his twenty-year reign. The largest, led by Lê Văn Khôi, broke out in July 1833 after Minh Mạng had the late viceroy Lê Văn Duyệt posthumously indicted; Khôi gained Siamese support, and Saigon fell in September 1835, when rebel commanders were put to death.

Minh Mạng was wary of Europe and refused the trade and diplomatic offers of France, Britain and the United States. In 1825 he banned Christian missionaries, and between 1833 and 1838 seven were sentenced to death, among them Pierre Borie, Joseph Marchand and Jean-Charles Cornay. He annexed Muang Phuan as Tran Ninh prefecture in 1832, completed the conquest of Champa, and incorporated Cambodia as the province of Tây Thành in 1834, then tried to impose Vietnamese culture there. A war with Siam over Cambodia was fought in 1833 and 1834. In 1827 he barred recently arrived Chinese of the Qing period from the bureaucracy, the rice monopoly and foreign trade.

Minh Mạng died on 20 January 1841. He was known for his scholarship, his poetry and his close attention to detail, which astonished his contemporaries, and he took an interest in Western mechanics, weaponry and navigation. He is reported to have fathered 142 children by 43 wives, and he set a poem from which his descendants' generation names were drawn. His son Thiệu Trị succeeded him. Later European demands on the pretext of the treatment of Catholic priests led, in the account given, to gunboat diplomacy and eventually to French colonisation.
minho-river: The Minho, or Miño in Spanish and Galician, is the longest river in Galicia, with a length of 340 km. By discharge it is the fourth largest river of the Iberian Peninsula after the Douro, Ebro and Tagus. It rises at Pedregal de Irimia in the Sierra de Meira, north of Lugo, about 695 metres above sea level. The lagoon Fonminhá was historically, and wrongly, regarded as its source. After about 73 km it passes just south of the walls of the Roman city of Lugo and flows south through canyons until the valley widens north of Ourense.

The name is recorded as Minius and Mineus and is thought to derive from an Indo-European root meaning to walk or go. The river receives its main tributary, the Sil, at Os Peares, about 20 km north of Ourense. After 260 km through Galicia it forms part of the border between Spain and Portugal for about 80 km, running mainly west. It reaches the Atlantic between A Guarda in Galicia and Caminha in Portugal.

The river has been dammed for hydroelectric power in a series of reservoirs from Portomarín to Frieira, and it also waters vineyards and farmland. Its lower valley is lush and green, producing corn, potatoes, cabbage and even kiwi fruit, with vines along the field edges. These vines yield the light, slightly sparkling Vinho Verde and the Ribeiro wine, and the best wine of the area, Alvarinho or Albariño, comes from around Monção, Arbo and Melgaço.

The medieval towns of Melgaço and Monção stand on the Portuguese bank. The Spanish town of Tui and the Portuguese Valença do Minho face each other across the river and guarded an important bridge for road and rail, and both preserve fortifications that are national monuments. The upper course has been declared a Biosphere Reserve. Oral tradition tells of mythological beings living in the basin, such as witches in the river and fish-men.
minie-rifle: The rifle took its name from the Minié ball, a bullet invented in 1849 by the French Army captain Claude-Étienne Minié of the Chasseurs d'Orléans and Henri-Gustave Delvigne. A version of the rifle was adopted in Britain for a short time in 1851, while the French Army adopted it officially only in 1857. Until then the smoothbore musket, often loaded with buck and ball, had been the only practical field weapon. Rifled muskets had existed since the Renaissance, but their bullets had to be hammered into the bore with a ramrod and mallet, and the short-lived carabine à tige system was hard to clean with the black powders of the period.
