The bullet was a conical-cylindrical piece of soft lead, slightly smaller than the bore, with three grease-filled grooves and a conical hollow in its base. On firing, the expanding gas spread the skirted base into the rifling, giving spin for accuracy, a better seal for longer range and a cleaner barrel. In a test at Vincennes in 1849 it passed through two boards of poplar at 15 yards. The large, easily deformed bullets, 14 to 18 mm across, caused terrible wounds.

The British Army used the Pattern 1851 Minié rifle from 1851 to 1855; built to a Belgian design with the approval of the Duke of Wellington, 34,000 were made. At the outbreak of the Crimean War neutral Prussia converted 300,000 older muskets for Minié-type ammunition. Similar rifles firing Minié bullets, such as the Pattern 1853 Enfield, the Springfield Model 1861 and the Lorenz rifle, were the main infantry weapons of the American Civil War. In Japan the Tokugawa shogunate and the Chōshū and Satsuma forces imported Minié rifles from 1862, and the fully equipped Chōshū troops won early victories in the Boshin War (1868–1869).

It is often said that the muzzle-loading Minié became obsolete in the Second Schleswig War of 1864, when Danes armed with it were beaten by Prussians carrying the bolt-action Dreyse rifle, and again in the Austro-Prussian War. Yet the Dreyse leaked gas and lost range, and the Bavarian army used the longer reach of its rifled muskets well, so the question is debated. In France existing Minié rifles were converted to breech-loading Tabatière (snuff-box) rifles, and the Chassepot that soon followed, with greater range and rate of fire, arguably ended the type.
ministerialis: The Latin word ministerialis meant at first simply a servant or agent. The origin of the class is obscure: one medieval chronicler traced it to Julius Caesar, who was said to have given Roman citizenship to the lesser knights of his Germanic allies. The first ministerials authoritatively recorded are the household serfs whom Abbot Adalard of Corbie, adviser to Emperor Charlemagne, praised in his De ordine palatii, and who trained their own successors. Lords needed such men because free nobles disliked entering servile relationships with other nobles, so bailiffs, officials and household warriors were drawn from the unfree.

Men and women alike held the status, and the laws made no distinction between them. Some, the casati, ran estates and lived from their proceeds, while others were paid in coin or from mills, tolls, ferries and port dues. By the 12th century greater ministerials, who had vassals of their own, were set apart from lesser ones who had none. Every arrangement included military service: in Bamberg ministerials were grouped in threes, one going on campaign while the other two equipped him, and in Cologne those with an income of 5 marks or more had to serve in person.

Their duties and rights were often recorded in a service code, the Dienstrecht. Some held allods, land of their own, and some even traded: Timo, burgrave of Salzburg around 1125, was also a merchant. A ministerial could not move without the lord's leave, and marriages between the people of two lords were bargained over, as when in 1213 the children of Gerhoch II of Bergheim-Radeck and Bertha of Lonsdorf were divided between the churches of Salzburg and Passau.

Under the Salian emperors, from 1024 to 1125, the ministeriales grew into a distinct and differentiated class, serving as stewards, castellans and judges, and as imperial ministerials they upheld the Salian and Hohenstaufen polity. In Salzburg ministerials and clergy together elected Archbishop Gebhard in 1060. By the end of the 12th century the word miles, until then kept for free warriors, was applied to them too. When Count Frederick of Isenberg murdered Archbishop Engelbert of Cologne in 1225, the archbishop's ministerials took the case to the royal court, which condemned him. In Gelderland, documents still told knights of noble and ministerial birth apart in the 15th century.
minkhaung-i: He was born Min Swe on 13 September 1373 at Gazun-Nyeint, in present-day northern Sagaing Region, to King Swa Saw Ke and a commoner, Saw Beza, whom the king made a junior queen. Bullied by his elder half-brother Tarabya, he was sent with his brother Theiddat to study under the chief primate near Pinle. In 1385, aged eleven, he was made governor of Pyinzi, which he held for 15 years. In the first invasion of Hanthawaddy that year he attacked King Razadarit against Tarabya's orders and was beaten back, a lost chance Ava came to regret. In 1389/90 he married Shin Mi-Nauk, daughter of the chief of Mohnyin.

After his father's death in April 1400 Tarabya was assassinated, and the court offered Min Swe the throne. He hesitated, fearing Governor Maha Pyauk of Yamethin, until Theiddat ambushed and killed Pyauk. Min Swe was proclaimed king by 25 November 1400 as Minkhaung, Foremost Lord.

In 1401–1403 Razadarit's river fleet invaded, but Ava's army defeated it south of Prome on 26 December 1402, and the treaty that followed fixed the border south of Prome and gave Ava a share of the Bassein customs and 30 elephants a year. Advised by his chief minister Min Yaza, Minkhaung then drew the nearer Shan states into Ava's orbit by 1406, a drive the Ming records describe as military expeditions, and on 29 November 1406 his son Minye Kyawswa took the Arakanese capital Launggyet.

Naming Minye Kyawswa heir drove Theiddat to flee to Pegu in 1407, and the war resumed. Minkhaung's own invasions of 1408 and 1409–1410 ended in disaster; his queen Mi-Nauk was captured, and he handed command to his son, who fought Hanthawaddy, Hsenwi and an army sent by the Yunnan government on several fronts until he was mortally wounded at Dala–Twante on 13 March 1415.

Heartbroken, Minkhaung made his middle son Minye Thihathu heir. Two more campaigns followed, a failed Hanthawaddy attack on Toungoo in 1416–1417 and an Ava invasion of the delta that could not break through to Pegu. The king spent his last years in piety and died c. October 1421; Razadarit is said to have lamented the news and died about two months later. Minkhaung ruled through semi-independent tributaries and governors on the old Pagan model. He failed to conquer Hanthawaddy or Arakan but brought most of the cis-Salween Shan states under Ava.
minnesang: Minnesang, love song, was a tradition of German lyric and song that flourished in the Middle High German period, from the 12th to the 14th century. Its name comes from minne, the Middle High German word for love, its main subject. A poet and performer was a Minnesänger and a single song a Minnelied. The Minnesänger are comparable to the Occitan troubadours and the northern French trouvères, but are described as an original German contribution to courtly lyric.

The earliest texts date from perhaps 1150, and the earliest named poets, Der von Kürenberg and Dietmar von Aist, wrote in a native German tradition called the Danubian. From about 1170 German poets came under the influence of the troubadours and trouvères and adopted the strophic form of the canzone; Friedrich von Hausen's Ich denke underwilen is regarded as a contrafactum of a song by Guiot de Provins.

Debate about the Minnesänger's social status rests on little reliable biography. Some belonged to the higher nobility: the Codex Manesse includes songs by dukes, counts, kings and the Emperor Henry VI. Others were educated commoners, as the title Meister shows, such as Konrad von Würzburg, and many are thought to have been ministeriales, vassals of lower nobility. They wrote for their own class at court and are better thought of as courtiers than as hired musicians. Friedrich von Hausen was in the entourage of Friedrich Barbarossa and died on crusade, and Walther von der Vogelweide received a fief from the Emperor Frederick II. Several, among them Heinrich von Veldeke, Wolfram von Eschenbach and Hartmann von Aue, are also noted for epic poetry.

From about 1190 the poets broke free of Franco-Provençal influence. Classical Minnesang, with Albrecht von Johansdorf, Heinrich von Morungen and Reinmar von Hagenau, reached its culmination in Walther von der Vogelweide, regarded in the Middle Ages and today as the foremost Minnesänger. The later Minnesang, from about 1230, turned partly away from the refined ethos and grew formally more elaborate; Neidhart von Reuental brought in characters from lower social classes, often for humour. Only a small number of melodies survive, mostly in manuscripts of the 15th century or later, and their rhythm is hard to read. In the 15th century Minnesang gave way to the Meistersänger, who were usually commoners. Richard Wagner's Tannhäuser and Richard Strauss's Guntram are operas about the tradition.
minnesota: Minnesota is the northernmost contiguous state, since the isolated Northwest Angle in Lake of the Woods County is the only part of the 48 contiguous states north of the 49th parallel. It borders Manitoba and Ontario to the north, Wisconsin to the east, Iowa to the south and North Dakota and South Dakota to the west. It is known as the Land of 10,000 Lakes, with 14,420 bodies of fresh water of at least ten acres each. About a third of the state is forested, and much of the rest is prairie and farmland.

The name comes from the Dakota name for the Minnesota River, either mní sóta, clear blue water, or Mníssota, cloudy water. The state seal carries the phrase Mni Sóta Makoce, the land where the water reflects the skies.

Native Americans have lived in Minnesota since the Woodland period of the 11th century BCE. The Upper Mississippian culture, made up of the Oneota and other Siouan speakers, emerged around 1000 CE and lasted until Europeans arrived in the 17th century. The Dakota lived in what is now Minnesota when French voyageurs and fur traders arrived, using the Grand Portage to reach trapping areas. The Anishinaabe, also called Ojibwe or Chippewa, were migrating in and formed an alliance with the Dakota. European powers destabilised the region, the alliance collapsed, and the Dakota-Ojibwe War followed.

The region was part of Spanish Louisiana from 1762 to 1802. The part east of the Mississippi became part of the United States at the end of the American Revolutionary War, and the part to the west came with the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. The Territory of Minnesota was formed in 1849, with Saint Paul as its capital, and Minnesota was admitted as the 32nd state in 1858. Its motto, L'Étoile du Nord, The Star of the North, is the only state motto in French.

Settlers came from across the country, and growth was based first on timber, agriculture and railroad construction. Into the early 20th century European immigrants arrived in large numbers, particularly from Scandinavia, Germany and Central Europe. The state was at the forefront of labour rights, women's suffrage and political reform.

Saint Paul is the capital and Minneapolis the most populous city, and the two form the Twin Cities, where more than half the state's people live. Minnesota has 11 federally recognised Native American reservations, seven Ojibwe and four Dakota, and its culture reflects Scandinavian and German influence.
mino-province: Mino Province was a province of Japan in what is today southern Gifu Prefecture. It was bordered by Ōmi to the west, Echizen and Hida to the north, Shinano to the east, and Ise, Mikawa and Owari to the south. The Sakai River separated Mino from Owari and gave the boundary its name, border river. Its abbreviated names were Nōshū and Jōshū. Under the Engishiki classification Mino ranked as one of the 13 great countries in importance and as one of the near countries in distance from the capital. The provincial capital and ichinomiya lay in what is now the town of Tarui.

Mino is an ancient place name, written 三野国 on wooden tags from the ruins of Asuka-kyō and Fujiwara-kyō. According to the Kujiki there were originally three separate countries, centred on what is now Ōgaki, Ōno and Kakamigahara, which together with Motosu and Mugetsu were joined under Yamato rule to form the province. The ancient Tōsandō highway linking the capitals with the eastern provinces ran through Mino, and in 713 it was widened to take increasing numbers of travellers. The Nihon Shoki and Shoku Nihongi indicate that many immigrants from the Hata clan and from Silla settled there in the Asuka and Nara periods.

In the Kamakura and Muromachi periods the Toki clan held the office of shugo of Mino, the Toki Yorisada serving from 1336 and the Toki Yorinari from 1519 to 1542. In the Sengoku period Saitō Dōsan usurped political power from the Toki, and the province was later conquered by Oda Nobunaga. The Battle of Sekigahara took place at the western edge of Mino, near the mountains between the Chūbu and Kinki regions. After the Tokugawa shogunate was established several feudal domains were set up in Mino. At the Meiji Restoration it was divided into 18 districts, 131 subdistricts and 1,561 villages, with a total assessed kokudaka of 654,872 koku.
minoan-civilisation: The Minoan civilisation was centred on Crete, with further settlements around the Aegean, and is often regarded as the first civilisation in Europe. It developed from the local Neolithic culture, whose oldest farming remains date to about 7000 BCE, and Early Minoan society shifted gradually from clan-based villages towards a more urban and stratified society. Crete lies on the sea routes between Europe, Africa and the Middle East and is poor in metals, which is believed to have encouraged overseas trade.

The name is a modern coinage from the mythical King Minos, whom the Greeks believed ruled Knossos, and was popularised by Arthur Evans. The people's own name for themselves is unknown, and the Egyptians called them the Keftiu.

The first palaces were built in the Middle Minoan period, in the decades after about 1925 BCE, at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, on sites used for communal ceremonies since the Neolithic. Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A developed in the following period, which ended in mass destructions usually attributed to earthquakes. Knossos, the largest site, had an estimated 18,000 people around 2000 BCE. The Late Minoan period produced many of the best-known objects, such as the snake goddess figurines and the La Parisienne fresco.

After about 1450 BCE the Minoans came under the cultural and perhaps political domination of the Mycenaean Greeks, forming a hybrid culture that lasted until about 1100 BCE. The civilisation was largely forgotten after the Late Bronze Age collapse and was rediscovered in the early twentieth century through excavation.

Little is known of Minoan society, and it is unclear whether there was ever a unified state. The buildings Evans called palaces are now thought to have served religious and economic purposes more than as royal residences. Minoan art shows no recognisable kings, and before about 1450 BCE a group of elite families may have controlled government and religion. Religion centred on peak sanctuaries and sacred caves, with symbols such as the bull, the double axe and the serpent.

The Minoans raised cattle, sheep, pigs and goats, grew wheat, barley and chickpeas, and cultivated grapes, figs and olives. They traded with Egypt, Cyprus, Syria, Anatolia and mainland Greece. Neither Linear A nor Cretan hieroglyphic has been deciphered, so the Minoan language is unknown.
minoan-eruption: The Thera volcano had erupted many times over several hundred thousand years. Each time it erupted violently and then collapsed into a roughly circular, seawater-filled caldera ringed by small islands, and the caldera slowly refilled with magma to build a new volcano. Immediately before the Minoan eruption the walls of the caldera formed a nearly continuous ring of islands, with the only entrance between Thera and the tiny island of Aspronisi. The eruption was centred on a small island just north of the present Nea Kameni.

Studies identify one minor precursory tephra fall and four major phases. The thinness of the first ash layer, and the lack of erosion of it by winter rains before the next was laid down, suggest that the volcano gave the island's people a few months' warning, and since no human remains have been found at Akrotiri the population probably fled. The first major phase deposited up to 7 metres of pumice and ash. The second and third brought pyroclastic surges and lava fountaining, and the third began the collapse of the caldera, which the fourth completed, producing tsunamis.

The eruption was of the Plinian type, with a column an estimated 30 to 35 kilometres high that reached the stratosphere. Its volume is uncertain because most of the material fell into the sea; analysis of marine sediments and seismic data gathered between 2015 and 2019 gave 28 to 41 cubic kilometres of dense-rock equivalent, a Volcanic Explosivity Index of 7. Tsunamis devastated the northern coast of Crete, 110 kilometres away, and ash lay 3 metres deep on Anafi.

Akrotiri was entombed in pumice and ash, and evidence suggests that survivors returned to recover their possessions. On Crete, earthquakes destroyed sites including Petras and tsunamis swept over coastal sites such as Palaikastro. The Minoans quickly recovered, and the following period is considered the high point of Minoan culture: Petras and Palaikastro were rebuilt and new palaces were constructed at Zakros and Phaistos, although Galatas and Kommos declined. Its longer-term effects remain debated.

Because the tephra is a marker horizon at archaeological sites across the eastern Mediterranean, the date matters greatly. Radiocarbon dating has favoured the late 17th century BCE, while archaeological correlation with Egypt points to between about 1550 and 1480 BCE. The revised calibration curve IntCal20 shifts the probable radiocarbon range to include most of the 16th century BCE, but the exact year is unsettled. Spyridon Marinatos linked the eruption to Plato's Atlantis, a view that current scholarship does not support.
minor-c-keith: Minor Cooper Keith was born on 19 January 1848 in Brooklyn, New York, the son of the lumber merchant Minor Hubbell Keith and his wife Emily, a sister of the railroad entrepreneur Henry Meiggs. At sixteen he worked as a store clerk on Broadway and then as a lumber surveyor. With $3,000 saved in a year he bought a cattle ranch on a river island near the mouth of the Rio Grande in southern Texas, which he ran until 1871, when his uncle invited him to Costa Rica.

Meiggs had contracted with the government of President Tomás Guardia Gutiérrez to build a railroad from San José to the Caribbean coast at Limón, giving Costa Rica's coffee a route to Europe, and Keith took the project over after Meiggs died in 1877. Poor financing, jungle, rain and disease made the work very hard: as many as four thousand people, among them Keith's three brothers, died building the first 25 miles of track, mostly of malaria. Keith brought in labourers from abroad, including Jamaicans, Chinese and Italians.

When the government defaulted in 1882, Keith raised £1.2 million himself and negotiated lower interest on Costa Rica's London loans. In return the Soto-Keith contract of 21 April 1884 gave him 800,000 acres of tax-free land along the line, about 6% of the country, and a 99-year lease on the railroad. In 1883 he married Cristina Castro Fernández, daughter of the former president José María Castro Madriz and niece of President Próspero Fernández Oreamuno.

Keith had begun planting bananas as early as 1873 and shipped them by steamboat from Limón to New Orleans through his Tropical Trading and Transport Company, later adding plantations in Panama and Colombia's Magdalena Department. A financial setback forced the 1899 merger with Andrew W. Preston's Boston Fruit Company that created United Fruit, of which he became vice-president. In 1904 he won from Guatemala's president Manuel Estrada Cabrera tax exemptions, land and control of the Atlantic railroads, and from 1912 he built 800 miles of track for the International Railways of Central America.

Keith also mined gold in Abangares and developed land around Panama City, Florida. He bequeathed his collection of ancient Native American gold to the American Museum of Natural History, and died of bronchial pneumonia at West Islip, Long Island, on 14 June 1929, before realising his plan for a line from Guatemala to the Panama Canal.
minos: In Greek tradition Minos and his brothers Rhadamanthys and Sarpedon were sons of Zeus and Europa, adopted and raised by King Asterion of Crete. When Asterion died, Minos claimed the throne, and according to some sources he banished his brothers. To justify his rule he prayed to Poseidon for a sign, and Poseidon sent a giant white bull from the sea. Minos was bound to sacrifice it but substituted another bull, and in rage Poseidon cursed his wife Pasiphaë with a mad passion for the animal. She bore the Minotaur, which Minos shut in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus.

Later poets and mythographers, among them Diodorus Siculus and Plutarch, reconciled the contradictions in his character by assuming two kings of that name: a good Minos I, son of Zeus, and a harsher grandson, Minos II, the Minos of the myths of Theseus, Pasiphaë and Daedalus. There is no evidence that Minos was a real person.

Homer shows Minos conversing with Zeus every nine years, and in Plato's reading of the Odyssey he took his laws from the god. Thucydides says he was the first known king to build a navy, which he used against piracy to secure his revenue, and that he reigned over Crete and the Aegean islands three generations before the Trojan War.

His son Androgeus was killed after winning the Panathenaic Games, by the bull at Marathon in one account and by jealous rivals in another. Minos made war on Athens, and the plague and hunger sent on the city ended when it agreed to send seven boys and seven girls to Crete every nine years to be fed to the Minotaur. The hero Theseus killed the Minotaur with the help of Minos's daughter Ariadne.

In the tale of his death Minos pursued Daedalus from city to city with a riddle about stringing a spiral shell, and learned where he was when King Cocalus at Camicus in Sicily had it solved. Cocalus's daughters and Daedalus then scalded Minos to death in a bath.

After death Minos became a judge of the dead alongside his brother Rhadamanthys and half-brother Aeacus, and held the deciding vote. Dante sets him at the entrance to the second circle of Hell, where he coils his tail to indicate each soul's circle. Arthur Evans named the Minoan civilisation after him.
minotaur: The Minotaur, also called Asterion or Asterius, is a mythical creature shown in classical antiquity with the head and tail of a bull and the body of a man. The name means Bull of Minos. According to the myth, Minos prayed to Poseidon for a snow-white bull as a sign of his favour, and then kept the bull instead of sacrificing it. To punish him, Poseidon arranged with Aphrodite for Minos's wife Pasiphaë to fall in love with the bull. She had the craftsman Daedalus make a hollow wooden cow and bore the Minotaur.
He grew ferocious and devoured humans, and on the advice of the oracle at Delphi Minos had Daedalus build the Labyrinth to hold him. The palace at Knossos has been found, but the Labyrinth never was.

All the stories agree that Androgeus, son of Minos, died through the fault of the Athenians. The common tradition holds that Minos waged a war of revenge and won, and that Athens then had to send seven young men and seven young women into the Labyrinth every nine years as victims. Pausanias says Minos simply harassed the Athenians until they agreed.

When the third sacrifice approached, the Athenian prince Theseus volunteered to kill the Minotaur. Minos's daughter Ariadne fell in love with him and in most accounts gave him a ball of thread to retrace his path. Classical sources say he killed the Minotaur with his sword, a club or his bare hands. On the way home he abandoned Ariadne on Naxos, and the crew forgot to change the black sail for the white one promised to his father Aegeus, who saw the black sail, presumed his son dead and leapt into the sea since named after him.

The contest of Theseus and the Minotaur was frequently shown in Greek art, and a didrachm of Knossos shows the Labyrinth on one side and the Minotaur among small balls, probably stars, on the other. Some nineteenth-century mythologists saw the Minotaur as a personification of the sun. In the Middle Ages some versions showed a man's head on a bull's body, the reverse of the classical form.

Dante places the Minotaur as guardian of the seventh circle in the Inferno. Pablo Picasso made etchings of the Minotaur, and Jorge Luis Borges told the story from the monster's perspective in The House of Asterion.
minox: Walter Zapp, a Baltic German born in Riga in 1905, conceived the camera in Reval, now Tallinn, where he had worked as an engraver and for a photographer. The idea of a camera that could always be carried grew out of talks with his friends Nikolai Nylander, who coined the name Minox and drew its mouse logo, and Richard Jürgens, who funded the project. Unable to find backing for production in Estonia, Jürgens approached the electrotechnical works VEF in Riga, where Zapp demonstrated his prototype with enlargements from its negatives. VEF secured patents on his inventions in at least 18 countries and kept producing the camera through the Soviet and German occupations of Latvia until 1943.

The Riga Minox had a brass chassis in a stainless steel shell that slid open to uncover the lens and viewfinder and closed to advance the film. It measured 80 by 27 by 16 mm and weighed 130 g. Its 15 mm f/3.5 Minostigmat lens focused as close as 20 cm and gave such depth of field that no diaphragm was needed, and a metal foil curtain shutter sat behind a protective window. Each frame measured 8 by 11 mm on unperforated film held in a twin-chamber cartridge of up to 50 exposures.

Zapp meant it as a camera for everyone, but its cost made it a luxury item, and its size and close focusing drew intelligence agencies in America, Europe, South Africa and the Soviet bloc. It was used by both Axis and Allied agents; one record shows the US Office of Strategic Services buying 25 in 1942, and the Soviet spy John A. Walker Jr. photographed US Navy ciphers with a Minox C. A measuring chain supplied with most cameras made copying letter-sized documents easy.

After the war Minox GmbH began making the aluminium-shelled Minox II in 1948 at Giessen near Wetzlar in West Germany. The Minox B, with a built-in Gossen meter, became the most widely produced model, and in 1969 the Minox C was the first camera of its kind with electronic exposure control. A Minox B in a protective housing was used in 1961 to inspect the inside of the US Army's SL-1 reactor after its explosion. The last TLX models were available until September 2014.
minsk: Minsk stands on the southeastern slope of the Minsk Hills, on the Svislach River and the now subterranean Nyamiha, at an average altitude of 220 metres. The Svislach flows through an ancient river valley formed by meltwater at the end of the last Ice Age, and six smaller rivers lie within the city limits. The city was first built on the hills, which allowed defensive fortifications, and its western parts are still the most hilly. Pine and mixed forests border its north and east, and the Zaslawskaye reservoir, built in 1956 and known as the Minsk sea, lies five kilometres from its north-western edge.

The Svislach valley was the boundary between two early East Slavic tribes, the Krivichs and the Dregoviches, and by 980 it was part of the Principality of Polotsk. The Primary Chronicle mentions the settlement as Měneskъ for the year 1067, in connection with the Battle on the River Nemiga. That year is now widely accepted as the founding date, and city authorities give 3 March 1067, though the town already had wooden walls and must have existed for some time. Kiev annexed the Principality of Minsk in 1129, the Polotsk dynasty regained it in 1146, and by 1150 Minsk rivalled Polotsk as the major city of the former principality.

The city was later annexed by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and received town privileges in 1499. From 1569 it was the capital of Minsk Voivodeship in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and Polish rule brought a massive migration of Jews to Belarusian lands. Minsk passed to the Russian Empire in 1793 after the Second Partition of Poland. In 1897 Jews were the largest religious group, 47,562 of 90,912 residents. From 1919 to 1991 it was the capital of the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, a republic of the Soviet Union from 1922.

Minsk is the capital and largest city of Belarus, with a special administrative status and a population of about two million. Since 1991 it has been the capital of the independent Republic of Belarus. The city is divided into nine districts. Among its historic churches are the Orthodox Cathedral of the Holy Spirit, a former Bernardine convent church, and the Cathedral of Saint Mary, built by the Jesuits. Its first theatres and libraries date from the middle of the 19th century.
minturnae: Minturnae was one of three towns of the Ausones that made war against Rome in 314 BCE, during the Second Samnite War, the others being Ausona, the modern Sessa Aurunca, and Vescia. A Roman settlement was founded there as a fort, Castrum Minturnae, about 296 BCE. The early town grew around the square fort, with polygonal stone walls along the river and the Appian Way as a military road, and in the 3rd century BCE it expanded with new tufa walls and towers. A Capitolium in the Italic style was built after 191 BCE next to the Appian Way and was probably an affirmation of Roman loyalty and identity.

The city was transformed when it became a colonia under Augustus. The stretch of the Appian Way through the town was given porticos, temples to Augustus and Julius Caesar were built, and the theatre was rebuilt. Under Hadrian it received thermal baths, a macellum, a nymphaeum and an aqueduct. The town was destroyed by the Langobards in 590 and was probably destroyed again by Saracens in 883. Its low site was increasingly abandoned for the hill town of Minturno, which until the 19th century was known as Traetto.

Many of the main buildings of the ancient city can be seen outside the modern town, mostly dating from the time of Hadrian. They include a theatre and an aqueduct in opus reticulatum, thermal baths with a large pool, two fora, a republican forum and an imperial one, the Appian Way with a colonnade, the macellum and the Capitolium.

The aqueduct was more than 11 km long from the springs of Capodacqua, and its distribution basin formed part of the central pier of the city gate. An amphitheatre is now almost entirely demolished. About 2 km away, near the river mouth, lay the sacred grove of the Italic goddess Marica, and a nearby sanctuary of Marica with a temple of tuff was built about 500 BCE.
mir-damad: Mir Damad worked in the Neoplatonizing Islamic Peripatetic tradition of Avicenna and was also a scholar of the traditional Islamic sciences. His chief contribution to Islamic philosophy was a new account of the gradations of time, in which the separate categories of time emanate as descending divine hypostases. With the notion of huduth-e-dahri, atemporal origination, built on the categories of Avicenna and Suhrawardi but going beyond them, he argued that everything except God, including the earth and the heavenly bodies, shares in both eternal and temporal origination.

His treatises include Taqwim al-Iman (Calendars of Faith), on creation and divine knowledge; Kitab Qabasat al-Ilahiyah (Book of the Divine Embers of Fiery Kindling), where he sets out atemporal origination; Kitab al-Jadhawat (Book of Spiritual Attractions); and Sirat al-Mustaqim (The Straight Path). He also wrote a few books on mathematics, of lesser importance. His philosophical prose is often counted among the densest and most difficult to understand, deliberately using and coining convoluted terms and neologisms that need systematic analysis and detailed commentary.

Mir Damad influenced the revival of al-Falsafa al-Yamani, the Philosophy of Yemen, which rested on revelation and the sayings of prophets rather than on the rationalism of the Greeks. The School of Isfahan that he founded embraced a theosophical outlook known as Hikmat-i Ilahi, Divine Wisdom. Besides Mulla Sadra, his students included Seyyed Ahmad ibn Reyn-al-A'bedin Alavi, Mohammad ibn Alireza ibn Agajanii, Qutb-al-Din Mohammad Ashkevari and Mulla Shams Gilani. His son was Seyed Ali Naghi Astarabadi and his grandson Sayyid Mahdi bin Sayyid Ali Naqi; a daughter married Sayyid Ahmad ibn Zayn al-Abidin Alavi. He was the ancestor of the Mirdamadi family, named after him.
mir-jafar: Mir Jafar was born in Delhi around 1691. His grandfather Syed Husayn Tabatabaei migrated from Najaf and settled in Delhi in 1675 at the invitation of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, married the emperor's niece and served as a qadi at court. Mir Jafar's paternal aunt, Begum Sharfunnisa, was the wife of Nawab Alivardi Khan of Bengal. When Raghoji I Bhonsle raided Bengal with Maratha forces from 1747, Mir Jafar, then subedar of Odisha, withdrew all his forces until Alivardi Khan arrived and routed Raghoji at the Battle of Burdwan. The angry nawab dismissed him.

Under Alivardi Khan's successor, Siraj ud-Daulah, Mir Jafar served as principal general and led the army to victory over the British on 19 June 1756. Siraj nonetheless favoured his rival Raja Manikchand, and the discontented Mir Jafar joined other opponents of the nawab, including the banking family of the Jagat Seths. They approached the East India Company, whose agent William Watts sent the Armenian Khwaja Petrus Aratoon to investigate. Mir Jafar, as paymaster of the Bengal army, offered 2.5 crore rupees for help in removing the nawab. Robert Clive, who thought Siraj universally hated, joined the plot.

Mir Jafar betrayed Siraj ud-Daulah at the Battle of Plassey in 1757, and the British installed him as a dependent nawab after Siraj's defeat and execution. He paid 17,700,000 rupees in compensation to the Company and the traders of Calcutta, and Clive received over two million rupees in bribes. Finding the Company's demands boundless, he turned to the Dutch, whom the British beat at the Battle of Chinsurah in November 1759. The Company then forced him to abdicate in favour of his son-in-law Mir Qasim.

Mir Qasim proved able and independent, and came into dispute with the Company over its refusal to pay taxes to him. The Company overthrew him and restored Mir Jafar, and Mir Qasim went to war with the help of Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II, who were defeated at the Battle of Buxar on 22 October 1764. Mir Jafar died in Murshidabad on 5 February 1765, after leprosy, prolonged ill health and an addiction to opium.

Many historians see his reign as the start of British expansion over the Indian subcontinent. The Company abolished the nizamat in 1793 and took complete control of the province. He is reviled as a traitor, especially among Bengalis, and the poet Muhammad Iqbal condemned Mir Jafar and Mir Sadiq as a stigma on humanity, on religion and on the country.
mir-jumla-ii: Mir Jumla was born Mir Mohammad Sayyid Ardistani in Safavid Iran in 1591, the son of Mirza Hazaru, a poor oil merchant of Isfahan. He learned to read and write, which probably led to work as a clerk for a diamond merchant with connections to the Golconda Sultanate, a region known for its diamond mines. He may have reached Golconda in 1630, though some scholars suggest 1615 or 1620. There he built a diamond business and a maritime trade, and gifts to the Qutb Shahi sultan, among them cabinets from China and elephants from Ceylon, won him a place at court.

In the 1630s Mir Jumla became Sar-i-Khail and administered trade at the port of Masulipatnam, where his strict collection of dues angered the English company, and he rose to be chief minister of Golconda. By the 1640s his own fleets sailed to Arakan, Aceh, Melaka, Bandar Abbas, Jeddah, Basra and the Maldives, and the historian Narayan Sarkar described his trade as a competitor of the East India Company.

From April 1642 he led Golconda armies into Karnatak, taking forts in the Nellore plains and Udayagiri, besieging the Dutch settlement at Pulicat and, in 1650, capturing Gandikota with the help of European gunners. He melted Hindu idols taken from temples to cast artillery. When the sultan demanded a share of his spoils and plotted to seize and blind him, he opened a secret correspondence with Prince Aurangzeb and entered Mughal service. After Aurangzeb's accession he pursued the rebel prince Shah Shuja, defeated at the Battle of Khajwa, and reached Dhaka on 9 May 1660, by which time Shuja had fled to Arakan.

As subahdar of Bengal he restored Dhaka as the capital in place of Rajmahal and dismissed dishonest qazis. His expedition against the Ahom kingdom took 12,000 cavalry, 30,000 infantry and 323 ships and boats crewed partly by Portuguese, English and Dutch sailors. Hunger and night attacks during the rains cost the Mughals two thirds of the army, and the peace bound the Ahom king to an indemnity, a yearly tribute of 20 elephants and the cession of the land from Guwahati to the Manas river.

Mir Jumla died on the march back on 30 March 1663 and was buried on a hillock at Mankachar in Assam, where his tomb survives. The traveller François Bernier wrote that his death was "a great sensation throughout the Indies". Parts of the roads, bridges and forts he built around Dhaka still stand.
mir-osman-ali-khan: Mir Osman Ali Khan was born on 5 or 6 April 1886 at Purani Haveli, the second son of Mahboob Ali Khan, Asaf Jah VI, and Amat-uz-Zahra Begum. He was educated privately and reportedly became fluent in Urdu, Persian, Arabic and English; from early 1899 Brian Egerton served for two years as his English tutor. His father died on 29 August 1911, and he was proclaimed Nizam the same day; the coronation was held at the Chowmahalla Palace on 18 September 1911. He lived at King Kothi Palace from the age of 13 until his death.

Hyderabad was the largest of the princely states of colonial India, and its ruler was one of only five princes entitled to a 21-gun salute. For his financial contribution to the British war effort in the First World War, amounting to nearly £25 million, King George V raised his style in 1918 to His Exalted Highness, and he was named Faithful Ally of the British Government. After the Great Musi Flood of 1908 he had two reservoirs, Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar, built on the advice of Sir M. Visvesvaraya. In 1919 he formed an Executive Council, and in 1941 the Hyderabad State Bank, which managed the state's own currency.

When the British withdrew in 1947 the Nizam ruled more than 16 million people. He refused to sign the instrument of accession, preferring a separate kingdom within the British Commonwealth, and signed a one-year standstill agreement instead. He negotiated openly with India and covertly with Pakistan, while his power was weakened by the Telangana Rebellion and by the Razakars, a Muslim militia he could not put down. In 1948 the Indian Army invaded in Operation Polo, under Major General Jayanto Nath Chaudhuri, and the annexation was over in 109 hours. The Nizam kept his personal wealth and title.

He served as Rajpramukh of Hyderabad State from 26 January 1950 to 31 October 1956, after which the state was partitioned. He gave 14,000 acres of his estate to the Bhoodan movement of Vinoba Bhave for distribution among landless farmers. He died on 24 February 1967 and was buried the next day, as his will asked, in the Masjid-e Judi, where his mother lay; the chief curator of the Nizam's Museum, D. Bhaskara Rao, put the funeral procession at an estimated one million people. His grandson Mukarram Jah succeeded him as titular Nizam.
mir-qasim: Mir Syed Qasim was the son of Mir Muhammad Razi Khan and claimed descent from Ali al-Ridha. His paternal grandfather, Sayyid Husayn Ridhwi, entered the Mughal Empire under Aurangzeb, received the title Imtiaz Khan and served as Waqia-navis, or intelligence minister, and then as Dewan of Bihar; he also wrote Persian poetry under the pen name Khalis. Qasim married Fatima Begum, a daughter of Mir Jafar and a granddaughter of Nawab Alivardi Khan, and served as Faujdar of Rangpur for roughly two decades before he became Nawab.

The Company had overthrown Mir Jafar after he sought an alliance with the Dutch East India Company, which the British defeated at Chinsura. On his accession Mir Qasim gave the Company lavish gifts and the right to collect the revenue of Burdwan, Midnapore and Chittagong. Disputes soon followed over his tariffs, in particular a 9% duty on all foreign traders, and over the Company's claim that its dastak, a Mughal licence, freed it from the taxes that local merchants paid at up to 40% of their revenue. He moved his capital from Murshidabad to Munger and paid for new troops by streamlining tax collection.

In 1763 he seized the Company's offices at Patna, massacring 45 Europeans, among them the Resident. The same year he sent his general Gurgin Khan into Nepal at the request of Kanak Singh Baaniya, chief minister of Makwanpur, whose king Bikram Sen had been taken hostage by Prithvi Narayan Shah; Gurgin was swiftly defeated and retreated.

After Buxar, Shuja-ud-Daula expelled him from his camp on 23 October 1764. He fled through Rohilkhand, Allahabad, Gohad and Jodhpur and settled around 1774 at Kotwal, near Delhi, where he died in obscurity and abject poverty, possibly of dropsy. His defeat at Buxar established the East India Company as a powerful force in Bengal in a much more real sense than Plassey had seven years earlier, and by 1793 the Company had abolished the Nizamat and taken full charge of the former Mughal province.
mir-sayyid-ali-hamadani: Hamadani was born around 1314 at Hamadan in Persia, into a Sayyid family claiming descent from the Prophet Muhammad through Ali ibn Abi Talib; his father Sayyid Shihabuddin was a local governor. He studied under Kubrawi masters, among them Sharafuddin Mahmud Mazdaqani, and spent his early years under Ala ad-Daula Simnani, the first Sufi to criticise the school of Ibn Arabi and its concept of the oneness of being, a debate Hamadani inherited. He was addressed by the honorifics Shāh-e-Hamadān, Amīr-i Kabīr, the Great Commander, and Ali Sani, the second Ali.

He travelled widely and preached in Afghanistan, Uzbekistan, China, Syria, Kashmir and Turkestan. In Kashmir he was welcomed by the ruler Qutb ad-Din Shah, then at war with Firuz Shah Tughlaq, the Sultan of Delhi, and brokered a peace between them. After Sharaf-ad-Din Abdul Rehman Bulbul Shah he was the second important Muslim to visit Kashmir. One account has him leaving Hamadan with 700 Sayyids to escape the wrath of Timur.

He wrote more than 70 treatises and books on Sufism, theology and ethics. His Zakhirat ul-Muluk, on politics, governance and social conduct, sets out twenty rules for non-Muslims under a Muslim ruler: they were not to build new temples or churches or rebuild ruined ones, dress like Muslims, take Muslim names, ride horses with saddles or carry swords, and any who broke these conditions forfeited their life and property. These efforts prepared the ground for the large-scale forced conversion of Kashmiri Hindus under Sikandar Shah Miri (1389–1413).

He died in 1384, accounts differing on whether in the Kunar Valley or in Swat, and his disciples carried his body to Kulob in Tajikistan, where his shrine remains a place of veneration. He is regarded as having brought crafts such as carpet weaving from Iran to Kashmir, and the growth of the textile industry drew Kashmiri Muslim groups to settle in Ladakh. His teachings influenced later Sufi orders in Kashmir, including the Rishi order, and the Eidgah of Srinagar is also named after him.
mirabai: Mirabai was born into a Rathore Rajput royal family at Kudki, in the present Beawar district of Rajasthan, and spent her childhood at Merta. She was the daughter of Ratan Singh Rathore and the granddaughter of Rao Dudaji of Merta, which made her a great-granddaughter of Rao Jodha. In 1516 she had an arranged marriage to Bhoj Raj, the crown prince of Mewar.

He was wounded in a war with the Delhi Sultanate in 1518 and died of his wounds in 1521. Both her father and her father-in-law Rana Sanga died a few days after their defeat by Babur at the Battle of Khanwa. After Rana Sanga, Vikram Singh became ruler of Mewar.

Her poems, often sung as bhajans, are lyrical padas in the Rajasthani language and describe love for Krishna, separation from him and dissatisfaction with the world. She often calls him Girdhar, the mountain lifter, and speaks of him as her only true husband. In poems of separation she sometimes portrays him as a detached yogi who leaves lovers in agony, and she presents herself as a yogini.

The earliest datable reference to her is a poem of praise in Nabhadas's Bhaktamal, composed about 1600. Millions of hymns are attributed to her in the Indian tradition, but scholars think only a few hundred authentic, and only two poems have been found in manuscripts older than the early 18th century. Poets who admired her probably composed many of the rest.
Poems attributed to her also appear in a copy of the Adi Granth made in 1604, which the Sikh gurus did not include in the standard edition, and in the Prem Ambodh Pothi of 1693.

The legends of her life vary widely. In the best known, her in-laws tried to kill her with poison sent as nectar and with a basket holding a snake, and she was saved by Krishna. Scholars doubt a story that Akbar and Tansen visited her, because Tansen joined Akbar's court 15 years after her death. The three oldest records that mention her all date from the 17th century.

Nancy Martin-Kershaw suggests that any persecution she met was likelier to come from political chaos and conflict between the Rajput kingdom and the Mughal Empire than from religious or social convention. Tradition holds that she spent her last years at Dwarka or Vrindavan and disappeared into an idol of Krishna in 1547 after being poisoned by her brother-in-law, which scholars contest for lack of evidence.
mirabal-sisters: The Mirabal family came from the central Cibao region and had a farm in the village of Ojo de Agua, near Salcedo. The parents, Enrique Mirabal Fernández and Mercedes Reyes Camilo, were landowners, and there were four sisters: Patria (1924), Dedé (1925), Minerva (1926) and María Teresa (1935). They attended primary school in the village and a Catholic boarding school, the Colegio Inmaculada Concepción, in La Vega.

The Mirabal house never displayed the customary picture of Rafael Trujillo, and the family was considered dissident. When Trujillo came to power the family lost almost its entire fortune. Minerva was the first woman to graduate from law school in the Dominican Republic, though her diploma was stripped of its honours and her licence to practise refused.

Minerva, who had the most active political role, and her husband Manolo Tavárez Justo founded the 14 June Revolutionary Movement, known as 1J4. María Teresa and then Patria joined, and the sisters called themselves Las Mariposas, the Butterflies, after Minerva's underground name. Patria lent her house to store weapons and tools. Dedé did not take part, partly because her husband did not want her to.

Minerva and María Teresa were imprisoned several times in 1960, including from 22 January to 7 February and from 18 May to 9 August, and were not tortured because of mounting international opposition to Trujillo.

On 25 November 1960 Patria, Minerva and María Teresa were returning from visiting their imprisoned husbands when Trujillo's men stopped them. The sisters and their driver, Rufino de la Cruz, were separated, strangled and clubbed to death, and their bodies were put in their vehicle, which was run off a mountain road to make it look like an accident. After Trujillo's assassination on 30 May 1961, General Pupo Román named members of his secret police as the killers. One historian wrote that such orders could only have come from Trujillo himself.

The historian Bernard Diederich wrote that the killings had a greater effect on Dominicans than most of Trujillo's other crimes and prepared the ground for his own assassination six months later. Their details were treated gingerly at the official level until 1996, and in 1997 the sisters were recognised as national martyrs in school history.

The surviving sister, Dedé, raised their six children, founded the Mirabal Sisters Foundation in 1992 and opened a museum in Salcedo in 1994. On 17 December 1999 the United Nations General Assembly designated 25 November the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women in their honour, and Salcedo Province was renamed Hermanas Mirabal Province in 2007. Julia Alvarez's novel In the Time of the Butterflies (1994) retells their story.
mirabeau-b-lamar: Lamar was born on 16 August 1798 in Louisville, Georgia, and grew up on Fairfield, his father's cotton plantation near Milledgeville. His uncle Zachariah named him after the comte de Mirabeau and Napoleon Bonaparte. He was accepted at Princeton but did not attend, failed as a merchant and a newspaper owner, and in 1823 became private secretary to Governor George M. Troup of Georgia. He then founded the Columbus Enquirer, served one term in the Georgia Senate, lost his wife Tabitha to tuberculosis in 1830, and was admitted to the bar in 1833.

Grieving his brother Lucius, Lamar reached Texas, then part of Mexico, in 1835. He joined Sam Houston's army in 1836 and, after rescuing two surrounded men on the eve of San Jacinto, was promoted from private to colonel and given the cavalry for the battle. He became Secretary of War in the interim government and was elected Vice President of Texas in 1836.

Inaugurated on 1 December 1838, Lamar told Congress that the Cherokee and Comanche should be driven from Texas even if they had to be destroyed, and he held that their total extinction was needed to open the land to whites. In 1839 Texian troops expelled the Cherokee at the Battle of the Neches, where about 500 Texans attacked some 800 people of several tribes, between 400 and 500 of them women, children and elders; Chief Bowles was killed. The Comanche resisted despite heavy losses.

He opposed annexation to the United States. A commission chose the village of Waterloo as the capital, renamed Austin, and he founded the Texas State Library. Peace talks with Mexico and recognition by Britain, France and Belgium failed. To fill the treasury he issued paper money, the Redbacks, which proved nearly worthless, and in 1841 he sent an expedition to Santa Fe without Congress's approval; its members were captured and marched to Mexico City, and many died. The public debt rose from $1.4 million to almost $7 million. He also set aside land for schools and two universities.

Lamar fought at the Battle of Monterrey in the Mexican–American War, sat in the Texas Legislature for Eagle Pass, and in 1857 was appointed minister to Nicaragua and Costa Rica. He published his poems as Verse Memorials the same year. He died of a heart attack at his Richmond plantation on 19 December 1859. Lamar County and Lamar University in Beaumont are named after him.
miracles-of-saint-demetrius: The Miracles of Saint Demetrius, in Latin Miracula Sancti Demetrii, is a collection of homilies written in Greek about the miracles of Saint Demetrius, the patron saint of Thessalonica. The first book was compiled between about 610 and about 620 by John, Archbishop of Thessalonica. The second was compiled in the 680s by an unknown author, who was either an eyewitness or drew on written annals and the testimony of eyewitnesses.

Book I tells fifteen episodes in which the saint intervened on behalf of the city, most of them under John's predecessor, Archbishop Eusebius: outbreaks of plague and a siege of Thessalonica by the Sclaveni and the Avars. They were written as sermons to be read aloud to the townspeople, to show that the saint was present among them and interceded for them. John portrays the Slavs only as generic barbarians.

Book II is closer to a historical account. It follows the Slavic invasion and settlement of the Balkans through a series of sieges of Thessalonica, ending in the great Slavic attack of about 677. Its author knew the Slavs far better than John did, named the tribes that had settled around the city and called them our neighbours. The book also describes the second basilica of Saint Demetrius before it burned in 629 or 634; some of its mosaics were reused when the church was rebuilt, and some scholars believe one of them depicts Archbishop John.

Because of its different style and focus, the second book was copied less often than the first and survives in a single manuscript. Historians value the collection as one of the few sources on the Slavic invasions of the late 6th and 7th centuries, which other writers of the time largely neglect. Dimitri Obolensky wrote that no other contemporary work gives so much precise, first-hand information on the defences and topography of Thessalonica and on the siege-craft of the Balkan wars of the period.

The standard critical edition is Paul Lemerle's, published in two volumes of text and commentary in Paris in 1979 to 1981. In 1997 the American writer Harry Turtledove published Thessalonica, a fantasy novel based on the Miracles in which the saint and figures of Christian, Greek and Slavic myth take part in the siege.
mirador-basin: The Mirador Basin lies in the remote rainforest of the northern department of Petén. It is described as two true basins of shallowly sloping terrain dominated by low-lying swamps called bajos, one draining into the San Pedro River and the other into the Candelaria River. Rugged karstic limestone hills to the east and south enclose a triangular trough of more than 2,169 square kilometres. Whether the landscape is a geological depression at all is disputed: data from NASA's Shuttle Radar Topography Mission show no depression in the area.

The major sites of the basin, among them El Mirador, Nakbe, El Tintal and Wakna, were first settled mainly in the Middle Preclassic period, about 1000 to 350 BCE, and the Late Preclassic, about 350 BCE to 150 CE. Because later building was comparatively light, their early remains lie under relatively little overburden from the large constructions of the Classic period (250 to 900 CE). Numerous smaller settlements, such as La Florida, Maaxte, Zacatal, Chan Kan, Tsab Kan, Pedernal, Isla, La Muerta and La Muralla, date mostly to the Classic period.

Archaeological work over the past two decades has also reached the sites of Xulnal and El Pesquero and the large city of Naachtun in the north-east corner, studied by a team from the University of Calgary. The Mirador Basin Project, directed by Richard Hansen and earlier known as the Regional Archaeological Investigation of the North Petén, Guatemala (RAINPEG) Project, has gathered evidence on the origins and early development of Maya civilisation in the area.

The basin belongs to the Maya Biosphere Reserve, the last large area of intact tropical rainforest in Mesoamerica. Illegal logging, fires from slash-and-burn farming and the looting of archaeological sites threaten it. Research is carried out with the Guatemalan Institute of Anthropology and History (IDAEH), the Ministry of Culture and Sports and the National Council of Protected Areas (CONAP), and with community organisations of Petén.
miraj: Miraj is part of the Sangli-Miraj-Kupwad metropolitan region in the Sangli district of Maharashtra. Marathi is the official language, while Kannada is also widely spoken and a form of Hindustani, Hyderabadi Deccani, is heard as well. The town grew into a vital junction of the railway network, and Miraj Junction was once the only junction to carry all three rail gauges: broad, narrow and metre gauge. The last narrow gauge train left on 1 November 2008.

At the end of the 9th century the Shilaharas of Kolhapur gained control of Miraj, and inscriptions describe their ruler Gonka as the conqueror of Karahata (Karad), Miraj and Konkan. In 1216 the town passed with other Shilahara lands to the Yadavas of Devagiri. One account relates that Hasan Gangu, founder of the Bahmani dynasty, raised an army with a treasure he found, defeated Rani Durgavati, the subedar of Miraj, and took its fort; in 1347 the town was renamed Mubarakabad. In 1490 it passed to the Sultanate of Bijapur, and Ibrahim Adil Shah I kept his son Ali Adil Shah I under house arrest there.

On 28 November 1659, soon after the death of the Bijapur general Afzal Khan at Pratapgad, the western Adil Sahi district was surrendered to Annaji Datto, finance minister of Shivaji, but the fort of Miraj held out. Netaji Palkar besieged it and Shivaji came to command the siege in January 1660, then abandoned it when attacks by Siddi Johar and Fazal Khan drew him back to Panhala. Shahu of Satara captured the town on 3 October 1739 after a campaign of two years, and in 1761 Gopalrao, son of Harbhat Patwardhan, took the Miraj jagir from Peshwa Madhavrao. In 1820 the state was split into Miraj Senior and Miraj Junior.

Miraj Senior acceded to the Dominion of India on 8 March 1948, and the town has been part of the state of Maharashtra since 1960. It supplies Indian string instruments such as the sitar, sarod and tanpura, a craft developed by Faridsaheb Shikalgar in the 18th century, whose descendants took the surname Sitarmaker. The singer Abdul Karim Khan of the Kirana gharana lies buried at a dargah in the town, where an annual music festival is held in his memory.
mirambo: Mirambo's own name was Mtyela Kasanda. He began as a trader and as his father's agent in the caravan business, owning caravans that ran from the Great Lakes region of western Tanzania to the coast and dealt mostly in ivory and slaves. His homeland was infested with tsetse fly, so goods were carried almost entirely by people rather than animals. Through trade with Europeans he gained firearms and money, which let him raise armies made up mostly of teenage orphans.

With this power he overthrew the traditional monarchy of Urambo and made himself ntemi, or king. The Nyamwezi aristocracy was appalled that a man not of royal birth held this religious and ceremonial office; other sources say he was the son of the ruler of Uyowa and that his accession broke the matrilineal rule of succession there. He learned the southern African age-grade system of military organisation from Mpangalala, leader of the Watuta, a group of Ngoni linked with Zwangendaba, and built on it his rugaruga force, about 10,000 strong by the early 1880s.

He expanded by war and by diplomacy. Some chiefdoms joined him of their own will and kept their rulers as long as they paid tribute and sent troops. His chief enemies were the Arab traders of Tabora in the kingdom of Unyanyembe, who had powerful allies in Zanzibar, and he never took the town. He allied closely with the Swiss merchant Philippe Broyon and welcomed the missionaries John Morton of the Church Missionary Society and Ebenezer Southon of the London Missionary Society, who saw him as building a stable state and persuaded John Kirk, the British consul at Zanzibar, to back him rather than Unyanyembe.

Mirambo opposed the Arab allies of Henry Morton Stanley, who called him "the African as Bonaparte" for his military talents. By his death he had united most of northern Unyamwezi in an alliance under his leadership, and he had built a capital at Iselemagazi. He fell ill near the end of his life and died at 44; it has been suggested that he was strangled, following an old Nyamwezi custom for a ntemi no longer fit to rule. The Urambo district of Tabora Region is named after him.
mircea-the-elder: Mircea the Elder (Romanian: Mircea cel Bătrân) was born about 1355 and died on 31 January 1418. He was a son of Radu I of Wallachia and his wife Calinichia, and so a descendant of the House of Basarab. He inherited the throne in 1386 after the death of his step-brother Dan I of Wallachia. Wallachia was then developing economically, administratively and religiously, and was exposed to the ambitions of Hungary and Poland, which sought to control the mouths of the Danube, and to those of the Ottoman Empire in the Balkans.

The byname elder was given after his death to distinguish him from his grandson Mircea II, though some historians think later generations used it as a mark of respect. Among his sons were Michael I of Wallachia and Vlad II Dracul, and Vlad Țepeș was his grandson.

Under Mircea Wallachia controlled the largest area in its history. It gained Dobruja in 1388 and the Banate of Severin in 1388 or 1389, and he held the fiefs of Amlaș and Făgăraș in Transylvania. He organised the high offices of state, raised revenue, and minted silver coins that circulated beyond the country. He gave trade privileges to merchants of Poland and Lithuania, renewed those of Brașov, fortified the Danube citadels and strengthened an army of townspeople and free and dependent peasants. He supported the Eastern Orthodox Church and built the Cozia Monastery about 1390.

Through Petru Mușat of Moldavia he concluded an alliance in 1389 with Władysław II Jagiełło of Poland, renewed in 1404 and 1410, and he kept close relations with Sigismund of Luxembourg, king of Hungary.

Mircea's support for the Bulgarians fighting the Ottomans brought conflict. Bayezid I crossed the Danube with about 40,000 men against Mircea's roughly 10,000. Mircea waged a war of starvation and small attacks, and the armies met at the Battle of Rovine on forested, swampy ground that kept the Ottomans from deploying their army. Mircea then had to retreat to Hungary, and the Ottomans installed Vlad the Usurper. In 1396 he joined the crusade begun by the king of Hungary, which ended in Ottoman victory at Nicopolis on 25 September.

In 1397, having defeated Vlad with help from Stibor, voivode of Transylvania, he stopped another Ottoman expedition, and he defeated a further one in 1400. After Timur defeated Bayezid at Ankara in 1402, Mircea exploited the Ottoman anarchy, regained Dobruja in 1404 and helped Musa ascend the Ottoman throne, reaching the height of his power. Late in his reign he agreed to pay a tribute of 3,000 gold pieces a year, and the Ottomans did not make Wallachia a province.
mireuksa: Mireuksa was the largest Buddhist temple of the Korean kingdom of Baekje. It was founded in 602 by King Mu, who reigned from 600 to 640. A legend told in the Samguk yusa says that the king and his queen saw a vision of Maitreya at a pond on Yonghwasan, and that the king had the pond drained to build the temple. The nine-storey wooden pagoda at its centre is said to have been the work of the Baekje master craftsman Abiji.

By 1910 only part of the western stone pagoda still stood, and in 1914 the Japanese government propped it up with concrete. The site was excavated in 1980, revealing much that had been unknown about Baekje architecture.

The complex had three pagodas in a line from east to west, a wooden one in the centre flanked by two of stone, each with a hall to its north and enclosed by covered corridors, so that it looked like three temples in the style called one hall, one pagoda. A causeway seems to have led to the outer gate of the walled precinct.

The western stone pagoda shows how Baekje builders carried the techniques of wooden construction into stone, with a low single-storey base, a massive central pillar and stone supports that imitate timber posts. It now has six storeys, and scholars are unsure how many it once had. In January 2009 a gold plate inscribed in Classical Chinese was found inside it, recording that a queen of King Mu, daughter of Sataek Jeokdeok, had founded the temple and enshrined relics there. Finds of tall foundation stones that once carried wooden floors point to the raised floor later typical of the Korean house.

Mireuksa is South Korean Historic Site No. 150 and has been partly restored, with a museum on the site. The western pagoda has been a National Treasure since 20 December 1962. Two stone flagpole supports, probably of the Later Silla period, are listed as Treasure No. 236.
mirgissa: Mirgissa stood at the Second Cataract of the Nile in Wadi Halfa, in what is now the Northern state of Sudan. Travellers from the north who reached Abusir had to leave their boats and go round the rapids to reach it, while boats from the south could dock in the calm waters of its harbour. Its high position let sentries watch the movement of troops for miles around. The region was occupied long before the fortress: a Mesolithic site at Akha, a few hundred metres east, dates back to 7500 BCE, and large stone tools from 3500 BCE show occupation in Neolithic times.

An open town existed before the great fort, about 1 kilometre north-northeast of it and spread over 75,000 square metres; its jars, millstones, bread moulds and beer mugs suggest a strictly Egyptian population. Senusret I probably founded the fortification within the northern enclosure, but the great fortress was mainly the work of Senusret III, who built eleven forts between the 2nd and 3rd cataracts, among them Shalfak, Uronarti, Askut, Semna and Kumma. Mirgissa was the largest, covering more than 40,000 square metres behind a double wall with bastions and towers. A stele of Senusret III's eighth year found near Semna forbade Nubians to pass north except those who came to trade at Mirgissa or on an embassy.

Occupation was most intense in the Thirteenth Dynasty and the Hyksos era. The fortress was abandoned under Neferhotep I, reoccupied in the Eighteenth Dynasty and then declined; the site was finally abandoned in the early Christian era. In the time of Thutmose II between 250 and 450 people lived there.

The English geologist Henry George Lyons was the first European to explore the site, in 1892. The French Egyptologist Jean Vercoutter excavated it from 1962 to 1969, uncovering two towns, a northern enclosure, cemeteries, a port and a boat slide more than 2 kilometres long, made of wooden cross beams set in silt and wetted mud. A small temple of Hathor yielded a stele naming the goddess mistress of Iken. In the desert nearby a pit held some 3,500 pottery fragments, some inscribed with execration texts naming foreign lands and rulers. The construction of the Aswan High Dam drowned the site.
miri: Miri is a coastal city in north-eastern Sarawak, on the island of Borneo, near the border of Brunei. It lies on the alluvial plain of the Miri River. Beach drift has built up Peninsula Road as a barrier beach between the river and the shore, so that the river runs parallel to the coast before breaking through into the South China Sea. The climate is tropical rainforest, with a dry southwest monsoon from April to September and a wet northeast monsoon from October to March. The town takes its name from a small ethnic group, the Jati Miriek, among the earliest settlers of the region; Europeans who came for oil mispronounced the name as Miri.

The first foragers visited the West Mouth of Niah Cave, about 110 kilometres southwest of Miri, 50,000 years ago. A modern human skull nicknamed the Deep Skull, found by Tom Harrisson in 1958, is the oldest in Southeast Asia and probably belongs to an adolescent girl.

In 1883 the Sultan of Brunei ceded the Baram region, including Miri, to Charles Brooke, Rajah of Sarawak. Miri was then a fishing village of about 20 scattered houses, a few Chinese shops and a lone Arab trader, and Claudetown, now Marudi, was the administrative centre. Miri was founded in 1910 when Royal Dutch Shell drilled the first oil well, and by 1929 it was the administrative centre of northern Sarawak.

As war approached, British forces withdrew to Singapore in 1941, and the Brooke government adopted a denial scheme to destroy the oil installations at Miri and Lutong, since the 48-kilometre coastline was impossible to defend. Miri was the first landing point of Japanese troops in Borneo. The occupation made it a target for Allied air raids, which destroyed refinery facilities. Oil exploration moved offshore from the 1950s, and Petronas, formed in 1974, began production-sharing contracts with Shell in 1976.

Miri is the second largest city in Sarawak, with a population of 356,900 in 2020, and the capital of Miri District. It received city status in 2005. It is the birthplace of the Malaysian petroleum industry, and timber, oil palm and tourism also matter. It is the gateway to Gunung Mulu National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and to the national parks of Niah, Lambir Hills and Loagan Bunut. The population includes Iban, Malay, Chinese, Melanau and many other groups, and the languages include Malay, Malaysian Mandarin and Iban.
miriam-makeba: Zenzile Miriam Makeba was born on 4 March 1932 in the Black township of Prospect near Johannesburg. Her Xhosa father, Caswell Makeba, was a teacher who died when she was six. Her Swazi mother, Christina, was a domestic worker. The name Zenzile comes from the Xhosa words her grandmother muttered after a difficult birth, which mean 'you brought this on yourself'.

Makeba began with the Cuban Brothers, a close-harmony group, and at 21 joined the Manhattan Brothers, the only woman among them. With them she recorded her first hit in 1953. In 1956 she joined the all-woman Skylarks, who blended jazz with traditional South African melodies, though she received no royalties from this work. These groups performed mbube, a style of vocal harmony drawing on jazz, ragtime, Anglican hymns and indigenous music.

She and Harry Belafonte received a Grammy Award for Best Folk Recording for An Evening with Belafonte/Makeba (1965). After she married Stokely Carmichael in March 1968, her popularity in the United States fell sharply and the government took an interest in her. While she was in the Bahamas she was refused a visa to return, and the couple moved to Guinea; she did not go back to the United States until 1987. Her daughter Bongi died in 1985, and Makeba moved to Brussels. In 1986 she joined Paul Simon's Graceland tour, which caused controversy because the album had been recorded in South Africa, in breach of a cultural boycott that she herself endorsed.

After Nelson Mandela's release in February 1990, Makeba entered South Africa on a six-day visa on 10 June 1990. In 1991 she recorded Eyes on Tomorrow with Dizzy Gillespie and Nina Simone, and in 1992 she played the mother in the film Sarafina! She died of a heart attack during a concert in Italy on 9 November 2008.

Makeba released more than 30 albums and was among the first African musicians to gain worldwide recognition. She said that what she sang was not politics but the truth, and she sang at independence ceremonies in Kenya, Angola, Zambia, Tanganyika and Mozambique. On her death Mandela said that her music inspired a powerful sense of hope in all of us.
mirian-iii-of-iberia: Mirian is the Georgian form of the Iranian name Mihrān, which Greek transliterates as Mithranes and which the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus gives as Meribanes. Mirian belonged to the House of Mihran, one of the Seven Great Houses of Iran. He was born in Iran and was originally a Zoroastrian.

The Sasanian King of Kings Bahram II, who ruled from 274 to 293, secured the Iberian throne for him. Bahram wished to strengthen Sasanian authority in the Caucasus and to use the Iberian capital Mtskheta as an entrance to the passes of the Caucasus Mountains. Mirian was then only seven, and Bahram sent a Mihranid grandee named Mirvanoz as his guardian.

The Life of the Kings recounts his reign in detail, though its claims that he pretended to the throne of Iran, controlled Colchis and Albania and operated as far as Syria are obviously fictional. As a Sasanian vassal he most likely took part in the brief war of Narseh against the Romans in 297 and 298, which ended in a crushing Sasanian defeat and the cession of Armenia and Iberia to Rome. Mirian adapted quickly and established close ties with Rome.

According to tradition, Mirian became a Christian through the ministry of Nino, a Cappadocian missionary. A legend says that while hunting near Mtskheta he was blinded by darkness, which lifted only when he prayed to Nino's God. His second wife, Nana, is said to have converted first. Christianity became the state religion, making Iberia the second kingdom after Armenia to do so. The monarchy confiscated the property of pagan temples and gave it to the nobles and the church, and it met resistance from the mountain people. Rufinus and the Georgian annals report that the Iberians asked Constantine for clergy, and that he sent priests and holy relics.

Georgian tradition relates that Mirian built a cathedral at Mtskheta and made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem shortly before his death. He and Nana are said to be buried at the Samtavro convent in Mtskheta. Nana bore him two sons, Rev and Varaz-Bakur, and a daughter. He is regarded as the founder of the Chosroid dynasty, a branch of the Mihranid family, and the Georgian Orthodox Church honours him as a saint, Equal to the Apostles.
mirko-petrovic-njegos: Mirko Petrović-Njegoš was born on 19 August 1820 in Njeguši, the son of Stanko Petrović-Njegoš and his wife Krstinja Vrbica; his uncle was Petar II Petrović-Njegoš. On 7 November 1840 he married Anastasia Martinović, daughter of Vojvoda Drago Martinović, in Njeguši. They had three children: Nikola, the future ruler of Montenegro, and two daughters, Anastasia, who married Savo Plamenac, and Maria. He held the title of veliki vojvoda, Grand Duke, of Grahovo and was known as Vojvoda Mirko.

In February 1857 he replaced his cousin Đorđije Petrović-Njegoš as President of the Governing Senate of Montenegro and the Highlands, and he held the office under his brother Danilo I and then his son Nikola until his death. He led the Montenegrin army that won the Battle of Grahovac on 1 May 1858. In the same period he led a campaign against the Kuči tribe, whose members had refused to obey the Petrović dynasty, in which 243 people were massacred, most of them old men, women and children. Historians disagree on the number of victims, and some suggest the atrocity was exaggerated by the chieftain Marko Miljanov.

In 1862, after the Convention of Scutari, he was sent into exile for having fought the Ottomans. His collection of epic poems, Junački spomenik (Heroic Monument), was published at Cetinje in 1864; it glorifies Montenegro and its people and tells of their victories over the Ottoman Empire.

Mirko died on 1 August 1867. He remains a disputed figure in Montenegro: many see him as a symbol of Montenegrin identity, pride and statehood, while others hold him responsible for the deaths of thousands of civilians. His son raised a monument to him in Podgorica in 1862, which was demolished in 1919 after the Petrović dynasty was dethroned. A new monument put up in the city in 2017 met with protests from ethnic Serbs, particularly those who trace their origins to the Kuči.
mirobriga: Despite some debate, the town is generally identified with the archaeological site of Castelo Velho de Santiago do Cacém, at Herdade dos Chão Salgados, one kilometre north-west of the modern town. The hill of Castelo Velho, 245 metres high, overlooks the northern plain of Chãos Salgados and lay on the ancient roads of the region, with access to the coast. The ruins were first described in the 16th century by André de Resende, who also linked them with the name Miróbriga, mentioned by Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy.

The site was occupied from the Iron Age, at least from the 5th or 4th century BCE and perhaps from the 9th century BCE, although the known structures go back only to the 4th–3rd century BCE. The early settlement covered only the hill and its slopes, about 11,800 square metres, and its material culture shows a strong continental Celtic influence, as does the suffix -briga. Only one building of that period has been excavated, the so-called Celtic temple, whose sacred function is still debated.

In Roman times the settlement grew into a town of about 28,000 square metres, its forum covering almost the whole hill. Baths and a paved road were built in the Flavian period, and in the 2nd century the eastern baths and the hippodrome were begun. The population fell markedly by the end of the 4th century, but some occupation continued into the Early Middle Ages, chiefly around the small Chapel of São Brás.

The ruins include the forum with an imperial temple and a temple of Venus, between them the remains of an older temple of a local divinity, a market, houses with peristyles, a single-arch bridge and two bath buildings set in an L, among the best preserved in Portugal. About 500 metres to the south lies the circus, 370 by 75 metres, the only one in Portugal whose whole ground plan is known. The heritage institute IPPAR took over the management of the site on 1 June 1992, and an interpretative centre designed by the architect Paula Santos was begun in 2000.
miroslav-gospel: The book was commissioned by Prince Miroslav, the knez of Hum and brother of Stefan Nemanja, the Grand Prince of Serbia. It was copied in Kotor, in present-day Montenegro, from an earlier text. Most of its pages are the work of an unknown scribe from Zeta, while the last few were written by Grigorije of Raška, also known as Grigorije the Scribe or the Pupil.

The manuscript runs to 362 parchment pages and is regarded as a masterpiece of illustration and calligraphy. Although it is one of the earliest manuscripts written in Cyrillic, it is later than other Serbian liturgical manuscripts written in Glagolitic. Its language is considered unique because it shows the transition between Old Church Slavonic and the first recognisably distinct form of Serbian.

The gospel was traditionally kept in the library of the Hilandar Monastery on Mount Athos, which Vukan's Gospel is presumed to have reached at the same time. In 1845 Archbishop Porphyrius Uspensky cut a leaf out of the book, and this leaf was first shown in public at an exhibition in Kiev in 1874. That same year three Russian scholars, Vladimir Stasov, Fyodor Buslayev and Nikodim Kondakov, became the first to study the manuscript.

In 1896 the book was presented to King Alexander I of Serbia on his visit to the monastery, and the first facsimile edition appeared in Vienna the following year. The gospel is now in the National Museum of Serbia in Belgrade, and it was inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2005.
miroslav-krleza: Miroslav Krleža was born in Zagreb on 7 July 1893, the son of a constable. He enrolled in a preparatory military school in Pécs and then in the Ludoviceum military academy at Budapest, both within Austria-Hungary. He defected to Serbia but was dismissed as a suspected spy. On his return to Croatia he was demoted in the Austro-Hungarian army and sent as a common soldier to the Eastern front in the First World War. After the war he established himself as a major Modernist writer and as a politically controversial figure in the newly created Yugoslavia.

Krleža was the driving force behind the leftist reviews Plamen (1919), Književna republika (1923–1927), Danas (1934) and Pečat (1939–1940).
