He joined the Communist Party of Yugoslavia in 1918 but was expelled in 1939 because of his unorthodox views on art, his opposition to socialist realism and his unwillingness to support the Great Purge openly. This followed a long polemic known as the Conflict on the Literary Left; the commissar sent to mediate was Josip Broz Tito. When the Independent State of Croatia was set up under Ante Pavelić he refused to join Tito's Partisans, and after 1945 he faced a brief period of social stigma before being rehabilitated.

In 1947 he became vice-president of the Yugoslav Academy of Science and Arts in Zagreb, and in 1950, with Tito's support, he founded the Yugoslav Institute for Lexicography, which he headed until his death. He was president of the Yugoslav Writers' Union from 1958 to 1961. His speech at the 1952 Congress of Yugoslav Writers signalled a new era of comparative freedom in Yugoslav literature.

Krleža's main interest was drama. He began with experimental expressionist plays such as Adam i Eva and Michelangelo Buonarroti, then turned to naturalist plays; the best known, Gospoda Glembajevi, is a cycle on the decay of a bourgeois family. His chief poetic work is Balade Petrice Kerempuha, centred on a plebeian prophet, a Croatian Till Eulenspiegel. The short story collection Hrvatski bog Mars (1922) is anti-war and follows Croatian soldiers sent to the battlefields.

His four novels are The Return of Philip Latinowicz, On the Edge of Reason, The Banquet in Blitva and The Banners, a multi-volume view of Croatian and Central European society before, during and after the First World War, which won the NIN Award in 1962. He died in Zagreb on 29 December 1981 and was given a state funeral.
miroslav-of-hum: Miroslav Zavidović was a son of Zavida, a Serbian royal of the Vukanović dynasty who had briefly ruled as Prince of Zahumlje. His brothers were Stefan Nemanja, Tihomir and Stracimir. Miroslav received Zahumlje as an appanage of the Grand Principality of Serbia, covering Herzegovina and southern Dalmatia, with his seat at Ston. In 1166 Stefan Nemanja rebelled against the eldest brother, Tihomir, who fled to Greece with Stracimir and Miroslav. Nemanja defeated their Byzantine mercenaries near Pantino in Kosovo, where Tihomir drowned in the Sitnica. The brothers lost their titles, but Nemanja pardoned them and they went on ruling their lands under him.

Miroslav married a sister of Ban Kulin of Bosnia. After the death of Emperor Manuel he took under his protection the Narentine Kačić family, who had organised the murder of Rajneri, Bishop of Split, and he kept the bishopric's money; reluctant to let Catholicism prosper in his lands, he was excommunicated by the Papacy in 1181, and the Bishop of Ston left his seat, which has remained vacant since.

In 1184 Miroslav set out to retake the islands of Korčula and Vis, but on 18 August 1184 his fleet was destroyed by the Ragusian navy at Poljice near Koločep. A peace with Dubrovnik in 1186 was followed by cordial relations, and on 27 September 1186 Stefan Nemanja and Miroslav signed a treaty with the Normans, who held Korčula, by which Hum renounced its claims to Korčula and Vis. In 1190-1192 Nemanja gave Hum to his son Rastko Nemanjić, the later Saint Sava, while Miroslav held the Lim region with Bijelo Polje; when Rastko took monastic vows, Miroslav ruled Hum again.

Miroslav died of old age. He had two sons by Ban Kulin's sister, Andrija Miroslavljević and Toljen Miroslavljević, who married a daughter of Berthold of Andechs, and possibly a third, Petar. To his church of Saints Peter and Paul in Bijelo Polje, on the Lim, he gave 20 villages. The Miroslav Gospel, the oldest known book written in Serbian in Cyrillic, was made for him and in his honour.
mirpur-khas: Mirpur Khas lies in the south-eastern part of Sindh on the Let Wah canal, 65 kilometres east of Hyderabad, 220 kilometres north-east of Karachi and about 170 kilometres from the Indian border. Its name in Sindhi and Urdu means town of the most high Mirs. The land around it is fertile and watered by canals linked to the Indus, which gave the district its farming economy.

The region has been inhabited for millennia. Excavations at Kahoo Jo Daro revealed a settlement of the Buddhist era, and Hindu temples also stood here. A bronze of the god Brahma from the Gupta period, of the 5th or 6th century, was found in the area and is described as the earliest known metal image of Brahma. In 712 the region was conquered by the armies of Muhammad Bin Qasim.

The Talpur dynasty conquered Sindh in 1784, and under Mir Fath Ali Khan the province was divided into three parts, centred on Hyderabad, Khairpur and Mirpur Khas. The Mankani branch under Mir Ali Murad Talpur inherited the Mirpur Khas region in 1801 and founded the city in 1806 as its capital. Mir Sher Muhammad Talpur, who ruled from 1829 to 1843, built a fort and held court in it. The rulers' tombs at Chitorri combine Islamic and Rajasthani architecture. Charles James Napier defeated Mir Sher Muhammad at Dubbo on 24 March 1843, and Sindh was annexed to British India; the defeated ruler is remembered as the Lion of Sindh.

Under British rule Mirpur Khas was part of the Bombay Presidency and was overlooked until a branch of the Scinde Railway reached it. The opening of the Jamrao Canal in 1900 set it apart from the district's other towns; it became a municipality in 1901, and in 1906 the district headquarters moved to it from Umerkot. Its population was 2,787 at the turn of the century. After the independence of Pakistan in 1947 it was the first city to receive refugees, and much of its Hindu population left, although Sindh did not see the rioting of Punjab and Bengal. By 1951 the population was 40,420, of whom 68 per cent were Urdu-speaking migrants from India.

Mirpur Khas had 267,833 inhabitants in the 2023 census. It is known for its mangoes, with an annual mango festival held since 1955, and the district also grows wheat, sugarcane, cotton and bananas. A disused Sikh temple, the Gurdwara Pehli Patshahi, stands nearby on a site where Guru Nanak is traditionally believed to have set his feet.
mirwais-hotak: Mirwais Khan Hotak, born about 1673, belonged to the Hotak sub-tribe of the Ghilji Pashtuns of Kandahar. Kandahar was then under Safavid rule, and the Safavid ruler Sultan Husayn, suspecting that the Ghilji had revolted, sent the Georgian general George XI of Kartli there as governor. The Ghilji were not in revolt, but George treated the land as conquered. He dismissed many high officials, taxed the local Sunni Afghans and seized goods, women and children. His largely Shi'ite Georgian soldiers reportedly desecrated Sunni mosques and abused and killed Afghan children.

Hotak was head of one of the tribes and one of the richest and most influential men in Kandahar. After a petition to Husayn failed, he advised submission for the time being. George had him arrested and sent to Isfahan, but Hotak persuaded the court of his innocence, portrayed George as a danger and obtained leave to make a pilgrimage to Mecca. There he asked religious leaders whether it was lawful to take up arms against a sovereign who broke his oath, and they answered yes.

Husayn restored Hotak to his position in Kandahar to watch George. When George demanded Hotak's daughter as a concubine, Hotak sent a disguised girl in her place and prepared a revolt. In 1709 he invited George and his Georgian troops to a banquet and killed them. Hotak and his allies put on the armour of the Georgians, entered Kandahar and attacked the Georgian garrison, and he declared the independence of the Kandahar region.

The Persian court sent ambassadors, who were imprisoned or rebuffed, and then armies. In 1710 a force under Muhammad Khan was defeated, and over the next eighteen months four more armies failed. George's nephew Khusru Khan marched on Kandahar with an army of 42,000, but Hotak cut his supply lines and laid waste to the land. The Persian army was destroyed and Khusru was killed. Later expeditions in 1712 and 1713 collapsed for lack of funds.

Hotak remained in power until his death in November 1715. His brother Abdul Aziz succeeded him and was later killed by Hotak's son Mahmud, allegedly for planning to return Kandahar to Persia. In 1717 Mahmud exploited Husayn's weakness and briefly conquered large parts of Persia. Hotak is buried in a mausoleum in the Kokaran section of Kandahar. Many Afghans, especially Pashtuns, regard him as one of Afghanistan's great national heroes, known in Pashto as Mirwais Baba, Mirwais the Grandfather, and Steven Otfinoski called him Afghanistan's George Washington.
mirza-ghalib: Mirza Ghalib was born in Kala Mahal, Agra, into a family of Mughals that had moved to Samarkand. His paternal grandfather, Mirza Qoqan Baig, a Seljuq Turk, came to India from Samarkand, worked in Lahore, Delhi and Jaipur and finally settled in Agra. His father, Mirza Abdullah Baig, married Izzat-ut-Nisa Begum, an ethnic Kashmiri, and served the Nawab of Lucknow and then the Nizam of Hyderabad; he died in a battle in 1803 at Alwar when Ghalib was a little over five. His uncle Mirza Nasrullah Baig Khan raised him, but died in 1806 after falling from an elephant.

Urdu was his first language, though Persian and Turkish were also spoken at home. He began composing poetry at eleven. At fourteen he met Abdus Samad, a newly converted Muslim from Iran who had been a Zoroastrian named Hormuzd, and who stayed with him for two years teaching him Persian, Arabic, philosophy and logic.

Until 1827 Ghalib received a monthly share of his uncle's government pension, and he travelled to Calcutta to petition the Governor-General to keep it. In 1850 the Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar gave him the title of Dabir-ul-Mulk, secretary of state, with the addition of Najm-ud-daula, star of the state, and the title Mirza Nosha, which marked his incorporation into the nobility of Delhi. In 1854 he became the emperor's poet tutor, and he was also tutor to the emperor's eldest son, Prince Fakhr-ud Din Mirza, and royal historian of the Mughal court.

Ghalib wrote in Urdu and Persian. His Persian Divan is at least five times longer than his Urdu one, but his fame rests on his Urdu poetry. Before him the ghazal was chiefly an expression of anguished love; Ghalib took up philosophy and the travails and mysteries of life, widening its scope. His first pen name was Asad, from his given name Asadullah Khan, and he later took Ghalib, meaning all-conquering.

He was also a gifted letter writer. Before him Urdu letters were highly ornamental, and he made his talk like conversation, sometimes writing just the name of the person addressed. His letters gave a foundation to easy and popular Urdu prose, and Ralph Russell translated them in The Oxford Ghalib. He followed Shia theology and wrote verses in praise of Ali ibn Abi Talib, and he placed more weight on seeking God than on ritual. A large part of his poetry consists of naʽats, poems in praise of Muhammad, among them the Persian Abr-i gauharbar.
mirza-hasan-shirazi: Born in Shiraz on 25 April 1815 into the Shirazi family, Shirazi lost his father, Mirza Mahmud Shirazi, while young and was raised by his maternal uncle, Sayyid Husayn Musawi. He began religious study at four, studied jurisprudence in the seminary of Shiraz and from 1832 in Isfahan, where he was granted ijtihad in 1835. In 1845 he moved to Najaf and studied under senior scholars including Sheikh Muhammad-Hassan Najafi, who gave him a second certificate of ijtihad. On the death of Murtadha Ansari in 1864 he was named the scholar best qualified to succeed him.

Based at Samarra, Shirazi came to be regarded as the leading marja' of the Shia world. Two scholars brought the tobacco concession to his notice, and on 26 July 1891 he sent a telegram to Naser al-Din Shah protesting the monopoly. The shah sent his ambassador in Iraq to argue that the deal served the nation. After a second appeal went unanswered, a fatwa began to circulate in Tehran declaring the use of tobacco equal to war against the Hidden Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi. Doubts about whether it was genuine faded when Shirazi did not disown it.

In Samarra his standing drew Sunnis into the Muharram mourning ceremonies, and he gave money to help them finish a seminary of their own. Sultan Abdul Hamid II answered by founding more Sunni madrasas in the town. In 1893 sectarian violence there killed his son Muhammad and a nephew. Shirazi restrained Shias from the south who wanted to come and fight, and he turned away British and Russian offers of support, calling the matter a dispute among brothers.

Shirazi died in Samarra on 20 February 1895 and was buried in the Imam Ali Shrine at Najaf. His duties left him little time to write, and he produced only a few works on the writings of Ansari. His students included Muhammad-Kadhim Khurasani, Muhammad-Kadhim Tabatabaei, Muhammad-Husayn Naini and Fadhlallah Nuri. Historians have described his part in the tobacco boycott as a striking demonstration of the power of the marja'-i taqlid, and the protest has been cited among the causes of the Persian Constitutional Revolution.
mirza-hosein-khan-sepahsalar: Mirza Hossein was born in Qazvin in 1828. His father was a friend of Amir Kabir, whose patronage brought the son into government service and sent him abroad, where he studied French and Arabic. In 1848 he was appointed consul in Bombay. There he reported to the Iranian government on the advantages of growing opium for export, and the government ordered its cultivation on the basis of his report. He returned after three years with a fortune of 150,000 rupees, which led to accusations of corruption.

After serving in Tiflis, where he came to know the reformist thinker Fatali Akhundov, he was appointed ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in 1856. His years in Constantinople coincided with the Tanzimat and the drafting of the first Ottoman constitution; there he met Mirza Malkam Khan and came under the influence of the secret society of the Young Ottomans. In 1870 he accompanied Naser al-Din Shah Qajar on a visit to the Ottoman Empire and discussed the reforms of Midhat Pasha with him. The following year the shah made him vizier.

As Grand Vizier Hosein Khan set out to reform the legislative and judicial systems and to reorganise the shah's army. His measures included limiting the power of provincial governors, safeguarding the civil rights of subjects, inviting an Austro-Hungarian military mission, reorganising the judiciary and founding a national postal system.

In 1872 he persuaded the shah to grant the Reuter concession to the entrepreneur Paul Reuter, placing railway construction and all of Iran's existing and future infrastructure and industry under his control. Merchants, clerics and nationalists condemned it at once, and opposition from bureaucratic factions and clerical leaders forced the shah to dismiss his Grand Vizier and revoke the concession. His years in office also saw opium cultivation spread and cotton production decline, among the causes of the economic crisis and famine that followed.
mirza-jani-beg-tarkhan: Mirza Jani Beg belonged to the Arghun family, heads of their clan in Turan, whose service Timur had rewarded with the title of Tarkhan. His ancestor Mir Dhu'n-Nun Beg revolted against the Timurid government in Herat and pushed towards Balochistan and Sindh, and Mirza Shah Arghun took Bhakkar and Siwistan and in 1520 became the first Arghun ruler in Sindh. Under Mirza Muhammad Baqi, Bhakkar in Upper Sindh was lost to Sultan Mahmud, and Siwistan also slipped from Tarkhan control, so that what Jani Beg inherited in 1585 was the land of Thatta.

Akbar set aside the Arghun claim of shared descent with the Mughals and, with the Portuguese presence growing, aimed to subdue them. In 1586 the Mughal governor of Bhakkar, Nawab Muhammad Sadiq Khan, besieged Tarkhan territory, but Jani Beg used his flotilla to rescue his troops and strike the Mughal rear from the river, forcing a settlement. Akbar then sent his chief noble, Khan-i-Khanan, to conquer Thatta. Jani Beg gathered local tribesmen and hired Portuguese mercenaries to build a fleet that could cut the Mughal supply line, and in the fighting he lost his father, Mirza Paynda, and his son Abu'l Fath.

The Dhakhirat al-Khawanin tells of a dream in which Muhammad awarded Thatta to Khan-i-Khanan; Jani Beg is said to have answered the saints who brought the message that the work would be done by the army of the day, not by the prayers of the night. The balance tipped towards the Mughals, and he handed over his lands.

Akbar gave him a mansab of 5,000, with Thatta and the sarkar of Siwistan, and held him in high regard. His standing fell in 1599-1600, when Bahadur Asiri surrendered Asir to Akbar without a fight and Jani Beg was rumoured to have said that in Asir's place he would have fought even the emperor. He continued in Mughal service until his death on 1 February 1601. A poet in Persian under the pen name Halimi, he wrote ghazals of which one is still sung by qawwals.
mirza-kuchik-khan: He was born Yunes in Rasht, the son of a merchant from Gilan known as Mirza Bozorg, and so was called Mirza Kuchak, the younger. After Mohammad Ali Shah Qajar shut down the Iranian Parliament in a coup in June 1908, uprisings followed in Tabriz, Ardabil and Rasht. Kuchik Khan tried to join Sattar Khan's forces in Tabriz but was prevented by illness, and he was wounded in the Constitutionalist war and travelled to Baku and Tbilisi for treatment. In July 1909 he was one of the lower-ranking commanders of the forces that took Tehran from the north.

The old privileged class soon regained control of the new regime, the revolutionaries were disarmed, and Russian and British interference deepened the unrest. With the Society of Islamic Union, Kuchik Khan began a rising in the forests of the southern Caspian, first based at Kasma, which drew on the new national bourgeoisie and the peasants. The Jangalis defeated local government and Russian troops, but at Manjil on 12 June 1918 they were beaten by British and White Russian forces under General Dunsterville and Colonel Lazar Bicherakhov, who used artillery, armoured cars and aircraft.

In May 1920 a Soviet fleet under Fyodor Raskolnikov entered the port of Anzali. Kuchik Khan agreed to cooperate on condition that a Socialist Republic of Gilan be proclaimed under his leadership without Soviet interference, but disputes with the Soviets and the Communist Party of Persia soon turned bloody, and a petition he sent to Lenin settled nothing.

In 1921, after an agreement with Britain, the Soviets withdrew their support, and government forces under Colonel Reza Khan overran the republic. Kuchik Khan and a companion, Gaouk, died of frostbite in the Talesh mountains. A local landlord cut off his head, which was shown in Rasht and sent to Reza Khan in Tehran; friends returned it to his tomb in Rasht during the Second World War. Historians such as Gregory Yeghikian and Ebrahim Fakhrayi trace the movement's fall to the communists' extremism and to his own cautious religious views.
mirza-muhammad-haidar-dughlat: Mirza Muhammad Haidar Dughlat Beg was a Chagatai Turco-Mongol general, governor of Kashmir and historian, a Dughlat prince who wrote in both Chaghatai and Persian. He and the first Mughal emperor Babur were first cousins on their mothers' side, sharing the grandfather Yunus Khan, and both belonged to the line of Genghis Khan. His mother was Khub Nigar Khanum, third daughter of Yunus Khan by Isan Daulat Begum and a younger sister of Qutlugh Nigar Khanum, Babur's mother.

Unlike Babur, Haidar considered himself more an ethnic Mongol of Moghulistan. In his Tarikh-i Rashidi he repeatedly mentions a distinct community of Moghuls there who, though reduced in numbers, preserved Mongol customs and, from the incidental Mongolian phrases and terms he gives, probably kept elements of the Mongolian language, despite the spread of Islam and of the Turki language that Haidar himself spoke naturally.

Haidar did not stay long on his first campaign in Kashmir. He left after making a treaty with the local sultan and striking coins in the name of Said Khan. He also attacked Tibet through Ladakh but failed to conquer Lhasa.

He returned to Kashmir in 1540, fighting for the Mughal emperor Humayun. On arriving he installed Nazuk, head of the Sayyid faction, as sultan. In 1546, after Humayun recovered Kabul, Haidar removed Nazuk Shah and struck coins in the name of the Mughal emperor. He governed Kashmir from 1540 until 1551, when he was killed in battle, and he was buried at Mazar-i-Salatin, Zaina Kadal, in Srinagar.

The Tarikh-i Rashidi is the work through which Haidar is best known. According to it, he regarded his Moghul Ulus as a people separate from the settled Turks of Transoxiania through the fifteenth century and the first half of the sixteenth. Vasily Bartold judged that there are some indications that the language of the Moghuls was Mongolian until the 16th century. For sedentary Mongols in Transoxiana, the nomadic Mongols to their east, in Xinjiang and Kashgar, stood for a bastion of true Mongol culture, which is the origin of the name Moghulistan.
mirza-reza-kermani: Mirza Reza was born in Kerman in 1854. With other followers of Jamal al-Din al-Afghani he demanded that the Qajar dynasty rule Iran justly, and after the Qajars expelled al-Afghani from the country he began to criticise Qajar officials openly and in public. His activity cost him dearly: he was imprisoned, his wife divorced him and his son was made a servant. In 1895 he visited al-Afghani in Istanbul, where the two planned the assassination of Naser al-Din Shah Qajar before Kermani returned to Iran.

He shot the shah at the Shah Abdol-Azim Shrine in Rey. He is reported to have said that he had an earlier chance to kill him but held back because Jews were holding their picnic after the eighth day of Passover, and he did not want them accused of the killing. It is said that the revolver was old and rusty, and that the shah would have survived had he worn a thicker overcoat or been shot from further away; shortly before he died he is reported to have said, "I will rule you differently if I survive!"

Kermani fled towards the Ottoman border. The new shah, Mozaffar ad-Din Shah Qajar, sent a detachment of troops on camels to find his father's killer, and Kermani was captured at the border. After months of interrogation he was hanged in public on 10 August 1896. The assassination and his execution are seen as a turning point in Iranian political thought, one that led in time to the Iranian Constitutional Revolution during Mozaffar ad-Din Shah's reign, the first major democratic movement in the modern Middle East after the First Constitutional Era of 1876–78 in the Ottoman Empire.
mirzhakip-dulatov: Dulatuly was born on 25 November 1885 in the village of Sarikopa in Turgay Oblast, into a Muslim family of the Argyn tribe of the Middle jüz. He lost his mother Demesh at the age of two and his father Dulat at twelve. After the village school he entered a Kazakh-Russian school in 1897 and qualified as a village teacher in 1902. In 1904 he met Ahmet Baitursynuly and Älihan Bökeihan at Karkaraly, and under their influence came to hold anti-colonial, anti-Russian views.

In 1907 he moved to St. Petersburg, became a delegate of the Constitutional Democratic Party and published his first poem, Jastarğa (To the Youth), in the journal Serke, which ran to only one issue. Oyan! Qazaq was confiscated as soon as it appeared in 1909 and was republished in 1911. His novel Baqytsyz Jamal (Jamal the Unfortunate, 1910), the story of a Kazakh girl who falls victim to patriarchal customs, was the first novel of modern Kazakh literature. Under surveillance he could hold no steady job, and after his arrest at Semey in 1911 he served a year and a half in prison.

He then wrote for the Kazakh periodicals Ayqap and Qazaq, criticising the conditions of Kazakhs under imperial rule, and published the collection Azamat (Citizen) in 1913. As one of the leaders of the Alash Orda government he sided with the Whites against the Bolsheviks from December 1917 to May 1919. When Admiral Aleksandr Kolchak turned down their requests for help, the Alash leaders realigned with the Bolsheviks in hope of autonomy, and Dulatuly worked as an editor and teacher under the new government.

Arrested on charges of nationalism in 1928, he died in the Solovki labour camp in 1935. He was rehabilitated after his death in 1988 and is considered a pioneer of modern Kazakh literature and a leader of Kazakh nationalism. He also wrote under the pen names Madiyar and Argyn, and the 1993 film Return of Mir-Yakub, made by the director Kalila Umarov, is dedicated to him.
mishneh-torah: The title Mishneh Torah means "repetition of the Torah" and was originally a name for the biblical book of Deuteronomy. The work is also called Sefer Yad ha-Hazaka, the "Book of the Strong Hand", because fourteen, written in Hebrew letters as yod and dalet, spells yad, hand. Maimonides compiled it between 1170 and 1180 while he was living in Egypt. He wrote it in Hebrew, as the Mishnah had been, since he was reluctant to use Talmudic Aramaic, which was not widely known; his earlier works were in Judeo-Arabic. He intended a complete statement of the Oral Law, so that someone who had mastered the Written Torah and then this work would need no other book.

The fourteen books are divided into sections, chapters and paragraphs. The first, HaMadda (Knowledge), covers belief in God, proper conduct, Torah study, idolatry and repentance, and further books treat love of God through prayer and blessings, the times of the Sabbath and festivals, and the laws of marriage and divorce. The work sets out all of Jewish observance, including the laws that apply only while the Temple in Jerusalem stands. The book almost never cites sources or arguments and states the final ruling for each case, with chapters following the subject matter rather than the Talmud's order. It also contains a widely quoted list of eight levels of charitable giving.

The work met strong opposition almost as soon as it appeared, chiefly because it gave no sources and seemed meant to replace study of the Talmud. The most influential critic was Abraham ben David of Posquières, whose comments are printed beside nearly every edition. Maimonides answered that he wanted brevity and a needed code, that he had not meant to end Talmud study, and that he regretted not adding sources. Yonah of Gerona took part in burning copies of the Sefer ha-Madda in the 1240s but repented after Talmud volumes were burned in Paris in 1244. The work soon won recognition as an authority for ritual decisions, and Meir HaKohen adapted it for Ashkenazi readers in the Haggahot Maimuniyyot.
misima: Misima, formerly called St. Aignan, is a volcanic island in the north-west of the Louisiade Archipelago, measuring about 40 by 10 km. It lies some 20 km north of the north-western end of the barrier reef of Vanatinai at Isu Raua Raua Island, and 80 km north-west of Vanatinai Island itself. The island is mountainous and densely forested, and Mount Koia Tau, 1,036 metres high, is the highest peak of the archipelago. The climate is tropical and humid, moderated by the north-east trade winds, with a dry and a wet season of about six months each.

Austronesian peoples have lived on Misima since about 1500 BCE. The French captain Louis Antoine de Bougainville sighted the island in 1768, and the French explorer Antoine Bruni d'Entrecasteaux explored it in 1793. The island owes its name to Élisabeth-Paul-Édouard de Rossel, a lieutenant on d'Entrecasteaux's voyage of scientific exploration. The British Empire annexed Misima in 1888, and it became part of British New Guinea, later the Territory of Papua administered by Australia. Gold was discovered late in 1888, and by March 1889 eighty men were digging on the island and a storekeeper had set up in business.

Since 1975 Misima has been part of independent Papua New Guinea. The modern gold and silver mine was a joint venture of Placer Dome Inc, which owned 80 per cent, and the state-owned Orogen Minerals Ltd, and it gave the islanders much work. It was officially closed in 2004 because of its heavy load on the environment and the hazards it posed to public health. In March 2012 Barrick closed its post-closure monitoring office in Bwagaoia after rehabilitating the mine and mill sites.

With 19,330 people in 78 villages, Misima is the most heavily populated island of the Louisiade Archipelago and the third largest by area, after Vanatinai and Rossel Island. Its main town, Bwagaoia on the south-east corner, is the seat of the Samarai-Murua District. The main language is Misiman, and many residents also speak English and Tok Pisin. Since the mine closed, artisanal gold mining has become a main source of income, with the Misima Alluvial Gold Mining Association founded in 2007, beside cash crops of coconuts, copra and cacao.
misiones-province: Misiones is one of the 23 provinces of Argentina, in the north-eastern corner of the country, in the region called Mesopotamia. Paraguay lies to the north-west, Brazil to the north, east and south and Corrientes Province to the south-west. It is the second-smallest province, after Tucumán. The Paraná, Uruguay and Iguazú rivers embrace it, and the Iguazú Falls are in its north-western corner, shared with the Brazilian state of Paraná. The soil of the Misiones plateau is reddish from iron in the rocks, and the native forest, the Selva Misionera, survives in Iguazú National Park.

Indigenous peoples lived in the area for thousands of years; at the time of European contact the Kaingang and Xokleng were there, later followed by the Guaraní. Sebastian Cabot reached Apipé Falls in December 1527, and Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca reached the Iguazú Falls in 1541. From 1609 the Jesuits, led at first by Diego de Torres Bello, founded a string of reductions, of which San Ignacio, founded in 1610, was the most notable. They soon had 30 mission villages and taught the Guaraní western-style agriculture and crafts. When the missions were abandoned, their trade vanished, and colonists imposed a brutal plantation economy that forced the Guaraní to work as slaves.

The territory was claimed by several countries and in practice governed itself. In 1830 Argentine forces from Corrientes took control, and in 1838 Paraguay occupied it. Paraguayan troops invaded again in 1865 in the War of the Triple Alliance, and after Paraguay's defeat it gave up its claim in a peace agreement signed in 1876. Academics tend to date Argentine possession from that war. On 22 December 1881 the national government detached the National Territory of Misiones from Corrientes. European colonists arrived under the Immigration and Colonization Law, many by way of southern Brazil, among them Poles, Ukrainians and Swedes, and the city of Eldorado was founded in 1919. The territory became a province on 10 December 1953.

Misiones has 1,280,960 people, according to the 2022 census. Yerba mate has long been its chief crop, and tea, citrus fruit and timber are also produced. In 1984 UNESCO designated the ruins of four mission sites in Argentina as World Heritage Sites. The Yacyretá dam, begun after a 1973 agreement, raised the Paraná along the province's shores in the 1990s.
misirlou: The earliest known recording was made in 1927 for Columbia by the rebetiko musician Theodotos (Tetos) Demetriades, an Ottoman Greek born in Istanbul in 1897 who had moved to the United States in 1921, when most of the Greek speaking population fled the emerging Turkish state. He probably knew the tune as a folk song before he left. As with almost all early rebetika, the composer was never identified and ownership rested with the band leader. The claim that the tune derives from Bint Misr by the Egyptian musician Sayed Darwish is thought to be incorrect.

The rebetiko version was meant for the Greek tsifteteli dance, at a slower tempo and in a different key from the Oriental performances known today. Michalis Patrinos recorded it in that style in Greece around 1930 and again in New York City in 1931. The melody moves up and down the Hijaz Kar, or double harmonic, scale, and people from Morocco to Iraq claim it as a folk song of their own country.

In 1945 Professor Brunhilde E. Dorsch organised an international dance group at Duquesne University in Pittsburgh to honour the allies of the United States in World War II. The Cretan dance Syrtos Haniotikos had no music, and the student Pat Mandros Kazalas suggested the slower Misirlou tune. The new dance, first performed on 6 March 1945, took the song's name and spread in the Greek-American community, at Serbian Orthodox church dances as a kolo, and in the Armenian-American community, for which Reuben Sarkisian wrote Armenian words in Fresno in the early 1950s.

In 1941 Nick Roubanis, a Greek-American music instructor, released a jazz instrumental arrangement crediting himself as composer; the claim was never challenged in law, so he is still credited everywhere except Greece, where credit goes to Roubanis or Patrinos. English lyrics followed, and the tune became an exotica standard. Harry James recorded it in 1941, Jan August in 1946 and Darío Moreno, in French, in 1951.

Dick Dale, whose Lebanese-American uncle had played the song on one string of the oud, turned it into a fast solo rock guitar piece in 1962. His surf version brought the song to a wider audience in the United States, was recorded by the Beach Boys in 1963 and opened the 1994 film Pulp Fiction. The Athens 2004 Olympics Organizing Committee selected it as one of the most influential Greek songs, and Anna Vissi sang it at the closing ceremony.
miskawayh: Miskawayh, whose full name was Abū ʿAlī Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb Miskawayh al-Rāzī, was born in Rey, then under Ziyarid control, and came from Parandak in Iran. He may have been a Zoroastrian convert to Islam, though it seems more likely that one of his ancestors converted. He was fluent enough in Middle Persian to translate some pre-Islamic texts in that language into Arabic.

In his early career Miskawayh lived in Baghdad, where he served as secretary to Muhallabi, the vizier of the Buyid emir Mu'izz al-Dawla. After long service to the Buyids of Iraq he moved to the court of Rukn al-Dawla, where he spent seven years working with the Buyid vizier Abu 'l-Fadl ibn al-'Amid. In 966 a group of ghazis marched on the Library of Rey, and Miskawayh managed to save it.

After Abu'l-Fadl's death in 970 he continued to serve his son Abu'l-Fath, and in 975 he left with him for Baghdad. He later worked as a secretary and librarian for a series of viziers, among them 'Adud al-Dawla. Some contemporary sources linked him with the Brethren of Purity, claiming that some of his writings were used in compiling their Encyclopedia. He died in 1030 at Ray, then under Kakuyid control.

Miskawayh was a Neoplatonist whose influence on Islamic philosophy lies chiefly in ethics. His Tahdhib al-Akhlaq, the Refinement of Character, was the first major Islamic work on philosophical ethics; written for students, it treats practical ethics, conduct and the refinement of character. He separated personal ethics from the public realm and contrasted the liberating nature of reason with the deception and temptation of nature.

His Tajārib al-Umam, the Experiences of Nations, is a universal history from the beginning of Islam that stops near the end of the reign of 'Adud al-Dawla, and is one of the first eyewitness chronicles of contemporary events by a Muslim historian, since he had access to the inner workings of the court. In Al-Fawz al-Akbar, Al-Fawz al-Akbar, he gave a Neoplatonic account of the soul's evolution through a chain of emanations from God, which Muhammad Hamidullah compared to Darwinian thought. He also made an Arabic translation of the Persian Eternal Wisdom.
missi-dominici: The office grew out of Merovingian ad hoc arrangements, under which a missus regis, the king's envoy, was sent out as needed. Charlemagne, who ruled from 768 to 814, made the envoys a regular part of his government. At first he chose them from his most trusted entourage, whatever their social rank. The Lorsch Annals record that in 802 he turned instead to archbishops, bishops and abbots, dukes and counts, men who had no need to take gifts from the people they judged, and the Capitulare missorum generale of that year set out their duties in detail.

Their circuits, called missatica or legationes, were drawn so as not to follow the lines of the existing dioceses or provinces, and the missi were to visit them for a month at a time, four times a year. They were chosen afresh each year and were usually strangers to their district, so that they would not put down local roots or act on their own initiative, as the counts were doing. Envoys sent for a single purpose were called missi ad hoc, and extraordinary missi represented the emperor on special occasions, sometimes beyond his borders.

Besides justice, they received oaths of allegiance to the king, made his will known, at times by distributing capitularies, and supervised the clergy of their region. The inhabitants had to provide for their keep, and at times the missi led the host to battle. They were protected by a triple wergeld, and resisting them was punishable by death.

Even under Charlemagne it was hard to find men who would carry out these duties impartially, and after his death it became almost impossible. Under Louis the Pious the nobles came to influence the choice of missi, who were then taken from the districts they served; the list of 825 shows circuits that matched the provinces. Their work merged with that of the bishops and counts. Louis the German is not known to have sent any out. The missi disappeared from France around the end of the 9th century and from Italy during the 10th, as hereditary fiefs took the place of central control.
mission-civilisatrice: In the 18th century Europeans came to see history as a linear process of sociocultural evolution led by Western Europe, and colonialists described non-Europeans as backward nations. In France the philosopher Marquis de Condorcet set out a European holy duty to help peoples who, in his words, waited "only to receive the means from us" to civilise themselves. English colonial charters used similar language: the First Virginia Charter of 1606 spoke of bringing "the infidels and savages" to "human civility".

According to the historian Jennifer Pitts, liberal thinkers of the 1780s such as Adam Smith, Jeremy Bentham, Edmund Burke and Denis Diderot were sceptical of empire. By the mid-19th century, however, John Stuart Mill and Alexis de Tocqueville endorsed empire on the basis of the civilising mission.

The French historian Raoul Girardet called the French ideology of civilising Africans colonial humanism. French colonists regarded the civilisations of the peoples they subjugated as backward and held colonisation to be good for them, and Jules Brévié, a former governor-general of French West Africa and French Indochina, presented the French as protectors of indigenous culture as well.

Other powers used the same reasoning. The British, who did not coin the term, invoked it above all where colonies paid little, and Rudyard Kipling's 1899 poem The White Man's Burden expressed it. The United States applied it after annexing the Philippines in 1898, with public health campaigns and a free public school system. The Russian Empire tied it to its conquest of Central Asia, and the Empire of Japan to its rule in Korea.

Portugal gave the idea legal form in the Estatuto do Indigenato of 1929, under the Estado Novo of António de Oliveira Salazar. It separated colonial citizens under Portuguese law from the indigenas, governed through customary authorities, with a small group of assimilados between them who had some formal education and were not subjected to forced labour.

Nineteenth-century elites of South American republics used the same rhetoric against indigenous peoples: when Chile ended the occupation of Araucanía in 1883, President Domingo Santa María said the region had been subjugated by "the moral and civilizing force of the republic". The historian Mary Renda argued that the American occupation of Haiti from 1915 served economic exploitation and strategic advantage. Critics of development see modern programmes that require societies to give up their native cultures and become Western as a continuation of the civilising mission.
mississippi-river: The Mississippi rises at its traditional source, Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota, and flows generally south for 2,340 miles (3,770 km) to the Mississippi River Delta in the Gulf of Mexico. Its main stem lies entirely within the United States, and its watershed drains all or parts of 32 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces. It is divided into the Upper Mississippi, from the headwaters to the Missouri at St. Louis; the Middle Mississippi, to the Ohio at Cairo, Illinois; and the Lower Mississippi, from there to the Gulf.

The name comes from Misi zipi, the French rendering of the Anishinaabe name Misi-ziibi, meaning Great River. The Laurentide Ice Sheet of the last Ice Age left sediment that made the valley flat and fertile. In March 1876 the river suddenly changed channel near Reverie, Tennessee, so that the state line still follows the old channel.

The basin was first settled by hunting and gathering peoples and is considered one of the few independent centres of plant domestication in human history. Early cultivation of sunflower and an indigenous squash dates to the 4th millennium BCE, and the Mound Builders formed agricultural and urban societies. Alonso Álvarez de Pineda was the first recorded European to reach the river, in 1519, and Hernando de Soto reached it on 8 May 1541. The French explorers Louis Jolliet and Jacques Marquette began exploring it in the 17th century. The Treaty of Paris of 1763 made it the border between the British and Spanish empires.

Steamboat commerce ran from about 1830 to 1870, and Mark Twain described it in Life on the Mississippi. In the American Civil War control of the river was a strategic objective of both sides: Union forces cleared Island Number 10 and Memphis and captured New Orleans in 1862, and the Siege of Vicksburg ended on 4 July 1863 with a Union victory. In the spring of 1927 the river broke out of its banks in 145 places and flooded 27,000 square miles.
missolonghi: Missolonghi lies between the Achelous and Evinos rivers, with a port on the Gulf of Patras and the Missolonghi-Aitoliko lagoons to the west. It is the capital of the Aetolia-Acarnania regional unit, and its municipality bears the title Sacred Town of Missolonghi. The town was first mentioned by a Venetian called Paruta, describing the naval Battle of Lepanto, fought nearby. Its name probably comes from the Italian mezzo and laghi, meaning in the middle of lakes. Remains of the ancient town of Pleuron, mentioned in Homer, lie to the north-west.

The settlement grew as a fishing and trading hub. The Venetians captured it in 1684 and held it through the Morean War, but it returned to the Ottoman Empire after the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699. It joined the Orlov Revolt in 1770, which was quickly put down.

When the Greek War of Independence began, Missolonghi was the first place in western Greece to join, on 20 May 1821, led by town notables. Protected by islands and its lagoon on the sea side and by a wall and marshes on the land side, it lay close to the Peloponnese and the Ionian Islands. Alexandros Mavrokordatos landed in July and on 4 November 1821 convened an assembly that set up the Senate of Western Continental Greece.

The defences were at first a shallow ditch and a low wall with fourteen guns. An Ottoman army of 7,000 to 8,000 besieged the town from 25 October 1822, but a garrison of about 500 held out until Greek ships brought reinforcements, and the siege was lifted on 31 December. A second attack in September 1823 was abandoned on 17 November. The third siege began on 15 April 1825 under Reşid Mehmed Pasha, with an army of 30,000, later reinforced by 10,000 under Ibrahim Pasha. After a year, facing starvation, the 10,500 people inside, 3,500 of them armed, left in a sortie on the night of 10 April 1826. Few survived after the plan was betrayed.

For its resistance and the massacre that followed, the town received the title Hiera Polis, the Sacred City. Lord Byron, who died there in 1824, is commemorated by a cenotaph holding his heart. The Entrance Gate and part of the fortification survive, and the Garden of Heroes holds graves of fighters of the sortie. The Exodus is remembered each year on Palm Sunday.
mitakshara: The Mitākṣarā is a vivṛti, or legal commentary, best known for its theory of inheritance by birth. Its author, Vijñāneśvara, lived at Marthur near Kalaburagi in present-day Karnataka, in the reign of Vikramaditya VI of the Cālukya dynasty of Kalyāni, and was a close student of Mimamsa, the system of interpreting the Vedas. The scholar Derrett held him to have been a judge; Kane argued that the passages on judges reflect Mimamsa interpretation rather than his own career.

Its exact date is uncertain. Derrett placed it between 1121 and 1125, a range Kane called arbitrary and unsupported; Kane himself held that no evidence fixes the exact time of writing, and Lingat was content to place it at the end of the eleventh century. Together with the text of the Yājñavalkya Smṛti it fills about 492 closely printed pages.

Vijñāneśvara set out to clarify the Yājñavalkya Smṛti while discussing earlier commentaries on it, citing among others Viśvarūpa, Medhātithi and Dhāreśvara. The commentary brings together many smṛti passages, explains away their contradictions by the rules of Mimamsa and gives each rule its proper scope, so that it resembles a nibandha, or digest. Its most important subjects are property rights, the division of property and inheritance.

Wanting to apply the law already customary among the people, British courts in India took the Mitākṣarā, with the Dāyabhāga, as a main authority on Hindu law. It prevailed in most of India, the Dāyabhāga in Bengal, Assam and parts of Odisha and Bihar. After Colebrooke translated its section on inheritance in 1810, it held the status of a legislative text in the courts of most of India.

W. Macnaghten translated the part on procedure in 1829, and J. R. Gharpure made a complete translation. Later sub-commentaries include the Subodhinī of Viśveśvara (c. 1375) and the Bālaṃbhaṭṭī (c. 1770), possibly written by a woman, Lakṣmīdevī, and the 13th-century Telugu Vijnaneshvaramu is based on it.
mitanni: Mitanni, also written Mittani, was known by other names to its neighbours. Babylonian texts called it Ḫabigalbat, the Assyrians Ḫanigalbat, the Egyptians Naharin and the Hittites Ḫurri. The Hurrians were in the region by the late 3rd millennium BCE, and the group that became Mitanni moved gradually south into Mesopotamia before the 17th century BCE. No histories, royal annals or chronicles have been found in its excavated sites, so knowledge of Mitanni depends largely on what its neighbours wrote.

At its maximum extent Mitanni reached west to Kizzuwatna by the Taurus Mountains, south to Tunip, east to Arraphe and north to Lake Van. Shaushtatar sacked the Assyrian capital Assur and carried its palace doors to Washukanni, and Assyria may have paid tribute to Mitanni for generations afterwards.

Egypt and Mitanni first fought over the Levant and later became allies. The daughter of King Artatama I married Thutmose IV, Gilukhipa, daughter of Shuttarna II, married Amenhotep III, and Tadukhipa, daughter of Tushratta, was also sent to Egypt. Mitanni was especially interested in Egyptian gold. Tushratta's son Shattiwaza later became a vassal of the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I. The Assyrian king Adad-nirari I took Washukanni and other cities, and Shalmaneser I defeated a rebellion by Shattuara II of Hanigalbat around 1250 BCE. Hanigalbat then came under direct Assyrian control.

The kingdom's organisation is poorly understood, even at its peak. Succession generally passed from father to son. Members of the royal family bore Hurrian names, and kings took an Indo-Aryan throne name. Its military power rested on a warrior elite, the maryannu, who specialised in the battle chariot, held the highest position in society and often owned large estates.

Indo-Aryan influence appears in names, in the technical terms of the horse-training text of Kikkuli, and in the gods Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatya, invoked in treaties found at Hattusa. The pottery most characteristic of the kingdom is Painted Nuzi Ware, found from about 1550 BCE.
mithra: The Avestan word miθra, like the Vedic mitra, derives from Proto-Indo-Iranian *mitrám, from a root meaning to bind, so that the name means that which causes binding: the Avestan word for a covenant, contract or oath. In Middle Iranian languages it became mihr, the source of New Persian mehr and Armenian Mihr.

Like most other divinities, Mithra is not named in the Gathas, the oldest Zoroastrian texts, traditionally attributed to Zoroaster. Scholars of the early 20th century took this silence to mean that Zoroaster had rejected him, a speculation no longer followed.

In the Avesta Mithra belongs to the ahuric triad with Ahura Mazda and Apam Napat. His stock epithet is "of Wide Pastures", and he is the protector of cattle and guardian of the waters. The Hymn to Mithra, the tenth Yasht, is the longest and one of the best preserved of the Yashts. It opens with Ahura Mazda's command that Mithra be venerated as much as himself, and describes him as guardian of the contract, patron of warriors and master of the Iranian countries, who punishes those who break their oaths. He has a solar aspect but is not the Sun itself, which is the god Hvare-khshaeta; later tradition came to identify the two.

Artaxerxes II was the first Achaemenid king to invoke gods other than Ahura Mazda by name, asking Ahura Mazda, Anahita and Mithra to protect him, and Artaxerxes III invoked Mithra at Persepolis. Several Parthian kings, and rulers of Pontus, Commagene, Armenia and Iberia, bore the name Mithridates, given by Mithra.

Under the Sasanian Empire, Mihr was one of the important gods beside Ahura Mazda and Anahita, and his festival, Mehregan, ranked with Nowruz. A relief at Taq-e Bostan shows him at the investiture of Ardashir II. In the Zoroastrian calendar the sixteenth day of each month and the seventh month are his, and in contemporary Zoroastrianism Mehregan is still held in the autumn.
mithridate-play: Racine wrote the tragedy in alexandrine verse, its five acts having five, six, six, seven and five scenes. It was first performed on 13 January 1673 at the Hôtel de Bourgogne and stands between Bajazet and Iphigénie in his work. Its subject comes from ancient history: Mithridates VI Eupator ruled Pontus around the Black Sea, accustomed himself to poisons, long resisted the Romans and finally killed himself after being betrayed by his own son.

The play sets several episodes of the king's life within a single day. Believing Mithridates dead, his son Xiphares declares his love to Monime, the king's betrothed, and fears his brother Pharnaces, who has always sided with the Romans. Mithridates returns, learns of the treachery of Pharnaces and plans to invade Italy. When Pharnaces refuses to marry a Parthian king's daughter, he is arrested, and Mithridates tricks Monime into confessing that she loves Xiphares.

Pharnaces reveals the plan of attack to the Romans, who land and attack the palace. A servant brings Mithridates and Monime poison, and a rumour spreads that Xiphares has died. Defeated and pierced by a sword, Mithridates pardons Monime; Xiphares meanwhile drives back the Romans, and before dying the king, proud of his son's victory, unites Monime and Xiphares and advises them to flee.

As usual in Racine, love intrigues carry great weight, but the epic element is stronger than in his other tragedies, and the play is marked by many long speeches and monologues. It was the favourite tragedy of Louis XIV. Over the centuries it has become rare on stage and is now one of the least performed of Racine's works. It formed the basis of Mozart's opera Mitridate, re di Ponto, of 1770.
mithridates-i-of-parthia: Mithridates was the son of Priapatius and the great-nephew of the first Arsacid king, Arsaces I. His name is the Greek form of the Iranian Mihrdāt, meaning given by Mithra. Parthian custom required a ruler to be succeeded by his own son, but his elder brother Phraates I broke the custom and named Mithridates as successor. The Roman historian Justin says Phraates had noticed his competence.

The kingdom he inherited was one of several medium-sized powers that had arisen as the Seleucid Empire declined. It covered present-day Khorasan Province, Hyrcania, northern Iran and the south of present-day Turkmenistan.

Mithridates first attacked the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, weakened by wars with its neighbours. Between 163 and 155 BCE he took Aria, Margiana and western Bactria from Eucratides I, and Merv became a Parthian stronghold. Turning west, he occupied Ecbatana in 148 or 147 BCE and conquered Media Atropatene. In 141 BCE he captured Babylonia, minted coins at Seleucia and held an investiture ceremony there. Elymais and Characene became vassals, and Parthian authority reached the Indus.

In about 140 BCE, while he fought the Saka in the east, the Seleucid king Demetrius II Nicator tried to retake Babylonia. He was captured in 138 BCE and sent to a palace in Hyrcania, where Mithridates treated him hospitably and married him to his daughter Rhodogune. Mithridates then punished Elymais for helping the Seleucids and made Persis a vassal.

He was the first Parthian king to take the Achaemenid title King of Kings. His later coins show a Hellenistic diadem and the title Philhellene, friend of the Greeks, aimed at his new Greek subjects. He renamed Nisa as Mithradatkert, and Ctesiphon was founded in his time.

Mithridates died in about 132 BCE and was succeeded by his son Phraates II. Historians such as Klaus Schippmann argue that his campaigns were more than raids for plunder and aimed at reaching Syria and the Mediterranean. Homa Katouzian has compared him with Cyrus the Great.
mithridates-i-of-pontus: Mithridates I Ctistes, also known as Mithridates III of Cius, was a Persian nobleman. He is said to have been of the same age as Demetrius Poliorketes, which would place his birth in the mid-330s BCE.

In 302 or 301 BCE, shortly after executing Mithridates II of Cius, the young man's father and predecessor, the diadoch Antigonus grew suspicious of the son who had inherited the family dominion of Cius and planned to kill him. Mithridates received timely notice of this from Demetrius Poliorketes and fled with a few followers to Paphlagonia, where he occupied a strong fortress called Cimiata.

Numerous bodies of troops from different quarters joined him, and he gradually extended his dominions in Pontus, laying the foundations of a new kingdom. It may be judged to have risen about 281 BCE, when Mithridates assumed the title of basileus, or king. In the same year he concluded an alliance with the town of Heraclea Pontica in Bithynia, to protect it against Seleucus.

At a later time Mithridates acquired support from the Gauls, who afterwards settled in Asia Minor, in order to overthrow a force sent against him by Ptolemy, king of Ptolemaic Egypt. These are the only recorded events of his reign.

Mithridates reigned from 281 to 266 BCE and was succeeded by his son Ariobarzanes. He seems to have been buried in a royal grave near the kingdom's capital, Amasia, and all the kings of Pontus were to be buried beside him until the fall of Sinope in 183 BCE. His epithet Ctistes means founder, literally builder, of the Kingdom of Pontus.

His ancestry is a matter of dispute. According to Appian, he was eighth in descent from the first satrap of Pontus under Darius the Great and sixth in ascending order from Mithridates Eupator. Plutarch, however, writes that eight generations of kings of Pontus stemmed from him before Roman subjection.
mithridates-ii-of-parthia: Mithridates II was crowned after the abrupt death of Artabanus I and inherited an empire under pressure from the east and the west, after humiliating defeats by eastern nomads. His parentage is uncertain. The Roman historian Justin makes him a son of Artabanus I, but a cuneiform tablet of 119 BCE calls the dead Artabanus his brother. Vesta Sarkhosh Curtis argues that he was a son of Priapatius, while Marek Jan Olbrycht holds that he was Artabanus's son and a middle-aged man at his accession.

In Mesopotamia he won the allegiance of Hyspaosines of Characene and then invaded Elymais, captured Susa and defeated its king Pittit. About 120 BCE he invaded Armenia and made King Artavasdes I accept Parthian suzerainty, taking Tigranes as a hostage. Iberia, and possibly Caucasian Albania, probably became vassal states too. In 114 or 113 BCE he captured Dura-Europos from the Seleucids. About 95 BCE Tigranes was released and made king of Armenia, and Adiabene, Gordyene and Osrhoene were conquered, moving the western border to the Euphrates.

In the east he reconquered western Bactria, avenging the nomads who had killed his predecessors. Sakastan, the land of the Saka, was recovered by a general of the House of Suren, who received it as a fiefdom, and the empire reached Arachosia. At the Euphrates the Parthians met the Romans for the first time: in 96 BCE Mithridates sent an official named Orobazus to Sulla, who apparently gained the upper hand in the talks. A Chinese delegation is attested at his court in 120 BCE, and the Silk Road opened to trade the following year.

Mithridates II used the title King of Kings regularly from about 109 BCE, and he stressed the dynasty's link to the Achaemenid Empire. His coins show him in an Iranian tiara instead of the Hellenistic diadem, and the omphalos on the reverse gives way to a high-backed Achaemenid throne. Justin says his achievements earned him the surname Great.

His son Gotarzes, who had served as satrap of satraps under him, was proclaimed king at Babylon after his death in 91 BCE. The period that followed, known as the Parthian Dark Age, is poorly documented, and political instability brought territorial losses, including land that Tigranes of Armenia seized. The crisis ended with the accession of Sinatruces.
mithridates-v-of-pontus: Mithridates V Euergetes, whose epithet means the Benefactor, was the seventh king of Pontus. He was of Greek Macedonian and Persian ancestry, the son of King Pharnaces I and Queen Nysa, and his sister was Nysa of Cappadocia. His mother is believed to have died in childbirth. He was born and raised in Pontus and succeeded his paternal aunt Laodice and his paternal uncle Mithridates IV on the throne, though the circumstances of his accession are uncertain.

Mithridates continued the alliance with Rome begun by his predecessors. He supported the Romans with some ships and a small auxiliary force in the Third Punic War, and later helped them in the war against Eumenes III, king of Pergamon, in 131–129 BCE. For this service the consul Manius Aquillius rewarded him with the province of Phrygia, although the Roman Senate rescinded the consul’s acts on grounds of bribery.

He also increased the power of Pontus by marrying his eldest child, his daughter Laodice, to King Ariarathes VI. The end of his reign can only be placed approximately, from statements about the accession of his son Mithridates VI, assigned to 120 BCE.

Mithridates V was assassinated at Sinope around 120 BCE, poisoned by unknown persons at a lavish banquet he gave. He was a benefactor of Hellenic culture, shown in surviving coinage and in honorific inscriptions recording his gifts at Athens and Delos, and he held the god Apollo in great veneration. A bilingual inscription dedicated to him is displayed at the Capitoline Museums in Rome. He was buried in the royal tombs of his ancestors at Amasya.

He married the Seleucid princess Laodice VI, a daughter of Antiochus IV Epiphanes, and they had seven children, among them Mithridates VI and Mithridates Chrestus. After the fall of Pontus in 63 BCE his daughters Roxana and Statira were compelled to poison themselves, and Nysa was made to march in the triumphs of two Roman generals.
mithridates-vi-of-pontus: Mithridates was born in Sinope on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia, the first son of Mithridates V Euergetes and the Seleucid princess Laodice VI. His name is the Greek form of the Iranian Mihrdāt, given by Mithra, and he claimed descent from Cyrus the Great and Darius the Great on his father's side and from Antigonus I Monophthalmus and Seleucus I Nicator on his mother's. His father was poisoned at a banquet in about 120 BCE. Laodice VI held power as regent and favoured the younger son, Mithridates Chrestus, and Mithridates escaped her plots and went into hiding. In 113 BCE he overthrew his mother and ruled alone.

Mithridates meant to make Pontus the dominant power of the Black Sea and Anatolia. He subjugated Colchis, and Tauric Chersonesus and the Bosporan Kingdom gave up their independence in return for protection against the Scythians. In Anatolia he divided Paphlagonia and Galatia with Nicomedes III of Bithynia, then fell out with him over Cappadocia. After Rome intervened twice for Nicomedes, from 95 to 92 BCE, he resolved to expel the Romans from Asia.

In 89 BCE Nicomedes IV of Bithynia, urged on by Roman advisers, invaded Pontus, and Mithridates defeated him while Rome was occupied with the Social War. In 88 BCE he ordered a massacre of Roman and Italian settlers in cities including Pergamon and Tralles, in which as many as 80,000 people are said to have died, an episode known as the Asiatic Vespers. He presented himself as protector of Greek culture against Rome and won over much of mainland Greece, including Athens. Sulla won a string of victories in the first of the Mithridatic Wars but offered a generous peace. The second war began in 83 BCE, and the third in 73 BCE.

After Pompey defeated him at the Battle of the Lycus in 66 BCE, Mithridates fled north of the Black Sea, hoping to raise a new army and invade Italy by way of the Danube. His preparations burdened the local nobles and people, who rebelled, and his son Pharnaces rose against him. He retreated to Panticapaeum and killed himself. According to Appian, after a failed attempt with poison he asked his Gallic bodyguard Bituitus to kill him with a sword.

He was said to have made himself immune to poison by taking small doses, and a universal antidote, mithridate, was named after him. Pliny the Elder reports that he spoke the languages of the twenty-two nations he ruled, and his name later gave titles to works on comparative linguistics.
mithridatic-wars: Mithridates VI Eupator came to the throne of Pontus in a coup around 113 BCE, imprisoning his younger brother Chrestus and his mother Laodice. At first he looked north and east, accepting hegemony over parts of Armenia and campaigning across the Black Sea to take Crimea. His partition of Paphlagonia with Nicomedes III of Bithynia and his intervention in Cappadocia drew Roman envoys and a senatorial decree forcing him out of Cappadocia, where Lucius Cornelius Sulla installed Ariobarzanes I as king.

An alliance with Armenia strengthened Mithridates, and while Rome was distracted by the revolt of its Italian allies he again overthrew the ruler of Cappadocia. When Roman commissioners under Manius Aquillius pressed the restored kings to invade Pontus, he drove Ariobarzanes out once more and declared war.

In the first war Mithridates overran the Roman province of Asia and ordered the Asiatic Vespers, the massacre of some 80,000 Romans and Italians in the occupied territories, which caused a financial panic in Rome. Athens and much of Greece went over to him. Sulla landed, took Athens on 1 March 86 BCE and destroyed the Pontic forces at Chaeronea and Orchomenus. The Treaty of Dardanos of 85 BCE forced Mithridates out of Roman Asia and Paphlagonia. It was lenient, probably because Sulla wanted a free hand against the regime at Rome. A second war began in 83 BCE when the governor Lucius Licinius Murena attacked Mithridates, and it ended inconclusively after Murena's defeat in 82 BCE.

The third war began in 73 BCE after Rome annexed Bithynia on the death of its king, Nicomedes IV. Lucius Licinius Lucullus relieved Cyzicus, drove Mithridates into Armenia and invaded it, winning at Tigranocerta on 7 October 69 BCE, but his troops protested the length of the campaigns and he was replaced. Pompey took command in 66 BCE, defeated Mithridates, forced Tigranes of Armenia to submit, and took Syria and Jerusalem. Mithridates fled to Crimea and killed himself when his son Pharnaces staged a coup.

Pompey's settlement annexed Pontus, joined to Bithynia as one province, and Syria, and set up client kingdoms on the Anatolian plateau, among them Cappadocia and Commagene. More than 36,000 talents of gold and silver were found in Mithridates' treasuries. Large parts of Anatolia came under Roman taxation for the first time, collected by publicani and enforced by garrisons.

The wars drew Rome far deeper into the eastern Mediterranean and shifted provincial policy permanently towards exploitation of the east. Pompey's difficulty in winning ratification of his settlements and land for his veterans led him into an alliance with Marcus Crassus and Julius Caesar.
mitma: The Quechua word mitma means to sprinkle, distribute or spread, and comes from mitmat, a man moved or transported, or an outsider. The Spanish mitimae, plural mitimaes, derives from the Quechua mitamaq, settler or newcomer, and names a person whose group the Incas resettled for political reasons. The word is related to mit'a, labour taken in turns, which the Spanish later used for forced native labour under colonial rule.

The Inca imperial state took shape early in the fifteenth century; its conquests began in the 1420s, after the Incas drove off the Chancas and rebuilt Cuzco. The policy grew with the empire and was used for a long time in all its border regions.

The ethnic Inca were outnumbered a hundred to one by the peoples they ruled, and resettlement helped weaken resistance to them. Rather than create new governments, they moved existing ethnic groups about, kept a census of the resettled, and promoted resettled elites to bureaucratic posts so that their status depended on the empire.

For two years the settlers drew on the state storehouses and the local population had to provide for them, so that they could become self-sufficient and keep their own social and productive order. The new settlements also depended on the Incas for defence, supplies and government. The policy may have been linked as well to the state's management of large herds of llamas, alpacas and vicuñas.

Conquered groups were made to adopt marks that set them apart from their neighbours; the Huancavelicas, for example, removed six of each settler's front teeth. Officials could thus tell at a glance who belonged where, and even failing to wear the traditional costume was a crime punishable by torture or death.

Mitma is well documented on the Altiplano, especially in the Titicaca Basin, and the coast and western slope between present-day Peru and Chile were settled by enclaves from the Altiplano. Place names such as Loa, Calama and Erqui in southern Bolivia are thought to reflect transfers from Chile. In present-day Ecuador population exchanges changed the mix of peoples greatly, almost completely around Tumipamba; the Cañaris, Saraguros, Salasacas and Puruhaes were among the groups moved.
mito-ibaraki: Mito lies in the centre of Ibaraki Prefecture in the northern Kantō region, about ten kilometres inland from the Pacific Ocean, near the Naka River. Immediately to the south is Lake Senba, a recreational area. The climate is humid subtropical, with warm summers and cold winters with light snowfall.

The Yamato people settled in Mito around the 4th century CE. Near the end of the Heian period Baba Sukemoto, a warlord of the Heike clan, built a castle there. Mito Castle changed hands several times and passed to the Satake clan in the Sengoku period, but the Satake had to surrender it to Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1603 after the Battle of Sekigahara. Ieyasu gave it to his son Tokugawa Yorifusa, who became head of one of the three gosanke branches of the Tokugawa family, qualified to provide a new shōgun if the main line failed. The Tokugawa ruled Mito until the Meiji Restoration.

Mito was the seat of the Mito School, nativist scholars of Confucian persuasion led by Aizawa Seishisai, who advocated Western learning as a way to develop Japan's technology and strength and to prove Japanese uniqueness among nations. The Kōdōkan was the largest of the domain schools. In 1842 Tokugawa Nariaki laid out the garden of Kairaku-en, known for its ume trees and counted among the Three Great Gardens of Japan.

The city of Mito was created on 1 April 1889, with 25,000 people, one of the first 31 cities in Japan, and was made capital of Ibaraki Prefecture. By 1900 the Jōban Line linked it with Tokyo. More than three-quarters of Mito burned in the air raid of 2 August 1945, shortly before the end of World War II. It is mainly a regional administrative and commercial centre, since most of Ibaraki's industry lies around Tsukuba and Hitachi. Visitors come mostly to Kairaku-en, Mito Castle, the Kōdōkan school and museums of the Tokugawa family.
mitridate-re-di-ponto: Mitridate, re di Ponto (K. 87) is an opera seria in three acts, written by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart while he toured Italy in 1770. The libretto by Vittorio Amedeo Cigna-Santi is based on Giuseppe Parini's Italian translation of Jean Racine's play Mithridate. According to the musicologist Daniel E. Freeman, Mozart composed it with close reference to the opera La Nitteti by Josef Mysliveček, whom Mozart and his father first met in Bologna in March 1770. Mysliveček visited the Mozarts often in Bologna that summer while Wolfgang worked on Mitridate, and Mozart incorporated some of his motifs. The opera was first performed at the Teatro Regio Ducale in Milan on 26 December 1770, during the Carnival.

The action is set in 63 BCE around the Crimean port of Nymphæum during the conflict between Rome and Pontus. Mitridate is presumed dead after a heavy defeat, and his sons Farnace and Sifare and his fiancée Aspasia hear the news. Farnace, who has ties to the Romans, presses his advances on Aspasia, while Sifare loves her. Mitridate returns with Princess Ismene, daughter of his ally the King of Parthia, whom he wants Farnace to marry. Learning of Farnace's plot with the Romans and of Aspasia's love for Sifare, he swears revenge, but the Romans attack. Defeated, Mitridate kills himself to avoid capture. He blesses Sifare and Aspasia and forgives Farnace, who agrees to marry Ismene.

The score has virtuoso arias for the principal roles but only two ensemble numbers: the duet that ends the second act, "Se viver non degg'io", and a short quintet that ends the opera in the manner of baroque opera seria.

The opera was a success, with 21 performances, despite doubts about Mozart's extreme youth at the age of fourteen. It was not revived until the twentieth century. In 1901 Charles Malherbe located previously uncatalogued works of Mozart, including a soprano aria from Mitridate, which Camille Fourrier sang in Paris that year. A recording from the Mozarteum in Salzburg dates from 1971, and a film directed by Jean-Pierre Ponnelle, with Nikolaus Harnoncourt conducting, appeared in 1986. Productions at the Royal Opera House in 1993 and the Salzburg Festival in 2006 have been recorded.
mixed-member-proportional-representation: Mixed-member proportional representation combines local winner-take-all elections with a compensatory tier of party lists, so that the result is proportional overall. Voters usually cast two votes, one for a constituency representative and one for a party. Constituency members, usually chosen by first-past-the-post voting, fill seats first, and the remaining seats go to party candidates by each party's share of the nationwide or regional vote. Each party's constituency wins are subtracted from its proportional entitlement, so that the list seats compensate. This differs from mixed-member majoritarian systems such as parallel voting. Two parties with 25 per cent of the votes each end up with about 25 per cent of the seats even if one wins more constituencies.

The system that is often called MMP originated in Germany, where it is known as personalised proportional representation. It came about in 1949 as a result of bargaining between parties. The original version gave voters a single vote, so that choosing a representative also chose that person's party, and Germany changed to two votes before the 1953 election. New Zealand later adopted it under the name MMP, and elsewhere similar systems have other names. Wales used a version called the Additional Member System from 1999, with 40 constituency seats and 20 list seats in five regions.

Many systems set a threshold for list seats. In New Zealand it is 5 per cent of the party vote, in Bolivia 3 per cent, and in Germany 5 per cent for federal and most state parliaments. In New Zealand a party that wins one constituency seat also qualifies, and in Germany three.

A party may win more constituency seats than its party vote entitles it to; these overhang seats are kept in most systems, while most German states add levelling seats so that the result stays proportional. Germany's electoral law was modified in 2023 so that constituency winners do not always keep their seats. Proposals for MMP were defeated in Prince Edward Island, in referendums in 2005 and 2019, and were examined in Canada in 2004 and 2016 without result. Some voters vote for one party in the constituency and another in the party vote, a tactic by which they may seek double representation.
mixtecs: The name Mixtec comes from the Nahuatl word mixtecah, meaning cloud people. The Mixtecs call themselves by several names, such as ñuù savi, all of which can be translated as the land of the rain. Their historic homeland, La Mixteca, covers roughly the western half of the state of Oaxaca and parts of Puebla and Guerrero. It is divided into the Mixteca Alta, the highlands, the drier Mixteca Baja and the humid Mixteca Costa on the Pacific coast.

The Mixteca Alta has been studied most by archaeologists, with evidence of settlement from the Archaic and Early Formative periods, and the first urbanised sites emerged there. For most of Mixtec history it was the dominant political force, with the capitals in the central highlands. The Mixtec culture is held to have lasted from around 1500 BCE until the Spanish conquest. Before it, the Mixtecs numbered around 1.5 million.

Mixtec kingdoms competed and allied with each other and with Zapotec kingdoms in the Central Valleys, and the Valley of Oaxaca was often a disputed border region. Important centres included Tilantongo, Achiutla, Cuilapan, Tlaxiaco and Tututepec, and the Mixtecs also made major constructions at Monte Albán, a city of Zapotec origin that they came to control. The Costa came under Mixtec control through the campaigns of the cultural hero Eight Deer Jaguar Claw, who set out from Tilantongo, conquered kingdoms on the way and established the capital of Tututepec in the lower Río Verde valley.

The Aztecs moved into Oaxaca in the 1450s and defeated the Mixtecs in 1458. In 1486 they founded a fort on the hill of Huaxyácac, now El Fortín, which let them collect tribute from Mixtecs and Zapotecs, though not every Mixtec town became a vassal. The Mixtecs were later subdued by the Spanish and their central Mexican allies in the 16th century.

The Mixtecs wrote their histories and genealogies in painted fold-books on deerskin. The best-known story is that of Lord Eight Deer, told in several codices including the Codex Bodley and the Codex Zouche-Nuttall. They were goldsmiths said to be the foremost of Mesoamerica, practising lost-wax casting, and their gold work formed part of the tribute they paid the Aztecs. Turquoise mosaic masks were given as gifts to seal alliances, worn by those impersonating a god, and fixed to funerary bundles seen as oracles.
The Mixtec languages form a major branch of the Oto-Manguean family. About 800,000 Mixtec people live in Mexico today, and many have migrated within Mexico and to the United States.
mixton-war: The Caxcanes, the heart of the rising, lived in what is now northern Jalisco, southern Zacatecas and Aguascalientes. Though the Spaniards counted them among the Chichimeca, they seem to have been settled farmers living in permanent towns, and probably spoke a Uto-Aztecan language; the Zacatecos also joined the revolt. Their first contact with the Spanish came in 1529, when Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán marched north from Mexico City with 300-400 Spaniards and 5,000 to 8,000 Aztec and Tlaxcalan allies. Over six years Guzmán killed, tortured and enslaved thousands, founded the province of Nueva Galicia with towns such as Guadalajara, and forced natives into servitude under the encomienda system.

The rising began in spring 1540, perhaps encouraged by the departure of Governor Francisco Vásquez de Coronado with more than 1,600 Spaniards and allies on his expedition north. Its spark seems to have been the arrest of eighteen native leaders and the hanging of nine. The rebels killed the encomendero Juan de Arze and two priests, and many fled to the hill fortress of Mixtón, where they repelled an assault by the acting governor Cristóbal de Oñate. Their most prominent leader was Tenamaztle of Nochistlán.

In June 1541 Pedro de Alvarado attacked Mixtón with 400 Spaniards without waiting for reinforcements and was beaten back by an estimated 15,000 defenders under Tenamaztle and Don Diego, a Zacateco; on 24 June a horse fell on him, and he died on 4 July. The rebels attacked Guadalajara in September but were repulsed. Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza then invaded with 450 Spaniards and 30,000-60,000 Aztec, Tlaxcalan and other allies, took the strongholds one by one in a war of no quarter, captured Nochistlán on 9 November 1541, and took Mixtón early in 1542.

Thousands of the defeated were sent in chains to the mines, and many survivors, mostly women and children, were moved to work on Spanish farms. On the viceroy's order many prisoners were executed, some by cannon fire, some torn apart by dogs, and the Council of the Indies opened a secret inquiry into his conduct. The victory gave the Spanish the region of Guadalajara and access to the northern silver deposits, and Spanish expansion led on to the Chichimeca War of 1550-1590. The Caxcanes were absorbed into Spanish society, though fiestas of the Tastuanes in Moyahua de Estrada and Apozol still commemorate the war.
miyagi-prefecture: Miyagi lies in the central part of the Tōhoku region, on Japan's eastern Pacific coast. It borders Iwate Prefecture to the north, Akita to the northwest, Yamagata to the west and Fukushima to the south. The Ōu Mountains, the longest range in Japan, bound it on the west, and there are also high mountains along the northeast coast, but the central plain around Sendai is fairly large.
