The Oshika Peninsula projects from the northern coastline. Miyagi was formerly part of the province of Mutsu.

Matsushima, a bay of about 260 small islands covered in pine groves, is counted among the Three Views of Japan. About 24 per cent of the prefecture's land is designated as natural parks, among them the Sanriku Fukkō National Park and the Kurikoma and Zaō Quasi-National Parks.

Sendai, the capital and the largest city in Tōhoku, was the castle town of the daimyō Date Masamune, and the remains of Sendai Castle stand on a hill above it. Rice and livestock were produced in the countryside, and the coast supported fishing. In the 20th century the prefecture's population grew most between 1940 and 1950 and continued to grow into the 21st century, with manufacturing, notably electronics, appliances and food processing, concentrating around Sendai.

Miyagi lies in a part of Japan that is prone to earthquakes, with large ones frequent offshore. On 11 March 2011 a magnitude 9.0 earthquake and a tsunami about 10 metres high struck the prefecture and caused major damage; Miyagi suffered the most damage of any prefecture in the country. A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck off its coast on 7 April 2011.

The prefecture is home to many universities, among them Tohoku University in Sendai. Its festivals include the Sendai Tanabata Festival in August, the Aoba Festival in May and the Shiogama Port Festival in July. The Tōhoku Shinkansen and expressways link it with Tokyo, and Sendai has a port and an airport.
miyamoto-musashi: The details of Musashi's early life are difficult to verify. In The Book of Five Rings he says he was born in the village of Miyamoto, and an early biography, the Niten Ki, gives the year as 1584. His father, Shinmen Munisai, was an accomplished martial artist, a master of the sword and the jutte, and his mother, Omasa, died giving birth to him. He gives his full name as Shinmen Musashi-no-Kami Fujiwara no Harunobu, and he was also called Shinmen Takezō and Niten Dōraku, his Buddhist name. Accounts say he never took a wife, cut his hair or entered a bath.

By his own account his first duel took place at the age of 12 or 13, against Arima Kihei, and he won. At 16 he beat Tadashima Akiyama, and in 1599 he left his village. At 21 he defeated several students of a sword school in Kyoto.

In 1600 Musashi probably served in the army of Kuroda Yoshitaka on the Eastern side. A popular theory put him with the Western Army at Sekigahara, but recent research suggests that he and his father were on the Eastern side, although whether he fought at Sekigahara or at the battle of Ishigakihara in Kyūshū is still debated. In 1608 he met the Tokugawa general Mizuno Katsunari and taught him the secrets of his sword style. He is said to have served in the Tokugawa army at the Siege of Osaka in 1614 and in the suppression of the Shimabara Rebellion in 1638.

His best-known duel was with Sasaki Kojirō on Ganryū Island, arranged through Hosokawa Tadaoki. Musashi, it is said, deliberately arrived late and had carved an oar into a wooden sword, and he killed Kojirō with one vertical stroke. From 1633 he stayed with Hosokawa Tadatoshi at Kumamoto Castle, and in 1640 he became a retainer of the Hosokawa lords.

In 1641 Musashi wrote the Hyōhō Sanjūgo, the "Thirty-five Instructions on Strategy", for Tadatoshi, which became the basis of The Book of Five Rings. In 1643 he retired to the cave Reigandō and wrote that book, finishing it in the second month of 1645. A week before his death he gave it, with the Dokkōdō, "The Path of Aloneness", to his student Terao Magonojō. He died around 13 June 1645, and sources disagree on whether it was in the cave or at a house in Kumamoto. He developed the two-sword technique Niten Ichi-ryū, and left calligraphy and ink paintings, recognised as masterpieces, in the style called sumi-e.
miyoshi-nagayoshi: Nagayoshi was born in 1522, the eldest son of Miyoshi Motonaga. In 1536 he became a commander under Hosokawa Harumoto and fought the rebels of Hosokawa Harukuni and the Hongan-ji militants at Nakajima in Settsu. In 1539 he led his army into Kyoto for the first time, and that year he made Koshimizu Castle in Settsu his base. Earlier heads of the Miyoshi had ruled from Awa on Shikoku and fallen back there in times of trouble; Nagayoshi never returned to Awa and became deputy governor of Settsu.

Collecting taxes in Settsu on his own authority, he fell out with Harumoto, and his power grew after the fall of Kizawa Nagamasa in 1542. He then rebelled against Harumoto in alliance with Hosokawa Ujitsuna and Yusa Naganori, defeated Harumoto's allies and entered Kyoto, while the shoguns Ashikaga Yoshiharu and Yoshiteru fled to Omi. The capture of Nagao Castle, the last stronghold of Yoshiteru's forces, in late 1550 brought down the Hosokawa government and began what historians call the Miyoshi government.

Yoshiteru tried to have him assassinated in 1551, and that July Nagayoshi's army of 40,000 under Matsunaga Hisahide fought Harumoto's men at Shokoku-ji in Kyoto. A peace of 1552 brought Yoshiteru back as shogun, but real power stayed with Nagayoshi; after a new clash in 1553 Yoshiteru spent five years in seclusion at Kutsuki. By 1561 Nagayoshi's influence reached ten provinces, and that year he issued a privilege for the Jesuit missionary Vilela. From the death of his brother Sogō Kazumasa in 1561 his fortunes declined: his brother Miyoshi Saneyasu was killed at Kumeda in 1562, though Nagayoshi won the Battle of Kyōkōji that May.

In 1563 he lost his only son, Miyoshi Yoshioki, and adopted his nephew Yoshitsugu. In 1564 he had his brother Atagi Fuyuyasu put to death, believing, according to the chronicle Ashikaga Kiseki, Matsunaga Hisahide's lie that Fuyuyasu meant to seize the clan's leadership. He died of illness that year, aged 42. From the mid-Edo period writers cast him as a weak backdrop to the villainous Hisahide, and Rai San'yō called him old, sick and ignorant. Modern historians such as Amano Tadayuki and Akira Imatani have revised this, Amano seeing his government as the forerunner of Oda Nobunaga's unification, while Thomas D. Conlan called him the brutal conqueror of Kyoto.
mizoram: Mizoram is a landlocked state of North East India. It borders Bangladesh to the west and Myanmar to the east and south, and the Indian states of Assam, Manipur and Tripura to the north and west. It covers 21,081 square kilometres, most of it forested, and the Tropic of Cancer runs through its middle. The name means land of the Mizos, from Mizo, the native inhabitants, and ram, land or forest. Excavations at Vangchhia, a large necropolis, have found human remains, ornaments and pottery dating from 600 BCE to 1750 CE.

Tibeto-Burman-speaking peoples migrated south from the Chin Hills in present-day Myanmar and formed autonomous chiefdoms, each village behaving like a small state under a hereditary chief called a Lal. Chiefdoms lived mainly by slash-and-burn jhum farming and by trade on routes linking Yunnan to the Bay of Bengal, using the sial, a tame bison, as a unit of wealth. By the eighteenth century the Sailo dynasty dominated much of the region. After the Lushai Expedition of 1870–71, the British conducted further expeditions and annexed the area in 1895 as the Lushai Hills District of Assam. Missionaries wrote the first script for Mizo about 1895 and opened the first primary school in 1898 at Aijal, and Christianity gradually replaced the Sakhua practices.

On 15 August 1947 no Indian flags were hoisted in the Lushai Hills, because of opposition from rival factions of the Mizo Union. The district stayed within Assam, and discontent over the state's handling of the mautam famine fuelled an uprising in 1966, led by the Mizo National Front. Mizoram became a union territory on 21 January 1972, although the Front continued its armed struggle for complete independence. In 1973 the central government expelled foreign missionaries, which unintentionally led to a revival of Mizo culture, including the festival Chapchar Kut. Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and the Front's leader Laldenga signed the Mizoram Peace Accord on 30 June 1986, and on 20 February 1987 Mizoram became India's 23rd state.

Aizawl is the capital and largest city. Mizo and English are the official languages, and about 87 per cent of the people are Christian, mostly Presbyterian and Baptist; the largest religious minority is Theravada Buddhist, mainly Chakma. The census of 2011 counted 1,091,014 people, nearly 95 per cent of them members of Scheduled Tribes, the highest share in India. Literacy reached 92 per cent in 2011. The bamboo that covers much of the state flowers about every fifty years, an event called mautam that sets off an explosion of rats; the plague of 1958–59 preceded the uprising of 1966.
mizpah-in-benjamin: The Hebrew name miṣpā means watchtower or lookout, and the town belonged to the tribe of Benjamin. Three sites have been proposed for it. Tell en-Nasbeh, first suggested by Yohanan Aharon, lies about 12 km north of Jerusalem on the main road leading out of the city. Nabi Samwil, some 8 km north-west of the Old City, stands on the highest hill of the area above the plain of Gibeon. Shuafat, a village on a flat spur from which Jerusalem is visible, has been put forward because its name, meaning prospect, is thought to preserve the old name.

The case for Tell en-Nasbeh rests on archaeology. Nabi Samwil has yielded no remains from Iron Age I or from the 6th century BCE, both periods in which Mizpah was occupied, while Tell en-Nasbeh has abundant remains from both and a massive fortification system that fits the building campaign of King Asa of Judah in the early 9th century BCE. Against it, the biblical account places Mizpah right next to Gibeon, and a fugitive from Tell en-Nasbeh would hardly have fled to Ammon by way of Gibeon, which lies to the west.

In the Book of Judges the Israelite tribes met at Mizpah after the men of Gibeah raped the Levite's concubine, and there decided to make war on the Benjaminites and to ban the marriage of Benjaminite men to Israelite women. After the return of the Ark of the Covenant, Samuel gathered all Israel at Mizpah to offer sacrifice; the Israelites drove off a Philistine raid on the assembly, and Samuel set up the stone Eben-Ezer between Mizpah and Shen. At a later gathering there Saul was chosen by lot as the first king.

King Asa built up Mizpah with the stones that King Baasha of Israel had used to fortify Ramah. After Gedaliah's appointment the prophet Jeremiah came there from Ramah, and when Ishmael, a member of the royal family, assassinated the governor, the people left for Egypt despite Jeremiah's warning. The Book of Nehemiah lists Mizpah among the towns resettled by returning exiles who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. According to 1 Maccabees, Judas Maccabeus camped at Mizpah before the Battle of Emmaus, held a religious ceremony there and chose a smaller force to ambush the Seleucid camp.
mkwawa: Mkwawa was born in Luhota, the son and successor of Sultan Munyigumba. His full name was Mkwavinyika Munyigumba Mwamuyinga, and the short form Mkwawa comes from Mukwava, itself a shortening of Mukwavinyika, meaning conqueror of many lands. As a small child he was called Ndesalasi, troublemaker, and as an adult he bore a long praise name describing a leader who takes control of the forests, is aggressive to men and polite to women, and whom only death can take away. His family descended from an immigrant from the north named Mufwimi, a name meaning a hunter.

Ruling from Kalenga in the Iringa region, Mkwawa opposed German colonisation. In July 1891 the German commissioner Emil von Zelewski led a battalion of 320 askaris, with officers and porters, to subdue the Hehe. On 17 August Mkwawa's army of 3,000, armed with spears and only a few guns, attacked them at Lugalo, quickly overpowered the column and killed Zelewski.

On 28 October 1894 the Germans under the new commissioner, Colonel Freiherr Friedrich von Schele, attacked the fortress at Kalenga. They took it, but Mkwawa escaped and waged a guerrilla campaign against them for almost four years. His brother Chambila, whose name roughly means hero, fought beside him to the end. On 19 July 1898, surrounded at the Mlambalasi Rock Shelter, Mkwawa shot himself to avoid capture, and his body was buried a few metres from the shelter.

German soldiers cut off his head, and the skull was sent to Berlin and probably ended up in the Übersee-Museum Bremen. In 1918 Horace Byatt, the British administrator of German East Africa, proposed demanding its return, both to reward the Hehe for their help in the war and as a sign that German power had ended, and Article 246 of the Treaty of Versailles of 1919 required Germany to hand it over. The Germans denied that it had been taken, and the British government held that it could not be traced.

After World War II, Sir Edward Twining, Governor of Tanganyika, took up the matter and visited the Bremen museum himself in 1953. Of its 2000 skulls, 84 came from German East Africa; from those whose measurements resembled living relatives of Mkwawa he chose the only one with a bullet hole. It was returned on 9 July 1954 and is kept in the Mkwawa Memorial Museum at Kalenga, near Iringa.
mljet: Mljet is the southernmost and easternmost of the larger Adriatic islands of Dalmatia. It lies south of the Pelješac peninsula, from which the Mljet Channel divides it, and is 37 km long with an average breadth of 3.2 km. Its area is about 98 square kilometres, and over 84 per cent of it is forest. The island is of volcanic origin, with chasms and gorges, and the limestone and dolomite form ridges and slopes. The north-west includes an inland lake with a small island in it, within the Mljet National Park, which was established on 12 November 1960.

Ancient geographers knew the island as Melite or Melita. It is described in the Periplus attributed to Scylax of Caryanda, and Appian reports that its people, islanders accused of piracy, revolted against Rome and were punished harshly in the Illyrian campaigns of Octavian, with the young men executed and the rest enslaved. The Roman emperor Septimius Severus is said to have banished Agesilaus, the father of the poet Oppian, to the island. Around 950 the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitos listed it in De Administrando Imperio among the islands held by the Narentines. A tradition first set out in the 10th century by Constantine VII holds that Mljet was the Melita where Paul the Apostle was shipwrecked, though the wreck is generally placed on Malta.

The Benedictines of Pulsano in Apulia became the feudal lords of the island in 1151. Between 1187 and 1198 Desa, Grand Prince of Serbia, built and gave them the Church and Monastery of Saint Mary on the islet in the Big Lake, and Pope Innocent III consecrated the church in 1198. The Benedictines gave up their rule in 1345, keeping a third of the land, and the island received a statute and a municipality at Babino Polje. It later came under the Republic of Ragusa.

In the 16th century the monastery was the centre of the Mljet Congregation of Benedictine houses in the territory of the Republic of Ragusa, and its abbots included the poets Mavro Vetranović and Ignjat Đurđević. The monastery was disbanded in 1809 under Napoleon.

Mljet is part of Croatia and had 1,062 residents in 2021 in fourteen settlements, the largest being Babino Polje. It has no airport and is reached by ferry from the Pelješac peninsula and from Dubrovnik. Small Indian mongooses, introduced in the early 20th century to control the venomous snake, ate most of the island's birds.
mo-li-hua: The song is generally dated to the Qianlong era of the Qing dynasty, though some argue it is of the Ming era, and the ethnomusicologist Frederick Lau notes that the earliest lyrics appeared in the Wanli period (1563–1620). It belongs to the xiaoqu or xiaodiao genre, usually of several stanzas with uniform phrases and equal numbers of words, and uses the pentatonic scale. Regional versions differ in words and melody: one describes the custom of giving jasmine flowers in the southern Yangtze delta, another the fear of plucking the flower, and in northern China it is sometimes called La Mei Hua or Yu Mei Hua.

The British diplomat John Barrow, of George Macartney's mission to the Qianlong court, copied the tune into Western notation in 1793 and published it in 1804, noting that it seemed one of the most popular songs in China. From 1896 Qing officials in Europe sometimes used it as a temporary national anthem, until Cup of Solid Gold was adopted in 1911. Anton Arensky arranged it in the 1890s, and Giacomo Puccini, who probably knew it from a music box given to him by a former Italian diplomat, made it the leitmotif of the princess's splendour in Turandot (1926).

In 1982 the song entered a UNESCO list of recommended songs. It was played at the handovers of Hong Kong in 1997, at the request of Jiang Zemin, and of Macau in 1999, and was sung at the closing ceremony of the 2004 Athens Olympics; an adaptation by Tan Dun and Wang Hesheng introduced the victory theme at the medal ceremonies of the Beijing 2008 Olympic Games.

During the 2011 pro-democracy protests, called the Jasmine Revolution, protesters reposted videos of officials singing the song and suggested playing it on mobile phones as a deniable form of protest. The authorities then placed it on the list of censored online material, blocking searches for its name and removing videos, among them one of Hu Jintao singing it in Kenya in 2006.
moamoria-rebellion: The followers of the Mayamara Satra were predominantly Morans, the mainstay of the Ahom militia, joined by Sonowal Kacharis, Chutias, professional castes such as potters, weavers and fishermen, and some Ahom nobles and officers. The Ahom state rested on the Paik system, under which any able-bodied man who was not a Brahmin or a noble could be called up for labour, service or the army. The satras gave refuge to those seeking to escape it, and the loss of manpower brought them into growing conflict with the kingdom. The Mayamara Satra belonged to the non-conformist Kala-samhati sect, which competed with the royalist satras.

On 15 September 1769 Raghav Moran, a leading disciple of the satra, was flogged by Ahom officials for not supplying the required number of elephants. The Morans gathered an army of about seven thousand, and on 21 November 1769 they occupied the capital, imprisoned King Sunyeophaa and placed Ramakanta, son of the rebel leader Naharkhora, on the throne. After four months, when the peasant soldiers had gone home for the spring festival, nobles in disguise killed Raghav Moran on 14 April 1770 and retook the capital.

In April 1782 the Moamorias attacked the convoy of the newly crowned King Suhitpangphaa and briefly held Rangpur; the royalists who drove them out killed several thousand people. A third rising began in 1786. The rebels surrounded Rangpur in January 1788, the king left for Guwahati, and the continuous fighting in Upper Assam brought a famine described as the severest in the history of Assam. The rebels struck coins in the names of their leaders Bharat and Sarbananda but set up no central administration. A British contingent under Captain Welsh captured Rangpur in March 1794, but it was recalled and the rebels took the city again.

After the king's death Purnananda Burhagohain became the effective ruler and raised a standing army of paid sepoys in place of the paik militia. In 1805 his forces fought those of Sarbananda in the Bengmara region. Both sides recognised a stalemate, and Sarbananda accepted peace: he received the title of Barsenapati and autonomous command of the region, which came to be called the Matak rajya and paid annual tribute to the Ahom kingdom.

The population fell to about half of what it had been and economic life was disrupted. The paik and khel systems broke down, compelling the state to move towards a money economy. The weakened kingdom later fell to a Burmese invasion, which ultimately led to British colonisation.
mobile-phone: A handheld radio telephone was imagined early in radio engineering. In 1917 the Finnish inventor Eric Tigerstedt filed a patent for a pocket-size folding telephone with a very thin carbon microphone. Early predecessors of cellular phones included analog radio communications from ships and trains. The race to build truly portable telephones began after the Second World War, and advances are traced in successive generations, starting with the zeroth-generation services such as the Bell System's Mobile Telephone Service. These systems were not cellular, supported only a few simultaneous calls and were very expensive.

A mobile phone connects over a radio link to the switching systems of an operator, which gives access to the public switched telephone network. The advantage of modern cellular networks over earlier systems is frequency reuse, which lets thousands of subscribers talk at once in an area. Feature phones have limited capabilities, while smartphones have advanced computing power and a full operating system. The first SIM card was made in 1991 by the Munich smart card maker Giesecke & Devrient for the Finnish operator Radiolinja.

The first SMS was sent from a computer to a mobile phone in the UK in 1992, and the first person-to-person message from phone to phone was sent in Finland in 1993. In 1998 Radiolinja sold ringtones, one of the first examples of selling media content through the phone. Apple's App Store, opened in July 2008, popularised manufacturer-hosted distribution of third-party applications. In Kenya the operator Safaricom's M-PESA lets customers hold cash balances recorded on their SIM cards and transfer money from person to person. In the UK the number of mobile phones overtook the number of houses in 1999.
mobutu-sese-seko: Mobutu, born Joseph-Désiré Mobutu on 14 October 1930 at Lisala in the Belgian Congo, belonged to the Ngbandi ethnic group. His mother, Marie Madeleine Yemo, was a hotel maid, and her husband, Albéric Gbemani, was a cook for a Belgian judge. Gbemani died when Mobutu was eight, and an uncle and a grandfather raised him.

He found discipline and a father figure in the colonial army, in Sergeant Louis Bobozo, and read European newspapers and books whenever he could, among them the writings of Charles de Gaulle, Winston Churchill and Niccolò Machiavelli. In 1956 he left the army and became a journalist in Léopoldville, writing for the daily L'Avenir. He later joined the Congolese National Movement of Patrice Lumumba and became his personal aide. Several accounts say he was also an informer for Belgian intelligence and for the Americans.

After the mutiny of the Force Publique on 5 July 1960 Mobutu helped negotiate the release of officers and their families. During the Congo Crisis, as Chief of Staff of the army, he deposed Lumumba's government with American and Belgian support. He installed a government that arranged for Lumumba's execution in 1961, and he continued to lead the armed forces.

In March 1965 parliament twice refused to confirm the prime minister-designate Évariste Kimba, and the government was in near-paralysis. On 24 November 1965 Mobutu took power in a bloodless coup. He assumed almost absolute powers under a state of exception, and in March 1966 his government permanently suspended parliament. In 1967 he made the Popular Movement of the Revolution the only legal party.

Mobutu pursued a campaign of cultural change called authenticité. From 1 June 1966 he renamed cities, so that Léopoldville became Kinshasa and Stanleyville Kisangani, and in October 1971 he renamed the country Zaire. People were ordered to take African names, Western dress was banned, and men wore the Mao-style abacost. He also put rivals to death: Kimba and three ministers were hanged on 30 May 1966 before an audience of 50,000. His rule involved a cult of personality, widespread corruption and the expropriation of foreign-held businesses under Zairianisation.

His opposition to communism won support from the United States, France and Belgium. In May 1990 he gave up the party's monopoly, and troops killed at least 290 students at Lubumbashi on 12 May, after which Western countries ended non-humanitarian aid. After the Rwandan genocide of 1994, Hutu refugees and fighters based in eastern Zaire destabilised the region. In May 1997 rebels under Laurent-Désiré Kabila overran the country. Mobutu left on 23 May, lived in Rabat, and died of prostate cancer on 7 September 1997.
moca-dominican-republic: Moca is the capital of Espaillat province in the Cibao region of the Dominican Republic, 18 kilometres east of Santiago, and has a population of 164,022 inhabitants. It covers 339.21 square kilometres and sits on a volcanic coral reef, with hills to the west and low mountains to the north that form part of the Cordillera Septentrional. The highest mountain in the municipality and the province is El Mogote, at 971 metres, and the city itself lies at an elevation of 183 metres. It is divided into eight municipal districts: San Víctor, Las Lagunas, José Contreras, Juan López, El Higuerito, La Ortega, Monte de la Jagua and Canca La Reina.

When the Spanish colonised the island, the land of what is now Moca belonged to the chiefdom of Maguá. Moca itself was founded in 1780. In 1845 it was designated a common of the department of La Vega, and in the later political division it became the head municipality of Espaillat province.

The city is known as La Villa Heroica, the Village of Heroes, because of the number of men and women from Moca who played a major part in the nation's history in bringing down two dictators, Ulises Heureaux and Rafael Trujillo, and in bringing democracy back to the country. Among the people of Moca is Trina de Moya, a poet who was First Lady of the Dominican Republic in 1899, 1902 to 1903 and 1924 to 1930.

Agriculture is the main livelihood of the inhabitants, with plantain and yucca the chief crops, and most crops are harvested by hand. Other produce includes bananas, pigeon pea, taro, yams, squash, beans, coffee, citrus fruit and papaya, and the city has a large poultry sector. Moca has an important banking sector, with branches of all the country's commercial banks, and a strong trade in shops, furniture, supermarkets and warehouses, along with factories making footwear, food and hardware. It also has the country's largest coffee manufacturing industry, Industries Banilejas.
The Cathedral of the Sacred Heart of Jesus stands in the city; its glass windows were brought from Italy and show the apostles and the path of Jesus to the crucifixion.
moctezuma-i: Moctezuma was the son of Huitzilihuitl and Queen Miahuaxihuitl, grandson of the first ruler of Tenochtitlan, and brother of Chimalpopoca and Tlacaelel I. After Chimalpopoca was assassinated, Moctezuma and Tlacaelel led a militant group of young nobles who chose their half-uncle Itzcoatl as ruler, and under Itzcoatl the two brothers served as generals. The same group elected Moctezuma in 1440, at the age of 42, after Itzcoatl died. He took the title Great Speaker because he spoke for the Aztecs and for the peoples under their control, and the ruler of Texcoco crowned him with a turquoise diadem known as the fire crown.

Moctezuma strengthened the alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan. Under its terms two fifths of the spoils went to Tenochtitlan, two fifths to Texcoco and one fifth to Tlacopan. With Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco he organised the building of a double aqueduct that brought fresh water to Tenochtitlan. His armies took the Aztec domain beyond the Valley of Mexico to the Gulf Coast, subjugating the Huastec and Totonac peoples. About 1458 he led an expedition against the Mixtec city-state of Coixtlahuaca and defeated it despite help from Tlaxcala and Huexotzinco. Most of the defeated princes kept their positions, but the Mixtec ruler Atonal was ritually strangled and his family enslaved.

Natural disasters struck. Locusts destroyed crops in 1446 and Lake Texcoco flooded the city in 1449. Frost and drought began in 1450 and lasted four years, and in the famine some sold their children or themselves into slavery. Believing the gods angry, Moctezuma supported more human sacrifices, which led to the Flower War against Huejotzingo, Tlaxcala and Cholula. He also issued rules fixing what each class could wear and how its houses could look, and kept the power of the death sentence for himself.

Moctezuma I was an ancestor of Moctezuma II, who met Hernán Cortés. He died in 1469. Several Southwestern Native American peoples, notably the Tohono O'odham and the Pueblo, tell of a hero-god Moctezuma whose legend differs from the historical ruler but probably grew from tales of him.
moctezuma-ii: Moctezuma Xocoyotzin, called Moctezuma II in European sources because the Aztecs used no regnal numbers, was a son of the emperor Axayácatl and a daughter of Nezahualcóyotl of Texcoco. Two of his uncles, Tízoc and Ahuizotl, were the emperors before him. His name is interpreted as meaning he frowns like a lord. Most historians place his coronation in 1502, though some argue for 1503, a date that appears on the Stone of the Five Suns.

After his coronation Moctezuma set up thirty-eight more provincial divisions and sent out bureaucrats with military garrisons to collect tax, uphold the laws and act as local judges. His reign began with a drought in 1505 that lasted three years. He and the rulers of Texcoco and Tlacopan used the food supplies to feed the population and raised tribute for one year. Through warfare he extended the empire south to Xoconosco in Chiapas and the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and brought the Zapotec and Yopi peoples into it.

He widened the divide between the pipiltin, or nobles, and the macehualtin, or commoners, by barring commoners from working in the royal palaces. He also fought Huejotzingo and Tlaxcala, sometimes in flower wars, which were arranged by the parties to capture warriors for sacrifice. Many of his dominions around Tlaxcala were reluctant to fight their former allies, so his support there was limited.

In 1518 Moctezuma learned of the landing at San Juan de Ulúa of the expedition of Juan de Grijalva and ordered extra watchtowers on the coast. After the arrival of Hernán Cortés he became a prisoner in his own house; the sources do not make clear why. During the fighting after Cortés returned he was killed, probably on 29 June 1520, and accounts differ on how and by whom. The Spaniards fled the city and made a treaty with Tlaxcala to conquer Tenochtitlan.

Portraits of him are divided. Spanish writers called him weak-willed and superstitious, and the historian James Lockhart suggests that he serves as a scapegoat for the defeat. Indigenous accounts of omens before the Spanish arrival are seen by many ethnohistorians as explanations made after the conquest. His name was later invoked in indigenous rebellions against Spanish rule, including in Chiapas in 1721.
modena: Modena lies on the south side of the Po Valley, between the rivers Secchia and Panaro, both tributaries of the Po. The Apennines begin about ten kilometres to the south. The territory was inhabited by the Villanovans in the Iron Age and later by Ligurian tribes, Etruscans and the Gaulish Boii. The Etruscan name was Mutna and the Latin Mutina. The settlement existed by the 3rd century BCE: in 218 BCE, during Hannibal's invasion of Italy, the Boii revolted and besieged it, and Livy described it as a fortified citadel where Roman magistrates took shelter.

Mutina was refounded as a Roman colony in 183 BCE as a military base for Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. The Ligurians sacked it in 177 BCE, but it was rebuilt and became the most important centre of Cisalpine Gaul, standing at the crossing of the Via Aemilia and the road to Verona. It was besieged in 78 BCE by Pompey and in 44 BCE by Mark Antony, when Octavian relieved it in the Battle of Mutina. It declined with the Empire and, according to tradition, a fog sent by its patron Saint Geminianus hid it from Attila, but a great flood buried it in the 7th century and it was abandoned.

Modena became a free comune from the 12th century. The Este were lords from 1288, when Obizzo d'Este held power, and the comune briefly reasserted itself after 1308, but by 1336 the Este were permanently in power. Borso d'Este made it a duchy. When Ferrara fell to the Pope in 1598, Modena became the primary ducal residence. Francesco I d'Este built the citadel and began the palace, and Francesco II embellished it. Napoleon made it part of the Cispadane Republic, and Francis IV received back the Este estates in 1814. Francis V was expelled in the Revolutions of 1848, restored by Austrian troops, and driven out again when Piedmontese forces annexed Modena to the Kingdom of Italy on 20 August 1859.

The Cathedral of Modena, the Torre della Ghirlandina and Piazza Grande have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. The University of Modena was founded in 1175 and expanded by Francesco II d'Este in 1686, and the Military Academy is partly housed in the Baroque Ducal Palace. The Biblioteca Estense holds 3,000 manuscripts. The city has 184,361 inhabitants and is known for its car industry and for balsamic vinegar.
modest-mussorgsky: Mussorgsky was born on 21 March 1839 in Karevo, in the Pskov Governorate, about 400 kilometres south of Saint Petersburg, into a wealthy landowning noble family. His mother, Julia Chirikova, a trained pianist, taught him from the age of six. At ten he and his brother were taken to Saint Petersburg to study at the Petrischule, and at thirteen he entered the Cadet School of the Guards. In 1856 he graduated and received a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment. That year he met Alexander Borodin and Alexander Dargomyzhsky, and he soon came to know Vladimir Stasov, César Cui and Mily Balakirev, who taught him musical form.

In 1858 he resigned his commission to devote himself to music. The emancipation of the serfs soon afterwards deprived his family of half its estate, and he spent much time in Karevo trying in vain to stave off its impoverishment.

In the 1860s Mussorgsky embraced artistic realism, depicting life as it is lived and the lower strata of society and rejecting repeating, symmetrical musical forms. His first realistic songs, including Hopak and Darling Savishna, date from 1866. In 1867 he finished the original orchestral version of Night on Bald Mountain, which Balakirev refused to conduct, so that it was never performed in his lifetime. Influenced by Dargomyzhsky's The Stone Guest, he set the first scenes of Gogol's Marriage in 1868, trying to render natural speech in music.

He then wrote Boris Godunov, shaping a text from Pushkin's play and Karamzin's history. The theatre rejected it in 1871, and he produced a revised and enlarged version, from which three excerpts were staged at the Mariinsky Theatre in 1873. The first production, in February 1874, was far from a critical success, but popular reaction in its favour made it the peak of his career. His other works of 1874 include the song cycle Sunless and the piano suite Pictures at an Exhibition, written in memory of his friend Viktor Hartmann. The cycle Songs and Dances of Death dates from 1877.

Mussorgsky's alcoholism worsened through the 1870s and he was dismissed from government service in 1880. Khovanshchina and The Fair at Sorochyntsi were left unfinished. After four seizures in early 1881, he died on 28 March 1881, a week after his 42nd birthday, and was buried at the Tikhvin Cemetery of the Alexander Nevsky Monastery. Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov completed Khovanshchina, which premiered in 1886, and re-orchestrated Boris Godunov in 1896, so that for many years his works were known mainly in revised versions. Maurice Ravel's orchestration made Pictures at an Exhibition widely known. Western views of him changed after the European premiere of Boris Godunov in 1908.
modhera-sun-temple: The temple stands on the bank of the river Pushpavati in Mehsana district. In 1024 and 1025 Mahmud of Ghazni invaded Bhima I's kingdom, and a force of around 20,000 soldiers tried without success to check his advance at Modhera. The historian A. K. Majumdar has suggested that the temple may have been built to commemorate this defence. It is built in the Maru-Gurjara, or Chaulukya, style, and the scholar Madhusudan Dhaky has suggested on grounds of style and construction that the assembly hall may have been a later addition.

The shrine hall, the assembly hall and the tank lie on one axis. The assembly hall stands a little apart on its own paved platform; its 52 carved pillars carry cusped arches, and its stepped pyramid roof, like the spire over the sanctum, has long since collapsed. The square sanctum, about 11 feet across inside, has an upper and a lower cell; the upper floor, which probably held the image of the god, has fallen in. On the summer solstice the sun stands directly over the temple at noon and casts no shadow.

The outer walls rise in carved bands of elephants, human figures and gods. Twelve niches show a different aspect of Surya for each month, standing with lotuses in his two hands and drawn by seven horses; several figures wear West Asian dress with belt and boots. Other panels show Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma, Ganesha, Saraswati and the eight guardians of the directions, and scenes from the Ramayana are carved on the ceilings. The tank measures 176 by 120 feet, with four terraces of steps and many small shrines.

No worship is offered at the temple now. It is a Monument of National Importance maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India, and in December 2022 it was added to the tentative list of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee. Since 1992 the Tourism Corporation of Gujarat has held a three-day festival of classical Indian dance, the Uttarardha Mahotsav, at the temple in the third week of January. In the 19th century a coloured engraving after a painting by David Roberts inspired a poem by Letitia Elizabeth Landon.
modibbo-adama: Adama, whose title Modibbo means learned man, was the son of Modibbo Hassana, an ardo or clan leader of the Yillaga (Yirlaɓe) clan, and was born at Wuro Chekke, in what is now Adamawa State. His father taught him until he was eleven; he then studied the Quran under Shehu Muhammad Tahir in Baghirmi and spent about a decade with the scholar Mallam Kiari at Birnin Ngazargamo, the capital of Bornu. Back in Fombina he joined the Ba'en Fulbe of the Faro valley under the scholar Modibbo Hamman, and the two became known across the upper Benue for their piety.

News of Usman dan Fodio's jihad, begun in 1804, reached Fombina through campaigners such as Buba Yero and through Fulbe refugees from Bornu. The ardo'en met at Guringa and chose Adama, seen as a learned man neutral among them, to lead a delegation to Sokoto. Usman told them to launch the jihad, appointed Adama Lamido Fombina, Lord of the South, and charged him to distribute flags among the ardo'en and to watch for signs of the coming of the Mahdi, whom Usman expected from the east.

Adama raised Fulani and Hausa cavalry, forbade pillage and indiscriminate killing, and offered enemy peoples conversion or tributary status; peoples without a central government faced conversion or enslavement. Some ardo'en resisted his primacy, since he came from a humble background and had little wealth. He created a new rank, the lamido, the leader of a territory rather than of a people, and appointed over 40 of them, who proved his most loyal lieutenants. He took the Mandara capital, Dulo, with little fighting, but a counterattack from Mora drove him out.

Maroua, Garoua and Ngaoundéré fell to Adama or his lieutenants, and by 1825 the Fulani had reached the Adamawa Plateau. Adama lived modestly, supported himself by making and selling ropes and preferred the scholar's title modibbo to that of lamido; the British explorer Hugh Clapperton saw him as the most modestly dressed of the emirs gathered before Muhammad Bello. He died in 1847 and was buried at Yola, where his tomb survives. His son Muhammadu Lawal succeeded him after a brief regency. Many peoples fled the conquests, and Fulani herding turned much former forest into savanna.
modibo-keita: Modibo Keïta was born in Bamako-Coura, a neighbourhood of Bamako, then the capital of French Sudan, in 1915. His Muslim family claimed direct descent from the Keita dynasty that founded the medieval Mali Empire. He was educated in Bamako and at the école normale William-Ponty in Dakar, where he was top of his class. From 1936 he worked as a teacher in Bamako, Sikasso and Tombouctou. In 1937 he coordinated an art and theatre group, and with Ouezzin Coulibaly he helped found the Union of French West African Teachers.

In 1943 he founded L'oeil de Kénédougou, a magazine critical of colonial rule, which led to three weeks' imprisonment in Paris in 1946. In 1945 he and Mamadou Konaté founded the Bloc soudanais, which developed into the Sudanese Union. When the African Democratic Rally was created at Bamako in October 1946, Keïta became its Secretary-General in French Sudan and head of its Sudanese affiliate, the US-RDA.

In 1948 Keïta was elected general councillor of French Sudan, and in 1956 mayor of Bamako and a member of the French National Assembly. He twice served as a secretary of state in French governments. In 1959 he became premier of the Mali Federation, made up of French Sudan and Senegal; on 20 July 1960 he was elected president of its constituent assembly. After the federation collapsed, the Sudanese Republic proclaimed full independence as the Republic of Mali, and Keïta became its first president.

He soon declared the US-RDA the only legal party and pursued socialist policies based on extensive nationalisation, including the state company SOMIEX, which held a monopoly on exports and many imports. The Malian franc, created in 1962, brought severe inflation and discontent among peasants and businessmen. Keïta left the French Community and kept close ties with the Eastern bloc, while also seeking good relations with Washington and meeting President John F. Kennedy in 1961. He imprisoned opponents such as Fily Dabo Sissoko. The economy kept deteriorating, and Mali rejoined the Franc Zone in 1967. In August 1967 he began the revolution active and suspended the constitution, and the militia of the US-RDA caused unrest.

A committed Pan-Africanist, Keïta helped draft the charter of the Organization of African Unity in 1963. That year he invited the king of Morocco and the president of Algeria to Bamako and, with Emperor Haile Selassie, negotiated the Bamako Accords, which ended the Sand War. He received the Lenin Peace Prize.

On 19 November 1968 General Moussa Traoré overthrew him and sent him to prison at Kidal. He was moved back to Bamako in February 1977 and died there as a prisoner on 16 May 1977. His reputation was rehabilitated in 1992, after Traoré's fall, and a monument to him was dedicated in Bamako in 1999.
modu-chanyu: According to the account of Sima Qian in the Shiji, Modu was a gifted child whose father Touman wanted the son of another wife to succeed him. Touman sent Modu to the Yuezhi as a hostage and then attacked them, hoping they would kill him, but Modu stole a fast horse and escaped, and was made commander of 10,000 horsemen.

He trained his followers with a whistling arrow, having them shoot at whatever it flew toward, and tested their loyalty by ordering them to shoot his favourite horse and then a favourite wife, executing those who hesitated. In 209 BCE he had them shoot his father on a hunting trip and proclaimed himself chanyu. He then executed his rival half-brother, his stepmother and officials who refused to support him.

The Qin invasion of the Ordos Plateau in 215 BCE had come as the Xiongnu confederation faced a leadership crisis, and Modu used the resulting militarisation to build a centralised political structure. By 208 BCE he had defeated the Donghu, whose remnants split into the Xianbei and Wuhuan, and he went on to subdue the Dingling and defeat the Yuezhi in 203 BCE. His empire reached from the Liao River in the east to the Pamir Mountains in the west and Lake Baikal in the north.

In 200 BCE Emperor Gaozu of Han led an army north and advanced to Pingcheng with 40,000 men, where Modu surrounded him with 40,000 cavalry. The Xiongnu withdrew some of their men, and Gaozu broke out. He then made peace through heqin, a marriage alliance with gifts of silk, wine and food. In 192 BCE Modu proposed marriage to Empress Dowager Lü Zhi, in a letter meant to intimidate and mock her. She refused humbly, and kept up the heqin policy and tribute.

Modu died in 174 BCE and was succeeded by his son Laoshang. Historians note that Han weakness gave Modu and his successors a steady flow of luxury and staple tribute to pass down to the aristocracy that supported them. Christopher Beckwith has pointed out that the story of his youth resembles a widespread class of folk tales of an abandoned young hero who proves his worth and becomes king. In Turkic languages Modu is known as Mete Khan, and the Turkish Land Forces take 209 BCE as their symbolic founding date.
moengo: Moengo is a town on the Cottica River in the Marowijne district of Suriname, between Paramaribo and the border town of Albina. In Eastern Maroon Creole its name is Mongo. It is also a resort, or municipality, of the district, and it was the capital of Marowijne District from 1932 to 1945. The site began as a Maroon village on a hill above the river, which was abandoned because houses were hard to build on the ground, rich in bauxite. In 2012 the Maroons formed the largest ethnic group, with a significant Javanese minority.

The modern town began in 1916, when Alcoa opened the first bauxite mine in Suriname. Moengo was designed in 1919 to house 4,000 people and became a major centre for mining and storing bauxite. It was a segregated town, with an American Quarter for Americans and Dutch, a Surinamese Quarter for Afro-Surinamese and Wonoredjo for Javanese Surinamese. Maroons were hired only for temporary work or trade and had to leave by sundown. The racial regulations remained in force until the 1960s.

In the 1980s the Surinamese Interior War reached Moengo. Troops of the Jungle Commando captured the town in 1988 and held it for nine months before the National Army retook it in June 1989. Much of the population fled, the mine stopped working and several buildings burned. In June 2014 Alcoa announced that the mine was almost depleted and that it wished to end operations in Suriname, and in 2017 ownership of its subsidiary Suralco passed to the Surinamese government.

Moengo could first be reached only by river. A road to Moengotapoe was begun in 1926 and extended to Paramaribo in 1929, and the East-West Link opened in 1964. The port was privately owned by Alcoa until 2008, when it was sold to Traymore Docks. The town has two first-division football clubs, Inter Moengotapoe and Notch. In 2009 the Kibii Foundation, chaired by the artist Marcel Pinas, founded the Tembe Art Studio, and the Contemporary Art Museum Moengo, the first of its kind in Suriname, followed in 2011. The Moengo Festival, held from 2013, drew 20,000 people in 2018. The freedom fighter Boni, who lived from about 1730 to 1793, is counted among its notable people.
moesia: Moesia was bounded to the south by the Haemus (Balkan Mountains) and Scardus (Šar) ranges, to the west by the river Drinus (Drina), to the north by the Danube and to the east by the Black Sea. It was later divided into Moesia Superior and Moesia Inferior, with the river Ciabrus (the modern Tsibritsa) as the boundary between them. The name itself is thought to have been a Roman invention of the age of Augustus: the Moesi are not mentioned in sources before his death in 14 CE and only by Ovid, Strabo and Livy, and the ethnonym was carried over from the Mysians of Asia Minor to replace that of the Dardani.

Before Roman rule the land was inhabited chiefly by Thracian, Dacian, Illyrian and Thraco-Illyrian peoples. The Dardani had their own kingdom in what became Moesia Superior, and the Dacian king Burebista ruled part of the region between 82 and 44 BCE. Augustus took up Julius Caesar's plan to advance the frontier to the Danube. Marcus Licinius Crassus, proconsul of Macedonia from 29 BCE, defeated the Moesi, drove back the Bastarnae and killed their king Deldo in single combat. Augustus proclaimed the victory in 27 BCE.

The region was not organised as a province until the last years of Augustus, and a governor, Caecina Severus, is mentioned in 6 CE. In 15 CE Tiberius placed Macedonia and Achaea under the governor of Moesia. After the Dacian king Duras attacked, Emperor Domitian reorganised it into Moesia Superior and Moesia Inferior, each under an imperial consular legate. Trajan's Dacian Wars of 101 to 102 and 105 to 106 were triggered by the constant Dacian threat to Moesia.

From the 3rd century the province was raided by the Carpi and the Goths, and in the Gothic War of 248 to 253 the Gothic king Cniva defeated the Romans at the Battle of Abrittus, where Emperor Decius was killed. Diocletian divided Moesia Superior into Moesia Prima and Dardania, and Moesia Inferior into Moesia Secunda and Scythia Minor. In 376 the Goths, pressed by the Huns, settled in Moesia with the permission of Emperor Valens; these Moeso-Goths received the Gothic Bible of Ulfilas. Slavs allied with the Avars destroyed much of the region in 583 to 587 and settled it in the 7th century. Bulgars conquered Lower Moesia by its end. The area returned to Byzantine control under Basil II in 1018.
mogao-caves: Dunhuang was founded as a frontier garrison by the Han emperor Wudi in 111 BCE to guard against the Xiongnu, and became a gateway to the West on the Silk Road. The Mogao Caves began, according to a book from the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, in 366 CE, when the monk Le Zun had a vision of a thousand Buddhas bathed in golden light at the site and decided to build a cave there. A second monk, Faliang, joined him, and a community of monks formed by the time of the Northern Liang. The caves first served hermit monks for meditation. Caves continued to be cut until the 14th century.

The cliff stretches nearly two kilometres. At its height under the Tang, more than a thousand caves existed, and 735 survive. The 487 in the southern section, which are decorated, were places of pilgrimage and worship, while 248 in the north were living quarters, meditation chambers and burial sites for monks. The murals cover about 46,000 square metres, from the 5th to the 14th century, and their quality peaked in the Tang period. About 2,400 clay sculptures survive. The largest, a Maitreya in cave 96, 35.5 metres high, was built in 695 under the orders of Empress Wu Zetian.

Early murals show strong Indian and Central Asian influence, and a distinct Dunhuang style emerged under the Northern Wei. Local rich clans built several caves as family caves, which show their devotion and social standing.

On 25 June 1900 Wang Yuanlu, a Taoist abbot who had made himself guardian of some of the temples, found a walled-up small cave, Cave 17, packed with manuscripts. It had been sealed in the 11th century and may originally have been a memorial cave for the monk Hongbian, who died in 862. It held up to 50,000 manuscripts dating from the 5th to the early 11th century, mostly Chinese and Buddhist but also in Tibetan, Uighur, Sanskrit, Sogdian and Khotanese. They include the Diamond Sutra of 868, the earliest dated printed book. The manuscripts were later scattered, with the largest collections now in Beijing, London, Paris and Berlin.
moghulistan: Moghulistan, also called the Moghul Khanate or the Eastern Chagatai Khanate, was a Turco-Mongol, Muslim khanate that broke away from the Chagatai Khanate. The name also describes a geographic area north of the Tengri Tagh range, now parts of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and north-western Xinjiang. In the 1340s the eastern tribes, who had earlier revolted against a khan who moved to Transoxiana, were virtually independent. In 1347 the most powerful of them, the Dughlats, raised the Chagatayid Tughlugh Timur to the throne as head of a tribal confederacy governing the Tarim Basin and the steppe of Moghulistan.

Tughlugh Timur converted to Islam in 1354 with some 160,000 followers, which marked the Islamization of Moghulistan. In 1360 and 1361 he invaded Transoxiana and installed his son Ilyas Khoja, but could not hold it, and the Moghuls were expelled by Amir Husayn and Timur.

The Dughlat Amir Qamar-ud-Din likely killed Ilyas Khoja in 1368, which set off near-constant civil wars, and Timur sent at least five victorious expeditions against him. The Ming dynasty opened caravan trade, and the khans grew rich collecting tax on the Silk Road. The Dughlats enthroned Khizr Khoja in the 1380s, and he forcibly converted the Uyghurs of Turfan and ended their polity. Uwais Khan restored Moghul rule from 1418, and Yunus Khan, who reigned from 1462, reunited the khanate and took Tashkent from the Timurids.

After Yunus died in 1487 his sons divided his lands, Ahmad Alaq ruling the east from Turpan and Mahmud Khan the west from Tashkent. The Uzbeks under Muhammad Shaybani defeated both brothers in 1503 and later executed Mahmud, and Kyrgyz tribes gradually took the western lands. In 1514 Sultan Said Khan conquered the western Tarim Basin and founded the Yarkent Khanate at Kashgar, so the khanate was permanently divided. Power then shifted to the khojas, Naqshbandi Sufi leaders, and by the early 18th century the Dzungar Khanate had conquered the region.

Unlike Mongols elsewhere, those of Moghulistan were steppe nomads from Mongolia, who kept their way of life for centuries and were among the last Mongols to convert to Islam. They adopted Turkic, forming the Chagatai Turkic language. Chieftains used Turkic and Turko-Persian titles such as Mirza, Bek and Amir, and the khans later adopted sharia in place of the Mongol Yassa. Local control rested with Dughlat amirs or Naqshbandi Sufis in their oases, and the towns declined under nomadic rule. Most knowledge of the state comes from the Tarikh-i-Rashidi, the only primary source.
mogilev: The city stands on the Dnieper, about 76 kilometres from the border with Russia's Smolensk Oblast, and was first mentioned in historical records in 1267. Its name may derive from the Russian mogila, grave, and lev, lion. According to folk legend it was named after the grave of a young peasant, known as the Tomb of the Lion, around which a fortress was built. Its founding has also been linked to the Galician prince Leo I.

From the 14th century Mogilev belonged to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and after the Union of Lublin of 1569 to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, where it was known as Mohylew. In the 16th and 17th centuries it was one of the main nodes of the east–west and north–south trade routes.

In 1654, during the Russo-Polish War, the townsmen agreed to surrender to the Russians if the Jews were expelled and their property divided. Tsar Aleksei Mikhailovitch accepted, but Russian troops led the Jews to the outskirts of the town and massacred them. Lithuanian forces besieged the city in 1655 and 1660. Peter the Great's forces set it afire in 1708, during the Great Northern War.

In 1897 the Russian census counted 21,500 Jews among 41,100 inhabitants, over half the total. In 1919 Soviet Russia incorporated the city into the Byelorussian SSR. In 1938 the Belarusian leadership decided to move the capital here from Minsk, which lay too close to the Polish border, and a government building was raised in 1938–1940. German forces took the city on 26 July 1941 and held it until 28 June 1944. The Jews were confined in a ghetto and systematically murdered by police and SS personnel, and Heinrich Himmler witnessed the shooting of 279 Jews on 23 October 1941. A plan for a death camp was dropped in favour of Maly Trostenets.

Mogilev is the administrative centre of Mogilev Region and the third-largest city in Belarus. After World War II it became a large metallurgical centre with steel mills and factories making cranes, cars and tractors, and it has an inland port on the Dnieper. Its convent of St. Nicholas has a cathedral built in 1668, with the original iconostasis, bell tower, walls and gates.
mogok: Mogok lies at 1,170 metres in a valley ringed by mountains, about 200 kilometres north of Mandalay; Taung Min Taung, the highest peak of the area, rises above 7,000 feet. Its name comes from the Shan Möng Kut, meaning winding valley. The city is made up of two towns, Mogok and Kyatpyin, which lies about 11 km to the south-west. Its climate is mild, with a dry season of cold mornings from mid-November to mid-April and a very wet season for the rest of the year, bringing about 2,700 millimetres of rain, three times that of Mandalay.

According to oral history, Mogok was founded in 1217 by three lost Shan hunters who found rubies at the foot of a collapsed mountain, later called Kyee Arr Taung, and offered them to the saopha of their home town, Momeik, who set up a village there. The city marked the 800th anniversary of its founding in 2018. After the Third Anglo-Burmese War of 1885 brought Upper Burma under British rule, the British sent a military expedition in 1886 to open the mines to British merchants. The gem expert George Skelton Streeter went with it and stayed on as a government valuer.

During the Myanmar civil war the town saw heavy fighting between the Ta'ang National Liberation Army and Myanmar's military. It fell to the rebels on 24 July 2024, and the TNLA withdrew after a China-brokered ceasefire on 29 October 2025.

Mogok has around 90,000 people, among them Bamar, Shan, Lisu, Palaung and Karen as well as Chinese, Indians and Gurkhas. Besides rubies and sapphires, the area yields spinel, lapis lazuli, garnet, moonstone, peridot and chrysoberyl, found in alluvial marble gravels by panning, tunnelling and digging pits by hand, with little machinery. Foreigners need special permits to visit, and gems may be bought for export only from licensed dealers.
mohamed-amin-didi: Mohamed Amin Didi was born on 20 July 1910, the son of Athireegey Ahmed Dhoshimeynaa Kilegefaan and Roanugey Aishath Didi, and through his father a descendant of the Huraa dynasty. In 1920 he was sent to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, to study at Saint Joseph's College in Colombo, and in 1928 he went to India for further studies at Aligarh Muslim University, returning to the Maldives a year later. He married Fathimath Saeed; their only child was a daughter, Annabeela Ameena Mohamed Amin.

In 1931 he was appointed to the Constituent Assembly convened by Sultan Muhammad Shamsuddeen III to draft the country's first written constitution. He went on to hold many posts: chief officer of customs, head of the post office, minister of trade, minister of education from 1933 to 1936 and from 1944 to 1952, minister of finance from 1942 to 1952 and minister of foreign affairs from 1944 to 1953. He sat in the first Maldivian parliament and was principal of Majeedhiyya School from 1946 to 1953.

He was appointed prime minister on 1 January 1947, at a time when the country was suffering widespread famine and exhausted resources after the Second World War. He led the first political party in the Maldives, the Rayyithunge Muthagaddim Party. His programme included the advancement of women and a ban on tobacco smoking. As prime minister he also wrote a booklet for foreigners, Ladies and Gentlemen: The Maldive Islands, on the life, culture and economy of the country.

According to a report in the newspaper Mihaaru, the revolt of 1953 was staged by Ibrahim Zaki, Mohamed Zaki and Ibrahim Nasir, who invited the vice-president, Ibrahim Muhammad Didi, to join; he agreed out of distaste for Amin's handling of state funds. A special assembly passed a vote of no confidence that handed all powers temporarily to Ibrahim Didi. Amin, in Sri Lanka, learned of events by letter but not of his removal. He returned by way of RAF Gan to Malé, was taken to Dhoonidhoo, where he was beaten by the army, and was then banished to Vihamanaafushi, where he died of health complications on 19 January 1954.

In September 2021 a member of parliament, Ibrahim Rasheed, lodged a case with the Office of the Ombudsperson for Transitional Justice seeking justice for his death and the overturning of his conviction as a traitor. The office's mandate expired on 19 November 2023.
mohamed-morsi: Mohamed Morsi was born on 8 August 1951 in the village of El Adwah in the Sharqia Governorate, north of Cairo, during the last years of the Egyptian monarchy. His father was a farmer. He studied engineering at Cairo University, graduating in 1975, and a government scholarship took him to the University of Southern California, where he received a doctorate in materials science in 1982. He taught at California State University, Northridge, until 1985, then returned to Egypt and taught engineering at Zagazig University.

Morsi sat in parliament from 2000 to 2005 as an officially independent member, since the Muslim Brotherhood was barred from fielding candidates under President Hosni Mubarak. In 2011 the Brotherhood chose him as first president of its new Freedom and Justice Party. When Khairat El-Shater was disqualified from the 2012 presidential election, Morsi became the Brotherhood's candidate. He narrowly defeated Ahmed Shafik, a former prime minister under Mubarak, and was sworn in on 30 June 2012, ending six decades of military rule.

In November 2012 he issued a declaration freeing his decisions from judicial review. He aimed to stop judges appointed under Mubarak from dissolving the constituent assembly. Critics called the move an Islamist coup, and protests followed; he rescinded the decrees as part of a compromise. A new constitution was approved by about two thirds of voters in a referendum with a turnout below a third of the electorate.

On 30 June 2013 protests across Egypt called for Morsi's resignation. The armed forces issued an ultimatum on 1 July, Morsi rejected it, and on 3 July General Abdel Fattah el-Sisi deposed him and suspended the constitution. Demonstrations by his supporters were crushed, with over 800 deaths. Morsi faced charges including inciting the killing of protesters and espionage. On 17 June 2019 he collapsed in court during a hearing and died; he was buried in Cairo.
mohammad-daoud-khan: Mohammad Daoud Khan was born in Kabul on 18 July 1909 into a Mohammadzai Pashtun family; his father, Prince Mohammad Aziz Khan, was assassinated in 1933 in Berlin while serving as Afghan ambassador to Germany. Daoud and his brother Naim Khan then came under the guidance of their uncle Mohammad Hashim Khan. Educated in France, Daoud served as governor of the Eastern Province and of Kandahar Province between 1934 and 1939. In 1939 he became Commander of the Central Forces. He led forces against the Safi in the tribal revolts of 1944-1947, which brought him national attention. He was Defense Minister from 1946 to 1948 and Interior Minister from 1949 to 1951.

Daoud became prime minister in September 1953 through an intra-family transfer of power. His decade in office saw a turn toward the Soviet Union, the completion of the Helmand Valley project and tentative steps toward the emancipation of women. He rejected the Durand Line and supported the reunification of Pakistan's Pashtuns with Afghanistan, which worried the Hazara, Tajik and Uzbek populations. Afghan incursions into Bajaur in 1960 and 1961 failed, and in 1961 Pakistan closed its border, which deepened dependence on the Soviet Union. Daoud asked King Zahir Shah to approve a one-party constitution. When it was rejected, he resigned in March 1963, and the border reopened in May.

After planning for more than a year, Daoud seized power on 17 July 1973 in a bloodless coup backed by army officers. For the first time in Afghan history he did not proclaim himself shah but established a republic with himself as president. The parliament was disbanded and replaced by a largely nominated loya jirga. Pro-communist Parchamite officers had taken part in the coup, but over time he removed communist influence from his cabinet. In 1977 a loya jirga approved a constitution creating a presidential one-party system under his National Revolutionary Party.

After the funeral of the Parchamite ideologue Mir Akbar Khyber on 19 April 1978, he ordered the arrest of leaders of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan, but acted too slowly. A coup began on 27 April, and Daoud and most of his family were shot in the Arg palace on 28 April. Their remains were found in mass graves in 2008, and he was given a state funeral in 2009.
mohammad-hasan-khan-qajar: Mohammad Hasan Khan was born in 1715 in Astarabad (now Gorgan), the son of Fath-Ali Khan Qajar, chief of the Qovanlu (Qoyunlu) branch of the Qajar Turkomans, who had lived near the Caspian coast for several centuries. His father died in 1726, when he was eleven, and for nearly twenty years he lived a nomadic life on the Gorgan Plain among the Yamut Turkmens, while Nader Shah Afshar held power. In 1744 he took Astarabad with 3,000 tribal troops, but Nader Shah's general Behbud Khan retook it and massacred the Ashaqeh-bash Qajars and other supporters.

After Nader Shah's assassination in 1747 he attacked Astarabad again, but the new ruler Adel Shah drove him off, and his five-year-old son Agha Mohammad Khan was captured, taken to Mashhad and castrated. By 1751 he held Gorgan, Mazandaran and Gilan. When Karim Khan Zand besieged him in Astarabad, he ambushed the Zand forces with Yamut help and seized the Safavid puppet king Ismail III. He beat Abdali Afghans near Sabzevar in 1755, and in 1756 defeated Zand troops at Kazzaz and Gulnabad and took Isfahan, minting gold coins there in his name.

In 1757 he drove Azad Khan Afghan into the Ottoman Empire and took Tabriz and Urmia without a fight, installing Agha Mohammad Khan as his deputy. In 1758 he besieged Karim Khan in Shiraz, but short of food and supplies he withdrew to Mazandaran in July, pursued by Sheikh Ali Khan Zand. The disobedience of his subordinates, above all Mohammad Hossein Khan Devellu Qajar, brought his defeat at Astarabad, and on 13 February 1759 he was killed by Mohammad Khan Savadkuh while fleeing.

The 19th-century scholar Etemad-os-Saltaneh listed him as Mohammad Hasan Shah, the first Qajar shah, reigning from 1751 to 1759, and the historian Hambly describes him as ruling as a sovereign until his death, after which Qajar rule paused until 1779. He kept his court at Ashraf (now Behshahr), repaired the Safavid palace there, and built the Mohammad Hassan Khan Bridge over the Babol river and a mosque at Barforush. He had nine sons and two daughters, and his example of Qajar rule was taken up by Agha Mohammad Khan.
mohammad-hatta: Hatta was born Athar on 12 August 1902 in Fort De Kock, now Bukittinggi, into a prominent and strongly Islamic family. His grandfather, Sheikh Abdurrahman, was a respected Naqshbandi-Khalidi murshid. His father died when he was eight months old, and in keeping with Minangkabau matrilineal custom he was raised in his mother's wealthy family. He studied Dutch and completed the Qur'an after school.

He attended the Dutch elementary school in Padang and then, from 1919, the HBS in Batavia, finishing with distinction in 1921. He went on to study economics in Rotterdam and earned a doctorandus degree in 1932. He completed the requirements for a doctorate but never finished his thesis, because politics had taken over his life.

In the Netherlands Hatta joined the Indies' Association, which became the Perhimpoenan Indonesia. He was its treasurer from 1922 to 1925 and its chairman from 1926 to 1930, and edited its magazine Indonesia Merdeka. In his inaugural speech he supported non-cooperation with the Dutch colonial government. Returning home in 1932, he became chairman of the New PNI, which concentrated on cadre training. He was imprisoned in the Boven Digoel camp for his activism.

On 16 August 1945 young activists took Hatta and Sukarno to Rengasdengklok to press them to declare independence. They returned to Jakarta that night and drafted the proclamation at Maeda's house. It was issued on 17 August 1945 in a short statement signed by both men. The next day Hatta was chosen first vice president.

In the early republic Hatta issued three decisions: giving the KNIP legislative powers, authorising political parties and transferring the role of head of government to a prime minister. He became prime minister and defence minister himself, and in August 1948 had to demobilise some soldiers. In December 1948 he stayed in Yogyakarta, was arrested by the Dutch and sent to Bangka. In 1948 he gave the speech Rowing Between Two Rocks, the origin of the Independent and Active foreign policy doctrine.

He announced his retirement from the vice presidency in 1955 and afterwards criticised Sukarno, whose Guided Democracy he called a form of dictatorship in his 1960 book Our Democracy. He died on 14 March 1980 in Jakarta, and was named a proclaiming hero in 1986. Soekarno-Hatta International Airport carries his name.
mohammad-mosaddegh: Mohammad Mosaddegh was born on 16 June 1882 in Ahmadabad, near Tehran, into a family of high officials. His father was finance minister under the Qajar dynasty, and his mother was a descendant of the reformist prince Abbas Mirza. In 1909 he went to Paris to study at Sciences Po, and in June 1913 he received a doctorate in law from the University of Neuchâtel, becoming the first Iranian to earn a doctorate in law from a European university.

His political career began in the Constitutional Revolution of 1905 to 1907, when at 24 he was elected to the Majlis from Isfahan but could not take his seat because he was under the legal age of 30. He later served as minister of justice, finance minister, foreign minister and governor of Fars and Azerbaijan, and was re-elected to the Majlis in 1923.

On 28 April 1951 the Shah confirmed Mosaddegh as prime minister after the Majlis elected him by 79 votes to 12. His government nationalised the Iranian oil industry, which had been run since 1913 by the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, later the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, and the clash with Britain became known as the Abadan Crisis.

On 16 July 1952 he resigned after the Shah refused to let him name the minister of war and the chief of staff. Ahmad Qavam was appointed in his place, but strikes and demonstrations in which over 250 demonstrators were killed or seriously injured brought Mosaddegh back. Parliament gave him emergency powers on 3 August 1952, and he cut the Shah's budget and transferred royal lands to the state. In October 1952 he cut diplomatic relations with Britain.

Britain, which had lost control of Iranian oil, looked to the United States for help. In March 1953 Secretary of State John Foster Dulles directed the CIA to draft plans to overthrow Mosaddegh, and on 4 April Allen Dulles approved $1 million for the purpose. Kermit Roosevelt Jr., chief of the CIA's Near East and Africa division, arrived in Tehran to direct the plot, known as Operation Ajax. The coup of August 1953 ended his government.

On 21 December 1953 Mosaddegh was sentenced to three years of solitary confinement in a military prison, well short of the death sentence the prosecutors asked for. He was then held under house arrest at Ahmadabad until his death from cancer on 5 March 1967. He was denied a funeral and was buried in his own living room. He remains one of the most popular figures in Iranian history. Some argue that the loss of support from the cleric Ayatollah Abol-Ghasem Kashani was fatal to his cause. The overthrow became a rallying point in anti-American protests in the 1979 revolution.
mohammad-nadir-shah: Nadir Khan was born in Dehradun, British India, on 9 April 1883, into the Musahiban branch of the ruling family, of the Mohammadzai section of the Barakzai Pashtuns. His ancestors had been exiled to British India by Emir Abdur Rahman Khan, who distrusted their ambitions. Nadir helped the Afghan government defeat the Khost rebellion in 1912, became a general under King Amanullah Khan, and led the Royal Afghan Army in the Third Anglo-Afghan War. He then served as Minister of War and, from early 1924 to 1926, as ambassador to France.

Disagreements with Amanullah led to Nadir's exile shortly after Habibullah Kalakani's rebellion against the monarchy. When Kalakani overthrew Amanullah, Nadir returned with an army of Mangal, Mahsud and Wazir tribesmen, with British support, and took most of the country. His forces captured Kabul by 13 October 1929 and sacked it, and he arrived on the 15th. Kalakani was shot on 1 November 1929 with his brother and nine of his circle.

As king, Nadir quickly abolished most of Amanullah's reforms. The army remained weak while religious and tribal leaders grew strong, and he faced many revolts, among them the Koh Daman revolt, the Shinwari rebellion of February 1930 and the Darre Khel revolt of November 1932. Most had been subdued by the end of 1931. A loya jirga of 286 members confirmed his accession in September 1930, and in 1931 he promulgated a constitution that, despite its constitutional appearance, in effect set up a royal oligarchy.

Nadir modernised more quietly than Amanullah. He improved roads, notably the Great North Road through the Hindu Kush, and helped establish Kabul University in 1931. He forged commercial links with foreign powers, began a banking system and long-range economic planning, and by 1933 had built a military force of 40,000.

On 8 November 1933 he was shot dead by Abdul Khaliq Hazara at a school graduation ceremony in Kabul. The assassin was executed along with most of his relatives, and the government used the occasion to arrest other rivals. Nadir was buried on Maranjan Hill, and Muhammad Iqbal wrote an elegy for him. His son Mohammad Zahir Shah succeeded him.
mohammad-najibullah: Mohammad Najibullah Ahmadzai was born on 6 August 1947 in Gardez, in Paktia Province, into the Ahmadzai clan of the Ghilji Pashtuns. He studied at Habibia High School in Kabul and at Kabul University, where he completed a medical degree in 1975 but never practised. In 1965 he joined the Parcham faction of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA), was twice imprisoned for political activity and served as a close associate and bodyguard of Babrak Karmal. After the Saur Revolution of 1978 the rival Khalq faction gained the upper hand, and he was briefly ambassador to Iran before going into exile in Europe until the Soviet intervention of 1979.

In 1980 Najibullah became head of the KHAD, the Afghan counterpart of the KGB, after lobbying by Soviet officials including Yuri Andropov. Its staff grew from 120 to between 25,000 and 30,000, and it reported directly to the KGB. He joined the PDPA Politburo in June 1981. Mikhail Gorbachev wanted Karmal to resign and supported Najibullah, who became General Secretary on 4 May 1986, although a Soviet military intelligence report had warned that he was a Pashtun nationalist.

In September 1986 he created a National Compromise Commission for his policy of National Reconciliation, calling a six-month ceasefire and offering talks that would lead to a coalition government. The programme failed, but some mujahideen commanders defected with their followers. He moved away from socialism towards Afghan nationalism, and the 1990 constitution made Islam the state religion and removed references to communism. On 18 February 1989, four days after the Soviet withdrawal, he declared a state of emergency, and 1,700 intellectuals were arrested that month.

With the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, Najibullah lost his foreign aid, and the defection of General Abdul Rashid Dostum to Ahmad Shah Massoud brought his government down. He resigned in April 1992. Dostum's troops blocked his flight to the airport, and he lived in the United Nations compound in Kabul, where he translated Peter Hopkirk's The Great Game into Pashto. The Taliban tortured and killed him on 27 September 1996, when they took Kabul. Supporters praise his efforts at reconciliation, while critics cite the abuses of the KHAD and alleged corruption under his government.
mohammad-reza-pahlavi: Mohammad Reza was born in Tehran on 26 October 1919, the son of Reza Khan, a brigadier general in the Persian Cossack Brigade, later Reza Shah, and his second wife, Tadj ol-Molouk. In 1931 he was sent to Institut Le Rosey in Switzerland, the first Iranian heir apparent educated abroad. On 15 March 1939 he married Princess Fawzia of Egypt in Cairo; the marriage ended in divorce on 17 November 1948.

After the Anglo-Soviet invasion of 1941 Reza Shah resigned, and on 17 September 1941 his son took the oath as shah. Iran became a main route for British and later American aid to the Soviet Union. On 11 December 1946 the army, led by the Shah in person, entered Iranian Azerbaijan, and the Soviet-sponsored government of Ja'far Pishevari collapsed with little resistance.

Mohammad Mosaddegh became prime minister in 1951 and nationalised the oil industry controlled by the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. He was overthrown in the 1953 coup, carried out by pro-monarchy forces with British and American involvement. In 1963 the Shah launched the White Revolution, whose referendum let women vote. Clerics objected, and demonstrations in 1963 and 1964, centred on Qom, killed at least 200 people; Ruhollah Khomeini was exiled to Iraq in October 1965. On 26 October 1967 the Shah took the title Shahanshah at a coronation in Tehran, and in October 1971 he marked 2,500 years of Persian monarchy since Cyrus the Great.

After a newspaper article attacking Khomeini appeared on 7 January 1978, protests began. On 8 September 1978 troops shot dead at least 64 people in Jaleh Square. Shapour Bakhtiar became prime minister on 6 January 1979, and on 16 January the Shah left Iran; the monarchy collapsed within a month, and Khomeini became supreme leader of the new Islamic republic. The Shah travelled through Egypt, Morocco, the Bahamas and Mexico, and died in exile in Egypt on 27 July 1980. Historians remain divided on his rule, some stressing repression and autocracy, others economic growth and modernisation.
mohammad-shah-qajar: Mohammad Mirza was born in Tabriz on 5 January 1808, the eldest son of the crown prince Abbas Mirza. He was a quiet and shy boy who became a skilled calligrapher and painter. A turning point came when the dervish Haji Mirza Aqasi was appointed his chief tutor and made him a devotee of Sufi teachings. In the Second Russo-Iranian War he led an army to protect Ganja and was defeated, but was praised and nicknamed Gazi.

After Abbas Mirza died in 1833, Mohammad became crown prince at Nowruz of 1834 and governor of Azarbaijan. Under the influence of his tutor Abol-Qasem Qa'em-Maqam, he imprisoned four brothers and later blinded them to remove their claims to the throne.

After Fath-Ali Shah died in 1834, claimants such as Hossein Ali Mirza rose against Mohammad, who suppressed them. He made Qa'em-Maqam his grand vizier, then arrested him on 22 June 1835 and had him executed four days later, and appointed Aqasi in his place. His chief aim was to bring the rebellious city of Herat back under Iranian rule. In 1837 he marched there and besieged it without success, withdrawing when the British government threatened to invade Iran.
