He also put down a revolt in Isfahan, led by the cleric Mohammad Bagher Shafti, who had declared a man named Ramazan Shah and struck coins in his name. Through British and Russian mediation he concluded the Second Treaty of Erzurum with the Ottoman Empire, after negotiations that ran four years from 1843. Pressed by the British envoy Justin Sheil, he refused to abolish the slave trade in the Persian Gulf, saying it would contradict Islamic tradition. He was the last Qajar king to attend a foreign war in person.

Mohammad suffered from gout and refused European doctors on Aqasi's advice, and in his last years he lost the will to rule and handed the government to Aqasi. He died on 4 September 1848 of gout and erysipelas and was buried at the Fatima Masumeh Shrine in Qom, and his son Naser al-Din Shah succeeded him.

He patronised Sufis, and the ulama became his firmest rivals. He refused to persecute the followers of the Báb despite a fatwa from Shiite clerics. He sent students to Europe, including the future grand vizier Mirza Hosein Khan Sepahsalar, and in 1837 ordered the first Iranian newspaper published in Tehran. Historians describe his reign as an interregnum between Fath-Ali Shah and Naser al-Din Shah, with Aqasi governing in his name and costly wars and maladministration.
mohammad-zahir-shah: Mohammad Zahir Shah was born on 15 October 1914 in Kabul, into the Musahiban branch of the Mohammadzai clan of the Barakzai Pashtuns. His father, Mohammad Nadir Shah, had been Commander-in-Chief of the Royal Afghan Army under King Amanullah Khan. Zahir was educated at schools in Kabul where subjects were taught in English and French, and then in France, at the Pasteur Institute and the University of Montpellier. On his return he helped his father and uncles restore order, and served as deputy war minister and minister of education.

He was proclaimed king on 8 November 1933, at the age of 19, after the assassination of his father. For his first twenty years he did not effectively rule, leaving power to his paternal uncles Mohammad Hashim Khan and Shah Mahmud Khan, who both served as prime minister. In 1934 Afghanistan joined the League of Nations and was recognised by the United States. Despite close relations with the Axis powers, the country stayed neutral in the Second World War, and from 1944 to 1947 it saw a series of tribal revolts.

After the war Zahir Shah recruited foreign advisers, and Afghanistan's first modern university was founded. He sought aid from both the United States and the Soviet Union, and the country was one of the few to receive it from both.

A new constitution promulgated in 1964 at his behest introduced free elections, a parliament, civil and political rights, women's rights and universal suffrage. His rule has been characterised as a lengthy era of peace. In July 1973 his cousin Mohammad Daoud Khan, a former prime minister whom Zahir had forced to resign a decade earlier, overthrew him in a coup while he was undergoing medical treatment in Italy. In August 1973 Zahir Shah sent a letter from Rome declaring his abdication.

He spent 29 years in exile near Rome. In 1983, during the Soviet-Afghan War, he was involved in plans for a government in exile, but they failed when he could not reach agreement with the Islamist factions. In 1991 he survived an attack by a knife-wielding man posing as a journalist. He returned to Kabul on 18 April 2002, after the end of Taliban rule, and was welcomed by Afghans of all ethnic groups.

Of the Loya Jirga he said he would accept the duties of head of state if it asked, but had no intention to restore the monarchy. Afterwards Hamid Karzai gave him the title Father of the Nation, which ended with his death. He died in the Arg, the old palace in Kabul, on 23 July 2007, at the age of 92, and was buried in the royal mausoleum on Maranjan Hill.
mohammed-abdullah-hassan: Mohammed Abdullah Hassan was born on 7 April 1856 in the Sacmadeeqa valley in the Ciid region, to a religious, pastoral family that traced its origins to the Ogaden clan on his father's side and the Dhulbahante clan on his mother's. He had memorised the entire Qur'an by the age of eleven and later studied at centres of learning in Harar, Mogadishu and Sudan under more than seventy teachers. In the early 1890s he completed the Hajj to Mecca, where he was influenced by the founder of the Salihiyya order, whose strict, reformist ideas shaped his militant outlook.

Returning to Somalia in 1895, he settled in Berbera, built a mosque and preached against the British colonial presence and Christian missionary activity. The Salihiyya clashed there with the established Qadiriyya, and in 1897 debates with Qadiriyya sheikhs, which the Qadiriyya reportedly won, left both sides accusing each other of heresy. The British banished him from Berbera.

In 1899 he founded the Dervish movement on Salihiyya principles, partly as a rebuke to the Qadiriyya's accommodation of the colonists. He framed his jihad as a defence of Somali sovereignty and Islam against foreign Christian encroachment, appealing to clans frustrated by colonial taxes, land seizures and missionary activity. The conversion of Somali children by the French Catholic mission at Berbera in 1899 was a spark.

Towards the end of 1900 the Ethiopian emperor Menelik proposed joint action with Britain. At Jidaale on 9 January 1904 General Charles Egerton killed 1,000 Dervishes. Around 1909 about 400 followers left him on receiving a letter of excommunication from the head of the Salihiyya, and in the same year the Dervish killed Sheikh Uways al-Barawi, a Qadiriyya rival. In 1909 and 1910 the Dervish capital moved to Taleh, where they built three stone forts. By 1913 they dominated much of the Somali hinterland. At Dul Madoba on 9 August 1913 they killed Colonel Richard Corfield, who commanded the Somaliland Camel Constabulary, together with others.

At the beginning of 1920 the British struck the Dervish settlements with a coordinated air and land attack and defeated them, damaging their forts and inflicting great losses. Hassan fled westward into the Ogaden and in October settled at Guano Imi in Arsi country with about four hundred followers. Hunger and sickness killed most of them. He died of influenza on 21 December 1920, and his grave is believed to lie near Imi, though its exact place is unknown.

The British called him the Mad Mullah, a pejorative; in 1917 the Ottoman Empire styled him Emir of the Somali People. Some regard him as an icon of Pan-Somalism and a father of Somali nationalism. He was also a poet, and several of his poems survive.
mohammed-al-shaykh: His father, Abu Abdallah al-Qaim, led the Saadi war against the Portuguese, and after his death in 1517 Mohammed and his brother Ahmad al-Araj took command of it. They conquered Marrakesh in 1524; Ahmad became Emir of Marrakesh, still recognising the Wattasid Sultan of Fez, while Mohammed remained ruler of Taroudannt. The Treaty of Tadla of 1527, agreed after the Wattasid defeat at the Battle of Wadi al-Abid, divided the two dynasties' lands at the Tadla region.

After 1536 the brothers came into conflict, Ahmad in effect allying himself with the Wattasids under the regent Ali Abu Hassun. Holding the south, Mohammed took Agadir and other coastal towns with the help of European artillery; the Portuguese at once evacuated Azamor and Safi, and Ahmad fled to Tafilalet. Having reorganised his army on the Ottoman model, he took Fez, ending Wattasid rule, and his son conquered Tlemcen in 1550, expelling its Spanish-backed Zayyanid sultan. The Portuguese left Ksar-el-Kebir and Asila in 1550, keeping only Ceuta, Tangier and Mazagan.

With Ottoman help Ali Abu Hassun retook Fez in early 1554, but Mohammed defeated the last Wattasids at the Battle of Tadla and recaptured the city in September 1554, and Ali Abu Hassun died that year. Allied with the Spanish, he captured Tlemcen from the Ottomans during their Siege of Oran in 1556. His victories over the Portuguese won him the support of the Andalusis as a man of jihad, though his relations with them were otherwise poor.

Ottoman soldiers who had entered his service posing as deserters killed him on 23 October 1557, on the orders of Hasan Pasha, son of Hayreddin Barbarossa, as he was preparing an alliance with Spain against the Ottomans. He was buried in the Saadian Tombs of Marrakesh. His son and successor, Abdallah al-Ghalib, defeated the Turks who invaded after the killing at the Battle of Wadi al-Laban in 1558.
mohammed-dib: Dib was born in Tlemcen, near the border with Morocco, into a middle-class family that had descended into poverty. After losing his father at a young age he began writing poetry at fifteen, and at eighteen he started work as a teacher in nearby Oujda in Morocco. In his twenties and thirties he worked as a weaver, teacher, accountant, interpreter for the French and British military, and journalist.

In 1952, two years before the Algerian revolution, he married a French woman, joined the Algerian Communist Party and visited France. In the same year he published his first novel, La Grande Maison. He belonged to the Generation of '52, a group of Algerian writers that included Albert Camus and Mouloud Feraoun.

Dib wrote over thirty novels, as well as many short stories, poems and children's books, in French. His concern was to bring the authentic experience of Algerian life to a wider, particularly French-speaking, world, and the Algerian revolution of 1954 to 1962 shaped his thinking and made him eager to draw attention to the struggle for independence.

La Grande Maison opened a trilogy about a large Algerian family. Its main character, Omar, is a boy growing up in poverty just before the Second World War. The second part, L'Incendie, appeared in 1954, the year the revolution began, and follows Omar through the war. The last part, Le Métier à tisser, published in 1957, deals with his adult life as a working man. The trilogy is partly autobiographical and naturalistic. Later works often added surrealistic elements, as in Qui se souvient de la mer (1962), which used science fiction and verse in his last novel, L.A. Trip.

In 1959 the French authorities expelled Dib from Algeria for his support of independence and because of the success of his novels, which depicted colonial life as most Algerians lived it. Rather than going to Cairo, as many nationalists did, he chose France, where he was allowed to stay after writers including Camus lobbied the government. He taught at the University of California at Los Angeles in 1976 and 1977 and was a professor at the Sorbonne. He won the Fénéon Prize in 1953, the grand prix de la Francophonie in 1994 and the Mallarmé prize in 1998. He died at La Celle-Saint-Cloud on 2 May 2003. French Culture Minister Jean-Jacques Aillagon called him a spiritual bridge between Algeria and France.
mohammed-iii-of-morocco: Sidi Muhammad bin Abdallah al-Khatib was the son of Mawlay Abdallah bin Ismail and a woman of the Chéraga Guich tribe. He governed Marrakesh around 1750 and had already been sultan briefly in 1748. On his accession in 1757 he restored the standing of the Arab guich, the tribal army, in place of the Black Guard, pacified the mountain Berbers who had raided the plains during the succession crisis, and cultivated a close relationship with the ulama, the religious scholars.

In 1760 he defeated a revolt of the Wadaya at Fes and broke them up into garrisons at Meknes. When in 1775 he ordered the Black Guard from Meknes to Tangier, they tried to proclaim his son Yazid sultan; Yazid was reconciled with his father, and the guard was scattered among several towns. Drought and famine from 1776 to 1782 and plague in 1779 and 1780 forced him to import wheat, cut taxes and hand out food.

Abroad, his forces defeated a French fleet at Larache in June 1765. He bombarded Spanish Melilla for 100 days from 9 December 1774 without taking it, and lost the Dutch–Moroccan War of 1775 to 1777 to a Dutch blockade. On 20 December 1777 Morocco became the first nation to recognise the United States, and the Treaty of Marrakesh of 28 June 1786 became the longest unbroken treaty relationship in American history.

He rebuilt many towns after the earthquake of 1755, among them Casablanca, which he renamed al-Dār al-Bayḍāʼ, and developed Essaouira in 1769 as the main port for foreign trade, to strengthen central authority and limit European intervention. In Rabat he built the Dar al-Makhzen palace and the As-Sunna Mosque. He died in Meknes on 9 April 1790 and was buried near the palace in Rabat; his son Yazid succeeded him. The historian Abdallah Laroui called him the architect of modern Morocco.
mohammed-v-of-morocco: Muhammad bin Yusef was born in Fes on 10 August 1909, the third and youngest son of Sultan Yusef and Lalla Yacout. In March 1912 the Treaty of Fes made Morocco a French protectorate, and the French enthroned his father in September of that year. He studied the Quran in the palace at Fes and, after the court moved to Rabat, with private teachers there, until he became a hafiz. He also studied French. He was enthroned on 18 November 1927, at the age of 17, after his father's death.

In May 1930 the young sultan signed the Berber Dahir, which changed the legal system in the areas where Berber languages were mainly spoken. Moroccan nationalists criticised it sharply, and it gave rise to the Moroccan nationalist movement. During the Second World War he took part in the Anfa Conference at Casablanca and met Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill on 22 January 1943. Most scholars stress his benevolence towards Moroccan Jews under Vichy, since he reportedly refused to approve measures to deport them, though he did sign two decrees barring Jews from certain schools and positions. The historian Michel Abitol holds that his role has been exaggerated.

After the war he became a central figure of the independence cause. In speeches at Tangier on 9 and 10 April 1947 he appealed for independence and stressed Morocco's ties with the Arab world. Relations with the French worsened, and on 20 August 1953 the French authorities deposed him and sent him to Corsica, later moving him to Madagascar. They installed Muhammad Ben Aarafa, a cousin, in his place. The deposition sparked active opposition, and he returned on 16 November 1955. In 1956 he negotiated Moroccan independence with France and Spain, and in 1957 he took the title of king.

Muhammad V died on 26 February 1961, aged 51, of cardiac arrest after an operation on his nasal septum. His son Moulay Hassan, who succeeded him as Hassan II, announced his death on national radio, and a seven-day period of mourning followed. A mausoleum for his remains was built in 1971. Many streets, schools, an airport and a university in Morocco bear his name, and historians often describe him as a moderate and conciliatory ruler.
mohamoud-ali-shire: Mohamoud Ali Shire bore the title of Sultan, also called Senior Akil, of the Warsangali, with his seat at Las Khorey. In 1886 he and other Warsangali elders signed a treaty with the British Empire establishing a protectorate over their territory, one of several such treaties with Somali clans. He had close dealings with Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, whose Dervish movement fought British, Italian and Ethiopian forces for two decades; the two leaders traded and intrigued, and Shire once sought to marry Hassan's daughter Faṭmah, offering ten camels loaded with draperies and silk, but was refused.

In the struggle between the Dervishes and the British, Shire threw in the Warsangali's lot with the Dervishes, and in January 1908 his men fired on a British ship about to land on their coast. After the Dervishes were defeated in 1920, as a direct result of Britain's new policy of aerial bombardment, the Secretary of State sentenced him to seven years' exile in the Seychelles, on the ground that he had exercised his own native authority. He was held at Berbera, from where he tried to escape, and was then shipped to the islands on HMS Odin.

On Mahé he lived in a house in the Anse Etoile district, reporting three times a day to the police station across the street, and he formed a friendship with another exile, Sa'ad Zaghloul Pasha, former Prime Minister of Egypt. His petitions for release, in which he promised to recognise British authority and gave up any wish to be Sultan, were refused, and he passed letters home through Somali sailors to evade censorship.

His exile ended in May 1928, when he was taken to Aden on the SS Karapara and returned to the Somaliland Protectorate. He still commanded his people's loyalty, the British in time restored his status as Sultan, and he later died peacefully in his sleep.
mohawk-river: The Mohawk is the largest tributary of the Hudson River. It begins where the West Branch and East Branch meet in north-central Oneida County, flows south past the city of Rome, where it enters the Erie Canal, and then runs east through the Mohawk Valley past Utica, Little Falls, Canajoharie, Amsterdam and Schenectady. It joins the Hudson at Cohoes, a few miles north of Albany. Its largest tributary, Schoharie Creek, supplies over a quarter of its watershed, and West Canada Creek adds about 16 per cent.

Around 13,350 years ago, in the last stage of the retreat of the ice, the catastrophic draining of the glacial Lake Iroquois passed through what became the Mohawk Valley. The torrent cut deep scour features such as the Potholes at Little Falls and laid down the sand and gravel of the Scotia Delta, also called the Great Flats Aquifer.

The river is named for the Mohawk Nation of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. In the 1700s and before, the Mohawk were based in the valley, and their name for the river is Teionontatátie, a river flowing through a mountain. It served as their highway, and it is a passage through the Appalachian Mountains between the Catskill Mountains to the south and the Adirondack Mountains to the north, easier than crossing the mountains. This made it strategically important in the French and Indian War and the American Revolutionary War, and several important battles were fought there.

The Dutchman Harman Meyndertsz van den Bogaert made the first recorded European exploration in 1634, going 100 miles upstream from Albany. Dutch colonists founded Schenectady in 1661. In 1712 the British built Fort Hunter at the mouth of Schoharie Creek and settled about 600 Palatine Germans along the river. In the early nineteenth century a corporation built the Erie Canal along the Mohawk to Lake Erie, which eased westward settlement and linked the port of New York with the Great Lakes at Buffalo.

Spring snowmelt brings the river's highest flows, and ice jams of some significance occur about every other year. The most severe flood on record was the spring breakup flood of 27 and 28 March 1914. The lower part of the river has five permanent dams, nine seasonal movable dams and five hydropower plants.
mohegan: The Mohegan are part of the Eastern Algonquian family of peoples and refer to themselves as the Wolf People. The name comes from an Algonquian term usually interpreted as People of the Wolf. They are distinct from the Mohican, or Mahican, who lived in the upper Hudson River Valley; English writers often confused the two, and the Dutch colonist Adriaen Block separated them in his writings as the Morhicans and the Mahicans.

The Mohegan and the Pequot are believed to share an ancestry in a coastal Algonquian-speaking population that moved south from the upper Hudson Valley and other inland regions. Both spoke Mohegan-Pequot, which was mutually intelligible with the speech of the Montaukett and the Narragansett. According to oral tradition and colonial records, Uncas broke from the Pequot sachem Sassacus and founded an independent community on the Thames River, centred on the fortified village of Shantok. Mohegan oral history says that Uncas broke the arrows of peace with Sassacus, and presents the split as a return to older values; colonial writers often saw it as opportunism.

Traditional Mohegan society traced descent through the mother's line, and women held influence in family and community decisions. A council of elders and sachems led by consensus rather than command. Families moved between river valleys, coast and inland forest with the seasons and lived in wigwams, domed dwellings framed with saplings and covered with bark or woven mats. Women grew corn, beans and squash, the Three Sisters, while men hunted deer and turkey and fished with weirs, nets and spears.

Mohegan belief centres on balance with the natural world. The Creator is often called Mundo in English, and decisions are guided by their effect on the seventh generation to come. The Trail of Life describes a path reaching seven generations back and seven forward. The Green Corn Ceremony, a harvest observance, was revived in the 20th century by Emma Fielding Baker.

The Mohegan language ceased to be spoken in daily conversation in the early 20th century, but the Mohegan do not regard it as extinct. Samson Occom, a minister born in 1723, used it in preaching, and Fidelia Hoscott Fielding kept four phonetic diaries of Mohegan words and phrases that now underpin its revival. Gladys Tantaquidgeon, an ethnobotanist who lived from 1899 to 2005, recorded Mohegan medicine and co-founded the Tantaquidgeon Museum. In 2022 Dartmouth College returned Occom's papers to the Mohegan Tribe. Mohegan identity is understood as cultural as well as legal, and many Mohegan live across the United States.
moheli: Mohéli, also called Mwali, lies in the Indian Ocean off the coast of Africa and is the smallest of the four major Comoro Islands. Its capital and largest city is Fomboni, where about 19,000 of the island's roughly 38,000 people lived at a count of 2006. Its main ethnic group, as on the other Comoro islands, is the Comorian people, a synthesis of Bantu, Arab, Malay and Malagasy culture, and its main religion is Sunni Islam.

Until 1830 Mohéli was part of the Ndzuwani Sultanate, which also controlled the neighbouring island of Anjouan. In 1830 migrants from Madagascar led by Ramanetaka, who later changed his name to Abderemane, took over the island and established the sultanate of Mwali. Its ruler in the mid-nineteenth century was Queen Jumbe-Souli. In 1886 France made the island a protectorate. Mwali kept its own French resident until 1889, when it was placed under the residency of Anjouan, and the sultanate was dismantled in 1909 after the French annexation of the island.

In 1975 Mohéli agreed to join the Comoros, together with Grande Comore and Anjouan. Political, economic and social turmoil followed. On 11 August 1997 Mohéli seceded, a week after Anjouan, under the leaders Said Mohamed Soefu, who became president, and Soidri Ahmed, who became prime minister. It rejoined the Comoros in 1998. In 2002 it ratified a new Comorian constitution that provided for a less centralised federal government and more power to the island governments, which helped to settle the turmoil.

Mohéli Marine Park, gazetted on 19 April 2001, was the first protected area in the Comoros. It came out of an arrangement negotiated between the government and the communities of the ten villages around its boundaries. It was redesignated Mohéli National Park in 2010 and in 2015 was enlarged to cover about three-quarters of the island's land area. A tract of 6,268 hectares in the western highlands, including Mount Mlédjélé, is an Important Bird Area for species such as the Comoro olive pigeon and the Moheli scops owl. The island's only airport lies between Fomboni and Djoièzi on the north coast.
mohenjo-daro: Mohenjo-daro lies off the right bank of the lower Indus in Larkana District, on a Pleistocene ridge in the river's flood plain, about 28 kilometres from the town of Larkana. The modern name, in Sindhi, means 'Mound of the Dead Men'. The city's original name is unknown; Iravatham Mahadevan, from a seal, speculated that it could have been Kukkuṭārma, 'the city of the cockerel'. At its height the Indus Civilisation spread from the Iranian border to Gujarat, with other great centres at Harappa, Lothal, Kalibangan, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi.

The city was divided into the Citadel, a mud-brick mound around 12 metres high, and the Lower City. The Citadel held public baths, a large residential structure for about 5,000 people and two large assembly halls. In 1950 Mortimer Wheeler identified a Great Granary, but Jonathan Mark Kenoyer pointed to the complete lack of evidence for grain and suggested a Great Hall of uncertain function. Repeated flooding led the builders to raise platforms of mud brick. Wheeler proposed that the city had been flooded and silted over perhaps six times and rebuilt each time on the same spot, while Gregory Possehl argued for frequent small floods combined with land worn out by crops and pasture.

The ruins were undocumented for around 3,700 years until R. D. Banerji of the Archaeological Survey of India visited in 1919 to 1920 and, finding a flint scraper, concluded that the site was ancient. Kashinath Dikshit excavated in 1924 to 1925 and John Marshall in 1925 to 1926, with later campaigns in the 1930s, in 1945 under Mortimer Wheeler and in 1964 and 1965 under George Dales. Excavation was banned after 1965 because exposed structures were weathering.

Finds include seated and standing figures, carved seals, balance-scales and weights, gold and jasper jewellery, and copper tablets bearing the undeciphered Indus script. Pakistan and India divided some 12,000 objects at independence; Pakistan received the Priest-king, and India kept the Dancing Girl, a bronze statuette 10.5 centimetres high found in 1926. The site is a World Heritage Site and is threatened by erosion and improper restoration.
mojmir-i: From the 570s the Avars dominated the region from the Eastern Carpathians to the Eastern Alps, and the Slavic tribes there paid them tribute. Charlemagne defeated the Avars between 792 and 796, and a series of Slavic principalities soon appeared on the Middle Danube. The Moravian principality first appears in the Royal Frankish Annals in 822, when the Moravians brought tribute to Emperor Louis the Pious.

Mojmir arose in Moravia in the 820s. It is uncertain whether he was the first ruler to unite the local Slavic tribes or simply rose to prominence in a changing political situation. A letter written around 900 by Bavarian bishops to the pope suggests that he had predecessors. Some scholars infer from the dating of a Christian church at Mikulčice that he was baptised between 818 and 824, but this remains debated. The History of the Bishops of Passau records a mass baptism of the Moravians by Bishop Reginhar of Passau in 831, yet the pagan sanctuary at Mikulčice stayed in use until the middle of the 9th century.

The frontiers of his state are not precisely known, but the Moravians were expanding in the 830s. A list known as the Catalogue of Fortresses and Regions to the North of the Danube, compiled between 844 and 862, credits them with eleven fortresses. According to the Conversion of the Bavarians and the Carantanians, written in 870, around 833 Pribina was driven across the Danube by Mojmir, duke of the Moravians. Pribina was either the head of another Slavic principality or one of Mojmir's rebellious subordinates, and most historians place his lands at Nitra.

In the 840s Mojmir used the civil war within the Carolingian Empire to plot a rebellion against Frankish overlordship, which made him a serious threat to Louis the German, king of East Francia. The Franks invaded Moravia in mid-August 846 and met little resistance. According to the Annals of Fulda, Louis arranged matters as he wished and set Rastiz, a nephew of Moimar, over the Moravians as duke. Modern scholarship credits either Mojmir or his successors with creating the early medieval state known as Great Moravia, and his house is named the House of Mojmir after him.
mokjong-of-goryeo: Born Wang Song on 5 July 980, Mokjong was the only son of King Gyeongjong of Goryeo and Queen Heonae of the Hwangju Hwangbo clan. When his father died he was too young to rule, so the throne passed to his uncle, Prince Gaeryeong Wang Ch'i, who reigned as King Seongjong. Mokjong became the seventh ruler of the dynasty on his uncle's death in 997 and chose his mother as regent.

Early in his reign Mokjong reformed the Jeonsigwa, the land-allotment system, worked to reorganise the military and had the castle of Pyongyang rebuilt to strengthen the northern defences of Goryeo. His later years were overshadowed by a plot of his mother and her lover Kim Ch'i-yang, who sought to put their own child on the throne, presenting the boy as a son of Gyeongjong. Mokjong tried to prevent this, since it would have ended the rule of the House of Wang. He had no heirs, and his homosexuality was later used to justify his removal.

To stop the coup, Mokjong called in General Kang Cho. Kang instead dethroned the king himself, charging that he had neglected the defence of a country in imminent danger of invasion by the Khitan Liao, and calling his homosexuality a sickness. Mokjong was sent into exile at Chungju but was killed on 2 March 1009, before he reached it.

His tomb was known as Gongneung, but its location is no longer known. His queen, Seonjeong of the Chungju Yu clan, and Palace Lady Yoseoktaek of the Kim clan bore him no children. He has been portrayed in the KBS2 television series Empress Cheonchu of 2009 and Korea–Khitan War of 2023.
moktar-ould-daddah: Moktar Ould Daddah was born on 25 December 1924 into an important marabout family of the Ouled Birri tribe in Boutilimit, in French West Africa. After attending elite Islamic academies he worked for the French colonial administrators as a translator. He studied law in Paris, becoming the first Mauritanian to hold a university degree, and was admitted to the bar at Dakar in 1955.

Back in Mauritania in the late 1950s he joined the Mauritanian Progressive Union. In 1959 he founded the Mauritanian Regroupment Party, which won every seat in the National Assembly in the last pre-independence elections that year, and he was appointed prime minister. He was known for building consensus among the White Moors, Black Moors and Black Africans, Mauritania's three main ethnic groups, and the French granted independence in 1960.

Named acting president of the new Islamic Republic, Moktar was confirmed in the first post-independence election in August 1961. In December the four largest parties merged as the Mauritanian People's Party, which became the sole legal party, and a constitution of 1964 formalised the one-party state, which he justified by saying Mauritania was unready for Western-style multi-party democracy. He was re-elected in uncontested elections in 1966, 1971 and 1976. He followed a policy of Islamic socialism with many nationalisations, joined the Non-Aligned Movement, kept strong links with the People's Republic of China and accepted French aid. In 1971 he was president of the Organization of African Unity.

Drought in the Sahel from 1969 to 1974 and falling iron prices lowered living standards. In 1975 Mauritania joined Morocco in the attempt to annex Western Sahara, which Moktar had claimed as part of Greater Mauritania since 1957. After the Madrid Accords with Spain it annexed a southern portion, but the Polisario Front's guerrillas defeated the small Mauritanian Army, attacked the iron mines at Zouerate and in 1976 attacked Nouakchott.

On 10 July 1978 a military coup led by Mustafa Ould Salek overthrew him. His successors withdrew from the war in August 1979. Moktar went into exile in France that month after a period of imprisonment, and founded the opposition Alliance pour une Mauritanie Démocratique in 1980. He was allowed to return on 17 July 2001, and died after a long illness in Paris on 14 October 2003. He was buried at the El Balatiya cemetery near Boutilimit. In his memoirs he expressed concern that slavery in Mauritania could lead to an armed conflict that would destroy the country.
mokvi-cathedral: Mokvi Cathedral is a Georgian Orthodox church in the village of Mokvi, in the Ochamchire Municipality of Abkhazia, a de facto independent republic internationally recognised as part of Georgia. It is a cross-in-square domed church of five naves, with chapels along the naves and three apses projecting on the east side. The middle apse of the altar is horseshoe-shaped inside and has five facets outside.

The dome rests on four pillars at the centre of the building, and its low neck has twelve facets. The church is faced with hewn stone; its plain facades carry no ornament and are divided into two tiers by a row of openings.

In the Catholicate of Abkhazia, Mokvi was the seat of a bishop at least until the 17th century. The eparchy was founded in the 10th century, but Mokvi flourished above all from the 13th century onwards as a centre of Georgian culture, where manuscripts were copied and old codices restored. Georgian literary sources preserve the names of its bishops, among them Grigol Mokveli, Daniel Mokveli, Abraam Mokveli, Eptvime Sakvarelidze and Pilipe Chkhetidze. Daniel Mokveli commissioned the Mokvi Four Gospels.

The church was substantially renovated and painted in the reign of David IV the Builder (1089-1125). An inscription, now lost, that Patriarch Dositheos II of Jerusalem found on his visit to Mokvi in 1659 dated the painting to the reigns of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos and David IV of Georgia. None of these murals survive, but in the 1980s fragments of murals thought to date from the 15th century were found, with many Georgian inscriptions. Of the church's once rich epigraphy only an inscription on the bell tower is preserved, while manuscripts from its library still survive.
moldova: Moldova is a landlocked country of 33,843 km2 between the Prut river on the west, which separates it from Romania, and the Dniester on the east. Most of it is hilly, with elevations that never exceed 430 metres, the highest point being the Bălănești Hill, and exceptionally rich Chernozem soil covers around three-quarters of the land. About 88% of the area lies in the Bessarabia region, and a narrow strip on the east bank of the Dniester is in the unrecognised breakaway state of Transnistria.

In 1999 Moldova acquired from Ukraine a 0.45 kilometre frontage on the Danube, which turned the village of Giurgiulești into a river port. The name comes from the Moldova River; a legend recounted by the chroniclers Dimitrie Cantemir and Grigore Ureche says that Prince Dragoș named it after his hound Molda, which drowned there.

In antiquity the area was a crossroads for invasions by the Scythians, Goths, Huns and other tribes, followed by periods of Roman and Byzantine control. The Principality of Moldavia emerged in the 1350s, reached prominence under rulers such as Stephen the Great, and was a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire from 1538. In 1812 the Ottoman Empire ceded the eastern half to the Russian Empire, which called it Bessarabia. Southern Bessarabia was returned to Moldavia in 1856, three years before Moldavia united with Wallachia to form Romania, but Russia restored its rule over the entire region in 1878.

Bessarabia declared independence in February 1918 and joined Romania later that year after a vote of its assembly, a decision disputed by Soviet Russia. In 1940, as a consequence of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, Romania was compelled to cede Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina to the Soviet Union, which created the Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic. It declared independence on 27 August 1991 and took the name Moldova, and the Transnistria War of 1992 left the breakaway region de facto independent.

Moldova adopted its constitution in 1994 and is a parliamentary republic with a 101-seat unicameral parliament. It was granted European Union candidate status in June 2022. The population was an estimated 2,423,300, and ethnic Moldovans were almost 77% of it in the census.
moldovita-monastery: The monastery lies in the commune of Vatra Moldoviței. Its founder, Petru Rareș, was the illegitimate son of Stephen the Great, prince of Moldavia from 1457 to 1504, who fought many battles against the Ottoman Empire and built churches after his victories. Petru Rareș ruled Moldavia from 1527 to 1538 and again from 1541 to 1546, and he founded the monastery as a protective barrier against the Ottoman conquerors. He also promoted a new vision for the churches of Bukovina, commissioning artists to cover their walls inside and out with frescoes of saints, prophets and scenes from the life of Jesus.

Moldovița's frescoes were painted by Toma of Suceava and are well preserved, mostly in yellow and blue. On the outer walls a procession of saints leads up to the Virgin enthroned with the Child above the narrow east window, and a Tree of Jesse rising from the reclining Jesse sets out the ancestry of Christ around the Holy Family. The Siege of Constantinople recalls the Virgin's intervention to save the city from a Persian attack in 626, though the siege shown is rather the Fall of Constantinople in 1453.

Tall arches open the porch to the outside and the daylight, and within it the Last Judgment covers the whole west wall, with its river of fire and the sea giving up its dead. Moldovița and Humor are the last churches built with an open porch, a hidden place above the burial vault, and Gothic-style windows and doors.

In 1993 Moldovița was placed on the UNESCO World Heritage List with the churches of Sucevița, Voroneț, Humor, Suceava, Pătrăuți, Arbore and Probota as the Painted churches of Moldavia. The monastery appeared on a Romanian postage stamp in 1968. Sister Maika, who has lived there for more than 50 years, calls its paintings "the holy scriptures in color".
mole-saint-nicolas: Môle-Saint-Nicolas is a commune on the north-western coast of Haiti and the chief town of the Môle-Saint-Nicolas Arrondissement in the department of Nord-Ouest. It lies on a wide bay sheltered from the winds. The production of charcoal has destroyed the forest that once covered the area, and the surrounding landscape now looks more like a high desert than a lush tropical island.

The town received its present name after France gained control of the western part of Hispaniola in 1697. In 1764, after the Grand Dérangement had exiled thousands of Acadians from their northern homelands, French authorities tried to settle them there, to strengthen Saint-Domingue and build a base for the French Navy. Disease and food shortages made it a disaster: within a year a reported 420 of the 700 settlers had died, and most of the survivors soon fled to Louisiana.

In 1889 the administration of President Benjamin Harrison appointed Frederick Douglass minister to Haiti, with instructions to encourage the acquisition of Môle-Saint-Nicolas as a coaling station for the American fleet. Douglass sought a lease, but the talks were wrecked by the United States Navy and by the New York businessman William P. Clyde, who wanted monopoly steamship access to Haitian ports. Admiral Bancroft Gherardi arrived with warships and declared it the destiny of the Môle to belong to the United States. The Haitians refused, Douglass resigned under attack, and seven years later the United States secured Guantánamo Bay in Cuba instead.

The town has about 4,000 inhabitants, with another 20,000 in the rural areas around it. Fishing and the making of charcoal, carried to larger cities in wooden sailing vessels, are its main industries. Remains of colonial forts survive, among them the Batteries de Vallières, Fort Georges, Saint-Charles and Le Fort Allemand, together with a powder magazine built in the 1750s.
molepolole: Molepolole is a large village in Kweneng District, Botswana, about 50 kilometres west of the national capital Gaborone, and serves as a gateway for exploring the Kalahari Desert. It is named after the Molepolole River. Its people are the Bakwena, one of the eight major tribes of Botswana, and it is the capital of the Bakwena. It has a large traditional kgotla, the assembly place of a community, and the Scottish Livingstone Hospital.

The Bakwena capital moved several times in the 19th century. Dimawe was settled in August 1851 and attacked by Boers in August 1852. Kolobeng, where Livingstone had a house and workshop and designed a square house for the chief Sechele I, was the capital until 1853. Livingstone arrived at Dithubaruba, the next Kwena capital, in 1853. A cave about 3 kilometres from Molepolole is linked with Livingstone and Sechele.

Ntsweng, a few kilometres south-east of Molepolole, was first occupied by the Bakwena under Sechele I in 1864. Visible house foundations of stones set on edge survive there, together with the ruins of the office of Sebele II, which stands beside the old royal kraal, now a royal cemetery. Analyses of the layout suggest that cattle were kept at the centre of each ward, as in the central cattle pattern of southern Bantu settlements. The chief Sebele I was one of three chiefs who went to England to seek British protection.

Molepolole is one of the largest traditional villages in Africa, with a population of over 74,674 at the 2022 count. It has a college of education, an institute of health sciences and eight government junior secondary schools. Nearby are rock paintings, iron smelting sites and caves in the Kopong hills, and the burial cairns of Sechele I, Sebele I and Sebele II.
moliere: Molière was born in Paris and baptised as Jean Poquelin on 15 January 1622, the first son of Jean Poquelin and Marie Cressé, from a prosperous bourgeois family. He lost his mother at 10. His father bought the post of valet of the King's chamber and keeper of carpets and upholstery in 1631, and the son took it over in 1641. He studied at the Jesuit Collège de Clermont and around 1642 as a provincial lawyer, though it is not documented that he qualified. In June 1643 he left his social class for the stage, joined the actress Madeleine Béjart, and founded the Illustre Théâtre.

Thirteen years as an itinerant actor refined his comic skill, and he began to write, combining commedia dell'arte elements with the more refined French comedy. Through aristocratic patrons, including Philippe I, Duke of Orléans, brother of Louis XIV, he gained a command performance before the King at the Louvre. He was granted the grande salle of the Petit-Bourbon and later the theatre in the Palais-Royal, where plays such as The Affected Ladies, The School for Husbands and The School for Wives succeeded. His troupe received a royal pension and the title Troupe du Roi.

His satires drew criticism. The Catholic Church in France denounced Tartuffe, a study of religious hypocrisy, and the Parlement banned it, while Don Juan was withdrawn and never restaged by Molière. His other plays include The Misanthrope, The Miser and The Learned Ladies. His health suffered from the work, and by 1667 he had to take a break from the stage.

Molière suffered from pulmonary tuberculosis. On 17 February 1673, while playing Argan in his last play, The Imaginary Invalid, he collapsed in a fit of coughing and haemorrhage. He finished the performance, collapsed again, and died at home a few hours later without the last rites: two priests refused to come and a third arrived too late. As actors could not then be buried in consecrated ground, his widow Armande asked the King for a normal funeral at night, and he was buried in the part of the cemetery reserved for unbaptised infants. In 1817 his remains were moved to Père Lachaise Cemetery.

He is considered the creator of modern French comedy. A tartuffe is a hypocrite, and a harpagon, after the miser of The Miser, is an obsessively greedy man. His works were translated into English prose by John Ozell in 1714, and the first complete English version, by Baker and Miller, appeared in 1739.
molina-de-aragon: Molina de Aragón is a municipality in the province of Guadalajara, in Castile-La Mancha, with five further settlements in its territory. It has a warm-summer Mediterranean climate with some semi-arid influences, and winters that are cold by Spanish standards, with temperatures often below freezing because of its altitude and inland position. It once held the record for the lowest temperature measured by a meteorological station in Spain, −28.2 °C. The mineral aragonite takes its name from the place, which is its type location.

During the Caliphate of Córdoba the area appears to have been very sparsely populated, with Arabized Berbers as its main inhabitants, according to Ramón Menéndez Pidal. After the caliphate broke up, a small taifa kingdom arose there, mentioned in the epic Cantar de mio Cid. It was captured during the Reconquista by Alfonso the Battler, king of Aragon, whose brother and successor Ramiro II ceded the lordship's lands to Castile; the region later returned to Muslim control under the Almoravids.

Around 1139 Manrique Pérez de Lara retook the lands and became the first Lord of Molina. On 21 April 1154 he issued a sweeping fuero to the town. He and his descendants claimed to rule Molina by the grace of God, and the lordship, made up of the town and four sexmas, remained independent of both Aragon and Castile for more than a century and a half.

In 1366, during the war between Castile and Aragon, the people of Molina rebelled against Henry II's grant of the lordship to Bertrand du Guesclin and placed themselves under Aragonese sovereignty, which was completed three years later; the name Molina de Aragón dates from then, the town having been Molina de los Caballeros. It returned to Castile in 1375 as part of the dowry of the Aragonese infanta Eleanor.

The town had 3,671 inhabitants at the 2009 census. In the Middle Ages it had a Jewish community, and remains of a medieval synagogue survive. During the Peninsular War the residents' resistance to Napoleonic troops led to the town being set on fire, and in recognition of their loyalty the Cortes granted it the title Muy Noble y Muy Leal Ciudad. Its main sights include a medieval alcazar of the 10th and 11th centuries, the largest in the province, a Roman bridge, the Convent of St. Francis and the churches of Santa Clara and Santa María de San Gil. It lies within the Molina-Alto Tajo Geopark.
molise: Molise covers 4,460.65 square kilometres, making it the second smallest region of Italy after the Aosta Valley. It is bordered by Abruzzo to the north, Apulia to the east, Lazio to the west and Campania to the south, and has 35 kilometres of sandy coastline on the Adriatic Sea. The countryside is mostly mountainous, with 55 percent covered by mountains and most of the rest by hills. The Volturno, the longest river of southern Italy, rises there. The name first appears in the High Middle Ages as that of a Norman county, taken from the name of the ruling family, the de' Moulins.

Evidence from the site of Isernia La Pineta shows that Molise was inhabited in the Paleolithic, with traces of human presence up to 700 000 years old. Before the Romans arrived it formed part of Samnium. The Pentri settled around Isernia and Campobasso from about the 7th century BCE. Roman expansion from the 4th century BCE brought the Samnite Wars. Isernia and Bojano, the Pentri capital, were captured, but the Samnites were completely defeated only after Sulla won the Social War.

The region declined in late antiquity, and the Lombards found it thinly populated. Around 667 Grimoald I, King of the Lombards, created the gastaldate of Bojano and gave it to the Bulgar commander Alzeco. In 1045 Rudolf of Moulins conquered what became the County of Bojano, which broke up into smaller fiefs after the family lost power at the end of the 11th century. In 1806 Joseph Bonaparte extended the French provincial model to the Kingdom of Naples, and by 1811 the Province of Molise had roughly its present area.

Molise has a population of 285,940 and its capital and largest city is Campobasso. Its two provinces are Campobasso and Isernia. It was formed in 1963 by separation from Abruzzo, with which it had been joined as Abruzzi e Molise. Emigration in 1951–71 emptied many small towns. Its two minorities are the Molisan Croats, who speak an old Dalmatian dialect of Croatian, and speakers of Arbëresh, a dialect of Albanian. Its sights include the Italic theatre at Pietrabbondante and the Roman site of Saepinum at Altilia.
molla-panah-vagif: He was born in the village of Salahly in the Kazakh Sultanate. His parents, Mehdi agha and Aghqiz khanum, sent him to the local cleric Shafi Effendi to learn Arabic and Persian, and in 1759 the family moved to the Karabakh Khanate after fighting between the Kazakh Sultanate and the Kingdom of Georgia. He settled in Shusha, the capital of the khanate, and founded a madrasa in its Saatli quarter.

In 1769 Ibrahim Khalil Khan, who had heard that he could predict lunar eclipses, invited him to court and, after he converted from Sunni Islam to Shiism, made him eshik aghasi, in charge of foreign affairs, an office he held for 27 years. He helped plan Shusha, visited Tbilisi several times, where he befriended Prince Iulon of Georgia, and began the khanate's correspondence with Catherine II of Russia. He tried without success to ally Karabakh, Georgia and the Erivan and Talysh khanates against Qajar Iran.

He organised the defence of Shusha when Agha Mohammad Shah Qajar besieged it in 1795. According to the historian Mirza Adigozal bey, in a tale that may be apocryphal, the shah shot a taunting couplet of Urfi into the town, playing on the likeness of Shusha to the word for glass, and Vagif answered it with a couplet of his own. After 33 days the shah lifted the siege.

When the shah returned in 1797, Shusha fell; Vagif was imprisoned, but the shah was assassinated that night. Muhammed bey Javanshir, a nephew of Ibrahim Khalil Khan, then had Vagif and his son Ali executed and his house plundered, and many of his verses were lost. His poems, first collected by Mirza Yusif Nersesov in 1856 and printed by Adolf Berge in Leipzig in 1867, turned from the abstract religious themes of Sufi-leaning verse to everyday feelings in a language close to the vernacular, and many are sung by ashiks. His mausoleum in Shusha, built in the 1970s, was destroyed in 1992 during the First Nagorno-Karabakh War.
molly-brant: Little is certain about Brant's early life. Named Mary, she was born to Christian Mohawk parents, possibly at Canajoharie or in the Ohio Country, where her family lived for a time. Her name Konwatsiʼtsiaiénni means Someone Lends Her a Flower; Degonwadonti, Two Against One, was given at adulthood. In 1753 her mother married Brant Kanagaradunkwa, a Mohawk royaner of the Turtle clan, whose name Molly and Joseph took. The family lived in a colonial-style frame house and attended the Church of England, and Molly spoke Mohawk and English, though she may have been only semi-literate.

She became the consort of Sir William Johnson, the Superintendent for Northern Indian Affairs, and bore their son Peter Warren Johnson in September 1759; eight of their nine children lived past infancy. At Fort Johnson and later Johnson Hall she ran the household and estate during his long absences, and Johnson used the tie in his dealings with the Haudenosaunee. After his death in July 1774 she returned to Canajoharie and prospered as a fur trader.

A Loyalist, she sheltered Loyalists fleeing to Canada. In August 1777 she sent runners to warn the British that Patriot militia were marching to relieve Fort Stanwix, which led to the ambush at the Battle of Oriskany. The Oneida and Patriots then plundered Canajoharie and she fled to Onondaga, where she urged the council to stay loyal to the Crown against the Seneca chief Sayenqueraghta. From Fort Niagara, Montreal and Carleton Island she worked as an intermediary between the British and the Haudenosaunee; the British commander there thought her influence far greater than that of all their chiefs together.

In 1783 she moved to Cataraqui, now Kingston, where the British gave her a house, a pension of £100 a year and land. New York ruled that she and her children, as Indians, could not own the land Johnson had left them. She died at Kingston on 16 April 1796 and was buried in St. Paul's Churchyard, the grave now lost. Long ignored by historians of the United States, she has drawn scholarly interest since the late 20th century; some criticise her as pro-British at the Haudenosaunee's expense, while others hold that she chose what she believed best for her people.
molly-malone: In the late 20th century a legend grew up that a historical Molly Malone lived in the 17th century, usually shown as a hawker by day and a part-time prostitute by night, though she has also been portrayed as one of the few chaste female street hawkers of her day. There is no evidence that the song is based on a real woman of that or any other time. Molly was a familiar form of Mary and Margaret, and many Molly Malones were born in Dublin over the centuries, but nothing connects any of them to the song. In 1988 the Dublin Millennium Commission nevertheless endorsed claims made for a Mary Malone who died on 13 June 1699, and proclaimed 13 June Molly Malone Day.

The song is not recorded earlier than 1876, when it was published in Boston, Massachusetts, in a section of a book titled Songs from English and German Universities, which suggests an Irish origin. A London edition of 1884 credited it to James Yorkston of Edinburgh and said it was reprinted from an edition that implies a first printing in Scotland, but no copy has been found. Siobhán Marie Kilfeather places it in the music hall style of its period and calls the story of a historical Molly nonsense, while not wholly excluding that it rests on an older folk song.

Several earlier pieces share elements with it. A song called Widow Malone was published as early as 1809, Pat Corney's Account of Himself as early as 1826, and Meet Me Miss Molly Malone in Glasgow in 1836. A copy of Apollo's Medley of about 1790, found again in 2010, holds a song to Sweet Molly Malone of Howth that otherwise resembles it not at all. In the 19th century Dublin's fair city was a common phrase for the city, and alive, alive O was a cry of street vendors selling oysters, mussels, fish and eels.

A statue of Molly Malone by the Dublin sculptor Jeanne Rynhart was unveiled on Grafton Street in 1988 by the Lord Mayor, Ben Briscoe, during the Dublin Millennium celebrations. Some artists objected to it, and it was nicknamed The Tart with the Cart. In 2014 it was moved to Suffolk Street to make way for Luas tracks. The Dubliners, Pete Seeger, Danny Kaye, U2 and Sinéad O'Connor are among those who recorded the song, and the Irish soap opera Fair City takes its title from the first line.
molokai: Molokaʻi is the fifth most populated of the eight major islands of the Hawaiian archipelago. It measures 38 by 10 miles (61 by 16 km) in length and width and lies south-east of Oʻahu across the 25-mile-wide Kaʻiwi Channel, and north of Lānaʻi. The island grew from two shield volcanoes, East Molokaʻi and the much smaller West Molokaʻi. The northern half of East Molokaʻi collapsed about 1.5 million years ago, and what remains of the volcano includes the highest sea cliffs in the world. The highest point is Kamakou, at 4,970 feet (1,510 m). The largest town is Kaunakakai.

It was long thought that Molokaʻi was first settled around 650 CE by people from the Marquesas Islands. A 2010 study using revised radiocarbon dating placed the settlement of the Marquesas much later, and later migrants likely came from Tahiti and other islands of the south Pacific. Captain James Cook sighted Molokaʻi in 1778, and the first European sailor to visit was Captain George Dixon of the Royal Navy in 1786. A Protestant mission was founded at Kaluaʻaha in 1832.

Rudolph Wilhelm Meyer, an immigrant from Germany who arrived in 1850, was the first to grow and mill sugar and coffee commercially on the island, and he built its only sugar mill in 1878. Ranching began in the first half of the 19th century, when King Kamehameha V set up a country estate that Meyer managed and that became the Molokai Ranch.

Leprosy reached the Hawaiian Islands with traders, sailors and workers from places where it was common, and sugar planters, worried for their labour force, pressed the government to act. A law required people with the disease to be quarantined, and settlements at Kalawao and then Kalaupapa served as a colony from 1866 to 1969. More than 8,500 people were sent there and declared legally dead. Father Damien, a Belgian priest, served the sufferers for 16 years and died at Kalaupapa in 1889; Mother Marianne Cope and her Sisters also worked there.

Molokaʻi is part of Maui County, except for the Kalaupapa Peninsula, which forms Kalawao County. The forced quarantine laws were abolished in 1969, and the Kalaupapa National Historical Park now preserves the former settlement. Molokaʻi is believed to be the birthplace of the hula, which is marked at the annual Molokaʻi Ka Hula Piko festival.
molokans: The Molokans are a Russian Spiritual Christian sect that evolved from Eastern Orthodoxy in the East Slavic lands. Their name, from the Russian moloko, milk, is an exonym used by Orthodox neighbours, who regarded them as heretics because they drank milk during the Orthodox fasts. They tend to call themselves Spiritual Christians. The term Molokan is first recorded in the 1670s, but it referred to a group not directly related to the later Molokans.

The Molokans of today split from the Doukhobors in 1779 and 1780, thinking that the Doukhobors neglected the Bible. Their founder, Semyon Matveevich Uklein, was the son-in-law of the Doukhobor leader Ilarion Poberokhin, and he insisted on reliance on the Gospel texts. Uklein's Molokans from Tambov spread the faith in Orenburg, Saratov and Astrakhan provinces, and he went on organising congregations until his death in 1809.

From the intervention of Count Nikolay Zubov in 1795 the Molokans were tolerated under Catherine the Great, but within strict rules meant to curb their growth; those who ignored them were punished as heretics. Forbidden to win converts, they turned to endogamy. The government sent them away from central Russia, to the Caucasus in 1833, to Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia in 1834, to Ukraine in the 1830s, and to Central Asia and Siberia. In 1833 a schism produced the Jumpers, who reported charismatic outpourings of the Holy Spirit, while the old Molokans were called Constants. The census of 1912 counted 133,935 Molokane and 4,844 Pryguny in Russia.

Roughly 3,500 Molokans left Russia between 1901 and 1911, many settling at Potrero Hill in San Francisco and in Los Angeles. In August 1917 thirty-five men who refused to register under the Selective Service Act of 1917 were sentenced to a year in prison. Jumper communities also settled in Mexico's Guadalupe Valley.

Molokans hold the Bible as their main guide and read it spiritually, treating sacraments such as water baptism as signs of spiritual truths. They reject the Orthodox priesthood, icons and the cross, elect councils of elders, advocate pacifism, hold meetings in homes and do not drink or smoke. They follow Old Testament laws, avoiding pork and shellfish, and do not obey Orthodox fasting rules. Beliefs varied sharply among their groups; some built chapels or revered saints and icons.

About 20,000 people in the former Soviet Union identify as Molokans, at least ethnically, with some 200 churches. About 25,000 live in the United States, mostly around Los Angeles and Fresno. There are also communities in Australia, Canada, Mexico and Uruguay. In the United States they keep Russian in church services and hold community dinners called obed.
molossians: The Molossians were a group of ancient Greek tribes of Epirus. Together with the Chaonians and Thesprotians they formed the main tribal groupings of the northwestern Greek group, and Strabo counted them among the foremost of the fourteen tribes of Epirus. In the Late Bronze Age they were probably located over much of the central and western ranges of the Pindos, and the area of Pogoni, with its many tumuli burials, has been regarded as their heartland.

They first lived in small unwalled settlements scattered through river valleys and lakeside areas. Their expansion in Epirus possibly began in the early 6th century BCE, mainly at the expense of the Thesprotians.

Around 370 BCE the Aeacid dynasty created the first centralised state in Epirus. In 359 BCE the Molossian princess Olympias married Philip II of Macedon and became the mother of Alexander the Great. Her brother Alexander the Molossian led an expedition to southern Italy and was defeated at the Battle of Pandosia in 331 BCE. After his death in 330 BCE the name Epirus appears for the first time as a single political unit, under the Molossian dynasty. Pyrrhus came to the throne in 295 BCE and defeated the Romans at the Battle of Heraclea in 280 BCE, but his costly victory at Asculum in 279 BCE gave the term Pyrrhic victory its meaning.

In 233 BCE Deidamia, the last of the Aeacid house, was murdered and a federal republic, the Epirote League, was set up. The Epirotes sided with Macedonia in the Third Macedonian War (171-168 BCE) and, after the Roman victory, 150,000 of them, mostly Molossians, were enslaved and sent to Italy by decision of the Roman Senate. Some recent research treats the figures of destruction as symbolic, and the Greek language remained vital in Epirus in later centuries.

The Molossians spoke a Northwest Doric dialect of Greek and worshipped the Greek gods, with Zeus supreme and the oracle of Dodona in their land. Many Greeks nevertheless regarded them as barbarians, because of their tribal organisation and pastoral economy. Their dynasty claimed descent from Molossus, a son of Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, and scholars see this genealogy as an effort to heroise the house.

Around 370-368 BCE their officials were the king, the prostatai, a secretary, the hieromnemones and ten damiourgoi, one for each tribe. Each year the king sacrificed to Zeus Areios and swore to rule according to the laws. The Molossians were also known for their hounds, and their coins showed a dog on a shield.
molotov-ribbentrop-pact: Talks between the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and France broke down after the Soviet Union was excluded from the Munich Agreement of September 1938. Britain and France had judged Soviet participation in the conference dangerous and useless, partly because of Hitler's anti-Soviet rhetoric, while the Soviet leadership believed that the West wanted to encourage German aggression in the East. Rapprochement between the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany began in early 1939. In May Stalin replaced his foreign minister Maxim Litvinov, who had advocated rapprochement with the West, with Vyacheslav Molotov. Contacts at first went through economic negotiations, and in early August the two sides began to discuss a political agreement, finding common ground in their opposition to the capitalist democracies.

The Treaty of Non-Aggression between Germany and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was dated 23 August 1939 and signed by Molotov and the German foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop. It ran for ten years and provided for consultation, arbitration of disagreements, neutrality if either party went to war with a third power, and no membership of any group aimed at the other.

The Secret Additional Protocol provided for the partition of Poland. Latvia, Estonia, Finland and Bessarabia were allotted to the Soviet sphere, and Lithuania, apart from the Vilnius region, to the German one. The existence of the protocol was rumoured in the West and was proved only when it was made public at the Nuremberg trials. The agreement stunned governments, the press, Germany's allies such as Japan and foreign Communist parties.

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. On 17 September, stating concern for ethnic Ukrainians and Belarusians there, Stalin ordered the Soviet invasion. The German–Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty of 28 September then drew a new border on former Polish territory and moved Lithuania into the Soviet sphere. After the Soviet Union attacked Finland on 30 November in the Winter War, Finland ceded parts of Karelia, Kuusamo and Salla, and Hanko was leased as a naval base. About 422,000 Finns, 12 per cent of the population, lost their homes.

In mid-June 1940 Soviet NKVD troops raided border posts in Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia. Their state administrations were replaced by Soviet cadres, who deported or killed 34,250 Latvians, 75,000 Lithuanians and almost 60,000 Estonians. Elections with a single pro-Soviet candidate for many positions produced assemblies that asked for admission to the Soviet Union, which was granted. Parts of Romania, among them Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina, were also annexed. The pact ended on 22 June 1941 with Operation Barbarossa. Ribbentrop was convicted at Nuremberg and executed in 1946.
molyvos: Mithymna, more commonly called Molyvos, is a town on the northern part of the island of Lesbos in the North Aegean, Greece. Since the 2019 local government reform it has belonged to the municipality of West Lesbos. The town had 1,399 inhabitants at the 2011 census and lies about 6 kilometres north of the beach town of Petra. The old Genoese fortress stands on the hill in the middle of the town, and the agora, on the road up to it, has many historic shops, cafés and restaurants. Its municipal unit is the island's smallest in land area, at 50.166 square kilometres.

As Methymna the city was once the prosperous second city of Lesbos. Epic tradition told that Achilles besieged it during the Trojan War, with the help of the Methymnian princess Pisidice, who opened the gates and whom he afterwards had stoned for treason. It had a long rivalry with Mytilene, and when all the other cities of Lesbos sided with Mytilene in the revolt of 428 BCE, Methymna sided with Athens; it was the only city spared a cleruchy and remained self-governing. In 406 BCE it held out against the Spartan commander Kallikratidas until traitors betrayed it. A tyrant, Kleommis, held power from at least the 340s BCE. In the Hellenistic period it fell under Lysimachus, then the Ptolemies, and later allied with Rome.

Roman writers praised the wine of Methymna; Galen ranked it first among the wines of Lesbos. A bishop is attested from 520 CE, and Cretan Arabs plundered the city in 840, after which its fortifications were strengthened. It became a possession of the Gattelusi family of Genoa in 1355, and from then was called Molyvos. It repelled an Ottoman attack in 1450 but fell to Admiral Ismael with 150 ships in 1458. It was the last castle on the island the Ottomans held in 1462, after strong resistance.
Under the Ottomans trade in olive oil, soap, wine and fish brought mansions and schools. After the First Balkan War of 1912 the Greek navy took Lesbos, and the town received its ancient name back.
momai-tamuli-borbarua: Momai Tamuli Borbarua, also known as Chiring Phiseng and Sukuti Tamuly, was born into a small family of Garhgaon and rose from humble origins. He first worked as a gardener, and his work so impressed the Ahom king Pratap Singha that the king took him into royal service. He held a series of royal offices before he was promoted to the newly created office of Borbarua, of which he was the first holder.

With the king's support, Momai Tamuli gave order to the paik system in 1609. The paik system was the machinery of the Ahom state: every adult man between the ages of 15 and 50 had to give service to the state. He also established model villages and made it compulsory for every adult to make a bamboo basket and to spin a set quantity of thread.

In 1638 he commanded the Ahom forces against the Mughals, who suffered a heavy setback at the Battle of Duimunsila and fell back to Guwahati. Long wars had drained the resources and manpower of both sides, and in 1639 he concluded the Treaty of Asurar Ali with the Mughal commander Allah Yar Khan. It fixed the boundary at Barnadi on the north bank of the Brahmaputra and at Asurar Ali on the south bank.

After the death of Pratap Singha he acted as the de facto administrator of the kingdom and conducted its dealings with the Mughal faujdar Allah Yar Khan. In 1641 he refused a proposed trade convention between Assam and the Mughal Empire, and he declined to inquire into a murder of members of a Mughal elephant-catching party by hill tribes. In 1643 the Ahoms held 63 Mughal traders and officials who had strayed into Darrang, and in November 1645 he imprisoned 107 Mughal sepoys who had entered Darrang and advanced to Singri on the pretext of catching elephants, refusing the faujdar's pleas for their release.

Momai Tamuli had seven children, the youngest of whom was Lachit Borphukan, who became an Ahom general. He is remembered above all for systematising the paik system, which organised the compulsory service of the kingdom's adult men, and for his years of service to the Ahom state, first under Pratap Singha and then as its administrator after the king's death.
momine-khatun-mausoleum: The tomb, also known as the Atabek Dome, replaced a modest building raised over Momine Khatun's grave right after her burial. Jahan Pahlavan of the Eldiguzids ordered a complex of grand buildings to keep her memory and gave the new mausoleum to Ajami ibn Abubekr Nakhchivani, already known for the mausoleum of Yusuf ibn Kuseyir. The rest of the complex was built later, when her youngest son Kyzyl-Arslan was atabeg. In the 19th century a Juma mosque 35–36 metres high still stood there with a portal and minarets, but only the mausoleum survives.

The tower stands on a low ten-sided platform covered with large polished diorite slabs, over a crypt that holds the grave and has no pedestrian access. In the crypt Ajami placed a thick ten-sided support in the middle, joined to the walls by pointed arches, a technique used 38 years earlier in the tomb of the Red Dome; brick ribs on it form a star-shaped frame. The tower is round inside, under a spherical dome with traces of a spiral staircase, while its outer pyramidal roof has been lost.

The architect did not set the eastern face with its entrance apart from the others: above the door, in a shallow lancet arch, a brick inscription in Kufic lines names him. Each face is a niche covered with Kufic script worked into geometric ornament, different on every side, with blue-turquoise tiles against the red brick. Aleskerzade read the inscriptions framing the faces as Surah Ya-Sin, running twice round the ten sides, and a band 98 centimetres high at the top carries the epitaph. Four medallions inside bear the names of Muhammad, Abu Bakr, Omar, Osman, Ali, Hasan and Huseyn.

Jafar Giyasi sees in it the end of a line of building on local traditions, running from the Red Dome tomb through the Gilan tomb, and the peak of the scientific and artistic progress of that period in Azerbaijan. Its rare ten-sided prism has parallels in the Gombede-Kavus at Gurgan, of 1006, and in a domed tomb built at Maragha ten years earlier. Its thick corner supports and narrow, deep and very high cornices make the tower look taller and thinner than it really is.
mon-people: The Mon descend from Proto-Austroasiatic people, who are believed to have migrated from the Yangtze valley in southern China to Southeast Asia between 3,000 and 2,000 BCE along the Mekong, Salween, Sittaung, Irrawaddy and Ping rivers, bringing riverine agriculture and wet rice. Their language belongs to the Monic branch of the Austroasiatic family and is close to Nyah Kur, spoken in northeastern Thailand.

The Mon were among the earliest peoples of mainland Southeast Asia and founded some of its earliest civilisations: Dvaravati in central Thailand, Sri Gotapura in central Laos, the Hariphunchai Kingdom in northern Thailand and the Thaton Kingdom in Lower Myanmar. They were the first to receive Theravada Buddhist missionaries from Sri Lanka, and they adopted the Pallava script; the oldest Mon inscription, found in a cave at Saraburi, dates to about 550 CE.

When the Pagan Kingdom collapsed in 1287, Wareru, born to a Mon mother and a Tai father, made himself king of the Mon at Martaban and later moved the capital to Pegu. His Hanthawaddy kingdom lasted from 1287 to 1539. Binnya U defended it against Lan Na in the mid-14th century, and his son Razadarit, who reigned from 1384 to 1421, repelled invasions from Ava and made contributions to the Shwedagon Pagoda.

In 1539 King Tabinshwehti of Taungoo took Hanthawaddy after a siege of Pegu lasting four years. Many Mon refugees fled to Ayutthaya, where the Mon aristocracy joined the court. The fall of Martaban in 1541 was accompanied by massacre and pillage on a large scale. In 1740 Mon rebels, joined by the Gwe Shan, restored a Hanthawaddy kingdom with French support, but King Alaungpaya conquered it in 1757. Tens of thousands of Mon civilians were killed, among them over 3,000 monks in the capital alone.

Under the Konbaung dynasty further rebellions, including one in 1814, were put down harshly, and large numbers of Mon migrated to Siam. The British took control of the Mon territories after the Second Anglo-Burmese War in 1852, but never restored the Mon kingdom.

Today the Mon are a major ethnic group in Myanmar and a minor one in Thailand, and the two Mon dialects are mutually intelligible. The Tai Tham and Burmese alphabets are adaptations of the Mon script, and Burmese has borrowed vocabulary from Mon, especially for administration, architecture, cloth, cuisine and flowers. Cities including Yangon and Lamphun were founded by Mon people or Mon rulers. Their symbol is the hongsa, a mythological water bird. Mon National Day, set up in 1947, commemorates the founding of Hanthawaddy.
mona-passage: The Mona Passage lies in the Greater Antilles, and together with the Windward Passage between Hispaniola and Cuba it is one of the channels joining the North Atlantic to the Caribbean. Mona Island lies near its middle, the much smaller Monito Island 5 km to the north-west of it, and Desecheo Island about 50 km to the north-east, only 21 km from the Puerto Rican mainland. Variable tidal currents created by the islands on either side, and sand banks reaching out from both coasts, make the crossing difficult.

Waters pass over a sill 400 to 500 metres deep that runs between Cabo Engaño in Hispaniola and the Cabo Rojo Shelf of Puerto Rico. Above about 300 metres, surface water flows from the Atlantic into the Caribbean; beneath it, the Tropical Central Water flows out towards the Atlantic. Tides striking a submarine ridge called El Pichincho raise internal waves 40 metres high, which stir nitrate up into the sunlit layer and sustain new biological production there.

The passage lies over a seismically active rift. Its eastern face, with a relief of 3 kilometres, is controlled by the north-south Mona Rift Fault, and to the north the 4-kilometre-deep Mona Canyon runs towards the Puerto Rico Trench. In 1918 an earthquake centred along the east or south-east edge of the rift, and the tsunami that followed, devastated western Puerto Rico. Small earthquakes are still frequent there.

The Mona Passage is an important shipping route between the North Atlantic and the Panama Canal. Its tides, internal waves and the exchange of water between ocean and sea make it a very dynamic environment, observed by underwater gliders, satellite imagery and photographs from the International Space Station.
monasterboice: The name Monasterboice is a partly anglicised form of the Irish Mainistir Bhuithe, the monastery of Buithe; older English spellings were Monasterboye and Monasterboyse, and Boice comes from Boecius, the Latin form adopted for the Irish name. Saint Buithe, or Buite, the founder, died around 521. The poet and historian Flann Mainistrech, known as Flann of Monasterboice, was lector there. Little else is known of the community beyond a list of abbots from 759 to 1122. After the Cistercian Mellifont Abbey was established nearby in 1142 the monastery fell into ruin, though a parish church was in use on the site by the 13th century.

The site holds the remains of two churches built in the 14th century or later, an earlier round tower and three high crosses. The tower stands about 28 metres tall and is in very good condition; it was probably built shortly after 968 and was damaged by fire in 1098. The three crosses date from the 10th century and belong to the scriptural group, carved with scenes from the Bible.

Muiredach's High Cross, 5.5 metres tall, is named after Abbot Muiredach mac Domhnaill, who died in 923. Its carvings include Adam and Eve from the Old Testament and the Adoration of the Magi from the New. The North and West crosses are of the same kind but have suffered far more from the weather. A copy of Muiredach's Cross is held in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

The ruins are a national monument of Ireland, owned by the National Monuments Service and open to the public. They give their name to the village and the civil parish of Monasterboice, and burials still take place in the graveyard around them.
monastery-of-irache: Santa María la Real de Irache, also written Hyrache and in Basque Iratxe, stands in the town of Ayegui in Navarre, beside the Way of Saint James. Next to it lies a winery, Bodegas Irache, which continues a tradition of viticulture dating from monastic times. The buildings that survive are later than the monastery's foundation. The monastery is cited in a donation made by King Sancho I Garcés in the 10th century.

The monastery became a landmark as a hospital for pilgrims travelling to Santiago. In the sixteenth century it set up a college that became Navarre's first university, the Universidad Real de Hyrache, made a pontifical university in 1615 and closed in 1824. Its role in caring for the wounded continued into the wars of the nineteenth century. In 1813 it gave medical care to the anti-Napoleonic parties, among them the one led by Francisco Espoz y Mina, and during the Third Carlist War of 1872-1876 the Carlists defeated at the Battle of Montejurra withdrew to Irache to have their wounded treated.

On 15 June 1936 Irache was the scene of a conspiratorial meeting between the Carlist leader Manuel Fal Conde and General Mola, who had been posted to Pamplona that year. The alliance agreed there, at first an unlikely one, became a springboard for the military rising against the Spanish Republic.

The monastery has been protected as a monument since 1877. In 2007 its buildings, apart from the church, were designated for conversion into a parador, a state hotel meant to lodge travellers on the Way of Saint James, but the economic crisis held the project back. In 2020 the monastery served as the setting of the boarding school in the television series The Boarding School: Las Cumbres.
monastery-of-san-juan-de-la-pena: The monastery stands at Santa Cruz de la Serós, in the province of Huesca, and its name means Saint John of the Cliff. The old monastery, built in 920, has a two-level church partly carved into the stone of the great cliff that overhangs it; the lower church keeps some Mozarabic architectural elements, but most of the buildings are Romanesque. The rock is sometimes linked with the Monte Pano of legend. In the 11th century the house joined the Benedictine Order, and it was one of the most important monasteries of medieval Aragon.
