The cloister, built around 1190 beneath the rock, has capitals carved with Biblical scenes that were first arranged in chronological order, a design found elsewhere in the region. After a fire in 1675 a new monastery was built in 1705 on a plateau higher up the mountain. The royal pantheon on the upper floor, with marbles and stucco medallions recalling historic battles, largely dates from 1770, under Charles III of Spain. It holds the remains of the kings of Aragon Ramiro I, Sancho Ramírez and Peter I of Aragon and Navarre. In August 2026 the bones of the three kings were removed for safekeeping as wildfires approached the site.

According to legend, the chalice of the Last Supper was sent to the monastery to keep it from the Muslim invaders of the Iberian Peninsula; it is said to be the cup that Alfonso V of Aragon gave to Valencia Cathedral in 1438. The Chronicle of San Juan de la Peña takes its name from the monastery, where it was partly researched and written. The old monastery was declared a National Monument on 13 July 1889 and the new one in 1923.
monastery-of-san-pedro-de-siresa: The abbey stands in the Valle de Hecho and is the northernmost monastery in Aragon. Excavations in 1991 suggested that buildings had stood on the site since perhaps Visigothic times, and a Roman road, whose remains survive, passed nearby, linking Zaragoza and Berdún with Béarn over the pass of Puerto de Palo at 1,970 metres. In 833 Galindo Garcés, Count of Aragon, and his wife Guldegrut made donations to build a monastery here. Its first abbot, Zechariah, organised it under the rules set by the synod of Aachen in 816.

In 852 the travelling monk and scholar Eulogius of Córdoba wrote to Guilesino of Pamplona of the splendour of the monastery and its library. There he found and copied Greco-Roman works that had been lost in the Caliphate of Cordoba, among them an Aeneid, poetry of Horace and Juvenal, the fables of Aviano and Augustine of Hippo's The City of God.

A donation completed in 864 gave the monastery the valley lands from Javierregay, now Puente la Reina de Jaca, up into the Pyrenees, and Count Galindo Aznárez I gave it the town of Hecho, dozens of vineyards and fields and the town of Surba. Grants and confirmations of the tenth century show its importance and its use of income to buy land. According to Fernando Romanos, the first reference to the Aragonese dialect of Hecho is found in a 13th-century inventory of the church.

None of the Carolingian monastery's buildings remains. Only the church survives, probably rebuilt in 1083 at the height of the monastery's wealth, when the old abbey was reformed; work resumed in the next century but petered out. It is a Latin cross with a crypt under a single semicircular apse, and the dome over the crossing, which fell after a fire, was replaced by vaults. Unusually for its area and period it has no sculpture: the Chi Rho on the door's tympanum is almost its only ornament. The church was declared a National Monument in 1931 and serves today as Siresa's parish church.
monastery-of-sant-joan-de-les-abadesses: Count Wilfred the Hairy, who had already founded the monastery of Santa Maria de Ripoll for his son Radulf, intended the house for the education of his daughter Emma, who became its first abbess. The bishop of Vic consecrated the church on 24 June 887. Until 945 it was the only female monastery in the area.

In 1017, at the request of Bernard I of Besalú, a papal bull suppressed the nunnery, and Bernard brought in a community of monks, the house now falling within the bishopric of Besalú. From 1083 to 1114 it was subject to the Monastery of St. Victor of Marseille, which sent a community of nuns of Greek origin. In 1114 papal intervention gave the monastery for good to a community of Augustinian canons. Local abbots ruled it until 1484, then commendatory abbots; in 1592 it was secularised as a collegiate church, which was suppressed in 1856. It was declared a Historical Monument in 1931.

The present church dates from the 12th century. An earthquake in 1428 brought down its dome and bell tower and damaged the building, which was largely restored. It has a single nave within a wide transept that opens onto five apses; because the church stood in the middle of the monastery, the transept once gave access to both the women's and the men's parts of the house.

Its works of art include the altarpiece of the White Virgin, made in 1343 by Florentine artists, and a Pietà by Josep Viladomat in the Baroque chapel of the Pains. The carved group known as the Descension, of about 1250, is regarded as one of the outstanding examples of Romanesque sculpture in Catalonia. A small two-storey Gothic cloister of the 15th century survives, with an abbot's palace of the same century.
monastery-of-santa-maria-de-ripoll: Count Wilfred the Hairy, Guifré el Pilós in Catalan, used the monastery as a centre for resettling the region after he conquered it. His son Ridulph was educated there and later became its abbot as well as bishop of Urgell. The church was reconsecrated in 935, 977 and 1032, and the monastery's offshoots included the abbeys of St. Martin-du-Canigou and Santa Maria de Montserrat. From 1070 to 1169 it was governed by the Abbey of St. Victor of Marseille.

Ripoll remained the main religious centre of Catalonia until the 15th century, when it began to decline, losing control of Montserrat in 1402. An earthquake damaged it severely in 1428, and it was restored with new parts in Gothic style. After it was secularised, fire destroyed the library and much of the archive in 1835. The architect Elias Rogent rebuilt it from 1886, and the basilica was consecrated in 1896.

The present church, from Rogent's rebuilding, keeps features of the original, which had a nave and four aisles ending in apses. Its transept holds the tombs of the counts of Besalú and of several counts of Barcelona, from Wilfred to Ramón Berenguer IV. The cloister keeps more of the old fabric. The portal's mid-12th-century relief, in seven bands, shows God enthroned with the symbols of the Four Evangelists and the Twenty-four Elders, the stories of David and Solomon and of Moses, and beasts identified with the visions of the prophet Daniel.

The library grew from 69 volumes in 979 to 121 by 1008 and 246 by the death of Abbot Oliba in 1046, most of them copied in the monastery's own scriptorium. Oliba acquired 71 manuscripts himself and threatened thieves with excommunication. Under Abbot Arnulf many copies were made, most of them translations of Arabic works on mathematics or astronomy. The great Bibles of Oliba's time include the Roda Bible, taken to France in 1693 and now in Paris, and the Ripoll Bible, now in the Vatican Library. In the 12th century its monks copied the Gesta comitum Barcinonensium and the Carmen Campi Doctoris, the earliest literary work on El Cid.
monastery-of-the-cross: The Monastery of the Cross stands in the Valley of the Cross near the Nayot neighbourhood of Jerusalem, below the Israel Museum and the Knesset. By legend it was raised on the burial spot of Adam's head, from which grew the tree that gave its wood to the cross of Christ, although two other places in Jerusalem claim the same honour.

It is believed that the site was first consecrated in the fourth century on the instruction of Constantine the Great, who later gave it to King Mirian III of Kartli after his kingdom's conversion in 327. Archaeologists have established that a first basilica was built at the end of the fourth century, and scholars name an Iberian prince, Bakur, as its founder. Few remains of that age survive, the most important being a fragment of a mosaic.

The monastery was built in the eleventh century, in the reign of King Bagrat IV, by the Georgian monk Prochorus the Iberian. The remains of the Crusader-period monastery form a small part of the present complex, which has been largely restored and rebuilt. Under Sultan Baybars the monks were executed after being accused of spying for the Ilkhanate Mongols. In 1305 an ambassador of the King of Georgia, supported by Andronikos II, won the monastery back from Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad.

In the early 1480s Felix Fabri found Georgian monks living there with their wives, and the high altar was said to stand where the tree of the cross had grown. Burdened by debt, the Georgians sold the monastery to the Greek Orthodox Patriarch Dositheos II in 1685, and monks of the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem still occupy it. Henry Maundrell, visiting in 1697, was shown a hole under the high altar where the stump of the tree was said to have stood.

The fortified monastery has a church with ancient murals and living quarters. In a side chapel a hole in the floor marks the place where, according to tradition, the tree grew. The library holds many Georgian manuscripts, and visitors can reach a museum.

In the 1970s and 1980s Georgian inscriptions on some murals were painted over and replaced with Greek ones, and later cleaning brought the Georgian ones back to light. In June 2004 the fresco of the poet Shota Rustaveli on a column was defaced, with its face and part of its inscription scratched out, and Georgia officially complained to Israel. The monastery has also been vandalised, in February and December 2012.
moncef-bey: Muhammad VII al-Munsif was born at La Manouba on 4 March 1881, the son of Muhammad V an-Nasir, and was the penultimate ruler of the Husainid dynasty. In April 1922 he supported the nationalist Destour movement and persuaded his father, Naceur Bey, to receive its representatives. In October 1900 he married his second cousin Lalla Traki Beya, daughter of Muhammad IV al-Hadi, who bore his four children. He was invested as Bey al-Mahalla on 30 April 1942 and succeeded his first cousin once removed, Ahmed Bey, on 19 June 1942.

Though the Vichy regime gave him the Grand Cross of the Légion d'honneur, Moncef Bey sent Marshal Pétain a memorandum on 2 August 1942 reasserting Tunisian sovereignty. He asked for a consultative legislative council with a Tunisian majority, civil service posts for Tunisians, measures against poverty, compulsory schooling in Arabic and the nationalisation of key enterprises. At the Eid al-Fitr ceremonies of 12 October 1942 the Resident General, Admiral Jean-Pierre Esteva, told him that only the French were suited to positions of authority, and the Bey asked in vain for his recall.

After Axis troops arrived on 16 November 1942, he proclaimed Tunisian neutrality while secretly assuring Roosevelt that Tunisia would support the Allies, and refused an Italian offer to repudiate the Treaty of Bardo. On 1 January 1943 he named Mohamed Chenik prime minister. Known as the Protector of the Jews, he worked to keep the Vichy decrees against the Jewish community from being applied and refused to sign others, among them those imposing the yellow star and forced labour.

When the Allies took Tunis, the French colonial lobby around Henri Giraud accused him of collaborating with the Axis. On 13 May 1943 General Alphonse Juin, the acting Resident General, demanded his abdication on Giraud's orders; he refused, was removed by Giraud's decree the next day and was flown out of the country. He formally abdicated at Laghouat in southern Algeria on 8 July, was moved to Ténès and, on 17 October 1945, to Pau, where he died. He was buried with full honours in the Jellaz Cemetery in Tunis, and the Place Moncef-Bey in La Marsa was named after him on 1 September 2012.
monckton-commission: The commission's official name was the Advisory Commission for the Review of the Constitution of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland. The British government set it up under Walter Monckton, 1st Viscount Monckton of Brenchley, to make proposals for the future of the Federation, also called the Central African Federation, which joined Southern Rhodesia, Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland, the present Zimbabwe, Zambia and Malawi. It had 20 members appointed to represent six interest groups. It toured the Federation in February 1960 with limited terms of reference, and was boycotted by the opposition Labour Party and by the black nationalists of Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia.

Released in October 1960, the report found widespread and sincere opposition to the Federation in the two northern territories and concluded that it could not be kept except by force or by massive changes in racial legislation. It proposed black African majorities in the legislatures of Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia, more voting rights for black Africans, less racial discrimination and the option for these territories to leave after five years. Because the commission seemed weighted towards keeping the Federation, its report disappointed the British government.

The Federal Prime Minister, Sir Roy Welensky, called the report the death knell of federation and rejected it. Black nationalists opposed it on other grounds, since they wanted an end to federation and independence under black majority rule. The British government broadly accepted the report. Over the objections of the Governor of Nyasaland, Sir Robert Armitage, Colonial Secretary Iain Macleod released Hastings Banda from detention on 1 April 1960 and opened talks with him on Nyasaland's constitutional future.

A Federal Review Conference, provided for in the act of 1953 that created the Federation, opened in London on 5 December 1960. Banda walked out on 12 December, and the federal talks were suspended on 16 December. The conference mainly made clear the views of Banda for Nyasaland and Kaunda for Northern Rhodesia that their peoples wanted to leave the Federation, and of Joshua Nkomo that the African majority of Southern Rhodesia wanted majority rule. After the Malawi Congress Party's victory in the elections of August 1961, Nyasaland became independent as Malawi on 6 July 1964.
monemvasia: Monemvasia stands on a tied island off the east coast of the Peloponnese, connected to the mainland by a sandy isthmus about 400 metres long. An earthquake in 375 CE separated the rock from the mainland. Most of the rock is a plateau about 100 metres above the sea. The upper town stood on the plateau, with a rectangular acropolis with four towers built in the sixth century, and the lower town lies on the southern slope. There are no natural springs, so the town depended on cisterns.

The name comes from two Greek words, moni, 'single', and emvasis, 'approach', meaning the city of the single entrance. Its Italian form, Malvasia, gave its name to malmsey wine, which was not grown locally but reached Europe through the town's extensive trade, mostly from the Peloponnese and the Cyclades, especially Tinos.

Monemvasia was founded in the sixth century by settlers from Sparta, then called Lacedaemon. A later local chronicle says that the city's inhabitants fled a Slav raid in 587 to 588, but archaeology does not support this, since the first level of the church of Christ Elkomenos dates from Justinian's reign, some decades earlier. While other settlements in the Peloponnese declined from the seventh century, Monemvasia grew into a commercial and cultural centre on sea routes such as the one to Sicily.

After Mehmed II took most of the Peloponnese in 1460 and 1461, Monemvasia fell to the Venetians by the end of 1463. In the Sixth Ottoman-Venetian War Francesco Morosini failed to take it in 1687 and 1689, but Girolamo Corner entered it on 12 August 1690. In the Greek War of Independence the fortress was besieged from 15 March 1821 and surrendered to the Greeks on 23 July after four months. The war left it nearly ruined, and the census of 1828 counted only 659 inhabitants.

The upper town has been uninhabited since the second Venetian occupation, but its Byzantine church of Hagia Sophia, built on a cross-in-square plan in the style of the twelfth century, survives, with parts of frescoes. A former mosque in Elkomenos square has housed the town's archaeological collection since 1999. From the 1970s Monemvasia revived as a tourist destination, as visitors bought and restored houses, and a bridge linked it to the road network in 1971.
mong-cai: Móng Cái lies on the south bank of the Beilun River, which here forms the frontier between Vietnam and China, facing the Chinese city of Dongxing. The city covers 519.28 square kilometres and was divided into wards, among them Ka Long, Hải Hòa and Trần Phúc, and rural communes such as Vạn Ninh and Vĩnh Thực. Near it lies the Sa Vĩ cape, one of the extreme points of Vietnam's frontier, from which the Chinese mainland can easily be seen across the water, and the beach of Trà Cổ, which draws visitors from Hanoi and Haiphong.

The name comes from Yue Chinese and means the market of Mong. It reflects the settlement's character on this coast in the Middle Ages, when Nùng, Tày and above all Tanka communities lived side by side there. The town grew as a meeting point of two countries, and the languages heard in it show this: Vietnamese, Cantonese in the central market and Mandarin in the commercial quarters.

Cross-border trade brought the city prosperity. Trade passing through the Móng Cái border gate reached US$2.4 billion in 2007 and US$4.1 billion in 2008, the highest of any crossing on the frontier, and the city's tax revenue in 2008 was 150 per cent of the previous year's. In 2008 it was classified as a Class-II provincial city. It became known as the Market City for the six large markets of its centre, where goods from China were sold wholesale and to visitors, and many of its merchants came across the border from China each morning and went home in the late afternoon.

Móng Cái had 108,553 inhabitants in 2019. It remains a centre of trade with China, with a night market on a walking street in Trần Phúc close to the border, and its seafood restaurants line the city's streets.
mongke: Möngke was born on 11 January 1209, the eldest son of Genghis Khan's son Tolui and Sorghaghtani Beki. A shaman, Teb Tengri Khokhcuu, claimed to see a great future for the child in the stars and gave him the name Möngke, meaning eternal. He was raised at the camp of his uncle Ögedei Khan's queen Angqui. In 1224 Genghis Khan performed the hunting ceremony on him and his brother Kublai near the Ili River, and in 1230 he went to war for the first time, against the Jin dynasty. Tolui died in 1232.

On his mother's advice Möngke went to Batu of the Golden Horde, who backed his election. A first kurultai at Ala Qamaq approved him, though its attendance was limited and its validity was questionable, and a second, organised by Sorghaghtani and Berke, proclaimed him Great Khan on 1 July 1251. He was the first khagan from the Toluid line and drafted his own decrees, limited costly gifts to princes by turning them into salaries, taxed merchants and punished commanders whose troops plundered civilians. He also paid the merchants' drafts issued under his predecessor Güyük, and favoured officials of Muslim, Chinese and Uyghur origin. Clergy of all faiths were exempted from tax.

His conquests were aimed at East Asia and the Middle East. Goryeo was ravaged by the Mongol army, which took 206,800 captives in 1254. Kublai took the Dali Kingdom in Yunnan in 1253 to 1254 and outflanked the Song, and in 1257 Uriyangkhadai sacked Thăng Long but withdrew after a Vietnamese counter-attack. In 1252 Möngke gave his brother Hülegü the conquest of Western Asia, with the Nizari Ismailis and the Abbasid Caliphate as priorities, and the Ismaili resistance in Iran was crushed by the end of 1256. In 1254 he received the envoy William of Rubruck at Karakorum.

In October 1257 Möngke set out against the Song, leaving Ariq Böke in charge at Karakorum. He took Paoning in 1258 and was last seen at the siege of Diaoyucheng near Chongqing, where he is generally agreed to have died on 11 August 1259. Sources disagree on the cause. Chinese accounts and Bar Hebraeus say a crossbow bolt killed him, the History of Yuan a stone projectile, and Persian accounts dysentery or cholera. He was buried at Burkhan Khaldun near Genghis and Tolui.

He left no designated successor. His brothers Kublai Khan and Ariq Böke fought the four-year Toluid Civil War, and that war and the later Kaidu–Kublai war led to the permanent division of the Mongol Empire.
mongkut: Mongkut, whose name means crown, was born on 18 October 1804, the second son of Prince Itsarasunthon, who was crowned Rama II in 1809, and Princess Bunrot. In 1824 he became a Buddhist monk, as Siamese custom asked of young men, and in the same year his father died. The nobility passed him over for the older and more experienced Prince Chetsadabodin, known as Nangklao, and Mongkut stayed in the monastery. In 1835 he began a reform movement that became the Dhammayut sect.

In 1836 he became first abbot of Wat Bowonniwet, where he studied Latin, English and astronomy with missionaries and sailors and became friends with Vicar Pallegoix. In 1829 at Phetchaburi he had met the monk Buddhawangso, who followed the vinaya, the monastic discipline, strictly.

Dit Bunnag, the most powerful noble of the previous reign, and British merchants backed Mongkut, who left the monkhood and took the throne in 1851 at the age of 47. He took the name Phra Chom Klao and crowned his brother Isaret as second king, Pinklao. The Bunnag family was at its height under him. He ordered nobles to wear shirts at court, ended the practice of sending envoys to the Qing court, banned forced marriages and the sale of wives to pay debts, and released many royal concubines. He had 32 wives and 82 children. He hired missionaries to teach English to the princes and urged a European-style education. Siamese forces failed to take Kengtung in 1855 after a siege of 21 days.

John Bowring came to Siam in 1854 to negotiate a treaty. It abolished the Royal Storage, which had held the monopoly on foreign trade since Ayutthaya, and limited import tax to 3 per cent, collected once. Trade, rice growing, milling and sugar production expanded, and coinage was introduced in 1860. The treaty also gave British subjects extraterritoriality, and more treaties with other powers followed, undermining national revenue and legal rights. In 1862 the court hired Anna Leonowens, whose memoir became the source of The King and I.

Mongkut studied indigenous astrology and Western astronomy and predicted the total solar eclipse of 18 August 1868. He invited European and Siamese officials to watch it at Wakor, south of Hua Hin, and his calculations proved accurate. He and his son Prince Chulalongkorn caught malaria on the expedition, and the king died six weeks later, on 1 October 1868. Chulalongkorn, who survived, succeeded him, and in 1902 gave the Thammayut sect royal recognition, making it one of the two major Buddhist denominations of modern Thailand.
mongol-conquest-of-the-jin-dynasty: The Jurchen rulers of the Jin dynasty took tribute from some of the steppe tribes and encouraged rivalries among them. When the Mongols were united under Khabul in the 12th century, the Jin urged the Tatars against them, and the Tatars later handed Khabul's successor Ambaghai to the Jin court, where Emperor Xizong had him executed. In 1210 an embassy announced the accession of Wanyan Yongji and demanded that the Mongols submit as vassals. Genghis Khan reportedly spat on the ground and rode away, and in early 1211 he summoned a kurultai on the Kherlen River and declared war.

In 1211 the Mongols broke through the Jin wall at Wushabao and defeated the Jin field army at Yehuling, while the general Jebe took the Eastern capital, present-day Liaoyang. Campaigns in 1212 and 1213 followed. In 1214, with Zhongdu besieged, the Jin agreed to pay tribute and gave Genghis Khan Princess Qiguo in marriage, but Emperor Xuanzong then moved the capital south to Kaifeng. The Mongols returned, and Zhongdu fell on 1 June 1215. They suppressed resistance in Shanxi, Hebei and Shandong from 1217 to 1223, while the general Muqali died besieging Feng County in Shaanxi.

Under Ögedei Khan the Jin, led by Emperor Aizong, won victories at Dachangyuan in 1229, Weizhou in 1230 and Daohuigu in 1231. The Mongols then converged on Kaifeng from three sides, Tolui's force passing through Song territory, and destroyed Wanyan Heda's army in a snowstorm at Sanfengshan. Aizong fled from Kaifeng to Guide, where Pucha Guannu's fire-lance troops won a night attack, and then to Caizhou. The Southern Song allied with the Mongols, and Caizhou was besieged from both sides. When its walls were breached Aizong killed himself, and his successor, Emperor Mo, was killed within a day, on 9 February 1234.

Many Han Chinese and Khitans had gone over to the Mongols during the war. Defectors such as Shi Tianze, Zhang Rou and Yan Shi commanded tumens of 10,000 men under Ögedei and helped build the administration of the new state. The Mongols spared cities that surrendered, and ordered that physicians, craftsmen and clerics be spared and brought to them. James Waterson cautions against blaming the fall in northern China's population on slaughter alone, since many people may have moved south to the Song or died of disease and famine. The fire arrows the Jurchens used at Kaifeng in 1232 were a weapon the Mongols adopted for later conquests.
mongol-conquest-of-the-song-dynasty: At his death in 1227 Genghis Khan left a plan to strike the Jin capital by passing through Song territory, and that spring a small Mongol force ravaged five prefectures of the Song Lizhou Circuit, the first armed clash between the two. In 1233 the Song allied with the Mongols, and Song troops under Meng Gong helped destroy the Jin at Caizhou. A year later Song armies advanced as far as Kaifeng to take the old capitals, but were repelled by the Mongol garrisons under Tachir.

From 1235 Köden attacked Sichuan through the Chengdu plain. Xiangyang, the gateway to the Yangtze plain, capitulated in 1236, but Meng Gong retook it in 1239, and the governor Yu Jie fortified mountain strongholds such as Diaoyucheng and held Sichuan for ten more years. Terrain unsuited to horses, new diseases and the need for naval warfare made this one of the most difficult wars of the Mongol conquests.

The attacks intensified after Möngke became Great Khan in 1251. The Mongols conquered the Kingdom of Dali in 1253, and Uriyangkhadai took the Đại Việt capital Thang Long in January 1258 before marching north through Guangxi. Möngke entered Sichuan in 1258 with two-thirds of the Mongol strength but died near the Diaoyu Fortress on 11 August 1259, and Kublai, elected Great Khan in 1260, first had to fight his brother Ariq Böke in the Toluid Civil War.

The strongholds of the Song loyalists fell one by one, Yangzhou in 1276, Chongqing in 1277 and Hezhou in 1279, and Wen Tianxiang was captured in February 1279. The war ended at Yamen on 19 March 1279, where 1,000 Song warships, roped together in a solid mass, could neither attack, manoeuvre nor escape when the Yuan fleet of Zhang Hongfan and Li Heng closed in.

The conquest is considered the last great military achievement of the Mongol Empire: with it the Mongols ruled all of continental East Asia under the Yuan dynasty. Cities that surrendered, such as Yangzhou and Hangzhou, were spared sacking, defecting Song troops formed the Newly Submitted Army and received land, and many Tusi chiefdoms of the south-west kept their integrity as Yuan vassals. Song officers and officials fled to Vietnam and Champa, and former Song soldiers served in the army Trần Thánh Tông prepared against the second Mongol invasion.
mongol-empire: The ancestors of the Mongols are first recorded in the late tenth century, migrating from eastern Manchuria onto the Mongolian Plateau and settling south-east of Lake Baikal. In the twelfth century their khans raided the Chinese Jin dynasty, but the killing of the khans Qutula and Ambaghai in the 1160s ended this first confederation. At a kurultai, an assembly, in 1206 the shaman Teb Tenggeri proclaimed Temüjin khan of the Great Mongol Nation, and he took the title Genghis Khan. He redistributed the tribal peoples into units of tens, hundreds and thousands, which the historian Timothy May calls a social revolution.

Genghis Khan died on 18 August 1227, when the empire ruled from the Pacific to the Caspian Sea, twice the size of the Roman Empire or the Umayyad Caliphate at their height. His son Ögedei was elected in 1229. After Ögedei's death in 1241 a stalemate over the succession lasted more than four years. In 1251 a kurultai proclaimed Möngke great khan, moving power from the Ögedeid to the Toluid line. In 1260 the Mamluks defeated the Mongol force under Kitbuqa at the Battle of Ain Jalut, the western limit of Mongol advance in the Middle East.

After Möngke died in 1259, rival councils elected his brothers Ariq Böke and Kublai Khan, who fought the Toluid Civil War from 1260 to 1264. Kublai prevailed but never regained control of the Chagatayid and Ögedeid families. On 18 December 1271 he issued an edict giving his regime the dynastic name Great Yuan. By his death in 1294 the empire had split into four: the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan dynasty. The Ilkhanate disintegrated between 1335 and 1353, and the Yuan lost China in 1368, when Ming forces took Dadu.

Every adult Mongol man was a soldier, and returned to pastoralism when not called up. Most were horse-archers, taking five or six horses on campaign. Genghis Khan imposed strict discipline, with officers responsible for training and equipment, and failure was often punished by execution.

Genghis Khan set up complete religious freedom, though he was himself a shamanist, and exempted religious leaders from taxation. A relay mail system, the Yam, had stations about 40 kilometres apart, and riders regularly covered 200 kilometres a day. Trade routes formed across the empire, and the Mongols supported merchants. The Secret History of the Mongols, the oldest surviving literary work in Mongolian, was written for the royal family after 1227.
mongol-invasion-of-central-asia: After Temujin united the Mongol and Turkic tribes of the Mongolian Plateau and was proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206, his rivals the Merkit and the Naimans fled west. In late 1208 or early 1209 a Mongol force under his eldest son, Jochi, caught them on a branch of the Irtysh, where the Merkit leader Toqto'a was killed. The survivors scattered: the Merkit towards the Qangli Kipchaks, the Naiman prince Kuchlug to Qara Khitai, whose throne he usurped in 1211.

The first Mongol contacts with Central Asia were peaceful. In 1209 Barchuq Art Tegin, ruler of the Uyghur kingdom of Qocho, killed the envoys of Qara Khitai and joined the Mongols of his own will, marrying Genghis Khan's daughter Al Altun; his kingdom later sent 18,000 troops to the western campaigns. In 1211 the Karluks under Arslan Khan also submitted, and by 1218 the Mongols held all of what is now Xinjiang.

When Kuchlug attacked the Karluk city of Almaliq, Genghis Khan sent his general Jebe against him in 1216. The Mongols defeated Qara Khitai at Balasaghun, and Kuchlug was captured and killed in Badakhshan in 1218. Around the same years, most likely 1217 or 1218, Subutai, Jebe and Tuqachar destroyed the last Merkit at the Chem River.

The war with Khwarazm followed. In 1218 Genghis Khan sent a large caravan of Mongol merchants, in which much of the Mongol elite seems to have invested. Inalchuq, governor of the Khwarazmian city of Otrar, seized its goods and executed its members as spies. Whether the charge was true, and how far the Shah was involved, is debated, but the Shah refused to punish Inalchuq, killed one Mongol envoy and humiliated the other two. Genghis Khan, who held envoys to be inviolable, left only a small army to continue his war against the Jin and gathered every man he could to invade Khwarazm.

By 1221 the Mongols controlled all the lands of the former Khwarazmian Empire. The nomadic peoples they had met in Central Asia may have been part of the reason Ögedei Khan launched a western campaign in 1235. In 1236 Batu Khan, son of Jochi, broke the Kipchaks and took their lands in Central Asia, Eastern Europe and Western Siberia into his appanage, which became known as the Golden Horde.
mongol-invasion-of-europe: The operations were planned by Subutai and commanded by Batu Khan and Kadan, grandsons of Genghis Khan. The army was ethnically mixed: Mongols formed the leadership and elite cavalry, but some historians estimate that 70 to 80 percent of the soldiers were Turkic nomads such as Cumans, Bashkirs and Volga Bulgars, whom European sources called Tatars. In 1223 the Mongols had routed a Rus' army of nearly 50,000 at the Battle of the Kalka River before turning back for almost a decade.

Ögedei Khan ordered Batu to conquer Rus' in 1235. Europe was divided. The papacy had preached a crusade against Kievan Rus' in 1238, and Emperor Frederick II was excommunicated four times by Pope Gregory IX and Pope Innocent IV.

The Mongols reached Ryazan in December 1237, sacked it and stormed Suzdalia. Grand Prince Yuri was killed on the Sit River on 4 March 1238, and Vladimir, Torzhok and Kozelsk fell. They then crushed the Kipchaks and Alans, and in 1239 sacked Pereyaslavl and Chernigov. Kiev was sacked on 6 December 1240.

In Central Europe the Mongols advanced with three armies. One defeated Henry II the Pious, Duke of Silesia, and his allies at the Battle of Legnica on 9 April 1241. Another crossed the Carpathians and a third followed the Danube. They regrouped on the Sajó river and defeated King Béla IV of Hungary at the Battle of Mohi on 11 April 1241. The invasion is said to have killed half of Hungary's population. Detachments raided Meissen, Moravia and Wiener Neustadt, and Duke Frederick II of Austria's forces defeated a small Mongol squadron near Vienna. Béla had received Batu's demand for surrender in 1237 and had not replied.

In late March 1242 the Mongols began to withdraw. The most common explanation is the death of the Great Khan Ögedei on 11 December 1241, which called the princes home to elect a successor, and Giovanni da Pian del Carpine reported this reason. Stephen Pow has pointed out that a messenger would have had to cover the distance very fast in winter. Other explanations are the exhaustion of pasture on the Hungarian plain, wet weather that muddied the ground and weakened the Mongol bows, and stone fortresses such as Esztergom that made a war of attrition hard to win.

Batu retreated to the Volga and founded the Golden Horde, and the next kurultai in Mongolia was not held until 1246. Much of Eastern Europe came under the Horde's rule, and raids continued into the late 13th century. After 1241 Béla IV built stone castles and reformed his army, and when Nogai Khan and Talabuga attacked Hungary in 1285 the invasion was repelled.
mongol-invasion-of-java: Kublai Khan had sent envoys demanding tribute, and when his envoy Meng-qi reached Singhasari, King Kertanegara branded his face and cut his ears. Kublai ordered a punitive expedition in 1292, hoping also to control the sea trade routes of the archipelago. According to the History of Yuan, 20,000–30,000 men from Fujian, Jiangxi and Huguang sailed in 500–1,000 ships under Shi Bi, Yighmish and Gao Xing. Meanwhile, with Singhasari's army away in Sumatra, Jayakatwang of Kediri revolted with the help of Arya Wiraraja and killed Kertanegara. Kertanegara's son-in-law Raden Wijaya submitted to Jayakatwang and was allowed to settle the Tarik timberland, which he named Majapahit.

The fleet sailed from Quanzhou, and on 22 January 1293 Yighmish went ahead with the emperor's order. When the force landed, Wijaya offered his submission and a tribute including two princesses in return for help against Jayakatwang. The Yuan troops gathered on the Kali Mas on 22 March and beat off an attack by Kediri's army on 15 April. On 26 April they stormed Daha, where some 5,000 Kediri soldiers were killed and thousands more drowned, and that afternoon Jayakatwang surrendered.

Wijaya then returned to Majapahit, ostensibly to prepare his tribute, and asked that the Yuan escort come unarmed. On 26 May he ambushed the two hundred soldiers sent to him and attacked the main camp, cutting Shi Bi off from his army. With the monsoon winds about to end, the Yuan forces killed Jayakatwang and his son and sailed for home on 31 May. Modern estimates put their losses at 12,000–18,000 men.

On their return Shi Bi received seventy lashes and lost a third of his property, and Yighmish was reprimanded and lost a third of his, though both were later pardoned; Gao Xing was rewarded for saving the army from total disaster. The expedition was the last of Kublai's reign, and a further invasion with a 100,000-strong army was dropped after his death. The campaign may have brought the first use of gunpowder to the archipelago, and Javanese shipbuilders took up Chinese techniques such as iron nails, watertight bulkheads and a central rudder.
mongol-invasion-of-kievan-rus: In 1207 Genghis Khan sent his eldest son Jochi to subdue the tribes north of the Selenga River and in the Irtysh valley, lands that included Eastern Europe in the Jochi Ulus. In 1222 to 1224 Subutai and Jebe led a force of 30,000 through Transcaucasia and south-eastern Europe, traditionally regarded as a reconnaissance. On 31 May 1223 they defeated a united Rus' army, together with the remnants of the Cumans, at the Battle of the Kalka River, and then withdrew. A kurultai of 1235 renewed the plan, and Batu, a son of Jochi, led the army that gathered in the Caspian steppes in the autumn of 1236.

The army first conquered Volga Bulgaria, which fell by the spring of 1237, and then defeated the Cumans and Alans. In November 1237 Batu sent envoys to Yuri II of Vladimir demanding submission. Yuri sent gifts but avoided open conflict. The Mongols attacked from several directions. Ryazan fell after three days, and a chronicler records that the Mongols killed its prince and princess and many of its people. They burned Kolomna and Moscow, besieged Vladimir on 4 February 1238 and took and burned it three days later. On 4 March the army Yuri had raised was destroyed at the Battle of the Sit River.

Batu then divided his force and ransacked fourteen cities of the north-east, among them Rostov, Yaroslavl, Tver and Torzhok. Kozelsk resisted for seven weeks. Novgorod was spared by an early decision to surrender. In the winter of 1239 Batu sacked Chernigov and Pereyaslavl. His army stormed Kyiv in December 1240 after many days of siege and pillaged it, although the Cathedral of Saint Sophia survived. The Mongols then moved into Hungary and Poland and took Esztergom on Christmas Day 1241.

The siege of Kyiv is generally held to mark the end of the state of Kievan Rus', which had already been fragmenting. The principalities became part of the Jochid appanage, the Golden Horde, whose capital Sarai lay on the lower Volga. Tribute demands continued until about 1480, though a Russian army defeated the Mongols at Kulikovo in 1380. Colin McEvedy estimates that the population fell from 7.5 million to seven million, and many cities took over a century to recover.

Moscow rose under Mongol rule. After the prince of Tver led an uprising in 1327, Ivan I of Moscow joined the Mongols in crushing it and received the title of Grand Prince. Most historians hold that the invasion accelerated a fragmentation already under way.
mongol-invasion-of-the-khwarazmian-empir: The Khwarazmian dynasty had expanded from its homeland to replace the Seljuk Empire in the late 12th and early 13th centuries. Tekish declared himself a sovereign in 1189 and was accepted by the caliph as Sultan of Iran and Khorasan in 1198, and his son Muhammad II, who became Khwarazmshah in 1200, subjugated the Qarakhanids and took Bukhara. Genghis Khan had meanwhile united the Mongolic peoples. Relations were at first cordial but soured through a series of diplomatic provocations.

The size of the armies is much disputed. The Secret History of the Mongols gives 100,000 to 135,000 for the Mongols, while the later chroniclers Rashid al-Din and Juzjani give far higher figures that modern historians regard as inflated. Muhammad distrusted most of his commanders and chose to divide his troops among his main cities.

Mongol princes Chagatai and Ögedei besieged Otrar, which held out for five months before a traitor opened its gate. Genghis Khan and his youngest son Tolui took about 50,000 men across the Kyzyl Kum desert and appeared at Bukhara, which fell after a break-out force was destroyed; a fire razed most of the city, and artisans were sent to Mongolia. Genghis reached Samarkand in March 1220. He exploited the quarrel between the shah and his mother Terken Khatun, and the city’s garrison surrendered on the fifth day. The siege of Gurganj proved the hardest of the campaign.

In 1221 Tolui devastated Khorasan. At Merv the townspeople surrendered on promises of fair treatment, but the population was driven onto the plain and put to the sword, apart from a few artisans and children. Ibn al-Athir put the dead at 700,000 and Juvayni at 1,300,000. Muhammad II fled before the generals Subutai and Jebe and died destitute on an island in the Caspian Sea. His son Jalal al-Din defeated a Mongol general at Parwan but was crushed by Genghis at the Indus.

Genghis returned to the war against the Jin dynasty in 1223. Jalal al-Din tried to rebuild the Khwarazmian kingdom and retook western Iran, but he was defeated by the Rum Seljuk sultan Kayqubad I at Yassıçemen in 1230 and died near Diyarbakir in 1231. The Mongols under Chormaghun came back in 1230 and 1231 to conquer the west of the former empire. The campaign was the first in which the Mongols defeated a non-sinicised state, and it gave them a base for later attacks on Georgia and Persia and for the invasion of Rus’. The Persian lands later passed to the Ilkhanate and the northern cities to the Chagatai Khanate.
mongol-invasion-of-volga-bulgaria: The Bulgar state on the Volga and Kama was for most of its history the centre of the fur trade in Eurasia. Before the Mongols came, Russians of Novgorod and Vladimir repeatedly raided the region, weakening its economy and military power. After the Mongol generals Subutai and Jebe defeated Russian and Cuman armies at the Battle of Kalka, their army met the Bulgars on its way back and, after several sharp skirmishes, withdrew down the Volga. The only account of this clash is a short one by the Arab historian Ibn al-Athir, writing in Mosul some 1,800 km away.

In 1229 Ögedei Khan sent another army under Kukday and Bubedey, which defeated the Bulgar frontier guards at the Ural River and occupied the upper Ural valley. In 1232 Mongol cavalry subdued south-eastern Bashkiria and occupied the southern parts of Volga Bulgaria. In 1236 Batu Khan led a force numbering 25-35,000 westward. The Mongols besieged and sacked Bilär, Bolghar, Suar, Cükätaw and most other towns and castles, killing or enslaving virtually all their inhabitants. The Laurentian Chronicle records that the godless Tatars took Bolgar, killed everyone from the old to the tiniest suckling, and burned it. When the Mongols moved on against the Russian lands, the Bulgar nobility rebelled, and the Mongols returned to put it down.

According to some historians more than 80% of the population was killed. Survivors left the steppe for the forests along the Kama and further north, in what are now Chuvashia and Tatarstan, and Kazan and Çallı became new political and trade centres. Some craftsmen were moved by force to Sarai. Volga Bulgaria became part of the Ulus Jochi, later the Golden Horde, divided into duchies with varying autonomy, and its rebuilt towns became trade and craft centres of the Horde.

The Muslim Bulgars took up the Kipchak language of the Horde, and the mixing of Kipchak and Bulgar produced Old Tatar, ancestor of modern Tatar. Non-Muslim Bulgars kept a Bulgar speech influenced by Mari, from which modern Chuvash developed.
mongol-invasions-of-anatolia: After the Mongol Empire conquered Persia in 1230, with Chormaqan as its military governor, there were at first no hostilities with the Seljuk Turks. Sultan Kayqubad I and his successor Kaykhusraw II swore vassalage to the Great Khan Ögedei and paid at least a token tribute. When Ögedei died in 1241, Kaykhusraw repudiated his vassalage. Chormaqan's successor Baiju summoned him to go to Mongolia in person, give hostages and accept a Mongol darughachi; when the sultan refused, Baiju declared war, and in 1241 his army besieged and took Erzurum after its inhabitants insulted his envoy.

In 1243 Baiju returned with Georgian and Armenian warriors under Avag and Shanshe and stormed Erzurum with twelve catapults when its governor Yakut refused to surrender. Kaykhusraw gathered his forces at Konya, with help from the Empire of Trebizond, the Ayyubid sultan at Aleppo and Frankish mercenaries; his army was larger than the Mongol force. He marched some 320 kilometres to Köse Dağ, where the Mongols had arrived in June 1243. After an indecisive first stage and heavy losses he withdrew at night, and Baiju received the submission of Erzincan, Divriği and Sivas and took Kayseri after a short resistance.

At Sivas the sultan's vizier accepted terms of resubmission and a yearly tribute in gold, silk, camels and sheep, but almost half of the sultanate stayed under Mongol occupation. Trebizond submitted to the Great Khan, and Hethum I of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia made peace in 1243 and sent his brother Sembat to Karakorum in 1247. Real power in Anatolia remained with the Mongols until the fall of the Ilkhanate in 1335, and a garrison was stationed near Ankara. The Turkmen beyliks did not mint coins in their own leaders' names while under Ilkhanid suzerainty; Osman I was the first to do so, in the 1320s.
mongol-invasions-of-georgia: When the Mongols first appeared in the autumn of 1220, Georgia dominated most of the Caucasus. About 20,000 Mongols under Subutai and Jebe, pursuing Shah Muhammad II of Khwarezm, entered Armenia, then under Georgian rule, and defeated some 10,000 Georgians and Armenians under King George IV and Ivane Mkhargrdzeli at the Battle of Khunan. Returning in January 1221, they destroyed Georgia's field army at Bardav before moving north to the Kalka River. The defeat kept Georgia out of the Fifth Crusade. Jalal al-Din Mangburni of Khwarezmia then attacked, taking Tbilisi in 1226 and leaving the kingdom largely defenceless.

In 1236 the commander Chormaqan led a large army against Georgia. Most nobles of the frontier submitted or held out in their castles, and Queen Rusudan left Tbilisi for Kutaisi, leaving eastern Georgia to Atabeg Avag Mkhargrdzeli and Egarslan Bakurtsikheli, who made peace and agreed to pay tribute. Ivane I Jaqeli of Samtskhe resisted until 1238, and in 1239 Chormaqan took Ani and Kars. The Mongols did not cross the Likhi Range, so western Georgia was largely spared. Avag arranged Rusudan's submission in 1243, and Georgia paid an annual tribute of 50,000 gold pieces and supplied an army.

Georgia became part of the Vilayet of Gurjistan, ruled through its own kings. After Rusudan's death in 1245 Güyük Khan made David VII Ulu and David VI Narin co-kings in 1247. Georgian contingents fought for the Mongols at Alamut, Baghdad and Ain Jalut, and in 1256 the kingdom passed to the Ilkhanate. David Narin's rising of 1259–1260 separated Imereti in the west, while eastern Georgia bore heavy tribute and repeated punitive expeditions.

Under George V the Brilliant, with the support of Chupan, the kingdom was reunited, and almost all Mongol troops withdrew in the 1320s. Its unity was finally shattered by the invasions of Timur between 1386 and 1403.
mongol-invasions-of-india: Mongol attacks on the Indian subcontinent began in 1221, when Genghis Khan pursued the Khwarazmian prince Jalal al-Din to the Indus and sent commanders to chase him through the Lahore region and Multan. Some time after 1235 a Mongol force made Kashmir a dependency under a darughachi, and on 30 December 1241 Mongols under Munggetu sacked Lahore. Under Möngke Khan's general Sali Noyan attacked Multan and Lahore, but Hulegu refused to sanction a full invasion of the Delhi Sultanate. Sultan Ghiyas ud din Balban (r. 1266-1287) made defence against the Mongols the chief concern of his reign.

From the 1280s the Chagatai Khanate under Duwa Khan pressed into India. In the winter of 1297 the noyan Kadar ravaged the Punjab, and the army of Alauddin Khalji under Ulugh Khan defeated him at Jaran-Manjur on 6 February 1298. In late 1299 Duwa sent his son Qutlugh Khwaja against Delhi; at Kili the general Zafar Khan attacked without orders and was killed, and the Mongols withdrew. Around August 1303 they ransacked Delhi while Alauddin held out in the unfinished Siri Fort. Malik Nayak defeated them at the Battle of Amroha after December 1305, and Malik Kafur routed another army near the Ravi in 1306.

Duwa died in 1307 and the raids ceased. Alauddin's governor of Dipalpur, Malik Tughluq, then raided Kabul, Ghazni and Kandahar each year. The siege of 1303 led Alauddin to strengthen the forts along the invasion routes and to carry out economic reforms to pay for a strong army. In 1327 Tarmashirin sacked Multan and besieged Delhi, the last large invasion. Delhi's chroniclers described the conflicts between the Tengrist Mongols and the Muslim community in binary terms, though many of the sultanate's own elites were of Turkic or Mongol descent, and they gave the Mongol armies at 100,000 to 200,000 riders where they probably numbered 10,000 to 30,000.
mongol-invasions-of-japan: After a series of Mongol invasions between 1231 and 1281, the Korean kingdom of Goryeo signed a treaty favouring the Mongols and became a vassal state. Kublai Khan was declared Khagan in 1260 and made Khanbaliq, now Beijing, his capital in 1264. Japan was then ruled by the Hōjō regents of the Kamakura shogunate. Between 1266 and 1273 Mongol and Korean diplomatic missions went to Japan six times to demand submission, and the Japanese ignored every demand.

In 1274 the invasion fleet left Hoppo, now Masan, on 2 November. It landed on Tsushima two days later and attacked Iki Island on 13 November, where the governor Taira no Kagetaka made a spirited defence before killing himself with his family. The fleet landed in Hakata Bay on 19 November, and the Battle of Bun'ei followed the next day. The Japanese were unused to Mongol tactics, and the invaders advanced behind shields and threw paper and iron casing bombs that frightened the Japanese horses. By morning most Yuan ships had gone. A storm is recorded, though it is uncertain whether it struck at Hakata Bay or on the way back, and of the 30,000-strong force 13,500 did not return.

The shogunate prepared for a second attempt, building a two-metre wall around Hakata Bay in 1276. Two sets of Yuan envoys, five in 1275 and five in 1279, were beheaded. In 1281 two fleets, one from Korea and one from southern China, sailed with a reported 142,000 soldiers and sailors. The Eastern Route army attacked Tsushima on 9 June and Iki on 14 June, then landed at Hakata, but could not get past the wall. Japanese night raids in small boats harassed the fleet. On 15 August a great typhoon, the kamikaze, struck the fleet at anchor, and the Japanese killed the survivors they found, except southern Chinese, who they believed had been coerced.

Thomas Conlan argues that the force of 1281 was exaggerated by an order of magnitude; Morris Rossabi suggests about 70,000. The defeated Mongol Empire lost most of its naval power, and Korea, which had built the ships, cut down much of its timber. Japan won no new land, so the Kamakura shogunate could not reward its gokenin, and its authority declined. Later Ming discussions of invading Japan were never carried out. The invasions are an early case of gunpowder warfare outside China, and bomb shells packed with gunpowder and scrap iron have been found in a wreck off Japan. The word kamikaze, divine wind, was first used for the typhoons, and the belief that Japan would never be invaded lasted into the twentieth century.
mongol-invasions-of-the-levant: The Mongol expansion rested on the idea that the eternal sky had destined the Great Khan to rule the world. The Ilkhanate was founded by Hulagu, a son of Tolui and loyal to his brother Kublai, while the Golden Horde under Berke disputed his conquests south of the Caucasus. In 1261 Berke allied with the Mamluk Sultan Baibars against the Ilkhanate, and Golden Horde attacks in the north repeatedly forced the Ilkhanate to recall troops from Syria within months. The Mongols of the Ilkhanate sought an alliance with the Franks of Europe without success.

A first raid under Yisaur in 1244 reached Hailan near Aleppo, whose ruler agreed to pay tribute, and in 1251 An-Nasir Yusuf made Syria a vassal of the Mongol Empire. After sacking Baghdad in 1258, Hulagu's army, joined by the Georgians, the army of Cilician Armenia under Hethum I and the Franks of Bohemond VI of Antioch, took Aleppo in January 1260, and Kitbuqa took Damascus on 1 March. When Möngke's death called Hulagu away, about 10,000 horsemen remained; the Mamluks defeated them at Ain Jalut in September 1260 and executed Kitbuqa.

Samagar took Aleppo in October 1271 but retreated before Baibars, and Abaqa Khan's army of 40,000 was beaten at the Second Battle of Homs in October 1281. In December 1299 Ghazan routed the Mamluks at the Battle of Wadi al-Khazandar and took Damascus, though not its citadel, but withdrew in February 1300, perhaps because the Chagatai Mongols threatened his eastern border or for want of grazing, which the Mamluks denied him by burning pastures. His next invasion ended in defeat at Marj al-Saffar in April 1303, and Öljaitü's siege of al-Rahba in 1312 failed after about a month.

As the Ilkhanate turned to Islam, peace became possible, and under Abu Sa'id, advised by Chupan, a treaty with the Mamluks was ratified in 1322/1323. The invasions brought upheaval and migration. Bar Hebraeus wrote that the entire population of northern Syria fled to Aleppo in 1259, and the pro-Mongol historian Rashīd al-Dīn that whole provinces were killed or fled. Harran, al-Ruha, Saruj and Raqqa were left abandoned, and many towns stayed empty for centuries. With Baghdad and Syria lost, the centre of Islamic power passed to the Mamluks in Cairo.
mongolia: Mongolia is a landlocked country between Russia to the north and China to the south, with an area of 1,564,116 square kilometres. Its landscape is grassy steppe, mountains in the north and west, and the Gobi Desert in the south, and the whole country is part of the Mongolian Plateau. The highest point is Khüiten Peak, at 4,374 metres. The climate is high, cold and windy, with long winters, and Ulaanbaatar is the world's coldest capital city. The country is subject to harsh conditions known as zud, in which large numbers of livestock die from starvation or freezing.

The Khoit Tsenkher Cave holds paintings dated to 20,000 years ago, and Neolithic agricultural settlements from about 5500 to 3500 BCE predate horse-riding nomadism, which became the dominant culture. The territory was ruled by nomadic empires, among them the Xiongnu, the Xianbei, the Rouran Khaganate, the First Turkic Khaganate, the Second Turkic Khaganate and the Uyghur Khaganate. In 1206 Genghis Khan founded the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous land empire in history. His grandson Kublai Khan conquered China proper and established the Yuan dynasty. After the Yuan collapsed, the Mongols retreated to Mongolia and resumed factional conflict, except in the era of Dayan Khan and Tumen Zasagt Khan.

Tibetan Buddhism spread to Mongolia in the 16th century, and by the early 20th century almost one-third of adult men were Buddhist monks. The Qing dynasty absorbed the country in the 17th century. Mongolia declared independence after the Qing collapsed in 1911 and achieved actual independence from the Republic of China in 1921, shortly after which it became a satellite state of the Soviet Union. The Mongolian People's Republic was founded as a socialist state in 1924.

After the anti-communist revolutions of 1989, Mongolia carried out its own peaceful democratic revolution in 1990, which led to a multi-party system, a new constitution in 1992 and a market economy. It is a semi-presidential democratic republic with a unicameral legislature, the State Great Khural, of 126 seats. The 2024 population was 3,544,835, and roughly half live in Ulaanbaatar.
About 30 per cent of the population is nomadic or semi-nomadic, and horse culture remains integral. Mahayana Buddhism is the majority religion, at 51.7 per cent. The traditional dwelling is the ger.
mongolian-peoples-party: In 1911 Outer Mongolia declared its independence from the Qing dynasty, but the independence of the Bogd Khanate was not recognised by its two neighbours, Russia and China. In 1919 the Chinese Beiyang government invaded Mongolia. During the occupation two underground resistance groups formed, the Consular Hill and the East Khuree. Their members included Dogsomyn Bodoo, Khorloogiin Choibalsan, Soliin Danzan and Damdiny Sükhbaatar, and together they became known as the First Seven. On 25 June 1920 the two groups united as the Mongolian People's Party and sent Danzan and Choibalsan to the Soviet Union, where they met Soviet representatives in Irkutsk in August.

On 18 March 1921 the Mongolian People's Militia under Sükhbaatar defeated Chinese forces and took Kyakhta. In May the White Russian Baron Ungern was defeated by joint Mongolian and Red Army forces, the revolutionaries entered the capital on 6 July, and independence was declared on 11 July. The party became the sole ruling party of the Mongolian People's Republic and, on the Communist International's advice, took the name Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party.

From 1928 politics turned sharply left. Herds were forcibly collectivised, and over seven million head of livestock died, leading to an uprising in 1932 that Mongolian and Soviet forces quelled. The purges began with the Lkhümbe Affair of 1933, and in a second wave from 1937 to 1939 officials arrested 25,437 people and executed 20,099, while the actual number of victims is estimated at over 35,000 to 100,000. Over 18,000 were lamas, and the Buddhist clergy was virtually destroyed.

The party followed Lenin's principle of democratic centralism. The Party Congress met every fifth year, the Central Committee met usually once a year, and most duties lay with the Politburo and its Standing Committee. After pro-democracy demonstrations began on 10 December 1989 and a hunger strike in Sükhbaatar Square on 7 March 1990, the party leader Jambyn Batmönkh dissolved the politburo and resigned on 9 March 1990.

In the first multi-party election in 1990 the party won 357 of 430 seats in the People's Great Khural, but it lost the 1996 parliamentary election. In 2010 members voted to restore the name Mongolian People's Party, with 99.3 percent of delegates to the 26th Party Congress approving, and the party moved from democratic socialism to social democracy. A faction led by Nambaryn Enkhbayar formed a new party under the old name, and the two parties reunited in 2021. The party returned to power in 2016 and kept its majority in the 2020 and 2024 elections.
mongoose-gang: The name goes back to the 1950s, when health officials in Grenada paid people who brought in mongoose tails to rid the island of the animal as a pest. Eric Gairy, then a member of the Legislative Council of the Colony of Grenada, found jobs on the eradication project for a number of men and women, and those who did the work became known as the mongoose gang. The name later passed to gangs of political thugs.

Officially the gang's members were Special Reserve Police or Volunteer Constables of the government of Gairy and his Grenada United Labour Party. They wore no distinctive dress, and a report of 1974 describes them as generally carrying thick pieces of wood and sometimes rifles. British MI5 reports called the gang ruthless and undisciplined, many of its men having criminal records. It silenced critics, broke up demonstrations and murdered opponents, among them Rupert Bishop, the father of Maurice Bishop, in January 1974; Maurice Bishop himself had been beaten and jailed in November 1973.

The violence of the gang and the police did more than the economy to stir unrest. In the general election of 1976, which international observers branded fraudulent, the gang threatened the opposition People's Alliance, and in 1977 it was used against protesters during the General Assembly of the Organization of American States, held in Grenada.

In 1979 a rumour spread that Gairy meant to use the gang to eliminate the leaders of the New JEWEL Movement while he was abroad, and Bishop overthrew him in March while he was visiting the United States. The gang then ceased to operate. Its leader, Mosyln Bishop, a taxi driver, was sentenced that year to fourteen years in prison for attempting to murder three people in November 1973. In a 1984 interview Gairy denied employing thugs or a secret police. The gang has often been compared to the Tonton Macoute of Haiti.
monks-mound: Monks Mound is a platform mound of the Mississippian culture at the Cahokia Mounds World Heritage Site near Collinsville, Illinois. Measured in 1988, it was about 291 metres long including the ramp at its southern end and 236 metres wide, close in base area to the Great Pyramid of Giza. It was raised almost entirely from layers of soil and clay carried in baskets, with bulwarks of clay and of sods from the Mississippi flood-plain that allowed steeper slopes. Botanical remains suggest it may have been built in a few decades rather than over centuries.

The first plan seems to have been a much smaller mound, now buried inside the northern end. Its flat top held rainwater, and slumping, the sliding of large sections of its sides, was a problem even during construction. The lower terrace at the south end was the last part added, some time before 1200, perhaps partly to check the slumping.

On a raised area at the north end of the summit stood a building over 30 metres long, the largest in the Cahokia urban zone. Several large ceremonial buildings on the southwest corner burned around 1150. Massive slumping from about 1200 lowered the western half of the summit and brought down the west end of the great building. Afterwards wooden buildings went up on the south terrace and rubbish was dumped at the foot. By about 1300 Cahokia was in serious decline. In 1735 French missionaries built a chapel on the south terrace, and the French Trappist monks who settled nearby from 1809 to 1813 grew wheat and garden produce on its terraces.

Henry Brackenridge published the first detailed description of the mound and gave it its name. Thomas I. Ramey, who bought the site in 1864, encouraged excavation. In the 1960s and 1970s Nelson Reed's cores traced its building stages, and his backhoe work revealed the outline of the summit building, though archaeologists objected that it destroyed centuries of stratification. After drying in the 1950s new slumps began about 1956, and in 2007 the eastern slump was dug out and rebuilt.
monkwearmouth-jarrow-abbey: Benedict Biscop founded St Peter's at Monkwearmouth, on the River Wear, on land given by King Ecgfrith of Northumbria. He meant it as a model monastery that would bring Roman practice to a region shaped by the Celtic Christianity of the missionaries of Melrose and Iona, and a papal letter of 678 exempted it from outside control. The king, pleased with its success, gave land at Jarrow on the River Tyne for St Paul's, and Ceolfrith led monks there, the young Bede among them. Benedict persuaded John, arch-cantor of St Peter's Basilica in Rome, to teach plainsong, and ruled that the two houses, 11 km apart, were to be one monastery in two places.

Under Abbot Ceolfrith the abbey became a centre of scholarship and book production with a house style of half-uncial script, and when he died in 716 its two houses had 600 monks. He had three pandect Bibles made; the one meant for the Pope survives as the Codex Amiatinus in Florence, the oldest surviving Vulgate Bible. The popularity of Bede's writings, above all the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, led to a faster insular minuscule script.

Vikings raided the abbey in 794, Danes destroyed it about 860 and it was abandoned in the late 9th century. In the early 1070s Aldwin, prior of Winchcombe Abbey, began to rebuild Jarrow with monks from Evesham Abbey, but they were recalled to Durham in 1083. Early in the 14th century both houses were refounded as cells of Durham, each with one or two monks, and in 1536 they were dissolved.

The two abbey churches survive as the parish churches of Monkwearmouth and Jarrow. St Peter's tower was built in stages from the 7th to the 10th century, and Rosemary Cramp's excavations of 1963 to 1978 found early Anglo-Saxon buildings and glass. At St Paul's the Anglo-Saxon chancel survives beside the ruins, and Jarrow Hall nearby holds a museum of Bede's age with a replica Anglo-Saxon farm. A bid for World Heritage status was later withdrawn.
monmouthshire: The centre of the county is the plain of Gwent, formed by the basin of the River Usk, with hilly land to the west. In the east the border with England largely follows the River Wye and its tributary the River Monnow, and the Wye Valley is a designated Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. The southern border is the Severn Estuary. The Gwent Levels along it are an almost entirely man-made landscape, reclaimed from the sea since Roman times and long vulnerable to flooding: the Bristol Channel floods of 1607 drowned some 2,000 people, many on this coast.

Remains from the Mesolithic period have been found across the county. In the Iron Age south-east Wales was held by the Silures, whom Tacitus called exceptionally stubborn. After the Roman conquest of Britain began in 43 CE they resisted under Caratacus, who was defeated in 50 CE, but the whole of south-east Wales was not subdued until about 75 CE. The ruins of Venta Silurum at Caerwent mark Roman rule. After the Romans left, the Kingdom of Gwent arose, with Caerwent as its capital.

From the late 1060s the Norman invasion destroyed the kingdom and replaced it with five Marcher lordships, based at Striguil (Chepstow), Monmouth, Abergavenny, Usk and Caerleon. Their castles began as earth and timber and were later built in stone, Chepstow's being begun by William FitzOsbern as early as 1067. The county's status was long disputed. A Laws in Wales Act formed the county from the Marches, but a later act of 1542 listed the counties of Wales and omitted Monmouthshire, which began a centuries-long dispute over whether it was Welsh or English.

The Local Government Act 1972 took effect in April 1974, abolished the historic county and created Gwent, confirming the area as part of Wales. The present county of Monmouthshire was re-created on 1 April 1996 with only the eastern three-fifths of the historic area. Its largest town is Abergavenny and its administrative centre is Usk. It has a fine collection of castles, among them Chepstow and Raglan, and Tintern Abbey became a focus of the Wye Tour in the late eighteenth century.
monnet-plan: France came out of World War II badly weakened. Its economy had stagnated even before the war, and by 1945 national income in real terms was little more than half that of 1929. Productivity per worker was a third of the U.S. level, chiefly because of low investment: France had one tractor for every 200 people on the land, the U.S. one for every 43. The plan, officially the Modernization and Re-equipment Plan, set out to raise investment and to change habits of thought along with machinery.

Charles de Gaulle, as chairman of the Provisional Government, set up the General Planning Commission on 3 January 1946, with Jean Monnet at its head. Monnet insisted that it be attached to the prime minister's office rather than an economic ministry. Its staff never exceeded thirty-five senior officials, but more than a thousand people from firms, unions and the civil service served on its eighteen Modernization Commissions. The plan set targets for 1950 in six basic sectors: coal, steel, electricity, rail transport, cement and farm machinery. It had no means of enforcement, but coal, electricity and rail were already nationalised and steel received state capital on condition of mergers.

In March 1946 a French delegation went to Washington, and on 28 May an agreement brought about $1 billion of new funding and the prospect of a $500 million loan from the World Bank, less than the $3 billion requested. The plan went to the government on 27 November 1946. After the harsh year of 1947 the Marshall Plan began in April 1948, and the Monnet Plan was extended to 1952 to match it. Just under $3 billion of French aid went to the plan's aims, through counterpart funds that supplied between 50 and 90 percent of its resources in 1949 and 1950.

Not every target was met, but Yergin and Stanislaw credit the plan with giving discipline and direction to France at a crucial time, and it set the country on the road to its economic growth of the 1950s. Its expected reliance on German coal led to the Schuman Plan of 9 May 1950 and so to the European Coal and Steel Community. The Planning Commission went on producing multi-year plans until 2006.
mono-river: The Mono River is the major river of eastern Togo. It is about 400 km long and drains a basin of about 20,000 square kilometres. It rises between the town of Sokodé and the border with Benin and flows south. Along its southern portion towards the mouth it forms the international boundary between Togo and Benin.

The river drains into the Bight of Benin through an extensive system of brackish water lagoons and lakes, including Lake Togo. Only the part nearest the mouth is navigable. About 35 km from the mouth there are six series of rapids. Below them the river runs slowly over a swampy floodplain, and a large area of contiguous wetland lies in both Togo and Benin. The wetland has a rich growth of reeds, sedges and grasses, and manatees, crocodiles and hippopotamuses occur in the river. Most of the basin on the upper tableland is cultivated for maize, yams, rice, cotton and cassava.

The Nangbeto Dam, a partnership between Benin and Togo, was completed in 1987, 160 km from the river's mouth. Studies have reported economic benefits, including tourism and fishing on the lake behind it. Its construction displaced between 7,600 and 10,000 people, and studies indicate that it substantially changed the ecology of the lagoon system at the mouth by reducing the natural seasonal fluctuations in the river's flow.

A second project, the Adjarala Dam, was proposed for the stretch between Nangbeto and the mouth during the 1990s but received no financing until 2017, when the China-Africa Development Fund agreed to support it. Its construction was part of a plan to raise Benin's domestic power generation capacity from 20 to 70 percent, since most of the electricity used in Togo and Benin was then imported from the Akosombo Dam in Ghana.
monothelitism: Monothelitism grew out of earlier disputes over the nature of Christ. The Council of Chalcedon defined Christ as having two natures in one hypostasis, while the non-Chalcedonians held that he had one nature. Since one nature seemed to imply one will, Eastern Roman rulers in the seventh century hoped a doctrine of one will would unite the quarrelling parties. Many provinces later lost to the Umayyad Caliphate were non-Chalcedonian: in Egypt about 30,000 Chalcedonian Greeks faced some five million Coptic non-Chalcedonians.

The first attempt was monoenergism, the teaching of one energy. Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople promoted it with Emperor Heraclius, who by 622 had written of Christ's single energy. By 630 three of the five patriarchates taught one theandric energy. A monk named Sophronius opposed it, became Patriarch of Jerusalem in 634 and attacked it as a disguised form of monophysitism. Support faded and Sergius and Heraclius dropped it.

Sergius then devised a new formula, which Heraclius issued as the Ecthesis in 638. It banned talk of one or two energies and declared that Christ had two natures but a single will, which could never oppose the divine will. The eastern patriarchs accepted it, but Pope Severinus and Pope John IV rejected it, producing a schism between Rome and Constantinople. Heraclius, old and ill, said on his deathbed that Sergius had pressured him into approving it.

Maximus the Confessor led the opposition in Africa. Constans II, who succeeded Heraclius, issued the Type of Constans, which forbade any discussion of one or two wills. Pope Martin I, at the Lateran Council of 649, condemned both the Ecthesis and the Type. The exarch Theodore I Calliopas seized Martin and took him to Constantinople, where he was imprisoned, tortured and banished to Chersonesus, where he soon died. Maximus lost his tongue and right hand.

After Constans died in 668, his son Constantine IV left the question to a church council. Pope Agatho held a synod at Rome in 680, and synods in the West condemned the doctrine. The Third Council of Constantinople, meeting in 680 and 681, condemned monothelitism and affirmed that Christ had two natural wills and two natural energies. It also anathematised Pope Honorius I, a point later debated in discussions of papal infallibility; Leo II's letter read the censure as aimed at his silence rather than at error of belief. The Oriental Orthodox deny that they ever held the doctrine.
monpazier: Monpazier, in Occitan Montpasièr, is a commune in the Dordogne department in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, in south-west France, 40 kilometres from Bergerac Airport. It belongs to the association Les Plus Beaux Villages de France, and in 2019 it received the designation Ville et Métiers d'Art because of the many artisans working in the village. From 1790 to 2015 it was the capital of the canton of Monpazier. Its inhabitants are called Monpaziérois in French.

Monpazier is a 13th-century bastide town founded by King Edward I of England. It was created by an act of paréage: the lord of Biron supplied the land and Edward the authority and permission, and any profits from taxes or commercial activity were split between the two. Like other bastides it was laid out on a grid pattern, with a square at its centre, one end of which contains an open market hall. It is one of the best preserved of its kind and keeps many original features.

The parish church of St. Dominique was built between the 13th and 16th centuries in a rectangular plot that adjoins a corner of the marketplace. Its apse was added in the fifteenth century and its choir is believed to have been completed in 1506.

The bastide draws visitors, among them guests of the four-star Hôtel Edward Premier, named after its founder. In summer the town holds a cycle race around the bastide, usually at the start of August, a medieval day, a kermesse and several specialist markets. Each July the Chorale of Monpazier gives a concert in the church. The actor Julien Guiomar (1928-2010) spent his last years in Monpazier.
monreale-cathedral: According to a legend, William II of Sicily fell asleep under a carob tree while hunting near Monreale, and the Virgin appeared to him in a dream and told him to build a church where he lay; a treasure of gold coins found among the roots was said to have paid for the work. It is thought more likely that the church belonged to a plan of large buildings in competition with Walter Ophamil, the bishop of Palermo, who had ordered the large cathedral of Palermo. Pope Alexander III approved the construction with a bull on 30 December 1174. The work, including an attached abbey, was finished only in 1267, when the church was consecrated in the presence of Pope Clement IV.

The church is 102 metres long and 40 metres wide. Its plan follows models of Clunian origin from northern France, and its façade is flanked by two towers, as at Cefalù Cathedral. The wide basilican nave has narrow aisles and is carried on columns of grey oriental granite, with one of cipolin marble, supporting eight pointed arches on each side. The main interior feature is the glass mosaic, 6,500 square metres in Byzantine style, executed between the late 12th and the mid-13th centuries by local and Venetian masters. Bronze doors by Barisano da Trani date from 1179.

The cloister, completed about 1200, covers about 2,200 square metres and has pointed arches carried on 216 white marble columns in pairs, alternately plain and decorated with bands of glass tesserae. Each marble capital is carved with foliage, biblical scenes or allegories, and no two are the same. The church holds the porphyry sarcophagus of William I and the tombs of Margaret of Navarre and her two sons. A fire in 1811 damaged some of the mosaics, which were restored a few years later, and a Renaissance portico by Giovanni Domenico and Fazio Gagini was added between 1547 and 1569.
monrovia: Monrovia lies along the Cape Mesurado peninsula, between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mesurado River, whose mouth forms a large natural harbour. The Saint Paul River lies directly north of the city and forms the northern boundary of Bushrod Island. The historic downtown, centred on Broad Street, is at the very end of the peninsula, and the market district of Waterside faces the harbour. The harbour was significantly expanded by United States forces during the Second World War.

Before 1816 the area around Cape Mesurado was called Ducor, a long-established crossroads of trade inhabited by fishing, trading and farming communities including the Dey, Kru, Bassa, Gola and Vai. The French cartographer and slave trader Chevalier des Marchais visited it in 1723. The American Colonization Society's representatives negotiated the purchase of land at Cape Mesurado from local leaders in December 1821, an agreement valued at about $300 in trade goods whose circumstances historians continue to debate.

On 7 January 1822 a ship took African American settlers to Dazoe Island, now Providence Island, and they went ashore at Cape Mesurado and founded Christopolis. In 1824 it was renamed Monrovia after President James Monroe, a supporter of the Society. A constitutional convention met there in 1845, and its document was adopted two years later as the constitution of the independent Republic of Liberia. At the start of the 20th century 2,500 of Monrovia's 4,000 residents were Americo-Liberian, living in houses reminiscent of the southern United States, while Krutown was inhabited mainly by Kru. By 1937 the population had grown to 10,000.

Monrovia is the capital and largest city of Liberia and the seat of its government, and the Freeport of Monrovia is the country's main port. Its name is one of only two world capitals taken from an American president, the other being Washington, D.C. The 2022 census counted 1,761,032 residents in the city. Capitol Hill holds the Temple of Justice and the Executive Mansion.
monsoon: The English word monsoon came from Portuguese monção, ultimately from Arabic mawsim, 'season', although partly by way of early modern Dutch monson; its etymology is not wholly certain. It was first used in English in British India and neighbouring countries for the big seasonal winds that blew from the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea in the southwest and brought heavy rainfall.
