There are also numerous Tiwanaku sites, and the area was an important colonial centre for the Tiwanaku state. It is the only area of Peru with both Wari and Tiwanaku ruins. The Chiribaya culture flourished in the Moquegua area and near the Pacific coast from about 1000 until 1360.

According to Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, the Inca emperor Mayta Cápac organised the military expedition that took Inca rule to the shore of the Pacific. The Inca overcame the peoples of the region in the 15th century, and in the next century the Spanish conquered them. The Spanish founded the city as Villa de Santa Catalina de Guadalcázar del Valle de Moquegua. Nothing definite is known of the year, but tradition holds that Pedro Cansino and his wife Josefina de Bilbao founded it on 25 November 1541.

Moquegua is the capital of the Department of Moquegua, of Mariscal Nieto Province and of Moquegua District, and lies 1,144 kilometres south of Lima. Its economy rests largely on mining, with copper, silver, gold and molybdenum; the Cuajone mine and part of the Toquepala mine are in the province, and a copper smelter and refinery in Ilo province treat their concentrates. The Pan-American Highway passes through the city. Its Plaza de Armas, said to have been designed in the 19th century by Gustave Eiffel, holds the José Carlos Mariátegui Museum and the Contisuyo Museum.
morant-bay-rebellion: Slavery in Jamaica was abolished on 1 August 1834, and the apprenticeship that followed ended by 1 August 1838. The freed population gained the vote, but a poll tax kept most of them from using it: in the election of 1864 fewer than 2,000 black men could vote in a population of more than 436,000. Floods in 1864, cholera and smallpox, a two-year drought and bankruptcies in the sugar industry deepened poverty, and rumours spread that the planters meant to restore slavery.

A letter of 1865 from Edward Underhill of the Baptist Missionary Society on the island's distress led to Underhill Meetings across Jamaica. In August 1865 Paul Bogle led a deputation on an 87-kilometre march to Spanish Town, but Governor Edward John Eyre refused to receive it.

On 7 October 1865 a fight broke out at the courthouse during the trial of a man charged with trespassing on an abandoned plantation, and warrants were issued for several men, Bogle among them. On 11 October Bogle marched on Morant Bay with hundreds of followers. The volunteer militia fired on the crowd, which burned the courthouse and nearby buildings, and more than 25 people died. Eyre declared martial law and sent troops under Brigadier-General Alexander Nelson, who met no organised resistance but killed indiscriminately; the historian Gad Heuman has called it a reign of terror. More than 600 men and women were flogged and thousands of homes burned.

George William Gordon, a member of the House of Assembly whom Eyre blamed for the rising, was arrested in Kingston, where martial law did not apply, tried at Morant Bay and hanged on 23 October, and Bogle on 25 October with fourteen others. In Britain the Jamaica Committee, whose members included John Bright and Charles Darwin, sought to have Eyre tried for murder, while Thomas Carlyle, John Ruskin and Charles Dickens supported him; a grand jury declined to indict him. Eyre was replaced by John Peter Grant in 1866, and the Assembly renounced its charter, ending two centuries of elected representation. In 1969 Bogle and Gordon were named National Heroes of Jamaica.
morava-river: The Morava rises on the slope of the Králický Sněžník mountain at an elevation of 1,371 m, close to the border with Poland. Its total length is 352 km, of which 269.4 km lie in the Czech Republic, and it carries an average of 110 cubic metres of water a second from a drainage area of 26,658 square kilometres. It is a lowland river and, unusually for Europe, a blackwater river. Its valley forms the Upper Morava Valley and the Lower Morava Valley in Moravia, the Marchfeld in Lower Austria and the Záhorie Lowland in Slovakia, which together make up a large part of the Vienna Basin.

Olomouc, Kroměříž, Otrokovice, Uherské Hradiště, Veselí nad Moravou and Hodonín stand on the river, and Brno lies within its basin. The Thaya, its longest tributary, joins it at the tripoint of the Czech Republic, Austria and Slovakia. The river enters the Danube just below Devín Castle on the outskirts of Bratislava.

The root of the name, mor-, comes from a Proto-Indo-European word for water or marsh. The river was first recorded as Maraha in a deed of 892, while the oldest record of the land of Moravia, from 822, is older than that of the river. The German name March derives from the Slavic one.

People have lived on the banks for a very long time: Stillfried, on the Austrian side, had a settlement 30,000 years ago, and farming began in the valley about 7,000 years ago. Below the confluence with the Thaya the river is one of the oldest national boundaries still in use in continental Europe. Around 800 it was the eastern boundary of the Carolingian Empire with the Avar Khaganate, and from the 10th century it divided the imperial marcha orientalis, later the Duchy of Austria, from the Kingdom of Hungary. In the Cold War it formed part of the Iron Curtain between Austria and Czechoslovakia.

The river links the Danube valley with the plains of northern Europe. Its gentle slope makes it meander and flood, and its floodplains are among the most biologically diverse in Europe, with some 12,000 species recorded. Much of the river, especially downstream from Litovel, was regulated in the 20th century, with the loss of floodplain. The central part has kept much of its natural character.
moravia: Moravia is one of the three historical Czech lands, with Bohemia and Czech Silesia, and takes its name from the Morava river. Its largest city and historical capital is Brno. Olomouc served as the capital until the Swedish army sacked it in the Thirty Years' War, and it is still the seat of an archdiocese. The depression between the Bohemian Massif and the Outer Western Carpathians gives an easy link between the Danubian and Polish regions, in a Central Europe where highlands otherwise make north-south movement difficult.

Human presence goes back more than 600,000 years at Stránská skála, and the Venus of Dolní Věstonice is the oldest ceramic figure in the world. Around 60 BCE the Celtic Volcae withdrew and were succeeded by the Germanic Quadi. Slavs established themselves in the 6th century, and a Moravian Principality became Great Moravia in 833 through the conquest of the Principality of Nitra. Rastislav, who ruled from 846 to 870, asked the Byzantine emperor Michael for missionaries, and the result was the mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius, who translated liturgical books into Slavonic. Great Moravia reached its largest extent in the 890s under Svatopluk I and ended when the Magyars overran it in 907.

After 955 Boleslaus I of Bohemia took control of Moravia, and in 1055 Bretislaus decreed that Bohemia and Moravia would be inherited together. From 1526 Ferdinand I of Austria ruled it as part of the Crown of Bohemia, and tension grew between the Habsburg rulers and the Protestant Moravian nobility. After 1918 it belonged to Czechoslovakia, and in 1928 it was merged with Czech Silesia. The Munich Agreement of 1938 gave German-speaking border areas to Nazi Germany, and Moravia as a land was dissolved in 1948.

Moravia lies in the east of the Czech Republic and has about 3.0 million of its inhabitants. It holds 94 per cent of the country's vineyards. Until the expulsions after 1945, significant parts of Moravia were German-speaking.
moravian-church: The Moravian Church traces its heritage to 1457 and the Lands of the Bohemian Crown, which included Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia. Its roots lie in the Hussite movement begun by Jan Hus in early 15th-century Bohemia. Hus objected to some practices and doctrines of the Roman Catholic Church: he wanted the liturgy in Czech, priests allowed to marry, and indulgences and the idea of Purgatory done away with. Because these actions predate the Protestant Reformation by a century, some historians claim the Moravian Church was the first Protestant church.

Under the Habsburg rulers the Counter-Reformation pressed on the Protestants of the Bohemian lands. The Jesuits were invited to found Roman Catholic schools, among them the university in the Moravian capital of Olomouc, and in 1582 they forced the closure of local Protestant schools.

In 1722 a small group of the Bohemian Brethren, called the Hidden Seed, arrived at the Berthelsdorf estate of Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf in present-day Saxony. They had lived in northern Moravia for nearly a hundred years as an illegal underground remnant in the Catholic setting of the Habsburg Empire. Their leader, the itinerant carpenter Christian David, asked that they be allowed to settle on Zinzendorf's lands in Upper Lusatia. Zinzendorf, a nobleman raised in the traditions of Pietistic Lutheranism, agreed out of a personal commitment to helping the poor and needy. The community they founded was Herrnhut, which gave the church its German name, Herrnhuter Brüdergemeine.

The church soon became a missionary movement. Together with the Royal Danish Mission College, its missionaries formed the first large-scale Protestant missionary effort, and the first were sent out when Herrnhut had only 300 inhabitants. Within thirty years hundreds had gone to the Caribbean, North and South America, the Arctic, Africa and the Far East. The Moravians were the first to send lay people as missionaries and the first Protestant denomination to minister to slaves, though some of their communities also owned slaves.

The church teaches the necessity of the New Birth, a personal conversion to Christ, together with piety, evangelism and good works. Its emblem is the Lamb of God with the flag of victory, and its motto runs: In essentials, unity; in nonessentials, liberty; and in all things, love. Bishops serve as spiritual leaders rather than administrators, and the church holds that it has preserved apostolic succession.
morbihan: Morbihan is one of the original 83 departments created on 4 March 1790 during the French Revolution. It was formed from part of the Province of Brittany and takes its name from the Morbihan, the enclosed 'small sea' in Breton that is the principal feature of its coastline. The Carnac stones, the megalithic alignments of Carnac, stand in the department and are noted as older and more extensive than Stonehenge in Wiltshire.

In 1945 cadets of the École Spéciale Militaire de Saint-Cyr, France's foremost military academy for officers, were relocated to Camp Coëtquidan at Guer. The camp was later developed to include the École militaire interarmes, for non-commissioned officers, and the École Militaire du Corps Technique et Administratif, so that three major military educational facilities now stand at Guer.

The department lies in the northwest of France and is bounded by Finistère, Côtes-d'Armor, Ille-et-Vilaine and Loire-Atlantique, with the Atlantic Ocean to the southwest. The Gulf of Morbihan holds many islands, 365 according to legend, though in fact there are between 30 and 40 depending on how they are counted, as well as islets too small for any development. All but two of them, l'Île-aux-Moines and l'Île-d'Arz, are privately owned.

Outside the gulf the department has four further inhabited islands: Belle Île, Groix, Houat and Hoëdic. Meaban, just outside the Port du Crouesty, is an ornithological reserve that visitors may not enter. The most populous commune is Lorient, and the prefecture, Vannes, is the second.

Many residents support the maintenance and use of the Breton language, and there are numerous advocates of bilingual education. The painter Raymond Wintz (1884–1956) depicted places around the Gulf of Morbihan.
mordvins: Mordvins is the official term used in Russia and the Soviet Union since 1928 for both the Erzya and the Moksha. The Mordvins do not use it as a self-designation, and when they speak of themselves as a whole they say Erzya and Moksha. The name is thought to come from an Iranian word, mard, meaning man. Possible early mentions include the Mordens in Jordanes' Getica and a land called Mordia in the De Administrando Imperio of Constantine VII, and the Russian Primary Chronicle names the Mordva in the 11th century.

Researchers distinguish the ancestors of the Erzya and the Moksha from the mid-1st century CE by the orientation of burials, costume and bronze jewellery. The two peoples did not intermarry before their conversion to Christianity.

The ancient Mordvins met the Bulgars around the 7th century and later paid tribute to Volga Bulgaria. In the 13th century the Mongols conquered the region and incorporated the Mordvins into the Golden Horde. In the late 14th century the Principality of Moscow took much of the western Mordvin lands, while the east was held by the Kazan Khanate. When Russia conquered the Kazan Khanate in 1552, all Mordvins became Russian subjects.

Under Russian rule the Mordvins suffered forced conversion to Christianity, displacement, migration and an influx of Russian settlers, which made them a minority in their own area. In the 17th century the Mordvins, Chuvash and Mari rose against Russian rule. After the revolt was suppressed many Mordvins fled east beyond the Volga, and those who stayed became serfs. Assimilation to Russian culture was rapid until a Mordvin nationalism appeared in the late 19th century. The Mordvins received an autonomous territory in the Soviet Union in 1928, but Russification intensified in the 1930s, and by the 1950s knowledge of their languages was declining rapidly.

The two Mordvinic languages, Erzya and Moksha, belong to the Uralic family and have about 275,000 native speakers together. They are not mutually intelligible, so Russian is often used between the groups. Their literary forms were standardised in 1922 and 1923, and both are written in the Russian alphabet. Both are official languages of Mordovia alongside Russian.

The Erzya and Moksha have no common mythology. In Erzya belief the gods hatched from an egg, with Ange Patiai as the mother of gods and the sun god Chipaz after her. In Moksha belief the supreme god is Viarde Skai. Many Mordvins also live outside Mordovia, in the Volga region and Siberia. The Erzya now practise Christianity and a native religion, and the Mordvins are known as skilled beekeepers.
morean-war: Venice had held islands in the Aegean and Ionian seas since the partition of the Byzantine Empire after the Fourth Crusade but lost most of them to the Ottomans, and in the Cretan War of 1645 to 1669 it lost Crete. During that war the Venetian commander Francesco Morosini made contact with the rebellious Maniots and in 1659 landed in the Morea and took Kalamata, but he had to return to Crete and the venture failed.

Venice declared war on the Ottomans in 1684, for the only time in the Ottoman-Venetian wars, on news arriving on 25 April of the formation of the Holy League. The Austrians and Poles valued the Venetian navy as a means of keeping the Ottomans from concentrating their forces. In the Senate the war party saw a unique chance for revenge while the Ottomans were occupied against the Habsburgs.

The Venetian fleet left Corfu on 18 July 1684 and took the fortress of Lefkada after sixteen days, on 6 August. In 1685 Morosini turned to the Peloponnese, where the Maniots sought his aid, but the Ottoman serasker Ismail Pasha invaded Mani with 10,000 men and forced them to submit. The conquest of the Morea went on through 1687.

On 21 September 1687 an army of 10,750 men under Königsmarck landed at Eleusis and the fleet entered Piraeus. The Ottoman garrison withdrew to the Acropolis, which the Venetians besieged from 23 to 29 September. The Ottomans used the Parthenon to store ammunition, and on the evening of 26 September a mortar shell hit it. The explosion killed 300 people and destroyed the roof and most of the walls. The garrison surrendered on condition of transport to Smyrna.

In Dalmatia the Venetians took Sinj in 1686 and Knin in 1688. Morosini was elected Doge on 3 April 1688 but kept his command, and died at Nauplia on 16 January 1694. The Ottomans recovered, and the Maniot freebooter Limberakis Gerakaris raided Venetian positions from 1689.

The Treaty of Karlowitz of January 1699 confirmed Venetian possession of Kephalonia and the Morea with Aigina, organised as the Kingdom of the Morea in four provinces. The war had cost the peninsula dearly: the first Venetian census counted 86,468 people against some 200,000 before the war. Venice did not win the trust of its Greek Orthodox subjects, who had been used to relative autonomy under the Ottomans, and an Ottoman campaign in 1715 reclaimed the Morea.
morelos: Morelos is landlocked and borders Mexico City to the north, the State of México to the northeast and northwest, Puebla to the east and Guerrero to the southwest. It is the second-smallest state of Mexico after Tlaxcala and has 36 municipalities. The region is a basin into which abundant water flows, and most of it has a warm climate year-round, suited to sugar cane and other crops. Visitors from the Valley of Mexico have come to it since Aztec times.

The first known inhabitants, from about 6000 BCE, were nomadic hunters and gatherers. After the Spanish arrived, agriculture shifted from maize and cotton to sugar cane and its refining in nearby mills, a system that remained largely intact until the Mexican Revolution. Conditions on the sugar plantations made Miguel Hidalgo's call to arms welcome, and rebellions began in 1811. José María Morelos y Pavón took over after Hidalgo's execution. In 1812 he and his men held Cuautla for 58 days under royalist siege, an early vital success; he was captured and executed in 1815. In 1869 President Benito Juárez separated the territory from the State of México and named it in his honour.

The state was ready for the Mexican Revolution. Emiliano Zapata, born at Anenecuilco, led its best-known movement. His victory in the Battle of Cuautla, 11 to 19 May 1911, brought about the abdication of Porfirio Díaz. After Francisco Madero's election, Zapata, feeling betrayed, called with his followers for agrarian reform in the Plan de Ayala. The motto Tierra y Libertad was first used by Ricardo Flores Magón in 1910.

Cuernavaca, about 90 km south of Mexico City, is the capital and is called the City of the Eternal Spring. It has the Palacio de Cortés, which now holds Diego Rivera's mural History of Morelos, Conquest and Revolution. The state is also home to Xochicalco and to the Monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl, a World Heritage Site.
morena-political-party: After the 2006 presidential election, in which Andrés Manuel López Obrador alleged fraud after narrowly losing to Felipe Calderón, many legislators of the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) began to distance themselves from him. In 2008 he organised a movement against an energy reform that he and his followers argued was a step toward privatising Pemex. On 10 January 2011 he announced a new organisation, the National Regeneration Movement, founded as a civil association on 2 October 2011 to create Voter Defense Committees in 66,000 electoral sections. After he lost the 2012 election to Enrique Peña Nieto, he left the PRD on 9 September 2012.

Morena held its first National Congress on 20 November 2012, with Martí Batres as president of its executive committee, and the National Electoral Institute approved it as a party on 10 July 2014. In its first legislative election in 2015 it won 35 seats in the Chamber of Deputies. In the 2017 State of Mexico gubernatorial election its nominee lost by about 2.8 percentage points.

In 2018 López Obrador won the presidency with 53 percent of the vote, and Morena and its allies gained majorities in both chambers of Congress. He called his programme the Fourth Transformation. It included pensions for the elderly, austerity for senior officials and projects such as the Tren Maya, the Dos Bocas refinery and the Felipe Ángeles International Airport. Claudia Sheinbaum won the presidency in 2024, the first woman to hold the office, and Morena and its allies obtained a supermajority in the Chamber of Deputies. In September 2024 López Obrador adopted a judicial reform for the direct election of judges, which supporters said would reduce corruption and critics said would erode checks and balances.

Morena describes itself as a social democratic party that opposes the neoliberal economic policies Mexico began adopting in the 1980s. It opposes the privatisation of Pemex and supports the 1996 San Andrés Accords. Its platform favours women's rights and the LGBT community, and it has focused on cutting the salaries of high officials rather than raising taxes on the wealthy. The party's name alludes to the Virgin of Guadalupe, known as La Morena. It publishes the newspaper Regeneración, named after a publication run by the Flores Magón brothers before the Mexican Revolution. Some critics have described it as a big tent party that follows its founder's decisions.
moreton-bay: The bay was formed when the rising sea flooded what had been the floodplains of the Brisbane River. It stretches some 125 km from Caloundra almost to Surfers Paradise, is 35 km across at its widest and covers 1,523 square kilometres, with an average depth of 6.8 metres. A chain of sand islands, Moreton, North Stradbroke and South Stradbroke, separates it from the Coral Sea, and it holds around 360 islands, among them Bribie, Coochiemudlo and the Southern Moreton Bay Islands. Shifting sandbanks fill its entrance, and a channel is kept open to the Port of Brisbane at the mouth of the river.

The bay and its islands were the country of the Quandamooka people, whose economy drew on rich oyster beds, the annual mullet catch and the bunya nut harvest. Captain Cook named Morton's Bay on 15 May 1770 after Lord Morton, president of the Royal Society; the spelling Moreton was an error in the first published account of his voyage. Matthew Flinders was the first recorded European to enter the bay, in 1799, and John Oxley explored the Brisbane River in 1823. A pilot station was set up at Amity Point in 1825, and convicts built a causeway and out-station at Dunwich in 1827, abandoned in 1831.

Contact brought conflict, as newcomers disregarded Aboriginal marriage rules, took bones and other artefacts and desecrated important sites. In the 1840s white administrators put the Aboriginal population of the area at around 4,000, and in 1843 Catholic missionaries chose Dunwich for the first Catholic mission to Australian Aborigines. The first immigrant ship from England, the Artemisia, arrived in December 1848, and some 3,000 European migrants landed between 1850 and 1855. Timber was rafted across the bay from the 1850s, and Peel Island served in turn as a quarantine station, asylum and leper colony.

Moreton Bay lies 14 km from central Brisbane and carries the shipping channel of the Port of Brisbane. Large areas of it were recognised as wetlands of international significance under the Ramsar Convention in 1993, the year the Moreton Bay Marine Park was declared, and Moreton Island is a national park. The bay is the only place in Australia where dugongs gather in herds, and it hosts tens of thousands of migratory shorebirds each year.
morgan-shuster: William Morgan Shuster was born in Washington, D.C., on 23 February 1877, the only son of William Shuster Jr., a prominent Washington attorney, and Caroline von Tagen of Philadelphia. He studied at George Washington University and its law school. He then became a customs collector for the United States government, serving with the Military Government in Cuba in 1899 after the Spanish–American War and in the Philippines. In 1906 he was appointed Secretary of Public Instruction in the Insular Government of the Philippine Islands and a member of the Philippine Commission.

Recommended by the United States government to the Iranian minister in Washington, Shuster was engaged by the second Majlis to put the finances of the constitutional government in order. Iran was burdened by debts the Qajars owed to Britain and Russia, which had divided the country into spheres of influence under the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907. Shuster oversaw the creation of a gendarmerie of 12,000 men to collect taxes. When he moved to seize the assets of Shu'a al-Saltaneh, the shah's brother and an ally of Russian aims, Russia landed troops at Bandar Anzali and demanded an apology.

Russia accused him of breaking the 1907 convention by sending gendarmes into the zone its army occupied and arresting Russian subjects. When the Majlis refused to dismiss him, Russian forces occupied northern Iran; under Russian and British pressure the regent expelled Shuster in December 1911 against the parliament's will, and the Majlis was suspended.

Back in the United States he wrote The Strangling of Persia, published in New York by the Century Company in 1912 and dedicated to the Persian people. It attacks British and Russian influence in Iran and has been praised as an eyewitness account, notably for its chapter on tax collection from payment in kind to tax farming. It was later translated into Persian. From 1915 Shuster headed the Century publishing house, which he led through mergers with D. Appleton & Company in 1933 and F. S. Crofts in 1947; he became chairman in 1952. He died in New York City on 26 May 1960, when the firm was known as Appleton-Century-Crofts. His papers are in the Library of Congress.
morgantina: The site lies in the province of Enna, sixty kilometres from the Ionian coast and two kilometres north-east of Aidone. It covers a two-kilometre ridge called Serra Orlando and a neighbouring hill to the north-east, Cittadella. The first major settlement, on Cittadella, lasted from about 1000/900 to about 450 BCE; the second, on Serra Orlando, from about 450 BCE to about 50 CE. Kenan Erim identified Serra Orlando as Morgantina from coins bearing the Latin word HISPANORUM and from passages of Livy. Strabo says the city was founded by the Morgetes of Rhegium.

After Ducetius took it in 459 BCE, Thucydides records that at the Congress of Gela Syracuse gave Morgantina to Kamarina for an indemnity. Dionysios of Syracuse recaptured it in 396 BCE, and in 317 BCE the exiled Agathocles found help there to return to Syracuse. Part of Hiero II's kingdom when he became a Roman vassal in 263 BCE, it went over to Carthage in 214 BCE and in 211 BCE was the last Sicilian town to fall to Rome, which gave it to Spanish mercenaries. Eunus, leader of the First Servile War, died there in 133 BCE. Strabo wrote that by his time the city had ceased to exist.

Its grape, the vitis murgentina, was praised by Cato, Columella and Pliny the Elder. Luigi Pappalardo dug the first trenches in 1884 and Paolo Orsi in 1912. Princeton University began a major project in 1955 under Erik Sjöqvist and Richard Stillwell, joined in the 1950s by King Gustaf VI Adolf of Sweden. From 1978 Malcolm Bell III of the University of Virginia led the work towards publication in the Morgantina Studies series. Excavations of the North Baths since 2003 have found one of the earliest examples of dome and barrel vault construction, and a 3rd-century BCE bouleuterion stood west of the agora.

Finds from the site are shown in the Archaeological Museum of Aidone, opened in 1980 in a 17th-century former Capuchin monastery. By the 1980s works looted from or near Morgantina had been sold through the dealer Robin Symes: an Aphrodite bought by the J. Paul Getty Museum, parts of two acroliths bought by Maurice Tempelsman and the Morgantina treasure bought by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. All were returned to Italy and are displayed in the museum.
mori-motonari: Mōri Motonari was born on 16 April 1497 under the childhood name Shōjumaru, the second son of Mōri Hiromoto, in a small domain of Aki Province. The Mōri clan claimed descent from Ōe no Hiromoto, an adviser to Minamoto no Yoritomo. In 1500 his father retired and handed the clan to his eldest son, Mōri Okimoto. Motonari was later called the Beggar Prince.

The clan lay between the powerful Amago and Ōuchi clans, and Motonari first made his name at the Battle of Arita-Nakaide, where a Mōri force of about 1,000 men, including 300 from the Kikkawa clan, defeated the Takeda, whose commander Takeda Motoshige was killed by an arrow. Around 1522 he married the daughter of Kikkawa Kunitsune, securing the friendship of the powerful Kikkawa clan.

In July 1523 Motonari's nephew Kōmatsumaru, the titular head of the clan, died at the age of nine, and the senior vassals offered the leadership to Motonari. He entered Yoshida-Kōriyama Castle on 10 August. In 1524 he crushed a conspiracy to put his half-brother Aiō Mototsuna in his place. In March 1525 he changed his allegiance from the Amago to Ōuchi Yoshioki. In 1546 he announced his retirement in favour of his son Mōri Takamoto, though all understood that he remained the true head.

In 1551 Sue Takafusa, who took the name Harukata, forced Ōuchi Yoshitaka to commit seppuku. Motonari rebelled against Sue to avenge Yoshitaka. In 1555 he lured Sue into occupying the island of Miyajima, home of the Itsukushima Shrine, by building the weak Miyao Castle and proclaiming that it could not hold out; in September Sue landed with the bulk of his army and fell into the trap. The Amago were weakened by their purge of the Shingūtō faction after the death of Amago Kunihisa. At the second siege of Toda Castle Amago Yoshihisa surrendered and became a monk.

Motonari fell ill in the first half of the 1560s, and the shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiteru sent his own doctor to treat him. He died at Yoshida-Kōriyama Castle in 1571, aged 74. Under his leadership the Mōri expanded from a few districts of Aki Province to rule ten of the eleven provinces of the Chūgoku region, and his descendants became lords of the Chōshū Domain.

He is best remembered for the 'lesson of the three arrows', an event that probably never took place: he gives each son an arrow to break, then three bundled together, which cannot be broken. In fact Motonari had nine sons and three daughters.
mori-terumoto: Terumoto was born Kotsumaru at Yoshida Koriyama Castle in Aki, the eldest son of Mōri Takamoto and grandson of the warlord Mōri Motonari. When his father died suddenly in 1563 he became heir, though Motonari kept real control of the clan's affairs. In 1564 he took the name Terumoto, the first part given by the shogun Ashikaga Yoshiteru. With his uncles Kikkawa Motoharu and Kobayakawa Takakage he put down an invasion of Suō by Ōuchi Teruhiro in 1569 and defeated Amago Katsuhisa at the Battle of Fubeyama in 1570. On Motonari's death in 1571 he inherited lands from Buzen to the borders of Harima and Bizen and a powerful navy.

Motonari had advised against further expansion, but within three years his grandson was at war with Oda Nobunaga. The Mōri backed the rebel Ukita Naoie and supplied the Ishiyama Hongan-ji; in 1576, at the First Battle of Kizugawaguchi, Terumoto's fleet under Murakami Takeyoshi defeated Kuki Yoshitaka and broke the blockade. In 1578 his uncles took Kōzuki Castle, where Amago Katsuhisa and Yamanaka Shikanosuke were killed, but the same year Kuki drove off the Mōri fleet, and the Hongan-ji surrendered in 1580. By 1582 Hashiba Hideyoshi had flooded Takamatsu Castle in Bitchu, and Terumoto's relief force hesitated to attack.

After Nobunaga's death in the Honnoji Incident, Terumoto made peace and in 1583 became Hideyoshi's vassal, sending troops to Shikoku and Kyushu and ships to Odawara. In 1592 he led the 7th Division of 30,000 men in Korea, fighting partisans in Gyeongsang. He sat on the council of Five Elders and at his height held 1.2 million koku, enough to field more than 40,000 men.

Reduced after Sekigahara to Nagato and Suō, worth 369,000 koku, Terumoto refused the Toyotomi's call in 1614 and sent troops to the shogunate's side at the Siege of Osaka. When a former vassal, Naito Motomori, was found to have fought for Osaka, suspicion fell on the clan until Motomori killed himself; Terumoto then forced Motomori's two sons to commit suicide. In 1616 he married his only daughter, Takehime, to Kikkawa Hiromasa to bind the two families. Resentment among his vassals led him to retire in favour of his son Mōri Hidenari, and he died at Yoshida on 2 June 1625. He was a noted patron of Hagi ware pottery.
morice-line: The barrier was built under French authority during the Algerian War to stop supplies from neighbouring Tunisia reaching the guerrillas of the National Liberation Front inside French-controlled Algeria. It went into effect in September 1957. Though not a fortification in the traditional sense, it was equipped with what were then state-of-the-art electronic systems.

Its centre was an electric fence 2.5 metres high that ran its entire length, carried 5,000 volts and had barbed-wire entanglements on one side. A minefield extended 45 metres on each side of the fence, and on the Algerian side a patrolled track ran beside it. Along the border with Tunisia it ran for 460 km, and a further 700 km of barrier followed the border with Morocco. Alarms, radars and searchlights, together with anti-personnel mines, allowed the forces assigned to the line to coordinate their response, and the combination made it almost impenetrable.

The line sharply reduced guerrilla activity by forces coming from Tunisia and proved effective in limiting the FLN's operations during the war. After the war ended in 1962, the new Algerian authorities set out to clear and dismantle it, in part by forcing captured harkis and other Muslim loyalists who had served with the French Army to do the work, and many of them were killed by mines.

For decades afterwards the heavily mined barrier went on causing casualties among the local population. Algeria joined the Ottawa Treaty banning landmines, and in 2017 it announced that after decades of work it had met its clearance obligation under the treaty, having cleared its last 93 mined or suspected areas, among them 78 former mine barrages of the Morice Line.
morioka: Morioka lies in the Kitakami Basin in central Iwate Prefecture, at the confluence of the Kitakami, the Shizukuishi and the Nakatsu. The Kitakami is the longest river in the Tōhoku region and the second largest on the Pacific side of Japan, after the Tone. It runs through the city from north to south. The active volcano Mount Iwate dominates the view to the north-west, and Mount Himekami lies to the north. The climate is cold and humid, with warm, short summers and long winters with heavy snowfall.

The area has been inhabited continuously since the Japanese Paleolithic, and tombs and remains of the Jōmon, Yayoi and Kofun periods have been found. The Emishi lived there into the Heian period. In 803 Sakanoue no Tamuramaro was ordered to Shiwa Castle, a military centre meant to extend imperial rule over Mutsu Province. The area was later ruled by the Abe clan until its destruction in the Former Nine Years War by the Minamoto and Kiyohara clans, and then by the Ōshū Fujiwara of Hiraizumi, until Minamoto no Yoritomo destroyed them at the start of the Kamakura period.

Several samurai clans disputed the region until the Nanbu clan, based at Sannohe to the north, expanded its territory in the Sengoku period and built Kozukata Castle. After the Battle of Sekigahara and the formal recognition of Morioka Domain under the Tokugawa shogunate, the castle was renamed Morioka Castle, and the town's name was rewritten from 森岡 to 盛岡, both read Morioka. During the Boshin War the domain was a key member of the pro-Tokugawa Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei.

The domain became Morioka Prefecture in 1870 and part of Iwate Prefecture in 1872. The city was established as the prefectural capital on 1 April 1889, and a railway joined it to Tokyo in 1890. It came through the Second World War with little damage, having suffered only two minor air raids.

The city had a population of 283,981 in August 2023. The site of Morioka Castle and the ruins of Shiwa Castle are National Historic Site, and the Bank of Iwate Red Brick Building is an Important Cultural Property. The Rock-Breaking Cherry Tree is a natural monument. Hōon-ji, a Sōtō Zen temple moved to Morioka by the Nanbu lords, holds statues of the 500 Rakan, among them figures of Kublai Khan and Marco Polo. Local dishes include jajamen, reimen and wanko soba.
moriscos: Muslims had lived in Spain since the Umayyad conquest of Hispania in the eighth century. By the end of the fifteenth century the Muslim population was estimated at 500,000 to 600,000 out of a Spanish population of 7 to 8 million, about half of them in the former Emirate of Granada, which surrendered to Catholic forces in 1492. The Treaty of Granada first guaranteed the Muslims their rights, but efforts at conversion, first by Archbishop Hernando de Talavera and then more forcefully by Cardinal Cisneros, led Granada's Muslims to rebel in 1499. The revolt lasted until early 1501, and the treaty's protections were abandoned.

In 1502 the Catholic Monarchs outlawed the practice of Islam, and Muslims in Castile had to accept baptism or go into exile. In Valencia, a revolt of Christian brotherhoods in the 1520s forced Muslims to become Christians, and King Charles V upheld those conversions and ordered the rest of the Muslims to convert. The label morisco appeared in texts in the first half of the sixteenth century. In their own texts the Moriscos more often called themselves simply Muslims.

Moriscos were a majority in some places, such as Hornachos, but elsewhere they lived among Old Christians. They made up about 20 per cent of the population of Aragon, where they did not speak Arabic and were allowed by their lords to practise their faith relatively openly. Many Moriscos became devout Christians, while others held on to Islam in secret. A legal opinion known as the Oran fatwa allowed them to conform outwardly to Christianity when necessary for survival while keeping their faith inwardly.

The Spanish crown mistrusted the Moriscos and feared they would support invasions from the Ottoman Empire. At the urging of the Duke of Lerma and Archbishop Juan de Ribera, Philip III expelled them between 1609, from Aragon, and 1614, from Castile, ordering them to leave on pain of death and to take nothing but what they could carry. Contemporary accounts give between 270,000 and 300,000 expelled, about 4 per cent of the Spanish population, most of them from the Crown of Aragon and above all from Valencia.

Most of the expelled settled on the western edge of the Ottoman Empire and in Morocco. The Hornacheros, who left Castile armed, founded the Corsair Republic of Bou Regreg and Salé in Morocco. Morisco mercenaries in the service of the Moroccan sultan, armed with arquebuses, crossed the Sahara and conquered Timbuktu in 1591, and their descendants formed the Arma. Historians agree that many more Moriscos avoided expulsion than was once thought, though the numbers are not known. The last mass prosecution of Moriscos for secret Islamic practice took place at Granada in 1727.
moro-people: The Moro people are 13 Muslim-majority ethnolinguistic Austronesian groups of Mindanao, Sulu and Palawan, a region known as the Bangsamoro, colloquially Muslim Mindanao. They include the Badjao, Iranun, Maguindanaon, Maranao, Sama, Tausūg, Yakan and others, and most are Sunni Muslims. The word Moro is a cognate of Moors, an exonym that the Spanish applied to Muslims in general, derived from Latin Mauru and a Berber word for the inhabitants of ancient Mauretania, and later to the Muslim communities they met in the Philippines. Some Muslim communities object to the term for its colonial origin, while separatist organisations adopted it for their own names.

Before Islam, the territories were ruled by leaders with titles such as rajah and datu. In the 13th century Muslim missionaries such as Makhdum Karim in Tawi-Tawi began the conversion of the native population, and trade with sultanates in what are now Brunei, Malaysia and Indonesia entrenched the faith. In 1457 the introduction of Islam led to the establishment of sultanates, including Rajah Buayan, the Sultanate of Maguindanao and the Sultanate of Sulu, regarded as the oldest Muslim government in the region and annexed by the United States in 1898. The Sultanate of Sulu kept diplomatic relations with Ming China.

Spanish colonisation began with Miguel López de Legazpi's expedition in 1564. The sultanates of Mindanao actively resisted, and the Spanish built garrisons and Catholic missions in Moro territory, notably at Zamboanga and Cotabato, and tried to suppress Islam. The Moros answered with raids on Catholic coastal towns, which peaked in 1754 under Datu Bantilan. The Moro states remained de facto independent until the Moro rebellion of the early 20th century. After Philippine independence in 1946 grievances grew, among them exclusion from mainstream society, the loss of ancestral land to settlers and corporations, settler militias and a policy of Filipinisation, and armed secessionist movements arose, chief among them the Moro National Liberation Front and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.

A ceasefire and peace talks between the Philippine government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front led to the creation of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao in 2018, with greater political autonomy and powers than the earlier autonomous region. The 2020 census counted about 7.1 million Moros, roughly 6.5 per cent of the Philippine population and the largest non-Christian population in the country. Moro culture has been shaped by Islam since the sultanates of Maguindanao and Sulu, and a traditional instrument is the kulintang, a set of gongs of bronze or brass. Moro communities also live in Sabah, Brunei and Indonesia.
moro-rebellion: Spain held only a few coastal garrisons in the Moro lands and occupied Jolo, seat of the Sultan of Sulu, in 1876. The treaty of 22 July 1878 gave Spain full sovereignty in its Spanish text but only a protectorate in the Tausug version, and Spain then ceded the islands to the United States in the Treaty of Paris. American forces took over Jolo on 18 May 1899 and Zamboanga that December. The Kiram–Bates Treaty guaranteed the Sulu Sultanate's internal autonomy if it stayed out of the Philippine–American War, freeing Brigadier General John C. Bates to fight in Luzon.

Under Brigadier General George Whitefield Davis, appointed in August 1901, the Americans followed a conciliatory policy, and Captain John J. Pershing won the friendship of Amai-Manabilang, the retired Sultan of Madaya, north of Lake Lanao. Relations broke down in March 1902, when Moros killed American soldiers near Parang and Malabang. Major General Adna Chaffee demanded the killers on 13 April 1902, citing the Treaty of Paris, but the Moros, who had never heard of it, held that Spain could not cede land it had never conquered.

As governor of Moro Province, Leonard Wood had the Kiram–Bates Treaty abrogated, reduced the sultan to a religious office, abolished slavery and imposed the unpopular Cedula poll tax of 1903. Tasker H. Bliss, from 1906, launched no punitive expeditions. Pershing, governor from 1909, ordered the Moros disarmed by Executive Order No. 24 of 8 September 1911; resistance on Jolo led to the Second Battle of Bud Dajo and the Battle of Bud Bagsak, fought from 11 to 15 June 1913 and usually taken as the end of the rebellion.

The last clash came at Talipao in October 1913, the month the civilian Frank Carpenter replaced Pershing, and in March 1915 Sultan Jamalul Kiram gave up all claims to political power, ending the Sulu Sultanate. The Americans lost 130 killed, 323 wounded and some 500 dead of disease, the Philippine Scouts 116 killed and the Philippine Constabulary more than 1,500 losses; Moro casualties were high, as Moros seldom surrendered in combat. Suicide charges by juramentados led the army to replace its .38 calibre revolvers with .45 calibre sidearms and contributed to the adoption of the M1911 pistol.
moroccan-army-of-liberation: The Army of Liberation, Jish Etteḥrir in Moroccan Arabic and Aserdas Uslelli in Berber, was a loose union of militias fighting for Morocco's independence from the French-Spanish protectorate. It was founded to organise the many factions of rural armed resistance that had spread across the country after the assassination of the Tunisian labour unionist Farhat Hached and the forced exile of King Mohamed ben Youssef. Abdelkrim El Khattabi played an important part in its creation through commanders such as Abbas Messaadi and Sellam Amezian.

In 1956 units of the army, which was moving its staff from northern Spanish Morocco, began infiltrating Ifni and other Spanish enclaves as well as Spanish Sahara, to claim them for Morocco, at first with important backing from the Moroccan government. In Spanish Sahara it rallied Sahrawi tribes and set off a large rebellion. Early in 1958 the king reorganised the units fighting there as the Saharan Liberation Army, also called the Southern Liberation Army, led by figures such as Abderrahmane Youssoufi, Fqih Basri and Bensaid Aït Idder.

A joint French and Spanish offensive put down the revolt in 1958. As the guerrillas retreated, the regular Moroccan Army hindered them, which allowed the Spanish and French forces to neutralise them. The king then signed an agreement under which Spain returned the province of Tarfaya, until then part of Spanish Sahara, to Morocco.

Morocco sees the army's battles in Western Sahara, and Sahrawis fighting under the Moroccan flag, as proof of the territory's loyalty to the Moroccan crown, while sympathisers of the Polisario Front see only an anti-colonial war against Spain. Sahrawi veterans are found on both sides of the Western Sahara conflict, and both Morocco and the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic celebrate the army as part of their history. Some parents of Polisario's founders had served in it, among them the father of Mohammed Abdelaziz, president of Polisario and of the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic.
morocco: Morocco has coasts on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, and covers about 446,300 km2. The Atlas Mountains run along the centre and south, the Rif Mountains lie in the north, and both ranges are mainly inhabited by Berber people. Most of the southeast lies in the Sahara Desert and is sparsely populated. The capital is Rabat, beside the Oued Bou Regreg River, and the largest city is the port of Casablanca. The English name Morocco comes from the Spanish Marruecos, itself derived from the name of Marrakesh, the capital of the Almoravid dynasty, the Almohad Caliphate and the Saadian dynasty.

People have lived in the region since the Paleolithic. Homo sapiens fossils from Jebel Irhoud were dated to roughly 315,000 years ago. At Oued Beht a Neolithic farming society of 3400–2900 BCE formed the largest known agricultural complex in Africa outside the Nile Valley at that time. Phoenicians later established trading colonies, the most substantial being Chellah, Lixus and Mogador.

The Moroccan state traces its origins to the Idrisid dynasty founded by Idris I in 788. It reached its height as a regional power in the 11th and 12th centuries under the Berber Almoravid and Almohad dynasties, which controlled the southern and eastern Iberian Peninsula and the Maghreb. In the 15th and 16th centuries Portugal seized some territory, but the Marinid and Saadi dynasties resisted foreign domination, and Morocco was the only North African nation to escape Ottoman rule. The Alawi dynasty, which still reigns, seized power in 1631. France and Spain established protectorates in 1912, and Morocco regained independence in 1956 under Sultan Mohammed V.

Morocco is a unitary semi-constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament of two chambers, and the 2011 constitutional reforms reduced the king's executive powers and enlarged the prime minister's. The king remains Commander of the Faithful and holds wide powers over the military, foreign policy and religious affairs. The population was about 37 million in the 2024 census. Arabic and Tamazight are the official languages, and Islam is the official religion.
morogoro: Morogoro lies in eastern Tanzania, about 196 kilometres west of Dar es Salaam, and is the capital of the Morogoro Region. The city stands at the foothills of the Uluguru Mountains and is a significant agricultural centre, with many sisal plantations around it. Its climate is warm and tropical, with hot days and cool nights. Informally it is sometimes called Mji kasoro bahari, which translates as the city short of an ocean or port.

The Mindu Dam on the Ngerengere River, begun in 1978, supplies about 80 per cent of the city's water. It has been controversial: the reservoir has raised rates of bilharzia infection, mining runoff has polluted the water with mercury, and deforestation nearby has increased sedimentation and reduced the dam's capacity.

Morogoro has many educational institutions. The Sokoine University of Agriculture is based there, together with the Muslim University of Morogoro, St. Joseph University College, Jordan University College, the Ardhi Institute, a teachers college and the Livestock Training Institute. Kilakala Girls High School, formerly Marian College, is one of the oldest secondary schools in the country, and the Morogoro International School, teaching in English, was established in 1975.

The city has a musical heritage. The Morogoro Jazz Band was established in 1944, and Salim Abdullah, founder of the Cuban Marimba Band, came from Morogoro. From the mid-1960s to the 1970s it was the home of Mbaraka Mwinshehe, a highly influential lead guitarist and singer-songwriter. The football club Mtibwa Sugar represents it in the Tanzanian Premier League. Local transport includes buses called dala dalas, motorcycles known as boda bodas and three-wheeled Bajaj vehicles. On 10 August 2019 a fuel tanker exploded in the town, killing 100 people.
morphou: Tradition holds that Morphou was founded by Spartans who brought with them the worship of Aphrodite. In the Middle Ages the town was called Morphou and also Theomorphou. In the 14th and 15th centuries it hosted royal casalia, estates where sugar was grown profitably with the encouragement of the kings of Cyprus. The Morphou area grew more than half of the citrus fruit of Cyprus. In the 16th and 17th centuries, under Ottoman rule, it was known for exporting linen. Between 1907 and 1948 it was one of the prominent stations of the Cyprus Government Railway.

Before 1974 Morphou was an almost entirely Greek Cypriot community: the census of 1960 counted 6,480 Greek Cypriots, 123 Turkish Cypriots and 32 Maronites. In the intercommunal violence known as Bloody Christmas, most of the Turkish Cypriot population fled in January 1964, though one third remained. After the Turkish invasion of Cyprus in 1974 all the Greek Cypriots of Morphou fled to the south of the island. Displaced Turkish Cypriots from villages of the Paphos district and the town of Paphos, and some from Limassol and its villages, settled in the town, which became a refugee town.

Morphou is known for its oranges, apples, vegetables, grapefruit and melons. Much of the citrus is exported and the rest is made into juice and canned. The town has held an annual Orange Festival, run by the municipality since 1977, lasting two weeks. It contains one of the many churches of Cyprus dedicated to Saint Mamas, who is popularly believed to have lived as a hermit in a cave near the town.

According to local legend he escaped soldiers who came to tax him by riding to town on a lion, and so won an exemption from tax. The church is now an icon museum, and it still hosts a Greek Cypriot liturgy each year. A museum of natural history and archaeology shows antiquities from the Neolithic to the Byzantine period.
morse-code: Early in the 19th century, European experimenters made progress with electrical signalling, using static electricity and Voltaic piles. The simple on-or-off nature of the signals made it desirable to find a way of sending natural language with only electrical pulses and the silence between them. Samuel Morse's first proposal for a telegraph code was replaced by an alphabet-based code developed by Alfred Vail, which was used for commercial telegraphy in North America.

Friedrich Gerke's 1848 proposal, the Hamburg alphabet, did away with the different-length dashes and spaces of American Morse, leaving two elements, the dot and the dash. It was first used between Hamburg and Cuxhaven. Gerke changed nearly half the alphabet and all of the numerals.

In International Morse, a dah lasts three times as long as a dit. The space between elements equals one dit, between letters three dits and between words seven. Vail designed his code so that the length of each symbol was roughly the inverse of the frequency of its letter in English, which is why E is a single dit. International Morse was standardised by the International Telegraph Convention in Paris on 17 May 1865, which formed the International Telegraph Union. Vail's version, known as American Morse or railroad code, remained in use only for land-line telegraphy in the United States and Canada.

In the original telegraph the receiver's armature clicked as it marked a paper tape. Operators soon learned to translate the clicks directly into dots and dashes, which made the tape unnecessary. In the 1890s Morse began to be used extensively for early radio, before voice could be transmitted, and in the late 19th and early 20th centuries most high-speed international communication used it on telegraph lines, undersea cables and radio circuits. Radiotelegraphy was vital in the Second World War.

The final commercial Morse transmission in the United States took place on 12 July 1999, signing off with Morse's 1844 message, What hath God wrought. Radio amateurs still use it, and radio navigation aids broadcast their identities in it.
mortimer-wheeler: Robert Eric Mortimer Wheeler was born in Glasgow on 10 September 1890, the first child of the journalist Robert Mortimer Wheeler and his second wife Emily, and was raised largely in Yorkshire before the family moved to London. In 1907 he won a scholarship to read classical studies at University College London, where A. E. Housman taught him. He switched for a time to the Slade School of Fine Art but returned to classics and graduated with a second class degree.

In the First World War he volunteered for the Royal Artillery, served on the Western Front, rose to major and was awarded the Military Cross. Afterwards he worked for the Royal Commission cataloguing the historic structures of Essex and published on Roman Colchester, and the University of London awarded him a Doctorate of Letters for research on Romano-Rhenish pots.

Wheeler joined the National Museum of Wales, first as Keeper of Archaeology and then as director, and with his first wife Tessa excavated the Roman forts of Segontium, Y Gaer and Isca Augusta. Influenced by Augustus Pitt Rivers, he argued that excavation and the recording of stratigraphic context needed a scientific and methodical approach, the Wheeler method. In July 1926 he became Keeper of the London Museum, where he reorganised the collection and began lecturing at University College London.

In 1934 he opened the Institute of Archaeology as part of the University of London, as honorary director, hoping to professionalise the subject and make it, in his words, a laboratory of archaeological science. He oversaw excavations at Lydney Park, Verulamium and Maiden Castle. In the Second World War he rose to brigadier, serving in the North African Campaign and the invasion of Italy. In 1944 he became director-general of the Archaeological Survey of India, where excavations at Harappa, Arikamedu and Brahmagiri took place and he reformed the establishment. His letters from that time contain racist remarks about Indians, and he beat some staff. After returning to Britain in 1948 he lectured and advised the government of Pakistan.

Knighted in 1952, Wheeler became a public figure through books, cruise ship lectures, radio and television, notably the BBC series Animal, Vegetable, Mineral?. He was president of the Society of Antiquaries from 1954 to 1959 and a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1968. He died on 22 July 1976. Archaeologists Gabriel Moshenska and Tim Schadla-Hall have called him the best-known British archaeologist of the twentieth century. He is regarded as a major figure in establishing South Asian archaeology, though many of his interpretations of particular sites have been discredited or reinterpreted. Colleagues divided over him: some loved him and others despised him.
mortmain: The term derives through Old French morte main. Sir Edward Coke offered several explanations of the name, and William Blackstone in 1765 thought the most probable to be that such purchases were usually made by ecclesiastical bodies whose professed members were reckoned dead persons in law, so that land held by them could properly be said to be held in mortua manu, in dead hands.

Limits on the Church's power to hold land in England appear before Edward I's statutes, in Magna Carta of 1215 and the Provisions of Westminster of 1259. Religious houses adjusted to the new rules: the chartulary of Chertsey Abbey records that shortly after "one of these statutes vulgarly called Mortmain" 11 acres in Ash, Surrey, were held by Robert de Zathe with common pasture for his flocks and herds, while Geoffrey de Bacsete and his brother William held 28 acres.

The prohibition shaped much early case law on charitable trusts. In Thornton v Howe (1862) a trust for publishing the writings of Joanna Southcott was held to be charitable as being for the advancement of religion, a decision often cited for setting a very low bar for such trusts; the statutes against mortmain were then still in force.

Corporate mortmain remains lawful in many countries, and where prohibitions on perpetual ownership survive they now apply mostly to companies and charitable trusts rather than to churches. In private trusts and settlements, laws against perpetuities still keep a founder's dead hand from prevailing beyond a fixed period, for example 80 years, and the common-law rule in Saunders v Vautier allows all the adult beneficiaries together to set aside the provisions of a trust. Such rules vary from one jurisdiction to another.
moruroa: Moruroa, also spelled Mururoa, is an atoll in the Tuamotu Archipelago of French Polynesia, about 1,250 kilometres south-east of Tahiti, and is part of the commune of Tureia. The first recorded visit was by Commander Philip Carteret on HMS Swallow in 1767, who named it Bishop of Osnaburgh Island. The British whaler Matilda was wrecked there in 1792. The atoll was not continuously inhabited: Frederick William Beechey found it empty in 1826, and a visiting ship in 1834 killed all but three of the inhabitants it found. Copra workers lived there briefly in the late nineteenth century and again in 1942 to 1943 and 1950 to 1952.

France established the atoll as a nuclear test site on 21 September 1962, and construction began in May 1963, with the atoll of Hao as a support base. The first test, Aldebaran, a plutonium fission bomb exploded in the lagoon, took place on 2 July 1966 despite objections from about 30 members of the Polynesian Territorial Assembly. President Charles de Gaulle was present for a test on 10 September 1966. Forty-one atmospheric tests were conducted between 1966 and 1974, after which France moved underground amid intense world pressure, to which New Zealand contributed by sending two frigates in July 1973.

The underground tests cracked the atoll and raised fears that radioactive material would escape. On 25 July 1979 a device stuck halfway down its 800-metre shaft was detonated at half the usual depth, causing a large submarine landslide, a tsunami and a crack two kilometres long. New tests on 5 September and 2 October 1995 caused worldwide protests, an embargo of French wine and riots in Polynesia. The last test at Moruroa took place on 27 December 1995, and the site was dismantled afterwards. In all 181 explosions took place there, though nuclear scientists working at the site claim 175.

The atoll has had no permanent inhabitants since 1952. In February 2021 the French National Institute of Health and Medical Research published a report on the health consequences of the atmospheric tests in French Polynesia for the general population and for civilian and military workers.
mosbach: Mosbach lies in the north of Baden-Württemberg, about 35 km east of Heidelberg, at the confluence of the Neckar and the Elz, south of the Odenwald mountains, at a height of 134 to 354 metres. It is the seat of the Neckar-Odenwald district and has about 25,000 inhabitants, spread over six boroughs: Mosbach Town, Lohrbach, Neckarelz, Diedesheim, Sattelbach and Reichenbuch.

The settlement developed around the Benedictine monastery of Mosbach Abbey, called Monasterium Mosabach, whose first written record dates from the 9th century. In 1241 Mosbach was granted the rights and privileges of an Imperial free city, which it lost in 1362 when it became part of the Electorate of the Palatinate. When the lands of King Rupert were divided in 1410, Mosbach became the capital of a small principality, Palatinate-Mosbach, the inheritance of his son Otto I. After the death of his brother John, Count Palatine of Neumarkt, in 1443, Palatinate-Neumarkt was added in a personal union, creating Palatinate-Mosbach-Neumarkt. The principality was dissolved with the death of Count Palatine Otto II in 1499.

The town and its territory reverted to the Electorate of the Palatinate, and Mosbach became the capital of the administrative district of Oberamt Mosbach. In 1806 it was made part of the Grand Duchy of Baden. In World War II the Mosbach area was the location of an underground Daimler-Benz factory for aircraft engines, codenamed Goldfisch. The 289th Combat Engineer Battalion occupied it in the immediate postwar period.

The historic town centre has a pedestrian area and timber-framed houses. Among them are the Palm House, built in 1610 and the town's emblem, and the Salzhaus, the oldest timber-framed house. The old town hall has a tower. The former collegiate church is now a parish church, its nave used by Protestants and its chancel by Roman Catholics. In the borough of Neckarelz stands the Tempelhaus, which has the character of both a castle and a church. Mosbach lies on two heritage routes, the Burgenstraße or Castle Road and the Deutsche Fachwerkstraße or German Half-timbered Road.
moscow: Moscow lies on the Moskva River, which flows for about 500 kilometres through the East European Plain in Central Russia, and 49 bridges span the river and its canals within the city. The city's name is thought to derive from the river's. The best-grounded theory traces it to a Proto-Balto-Slavic root meaning 'wet', so that Moskva would mean a river at a marsh. A Finno-Ugric hypothesis holds instead that the Merya and Muroma, pre-Slavic peoples of the area, called it Mustajoki, 'Black River'.

The site has been inhabited since prehistoric times, and around 950 CE two Slavic tribes, the Vyatichi and Krivichi, settled there. Chronicles first mention Moscow in 1147, as a minor town on the western border of the principality of Rostov-Suzdal and a meeting place for Yuri Dolgorukiy and Sviatoslav Olgovich. It was fortified in the 1150s, when the first walls of the Kremlin were built, and was sacked during the Mongol invasions of 1237–1238 after the destruction of Ryazan.

The Grand Principality of Moscow led the unification of Russian lands in the 15th century, and the Kremlin was rebuilt then, with towers and churches by Italian architects. After the Tsardom of Russia was proclaimed in 1547, Moscow remained its political and economic centre until Peter the Great moved the capital to the newly founded Saint Petersburg in 1712. The capital returned to Moscow in 1918, after the establishment of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic.

Moscow had 13,010,112 residents in the 2021 census, up from 11,503,501 in 2010. It is a federal city, divided into 12 administrative okrugs and 125 districts. Its road system radiates from the Kremlin and crosses circular roads that began as lines of fortification, among them the Boulevard Ring, on the line of the 16th-century wall of Bely Gorod, and the Garden Ring.

The Moscow Metro opened in 1935, and its original stations were decorated to impress and instruct the population. The city also holds Lomonosov Moscow State University, founded in 1755, and the Tretyakov Gallery, which has works by the icon painter Andrei Rublev.
moscow-kremlin: The Kremlin comprises five palaces, four cathedrals and an enclosing wall with numerous towers. It overlooks the Moskva River to the south, Red Square to the east and Alexander Garden to the west. In Russian, kreml' means a fortress within a city, but the Moscow Kremlin has also become a metonym for the Russian government; during the Cold War the term meant the government of the Soviet Union.

The site was inhabited by the Meryans from the 2nd century BCE, and Slavs held part of Borovitsky Hill by the 11th century. The word Kremlin was first recorded in 1331. The Mongols destroyed the fortress in 1237, and Ivan I Kalita rebuilt it in oak in 1339. Dmitri Donskoi replaced the palisade with a white limestone citadel in 1366 to 1368, which withstood a siege by Khan Tokhtamysh. Ivan III invited Italian architects, among them Pietro Antonio Solari, who designed the wall and towers, built between 1485 and 1495.

Polish forces held the Kremlin from 1610 to 1612, and its liberation made possible the election of Mikhail Romanov as tsar. Peter abandoned it for Saint Petersburg in 1703. French forces occupied it from 2 September to 11 October 1812, and Napoleon on retreating ordered it blown up; rain damaged the fuses and the damage was less than intended.

The Soviet government moved to Moscow on 12 March 1918, and Lenin chose the Senate building as his residence. In all 28 of the 54 historic buildings in the Kremlin were destroyed during Soviet rule, among them the Chudov Monastery and the Ascension Convent.

The Grand Kremlin Palace, built in 1839 to 1849, is the residence of the president of the Russian Federation. The complex was closed to tourists until 1955, the Kremlin Museums were established in 1961, and it was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1990.
moscow-mathematical-papyrus: The papyrus is also called the Golenishchev Mathematical Papyrus after its first non-Egyptian owner, the Egyptologist Vladimir Golenishchev, who bought it at Thebes in 1892 or 1893. It later entered the collection of the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts in Moscow. From its hieratic text it was most likely written in the 13th Dynasty from older material probably dating to the 12th Dynasty, around 1850 BCE. It is around 5.5 metres long, and in 1930 the Soviet Orientalist Vasily Struve divided it into 25 problems with solutions. It is older than the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus, though the Rhind is the larger.

The problems follow no particular order, and their solutions give much less detail than those of the Rhind Papyrus. Ten of the 25 are pefsu problems, which use the pefsu, a measure of the strength of beer or bread made from a hekat of grain; a higher number means weaker bread or beer. Problems 1, 19 and 25 are aha problems, which find an unknown quantity, called aha, or stack, from its sum with parts of itself. Parts of a ship are the subject of problems 2 and 3. Problems 11 and 23 concern the output of workers, the latter a shoemaker cutting and decorating sandals. Seven problems deal with geometry, from areas of triangles to the volume of a frustum.

The papyrus is known above all for two geometry problems. Problem 14 gives a truncated pyramid with a height of 6, a base of 4 and a top of 2, and finds a volume of 56, which is correct, so the Egyptians knew the right rule, though the papyrus does not say how it was derived. Problem 10 asks for the surface of a basket with a mouth of 4 1/2; Struve and Gillings read it as the area of a hemisphere, while Peet suggested a semi-cylinder. With the Rhind Papyrus, it is usually cited as a main source for Egyptian mathematics.
moscow-nights: Moscow Nights is a Soviet patriotic song with words by Mikhail Matusovsky and music by Vasily Solovyov-Sedoy. The two wrote it in 1955 under the title Leningrad Nights. At the request of the Soviet Ministry of Culture the song was renamed Moscow Nights, with corresponding changes to the words. In 1956 the young actor Vladimir Troshin of the Moscow Art Theatre recorded it for a scene in a documentary about the Spartakiad of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic, in which the athletes rest in Podmoskovye, the Moscow suburbs. The film did nothing to promote the song, but it gained popularity through radio broadcasts.

The song was soon covered abroad. In Finnish it was performed as Unohtumaton Ilta, Unforgettable Evening, by many artists, among the earliest the Estonian singer Georg Ots in 1958, who also sang it in Russian. The Dutch jazz group New Orleans Syncopators recorded an arrangement by Jan Burgers as Midnight in Moscow on 4 January 1961, and Kenny Ball and his Jazzmen recorded it in November 1961 under the same title. That version peaked at number two on the UK Singles Chart in January 1962 and at number two on the American Billboard Hot 100 in March, kept from the top by Hey! Baby by Bruce Channel; it spent three weeks at number one on the American Easy Listening chart.

In 1962 the Chad Mitchell Trio recorded it on their live album At the Bitter End and introduced it in Russian to a mainstream American audience during the Cold War, and Ketty Lester recorded it the same year. In 1964 Anatoliy Solovianenko's rendition took third place in the Italian television show Napoli contro tutti, and Italian choirs recorded a version, Mezzanotte a Mosca. Jan Johansson made a jazz version in 1967, and the Chinese composer Gao Ping used the melody in 2003. Since 1978 Radio Moscow's English-language service has played an instrumental jazz big-band version between announcements, and in 2015 the Massed Bands of the Moscow Garrison played a march arrangement in the Victory Day Parade.
moscow-peace-treaty: The Winter War began on 30 November 1939 with the Soviet invasion of Finland. On 29 January 1940 the Soviet foreign minister Vyacheslav Molotov dropped the puppet Terijoki Government and recognised the Ryti–Tanner government as the legal government of Finland, saying the Soviet Union was willing to negotiate. The first tentative conditions reached Finland through Stockholm two days later and were larger than the claims made before the war. They demanded the Karelian Isthmus, including the city of Viipuri, and Finland's shore of Lake Ladoga, with the Hanko Peninsula leased for 30 years. Finland rejected them and appealed to Sweden, France and the United Kingdom for troops.

In February 1940 the commander-in-chief, Marshal Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim, expressed pessimism about the military situation, and the government began peace talks on 29 February, the day the Red Army began an attack on Viipuri.

A Finnish delegation led by Prime Minister Risto Ryti travelled to Moscow on 6 March, while the Red Army was close to surrounding Viipuri. President Kyösti Kallio resisted giving up any territory but agreed to sign, and is said to have exclaimed: Let the hand wither that signs this monstrous treaty! The treaty was signed on the evening of 12 March, Moscow time, for the Soviet Union by Molotov, Andrei Zhdanov and Aleksandr Vasilevsky and for Finland by Ryti, Juho Kusti Paasikivi, Rudolf Walden and Väinö Voionmaa.

Finland ceded approximately half of Finnish Karelia, more than the Soviets had demanded before the war. The area included Viipuri, Käkisalmi, Sortavala, Suojärvi and the whole of Viipuri Bay, along with a part of the Salla area, the Finnish part of the Rybachi Peninsula and several islands in the Gulf of Finland. The Hanko Peninsula was leased to the Soviet Union as a naval base for 30 years at an annual rent of 8 million marks. Petsamo, captured by the Russians during the war, stayed in Finnish hands.

Troops and the remaining civilians were hastily evacuated inside the new border: 422,000 Finns, 12 per cent of the population, left their homes. The Soviet demand for rail transit rights to Hanko came only on 9 July, after Sweden had allowed Wehrmacht troops to cross its railways to occupied Norway. The Winter War and the treaty were core factors leading to the Continuation War, when hostilities resumed in 1941. The terms were not reversed after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, and the debate in Finland over regaining the ceded territory is known as the Karelian question.
moselle: The Moselle rises at 715 m on the Col de Bussang, on the western slopes of the Ballon d'Alsace in the Vosges. Of its length, 313 km lie in France, 39 km form the border between Germany and Luxembourg, and 208 km are wholly within Germany. It flows through Lorraine and joins the Rhine at the Deutsches Eck in Koblenz, where it is the second largest tributary of the Rhine by volume after the Aare.

Below Trier it separates the Eifel to the north-west from the Hunsrück to the south-east, in wide meanders cut deeply into the Rhenish Massif, the most striking being the Cochemer Krampen. Its largest tributaries are the Meurthe, the Saar and the Sauer. The Meurthe was once the upper course of the Moselle, until the Moselle captured the former upper reaches of the Meuse.

The name comes from the Celtic Mosela by way of the Latin Mosella, a diminutive of Mosa, the Latin name of the Meuse, so that the Mosella was the Little Meuse. Tacitus first records the river in his Annals and Histories. About 371 the poet Ausonius, a teacher at the imperial court in Trier, made it the subject of his poem Mosella, of 483 hexameters, describing a journey from Bingen to Trier and the rich landscapes along the valley under Roman rule. After the division of Lotharingia in the later 10th century, Upper Lotharingia along the river was often called Mosellania.

From 1815 the Moselle formed the border between the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg and Prussia. In September 1944 it was a barrier to the Allied advance, and the American 80th Infantry Division won a bridgehead at Dieulouard, allowing armour to move on Nancy. At the tripoint near Schengen the Schengen Agreement was signed in 1985.

The Moselle valley between Metz and Thionville is an industrial area of coal mining and steel. Further downstream the terraced hillsides carry vineyards, producing Riesling, Elbling, Müller-Thurgau and other wines, with many castle ruins above the villages. A treaty of 27 October 1956 between France, Germany and Luxembourg led to the canalisation of the river, officially opened from Metz to Koblenz on 26 May 1964; 394 km are now navigable through 28 locks, up to Neuves-Maisons south of Nancy. The Moselle Commission, founded in 1962, has its seat in Trier.
moses: According to the Book of Exodus, Moses was born to Amram, a descendant of Kehath the Levite, and Jochebed, when the Israelites were an enslaved minority in Egypt. He had an older sister, Miriam, and an older brother, Aaron. Pharaoh had ordered all newborn Hebrew boys drowned in the Nile, so his mother hid him in an ark among the bulrushes, and Pharaoh's daughter adopted him. After he killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew, Moses fled to Midian and married Zipporah. On Mount Horeb God appeared to him as a burning bush and commanded him to bring the Israelites out of bondage. The Egyptian root msy, child of, as in Thutmose, has been proposed as the origin of his name.

After God sent ten plagues Pharaoh relented, and Moses led the Exodus across the Red Sea, where Pharaoh's army was destroyed. At Mount Sinai he received the Ten Commandments. After 40 years of wandering in the desert he died on Mount Nebo at the age of 120, within sight of the Promised Land.

Scholars disagree about his historicity. William G. Dever describes the modern consensus as that the biblical Moses is largely mythical, while allowing that a Moses-like figure may have lived in the southern Transjordan in the mid to late 13th century BCE. No Egyptian source mentions him before the fourth century BCE, and no archaeological evidence in Egypt or Sinai supports the story. Others hold that his leadership is too firmly rooted in Israel's collective memory to be pious fiction.

Jewish tradition considers Moses the foremost prophet, though Judaism stresses that he was a human being and not to be worshipped. He is also a major prophet in Samaritanism, Christianity and Islam. Hecataeus of Abdera, in the fourth century BCE, wrote the earliest reference to him in Greek literature. The Sistine Chapel has six frescoes of his life, painted in 1481-82 by artists including Sandro Botticelli and Pietro Perugino. Because the Hebrew word keren can mean horn or ray, Jerome's Latin Vulgate describes his face as horned, and Western art until the Renaissance often shows him with small horns, as in Michelangelo's statue of 1513 to 1515.
moshoeshoe-i: Moshoeshoe was born Lepoqo at Menkhoaneng in the north of modern Lesotho, the first son of Mokhachane, a minor chief of the Bamokoteli lineage, a branch of the Bakoena clan, and his first wife Kholu. His name literally means dispute, after accusations of witchcraft made against a man in the village around the time of his birth. Estimates of the year of his birth range from 1780 to 1794, with 1786 the most commonly agreed. After his initiation in 1804 he led a cattle raid on the village of Chief RaMonaheng, and a praise poem likened him to a razor that had shaved RaMonaheng's beard, so he became known as Moshoeshoe, the Shaver.

He succeeded his father as chief of the Bamokoteli in 1820 and settled with his followers at Butha-Buthe. The wars of the time of troubles, marked by attacks of invading Nguni clans on the Sotho, forced him to move to the Qiloane plateau, later called Thaba Bosiu, which proved an impassable stronghold.

In the 1820s the Basotho faced cattle raids from the Koranna and first met horses and guns in battle. They captured or acquired their own, and by 1843 Moshoeshoe had more horses and guns than any other chieftain in South Africa. In 1833, at his invitation, missionaries of the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society began setting up outposts in Basotho lands. In 1843 he signed a treaty with Sir George Napier, governor of the Cape Colony, by which the British recognised the Basuto as allies.

On 30 June 1851 a Basotho and Taung army defeated a mixed force under the British Resident, Major Henry Douglas Warden, at the Battle of Viervoet. At the Battle of Berea on 20 December 1852 British forces withdrew, and Moshoeshoe sued for peace on favourable terms. After the British left in 1854, the Boer Orange Free State was formed, and war with it broke out in 1858. The Basotho won the first war but lost the two that followed. By the Treaty of Thaba Bosiu in 1866 Moshoeshoe ceded most of his arable land, and when fighting resumed the Boers used a scorched earth policy, which led to starvation.
