Moshoeshoe, his sons and local missionaries appealed to the British High Commissioner, Sir Philip Wodehouse, and to Natal for protection. Wodehouse blocked ammunition supplies to the Free State and on 12 March 1868 proclaimed Basotho land a royal dominion. Moshoeshoe died on 11 March 1870 and was succeeded by his eldest son Letsie I. Only the children of his senior wife 'MaMohato formed the royal line, though he practised polygamy. Moshoeshoe Day, 11 March, is a national holiday in Lesotho.
moshoeshoe-ii: Moshoeshoe II was born Constantine Bereng Seeiso on 2 May 1938, a descendant of the founder of the nation, Moshoeshoe I, from whom he took his royal name. He succeeded Paramount Chief Seeiso. He was educated at Roma College in Lesotho and then, apparently fleeing rumours that his stepfather planned to poison him, was sent to England, first to Ampleforth College and later to Corpus Christi College, Oxford. There he took to the life of an English country gentleman, with hunting, shooting and fishing. In 1962 he married Princess Tabitha 'Masentle Lerotholi Mojela, later known as Queen 'Mamohato, and they had two sons and a daughter.

He was Paramount Chief of Basutoland from 1960 until independence from Britain in 1966, when he was crowned King Moshoeshoe II of Lesotho. His political power was always limited, and his reign was interrupted twice. Early on, Chief Leabua Jonathan became Prime Minister and gained control of the government. In 1970, after his party lost the election, Jonathan suspended the king to reestablish his own control, and Moshoeshoe went into temporary exile in the Netherlands. A few months later Jonathan allowed him to take the title of King again.

After Jonathan was overthrown in 1986, the king gained some power, but in February 1990 he was stripped of his constitutional powers. In November 1990 he was deposed and his son Letsie III was forced to take his place. Moshoeshoe went into exile in the United Kingdom, and was reinstated as king in January 1995. During the turmoil of 1970 and 1990 his wife 'Mamohato acted as regent.

Moshoeshoe II died at the age of 57 in a road accident in the early hours of 15 January 1996, when his car plunged off a mountain road in the Maloti Mountains. The driver was also killed. According to a government statement, he had set out at 1am to visit his cattle at Matsieng and was returning to Maseru. His son became King Letsie III again a month later, with 'Mamohato acting as regent in the interval.

He was Grand Master of five Lesotho orders, among them the Order of Dignity named for Moshoeshoe, and received the Commemorative Medal of the 2500th Anniversary of the founding of the Persian Empire in 1971. South Africa awarded him the Order of the Companions of O. R. Tambo after his death, in 2006.
moskva-river: The river rises about 140 kilometres west of Moscow, crosses Smolensk and Moscow Oblasts and reaches the Oka about 110 kilometres south-east of the capital. Its length is given as 473 kilometres, or by another measure 502, its basin covers 17,600 square kilometres, and it falls 155 metres along its course. An estimated 61 per cent of its water comes from thaw, 12 per cent from rain and 27 per cent from underground sources. It normally freezes around November or December and begins to thaw in late March. On its banks, besides Moscow, stand Mozhaysk, Zvenigorod, Zhukovsky, Bronnitsy and Voskresensk.

Recent studies suggest that the river has occupied its present bed for about 12,000 years. Finnic peoples lived along it, as did Slavic tribes such as the Vyatichi. The name of the city is thought to come from that of the river. The most widely accepted explanation derives it from a Proto-Balto-Slavic root connected with wetness, so that it may have meant a river in a marsh or wetland. One Finno-Ugric hypothesis holds instead that the Merya and Muroma, pre-Slavic peoples of the area, called it Mustajoki, black river. To tell the two apart, Russians usually call the river Moskva-reka.

The first stone bridge across it, the Bolshoy Kamenny Bridge, was built in 1692. The Vodootvodny Canal, dug in the 1780s, created the island opposite the Kremlin that Muscovites informally call Bolotny Ostrov, Bog Island. Dams built in 1785, 1836 and 1878 failed to keep the river navigable through summer droughts. The highest recorded water level in central Moscow, 127.25 metres above sea level against a usual 120, was reached in the flood of 1908.

Since the Moscow Canal was completed, in 1932–1937, the river has also carried a share of water from the upper Volga, which has made commercial shipping reliable. The average discharge, Volga water included, rises from 38 cubic metres a second near Zvenigorod to 250 at the mouth. As of 2007 there were 49 bridges over the river and its canals within the city, where it is 120 to 200 metres wide and narrowest under the Kremlin walls. Moscow draws its drinking water from five stations on the river and from the upper Volga reservoirs. The stretch within the city freezes only occasionally, on account of contamination.
mosque-cathedral-of-cordoba: According to traditional accounts, a Visigothic church dedicated to Vincent of Saragossa stood on the site and was shared by Christians and Muslims after the Umayyad conquest; scholars have debated this. The accounts say Abd al-Rahman I bought the Christian half for a hundred thousand dinars, demolished the church and built the mosque, allowing Christians in return to build churches outside the walls. Abd al-Rahman was a fugitive of the Umayyad family overthrown in the Abbasid Revolution of 750, and he founded the Umayyad Emirate in 756 with Córdoba as capital.

Hisham I added a shelter for the muezzin in 793, and Abd al-Rahman II extended the prayer hall eight bays to the south between 833 and 848, making it 64 metres long. Abd al-Rahman III added a minaret, finished in 958, and his son al-Hakam II a richly decorated mihrab and maqsurah, finished in 971. The hypostyle hall served for the daily prayers and Friday sermon, and for teaching and legal cases. The courtyard, now the Patio de los Naranjos, was planted with citrus and palm trees and had fountains for ritual ablutions. After the caliphate collapsed early in the 11th century the mosque was looted and damaged in the civil conflict that followed, and no more expansions were made.

Ferdinand III of Castile conquered Córdoba in 1236, and the mosque became a cathedral dedicated to the Virgin Mary, with its first mass on 29 June. For centuries it changed little. In 1523, under Bishop Alonso de Manrique, a Renaissance nave and transept began to rise in its middle, over the opposition of the city council, after the cathedral chapter won the permission of Charles V. He is reputed to have said, on seeing the result, that the builders had destroyed something unique in the world. The old minaret was encased in a bell tower built between 1593 and 1617.

The original mihrab was uncovered in 1816, and restoration between 1879 and 1923 recovered more of the Islamic structure. It was declared a National Monument in 1882 and a World Heritage Site in 1984, and it strongly influenced later Moorish architecture. The poet Muhammad Iqbal visited in 1931–32 and wrote The Mosque of Cordoba.
mosque-of-ibn-tulun: The mosque was commissioned by Ahmad ibn Tulun, the Abbasid governor of Egypt from 868 to 884, who made himself a de facto autonomous ruler over Egypt and parts of the Levant. In 870 he began a new administrative capital, al-Qata'i, north-west of Fustat and al-'Askar, and the mosque served as its congregational mosque, the third in what is now Cairo. Al-Maqrizi says construction began in 876, while an original inscription slab gives the completion as Ramadan 265 AH, April–May 879. According to the 10th-century author Balawi, the architect was a man named al-Nasrani, a non-Muslim, possibly Christian. It stands on a small hill called Gebel Yashkur, and Ibn Tulun's palace, the Dar al-Imara, adjoined it behind the qibla wall.

The design is modelled on the mosques of Samarra, the Abbasid capital where Ibn Tulun had spent much of his early career, making it one of the best surviving examples of Abbasid architecture. A spacious courtyard is surrounded by roofed galleries divided into aisles by pointed arches on brick piers, five aisles deep on the qibla side and two on the others. The arches carry carved stucco in the Samarra styles. A Kufic inscription on a wooden frieze runs nearly 2 kilometres round the walls and reproduces about one fifteenth of the Qur'an, the oldest surviving Islamic monument with religious inscriptions of such length. With its outer enclosure, the ziyada, it covers 26,318 square metres.

The stone minaret has a cuboid base, a cylindrical section and an external spiral staircase. Scholars disagree about its date: K. A. C. Creswell took it as a reconstruction by Sultan Lajin in 1296, while Doris Behrens-Abouseif argues that much of the Tulunid tower survives.

Abbasid forces razed al-Qata'i in 905, leaving only the mosque and the Dar al-Imara, which the mosque's religious function had spared. The Fatimid vizier Badr al-Jamali restored the mosque, and by the 12th century it served as a caravanserai for North African pilgrims bound for the Hijaz. Lajin, in hiding in the ruins after the murder of Sultan Al-Ashraf Khalil, vowed to restore it if he became sultan, and he did in 1296, adding the present fountain and kiosk and a wooden minbar. Under Muhammad Ali in the early 19th century it became a military hospital, salt warehouse, asylum and poorhouse. A government committee began restoration from 1890, and a full restoration was carried out between 2002 and 2004.
mosquito-coast: The Mosquito Coast, also known as Mosquitia or the Mosquito Shore, lies along the coast of eastern Nicaragua and south-eastern Honduras. It takes its name from the Miskito nation and was long dominated by British interests, which knew it as the Mosquito Kingdom. Because it was defined as the domain of that kingdom its extent changed with the kingdom's. The British and Miskito definition covered the whole eastern seaboard of Nicaragua and La Mosquitia in Honduras as far west as the Río Negro or Tinto. Before the arrival of Europeans the area was divided among many small, egalitarian groups.

Christopher Columbus visited the coast briefly on his fourth voyage. Spanish authorities issued licences to conquer the region in 1545, 1562, 1577 and 1594, but no settlement or conquest resulted, and missionary efforts by Franciscans between 1604 and 1675 also failed. The region stayed independent, and English and Dutch privateers found refuge there. Agents of the Providence Island Company made friendly contact from about 1630, and a Miskito leader visited England about 1638 and sealed an alliance. The king's son placed the country under English protection.

In the 19th century Miskito kings renewed the alliance with Britain, with Belize replacing Jamaica as the principal British connection, and George Frederic Augustus I was crowned in Belize in 1816. Between 1820 and 1837 the Scottish confidence trickster Gregor MacGregor, claiming to have been named Cacique of Poyais, sold forged land rights to settlers and investors in Britain and France, and most of the settlers died of tropical diseases.

By the Treaty of Managua of 28 January 1860 Britain transferred suzerainty over the coast between Cabo Gracias a Dios and Greytown to Nicaragua, and the kingdom became an autonomous Mosquito Reserve. Its ruler was confirmed as hereditary chief, not king, advised by a council of 41 members. In November 1894 the coast was militarily incorporated into Nicaragua.

The former Miskito coast of Nicaragua has about 400,000 inhabitants, most of them Miskito, with Creoles, Ladinos, Sumu, Garifuna and Rama. Anglicanism and the Moravian Church gained a significant following there. Under Nicaraguan rule the Miskito kept a degree of autonomy, though with tension between their claims and those of the state, and during Sandinista rule they were allies of the Contras.
mostaganem: Mostaganem is a major port on the Gulf of Arzew in the Mediterranean, 72 km east-northeast of Oran and about 280 km southwest of Algiers. A ravine, the Wadi Ain Sefra, divides the city into a modern eastern quarter and an older western quarter that includes the historic Muslim city of Tidgit. The port and beaches lie in the south. The Ain Sefra flooded the city in 1900, and flooding of the Cheliff River caused damage in later years. The climate is mild and Mediterranean, with more rain in winter than in summer.

Mostaganem is said to correspond to the ancient Punic port of Murustaga, the name by which it was known when it became a Christian bishopric. The name Cartennae, given to a Roman city renamed under the emperor Gallienus, belongs instead to modern Ténès, 50 km to the east. The Zirid dynasty ruled Mostaganem between 973 and 1146. The Almoravid dynasty then conquered it, and it reached its high point of power under Yusuf ibn Tashfin. It was later ruled by the Zayyanid dynasty of Tlemcen, which was conquered by the Marinid dynasty of Fes, until the Zayyanid dynasty took back control of the city.

In the 16th century the town resisted a Spanish invasion but was captured by the Ottoman admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa, and it became a harbour for Mediterranean corsairs as well as an important commercial port. By 1700 it was under Ottoman rule. France took the city in 1833 and established a garrison. In April 1943 the US Navy's D Company arrived to build an amphibious port, and the Allied forces turned the city into the largest base of its kind, with electricity, running water, roads, a hospital and pontoon shops. Algeria became independent in 1962.

Mostaganem is the capital of Mostaganem province and the second-largest city of north-western Algeria after Oran. It had 406,190 inhabitants at the 2019 census. The University of Mostaganem, founded in 1979, is known locally as the University of Abdelhamid Ibn Badis, after a figure of the Muslim reform movements of Algeria. The religious figure Ahmad al-Alawi was born and buried in Mostaganem.
mostar: Mostar stands on the Neretva between Mount Hum and the Velež Mountain. People have lived on the river since prehistory, as fortified enclosures and cemeteries show, and there is evidence of Roman occupation beneath the present town. It is the historical capital of Herzegovina and the administrative centre of Herzegovina-Neretva Canton. The name comes from the mostari, the bridge-keepers who guarded the Old Bridge in the Ottoman era.

The name Mostar first appears in a document of 1474, which refers to a wooden bridge used by traders, soldiers and others. The town was then also the seat of a kadiluk, a district with a regional judge. It lay on the trade route between the Adriatic and the mineral-rich regions of central Bosnia, and the settlement spread to the right bank. The region came under Ottoman rule in 1468. The Ottomans called the place Köprühisar, 'fortress at the bridge', and organised it into the čaršija, the crafts and commercial centre, and the mahala, the residential area.

Austria-Hungary took control of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1878 and held it until 1918, after which Mostar belonged to the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs and then to Yugoslavia. In 1881 it became the seat of the Catholic diocese of Mostar-Duvno. After Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence in April 1992, the Yugoslav People's Army besieged the town following clashes with Croat forces, and Mostar became the capital of the Croatian Republic of Herzeg-Bosnia. The Old Bridge was destroyed in the war. Its reconstruction began in 1999 and was mostly complete by spring 2004, funded by donations from Spain, the United States, Turkey, Italy, the Netherlands and Croatia.

The Old Bridge, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, was commissioned by Suleiman in the 16th century and is considered an exemplary piece of Islamic architecture in the Balkans. The city also has an Italianate Franciscan church, the Ottoman Muslibegovića house, the Dalmatian Ćorović House and an Orthodox cathedral built as a gift from the Sultan.
mosul: Mosul stands on the Tigris, and the ruins of the ancient Assyrian city of Nineveh lie on its east side. The Arabic name Mawsil means linking point, or Junction City, and its strategic and central location made it a hub of trade and travel. Assyrians still call the whole city Nineveh. Xenophon mentions a small Assyrian town called Mépsila on the Tigris in 401 BCE, though it may be safer to identify it with Iski Mosul, about 30 kilometres north, where the Sasanian centre of Budh-Ardhashir was built six centuries later. The area was part of Assyria from as early as the 25th century BCE.

After the Muslim conquests of the mid-7th century, Arab, Kurdish and Turkic peoples gradually settled in the region. In the late 9th century the Turkic dynasts Ishaq ibn Kundaj and his son Muhammad seized Mosul, and in 893 it came again under direct Abbasid control. In the early 10th century the Arab Hamdanid dynasty took it. Under Abdallah ibn Hamdan and his son Nasir al-Dawla the Hamdanids expanded their control over Upper Mesopotamia, first as Abbasid governors and later as de facto independent rulers. A century later the Uqaylid dynasty supplanted them. In 969 the geographer Ibn Hawqal called it a fine town with excellent markets.

In the 13th century Mosul was a wealthy capital, first of the Zengids and then of Badr al-Din Lu'lu', and made luxury brass vessels inlaid with silver. Of all medieval Islamic artefacts, Mosul brasswork has the most inscriptions. The Andalusian geographer Ibn Sa'id, who passed through about 1250, is the only contemporary source to mention the industry. Sultan Suleiman captured Mosul from Safavid Persia in 1538 and the city was governed by a pasha. It was famed for its walls, with seven gates, a hospital and a covered market. British forces occupied it in October 1918. Turkey contested the mandate, and in 1926 an agreement brokered by the League of Nations confirmed Iraq's possession.

Mosul is the capital of Nineveh Governorate in northern Iraq. Its people are mostly Arabs, with Kurds, Assyrians, Turkmens and Shabaks, and Sunni Islam is the largest religion, and there are many Christians and Yazidis. The local dialect is North Mesopotamian Arabic, called Maslawi. The city has historic mosques, Christian sites and synagogues, and the University of Mosul. The metropolitan area spreads over both banks of the Tigris.
mot-god: Mot, also called Maweth, was the Canaanite god of death and the underworld, known at Ugarit and in Phoenicia. His name, written mt in Ugaritic, belongs to a large family of words for death across the Semitic and Afro-Asiatic languages, among them Arabic mawt, Hebrew mot or mavet, Akkadian mutu, Ge'ez mot and Hausa mutuwa. The main source for him is the texts found at Ugarit; he also appears in the surviving fragments of Philo of Byblos's Greek translation of the Phoenician writer Sanchuniathon.

In the Ugaritic texts Mot is a son of El. Baal, also called Hadad, instructs his messengers that Mot lives in a city named Mirey, that a pit is his throne and filth the land of his inheritance, and warns them not to come near him, lest he take them like a lamb in his mouth. Mot answers that his appetite is like that of lions in the wilderness and of dolphins in the sea, and threatens to devour Baal. Gaps in the tablets leave the next part obscure, but Mot seems to carry out his threat, or to believe he has done so; the sun goddess Shapash joins Anat in burying Baal.

Anat then seizes Mot, splits him with a blade, winnows him in a sieve, burns him, grinds him under a millstone and scatters what remains over a field for the birds. El dreams that Baal lives and, as the land has dried up, sends Shapash to bring him back. Seven years later Mot returns, seeking vengeance and complaining that Baal has given him his own brothers to eat. The two fight in single combat until Shapash warns Mot that El will overturn his throne, and the conflict ends.

In the Phoenician account preserved by Eusebius, Muth is a son of El who after his death is deified and called Thanatos and Pluto. Sanchuniathon's creation myth names a distinct Mot, a kind of mud or watery decay from which the seeds of creation came. In the Hebrew Bible death is sometimes personified, as in Habakkuk 2:5 and Job 18:13. A few scholars have proposed that Passover began as a rite tied to the myth of Mot and Baal; others reject this and see the biblical authors as deliberately overturning the myth for an audience that knew it.
motagua-river: The Motagua River is 486 kilometres long and rises in the Western Highlands of Guatemala. It runs in an easterly direction along the Atlantic slope to the Gulf of Honduras, passing through 14 of Guatemala's departments and seven distinct ecoregions, and 29 other major rivers flow into it. Its basin covers 12,670 square kilometres and is the largest in Guatemala. The final few kilometres form part of the Guatemala-Honduras border, and the mouth opens at El Quetzalito Beach. The valley also marks the Motagua Fault, the tectonic boundary between the North American and the Caribbean plates, which has been the source of several major earthquakes in Guatemala.

The valley holds the only known source of jadeitite in Mesoamerica. The green jade used by the Aztec and Maya peoples was rediscovered in the 1950s by the American geologist William Foshag, who was directed by a local tomato farmer. The rarer blue-green jade used by the Olmec was rediscovered further north of the river in 2002. The Olmecs are believed to have first settled in the valley around 3000 BCE and made figures, masks and ornaments from the blue-green jade. The Maya likely settled there around 2000 BCE and made beads and amulets from green jade, used in religious rituals or to signify wealth.

The Maya site of Copán lies along the river, and the important site of Quiriguá is near its north bank, as are smaller sites with jade quarries and workshops. In pre-Columbian times the river was also an important trade route for goods, ideas and people, as jade items and particular pottery methods found across many regions of Mesoamerica indicate.

Pollution is reported to have first affected the river in 2003, when industrial waste from a power plant in Guatemala City was carried down the Río Las Vacas, one of its tributaries, and residents along the river were told not to use the water. The river carries untreated sewage, industrial waste and rubbish from Guatemala City, and the pollution reaches the Caribbean, harming marine protected areas in Honduras and Guatemala and the fishing and tourism of coastal communities. The Guatemalan government built bio-fences to filter waste, and in May 2023 The Ocean Cleanup installed an Interceptor barricade on the river downstream from Guatemala City.
mothers-of-the-plaza-de-mayo: The association arose in response to the abuses of the National Reorganization Process, the military dictatorship under Jorge Rafael Videla. On 30 April 1977 Azucena Villaflor de De Vincenti and about a dozen other mothers walked to the Plaza de Mayo in front of the Casa Rosada. Each mother had thought her child's disappearance a unique case, but while visiting prisons, hospitals and police stations they met others and came to see that the disappearances were systematic. Most came from working-class backgrounds and had little knowledge of politics. In September 1977 they joined the pilgrimage to Our Lady of Luján wearing nappies as headscarves, and afterwards they kept the scarves, embroidered with their children's names and the demand Aparición con Vida.

The women demonstrated on Thursdays, holding photographs of their missing children, and the government dismissed them as las locas, the madwomen. On 10 December 1977 they published a newspaper advertisement listing the names of the missing, and that night Villaflor was kidnapped from her home in Avellaneda. Founders Esther Ballestrino and María Ponce de Bianco, and the French nuns Alice Domon and Léonie Duquet, who supported them, also disappeared. In 2005 forensic anthropologists identified remains from an unmarked grave near Santa Teresita, among them Villaflor and Duquet, and Villaflor's ashes were buried in the Plaza de Mayo.

After civilian government returned in 1983 the Mothers pressed for trials, which led to the Trial of the Juntas in 1985. Since 1986 the movement has been divided into the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo Association, led by Hebe de Bonafini, and the Founding Line. In January 2006 the Association announced a final annual March of Resistance, after the laws that had stopped prosecutions were repealed and declared unconstitutional.

The Mothers were the first major group to organise against the regime's abuses, and they politicised their role as mothers. The group remained women-only, partly so that their voices would not be lost in a male-dominated movement. With the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo they have helped identify children born to mothers who disappeared and were illegally adopted. In 1992 the members of the association received the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought.
motobu-peninsula: The peninsula, Mutubu in Okinawan, lies in the Yanbaru region of Okinawa Island, bounded by Nago Bay to the east, the Haneda Inland Sea to the north and the East China Sea to the west. It is mostly mountainous with a few plains, its north-eastern tip is Cape Bise, and its highest point is Mount Yae, 593 metres high. The Nago fault cuts off its eastern side; the area is made of Paleozoic metamorphic and igneous rocks, with the Pleistocene Ryukyu Group in the north.

In medieval times the peninsula was the centre of power of the kingdom of Hokuzan, and in 1416 it was the scene of the invasion of Hokuzan. In 1609 it saw the first Japanese landing of the invasion of Ryukyu. During the Battle of Okinawa in 1945 it was the scene of heavy fighting, especially on Mount Yae, and it had been mostly secured by United States forces by 10 April 1945. Motobu Airfield, on the peninsula, was decommissioned after 1945. Kanbun Uechi, founder of Uechi-ryū, one of the main karate styles of Okinawa, came from the peninsula.

The peninsula is divided between Motobu, Nago and Nakijin. Its historic sites include Nago Castle and Nakijin Castle, and it hosted Expo '75. Bridges link it to Sesokojima and Yagaji Island, and Iejima lies offshore. The summit of Mount Yae is closed to the public because of a United States military communications tower.
motsu-ji: Mōtsū-ji was founded in 850 by the monk Ennin, known as Jikaku Daishi, when Hiraizumi lay on the frontier between Yamato Japan and the Emishi of the Tōhoku region. In the mid-12th century Fujiwara no Motohira, the second lord of the Northern Fujiwara, built a temple called Enryū-ji on the site, around 1150. His father Fujiwara no Kiyohira, who died in 1128, may have built an earlier Enryū-ji there that burned soon after completion in the war of succession between Motohira and his brother Koretsune.

The main hall of Motohira's temple held a monumental statue of Yakushi Nyōrai, the Buddha of Healing, and statues of the Twelve Divine Generals carved by Unkei with crystal eyes, then a new technique. The hall was brightly painted and adorned with precious woods, gold, silver and jewels, and was surrounded by a lecture hall, a two-storey gate, a bell tower and a sutra repository. Its name placard was written by Fujiwara no Tadamichi. At its height the temple is said to have had 40 buildings and up to 500 subsidiary chapels.

Motohira then ordered a near copy, Kashō-ji, beside it, completed by his son Hidehira, its walls painted with scenes from the Lotus Sutra. After the fall of the Northern Fujiwara every building burned, and the temple lay wholly in ruins by 1226.

The present temple, with a Hondō enshrining Yakushi Nyōrai and a Jogyō-dō meditation hall, was built in the Edo period away from the old foundations and does not reproduce the earlier buildings. The Oizumi-ga-ike pond and its Pure Land garden survive much as they were 800 years ago. Their unknown designer clearly knew the Sakuteiki, an 11th-century treatise on garden making. The pond has two islands and peninsulas, and its beach and rugged rocks are thought to represent a seacoast. Bridges once joined the main hall on the north shore, whose foundations remain, to the central island and the great south gate.

Mōtsū-ji is a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and a Special National Historic Site, and in June 2011 it was listed by UNESCO among the Historic Monuments and Sites of Hiraizumi. The Ennen no Mai dance is performed at its festivals in January, May and November.
motya-charioteer: The figure stands in a swinging contrapposto, right foot forward, left hand on the hip and right arm raised. He wears a very long chiton with a broad flat belt high on the chest. The sculptor made the muscles, genitals and buttocks appear through the sheer cloth. The face is impassive, with puffy lids and almond-shaped eyes, and the hair is rendered as three rows of snail curls below a smooth dome that probably carried a metal cap or helmet. Both arms and the legs below the shins are lost, and the head, broken at the neck, has been reattached.

The statue lay in a layer linked with the destruction of Motya in 397 BCE, so it is older than that. The snail curls are an Archaic feature; bulging veins of the kind on its upper arms were first carved by Pythagoras of Rhegium around 480–470 BCE; and the face resembles the pediment figures of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia. These features mark it as an early work of Classical sculpture.

Its subject is strongly disputed, because it is a Greek work found in a Punic city. Scholars who stress the Punic setting see a Punic priest, and some identify him with Hamilcar I of Carthage, who led the invasion of Sicily that ended at the Battle of Himera in 480 BCE. Others, among them R. R. R. Smith, see a charioteer celebrating a victory at the Panhellenic Games in the charioteer's traditional costume, as worn by the Charioteer of Delphi; Smith explains the very different pose by arguing that the figure is an owner who drove his own chariot.

Those who favour the Greek reading often take the statue as booty from one of the Greek cities of Sicily destroyed in the Carthaginian invasion of 410–404 BCE. Smith argues that this explanation may not be needed, since Motya had a large Greek population and its Punic inhabitants knew Greek culture well.

Archaeologists found it in October 1979 in the north-east of the island, in an open area between a potters' workshop and a sanctuary, filled with rubble that may have formed barricades during the siege of Motya by Dionysius I of Syracuse. It lay on its back with the head detached beside it; the arms, metal fittings and base were missing, and it may have stood in the nearby sanctuary until it was thrown down in the siege. It is in the Museo Giuseppe Whitaker on the island.
moulay-ismail: Moulay Ismail was a son of Sharif ibn Ali, Emir of Tafilalt and first sovereign of the 'Alawi dynasty, whose clan claimed descent from the Prophet Muhammad through Hassan Ad-Dakhil. According to the historian Ibn Zaydan, his mother Mubarka was a black slave of the Saharan Mghafra tribe. He governed the province of Fez and the north of Morocco from 1667 until the death of his half-brother Sultan Moulay Rashid in 1672.

Proclaimed sultan at Fez, Ismail faced rebellions from his nephew Moulay Ahmed ben Mehrez, who claimed the throne until his death in 1687, from his brothers, one of whom took the title King of Tafilalt, and from the Tetouan warlord Khadir Ghaïlan. Around 1677 he began to assert his authority over the whole country. He built his power on the Abid al-Bukhari, or Black Guard, black slaves devoted to him, and on the jaysh tribes, so that the central power relied less on tribes that often rebelled.

He expelled Europeans from Larache, Asilah, Mehdya and Tangier, took thousands of Christians prisoner and nearly took Ceuta. Corsairs based at Salé supplied him with European captives and weapons. He had mixed fortunes against Ottoman Algeria: a large army sent in 1692 was defeated, the Algerians advanced as far as Fez, and the border was fixed at the Moulouya River. His army was routed at the Battle of Chelif in 1701, and a treaty of that year held until his death.

Ismail made Meknes his capital in 1672 and built a citadel and palace complex there, with gates, mosques, gardens, madrasas and more than forty kilometres of walls. Fittings were stripped from the Saadian El Badi Palace in Marrakesh and marble was taken from the Roman ruins at Volubilis. At least 25,000 workers were employed, mostly paid labourers and some conscripted Christian prisoners. Europeans compared him with Louis XIV, and called him the bloody king for his cruelty to Christian slaves.

He died on 22 March 1727 after an illness, having reigned 55 years, the longest reign of any sultan of Morocco. Chroniclers such as Ahmad ibn Khalid al-Nasiri describe his rule as a period of peace after nearly a century of division. After his death his supporters grew so powerful that they enthroned and deposed sultans at will.
moulouya-river: The Moulouya is a river 520 kilometres long in Morocco. Its sources lie on the Ayashi mountain in the Middle Atlas, and it empties into the Mediterranean Sea near Saïdia, in the north-east of the country. Its water level often fluctuates. The river is used for irrigation and is dammed by the Hassan II and Mohamed V Dams. It also receives domestic wastewater from nearby populations and agricultural pollutants from the upper valley of its headwaters.

The river was historically known as Malva, Malua, Malvam, Mulva, Mulucha or Molochath flumen. The names are possibly related to the Semitic root melach or malach, meaning 'salt', and Maurice Besnier suggested that its lower parts were used for salt production, though no material confirmation has been found. From the end of the fourth to the beginning of the third century BCE the Mulucha formed the boundary between the Kingdom of the Mauri to the west and the Kingdom of the Masaesylli to the east, and Livy mentions it under that name.

In the Historia Brittonum, around 828, it appears as the River Malvam along the route of the Scoti from Egypt to Hispania. In Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae, around 1136, Brutus of Troy follows a similar route and passes the River Malvam before entering Mauretania. Before French colonisation the Moulouya was sometimes considered the border between the Regency of Algiers and the dynasties that controlled Morocco, and a battle between the Algerians and the Alawites took place at its ford in 1692.

In the 1920s the Moulouya formed the eastern border of the Rif Republic. A small part of Morocco containing important cities such as Saïdia and Oujda lay east of the river, between it and the border with Algeria. Until 1956 the river also formed the eastern border of the Spanish Protectorate of Morocco.
mound-key: Mound Key lies in Estero Bay near the mouth of the Estero River. The island covers one hundred and twenty-five acres and is a complex of mounds and middens of shell, fish bone and pottery that rises more than 30 feet above the bay. It probably began as a low-lying oyster bar rich in marine food. As the Calusa population grew, their food waste was heaped into the middens that form the island, and they built a system of mounds, water courts and canals whose features still survive. Such mounds were not simply refuse heaps: they served as displays of power, religious monuments and burial places.

Calusa culture at Mound Key has been carbon-dated to 1150 BCE. The island served for many years as the ceremonial centre of a Calusa kingdom that reached from Tampa Bay south to the Ten Thousand Islands and east to Lake Okeechobee, and most researchers believe it was the capital, Calos. Here King Carlos held the wedding of his sister, later baptised as Antonia, to Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, a political marriage meant to secure an alliance with the Spanish.

The Spanish built a fort and settlement on the island, and the Jesuit Juan Rogel founded the mission of San Antón de Carlos. Conflict with the Calusa was frequent, and the Spanish abandoned the island in 1569 after the alliance broke apart. Disease brought by the Spanish and warfare ended Calusa civilisation around 1750. In 2020 archaeologists confirmed that Mound Key was the site of Fort San Antón de Carlos, the oldest known North American example of tabby concrete.

Pirates, Cuban, Portuguese and Spanish fishermen and American pioneers later used the island. Frank Johnson and his wife received a homestead there in 1891 and sold the island in 1905 to the Koreshans, a utopian community that had settled nearby in 1894. After the death of their leader Cyrus Teed in 1908 their numbers declined, and in 1961 they gave the key to the state.

Mound Key Archaeological State Park manages one hundred and thirteen of the island's acres and is administered by the Koreshan State Historic Site. The Mound Key Site was added to the National Register of Historic Places on 12 August 1970. The island can be reached only by boat, and a trail of 0.75 miles crosses two large shell mounds.
moundville-archaeological-site: The site stands on a bluff overlooking the Black Warrior River in Hale County, near the city of Tuscaloosa. Moundville and its affiliated settlements lay in a stretch of the valley beginning below the fall line and running about 40 km downriver, where the transition between the Piedmont and the Coastal Plain gave the land a wide range of forests and wildlife. The palisade enclosed three sides of the town; the river bluff guarded the fourth.

The largest platform mounds stand on the northern edge of the plaza and grow smaller towards the south. Mound B, the tallest, is a steep pyramid 18 m high with two ramps. Archaeologists read the plan as a sociogram: ranked clans occupied precincts whose standing was shown by the size and position of their paired mounds, the highest on the north side. Remote sensing has shown that the plaza held the remains of hundreds of buildings.

The people of Moundville grew maize in surplus, which supported a dense population and craft specialists. Copper, mica, galena and marine shell were brought in from afar, and the site is known for its pottery, stonework and embossed copper, including the locally made Hemphill engraved ware. Christopher Peebles, studying the burials excavated in the 1930s, found that some children were buried with rare ornaments and concluded that the highest status was inherited.

People began to leave in the 14th century, when mound building stopped and single-mound sites were founded nearby; they still returned to bury their dead. Clarence Bloomfield Moore dug extensively in 1905 and 1906, and looters damaged the mounds over the next two decades. Walter B. Jones of the Alabama Museum of Natural History led the effort to buy the land, and workers of the Civilian Conservation Corps stabilised the mounds in the 1930s.

The University of Alabama Museums administer a park of 75 ha with 29 platform mounds around the plaza, a museum named after Jones and an archaeological laboratory. The site became a National Historic Landmark in 1964. In 2024 the human remains excavated there and many of the objects buried with them were returned to the tribes that claim descent from its people.
mount-aragats: Aragats is an isolated volcanic massif with four summits, standing about 40 kilometres northwest of Yerevan. Its northern summit, at 4,090 metres, is the highest point of the Lesser Caucasus and of Armenia. The other peaks are the western at 3,995 metres, the eastern at 3,908 and the southern at 3,888. The massif is bounded by the Kasagh River on the east, the Akhurian on the west, the Ararat Plain on the south and the Shirak Plain on the north. It is about 200 kilometres around and covers some 6,000 square kilometres, around a fifth of the area of Armenia.

The volcano was built in four phases, from a first phase possibly 2.5 million years ago to a fourth between 0.56 and 0.45 million years ago, and its lava flows range in age from the middle Pleistocene to 3,000 BCE. Rock paintings in the Kasagh River valley may date to the early Holocene, and petroglyphs showing animals at Aghavnatun were possibly made between the 4th and 1st millennia BCE. According to Armenian tradition the name means Ara's throne, after the hero Ara the Handsome, though this is almost certainly a folk etymology. The early medieval historian Movses Khorenatsi says the mountain was named after Aramaneak, son of the patriarch Hayk.

A later name, Alagöz, meaning variegated eye in Turkish and Azerbaijani, was widely used until the mid-20th century. Legend tells that Aragats and Mount Ararat were sisters who parted after a quarrel, and that Gregory the Illuminator, who converted Armenia to Christianity in the early 4th century, prayed on the peak by the light of a lamp hanging from heaven without a rope. Both Aragats and Ararat are held sacred by Armenians. A 4th-century mausoleum of the Arsacid dynasty stands at the village of Aghtsk, and the fortress of Amberd and the 11th-century Vahramashen Church lie on the slopes at 2,300 metres.

Glaciers in the crater, which covered 5.5 to 5.8 square kilometres in 1896, have retreated since. The Aragats Cosmic Ray Research Station, near Lake Kari at about 3,200 metres, was founded in 1943 by the brothers Artem Alikhanian and Abram Alikhanov. The Byurakan Observatory, established in 1946 by Victor Ambartsumian on the southern slopes, made Armenia one of the world's centres of astrophysics in the 20th century. The settlements on the slopes include Ashtarak, Aparan and Talin, and the mountain appears on the coat of arms of Gyumri.
mount-ararat: Mount Ararat, officially Mount Ağrı and called Masis in Armenian, is a dormant compound volcano in easternmost Turkey, between the provinces of Ağrı and Iğdır and between the Aras and Murat rivers. It has two cones, Greater Ararat at 5,137 metres, the highest peak in Turkey and the Armenian highlands, and Little Ararat at 3,896 metres. A lava plateau at about 2,600 metres separates them. The massif forms a near-quadripoint between Turkey, Iran, Armenia and the Nakhchivan exclave of Azerbaijan.

The volcano has erupted several times. Archaeological evidence shows that explosive eruptions from its north-western flank around 2500 to 2400 BCE destroyed and buried at least one settlement of the Kura–Araxes culture. Oral histories speak of an eruption in 550 BCE, and a definite eruption and a landslide occurred in 1840. The name Ararat is the Biblical Hebrew rendering of Urartu, the Iron Age kingdom, and none of the peoples of the region traditionally used it for the mountain. Robert W. Thomson argued that it came to be so called through confusion with Ayrarat, the central province of ancient Armenia.

Since the 11th century the mountain has been linked to the Book of Genesis, which says that Noah's Ark landed on the mountains of Ararat. Scholars generally agree that the phrase meant the wider region of Urartu, and the Vulgate renders it as the mountains of Armenia. Armenians began to identify Ararat as the ark's landing place in the 11th century, and the ark on Ararat appears on world maps from that time. Searches for the ark have continued since the 19th century, and scholars regard them as an example of pseudoarchaeology.

The Armenian Apostolic Church historically opposed ascents on religious grounds. The 13th-century missionary William of Rubruck wrote that many had tried to climb it and none had succeeded. The first recorded ascent took place on 9 October 1829, when the naturalist Friedrich Parrot of the University of Dorpat climbed it with the writer Khachatur Abovian as interpreter and guide, assigned by Catholicos Yeprem. Later climbers included Otto Wilhelm Hermann von Abich in 1845 and James Bryce in 1876.

Though outside the borders of modern Armenia, the mountain is the principal national symbol of Armenia and has been held sacred by Armenians. Movses Khorenatsi linked the Genesis flood to the Armenian myth of origin, writing that Hayk, a descendant of Noah's son Japheth, returned to the area round Ararat and founded the Armenian nation. After the Armenian genocide of 1915 it also came to stand for the lost homeland. Ararat has appeared on the coat of arms of Armenia since 1918, together with the ark, and the arms were readopted in 1992.
mount-athos: The Athos peninsula is the easternmost leg of Chalkidiki, in central Macedonia. It runs 50 km into the Aegean Sea at a width of 7 to 12 km and covers 335.6 km2. The mountain itself has steep, densely forested slopes rising to 2,033 m. Unlike Sithonia and Kassandra, the peninsula is a geological continuation of the Rhodope Mountains. Sweet chestnut, holm oak and black pine grow on it, and at least 35 plant species are endemic.

In antiquity the mountain was Athos and the peninsula Akte. Herodotus records that in 492 BCE a storm wrecked the Persian fleet of Mardonius off the peninsula, with a loss of 300 ships and 20,000 men, and that Xerxes I had a canal dug across the isthmus for his fleet in 483 BCE.

According to Athonite tradition the Virgin Mary was blown ashore here on her way to Cyprus, blessed the mountain and asked her son for it as her garden, which is why it is held to be closed to other women. The cities named by Herodotus and Strabo, among them Sane and Akrothoon, are believed to have been deserted by the time monks began to arrive. Some monks may have come from Egypt after the Islamic conquest of the 7th century, building huts of wood with roofs of straw.

Monastic life grew considerably under the Byzantine emperors, who granted the settlements privileges and protection. In 963 Athanasius the Athonite founded the Great Lavra with the support of Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas, marking the move from scattered hermitages to large communal monasteries and providing a model for later ones. Rulers across the Orthodox world gave patronage, among them those of the Kingdom of Georgia and various Slavic states, so that monasteries of different traditions arose.

After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 the monasteries kept working under Ottoman rule, with some autonomy, although they met periods of hardship. In the 19th century the monastic population grew with donations from Russia, Serbia and Romania. In the 20th century the peninsula was brought into the modern Greek state with its autonomous monastic status.

The mountain and most of the peninsula are governed as an autonomous region of Greece by the monastic community, which is under the direct jurisdiction of the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. By Greek law and religious tradition women may not enter. Visitors need a permit called a diamonitirion and usually arrive by boat from Ouranoupoli. The monastic community was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1988.
mount-batten: Mount Batten is a rocky outcrop 24 metres tall on a peninsula about 600 metres long in Plymouth Sound. It was once called How Stert and takes its present name from Sir William Batten, MP and Surveyor of the Navy. To the west the Mount Batten Breakwater, built by the Cattewater Commissioners between 1878 and 1881 at a cost of £20,000 and 915 feet long, shelters the Cattewater and Sutton Harbour. Before it and the Plymouth Breakwater of 1841 were built the peninsula suffered heavy erosion, and its isthmus was breached in 1633 and 1634.

Excavations reported by Barry Cunliffe in 1988 showed that the site traded with the continent from the late Bronze Age, peaked in the late Iron Age and remained in use through the Roman era. It seems to have been a main route by which goods such as wine entered Britain, and it has been suggested as the trading centre Ictis named by Diodorus Siculus. Three British-made bronze mirrors found there were lost in the Plymouth Blitz.

In the later Middle Ages the peninsula became a defensive point for Plymouth, commanding the Cattewater, and in 1652 the circular artillery fort of Mount Batten Tower was built. Quarrying from 1839 to the mid-1860s supplied stone for the steam yards at Devonport and threatened the tower until the landowner, Lord Morley, restricted it after a petition from 53 citizens. Seaplane trials began in 1913, and the air station was RNAS Cattewater, then RAF Cattewater and from 1928 RAF Mount Batten. T. E. Lawrence served there under the name Aircraftsman Shaw, and Royal Australian Air Force Sunderland flying boats flew from it in the Battle of the Atlantic. The RAF left in 1986.

After the Plymouth Development Corporation took over the site, the peninsula gained a marina and a centre for sea sports, and the refurbished breakwater reopened to the public in 1995. Mount Batten Tower is a Scheduled Ancient Monument. Nearby lies the Cattewater Wreck, a merchant ship of the early 16th century and the first wreck protected under the Protection of Wrecks Act 1973.
mount-bischoff: Mount Bischoff stands beside Savage River National Park, close to the town of Waratah. It was named in the early nineteenth century after James Bischoff, chairman of the Van Diemen's Land Company. Between 1900 and mid-1940 the mine on its face was linked to the Emu Bay Railway by the Waratah Branch, which ran from Guildford Junction to Waratah.

The first operator of the mine was the Mount Bischoff Tin Mining Company, which worked the ore with a sluice fed by water from the top of the waterfall at Waratah. In June 1883 the mine installed one of the first hydro-electric generators in Australia, lighting its offices, workshop and manager's house. The easy ore was exhausted by 1893, when sluicing stopped, and mining went on in an open cut on the face of the mountain and underground.

John Dunlop Millen, manager from 1907 to 1919, was credited with modernising the mine's facilities. The underground mine closed in 1914, and surface working ended after the price of tin slumped in 1929. The Commonwealth Government reopened the mine in 1942 to support the war effort, but it closed again in 1947.

In 2008 Metals X Limited, a Perth-based company, decided through its subsidiary Bluestone Mines Tasmania, operator of the Renison Bell tin mine, to work the remaining ore. A large open cut took in all the old workings, and the ore was trucked 80 kilometres to the Renison Bell plant to be blended with its own. Reserves were then estimated at 845,000 tonnes grading 1.20 percent tin, and in 2009/10 the open cut yielded 198,000 tonnes of ore and 6,267 tonnes of tin in concentrate. By 2015 the mine was on care and maintenance, while exploration continued.
mount-cameroon: Mount Cameroon is a stratovolcano in the Southwest Region of Cameroon, next to the city of Buea and near the Gulf of Guinea. It is also called Cameroon Mountain or Fako, the name of its higher peak, and has an indigenous name, Mongo ma Ndemi, meaning Mountain of Greatness. It belongs to the Cameroon Volcanic Line, a belt of oceanic and continental volcanoes about 1,600 kilometres long that stretches from Pagalu Island in the Gulf of Guinea to northern Cameroon and includes Lake Nyos, the site of a disaster in 1986.

The volcano is elliptical, about 50 by 35 kilometres, and sits on a horst of Precambrian granite and gneiss. Dating along the line gives ages from about 51.8 million years to the present, and Mount Cameroon is the youngest and the only presently active volcano on it.

Historical records document major eruptions in 1909, 1922, 1925, 1954, 1959, 1982, 1999, 2000 and 2012. The eruption that began on 28 April 1909 and lasted into June caused the German colonial government of Kamerun to move temporarily from Buea to Douala. In 1922 a flank eruption sent lava to the Atlantic coast, and in 1999 the lava came within 200 metres of the sea.

The 1959 eruption, in February and March, ran from a fissure on the north-eastern flank and produced a lava flow about 7.75 kilometres long. The eruptions of 1999 and 2000 created more than 100 cones and vents. The volcano has erupted basanite and alkali basalt, and it counts among Africa's most active, with eight major eruptions in the twentieth century. English explorer Mary Kingsley was one of the first Europeans to climb it and described her expedition in her 1897 book Travels in West Africa.

Lowland rain forest covers the lower slopes up to 800 metres, giving way to montane forest, scrub and grassland, with sub-alpine grassland above 3,000 metres. Much of the lowland forest has been turned into agriculture, including oil palm plantations. Forest elephants, chimpanzees, drills and two endemic birds live on the mountain. Mount Cameroon National Park, created in 2009, covers 581.23 square kilometres. In 2022 the International Union of Geological Sciences listed the volcano among its 100 geological heritage sites. Hikers climb the peak often, and the annual Mount Cameroon Race of Hope scales it.
mount-carmel: The name Mount Carmel is used for three areas: the whole range of about 39 km that runs to Jenin, its northwestern 19 km, or the headland at the northwestern end. The range is 6.5 to 8 kilometres wide and slopes gradually to the southwest, while its northeastern face forms a steep ridge 546 metres high. The Jezreel Valley lies immediately to the northeast. The range is a natural barrier, as the valley is a natural passageway, and together they have shaped migration and invasion through the Levant.

Between 1930 and 1932 Dorothy Garrod excavated caves and rock shelters at el-Wad, el-Tabun and Es Skhul, finding Neanderthal and early modern human remains, among them the Neanderthal female known as Tabun I. The Tabun cave has the longest stratigraphic record in the region, spanning 600,000 years or more of human activity. In Roman and Byzantine times a belt of Jewish villages flourished across the range, including Horvat Sumaqa, with its monumental synagogue of the 3rd and 4th centuries CE.

The mountain was held sacred in antiquity. Thutmose III lists a holy headland among his Canaanite territories, and if this is Carmel, as some Egyptologists believe, the mountain was sacred from at least the 15th century BCE. A Greek inscription published by Michael Avi-Yonah in 1952 is dedicated to Heliopolitan Zeus of Carmel, and Suetonius states that an oracle there was consulted by Vespasian.

In the Books of Kings, Elijah challenges 450 prophets of Baal to a contest at an altar on the mountain, to show which deity truly ruled Israel. When the prophets of Baal failed to light their sacrifice, Elijah had water poured over his own and prayed, and fire consumed it. The Druze venerate Elijah, and their towns of Daliyat al-Karmel and Isfiya stand on the eastern slopes.

A Catholic order, the Carmelites, was founded on the mountain in 1209 and named for it. Its founder is unknown; the early Rule, given by Albert, the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, calls him only Brother B. The monastery, dedicated to Mary as Star of the Sea, often changed hands during the Crusades, was made a hospital by Napoleon in 1799 and was destroyed by the pasha of Damascus in 1821.

Haifa lies on the northern and western slopes, and the range is a UNESCO biosphere reserve. The caves of Tabun, Jamal, el-Wad and Skhul were added to the World Heritage List in 2012. The mountain is also sacred to the Baháʼí Faith: the remains of the Báb were laid to rest there on 21 March 1909, and the Shrine of the Báb and the Baháʼí World Centre stand on its slope.
mount-cithaeron: Cithaeron, also written Kithairon, is a mountain range about sixteen kilometres long in Central Greece. It forms the physical boundary between the region of Boeotia in the north and Attica in the south. It is mainly composed of limestone and rises to 1,409 metres. The north-east side of the range is formed by the mountain Pastra.

The range was the scene of many events in Greek mythology and was especially sacred to Dionysus. In Euripides' Bacchae, Dionysus carries out his dances and rites on Cithaeron with his bacchants, his priestesses. Oedipus was exposed on the mountain, while Actaeon and Pentheus were both dismembered on its slopes, and Heracles or Alcathous hunted and killed the Lion of Cithaeron there. In one tale the mountain, personified as Cithairon, entered a singing contest with Helikon, judged by the Muses. Cithairon won and was adorned with garlands. The angry Helikon smashed one of the large rocks on his own slopes.

The people of Plataea personified the mountain as their primal king. As the account puts it, they knew of no king except Asopus and, before him, Cithaeron, who gave his name to the mountain as Asopus did to the river. In historic times the mountain was the backdrop to the Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE and the scene of much skirmishing before the battle itself. Later, because the mountain formed the disputed natural border between Athens and Thebes, fortifications were built at both Plataea and Erythrai. In the Middle Ages the village of Myoupolis on its slopes was the site of a monastery founded by Meletios the Younger.
mount-damavand: Mount Damavand is a stratovolcano standing in the middle of the Alborz range, near the southern coast of the Caspian Sea. It lies in Amol County, Mazandaran Province, 66 kilometres north-east of Tehran. It is the highest peak in Western Asia and the highest volcano in Asia. The Alborz rises from the collision of the Arabian and Eurasian tectonic plates, a collision that does not usually produce volcanoes, but recent research suggests that a hot region created by it caused this one to form.

Volcanic activity in the area began in the Pleistocene, almost 1.78 million years ago, and the present cone has been built over about 600,000 years. Its steep cone is made of ash and lava flows, mainly trachyte, andesite and basalt. Its last eruption was around 5300 BCE. Hot springs at the base and on the flanks, and fumaroles near the summit, show that heat remains beneath it.

Damavand holds a special place in Persian mythology. In Zoroastrian texts the three-headed dragon Aži Dahāka was chained inside the mountain, to stay there until the end of the world. A later version of the legend puts the tyrant Zahhak in a cave on the mountain after Kāveh and Fereydūn defeated him. In the Iranian legend of Arash, as recounted by Bal'ami, the hero shot his magical arrow from Damavand to mark the border of Iran during its dispute with Turan.

In Persian poetry and literature the mountain became a symbol of Iranian resistance against despotism and foreign rule. Mohammad Taqī Bahār's poem Damāvand opens with the line, in translation, O white giant with feet in chains, O dome of the world, O Damāvand.

Glaciers survive on the upper slopes, the largest being the Yakhar Glacier, and the meltwater feeds some of the few permanently flowing rivers in Iran. Its slopes shelter brown trout in the streams, wild goat, Persian leopard and Syrian brown bear, and an iris named after the mountain. The Larijan hot spring on its flank is bottled for sale across Iran.

Climbers use at least 16 known routes to the summit. The southern route is the most popular, with a shelter at 4,220 metres. Since 2008 the day of the Tirgan festival has been named Damavand National Day, and the mountain was the first natural site registered as national heritage in Iran.
mount-ebal: Mount Ebal is one of the two mountains near the city of Nablus, biblical Shechem, in the West Bank. It forms the northern side of the valley in which Nablus lies, and Mount Gerizim forms the southern side. It rises to 935 metres above sea level, some 60 metres higher than Gerizim, is about 17 square kilometres in area and consists mainly of limestone. Its slopes hold several large caverns, probably once quarries, and at the base to the north there are several tombs. On the higher western part are the ruins of massive walls called Al-Kal'ah, and to the east a site called Kunaisah.

In Deuteronomy 11:29 Moses directs that, once the Israelites enter the land, the blessing is to be put on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. In the Masoretic Text and the Septuagint version of Deuteronomy 27, there is an instruction to build an altar of uncut stones on Ebal, to whiten stones with lime, to make peace offerings and to write the words of the law on the stones. The Samaritan Pentateuch and a Qumran fragment place this instruction at Mount Gerizim instead, which the Samaritans hold holy. Some scholars think the Samaritan reading probably more accurate, and a study of 2018 argued that the Gerizim reading is older and the Ebal reading a later, polemical revision.

The tribes of Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph and Benjamin were to stand on Gerizim, and Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan and Naphtali on Ebal, where twelve curses were pronounced by the Levite priesthood and answered by the people with Amen. In the Book of Joshua, after the Battle of Ai, Joshua builds an altar of unhewn stones, the Law of Moses is written on stones and the people pronounce blessings and curses as Deuteronomy instructs. Scholars debate whether that account joins two earlier ones, and generally hold that Joshua's sources are older than Deuteronomy.

In 1980 the Israeli archaeologist Adam Zertal discovered a structure on Mount Ebal, at northern el-Burnat, during the Manasseh Hill Country Survey. The University of Haifa and the Israel Exploration Society excavated it over eight seasons from 1982 to 1989 and found scarabs, seals and animal bones of the Iron Age I period. Most archaeologists now agree that it was a site of early Israelite cultic activity. Zertal proposed that it was the altar that Joshua built to Yahweh, where the Covenant was renewed, but a number of archaeologists have disputed this identification.
mount-erciyes: Mount Erciyes is a large stratovolcano in Kayseri Province, surrounded by many monogenetic vents and lava domes and one maar. Most of its bulk is formed by lava flows of andesitic and dacitic composition. It is the most voluminous volcano of central Anatolia and rises about 900 metres above the Sultansazlığı basin. Its height is given as 3,864, 3,918 or 3,917 metres. Kayseri lies 15 to 25 kilometres to the north, and some lava domes lie within the city limits.

The volcano is part of the Central Anatolian Volcanic Province, which formed where the Anatolian block was squeezed between the Eurasian, African and Arabian plates. Volcanism there began in the Miocene. A volcano named Koç Dağ formed first, then large explosive eruptions made a caldera, and in the Pleistocene Erciyes itself grew inside it. Part of the summit later collapsed towards the east.

The name Erciyes is the Turkish adoption of the Greek Argaios, meaning bright or white. It was spelled Erciyas until vowel harmony changed it in the 1940s to 1960s. Assyrian sources name a mountain and god Aškašipa, and the Bronze Age Mount Harhara of Anatolian inscriptions, which may be Erciyes. The Hittites left rock carvings and an artificial tunnel on the mountain.

The geographer Strabo said the mountain was forested in antiquity and mentioned the view from its summit, from which climbers were said to see both the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Strabo and Claudian report volcanic activity, and Roman coins found in Cappadocia show the mountain smoking, but these may refer to gas from swamps. The last eruptions occurred in the early Holocene. In the eleventh century Lazaros of Mount Galesios is said to have climbed it in midwinter singing psalms. A story of Cis Hatun tells that her wedding dress, left on the mountain, forms its snow cover.

The volcano is considered dormant. One regular glacier remains and is receding, and the volcano was glaciated in the Pleistocene. Its eruption 2.8 million years ago produced the Valibaba Tepe ignimbrite, the last of the Cappadocian ignimbrites. The Erciyes Ski Resort lies in the Üçker valley, and the wetlands of the Sultansazlığı basin are protected under the Ramsar Convention.
mount-etna: Etna is a stratovolcano in the Metropolitan City of Catania, between Messina and Catania, above the convergent boundary of the African and Eurasian plates. It covers 1,190 square kilometres, with a base 140 kilometres around, and is about two and a half times the height of Vesuvius, the next largest of Italy's four active volcanoes. Its fertile volcanic soils carry vineyards and orchards on the lower slopes and the Plain of Catania. Most eruptions come from five summit craters, while the flanks hold more than 300 vents.

Volcanic activity began about 500,000 years ago under the sea off the ancient Sicilian coast. A catastrophic collapse of the eastern flank, thought to have happened around 8,000 years ago, left the Valle del Bove and may have caused a tsunami in the eastern Mediterranean. The mountain is moving towards the sea at an average of 14 millimetres a year.

The first recorded eruption is reported by Diodorus Siculus at about 1400 BCE. An eruption in 396 BCE reportedly stopped the Carthaginians advancing on Syracuse. A violent summit eruption in 122 BCE brought tephra that collapsed roofs in Catania, and the Roman government exempted its people from taxes for ten years. Virgil probably described an eruption at first hand in the Aeneid. The name may derive from the Greek verb meaning to burn, or from a Phoenician word for furnace. Greek and Roman myth placed the forge of Vulcan, or Hephaestus, beneath it and said that Zeus trapped the monster Typhon under the mountain.

The mountain was also called Mongibello, a name tied to Arthurian romance, in which it became the otherworld realm of Morgan le Fay and Arthur. The eruption that began on 11 March 1669 destroyed at least ten villages and reached Catania's walls on 15 April, filling its harbour. Reports of up to 15,000 dead are not supported by contemporary accounts, which mention no deaths, and only 77 deaths are attributed with certainty to Etna's eruptions. In 1928 lava almost completely destroyed Mascali, and the regime of Benito Mussolini used the rebuilding for propaganda. Operation Hot Rock diverted lava from Zafferana Etnea in 1992.

Etna remains one of the world's most active volcanoes and is almost constantly active. It has been designated a Decade Volcano by the United Nations and was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in June 2013. The Circumetnea railway, built between 1889 and 1895, runs 110 kilometres round it from Catania to Riposto, and the Sapienza Refuge on the south side is the base for a cableway and ski slopes.
mount-everest: Mount Everest lies in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas, and its summit marks part of the China–Nepal border. A joint survey by Nepalese and Chinese authorities in 2020 measured its height as 8,848.86 metres above sea level. Because that height is taken from the geoid, which approximates sea level, climbers ascend only part of it; the nearest sea, the Bay of Bengal, is almost 700 kilometres away. The mountain has an ice cap climate, with every month averaging well below freezing, and very little native life: a moss grows at 6,480 metres, and a small black jumping spider has been found as high as 6,700 metres.

The Nepali name is Sagarmāthā, literally 'head in the sky'. The Tibetan name Qomolangma means 'holy mother'; it was first recorded in a Chinese transcription in the 1721 Kangxi Atlas and reached the West in 1733 on a map by the French geographer D'Anville. The official Chinese form is a phonetic rendering of the Tibetan, adopted after a decree of May 1952 that chose a single name.

In 1802 the British began the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India to fix the positions, heights and names of the world's highest mountains. The teams, using theodolites that each weighed 500 kilograms and needed 12 men to carry, reached the Himalayan foothills by the 1830s. Nepal, suspicious of British intentions, refused their requests to enter, so the surveyors worked from the Terai to the south, where torrential rain and malaria killed three survey officers and forced two others to retire.

Nepal also barred foreigners from climbing, so the first recorded attempts were British expeditions on the North Ridge from Tibet. The reconnaissance of 1921 reached 7,000 metres on the North Col. In 1922 climbers went above 8,000 metres for the first time, reaching 8,321 metres. On 8 June 1924 George Mallory and Andrew Irvine made a final summit attempt and never returned, and it remains debated whether they reached the top. Tenzing Norgay, who had reached 8,595 metres with the Swiss expedition of 1952, made the first documented ascent in 1953 with Edmund Hillary by the Southeast Ridge.

Only about 200 people had reached the summit by 1987. Large national expeditions were the norm until commercial expeditions began in the 1990s. The mountain's dangers include winds beyond 320 kilometres an hour when the jet stream descends, blizzards and avalanches. Climbers usually start from base camps above 5,000 metres; on the Nepalese side they fly to Lukla and trek to the South Base Camp, while on the Tibetan side most drive to the North Base Camp. Nepal and Tibet each manage climbing through permits.
mount-fuji: Mount Fuji stands near the Pacific coast of central Honshu, about 100 km southwest of Tokyo, and straddles the boundary of Shizuoka and Yamanashi prefectures. Its summit is 3,776.24 m, and it is the highest mountain in Japan and the seventh-highest peak of an island on Earth. It has an exceptionally symmetrical cone, covered in snow for about five months of the year. Five lakes lie around it: Kawaguchi, Yamanaka, Sai, Motosu and Shōji. It lies where the Eurasian, North American and Philippine Sea plates meet, with the Pacific Plate subducting beneath them.

Fuji was formed in phases. An andesite core, Sen-komitake, lies deep within the mountain, followed by a basalt layer, Komitake Fuji. Old Fuji formed over it about 100,000 years ago, and the modern New Fuji over Old Fuji around 10,000 years ago. Ten eruptions can be traced to reliable records. The last, the Hōei eruption, began on 16 December 1707 and ended about 1 January 1708. It formed a new crater and a second peak, Mount Hōei, on the southeastern side, and cinders and ash fell like rain in Izu, Kai, Sagami and Musashi.

The summit has been thought sacred since ancient times and was forbidden to women until an edict of 4 May 1872 abolished the exclusion; Tatsu Takayama is the first woman on record to have reached it, in autumn 1832. The mountain has been a frequent subject of art, especially after 1600, when Edo became the capital and travellers on the Tōkaidō road saw it. Samurai used its base as a training area, and the shōgun Minamoto no Yoritomo held archery contests there in the early Kamakura period. Sir Rutherford Alcock made the first ascent by a foreigner in September 1860.

Mount Fuji is one of Japan's Three Holy Mountains, with Mount Tate and Mount Haku, and a Special Place of Scenic Beauty. It was added to the World Heritage List as a Cultural Site on 22 June 2013; UNESCO recognises 25 sites of cultural interest within it, including the Shinto shrine Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha. Climbers usually start from the fifth stations and walk to the summit, the tenth station, on one of four routes, Yoshida, Subashiri, Gotemba and Fujinomiya. Most go at night to see the sunrise, called goraikō, the arrival of light.
mount-gerizim: Mount Gerizim rises to 881 metres above sea level, 70 metres lower than Mount Ebal. It forms the southern side of the valley in which Nablus lies, and it is steep on its northern side, with a spring of fresh water lower down. In the Hebrew Bible it is where the Israelites, on first entering the Promised Land after the Exodus, pronounced blessings, as Moses had instructed, while curses were pronounced on Mount Ebal. In the Book of Judges it is where Jotham delivered the Parable of the Bramble King to the people of Shechem. Its name may mean mountain of the Girzites, or mountain cut in two.

The Samaritans hold Gerizim to be the oldest and most central mountain in the world, which rose above the Flood and gave Noah his first landing, and the place where Abraham almost sacrificed Isaac. Jews place that event on Mount Moriah. The Samaritan Pentateuch and a manuscript from the Qumran caves read Gerizim where the Masoretic Text of Deuteronomy reads Ebal as the site of Moses's commanded altar. Excavations show a Samaritan temple on the summit by the mid-5th century BCE, with a city of more than 10,000 inhabitants named Luzah beside it. It was destroyed and rebuilt in the early 2nd century BCE.

In 168 BCE Antiochus IV Epiphanes built a temple of Zeus Xenios on the mountain. John Hyrcanus destroyed the Samaritan temple in the late 2nd century BCE, but the mountain remained the holiest place for the Samaritans.

In 36 CE a Samaritan prophet rallied followers on the mountain, promising to show the sacred vessels Moses had buried. Pontius Pilate sent troops, there were deaths, and Lucius Vitellius deposed Pilate after Samaritan leaders complained. Roman troops dispersed an armed Samaritan gathering in the summer of 67. In the late 4th century Samaritans were barred from worshipping on the mountain, and a church was built on the summit in 475, followed by an octagonal church of the Theotokos in 484. Justinian I made Samaritanism illegal in 529, which led to a Samaritan revolt under Julianus ben Sabar. It was crushed in 531, and in 533 Justinian had a castle built to protect the church.

Excavations ran from 1983 to 2006 and yielded tens of thousands of finds, among them thousands of pottery vessels, burned animal bones from sacrifices and stones inscribed with the name of God. Visible remains include walls, streets, houses, the octagonal Byzantine church and its fortifications. The mountain is still the centre of Samaritan religion, and Samaritans ascend it three times a year, at Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. About half of the remaining Samaritans live near it, mostly in the village of Kiryat Luza.
mount-helicon: Mount Helicon lies in the region of Thespiai in Boeotia and stands 1,749 metres high. It is located approximately 10 kilometres from the north coast of the Gulf of Corinth. Some researchers maintain that Helicon was also the Greek name of a mountain in Sicily, Rocca Salvatesta, since a river that started from it was also called Helikon. The monastery of Hosios Loukas, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, stands on the mountain.

Greek myth placed two springs sacred to the Muses on Helicon, the Aganippe and the Hippocrene, both of which carry the Greek word for horse, hippos, in their names. In a related myth the Hippocrene burst from the rock when the winged horse Pegasus struck it with his hoof.

Poets returned to the mountain again and again. Hesiod, in the late eighth or early seventh century BCE, placed a reference to the Muses on Helicon at the start of his Theogony. The Homeric Hymn to Poseidon, generally dated to the seventh century, hails the god as Lord of Helicon. In his Aitia the third-century BCE poet Callimachus tells of a dream in which he was young again and talked with the Muses there, explicitly following Hesiod, and he set on Helicon the episode in which Tiresias came upon Athena bathing and was blinded but given the art of prophecy. The Roman poet Ovid, in his Metamorphoses, writes of Minerva visiting the Muses on the mountain.

Cult centres were established in the Valley of the Muses, a fertile valley near Thespiai and Ascra, under the influence of Hesiod's texts, in Hellenistic times if not before. Pausanias visited them in the second century CE and described the sacred grove by the spring Aganippe, with its statues of Apollo, Dionysus and famed poets and an image of Linus in a small rock worked into the manner of a cave. The tripod Hesiod won at a contest in Chalcis in Euboea was still on view there.

The image of Helicon fixed by the Roman poets became an emblem of cultural inspiration again with the Renaissance and is often referred to in poetry. John Milton calls it the Aonian mount at the opening of Paradise Lost, and Torquato Tasso names it Elicona in the second verse of Gerusalemme Liberata. The Hungarian composer Leó Festetics held Helicon balls at his Festetics Palace near Keszthely and named the library he founded the Helikon Library.
mount-hermon: Mount Hermon is a cluster of three summits of about the same height at the southern end of the Anti-Lebanon Mountains, with the boundary between Lebanon and Syria running along its spine. The range extends for 70 km and covers about 700 square kilometres. The highest summit reaches 2,814 metres and is the highest point in Syria. Winter and spring snow covers all three peaks for most of the year. The mountain captures a great deal of precipitation in a dry region, and meltwater that seeps through its Jurassic limestone feeds springs at its base which merge to become the Jordan River. Vineyards, pines, oaks and poplars grow below the snow line.

Egyptian execration texts of the 19th century BCE mention Siryon, one of the mountain's names, and Siryon and Lebanon appear as the dwelling of the Anunnaki in a version of the Epic of Gilgamesh and as gods witnessing a treaty of the Hittite king Muršili II. The name Hermon is unattested before the Bible and has been related to the Semitic root ḥrm, meaning taboo or consecrated. The Bible gives it as the northern limit of the Amorite kingdom and says in Deuteronomy that the Sidonians call it Siryon and the Amorites Senir. Shalmaneser III wrote that Hazael fortified the peak he called Saniru.

Many temples stand in villages on its slopes. Qasr Antar, on the summit, is a building of hewn stone documented by Sir Charles Warren in 1869, and an inscription recovered from it speaks of those who take an oath proceeding from the place. In the apocryphal Book of Enoch, a class of fallen angels descended to Earth on Hermon. Eusebius wrote in the first quarter of the 4th century that nations respected the mountain as a sanctuary.

Its southern slopes extend into the Golan Heights, where a ski resort has operated since 1972. Fighting took place on the mountain during the Six-Day War of 1967 and the Yom Kippur War of 1973. The mountain remains one of the area's chief water resources.
mount-hiei: Mount Hiei lies north-east of Kyoto, on the border between the Kyoto and Shiga prefectures. Its position north-east of the ancient capital of Heian-kyō meant that, in ancient geomancy, it was thought to be a protective bulwark against negative influences on the capital. It was first thought to be the home of indigenous gods and spirits, and a shrine to Oyamakui no Kami, known in the shinbutsu-shūgō system as Sannō Gongen, stood there. From the mountain there are views of Kyoto, Ohara and Lake Biwa.

The temple of Enryaku-ji, the first outpost in Japan of the Tendai sect (Tiantai), was founded on the summit by Saichō in 788 and grew rapidly into a sprawling complex of temples and buildings. It came to be divided into three areas: the Saitō, or West Pagoda, near the summit and technically in Kyoto Prefecture; the Tōdō, or East Pagoda, where the temple was first founded, just within Shiga Prefecture; and the remote Yokawa near the northern end, which went through periods of revival and decline, from Ennin to Ryōgen and the scholar-monk Genshin.

With the rise of the Tendai sect in the Heian period, the mountain and its temple complex were politically powerful and influential.
