Later schools of Buddhism in Japan were almost entirely founded by former Tendai monks such as Hōnen, Nichiren, Dōgen and Shinran, who all studied there before leaving to begin their own practices. In 1571 Oda Nobunaga razed the complex to quell the rising power of Tendai's sōhei, its warrior monks. It was rebuilt and remains the headquarters of the Tendai sect.

Enryaku-ji is the main attraction, concentrated in three areas connected by foot trails, with smaller temples and shrines on the slopes. The mountain is also known for the marathon monks, whose practice of the kaihōgyō involves long walks, up to 52 miles in a day for 100 days in a row, in an effort to attain enlightenment; the sennichi kaihōgyō, the thousand-day form, is 1,000 days of walking meditation and prayer over seven years. Visitors reach the summit by toll road, bus, funiculars on the Kyoto and Shiga sides and an aerial tramway. Ships were named after the mountain, among them a 19th-century ironclad and the World War II-era battleship Hiei.
mount-ida-crete: Mount Ida, with the Greek name Ἴδα, is known also as Idha, Ídhi, Idi and Ita; the massif that includes it is called Psiloritis. It lies in the Rethymno regional unit, on the water divide between the southern part of Crete, which drains to the Libyan Sea, and the northern basin facing the Aegean. A saddle at 2,321 m east of the summit connects it with Mount Agathias, while westward the ridge continues to Mount Stolistra, at 2,336 m.

East of the mountain lies the Nida plateau, with shepherds' huts built only of local stone and used for shelter and for cheesemaking. On Skinakas Peak stands the Skinakas Observatory of the University of Crete, with a 1.3 m telescope. Beneath it the Vromonero plateau holds a holly and maple grove with many endemic and endangered species, now a Natura 2000 protected area.

On the northern foothills lies the plateau of Zominthos, which has the highest Minoan villa yet found. A study of plant remains from the villa showed a rich range of food plants, supplying carbohydrates, protein and vitamins. The Kamares cave was used as a cave sanctuary in ancient times, and the Minoan pottery called Kamares ware is named after it, since some of the first examples were found there.

In antiquity the Idaean Cave, the cave of the Goddess, was venerated by Minoans and Hellenes alike, and by Greek times it was rededicated to Zeus. Votive seals and ivories have been found in it. Like the Dictaean cave it was a place of initiations and may have housed an oracle, which the frequent tripod on the coins of nearby Axos, which presumably controlled the territory around the cave, may symbolise. Legend places the birth of Zeus in this cave, though other legends name Psychro Cave on the Lasithi Plateau.

Mount Ida is the highest mountain on Crete, at 2,456 m, and has the highest topographic prominence of any mountain in Greece. A natural park that includes it is a member of UNESCO's Global Geoparks Network. In Greek myth it was sacred to the Titaness Rhea and was the home of the Dactyls, a mythical race of metalworkers.
mount-ithome: Ithome is the northern of twin peaks, joined by a thin ridge about 0.80 kilometres long to Mount Eva, 700 metres high. It stands 25 kilometres north of Kalamata and 60 kilometres east of Pylos, and from its flat summit the whole valley of the Pamisos river can be seen, east to Mount Taygetus and south to the Gulf of Messenia. Before Greek independence it was known as Vourkano or Voulcano, a name the Archaeological Museum of Messenia dates to the 10th century.

The Homeric village of Ithome was probably on the summit, where Zeus Ithomatas was honoured with an annual festival, the Ithomaea, at first a musical contest. As the most defensible point of the region, Ithome was the centre of Messenian resistance to Sparta in the Messenian Wars of the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, and of the helot revolt after an earthquake in Sparta, known as the Third Messenian War. The classical town lay in a bowl on the lower west flank, where Epaminondas rebuilt Messene; its walls, probably restored rather than newly built by him, enclose the zig-zagging road to the summit.

No later than the early 14th century the temple on the summit was pulled down and its stone reused for a Christian church and monastery, Panagia Voulkanou, which was closed in the 17th century except for a caretaker.

A newer monastery on the lower east slope of Mount Eva served as a staging point in the Greek War of Independence and keeps a library of ancient manuscripts. The village of Mavromati, named after a spring whose ancient channels ran down to the city, occupies part of ancient Messene, where excavations have found evidence of settlement back to the Stone Age.
mount-kailash: The mountain stands in the Gangdise Shan, also called the Kailash Range, near the western trijunction of China, India and Nepal. It lies close to the lakes Manasarovar and Rakshastal, and the sources of four rivers, the Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra and Ghaghara, lie within a stretch of about 60 kilometres around it. The mountain itself consists of thick conglomerate resting on granite. Its Sanskrit name Kailāsa may derive from kelāsa, crystal. In Tibetan it is Gang Rinpoche, the snow jewel mountain.

In Hindu art and literature the mountain is the abode of Shiva, who sits there in meditation with his consort Parvati and their children Ganesha and Kartikeya, and the Ramayana and the Mahabharata mention it. Buddhist texts identify it with the mythological Mount Meru, and in Buddhism Kailash represents the father of the world and Lake Manasarovar the mother. Vajrayana Buddhists tell that Milarepa, who lived about 1052 to 1135, won a contest with the Bon follower Naro Böncham by reaching the summit riding on the rays of the Sun. For Bon it is the abode of the sky goddess Sipaimen and was the centre of the ancient empire of Zhang Zhung. Jains hold that Rishabhadeva, the first Tirthankara, attained liberation there.

Pilgrims walk a circuit of 53 kilometres from Darchen, over the Drölma pass at 5,650 metres. Hindus, Buddhists and Jains go clockwise and Bönpos counterclockwise, and the walk takes about three days, or about three weeks with full-body prostrations. Many cultural artifacts along the route were destroyed during the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976. China permitted pilgrimages after its occupation of Tibet in 1950–51, and pilgrimage from India, closed after the Sino-Indian War of 1962, resumed in 1981.

Hugh Ruttledge circumambulated the mountain in 1926 and judged it unclimbable. When Herbert Tichy asked local people in 1936 whether it could be climbed, a Garpön replied that only a man entirely free of sin could climb Kailash, by turning himself into a bird. Reinhold Messner reportedly declined an offer to climb it in the mid-1980s.

Mount Kailash lies in Ngari Prefecture in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, and its summit has never been successfully ascended. Climbing it is prohibited by the Chinese authorities because of its religious significance.
mount-kilimanjaro: Kilimanjaro is a dormant stratovolcano made up of three volcanic cones: Kibo, the highest, Mawenzi at 5,149 metres and Shira, the lowest at 4,005 metres. Mawenzi and Shira are extinct, while Kibo is dormant and could erupt again. It is the highest free-standing mountain above sea level in the world and one of several mountains arising from the East African Rift, formed by volcanic activity over two million years ago. Eruptive activity at Shira began about 2.4 million years ago, and Mawenzi and Kibo began erupting about 1 million years ago.

Its slopes carry montane forests and cloud forests, and several species are endemic to the mountain. Kibo bears a large ice cap and the largest glaciers in Africa, and the ice cap has lost over 80% of its extent in the 20th century. Geological evidence shows five successive glacial episodes in the Quaternary period.

The Chagga people traditionally lived on the southern and eastern slopes in sovereign Chagga states, known as the Chagga Kingdoms until their abolition in 1963 by Julius Nyerere. The Chagga have no name for the mountain itself, but call its two peaks Kipoo and Kimawenze, usually rendered Kibo and Mawenzi, meaning spotted and broken top. The origin of the name Kilimanjaro is disputed. It may come from the Chagga calling the mountain unclimbable, which explorers misunderstood as its name. A Chagga tale tells how Tone, who provoked the god Ruwa, was pursued by fleeing cattle that threw up hills, including Mawenzi and Kibo.

The mountain may have been known to non-Africans since antiquity, since Ptolemy records sailors' reports of a moon mountain and a spring lake of the Nile, though these could refer to other East African mountains. The German missionary Johannes Rebmann is credited as the first European to report its existence, in 1848, when he took the white summit for snow, which his guide called cold. After several attempts by Europeans, Hans Meyer reached the highest summit in 1889. Two German climbers made the first ascent of Mawenzi's highest summit on 29 July 1912, and the mountain gave its name to the 1914 Battle of Kilimanjaro.

Kilimanjaro lies in Tanzania and has been part of Kilimanjaro National Park since 1973. Uhuru Peak, on the rim of Kibo's crater, is its highest point, at 5,895 metres by the figure of a British survey of 1952 that Tanzanian authorities still list. It is one of the Seven Summits and a major hiking destination, with seven established routes to Uhuru Peak. Although not technically challenging, its height carries a serious risk of altitude sickness.
mount-koya: Mount Kōya, Kōya-san in Japanese, is a large temple settlement in Wakayama Prefecture to the south of Osaka. In the strictest sense the name is the mountain name, or sangō, of Kongōbu-ji Temple, the ecclesiastical headquarters of the Kōyasan sect of Shingon Buddhism. The monk Kūkai first settled it in 819. He chose a plain 800 metres high among eight peaks because the terrain was supposed to resemble a lotus plant, and the original monastery has since grown into the town of Kōya.

The settlement has a university dedicated to religious studies and 120 sub-temples, many of which offer lodging to pilgrims. It is also a common starting point for the Shikoku Pilgrimage associated with Kūkai. Kongōbu-ji, the head temple, stands roughly in the middle of the sanctuary and is colloquially known as Kōyasan-Issan, the mountain of Kōya. The warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi built it for his mother's benefit when she died, and it was originally named Seigan-ji.

In the middle of the settlement lies the Danjō Garan, an area of the main sacred buildings: a main hall, several pagodas, a scripture storage, a bell tower and a lecture hall. The Konpon Daitō, or Basic Great Pagoda, stands 48.5 metres tall in the middle of Kōyasan. According to Shingon doctrine it represents the central point of a mandala covering all of Japan, and it was built as a seminary for the esoteric practices of the sect. The main gate, the Daimon, is flanked on each side by Kongō warriors who guard the mountain.

Okunoin is the mausoleum of Kūkai, surrounded by the largest graveyard in Japan. His spirit is considered to be alive and is treated as a living deity, attended daily by Buddhist priests. The Tokugawa family tomb was built by the third shōgun, Tokugawa Iemitsu, took ten years to build and is architecturally representative of the Edo period; the first shōgun, Ieyasu, is enshrined on its right and the second, Hidetada, on its left.

In 2004 UNESCO designated Kongōbu-ji on Mount Kōya as part of the World Heritage Site Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range, and the Kōya Sankeimichi pilgrimage route was inscribed with it. Visitors usually come by the Nankai Electric Railway from Namba Station in Osaka to Gokurakubashi, then by a cable car that takes five minutes. Many monasteries on the mountain serve as lodgings, with an evening meal and breakfast, and guests may join the morning services.
mount-lebanon: The Mount Lebanon range runs about 170 kilometres along the whole country, parallel to the Mediterranean coast, with its highest peak, Qurnat as Sawda', at 3,088 metres. The name Lebanon comes from a Semitic root meaning white, likely a reference to the snow-covered tops. The Beqaa Valley separates it from the Anti-Lebanon Mountains. The mountains long protected the local population. They produced too little wheat, which came from the Beqaa and the Hawran, while silk from the mountain was sold in Damascus, and the Beirut to Damascus road crossed the range.

The Phoenicians used the cedar forests to build ships, and the Old Testament says Hiram I of Tyre sent cedar wood to build Solomon's Temple. After Pompey's conquest in 64 BCE the range became part of the Roman province of Syria. After the 5th century monks following a hermit named Maron came from the Orontes valley and preached in the north. In the late 8th century the Mardaites, sent by the Byzantine emperor to raid Islamic territories in Syria, settled in the north and became part of Maronite society. Muslim ascetics and Sufis lived there from the 7th century, and in the 9th century the Tanoukhiyoun settled the south, converting to the Druze faith in the 11th.

In the early 17th century Emir Fakhr al-Din II, tax-collector of the Druze Chouf, opened it to Maronite settlement after the Ottoman expedition of 1585. The Battle of Ain Dara in 1711 ended a rivalry between Druze clans with the near-complete exodus of the Yamani Druze. Within the Ottoman Empire the mountain had relative autonomy. From the 18th century Maronite settlement spread into Druze districts, and tensions rose after the peasant uprising of Kisrawan in 1858. The Druze won militarily, but France and Britain intervened for the Maronites and the Druze, and in 1861 the autonomous district of Mount Lebanon was set up under an international guarantee.

Historically the name meant the mountain range, not one administrative territory; the south was known as Jabal al-Shuf and the north as Jabal Kisrawan. After the First World War, France expanded the borders of Mount Lebanon in 1920 to form Greater Lebanon. The last old-growth groves of the Cedar of Lebanon grow on its high slopes in the Cedars of God World Heritage Site, and Christian and Druze communities have lived together in the mountains for roughly a thousand years.
mount-li: Mount Li lies northeast of Xi'an and forms part of the Qinling range, rising to 1,302 metres. It is counted among the eight scenic spots of the Guanzhong Plain and is popularly said to shine like a beacon in the evening sunlight. Its Chinese name means Black Steed Mountain; some old tales say it resembles a horse, others that a Black Steed Tribe lived there under the Shang and Zhou dynasties. Legend also makes it the place where the goddesses Lishan Laomu and Nüwa, creator of mankind, repaired the wall of heaven, and the two have long been worshipped on the mountain.

King You of Zhou died at its foothills in 771 BCE together with his vassal Duke Huan of Zheng, an event that marked the collapse of the Western Zhou and opened a long age of conflict on the Central Plains. The necropolis of the first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, with his mausoleum and the Terracotta Army, lies at the mountain's foot. The Northern Wei geographer Li Daoyuan wrote in the Shui Jing Zhu that the mountain was famed for its jade mines and gold, and that the first emperor chose to be buried there for that reason. The Huaqing Pool, a hot-spring complex of the Tang emperors, also stands at its foot.

On 4 December 1936 Chiang Kai-shek came to Shaanxi and stayed at Huaqingchi. In the Xi'an Incident that followed he was seized while hiding in a crevice on the mountain. The Kuomintang government built a pavilion at the foot of the crevice to commemorate the event, rebuilt in steel and concrete in 1946 with funds from students of the Whampoa Military Academy and renamed the Zhengqi Pavilion.

After the Communist victory of 1949 the pavilion was for a time called the Seizing Chiang Pavilion, and since 1986 it has been the Bingjian Pavilion, a name that also refers to the Xi'an Incident. The mountain is protected as Li Mountain National Forest Park.
mount-lu: Mount Lu, also known in ancient times as Kuanglu, rises in Jiujiang, Jiangxi. Its oval-shaped massif is about 25 kilometres long and 10 kilometres wide, bounded by the Yangtze River and Jiujiang to the north, Nanchang to the south and Poyang Lake to the east. The highest point is Dahanyang Peak, at 1,474 metres above sea level. A sea of clouds can cover the mountain for almost 200 days each year, and the mountain is cooler than the surrounding lowlands in summer.

Mount Lu holds important sites of Mahayana Buddhism, Daoism and Confucianism, and later of Christianity. Between 386 and 402, under the Jin dynasty, Huiyuan founded Pure Land Buddhism and Donglin Temple on its slopes. Under the Tang dynasty Daoist temples were built nearby to house sacred scriptures. The White Deer Grotto Academy, founded in 940, became a centre of academic research in the Song dynasty under the Confucian scholar Zhu Xi and stayed open until at least the nineteenth century.

The Song poet Su Shi wrote of the difficulty of conveying its beauty: "Why can't I tell the true shape of Lushan? Because I myself am in the mountain." The grave of the Tang poet Tao Yuanming also lies there.

Kuling became a summer resort for Western missionaries; Absalom Sydenstricker, father of Pearl Buck, was one of the first five to acquire property there. In the twentieth century the mountain served as a summer seat of the Republic of China. In June 1937 Zhou Enlai met Chiang Kai-shek there to discuss a united front against the Japanese invasion, and in July 1937 Chiang announced full mobilisation for war with Japan from the mountain. Mao Zedong convened conferences of senior party officials there in 1959, 1961 and 1970. The 1959 meeting, known as the Lushan Conference, saw the purge of Peng Dehuai, who had criticised the Great Leap Forward.

The mountain and its surrounding area form Lushan National Park, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996. Among its sights are the Five Old Men Peaks, the Three Tiled Springs, the White Deer Grotto Academy and the town of Kuling, at more than a kilometre above sea level. Lushan Botanical Garden holds tens of thousands of plant species, and Lushan clouds and mist tea is grown on the slopes.
mount-lykaion: The mountain has two peaks: Stefani to the north, 1,421 metres high, and St. Ilias to the south, 1,382 metres, where the altar of Zeus stands. The altar is a circular mound of blackened earth about 30 metres across and 1.5 metres high, made of the burned ash of offerings. Beside it lay the temenos, a sacred precinct no one was allowed to enter; it was believed that anyone who did would die within a year. Lower down, in a valley to the north-east, lay the sanctuary where the Lykaia games were held every four years, and Pausanias also describes a sanctuary of Pan in a grove.

Myth made Lycaon, son of Pelasgus, the founder of the cult. The Bibliotheca says he tried to trick Zeus into eating human flesh and was slain with his fifty sons; Ovid and others say he was turned into a wolf. In antiquity it was alleged that the rite involved a human sacrifice. Excavation in 2007 found activity at the altar from as early as 3000 BCE and continuous use from about 1500 BCE to the Hellenistic period, with Mycenaean drinking vessels and the bones of sheep and goats, and a Late Minoan seal ring.

Thucydides writes that the Spartan king Pleistoanax lived in exile on the mountain from the mid-440s BCE until 427 BCE, in a house straddling the temenos. Polyaenus describes a battle there in 294 BCE in which Demetrius of Macedon defeated the Spartans. The Lykaia included footraces for men and boys, chariot races, boxing, wrestling and a pentathlon, and Pindar recorded several of its victors. Aristotle is said to have ranked the games fourth after the Eleusinia, the Panathenaia and the Argive games.

The Greek Archaeological Service dug at the site in 1897, 1902 and 1909. Since 1996 David Gilman Romano of the University of Pennsylvania has surveyed it, and the Mt. Lykaion Excavation and Survey Project of the University of Pennsylvania and the University of Arizona has excavated from 2006. Its finds include the stadium with seven stone starting blocks, the Hagno fountain, a bathhouse, a stoa, a hotel and a 250 by 50 metre hippodrome, said to be the only one surviving from Greek antiquity.
mount-merapi: Mount Merapi lies on the border between the province of Central Java and the Special Region of Yogyakarta, about 28 kilometres north of Yogyakarta city. Its name, in Javanese, means Fire Mountain, and it has erupted regularly since 1548. It is the youngest in a group of volcanoes in southern Java, at a subduction zone where the Indo-Australian plate passes under the Sunda plate. Villages stand on its flanks as high as 1,700 metres above sea level.

Eruptions in the area began about 400,000 years ago. Until about 10,000 years ago they were mostly effusive, with basaltic lava. Since then they have become more explosive, with viscous andesitic lavas that often build lava domes. The collapse of a dome produces pyroclastic flows, which the people of the region call wedhus gembel, shaggy goat.

Small eruptions come every two to three years and larger ones every 10 to 15 years or so. Notable eruptions, often with many deaths, occurred in 1006, 1786, 1822, 1872 and 1930. The eruption of 1006 is claimed to have covered all of central Java with ash. In 1930 pyroclastic flows destroyed thirteen villages and killed 1,400 people. On 22 November 1994 a pyroclastic flow killed 27 people, mostly in the town of Muntilan.

On 25 October 2010 Merapi erupted on its southern and south-eastern slopes. Over the next month 353 people died and 350,000 fled their homes, most of the damage coming from pyroclastic flows, with lahars after heavy rain on 4 November. The eruption lowered the summit by 38 metres to 2,930 metres. Seismic monitoring began on the mountain in 1924, and the volcano is one of the Decade Volcanoes chosen for special study. After 2010 a zone in nine villages in Cangkringan district was closed to permanent settlement.

Merapi is important to the Javanese people, especially those living near its crater. Villagers hold that a spirit palace lies inside it, ruled by the armourers Empu Rama and Empu Permadi, a counterpart to the Yogyakarta Sultanate. In one widely told origin story the gods moved Mount Jamurdipo to the centre of Java to balance the island and buried the two armourers, who had refused to leave their forge, beneath it.

For the Sultanate the mountain marks the northern end of a sacred axis running through the Tugu monument, the sultan's palace and the Indian Ocean coast. An area of 6,410 hectares around the mountain has been a national park since 2004.
mount-morgan-queensland: Mount Morgan lies on the Dee River, 38 kilometres south of the city of Rockhampton and 680 kilometres north of the state capital, Brisbane, on the traditional lands of the Kangulu people. The town takes its name from the family who took out the first gold mining leases there: Frederick Augustus Morgan and his brothers Thomas Squire Morgan and Edwin Francis Morgan. Clay mined from a nearby hill for furnace bricks left the Fireclay Caverns, in whose ceilings dinosaur footprints of the Early Jurassic were later found.

Mount Morgan was founded as a gold mining town in 1882 and grew haphazardly around the entrance to the mining lease near the Dee River. Its name was formally changed from South Calliungal to Mount Morgan in 1889, and the census of 1891 counted 3,514 people. Until the railway arrived, everything travelled by horse team; the line to Rockhampton opened on 26 November 1898 and included one of the few rack railways to work in Australia. Mount Morgan State High School, opened on 22 January 1912, was the first school of its kind in Queensland.

Over its life the mine yielded gold, silver and copper: 250 tonnes of gold and 360,000 tonnes of copper in all, leaving 134 million tonnes of waste rock and tailings. Most of the mountain was mined away, and the town now stands beside a pit 43 metres deep filled with acid water, which the Queensland Government has begun to rehabilitate. In 1900 the town marked the relief of Mafeking with bonfires and hung a Mafeking bell, cast at the mine, beside the town hall.

Mount Morgan was the administrative centre of the Mount Morgan Shire until March 2008, when the shire was merged into the Rockhampton Region. The census of 2021 counted 2,487 people in the town. The mine, the high school, the railway station and several hotels and churches are heritage-listed, and the old station serves as a museum and tourist information centre.
mount-mycale: Mycale, called Samsun Dağı or Dilek Dağı in Turkish, rises north of the mouth of the Maeander and is divided from Samos by the Mycale Strait, 1.6 km wide. Its ridge ends in the promontory known in antiquity as Trogilium, with beaches on the north shore and a steep escarpment to the south. In classical times Priene stood on the coast below its southern flank, with Miletus across the bay into which the Maeander drained; silt from the river has since left both ruins several miles inland, and the end of the bay survives as Lake Bafa.
The mountain belongs to a fault-block ridge that continues on Samos and is part of the Menderes Massif. Its marble, limestone and schist served the builders and sculptors of Ionia.

The Iliad places Mycale among the lands of the Carians, and the Hymn to Apollo names its steep heights. In the Late Bronze Age it may have been the Arrinnanda of Hittite records. An inscription from Priene recalls a Meliac War against a state on the mountain, Melia, whose fortified town Carium was taken by the Ionians, who expelled the Carians; Priene and Samos later disputed its lands before jurors from Rhodes.

Beside Carium the Ionians built the Panionium, a temple of Poseidon Heliconius put up around 540 BCE, where the Ionian League met and held the festival called the Panionia. After several false identifications, the remains of Melia and the Panionium were found in 2004 on a lesser peak, 15 km north of Priene. In 479 BCE the Greek fleet under the Spartan Leotychides defeated the Persian fleet and army at Mycale, on the same day, according to Herodotus, as the Greek victory at Plataea.

The whole ridge became the Dilek Peninsula National Park in 1966, covering 109.85 km², part of it a military reservation. About 60% of it is maquis shrubland, and it shelters species once commoner in the region, among them the monk seal, Monachus monachus, which breeds in caves along its shores.
mount-nemrut: Mount Nemrut lies in the Anti-Taurus range in Adıyaman Province. In 62 BCE King Antiochus I of Commagene built a tomb-sanctuary on its summit, flanked by statues 8 to 9 metres high of himself, two lions, two eagles and composite Greek and Iranian gods, among them Heracles-Artagnes-Ares, Zeus-Oromasdes and Apollo-Mithras-Helios-Hermes. The sanctuary was part of a programme to revive the Persian traditions of Commagene. Following the Mithridatic rulers of Pontus, Antiochus stressed his descent from the Achaemenids and Seleucids and claimed the royal legacy of Armenia, merging the traditions of Cappadocia, Pontus and Armenia into a new Greco-Iranian pantheon.

The statues were once seated, each with the name of its god inscribed. Their faces look Greek, but their clothing and hair are Persian. The heads were removed at some point and now lie scattered over the site; the damage, especially to the noses, suggests deliberate iconoclasm. Stone slabs with bas-reliefs, probably part of a frieze, show Antiochus' Greek and Persian ancestors. The tumulus of loose rock is 49 metres tall and 152 metres across, and may have been meant to protect a tomb from robbers, since any excavation would quickly fill in.

On the western terrace a slab with a lion shows stars and the planets Jupiter, Mercury and Mars, taken as a chart of the sky on 7 July 62 BCE, which may mark when building began. The site is thought to have served for religious ceremonies.

Karl Sester, a German engineer assessing transport routes for the Ottomans, excavated the site in 1881. After her first visit in 1947 Theresa Goell devoted her life to it, beginning campaigns in 1954. Later excavations have not revealed the tomb of Antiochus, though the mountain is still believed to be his burial place. UNESCO listed the site in 1987, calling the mausoleum one of the most ambitious constructions of the Hellenistic period, whose royal lineage, traced through Greek and Persian legends, shows the dual origin of the kingdom's culture.
mount-paektu: Mount Paektu is a stratovolcano whose cone is cut by a large caldera, about 5 kilometres wide and 850 metres deep, partly filled by Heaven Lake. Sixteen peaks over 2,500 metres line the rim; the highest, Janggun Peak, belongs to North Korea and is covered in snow about eight months of the year. The lake is the source of the Songhua, Tumen and Yalu rivers, and the Tumen and Yalu form the northern border of North Korea with Russia and China. China calls the mountain Changbai, meaning ever white mountain, and the Korean name Baekdu means white-head mountain.

Eruptions began about 5 million years ago with basaltic lava flows, and the cone began to grow about 1 million years ago. The caldera was created in 946 by the Millennium or Tianchi eruption, a VEI 6 event that released about 100 to 120 cubic kilometres of tephra. Its ash reached southern Hokkaido and Greenland, and the Goryeosa records thunder from heaven's drum heard at Kaesong, then the capital of Goryeo.

After the great eruption the volcano had at least three smaller ones, in 1668, 1702 and 1903. The name Changbai was first used under the Liao dynasty and then the Jin dynasty of the Jurchens, who gave the mountain titles as a king and then an emperor. The Manchus and their ancestors held it the most sacred mountain of their shamanism, and the clan Aisin Gioro, who founded the Qing dynasty, claimed that their progenitor Bukūri Yongšon was conceived near it.

Koreans have held the mountain sacred throughout history. In Korean mythology it was the birthplace of Dangun, the founder of Gojoseon, whose parents were Hwanung, the Son of Heaven, and Ungnyeo, a bear transformed into a woman. The Gando Convention of 1909 between China and Japan recognised the north and east of the mountain as Chinese territory. In 1962 and 1964 China and North Korea made border treaties that gave North Korea 9 of the 16 peaks and 54.5 per cent of Heaven Lake.

Mount Paektu is mentioned in the national anthems of both North and South Korea and in the folk song Arirang. Dense forest on its slopes gave bases to Korean armed resistance against the Japanese occupation. The peak has been on the state emblem of North Korea since 1993.
mount-pagus: Mount Pagus, Pagos in Greek, rises to 186 metres about 2 kilometres from the shore and commands a view over much of İzmir and the Gulf of İzmir. Its summit castle, Kadifekale, the velvet castle in Turkish, was first built in the 3rd century BCE. Strabo records that only a small part of ancient Smyrna stood on the hill, with most of the city around the harbour on the flat land below; the stadium and the theatre lay on the slopes just beneath the summit.

The first recorded walls on the hill were the work of Lysimachos, a successor of Alexander the Great and later king in Thrace and Asia Minor. They belonged to the refounding of Smyrna away from the old city on a small mound at the corner of the inner gulf, which could hold only a few thousand people. A legend told by Pausanias says that the goddesses called the two Nemeseis appeared to Alexander as he slept under a plane tree after hunting and told him to found a city there, and that the oracle at Klaros blessed those who would dwell on Pagus beyond the sacred Meles. The legend often appears on ancient coins.

The stadium west of the castle, scene of the martyrdom of St. Polycarp, and the theatre east of the gates were rebuilt after an earthquake in 178; both are now built over, though traces of the theatre remain. In the 14th century the hill castle fell to the Aydinids while the port, with a castle of its own, was held by others until Tamerlane took it in 1403. In the 19th century Kadifekale belonged to the Turkish core of İzmir on the slopes, while the city below was cosmopolitan.

The present walls are medieval. Beside the castle lie Roman cisterns, renovated in Byzantine and Ottoman times, which formed the centre of Smyrna's water supply. The city began restoration work in 2007, and in 2020 the castle became a Tentative World Heritage Site as part of the Historical Port City of Izmir.
mount-parnassus: Parnassus is one of the largest mountain regions of mainland Greece, spread across Boeotia, Phthiotis and Phocis, where its largest part lies. Its highest peak, Liakoura, reaches 2,457 metres. To the north-west it joins Mount Giona and to the south Mount Kirphi, and the valley of the Boeotian Cephissus bounds it on the east and that of Amfissa on the west. The Oracle of Delphi stood on its southern slopes in a rift valley north of the Gulf of Corinth. Its melting snows supply water to the surrounding communities, and its limestone holds rich deposits of bauxite, mined systematically since the end of the 1930s.

The mountain appears in early Greek literature, and many of its communities are named in Homer's Iliad. It was home to the Dorian states of Phocis, whose people spoke Phokian, a Doric dialect. Ancient Greeks held it sacred to Apollo and the Corycian nymphs, to Dionysus and his mysteries, and to the Muses, and Delphi, on its slope, was the site of the navel of the world. Some traditions placed the spring of Castalia and the home of the Muses there, though others gave that honour to Mount Helicon, so that Parnassus came to be seen as the home of poetry, music and learning.

The name is not recorded in Linear B, although Mycenaean settlements were abundant to the south and east. The philologist Leonard Robert Palmer suggested a Luwian origin, meaning the mountain of the house of the god, but no archaeological evidence ties the name to an Anatolian presence. The mountain also sheltered partisans resisting the Axis occupation and was a theatre of the Greek Civil War; it had served as a centre of resistance in the Greek war of independence.

Parnassus National Park was founded in 1938 and covers about 150 square kilometres, and a larger area of about 344 square kilometres is protected under Natura 2000. Endemic plants include the Parnassian peony, and wolves, boars and badgers live there. The slopes hold the largest ski centre in Greece, built from 1975 and 1976, with the resorts at Kellaria and Fterolakka. The French Parnassism movement took its name from the mountain, and the Paris quarter of Montparnasse was named after it.
mount-pelee: Mount Pelée is a stratovolcano at the northern end of Martinique, in the Lesser Antilles Volcanic Arc, a curved chain of volcanoes about 850 kilometres long between Puerto Rico and Venezuela. The arc exists because the Caribbean Plate meets Atlantic oceanic crust belonging to the South American Plate. Other volcanoes of the arc include La Soufrière on Saint Vincent, the Soufrière Hills on Montserrat and the submarine volcano Kick 'em Jenny. Pelée's cone is made of stratified layers of hardened ash and solidified lava.

Volcanologists distinguish three phases. In the Paléo-Pelée stage it was an ordinary stratovolcano. The intermediate phase began about 100,000 years ago and produced pyroclastic flows like those of 1902; about 25,000 years ago a large collapse of the south-west sector caused a landslide. In the modern phase, which built most of the present cone, more than 30 eruptions have been identified in the last 5,000 years. Three thousand years ago the Étang Sec caldera formed after a large pumice eruption. Minor steam eruptions occurred in 1792 and 1851.

The main eruption of 8 May 1902 destroyed Saint-Pierre in a few minutes and left only three known survivors. Ludger Sylbaris survived in a poorly ventilated, dungeon-like jail cell, Léon Compère-Léandre, who lived at the edge of the town, escaped with severe burns, and a young girl, Havivra Da Ifrile, fled by boat to a sea cave. The eruption formed pyroclastic flows and a dome that filled the caldera, and activity continued until 4 July 1905. A new eruption began on 16 September 1929, when the authorities at once evacuated the danger area, and ended in late 1932.

Saint-Pierre was never fully rebuilt, though villages grew up in its place. The volcano is regarded as active and is under continuous observation by geophysicists. The Martinique volcano frog lives nowhere else, and a largely forested tract of about 9,262 hectares around the mountain is an Important Bird Area. The volcanoes and forests of Mount Pelée and the pitons of northern Martinique were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
mount-sinai: Mount Sinai, also called Jabal Musa, Arabic for the Mountain of Moses, lies near the city of Saint Catherine on the Sinai Peninsula. It is one of several places claimed to be the biblical Mount Sinai. It is surrounded on all sides by higher peaks of the same range and stands next to Mount Catherine, which at 2,629 m is the highest peak in Egypt.

Its rocks formed late in the evolution of the Arabian-Nubian Shield. The mountain shows a ring complex of alkaline granites intruded into diverse rock types, including volcanics, and it is not the tallest peak of its range.

In Judaism the mountain is where God gave Moses the Ten Commandments on the Tablets of Stone and the rest of the Torah. The festival of Shavuot marks the giving of the Torah, and its special reading includes the Ten Commandments. In Rabbinic Judaism Moses received the Oral Torah as well as the Written Torah. Jewish views differ on the exact location of Sinai, and the traditional site on the peninsula may not be the mountain described in Jewish tradition.

Immediately north of the mountain stands the 6th-century Saint Catherine's Monastery. On the summit is a Greek Orthodox chapel, built in 1934 on the ruins of a 16th-century church and closed to the public, which encloses the rock considered the source of the Tablets of Stone. Nearby is Moses' cave, where Moses is believed to have waited to receive the commandments. In Islam the mountain is associated with the prophet Mūsā ibn ʿImrān, and the Quran refers to it as Ṭūr Saināʾ, Ṭūr Sīnīn and aṭ-Ṭūr. The adjacent Valley of Tuwa is held to be sacred, and part of it is called the Blessed Place.

Two main routes lead to the summit. The longer, shallower Siket El Bashait takes about 2.5 hours on foot, and camels can be used. The steeper Siket Sayidna Musa climbs 3,750 steps of penitence in the ravine behind the monastery. Many visitors ascend after midnight to reach the summit for sunrise.
mount-tai: Mount Tai, or Taishan, lies in central Shandong, just north of the city of Tai'an and south of the provincial capital Jinan. It is the highest point in the province and covers 426 square kilometres at its base. It is a tilted fault-block mountain that rises abruptly from the plain, and its slopes are about 80 per cent covered with vegetation. Six streams flow from the summit. Some trees are notable, among them cypresses said to have been planted by Emperor Wu of Han about 2,100 years ago.

People lived near the mountain from the Paleolithic and Neolithic periods; the Dawenkou culture lay to its south and the Longshan culture to its north. Worship of Mount Tai dates back at least 3,000 years, from the Shang to the Qing dynasty, and developed into the Feng and Shan sacrifices, an imperial rite in which the emperor paid homage to Heaven on the summit and to Earth at the foot of the mountain. Carving an inscription marked the attainment of great peace.

Under the Zhou the sacrifices became highly ritualised, and the spirit of the mountain was held to accept offerings only from a feudal lord, which led Confucius to criticise ministers who sacrificed there after usurping power. In the Warring States period the State of Qi built a wall of about 500 kilometres, whose ruins can still be seen.

In 219 BCE Qin Shi Huang held a ceremony on the summit and proclaimed the unity of his empire in a well-known inscription. Under the Han the Feng and Shan sacrifices were considered the highest of all sacrifices. In 666 Emperor Gaozong of Tang held the sacrifices, attended by representatives from Japan, India, Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla, the Turks, Khotan, the Khmer and the Umayyad Caliphate. A total of 72 emperors are recorded as visiting the mountain. Writers also climbed it for inspiration, leaving stone inscriptions and tablets, and the mountain was important in the development of both Buddhism and Taoism.

Mount Tai was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. The Dai Temple at its foot, first built under the Qin and modelled since the Han on an imperial palace, covers 96,000 square metres and holds a mural of 1009 showing the god of the mountain on a journey. The Shrine of the Blue Dawn near the top honours the goddess Bixia Yuanjun. About 6,660 stone steps lead from the red gate at the foot to the South Heaven Gate at the top, and the mountain carries many temples, stone tablets and cliff inscriptions.
mount-tambora: Mount Tambora, also called Tomboro, is an active stratovolcano in the northern part of Sumbawa, in the Lesser Sunda Islands. It forms its own peninsula, the Sanggar peninsula, between the Flores Sea to the north and Saleh Bay to the south. Its volcanism results from the Australian Plate moving beneath the Sunda Plate, and estimates for its onset range from 57 to 43 thousand years ago. Before 1815 it was a high cone with a single central vent and a base 60 kilometres across.

After lying dormant for several centuries, the volcano began to rumble in 1812. A moderate eruption on 5 April 1815 was followed by thunderous detonations heard in Ternate, 1,400 kilometres away. The climax came days later, and the explosions were heard on Sumatra, more than 2,600 kilometres away, and possibly in Thailand and Laos.

Ash fell as far away as Borneo, Sulawesi, Java and the Maluku Islands, and the mountain's height dropped from about 4,300 to 2,850 metres. The eruption ejected up to 150 cubic kilometres of material, rated VEI-7, and killed at least 71,000 people, though estimates vary.

The eruption cooled the global climate, and 1816 became known as the Year Without a Summer in North America and Europe, where crops failed, livestock died and the worst famine of the century followed.

In 2004 a team led by Haraldur Sigurðsson found a village buried about 25 kilometres west of the caldera, with a house holding the remains of two adults, bronze bowls, ceramic pots and iron tools. The finds suggested well-off traders, and the site was called the Pompeii of the East. The Tambora language was lost; remaining word lists suggest it was not Austronesian, but possibly a language isolate or related to the Papuan languages far to the east. Local folklore explained the disaster as divine punishment of a ruler who had killed a hajji.

The Swiss botanist Heinrich Zollinger reached the summit in 1847, the first to do so after the eruption, and found smoking sulphur and some regrown vegetation. Resettlement began in 1907, and a coffee plantation was set up in the 1930s at Pekat. A dense rain forest of Duabanga moluccana trees covers up to 80,000 hectares of the slopes. The Directorate of Volcanology monitors the mountain from a post at Doro Peti village.
mountain-autonomous-soviet-socialist-rep: The Mountain Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, or Mountain ASSR, was a short-lived autonomous republic within the Russian SFSR in the Northern Caucasus. It existed from 20 January 1921 to 7 July 1924. It grew out of the Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus, which indigenous nationalities had created from parts of the Kuban and Terek Oblasts after the Russian Revolution. Soviet rule was installed after the Red Army conquered the Northern Caucasus in the Russian Civil War.

The republic covered over 73,000 square kilometres and had about 800,000 people. It comprised six okrugs, Balkar, Chechen, Kabardian, Karachay, Nazran (Ingushetia) and Vladikavkaz (Ossetia), and had two cities, Grozny and Vladikavkaz. The Terek Cossacks had a special autonomy as the Sunzha Cossack Okrug.

On 1 September 1921 the Kabardin Okrug was split off as the Kabardin Autonomous Oblast. The Karachay Okrug became the Karachay-Cherkess Autonomous Oblast on 12 January 1922, and the Balkar Okrug was merged with the Kabardin oblast on 16 January 1922. The Chechen Okrug became the Chechen Autonomous Oblast on 30 November 1922. A decree of the Supreme Soviet of 7 July 1924 divided the rest into the North Ossetian and Ingush Autonomous Oblasts, and on 17 October 1924 the North Caucasus Krai took in all of the former republic.

During the Cold War many Western historians saw the break-up as a Soviet strategy of divide and conquer. Archives opened in the 1990s showed that it began in March 1921, when Kabardian leaders protested at being included, citing the lack of economic links with the other mountain peoples. A Kabardian congress that spring voted overwhelmingly, with only 28 of its 140 delegates Bolsheviks, to demand autonomous republic status, and Joseph Stalin had to dissuade the leader Betal Kalmykov from applying for union republic status.

In the 19th century the best land in the region had been given to Cossacks, Russian and Ukrainian military colonists, while many natives were driven into the mountains. In 1920 the Soviet government decided to deport the Terek Cossacks and give their farms to the native peoples, and 34,637 people were deported to Vladikavkaz, Arkhangelsk and the Donbas. In 1882, 24.7 per cent of the Ingush had lived in the mountains, and by 1924 only 2.1 per cent did.
mountainous-republic-of-the-northern-cau: The February Revolution of 1917 swept away the military-civil administration of the North Caucasus and left competing bodies: local councils of the ethnic groups and soviets in the Russian-populated towns. In March 1917 representatives of the region's national intelligentsias met to prepare a federation, and in May about 300 delegates met at Vladikavkaz to found the Union of the Mountaineers of the North Caucasus and Dagestan. They elected the Chechen former officer and oil magnate Abdulmajid Tapa Tchermoev chairman of its Central Committee and the Avar scholar Nazhmuddin Gotsinskii as mufti. The Union declared itself an inseparable part of Russia, with autonomy in a federal state, and tensions between its secularist and Islamist factions appeared by September 1917.

After the Bolsheviks seized power the Union declared itself a republic, and in December 1917 it formed a joint government with the Terek Cossacks. Disorder, clashes over land and the Red Army's advance forced its government out of the North Caucasus in early 1918, first to Temir-Khan-Shura and then to Tiflis. On 11 May 1918 it formally declared independence from exile in Istanbul and made a treaty of friendship with the Ottoman Empire. With Ottoman help it took Temir-Khan-Shura, and its re-establishment was marked at Derbent on 13 October 1918, but the Ottomans soon withdrew.

Anton Denikin's Volunteer Army refused any cooperation, and by May 1919 it had captured Petrovsk-Port and Derbent; after his ultimatum the government at Temir-Khan-Shura was dissolved and the Kotsev government fled to Tiflis. A revolt against Denikin began in Dagestan in June 1919, and in September Usun-Khadzhi proclaimed the North Caucasian Emirate. In 1920 the 11th Red Army and the Muslim clergy drove out Denikin's forces and ended the emirate. The Bolsheviks created the Mountain Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic in 1921, though the uprising lasted until 1925.

The republic claimed seven constituent states, Dagestan, Ingushetia, Chechnya, North Ossetia, Circassia, Karachay-Balkaria and the Nogai steppes, and was recognised by the Central Powers, Ukraine, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United Kingdom, while the Bolsheviks declined to recognise it on 30 May 1918. A delegation led by Tapa Tchermoeff went to Paris in March 1919 seeking recognition. In 1984 the United States Congress passed a resolution marking the 66th anniversary of its declaration of independence, and a political organisation, the Congress of the Peoples of the North Caucasus, has invoked it to urge cooperation among North Caucasian separatist groups.
mountstuart-elphinstone: Mountstuart Elphinstone was born in Dumbarton on 6 October 1779 and educated at the Royal High School. He was the fourth son of the 11th Baron Elphinstone. Appointed to the civil service of the East India Company, one of whose directors was his uncle, he arrived at Calcutta early in 1796. In 1799 he escaped a massacre at Benares by followers of the deposed Nawab of Awadh, Wazir Ali Khan. In 1801 he moved to the diplomatic service as assistant to the British resident Josiah Webbe at the court of the Peshwa Baji Rao II.

Elphinstone was attached to the mission of Sir Arthur Wellesley to the Marathas and, when war broke out, acted as virtual aide-de-camp to Wellesley, showing at the Battle of Assaye such courage that Wellesley told him he ought to have been a soldier. In 1804 he became British resident at Nagpur. In 1808 he was appointed the first British envoy to the court of Kabul, to secure an alliance against Napoleon's planned advance on India. The alliance proved of little value because Shah Shuja was driven from the throne, but Elphinstone's Account of the Kingdom of Cabul, of 1815, was the lasting result.

In 1811 he became resident at Pune. When the Marathas declared war on the British in 1817 he assumed command at the Battle of Khadki despite his non-military background and secured a victory. The Peshwa's territories were annexed, and he became Commissioner of the Deccan in 1818. From 1819 to 1827 he served at Bombay, where he promoted education, was credited with the Elphinstone code of criminal law, and returned many lands to the Raja of Satara.

Back in Britain in 1829, Elphinstone was one of the seven founders of the Royal Geographical Society on 16 July 1830. He twice refused appointment as Governor-General of India in order to finish his two-volume History of India, published in 1841. He died in Hookwood, Surrey, on 20 November 1859 and was buried in Limpsfield churchyard. Elphinstone College was endowed in his memory, and there is a memorial to him in the crypt of St Paul's Cathedral. James Sutherland Cotton wrote his biography in 1892.
mouseion: The word mouseion originally meant any place dedicated to the Muses, often connected with the study of music or poetry, and later it came to be associated with sites of learning such as Plato's Academy and Aristotle's Lyceum. According to Johannes Tzetzes, the Mouseion of Alexandria was founded by Ptolemy I Soter, though it more probably took shape under Ptolemy II Philadelphus. It arguably included the Library of Alexandria. The Ptolemies reputedly set out to bring together some of the best scholars of the Hellenistic world and to collect all the books then known.

The Mouseion was a community gathered under the protection of the Muses, supported by the patronage of the Ptolemies and later of the Roman emperors. It held no collection of sculpture and painting, unlike the one that their rival Attalus assembled at the Library of Pergamum. It was rather an institution of learning, compared by Germain Bazin to the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. Reports are few, but scholars and staff appear to have been salaried by the state and to have paid no taxes; according to Strabo they also received free room and board and free servants.

Strabo, in the first century CE, described it as part of the Brucheion, the palace complex, with a lobby, a columned hall and a large dining hall for the common table of its members, under a priest once appointed by the kings and now by Caesar. Scholars there evidently pursued literary criticism, and translated some foreign texts from Egyptian, Assyrian, Persian, Jewish and other languages. Many editions of the Greek canon, from Homer and Hesiod onwards, rest on texts collated and corrected by scholars presumably linked to it.

Under Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, in a time of political turmoil, most intellectuals were killed or expelled from the city, among them the last recorded head librarian, Aristarchus of Samothrace, who is said to have resigned in 145 BCE. The Mouseion continued under Roman rule but never regained its former standing, and its membership came to include politicians and athletes rewarded for service to the state. The Brucheion was probably destroyed by fire on the orders of Emperor Aurelian in 272 CE.

Its members included Callimachus, who produced the first comprehensive book catalogue, the Pinakes, Zenodotos, the first head librarian, Apollonius of Rhodes, author of the Argonautica, and Eratosthenes of Cyrene, who measured the Earth's circumference. Through their work the writings of Homer and the tragedians survive. The word mouseion is the root of the modern museum.
moutier-grandval-abbey: The abbey was a Benedictine house near the villages of Moutier and Grandval in the present Bernese Jura. Grandval already existed when it was founded, while Moutier grew up around the abbey. It began as a dependency of Luxeuil Abbey, on land granted by Gundoin, Duke of Alsace, on the old route to the Pierre Pertuis Pass. Saint Waldebert, abbot of Luxeuil, sent Saint Germanus of Granfelden, who served 35 years as first abbot, with Saint Randoald of Grandval as his prior. Both were martyred in 675 by Adalrich, Duke of Alsace, after protesting against his expulsion of the people of the Sorgenau valley.

Like some other abbeys, it became the secular ruler of a territory, and by the 9th or 10th century its property and influence reached Lake Biel and the Balsthal valley, though it was held as a fief of the king of Burgundy. In 968 Conrad of Burgundy granted it in benefice to Count Luitfrid, who divided it among his sons as if it were his own; after a court case it returned to the king. When Rudolph III of Burgundy gave the abbey to the bishop of Basel in 999, its lands measured 540 square miles, and disputes with the prince-bishops continued.

From 1486 the abbey was also part of the Protectorate of Bern in the Old Swiss Confederacy while remaining subject to Basel, and from 1475 the Alsatian-born chronicler Johann Burchard, living in Rome, was its provost. After the Swiss Reformation the monks fled to Delémont, whose parish church served them from 1534 to 1792. The arrival of French Revolutionary armies in 1792 ended both the abbey and the Prince-Bishopric.

The abbey's buildings have disappeared, though remains of the 12th century were found under the town in 2008. The small chapelle de Chalière, now the cemetery chapel at Perrefitte, is a Carolingian building of the abbey with faded wall paintings of the 11th century. The church at Delémont keeps the bodies of Saints Germanus and Randoald, and its museum his reputed cross, sandals and chalice. The abbey's Bible of about 840, probably written in Tours, was apparently forgotten after the dissolution and found in Delémont by children; its miniatures include the story of Adam and Eve and Moses receiving the Tablets of the Law.
movable-type: Movable type uses individual, reusable components, usually single characters or punctuation marks, to reproduce a document. Metal punches were used for imprinting symbols around 3000 BCE in Sumer, and some archaeologists conjecture that stamps from Uruk and Larsa, dating from the 2nd millennium BCE, show the use of movable type.

In China, paper made writing materials more economical, but copying books by hand remained laborious. Woodblock printing was invented by about the 8th century under the Tang and reached its height under the Song. Carving a plate took much time, labour and material, plates were inconvenient to store and mistakes were hard to correct.

Bi Sheng (990 to 1051) developed the first known movable-type system around 1040 in the Northern Song, using ceramic type. The scholar Shen Kuo described how he set the type in an iron frame, warmed it so that the paste at the back softened, and pressed it level with a smooth board. For two or three copies the method was not worth the trouble, but for hundreds or thousands it was very quick, because two forms alternated, one printing while the other was set.

Bi Sheng also tried wooden type, but the grain and its unevenness once soaked in ink led to its replacement by clay. Bronze type was in use in China no later than the 12th century, for anti-counterfeit markers on paper money of the Jin and Southern Song, and a book of 1193 documented copper type.

The oldest surviving book printed in movable metal type, the Jikji, was printed in Korea in 1377 under the Goryeo dynasty. Both systems stayed mostly within East Asia. Around 1450 the German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg invented the metal movable-type press and ways of casting type from a matrix and hand mould, using an alloy of lead, tin and antimony that remained standard for 550 years. The small number of letters in European alphabets helped.

For alphabetic scripts, setting type was quicker than woodblock printing, and metal type was more durable and uniform, which led to typography and fonts. The quality and relatively low price of the Gutenberg Bible of 1455 established the superiority of movable type in Europe, and presses spread rapidly. The printing press may be regarded as one of the main factors that encouraged the Renaissance.
movilla-abbey: Movilla, in Irish Mainistir Mhaigh Bhile, takes its name from the plain of the ancient tree: a sacred tree is said to have been worshipped on the site before the monastery was built. Saint Finnian founded it under the patronage of the king of the Dál Fiatach, and by his death in 579 it was a great monastic house. The Book of Armagh remembers him as a man of venerable life who reposes in many miracles in his city of Movilla. It should not be confused with Moville in County Donegal.

By the seventh century Movilla was among the leading monasteries of Ireland, a centre of worship, study, mission and trade. Its standing rested partly on a complete copy of the Latin Vulgate Bible that Finnian had obtained from Rome. Tradition holds that Columba, Finnian's pupil, secretly copied it on a visit in the 550s, and that the High King Diarmait mac Cerbaill ruled that the copy belonged to Finnian: to every cow her calf, to every book its copy. Excavations in 1980–81 found the work of craftsmen in iron, bronze and glass, including a bronzesmith's trial piece.

Bede names a Cromanus, thought to be St. Cronan of Movilla, among the churchmen to whom Pope Honorius I wrote about the date of Easter. Early in the eighth century its bishop Colman, son of Murchu, wrote a hymn to the archangel Michael. The Danes sacked the monastery in 823, and in the tenth century it was united with Bangor Abbey. Saint Malachy of Armagh placed Augustinians there in 1135, but it stayed poor, valued at two and a half marks in 1306. Henry VIII dissolved it in 1542, and in the reign of Elizabeth I Brian O'Neill of Clandeboye burned it.

Nothing visible remains of Finnian's monastery. The standing ruins are those of the fifteenth-century Augustinian church, two gables about 150 feet apart, with a Romanesque window in the east wall and carved grave slabs on the north wall. The ruins stand within Movilla Cemetery, still in use, and are a State Care Historic Monument.
movses-kaghankatvatsi: The name Movses Kaghankatvatsi means Moses of Kaghankatuk, and Movses Daskhurantsi Moses of Daskhuran. Earlier Armenian authors attach no name to the History. Early in the 13th century the legal scholar Mkhitar Gosh named Movses Daskhurantsi as its author, and the later historian Kirakos Gandzaketsi drew the name Kaghankatvatsi from a passage in Book II, chapter 11, where the writer says he comes from the province of Uti, in which the large village of Kaghankatuik lies. The earliest surviving manuscript, of 1289, bears no author's name, and the first to bear the name Movses Kalankatuaci was copied by the scribe Lunkianos in 1761.

The History deals with Caucasian Albania and the eastern provinces of Armenia. Books I and II narrate events up to the seventh century, among them the Khazar invasion of Transcaucasia. Book III differs from them in style and date and describes the Caspian expeditions of the Rus' and their conquest of Partav in the tenth century. Because of the gap in time and the change of style, attribution to a single author seems doubtful, and it has been common to assume two writers: Kaghankatvatsi in the seventh century as author of Books I and II, and Daskhurantsi in the tenth as editor of that text and author of Book III.

The Old Armenian text was printed in Moscow and in Paris in 1860, and Varag Arakelian published a critical text in Erevan in 1983, after his modern Armenian translation of 1969. K. Patkanov translated the work into Russian in 1861 and Sh. V. Smbatian in 1984, and L. Davlianidze-Tatishvili into Georgian in 1985. The English translation by C. J. F. Dowsett, The History of the Caucasian Albanians, appeared in 1961, and Robert Bedrosian's The History of the Aghuans in 2010.
moynaq: Moynaq, also spelled Muynak, is a city in northern Karakalpakstan, an autonomous republic in Uzbekistan, and the seat of the Moynaq district. It was formerly a seaport on the Aral Sea and now lies about 150 km from the water, in the Aralkum Desert. Its population was 13,000 in 1991 and 18,196 in 2012. Most inhabitants are Karakalpaks, with many Uzbeks and Kazakhs and smaller groups of Tatars and Turkmens. Uzbek and Karakalpak have official status, and Russian serves as a language of interethnic communication.

Moynaq was a bustling fishing community, once Uzbekistan's only port city, with tens of thousands of residents. Fishing had always been part of the regional economy, and the town became a centre of industrial fishing and canning. In the 1960s the Soviet government diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate a regional monoculture of cotton, which starved the Aral Sea of its inflows. Agricultural chemical runoff caused severe pollution, the sea evaporated, and the remaining water became highly saline and toxic. The shoreline receded dozens of kilometres from the town and the economy collapsed.

Dust storms from the dried and polluted seabed cause chronic and acute illnesses among the few residents who remained, and weather no longer moderated by the sea brings hotter summers and colder winters.

The town's main attractions are the rusting hulks of its former fishing fleet, which stand beside the Aral Sea Memorial at its northern end, and a one-room museum with paintings and photographs of its more prosperous days, including fur farming and rush mat manufacture. Saiga antelope still live wild around Moynaq, and about 230 species of birds are recorded in the region, around half of which breed in the Sudochye Wetland. The Stihia electronic music festival has been held among the ships since 2018 to draw attention to the Aral Sea disaster. Water transport has ceased, and the port is not functioning.
mozabites: The origin of the name is debated. Ibn Khaldun derived Mzab from a supposed ancestor, Maṣʿab ibn Sadmān, while the Ibadi author Amhammad Atfayyash linked it to the Arabic mīzāb, gutter, perhaps to tie the people to the gutter of the sanctuary at Mecca. The Mozabite anthropologist Brahim Chérifi traces it to the Berber At n-Zab, people of the Zab. Most of the region's Berber population adopted Ibadi Islam after a Persian Ibadi refugee founded the Rustamid dynasty in 767. Defeated at Tiaret by the Fatimid Caliphate in 911, the Ibadis withdrew to Ouargla and later, in the face of further persecution, to the M'zab.

The valley long remained beyond the reach of its neighbours. In the 1500s the Mozabites recognised nominal Ottoman authority. After the French captured Laghouat in 1852, they concluded a convention in 1853, agreeing to pay 1,800 francs a year in return for their independence, but in November 1882 the M'zab was annexed to French Algeria. Under French rule Beni Isguen became the depot for goods from Europe.

The valley also had a small Jewish community, which according to one theory was brought from Tunisia by the Ibadi leadership in the 14th century as part of a merchant route. In 1881 it numbered an estimated 3,000 of Algeria's 30,000 Jews. Unlike the Jews of the north, whom the French made citizens under the Crémieux Decree of 1870, many Mozabite Jews were kept under the indigenous code and Mosaic law, which limited their political and social power, and only French Law 61-805 of 1961 gave them common law civil status and citizenship.

The Mozabites, numbering about 150,000 to 300,000, live mainly in five oases, Ghardaïa, Beni Isguen, El Atteuf, Melika and Bounoura, and in the two more isolated oases of Berriane and El Guerrara to the north. Ghardaïa is the capital of their confederation and Beni Isguen its chief commercial centre. They speak the Mozabite language, one of the Zenati Berber languages, and many also speak Algerian Arabic. Mozabite engineers built irrigation works that made the oases much more fertile than before.
mozaffar-ad-din-shah-qajar: Mozaffar ad-Din was born on 23 March 1853 in Tehran, the fourth son of Naser al-Din Shah Qajar. His mother was Shokouh al-Saltaneh, a daughter of Fathollah Mirza and a granddaughter of the second Qajar shah, Fath-Ali Shah. He was named crown prince and sent as governor to the northern province of Azerbaijan in 1861.

He spent some 35 years as crown prince, in the pursuit of pleasure. His relations with his father were frequently strained, and he was not consulted in important matters of state, so that when he came to the throne in May 1896 he was unprepared for the burdens of office.

Iran faced a financial crisis at his accession, with annual government expenditure far above revenue. Mozaffar ad-Din attempted some reforms of the central treasury, but the debts to England and Russia incurred by the Qajar court undermined them. He borrowed further from Britain, France and Russia, and the later loans went to pay off earlier ones rather than to fund economic development. To meet the costs of the state and of his own extravagant life he also signed concessions that gave foreigners monopoly control over various industries and markets.

Like his father he visited Europe three times. On the urging of his chancellor Amin-os-Soltan he borrowed from Nicholas II of Russia to pay for the journeys. In Paris he saw the cinematographe and ordered his photographer to bring the equipment to Tehran, which began Persian cinema. On his visit to the United Kingdom in August 1902 he hoped for the Order of the Garter, but King Edward VII refused it to a non-Christian; in 1903 the king gave way and the shah was appointed a member.

Fear among the aristocracy, the educated elite and the religious leaders of foreign control led to protests in 1906. The shah then agreed to the creation of a Majles, a National Consultative Assembly, granting a constitution and a parliament that curtailed the monarch's power. He died of a heart attack 40 days after granting the constitution, on 8 January 1907, and was buried in the Imam Husayn Shrine in Kerbala.

Contemporaries judged his character in varied terms. The historian Abbas Amanat describes a man of gentle disposition with an earnest wish to open the country to social and educational reforms, who lacked his father's panache and political skill in playing the European powers against each other. The British diplomat Mortimer Durand, who knew both shahs, wrote that he was more amiable than his father but weak and easily misled. He suffered ill health from youth, including a weak heart and a chronic kidney infection, yet enjoyed riding, hunting and shooting. He is often credited with the Persian Constitution of 1906.
mozambique: Mozambique lies on the southeast coast of Africa, bordered by the Indian Ocean, Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Eswatini and South Africa. The Zambezi River divides it into two topographical regions. North of the river a narrow coastal strip gives way to inland hills, low plateaus and rugged highlands covered with miombo woodlands. South of it the lowlands are broader. The climate is tropical, with a wet season from October to March and a dry season from April to September.

The country was named Moçambique by the Portuguese after the Island of Mozambique. The island's name is derived from Musa ibn Bique, an Arab trader who first visited it, later lived there and was its ruler when Vasco da Gama called in 1498. The island-town was the capital of the Portuguese colony until 1898, when the capital moved south to Lourenço Marques, now Maputo.

Bantu-speaking peoples migrated into Southeast Africa as early as the 4th century BCE. Between the 1st and 5th centuries CE waves of migration passed through the Zambezi valley into the plateau and coastal areas. They established agricultural communities and herding societies and brought the technology of iron smelting and smithing. From the late first millennium CE, Indian Ocean trade networks reached as far south as the port town of Chibuene. From the 9th century, port towns grew along the East African coast and shared in an incipient Swahili culture. Islam was often adopted by urban elites, which facilitated trade.

Sofala, Angoche and Mozambique Island were regional powers by the 15th century. Inland states such as the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe and the Mutapa Empire supplied gold and ivory, which were exchanged up the coast to larger ports such as Kilwa and Mombasa. Vasco da Gama's voyage of 1498 marked the Portuguese entry into the region. They gained control of the Island of Mozambique and of Sofala in the early 16th century, and by the 1530s traders and prospectors seeking gold had set up garrisons and trading posts at Sena and Tete on the Zambezi. Portuguese posts and forts displaced Arab commercial and military dominance.

Mozambique is the Republic of Mozambique, a presidential republic with its capital and largest city at Maputo. It became independent in 1975 after more than four centuries of Portuguese rule, and a civil war followed from 1977 to 1992. Portuguese is the only official language, alongside local languages such as Tsonga, Makhuwa and Sena. The Makonde are known for their wood carving and masks, and the Chopi for their marimba music and dance.
mozambique-island: The Island of Mozambique lies between the Mozambique Channel and Mossuril Bay and belongs to Nampula Province. It is about 3 kilometres long and between 200 and 500 metres wide. Most of the historic buildings stand at the northern end, in what is now called Stone Town, while most residents live in reed houses in Makuti Town at the southern end. The island is entirely urbanised, and since the 1960s a bridge of 3 kilometres has joined it to the mainland. The country takes its name from the island.

Pottery shows that the town was founded no later than the fourteenth century, and tradition says its first Swahili population came from Kilwa. By the fifteenth century its rulers had links with those of Angoche and Quelimane. In 1514 Duarte Barbosa noted that its people were Muslim and spoke the same Swahili dialect as Angoche. The name Moçambique derives from Ali Musa Mbiki, called Mussa Bin Bique, the sultan of the island at the time of Vasco da Gama.
The Portuguese established a port and naval base in 1507 and built the Chapel of Nossa Senhora de Baluarte in 1522, now considered the oldest European building in the Southern Hemisphere.

In the 16th century they built Fort São Sebastião, and their settlement became the capital of Portuguese East Africa and an important missionary centre. The island withstood Dutch attacks in 1607 and 1608 in a defence led by the captain-general Dom Estêvão de Ataíde. It was a major post on Portuguese voyages to India and a place where slaves, spices and gold were traded. The opening of the Suez Canal reduced its fortunes, the capital moved to Lourenço Marques, now Maputo, in 1898, and by the middle of the 20th century the new harbour of Nacala took most of the remaining business.

The island is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with a permanent population of about 14,000. Besides the old fortifications, its buildings include the Palace and Chapel of São Paulo, built in 1640 as a Jesuit college and later the governor's residence, now a museum. The Museum of Sacred Art, in the Church of the Misericórdia, displays a Makonde crucifix. A neo-classical hospital of 1877 survives, and the island also has mosques and a Hindu temple.
mozarabs: The name Mozarab comes from the Arabic musta'rab, meaning Arabized. It is first documented in Christian sources from the 11th century, and Muslims did not use it for Christians; Arabic sources called them Nazarenes or described them by their legal status as people of the covenant. More precisely they were Andalusi Christians, the Christians of the territories of Iberia under Muslim rule after the Umayyad conquest of the Visigothic Kingdom. Most were descendants of local Christians who spoke Romance varieties, together with members of the former Visigothic ruling elite who neither converted nor emigrated north.

As dhimmi, Christians paid the jizya, a personal tax, and kept their own judges, tribunals and Roman-derived civil law. Some held high office: Recemundus, a palace official, wrote the Calendar of Córdoba for Abd ar-Rahman III, and in 1064 the emir of Zaragoza sent the Mozarabic bishop Paternus of Tortosa as an envoy to Ferdinand I of León. Their guarantees, at first fairly broad, steadily diminished. The building of new churches and the ringing of church bells were eventually forbidden. An estimated 50 per cent had converted to Islam by 951.

Mozarabs took Arabic names and learned Arabic, and Petrus Alvarus of Córdoba lamented the decline of spoken Latin among them. Latin remained the language of the liturgy and of culture. Their Romance dialects, today called the Mozarabic language, are first written down in the kharjas, the closing choruses of Arabic and Hebrew muwashshah poems, and passed many words of Andalusi Arabic origin into Portuguese, Spanish and Catalan.

Between 850 and 859 a movement in Córdoba brought Christians to seek martyrdom by insulting Muhammad and criticising Islam. Eulogius of Córdoba, beheaded in 859, recorded their deaths and opposed the Arabization of the Christians, while Albarus of Córdoba defended the martyrs in his Indiculus luminosus. Kenneth Baxter Wolf concludes that Eulogius was a hagiographer rather than the instigator, and records further executions in Córdoba in 860, in 888–912, in 913–920.

Mozarabs migrated north to the Christian kingdoms, and this northward movement explains Arabic place names in areas where Muslim rule did not last long. Many who lived under Christian rule kept their distinctive rite until the 14th century. How many Christians lived in al-Andalus is debated: one scholar puts them at about 75,000, roughly 15 per cent of the population of Islamic Iberia, at the end of the 11th century.
mozdok: Mozdok stands on the left shore of the Terek River in North Ossetia–Alania, 92 kilometres north of Vladikavkaz, and is the administrative centre of Mozdoksky District. Its name comes from a Kabardian phrase, mez degu, meaning the deaf forest.

The Russians established the fort in 1763 on the site of a Kabardian village founded four years earlier, and settled families of Volga Cossacks in stanitsas around it. In 1764 one of the first Ossetian schools opened there, and the Kabardian leaders' request that the fortress be destroyed went unanswered. The Kabardians later tried to besiege the town but were compelled to retreat. Russian authorities encouraged Ossetians, Georgians, Armenians and other Christians to settle, and the town became a key military outpost linked to Kizlyar by a fortified line and a centre of trade. A census of 1777 counted 674 Georgians, 565 Armenians, 180 Kabardians, 95 Ossetians and 21 Greeks.

Mozdok was the northern end of the Georgian Military Road to Tbilisi until Vladikavkaz, founded in 1784, took its place. Ossetian settlement grew in the 1820s when the Russian commander Yermolov began removing Kabardians from the area of the road and settling Ossetians there. Muslim Ossetian families from Digoria also settled early in the 19th century. The brothers Dubinin built the first oil-refining apparatus in the world there in 1823. German troops took the town on 23 August 1942 during Case Blue, and the Red Army recaptured it on 3 January 1943.

Under the Russian Empire Mozdok was the seat of the Mozdoksky Otdel of the Terek Oblast. The census of 2002 recorded 62.7 per cent Russians, 7.7 per cent Ossetians and 6.1 per cent Armenians. From 1961 to 1998 the 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, flying Tupolev Tu-95s, was based at the nearby airbase.
mozhaysk: Mozhaysk lies 110 kilometres west of Moscow on the historic road leading to Smolensk and then to Poland. It is the administrative centre of Mozhaysky District. One theory holds that its name comes from the Mozhay river, whose name may be of Baltic origin, compared with the Lithuanian mažoji, small, in contrast to the larger Moskva river nearby. The town was frequently the last major obstacle on the way to the capital, and gave rise to the Russian expression to push beyond Mozhay, meaning to crush an enemy completely and drive them far away. It is said to have originated when the Polish army retreated to Mozhaysk after the Battle of Moscow in 1612.

Mozhaysk is first mentioned in 1231 as an appanage of Chernigov. It became an important stronghold of the Smolensk dynasty and in the 13th century was ruled by Duke Theodore the Black, later a saint. The Muscovites seized it in 1303, but during the following century they had serious trouble defending it against Algirdas, Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1345 to 1377. A younger brother of the ruling Grand Duke of Moscow usually held the Principality of Mozhaysk. In 1562 Denmark and Russia signed the Treaty of Mozhaysk there during the Livonian War, and in 1708 the administration of Peter the Great granted the town its status.

The town helped defend the western approaches to Moscow in the 19th and 20th centuries. During the French invasion of 1812 the Battle of Borodino was fought 12 kilometres away. German forces took Mozhaysk on 18 October 1941 and the Red Army recaptured it on 20 January 1942.

A first fortified settlement existed in the 12th century. After the great fire of 1541 Ivan the Terrible ordered it rebuilt, and a brick kremlin replaced the stone fortress in 1624 to 1626. The Cathedral of St. Nicholas, in Gothic Revival style by Aleksei Bakarev, was begun in 1802, ransacked by the retreating French in 1812 and consecrated in 1814. The Luzhetsky Monastery was founded in 1408 by Saint Ferapont and rebuilt in brick in the 16th century. The 2010 census counted 31,363 inhabitants.
mpande: Mpande was born in Babanango, Zululand, the son of Senzangakhona kaJama and his ninth wife Songiya kaNgotsha Hlabisa.
