Considered weak beside his contemporaries and showing no interest in Zulu power politics, he was allowed to live when Dingane assassinated Shaka in 1828 and other half-brothers were eliminated. After Dingane's defeat at the Battle of Blood River in December 1838, Mpande defied him in September 1839, refusing to join a war against the Swazi, and led thousands of Zulus into the Boer republic of Natalia.

The Boers under Andries Pretorius and Gert Rudolph backed him in the hope of concessions. In January 1840 his army under Nongalaza defeated Dingane at the Battle of Maqongqo, and Mpande, arriving with Pretorius's force, was proclaimed king; the Boers were at once granted a large stretch of territory. In 1843 he had his brother Gqugqu killed, with his wives and children, for allegedly plotting against him, and many refugees fled into Natal. The same year the British commissioner Henry Cloete negotiated a treaty defining the borders of Natal and Zululand.

In the early 1850s Mpande raided the lands around his kingdom, culminating in the invasion of Swaziland in 1852; according to the historian Philip Bonner, he wanted control of it because he feared Boer expansion from Natal. British pressure made him withdraw. His eldest son Cetshwayo, who had led well in the campaign, came into conflict with the favourite son, Mbuyazi, as Mpande declared neither mother his Great Wife, and Cetshwayo crushed Mbuyazi's followers at the Battle of Ndondakusuka, massacring survivors, among them five of his brothers.

From then on Cetshwayo was the de facto ruler and Mpande kept only ceremonial functions; in 1861 Cetshwayo had Mpande's favourite wife Nomantshali and her children killed. Mpande died in late 1872, the exact date kept secret to secure a smooth succession. J. Y. Gibson called him the fool of the family, while James O. Gump describes him as a savvy survivor in the Machiavellian world of Zulu politics. He allowed John Colenso to codify Zulu grammar and translate the Bible into Zulu, and Colenso's associate Magema Fuze praised his peaceful rule.
mpla: The movement grew out of two organisations: the Party of the United Struggle for Africans in Angola, founded in 1953 by Viriato da Cruz and Matias Miguéis, and the Angolan Communist Party, founded in December 1955 as a Luanda cell of the Portuguese Communist Party. Viriato da Cruz belonged to both and arranged their merger into a broad nationalist front. On 10 December 1956, at the house of Ilídio Machado in Luanda, Machado, da Cruz and Mário Pinto de Andrade wrote the Manifesto of 1956 calling for a broad Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola. Machado was the first president until his arrest in 1959, and part of the leadership moved to exile in Paris and Frankfurt from 1957.

The MPLA took up arms against the Portuguese in 1961. In the early 1970s its guerrilla activity declined under Portuguese counter-insurgency, and internal conflict split it for a time into three factions. After the Carnation Revolution of 1974 the Angolan independence coalition broke down, and on 11 November 1975 Agostinho Neto, holding Luanda and the oil fields of the Atlantic coast, declared the People's Republic of Angola. UNITA and the FNLA declared independence separately at Huambo. South Africa and Zaire intervened for the FNLA and UNITA, Cuba intervened for the MPLA, and the Soviet Union aided Cuba and the MPLA.

At its first congress in 1977 the MPLA adopted Marxism-Leninism and added Partido do Trabalho to its name. After Nito Alves's attempted coup that year, Neto ordered the killing of suspected followers of orthodox communism; estimates of the dead range from 2,000 to 70,000, with some placing the toll at 18,000. In December 1990 the party declared social democracy its ideology. After it won the 1992 election, fighting resumed, and tens of thousands of UNITA and FNLA sympathisers were killed in what is called the Halloween Massacre. The war ended in 2002 with the death of Jonas Savimbi and a ceasefire; more than 500,000 civilians died in it.

The MPLA's core base is the Ambundu ethnic group and the educated intelligentsia of Luanda. Its armed wing, the People's Armed Forces for the Liberation of Angola (FAPLA), became the national armed forces from 1975 to 1991. Its mass organisations include the Angolan Women's Organization, the National Union of Angolan Workers, the Agostinho Neto Pioneer Organization and the Youth of the MPLA.
mpondo: In Mpondo oral tradition the people descend from King Mpondo, grandson of Sibiside, leader of the Embo or Aba-Mbo nation, who are thought to have migrated south into present-day South Africa. Mpondo and Mpondomise are remembered as twins; tradition holds that Mpondo, generally taken as the senior, killed a lion and refused to hand its skin to his brother, and then led his followers away to settle elsewhere. The Mpondo share their lineage with the amaMpondomise, amaXesibe, the Mkhize, the amaBomvu and the amaBomvana. The royal clan, the amaNyawuza, takes its name from King Nyawuza, a later descendant of the founder.

Mpondo tradition remembers the reign of King Faku for the defeat of Zulu invasions during the Mfecane. The first, in 1824, ended with the Zulu army short of food and foraging for wild watermelons, so that it became known as Impi yama Bhece. Before a second invasion in 1828 Faku moved women and children into the Mngazi forests west of the Mzimvubu River while his son Prince Ndamase led the army, and a third attempt was turned back at the Mthavuna River. The kingdom also fought neighbours such as the Abathembu, the amaMpondomise and the Amabhaca.

In the 1950s the land rehabilitation programme, the Bantu Authorities system, which gave chiefs a limited, state-sanctioned power in place of consultation at the inkundla, and higher taxes provoked growing resistance. In June 1960 police fired on a meeting at Ngquza Hill, killing 11 people and arresting 23. Chiefs seen as collaborators were attacked, and a boycott of white-owned stores followed. By the end of November 1960 a state of emergency covered Flagstaff, Bizana, Tabankulu, Lusikisiki and Mount Ayliff, and heavy policing and military force put the revolt down; 4,769 people were imprisoned, 2,067 brought to trial, and 30 sentenced to death in 1961.

The great house of the kingdom has its palace, Ndimakude, at Flagstaff, and the right-hand house its Nyandeni Great Place at Libode; Nyandeni long enjoyed autonomy as western Mpondoland, while the Qawukeni house was called eastern Mpondoland. Towns of the kingdom include Lusikisiki, Mbizana, Ntabankulu, Port St. Johns and Ngqeleni. Besides the royal clans, the kingdom holds older Aba-Mbo clans and clans that settled later and pay tribute. The Mpondo perform ukusina and their own imfene, or baboon dance, to maskandi music; in the old calendar the year begins in September, the month of the annual Mpondo Culture and Heritage Festival at Ntabankulu.
mpondomise: The Mpondomise, also called the Ama-Mpondomise, are a Xhosa-speaking people whose homeland is in the Eastern Cape of South Africa and, in the apartheid period, lay in the Transkei. Like the Thembu and the Mpondo, they are a separate kingdom and are sometimes mistaken for part of the Xhosa people. They belong to the AbaMbo group. The name means to hold your horns upright, a description of the mountainous country they occupied and of their fighting strength, and it is also read as a sign of being both diplomatic and ready to attack.

Their traditions trace them to King Mpondomise, son of Khubazi and grandson of King Sibiside of the Embo nation. Mpondomise and Mpondo were twins, and it is held that the Mpondo prince killed a lion and refused to hand the skin to his senior twin as custom required, after which he and his followers left to settle elsewhere. Which twin was older is still argued, but most hold that Mpondomise was the senior. The Mpondomise also intermarried with the San, as their language's clicks and their clan names show, and the royal Jola or Majola clan descends from such marriages.

According to the Mpondomise counsellor Vethe Mziziba, the Bhaca found the Mpondomise at Mcuthu and defeated them. The Mpondomise sought help from the Thembu, and King Ngubengcuka joined them against the Bhaca, but both were defeated again until Ngubengcuka reached a diplomatic settlement with the Bhaca king Madzikane. The Bhaca were later defeated by a combined force of Thembu, Gcaleka, Qwathi and Mpondomise, with some Irish mercenaries who had left the Cape Colony.

In 1880–81 the Mpondomise rose in revolt, and King Mhlontlo ka Matiwane was accused of killing a Qumbu magistrate, Hamilton Hope, and two white policemen. He was acquitted of murder but lost his kingship by administrative action, and the nation's royal status was removed in 1904. In 2005 the Nhlapo Commission found that they had no claim to a kingship. The Eastern Cape High Court at Mthatha later recognised the kingship and ordered it reinstated, setting aside the commission's decision.

Because of colonial conquest most Mpondomise now speak Xhosa, and a minority are bilingual, with Isi-Mpondomise as their home language. The language is dying out, and some regard it as a dialect of Xhosa. The Mpondomise kings are recorded in a long genealogy that includes King Myeki, the most prominent of them.
mpumalanga: The name means East, or literally the place where the sun rises, in the Nguni languages. The province borders Limpopo to the north, Gauteng to the west, the Free State to the south-west and KwaZulu-Natal to the south, and takes up 6.3 percent of South Africa's land. The Drakensberg escarpment divides it into a western half of high-altitude grassland, the Highveld, and an eastern half of low-altitude subtropical Lowveld, mostly savanna, where the southern half of Kruger National Park lies. Some of the oldest rocks on earth have been found in the Barberton area.

Archaeological sites show human settlement going back 1.7 million years, and the Lion Cavern at Ngwenya on the Eswatini border shows iron ore being mined at least 28,000 years ago. The Lydenburg Heads, from about 500 CE, are the oldest Iron Age artworks south of the equator. Stone-walled Mbayi sites on the Highveld point to a large agropastoral society between about 1500 and 1820, connected to the Portuguese trading post in Maputo Bay. The groups that became the Swazi, Pedi, Ndebele and Tsonga peoples settled in the area.

The first Dutch-speaking settlers arrived in 1845 in the Great Trek, and in 1852 the Boers established the South African Republic. The Pedi, Swazi and Zulu kingdoms offered significant resistance, and the Pedi fought the Boers in the Sekhukhune Wars of 1876. Gold was first found near Barberton in 1883, and the region became a thoroughfare for trade between Johannesburg and Delagoa Bay. Under a system known as Inboekstelsel, Boers raided to capture children and force them into indentured labour. Kruger National Park was established in 1898.

After 1948 apartheid policy moved Black South Africans by forced removals into homelands, among them KaNgwane, KwaNdebele, Lebowa and Gazankulu. In 1959 the town of Bethal was the centre of a consumer potato boycott against conditions on local farms. In 1986 a disaster at Kinross Mine killed 177 mine workers. The province was formed on 27 April 1994, the day of South Africa's first democratic elections, from the Eastern Transvaal and the former homelands, and was renamed Mpumalanga on 24 August 1995.

The capital is Mbombela. The province is home to Swazi, Ndebele, Afrikaans, Tsonga, Zulu, Mapulana, Portuguese and Pedi communities, and the Ndebele Cultural Village at Botshabelo displays Ndebele house painting. At the 2011 census it had about four million people, 30 percent of whom spoke siSwati.
mrauk-u: Mrauk U is a town in northern Rakhine State, Myanmar, and the capital of Mrauk-U Township. It lies about 11 kilometres east of the Kaladan River on the banks of minor tributaries, on a small outcrop of the Rakhine Yoma, and the countryside around is hilly but holds marshes, mangroves and lakes. The climate is tropical monsoon, with over 3,600 millimetres of rain a year from the southwest monsoon. Some Rakhine scholars hold that the name means The First Accomplishment in archaic Arakanese, after a prince of the Mro people who crushed a Pyu invasion in the mid-10th century. A story dismissed as myth derives it instead from Monkey’s Egg.

In 1430 King Min Saw Mon established Mrauk U as the capital of the last unified Arakanese kingdom, and it remained the capital of the Mrauk U Kingdom and its 49 kings until the Burmese Konbaung dynasty conquered the kingdom. The city reached a population of 160,000 in the early 17th century. Its history is divided into three periods: 1430–1530, 1531–1638 and 1638 onward. It was fortified by a wall 30 kilometres long and a network of moats and canals, and its waterways earned it comparison with Venice. At its height the kingdom stretched from the Ganges to the western reaches of the Ayeyarwady, and its kings minted coins inscribed in Arakanese, Kufic and Bengali.

The city was a trade hub on the Bay of Bengal. Goods passing through included rice, ivory and elephants from Ava, and cotton, horses, spices and textiles from Bengal, India, Persia and Arabia. The Portuguese came first, and the Dutch East India Company began trading in 1608 and kept a permanent factory from 1635 to 1665. Much of what is known of the city comes from Friar Sebastian Manrique, a Portuguese Augustinian who lived there from 1630 to 1635.

Mrauk U has a rich collection of temples and pagodas, second in Myanmar only to Bagan, most built of hewn stone rather than brick. The best known are the Shite-thaung, Htukkanthein and Koe-thaung temples. Manrique also mentions a Roman Catholic church and foreign-born converts, and Japanese warriors who had left Japan served in the royal guard. In 2017 an international commission urged Myanmar to nominate the town for World Heritage status.

On 16 January 2018 police fired live ammunition at Rakhine protesters rioting near a government building, killing seven and wounding twelve. The Arakan Army captured the city from the Tatmadaw on 8 February 2024. On 10 December 2025 a hospital in Mrauk U was bombed by the Myanmar military, killing 33 people and injuring about 80.
msallata: Msallata, also called Al Qasabat, Cussabat or El-Gusbát, lies in the Murqub District. Its winters are very wet, and its economy rests mainly on olives, wheat and barley, with as many as 19 olive mills, the herding of sheep and goats and the manufacture of cement. The origin of the name is unknown: some derive it from masallat, the plural of the Arabic masalla, obelisk, after the town's 22 tall buildings called qasaba, others from a word for scrubbing olives from the tree, but none of these ideas has been substantiated.

In Roman times the place was a station called Misfe between Leptis Magna and Tarhunah. At the end of the First World War the agreement establishing the Tripolitanian Republic was signed in the town on 16 November 1918. During the anti-Jewish riots in British-administered Tripolitania in November 1945, many Jews in al-Kusbat converted to Islam to protect themselves from being massacred, and Jewish refugees from Msallata founded Ahisamakh in Israel in 1950.

In the civil war of 2011 Reuters reported clashes in the town on 3 August in which three people were killed. By 5 August AFP was reporting that the town, whose residents had joined the rebellion in its early stages, was under siege: government troops held the roads into it, had cut off electricity and communications and had begun arresting people in the suburbs.

Msallata was historically a centre of Islamic studies and still draws Libyan and Sub-Saharan students who come to learn the Quran at schools such as Zawiyat Al-Jourani, the Mejabra Mosque and Zawiyat Al-Dokaly. It has a branch of Almergheb University of Arts, a religious sciences college and an engineering faculty. With the city of Tarhuna it gave its name to the former district of Tarhuna wa Msalata.
msiri: Msiri, whose full name was Mwenda Msiri Ngelengwa Shitambi, was a Nyamwezi from Tabora. Like his father Kalasa he traded in copper, ivory and slaves along the routes controlled by the Sultan of Zanzibar and his Arab and Swahili agents, which ran by Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika to Lake Mweru and Katanga. He saw that guns were the key to power and that Katanga's copper and ivory could buy them. He formed a militia, conquered his neighbours and married into the Luba royal family.

Because supplies from the east coast passed through his rivals' lands, Msiri sent his nephew Molenga west to the Ovimbundu and to Portuguese traders near Benguela, and a trader called Coimbra became his supplier. He thus traded with both coasts of Africa and dealt almost as an equal with Tippu Tip and Mirambo. In 1870 he joined Tippu Tip in killing Mwata Kazembe, and he then influenced the choice of Kazembe's successors. He held his subject chiefs through his more than 500 wives, taking one from each chief's village to serve as a spy and, if needed, a hostage.

European sources describe his rule as cruel, with mutilations and executions, while the missionary Frederick Stanley Arnot, whom he invited to Bunkeya and who arrived in 1886, called him a thorough gentleman.

In 1890 Alfred Sharpe brought a British protectorate treaty, which Msiri rejected once the missionary Charles Swan had it translated. In 1891 Congo Free State expeditions led by Paul Le Marinel and then by Delcommune also failed to win his submission.

On 20 December 1891 Lieutenant Omer Bodson of the Stairs Expedition confronted Msiri at Munema and shot him; Bodson was himself mortally wounded. The expedition cut off Msiri's head, and its fate is unknown. The askaris massacred many of his people at Munema, and the population of Bunkeya, estimated at 60,000 to 80,000 in 1891, fell within a year to 10,000 to 20,000. His descendants keep the Garanganze chieftaincy at Bunkeya under the name Mwami Mwenda.
mstislav-i-of-kiev: Mstislav Vladimirovich was born in Turov in February 1076, the eldest son of Vladimir II Monomakh and Gytha of Wessex. His Christian name was Theodore (Fedor). As his father's future successor he reigned in Novgorod from 1088 to 1093 and, after a brief stint at Rostov, from 1095 to 1117, and he built numerous churches there, of which St. Nicholas Cathedral (1113) and the cathedral of St Anthony Cloister (1117) survive. In 1095 he married Princess Christina Ingesdotter, daughter of King Inge I of Sweden. Their children included Ingeborg, mother of Valdemar I of Denmark, and Eupraxia, who married Alexius Comnenus. After Christina died on 18 January 1122 he married Liubava Dmitrievna Zavidich of Novgorod.

After 1117 Mstislav was co-ruler with Monomakh at Belgorod Kievsky and inherited the Kievan throne at his father's death. He also built churches in Kiev, among them his family sepulchre at Berestovo and the church of the Assumption of the Mother of God in Podol. His life was spent in constant warfare, against the Cumans (1093, 1107, 1111 and 1129), the Estonians (1111, 1113, 1116 and 1130), the Lithuanians (1131) and the princedom of Polotsk (1127 and 1129). In 1096 he defeated his uncle Oleg of Chernigov on the Koloksha River, which was the root of centuries of enmity between his descendants and Oleg's. The Norse sagas know him as Harald, an allusion to his grandfather Harold II of England.

Mstislav died in Kiev on 14 April 1132 and was the last ruler of a unified state; as the chronicler put it, the land of Rus was torn apart. When Monomakh died the princely family had two main groups, the Monomakhovichi and the Olgovichi, but as it multiplied it broke up into local branches and sub-branches, and the state quickly disintegrated into rival principalities. The Russian Orthodox Church canonised him as a saint, and the Eastern Orthodox Church commemorates him on 15 April.
mstislav-mstislavich: Mstislav Mstislavich was the son of Mstislav Rostislavich, called the Brave, of Smolensk, and a princess of Ryazan; his grandfather was Rostislav I of Kiev. In 1193 and 1203 he was praised for his bravery in the Kipchak wars, which made his name across Kievan Rus', and at about that time he married Maria, a daughter of the Kipchak khan Kotyan. In 1209 he is recorded as ruler of Toropets.

A year later he took the throne of Novgorod and seized the men of Prince Sviatoslav Vsevolodovich. On the way he relieved Torzhok from a siege by Vsevolod III of Vladimir. He led two successful Novgorodian campaigns against the Chudes in 1212 and 1214, and in 1215 he drove Vsevolod IV out of Kiev and set his uncle Mstislav Romanovich on its throne. After the victory at Lipitsa in 1216 he made his ally Konstantin of Rostov Grand Prince of Vladimir and married his daughter to Yaroslav of Suzdal. Meanwhile his enemies deposed him in Novgorod, and he left northern Rus' for Galicia.

In 1219 he made peace with his chief rival, Daniel of Galicia, who married his daughter Anna. At the Kalka River in 1223, where a coalition of perhaps 18 princes and their Cuman allies fought the Mongols, he is the only prince named among the nine or so who escaped; he cut loose the boats on the Dnieper so that he could not be followed. In 1224 the forces of Leszek the White defeated him in the Polish-Ruthenian War.

Mstislav ruled Galicia until 1227, when intrigues of the boyars forced him to leave the city to his son-in-law, Andrew of Hungary. He withdrew to Torchesk, where he died. Through his daughters he was the maternal grandfather of Alexander Nevsky, Prince of Novgorod and Grand Prince of Vladimir, and of Leo I of Galicia.
mswati-ii: Mswati, also known as Mavuso III, was born around 1820, a son of King Sobhuza I (Somhlolo) and Tsandzile Ndwandwe, known as LaZidze, daughter of Zwide kaLanga of the powerful Ndwandwe clan south of the Pongola River. Sobhuza had sought the marriage to make peace with the Ndwandwe, and Tsandzile was chosen to bear his successor. After Sobhuza's death the kingship was disputed by Mswati's brothers Fokoti, Malambule and Somcuba, so that Mswati and his mother were installed before either was properly prepared. His half-brother Malambule, who held the government until Mswati became king, hid royal cattle and later fled to Zululand.

Mswati's military power grew from the late 1850s. His regiments, among them the Nyatsi, Umbhula and Malalane, raided as far as Zimbabwe and Mozambique, at first for cattle and captives rather than to incorporate the peoples they attacked. In 1852 they drove the Mbayi, or Maseko, out of the Drakensberg foothills. He built a line of outposts along the Kaap River, including Mbhuleni and Mekemeke, to keep the Bapedi from returning, moved his capital to Hhohho, influenced events in the Gaza kingdom, and resisted Zulu encroachment. The writer A. T. Bryant called him a veritable Shaka of the north.

Distant groups sought his protection. He set loyal groups under their own leaders in thinly peopled chiefdoms and placed royal princes and trusted commoners in others; these newcomers became known as Emafikamuva, those who arrived after. The arrival of the Trekboers in what became the Transvaal brought the first contact between the Swazi and European settlers.

Mswati died at his royal residence at Hhohho, aged about forty, having danced the annual incwala 19 times, and was buried at Mbilaneni beside Sobhuza I and Ngwane III. His death ended the era of Swazi conquest and expansion. His successor, the eleven-year-old Ludvonga II, died in 1874, and Mbandzeni became king in June 1875. The country takes its name, Eswatini, from him.
mtskheta: Mtskheta lies on a lowland surrounded by mountains, at the confluence of the Kura, called the Mtkvari in Georgian, and the Aragvi. The Greater Caucasus rise to the north and the Lesser Caucasus to the south. Archaeology traces settlement in the area from the 2nd millennium BCE to the early 1st millennium CE, and numerous Bronze Age burials show that it was already a significant settlement at the start of the 1st millennium BCE.

The Georgian Chronicles say that Mtskheta was founded by Mtskhetos, son of Kartlos, the eponymous ancestor of the Georgians. Historians more readily accept another account, that the Meschian tribes founded it in the 5th century BCE. It was the capital of the early Georgian Kingdom of Iberia from the 3rd century BCE, and the chronicles have Alexander the Great conquering it, which some historians do not accept. At the start of the 3rd century BCE the first Georgian king, Parnavaz, built a new wall around it, and his son Saurmag strengthened it. The city was strongly fortified, with the citadel of Armazi on Mount Bagineti and forts at Tsitsamuri and Sarkine.

Mtskheta was a site of early Christian activity, and in 337 Christianity was proclaimed the state religion of Iberia. A small wooden church built in the centre of the city soon after the conversion became Svetitskhoveli Cathedral, and in the 5th century Vakhtang Gorgasali built a large basilica on the site. The first katolikos was elected in the 5th century and resided in Mtskheta. Vakhtang's successor, King Dachi, moved the capital to the more defensible Tbilisi in the early 6th century, following his father's will. Mtskheta nevertheless remained the coronation and burial place of most Georgian kings until the end of Georgian political independence in the 19th century.

The city was heavily damaged during the Umayyad defeat of the Khazars between 736 and 739. It regained its standing under King George I and Katolikos Melchizedek I, who oversaw the building of the present Svetitskhoveli and Samtavro cathedrals. Timur burned the city in the 15th century, and Alexander I rebuilt Svetitskhoveli in 1425. Further attacks, including one in 1625, reduced it so that by 1801, when Georgia became part of Russia, it was little more than a village.

Mtskheta remains the seat of the Georgian Orthodox Church. Svetitskhoveli Cathedral, the Samtavro Monastery and the Jvari Monastery are among the most significant monuments of Georgian Christian architecture, and their early inscriptions are a valuable reference for the origins of the Georgian alphabet. The Historical Monuments of Mtskheta became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994. Nearby lie the ruins of the Armaztsikhe fortress.
mu-of-balhae: Tae Muye was the eldest son of Tae Choyŏng, the founder of the kingdom of Balhae, and came to the throne on his father's death in 719. The Tang Emperor Xuanzong gave him the title of King of the Kyeru Province, and he in turn gave his father the posthumous title King Go. He then declared the era name Inan, an act of independence from the Tang dynasty, yet he also sent frequent embassies to the Tang court, among them his own sons and brothers.

The aggressive expansion of Balhae under King Mu caused friction with Tang China, with Silla in southern Korea, and with the Khitans, the Xi, the Göktürks and several Mohe tribes. When the Heishui Mohe to the north of Balhae came under the direct control of the Tang in 727, he attacked them, fearing that his kingdom would be caught in a pincer between two enemies.

In 732 he sent the Balhae navy under Chang Munhyu against Tang territory in present-day Shandong. The assault on Dengzhou, in which the local governor Wei Jun was killed, was largely an act of piracy, but the governor's death turned it into an international conflict. In the same year the king led troops to Madushan near Shanhaiguan and occupied the towns nearby. In 733 Emperor Xuanzong ordered Tae Munye to attack Balhae together with forces from Silla, but the allied advance was held up by heavy snow and the attack was repelled.

From 727 Balhae also sent embassies to Japan, so as not to stand alone among its neighbours. The king's letter to the court of Japan declared that Balhae had recovered the lands of Goguryeo and carried on the culture of Buyeo, and Japan, whose relations with Silla were strained, welcomed the mission as a revival of Goguryeo. Mu was succeeded in 737 by his son Dae Heummu.
muallaqat: The Mu'allaqat is a compilation of seven long pre-Islamic Arabic poems, whose name means the Suspended Odes or the Hanging Poems. Together with the Mufaddaliyat, the Asma'iyyat and the Hamasah, among others, they are counted a primary source for early written Arabic poetry; Peter N. Stearns calls them the most sophisticated poetic production in the history of Arabic letters. The original compiler may have been Hammad al-Rawiya, of the 8th century. The grammarian al-Nahhas, who died in 949, tells that Hammad, seeing how little men cared for poetry, collected these seven pieces and urged people to study them.

The seven poets are Imru' al-Qais, Tarafa, Zuhayr, Labid, 'Antara ibn Shaddad, 'Amr ibn Kulthum and Harith ibn Hilliza. Some early authorities gave poems by al-Nabigha and al-A'sha in place of those of 'Antara and Harith, and Ibn Qutaiba mentioned a poem by 'Abid ibn al-Abras; the variation may reflect tribal rivalries.

Ibn Abd Rabbih wrote that the Arabs valued poetry so highly that they wrote seven long pieces in gold on folded Coptic linen and hung them on the curtains of the Kaaba. Al-Nahhas denied this, saying it was not known to any who had handed down ancient poems. No trace of the story appears in early sources on Mecca, and most scholars doubt the poems were physically hung. The story may have grown from the phrase golden poems, a figure for excellence, and the word suspended may be figurative too, or may mean the poems were raised to an honoured position. Robson proposed that Hammad meant the poems were suspended from their proper place, a diwan.

The poets' lives spread over more than a hundred years. Imru' al-Qais, regarded by many as the most distinguished of them, was a prince of the house of Kinda, and the best part of his career probably fell in the middle of the 6th century. 'Amr ibn Kulthum's poem defies the king of al-Hirah, 'Amr III ibn al-Mundhir, whom the poet afterwards killed. Labid is the only one of the seven still alive when Muhammad began preaching, and he later converted to Islam, though his poem belongs to the pre-Islamic period.

The poems cover almost every type of ancient Arabian poetry in the qasida form. Tarafa's includes a long, anatomically exact description of his camel, those of 'Amr and Harith boast of their tribes, and Zuhayr's offers practical wisdom. 'Antara's has a warlike tone and Labid's peaceful themes. The poems were almost certainly transmitted orally before being written down.
muammar-gaddafi: Muammar Gaddafi was born about 1942 near Qasr Abu Hadi, outside Sirte in Tripolitania, during Italian colonial rule. His family belonged to a small, relatively uninfluential tribe, the Qadhadhfa. As a boy he saw the Arab–Israeli War of 1948, the Egyptian Revolution of 1952 and the Suez Crisis of 1956, and he became an Arab nationalist at school in Sabha. In October 1961 he led a demonstration there against Syria's secession from the United Arab Republic, and the authorities expelled him and his family from the town. He later enrolled in the Royal Military Academy in Benghazi.

Gaddafi founded a revolutionary group, the Free Officers, which deposed the Senussi monarchy of King Idris in the coup of 1969. Its central committee became the Revolutionary Command Council, with Gaddafi as chairman and de facto head of state. Ruling by decree, he deported Libya's Italian population and ejected Western military bases. He nationalised the oil industry and used the revenue to build up the military, fund foreign revolutionaries and expand housing, healthcare and education.

On 2 March 1977 the General People's Congress established the Jamahiriya, a state of the masses. Gaddafi gave up his formal post in 1979 and took the title Leader of the Revolution, remaining commander-in-chief and head of the Revolutionary Committees that policed and suppressed dissent. Border conflicts with Egypt and Chad, support for foreign militants and alleged responsibility for the Pan Am Flight 103 bombing isolated Libya, and the United States bombed it in 1986, followed by United Nations sanctions. After 1999 he turned from pan-Arabism to pan-Africanism and chaired the African Union from 2009 to 2010.

Protests against corruption and unemployment began on 17 February 2011, during the Arab Spring, and became a civil war in which NATO intervened on the side of the National Transitional Council. After the fall of Tripoli in August 2011, Gaddafi retreated to Sirte, where he was captured, tortured and killed by militants of the Council on 20 October 2011.

He dominated Libyan politics for four decades. Supporters praise improvements in housing, education and free healthcare. Critics point to human rights abuses, persecution of Berbers, Jews, migrants and foreign workers, and the financing of terrorism.
muara-takus: The complex is thought to have been built by the maritime Srivijaya Empire in the 11th century, and the architecture and design of its temples point clearly to a Mahayana Buddhist origin. The scholar Schnitger suggested that the main temples may have been extensively renovated in the 12th century. The area is thought to have served Srivijaya as both a religious and a trade centre. It is one of the largest and best-preserved ancient temple complexes in Sumatra.

The site was abandoned for many centuries until Cornet De Groot rediscovered it in 1860. W. P. Groenveld explored and surveyed it in 1880, and excavations have taken place from time to time since. Research in 1983 mapped the remains of an ancient embankment, the Mahligai temple compound and other structures. The site is now protected as a national monument.

A stone wall about 1 metre high, 74 by 74 metres, surrounds the complex, entered by a gateway on the north side. Inside stand the remains of four substantial temples. Candi Mahligai is a lotus-shaped stupa on an octagonal base, 14.30 metres high, unique in Indonesia though similar structures survive in Thailand and Myanmar; lion figures, barely visible from below, decorate its top level. East of it lies the base of Candi Palangka, built of red stone and now 1.45 metres high; its upper terraces, reportedly taller at the time of the first colonial expeditions, have collapsed.

Candi Bungsu, now 6.20 metres high, is built partly of red stone and partly of sandstone. Candi Tua has a base of 32.80 by 21.80 metres and rises 8.50 metres in terraces, recalling in its design the much larger stupa of Borobudur in Java. All the temples carry little decoration, the seated lions on the upper terraces being the most notable.
muawiya-i: Early Islamic sources give Mu'awiya's year of birth as 597, 603 or 605. His father, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, was a prominent Meccan merchant who led trade caravans to Byzantine Syria and became leader of the Banu Abd Shams clan of the Quraysh. Mu'awiya and his father opposed Muhammad until Muhammad captured Mecca in 630, after which Mu'awiya became one of his scribes. Caliph Abu Bakr appointed him a deputy commander in the conquest of Syria, and he rose through the caliphate of Umar until Uthman made him governor of Syria. There he allied with the Banu Kalb tribe, marrying a daughter of its ruling house about 650. He also launched the first Muslim naval campaigns against Byzantium, with Uthman's permission, beginning with Cyprus.

After Uthman was killed in 656, Mu'awiya took up the cause of avenging him and withheld allegiance from Ali. Their armies met at Siffin in 657 and reached a stalemate, and arbitration talks failed. In April or May 658 the Syrians pledged allegiance to Mu'awiya as caliph, and his ally Amr ibn al-As conquered Egypt from Ali's governor.

After Ali was killed in 661, Mu'awiya marched on Kufa, where Hasan, Ali's son, abdicated in return for a financial settlement. Mu'awiya entered the city in July or September 661, and early sources call that year the year of unity.

He made Damascus his capital and moved the treasury there from Kufa. He relied on a Syrian tribal army of about 100,000 men and ruled the provinces indirectly through governors with full civil and military authority, preferring agreements and bribes to confrontation. Armenia became a tributary of the Caliphate, and almost every year his troops raided Byzantine territory across the Anatolian frontier. In 670 the commander Uqba ibn Nafi began the conquest of Ifriqiya. He nominated his son Yazid as his successor, a move without precedent, making the caliphate hereditary.

Mu'awiya died of an illness in Damascus in April or May 680, at about the age of 80, and was buried by the Bab al-Saghir gate. The surviving Muslim histories come from Abbasid-era Iraq and are mostly hostile to the Umayyads, yet they portray him in a relatively balanced way, stressing his hilm, meaning mildness and the skilful management of people. Sunnis do not count him among the rightly-guided caliphs, since he gained the caliphate through civil war and made it hereditary, but they honour him as a companion of Muhammad and a scribe of the revelation. In Shia Islam he is reviled for opposing Ali.
muayyad-al-dawla: Abu Mansur Buya, later known by the honorific Mu'ayyad al-Dawla, meaning Helper of the State, was the third son of Rukn al-Dawla. His mother was a daughter of the Daylamite Firuzanid nobleman Al-Hasan ibn al-Fairuzan, a cousin of the military leader Makan ibn Kaki. He grew up in Isfahan, and in 955, when the Daylamite officer Muhammad ibn Makan attacked the city, he and his family had to flee. They returned after his eldest brother, Adud al-Dawla, and Rukn al-Dawla's vizier Abu 'l-Fadl ibn al-'Amid defeated the attacker.

Around 958 he went to Baghdad and married Zubayda, a daughter of Mu'izz al-Dawla, and brought her back to Isfahan, the city his family had been forced to leave in 955. In 966 he received the honorific title of Mu'ayyad al-Dawla, by which he is known.

Under the settlement Rukn al-Dawla made with Adud al-Dawla in early 976, Mu'ayyad al-Dawla was to receive Hamadan on his father's death in return for recognising Adud al-Dawla as the senior amir. When their brother Fakhr al-Dawla, who ruled in Ray, rose against Adud al-Dawla's authority, Mu'ayyad al-Dawla took the field on Adud al-Dawla's side and forced Fakhr al-Dawla to take refuge with the Ziyarids of Gorgan and Tabaristan. The two brothers then took the Ziyarid lands as well, and Mu'ayyad al-Dawla held the conquered provinces as Adud al-Dawla's subordinate, ruling Hamadan, Jibal, Tabaristan and Gorgan.

Adud al-Dawla died in March 983, and Mu'ayyad al-Dawla died shortly afterwards. His vizier, Sahib ibn 'Abbad, then gathered the army and persuaded its leaders to proclaim Fakhr al-Dawla, the brother the two had driven out, as his successor, so that the lands Mu'ayyad al-Dawla had held passed to him.
mubadala-investment-company: The older of Mubadala's two parents, the International Petroleum Investment Company (IPIC), was set up in 1984 to put Abu Dhabi's petroleum wealth to work for the emirate's development. Mubadala Development Company followed in 2002 to diversify the economy further. The merger of the two was announced in June 2016, and in 2017 ownership of both passed to a newly created parent, Mubadala Investment Company, a wholly owned investment vehicle of the government of Abu Dhabi, with offices in London, Rio de Janeiro, New York, San Francisco and Beijing. It works through four platforms: direct investments, UAE investments, disruptive investments, and real estate and infrastructure.

Its technology holdings grew from the Advanced Technology Investment Company (ATIC) of 2008, which owned the chip foundries GlobalFoundries and Chartered Semiconductor Manufacturing; in 2011 ATIC announced $5.5 billion of investment in chip manufacturing in Singapore, Dresden and New York, and in 2014 it became Mubadala Technology. Mubadala first invested in AMD in 2007 and sold its entire stake in 2019.

Later purchases included MetrôRio, operator of the Rio de Janeiro metro, in 2021; a majority stake in Fortress Investment Group, bought from the SoftBank Group in a $3 billion takeover that the Committee on Foreign Investment in the US (Cfius) reviewed over concerns about the UAE's ties with China and approved in May 2024; and the Canadian asset manager CI Financial Corp., which Mubadala Capital acquired for $8.9 billion in August 2025.

Some investments drew criticism. Mubadala Capital put €50 million into the Novalpina Capital fund that bought the Israeli security company NSO Group in 2019, at a time when reports said the UAE had used the Pegasus spyware against human rights activists, journalists and Princess Haya. In 2023 the former British minister Gerry Grimstone was criticised for not declaring 13 meetings with Mubadala after becoming an adviser at Investcorp, in which Mubadala had become the biggest external shareholder in 2016.
mubarak-al-sabah: Mubarak was born into the al-Sabah family in 1837, a son of Sheikh Sabah II Al-Sabah, who ruled Kuwait from 1859 to 1866. As a grown man he served mainly as cavalry commander of Kuwait's forces, including in several Ottoman campaigns, most notably those of 1871, 1892 and 1894 into Hasa, Qatar and southern Iraq. In August 1879 the Ottomans gave him the rank of Grand Equerry for a campaign into Qatif and southern Iraq. He met Sir Lewis Pelly, the British political resident in Persia, in 1863, and in 1883 he went on an Ottoman diplomatic mission to Bahrain.

His half-brothers Muhammad and Jarrah were killed on 8 May 1896. Accounts of the killing vary: Jill Crystal holds that Mubarak, his sons Jabir and Salim and loyal supporters killed them in secret during the night. Mubarak then spent his late brother's wealth on gifts to the Ottoman bureaucracy to win recognition. The Ottoman Council hesitated, and Hamdi Pasha, the Wali of Basra, proposed military intervention, but in December 1897 Mubarak was named kaymakam, or sub-governor, of Kuwait, since force threatened to destabilise the region further.

Under British protection he invaded Najd in 1901 against the Rashidi, but most of his army was destroyed at the Battle of Sarif on 17 March 1901, his brother and two nephews among the dead. After a stand-off between an Ottoman and a British warship, the Status Quo Agreement of September 1901 barred troops of either power from Kuwait and left Ottoman authority nominal. In October 1907 Mubarak sold Britain the rights to any railway terminus, for £4000 a year, blocking the German-Ottoman plan to bring the Berlin-Baghdad Railway to the port. The Anglo-Ottoman Convention of 1913 recognised Kuwait as an autonomous kaza of the Ottoman Empire.

When World War I began Mubarak sided with Britain. In November 1914 he sent a force to expel the Ottomans from Umm Qasr, Safwan, Bubiyan and Basra, and Britain recognised Kuwait as an independent government under British protection. He removed the Ottoman symbol from the Kuwaiti flag and put the word Kuwait in Arabic script in its place. Weakened by illness in his last years, he died in November 1915 of malaria aggravated by a bad heart. His sons Jaber and Salim succeeded him, and the constitution of Kuwait requires the Emir to be his descendant.
mubariz-al-din-muhammad: Mubariz al-Din Muhammad was born in 1301 into a family of Arab origin that had settled in Khurasan during the Islamic conquest; his mother was probably Mongol. His father, Sharaf al-Din Muzaffar, served the Ilkhanids, and on his father's death in 1314 Mubariz inherited his offices. He lived at the court of the Ilkhanid ruler Öljaitü until Öljaitü's death and then left for Maibud. He married Qutlughkhan Makdumshah, daughter of Qutb al-Din Shah Jahan, the Khitan ruler of the Qutlugh-Khanids.

In 1319 he took Yazd from its atabeg, Hajji Shah ibn Yusuf Shah. Ordered to put down a rising in Sistan, he did so, and when the province rebelled again he reportedly fought 21 battles before it was subdued. After the death of Abu Sa'id ended Ilkhanid authority in central Iran, he declared his independence. In 1339 or 1340 he seized Kirman from its Mongol governor, Kutb al-Din ibn Nasir, who briefly retook it with help from the Kartid dynasty of Herat; Mubariz al-Din held the province for good from late 1340, and later besieged and took Bam.

Rivalry with the Injuids, who held Shiraz and Isfahan, followed. In 1347 Abu Ishaq Inju began a long war to win Kirman, but he failed to take Yazd in 1350-1351 and an army he sent to Kirman was defeated. After taking Shiraz in 1353, Mubariz al-Din pursued Abu Ishaq to Isfahan, took the city and executed him, which left Fars and western Iran in his hands and made Shiraz the Muzaffarid capital.

Strong enough to decline when the Golden Horde khan Jani Beg offered to take him as a vassal, he pushed into Azerbaijan, defeated the khan's governor Akhichuq and occupied Tabriz, but withdrew before Jalayirid troops marching from Baghdad. Remembered as a cruel ruler, he was blinded and imprisoned in 1358 by his son Shah Shuja. A reconciliation did not last, and he died in prison.
mubariz-khan: Mubariz Khan was born Khwaja Mohammad in Balkh and served Aurangzeb as a Turani officer. Of a relatively obscure background, he entered Mughal service as a clerk; his career rose after he married the daughter of Inayat Khan Kashmiri, a noble in Aurangzeb's favour. He was bakshi of Prince Kam Baksh and faujdar of Sangamner, and in 1703-1704 received the title Amanat Khan as faujdar of Baizapur. Under Bahadur Shah he held Surat and then Gujarat, under Jahandar Shah he was moved to Malwa as Shahamat Khan, and in 1713, under Farrukhsiyar, he became governor of Hyderabad with the title Mubariz Khan.

He received wider powers than his predecessors in a province that had lost its splendour after Aurangzeb's death, suffered Maratha raids to extract chauth and saw its trade decline. In the early months of 1714 he defeated a Maratha raiding party near Hyderabad. His methods were violent: after a 40-day siege of the fort of Changapettah, held by the Telugu Nayak Venkat, he raised a tower of skulls, renamed the fort Farrukhnagar and sent Venkat's head to the emperor at Delhi.

He sided with Hussain Ali Khan Barha, the viceroy of the Deccan, rather than the emperor, and in December 1715 was confirmed as governor and made diwan, which removed the central Mughal regime from Golconda's finances. He then punished zamindars slow to pay their taxes, led a nine-month circuit through the country of the Godavari and, after a five-month siege of the fort of Cankoll, in which gunners sent by the English factory at Masulipatnam manned his guns, controlled the whole Andhra coast. The Maasir-ul-Umara praised him for driving off large Maratha armies with no more than 3,000 horse.

In 1722 Nizam-ul-Mulk, Asaf Jah I, then wazir, found large arrears in the appointments of Mubariz Khan and his sons. When the Nizam left Delhi for the Deccan, Emperor Muhammad Shah issued a farman granting Mubariz Khan the governorship of the six provinces of the Deccan. Busy with a siege, Mubariz Khan was slow to respond and camped at Shakar Kheda while the Nizam, allied with Bajirao I, reached Aurangabad first. He died fighting the Nizam on 11 October 1724 and was buried the next day with all his followers. The historian John F. Richards describes him as a proto-dynastic figure.
much-wenlock: Much Wenlock is a market town and parish in Shropshire, England, on the A458 road between Shrewsbury and Bridgnorth, with the Ironbridge Gorge and Telford to the north-east. Much was added to the name to distinguish it from the nearby Little Wenlock. Wenlock probably comes from a Celtic name, Wininicas, meaning white area, after the limestone of Wenlock Edge, plus the Old English loca, an enclosed place. The Domesday Book of 1086 records it as Wenloch, already a fairly large settlement with 73 households.

The town grew up around an abbey or monastery founded around 680 by Merewalh, a son of King Penda of Mercia. Penda installed his daughter Milburga, also called Mildburh, as abbess, and she was credited with many miraculous works. The abbey flourished until around 874, when a Danish Viking attack is thought to have occurred. In the 11th century Leofric, Earl of Mercia, and his wife Godiva built another religious house on the site, and in the 12th century Roger de Montgomery established a Cluniac priory in its place after the Norman Conquest. Its ruins are in the care of English Heritage. The manor belonged to the priory until the dissolution of the monasteries in 1540.

In 1468 Edward IV granted the men of Much Wenlock a charter forming the Borough of Wenlock, at the request of Sir John Wenlock, in consideration of their services in helping the king gain the crown. Henry VIII confirmed it in 1547 and Charles I in 1631. The borough asserted jurisdiction over the liberty of Wenlock, whose lands included detached parts well outside the town, and at its height it covered 71 square miles, including Little Wenlock, Broseley and Ironbridge. It was reformed in 1836 and abolished in 1966.

The Wenlock Olympian Games were set up in the town in 1850 by William Penny Brookes and his Wenlock Olympian Society, and are still held each July. Brookes is credited as a founding father of the modern Olympic Games, and in 1890 Baron Pierre de Coubertin was guest of honour at the Games dinner. The mascot of the London 2012 Summer Olympics was named Wenlock after the town, and the Olympic flame passed through it on 30 May 2012.

Holy Trinity Church dates from 1150 and was built by the Cluniac monks of Wenlock Priory. Medieval pilgrims came to the shrine of Milburga and her well, which was thought to cure eye diseases. The nearby Wenlock Edge and the town feature in A. E. Housman's A Shropshire Lad, and Vaughan Williams set six of its poems to music in 1909 as On Wenlock Edge.
mudaito-dynasty: The Mudaito, also written Modaytó, were the Asaihemara Modaito clan of the Afar, who came from the La'o and Doobi areas. Their sultanate succeeded the Imamate of Aussa, which had come into being in 1577, when Muhammad Gasa moved his capital from Harar to Aussa (Asaita) as the Adal Sultanate split into the Imamate of Aussa and the Emirate of Harar. Some time after 1672 the imamate declined and for a while came to an end.

On 26 September 1725 the Mudaito Afars and their Harla allies invaded Aussa from the north-east and the centre-west and burned the state of Awsa. They spread through Dobi and Kalo, ransacking Adali settlements, and the following month defeated the soldiers of Imam Salman, killing 200 of them. By 1734 Kedafu had prevailed over the imamate as Amoyta, the title of the dynasty's rulers. The sultan's chief symbol was a silver baton believed to have magical properties.

In June 1764 the Mudaito extended their control by overpowering the tribes loyal to the imamate in and around Awsa. In July 1809 Amir Mahammad bin A'as Ali tried and failed to avenge his father's killing in Awsa. In the years that followed the Mudaito dealt heavy blows to the pro-imamate warriors of the Adali Debne We'ima when the Adals tried to halt their advance, and in 1814 they invaded Tadjourah, the capital of the Adali Dardars, killing its rulers and destroying homes. These victories turned the struggle for power among the Afar in the Mudaito's favour, and their Sultanate of Awsa lasted until the colonial reorganisation of 1936.
mudbrick: A mudbrick, also called an unfired brick, is an air-dried brick made from a mixture of mud containing loam, clay, sand and water with a binding material such as rice husks or straw. From around 5000–4000 BCE mudbricks evolved into fired bricks, which are stronger and more durable. In some warm regions with little timber to fuel a kiln, mudbricks stayed in use, and they remain the standard of vernacular architecture in parts of Africa and western Asia. In the 20th century the compressed earth block was developed, using high pressure to make a cheap non-fired brick stronger than the simpler air-dried kind.

Mudbrick production in the southern Levant goes back to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, as at Jericho, where dwellings of about 9000 BCE were built of mudbricks set in mud. Mixtures of sand, clay and water, often tempered with chopped straw and chaff, were the most common material for earthen buildings across the ancient Near East for millennia. Well-preserved bricks from Tel Tsaf in the Jordan Valley date to 5200 BCE, and their composition stayed stable for at least 500 years. The people of Mehrgarh in South Asia lived in mudbrick houses between 7000 and 3300 BCE, and more than 15 sites of the Indus Valley civilisation in the 3rd millennium BCE used them, though the Mature Harappan phase used fired bricks.

Mesopotamians built cities of sun-dried bricks, typically flat below and curved on top, called plano-convex, and some walls had a few courses of fired brick at the base to protect them from splashing. Sun-dried bricks were found in Neolithic Knossos. They were the most common building material in pharaonic Egypt, where workers trampled Nile mud with straw in a pit; because the bricks were chemically suitable as fertiliser, many ruins such as Edfu were destroyed, while Amarna is a well-preserved site. Greeks used mudbrick for walls and citadels, including Troy II.

In areas of Spanish influence the technique is called adobe. The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali, the world's largest mudbrick structure, is built of banco, a fermented mixture of mud and grain husks whose plaster must be reapplied annually.
mudejar: From the eleventh century, as Christian kingdoms retook larger regions that had been under Muslim control, treaties defined the status of the remaining Muslim population as Mudéjar. Modelled on the dhimmi, the status established a parallel society with its own religious, legal, administrative and fiscal autonomy and institutions, while Muslims remained subject to their Christian kings and lords. The surrender treaty at the conquest of Toledo was especially influential, since the Muslims there were a numerical majority and shaped its wording.

In the mid-thirteenth century, regions from the Algarve to Murcia and Valencia passed to Christian rule. Those who accepted surrender terms might stay, while those who held out were expelled, though there were exceptions. The word is a medieval Castilian borrowing of the Arabic mudajjan, meaning subjugated or tamed, and probably began as a taunt, since it was usually applied to domestic animals.

The Mudéjar of Andalucia rebelled in 1264 at the instigation of the emirate of Granada, and Castilian and Aragonese forces quelled the revolt by 1267. King Alfonso X of Castile then tried to rebuild Andalucia and Murcia by expelling Mudéjar and settling Christians, yet the conquered were treated with relative tolerance, and Fernando III and Alfonso X each styled themselves King of the Three Religions. In Valencia the Mudéjar were two thirds of the population in the late fourteenth century and rebelled several times in the thirteenth. The crises of the mid-fourteenth century, among them the Black Death, which killed about 30 per cent of the peninsula's people, ended their stable position, and by 1450 they were only 30 per cent of Valencia's population.

After the fall of Granada in 1492, policy changed. By 1498 Mudéjar were banned from living in Granada, and Cardinal Cisneros, seeking to coerce conversion, burned Islamic religious texts in public. Granada's Mudéjar rebelled, and the region was not subdued until 1501. Ferdinand and Isabella decreed in 1502 that all Muslims in the Crown of Castile must convert or leave. In 1526 Carlos I ordered the suppression of Islamic worship in the Crown of Aragon. The newly baptised, suspected of being crypto-Muslims, were known as Moriscos, and they too were expelled in 1609 to 1614.

Muslim administrators oversaw the Mudéjar, Muslim tax collectors gathered their taxes, and they were governed by Islamic law and could practise their faith. In some ways they enjoyed protections that Christian commoners lacked, such as against torture and execution and a right to appeal to the royal court. Both societies kept Muslims and Christians apart. Mudéjar in Castile and Aragon spoke the Romance languages of their Christian neighbours, while most in Valencia were Arabic-speaking peasants. The term also names Mudéjar art, shaped by Islamic art but typically made by Christian craftsmen for Christian patrons.
mudejar-revolt-of-1264-1266: In the early thirteenth century the Almohad Caliphate fell into dynastic struggles and al-Andalus broke into small kingdoms. Ferdinand III, who united Castile and León in 1231, conquered the Guadalquivir basin and Murcia; the city of Murcia surrendered to Infante Alfonso, the future Alfonso X, on 2 April 1243 and became a semi-independent vassal, and Jerez fell in 1261. Muslims of these newly conquered lands were often relocated by their conquerors, a policy they found oppressive and protested to the Pope. Muhammad I ibn al-Ahmar of Granada had paid tribute to Castile since 1246, but the historian L. P. Harvey suggests he sought to weaken Castilian rule after the fall of Niebla in 1262.

The revolt began almost at once in Lower Andalusia and Murcia, probably between April and June 1264. The Muslims of Jerez, aided from Algeciras and Tarifa, took its alcázar on 8 August 1264 after its commander, Nuño González de Lara, deserted. Lebrija, Arcos and Medina-Sidonia followed, while in Murcia the rebels ousted the royal garrison and declared for Muhammad I. The Mudéjars of Old and New Castile largely stayed out. Castile retook Jerez late in 1264 and expelled its Muslims, and early in 1265 Alfonso won a major battle and raided towards Granada.

Queen Violant asked her father, James I of Aragon, for help. After winning over his nobles he invaded Murcia in October 1265, defeated a relieving column of 2,800 men from Granada and besieged the city from 2 January 1266; it surrendered on 31 January. When the Banu Ashqilula rose against Muhammad I at Málaga, Alfonso sent them 1,000 men, and Muhammad sued for peace.

By the treaty of Alcalá de Benzaide, dated variously from 1265 to 1267, Granada became Castile's vassal with a tribute of 250,000 maravedís a year. Castile annexed Murcia outright, except Orihuela and Elche, which went to Aragon. In Andalusia the victors carried out mass expulsion and ethnic cleansing, settling Christians on the land, so that Muslims became almost non-existent there. In Murcia the Muslims kept their religious rights but were moved to the suburb of Arrixaca. Granada survived as the sole independent Muslim state in the peninsula, strengthened by refugees.
mufarrij-ibn-daghfal: Mufarrij was the son of Daghfal ibn al-Jarrah, the first of the Jarrahid family of the Banu Tayy to rise to prominence, as an ally of the Qarmatians against the Fatimids in the early 970s; some sources wrongly call him Daghfal ibn Mufarrij.

He first appears after the Battle of Ramlah in 977, when he found the defeated Turkish ruler of Damascus, Alptekin, near death in the desert, took him home and then handed him over to the Fatimid caliph al-Aziz for a promised reward of 100,000 gold dinars. In 979 he defeated and captured the Hamdanid emir Abu Taghlib, who had attacked Ramlah, paraded him through the town on a camel and killed him with his own hands.

Mufarrij rebelled openly on 7 July 981, but a Fatimid army under Rashiq al-Azizi routed him. He fled to the Hejaz, attacked a Hajj caravan, destroyed a pursuing army at Ayla, was beaten again in Palestine and found refuge with Bakjur at Homs.

In 983 his Tayy fought for the Byzantine emperor Basil II under Bardas Phokas. After a pardon he allied with Bakjur against the vizier Ibn Killis, and when Bakjur was driven from Damascus in 988 Mufarrij followed him north. Only after Ibn Killis died in 991, having urged al-Aziz on his deathbed to execute Mufarrij if he were caught, could he return to Palestine.

In the factional struggle after al-Aziz's death in 996 he sided with the Turkish general Manjutakin, then deserted to the victorious Berber commander Sulayman ibn Ja'far ibn Fallah. Driven to the Hejaz again in 997, he won a pardon by sending the old women of his tribe to ask for it.

In the revolt that began in 1011 his son Hassan ambushed and captured the governor Yarukh, and the Bedouin took and plundered Ramlah. Mufarrij sponsored restorations of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the reappointment of a patriarch, Theophilus I; according to Yahya of Antioch his family held the interior from al-Farama to Tiberias. But al-Hakim's bribes divided the Jarrahids, Abu'l-Futuh returned to Mecca, and in July or August 1013 a Fatimid army of 24,000 defeated them. Mufarrij died, possibly poisoned by the caliph's agents, and Hassan kept his father's lands under a pardon.
mughal-empire: The empire is conventionally said to have been founded in 1526 by Babur, a Timurid prince from the Fergana Valley. He descended from Timur on his father's side and from Genghis Khan on his mother's. Driven from Central Asia, he established himself in Kabul and pushed south through the Khyber Pass. At the First Battle of Panipat he defeated Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, with firearms and cannon despite being outnumbered, using a formation taught by the Ottoman expert Ustad Ali Quli. The Battle of Khanwa against Rana Sanga of Mewar in 1527 was a second decisive victory, and the centre of Mughal power shifted to Agra.

Akbar reigned from 1556 to 1605, first under the regent Bairam Khan. Through a series of wars he controlled almost the whole subcontinent north of the Godavari River and set up the centralised administration. He allowed freedom of religion at his court and tried to bridge differences by founding a new religion, Din-i Ilahi. The empire reached its maximum extent under Aurangzeb, and historians date its imperial structure from about 1600 to 1720.

After Aurangzeb's son Bahadur Shah I died in 1712 the dynasty sank into feuds, and in 1719 alone four emperors came to the throne as figureheads under the Sayyid brothers. Historians cite weak rulers, succession wars and imperial overstretch. The empire was reduced to the region around Old Delhi by 1760 and formally dissolved by the British Raj after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

Below the emperor stood four ministries: finance under the diwan, the military under the mir bakhshi, law and religious patronage under the sadr as-sudr, and the imperial household under the mir saman. The empire was divided into subahs under governors. The capitals were Agra, Delhi, Lahore and Fatehpur Sikri. Agricultural taxes, which amounted to well over half a cultivator's output, were paid in a regulated silver currency. Persian became the official and courtly language, and Hindustani developed in Delhi in the late Mughal era. Mughal monuments listed as World Heritage Sites include Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, the Red Fort, Humayun's Tomb, Lahore Fort and the Taj Mahal.
muhammad: The early sources for Muhammad's life are Muslim authors of the 8th and 9th centuries CE, and scholars dispute how far they can be trusted because of the gap between his life and their writing. Western historians describe the early biographies as written largely to convey a message rather than to record history exactly. What follows is the traditional account.

According to it, Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 into the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh, the leading tribe of western Arabia. His father Abdullah died around the time of his birth and his mother Amina when he was six, and his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and then his uncle Abu Talib brought him up. At 25 he married Khadija, a wealthy woman of 40. He would withdraw for nights of prayer to a mountain cave named Hira, where, at about 40, around 610, he reported that the angel Gabriel gave him his first revelation from God.

In 613 Muhammad began to preach publicly that God is One and that complete submission, Islam, to God is the right way of life. His followers were few and were persecuted by Meccan polytheists for 13 years. In 622 he and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina, then called Yathrib. This migration, the Hijrah, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. In Medina he united the tribes under the Constitution of Medina.

After years of intermittent fighting with Meccan tribes, he marched on Mecca in 630 with 10,000 converts and seized the city with minimal casualties. He declared an amnesty for past offences, except for ten men and women, and had the statues of Arabian gods in and around the Kaaba destroyed. By his death most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam.

Muhammad fell ill in June 632 and died on 8 June in the house of his wife Aisha, where he was buried. A dispute over succession followed. Umar ibn al-Khattab nominated Abu Bakr, who was confirmed as the first caliph, while some companions held that Muhammad had designated his cousin and son-in-law Ali ibn Abi Talib. Within a decade Muslims conquered Mesopotamia, Byzantine Syria and Egypt and large parts of Persia. Muslims hold that he was the last prophet sent by God and that his revelations form the Quran. His sayings and practices, preserved in the hadith, make up the sunnah, which supplies many details of prayer, fasting and pilgrimage not found in the Quran.
muhammad-abduh: Muhammad Abduh was born in 1849 in the Nile Delta, to a father of Turkish ancestry and an Egyptian mother; his family belonged to the Ottoman Egyptian elite. He was educated at a private school in Tanta and at the Ahmadi mosque, and in these years studied under his Sufi uncle Darwish, a member of the reformist Madaniyya order, which stressed adherence to foundational teachings and shunned taqlid, the imitation of earlier authorities. In 1866 he entered al-Azhar in Cairo, where he criticised the traditional curriculum and chose Jamal al-Din al-Afghani as his guide. Their relationship lasted eight years, and al-Afghani gave his mysticism a philosophical basis and drew him towards a rationalist reading of Islam.

Abduh received the degree of alim in 1877 and began teaching logic, theology and ethics at al-Azhar. In 1878 he became professor of history at the teachers' training college Dar al-Ulum and also taught Arabic. In 1880 he became editor-in-chief of the official gazette, the official gazette, which he used to spread anti-colonial ideas and calls for social and religious reform. British forces exiled him in 1882 for six years for supporting the Urabi revolt. He spent several years in Ottoman Lebanon, helping to establish an Islamic educational system, and in 1884 joined al-Afghani in Paris to publish al-Urwa al-Wuthqa.

After returning to Egypt in 1888 he served as a judge in the Courts of First Instance of the Native Tribunals and became a consultative member of the Court of Appeal in 1891. As Grand Mufti from 1899, he was involved in decisions considered liberal, such as allowing meat butchered by non-Muslims and accepting loan interest. This endeared him to Lord Cromer but caused a rift with the khedive Abbas Hilmi and the nationalist leader Mustafa Kamil Pasha. He proposed reforms to al-Azhar's examinations, curriculum and working conditions, and in 1900 founded the Society for the Revival of Arabic Literature. He died of renal cell carcinoma in Alexandria on 11 July 1905.

Abduh wrote the Risalat al-Tawhid, a commentary on the Quran, and articles in al-Manar and al-Ahram. He argued that Islam reproved slavish imitation of tradition and gave humans independence of will and thought, and he held that education, religious and scientific, was the best means of reform. He opposed polygamy where it led to injustice between wives and criticised superstition and the veneration of saints, while remaining sympathetic to Sufism. He urged friendship among the schools of thought within Islam and between Muslims, Christians and Jews. Opponents accused him of being an unbeliever; followers regarded him as a reviver of Islam.
muhammad-ahmad: Muhammad Ahmad was born on Labab Island, Dongola, in northern Sudan, into a notable religious Arabized Nubian family from the Danagla tribe, who traced their descent from the Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Hassan. His father was a boat-builder. While his brothers joined the trade, he turned to religious study and in 1861 sought out Sheikh Muhammad Sharif Nur al-Dai'm of the Samaniyya Sufi order. After seven years he was recognised for his piety and given the title of sheikh. In 1870 he settled on Aba Island, built a mosque and taught the Quran. In 1878 his teacher expelled him from the order, and when Sheikh al-Qurashi wad al-Zayn died on 25 July 1878 his followers recognised Muhammad Ahmad as their leader.

On 29 June 1881 he claimed to be the Mahdi, the redeemer who would prepare the way for the second coming of Jesus. The Samaniyya already expected a Mahdi from its own line. He said that a prophetic assembly, a hadra, had appointed him, and he called his followers Ansār, after the people of Medina who welcomed Muhammad, in place of darwish. Some scholars loyal to the Ottoman Sultan rejected his claim. When the governor general sent a party to arrest him, it was overwhelmed on 11 August 1881. Late in 1883 his forces, armed with spears and swords, overwhelmed a 4,000-man Egyptian force near El Obeid, and then defeated the 8,000-man force of William Hicks at the Battle of Shaykan.

General Charles George Gordon reached Khartoum in February 1884, and the Ansār besieged the city from April. A British relief force arrived on 28 January 1885 to find that Khartoum had fallen two days earlier. The garrison was killed, the male population massacred, and women and children enslaved. Gordon was killed at the palace.

Muhammad Ahmad died of typhus a few months after Khartoum and was buried at Omdurman. He had chosen three deputies, and Abdallahi ibn Muhammad succeeded him. After the British under Kitchener defeated the Khalifa in 1898, his tomb was destroyed and his bones thrown into the Nile, to stop it from becoming a rallying point; it was later rebuilt.

His posthumous son Abd al-Rahman al-Mahdi led the neo-Mahdist movement and sponsored the Umma Party before Sudan's independence in 1956. Some Sudanese regard the Mahdi as a precursor of Sudanese nationalism. His collected works, about 1,000 letters, proclamations, sermons, prayers and rulings written between 1881 and 1885, were published in 1993.
muhammad-al-amin-bey: Born on 4 September 1881, he married Lalla Jeneïna Beya, the daughter of a Tripolitanian merchant of Tunis, in 1902. On 25 June 1942 Moncef Bey named him Bey al-Mahalla, the heir apparent. A month later he warned Moncef that the court counsellor General M'hammed Belkhodja was urging the French Resident General Jean-Pierre Esteva to depose him.

In May 1943 General Alphonse Juin came to Tunis with orders to remove Moncef Bey for alleged attempts to collaborate with the Axis forces. Juin found no grounds for condemning him. Lamine at first refused to promise that he would accept the throne and agreed largely because of the benefits to his family. Juin installed him at the Bardo palace on 15 May 1943. Moncef abdicated only on 6 July.

For most Tunisians he remained a usurper, the Bey of the French. The other Husainid princes boycotted him. The death of Moncef Bey in exile on 1 September 1948 removed the possibility of a restoration, and his subjects began to regard him as their legitimate ruler.

He then worked clandestinely with Habib Bourguiba and Salah Ben Youssef for self-government. In 1952 the Resident General Jean de Hauteclocque imprisoned Bourguiba and had the Bey's ministers arrested; the Bey refused to sign decrees, bringing government to a standstill, and gave way after the trade union leader Farhat Hached was assassinated in December 1952. In 1954 he accepted a reform package negotiated by Muhammad Salah Mzali while Bourguiba was still confined. After the French Prime Minister Pierre Mendès France announced internal autonomy on 31 July 1954, France dealt with the Neo Destour alone.

As king he signed without protest the decree of 31 May 1956 that abolished the privileges of the ruling family. On 15 July 1957 the Tunisian army replaced the Royal Guard around the palace, and on 25 July the Constituent Assembly voted by a show of hands to abolish the monarchy.

He was taken with members of his family to an abandoned palace in Manouba without water or electricity; two of his sons and his son-in-law were imprisoned. In October 1958 he and his wife were moved to a small villa in La Soukra, still under house arrest. She died two days after three days of interrogation about the family jewels, and his confinement was then lifted. He died in Tunis on 30 September 1962 and was buried beside her in the cemetery of Sidi Abdelaziz in La Marsa, not in the dynasty's mausoleum of Tourbet el Bey.
muhammad-al-badr: Muhammad al-Badr was the oldest son of Ahmad bin Yahya, later Zaydi imam and king of North Yemen. After the assassination of Imam Yahya in February 1948, al-Badr reached Sanaa but apparently gave only tacit support to the new regime. His father gathered the tribes around Hajjah, proclaimed himself imam and regained Sanaa within a month, executing the main perpetrators.

By late 1949 the prince, now called Sayf al-Islam al-Badr, was deputy over the port of Hodeida and Minister of the Interior. He played a prominent part in putting down the revolt of 1955 led by his uncle Sayf al-Islam Abdullah, and was then declared Crown Prince. He later became Minister of Foreign Affairs and, from 1958, the Imam's deputy over Sanaa. On 8 March 1958 he signed a pact with Gamal Abdel Nasser creating the United Arab States, a federation linking Yemen with Egypt and Syria in which Yemen kept its independence.

A great admirer of Nasser, al-Badr arranged for Egyptian experts to come and modernise Yemen in 1959, when he governed for a few months while his father was in Italy for medical treatment; his father annulled this on return. After an assassination attempt in March 1961 left Imam Ahmad gravely crippled, al-Badr took effective control of the government in October.

Ahmad died in his sleep on 19 September 1962, and al-Badr was proclaimed imam and king with the title al-Mansur. A week later, on 26 September, rebels shelled his residence, Dar al-Bashair, in Sanaa. Abdullah as-Sallal, whom he had appointed commander of the royal guard, staged a coup and declared himself president of the Yemen Arab Republic. The revolution announced that al-Badr had died under the rubble, but he had escaped unhurt to the north.

Tribes there pledged loyalty to him as Amir al-Mumineen, Leader of the believers, because the Zaydi Shia held loyalty to an imam descended from the Prophet's family to be a religious obligation. His uncle Sayf al-Islam al-Hassan, who had been proclaimed imam on the false news of his death, gave him allegiance, as did the Bakil confederation and most of the Hashid. The North Yemen Civil War began, with Saudi Arabia supporting al-Badr and Egypt the republicans.

In 1970, though most of Yemen's territory was still under al-Badr and the Hamid al-Din family, Saudi Arabia recognised the Yemen Arab Republic without consulting him, and the United Kingdom and other nations followed. He demanded to leave Saudi Arabia and went to England, where he lived quietly in Kent. He died in London in 1996 and was buried in Medina.
muhammad-al-idrisi: Al-Idrisi came from the Hammudid dynasty of North Africa and Al-Andalus, which claimed descent from Muhammad through the Idrisid dynasty. He is believed to have been born in Ceuta in 1100, at that time held by the Almoravids, where his great-grandfather had been forced to settle after Hammudid Málaga fell to the Zirids of Granada. He spent much of his youth travelling through North Africa and Al-Andalus and acquired detailed information on both regions. He visited Anatolia when he was barely sixteen and studied at the university in Córdoba. His travels also took him to Portugal, the Pyrenees, the French Atlantic coast, Hungary and Jórvík, now York.

Because of conflict and instability in Al-Andalus, al-Idrisi joined contemporaries such as Abu al-Salt in Sicily, where the Normans had overthrown Arabs who had been loyal to the Fatimids. He drew the Tabula Rogeriana in 1154 for King Roger II after a stay of eighteen years at the court, during which he worked on the commentaries and illustrations of the map. Its legends are in Arabic. It shows the Eurasian continent in its entirety but only the northern part of Africa, and it lacks detail for the Horn of Africa and Southeast Asia. For Roger the map was also inscribed on a massive disc of solid silver two metres in diameter.

Al-Idrisi combined knowledge of Africa, the Indian Ocean and the Far East gathered by Islamic merchants and explorers, recorded on Islamic maps, with the information brought by Norman voyagers. The map illustrates his Kitab nuzhat al-mushtaq, which may be translated A Diversion for the Man Longing to Travel to Far-Off Places. It survives in nine manuscripts, seven of them with maps. In its introduction he names Ptolemy and an astronomer, probably Ishaq ibn al-Hasan al-Zayyat, as sources for geographical coordinates and says he cross-checked oral reports from different informants. It records Chinese trade, mentioning the glassware of Hangzhou and the silk of Quanzhou. He also compiled a medical dictionary listing drugs and plants with their names in as many as twelve languages.

His work influenced Islamic scholars including Ibn Sa'id al-Maghribi, Hafiz-i Abru and Ibn Khaldun, but it was unknown in Western Europe and had little effect on Renaissance cartography. An abridged Arabic text was printed in Rome in 1592, one of the first Arabic books ever printed. An abridged Latin translation appeared in Paris in 1619, and a complete French translation by Pierre Amédée Jaubert in the middle of the 19th century.
muhammad-al-nasir: Muhammad al-Nasir, born around 1182, was the fourth Almohad caliph. Christians of his time called him Miramamolín, and he took the regnal title al-Nasir li-Din Allah. His father, Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur, died on 25 January 1199, and al-Nasir was proclaimed caliph that same day. He inherited an empire showing signs of instability. His father’s victories against the Christians in the Iberian Peninsula had relieved him for a time of serious threats there, and he was able to concentrate on defeating the attempts of the Banu Ghaniya to seize Ifriqiya, now Tunisia.

To deal with problems elsewhere in the empire he appointed Abu Muhammad Abd al-Wahid as governor of Ifriqiya, and so, without intending it, began the rule of the Hafsid dynasty there, which lasted until 1574. In October 1205 Abd al-Wahid led 4,000 cavalry and crushed Yahya ibn Ghaniya at Jabal Tajra, and in January 1206 he obtained the surrender of al-Mahdia, whose governor rallied to the Almohad cause.

The caliph then turned back to Iberia, where Pope Innocent III proclaimed a crusade at the request of King Alfonso VIII of Castile. A Christian coalition defeated him at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. He died the following year and was succeeded by his young son Yusuf al-Mustansir, born of a Christian slave named Qamar.

A story told by the chronicler Matthew Paris, writing two decades after the events, claims that King John of England, under pressure after a quarrel with Innocent III that placed England under an interdict, sent envoys to al-Nasir offering to convert to Islam and make England a Muslim state in return for help.
