The caliph was said to be so disgusted by the plea that he sent the envoys away. Historians doubt the story because no other contemporary evidence supports it.
muhammad-ali-al-abid: Muhammad Ali al-Abid was born in Damascus, then in the Ottoman Empire. His father, Ahmad Izzat al-Abid, worked in the administration of Damascus Vilayet and founded a periodical, then in 1887 moved with his family to Constantinople, where Muhammad Ali attended Galatasaray High School. He went on to study law in Paris and Islamic jurisprudence, graduating in 1905. From 1894 his father was an adviser of the sultan, head of his intelligence services and governor of Mosul.

Fluent in Arabic, French and Turkish, with a good knowledge of English and Persian, al-Abid entered the foreign affairs administration and in 1907 became the Ottoman Empire's ambassador to Washington. He returned soon after the constitution was declared on 23 July 1908, when the Young Turks revolted against the sultan. His father fled to London, and al-Abid travelled with him through England, Switzerland and France, reaching Egypt on the eve of World War I.

Al-Abid moved back to Damascus in the summer of 1920, when Syria came under the French Mandate, and in 1922 he became Minister of Finance. Elected to the parliament in Damascus as a nominee of the National Bloc on 30 April 1932, he was raised on 11 June to the presidency, after France had granted Syria partial recognition of its sovereignty. He was made a Commander of the Legion of Honour in 1932. After a free parliament was elected in 1936 he resigned and went to Paris. Hashim al-Atasi, the nominee of the National Bloc, replaced him, though French troops did not leave Syria completely until 1946.

Al-Abid died of a heart attack at a hotel in Rome on 22 October 1939, a few months after Bahij al-Khatib had become head of state in Syria. His body was taken to Beirut, and on 16 November his funeral procession left from there for Damascus. In French he spelled his own name Mehmed Ali Abed.
muhammad-ali-jinnah: Jinnah was born Mahomedali Jinnahbhai, probably on 25 December 1876, at Wazir Mansion near Karachi, then in the Bombay Presidency. His family came from Gujarat and had followed the Nizari Isma'ili branch of Shia Islam; he later followed Twelver Shia teachings, and after his death relatives and other witnesses claimed that he had turned to Sunni Islam. In 1892 a business associate of his father offered him an apprenticeship in London. He accepted despite his mother's opposition, and before he left she had him marry a cousin, Emibai. Both women died while he was in England, where he trained as a barrister at Lincoln's Inn.

Jinnah began practice in Bombay at the age of 20, the only Muslim barrister in the city. His first three years brought few briefs, but he later earned large fees. He also took an interest in labour causes: he was elected president of the All India Postal Staff Union in 1925 and helped to pass the Trade Union Act of 1926. In politics he rose in the Indian National Congress and worked to bring Congress and the Muslim League together. As president of the League in 1916 he signed the Lucknow Pact, which set quotas for Muslim and Hindu representation in the provinces, and Sarojini Naidu called him an ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity.

In 1920 he left Congress, which had agreed to a campaign of satyagraha that he regarded as political anarchy. In 1923 he was elected Muslim member for Bombay in the Central Legislative Assembly, and in 1925 he declined a knighthood from Lord Reading, saying he preferred to be plain Mr Jinnah. In the early 1930s Muslims urged him to resume leadership of the inactive League. Muhammad Iqbal, with whom he corresponded in 1936 and 1937, urged Muslims to strengthen his hands, and Jinnah later called Iqbal his mentor.

Until the late 1930s most Muslims of British India expected to belong to a single state after independence. After the Second World War began, the British increasingly treated Jinnah and the League as the representatives of India's Muslims, and the League passed the Lahore Resolution in 1940. Talks between Congress and the League failed to find a formula that would keep British India united, and the parties agreed instead to the independence of a Hindu-majority India and of Pakistan.

As first Governor-General, Jinnah worked to set up the new government and personally supervised refugee camps for the millions of Muslims who migrated to Pakistan. He fixed his salary at 1 rupee a month. He died on 11 September 1948, aged 71. He is revered in Pakistan as Quaid-e-Azam and Baba-e-Qaum, universities and public buildings bear his name, and his birthday is a national holiday.
muhammad-ali-khan-wallajah: Wallajah was born on 7 July 1717, the son of Anwaruddin Muhammed Khan, Nawab of the Carnatic, whose family was of Qannauji Sheikh origin. Muhammad Ali Khan later claimed Arab and Sayyid descent, but a modern study of the Walajah dynasty argues that the family was of indigenous origin and that he deliberately built a genealogy linking it to the Quraysh and the second caliph, Umar ibn al-Khattab. His mother, Fakhr un-nisa Begum Sahiba, was the niece of Sayyid Ali Khan Safavi ul-Mosawi of Persia.

When his father was killed at the Battle of Ambur in 1749, Wallajah fled to Trichinopoly, and his claim was contested by Chanda Sahib, backed by Joseph François Dupleix and the French. British reinforcements under Stringer Lawrence and Robert Clive came to his aid in April 1752, forcing the besiegers of Trichinopoly to withdraw to the island of Srirangam, and Chanda Sahib surrendered to Maratha forces from Tanjore. Emperor Shah Alam II gave Wallajah further titles in 1760, and the Treaty of Paris recognised him as an independent ruler in 1763.

He harboured ambitions of his own in a south India where Hyder Ali of Mysore, the Marathas and the Nizam of Hyderabad were constant rivals, and his failure to surrender Tiruchirappalli to Hyder Ali as promised lay at the root of many later conflicts between Mysore and the British. Much of the war that followed Hyder Ali's invasion of the Carnatic on 23 July 1780 was fought on the Nawab's lands. For the defence of his territory he paid the British 400,000 pagodas a year, about £160,000, and 10 of the 21 battalions of the Madras army garrisoned his forts.

In 1764 Wallajah planned a palace inside Fort St. George, but there was no room, and Chepauk Palace was built for him instead by Paul Benfield, an East India Company engineer turned contractor, and completed in 1768. One of the first buildings in India in the Indo-Saracenic style, it replaced Arcot as the capital until 1855. The Nawab borrowed heavily, and because many Company officials were his creditors his affairs became a factor in Westminster politics. He died of gangrene at Madras on 13 October 1795 and was succeeded by his son Umdat ul-Umara.
muhammad-ali-of-egypt: Muhammad Ali was born on 4 March 1769 in a village in Albania, to ethnic Albanian parents from the Korça region. His family moved to Kavala, where his father Ibrahim Agha, a tobacco and shipping merchant, commanded a small Ottoman unit. After his father died, his uncle raised him and made him a collector of taxes. He then became second-in-command of the Kavala contingent of Albanian mercenaries sent in 1801 to retake Egypt from the French after the withdrawal of Napoleon Bonaparte.

Between 1801 and 1805 he worked with both the Ottomans and the Mamluks, allied himself with the Egyptian leader Umar Makram, and won the support of the public. In 1805 a group of prominent Egyptians led by the ulama demanded that Governor Hurshid Pasha be replaced by Muhammad Ali, and the Ottomans yielded. His aim was an Egypt ruled by his own hereditary dynasty, which required a reorganised society, a streamlined economy, a professional bureaucracy and a modern army. Recruits were housed in barracks under close surveillance, and each soldier was given a number identifying his unit and role.
He sent the first educational mission of Egyptian students to Europe in the 1820s, and the Bulaq Press, the first indigenous press in the Arab world, was founded in 1819 or 1821.

His first campaign was in Arabia, where his son Tusun led an expedition in 1811 and Hejaz was retaken in 1812; his son Ibrahim then crushed the Saudis, and their leader Abdullah ibn Saud was sent to Constantinople and executed. In 1820 an army of 5,000 under his son Ismail marched into Sudan, which he valued for territory, gold and slaves. In 1821 Sultan Mahmud II offered him Crete in return for help against the Greek rebels. Ibrahim led 16,000 soldiers to Greece, and on 20 October 1827 the entire Egyptian navy was sunk at Navarino by a fleet of Britain, France and Russia. On 31 October 1831 Ibrahim invaded Syria, beginning the First Turko-Egyptian War.

In his last years Muhammad Ali grew paranoid, and whether the cause was senility or the silver nitrate he had once been given for dysentery remains debated. He governed until 1848 and died on 2 August 1849. The prevailing view calls him the Father of Modern Egypt, the first ruler since the Ottoman conquest of 1517 to remove the sultan's power there for good. His central bureaucracy, schools and cotton economy lasted, and his descendants ruled Egypt and Sudan for nearly 150 years. Others see him as a conqueror: he was of Albanian origin, his court used Ottoman Turkish, and critics argue that he took Egyptian manpower for his own ends. Sudan remembers his rule there as brutal.
muhammad-alwali-ii: Muhammad Alwali, also called Muhammad Dan Yaji, was a son of Sultan Yaji II and Baiwa. In 1781 he succeeded his brother Dauda Abasama II, the third son of Yaji in succession to take the throne of Kano. He came to power in a state constantly at war over trade routes, struck by famine and burdened with heavy taxes, from which traders were leaving for the Sahel. He collected stores of sorghum and millet against war and famine, but famine devastated the city soon after.

The Kano Chronicle tells that he refused his chiefs forty cattle for the sacrifice to Dirki, a sacred object of hide wrapped around a Quran, and had it broken open with axes. The royal house was divided, and he stripped Dan Mama of the title of Ciroma, crown prince, in favour of his own son. According to tradition, Dan Mama dissuaded him from accepting the call of Shehu Usman Dan Fodio and then offered his own support to the Shehu in exchange for a hundred towns.

When the Fula clans of Kano and their Hausa Muslim allies rose in jihad, Alwali at first underestimated them. His forces were beaten at Kwazzazabo and town after town fell, Karaye first among the major ones. Tuareg fighters of Adar under Tambari Agumbil, hired for four million cowries, were routed at Tatarawa. At Dan Yaya, joined by the Sultans of Katsina and Daura, Alwali fought the rebels for three to four months, but after Ciroma Dan Mama and the Fula chief of Dambarta went over to them, the Fula set fire to his camp in a night battle and his army broke.

His offer to remain in office as a tributary was rejected, and he fled to Zazzau. When Gaya, which had stayed loyal to him, fell to Muhammad Bakatsine, he went to Burum-Burum, which withstood the Fula for several weeks before it fell. Alwali died there in 1807, while his son Umaru escaped towards Damagaram. His death ended the Kutumbawa line. Dan Fodio appointed Suleiman Abahama the first Fula Emir of Kano, subject to the Sokoto Caliphate, and in exile at Maradi Alwali's descendants kept the title Sarkin Kano.
muhammad-amin-bughra: Muhammad Amin Bughra, also known by the Chinese name Mao Deming and the Turkish name Mehmet Emin Buğra, was a Jadidist. After the fall of the Turkish Islamic Republic of East Turkestan he lived in exile in Afghanistan, where in 1935 he put to the Japanese ambassador a plan for an Eastern Turkestan Republic under Japanese sponsorship, with Mahmud Sijang, a Uyghur division commander at Kashgar, as its leader. The plan collapsed when Mahmud fled to India on 2 April 1937.

In 1940 Isa Yusuf Alptekin and Ma Fuliang, sent by Chiang Kai-shek, asked him to come to Chongqing. Arrested by the British in 1942 for spying for Japan, he was released through the Kuomintang, and he and Isa Yusuf edited Kuomintang Muslim publications.

In 1940, in exile in Kashmir, he published Sharkiy Turkestan Tarihi (East Turkestan History), a history of the region from ancient times that analysed why it had lost its independence in the middle of the eighteenth century. With his fellow Pan-Turkic Jadidist Masud Sabri he rejected the name Uyghur, which they saw as a Soviet imposition, and demanded Türk or Türki as the true name of his people. He attacked Sheng Shicai for dividing the Turkic Muslims into separate ethnicities, which he held would sow disunion among them.

Under Zhang Zhizhong's administration of Xinjiang he served as a provincial commissioner, and in December 1948 Chiang Kai-shek made him vice-chairman of the provincial government under Burhan Shahidi; his wife Amina had been elected to the Legislative Yuan that year. With Isa Yusuf Alptekin and Masud Sabri he was one of the three Effendis, whom the Second East Turkestan Republic attacked as Kuomintang puppets. As the People's Liberation Army approached in September 1949 he fled to India and then Turkey. In 1954 he and Alptekin went to Taiwan to ask the Republic of China to drop its claim to Xinjiang, but it refused. He died in Turkey in 1965.
muhammad-baqir-majlesi: Mohammad Baqer Majlesi was born in Isfahan, the son of Mulla Mohammad Taqi Majlesi (1594–1660), a cleric of the Ja'fari school and the first of the family to bear the name Majlesi; the son is therefore also called Majlesi the Second. His first certain ancestor was Kamal al-Din Darvish Mohammad ibn Hasan Ameli, of Lebanese origin, the first scholar to spread the Usul of Shia hadith in Isfahan after the rise of the Safavids. By the age of 25 Majlesi had a certificate from Mulla Sadra to teach. He is said to have studied under 21 masters and to have trained 181 students.

In 1687 Shah Suleiman appointed him Shaykh al-Islām of Isfahan, the Safavid capital, with a free hand to encourage and punish as he saw fit. He worked to suppress Sufism, philosophy, which he held contrary to Islam, and Sunnism, and he persuaded the shah to exclude Sunnis from Isfahan. According to the scholar Moojan Momen, Shiism and Sufism had been closely linked until his time; afterwards Sufism ceased to shape mainstream Shia thought and philosophy lost its place in the religious colleges. He is credited with spreading rituals such as Azadari, the Arba'in pilgrimage, Alam processions, Ta'ziyah and Latmiya, and he issued rulings on everyday conduct down to dress, sleep and hygiene.

Majlesi wrote more than 100 books in Persian and Arabic, in a plain style meant for ordinary believers; besides the Bihar al-Anwar in 110 volumes they include Hayat al-Qulūb. He defined knowledge narrowly as knowledge of the clear, secure ayat, of religious duties and the hadith, warning that further learning wasted one's life and led to heresy. He died on 29 March 1699 and was buried beside his father in the family mausoleum next to the Jameh Mosque of Isfahan. His hostility to Sunnism may have contributed to the circumstances of the Afghan invasion of 1722, and the Qajar dynasty later endorsed his religious programme.
muhammad-bello: Muhammad Bello was born on 3 November 1781, the son of the preacher and scholar Usman dan Fodio and his fourth wife, Hauwa. His nickname Bello means assistant or helper in Fulfulde, probably because he went everywhere with his father from an early age and later became his wazir. His family belonged to the Torodbe, a clerical clan that spoke Fula and claimed partly Arab descent. He studied under his father at Degel until the family went into exile in 1804, and in 1809 he founded Sokoto, which became the capital of his father's conquest of the Hausa lands in the Fulani War.

In 1815 Usman retired from government and put Bello in charge of some of the eastern emirates, which he ruled from Wurno near Sokoto. On his father's death Bello's supporters sealed the gates of Sokoto against rival claimants, among them his uncle Abdullahi dan Fodio. Facing dissent from both the Fulani and Hausa aristocracies, Bello tolerated more of the older Hausa institutions than his father had, and encouraged the pastoral Fulani to settle around fortified ribats with schools and mosques. When Dan Tunku of Kazaure rebelled after Bello named Ibrahim Dabo Emir of Kano in 1819, Bello helped Dabo defeat him.

He then consolidated the state through building, settlement and uniform courts of justice, and widened education for both men and women, with his sister Nana Asma'u as teacher and link to rural women. Umar Tall, later founder of the Toucouleur Empire, settled at Sokoto in 1822, married one of Bello's daughters and served him as judge and commander. The explorer Hugh Clapperton visited his court in 1824. In 1836 the kingdom of Gobir revolted, and Bello crushed the rising at the Battle of Gawakuke on 9 March 1836.

Bello wrote hundreds of works on history, Islamic studies and poetry. His Infaku'l Maisuri, The Wages of the Fortunate, is often considered the definitive history of the Fulani wars and of his father's empire. He died of natural causes at Wurno on 25 October 1837 and was succeeded by his brother Abu Bakr Atiku and later by his son Aliyu Babba.
muhammad-bey-abu-al-dhahab: Muhammad Abu al-Dhahab was born in 1735 in the North Caucasus, in Circassia or in Abkhazia. He was kidnapped and sold to the Mamluk emir Ali Bey al-Kabir in Egypt, and became Ali Bey's closest companion, his most trusted general and his brother-in-law, though other sources make him a son-in-law or an adopted son. His name, father of gold, was apparently given to him for his generosity and wealth.

During the Russo-Turkish War, Ali Bey declared Egypt independent of the Ottoman Empire and tried to restore the Mamluk Sultanate that the Ottomans had conquered 250 years before. On his behalf Abu al-Dhahab put down a revolt in Upper Egypt in 1769 and seized the Hejaz in 1770. Allied with the Palestinian emir Daher al-Umar, he conquered large parts of Ottoman Syria and took Damascus from its Ottoman governor, Uthman Pasha al-Kurji.

He then changed sides. Handing all the conquered lands over to the Ottomans, he marched on Cairo, and Ali Bey fled to Daher al-Umar at Acre. Abu al-Dhahab became Shaykh al-Balad, the civil governor, and de facto ruler of Egypt. When Ali Bey returned to recover his position, Abu al-Dhahab's forces defeated and killed him near Cairo in 1773.

Acting on Ottoman orders, Abu al-Dhahab invaded Palestine to defeat Daher al-Umar and took Gaza, Jaffa and Acre, but he died suddenly of the plague during the campaign. Power in Egypt passed to his comrades Murad Bey and Ibrahim Bey, the leaders of his Mamluk faction, known as the Abu-Dhahab faction or Muhammadiyya, who then fought repeated conflicts with Ismail Bey.
muhammad-bin-thani: He was born in Fuwayrit, the second eldest son of Sheikh Thani bin Mohammad. He began to gain influence over the peninsula after his family moved from Fuwayrit to Al Bidda in 1848. Until then each tribe and settlement had its own leader, and with his arrival Qatar began to gain economic and political weight, though it remained under the suzerainty of Bahrain.

In May 1851 Faisal bin Turki, Imam of the Emirate of Najd, marched on Al Bidda as a base for invading Bahrain. Muhammad and his son were among the leaders of the Qatari forces in the Battle of Mesaimeer from 2 to 4 June 1851, during which the Bahraini and Abu Dhabi forces withdrew to their ships. He then made a separate peace with Faisal, accepting Wahhabi rule on condition that he remained chief of Al Bidda, and on 8 June his men took the Burj Al-Maah watchtower, whereupon the allied commanders fled to Bahrain. Under a treaty of 25 July 1851 negotiated by Saeed bin Tahnun, Faisal renounced his claims to Qatar and Muhammad gave up his position.

The enmity left by the battle fed into the Qatari–Bahraini War of 1867, and on 12 September 1868 a treaty signed with the British representative Lewis Pelly marked Qatar's emergence as a separate political entity. In 1871 he asked the Ottomans at Al Hasa for protection against outside attack, though in the same decade the Ottomans themselves turned hostile to the Qataris. He died of natural causes on 18 December 1878, a date now kept as a national day in Qatar. He had six sons and two daughters.
muhammad-bin-tughluq: Muhammad was the eldest son of Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq, founder of the Tughlaq dynasty, and was known as Fakhr Malik Jauna Khan before he became sultan. In 1321 his father sent him to the Deccan to campaign against the Kakatiya dynasty, and in 1323 he besieged and took their capital Warangal, ending the dynasty and defeating King Prataparudra. He was skilled in Persian, Hindavi, Arabic, Sanskrit and Turkic and had an interest in medicine.

He ascended the throne on 4 February 1325, three days after his father's death. In his reign the sultanate took Warangal, Ma'abar and Madurai and reached the south of present-day Karnataka. In 1327 he ordered the capital moved from Delhi to Daulatabad, a more central site, and many who made the journey died of hunger and exhaustion on the road. In 1334 a rebellion in Mabar led by Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan founded the Madurai Sultanate. Plague struck his army at Bidar, and Mabar and Dwarsamudra broke away, followed by a revolt in Bengal. In 1335 he moved the capital back to Delhi.

In 1330 he issued token currency of brass and copper, with the value of gold and silver coins. Forgeries multiplied and the coins lost their value, and the experiment had ended by 1333. His expedition to Kumaon in 1333 ended in the near-destruction of his army, and his own generals rebelled. One of them, Hasan Gangu, went on to found the Bahmani Sultanate in the Deccan.

Muhammad died in 1351 on the way to Thatta in Sindh, while campaigning against the Taghi. During his reign the sultanate lost ground in Rajputana, and Harihara and Bukka founded the Vijayanagara Empire in the south.

Medieval writers such as Ziauddin Barani and Ibn Battuta, who visited his court, say Delhi was emptied by the move, though modern historians regard this as exaggeration. Historians disagree on his religious policy: some sources report intolerance, while Peter Jackson notes that he took part in Hindu festivities, and Jain writers record cordial relations with Jain scholars. Later historians called him the Wisest Fool.
muhammad-haji-ibrahim-egal: Egal was born on 15 August 1928 at Odweyne in the British Somaliland Protectorate, the son of a wealthy merchant. He belonged to the Issa Musse division of the Habar Awal, part of the larger Isaaq clan. He completed primary, intermediate and secondary schooling in British Somaliland and was then sent to the United Kingdom to continue his studies, which was unusual at the time. He married Asha Saeed Abby, and they had five children, three sons and two daughters.

On 26 June 1960 Egal became prime minister of the newly independent State of Somaliland, which merged five days later with the former Trust Territory of Somalia to form the Somali Republic on 1 July 1960. He served the republic as minister of defence from 1960 to 1961 and minister of education from 1962 to 1963. In 1967 President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke appointed him prime minister. His rise was reportedly financed largely by covert support from the American Central Intelligence Agency to him and other pro-Western members of the Somali Youth League. In 1968 he publicly said that Somalia would not drop its aim of uniting all Somalis, but he provoked popular anger when he later gave up claims to the Ogaden.

Shermarke was assassinated on 15 October 1969, while Egal was in the United States. A Supreme Revolutionary Council led by Major General Siad Barre seized power, renamed the country the Somali Democratic Republic, banned political parties and dissolved parliament. Egal was detained, released, and served as ambassador to India from 1976 to 1978, before the Barre government imprisoned him again on charges of conspiracy until 1985.

As second president of Somaliland, from 1993 until his death, Egal disarmed and rehabilitated rebel groups and introduced the Somaliland shilling, a passport and a national flag. In 1995 he wrote to Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin seeking diplomatic ties; Abdirahman Tuur, the first president, said Egal hoped this would help win recognition from the United States. Hardliners in the Somali National Movement doubted his commitment to separation, and in August 2001 he survived by one vote a motion charging him with pursuing it half-heartedly.

Egal died on 3 May 2002 in Pretoria, South Africa, during surgery at a military hospital. After a state funeral he was buried at Berbera beside his father, with about 4,000 mourners reported, and parliament declared seven days of mourning. Dahir Rayale Kahin was sworn in as president the next day.
muhammad-i-al-mustansir: Al-Mustansir was the second Hafsid sultan of Ifriqiya. He had been a vassal of the Kingdom of Sicily but threw off that allegiance when King Manfred was overthrown by Charles I. After the Siege of Baghdad ended the Abbasid Caliphate, his claim to the caliphate was recognised by the Marinid sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub of Morocco in 1258, the Sharif of Mecca Abu Numayy in 1259 and the emir of Granada in 1264, and perhaps by the Mamluk Sultanate in 1260. According to Ibn Khaldun, the ruler of the Kanem–Bornu Empire sent him a giraffe as a diplomatic present in 1257.

In 1267, after the Mamluk sultan Baibars had taken Nazareth, Haifa, Toron and Arsuf from the Crusader states, Louis IX of France called a new crusade. His brother Charles I, King of Naples and Sicily, persuaded him to strike first at Tunis, as a base against Egypt. Al-Mustansir was rumoured to be sympathetic to Christianity through his links with Christian Spain, and Charles suggested that a crusade might bring about his conversion.

Louis landed in July 1270, but disease spread through the army from poor drinking water, and Louis died a day after Charles arrived. Charles, leading the crusade for the young Philip III, abandoned the siege on 30 October under an agreement with al-Mustansir that gave the Christians free trade with Tunis and guaranteed residence there for monks and priests. Hearing of the evacuation, Baibars cancelled his plan to send troops to Tunis.

In 1247 he wrote a book, On Hunting, on the ways of hunting in North Africa at the time. A chapter teaches the hunter how to manage and hunt with salukis, and other parts deal with the training and keeping of falcons and with the techniques used on his estate at Bizerte.
muhammad-i-of-granada: Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Nasr, known as Ibn al-Ahmar, the Son of the Red, was born around 1195 at Arjona, a small frontier town south of the Guadalquivir. His background was humble, and the Castilian First General Chronicle says he had at first no other occupation than following the oxen and the plough. He became known for leadership on the frontier and for an ascetic image that he kept after he became a ruler. His clan, the Banu Nasr, was said by the later vizier Ibn al-Khatib to descend from a companion of the Prophet, Sa’d ibn Ubadah, but this genealogy appears to be a later invention meant to glorify the dynasty.

The Almohad caliphate had split after 1224, and Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Hud, ruling from Murcia, became the leading figure in al-Andalus. When his defeats by the Christians eroded his credibility, a mosque assembly at Arjona declared the town independent on 16 July 1232 and chose Muhammad as its leader. He briefly held Córdoba and Seville, lost both, and turned against Ibn Hud in 1236 to help Ferdinand III of Castile take Córdoba. He entered Granada in May 1238 and began work on the Alhambra, and he gained Almería and Málaga without force, through political manoeuvre.

Ferdinand besieged Jaén, and in March 1246 Muhammad surrendered it and agreed to pay an annual tribute of 150,000 maravedíes. Castilian sources present this as vassalage; Muslim sources describe a relationship between equals.

Peace held for about twenty years. In 1248 he sent a contingent to help Castile take Seville. When Alfonso X of Castile pressed for the ports of Tarifa and Algeciras, Muhammad called on Marinid troops and in 1264 attacked Castile as the Mudéjars rose in revolt. The revolt failed, and he had to pay 250,000 maravedíes a year. In 1266 the Banu Ashqilula, his allies from Arjona, rebelled at Málaga.

The conflict with Castile and the Banu Ashqilula was still unresolved when Muhammad fell from his horse and died on 22 January 1273. He was buried on the Sabika Hill, east of the Alhambra, and his son Muhammad II succeeded him as he had planned. The Emirate of Granada survived two more centuries until Castile annexed it in 1492. The historian L. P. Harvey says he managed to snatch from disaster a relatively secure refuge for Islam in the peninsula. His religious outlook shifted from that of an ascetic frontiersman towards mainstream Sunni orthodoxy and the Maliki jurists, bringing Granada into line with the rest of the Islamic world. The Alhambra is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
muhammad-i-tapar: Muhammad I Tapar was born on 20 January 1082, a son of Malik-Shah I and Taj al-Din Khatun Safariyya. His brother Ahmad Sanjar in Khorasan held more practical power than he did within the dynasty. After a civil war with his half-brother Berkyaruq he was given the title of malik and the provinces of Armenia and Azerbaijan. Dissatisfied, he revolted again but had to flee back to Armenia. By 1104 Berkyaruq, ill and tired of war, agreed to divide the sultanate with him, and Muhammad became sole sultan when Berkyaruq died in 1105.

Muhammad probably allied himself with Ridwan of Aleppo at the Battle of the Khabur River in 1107, in which Kilij Arslan I, the sultan of Rum, was defeated and killed. In 1106 he conquered the Ismaili fortress of Shahdiz and ordered the Bavandid ruler Shahriyar IV to join his campaign against the Ismailis. Shahriyar refused, and an army sent against him was defeated by Shahriyar and his son Qarin III. Muhammad then asked for one of Shahriyar’s sons to be sent to his court at Isfahan, and Qarin III later married his daughter.

Around 1106 or 1107 he appointed Ahmad ibn Nizam al-Mulk, son of the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, as his own vizier, mainly because of the father’s reputation. Muhammad and Ahmad campaigned in Iraq and defeated and killed the Mazyadid ruler Sadaqa ibn Mansur, who bore the title king of the Arabs. A later attempt to take the Ismaili fortresses of Alamut and Ostavand failed to achieve a decisive result.

Muhammad died on 18 April 1118 and was succeeded by Mahmud II, though Sanjar was clearly the chief power in the Seljuk realms afterwards. He is regarded as the last Seljuk ruler with strong authority in the western part of the sultanate. The bureaucrat Anushirvan ibn Khalid wrote that under him the kingdom was united and secure, and that under his son Mahmud it split. Imad ad-Din al-Isfahani called him the perfect man of the Seljuk dynasty. His campaigns inspired his poet Iranshah to compose the Persian epic Bahman-nama. He was remembered as a devout Sunni and a friend of the clergy, and he abolished taxes not sanctioned by religious law.
muhammad-ibn-abd-al-wahhab: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab was born in 1703 into the Banu Tamim clan in Uyayna, a village in Najd in central Arabia. His father was the Hanbali jurisconsult of Najd and his grandfather a judge of Hanbali law. He left Uyayna around the age of twenty, in circumstances that are unclear, made the pilgrimage to Mecca and spent time in Medina, where he studied under Abdallah ibn Ibrahim ibn Sayf and Muhammad Hayat al-Sindi, who taught him to reject practices associated with saints and their tombs and to reject rigid imitation of medieval legal commentaries.

He then studied in Basra for four years, where his preaching against such practices brought a strong backlash and he was driven out of the town. He went on to Baghdad, where he married a wealthy woman, and travelled on before settling in Huraymila, where his father was judge. There he wrote the Kitab al-Tawhid, the Book of Oneness,.

Ibn Abd al-Wahhab taught that the primary doctrine of Islam was the oneness of God, tawhid. He judged much of the folk religion of Najd, including visits to the tombs of Companions, sacred trees and sacrifices before a blind sage, to be polytheism, shirk, resembling the pre-Islamic age. He called for a return to the Quran and hadith, opposed taqlid, the imitation of established opinion, and urged ijtihad, independent legal reasoning, by qualified scholars. His followers called themselves al-Muwahhidun, the Unitarians, and opponents named them Wahhabis after his father's name, a label many adherents reject. Some of his contemporaries, including Hanbali scholars, rejected his views.

Driven from Uyayna, he was invited to Diriyah by its ruler Muhammad ibn Saud. After some time in Diriyah the two agreed to bring the Arabs of the peninsula back to what they saw as the true principles of Islam. The alliance gave the Al Saud a religious mission and drove the expansion of the first Saudi state. A war with the chieftain of Riyadh lasted nearly thirty years until Abd al-Aziz conquered the town in 1773. Ibn Abd al-Wahhab then left government to Abd al-Aziz and devoted himself to teaching, preaching and worship. In 1787 he called on the people to swear allegiance to Saud, Abd al-Aziz's son, as heir. He died in 1792.
muhammad-ibn-abil-saj: Muhammad was the son of Abi'l-Saj Devdad, and like his father he and his brother Yusuf had long military careers. In 879 the Saffarid Amr ibn al-Layth made him his representative in Mecca, and the Abbasids later appointed him governor of Anbar and Rahba. After the death of Ahmad ibn Tulun, the amir of Egypt, in 884, he allied with the Abbasid general Ishaq ibn Kundaj to take lands in Syria from Ibn Tulun's young heir Khumarawayh, but quarrelled with the future caliph al-Mu'tadid and left before the Tulunids routed the Abbasid army at the Battle of the Mills.

Muhammad then went over to Khumarawayh, crossed the Euphrates with Egyptian aid and defeated Ishaq in 886–887, bringing the whole Jazira under Tulunid control; he was later given Mosul in Ishaq's place. In 888–889 Ishaq defeated him at Damascus, and Muhammad fled to the regent al-Muwaffaq, who made him governor of Azerbaijan. There he persuaded the rebel Abd-Allah ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Hamdani to surrender Maragha in 893 on a promise of safety, then executed him, and made Maragha his capital.

When the Bagratid Smbat I became king of Armenia in 890, Muhammad sent him a crown in the caliph's name, asserting his own authority. After Smbat invaded Georgia and Albania, Muhammad seized Nakhchivan and Dvin but was defeated and made peace. In 898 he took the title al-Afshin, once used by the rulers of Ushrusana, his family's home, probably while withholding revenue from Baghdad, before returning to loyalty and being confirmed as governor of Azerbaijan and Armenia.

In a new campaign he took Kars and captured Smbat's wife and part of his treasury, exchanging her in 899 for Smbat's son Ashot, and forced Ashot-Sargis Artsruni of Vaspurakan to submit. In 900 he invaded Vaspurakan again and left a garrison there. He died of an epidemic in 901 while preparing another campaign against Smbat, and was succeeded by his son Devdad.
muhammad-ibn-ilyas: Muhammad ibn Ilyas first appears as a commander in the service of the Samanids. In 929 he was imprisoned after angering the Samanid amir Nasr ibn Ahmad, but he was freed with the support of the vizier Abu'l-Fadl al-Bal'ami and sent on campaign in Gurgan. He then joined a rebellion of Nasr's brothers led by Yahya ibn Ahmad, and when the rebels began to lose he went to Nishapur. Its governor, Makan ibn Kaki, refused him entry but took him into his service, and when Makan left for Gurgan, Muhammad let Yahya into the city.

When Nasr's army approached Nishapur in 932, Muhammad went to Kerman, a province loosely held by the Abbasids, and made himself master of its northern part; the Qufs and Baluch tribes of the south and east kept their autonomy. In 934 Nasr sent Makan against him. Muhammad failed to win the support of the Abbasid general Yaqut, was defeated and fled, but returned once Makan left and drove out the Samanid garrisons. When the Buyid Ahmad was sent to take Kerman two years later, Muhammad withdrew to Sistan, and he came back after the Buyids recalled Ahmad.

Little is recorded of the next thirty years. He may have acknowledged the Samanids or the Buyids as overlords, but in 959 or 960 the caliph sent him a banner and robe, signs of an independent ruler. He reportedly plundered the caravans coming from Fars and grew rich, and he also paid for buildings and charities.

While travelling to collect his share of plunder from the Qufs he suffered a stroke that left him paralysed. He named his son Ilyasa heir and commander of the army, with Ilyas next in line. A third son, Suleiman, rebelled with the Qufs and took Sirajan, but Ilyasa defeated him and Suleiman fled to Khurasan.

Courtiers later turned Muhammad against Ilyasa, whom he dismissed and imprisoned. The mothers of Ilyasa and Ilyas freed him, the army took his side, and Muhammad agreed to abdicate in his favour. Allowed to leave with all his wealth, he went to the Samanid court at Bukhara, where he urged the amir Mansur ibn Nuh to act against the Ziyarids and Buyids. He died soon afterwards.
muhammad-ibn-musafir: Muhammad was the son of Musafir, and his original name seems to have been Sallar or Salar, Persian for commander, which his successors later used as a title. Some time before 916 he became ruler of Tarom. Like his predecessors he married into the Justanid dynasty of Dailaman, taking Kharasuya, daughter of King Justan III, as his wife, and the marriage gave him a footing in Justanid affairs.

In 919 Muhammad killed Ali of Dailam, who had murdered Justan to seize the throne. He also killed Khusrau Firuz in battle, though Khusrau Firuz's son Siyahchashm still succeeded him, and the power of the Sallarids grew at the Justanids' expense. Muhammad was also remembered for building up the fortress of Shamiran, hiring skilled workmen on promises of high pay and then reducing them to forced labourers.

In 930 the Dailamite leader Asfar ibn Shiruya sent Mardavij to take Tarom, and Mardavij besieged Shamiran. Muhammad persuaded him instead to turn on Asfar. With Sallarid support Mardavij killed Asfar's brother Shirzad and then Asfar himself, took his lands and founded the Ziyarid dynasty of northern Iran.

His harsh rule made him unpopular even within his family, and in 941 his sons Marzuban and Wahsudan confined him in a castle. Wahsudan took over Tarom, while Marzuban went on to conquer Azerbaijan. When the Buwayhids captured Marzuban in 949, Marzuban's Dailamite captains freed Muhammad and set him up at Ardebil, but he soon offended them and fled to Tarom. There Wahsudan imprisoned him again, and he remained a prisoner until his death some time before 953.
muhammad-ibn-qasim: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Thaqafi belonged to the Banu Thaqif, an Arab tribe centred on the city of Taif in western Arabia. His first assignment was in the province of Fars, where he subdued a group of Kurds and was appointed governor, probably succeeding his uncle Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi.

Umayyad interest in Sindh was stirred by pirates, among them the Meds, who preyed on shipping from bases at Kutch, Debal and Kathiawar. Muslim sources say that the kidnapping of Muslim women travelling from Sri Lanka by the Meds of Debal gave the pretext, and that Raja Dahir, the ruler, refused to release prisoners or pay compensation, saying that he had no control over the raiders.

Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, the governor in Iraq, sent Muhammad against Sindh in 711, when he was in his teens, after two earlier commanders had failed. The army that left Shiraz held 6,000 Syrian cavalry and detachments of mawali, joined by camel cavalry and by reinforcements and catapults sent by sea to Debal, at the mouth of the Indus. Towns were given the choice of submitting peacefully or being attacked. Where they were taken by force, fighting men were executed and surviving dependants enslaved.

As governor of Sindh from 712 until his death he asked for acceptance of Muslim rule in return for non-interference in religious practice, so long as taxes and tribute were paid. Villages kept their headmen and their own laws, non-Muslims paid the jizya and Hindus and Buddhists were taken into the administration.

Al-Hajjaj died in 714 and Caliph al-Walid I a year later. The new caliph, Sulayman, took revenge on the generals close to al-Hajjaj. Muhammad was put in chains and died in Mosul on 18 July 715. Al-Baladhuri says that he was tortured to death by officials who had a grievance against al-Hajjaj's family; some sources place his burial in Makran. Dahir's son soon recaptured Brahmanabad.

Historians disagree about the conquest. Stanley Lane-Poole called it liberal, while early historians such as Elliot and Majumdar held that the conversion of Sindh was coercive. Others, among them Thomas W. Arnold, argue that it was largely peaceful. Conversion was in fact slow, and most of the population stayed Hindu. Port Qasim is named after him.
muhammad-ibn-sulayman-al-katib: Muhammad ibn Sulayman was an Egyptian, born and raised in Egypt. His surname al-Katib, the secretary, recalls his first post as secretary to the Tulunid general Lu'lu', who governed northern Syria from Raqqa on behalf of Ahmad ibn Tulun. When Lu'lu' went over to the Abbasid regent al-Muwaffaq in 882, Muhammad followed him and entered the central caliphal administration.

In 891 al-Tabari names him as secretary to the vizier Abu'l-Saqr Isma'il ibn Bulbul, who backed a failed attempt to depose al-Muwaffaq and restore power to Caliph al-Mu'tamid. In the riots that followed in Baghdad, a mob burned down Muhammad's house.

By 896 he was an army commander, charged with enrolling the many officers who had left the Tulunids after plotting to kill the emir Jaysh ibn Khumarawayh. In 903 he headed the department of the army, the diwan al-jaysh, and was given the war against the Qarmatians, a radical Isma'ili sect whose raiders from Bahrayn and the Syrian Desert had besieged Damascus and ravaged Syria.

Caliph al-Muktafi nominally led the campaign but stayed at Raqqa while Muhammad commanded in the field. On 29 November 903, some 24 km from Hamah, he crushed the Qarmatian army and captured its leaders, among them the Sahib al-Shama. He entered Baghdad in triumph on 2 February 904 and presided over their public execution eleven days later.

In May 904 he set out again, with an army of 10,000 according to al-Tabari, to recover southern Syria and Egypt. A fleet from Cilicia under Damian of Tarsus sailed up the Nile and cut the supplies of the Tulunid forces. Weakened by factional strife, defections and the murder of the emir Harun ibn Khumarawayh by his uncles, the Tulunid state offered little resistance, and its leading family and supporters were deported to Baghdad. Muhammad handed Egypt to the new governor, Isa al-Nushari, and returned to Syria, where he was soon arrested for embezzling much of the booty of the conquest.
muhammad-ibn-tahir: Muhammad was the son of Tahir ibn Abdallah, governor of Khurasan, and belonged to the Tahirid family that held the province for the Abbasid caliphs. When his father died in 862, the caliph first offered the post to Tahir's brother, Muhammad ibn Abdallah ibn Tahir, who refused it. The younger Muhammad was appointed instead, but the military governorship of Iraq and Baghdad (sahib al-shurta), usually held by the Tahirid governor of Khurasan, went to his uncle. He was young and inexperienced, and held office through the civil war of 865–866 under four caliphs, al-Musta'in, al-Mu'tazz, al-Muhtadi and al-Mu'tamid.

Only two years after his accession, Tabaristan was lost to the Zaydi revolt of Hasan ibn Zayd ibn Muhammad and never recovered. In 867 Ya'qub al-Saffar, the Saffarid amir of Sistan, took Herat and imprisoned its Tahirid governor; an army sent under the Samanid Ibrahim ibn Ilyas was defeated, and Muhammad had to come to terms. He also contested the western offices with his kin, sending another uncle, Sulayman ibn 'Abdallah, to Iraq against 'Ubaydallah, who had taken them over in 867 and later won them back.

When Ya'qub marched on Nishapur in 873, Muhammad refused to flee. He spent three years as a prisoner of the Saffarids, until caliphal forces defeated them at the Battle of Dair al-'Aqul in 876 and freed him. The caliph restored him as governor of Khurasan, but he never asserted his authority there, although anti-Saffarid leaders such as Ahmad al-Khujistani and Rafi' ibn Harthama placed his name in the khutba in the lands they held.

Muhammad then lived in Baghdad. After Ya'qub's death in 879 his brother Amr bin Laith came to terms with the caliph and was invested with Khurasan in Muhammad's place, named 'Ubaydallah to the western offices and had Muhammad arrested for supposedly backing al-Khujistani, on little evidence. When peace between the caliphate and the Saffarids broke down around 884, Muhammad regained favour: he was made governor of Baghdad, serving from 885 to 889, and was again named governor of Khurasan without ever ruling it. He died around 910.
muhammad-ibn-tughj-al-ikhshid: According to the biographical dictionary of Ibn Khallikan, Muhammad ibn Tughj was born in Baghdad on 8 February 882. His family was of Turkic origin from the Farghana Valley and claimed royal descent. His grandfather Juff and father Tughj served the Abbasids, and Tughj later served the Tulunids as governor of Tiberias, Aleppo and Damascus, holding Damascus for seven months against the Qarmatians in 903. Muhammad spent much of his youth in the Levant at his father's side and served as his sub-governor of Tiberias.

His early career was turbulent. He was imprisoned with his father in 905, released in 906, took part in the murder of the vizier al-Abbas ibn al-Hasan al-Jarjara'i in 908, and fled Iraq to serve Takin al-Khazari, governor of Egypt. The patronage of the commander-in-chief Mu'nis al-Muzaffar later brought him the governorships of Palestine and of Damascus.

In 933 he was briefly named governor of Egypt, but the appointment was revoked after Mu'nis was murdered. Re-appointed in 935, he invaded Egypt by land and sea, his fleet took Tinnis and the Nile Delta, and he entered Fustat on 26 August 935. He defeated a Fatimid invasion and restored a rare period of domestic peace, with only a minor Shi'ite revolt in 942. He asked Caliph al-Radi in 938 for the title al-Ikhshid, once borne by the kings of Farghana, and approval was formally given in July 939. He built up a large military force of his own, including Turkic and Black African slave soldiers.

Al-Ikhshid was a cautious man who preferred diplomacy to battle. He declined the post of amir al-umara when Caliph al-Mustakfi offered it. Control of Syria was contested: he was forced to cede its northern half to Ibn Ra'iq between 939 and 942, and later faced the Hamdanids, whose prince Sayf al-Dawla seized Aleppo in 944 and was driven out the next year. At Raqqa in 944 Caliph al-Muttaqi recognised his hereditary rule over Egypt, Syria and the Hejaz for thirty years.

Al-Ikhshid died in Damascus on 24 July 946 and was buried in Jerusalem. His son Unujur succeeded peacefully under the commander Kafur, a Black African slave recruited by al-Ikhshid, who remained the paramount minister for 22 years and held power in his own right from 966 until his death two years later. In 969 the Fatimids conquered Egypt.

Unlike Ibn Tulun, al-Ikhshid was neither a patron of artists and poets nor a major builder. Medieval chroniclers, according to Thierry Bianquis, described him as choleric, gluttonous, shrewd and inclined to avarice, with a fondness for eastern luxuries, especially perfumes, whose fashion spread among the upper classes of Fustat.
muhammad-ibn-zayd: Nothing is known of Muhammad's early life; the Iranologist Wilferd Madelung suggests the family lived in Iraq, and Muhammad seems to have come to Tabaristan in 867, three years after his brother Hasan ibn Zayd took power there. He served Hasan as general and governor. Captured by the Saffarid Ya'qub ibn al-Layth during his invasion of 874, he was released at Gurgan in 876, suppressed the rebellion of the Bavandid Rustam I in 880 and probably governed Gurgan until Hasan died on 6 January 884. Hasan's brother-in-law Abu'l-Husayn Ahmad ibn Muhammad then seized power, and only in October 884 could Muhammad take the capital, Amul, and behead the usurper.

Taking his brother's regnal name, al-Dāʿī ilaʾl-Ḥaqq, he was known as al-Dāʿī al-Ṣaghīr, the Younger Missionary. His campaigns met mixed fortune: an attack on Rayy in August 885 was driven back, and in 888 or 889 Rafi' ibn Harthama, the ruler of Khurasan, conquered most of his lands, forcing him into the mountain fortresses of the west, where Justan ibn Vahsudan, lord of Daylam, supported him.

When the new Caliph al-Mu'tadid gave Khurasan to the Saffarid Amr ibn al-Layth in 892, Rafi' made peace, returned Tabaristan and pledged allegiance to the Zaydid cause. Muhammad re-entered Amul on 24 June 893 and recovered Gurgan after Rafi' was killed. In 900, after the Samanids defeated Amr, he planned to invade Khurasan, but was beaten at Gurgan by the Samanid army of Muhammad ibn Harun al-Sarakhsi and died of his wounds the next day, 3 October 900. His head was sent to Bukhara and his body buried at the gate of Gurgan, where his tomb soon drew pilgrims.

His heir Zayd was taken to Bukhara, and dissension among the Zaydid leaders let the Samanids take the province and restore Sunni Islam there, until Hasan al-Utrush restored Zaydid rule in 914. Like his brother, Muhammad promoted Zaydi Shi'ism and Mu'tazilism and repressed Sunni opposition; this, with the conduct of his Daylamite troops, estranged much of the population. He sponsored the rebuilding of the shrine of Ali and Husayn, gave generously to members of the Alid family across the Muslim world and wrote poetry, of which a few lines survive, yet later Zaydis did not count him a legitimate imam.
muhammad-ii-of-cordoba: Muhammad II al-Mahdi was the fourth Caliph of Córdoba of the Umayyad dynasty in al-Andalus. In early 1009 he, an Umayyad prince and pretender to the throne, led a rebellion against the existing caliph, Hisham II, whom he deposed and imprisoned. He then took the throne but oppressed, slaughtered and ultimately expelled many Berbers from the city. Great numbers of them went north to Calatrava, where they formed a fighting force and chose Sulayman ibn al-Hakam as their candidate for caliph.

In November 1009 Sulayman led a Berber and Castilian army that defeated Muhammad's forces at Qantish and Alcolea Bridge. Sulayman entered Córdoba on 9 November, and Muhammad and his loyalists fled to Toledo. There, with his prime minister Wāḍiḥ al-Ṣiqlabī, he rebuilt his army, and Wāḍiḥ formed an alliance with some of the Ṣaqāliba in the east and with the Frankish counts Ramon Borrell of Barcelona and Ermengol I of Urgell. The armies met at Espiel on 22 May 1010, where Sulayman's Berber force was defeated, and Muhammad was installed as caliph again.

Muhammad tried to win the support of the Berbers, but his regime remained unstable. A military strike to the south ended badly when Wāḍiḥ and the Frankish allies were defeated in June 1010 at Marbella and Guadiaro. The Ṣaqāliba under Wāḍiḥ then abandoned him to work for the restoration of Hisham II, the Frankish alliance fell apart and the Franks went home. Wāḍiḥ returned to Córdoba and organised a coup. Muhammad tried to flee, reportedly disguised as a woman, but Wāḍiḥ arrested him, and he was tried and executed on 23 June 1010. Later Muslim historians also accused him of taking women from the Amirid harem during the revolution of 1009.
muhammad-ii-of-granada: Muhammad was born in 633 AH, 1235 or 1236 CE, into the Nasrid clan of Arjona, which according to Ibn al-Khatib descended from Sa'd ibn Ubadah, a companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. His father, Muhammad I, made Arjona independent in 1232 and built a state centred on Granada. After the death of his elder brother Faraj in 1257, Muhammad and his brother Yusuf were named heirs, and with Yusuf's death he became sole heir. He served for a time as vizier, and when his father died after a fall from his horse on 22 January 1273 he was 38 and experienced in war and diplomacy.

Granada lay between Castile, which demanded a tribute of 300,000 maravedís, about half its revenue, and the Marinids of Morocco, while the Banu Ashqilula, former allies of the Nasrids, held Málaga in rebellion. In late 1273 Muhammad promised Alfonso X vassalage and tribute in return for an end to Castilian support for the rebels, but Alfonso took the money and kept backing them. Muhammad turned to the Marinid sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub, whose army won at Ecija in September 1275, though he was offended to be treated as the equal of the Banu Ashqilula.

When the Banu Ashqilula handed Málaga to the Marinids, Muhammad encouraged Yaghmurasen of Tlemcen and Castile to attack them, and regained the city on 31 January 1279. In 1280 he faced Castile, the Marinids and the Banu Ashqilula at once, but held out with the Volunteers of the Faith and the rift between Alfonso and his son Sancho. In 1288 the Banu Ashqilula left for North Africa. Castile took Tarifa in 1292 with Granada's help but kept it, and a joint siege with the Marinids in 1294 failed. After Sancho's death in 1295 Muhammad took Quesada and, in 1299, Alcaudete.

He died on 8 April 1302, before a planned offensive with Aragon, and was succeeded by his son Muhammad III; allegations that his son had poisoned him were never confirmed. He instituted the Nasrid royal protocol and the court chancery, built frontier strongholds held by governors whom the court appointed, and enlarged the Alhambra, where he built the Tower of the Ladies and the Tower of the Points. His epithet al-Faqih reflects his learning: he wrote poetry and drew scholars such as Muhammad al-Riquti and Muhammad ibn al-Raqqam to his court.
muhammad-iii-as-sadiq: Muhammad as-Sadiq, commonly known as Sadok Bey, was born on 7 February 1813. He was invested as Bey al-Mahalla, the heir apparent, on 10 June 1855, the same day he was named a divisional general in the Ottoman army, and he succeeded his brother Muhammad II ibn al-Husayn on 23 September 1859. On 10 December 1859 he was promoted to the rank of marshal.

In July 1860, persuaded by the British consul Richard Wood, the bey allowed a British subject named Holt to set up the country's first official printing press and its first Arabic-language newspaper, ar-Ra'id at-Tūnisi. The constitution of 23 April 1861 divided executive, legislative and judicial power among a Supreme Council, a legislature and new courts, limited the bey's powers and gave Muslims, Christians and Jews equal rights, above all in owning property, which drew French traders and religious schools to Tunisia. Three days later he changed the succession, so that the oldest prince of the family would inherit rather than the late ruler's eldest son.

He had the Marseille engineer Colin repair the Zaghouan aqueduct that supplied the capital, and in 1865 began demolishing the walls of the medina, when Tunis lost gates such as Bab Cartagena, Bab Souika, Bab Bnet and Bab El Jazira. Meanwhile intrigues among his ministers, notably Mustapha Khaznadar and Mustapha Ben Ismaïl, the pressure of the European consuls and the approaching bankruptcy of the state brought on the Mejba Revolt of 1864 and debts he could not repay, despite the efforts of his Grand Vizier Kheireddine Pacha.

In April 1881 raids by Khroumire tribesmen across the border of French Algeria gave France its pretext. A French expeditionary force took El Kef, troops landed at Bizerte on 1 May, and the French army occupied Tunis on 11 May.

His main residence was the Ksar Said palace, built in an Italianate style in front of the Bardo palace, and it was there, on 12 May 1881, that the French consul Théodore Roustan brought General Jules Aimé Bréart to obtain his signature on the Treaty of Bardo. In his later years the bey fell under the influence of Mustapha Ben Ismaïl. He died on 27 October 1882 without children, was buried in the Tourbet el Bey mausoleum in the medina of Tunis and was succeeded by his brother Ali III ibn al-Husayn.
muhammad-iii-of-granada: Muhammad was born in Granada on 15 August 1257, in the reign of his grandfather Muhammad I, the founder of the dynasty. His father, the future Muhammad II, encouraged learning in his children: Muhammad gave himself to poetry, his sister Fatima studied the lives of Islamic scholars, and their much younger half-brother Nasr astronomy. As heir he took part in affairs of state, and he once nearly had his father's secretary Ibn al-Hakim executed over satirical verses wrongly attributed to him. He came to the throne at about 45, on 8 April 1302; the historian Ibn al-Khatib cites a rumour, never confirmed, that he had poisoned his father.

Muhammad at first kept up his father's war with Castile and his alliances with Aragon and the Marinids. His troops took Bedmar, near Jaén, two weeks after his accession, and in 1303 he suppressed a revolt by his relative Abu al-Hajjaj ibn Nasr, governor of Guadix. In August 1303, at Córdoba, he made a three-year peace with Castile that confirmed Granada's conquests, including Bedmar, Alcaudete and Quesada, in return for his vassalage to Ferdinand IV and the payment of tribute. The peace angered the Volunteers of the Faith, North African warriors of holy war, and he dismissed 6,000 of his North African troops.

His failing sight left power increasingly with Ibn al-Hakim, who from 1303 held both the vizierate and the chancery and was styled holder of the two vizierates. The occupation of Ceuta and the Marinid ports of Ksar es-Seghir, Larache and Asilah, with Gibraltar and Algeciras, gave Granada command of the Strait. On 19 December 1308 Aragon and Castile agreed at Alcalá de Henares to conquer and divide Granada, and Aragon made a pact with the Marinid sultan Abu al-Rabi to retake Ceuta.

The coup of 14 March 1309, on the feast of Eid al-Fitr, was led by Atiq ibn al-Mawl, who killed Ibn al-Hakim, while the people of Granada sacked the palaces of sultan and vizier. Muhammad abdicated before jurists and lived at Almuñécar. After plots to restore him he was held in the Dar al-Kubra of the Alhambra and drowned in one of its pools on 21 January 1314, probably at Nasr's order. He was known as al-Makhlu, the Deposed. Ibn al-Khatib tells of his cruelty to his father's household troops, but also preserves his poems, and the Partal Palace and a bathhouse that endowed the Alhambra's mosque were his work.
muhammad-iqbal: Iqbal came from a Punjabi family of Kashmiri ancestry and studied at Government College in Lahore, where he took his Master of Arts in 1899. He taught Arabic at the Oriental College, Lahore, and then philosophy at Government College. Encouraged by his teacher Sir Thomas Arnold, he went to England in 1905, took a second Bachelor of Arts at Trinity College, Cambridge, and was called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn. In Germany he studied under Friedrich Hommel, and his thesis, The Development of Metaphysics in Persia, was published in London in 1908.

On his return he practised before the Chief Court of Lahore, where more than 100 reported judgements bear his name, but he gave most of his time to writing. He joined the Punjab Muslim League as one of its first joint secretaries, was elected to the Punjab Legislative Council in 1927 and criticised the Indian National Congress as dominated by Hindus. He became convinced that Muhammad Ali Jinnah alone could keep the League united, and corresponded with him.

Of his roughly 12,000 verses, about 7,000 are in Persian. Asrar-i-Khudi (Secrets of the Self, 1915) sets out his idea of khudi, the self, whose aim is self-realisation and which passes through stages toward becoming a vice-regent of God. Reynold Alleyne Nicholson's translation introduced his writing to Western readers. His first Urdu collection, Bang-e-Dara (1924), has three phases: patriotic and nature poems to 1905, poems on European society written in Europe, and poems on the heritage of the Muslim community, addressed to the Ummah.

His six English lectures, delivered at Madras, Hyderabad and Aligarh, appeared in 1930 as The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam. In the same year, in the Allahabad Address to the Muslim League, he outlined a political framework for the Muslim-majority regions of northwestern India. In the late 1930s he debated nationalism with Hussain Ahmad Madani, who defended a culturally plural India while Iqbal looked first to a Muslim community in Muslim-majority lands.

After a throat illness that began in 1933, Iqbal stopped practising law in 1934 and received a pension from the Nawab of Bhopal. He died in Lahore on 21 April 1938 and is buried in Hazuri Bagh, between the Badshahi Mosque and the Lahore Fort.

In Pakistan he is honoured as national poet, and 9 November, his birthday, is a public holiday. Many institutions bear his name, among them Allama Iqbal Open University and Allama Iqbal International Airport in Lahore. In Iran he is known as Iqbal of Lahore, and the Indonesian president Sukarno was among his admirers.
muhammad-iv-of-granada: Muhammad was born in the city of Granada on 14 April 1315, the first son of Sultan Ismail I and of Alwa, a Christian. On 8 July 1325 his father was assassinated by a relative, and the ten-year-old Muhammad was proclaimed sultan the same day. The wounded vizier Abu al-Hasan ibn Mas'ud rallied the court to swear allegiance, and his grandmother Fatima bint al-Ahmar, through whom he descended from earlier sultans, lent his accession crucial support. The Castilian Chronicle of Alfonso XI claims the murder was secretly planned by Uthman ibn Abi al-Ula, commander of the Volunteers of the Faith.

In the first years ministers vied for control. Uthman and the vizier Muhammad ibn al-Mahruq fell out, and in January 1327 Uthman proclaimed Muhammad's uncle, Muhammad ibn Faraj, a rival sultan at Almería and won the support of Alfonso XI of Castile, who seized Olvera and other frontier fortresses. To obtain Marinid troops the court gave up Ronda, Marbella and Algeciras to the Marinid Sultan Abu Said Uthman II. In 1328 Muhammad, now taking charge himself, reconciled with Uthman and had Ibn al-Mahruq killed, ending the civil war. In 1329 he made his former tutor Abu Nuaym Ridwan hajib, the first holder of that office among the Nasrids.

In 1330 Castile and Aragon invaded together: Alfonso XI took Teba after defeating a Granadan army, and crusading forces ravaged the countryside. Muhammad made peace with Castile at Seville on 19 February 1331, agreeing to pay tribute, but Alfonso soon stopped the promised food exports, and war with Aragon went on. In September 1332 Muhammad sailed to Fez, and the Marinid Sultan Abu al-Hasan Ali sent 5,000 troops under his son Abu Malik Abd al-Wahid. Gibraltar surrendered on 17 June 1333 after about five months of siege, and a truce of 24 August lifted Alfonso's siege of the town.

The next day, 25 August 1333, Muhammad was killed near the mouth of the Guadiaro on the orders of Uthman's sons Abu Thabit and Ibrahim; a slave named Zayyan carried out the killing. Muslim sources such as Ibn Khaldun blame the brothers' hostility to his Marinid alliance, while Castilian sources say he was killed for his friendliness with Alfonso XI. He was buried in Málaga, later under a domed mausoleum. Aged about 18, he left no descendants. His biographers describe him as a keen hunter and rider, interested in literature and poetry.
muhammad-ix-of-granada: Muhammad IX, known in Castilian as El Zurdo, was a grandson of Muhammad V and a nephew of Yusuf II. He was probably born in Granada around 1384, the year his grandfather held his circumcision ceremony, and in his youth he was imprisoned at Salobreña, probably after Muhammad VIII came to the throne. Of his two known wives, Zahr al-Riyad and Umm al-Fath, the second was a frequent adviser on matters of state. He had no son, and his three daughters married Muhammad X, possibly Yusuf V, and Abu l-Hasan Ali.

Provincial governors and the Banu al-Sarraj freed him in 1419 and proclaimed him sultan, after a fatwa declared the eight-year-old Muhammad VIII unfit to rule. Taking the epithet al-Galib bi-llah, he made Abu al-Hajjaj Yusuf ibn al-Sarraj vizier, kept truces with John II of Castile and courted the Hafsid ruler Abu Faris of Tunis, who sheltered him when he was overthrown in January 1427. He returned in 1429 and took the Alhambra in March 1430, then had Muhammad VIII executed. After the Castilian victory at La Higueruela on 1 July 1431 he lost the throne to Yusuf IV, but his supporters took the Alhambra back in 1432.

His third reign brought frontier raids, the loss of Huelma in 1438 and a truce in 1439; he refused formal vassalage to Castile. Faced with the revolt of his nephew Yusuf V he abdicated in 1445, but returned in 1447 after Yusuf's fall. In 1448 his forces defeated Juan de Saavedra at Río Verde near Marbella, a battle remembered in Castilian ballads, and in 1450 he retook Málaga from the pretender Ismail III.

Granadan commanders died in the defeat at Alporchones in 1452, and he agreed a five-year truce with Castile from 1 September 1452. He died in July 1453, aged more than sixty-nine by the grand vizier's official letter. With about 28 years on the throne he ruled longest of the 15th-century sultans, though he never had wide popular support.
muhammad-khan-bangash: Muhammad Khan Bangash, titled Ghazanfar-Jang, was the son of Ain Khan Bangash of the Karlani Khaghzai clan of the Pashtun Bangash tribe. His father had migrated from his homeland in the time of Aurangzeb, settled at Mau Rashidabad, entered the service of the descendants of Khwaja Bayazid Ansari, founder of the Roshaniyya movement, and married there. Muhammad Khan became one of the most powerful Indo-Afghan mercenaries of that part of Hindustan, a commander of 52,000 men in the Mughal army. He was illiterate and could not understand Persian, Turki or Pashto, so one of his sons had to accompany him, and contemporaries were struck by his simple habits beside his great wealth.

In 1713 Emperor Farrukhsiyar made him a courtier. He received the jagir of the Farrukhabad area and part of Bundelkhand, and he also founded Mohammadabad, named after himself, and Qaimganj, named after his son Qaim Khan. Since his Afghan followers were few, most of his soldiers were elite slaves called disciples, mostly former Hindu Rajputs and sometimes Brahmins, who were adopted, converted to Islam, renamed and trained, and counted as brothers of his natural sons.

He served in the campaign of the Sayyid Brothers against the Jat leader Churaman in 1722 and 1723. In December 1728 he besieged Chhatrasal, who had founded an independent kingdom in Bundelkhand, in his fort, but in March 1729 the Peshwa Baji Rao I marched to Chhatrasal's aid and Bangash was defeated and withdrew from Bundelkhand. Emperor Muhammad Shah made him subahdar of Malwa in 1730, but he could not stop the repeated Maratha raids and was removed in 1732. He also lost the governorship of Allahabad after his second failure against Chhatrasal.

At his death his lands covered the Doab from Koil in the north to Kora in the south, including Farrukhabad and parts of Cawnpore, Shahjahanpur, Budaun and Aligarh. His eldest son Qaim Khan succeeded him in 1743, followed by his second son Ahmad Khan Bangash. He married Malaha Banu, daughter of Kasim Khan Bangash, and had twenty-two sons and at least twenty-two daughters. Before his death the divisions between the tribes and castes among his followers had broken down, so that he had in effect founded an Indian Muslim tribe or caste of his own.
muhammad-naguib: Muhammad Naguib was born on 19 February 1901 in Khartoum, in Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, the eldest of nine children. His father was a ranking officer of the Egyptian Armed Forces, and his mother came from an Egyptian military family living in Omdurman. He attended secondary and military schools at Gordon Memorial College in Khartoum, graduating in 1918, and joined the Egyptian Royal Guard in 1923. In 1927 he became the first Egyptian military officer to obtain a law licence, and he took postgraduate degrees in political economy in 1929 and in civil law in 1931.

Naguib was promoted to captain in December 1931 and to major on 6 May 1938. In 1937 he founded a newspaper for the Egyptian Armed Forces in Khartoum. He became regional governor of the Sinai Peninsula in 1944 and a brigadier general in 1948. In the 1948 Arab-Israeli War he was wounded seven times and received the first military star of Fuad and the title of Bey. He was then made director of the Egyptian Military Academy, where Abdel Hakim Amer introduced him to the Free Officers.

Gamal Abdel Nasser had led the movement and felt it needed an older officer of distinguished record in order to be taken seriously. Naguib was invited to lead it. Historians note that he saw himself as its true leader, while the younger officers regarded him as a figurehead who would yield to their collective decisions. When the coup began on 23 July 1952 he was appointed Commander in Chief of the Army. On 26 July Ali Maher presented King Farouk with Naguib's ultimatum to abdicate, and Farouk sailed from Egypt the next day. Naguib became prime minister in September 1952, and when the republic was declared on 18 June 1953 he was sworn in as its first president.

He began to show independence from Nasser by distancing himself from the land reform decrees and drawing closer to the Wafd Party and the Muslim Brotherhood. In late 1953 Nasser accused him of supporting the outlawed Brotherhood and of dictatorial ambitions. Nasser won the struggle that followed and forced Naguib to resign in November 1954, then placed him under informal house arrest in a suburban Cairo villa. President Anwar Sadat released him in 1971.

Naguib died in Cairo on 28 August 1984 of liver cirrhosis, at the age of 83, and was given a military funeral attended by President Hosni Mubarak. Shortly before his death he published memoirs, which appeared in English as Egypt's Destiny. A Cairo Metro station and a major road in the Al Amarat district of Khartoum are named after him.
muhammad-of-ghor: Muhammad of Ghor, also called Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad ibn Sam, was born in Ghur in what is now west-central Afghanistan, the son of the Ghurid ruler Baha al-Din Sam I, who died in 1149. His birth year, about 1144, is worked out from the writings of Juzjani, who makes him three years and a few months younger than his brother Ghiyath al-Din, born in 1140. Their uncle Ala al-Din Husayn imprisoned both brothers, suspecting their loyalty, until his son freed them after his death in 1161. The brothers then ruled as a dyarchy. Ghiyath al-Din governed the west from Firozkoh and was engaged against the Khwarazmians, while Muhammad extended Ghurid rule eastwards from Ghazni.

Muhammad crossed the Indus in 1175 and took Multan from the Qarmatians. Near Mount Abu he was wounded and routed by a coalition of Rajput chiefs led by the Chaulukya king Mularaja, so he changed his route. He expelled the Ghaznavids by 1186, taking the upper Indus plain and most of Punjab, and secured the Khyber Pass.

In 1191 he was wounded at the first Battle of Tarain, defeated by the Rajput Confederacy under Prithviraj Chauhan, and returned to Khurasan. A year later he came back with a large army of mounted archers and won the second battle at the same place, and he executed Prithviraj shortly afterwards. In 1194 he defeated the Gahadavala king Jayachandra at Chandawar, and Varanasi was looted and Kanauj annexed in 1198. Most operations in India were left to slave commanders such as Qutb ud-Din Aibak, who pushed the frontier as far as Bengal and Bihar.

After Ghiyath al-Din died on 13 March 1203, Muhammad became supreme sultan. He suffered a heavy defeat at Andkhud against the Khwarazmians, who were aided by the Qara Khitai, and lost most of Khurasan.

While Muhammad was planning to avenge Andkhud, a rebellion by the Khokhars drew him to the Salt Range, where he crushed it. On 15 March 1206 he was assassinated at Dhamiak while at evening prayers. Sources name the Khokhars or Isma'ili emissaries. His only child, a daughter, had died before him, and his slaves and the Ghurid elite quarrelled over the succession. Muhammad II of Khwarazm annexed the Ghurid lands west of the Indus by 1215, but the conquests east of the Indus became the Delhi Sultanate under Aibak. At their height the Ghurids ruled a territory 3,000 km across, from Gorgan to Lakhnauti.
muhammad-quli-qutb-shah: Muhammad Quli was the third son of Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah Wali and succeeded him in 1580 at the age of 15. In the first years of his rule he put down rebellions on the eastern and western fronts of the sultanate, leading the troops himself against Ali Khan Loor and Yashwant Raj, and in 1592 his commander Aitbar Khan defeated Shah Saheb, who had risen to seize the throne.

Crowding in Golconda since his father's time created the need for a new city, and the building of Hyderabad began in 1591 on the southern bank of the River Musi. He is said to have prayed that the city be kept as full of people as the river is of fish; the story that he chose the site on his way back from a hunt is thought to be romanticised. The city was laid out on a grid with the Charminar at its centre and palaces and offices along the axes, and the Dar-ul-Shifa, the Mecca Masjid and the Badshahi Ashurkhana followed, along with several gardens.

He wrote poetry in Persian, Telugu and Urdu, and is held to be one of the first poets of Deccani Urdu and the first Urdu poet to compile a diwan. His verse ranged from the religious to the romantic and the profane, often in the gazal-i musalsal, a sequence of verses on a single theme, and was gathered as the Kulliyat-e-Quli Qutub Shah, of some 1800 pages, more than half of them gazals.

He was also a patron of painting, calligraphy and architecture; an inscription in Nastaliq script on the Mecca Masjid is unknown elsewhere in the Deccan. Physicians of his reign wrote Persian books on Unani medicine, among them Mir Momin's Ikhtiyarat-i Qutub Shahi and Abdullah Tabib's Tibb-i Farid.
muhammad-rumfa: Rumfa's birth name was Muhammad dan Yakubu. His lineage is much debated. The Kano Chronicle calls him the son of Yakubu, the nineteenth ruler of Kano, and of Fasima Berana, a Kanuri name, while other sources make Rumfa, Yakubu and Abdullahi Burja half-brothers and give his mother as Fatima, a woman from Rano. Some historians think the line came from Daura by way of Gaya, and that it took power with the help of Gaya and possibly of Bornu. Oral tradition explains the name Rumfa by the sheds (rumfa) built in his time to keep food out of reach of wild dogs.

Rumfa succeeded his father in 1463 and inherited a growing economy that drew scholars and traders of Arab, Kanuri, Berber and Fula descent. The best known was Muhammad Al-Maghili, who came to Kano after a stay in Katsina. Under his guidance Rumfa built mosques, cut down a sacred tree of the Abagayawa and raised a minaret on its site, banned pagan practices, and in his reign Eid al-Fitr was first held in Kano. Al-Maghili wrote On the Obligation of Princes as a guide for him.

The Kano Chronicle credits him with twelve innovations. Among them were the Taran Kano, a council of nine advisers and kingmakers, the practice of kulle or purdah, and the giving of offices of state and the treasury to eunuchs and slaves. He began the custom of taking every first-born virgin among the Indabawa for himself and is said to have had a thousand wives. His court used the kakaki trumpet and ostrich-feather sandals. He fought the first war between Kano and Katsina, which lasted eleven years without a victor.

Leo Africanus's account of Kano is thought to describe Rumfa's time, with its wealthy merchants, skilled craftsmen and cavalry. Leo also reported a conquest of Kano by the Songhai under Askiya the Great, but the Kano Chronicle does not mention it, and historians such as Humphrey J Fisher doubt that it happened or think it had no lasting effect.

The Kano Chronicle calls him just and learned and says that there was no Sarki more powerful. The Rumfawa, the rulers of his line, held Kano until the Kutumbawa replaced them in 1623, and the first Kanoan Empire arose under his grandson Muhammad Kisoki. Kano's palace still bears his name.
muhammad-shah-of-brunei: According to tradition, Awang Alak Betatar and his half-brother Awang Semaun were among the 14 children of Dewa Emas Kayangan, born of a Murut woman from Limbang, and he was crowned though he was not the firstborn. His descent remains unclear, and it has been disputed whether his father was Dewa Emas Kayangan or Sultan Ibrahim Shah of Kedah. His story is told chiefly in the Syair Awang Semaun, an oral poem first written down in 1947, and the Salasilah Raja-Raja Brunei, the royal genealogy.

He first founded a village at Negeri Garang, in the present Temburong District, before moving to the waters around Kota Batu, where the river let him control the rural areas. Brunei had been a vassal of the Majapahit Empire; as Majapahit declined, his forces under Awang Jerambak defeated the Melanau leader Basiung at Igan, took Oya, Matu, Mukah and other Melanau lands and pressed on to Sambas, so that his frontier ran from the Tutong River to the Rejang delta.

The Syair Awang Semaun and the Salasilah say he embraced Islam to marry Puteri Dayang Pingai, daughter of the Sultan of Johor; since Johor was not created until 1512, Jamil Al-Sufri reads it here as Tumasik, ancient Singapore. Islam did not yet reach deeply into a society shaped by Hindu-Buddhist ways. Envoys of the Hongwu Emperor reported in 1371 that he was cold towards them and spoke of an invasion by Sulu, but the mission brought letters acknowledging Chinese authority, carried by his envoy Ismail.

Later rulers of Brunei were styled sultans, and he is also regarded as the first sultan of Sarawak, Labuan and Sabah. Tradition says his daughter Princess Ratna Dewi married Ong Sum Ping, a Chinese immigrant who set up a trading station on the Kinabatangan River. The early succession is uncertain: Chinese records name rulers such as Raja Ma-na-je-chia-na whom the royal genealogy omits, naming Sultan Ahmad after him.
muhammad-shah-of-pahang: Known before his accession as Raja Muhammad, he was the second of two sons of Sultan Mansur Shah of Malacca by Putri Wanang Sri Lela Wangsa, daughter of Dewa Sura, the last pre-Malaccan ruler of Pahang, who was related to the King of Ligor; mother and grandfather had been captured and brought to Malacca after the conquest of Pahang in 1454. His father favoured him over his elder brother, Raja Ahmad, and named him Raja Muda, heir apparent, but the boy had a reputation for a hot temper.

When he was about fifteen he rode past boys playing sepak raga, and a ball kicked by Tun Besar, son of the Bendahara Tun Perak, knocked off his headdress.
