In a rage he drew his kris and killed Tun Besar. The Bendahara restrained his people from taking revenge, reminding them that Malay folks never commit treason, but they vowed that Raja Muhammad should never rule over them. Sultan Mansur agreed to send him away and ordered Sri Bija Diraja to escort him to Pahang and install him there.

He brought the trappings of the Malaccan court with him: Tun Hamzah, the former governor of Pahang, as his first Bendahara, Seri Akar Raja as chief Hulubalang, a chief treasurer, a Temenggong, and 100 boys and 100 girls of noble family. Installed as Sultan Muhammad Shah in 1470, he modelled his government on Malacca's, following the Undang-Undang Melaka and the Undang-Undang Laut Melaka. Pahang remained a vassal of Malacca. His realm stretched from Sedili Besar to the borders of Terengganu, and his court is said to have stood at Tanjung Langgar, Pekan. He married Mengindera Puteri, a granddaughter of Sultan Iskandar Shah of Kelantan, and had three sons.

He died on 17 September 1475, possibly of poison according to Portuguese records, and was buried at Langgar, Dusun Pinang, which gave him his posthumous name, Marhum Langgar. His son Raja Jamil succeeded him. The Arabic epitaph on his tombstone records his descent from Sultan Mansur Shah, Muzaffar Shah and Muhammad Shah and the date of his death, and confirms the genealogy of the Malaccan sultans given in the Malay Annals.
muhammad-shaybani: Muhammad Shaybani was a Shaybanid, a descendant of Shiban, son of Jochi Khan and grandson of Genghis Khan. His father was Budaq Sultan, one of the eleven sons of Abu'l-Khayr Khan, ruler of the Uzbek ulus, and his mother was Aq Quzi Begum. According to the historian Kamal ad-Din Binai, his father nicknamed him Shibägh, wormwood. Budaq Sultan was an educated man who had Persian works translated into Turkic, and Shaybani was fluent in both languages. He was fond of history in his youth, and in 1475 was presented with the Alexander Romance of Nizami Ganjavi.

He first appears leading 3,000 men in the army of the Timurid ruler of Samarkand, Sultan Ahmed Mirza. When Ahmed went to war with Sultan Mahmud Khan of Moghulistan over Tashkent, Shaybani secretly agreed with the Moghul khan to betray and plunder Ahmed's army, which he did at the Battle of the Chirciq River in 1488. Mahmud Khan rewarded him with Turkistan. There he oppressed the local Kazakhs, which led to a war between Moghulistan and the Kazakh Khanate that Moghulistan lost, while Shaybani's standing among the Uzbeks grew.

He ousted the Timurids from Samarkand in 1500, retook it in 1501, conquered Bukhara the same year and founded the Shaybanid dynasty of the Khanate of Bukhara. He fought successfully against Babur, later founder of the Mughal Empire, and married Babur's sister Khanzada Begum; Babur's freedom to leave Samarkand depended on his consent. Against the Shia Safavids he aligned himself with the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II. He patronised the Yemeni religious figure known as Mir-i Arab and wrote religious and philosophical works in Chagatai, among them the Bahr ul-Khudo of 1508. Raids on Kazakh lands in 1508–09 ended in a major defeat by Kasym Khan in 1510.

In 1510 Ismail I invaded western Khorasan. Shaybani had lost most of his cavalry in a campaign against the Hazaras, so he withdrew behind the walls of Merv. Ismail besieged the city for a month without result and then feigned a retreat. According to some sources the khan's emirs advised waiting for reinforcements, but his wife Aisha Sultan Khanum shamed the council into fighting. His army was surrounded by Ismail's 17,000 men and destroyed, and Shaybani was killed trying to escape, on 2 December 1510. Shaybani was succeeded by an uncle, a cousin and a brother, whose descendants ruled Bukhara until 1598 and Khwarezm until 1687.
muhammad-tayrab: Tayrab was the son of Sultan Ahmad Bukr and of Kaltuma, a Zaghawa Kobe of the ruling Angu clan. He came to the throne after his brother Abu'l-Qasim had been deserted on the battlefield in a war against Wadai, having tried to lessen his reliance on the Keira, the ruling family, and on the Fur. Abu'l-Qasim survived and returned to Darfur, and Tayrab wished to abdicate, but the title-holders had Abu'l-Qasim executed instead. The historian Rex O'Fahey found it unclear why they chose Tayrab, given his Zaghawa descent.

Tayrab gave offices to Zaghawa relatives, making his uncle Sultan of Kobe and a nephew the main intermediary at his itinerant courts, the fashirs. His first main fashir was at Shoba near Kabkabiya, where he built a redbrick palace and mosque. Finding Wadai too strong, he turned the sultanate east towards Kordofan and the Musabba'at, an exiled branch of the Keira, and around 1770 moved his main fashir to Ril near Nyala.

He suppressed a rebellion of the Birged of south-eastern Darfur, who reportedly accused him of selling Birged girls sent as tribute into slavery, and a major revolt led by the Tunjur sultan al-Mur. He strengthened his hold over the Beigo and the Berti but failed to subdue the Rizayqat nomads, who moved further south.

In 1782 the Funj Sultanate took Kordofan from Hashim of the Musabba'at, whose followers then raided Darfur. When the Funj withdrew amid a civil war around 1785, the elderly Tayrab invaded, drove Hashim east to the Shaiqiyya and advanced as far as the Nile near Shendi. His exhausted forces then fell back to Bara.

Knowing he was dying at Bara, Tayrab wrote to his son Ishaq to join him, and the title-holders swore to hand the army to Ishaq. After his death they did not, and Ishaq was defeated and killed in the civil war that brought Abu al-Rahman to the throne. Abu al-Rahman reportedly shared out Tayrab's former wives and possessions among his supporters. Tayrab was buried at Turra, as was the custom for Darfur's sultans.
muhammad-v-of-granada: Muhammad, who took the regnal name al-Ghani bi'llah, was the eldest son and heir of Yusuf I by his slave Butayna. When Yusuf I was murdered at prayer in the congregational mosque of Granada in 1354, his son was still a minor, and the state was run by the hajib Ridwan, the vizier Ibn al-Khatib and Yahya ibn Umar ibn Raḥḥu, commander of the Ghazis. They kept peace with Castile, paying tribute and sending troops against its enemies when asked, as against Aragon in 1359.

A palace coup in August 1359 put his half-brother Isma'il II on the throne. Muhammad fled to Guadix and then to the Marinid ruler Abu Salim in Fez, with Ibn al-Khatib, and there both men met Ibn Khaldun. Isma'il II was killed in June 1360 by his cousin, who reigned as Muhammad VI. In 1362 Muhammad V returned with Peter I of Castile, and their forces took Málaga; Muhammad VI surrendered to Peter, who executed him.

In his second reign Muhammad V steered through the Castilian Civil War, backing Peter against Henry of Trastámara, making peace with Henry when he took Seville in 1366 and renewing his loyalty to Peter in 1367. After Peter was assassinated in 1369 he recaptured Algeciras and destroyed it. In 1370 he abolished the office of chief of the Ghazis, placing the Zenata troops under the direct command of the Nasrid family for the first time. The emirate was relatively free of internal conflict in these years.

Besides the Palace of the Lions, he rebuilt the Mexuar and refurbished the Comares Palace with the ornate façade of the Patio del Cuarto Dorado. Between 1365 and 1367 he built the Maristan of Granada, one of the earliest European hospitals to care also for the mentally ill. He sent Ibn Khaldun as an ambassador to Seville in 1363, and Peter I built his palace in the Alcazar of Seville in the style of Granada. Muhammad V died on 16 January 1391 and was succeeded by his son Yusuf II; in the century before Granada fell, the dynasty was torn by succession disputes and assassinations.
muhammad-vi-of-granada: Muhammad was a grandson of Muhammad ibn Faraj, the brother of Sultan Ismail I, who had claimed the throne at Andarax in 1327 and lost the civil war that followed to Muhammad IV. He was a second cousin of the sultans Muhammad V and Ismail II, and some time before 1354 he married a daughter of Yusuf I, a full sister of Ismail. Their daughter married Muhammad ibn al-Mawl, and their grandson became Sultan Yusuf IV ibn al-Mawl. His nickname, el Bermejo, apparently referred to his reddish hair and beard.

With money from Ismail's mother Maryam, el Bermejo led about 100 men over the walls of the Alhambra on 23 August 1359, during Ramadan. They killed Muhammad V's hajib, Abu Nu'aym Ridwan, and proclaimed Ismail II, while Muhammad V escaped to Guadix and later went into exile in North Africa. El Bermejo became the real power behind the throne, and when Ismail began to oppose him he led a second coup in June or July 1360. Ismail was executed in a dungeon, as were his young brother Qays and his ministers.

Muslim chroniclers describe Muhammad VI as coarse in dress and manners, and Ibn al-Khatib, a minister of Muhammad V, as addicted to hashish. He persecuted suspected supporters of Muhammad V, stopped the tribute to Castile and on 9 October 1360 allied with the Crown of Aragon in the War of the Two Peters. When Aragon made peace in May 1361, Peter I of Castile backed Muhammad V, who returned in August. Muhammad VI won a victory near Guadix on 15 January 1362, taking 2,000 prisoners, but from February Peter and Muhammad V took fortress after fortress, and Muhammad V seized Málaga.

On 13 April 1362 Muhammad VI fled Granada with most of the treasury and unexpectedly surrendered to Peter at Seville, offering to rule as his vassal. Peter arrested him after a feast and had him led to a field at Tablada, where the king struck him with a lance, blaming him for the poor peace he had been forced to make with Aragon. Along with him 36 of his followers were killed, and about 300 were imprisoned and later poisoned. Many at the Castilian court called the killing an atrocious betrayal. Peter sent the heads to Muhammad V, who hung them near the wall Muhammad VI had scaled in 1359.
muhammad-zia-ul-haq: Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq was born on 12 August 1924 in Jullundur, Punjab, into an Arain family. His father worked at the Army General Headquarters in Delhi and was noted for his religiousness. Zia studied history at St. Stephen's College in Delhi, graduating in 1943, and was commissioned into the British Indian Army, serving in a tank unit, the 13th Lancers, in the Burma campaign. After the Partition of India in 1947 he joined the army of Pakistan. He took part in the Indo-Pakistani War of 1965 as a tank commander, and from 1967 to 1970 headed a Pakistani training mission in Jordan.

In 1975 Zia commanded the II Corps at Multan, and on 1 March 1976 Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto made him Chief of Army Staff, choosing the most junior of eight lieutenant generals. Following civil disorder after the 1977 general election, Zia carried out a coup on 5 July 1977, codenamed Operation Fair Play, and Bhutto and his cabinet were arrested. Zia promised elections within 90 days, but they were postponed. The Supreme Court upheld the coup under the doctrine of necessity. Bhutto was arrested again on 3 September 1977 for authorising the murder of a political opponent, and on 18 March 1978 he was sentenced to death. Zia declared himself president on 16 September 1978.

In 1979 he banned all political parties and disbanded parliament, and at the end of 1981 set up a nominated consultative council, the Majlis-e-Shoora. After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan on 25 December 1979 he decided to support the Afghan mujahideen with American help, and Pakistan became the main base of the war against the Soviet forces. He lifted martial law in 1985, after non-partisan elections, but kept wide presidential powers through the Eighth Amendment, and in 1988 dismissed the government of Prime Minister Muhammad Khan Junejo.

On 17 August 1988 Zia left Bahawalpur, where he had watched a tank demonstration, in a C-130B Hercules. Soon after take-off contact was lost, and witnesses said the plane flew erratically before it crashed. Twenty-nine others died, among them General Akhtar Abdur Rahman and the American ambassador Arnold Lewis Raphel. The cause has given rise to many conspiracy theories. Zia remains a polarising figure: some credit him with checking Soviet advance towards Pakistan, while critics hold that he weakened democratic institutions and passed laws that encouraged religious intolerance.
muhammadiyah: Muhammadiyah, officially the Muhammadiyah Society, was established on 18 November 1912 in Yogyakarta by Ahmad Dahlan, a court official of the kraton of the Yogyakarta Sultanate and an educated Muslim scholar from Mecca. Among the motives were what he saw as the backwardness of Muslim society and the penetration of Christianity. Much influenced by the Egyptian reformer Muhammad Abduh, Dahlan held that modernisation and the purification of religion from syncretic practices were vital, and the movement has stressed tawhid, strict monotheism, from its beginning.

From 1913 to 1918 Muhammadiyah established five Islamic schools, and in 1919 an Islamic high school, with teachers supplied by the nationalist movement Budi Utomo. At Dahlan's death in 1923 it reported 2,622 men and 724 women as members, mostly in Yogyakarta. By 1925 it had built 55 schools and two clinics in Surabaya and Yogyakarta. After Abdul Karim Amrullah introduced it to the Minangkabau, it grew rapidly, and Minangkabau businesspeople spread it across Indonesia. In 1938 it claimed 250,000 members, 834 mosques, 31 libraries and 1,774 schools.

It has generally avoided politics and never formed a political party, unlike the traditionalist Nahdlatul Ulama. In 1965 and 1966 it declared the extermination of the Communist Party of Indonesia a holy war, a view other Islamic groups endorsed, which contributed to the Indonesian mass killings of those years. Around the fall of Suharto in 1998 its chairman, Amien Rais, founded the National Mandate Party, which has no official relationship with the organisation. It had 29 million members in 2008.

Muhammadiyah promotes ijtihad, the derivation of Islamic law directly from the Qur'an and sunnah, and rejects taqlid, blind adherence. It is Sunni in theology and opposes syncretism with animism and with Hindu and Buddhist elements, as well as the Sufi tradition that makes a shaykh the formal authority over Muslims. Its schools combine religious and secular education, and some are open to non-Muslims.

Beneath its Central Board stand boards at the provincial, regency or city, sub-district and village levels, and there are boards overseas. Its autonomous organisations include Aisyiyah for women, Pemuda Muhammadiyah for youth and the scouting body Hizbul Wathan. Its magazine Suara Muhammadiyah, begun by Dahlan in 1915, is one of the oldest publications in Indonesia. It was said to have 60 million members in 2019, largely urban and middle-class, and it had 89 universities in 2024. Its headquarters were first in Yogyakarta, but by 1970 several committees had moved to Jakarta.
muhammadu-attahiru-i: Attahiru became the twelfth sultan of Sokoto in October 1902, on the death of Abderrahman dan Abi Bakar. British forces had already taken parts of the caliphate: in Abderrahman's last year General Frederick Lugard had used the rivalries between the southern emirs and Sokoto to prevent a united defence. As a force led by the British approached the capital, Attahiru organised a hasty defence and chose to meet it outside the city. The battle was soon over, the superior British firepower causing heavy losses among his men, and his reign as sultan ended on 15 March 1903.

Attahiru and many followers left Sokoto on what he called a hijra, made to prepare for the coming of the Mahdi. The British entered the largely emptied city and on 21 March 1903 installed Muhammadu Attahiru II. Lugard in effect abolished the office of caliph, keeping the title of sultan as a symbolic position in the new Northern Nigeria Protectorate.

Pursued by the British, Attahiru travelled through the countryside of the caliphate gathering supporters. The numbers who joined him, eventually thousands, alarmed both the British and the emirs who had sided with them, as the movement marched through Zamfara and Kano. On 29 July the British attacked at the Mbormi battle ground, near present-day Gombe, and Attahiru was among those killed.

The British cut off his head, photographed it and showed the photographs across Northern Nigeria to convince the diehards of the futility of fighting. His son Muhammad Bello bin Attahiru, called Mai Wurno, led those who remained of the movement and eventually settled in Sudan, where many of their descendants still live.
muhammadu-dikko: Muhammadu Dikko, also called Muhammad Dikko dan Gidado, was born in the reign of Emir Muhammadu Bello to Muhammadu Gidado, who held the title of Durbi, one of Katsina's kingmakers, and his wife Ta-Malamai. He studied with the scholars of Katsina at Tsagero. When Musa became emir in 1882 he stripped Gidado of his title and seized the family's property, but under Musa's successor Abubakar the family recovered. Dikko fought bravely in Katsina's wars with Maradi, and Abubakar made him Durbi and district head of Mani.

In April 1903 a British force under Lord Frederick Lugard reached Katsina, which surrendered without a fight. Emir Abubakar made Dikko his liaison with the British and responsible for their supplies, and Dikko worked to win their trust. The British exiled Abubakar to Ilorin in January 1905 and installed Yero, who resisted them. While Dikko was in Agadez buying camels and firearms for the British, the resident Herbert Richmond Palmer deposed Yero on 9 November 1906 and named Dikko interim emir, passing over the heirs of the ruling Dallazawa. The acting High Commissioner William Wallace confirmed him on 25 January 1907.

The Dallazawa and their followers saw Dikko as a usurper imposed by the British. He placed loyal men in key posts, among them Mallam Haruna as Katsina's first Waziri, and married his daughters to district heads and nobles. His reign saw new taxes, the division of the native authority into departments, the move of district heads out of Katsina to their districts, a hospital and, in 1922, Katsina College, the first secondary school in Northern Nigeria.

In 1921 he went to Mecca by car and from there to England, where he met King George V; he returned to England in 1924 and 1937. In 1935 he rebuilt the mosque of Ummarun Dallaje, later called Masallacin Dutsi, and he turned Katsina's war horses to racing and polo.

Dikko died after an illness in 1944, setting off a contest between the Dallazawa princes and his own sons. In March 1944 the kingmakers chose his son Usman Nagogo, the British candidate, who was turbaned on 19 May 1944. Dikko is buried in a garden of the emir's palace, and the Muhammadu Dikko Stadium in Katsina bears his name.
muhammadu-kanta: According to tradition, his father Makata migrated from the east to Bawa, then part of the Hausa kingdom of Katsina, where he became village head with the title Magaji, and his mother Tamatu was a Katsina princess. Passed over as his father's successor, Kanta became a cattle grazer, crossed Gobir and Zamfara to the Rima River and settled in a village that some historians identify as Surame and others as Leka. His strength in boxing and wrestling earned him the epithet Kotal, no challenger, and a following with which he overthrew the village's Fulani Magaji and took the title Sarki.

He joined Askia the Great's campaign against the Hausa states in 1513 and rose to be a barde, a captain, in the Songhai army. The Tarikh al-Sudan relates that after the expedition against Agades he and his followers were refused their share of the spoils and rose in revolt. Kanta repelled the army sent against him, and Kebbi became the last of the Hausa states to emerge. He conquered Asben and Aïr, Nupe and Borgu, Zamfara and Zazzau, Arewa and Zaberma, and controlled Gobir, Katsina and Kano. After Askia Muhammad Benkan barely escaped a defeat, Songhai made peace.

Bornu was his strongest rival. Tradition tells that a Bornu army besieged Surame and withdrew when it saw dead defenders propped on the walls, their lips slit to look as if they were grinning; in another war Mai Muhammad Aminami reportedly fielded about 100,000 men. Kanta built fortified towns, among them Birnin Leka, Gungu and Silame, and his final capital, Surame, of seven concentric towns with forty-foot walls, parts of which still stand.

Years after the siege of Surame he marched against Bornu, and is said to have won seven pitched battles before he was halted short of its capital. On the way back he was struck by a poisoned arrow at Rimin dan Ashita, near Ingawa in Katsina, and died at Jiruwa in 1561. Twelve tombs were built along the road to Kebbi to hide his burial place. His successors could not hold his conquests: by the end of the 16th century Hausaland had stopped sending tribute, and Kebbi had shrunk to a local kingdom.
muhanga: Muhanga, called Gitarama until it was renamed in 2006, lies in central Rwanda although it is officially part of the Southern Province. It stands 1,812 metres above sea level, about 45 kilometres by road south-west of Kigali, and about 40 kilometres by road north of Nyanza, the provincial headquarters. It is the capital and largest urban area of Muhanga District, and serves as a gateway to the west and south of the country. The city is known for its mineral resources, including coltan, wolfram and cassiterite, and has several open-pit mines for gravel and sand.

During the 1994 Rwandan genocide the district, then known as Gitarama, was one of twelve provinces of Rwanda, and the town became the seat of the provisional government. Its centre of Catholic life is Kabgayi, where the Kabgayi Minor Basilica, a major and a minor seminary, a hospital and several colleges stand, among them the Catholic Institute of Kabgayi and the Catholic University of Rwanda. Muhanga also has Adventist and other secondary schools and the St. Elizabeth Nurses and Midwives College.

Muhanga is an industrial and minerals-processing hub and one of three satellite cities in the country, a target of the government's regional growth strategy because of its closeness to Kigali. It is the fourth-largest city in Rwanda, and the 2022 national census put its population at 85,000. The city holds the offices of the district administration and council, the district prison, a high court building and a cultural centre. It has a farmers' market and several bank branches, and Zipline delivers supplies from Muhanga to medical centres in the surrounding area by drone. People from Muhanga include Dominique Mbonyumutwa and Fred Rwigyema.
muharram: Muharram, meaning sacred, is the first month of the Islamic calendar, with at most thirty days. Warfare in it was forbidden before the advent of Islam. The word is short for Muharram Safar, the sacred Safar, which in the ancient Arab calendar distinguished Safar I, which was sacred, from Safar II, which was not. Over time the adjective itself became the name of the first month of the year.

The Islamic calendar is lunar, and months begin when the first crescent of a new moon is sighted. Because the lunar year is eleven or twelve days shorter than the solar year, Muharram falls on different days in successive solar years.

The tenth day of Muharram is Ashura. For Sunni Muslims it marks the parting of the Red Sea by Moses and the salvation of the Israelites, and tradition also places on this day Noah's disembarking from the Ark, God's forgiveness of Adam and the release of Joseph from prison. It is observed by voluntary fasting and other pious acts. Some Sunni communities hold carnivals, bonfires and special dishes, though some Sunni scholars have criticised such practices.

For Shia Muslims Ashura is a day of mourning for Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad and the third imam. Husayn refused on moral grounds to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid ibn Mu'awiya and was killed, with most of his male relatives and his small retinue, by the Umayyad army at the Battle of Karbala on Ashura in 61 AH (680 CE). Sunnis also regard the killing of Husayn as a tragic event, and Husayn and his companions are widely regarded as martyrs by all Muslims.

The events of Karbala are remembered day by day. Husayn arrived there on 2 Muharram and was forced to camp in the desert; on 7 Muharram the Umayyad army cut off his access to the Euphrates; on 9 Muharram, called Tasu'a, negotiations failed and the commander Umar ibn Sa'd was persuaded to delay the attack until the next day. After the battle the women and children of the camp were taken prisoner and marched to Damascus.

Most Shia mourning takes place in the first ten days, ending with processions in major Shia cities on the tenth. Practices include gatherings in mosques and husayniyyas where scholars and maddahs recount Karbala, the recitation of elegies, charitable distribution of food and water, reenactments, and ritual chest-beating, called latmiyya or sīnah-zanī. Among the Shia, mourning for Husayn is viewed as protest against oppression and as a struggle for God.
muhlhausen: Mühlhausen lies in the northwest of Thuringia on the Unstrut river, on the eastern edge of the Hainich hills, in the flat and fertile Thuringian Basin at about 215 metres above sea level. It is 50 km north-west of Erfurt and 5 km north of Niederdorla, the geographical centre of Germany. Archaeological finds near St. George's Church show a large settlement of the Thuringii and Francia period, from the 6th to the early 10th century, which is seen as the origin of the town. After 1815 Mühlhausen belonged to the Prussian Province of Saxony, and industrialisation reached it late, around 1870, with the railway.

The town was first mentioned in 967, in a territory given by Otto II to his wife Theophanu. It belonged to the imperial estate, and emperors from Otto III to Henry III visited its Kaiserpfalz in the 10th and 11th centuries. The election of Philip of Swabia in 1198 ended with a homage there. Mühlhausen became a Freie Reichsstadt, an independent and self-ruled member of the Holy Roman Empire that controlled about 220 square kilometres and 19 villages, and with its long-distance trade it was prosperous, with some 10,000 inhabitants around 1500.

The Reformation brought disturbances. The monk Heinrich Pfeiffer preached at St. Mary's in 1523, and Thomas Müntzer in August 1524. They made political demands as well as religious ones, aimed at the privileges and oligarchic rule of the magistrates, and the council was replaced by an Eternal Council. During the German Peasants' War of 1524 and 1525 the monasteries were looted and churches stripped. After the imperial army defeated the uprising, Müntzer and Pfeiffer were executed, Müntzer on 27 May 1525 just outside the city. The city paid a fine of 40,000 guilders and lost part of its independence. The Reformation was introduced by force in 1542.

Because it was spared later destruction, Mühlhausen has one of the largest medieval city centres remaining in Germany, with eleven Gothic churches and an almost completely preserved fortification. St. Blaise's, first mentioned in 1227, is a major 13th-century church where Johann Sebastian Bach was organist in 1707 and 1708. St. Mary's, from the early 14th century, has the highest steeple in Thuringia and now houses a Müntzer memorial, opened in 1975. John A. Roebling, who built the Brooklyn Bridge, was born in the town.
muhtasib: Islamic tradition holds that the Prophet Muhammad himself appointed overseers of the markets of Mecca and Medina, among them Saʿid b. Saʿid b. al-As over the market of Medina after the conquest of Mecca in 629, and that the caliph Umar had two men working over that market. During the Umayyad period market inspectors are reported at Mecca and Wāsit, and in Spain the post was called Sāḥib al-Sūq. According to R. P. Buckley, the first muhtasibs are mentioned in the early years of the Abbasid Caliphate, and the new name may have been intended to indicate an Islamicizing of the post.

Willem Floor argues that the conquered societies already had such market inspectors, that the practical manuals came before those setting the office in a religious and legal frame, and that the jurists imposed that frame on an existing institution. Al-Ghazali (d. 1111) used the word muhtasib in a wider sense, for anyone who forbids wrong, which the historian Michael Cook sees as a source of confusion.

The muhtasib stood roughly between a qadi and a court magistrate: he could not hear cases, only settle disputes and breaches of the law where the facts were admitted or guilt confessed. Besides prices, weights and food, he inspected public eating houses and kept a check on doctors, surgeons and apothecaries, and craftsmen and builders answered to him for the standards of their craft. After 950, under the Buyids, the office was sold, in 961 for 20,000 dirhams a month, and Floor thinks its holders took bribes to recover the cost. Nizam al-Mulk wrote that the post was usually given to a noble, a eunuch or an old Turk.

Under the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, who ruled from 1658 to 1707, muhtasibs acted as censors of morals enforcing his orders, including the destruction of Hindu temples and shrines. The office was renewed in the Ottoman Empire in 1855 and in the Republic of Syria in 1925. In Iran it was abolished in Shiraz around 1852 and in Isfahan in 1877, while in Tehran it survived as a city cleaning department until 1926. Among the Tatars of the Russian Empire the möxtäsip enforced Sharia until the 1920s. In post-Soviet Russia a muhtasib is a regional representative of a muftiate, and in Pakistan the Mohtasib is an ombudsman.
muhu: Muhu is an island of Estonia in the West Estonian archipelago of the Baltic Sea. It has an area of 208 square kilometres and is the third largest island of Estonia, after Saaremaa and Hiiumaa. The Big Strait divides it from the mainland and the Little Strait from Saaremaa. The German and Swedish name for the island is Moon, and the waters to its north are called the Sea of Straits, or Moon Sound. With four neighbouring islets, Muhu forms a rural municipality in Saare County, whose main settlements are Kuivastu, Liiva and Koguva. Muhu is linked to Saaremaa by the Väinatamm causeway, opened in 1896.

In January 1227 an army of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, with Letts, Germans of Riga and native Livonians, 20,000 men commanded by William of Modena, crossed on sea ice from the mainland and attacked Saaremaa, the last holdout of the pagan Estonians. The Estonians surrendered on Muhu at a circular stronghold called Mona, whose earthworks are still preserved near the causeway between the islands. This ended the Estonian Crusade.

The Battle of Karuse, also called the Battle on the Ice, was fought on 16 February 1270 on the frozen Baltic Sea between Muhu and the mainland. The Grand Duchy of Lithuania won a decisive victory over the Livonian Order, in what was the fifth-largest defeat of the Livonian or Teutonic Orders in the 13th century. The same waters saw the Battle of Moon Sound between Russian and German naval forces in September and October 1917, during the First World War.

The island has a medieval Lutheran church, St. Catherine's, and the traditional village of Koguva, where the Muhu Museum stands. Muhu is known for having the only traditional windmills in Estonia that are still operational and for its traditional knitted stockings.
muhyiddin-of-brunei: Muhyiddin was the fourth son of Sultan Abdul Jalilul Akbar and a younger brother, by the same mother, of Sultan Abdul Jalilul Jabbar. He was also the nephew and son-in-law of Sultan Muhammad Ali, whose daughter Pangiran Anak Putri Siti Maria he married. After Muhammad Ali was murdered, the new sultan, Abdul Hakkul Mubin, gave Muhyiddin, then known as Pengiran Bongsu Muhyiddin, the title of Pengiran Bendahara Seri Maharaja Permaisuara in order to appease the supporters of the dead ruler.

Resentment of Abdul Hakkul Mubin persisted, and Muhammad Ali's supporters pressed Muhyiddin to overthrow him. He at first declined but then helped to arrange the ouster. When Abdul Hakkul Mubin moved his administrative centre from Kota Batu to Pulau Cermin, Muhyiddin stayed behind in Kampong Ayer, raised the sultan's yellow flag for himself and declared himself sultan, beginning Brunei's first civil war.

His warriors failed in their attacks on his rival's fort at Kinarut, which was defended with the help of Bajaus and Dusuns, and he asked the Sultan of Sulu for aid in exchange for the province of eastern Sabah. His forces finally bombarded Pulau Cermin from Tanjung Kindana, destroying most of its defences, and Abdul Hakkul Mubin was executed at the island's Great Mosque, which ended the war. A letter of Muhyiddin to an English captain who oversaw English trade in Jambi, studied by the Brunei History Centre in 2017, points to links with Jambi, and the purchase of gunpowder is credited with his victory on Pulau Cermin.

Once in power, Muhyiddin sought to return the succession to Muhammad Ali's line. He recalled Pengiran Muda Bongsu, who had fled to Sambas at the outbreak of the war, and named him Raja Bendahara, but Pengiran Muda Bongsu died first, and the title passed to his son, Pengiran Anak Muhammad Alam. Muhyiddin died in 1690 and was succeeded by Sultan Nasruddin.
muin-al-din-unur: Unur began as a mamluk, a slave soldier, in the army of Toghtekin, the founder of the Burid dynasty of Damascus. When Zengi, the atabeg of Aleppo, besieged Damascus in 1135, he commanded the army defending the city. The Burid Shihab ad-Din Mahmud then sent him to govern Homs, with Yusuf ibn Firuz as his lieutenant, and he still held it when Zengi besieged the city briefly in 1137. In 1138 Shihab ad-Din made him atabeg of Damascus with the title Isfahsalar, but when Zengi received Homs in a marriage settlement later that year, Unur was given the castle of Barin instead.

After Shihab ad-Din's assassination on 22 June 1139, Unur governed Baalbek for the new emir, Jamal ad-Din, and defended it until Zengi took the city with 14 catapults. From 1140 he ruled Damascus as regent for Jamal ad-Din's son Mujir ad-Din Abaq. That year he besieged Banias with King Fulk of Jerusalem and Prince Raymond of Antioch and handed it to Fulk, and on a visit to Jerusalem with the future chronicler Usamah ibn Munqidh he negotiated a fuller alliance against Zengi.

After Zengi was assassinated in 1146, Unur took Baalbek from Najm ad-Din Ayyub, father of Saladin, and asserted control over Homs and Hama. In 1147 he allied with Nur ad-Din, and when Altuntash, governor of Bosra and Salkhad, joined Jerusalem against him, the army of Aleppo forced the crusaders to withdraw. In August 1147 the caliph Al-Muqtafi, the Seljuk sultan Mas'ud and the Fatimid caliph al-Hafiz recognised him as governor. Against the crusaders in 1148 he reluctantly called on Nur ad-Din and Saif ad-Din Ghazi I, and he may have bribed the besiegers to leave.

Afterwards he had to acknowledge Nur ad-Din as his overlord. In 1149 he raided crusader lands, agreed a two-year truce with King Baldwin III, and patrolled the Hauran while Nur ad-Din defeated Antioch at the Battle of Inab. Back in Damascus in July he fell ill with dysentery; he died on 28 August 1149 and was buried in the university he had founded in the city. Both Ibn al-Qalanisi and the Christian chronicler William of Tyre praised him, William calling him "a man of much wisdom and a lover of our people." By 1154 Nur ad-Din held Damascus.
muirchertach-ua-briain: Muirchertach was a son of Toirdelbach Ua Briain, the Dalcassian king of Munster, and of Derbforgaill, daughter of Tadhg Mac Giolla Pádraig of Osraige. The Annals of Tigernach give his birth as 1050, but he next appears only in 1075, defeated with heavy losses by the Kingdom of Airgíalla near modern Ardee during his father's campaigns in the north. After the death of the King of Leinster that year, Toirdelbach took control of Dublin, valued for its trade and its fleet, and made Muirchertach its king or governor.

On his father's death in 1086 Munster was divided among three sons. Tadc died the next year, Muirchertach banished his brother Diarmuit, and he defeated Diarmuit and his Leinster allies at Raith Etair, possibly on Howth Head. In 1088 his fleets sent against Ruadhrí na Saide Buide Ua Conchobhair of Connacht were destroyed, and Ruadhrí and Domnall Mac Lochlainn burned Limerick, Killaloe and Emly and took over 160 hostages, whom Muirchertach had to buy back. In 1094 he drove Gofraid Crobán out of Dublin, and in 1095 he gained overlordship of the Isles through his nephew Diarmuit's marriage to a Manx princess.

His annual campaigns against Domnall in the north were often halted by truces that the abbot of Armagh arranged. Facing Magnus Barefoot of Norway, he made an alliance sealed by the marriage of his daughter Bjaðmunjo to Magnus's son Sigurd, and the two campaigned in Ulster in 1102 and 1103, with little success by the account of the Irish annals. Domnall defeated him at the Battle of Mag Coba on 5 August 1103. He also sent his daughter Lafracoth with a fleet to Arnulf, Earl of Pembroke, in his quarrel with Henry I of England, and in 1105 King Edgar of Scotland sent him a camel.

In 1114 he fell so ill that he was described as a living skeleton, and Diarmuit seized the kingship and banished him. He recovered the next year and captured Diarmuit in 1115, but his high kingship was breaking apart. The historian Anthony Candon described him as an ambitious, modernising and outward-looking king who sought to involve Ireland in the international politics of Europe, through marriages with the king of Norway and the de Belleme family and dealings with the kings of Scotland and England and aid to the Welsh princes.
muizz-al-dawla: Ahmad was a son of Buya, a fisherman of Lahijan in Daylam who had left the Zoroastrian faith for Islam. Around 928 his brother 'Ali entered the service of Makan ibn Kaki and found military posts for Ahmad, then about thirteen, and their brother Hasan; the brothers later went over to the Ziyarid prince Mardavij. Sent to conquer Kerman in 935 or 936, Ahmad was wounded in the head and lost a hand and several fingers of the other. He then took Khuzestan from the Baridis and from there campaigned into Iraq on his own initiative.

He entered Baghdad without a struggle on 19 December 945 and took the post of amir al-umara', though he remained largely subordinate to 'Imad al-Dawla in Shiraz. In January 946 he deposed and blinded the caliph al-Mustakfi and set up al-Muti'. The Hamdanid Nasir al-Dawla then seized eastern Baghdad, and for three months the Tigris divided the city; the western side was blockaded until starving people ate grass and carrion. On the night of 1 August his secretary Saymari crossed the river while Ahmad made a diversion with torches and trumpets, and the Hamdanids withdrew; his Daylamite troops then looted the eastern quarters and killed civilians.

He took Basra and Wasit from the Baridis in 947, but the Batihah marsh amirate of 'Imran ibn Shahin defeated his armies and was made a vassal. In 957 his Turkic ghulams defeated the rebel Daylamite officer Ruzbahan, who was later drowned in the Tigris. Twice, in 958 and 964, he took Mosul and Nasibin, but could not hold them against a hostile population, and made peace in return for tribute.

With help from 'Adud al-Dawla he annexed Oman, and he died during a campaign against the Shahinids of the Mesopotamian marshes, on 8 April 967. His son 'Izz al-Dawla, named his successor during a serious illness in 955, followed him. His entry into Baghdad began more than a century of Buyid rule in Iraq and of Shi'ite Buyid control over the Sunni caliphate, but he left the rivalry between Baghdad and Shiraz and the hostility between Turks and Daylamites unresolved.
mujahid-al-amiri: Mujahid was a saqlabi, a slave of Slavic origin; his patronymic, Ibn Abd Allah, does not name his real father, and his mother was a captured Christian. The hajib al-Mansur bought him, converted him to Islam and had him educated. He may have governed Dénia for al-Mansur's sons after 1002, and he took control of the town after the death of al-Mansur's second son, Sanchuelo. Within a few years he had set up a puppet caliph of his own, al-Muʿayṭī.

In 1015 he sailed for Sardinia with 120 ships in al-Muʿayṭī's name and occupied the southern coastal plain, but Pisan and Genoese forces defeated him. The next year he returned with a large cavalry force, beat the army of the judge of Cagliari and even sent a raid against Luni on the Italian coast. The chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg tells that he sent the pope a sack of chestnuts to show the number of his soldiers, and that Benedict VIII answered with a sack of millet. In May 1016, facing mutiny, he fled by sea; a storm wrecked his fleet, the Pisan and Genoese fleets took the remaining ships, and his mother and his son Ali were captured.

Back in Dénia he sent al-Muʿayṭī, who had tried to seize power in his absence, into exile in Africa. His later rule is poorly recorded, and few of his coins survive. He shared rule of the taifa of Valencia with Labib al-Fata al-Saqlabi in 1019–1020, and in 1033 accepted the nominal authority of an impostor Hisham II put forward by Seville. Late in life he briefly occupied Murcia and quarrelled with his younger son Hasan. Ali succeeded him.

Mujahid patronised theological and literary study, above all qirāʾāt, recitation. Ibn Gharsiya wrote at his court his treatise on the shu'ubiyya, which criticised Arab dominance in Spain and praised Berbers and Slavs, and Ibn Burd al-Asghar dedicated a work to him. The polymath Ibn Hazm and the jurist Ibn Abd al-Barr spent time there. Mujahid himself wrote a book on Arabic metre, now lost.
mujir-al-din-abaq: Mujir al-Din was the eldest son of Jamal al-Din Muhammad, the Burid emir of Damascus. His honorific Mujir al-Din means protector of the faith. When his father died in 1140 he succeeded him while still a minor, and Mu'in al-Din Unur was named vizier to govern for him.

Zengi attacked Damascus at once, hoping to profit from Jamal al-Din's death, but Unur organised the defence of the city. Only when Unur died in July 1149 did Mujir al-Din take his place as ruler in his own right. He proved a weak ruler, and the city fell under the influence of Nur al-Din Zengi, emir of Aleppo and Mosul, who had imposed his dominance over Damascus after the Second Crusade.

Nur al-Din recognised Mujir al-Din as ruler of Damascus in 1150. In 1151 Mujir al-Din joined the crusaders against Bosra, angering Nur al-Din, and later that year travelled to Aleppo to swear loyalty to him. In 1152 he besieged Bosra again until its governor accepted his demands, and in 1153 he joined Nur al-Din's attempt to take the crusader castle of Banias. In 1154 the two were again at odds, and Nur al-Din took Damascus and with it control of all of Syria.

Expelled from Damascus, Mujir al-Din was sent to Homs. He later left Homs for Baghdad, where he settled and died in 1169. With his removal the Burid line that had ruled the emirate of Damascus came to an end, and the city passed into the hands of Nur al-Din.
mukachevo: Mukachevo lies in the valley of the Latorica River in Zakarpattia Oblast, close to the borders of Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania. It is a rail terminus and highway junction. The name most probably derives from the Hungarian surname Muncas, from munkás, worker, though another theory points to a Proto-Slavic root meaning flour. Ukraine's parliament officially renamed the city from Mukacheve to Mukachevo in 2017, after it emerged that the former spelling, in use since 1947, had come about by a mistake.

Excavations have found a Celtic oppidum of the 3rd to 1st century BCE and an Iron Age Thracian fort in the area. Slavs settled it in the 6th century, and Hungarian tribes entered the Carpathian Basin in 895. In 1397 Sigismund, Holy Roman Emperor, granted the town to the exiled prince of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania Fyodor Koriatovych, who settled many Ruthenians there; other sources say he bought it in 1396. It became a Hungarian royal free city in 1445 and later part of the Principality of Transylvania. Imre Thököly's revolt against the Habsburgs started from Munkács in 1678, and Palanok Castle was important in Ferenc II Rákóczi's war of independence.

After 1711 the city came under Austrian control. In 1726 the Habsburgs gave the castle and town to the Schönborn family, who settled many Germans there. The castle served as a prison from 1796 to 1897 and held the Greek leader Alexander Ypsilanti from 1821 to 1823.

Mukachevo became part of Czechoslovakia on 4 June 1920, was re-annexed by Hungary in 1938 by the First Vienna Award, passed to the Soviet Ukraine in 1945 and is now in Ukraine. Jews made up about half the town's population before the Second World War, and it was known for its Hasidic community under Chief Rabbi Chaim Elazar Spira, who led it from 1913 until his death in 1937. The remaining Jews, nearly 15,000 in the spring of 1944, were deported to Auschwitz. A new synagogue was dedicated in 2006. Palanok Castle dates from the 14th century.
mukalla: Mukalla lies on the Gulf of Aden, on the shores of the Arabian Sea, about 480 kilometres east of Aden, and is the most important port of the Hadhramaut region. It is not far from Qana, the ancient principal Hadrami trading post between India and Africa, with incense-producing areas in its hinterland. The name comes from the Arabic verb kala, to preserve or nurture, reflecting its role as a sheltered harbour. Earlier names include Al-Kheesa, meaning bay or cove, Bandar Yaqoub, after the saint Yaqoub bin Yusuf, who settled there about the 12th century, and Bandar Al-Naqeeb, after Captain Salah bin Hamad Al-Kassadi of the dynasty that governed the town in the 18th century.

Mukalla was founded in 1035 as a fishing settlement. In the 19th and 20th centuries the Kathiri and Qu'aiti sultanates struggled for control of it, and it became the capital of the Qu'aiti State of Hadhramaut. The Qu'aiti Sultanate belonged to the Eastern Aden Protectorate, and a British Resident Advisor was stationed in the town. The sultanates' other major cities were Ash-Shihr and Shibam.

Captain Haines, a British officer who surveyed Yemen in the 1830s, described Mukalla as a town of 4,500 inhabitants with a significant trade in slaves. Theodore Bent and Mabel Bent used it several times in the 1890s to enter and leave the Wadi Hadhramaut, and Theodore Bent called it the only spot between Aden and Maskat with any claim to the name of port.

In 1967 Mukalla lost its status as capital of the Qu'aiti Sultanate when it became part of the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen. After Yemeni unification in 1990 it became part of the present state of Yemen.

Mukalla is the capital city district of Hadhramaut, Yemen's largest governorate. The port lies east of the town, with an oil pipeline for tankers and a cement factory of an Omani-Yemeni company, and the main market souq is a commercial hub. The old town has the sultan's royal palace and guard towers that once served as outposts, and the Hadhramaut Mountains, such as Husn Ghuraf, lie nearby. The College of Medicine of Hadhramout University is in the city, and Riyan International Airport serves it.
mukden-incident: Japan's economic and political interest in Manchuria had grown since the end of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905. The Treaty of Portsmouth gave Japan the lease of the South Manchuria Railway, and Japanese railway guards were stationed along it, though they often carried out manoeuvres outside the railway zone. Meanwhile the newly formed Chinese government sought to reassert its authority and challenged treaties with Japan. The Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin was assassinated by the Kwantung Army, and his son Zhang Xueliang joined the Nanjing government of Chiang Kai-shek. In 1929 the Soviet Red Army defeated Zhang Xueliang's forces in a conflict over the Chinese Eastern Railway, which revealed Chinese military weakness to Kwantung Army officers.

Colonel Seishirō Itagaki and Lieutenant Colonel Kanji Ishiwara planned to provoke an incident in order to prompt Japan to invade Manchuria. When the Minister of War sent Major General Yoshitsugu Tatekawa to curb the army's insubordination, they decided to stage the incident themselves. They chose a spot near Liutiao Lake, only eight hundred metres from the Chinese garrison at Beidaying. At about 10:20 p.m. on 18 September 1931, Lieutenant Suemori Kawamoto of the unit guarding the railway set off explosives beside the track. The blast damaged only a 1.5 metre section of one rail, and a train passed over it within minutes.

The army blamed Chinese dissidents and on 19 September opened fire on the Chinese garrison near Mukden. Five hundred Japanese troops attacked a garrison of around seven thousand, and by evening Mukden was occupied at the cost of five hundred Chinese lives and only two Japanese dead. General Shigeru Honjō, the commander of the Kwantung Army, at first objected that the plan had been carried out without his permission but then approved it. Zhang Xueliang had ordered his men not to resist. Within five months the Japanese army had overrun all the major towns of Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang.

China appealed to the League of Nations, which on 24 October demanded Japanese withdrawal, but Japan refused. In March 1932 Japan established the puppet state of Manchukuo, with Puyi as head of state. The Lytton Report of 2 October 1932 rejected the claim that the invasion was self-defence, but did not say that the Japanese had set off the explosion. The League refused to recognise Manchukuo, and Japan left it in March 1933.

Strong evidence points to young Kwantung Army officers having plotted the blast, with or without orders from Tokyo. Historians differ over whether the Tokyo leadership shared their aims, the historian James Crowley arguing that the officers and the civilian leaders held the same overall intentions.
mukhalingam: Mukhalingam, also called Srimukhalingam or Mukhalinga, is a village and gram panchayat in Jalumuru mandal of Srikakulam district, on the left bank of the Vamsadhara river, 48 kilometres from the town of Srikakulam. Before 1936 it belonged to the undivided Ganjam District, and it lies close to Paralakhemundi, the headquarters of Gajapati District in Odisha. The origin of its name is debated: it has been read as a corruption of Mohalingam, a Prakrit form; as a reference to the faceted linga of the Madhukeshwara shrine, mukha meaning face in Odia; or as Mudu-Kalingam, a Telugu rendering of the Sanskrit Tri-Kalinga.

The town was the main city of Kalinga, a region known in antiquity as Tri-Kalinga because it was divided into three parts, and it served as the capital of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. In 1122 King Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva conquered Utkala and moved his capital from Mukhalingam to Kataka, the modern Cuttack. The principal temple of Sri Mukhalingam had been built under the patronage of the Eastern Ganga king Kamarnava Deva II, Anantavarman Chodaganga's great-grandfather.

Mukhalingam keeps a group of three Śaiva temples, the Madhukeshwara, Someswara and Bhimeswara, whose dates historians have long contested. In the 17th century the Maharaja of the Paralakhemundi Estate renovated the temple. Every year pilgrims from Odisha and Andhra Pradesh come in great numbers for the Chakratirtha Snana, a holy bath, to seek the blessings of Shiva. The 2011 census counted 3,022 people in 837 households.
mukteshvara-temple-bhubaneswar: The temple is dated to 950–975 CE and is held to be the earliest work of the Somavamshi period. Most scholars place it after the Parashurameshvara Temple and before the Brahmeswara Temple of 1060 CE. Percy Brown dated its construction to 950 CE, while K. C. Panigrahi placed it in 966 CE and proposed that the Somavamshi king Yayati I built it, though no historical evidence confirms this. Its design gathers the earlier developments of Odishan temple building and opens a century of experiment seen in later temples of Bhubaneswar such as the Rajarani Temple and the Lingaraj temple.

The temple faces west and stands on a lower level among a group of temples, inside an octagonal compound wall with elaborate carvings. It has two main parts on a raised platform: the vimana over the sanctum, whose shikara rises 10.5 metres and bears four Natarajas and four kirtimukhas, and the jagamohana, the hall in front. The pyramidal roof of the jagamohana was the first of its kind, and the temple is the earliest of the pithadeula type. A new ornament, the bho, a richly carved chaitya window crowned by a demon mask and dwarf figures, may have been developed here and became common in later Odishan temples.

The arched torana before the jagamohana, unique in the region, shows the influence of Buddhist architecture; its thick pillars carry carved beads and reclining women, and its sculptures range from scrolls to monkeys and peacocks. The red sandstone walls show lean sadhus and jewelled women, Ganga and Yamuna, Gajalakshmi, Rahu and Ketu, and Lakulisa on the lintel.

The name Mukteshvara means Lord of Freedom, from the cycle of births and deaths, and the temple is dedicated to Shiva. Many carvings show skeletal ascetics teaching or meditating, and some scholars link the name to a role as a centre of Tantric initiation. Niches on the compound wall hold Saraswathi, Ganesha and Lakulisha, founder of the Pashupata sect. According to tradition, childless women who bathe in the Marichi Kunda tank on the night before the Ashokashtami car festival will bear sons. The state's Department of Tourism holds a yearly three-day festival of Odissi dance in the temple grounds.
mukunda-deva: Mukunda Deva, also called Mukunda Harichandana, traced his descent from the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, and the traditions of Odisha call him Telinga Mukundadeva. His Bhimeswara temple inscription names his father as Saravaraju and his grandfather as Singaraju. He took the throne at Kataka in 1559 after killing Raghuram Raya Chotaraya, the last ruler of the Bhoi dynasty, and is counted as the founder and only monarch of a Chalukya dynasty of Odisha.

As king he tried to revive the power of Odisha. He laid out two streets from the Lion's Gateway to the Gundicha Temple and made the road smooth by filling its pits and holes. On the outer side of the southern walls he raised a swing arch, the Dola Mandap, on which the deities are swung during the Dola festival in the last five days of the month of Falguna. He also built a chain of forts at Raibania, in the present Balasore district.

His foreign relations were shaped by two powers: the Sultan of Bengal, his enemy, and the Mughal emperor Akbar, his ally. In 1560 Sultan Ghiyasuddin Jalal Shah of Bengal invaded and marched as far as Jajpur, and Mukunda Deva defeated him and drove him out.

In 1567, while Akbar was occupied with the invasion of Chittorgarh, the Karrani sultan of Bengal invaded. Mukunda Deva was defeated and took shelter in the fort of Kotsima, and the Bengal army under the general Kalapahada made a devastating attack on the capital, Cuttack. In the king's absence Ramachandra Bhanja, a feudatory of Sarangagarh, declared himself king. Mukunda Deva hurried back and met him in battle at Gohiratikiri, near Jajpur, where Mukunda Deva was killed.

Ramachandra Bhanja was himself later executed by the sultan's forces. Afterwards Ramachandra Deva I of the Bhoi dynasty, son of Danai Vidyadhara, allied himself with Akbar to avoid an Afghan invasion and continued to rule as a subordinate king of Odisha.
mularaja: The Kumarapala-Bhupala-Charita of Jayasimha Suri gives Mularaja a mythical descent from Chulukya, a warrior said to have ruled at Madhupadma, and names his parents as Raji and Liladevi. The 14th-century chronicler Merutunga says he was named after the Mula nakshatra under which he was born, and that his mother, sister of the Chapotkata (Chavda) king Samanta-simha, died while pregnant, the child being cut from her womb. Merutunga also tells that the king, when drunk, would make his nephew king and depose him when sober, until Mularaja killed him.

Historians weigh these stories differently. Georg Bühler dismissed Merutunga's tale as chronologically impossible and saw Mularaja as an outsider who seized the kingdom; Asoke Majumdar held that he was the king's relative and won support by lowering taxes and sharing the Chapotkata wealth. His own inscription says he conquered the land watered by the Sarasvati by the strength of his arms.

His first kingdom was probably the Sarasvata-mandala, around present-day Mehsana, Radhanpur and Palanpur. Hemachandra describes a war against Graharipu, the Chudasama king of Saurashtra, whom Mularaja overcame on the Jambumali River, and the killing of his ally Laksha, possibly the Lakha Phulani whom the Jadeja princes of Kutch count among their ancestors. By the end of his reign the kingdom ran from Mount Abu to the Lata region.

Merutunga tells of simultaneous invasions by the Chahamana king Vigraharaja II from the north and the Lata Chalukya Barapa from the south, after 973. Mularaja killed Barapa, but historians such as Dasharatha Sharma think the struggle with Vigraharaja ended to the Chahamana's advantage.

A Shaivaite who is said to have been consecrated with a Vedic Vajapeya sacrifice, Mularaja also supported the Jains, building the Mulavasatika temple for the Digambaras and the Mulanatha-jinadeva temple for the Svetambaras. Tradition credits him with the first Rudra Mahalaya Temple at Siddhpur, which stood by 987, and he built temples at Anahilapataka (Patan) and Mandal. He settled Brahmins from northern India at Vadnagar, and he probably rebuilt the great temple at Somnath after his victory in Saurashtra.
mularaja-ii: Mularaja, known as Bala Mularaja, the Child Mularaja, succeeded his father Ajayapala on the Chaulukya throne at Anahilapataka (modern Patan) while still a young child. His mother Naikidevi was the daughter of a ruler named Paramardin, identified by one theory with the Goa Kadamba king Shivachitta Paramadideva and by another with the Chandela king Paramardi. The 14th-century chronicler Merutunga says that Naikidevi fought the Muslims at Gadararaghatta, which appears to be the Kasahrada where the Chaulukya army defeated the Ghurids in 1178, when the king was thirteen.

The Paramara kingdom of Malwa had come under Chaulukya control under Mularaja's predecessors. During his reign a severe famine struck Gujarat, and the Paramara king Vindhyavarman took the chance to try to win Malwa back. According to the Surathotsava, written by the poet Someshvara, his father Kumara, the royal priest, persuaded the king to give his subjects a tax break during the famine and also commanded the army against Vindhyavarman.

Someshvara says Kumara defeated the Paramara king, destroyed his town of Gogasthana, sank a well where the Paramara palace had stood and plundered Malwa, giving the wealth at Gaya during a shraddha ceremony; he also defeated a mlechchha army near Rajnisara. Vindhyavarman nonetheless regained Malwa in the end. R. C. Majumdar held that this happened during Mularaja's reign, while A. K. Majumdar believed Malwa stayed under Chaulukya control until after it.

Mularaja died at a very young age in 1178, the year of the victory over the Ghurids, and was succeeded by his brother Bhima II. The regency of his mother Naikidevi, the famine, the tax relief and the campaigns in Malwa are known mainly from Merutunga and from the Surathotsava Mahakavya of Someshvara, the son of Kumara.
mull-of-kintyre: The Mull of Kintyre is the south-westernmost tip of the Kintyre peninsula, formerly spelled Cantyre, in south-west Scotland. It lies about 16 kilometres from Campbeltown in Argyll and Bute and about 13 kilometres beyond Southend, the southernmost village of the peninsula, and is reached by a single-track road. The name is an anglicisation of the Gaelic Maol Chinn Tìre, meaning Rounded or Bare Headland, from maol, bald or bare, and the headland of the land. Mull is a term found chiefly in south-west Scotland for a headland or its tip, a landform bare of trees.

From the Mull the County Antrim coast of Northern Ireland, Rathlin Island and Ailsa Craig are clearly visible, and on clearer days Malin Head in County Donegal and the Ayrshire coast can be seen. At its closest point mainland Ulster is 19 kilometres away. The Straits of Moyle, part of the North Channel, give sea passage from the Irish Sea to the Atlantic, and strong currents around the tip are a hazard to unmotorised craft.

The Mull has been an important land bridge throughout history. It is thought that early humans used it on their way from continental Europe to Ireland through Scotland. In more recent times the Scotti crossed from Ireland to establish the kingdom of Dál Riata in what is now Argyll.

A historic lighthouse, the second commissioned in Scotland, guides shipping in the North Channel. The steep cliffs and hills that rise from the sea on all sides, together with frequent sea mists, have made the area a hazard to flight, and it has been the site of numerous air crashes, the remains of some of which still lie there. The best known was the crash of an RAF Chinook helicopter on 2 June 1994. On 13 June 1858 the SS New York, a steamship converted to sail, was wrecked at the south end of the Mull.

The area was made well known by the 1977 song Mull of Kintyre by Wings, the band of Paul McCartney, who lived on the peninsula. A persistent urban legend, which the British Board of Film Classification has denied, holds that an unofficial rule of the Board once measured what could be shown in film against the angle of the Kintyre peninsula on maps of Scotland.
mullah-mohammad-omar: Mohammad Omar was born into a poor Pashtun farming family in Kandahar Province, in a year that is uncertain: sources give a date between 1950 and 1962. He came from a line of Islamic scholars; his father, a poor, landless itinerant teacher of the Quran, died when Omar was a small child, and his uncles raised him. After the Soviet invasion of 1979 he joined the mujahideen and fought in the districts of Maiwand, Zhari, Panjwai and Dand, and was wounded four times. He lost his right eye to shrapnel.

With the country in chaos as factions fought for control, Omar began a movement in 1994 with fewer than 50 armed madrasa students, who were known simply as the Taliban, Pashto for students. They fought warlord rule and corruption and were at first welcomed by Afghans weary of it. On 4 April 1996 his supporters gave him the title Amir al-Mu'minin, Commander of the Faithful. The Taliban formed a Sunni Islamic theocracy, the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, which strictly enforced Sharia. It was widely condemned for massacres of civilians, discrimination against minorities, and banning women from school and most employment.

In July 1999 Omar issued a decree in favour of preserving the Buddhas of Bamiyan, but in March 2001 an edict from him ordered that all the statues in Afghanistan be destroyed, and they were. In July 2000 he declared the growing of poppies un-Islamic, and opium cultivation in Taliban areas fell by 99 per cent. After the September 11 attacks of 2001, he refused to hand over Osama bin Laden. The American-led invasion began in October 2001, and on 5 December 2001 he handed the leadership to Mullah Obaidullah and two days later left Kandahar for Zabul Province.

Omar was the subject of an international manhunt, and the United States offered a reward of US$10 million. Research published in 2019 by the journalist Bette Dam indicates that he spent the rest of his life in Zabul Province. He died of tuberculosis on 23 April 2013, a fact first announced officially in July 2015 by Afghanistan's National Directorate of Security and confirmed by the Taliban the next day.

Little was publicly known of him; he made only one public speech and refused to meet foreigners, and only one confirmed photograph existed before his death. Taliban members regard him as a freedom fighter who defended Afghanistan's Islamic principles, while others criticise his method of governing and his religious dogmatism.
multan: Multan lies on the eastern bank of the Chenab River in the Punjab province of Pakistan and is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Asia. The region holds archaeological sites of the early Harappan period of the Indus Valley Civilisation, dated between 3000 and 2800 BCE. Hindu texts say the sage Kashyapa founded it and that it was the capital of the Trigarta Kingdom during the Kurukshetra War of the Mahabharata. In the time of Alexander the Great the city stood on an island in the Ravi River, which has since shifted course many times. The origin of its name is unclear; an ancient name was Malli-istan, after the Malli tribe.

Multan is believed to have been the Malli capital that Alexander besieged in 326 BCE. During the siege of the citadel Alexander was wounded by an arrow that penetrated his lung. A Muslim army first invaded after the reign of the caliph Ali, in 664, but the expedition seems to have been one of exploration. Muhammad ibn Qasim took the city in 712 after a two-month siege, and its subjects remained mostly non-Muslim for some decades under the Umayyad Caliphate.

The Banu Munabbih came to rule Multan by the mid-800s, and in 855 it became capital of the Emirate of Multan. Multan attracted many Sufi mystics in the 11th and 12th centuries and is called the City of Saints. In 1445 it became capital of the Langah Sultanate. Akbar made it the headquarters of the Multan Subah, one of the Mughal Empire's largest provinces, and Mughal rule was re-established there in 1557.

Ahmad Shah Durrani captured Multan in 1752, and after repeated invasions following the collapse of the Mughal Empire the city declined from an important early-modern commercial centre to a regional trading town. The Sikh Empire ruled it from 1818 to 1849. By December 1848 the British had taken parts of the outskirts and destroyed the Multan Fort in bombardment; on 22 January 1849 they breached its walls and Diwan Mulraj surrendered. Between the 1890s and 1920s the British laid a vast network of canals across the region.

Multan is the administrative headquarters of its division and district, and a major cultural, religious and economic centre of the Punjab. With nearby Uch it is known for its large number of Sufi shrines, many dating from the medieval period. The old city, like other ancient cities in South Asia, had a walled town and a royal citadel, but Multan lost its citadel, largely destroyed by the British in 1848.
multatuli: Eduard Douwes Dekker was born in Amsterdam on 2 March 1820, the fourth of five children of a Mennonite family. His father, Engel Douwes Dekker, was a sea captain from the Zaan district, and his mother, Sietske Eeltjes Klein, was born on Ameland. He attended the Latin school on the Singel, and his father at first intended him to become a minister. He worked for a time as a clerk at a textile firm, and in 1838 sailed on one of his father's ships to Batavia, where he held colonial posts over the next two decades, starting in the accounting department, work he disliked.

In 1842 he became comptroller of the troubled district of Natal on Sumatra. A deficit in the funds, partly older than his time in office, brought a serious reprimand from General Andreas Victor Michiels and a temporary suspension. He refunded the deficit himself and was transferred, acknowledging that he was not well suited to administration. He married Everdine Hubertina van Wijnbergen on 10 April 1846.

In 1848 he became secretary to the Resident of Menado, Reinier Scherius, who shared his sense of fair play towards the indigenous population. He was promoted to Assistant Resident of Ambon at the end of 1851 but soon went on health leave to the Netherlands, where he stayed from 1852 to May 1855, gambling and running up debts. As Assistant Resident of Lebak on Java he protested openly against colonial abuses and was threatened with dismissal; he resigned and returned to the Netherlands.

Max Havelaar appeared in 1860 under the pen name Multatuli, Latin for "I have suffered much". His friend Jacob van Lennep had identifiable place names changed, yet the book caused great controversy. Defenders of colonialism accused him of exaggeration, and he was unsuccessfully pressed to withdraw it. It was read across Europe.

He followed it with Minnebrieven (1861), a satire in the form of a fictitious correspondence, and seven volumes of Ideën between 1862 and 1877, which first printed his novel Woutertje Pieterse. His play Vorstenschool was staged three years after publication, for fear of offending the king. He stopped writing in 1877, having settled about ten years earlier at Ingelheim am Rhein. In 2002 the Society of Dutch Literature named him the most important Dutch writer of all time.
mumadona-dias: Mumadona, also written Muniadomna Díaz, was one of the three daughters of Count Diogo Fernandes and Countess Onega, who had been tutors of the future King Ramiro II of León. She married Count Hermenegildo González, probably between 915 and 920 and certainly by 926, when the couple first appear together, receiving the villa of Creximir near Guimarães from King Ramiro II. She ruled the County of Portugal jointly with her husband before governing it alone after his death, which came between 943 and 950.

Her many estates covered an area that roughly matched the later counties of Portugal and Coimbra. In July 950 they were divided among her six children, and Gonzalo Menéndez received the County of Portugal. In 950 or 951 she founded a monastery dedicated to São Mamede on her property at Vimaranes, the Monastery of Guimarães, where she later took her vows herself.

Her will, dated 26 January 959, gave her domains, cattle, incomes, religious objects and books to the monastery, and it is an important record of the castles and villages of the region. The castle she began, around which the burgh of Guimarães grew, was handed to the monastery for its protection in 968, the year of her death, and later became the seat of the court of the counts of Portugal. Several Portuguese cities commemorate her.
mumbai: Mumbai lies on the Konkan coast of western India, on a narrow peninsula of Salsette Island bounded by the Arabian Sea, Thane Creek and Vasai Creek, at the mouth of the Ulhas River. It has a deep natural harbour. The city grew from an archipelago of seven islands: the Isle of Bombay, Parel, Mazagaon, Mahim, Colaba, Worli and Old Woman's Island, also called Little Colaba. Greater Mumbai covers 603 square kilometres in two districts, Mumbai City, the southern Island City, and Mumbai Suburban.

The islands were inhabited since the South Asian Stone Age. They became part of the Maurya Empire under Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE, followed by the Satavahana dynasty in the 2nd century BCE, and Ptolemy mentioned them in 150 CE. The Koli fishing community, whose goddess Mumbadevi is believed to have given the city its name, settled the region around the beginning of the Common Era. The Delhi Sultanate and then the Gujarat Sultanate ruled them in the Middle Ages. The islands were ceded to the Portuguese in 1535 and in 1661 passed to the British Crown, which leased them to the East India Company in 1668.

Under British rule Bombay became the capital of the Bombay Presidency and a major trading and administrative centre. The Hornby Vellard project, begun in 1782 and completed in 1845, reclaimed land between the seven islands from the Arabian Sea and unified them. With new roads and railways and the cotton boom of the 19th century, it made the city a major seaport. The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation was established in 1888. The city played a major part in the Indian independence movement. After 1947 it became the capital of Bombay State, and after the Samyukta Maharashtra movement the capital of Maharashtra in 1960.

Mumbai is the capital of Maharashtra and the financial and commercial capital of India. Its population was 12,442,373 at the 2011 census, with more than 18 million in the metropolitan region. Its buildings from the British period, such as Victoria Terminus, are largely in the Gothic Revival style, while the Gateway of India is Indo-Saracenic and Marine Drive has many Art Deco buildings. The city is also the centre of Bollywood, the Hindi film industry, whose name blends Bombay and Hollywood.
mumuye: The Mumuye speak the Mumuye language and are the predominant people of the Zing, Yorro, Jalingo, Ardo-Kola, Lau, Gassol, Bali and Gashaka local government areas of Taraba State; many also live in neighbouring Adamawa State. They had no central government in the past. Today they live in small villages of extended families called dola, each governed by a council of elders and an elected leader, and because these groups are isolated from one another their customs vary, though they share one language in its variations and a common culture.

Masquerades strengthen ties within the community, among them the Vabon funeral masquerade, and the Ushavuko ceremony is held twice a year. Scarification marks initiation, and women are scarified before marriage; one pattern of three horizontal rows of cuts divides the face into thirds. A secret society, the Vabong, with seven levels, governs spiritual life, and its initiation, often harsh, includes the explanation of the masks and divination objects. Rainmakers are held to be the most powerful protectors of the community, and zigzag rainmaking rods, shaped like lightning or a snake, stand for the fertility of the land and the people.

The Mumuye are known above all for their figure sculpture, the iagalagana. Carved by blacksmiths or weavers, crafts of high standing, the figures serve for divination, healing, rainmaking and warding off evil, and are kept in a separate hut by someone thought to have magical powers; they are also said to greet visitors to the rainmaker's hut, guard homes and act as judges in trials. They vary from short and squat to elongated, but share a style: large earlobes from the custom of inserting discs into the ears, which the Mumuye read as female, an exaggerated navel and understated genitalia.

Two kinds of mask are made: the Sukwava, with a long neck and large ears, once worn before war and now for healing and rainmaking, and an initiation face mask with hollowed eyes and animal features. The Sukuru mask of an old woman with pierced ears is sometimes worn in rainmaking rites. Some Mumuye figures were long attributed to the neighbouring Chamba. A great number of sculptures left the country at the height of the Biafran war, when border controls were at their weakest.
mun-of-balhae: Mun was born in 715, the son of King Mu and the grandson of Tae Choyŏng, the founder of Balhae. He came to the throne on his father's death in 737 and became the longest-reigning ruler of the kingdom. His wife is remembered as Empress Hyoŭi, and his younger brother was Tae Wŏnŭi. His first son, Tae Koengnim, who died in 780, was the father of the later King Sŏng, and his fourth son became King Kang.

The tomb of his fourth daughter, Princess Chŏnghyo, who lived from 757 to 792, was discovered in 1980, and the tombstone of his second daughter, Princess Chŏnghye, who lived from 737 to 777, has also been found. A first daughter, born in 732, died young.

Under Mun diplomatic ties with the Tang dynasty were established, and many Balhae scholars went to study under the Tang, spreading the influence of Buddhism and Confucianism in the kingdom's government. He founded the Chujagam, a national academy modelled on that of the Tang. He also strengthened relations with Silla, which had unified the Korean Peninsula to the south, and oversaw the development of the trade route known as the Silla-road, while Balhae's diplomacy and trade with Japan grew.

He moved the capital several times, to Sanggyeong and to Donggyeong, and strengthened central rule over the various tribal peoples of a realm that for a time grew larger. Although the Tang recognised him only as a king, at home he bore titles such as Taehŭng poryŏk hyogam kŭmnyun sŏngbŏp taewang, Kadokpu, Seongwang and Kiha, and Balhae spoke of him as the posterity of heaven and as an emperor. His reign used the era names Taehŭng, Great Happiness, and Poryŏk.
munda-people: The Munda are an Austroasiatic-speaking people of the Indian subcontinent whose native language is Mundari. They live mainly on the Chotanagpur Plateau in Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal, with others in Madhya Pradesh, Bangladesh, Nepal and Tripura, and in the tea valleys of Assam, where they migrated to work on plantations in colonial times. Munda means headman of a village; they call themselves horoko or ho ko, meaning men. According to the linguist Paul Sidwell, Munda languages reached the coast of Odisha from Southeast Asia about 4,000 to 3,500 years ago. The Munda claim an origin in Uttar Pradesh, but a Munda presence in the upper Gangetic plain has no linguistic or genetic basis.

In the late 1800s, under British rule, the Munda were forced to pay rents and work as bonded labourers for the zamindars. During the Kol uprising of 1823 to 1833 some Manki Munda revolted, and the rising was suppressed by Thomas Wilkinson. Birsa Munda later led protest marches calling for the non-payment of rents and the remission of forest dues, and waged guerrilla warfare to overthrow British rule and establish a Munda Raj. He was caught with his supporters and died in jail, and he is still revered in Jharkhand.

The Munda are patrilineal and divided into exogamous clans called killi, each of totemic origin. In the Kolhan region villages were governed by the Munda-Manki system: the Munda is the village head, the Pahaan the village priest and the Manki the head of fifteen to twenty villages. Farming people, they celebrate the seasonal festivals of Mage Parab, Phagu, Karam, Baha parab, Sarhul and Sohrai, and their deity is Singbonga. Many practise patthalgari, the erecting of a large stone at a grave or at the entrance to a village, inscribed with the family tree of the dead. The Jesuit John-Baptist Hoffmann published the first Mundari grammar in 1903.
munger: Munger lies on the south bank of the Ganges in Bihar, about 180 km east of Patna and 480 km west of Kolkata. It forms a twin city with Jamalpur and is the headquarters of Munger district and division. Historically it sat at a strategic bottleneck on the main route into Bengal from the west: steep hills blocked travel to the south, and the many tributaries of the Ganges were the obstacle to the north.

The town is said to have been founded by the Guptas in the fourth century CE. In the classical period it was called Guptagadh or Guptagarh, and an inscription on a rock at the kasta-harani ghat, near the north-western side of the present fort, names it as founded by Chandragupta Vikramaditya. In early medieval times it was Mudgagiri, from the Sanskrit mudga, the mung bean, and giri, hill. It was a royal residence of the Pala Empire, and a significant battle between the Palas and the Pratiharas was fought there as part of a Pratihara invasion of Bengal.
