It was later mentioned as the residence of the Pala ruler Ramapala. In the twelfth century it seems to have been under Sena rule, and in April 1146 the Gahadavala ruler Govindachandra advanced as far as Mudgagiri and bathed in the Ganges, probably on an unsuccessful expedition to Bengal.

At the end of the twelfth century Bakhtiyar Khalji conquered Munger and Patna. The region was a province of Bengal until 1330, when Muhammad Tughlaq annexed it, and from 1397 it belonged to the Jaunpur Sultanate until Sikander Lodi overran Bihar before 1499. In 1521 Nusrat Shah annexed a few of its forts, and it later fell to Sher Shah Suri. From 1545 the Karrani dynasty held it until Akbar's invasion of Bengal.

In 1763 the Nawab of Bengal Mir Qasim made Munger his capital and built an arsenal and several palaces. The British, who took Bihar in the 1760s, made it a municipality in 1864 and set up the railway workshops at Jamalpur in 1862.

The fort covers about 222 acres and holds the tomb of the Muslim saint Shah Mushk Nafā, who died in 1497. Munger is also known for the Bihar School of Yoga, founded in 1964, and for the Sitacharan temple on a boulder in the Ganges, a centre of the Chhath festival.
muniadona-of-castile: Muniadona was the eldest child of Count Sancho García of Castile and his wife Urraca, who was probably a member of the Banu Gómez family. She was also called Mayor or Munia. She married King Sancho Garcés III of Pamplona before 27 June 1011, when both appear confirming privileges of the Monastery of San Millán, and she was queen of Pamplona from 1011 until 1035.

Her marriage gave her husband claims through her dynastic rights. In 1017 William Isarn, Count of Ribagorza, was assassinated. His county had been partitioned with his cousin Mayor García, and she and her husband Raymond III of Pallars Jussà claimed all of it. Sancho Garcés III contested this, asserting the rights of Muniadona, who as eldest daughter of Mayor García's brother could claim to be heiress of her grandmother Ava de Ribagorza. His troops invaded in 1017 and took William's half.

In 1025 Mayor García, repudiated by her husband, transferred most of the rest to Sancho, and Raymond kept only the Noguera Ribagorçana basin. Muniadona may have taken the name Mayor in recognition of this. Her rights were invoked again in 1028, when the Vela family assassinated Count García Sánchez of Castile at León. Because she was his eldest sister, Sancho III took control of Castile, and their son Ferdinand Sánchez was named count in 1029. Her children were García Sánchez III, king of Pamplona from 1035 to 1054; Ferdinand Sánchez, king of León; Gonzalo Sánchez, king of Sobrarbe and Ribagorza; and Jimena Sánchez, queen of León through her marriage to Bermudo III.

Muniadona outlived her husband, who died in 1035, and most of her children. As a widow she founded the monastery of San Martín de Tours de Frómista, where she asked to be buried in her testament of 13 June 1066, and she probably died soon afterwards. The will freed the Saracens who had converted to Christianity and were dependent on her, gave the monastery estates in Bobadilla and Agero and a share of the tithes of Frómista and Población de Campos, and divided her sheep, cows and horses among the churches of Santa María, San Juan Bautista and San Martín.
munich: Munich lies on the elevated plains of Upper Bavaria, in the Northern Alpine Foreland, about 50 kilometres north of the Alps and about 520 metres above sea level. The rivers Isar and Würm flow through the city. The northern part of the plateau is a fertile flint area, the southern part is covered with morainic hills, and between them lie outwash plains where groundwater rising through the gravel has formed marshes in the north.
The name goes back to a tiny monastic settlement of the 10th century called zu den Munchen, 'to the monks'; the Old High German Munche is the base of the modern München.

The Isar was a prehistoric trade route, and in the Bronze Age Munich was among the largest raft ports in Europe; settlements up to four thousand years old have been found, along with Celtic settlements of the Iron Age. The Roman road Via Julia, linking Augsburg and Salzburg, crossed the Isar south of the city. From the 6th century the Baiuvarii settled the area, and the first known Christian church was built in Fröttmanning around 815. Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, founded the town to control the salt trade after burning down Föhring and its bridges over the Isar; historians date this to about 1158.

Munich remained Catholic during the Reformation and became the capital of the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806. Its population, only 24,000 in 1700, doubled about every 30 years: 100,000 in 1852, 250,000 in 1883 and 500,000 in 1901. The House of Wittelsbach ruled until 1918, when the German revolution of 1918–1919 ended its reign and brought the short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic. In the 1920s the city became a centre of political movements, including the rise of the Nazi Party, and it was known as the Capital of the Movement. Munich was heavily bombed in the Second World War, though much of its historic architecture has since been restored. It passed one million inhabitants in 1957 and hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics.

Munich is the capital of Bavaria and the third-largest city in Germany, with about 1.5 million inhabitants. It is the seat of the Bavarian Landtag and of institutions such as the Federal Finance Court and the European Patent Office. The old town centres on the Marienplatz, with the Old Town Hall and the New Town Hall, and includes the Frauenkirche, the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising, and the Michaelskirche. Nymphenburg Palace was begun in 1664, the Englischer Garten was laid out between 1789 and 1807, and the city is known for the annual Oktoberfest.
munich-agreement: Czechoslovakia was created in 1918 after the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Its population included more than three million Germans, 22.95 percent of the total, who lived mostly in the border regions that came to be called the Sudetenland. They had not been consulted on becoming citizens, and although the constitution promised equality they remained underrepresented in the government and the army. By 1936 60 percent of the unemployed in Czechoslovakia were Germans.

Britain and France wished to avoid war. The French government followed the British government of Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, who considered the Sudeten German grievances justified. Both advised Czechoslovakia to give way to German demands. President Beneš resisted and ordered a partial mobilisation on 19 May 1938. Hitler later signed a secret directive for war against Czechoslovakia to begin no later than 1 October.

Chamberlain asked Hitler for a personal meeting and flew to Germany on 15 September. At Berchtesgaden Hitler insisted that the Sudeten Germans be allowed national self-determination and union with Germany. On 17 September Germany began a low-intensity undeclared war on Czechoslovakia, and on 20 September Britain and France formally asked Czechoslovakia to cede the Sudetenland. Poland and Hungary made territorial demands on 21 and 22 September.

The emergency meeting of the main European powers took place in Munich on 29 and 30 September. Czechoslovak representatives were in the town but were not admitted. A deal was reached on 29 September, and at about 1:30 a.m. on 30 September 1938 Hitler, Chamberlain, Benito Mussolini and Édouard Daladier signed the agreement. The German army was to complete the occupation of the Sudetenland by 10 October, and an international commission would decide the future of other disputed areas. Britain and France told Czechoslovakia it could resist Germany alone or submit, and on 30 September its government reluctantly capitulated.

Many Czechs and Slovaks call the agreement the Munich Diktat or the Munich Betrayal. Czechoslovakia lost its defensible border and fortifications, 70 percent of its iron and steel industry and 3.5 million citizens. On 2 November the First Vienna Award gave southern Slovakia and southern Subcarpathian Rus' to Hungary, and on 30 November Poland received small areas in Spiš and Orava. In March 1939 the First Slovak Republic declared independence as a German puppet state, and Hitler broke his promise to respect the country's integrity by occupying the rest and creating the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia.

Much of Europe welcomed the agreement as a way of preventing a major war. Later it came to be regarded as a failed act of appeasement. Chamberlain was attacked as one of the Men of Munich in the 1940 book Guilty Men,.
munich-secession: By the end of the 19th century more artists lived in Munich than in Vienna and Berlin together, but its art world was dominated by the conservative Munich Artists' Association and its allies in government, whose outlook was set out by the so-called Prince of Painters, Franz von Lenbach. In 1891 Prince-Regent Luitpold of Bavaria founded an art foundation devoted to traditional history painting in the service of the state and opposed to impressionism, symbolism and other new trends. The complete financial failure of the association's exhibition of 1888 at the Glaspalast had already led to a bitter dispute that drew in the Ministry of State for Science and Art.

On 4 April 1892 ninety-six artists who had resigned from the official association founded the Association of Visual Artists of Munich, with Bruno Piglhein as president and Paul Hoecker as secretary; within months the name Munich Secession took over. Its first backers were the journalist Georg Hirth, who coined the word secession for the spirit of the new art movements, the socialist editor Georg von Vollmar and the liberal Hans Veit zu Toerring-Jettenbach. The founders called for artists' freedom to present their work directly to the public and acted as a cooperative to secure commissions and their livelihood.

After a first exhibition at Berlin's National Exhibition Building early in 1893, the group opened its own building on land given by Franz von Brandl at the corner of Prinzregentenstraße and Pilotystraße. Its debut there on 16 July 1893 showed 876 works by 297 artists. In 1897 it received the exhibition building on the Königsplatz. Dissatisfied members left to form Phalanx in 1901, and another split in 1913 produced the New Munich Secession. After the National Socialist party brought the arts under their control from 1933, the Secession was dissolved in 1938 as part of the so-called cultural cleansing.

Painters such as Lovis Corinth, Lesser Ury and Gabriel von Max exhibited with the Secession and counted themselves part of it without being founding members. After the Second World War new groups founded in 1946 led to the Federal Association of Visual Artists. The Secession marked its centenary in 1992, and in March of the following year a society of friends and sponsors was created to keep its gallery and exhibitions going.
munis-al-muzaffar: According to the fourteenth-century historian al-Dhahabi, Mu'nis was 90 years old when he died. He was called al-Khadim to tell him apart from his contemporary, the treasurer Mu'nis al-Fahl. Though a harem eunuch, he first appears as a ghulam of the future caliph al-Mu'tadid during the suppression of the Zanj Rebellion in 880/1, and by 900 he was chief of police of the field army, deputy to the commander-in-chief Badr al-Mu'tadidi. His banishment in 901 was probably tied to the struggle between Badr and the vizier al-Qasim ibn Ubayd Allah, and possibly to harem intrigues in favour of al-Muqtadir.

After he defended the Hasani Palace against the coup of December 908, which aimed to put Abdallah ibn al-Mu'tazz on the throne, al-Muqtadir's mother Shaghab gave him command of the caliphal guard, the Hujariyya. The vizier Ibn al-Furat, hostile to his rise, kept him on the frontiers. He raided Byzantine Asia Minor from Malatya in 909, recovered Fars from the Saffarids and supervised prisoner exchanges with the Byzantines. His victory in Egypt in 915 earned him the title al-Muzaffar, the Victorious. In 918 he was defeated before Ardabil by the Sajid Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, but beat him there the next year and took him captive to Baghdad.

He was a staunch rival of Ibn al-Furat and ally of Ali ibn Isa al-Jarrah. During Ibn al-Furat's third vizierate in 923-924 he was sent into quasi-exile at Raqqa, but a military coup brought him back and the vizier and his son were executed. Mu'nis now had a decisive voice in naming viziers, and his rift with al-Muqtadir widened until the caliph plotted to kill him in 927. That year the Byzantines surprised his army near Samosata and killed 400 men.

In 928, after his favourite Ali ibn Isa was dismissed, Mu'nis deposed al-Muqtadir and set up al-Qahir, but reversed this within days. In 933 al-Qahir lured him and his main lieutenants to the palace and had them executed. Michael Bonner wrote that he "kept the remnants of the army together and saved the caliphate on several occasions", and Harold Bowen judged his influence on the whole good but too weak to halt the decline. His seizure of power and the killing of a caliph, the first since the Anarchy at Samarra, set a precedent: military strongmen later contended for the title amir al-umara until the Buyids took Baghdad in 946.
munjamyeong-of-goguryeo: Munjamyeong was the 21st monarch of Goguryeo, the northernmost of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His father, Gochudaega Joda, had been named Crown Prince by Taewang Jangsu but died before he could take the throne, so the succession passed to the grandson. In 427 Goguryeo had moved its capital from the area of modern Ji'an on the upper Yalu River to Pyongyang, amid rising rivalry with the allied kingdoms of Silla and Baekje.

Munja kept up Jangsu's long-distance diplomacy and cultivated close ties with the Chinese dynasties of Northern Wei, Southern Qi and Liang; the Book of Qi records a title granted to the king of Goguryeo. His friendship with Northern Wei helped him hold the Liaodong peninsula. According to the 12th-century history Samguk sagi, the remnants of Buyeo submitted to Goguryeo in 494 after being defeated by the Mohe people, completing the conquest of the Buyeo lands begun under Gwanggaeto.

Baekje and Silla drew closer against him. Under King Muryeong, Baekje attacked Goguryeo's northern frontier, in 505 with more than 3,000 soldiers, and a counterattack by Munjamyeong in 506 achieved nothing because of severe famine. Munja also furthered Buddhism, which had entered Goguryeo under Sosurim. Nine monks are said to have been sent to Northern Wei to study Buddhist books, and in 498, his seventh year, he built the temple of Geumgangsa.

Munjamyeong died in 519 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Anjang of Goguryeo. Two other sons are recorded, Prince Heungan, who died in 531, and Prince Boyeon, who died in 545. He is counted among the rulers of Goguryeo at its height, the age that began with Gwanggaeto the Great.
munmu-of-silla: Munmu was born as Kim Pŏmmin and took the name Munmu when he succeeded his father, King Muyeol. His mother, Munmyeong, was the younger sister of the general Kim Yu-sin. Under his father he held the office of pajinchan, which apparently was responsible for maritime affairs, and he played a key part in developing the kingdom's diplomatic links with Tang China. He is usually considered the first ruler of the Unified Silla period.

Munmu took the throne in the midst of a long conflict with Baekje and Goguryeo, soon after General Kyebaek and the Baekje army had been defeated at Sabi by Kim Yu-sin in 660. Silla was heavily aided by the Tang in these struggles. The first years of the reign went on trying to defeat Goguryeo, after an abortive attempt in 661. In 667 he ordered a further attack, which led to the fall of Goguryeo in 668.

After Goguryeo fell, Tang created the Protectorate General to Pacify the East and tried to place the whole peninsula, Silla included, under its rule. Munmu allied with Goguryeo resistance leaders such as Geom Mojam and Anseung and attacked the Tang forces in the former Baekje lands. By 674 Silla and its former ally were in constant battle. Emperor Gaozong, in anger, declared Munmu's brother Kim In-mun to be king, but Munmu apologised formally and offered tribute, and Gaozong recalled Kim In-mun. In 675 Silla defeated Tang forces led by Li Jinxing, who had arrived with Mohe troops, at the Maeso fortress. Gaozong then ordered all Tang forces to leave the peninsula and moved the Protectorate General to Liaodong.

Munmu ruled the unified kingdom for twenty years and fell ill in 681. On his deathbed he left a will and passed the crown to his son, Prince Sinmun, asking that his body be cremated and the ashes scattered in the sea where the whales live, so that he might become a dragon and thwart foreign invasion. Sinmun built the Gomun Temple in his honour, a waterway for the sea dragon to pass between sea and land, and a pavilion overlooking the islet of Daewangam, where later kings could pay their respects.

Many modern Korean scholars, particularly in North Korea, doubt that Silla was the first state to unify the Korean people, since it did not conquer parts of Goguryeo and Balhae in the northeast; some regard Goryeo as the first. Silla's victory over Tang is generally regarded as a critical turning point in Korean history.
munuza: Munuza appears in conflicting chronicles of the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula, and is believed to have been a companion of the Berber leader Tariq ibn Ziyad. One account makes him governor of Gijón, or possibly León, after Musa ibn Nusayr raided north-western Iberia, including Asturias but not Cantabria, in the first decade of the Umayyad conquest of Hispania. He was subject to the wali of Al-Andalus, Anbasa ibn Suhaym Al-Kalbi.

Late Asturian chronicles tell that he fell in love with Ormesinda, sister of Pelayo of Asturias, and with Kazim seized and married her; the chronicle of Alfonso III speaks of a compulsory marriage whose failure drove Pelayo to rebel. The background can only be guessed at. Pelayo may have hoped to win a favoured place among the local nobles by marrying his sister to the new power in the region, or the match may have served as a counterweight to Peter of Cantabria and a sign of nominal submission.

After a Muslim garrison was lost on a punitive expedition, Munuza may have held the whole Asturian coast while keeping court in the western districts nearer to Galicia. Defeated in his attempt to secure León, he may have fled from Gijón, and Christian chronicles report that he was killed with all his soldiers at Trubia or La Felguera.

He may be the same man as Uthman ibn Naissa, a Berber commander whom other contemporary chronicles call Munuza and who led Umayyad operations in Cerdanya, in the eastern Pyrenees, a decade later. As deputy governor of Catalunya he made peace in 730 with Odo the Great, Duke of Aquitaine, and married his daughter Lampegia. He then rebelled against the governor-general of al-Andalus, killed Nambaudus, bishop of Urgell, and was defeated and executed by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi. Whether the two were one man is uncertain.
muqaddimah: Ibn Khaldun wrote the first version of the Muqaddimah in Qalʿat ibn Salama, where he secluded himself for almost four years after withdrawing from political life. It was the first of three parts of a project on which he worked for almost thirty years, the Kitab al-ʿIbar, or Book of Lessons, a universal history that fills seventeen volumes of 500 pages each in its modern edition. A draft of the Muqaddimah was completed in 1377. Manuscripts copied in his lifetime survive, some with his own marginal notes, and already in his lifetime it came to be regarded as a work in its own right.

Ibn Khaldun begins with a criticism of the errors his fellow historians regularly commit. He lists seven, among them partisanship towards a creed or opinion, over-confidence in sources, failure to place an event in its context, the wish to flatter the powerful, and, most important, ignorance of the laws governing the transformation of human society. Against this seventh point he sets out his theory of society.

Its best known concept is ʿasabiyyah, group feeling or social cohesion. As it declines, a more compelling ʿasabiyyah may take its place, so that civilisations rise and fall. Ruling houses tend to emerge on the peripheries of great empires and use the unity found there to bring about a change of leadership. Once settled at the centre, the rulers grow lax and concerned with their lifestyles, and a new dynasty emerges at the periphery to begin the cycle again. His framework contrasts nomadic life with sedentary life. The book also discusses economics, political theory, theology, law, and alchemy, which he refutes on social, scientific, philosophical and religious grounds.

The Muqaddimah is held to be a foundational work for historiography, cultural history and the philosophy of history. Ibn Khaldun criticised idle superstition and uncritical acceptance of historical data, and called his approach a new science. He treated the past as strange and in need of interpretation, and he questioned the sizes of armies in earlier accounts by considering military logistics, including those given by the historian al-Masudi.

Some modern thinkers view it as the first work to deal with sociology, demography and cultural history. Dawood described it as the earliest attempt by any historian to discover a pattern in changes in political and social organisation. Its attention to systemic bias in the making of history is said not to have been matched, apart from al-Maqrizi, until Hegel, Marx and Nietzsche in nineteenth-century Germany.
muqan-qaghan: Muqan Qaghan, born Ashina Yandu, was the third qaghan of the First Turkic Khaganate. He held the rank of irkin under his father and succeeded his elder brother Issik Khagan in 553 in a lateral succession, appointing his younger brother Ashina Kutou lesser khagan in the east. The Sogdian Bugut Inscription names him, and several scholars, among them Talat Tekin and Christopher Beckwith, reconstruct his Turkic regnal name as Buqan and identify him with the Bokhanos of Menander Protector.

Around the new year of 554 the last Rouran sought the protection of the Northern Qi, whose Emperor Wenxuan fought off Muqan's army and settled them at Mayi; under Göktürk pressure the last Rouran khagan, Yujiulü Dengshuzi, was executed in 555. In 556 Muqan joined the Western Wei in an attack on the Tuyuhun that captured the family and treasure of their king. In 557 the Göktürks and Khosrow I defeated the Hephthalites near Bukhara, in a campaign largely led by Istami. Muqan also annexed the Kyrgyz, and the expansion drove the Avars west towards the Danube.

He allied with the Northern Zhou against the Northern Qi in 563, promising his daughter to Emperor Wu, and their armies struck at Jinyang and Pingyang that winter. In 565 he broke the agreement and held the Zhou envoys, but after a storm damaged his headquarters in 568 he took it as a sign of divine displeasure and sent his daughter, who became Empress Ashina.

Muqan died in 572 and the title passed to his younger brother Taspar. His reign marked the height of Sogdian influence in the khaganate: Sogdian merchants from Turpan served as envoys and advisers, and the Sogdian language and script were used in government. He is credited with first introducing Buddhism to the Türks and promoted a Türkic Buddhist temple in Chang'an, though it is not known whether he converted. His son Talopien later claimed the throne as Apa Qaghan without success.
muqarnas: Muqarnas most likely first developed in 11th-century Iraq, although the earliest preserved examples are found elsewhere. The earliest monuments to use it date from the 11th century and stand in Iraq, North Africa, Iran, Central Asia and Upper Egypt. Early scholars such as K. A. C. Creswell and Georges Marçais held that it developed in parallel in different regions, while others propose that it began in one place at least a century earlier. The earliest in situ examples are tripartite squinches, among them the Arab-Ata Mausoleum at Tim (977–978) and the Gunbad-i Qabus (1006–1007). Some scholars argue for northeastern Iran and Great Seljuk architecture, others, such as Yasser Tabbaa, for Abbasid Baghdad.

Muqarnas consists of niche-like cells combined in a geometrical framework with a few axes of symmetry, arranged in tiers that project over those below like corbels. Its main function is ornamental. It fills transitions, above all between a square chamber and a round dome, as an evolution of the squinch, and it appears on domes, vaults, cornices, mihrabs and entrance portals. The material varies by region: stone in Syria, Egypt and Turkey, plaster or wood in North Africa, and brick, sometimes covered in plaster or ceramic, in Iran and Iraq. Western writers often compare the effect to stalactites or honeycombs.

By the 12th century muqarnas had spread across the Islamic world and developed regional styles. Carved stone portals were characteristic of Ayyubid and Mamluk Egypt, and the Seljuks associated the muqarnas portal with royal patronage in 13th-century Anatolia. In the Maghreb and al-Andalus it was introduced under the Almoravid emir Ali ibn Yusuf, and it reached its highest sophistication in the Alhambra of Granada, where one dome in the Palace of the Lions contains at least 5,000 cells. Christian patrons also used it, as in the Cappella Palatina in Palermo (c. 1140). The oldest surviving written work on muqarnas is al-Kashi's Miftāḥ al-ḥisāb, from 1427. Oleg Grabar suggested the domes represent the rotating heavens.
muqrin-ibn-zamil: Muqrin came to power after the death of Ajwad ibn Zamil, the most powerful of the Jabrid rulers, who was possibly his grandfather. He was one of three Jabrid brothers who between them ruled a kingdom made up of Oman, the north coast of Oman and the Bahrain-Qatif area. Muqrin governed the last of these, which included al-Hasa, al-Qatif and Bahrain, from his capital at al-Hasa, and he was the last Jabrid ruler of Bahrain and eastern Arabia.

By his time the Portuguese, in alliance with the Kingdom of Hormuz, had come to dominate the sea lanes. Muqrin refused to pay them tribute, and the allies sent an invasion force to subdue Bahrain. In the account given by the 19th-century English traveller James Silk Buckingham, drawing on the Portuguese histories, the islands were taken by the combined Portuguese and Hormuzi forces while the Persian admiral, called Xarafo or Asharoff, watched from his ship. Muqrin was shot through the thigh, captured, and died of his wounds six days later.

When his body was being taken to al-Hasa for burial, the Hormuzi admiral cut off the head and sent it to Ormuz, an act Buckingham condemned as disgraceful. The Portuguese commander, Antonio Correia, added the title of Bahrain to his name and was authorised to bear Muqrin's severed head on his coat of arms, which remains a feature of the arms of the Count of Lousã, his descendant in Portugal. Muqrin's defeat began nearly eighty years of Portuguese rule over Bahrain.
murad-giray: Murad Giray was born in 1627, a son of Mubarek, one of the many sons of Khan Selâmet I Giray; three of his uncles became khans. He grew up in Yambol as one of the many Giray princes whom the Ottoman Empire supported and controlled, and after his father's death he was cared for by his uncle Rezmi Bahadır Giray. From 1659 to 1663 he served as nureddin, the third office of the khanate, during the second reign of Mehmed IV Giray, and then retired to Istanbul.

In 1678, during the Russo-Turkish War of 1676 to 1681, the Ottomans made him khan in place of his cousin Selim I Giray, who had performed poorly at the siege of Chyhyryn. Crimea took part in the further fighting, which ended with the Treaty of Bakhchisarai of 1681, recognising Ottoman control of western Ukraine. His nureddin was the future khan Saadet III Giray, and his kalga was Tokhtamysh, a brother of the future khan Safa Giray.

According to the chronicle of Mehmed Seyyid Riza, Murad set out to replace sharia with Mongol law, replacing the chief judge called the kadıasker with a new officer, the töre başı, who applied Chingisid law. The change was meant to strengthen his hand against the Ottomans and to push back Islamic and Ottoman influence over Tatar society, but it proved unpopular and short-lived, and the dervish Vani Mehmed Efendi had a part in his return to Islamic law.

After the defeat at the Battle of Vienna in 1683, Ottoman officials looked for someone to blame, and on the advice of Kara Mustafa Pasha Murad was removed. He made the hajj, then retired to an estate near Yambol, in present-day Bulgaria, where he died in 1696. Haci II Giray reigned briefly after him before Selim was restored. None of his descendants became khan.
murad-i: Murad I was the son of Orhan Gazi and Nilüfer Hatun, a slave concubine of ethnic Greek descent. He took the nickname Hüdavendigâr, from a Persian word meaning sovereign. He came to the throne after the death of his elder half-brother Süleyman Pasha. Ottoman sources give him many titles, among them Bey, Great Emir, Ghazi, Khan, Padishah and Sultan of sultans, while Bulgarian and Serbian sources call him Tsar and a Genoese document names him master lord of the Turks.

Murad conquered Adrianople in the 1360s and made it the Ottoman capital. He then brought most of the Balkans under Ottoman rule and forced the princes of Serbia, the emperor of Bulgaria and the Byzantine emperor John V Palaiologos to pay him tribute. He divided his realm administratively into two provinces, Anatolia and Rumelia, the Balkans. He fought the beylik of Karaman in Anatolia, and in Europe the Serbs, Albanians, Bulgarians and Hungarians.

On 26 September 1371 a Serbian expedition to drive the Turks from Adrianople, led by King Vukašin and Despot Uglješa, was defeated by Murad's lieutenant Lala Şâhin Paşa, the first governor of Rumeli. Sofia fell to the Ottomans in 1385. In 1386 Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović beat an Ottoman force at the Battle of Pločnik, where the Ottomans suffered heavy casualties and could not take Niš on the way back. In 1378 he married his daughter to the ruler of Karaman in an unsuccessful attempt to stop the war with it.

Murad's army met the Serbian army and its allies under Lazar at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, and both Lazar and the sultan died there. Accounts of how Murad was killed were recorded decades later, in the 15th century and after. Some name the Serbian knight Miloš Obilić, who stabbed him, either early in the battle or, in most Ottoman chronicles, while he inspected the field after it had ended. His son Bayezid I, who commanded the left wing, took charge and had his brother Yakub strangled, so that he alone claimed the throne.

Murad's internal organs were buried on the battlefield, at a place called Meshed-i Hudavendigar, and the rest of his remains were taken to Bursa, to a tomb in the complex built in his name. Ottoman sources describe a charitable, just ruler devoted to holy war, while Byzantine sources remember a man who spoke little but eloquently, was fond of hunting, was merciful to Christians and was always successful against his enemies.
murad-ii: Murad was born in June 1404 to Mehmed I. The identity of his mother is disputed: a 15th-century historian called her a concubine, a 20th-century writer named Şahzade Hatun, daughter of Divitdar Ahmed Pasha, and the most widely accepted view is that she was Emine Hatun of the Dulkadirid Beylik. He spent his early childhood in Amasya, came to the capital Edirne with his father in 1410, and was made governor of the Amasya Sanjak after Mehmed became sultan. When Mehmed I died in 1421 Murad was recognised as sultan at 16 and girded with the Sword of Osman at Bursa.

His reign was troubled by insurrection from the start. The Byzantine Emperor Manuel II released a pretender, Düzmece Mustafa, who defeated Murad's general Bayazid Pasha and declared himself Sultan of Adrianople. Murad out-manoeuvred him, his troops defected, and with help from a Genoese commander named Adorno he besieged and stormed Gallipoli, where Mustafa was taken and put to death. Murad then formed a new army, the Azeb, and besieged Constantinople, but had to abandon the siege when the Byzantines, in league with Anatolian states, sent his 13-year-old brother Küçük Mustafa to rebel and besiege Bursa. Küçük Mustafa was executed, and Murad annexed the Aydinid, Germiyanid, Menteshe and Teke states.

He defeated the Karamanids in 1428, and Venice withdrew in 1432 after Murad took Thessalonica in 1430. In the 1430s he captured large territories in the Balkans and annexed Serbia in 1439. He won the Crusade of Varna against John Hunyadi in 1444, and at Varna, according to the chronicles, he dismounted to pray as the Hungarians gained ground, and Władysław III of Poland, King of Hungary, was killed in a charge. Exhausted by war and by the death of his son Shehzade Alaedin, he signed the Peace of Szeged and abdicated in favour of his son Mehmed II, then 12. A rebellion at Edirne in 1446, probably sparked by debasement of the akçe, brought about Murad's return to the throne.

He presented himself as a ghazi sultan, modelling his conduct on the caliph of the epic Battalname, and a collection of his campaigns was given the title The Ghazas of Sultan Murad. His reign saw an increase in trade and the growth of cities; in 1432 the traveller Bertrandon de la Broquière noted that Ottoman annual revenue had risen to 2,500,000 ducats.
murad-iii: Murad was born in Manisa on 4 July 1546 to Şehzade Selim and his powerful consort Nurbanu Sultan, and was a grandson of Suleiman I and Hürrem Sultan. He learned Arabic and Persian, and after his ceremonial circumcision in 1557 Suleiman appointed him governor of Akşehir in 1558. In 1564 he became governor of Saruhan with Manisa as his seat, and he remained there during his father's reign, continuing his education under the historian Hoca Sadeddin Efendi. Contemporary accounts describe him there as highly educated, talented and deeply religious.

Murad succeeded Selim II in December 1574. His authority was increasingly influenced by the imperial harem, above all by his mother and later by his favourite consort Safiye Sultan, often at the expense of the Grand Vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, who served until his assassination in October 1579. In 1576 Abd al-Malik and Ramazan Pasha set out from Algiers with an army of about 10,000, mostly Ottoman Turks, and restored Abd al-Malik to the Moroccan throne as an Ottoman client. His brother Ahmad al-Mansur at first recognised Ottoman suzerainty but declared full independence in 1582.

The Ottomans had been at peace with the Safavids since the Treaty of Amasya of 1555. In 1577 Murad declared war to take advantage of the disorder at the Safavid court after the death of Shah Tahmasp I, influenced by the viziers Lala Kara Mustafa Pasha and Sinan Pasha and against the counsel of Sokollu. The Ottoman–Safavid War of 1578 to 1590 ended with the Treaty of Constantinople, which brought temporary significant gains. Admiral Mir Ali Beg established Ottoman supremacy in cities on the Swahili coast between Mogadishu and Kilwa, and Ottoman suzerainty was recognised in Mogadishu in 1585.

By 1580 an influx of silver from the New World had caused high inflation and unrest, especially among the Janissaries and officials paid in debased currency. Ottoman and Habsburg sources accuse Murad himself of taking large bribes. He exchanged letters and envoys with Elizabeth I, and England exported tin, lead and ammunition to the Ottomans. Like his father, Murad never went on campaign; in his last years he did not leave Topkapı Palace, and the historians Mustafa Âlî and Mustafa Selaniki disapproved of his sedentary life. He commissioned the Siyer-i-Nebi and other illustrated manuscripts.
muradid-dynasty: The founder, Murad I Bey, was of Corsican origin and had been sponsored since his youth by Ramdan Bey, ruler of Tunis. On Ramdan's death in 1613 Murad followed him into the office of bey, which he held effectively until 1631. The Ottoman sultan also named him pasha, though as bey he still ranked below the dey. He then resigned his offices, and his son Hamuda Bey inherited both titles with the support of the notables of Tunis, ruling from 1631 to 1666.

The title of pasha gave the beys the prestige of a link with the Sultan-Caliph in Constantinople. When the dey died in 1640, Hamuda Bey manoeuvred to control the appointment of his successors. Under Hamuda's son Murad II Bey, who reigned from 1666 to 1675, the Diwan again worked as a council of notables. In 1673 the janissary deys, seeing their power ebb, rose in revolt. Their urban troops fought the largely rural forces of the Muradids, led by tribal shaykhs and backed by city notables.

The beys won, and with them the rural Bedouin and the Tunisian notables. Arabic returned to local official use, while the Muradids kept Turkish in the central government as a mark of their elite status and Ottoman connection. After Murad II's death in 1675, discord within the family turned into armed struggle, the Revolutions of Tunis, which lasted until 1705.

The Turkish rulers of Algeria intervened for one side in the family's wars, and their forces stayed in the country and proved unpopular. The last Muradid bey, Murad III, was assassinated in 1702 by Ibrahim Sharif, who ruled for several years with Algerian backing. In 1705 Al-Husayn I ibn Ali at-Turki took power and founded the Husainid dynasty.
murano: Murano is made up of seven islands in the Venetian Lagoon, linked by bridges over eight channels. It measures about 1.5 kilometres across. It was once an independent comune but is now a frazione of the comune of Venice. Its countryside was known for orchards and vegetable gardens until the nineteenth century, when more housing was built.

Murano was first settled by the Romans and, from the sixth century, by people from Altinum and Oderzo. At first it prospered as a fishing port and through the production of salt. From the eleventh century it began to decline as islanders moved to Dorsoduro. It had a Grand Council like that of Venice, but from the thirteenth century it was governed by a podestà from Venice. Unlike the other islands of the lagoon, Murano minted its own coins.

Early in the second millennium hermits of the Camaldolese Order founded the Monastery of St Michael, which became a great centre of learning and printing. The cartographer Fra Mauro, whose maps were important to European exploration, was a monk there. French forces under Napoleon suppressed it in 1810 and the grounds became Venice's major cemetery.

In 1291 all the glassmakers of Venice were required to move to Murano, since the Republic feared fire among the city's mostly wooden buildings. Exports began in the following century, at first of glass beads and mirrors. Aventurine glass was invented on the island, and for a while Murano was the main producer of glass in Europe.

By the fourteenth century glassmakers were allowed to wear swords, were immune from prosecution by the Venetian state, and saw their daughters marry into Venice's wealthiest families, but they were forbidden to leave the Republic. Many took the risk and set up furnaces in other cities, sometimes in England and the Netherlands.

Murano held a monopoly on high-quality glass for centuries and developed or refined optically clear glass, enamelled glass, aventurine, multicoloured millefiori, milk glass called lattimo and imitation gemstones. The Republic partly lost its monopoly at the end of the sixteenth century, when some glassmakers let the secrets be known in other European countries. Decline set in during the eighteenth century, yet glassmaking is still the island's main industry. The Murano Glass Museum is housed in the Palazzo Giustinian.
murasaki-shikibu: Murasaki Shikibu is a descriptive name, and her personal name is unknown, though she may have been the Fujiwara no Kaoruko mentioned in a court diary of 1007. She was born in Heian-kyō around 973 into the northern Fujiwara clan. Her branch of the family had declined from the top tier of the aristocracy by the time of her birth. Her father, Fujiwara no Tametoki, was a respected scholar of Chinese classics and poetry who entered public service around 968 and held a governorship from 996 to about 1018.

Heian women were excluded from learning Chinese, the written language of government, but Murasaki, raised in her father's household, showed an aptitude for the Chinese classics and acquired fluency. In 996 she went with her father to his governorship in Echizen Province. She returned to Kyoto probably in 998 to marry Fujiwara no Nobutaka, a much older second cousin. Her husband died after two years of marriage.

It is uncertain when she began The Tale of Genji, but it was probably while she was married or soon after she was widowed. About 1005 Fujiwara no Michinaga invited her to serve as a lady-in-waiting to his daughter, Empress Shōshi, probably because of her reputation as a writer. She continued to write at court, adding scenes of court life to her work. Michinaga probably wanted Shōshi to surround herself with skilled women such as Murasaki to build a rival salon.

Murasaki taught Shōshi classical Chinese in secret, since written Chinese was regarded as the language of men; the scholar Richard Bowring calls it almost subversive. A lady-in-waiting who disliked her nicknamed her The Lady of the Chronicles after chapters of Genji were read aloud to the Emperor and one courtier remarked on the author's learning. When Emperor Ichijō died in 1011, Shōshi retired to a Fujiwara mansion near Lake Biwa, and Murasaki most likely went with her. Most scholars date her death to 1014, while others suggest she lived with Shōshi until about 1025.

Three works are attributed to her: The Tale of Genji, The Diary of Lady Murasaki and Poetic Memoirs, a collection of 128 poems. Her work reflects the shift of Japanese from an unwritten vernacular to a written language, after the development of the kana script in the mid-to-late 9th century. Within a decade of its completion Genji was circulating in the provinces, and within a century it was recognised as a classic of Japanese literature. Since the 13th century Japanese artists have illustrated her works.
murata-seifu: Murata was born in Misumi Village, in Otsu District of Nagato Province, the eldest son of Murata Mitsukata, a retainer of the Chōshū Domain with a stipend of 91 koku. He did well at the domain school, the Meirinkan, and in 1808 became a page to the daimyō Mōri Narifusa. In Edo he studied warfare and coastal defence under Hanawa Hokiichi and others, and economics through the writings of Kaiho Seiryō. He became head of the Murata family in 1819 and went on to hold important posts under five successive daimyō, from Mōri Narihiro to Mōri Takachika.

From 1838 Murata held the real power in the domain's administration under Mōri Takachika, alongside the Tenpō Reforms that the shogunate introduced under Mizuno Tadakuni between 1841 and 1843. In 1843 he worked out a plan to pay off the domain's heavy debts and their interest over 37 years. He taxed the shipping that passed through the Kanmon Straits between Honshu and Kyushu and built up a domain-owned financial and warehousing centre in the port of Shimonoseki. He also promoted education among the common people and enlarged the Meirinkan in 1849.

The reforms met resistance. Local merchants resented the new taxes and the slow repayment of debts, and the merchants of Osaka feared that Shimonoseki would draw trade away from them. When Mizuno Tadakuni fell from power in 1845, most of his national reforms were repealed. Murata resigned after a stroke left him partly paralysed.

After recovering, Murata gave his time to education and wrote a number of books. He returned to the domain's administration in 1855 but suffered another stroke that year and died aged 73. His reforms were only partly successful, yet he is credited with laying the foundations that allowed Chōshū to play an active part in the Meiji Restoration. The house in present-day Nagato, Yamaguchi, where he was born and where he lived from 1845, survives with its rice storehouse, stable and bath around a thatched main building; it and his grave nearby were designated a National Historic Site in 1941.
muravsky-trail: The route was described in the Book to the Great Chart of Muscovy of 1627. It left the Tatar fortress of Or Qapı at Perekop, the gateway of the Crimean peninsula, ran east of the Dnieper and made an almost straight line from the Dnieper bend towards the Russian fortress of Tula, 193 km south of Moscow. It crossed thinly populated tallgrass steppe; the name comes from murava, an old Slavic word for grassland.

According to the historian Davies, the trail ran north-east parallel to the coast of the Sea of Azov, then swung north along the watershed of the Dnieper and the Donets. In Sloboda Ukraine it split into three branches, the Muravsky proper, the Izium Trail and the Kalmius Trail, which met again near Stary Oskol and Livny. From Livny it led north to Tula and crossed the Oka at Serpukhov.

Between 1500 and 1550, 43 Tatar raids used the trail. The raiders preferred to come at harvest time, when forage was plentiful, and made smaller raids in early winter over frozen rivers. Larger raids were led by the khan himself with a guard of musketeers and light artillery around a main body of horse archers, each with one or two spare horses, who lived off the land.

Near enemy territory the columns sent out wings of up to 10,000 men to sweep the country, taking women, children, livestock and men who did not resist, and withdrew by another route. They avoided fortified towns and organised armies. After the Russo-Crimean War of 1571 Moscow concluded that only a line south of the Great Zasechnaya cherta would stop the yearly incursions. Under Boris Godunov a chain of eleven forts was built, among them Livny and Voronezh in 1586, Kursk in 1587, Yelets in 1592, Stary Oskol and Valuyki in 1593 and Belgorod in 1596. After this the Tatars began to avoid the route, and it later became the main way by which the Cossacks raided Crimea.
murcia: Murcia lies on the Segura River in the south-east of the Iberian Peninsula, near the centre of a low-lying fertile plain known as the huerta, the orchard of Murcia. The river has flooded the city many times, in 1651, 1879, 1946 and 1948 among other years, and a levee was built. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with mild winters and very hot summers. Because of its long agricultural tradition and its fruit, vegetables and flowers, the city is called Europe's orchard.

The city on its present site was founded in 825 as Madinat Mursiyah by Abd ar-Rahman II, then emir of Córdoba. Umayyad planners used the course of the Segura to create a complex network of irrigation channels that made the town's agriculture prosperous. The name is widely thought to come from the Latin myrtea, land of the myrtle.

After the fall of the Caliphate of Córdoba in 1031 Murcia became the capital of its own kingdom under Ibn Tahir. Ibn Mardanis made it the capital of a new independent kingdom after the fall of the Almoravid empire. It was famed for ceramics exported to Italian towns and for silk and paper industries, and the mystic Ibn Arabi (1165-1240) was born there. The Almohades conquered it in 1172.

By the Treaty of Alcaraz in 1243 Ferdinand III of Castile made Murcia a protectorate. Christians became the majority as immigrants arrived, while Muslims were confined to the suburb of Arrixaca. A Muslim revolt in 1264 was put down by James I of Aragon in 1266, and in 1304 the Treaty of Torrellas incorporated the city finally into Castile. Murcia flourished after the conquest of Granada in 1492 and again in the 18th century, with a boom in silk. Napoleonic troops looted it in 1810. An earthquake in 1829 killed an estimated 6,000 people across the province.

Murcia is the capital of the autonomous community of the Region of Murcia, created in 1982, and is mainly a services city and a university town. Its main sights are the Cathedral of Murcia, baroque buildings and the works of the sculptor Francisco Salzillo. The Holy Week procession and the Fiestas de Primavera are its main festivals.
mures-river: The Mureș rises in the Hășmașu Mare Range, close to the headwaters of the river Olt, and joins the Tisza at Szeged in south-eastern Hungary. Its drainage basin covers about 30,332 square kilometres. It flows through the Romanian counties of Harghita, Mureș, Alba, Hunedoara, Arad and Timiș and the Hungarian county of Csongrád. Its largest cities are Târgu Mureș, Alba Iulia, Deva and Arad in Romania and Makó and Szeged in Hungary. For 73 kilometres in its Hungarian reach it forms the state border, and part of the northern bank there belongs to the Körös-Maros National Park.

Since ancient times the Mureș has been a heavily used waterway for trade and for military purposes, a kind of highway for the area north of the Danube. Herodotus is the first to mention it, as Maris, Strabo calls it Marisos, and a document of the Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII from 948 calls it Morisis. It was known in German as the Mieresch, because of the Transylvanian Saxon settlements and Habsburg rule, and in Turkish as the Maroş under the Ottomans.

From the Dacian-Roman wars onward control of the river was a key aim of the Roman army against the defences of the Dacian Kingdom. In the opening operations of Trajan's Second Dacian War a force from Pannonia Inferior under Aelius Hadrianus, the later Emperor Hadrian, is thought to have advanced into Dacia by the Mureș valley, probably using the river fleet, the Classis Flavia Pannonica. Gold, iron, salt and wood went by water to Rome and the western provinces. Apulum, where the river route met the main imperial road of the province, was the most important civilian river port of Roman Dacia. In medieval times salt was still traded down the river on large rafts.
muri-abbey: The monastery was dedicated to Saint Martin of Tours and lay in the Diocese of Basel, originally in that of Constance. Its first monks came from nearby Einsiedeln Abbey under Prior Reginbold, on land given by a daughter of Frederick, Duke of Lower Lorraine, and by Werner, Bishop of Strasburg. On Reginbold's death in 1055 Burchard was chosen as the first abbot, and the abbey church was consecrated under him in 1064. A further colony of monks came from the Abbey of St. Blaise in the Black Forest; one of them, the Blessed Luitfrid, governed both communities until his death on 31 December 1096.

Under Abbot Henry de Schoenwerd a whole family took vows, the father and sons in the abbey and the mother and daughters in the neighbouring convent of nuns, later moved to Hermetschwil. In 1114 Emperor Henry V took Muri under his protection, and it held lands and rights in Unterwalden, in Stans and Buochs and in the mountains around Engelberg. Fires in 1300 and 1363 and the war between the Swiss Confederacy and the Habsburgs set it back. Abbot George Russinger, who had attended the Council of Constance, joined it to the reforming Congregation of Bursfelde, and Pope Julius II granted its abbots the use of pontificalia.

In the 1530s troops from Bern, newly Protestant, attacked the abbey, which survived under Abbot Laurentius von Heidegg, a friend of the Zürich reformer Heinrich Bullinger. After the rule of Abbot Jakob Meyer proved an economic disaster, he was forced out in 1596 and replaced by John Jodoc Singisen, who restored discipline and helped found the Swiss Congregation of 1602. His successor Dominic Tschudi wrote the Origo et genealogia comitum de Habsburg. Emperor Leopold I raised Abbot Placid Zurlauben and his successor to princes of the Holy Roman Empire and paid for rebuilding the monastery and church.

The abbey church holds the oldest burial place of the Habsburgs, and the bodies of Rudolf and Felix, sons of the last emperor, lie with their parents' hearts in the family crypt of the Loreto Chapel. The former abbey is now a museum and cultural centre, showing the treasures of the monastery and the work of the Swiss landscape painter Caspar Wolf, and it is a heritage site of national significance.
muridun: The Muridun were a Sufi order founded and led by Abūʾl-Qāsim Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Qasī, a convert from Christianity from the city of Silves in the far west of al-Andalus. Among his followers was Muhammad ibn Umar ibn al-Mundhir, a correspondent of the Sufi teacher Ibn al-Arif of Almeria. Alarmed by the spread of Sufi teaching in Almeria, the Almoravid authorities arrested Ibn al-Arif and his colleague Ibn Barrajan. Ibn Barrajan died in prison and Ibn al-Arif died suddenly, poisoned it was said. These deaths, presumably at the hands of the authorities, convinced Ibn Qasi to proclaim himself imam and lead his followers into open revolt.

Early in the rebellion Ibn al-Mundhir seized Silves, and Sidray ibn Wazir, the governor of Beja, went over to the rebels. Together they took the fort of Monchique and killed its Almoravid garrison. On 12 August 1144 a force of seventy Muridun captured Mértola, which Ibn Qasi made his capital, and Yusuf ibn Ahmad al-Bitruji, the governor of Niebla, joined them.

Holding Silves, Mértola, Beja and Niebla, the Muridun marched on Seville but were defeated by the Almoravid general Yahya ibn Ali ibn Ghaniya. The Almoravid counter-attack was cut short by the rebellion of Ibn Hamdin in Cordoba, but it had already split the movement, with Ibn Qasi and Ibn al-Mundhir on one side and Ibn Wazir on the other.

In September 1145 Ibn Qasi went to Marrakesh to seek help from the Almohad caliph, an enemy of the Almoravids. He returned to the Algarve in the summer of 1146 with Almohad support but refused to place the Muridun under Almohad control. To escape his overbearing allies he negotiated the handover of Silves to the Christians, and the people of Silves killed him in his palace in August or September 1151. Ibn al-Mundhir then placed the city under Almohad control, which ended the Muridun's taifa.
muriq-shpata: Muriq, also known as Maurice Shpata, was a grandson of Gjin Bua Shpata, the first Albanian ruler of Arta, and was born there in the 14th century. He had a full brother, Yaqub, and two half-siblings, Charles Marchesano and Maddalena, from his mother's second marriage. Shortly before his death on 29 October 1399, Gjin named his own brother Skurra Bua Shpata, ruler of Naupactus, as his successor, but within days the adventurer Vonko seized Arta. Muriq drove Vonko out, possibly as early as December 1399, and took over the city.

Much of his rule was taken up by war with Carlo I Tocco. In 1402–03 he helped Skurra repel Tocco's general Galasso Peccatore at Angelokastron, and in 1406, when Tocco and the rival Bua brothers ravaged Acarnania and the country round Arta, he held the city. He refused to help his cousin Pal Shpata, who then ceded Angelokastron to the Ottomans and sold Naupactus to Venice in 1407–08. Around 1410 Muriq allied with Esau de' Buondelmonti, Despot of Ioannina, who had married and then divorced his mother Irene, and sealed the pact by marrying a daughter to Esau's son Giorgio.

Esau's death on 6 February 1411 opened a contest for Ioannina. With Gjon Zenebishi, lord of Gjirokastër, Muriq besieged the city twice in vain, and its people, opposed to an Albanian or Serbian ruler, surrendered it to Tocco. In spring or summer 1412 the two Albanian lords almost destroyed Tocco's army at Kranea, in the district of Mesopotamon, but still could not take Ioannina. Tocco then allied with the Ottoman prince Musa Çelebi, while Muriq turned to Centurione II Zaccaria, Prince of Achaea. A scandal involving Zenebishi's son and a son-in-law of Muriq broke the alliance, and Zenebishi made peace with Tocco.

On his death Muriq was succeeded in Arta by his brother Yaqub, while Charles Marchesano received the governorship of Rogoi. His successors could not hold off Tocco: in October 1416 Yaqub was captured and killed in an ambush, and Arta surrendered, ending Albanian rule in the area. From his marriage to Nerata, a Serbian woman, Muriq had daughters, usually counted as three, who married Giorgio de' Buondelmonti, Simon Zenebishi and, after their father's death, Carlo II Tocco.
murom: Murom lies on the Oka River in Vladimir Oblast, close to the border with Nizhny Novgorod Oblast and 137 kilometres from the oblast's administrative centre, Vladimir. Its name comes from the Muroma, a Finnic tribe that lived in the area. In the 9th century it was the easternmost settlement of the East Slavs in the land of the Muroma.

The Primary Chronicle mentions Murom as early as 862, which makes it one of the oldest cities in Russia. Around 900 it was an important trading post on the route from Volga Bulgaria to the Baltic Sea. Between 1010 and 1392 it was the capital of a separate principality. Its rulers included Gleb, who was assassinated in 1015 and canonised in 1071, Konstantin the Blessed, and Peter and Fevronia of Murom, who are the subjects of an opera by Rimsky-Korsakov. The town was also believed to be the home of the epic hero Ilya Muromets.

With the Principality of Ryazan, Murom bore the brunt of attacks from the east, since it formed the south-eastern border of Russia, and as a result it became dependent on the other Russian principalities. Vasily I of Moscow received the patent for the throne of Murom in 1392, and the principality was incorporated into the Grand Principality of Moscow.

Murom keeps many marks of antiquity. The Transfiguration Monastery, one of the oldest in Russia, was first chronicled in 1096, when Oleg of Chernigov besieged it and killed Vladimir Monomakh's son Izyaslav, who is buried there. Ivan the Terrible visited it in 1552 and commissioned a stone cathedral. The Trinity Convent displays the relics of Saints Peter and Fevronia and has a cathedral of 1642 to 1643. The tent-like church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, built in 1565 on the bank of the Oka, commemorates the Russian conquest of Kazan. A statue of Ilya Muromets shows him holding his sword's hilt in one hand and a cross in the other.
murong-bao: Murong Bao was the fourth son of Murong Chui, by his first wife Princess Duan, who died in prison in 358 after being falsely accused of witchcraft. In 369 he fled with his father's household to Former Qin, and when his elder brother Murong Ling was lured back to Former Yan and killed, he became his father's heir. After the defeat at the Battle of Fei River in 383 he urged his father to kill the Former Qin emperor Fu Jiān and rebel, and in 384 he took part in the massacre of Fu Feilong's Di soldiers that began the rising.

As crown prince of Later Yan from 384 he won a name as a studious learner and talented writer and cultivated his father's officials, and Murong Chui kept him as heir though Empress Duan Yuanfei warned that Murong Nong or Murong Long would be better. He usually guarded the capital Zhongshan during his father's campaigns, and from 388 held most of the imperial authority. Traditional historians record that in 391 Murong Chui's sons detained Tuoba Gu, envoy of Northern Wei, to extort horses from his brother Tuoba Gui, which broke the alliance and led to the disastrous expedition of 395.

On his accession in 396 Murong Bao forced his stepmother Duan Yuanfei to commit suicide and made his young son Murong Ce crown prince over the favoured Murong Hui. When Tuoba Gui invaded, he chose to hold Zhongshan, and the garrisons of the other cities, except Yecheng and Xindu, abandoned their posts. He wavered over battle and peace, and when Murong Lin rebelled he left Zhongshan for Longcheng. On the way Murong Hui rebelled, killing Murong Long before he was defeated by Gao Yun, while Murong De broke away to found Southern Yan.

In 398 the general Duan Sugu rebelled as soon as Murong Bao set out to recover his lands, and Longcheng fell after Murong Nong surrendered. Murong Bao wandered south and back, and as he returned to Longcheng in early summer he was killed outside the city by Lan Jia'nan, brother of his granduncle Lan Han. Lan Han slaughtered most of the Murong clan, but Murong Sheng overthrew him two months later. Historians largely blamed Murong Bao's irresolution for the losses, and Later Yan never regained its power.
murong-chao: Murong Chao's father Murong Na, Prince of Beihai under Former Yan and a brother of Murong De, was executed with all the sons of both brothers by the Former Qin governor of Zhangye, Fu Chang, after Murong De and Murong Chui rebelled in 384. His mother Lady Duan was spared because she was pregnant. The jailer Huyan Ping, once a subordinate of Murong De, escaped with her and her mother-in-law Lady Gongsun to the Qiang tribes, where Murong Chao was born. They later moved to Later Liang, and in 403 they were forcibly resettled at the Later Qin capital Chang'an.

There he married Huyan Ping's daughter and, fearing discovery, lived as a beggar who feigned madness, deceiving even the emperor Yao Xing. In 405 Murong De learned of him and sent secret messengers, and Murong Chao fled to the Southern Yan capital Guanggu, where he presented the golden knife his uncle had left with Lady Gongsun. Created Prince of Beihai, he behaved with care and won general approval, and on Murong De's deathbed that autumn he was made crown prince and succeeded him.

As emperor he proved capricious and unwilling to hear criticism, promoting his associate Gongsun Wulou and setting aside the officials Murong De had trusted. In 406 a plot by Murong Zhong, Murong Fa and Duan Hong was revealed, and they fled. To recover his mother and wife from Later Qin in 407 he became Yao Xing's vassal and handed over 120 court musicians. In 409, lamenting the lack of musicians, he raided Eastern Jin, capturing Suyu and 2,500 men and women to be taught music.

Liu Yu answered with a major campaign. Murong Chao refused advice to hold the Daxian Mountain pass or burn the crops and jailed Murong Zhen for objecting; his forces were beaten near Linqu and he fell back to Guanggu, where he executed anyone who proposed surrender. Later Qin aid never came. Guanggu fell in spring 410, and Murong Chao was taken to Jiankang and executed with some 3,000 Southern Yan officials and nobles.
murong-chong: Murong Chong was a son of the Former Yan emperor Murong Jun and a younger brother of the emperor Murong Wei. His birth date is unknown: since Murong Wei was born in 350 and Chong was made Prince of Zhongshan in 359, he was born between those years. In 368, after the death of his uncle the regent Murong Ke, he succeeded to Ke's post as commander of the armed forces, though there is no evidence that he ever led armies.

When Former Qin destroyed Former Yan in 370, he and his brothers were made local officials across the Qin realm. Historical accounts say that he had a sexual relationship with the Former Qin emperor Fu Jian, and that the emperor's favour to him and to his sister Consort Murong, whom Fu Jian took as a concubine, was the talk of Chang'an.

By 384 he was governor of Pingyang Commandery. When his uncle Murong Chui and his brother Murong Hong rebelled after Fu Jian's defeat at the Battle of Fei River in 383, he rose too, was beaten by the Qin general Dou Chong, and joined Hong. In summer 384 Hong's strategist Gao Gai and other officials, judging Hong's punishments too harsh, killed him and made Chong ruler. With Murong Wei still a captive in Chang'an, Chong took the title of crown prince and rejected a peace overture from Fu Jian.

Around the new year of 385 Murong Wei and his cousin Murong Su plotted a rising inside Chang'an; Fu Jian discovered it, executed them and slaughtered the Xianbei in the city. Chong then declared himself emperor. He became capricious in rewards and punishments, let his soldiers pillage the Guanzhong region, and kept up the siege until famine struck the city. In summer 385 Fu Jian broke out to look for food, leaving his crown prince Fu Hong to hold Chang'an, and the city fell as soon as he had gone.

His Xianbei followers wanted to go home to the east, but Murong Chong chose to stay in Chang'an, because he liked the city and feared Murong Chui, who had founded Later Yan. In spring 386 his general Han Yan killed him in a coup and made another general, Duan Sui, Prince of Yan. He is known formally as Emperor Wei of Western Yan; his son Murong Yao later became emperor.
murong-chui: Murong Chui, courtesy name Daoming, was born in 326, the fifth son of Murong Huang by his concubine Consort Lan. His father favoured him and wished to make him heir, but accepted his officials' advice to choose the eldest son of his wife, Murong Jun, and instead named the boy Murong Ba, meaning hegemon. Murong Jun, jealous, renamed him after he succeeded in 348, first Murong Que and then Murong Chui. As a young general Murong Chui fought in the conquest of the Yuwen tribe in 344 and held the border against the Later Zhao.

Under Murong Jun he helped take the eastern half of the former Later Zhao lands and was made Prince of Wu in 354, but the emperor kept him at a distance. In 358 his wife Princess Duan was falsely accused of witchcraft, tortured and died in prison. Murong Chui helped the regent Murong Ke capture Luoyang in 365, and in 369 he and his brother Murong De defeated the Jin general Huan Wen near Yecheng. The regent Murong Ping and Empress Dowager Kezuhun then considered executing him, and he fled.

Fu Jian of the Former Qin welcomed him and made him Marquess of Bintu, despite the doubts of the prime minister Wang Meng. In 370 Wang Meng tricked Murong Chui's son Murong Ling into defecting back to Yan, but Fu Jian pardoned the father. When Fu Jian's army collapsed at the Fei River in 383, Murong Chui's troops stayed intact and Fu Jian took refuge with him; Murong Chui refused his son's and brother's urging to kill him, before turning to rebellion himself.

After taking Yecheng late in 385 he made Zhongshan his capital. In 386 Tuoba Gui of the Northern Wei became his vassal, but relations broke down in 391. Murong Chui conquered the Dingling state of Wei at Huatai in 392 and then took Zhangzi, capital of the Western Yan, killing its emperor Murong Yong.

After Northern Wei destroyed a Later Yan army at the Battle of Canhe Slope in 395, he led a new campaign and took Pingcheng, but on passing the battlefield, with its bodies, he fell gravely ill and died at Shanggu on 2 June 396. Historians count him a general who never lost a battle, but blame him for betraying Fu Jian and for leaving a weak state to his heir Murong Bao.
murong-de: Murong De was born in 336 to Murong Huang and his concubine Consort Gongsun; in 337 his father claimed the title Prince of Yan, an act generally taken as the founding of the independent Former Yan state. His brother Murong Jun, after claiming the imperial title in 354, made him Duke of Liang, and he later became Prince of Fanyang. In 369 he served under his brother Murong Chui in the defeat of the Jin general Huan Wen near Yecheng, but when Murong Chui fled to Former Qin that year, Murong De lost his post as mayor of the capital.

After Former Qin conquered Former Yan in 370 he served its emperor Fu Jiān as governor of Zhangye Commandery. After Fu Jiān's defeat at the Battle of Fei River he urged Murong Chui to kill him and restore Yan. When Murong Chui did rebel in 384 and founded Later Yan, the governor at Zhangye executed Murong De's brother Murong Na and all of Murong De's sons. Under Murong Chui he was a chief official and general, campaigning near the Yellow River and against the Xianbei Helan tribe in 389. He served at the disastrous Battle of Canhe Slope in 395, and under Murong Bao he was viceroy at Yecheng, which he held against several attacks by Northern Wei.

On the advice of his nephew Murong Lin he abandoned Yecheng in spring 398 for Huatai, south of the Yellow River, where he declined the imperial title but founded Southern Yan; he soon executed Murong Lin for plotting rebellion. After losing Huatai to Northern Wei in 399 he advanced east and that autumn took Guanggu, capital of the Jin province of Qing, from its governor Pilü Hun. He claimed the imperial title in 400, changing his name to Murong Beide to ease the naming taboo, and thereafter carried out few campaigns. He refused a proposal to attack Jin in 403 and survived a plot against him in 404.

In 405 Murong Na's posthumously born son Murong Chao reached Southern Yan and proved who he was with the golden knife that Murong De had given his mother. Having no surviving sons, Murong De made him crown prince shortly before his death. His burial was secret: more than 10 caskets were carried out of the gates of Guanggu, only one of them holding his body.
murong-huang: Murong Huang, courtesy name Yuanzhen, was born in 297 to the Xianbei chief Murong Hui and a daughter of Duan Jie of the Duan tribe. As the Jin dynasty collapsed in infighting and rebellion, Han refugees settled in his father's relatively safe domain, which became the only part of northern China still under titular Jin rule. Murong Huang fought the Yuwen tribe for his father in 320 and 325 and was named heir apparent in early 322, but grew jealous of his favoured brothers Murong Ren, Murong Zhao and above all the general Murong Han.

When Murong Hui died on 4 June 333, Murong Huang took over as Duke of Liaodong. His harsh enforcement of the laws and his suspicion of his brothers drove Murong Han to the Duan, while Murong Ren seized the Liaodong Peninsula and claimed the dukedom. In early 336 Murong Huang led his army over the frozen Bohai Sea to Pingguo, captured Murong Ren and forced him to commit suicide. In November 337 he took the title Prince of Yan and set up a government modelled on the Jin court, the traditional founding of Former Yan.

Allied with Shi Hu of Later Zhao, he raided the Duan in 338, but Later Zhao then turned on him; he held Jicheng for nearly 20 days, and his son Murong Ke defeated the retreating army. He absorbed the remaining Duan forces, allied with Tuoba Shiyiqian of Dai by marrying him to his sister, and received formal recognition of his title from Emperor Cheng of Jin in 341. He moved his capital to the new city of Longcheng. In 344, with Murong Han as his deputy, he defeated the Yuwen and moved the tribe into his own population, then forced Murong Han to kill himself.

In 345 he stopped using the Jin era names, which some see as Former Yan's formal independence, and in early 347 he attacked Buyeo and captured its king. He fell ill and died in October 348 and was succeeded by his son Murong Jun, who proclaimed himself emperor in January 353 and gave his father the posthumous title Emperor Wenming. Among his other sons were Murong Ke, Murong Chui and Murong De.
murong-hui: Murong Hui was a son of Murong Shegui, chanyu of the Murong Xianbei. His elder brother Murong Tuyuhun led part of the people away from their original settlements on the Liaodong Peninsula to the Yin Mountains and on into the eastern region of modern Qinghai, where his tribe later became the Tuyuhun. The Book of Jin describes Murong Hui as tall, physically strong and handsome. He fought Jin forces late in the reign of Emperor Wu of Jin before submitting as a Jin vassal in 289.

Under constant attack from Duan Jie of the Duan tribe, a fellow Xianbei chief, Murong Hui sought peace and married one of Duan Jie's daughters, who bore him Murong Huang in 297 and the younger sons Murong Ren and Murong Zhao. As the Jin government fell into infighting and the Xiongnu state of Han-Zhao advanced, refugees reached his domain, and because he treated the Han refugees kindly most of them stayed, greatly strengthening his power. When Jin forces in the north fell to Shi Le, his domain became the only one in northern China still under titular Jin rule.

He entrusted Murong Huang with campaigns against the powerful Yuwen tribe in 320 and 325 and named him heir apparent in early 322. He also greatly favoured Murong Huang's brothers, above all Murong Han, a highly regarded general, and Murong Huang's jealousy of them sowed the seeds of later conflict. One of Murong Hui's daughters married Tuoba Shiyiqian, a son of Tuoba Yulü. Murong Hui died on 4 June 333 and was posthumously honoured as Emperor Wuxuan.
murong-jun: Murong Jun, whose Xianbei name was Helaiba, was born in 319, while his father Murong Huang was still heir to Murong Hui, the Jin-created Duke of Liaodong. He was made heir apparent after his father succeeded in 333, and kept that rank when Murong Huang claimed the title Prince of Yan in 337. Accounts say his father once thought of naming his younger brother Murong Ba instead, which left Murong Jun jealous of him. He led an army against Dai in 344 with his uncle Murong Ping, and in 346 nominally commanded the army, led in fact by his brother Murong Ke, that captured the capital and king of Buyeo.

After the Later Zhao emperor Shi Hu died in 349 and his state fell into civil war, Murong Jun attacked in the spring of 350, took Jicheng in modern Beijing, moved his capital there from Longcheng and soon held all of Youzhou. In the summer of 352 Murong Ke drew the infantry of Ran Min, founder of Ran Wei, onto the plains and broke it with cavalry; Ran was whipped, exiled and beheaded, though later buried with honours. Former Yan forces then breached Ye and captured Ran Zhi and Empress Dong, ending Ran Wei, and Murong Jun broke openly with the Jin.

As emperor he made his wife Kezuhun empress in 353. In 356 Murong Ke took Guanggu in Shandong from his cousin Duan Kan, whom he executed in 357. In 358 he ordered large-scale conscription for war on Former Qin and Jin, scaled back after a petition by Liu Gui, and his rivalry with Murong Chui, as Murong Ba was now named, flared when Chui's wife Princess Duan was falsely accused of witchcraft and died in prison. A Jin attack in 359 under Zhuge You and Xie Wan was defeated, opening the Henan region to Former Yan.

Falling ill early in 360, Murong Jun offered the throne to Murong Ke rather than to his 10-year-old son Murong Wei, but Murong Ke declined. He entrusted the crown prince to Murong Ke, Yang Wu, Murong Ping and Muyu Gen and died on 23 February 360. During his reign the state grew from modern Liaoning and part of Hebei to nearly all the land north of the Yellow River, with substantial holdings south of it.
murong-ke: Murong Ke was the fourth son of Murong Huang, by his concubine Consort Gao, and his father at first thought little of him because he did not favour his mother. The Book of Jin describes him as over 2.1 metres tall. Before 345 he held the defence of Liaodong against Goguryeo, which he attacked successfully in 345, and in 346 he took the capital of Buyeo and its king, Hyeon of Buyeo.

When the Later Zhao state collapsed, Murong Ke was among the main generals of the Former Yan invasion of the North China Plain. His army was said to be so disciplined that it harmed not even trees and grass. Against Ran Min's infantry he feigned repeated defeats to draw the enemy into the plains, then broke them with cavalry chained in square formations. After the fall of Yecheng late in 352, his brother Murong Jun claimed the imperial title and made him Prince of Taiyuan in 353.

In the following years he subdued former Later Zhao generals, forced the surrender of Duan Kan at Guanggu in 356 and took Jin commanderies south of the Yellow River in 358. Around the new year of 360 the dying Murong Jun offered him the throne; Murong Ke declined and became regent for the ten-year-old Murong Wei.

As regent he executed the senior official Muyu Gen, who had accused him of plotting rebellion, and consulted his uncle Murong Ping on all important decisions. Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian credits him with ruling his soldiers through kindness rather than punishment, and no recorded battle of his ended in defeat. He took Luoyang from Jin in 365.

Falling ill in 367, he urged that command of the armies go to Murong Chui, whose abilities he admired. After his death Murong Ping took most of the power and gave the post instead to Murong Chong. Former Qin destroyed Former Yan in 370, three years later. The Eastern Wei general Murong Shaozong was among his descendants.
murong-nuohebo: The year of Murong Nuohebo's birth is not known. In 635 his grandfather, the Busabo Khan Murong Fuyun, whose border raids had provoked the Tang, was killed in flight from an army under the general Li Jing. His father Murong Shun surrendered and was made khan, but he had spent years at the Sui court, his mother was the Sui princess Guanghua, and the Tuyuhun thought him too Chinese; late in 635 he was assassinated. Nuohebo, said to be young and holding the title Prince of Yan, succeeded, and Emperor Taizong sent the general Hou Junji to help him pacify his people.

In 636 Nuohebo submitted to the Tang as a vassal and sent a younger brother as a hostage, and Taizong made him Prince of Heyuan and Ledou Khan. From 638 the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo, who believed Nuohebo had blocked his request for a Tang bride, attacked Tuyuhun and drove its people north of Qinghai Lake. In 639 Nuohebo visited Chang'an and married Princess Honghua. By 641 his chief minister, the Prince of Xuan, plotted to seize them both and go over to Tibet; Nuohebo fled to the general the Prince of Weixin at Shanshan, and the Tang officer Xi Junmai killed the plotter.

Tibetan attacks resumed in 660 under Gar Trinring Tsendro, son of the minister Gar Tongtsen. In 663 the official Suhe Gui fled to Tibet with Tuyuhun secrets, Tibetan forces defeated the Tuyuhun, and Nuohebo and Princess Honghua led their people to Tang's Liang Prefecture, near modern Wuwei.

Emperor Gaozong made Nuohebo Prince of Qinghai around 666, perhaps to show Tibet that he still meant to restore Tuyuhun, but declined to fight for it until 670, when Xue Rengui's army was routed at the Battle of Dafeichuan. In 672 the Tuyuhun were settled at Shanzhou and soon moved to Lingzhou, where a prefecture, Anlezhou, was made for them with Nuohebo as prefect. He kept the title of khan until his death in 688. His son Murong Zhong inherited his titles, which passed down at least four more generations.
murong-wei: Murong Wei, courtesy name Jingmao, was born in 350, a son of Murong Jun and Empress Kezuhun. He was made Prince of Zhongshan in 354 and crown prince in 357, after the death of his able elder brother Murong Ye, probably because he was the empress's son, though his father had older sons. At a feast in 359 the official Li Ji praised him but warned of his overindulgence in hunting and music, and Murong Wei bore him a grudge ever after. When Murong Jun fell ill in early 360, his brother Murong Ke declined the throne and became regent for the boy.

Murong Ke was an able regent who made all major decisions, executed the plotting official Muyu Gen and took Luoyang from Jin in 365. The young emperor still sent Li Ji away into exile. When Murong Ke died in 367 he recommended Murong Chui, but Empress Dowager Kezuhun and the jealous, corrupt Murong Ping kept power instead. Murong Ping refused to help the rebel dukes of Former Qin, though the reformer Yue Wan restored over 200,000 people to the tax rolls in 368. In 369 the Jin general Huan Wen advanced to Fangtou near Yecheng before Murong Chui and Murong De defeated him.
