The court then denied Murong Chui his rewards and considered killing him, so he fled to Fu Jiān of Former Qin, and it broke a promise to cede the Luoyang region. Wang Meng invaded with 60,000 men, and in 370 crushed Murong Ping's army of 300,000, whose morale had collapsed after Murong Ping charged his own soldiers for firewood and water. Murong Wei fled Yecheng, was deserted by his guards and was captured.

Fu Jiān made him Marquess of Xinxing and a general in Chang'an, and he served in the siege of Xiangyang in 378 and the campaign of 383. After the defeat at the Fei River his brothers Murong Hong and Murong Chong rebelled. Murong Wei wrote secretly to Murong Hong that he was a man in an iron cage, and with his cousin Murong Su planned to kill Fu Jiān at a feast for his son's wedding. The plot leaked, and Fu Jiān executed them and the Xianbei of the city. Southern Yan later named him Emperor You.
murong-xi: Murong Xi, courtesy name Daowen and known after death as Emperor Zhaowen, was born in 385 to Murong Chui, founder of the Xianbei-led Later Yan, and his concubine Consort Duan. He was made Prince of Hejian in 393. After his father's death in 396, Northern Wei forces under Tuoba Gui besieged the capital Zhongshan, and in 397 his brother Murong Bao moved the court to Longcheng. In the mutiny of 398 many princes were killed, but Murong Xi was spared through his friend Murong Chong. Under his nephew Murong Sheng he served as forward general against Goguryeo in 400.

During Murong Sheng's reign Murong Xi began an affair with the emperor's mother, Empress Dowager Ding. When Murong Sheng was assassinated in 401 she insisted that Murong Xi succeed, and he took the title Heavenly King. Within days he ordered Murong Sheng's brother Murong Yuán to commit suicide, and soon after the former crown prince Murong Ding. In 402 he took two daughters of the official Fu Mo, Fu Song'e and Fu Xunying, as concubines; when the neglected Empress Dowager Ding plotted against him, he forced her to commit suicide.

His building works cost many lives. Longteng Chateau, begun in 403, took the forced labour of 20,000 men, and more than half the soldiers who built Xiaoyao Palace in 404 were said to have died of heat and exhaustion. On a winter hunt with Empress Fu Xunying more than 5,000 escorting soldiers died. In 405 he nearly took the Goguryeo city of Liaodong but delayed the final entry, and the defenders refortified it.

When Empress Fu died in 407, Murong Xi forced Princess Zhang of Gaoyang to commit suicide so that she could be buried with her, and he left Longcheng with the funeral procession. The general Feng Ba and his brother Feng Sufu then rose and made Murong Yun, an adopted son of Murong Bao, Heavenly King. Murong Xi panicked and fled; he was found in civilian clothes in a forest and beheaded with his sons. Because Murong Yun later took back the surname Gao, historians differ on whether Murong Xi was the last emperor of Later Yan.
murong-yong: Murong Yong, courtesy name Shuming, was a grandson of Murong Yun, an uncle of the Former Yan founder Murong Huang. As a member of the imperial clan he was moved to Guanzhong, the capital region of Former Qin, when Former Qin destroyed Former Yan in 370. He was described as poor, and he and his wife made their living by selling boots.

He apparently became a Western Yan general in 384, when Murong Hong and Murong Chong rose against Former Qin. In 386, after Murong Chong was assassinated, Murong Yong took part in a rapid series of killings and depositions among the Xianbei leaders as they abandoned Chang'an and headed east. When the general Diao Yun killed Murong Zhong, he raised Murong Yong in his place, and Murong Yong first styled himself Prince of Hedong and sought to be a vassal of the Later Yan emperor Murong Chui.

Refused a passage east by the Former Qin emperor Fu Pi, Murong Yong defeated him, killed his prime minister Wang Yong and captured his officials and his wife, Empress Yang, who later tried to stab him and was killed. He took Fu Pi's lands in central and southern Shanxi, set his capital in what is now Changzhi and claimed the imperial title, breaking with Murong Chui. In 387 or 388 he ordered the slaughter of all descendants of Murong Chui and of the Former Yan emperor Murong Jun.

Once settled, he campaigned little. He was twice repelled from the Jin city of Luoyang, in 390 by the Jin general Zhu Xu and again in 391. In 392 he refused aid to the Dingling chief Zhai Zhao, besieged by Murong Chui, hoping the two would wear each other out; Murong Chui took Zhai's Wei lands easily, and Murong Yong later killed Zhai on suspicion of treason.

In 394 Murong Chui, advised by his brother Murong De, attacked by three routes. Murong Yong was defeated in the field, fled to his capital and appealed to Jin and Northern Wei, but the city fell before help came. His sons, the crown prince Murong Liang and Murong Hong, Duke of Changshan, died the same year, presumably with him, and Western Yan was annexed to Later Yan.
murray-maclehose: Crawford Murray MacLehose was born in Glasgow on 16 October 1917, the son of Hamish Alexander MacLehose, who owned a printing business, and Margaret Bruce Black. He went to Rugby School and Balliol College, Oxford, where he read modern history, and joined the colonial administration of British Malaya in 1939. Sent to the consulate in Xiamen in 1940 to learn Hokkien, he trained Chinese guerrillas for sabotage behind Japanese lines under cover as vice-consul, was detained by the Japanese in December 1941 and repatriated in 1942, then returned to China with British naval intelligence.

After the war he was acting consul in Fuzhou and from 1948 consul general in Hankou, where he learned Mandarin. He was principal private secretary to the Foreign Secretary George Brown and ambassador to South Vietnam from 1967 to 1969, surviving a lapse when he left a confidential telegram between Harold Wilson and Lyndon Johnson in a bank. He became governor in November 1971, after the 1967 riots, and served until May 1982, ten years and six months.

His reforms made Chinese an official language beside English, expanded welfare, began the Ten-year Housing Programme in 1972, introduced nine years of compulsory education, and built new towns such as Sha Tin and Tuen Mun, the Country Parks and the Mass Transit Railway. He set up District Boards and, under strong public pressure, the ICAC. In his first two years government spending rose by over 50%. He was convinced China would reclaim Hong Kong and opposed moves towards constitutional democracy. In 1979, as the first governor to visit the People's Republic officially, he raised the lease of the New Territories with Deng Xiaoping.

He is generally regarded as one of Hong Kong's most popular governors, and the 1970s became known as the MacLehose Era. Members of the pro-democracy camp, among them Martin Lee, criticised him for not pressing for democratic reform, while he insisted he had not given Hong Kong away. He became a life peer as Baron MacLehose of Beoch in 1982 and a Knight of the Thistle in 1983. He died in Ayrshire on 27 May 2000, and the 100-kilometre MacLehose Trail bears his name.
murrough-obrien-1st-earl-of-thomond: Murrough, in Irish Murchadh an Tánaiste Ó Briain, was a lineal descendant of Brian Boru, High King of Ireland, and the third or fourth son of Turlough O'Brien, Lord of Thomond, and Raghnailt, daughter of John MacNamara. When his brother Conor O'Brien died in 1539 he succeeded to the lordship of Thomond and the chieftainship of the Dal Cais by the custom of tanistry. Conor had tried in vain to pass the succession to his sons by his second wife, Ellen, sister of James Fitzjohn Fitzgerald, fourteenth earl of Desmond, and the attempt had caused much dissension between the brothers.

He first joined Con O'Neill and Manus O'Donnell in a confederacy against the English government, but Sir William Brereton foiled it, and when Sir Anthony St Leger arrived as viceroy O'Brien asked to parley. Meeting him at Limerick early in 1541, he readily acknowledged Henry VIII as his sovereign and renounced the supremacy of the Pope, but asked for time over terms that would confine his authority to the west of the River Shannon. Con O'Neill's submission in December 1541 moved him to accept them.

Reconciling succession by tanistry with inheritance by the eldest son took some time. Under the settlement O'Brien was made Earl of Thomond for life, the title passing at his death not to his eldest son but to his nephew Donough, created Baron Ibrickan. At his own request he served on the commission for suppressing the religious houses of Thomond, and St Leger lent him £100 in harp-groats for his journey to England. He reached court in June 1543 with Ulic de Burgh, 1st earl of Clanricarde, and Henry also granted him a house and lands in Dublin.

Back in Ireland he still quarrelled with his neighbours, the Burkes and the Munster Geraldines, but he held St Leger in sincere regard, saw him off in April 1546 and welcomed him back in 1550. He died on 7 November 1551. Donough succeeded him, surrendered the patent and on 7 November 1552 received a new one granting the title to him and the heirs male of his body. Murrough married Eleanor FitzGerald, daughter of Thomas FitzGerald, Knight of the Valley, and they had three sons and four daughters.
murshid-quli-khan: According to the historian Sir Jadunath Sarkar, Murshid Quli Khan was born a Hindu Brahmin named Surya Narayan Mishra in the Deccan; the 18th-century compendium Ma'asir al-umara also gives him a Brahmin origin. At about ten he was sold to a Persian, Haji Shafi, who converted him to Islam and raised him as Mohammad Hadi. He went with Shafi to Persia around 1690 and, some years after his master's death, returned to India to serve Abdullah Khurasani, the diwan of Vidarbha, where his skill in revenue matters drew the notice of Emperor Aurangzeb.

As diwan of Bengal from about 1700 he quarrelled with the governor, Prince Azim-us-Shan, who wanted the revenue for his own bid for the throne and, by one account, plotted to have him stabbed by unpaid soldiers. Murshid Quli wrote to Aurangzeb, who warned the prince. Feeling unsafe in Dhaka, he moved his office to Mukshudabad, and Aurangzeb, pleased with the revenue brought to him at Bijapur, gave him the title Murshid Quli and leave to rename the town. Historians differ over the year of the renaming, 1703 or about 1704; the town's first coins date from 1704.

After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 he was sent away as diwan of the Deccan, but returned to Bengal in 1710. Emperor Farrukhsiyar made him governor in 1717, and the capital moved from Dhaka to Murshidabad. He replaced the jagirdari system with the mal jasmani, under which revenue contractors, later known as zamindars, squeezed out the jagirdars, and he sent 1 crore 30 lakh rupees to the emperor each year.

He built a palace, a revenue office, a mint in 1720 and the Katra Masjid in 1724. He died on 30 June 1727 and was buried, as he had wished, under the stairs of that mosque. His grandson Sarfaraz Khan was named to succeed him, but gave way without a fight to his son-in-law Shuja-ud-Din Muhammad Khan.
murshidabad: Murshidabad lies on the eastern bank of the Bhagirathi River in West Bengal and is the headquarters of the Lalbag subdivision of Murshidabad district. The area was part of the Gauda Kingdom and the Vanga Kingdom in ancient Bengal. The Riyaz-us-Salatin credits the initial development of the town to a merchant named Makhsus Khan. In the 17th century the area was well known for sericulture, and in 1621 English agents reported large quantities of silk available there.

In the early 18th century Murshid Quli Khan, prime minister of the Bengal Subah, had a bitter rivalry with Prince Azim-ush-Shan, the viceroy of Bengal, who even tried to have him killed. With the Mughal court in Delhi losing authority, Emperor Farrukhsiyar promoted Khan to the status of a princely Nawab. He moved the capital of Bengal from Dhaka, which had lost its strategic importance after the expulsion of the Arakanese and Portuguese from Chittagong, and founded Murshidabad. It became the centre of political, economic and cultural life, and the Nawab's jurisdiction covered Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. The capital of the Bengal Subah stayed there for seventy years.

The princely court, the Mughal Army, artisans and merchants of many origins brought wealth. The Murshidabad mint became the largest in Bengal. Murshid Quli Khan built a palace and a caravanserai with a grand mosque, the Katra Masjid, and the third Nawab, Shuja-ud-Din Muhammad Khan, built a compound called Farrabagh with a revenue office, a durbar hall and a treasury. Siraj-ud-Daulah built a palace near the Motijhil. Jain traders, Armenian financiers and the banking family of the Jagat Seth family settled in the city, and the French, Dutch, Danish and British East India Companies and the Ostend Company operated factories nearby.

Siraj-ud-Daulah, the last independent Nawab, was defeated at the Battle of Plassey in 1757, betrayed by his commander Mir Jafar. The British installed Mir Jafar's family as a puppet dynasty and reduced the Nawab to a zamindar. Warren Hastings moved the supreme civil and criminal courts to Calcutta in 1772, and in 1790 Lord Cornwallis moved the whole revenue and judicial staff there. The Hazarduari Palace was built in 1837.
The Hazarduari Palace and its associated sites in the Kila Nizamat area, with the Katra Masjid, the Fauti Mosque, the Jama Masjid and the Motijhil, are the town's main attractions.
mursili-i: Mursili I, also transcribed Mursilis or Murshili, was a king of the Hittites and was likely a grandson of his predecessor, Hattusili I. His sister was Ḫarapšili and his wife was Queen Kali. He came to the throne as a minor, and on reaching adulthood he renewed Hattusili I's warfare in northern Syria. The dates of his reign depend on the chronology used: the middle chronology, the most widely accepted, places it from about 1620 to about 1590 BCE, and the short chronology from about 1556 to 1526 BCE.

Mursili invaded Yamhad and its capital Aleppo, which had eluded Hattusili I. He then led a march of 2,000 km southeast into Mesopotamia, the first of its kind, where around 1595 BCE he sacked Babylon. His motive is unclear. William Broad has proposed that he wanted grain, because clouds from the Minoan eruption had reduced the Hittite harvests. The raid cannot have been meant to establish rule, since Babylon was too far from Anatolia. It is thought to have ended the Amorite dynasty of Hammurabi and allowed the Kassites to take power, and may have arisen from an alliance with them or a wish to outdo his predecessor.

When Mursili returned to his kingdom he was assassinated in a conspiracy led by his brother-in-law Hantili I, who took the throne, and by Hantili's son-in-law Zidanta I. His death began a period of social unrest and decay of central rule, followed by the loss of the conquests made in Syria.
mursili-ii: Mursili was the fifth son of King Suppiluliuma I and Queen Henti, and the younger brother of Arnuwanda II. He also had a sister and three more brothers. Two surviving elder brothers served as viceroys of Carchemish and Aleppo, among them Sarri-Kush. The plague that ravaged the Hittites in the 1330s BCE killed both his father and Arnuwanda, and Mursili assumed the throne in 1321 BCE, after Arnuwanda's premature death. Dates for his reign vary with the chronology used: about 1330 to 1295 BCE in the middle chronology, or 1321 to 1295 BCE in the short chronology.

Hatti's enemies greeted him with contempt, since he was seen as an inexperienced ruler who had become king only through Arnuwanda's early death, and he faced numerous rebellions early in his reign. The most serious were those begun by the Kaskas in the mountains of Anatolia, by the Arzawa kingdom in south-western Asia Minor and by the Hayasa-Azzi confederation in eastern Anatolia. His Annals record the scorn of one foe: "You are a child; you know nothing and instill no fear in me." Young and inexperienced as he was, he was almost certainly not a child: had he been one, other arrangements would have been made to secure the empire's stability.

The Annals for his first ten years survive. In the first two years he carried out punitive campaigns against the Kaska tribes to secure the northern borders. He then turned west to resist Uhhaziti, king of Arzawa, who was trying to lure Hittite allies into his camp. In his ninth year his cupbearer Nuvanza decisively defeated the Hayasan forces at the Battle of Ganuvara, after which the Hayasa-Azzi were reduced to Hittite vassals. The Annals also record an omen of the sun, a solar eclipse, in his tenth year, as he was about to launch his campaign against the Hayasa-Azzi.

This eclipse matters for dating the Hittite Empire within the chronology of the ancient Near East. Only two dates are possible, 24 June 1312 BCE or 13 April 1308 BCE. Trevor R. Bryce accepts the earlier, and most scholars follow, because it was near total over Anatolia around noon, while Paul Åström suggested the later.

His highest confirmed date is his twenty-second year. He is believed to have lived a few years beyond it and to have died after a reign of about 25 to 27 years, and his son Muwatalli II succeeded him. Another son, Hattusili III, also became a king. Mursili is known from many cuneiform texts, among them the Annals, treaties with Duppi-Teššup of Amurru, Niqmepa of Ugarit, Targašnalli of Ḫapalla and Manapa-Tarḫunta of Šēḫa, decrees on the borders of Ugarit, plague prayers and hymns to the Sun Goddess of Arinna.
murska-sobota: Murska Sobota lies near the Mura river in north-eastern Slovenia and is the regional capital of Prekmurje and the centre of its own municipality. Inhabitants usually call it simply Sobota, while people from other parts of Slovenia say Murska. Its German name is Olsnitz, derived from an old Slovene name, Olšnica. The modern Slovene name translates the Hungarian Muraszombat, the official name until 1919; szombat means Saturday and refers to the weekly fairs held on that day. The settlement is first attested in writing in 1297 as Belmura, and later as Murazombatha in 1348 and Murazumbota in 1366.

The town was part of the Balatin Sanjak under Ottoman rule, which belonged first to the Budin Eyalet and later to the Kanije Eyalet, until the Treaty of Karlowitz. In the Kingdom of Hungary it was a district town of Vas County until 1918. In 1919 a republic of Prekmurje was declared here, and the town was its capital. Murska Sobota later stood as the northernmost town of Yugoslavia, and its borders shifted repeatedly between Slovenia, Yugoslavia and Hungary. Hungary annexed most of Prekmurje from 1941 to 1944, German forces occupied it in 1944 and 1945, and Soviet troops captured the town in May 1945.

The town had a significant Jewish community. Its synagogue, built by Lipót Baumhorn, was consecrated on 31 August 1908. On 26 April 1944 all the Jews of the town were ordered to gather there with hand luggage only and were locked in overnight without food or water. The next morning they were sent to Čakovec and then to Nagykanizsa, the main camp before Auschwitz, where the last rabbi, Lazar Roth, was murdered. The community was destroyed, and the local communist authorities, having bought the building from the decimated congregation, demolished the synagogue in 1954.

Hungarians still form a minority of about 3,000 in the town. Its economy rests on regional administration, light industry, commerce and spa tourism. In April 2006 it became the seat of the newly created Roman Catholic Diocese of Murska Sobota, a suffragan of the archdiocese of Maribor. A memorial to the Jews of Prekmurje, the first Holocaust memorial in Slovenia, was unveiled at its railway station on 29 January 2010.
muryeong-of-baekje: Muryeong was the 25th king of Baekje, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea. His tomb calls him King Sama, and the Samguk sagi gives his personal name as Sama and describes him as the second son of the 24th king, Dongseong; the Nihonshoki instead makes him the son of Prince Gonji, and so Dongseong's half-brother. The Liang shu of China names him Yeo Yung. He came to the throne when Dongseong was assassinated by the court official Baek Ga, whose planned rebellion he crushed the following year.

Baekje remained allied with Silla against Goguryeo. In 501 he sent an army against Goguryeo's Sugok-seong, in 503 he repelled an attack by the Mohe, and in 507 he turned back a joint Goguryeo and Mohe attack. When Goguryeo took two castles in 512, he led 3,000 men in person to destroy its army, and in 523 he ordered a fortified wall built along the northern border.

In 512, according to the Liang shu, he sent Baekje's first mission to the new court of the Liang dynasty, and a second in 521 announced his victories over Goguryeo. The Liang emperor gave him titles including Great General Tranquilizing the East and King of Baekje, which were also found engraved in his tomb. To Japan he sent a bronze mirror in 503 and Confucian scholars in 513 and 516.

His tomb at Songsan-ri in Gongju, excavated in 1971, held him and his queen. His son Seong succeeded him; another son, Prince Junda, settled in Japan and died there in 513. The Shoku Nihongi makes Takano no Niigasa, mother of Emperor Kanmu, a descendant of Junda, and in 2001 Emperor Akihito referred to this, the first time a Japanese emperor spoke publicly of Korean blood in the imperial line.
murzuq: Murzuq, also spelled Murzuk, is an oasis town and the capital of the Murzuq District in the Fezzan region of south-western Libya. It lies on the northern edge of the Murzuq Desert, an extremely arid region of ergs, or great sand dunes, that forms part of the Sahara.

The town developed around an oasis that served as a stop on the north-south trade route across the Sahara. From the 5th century BCE to the 5th century CE the area was home to the Garamantian Empire, a city state that operated the trans-Saharan routes between the Carthaginians, and later the Roman Empire, and the states of West and Central Africa. By 1300 the Arab Banu Sulaym tribe ruled the area. By 1400 it was ruled by the Bornu Empire, whose legacy survives in street names in the Kanembu and Kanuri languages, and in the later 15th century it became a tributary of the Hafsid dynasty of Tunis.

Early in the 16th century Muhammad al-Fasi founded the Awlad Muhammad dynasty, which held power in the city until 1812. Tradition holds him to be a Moroccan sharif. His dynasty reinvigorated pilgrim traffic and the slave trade, and Murzuq became part of a slaving network reaching into present-day Chad and the Central African Republic. By the late 16th century it was more important than Ghat and Ghadames.

Under Ottoman rule, from 1574 to 1912, Murzuq was at times the capital of Fezzan and enjoyed a long period of prosperity. It had a major fort and was termed the Paris of the Sahara. An Ottoman garrison was usually kept there, but local control stayed with the Sultan of Fezzan.

In the early nineteenth century Murzuq was the jumping-off point for British expeditions in search of Lake Chad and Timbuktu. The expedition of Denham, Oudney and Clapperton travelled there from Tripoli in 1822. Many British explorers thought the town unhealthy: James Richardson, in 1846, reported that three quarters of the Europeans who came there fell ill with what was called Mourzuk fever.

The town declined as modern transport replaced the caravan routes. The Ottomans ceded Fezzan to the Italians in 1912, though the town was not occupied until 1914. On 11 January 1941 about 70 men of the British Long Range Desert Group and a few Free French soldiers from Chad raided the town and its small Italian airbase, and the Italian garrison in the old fort eventually surrendered.
mus: Muş is one of the principal cities of the predominantly Kurdish-inhabited region of eastern Anatolia. It is the seat of Muş Province and Muş District. The town and the surrounding plain are often covered in fog in the mornings, and the name is sometimes linked to the Armenian word mshush, meaning fog. The 17th-century traveller Evliya Çelebi tells of a giant mouse, created by Nimrod, that destroyed the city, which was then called Muş, the Persian word for mouse. Others connect the name with the Mushki or the Mysians.

The date of foundation is unknown, but a settlement is believed to have existed by the time of Menua, king of Urartu, around 800 BCE, whose cuneiform inscription was found near the city. An inscription of the Urartian king Argisti I, who reigned from 785 to 765 BCE, was found near Kepenek Castle. In the Middle Ages the city was the centre of the Taron region of Armenia and is first mentioned as a city in Armenian manuscripts of the 9th and 10th centuries.

Taron came under the Bagratid dynasty in the late 8th century and was annexed to the Byzantine Empire in 969. After the Seljuk victory at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 it passed to the Ahlatshahs, and later to the Ayyubids, Ilkhanids and Kara Koyunlu. Between the 10th and 13th centuries Muş grew into a major city of an estimated 20 to 25 thousand people. Timur apparently took it without a battle in 1387. The Safavids held it before the Ottoman sultan Selim I took the town and region in the early 16th century, and it kept a large Armenian population under Ottoman rule.

At the turn of the twentieth century the city had around 20,000 inhabitants, of which 11,000 were Muslims and 9,000 were Christian Armenians. In June and July 1915, during the Armenian genocide, over 140,000 Armenians of the Muş sanjak, in 234 villages and towns, were targeted; the city's Armenians were killed only after the surrounding villages had been destroyed. Russian forces captured the town in February 1916, and the Second Army under Mustafa Kemal Pasha retook it in 1917.

The municipality had about 120,699 inhabitants in 2022, a majority of them Kurds, with Arabs and Hidden Armenians among them. Sights include the Murat Bridge, Muş Castle, Kepenek Castle and mosques showing Seljuk influence, among them the Ulu Mosque of the 14th century, once an Armenian church. Medieval Armenian monasteries and churches near the city, such as Arakelots and Surb Karapet, are mostly ruins; Arakelots was dynamited by local officials in the 1960s.
musa-dagh: The mountain's name means Moses Mountain: it is Musa Dağı in Turkish, Musa leṛ in Armenian and Jebel Musa in Arabic. Until after the First World War it lay in the Aleppo Vilayet of the Ottoman Empire. Six Armenian villages stood in the Musa Dagh region: Kabusie, Yoghunolukh, Bitias, Vakef, Khederbeg and Haji-Habibli. After the war the French took possession of the area and placed it in the Sanjak of Alexandretta, part of the Mandate of Syria.

The Ottoman government's orders for the deportation of the Armenian population reached the six villages in July 1915. As Ottoman Turkish forces converged, the villagers refused deportation and withdrew onto the mountain, where they held off assaults from July to September 1915. One of the leaders of the resistance was Movses Der Kalusdian, whose Armenian first name was the same as the mountain's. Ships of the French 3rd Squadron in the Mediterranean, under Vice Admiral Louis Dartige du Fournet, sighted the defenders just as their ammunition and food were running out.

Five French ships took the survivors to Port Said: the protected cruiser Guichen under Captain Jean-Joseph Brisson, which came first, the seaplane carrier Foudre, the protected cruiser D'Estrées and the armoured cruisers Amiral Charner and Dupleix. They carried 3,004 women and children and over 1,000 men. From 1918, when the Sanjak of Alexandretta came under French control, the villagers returned to their homes, and in 1932 a monument to the defence was raised on the summit. On 29 June 1939, under an agreement between France and Turkey, the province passed to Turkey.

Vakıflı, whose residents partly chose to stay in 1939, is the only remaining ethnic Armenian village in Turkey, with about 140 Turkish-Armenian inhabitants. Those who left settled mostly in the town of Anjar in Lebanon, which is divided into six districts named after the villages of Musa Dagh. Franz Werfel, who said he wished to aid the Armenian people by bringing their struggle to the world, published his novel in 1933. When Nazi Germany began conquering Europe it was read in the Warsaw and Vilna ghettos, and the resisters of the Bialystok ghetto spoke of their own Musa Dagh moment.
musa-ibn-musa: Musa ibn Musa, nicknamed the Great, descended from Cassius, who converted to Islam after the Muslim conquest of Iberia. His mother, whose name is not known, was by another husband the mother of the Basque chieftain Íñigo Arista, according to the chronicler Ibn Hayyan. His early years are obscure, but he is presumed to have supported the Basques against the Franks at the Second Battle of Ronceveaux, a battle generally credited with giving birth to the Kingdom of Pamplona.

He first appears in 840/41, rising with Íñigo against Emir Abd ar-Rahman II after attacks on Íñigo's lands and the expulsion of a kinsman by the governors of Zaragoza and Tudela. Over the next decade he rebelled and submitted again and again. In 842, believing himself mistreated in the emir's army, he joined his nephew García Íñiguez of Pamplona in defeating a Cordoban force; the emir's campaigns of 843 and 844 defeated the allies, and in November 844 Musa helped defeat the Viking raiders who had sacked Seville. His brother Yunus ibn Musa stayed loyal to Córdoba and fought him for about 30 years.

In 851/2 Íñigo Arista and Abd ar-Rahman II both died, and Musa won a two-day battle near Albelda over Basque or Gascon forces. The new emir, Muhammad, named him Wāli of Zaragoza and governor of the Upper March. Holding Zaragoza, Tudela, Huesca and Toledo, he ruled what was in effect a state from Nájera to Zaragoza and Calatayud. He attacked Álava for Córdoba in 855 and Barcelona and Terrassa on his own account in 856, and later let a Viking force pass to attack Pamplona, where they captured García Íñiguez, who then joined Ordoño I of Asturias against him.

Christian sources remembered his defeat at Albelda as the Battle of Clavijo, a battle of legend. In 860 Emir Muhammad removed him as wali and governor. In 862, moving against his son-in-law Azraq ibn Mantil ibn Salim, he attacked Guadalajara and was wounded so badly he could not mount a horse, and he died at Tutila on 26 September 862. The family vanished from politics for a decade, then ruled a shrinking territory for another half-century, until the last of his principality was gone by the end of the 920s.
musa-ibn-nusayr: His ancestry is variously reported. Al-Tabari says his father was an Arab Christian of the Banu Yashkur held hostage after the fall of Ayn al-Tamr in 633, while al-Baladhuri calls him an Arab of the Balī tribe from Palestine. As a slave his father entered the service of Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan, governor of Egypt, who freed him, and Musa was born in Syria, with the date given as 640. The caliph Abd al-Malik made him co-governor of Iraq. After a quarrel over missing tax money he was told to pay a huge fine or lose his head, and Abd al-Aziz paid the ransom and later had him appointed governor of Ifriqiya.

In 698 Musa became governor of Ifriqiya, the first not subordinate to the governor of Egypt, and he completed the conquest of North Africa. He did not impose Islam by force but respected Berber traditions and used diplomacy, and many Berbers converted and entered his army, possibly including Tariq ibn Ziyad. He took Tangiers and the Sous, and built a navy that conquered Ibiza, Mallorca and Menorca.

Sources say he decided to cross to Hispania when Julian, Count of Ceuta, encouraged him with accounts of the injustice of King Roderic. After a successful raid of 400 men at Tarifa he sent Tariq with about 7,000 Berbers and Arabs, who defeated Roderic's much larger army at the Battle of Guadalete. Musa then landed with 18,000 men, took Seville after a siege of three months and Mérida after five, and met Tariq at Toledo. When Caliph al-Walid I ordered him to report to Damascus, he delayed in order to continue north, taking Zaragoza, Oviedo and reaching the Bay of Biscay before he placed governors across al-Andalus.

In Damascus Musa entered the city in spite of a request to delay, and brought the booty before the ailing al-Walid. After al-Walid's death his brother Sulayman stripped Musa of his rank and confiscated the spoils. His son Abd al-Aziz, who had married Roderic's widow Egilona, was assassinated, and another son, Abd Allah, was executed on the caliph's orders. Musa died naturally while on the Hajj with Sulayman in about 715 or 716. Because of his disgrace, some medieval historians of the Maghreb gave his deeds to Uqba ibn Nafi. Legend made him the hero of a tale of the city of brass, told in the One Thousand and One Nights, and the Moroccan peak Jebel Musa is said to be named for him.
musa-molo: Musa Molo Balde came of a family descended from slaves and originally from Bundu. His father Alfa Molo founded Fuladu after the Battle of Kansala in 1867, having led a Fula rebellion against the Mandinka rulers of Kaabu, and Musa had great influence in his government as a military leader and as Fuladu's representative in meetings with the British. On his father's death in 1881 he accepted, as custom required, the nominal rule of his uncle Bakary Demba, while keeping political and military control over much of what is now the Senegalese region of Kolda. He came to power in his own right in 1893.

While still the power behind his uncle's throne, he repressed rebellions in the south of Fuladu, killing his rivals and enslaving their families, and removed challengers within his family with French support. He built a more centralised government than his father's, though weak transport and communication limited its reach, twice invaded Kantora and imposed heavy taxes for his wars. His harsh rule drove Fula and minority peoples to emigrate, often to European trading posts; he raised the taxes of those who stayed, arrested those who could not pay, enslaved people where he could and cut off the limbs of those who angered him, above all Mandinka.

The British first contacted him in 1880, and the French signed a treaty with him three years later. The British, the French and the Portuguese drew lines on maps dividing Fuladu among them, but he used his treaties with all three to strengthen his own power. With French help he defeated and killed the Mandinka warlord Fode Kaba in 1901 and conquered Niani and Kantora, but in return he gave up half his tax revenue and accepted a French resident at Hamdallaye. The British and French divided Fuladu into spheres of influence in 1900, and the British annexed their share into the Gambia Colony and Protectorate in 1902.

In May 1903, rather than submit to the French, he led about 3,000 people, some of them forced to come, to the British side. The British made him a chief in Fulladu West with a stipend of 500 pounds a year. Exiled to Sierra Leone after a local revolt in 1919, he returned four years later and relied on marriage alliances with Fula and Mandinka notables. He died at Keserekunda in 1931. His son was district chief from 1924 to 1952 and his grandson from 1964 to 1997.
musab-ibn-al-zubayr: Mus'ab was a son of Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, a prominent companion of the Prophet Muhammad, and of Rabab bint Unayf, a daughter of a chieftain of the Banu Kalb. In the last years of the caliph Mu'awiya I he belonged to a group that met in the mosque of Medina, among them his half-brother Urwa and the future Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. His wives included A'isha, a daughter of Talha ibn Ubayd Allah, and Sukayna, a daughter of Husayn ibn Ali.

After the death of the caliph Yazid in November 683, Mus'ab's half-brother Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr was recognised as caliph in most of the Caliphate. Mus'ab led an expedition against Umayyad Palestine in 684/685, which Amr ibn Sa'id al-Ashdaq repulsed, and then governed Medina. When Mukhtar al-Thaqafi seized Kufa in 685, Ibn al-Zubayr made Mus'ab governor of Basra in 686 to recover Kufa and fight the Kharijites, and Mus'ab sent his commander Muhallab ibn Abi Sufra against the Azariqa in Fars and Kirman.

After defeating Mukhtar's army at Madhar and Harura, Mus'ab besieged him in the palace of Kufa for four months. Between 6,000 and 8,000 of Mukhtar's supporters surrendered, and under pressure from the vengeful tribal nobles Mus'ab executed them all, which left Kufa resentful. Briefly removed by his brother after complaints and then restored, he put down the rebellion of Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hurr al-Ju'fi, faced Abd al-Malik in campaigns of 689 and 690 that ended without battle, and harshly punished Umayyad loyalists in Basra after a revolt there.

In 691 Abd al-Malik camped at Maskin. Mus'ab could raise only a small army, and Abd al-Malik won over most of his commanders with promises of money and governorships. Mus'ab ignored a warning from Ibrahim ibn al-Ashtar, and when Ibn al-Ashtar fell early in the battle the rest refused to fight or defected. His son Isa was killed before his eyes. Mus'ab refused an offer of amnesty and was killed by Za'ida ibn Qudama al-Thaqafi, a follower of Mukhtar. He was buried at Dayr al-Jathaliq, where a mausoleum over his grave became a pilgrimage site.
musavat: Musavat was founded in 1911 in Baku as a secret organisation by Mahammad Amin Rasulzade, his cousin Mahammad Ali Rasulzade, Abbasgulu Kazimzade and Taghi Nagioglu, under the name Muslim Democratic Musavat Party. The initiative came from Rasulzade while he was living in exile in Istanbul. Before the First World War it was a small underground group working, like counterparts across the Middle East, for the prosperity and political unity of the Muslim and Turkic-speaking world. Though it espoused pan-Islamic ideas and its founder sympathised with the pan-Turkic movement, it supported the tsarist regime during the war.

After the Amnesty Act of 1913, Rasulzade returned to Azerbaijan and took the leadership. On 17 June 1917 the party merged with the Party of Turkic Federalists, and at its first congress in October 1917 it adopted a programme of 76 articles calling for a federative democratic republic in Russia based on national and territorial autonomy. In February 1918 it entered the Transcaucasian Sejm with 30 of 125 deputies.

After the Declaration of Independence, Musavat became the leading party of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic and held the majority of seats in its National Council and then in its parliament. Rasulzade was its first head of state, from 28 May to 7 December 1918. Under Musavat's leadership the name Azerbaijan, previously used only for the adjacent region of north-western Iran, was adopted. In 1919 women were granted the right to vote. Nasib bey Yusifbeyli, a party member, was prime minister from March 1919.

The Bolshevik invasion ended the republic in April 1920. Musavat returned to secret activity, prepared Rasulzade's flight to Finland and organised armed uprisings at Ganja, Karabakh, Zagatala and Lankaran. The Soviets arrested at least 2,000 of its members up to 1923, and the party ceased all activity within Azerbaijan that year. Rasulzade set up a Foreign Bureau in 1923, centred on Istanbul in the 1920s and early 1930s and on Ankara from the late 1940s.

Musavat was revived in Azerbaijan in 1989, when a group of intellectuals created the Azerbaijan National Democratic New Musavat Party, which was recognised by the exile party. In 1992 delegates of both gathered at the III Congress of Musavat and formally re-established it, with Isa Gambar, a leader of the Popular Front, as chairman. The party was barred from the parliamentary elections of 1995 and 2000. In the 2000 and 2001 elections it won 4.9 per cent of the vote and two of 125 seats, and Gambar won 12.2 per cent in the presidential election of 15 October 2003. It is the oldest existing political party in Azerbaijan.
musaylima: Musaylima, whose full name was Muslima ibn Habib al-Hanafi, was the son of Habib of the Banu Hanifa, one of the largest tribes of Arabia, which lived in the region of Najd. Muslims changed his name Maslama to the diminutive Musaylima and call him Musaylima al-Kadhab, the arch-liar. He first appears in the late 9th Hijri year, the Year of Delegations, when he accompanied a delegation of his tribe to Medina. He stayed behind to look after the camels while the others met Muhammad, and the delegation embraced Islam before returning home.

Historians differ over how reliable the later story is: Christian J. Robin argues that the political events were too notable to have been invented, while Gerald Hawting regards reports of activity before or independent of Muhammad as a later fabrication.

Muslim historians describe him as a skilled magician who performed feats that amazed onlookers, and he shared verses that he presented as revelations from God. According to al-Tabari, in 10 Hijri he wrote to Muhammad proposing a division of power, saying that half the earth belonged to his people and half to the Quraish; Muhammad is said to have replied by calling him the arch-liar. Al-Tabari also records that he set up a sacred enclave in the Yamamah. He is said to have composed in saj', a rhymed prose common in pre-Islamic speech.

After the death of Muhammad he led one of the tribal rebellions of the Ridda wars. Sajah bint al-Harith, who had declared herself a prophetess, planned to march on Medina but called off the attack when Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated Tulayha al-Asadi, another claimant. She then sought cooperation with Musaylima and the two married; she accepted his prophethood, though she later recanted and died a Muslim. Khalid defeated the remaining rebels around Sajah and then moved against Musaylima.

Musaylima fought at the Battle of Yamama and was killed by Wahshi ibn Harb. His career has been compared with that of other prophet claimants of the sixth and seventh centuries, among them Khalid ibn Sinan, al-Aswad al-Ansi and Ibn Sayyad. A 17th-century work on the religions of India, the Dabestan-e Mazaheb, describes a group called the Sadakiyya who followed him and attributes to him teachings such as three daily prayers facing any direction and the freeing of any slave who converted. A discussion of the Sadakiyya is said to have taken place at the Mughal ruler Akbar's council of religions.
muscat: Muscat lies in northeast Oman on the Gulf of Oman, near the Strait of Hormuz, with the Hajar Mountains rising behind it. The water along its coast is deep, forming two natural harbours, at Muttrah and at Muscat itself. Muttrah, with its corniche and harbour, lies at the northeastern edge of the city. The climate is hot and arid, with about 10 centimetres of rain a year.

Ptolemy knew Muscat as a port in the 1st century CE, calling it Cryptus Portus, the Hidden Port, and Pliny the Elder called it Amithoscuta. It fell to a Sassanid invasion in the 3rd century under Shapur I, and conversion to Islam came in the 7th century. Coastal ports such as Muscat prospered from maritime trade and ties with the Indian subcontinent.

The Portuguese admiral Afonso de Albuquerque sailed to Muscat in 1507 to establish trade, but his ships were fired on as he approached, and he decided to conquer it. Most of the city burned. The Portuguese held it for over a century, despite a bombardment by the Ottoman Turks in 1546, and the Turks captured it twice, in 1552 and in 1581–88. The election of Nasir bin Murshid Al-Ya'rubi as Imam in 1624 shifted power to local Omanis. On 23 January 1650 the Imam's troops forced a Portuguese surrender.

A civil war and repeated incursions by the Persian king Nader Shah in the 18th century left a power vacuum, from which the Al Bu Sa'id dynasty emerged, and it has ruled Oman ever since. In 1793 the capital was transferred from Rustaq to Muscat. Said bin Sultan, who restored its naval strength in the 19th century, moved his capital to Zanzibar in 1840. On 23 July 1970 Qaboos bin Said took power in a bloodless coup, and Muscat then developed rapidly.

Muscat is the capital and most populous city of Oman, and the seat of the Governorate of Muscat, which has six wilayat. Arabic is the predominant language, and Islam, mostly Ibadi, is the main religion. The Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque is among its many mosques, and Old Muscat and the Old Palace, with the forts, hold its past.
muscogee: The Muscogee, or Mvskoke, are a group of related Indigenous peoples of the Southeastern Woodlands. Their historical homelands lie in what is now southern Tennessee, much of Alabama, western Georgia and parts of northern Florida. Their ancestors were part of the Mississippian cultures, which between 800 and 1600 CE built complex cities with earthwork mounds, surrounded by satellite towns and farmsteads. The Muscogee are associated with mound sites such as Ocmulgee, Etowah and Moundville.

Spanish explorers met their ancestors in the mid-16th century. The Spanish expedition brought epidemics of smallpox and measles, and the Indian slave trade conducted by colonists in the 17th and 18th centuries added to the losses. As survivors and their descendants regrouped, the Muscogee Creek Confederacy arose as a loose alliance of Muskogee-speaking peoples.

The English founded Charles Town in 1670, and traders from Carolina visited Muscogee towns to exchange firearms, gunpowder, axes, glass beads, cloth and rum for deerskins and Indian slaves. Spain built missions, while the British and French preferred trade to conversion. In the American Revolutionary War the Muscogee leaned towards the British, but, divided by factions, generally avoided sustained fighting. Many leaders of the period, among them Alexander McGillivray and William McIntosh, bore British names through intermarriage.

In 1811 the Shawnee leader Tecumseh visited Tuckabatchee, telling the Muscogee that a comet signalled his coming. Upper Towns, inspired by him and by their own religious leaders, resisted American encroachment. The result was the Red Stick War, or Creek War, of 1813-1814, which began as a civil war and became entangled with the War of 1812. General Andrew Jackson put down the rebellion with the help of Southern Muscogee, and the nation was forced to sign the Treaty of Fort Jackson on 9 August 1814, ceding land even from those who had fought beside him.

Under Jackson's presidency from 1829 the government pursued the removal of all tribes east of the Mississippi River to Oklahoma. In the 1830s most of the Muscogee were forcibly relocated to Indian Territory. A small group remained in Alabama, and others had earlier moved into Florida, where they helped form the Seminole.

The Muscogee are matrilineal: each person belongs to the clan of their mother, and inheritance and property pass through the maternal line. Hereditary chiefs were born into certain clans. Town networks were laid out around plazas, ballparks and square ceremonial dance grounds. The Stomp Dance and the Green Corn Ceremony remain revered gatherings, and stickball games, festivals and language classes continue to sustain a tribal identity.

The Muscogee language belongs to the Eastern Muskogean branch of the Muskogean family. Today the Muscogee (Creek) Nation is headquartered at Okmulgee, Oklahoma, and the Poarch Band of Creek Indians is federally recognised in Alabama.
muscovite-lithuanian-wars: Lithuania had grown after the Mongol invasions to hold vast lands from Kiev to Mozhaysk, having absorbed Chernigov and Severia by the mid-14th century. Its ruler Algirdas led three expeditions against Moscow, the first in 1368, and Vytautas the Great kept Smolensk after a standoff on the Ugra River in 1402. In the late 15th century Ivan III of Moscow proclaimed himself sovereign of all Russia and claimed the former lands of Kievan Rus’. After the Golden Horde’s supremacy ended in 1480 he annexed Novgorod in 1477 and Tver in 1483, and his ambitions then clashed with Lithuania.

Around 1486 and 1487 the border on the upper Oka came under attack from Moscow and its ally Meñli I Giray, Khan of Crimea, and in August 1492 Ivan III began large operations. An eternal peace of 5 February 1494 gave Moscow Vyazma and a region on the upper Oka. War resumed in May 1500; the Lithuanians lost the Battle of Vedrosha on 14 July 1500, and a truce of 25 March 1503 cost them about a third of their territory, including Chernigov, Novgorod-Seversk and Starodub. In 1508 Michael Glinski rebelled and joined Moscow, and a peace of 8 October 1508 kept the 1503 terms.

In December 1512 Moscow invaded to take Smolensk, which fell in July 1514. On 8 September 1514 the Russians suffered a major defeat at the Battle of Orsha, yet the Lithuanians could not recapture Smolensk, and a treaty of 1522 left it with Russia. A last war in 1534–1537 centred on Starodub, and a five-year truce left Gomel with the king and Sebezh and Zavoloche with Moscow.

After repeated defeats Lithuania relied increasingly on Polish aid, which became an important factor in the creation of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. The Livonian War, fought from 1558 over the lands around the Baltic, continued the contest, and the Union of Lublin of 1569 formed the Commonwealth. Stefan Batory took back Polatsk in 1579, and the Peace of Jam Zapolski ended that war, with the tsar giving up his claims to Livonia and Polotsk. The historian Edvardas Gudavičius saw in the terms of 1503 a planned political aggression, since Ivan III’s concept of a sovereign of all Russia left no room for the Lithuanian state.
muscovy-company: The company traces its roots to the Company of Merchant Adventurers to New Lands, founded in 1551 by Thomas White, Richard Chancellor, Sebastian Cabot and Sir Hugh Willoughby to look for a Northeast Passage to China. Its first expedition of three ships left London on 10 May 1553 under Willoughby, with Chancellor as navigator, and a storm separated Chancellor's ship from the others. Willoughby's ship became trapped in ice at the mouth of the Varzina River, and Russian fishermen later found the crew dead.

Chancellor entered the White Sea and reached the Northern Dvina. Ivan IV invited him to Moscow, where he found a city larger than London and built almost wholly of wood. He returned in 1554 with letters from the tsar offering trade privileges.

Mary I rechartered the company as the Muscovy Company in 1555, and Chancellor sailed again for Russia, where he secured free passage, control of English settlement and freedom from arrest. On the voyage home in 1556 his ship was wrecked off the Scottish coast and he drowned.

Anthony Jenkinson succeeded Chancellor as the main trader. He travelled overland from Moscow as far as Bukhara and sought a route through Russia to Persia, which was abandoned in 1573. In 1571 Ivan IV revoked the company's right to free trade down the Volga, offended by English demands to close Russian trade to other European nations, and Jenkinson largely restored the privileges in 1572. Elizabeth I granted a whaling monopoly in 1577, and the charter of 1613 gave a monopoly of whaling at Spitsbergen. Henry Hudson made two unsuccessful voyages for the company in 1607 and 1608.

In 1646 Tsar Alexei I rescinded the company's exemption from Russian customs, in response to its alleged support for the Parliamentarians in the English Civil War, and after the execution of Charles I he expelled English merchants from Russia except at Arkhangelsk. Dutch merchants replaced the English as the leading traders. The company held a monopoly on English-Russian trade until 1698, when it lost its privileges to political opposition. It continued until the Russian Revolution of 1917 and has since operated mainly as a charity. It helped provide churches and Anglican ministers in Russia, and its headquarters, the Old English Yard, stands near the Kremlin.
muse-myanmar: Muse is the capital of Mu Se District and the principal town of Mu Se Township. A bridge across the Shweli River, also called the Nam Mao, joins it to Ruili in Yunnan Province. National Highway 3, part of Asian Highway route 14, runs 450 km to Mandalay by way of Lashio, and the old Burma Road links it to Bhamo in Kachin State and on to the Ledo Road. The Mandalay–Lashio–Muse road, which included part of the Burma Road, was rebuilt for heavy traffic in 1998 by the Asia World Company, cutting the journey from two days, or a week in the rains, to 12–16 hours.

Ne Win banned cross-border trade after the military took power in Burma in 1962, and the ban was lifted after negotiations in 1988. One of five official border trade posts with China opened at Muse on 21 January 1998, and the 150-hectare 105th mile Trade Zone, the first and largest of its kind in Burma, followed in April 2006. In 2007 the local militia, on the orders of the military authorities, seized 10,000 acres of tea and orange plantations and small farms, with little or no compensation, to grow physic nuts for biodiesel. The old bridge, which locals called the Gun Bridge for the arms smuggled across it, was closed in 2005.

Drug addiction was a major problem in the area, where the opium poppy harvest had grown, and the World Food Programme gave emergency food to former poppy farmers in 2004 and 2005. The People's Defense Force of the National Unity Government clashed with Tatmadaw forces in Muse on 23 May 2021, killing 13 security guards. During Operation 1027 the Three Brotherhood Alliance fought the Tatmadaw for control of the town, whose main defence was the 105th tactical command base on a hill to the east.

Muse is a major hub of Myanmar's trade with China, handling about 70% of the cross-border trade between the two countries. Burma sends mainly agricultural produce, fish, timber, gems and minerals across the border and receives consumer goods, electronics, machinery and processed food. A trade fair has been held every December since 2001, alternating between Muse and Ruili.
museo-di-capodimonte: The building goes back to 1738, when King Charles VII of Naples and Sicily, later Charles III of Spain, decided to build a hunting lodge on the Capodimonte hill. He then chose a grand palace instead, partly because his residence in the centre of the city, the Palace of Portici, was too small for his court, and partly to house the Farnese collection he had inherited from his mother, Elisabetta Farnese, the last descendant of the ruling ducal family of Parma. The palace was enlarged and filled with more art over the years, and in 1787, on the advice of Jacob Philipp Hackert, a laboratory for restoring paintings was created.

When the Parthenopaean Republic was declared in 1799, King Ferdinand IV fled to Palermo on Nelson's Vanguard, taking the most valuable items. French troops under General Jean Étienne Championnet, billeted in the palace, looted what remained. During the French occupation from 1806 to 1815 the collection was moved to the Naples National Archaeological Museum. Ferdinand returned in 1815 and employed many painters and sculptors on the redecoration, which was finished in 1840, with a gallery of contemporary art added.

In 1861 the palace passed to the House of Savoy, who added further pieces, with Domenico Morelli as consultant for acquisitions, and a collection of historic firearms. In 1866 the boudoir of Maria Amalia of Saxony was brought from the Palace of Portici, and in 1877 a Roman marble floor from a villa on Capri. After the end of the monarchy the palace became purely a national museum in 1950, with many exhibits returned from the archaeological museum; in its present form the museum was inaugurated in 1957.

The museum is the prime repository of Neapolitan painting and decorative art, with works from other Italian schools and some Roman sculpture, and is among the largest museums in Italy. The first and second floors house the Galleria Nazionale, with paintings of the 13th to 18th centuries by Caravaggio, Raphael, Titian, El Greco, Giovanni Bellini, Simone Martini, Masaccio and Lorenzo Lotto, and large holdings of Jusepe de Ribera, Luca Giordano and the Neapolitan Caravaggisti. Much of the ground floor holds part of the Farnese collection of Roman monumental sculpture. The royal apartments are furnished with 18th-century furniture and porcelain and majolica from the royal residences. In 2022 the art dealer Lia Rumma donated more than 70 works by 30 Italian artists.
muses: The earliest known records of the Muses come from Boeotia, and some ancient authorities regarded them as Thracian in origin. Their number and names differed by region. Pausanias reports three original Muses worshipped on Mount Helicon: Aoide, Melete and Mneme, 'song', 'practice' and 'memory'. At Delphi three were worshipped as Nete, Mese and Hypate, the names of the chords of the lyre.

From the Classical period the number was standardised at nine, the daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne in Hesiod's Theogony, from about 700 BCE. Diodorus Siculus noted that writers disagreed whether there were three or nine, and that nine prevailed on the authority of Homer and Hesiod. Alcman and Mimnermus made them children of Uranus and Gaia. They were also seen as water nymphs of the springs of Helicon and Pieris.

Not until Hellenistic times were functions assigned systematically: Calliope to epic poetry, Clio to history, Polyhymnia to hymn and mime, Euterpe to song and elegiac poetry, Terpsichore to chorus and dance, Erato to lyric choral poetry, Melpomene to tragedy, Thalia to light verse and comedy, and Urania to astronomy. Classical writers made Apollo their leader, and their cult was commonly connected with his.

In myth, Thamyris boasted that he could beat them in song; they defeated him and took away his gift of song and his sight. The Pierides, nine daughters of Pierus of Macedon, challenged them and, in Ovid's Metamorphoses, were turned into magpies. The Muses also gathered the body of Orpheus, the son of Calliope, and buried it in Leibethra.

The Greek word mousa meant 'art' or 'poetry', and mousike, source of the word music, was only one of the arts of the Muses, which also covered science, mathematics and philosophy. Before books were widely available this included nearly all learning. Alexandrian editors divided the Histories of Herodotus into nine books named after the Muses, and Solon called them the key to the good life.

Ancient poets invoked the Muse near the start of a work, as Homer does in the Odyssey. In Renaissance art, emblem books such as Cesare Ripa's Iconologia of 1593 standardised their props: a writing tablet for Calliope, a tragic mask for Melpomene and compasses and a globe for Urania.
mushika-dynasty: The name Mushika or Mushaka Parvata is a Sanskrit rendering of the Tamil Ezhimalai, the hill of Ezhimala; mispronounced as Elimala, it came to be read as the Mountain of the Rats. Early Tamil poems of the Sangam literature describe Ezhimalai on the north-western edge of the Tamil country and its rulers, a chiefly lineage called the Muvan, as enemies of the early Chera rulers who also made marriage alliances with the Chera, Pandya and Chola families. The Mahabharata lists the Mushikas among the kingdoms of the far south.

The poems celebrate rulers named Nannan. One, active around 180 CE, was known for his gold ornaments and gilded chariots; his warriors under Njimili killed the Satiyaputra ruler Neduman Anji at the battle of Pazhi, and he was finally defeated and killed by the Chera ruler Narmudi Cheral, who cut down Nannan's sacred Vaka tree.

In the early medieval period the polity became a monarchy known as Kolla-desham, along the Kavvai, Kuppam and Valappattanam rivers, and came under Chera influence, probably in the reign of Vijayaraga in the late 9th century. Its rulers supplied troops to the Cheras against the Cholas. In 1005 the Senur inscription of the Chola emperor Rajaraja I records the defeat of the kings of Kollam, Kolladesam and Kodungallur, through what seem to have been naval raids for plunder, and the Eramam inscription of about 1020 attests Chola officers in northern Kerala.

The Mushaka Vamsa Kavya, composed by the poet Athula at the court of King Srikantha, traces the line to a king consecrated by Parashurama. It tells of a king restored with Pandya help, of one who killed a Pallava royal and married his daughter, and of marriages and wars with the Chera king Jayaraga. After the Chera state declined, the kingdom lived on as Kolathunad.

Both the early chiefdom and the medieval kingdom rested chiefly on the Indian Ocean trade in pepper, cardamom and other hill produce rather than on wet-rice farming. Ezhimala Hill was the first landfall on the Malabar Coast for ships crossing the Arabian Sea, and the port of Naravu is often identified with the Naura of the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. Medieval ports such as Madayi, Valapattanam and Dharmapattanam hosted the merchant guilds anjuvannam, manigramam, valanchiyar and nanadeshikal, and probably Jewish traders. Unlike other Chera subordinates, the ruler commanded his own guard of companions called the Thousand.
mushikavamsa: The poem is believed to have been written in the reign of the Mushika ruler Shrikantha, thought to be a contemporary of the Chola king Rajendra I. If so, it is the earliest known historical mahakavya in Sanskrit, a few decades older than Kalhana's Rajatarangini. The Indologist A. K. Warder classes Atula's style as Vaidarbhi and sees the influence of the 6th-century poet Bharavi, among others. The surviving text breaks off in its account of Shrikantha's reign.

Atula traces the dynasty to a pregnant Heheya queen who escaped Parashurama's slaughter of the Kshatriyas and fled south to the Eli mountain (Ezhimala). There she burned a huge rat (mushika), in truth the cursed spirit of the mountain, and her son was later crowned by Parashurama himself as Rama-ghata-mushika. The first six cantos tell how Rama founded the fortified city of Kolam, killed the Magadha king Suvarman and became a universal emperor; the next four describe the amorous exploits of his son Nandana, and Canto 11 lists 51 further rulers.

From Canto 12 the kings can be identified as historical figures. Ishanavarman married Nandini, daughter of a Chedi king, and in a damaged passage the goddess Bhadrakali seems to promise the throne to the sons of her family's women; from then on the crown passes to sisters' sons. Later rulers fight the Kerala kingdom, Ganga invaders and rebel chiefs and build Shiva and Vishnu temples, and Vallabha II founds the port of Marahi and the fort of Vallabhapatnam.

Atula wrote chiefly to praise his patrons, and nothing supports the claim that a ruler from Kerala conquered Magadha. M. G. S. Narayanan nevertheless reads the origin story as a sign that the family came from the Heheya country of Central India, perhaps at the beginning of Mauryan rule. Warder notes that Shiva's boon of long life to Sharmadatta and his 20 successors smooths over the chronology, and those kings appear imaginary. Shrikantha is identified with Kandan Karivarman of the Eramam inscription; Atula seems to have left out the Chola invasion of about 1020 that preceded his restoration of plundered temples.
musket: The musket was a muzzle-loaded long gun that fired black powder and appeared as a smoothbore weapon in the early 16th century, at first as a heavier variant of the arquebus capable of penetrating plate armour. The word is first recorded in Europe in 1499, but evidence of the musket as a type of firearm dates from 1521, when it described an arquebus so heavy that it had to be rested on a forked stick. The historian David A. Parrot thinks the musket as a genuine innovation uncertain, perhaps only a change of name. The heavy type went out of use by the mid-16th century as heavy armour declined, but the word remained the general term for smoothbore shoulder arms into the 19th century.

Musketeers were the first infantry to give up armour entirely. They took cover behind walls or in sunken lanes and sometimes acted as skirmishers, and their numbers rose relative to pikemen because they were more mobile. Matchlock firearms were used in India by 1500, in Đại Việt by 1516 and in Southeast Asia by 1540. In Sri Lanka the kingdoms of Sitawaka and Kandy made hundreds of muskets with a bifurcated stock, a longer barrel and a smaller calibre.

Slow reloading made volley fire important, with each row firing and reloading in turn. Matchlock volley fire was first used in 1526 when the Ottoman Janissaries fired in volleys at the Battle of Mohács, and appeared next in China under Qi Jiguang and in late 16th-century Japan. In China and Japan matchlocks stayed in use until percussion locks arrived in the 19th century.

Smoothbore muskets remained the main firearm of most armies until the mid-19th century, because rifles, known in Europe by the late 15th century, fouled quickly and loaded slowly. In New Zealand, between 1805 and 1843, at least 500 conflicts took place among Māori groups that often used trade muskets alongside traditional weapons. The Minié ball, invented by Claude-Étienne Minié in 1849, brought the rifled musket into wide use, and breech-loading weapons, the Henry rifle of 1860 and its descendant the Winchester ended the era of the musket.
muslim-brotherhood: Hassan al-Banna founded the Society in the city of Ismailia in March 1928 with six workers of the Suez Canal Company. They appointed him their leader and vowed to work for Islam through jihad, taking the pledge that its members would be soldiers in the call to Islam. The Brothers regard their movement as the practical extension of the pan-Islamist movement of Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida, and al-Banna was seen as its builder. He described the movement as a Salafiyya message, a Sunni way, a Sufi truth, a political organisation, an athletic group, a cultural-educational union, an economic company and a social idea.

After the Second World War the Brotherhood established a Palestinian branch in October 1945, and a small branch appeared in Jordan around the turn of 1946. Governments in Egypt have cracked down on it repeatedly since 1948. Al-Banna led it until 1949, followed by Hassan al-Hudaybi until 1972 and Umar al-Tilmisani until 1986. The group remained on the fringe of Arab politics until the Six-Day War of 1967, when Islamism replaced secular Arab nationalism as a popular current after the Arab defeat. Under Hosni Mubarak it was the largest opposition group in Egypt and had built a wide network of support through Islamic charities working among poor Egyptians.

The movement spread beyond Egypt. It reached Algeria in the last years of French rule, where Ahmad Sahnoun led it in 1953–1954 and its members took part in the uprising of 1954–1962, but it was marginalised under the one-party rule of the FLN after independence in 1962. In Europe, the first members arrived from the Middle East in the late 1950s and early 1960s, among them leaders who had fled Gamal Abdel Nasser's rule. Student groups grew into organisations, and mosques were run as community centres.

After the fall of Mubarak in 2011 the Egyptian Brotherhood was legalised. On 30 April 2011 it launched the Freedom and Justice Party, which won 235 of the 498 seats in that year's parliamentary elections, and in 2012 its candidate Mohamed Morsi won the presidency. Morsi was overthrown in 2013 and the group was banned in Egypt.

The Brotherhood's best-known slogan is Islam is the Solution. Its English-language website lists among its principles the Islamic Sharia as the basis for controlling the affairs of state and society and the unity of Islamic countries. Views of the group differ. Authors in Foreign Affairs wrote that it has at times used or supported violence but, since the 1970s, has disavowed it and sought to take part in Egyptian politics, while others question the sincerity of its statements. Many Islamist movements and parties have drawn on al-Banna's teachings.
muslim-conquest-of-persia: In the early 7th century the Sasanian Empire was under strain. The Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628 had exhausted its army, and after the execution of the shah Khosrow II in 628 ten claimants were enthroned within four years. A civil war, the Sasanian Interregnum, left the government decentralised by 632. Yazdegerd III came to the throne aged about eight and did not rebuild the army. The empire was in effect a confederation with Parthian families, some of whom wished to withdraw, and the northern and eastern houses later made peace with the Arabs rather than fight beside the Sasanians.

Muhammad died in June 632 and Abu Bakr became caliph at Medina. The Ridda Wars kept the caliphate occupied until March 633, after which the Arab chief al-Muthanna ibn Haritha raided Sasanian towns in Mesopotamia with light cavalry, and his success led Abu Bakr to consider expansion.

Under Caliph Umar the Muslims lost ground in Mesopotamia after Khalid ibn al-Walid left for Syria with half his army, and the Persians defeated Abu Ubaid al-Thaqafi in the Battle of the Bridge. Al-Muthanna won at Buwayb, and in 635 Yazdegerd III sought an alliance with the Byzantine emperor Heraclius. By 638 the Tigris and Euphrates valleys were under Muslim control, with the Persians withdrawn east of the Zagros. In Khuzestan the Persian chief Hormuzan signed and broke two treaties before he was defeated and captured at Tuster.

Umar was wary of attacking what remained of the empire, but a new offensive followed, and the Battle of Nahavand in 642 proved the key to Persia. Yazdegerd fled to raise another army with limited success. Isfahan fell after a siege of a few months, Fars was taken in stages, and expeditions went to Kerman, Sakastan, Azerbaijan and Armenia. In 651 Ahnaf ibn Qais took Nishapur, Herat and Merv, where Yazdegerd had held court; the remainder of his army was beaten at the Battle of Oxus River and retreated across the Oxus. Umar was assassinated in November 644 by an Iranian slave, Abu Lu'lu'a Firuz.

The conquerors settled in garrison towns. Non-Muslim subjects were tolerated as dhimmi and paid the jizya, and mass conversion was neither wanted nor allowed in the first centuries. Conversion was slow and incomplete, stretching over many centuries, with a majority of Persians still following Zoroastrianism at the turn of the millennium. Middle Persian stayed the official language under the Rashidun, but Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf later changed the administrative language of Iraq to Arabic. Persian survived as New Persian, with many Arabic words and the Arabic alphabet.

Historians have long relied on Arabic accounts written well after the events and on the Armenian bishop Sebeos. Parvaneh Pourshariati, in a 2008 study, questions the traditional narrative, including its timeline and specific dates.
muslim-conquest-of-the-maghreb: By 642 Arab Muslim forces under Caliph Umar had taken Mesopotamia, Syria and Egypt. Soon after the fall of Alexandria, Amr ibn al-As led about 4,000 troops west into Cyrenaica and Tripolitania. Barqa fell without opposition, the Luwata Berbers agreed to pay 13,000 dinars in tribute, and Tripoli fell after about a month. In late 645 the Byzantines briefly retook Alexandria and were stopped at Nikiou in May 646, which showed that the Muslim hold on Egypt was still insecure.

In 647 Abd Allah ibn Sa'd, governor of Egypt, led some 20,000 men into Africa and defeated the Byzantine army at Sufetula in southern Tunisia, exacting a large tribute. After the First Fitna the Muslims had to begin again. Campaigns resumed in 665, and in 670 Uqba ibn Nafi founded Qayrawan. His successor Abu al-Muhajir Dinar began a policy of rapprochement with the Berbers and recruited them in large numbers. Uqba returned in 682, arrested Abu al-Muhajir and the Berber leader Kusaila, and led some 15,000 troops west. In 683 he reached the Atlantic but was defeated on his return, which reversed all Muslim gains.

Kusaila then entered Qayrawan unopposed and ruled most of Byzacena and Numidia for several years, until Zuhayr ibn Qays defeated and killed him at the Battle of Mamma. In 694 Caliph Abd al-Malik, having won the civil war, sent Hassan ibn al-Nu'man with 40,000 troops. They took Carthage, ending the Byzantine presence by 698. In 704 or 705 Musa ibn Nusayr replaced Hassan and conquered what are now Algeria and Morocco over the next decade, recruiting Berbers on a great scale. In 709 the Byzantine Empire lost its last strongholds in the Maghreb to Caliph al-Walid I.

In 705 the region became a province separate from Egypt, divided into five provinces: Ifriqiya, Tripolitania, Zab, Near Sus and Far Sus. Most of its 50,000 Arab troops were in the east, so in the west the Caliphate depended on Berber manpower. In 711 Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the strait into Iberia with 12,000 men, mostly Berbers.

The loss of Africa deprived the Byzantine Empire of a large granary and of tax revenue. Arabization was gradual: Latin did not disappear at once, and Christianity is documented after the conquest, though its communities faded by the 14th century. Later governors imposed the jizya on the Berbers, taking it by money and by enslavement, which provoked the Great Berber Revolt, and many Berbers turned to the Kharijite movement.
muslim-conquest-of-transoxiana: After the Battle of Nahavand in 642 the Arabs took Sistan and Khorasan, and with the fall of Marw to Abd Allah ibn Amir in 651 the Caliphate's border reached the Oxus. The land beyond the river, mā wara al-nahr to the Arabs, was divided into many small principalities. In Tokharistan local shads, many of them Turkic chieftains, owed nominal allegiance to the Yabghu at Kunduz. Sogdia, an Iranian-speaking land with its own script, was led by Bukhara and Samarkand, whose ruler bore the title ikhshid; Khwarizm was ruled by the Khwarizmshah, and Ustrushana, Chach and Fergana lay further north and east.

The first Arab campaigns were mostly raids for booty and tribute, launched every year from a small garrison at Marw. Under Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan's government of the east, his deputy al-Hakam ibn Amr al-Ghifari led Arab armies across the Oxus into Chaghaniyan. The Second Fitna then halted expansion for a generation, while Khorasan's Arab settlers fought among themselves and Abd Allah ibn Khazim al-Sulami held the province until 691.

Qutayba ibn Muslim, backed by al-Hajjaj, consolidated Khorasan and recruited large bodies of native troops, converts and non-Muslims alike. In 707 he took Numushkat and Ramithna and defeated a coalition from Fergana and Sogdiana, and in the reign of al-Walid I he conquered most of Transoxiana. In 719 local rulers asked the Chinese and the Türgesh for help, and from 720 the Türgesh attacked while the Sogdians rose. The governor Sa'id ibn Amr al-Harashi suppressed the revolt harshly; the rebel leader Divashtich, captured at his fortress on Mount Mugh, was crucified. Fergana was lost, and in 717 a Tang army had defeated an Arab, Tibetan and Türgesh attack at Aksu.

Conversion was slow under the Umayyads, who treated local non-Muslims as second-class subjects and did not encourage them to convert, so that few Sogdian commoners became Muslims. In the Abbasid period non-Arabs gained equal status on conversion, and Islam spread across Central Asia. The region conquered then covers all or part of present-day Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.
muslim-ibn-quraysh: Muslim, whose full name was Abu'l-Makarim Muslim ibn Quraysh, was the son of Quraysh bin Badran, called Alam al-Din, the Arab emir of Mosul. Quraysh acknowledged the Seljuks but later quarrelled with them, was for a time driven from Mosul, and joined the Mamluk soldier Basasiri when he took Baghdad at the end of 1058. On his father's death in 1061 Muslim succeeded him. A Shiite, he at first recognised the Fatimid caliph in Cairo, but around 1066 he allied with the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan and married Safiyya, an aunt of the later Sultan Malik-Shah.

In 1077 Muslim joined, as Malik-Shah's vassal, the campaign of the sultan's brother Tutush I against Aleppo, held by the Mirdasid Sabiq ibn Mahmud. He disliked the attack, persuaded the Kilab tribesmen to leave Tutush's army, let his troops sell food to the besieged city, and withdrew. On his way home he warned Sabiq of 1,000 Seljuk reinforcements at Sinjar, which an Arab coalition under Abu Za'ida Muhammad ibn Za'ida then routed at Wadi Butnan, and Tutush gave up the siege.

In 1080 Sabiq ceded Aleppo to him, its people hoping he could protect them from Seljuk raids, and in the next year he took Harran from the Numayrids. He then fell out with the Seljuks and was defeated by Malik-Shah's forces, but pardoned. When Suleiman ibn Qutalmish took Antioch in December 1084, Muslim demanded the tribute that Philaretos Brachamios had paid him, and Suleiman refused it.

In June 1085 Muslim was killed fighting Suleiman's forces after his Turkoman mercenaries went over to the enemy and his Arab troops fled. His brother Ibrahim ibn Quraysh, released from prison, succeeded him, followed later by Muslim's son Ali ibn Muslim. Muslim was regarded as the last strong Arab king of northern Mesopotamia, and the last Arab ruler whose lands included parts of modern Turkey; after his death Turkoman nomads came to dominate the region. The Imam Dur Mausoleum in Samarra is said to be his tomb, though its inscription names Imam Muhammad al-Durri.
musov: Mušov, Muschau in German, is a cadastral area and a defunct village in the municipality of Pasohlávky, in the South Moravian Region, covering 1,420 hectares. It was the lowest-lying village of the Břeclav District, set in the riparian forest along the river Thaya. The Roman site lay on the hill called Burgstall, today Hradisko, above the former village and 80 km from Vindobona, the Roman forerunner of Vienna.

Research on Burgstall began in 1927. Excavators found two masonry buildings, a praetorium and a bath with a hypocaust, bricks stamped by the Xth legion and coins of the emperors Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius and Commodus; the youngest coins date from the reign of Septimius Severus. The legion is thought to have watched over the Germanic tribes defeated in the Marcomannic Wars. The chieftain buried in the tomb of 1988 was apparently a Roman ally in that war, and the area has also yielded a Slavic burial and finds from many periods of prehistory.

In the late 1970s the socialist authorities decided to build the Nové Mlýny reservoirs, and the village was destroyed despite its inhabitants' opposition. It was merged with Pasohlávky in 1976, its residents were offered apartments or plots there, the post office last opened on 30 June 1978, and the land was flooded between 1981 and 1987.

The medieval church of St Leonard was preserved at the conservationists' urging and now stands on a small island in the Věstonice Reservoir. Built in the late 12th century as a late Romanesque church and rebuilt in Gothic style in the 14th, it is a bird nesting site within the Natura 2000 network and opens to visitors in summer. The wine cellars north of the dam survive intact, and an exhibition on the Roman presence is shown at the ATC Merkur camp in Pasohlávky.
mustafa-barzani: Mustafa Barzani was born on 14 March 1903 in Barzan, a village in southern Kurdistan. When he was a few months old Ottoman Hamidiye Horsemen attacked the village and his family was deported to Diyarbakır and imprisoned. His father, grandfather and a brother were later executed by the Ottoman authorities for other insurrections.
