In 1931 he followed his older brother, the chieftain Sheikh Ahmed Barzani, in an insurrection against Baghdad's attempts to break up tribal power. Iraq, helped by British aerial warfare, forced Sheikh Ahmed to surrender in June 1932, while Mustafa fought on for another year. In 1943 he broke out of exile in Sulaymaniyah and rebelled, and in October 1945 he crossed into Iran with Sheikh Ahmad and about three thousand followers.

In December 1945 Qazi Muhammad declared the Kurdish Republic of Mahabad, under Soviet military control, and Barzani became its minister of defence and army commander. After Soviet troops withdrew in May 1946, Iranian troops overran Mahabad in December. Barzani and his followers fled to the Soviet Union, where they were held in camps and he was separated from his followers for three years until a Soviet investigation in 1951 found them unfairly treated. Meanwhile the Kurdish Democratic Party, founded at Baghdad on 16 August 1946, elected him president in his absence.

After the republican coup of 1958 he returned to Iraq in October. Relations with the prime minister Qasim soured, and from December 1961 he fought Baghdad. In 1964 he took control of the party by expelling Jalal Talabani and Ibrahim Ahmad. Negotiations with the Ba'ath government, with Saddam Hussein acting for it, produced the agreement of 11 March 1970, which made Kurdish a second official language and promised autonomy excluding Kirkuk and Khanaqin. It collapsed amid Barzani's accusations of Arabification and an attempt on his life in September 1971, and he rejected the autonomy law of 11 March 1974.

The Algiers Agreement between Iran and Iraq in March 1975 ended Iranian support for the peshmerga, and on 23 March Barzani and nearly 100,000 followers left for Iran. Barzani went to the United States for lung cancer treatment and died on 1 March 1979 at Georgetown University Hospital in Washington, D.C. He was buried at Oshnavieh, and in October 1993 his remains were moved to Barzan. His sons Masud and Idris took over the leadership of the Kurdistan Democratic Party.

Critics, among them Talabani, accused him of tying the Kurdish national movement too closely to tribal structures and of acting to gain power for himself. Many Kurds nonetheless regard him, for his charisma and inflexibility, as a prominent figure of the Kurdish independence movement.
mustafa-chokay: Mustafa Shokay was born on 25 December 1890 into a wealthy Kazakh family of the Middle Juz at Ak-Meshit, the present Kyzylorda. His grandfather had served as datkha, a chief minister, to the khan of Khiva, and his mother Bakty, who knew Kazakh, Arabic and Persian, taught her children to read and write. He went to a Russian school, entered a Tashkent gymnasium in 1902 and graduated in 1910 with its gold medal, which General Alexander Samsonov tried to give to a Russian student instead. He then studied law at the university of St. Petersburg from 1910 to 1917, interrupted when his father died in 1912.

Recommended by Alikhan Bukeikhanov, he worked as secretary and translator of the Muslim faction of the State Duma, where he befriended Ahmad Zeki Velidi and helped prepare the protests against the decree of 25 June 1916 drafting Central Asians for labour behind the front, which set off a great uprising. In 1917 he was a delegate to the Muslim congress in Moscow, sat on the Provisional Government's Turkestan committee and was elected chairman of Turkestan's national committee. When Bolshevik troops sent on 11 February 1918 destroyed Kokand, he fled through Fergana to Tashkent with a price of 1000 roubles on his head, and in April 1918 he married Maria Gorina.

By way of Baku the couple reached Tbilisi, where they lived until the Red Army took the city in February 1921, and then Istanbul. With the help of Alexander Kerensky they moved to Paris in the summer of 1921, and in 1923 to Nogent-sur-Marne. Shokay wrote for émigré papers, founded Yash Turkistan in Istanbul in 1927 and edited the journal Yash Turkestan, which ran to 117 issues before the Second World War. His books included Chez les Soviets en Asie Centrale of 1928.

On 22 June 1941 the German occupiers in Paris interned him at Compiègne and then took him to Berlin, where he was asked to lead the Turkestan Legion of Turkic Soviet prisoners. Accounts of his life say he was shocked by the prisoners' conditions and wrote to Joachim von Ribbentrop refusing further cooperation. He died in a Berlin hospital on 27 December 1941, officially of blood poisoning after typhus, though his wife held that he had been immune and poisoning has been suspected. A memorial stele stands in Nogent-sur-Marne, and streets in Kyzylorda and Almaty bear his name.
mustafa-kemal-ataturk: Shortly after graduating from military school he was arrested for activities against the regime of Sultan Abdul Hamid II, and he was released after months only with the support of his former school director. He was posted to the Fifth Army in Damascus as a staff captain, joined a small secret society of reformist officers called Vatan ve Hürriyet, and later joined the Committee of Union and Progress, though he became known for his criticism of its leaders.

He took part in the suppression of a tribal rebellion in Tripolitania in 1908 and in the suppression of the counter-revolution of April 1909, the 31 March Incident, which ended with the deposition of Abdul Hamid II. He fought in the Italo-Turkish and Balkan Wars and rose to prominence in the Defence of Gallipoli during the First World War. After the Ottoman defeat he directed the Turkish National Movement against the partition of the country by the victorious powers, set up the provisional Ankara government and won the war against Greece, Armenia, France and the United Kingdom, a result confirmed in the Treaty of Lausanne.

During and after the war the ethnic cleansing of Armenians and Greeks from Anatolia outside Istanbul was largely completed through massacres, flight, expulsions and the population exchange between Greece and Turkey. His government abolished the Ottoman sultanate in 1922 and proclaimed the Republic of Turkey in 1923, with Atatürk as its first president until his death on 10 November 1938 at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul, aged 57. He was succeeded by İsmet İnönü.

As president he sought complete independence, which he defined as economic, financial, juridical, military and cultural. He led reforms to build a republican and secular nation-state with a Western facing society. The Ottoman Caliphate was abolished, a fully secular civil code replaced the semi-secular Mecelle, the fez was banned, thousands of schools were opened and a Latin-based Turkish alphabet was introduced. State-owned enterprises were set up and the first five-year plan was begun. Turkish women received equal civil and political rights.
mustafa-pasha-bushati: Mustafa Pasha Bushatli, called Ishkodrali, from Scutari, was the son of the powerful Kara Mahmud Bushatli. Around 1810 he succeeded his uncle, Ibrahim Pasha, as governor of the Pashalik of Scutari, received the rank of vizier in 1812 and went on ruling as an independent lord. In 1820 the sanjak of Berat was given to him, and in 1824 the sanjaks of Ohrid and Elbasan, together with the title of serasker. In English he is usually known as Mustafa Pasha Bushatli, in Serbian as Mustafa-paša Bušatlija.

Mustafa led a mercenary army early in the Greek War of Independence. In 1823 he and Omer Vrioni led a campaign of 8,000 Albanian troops, according to the historian Finlay, in western Greece, and on 24 August 1823 Markos Botsaris and 350 Souliotes attacked his army near Karpenisi; Botsaris was killed. Like his father, Mustafa sought greater independence, and when Mahmud II's military reforms threatened his hereditary rights he kept friendly relations with Prince Miloš Obrenović of Serbia, the discontented Bosniaks and Muhammad Ali of Egypt. In the Russo-Turkish War of 1828-1829 he stayed passive, reaching the Danube only in May 1829 and avoiding battle.

In 1831 the Porte demanded that he hand Dukakin, Debar, Elbasan, Ohrid and Trgovište to the grand vizier and carry out reforms in Scutari. With money and support from Prince Miloš he marched against the grand vizier in mid-March, joined by other pashas of northern Albania and Kosovo, and took Sofia, but regular troops routed the rebels at Skopje early in May. He fell back on Scutari and surrendered after a six-month siege.

At the request of Metternich he was pardoned and taken to Constantinople. Fifteen years later he was again a governor, of the Ankara Eyalet from 1846, and then of the Herzegovina Eyalet, where he arrived on 22 May 1853; Serbian sources describe him as fair. During his rule there the hajduk bands grew so numerous that he feared being seized at night in Mostar. His last post was in Medina, where he died on 27 May 1860.
mustafa-resid-pasha: Mustafa Reşid was born in Constantinople on 13 March 1800. His father, a civil servant, died when he was ten, and he left his madrasa to live with his uncle Ispartalı Ali Pasha, a court chamberlain under Sultan Mahmud II and later Grand Vizier. He studied at a scribal institution and went with his uncle when the latter became governor of the Morea in 1816. During the Greek War of Independence he noted that Ottoman institutions needed reform and that foreign European support was essential. After his patron fell he worked as a clerk under the foreign minister and was secretary to the Ottoman delegation at the peace talks at Adrianople in 1829.

He became ambassador to France in 1834 and to the United Kingdom in 1836, and minister for foreign affairs in 1837. In London he won British support for the sultan against Muhammad Ali of Egypt and negotiated the Treaty of Balta Liman, a commercial treaty with Britain. In the Oriental Crisis of 1840 he stayed with the Great Powers and refused a direct settlement with Egypt. Muhammad Ali later bribed the Porte to remove him as foreign minister, and he returned to Paris as ambassador.

In 1853, out of office, he regained the foreign ministry, helped to draft the Ottoman response to Russian demands and persuaded the officials who favoured war; the empire declared war on Russia on 4 October 1853.

His part in the Edict of Gülhane was central. On 11 August 1839 he sent a private memorandum from London to Lord Palmerston arguing that reform was needed and that the protection and security of the people were required.

The Edict of Gülhane, read in the rose garden of Topkapi Palace before Sultan Abdulmecid and foreign diplomats, opened the Tanzimat era and called for the protection of individual rights and property, while new laws were to stay within sharia. Between 1845 and 1857 Reşid held the office of Grand Vizier six times. He set up commercial courts and a commercial code based on French models, founded the Meclis-i Maarif, a committee of education meant to reduce the ulema’s influence, in 1846, and the Academy of Sciences in 1852.

French and other pressure repeatedly removed him, and he opposed the 1856 Reform Edict, which he saw as foreign interference. He died of a heart attack in Constantinople on 7 January 1858. His protégés Fuad Pasha and Mehmed Emin Âli Pasha carried the reforms forward.
mustansirite-hardship: For several years before the crisis the Nile failed to rise high enough to irrigate the fields, and harvests fell. In 1066 a quarrel between Turkish Mamluk slave soldiers and Sudanese slave soldiers in the Fatimid army grew into open civil war, each side trying to control the weak Caliph al-Mustansir Billah. The caliph's mother, herself an African slave concubine, used her influence for the African faction, while the Turks were led by the general Nasir al-Dawla ibn Hamdan. The fighting between them, which included a siege of Cairo, made the shortage of food worse, until Nasir al-Dawla routed the African forces and took control of the vizierate.

A run on wheat and bread drove prices up rapidly and emptied the treasury of the Fatimid state, and food became too dear, or impossible to obtain, for the average Egyptian. The 14th-century Egyptian historian al-Maqrizi records the desperate measures of the starving: cannibalism became common, kidnappers lowered hooks from rooftops to seize passers-by and eat them, and the bodies of executed criminals were eaten. Dogs sold for 5 silver dirhams each until there were none left, and al-Maqrizi tells of a woman who had strips of flesh cut from her thighs by hungry captors.

Around 40,000 people are estimated to have starved to death. Several towns, among them al-Askar and al-Qata'i, were completely emptied of people, and others lost most of their inhabitants. The famine is named after the reigning caliph, ash-Shiddatu l-Mustanṣiriyya in Arabic, and some Arab historians compared it with the seven-year famine of Egypt described in Judeo-Christian and Islamic tradition.
mustapha-bouchelaghem: Mustapha ben Youcef ben Mohamed ben Ishaq el-Mesrati was the first-born of the eight children of Youcef el-Mesrati, a Zenetian Berber noble from the Kalaa of Beni Rached, and an Algerian woman. His father had served as khalifa, or lieutenant-governor, to the Bey of Constantine before moving back to Mostaganem, where the family was raised. Several of Mustapha's brothers later became beys of Oran themselves. The name Bouchelaghem, rendered in Spanish as El Bigotillos, was an epithet referring to his moustache.

He was elected bey of the Western Beylik in 1686, after his predecessor Chaban-ez-Zenagui was killed in front of Oran. In 1701 he moved his seat to Mascara for its more central position, built a garrison there and gathered a large army drawn mainly from thousands of Arab and Berber tribal levies. Moroccan forces led by a son of Moulay Ismail invaded his territory in 1699, early in the Maghrebi war, and looted his palace; in 1701, with the help of Hajj Mustapha Dey, he defeated the Moroccan armies at the Battle of Chelif, and in 1707 he drove back a further expedition.

Relations with Spain soured after Spanish troops attacked the Beni Ameur, a tribe loyal to Algiers, in 1703, and he had the tribes around Oran harass the Spanish. In 1707, while Spain was occupied by the War of the Spanish Succession, he and Ouzoum Hassan, a commander sent from Algiers, took the fort of Saint-Philippe and laid siege to the city; after six months Oran and Mers el Kébir fell.

He made Oran a base for Barbary pirates and built a small fleet to protect it. When a revolution led by Baba Ali Chaouch in Algiers in 1710 brought purges of the provincial beys, he kept his office, thanks mainly to his popularity and neutrality, and he spent the following years strengthening the defences and investing in the region's wealth.

In 1732 a Spanish force defeated the Algerian ships guarding Oran and Mers el Kébir, landed, and took the city after a hard siege. Bouchelaghem withdrew to Mostaganem and is said to have fallen into depression after the loss. He was succeeded by his brother, and his long tenure made him the longest-serving of the beys of the West. He is buried in a mausoleum of his own.
mustapha-harun: Mustapha was born Datu Badiozaman on 31 July 1918 at Kampung Limau-Limauan, Kudat; his name was changed in his youth in the local belief that this would help him overcome frequent illness. His father was Datu Harun bin Datu Nasaruddin, and the family traced its ancestry to the Sultans of Sulu. During the Japanese occupation he led rebellions against the Japanese around Kudat; unable to find him, they caught and killed his younger brother. Albert Kwok invited him to join the Jesselton Revolt, but Mustapha advised him to wait and prepare.

Mustapha founded the United Sabah National Organisation (USNO) and became Sabah's first Yang di-Pertua Negeri, or head of state, on the formation of Malaysia, while Donald Stephens became chief minister. After USNO won the 1967 state election he became the third chief minister. His relations with the federal government were strained by his threats to take Sabah out of Malaysia and by his refusal to sign an oil agreement giving the state 5 percent of its oil revenue, when he demanded at least 30 percent. He proposed the Sabah Foundation (Yayasan Sabah) and helped set up the Sabah campus of Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia.

He sponsored the United Sabah Islamic Association, founded on 14 August 1969, and campaigned for conversion to Islam, holding that unity required a common religion and language; by February 1974 about 75,000 non-Muslim Sabahans had converted. He enforced Malay as the language of Sabah and banned radio broadcasts in English and the vernaculars. In December 1972 police acting on his orders raided Catholic missions and arrested foreign priests who lacked permanent residency. He was also believed to have aided the Moro rebels of the southern Philippines with arms and training.

In 1975 USNO's secretary-general Harris Salleh left to form BERJAYA, which won the 1976 state election. Mustapha led USNO in four later state elections without winning again, and after 1990 its merger with BERJAYA created the Sabah chapter of the United Malays National Organisation, of which he became the first chief. He died at Kota Kinabalu on 2 January 1995 and was buried at Putatan, and the Sabah Foundation Building was renamed Tun Mustapha Tower.
musunuri-nayakas: Little is known of the family, which historians often call obscure. Prolaya Nayaka appeared as a new ruler at Rekapalle, near Bhadrachalam, around 1330, claiming descent from the Kakatiyas. Rekapalle, at the edge of the Papikondalu hills of the Eastern Ghats, commanded the narrow Sabari River valley and traffic on the Godavari. Some Andhra historians assign the family to the Kamma caste, though the modern castes of the region arose only late in the Vijayanagara period. The Nayakas were Shaivites.

After the fall of the Kakatiyas their lands were annexed by the Delhi Sultanate, and a former Kakatiya commander, renamed Malik Maqbul, governed Warangal. In 1330 Prolaya Nayaka issued the Vilasa grant, a copper-plate grant near Pithapuram that lamented the devastation of the Telugu country by northern armies and presented him as the restorer of order. Historian M. Rama Rao suggests he acted jointly with Prolaya Vema Reddi of Addanki.

Prolaya Nayaka left no children and was succeeded by his cousin Kapaya Nayaka, who led a larger rebellion. Muhammad bin Tughluq faced risings across his realm, and in 1334-35 an epidemic struck the army he led into the Deccan. Ferishta, writing around 1600, says Kapaya Nayaka sought help from the Hoysala ruler Veera Ballala III, and with part of his army drove the governor to Daulatabad. Historian R. C. Majumdar called it a national revolt.

Kapaya Nayaka supported other rebels, among them Alauddin Bahman Shah, who later turned against him. In the wars with the Bahmani Sultanate that followed he ceded forts and lands, including Golconda, and in 1361 gave the Bahmani sultan Mohammed Shah I the Turquoise throne of Warangal under a treaty. The Reddis of Kondavidu and the Recherla Nayakas exploited his weakness, and the Recherla Nayakas killed him in battle at Bhimavaram near Warangal.

Kapaya Nayaka kept using the Kush Mahal built by the sultans at Warangal, took the Persianised title Sultan of the Andhra country, and claimed to have been appointed by the god Visweswara of Kashi to protect the dharma. After his death his allied Nayakas went back to their own towns, and the Recherla Nayakas dominated Telangana until 1435.
mutahharten: Erzincan lay south of the Empire of Trebizond and traded closely with it; most of its people were Christian Armenians under a Muslim ruler. Its earlier emirs, Ahi Ayna and then Pir Husayn, held it as vassals of the Eretnids. Early Ottoman sources call Mutahharten a Tatar, while the historian Astarabadi made him a nephew of Eretna, and the historian Göde identifies his father as Eretna's brother Burak Beg, appointed emir of Erzincan with Eretna's approval.

Taking power on Pir Husayn's death in 1379, Mutahharten struck his own coins and had the khutbah read in his name. The Eretnid sultan Ala al-Din Ali marched against him; defeated in a first battle, Mutahharten called in the Dulkadirids and the Aq Qoyunlu, and Ali retreated to Sivas. Ali's vizier Kadi Burhan al-Din, who declared himself sultan in 1381, then fought him for years, razing parts of Erzincan in 1384–5 before the two agreed to recognise each other's sovereignty.

Often outmatched, Mutahharten changed sides freely. He executed his brother-in-law and ally Zannun and massacred the people of Koyulhisar, broke with the Aq Qoyunlu in 1389 and was twice defeated by them. When Timur arrived in late 1386 he quickly accepted his rule, and in 1393–4 he put Timur's name on his coins and in the khutbah. He defeated Burhan al-Din at Pulur on 27 October 1395, and the war ended only with Burhan al-Din's death in 1398.

With Trebizond relations stayed close: he took kharāj from the empire and married a daughter of its emperor. Around 1400, when Timur ordered the Christians of Erzincan massacred after a priest refused to convert, Mutahharten had the order reversed by paying 9,000 aspers.

Refusing the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I's demand for submission, he relied on Timur. Bayezid took Erzincan in 1401 and briefly held him and his Trapezuntine wife captive, but he was restored and joined Timur's campaign that ended at the Battle of Ankara. He died in late 1403 with no surviving legitimate son. His grandson Yar Ali ruled for a time, before the emirate ceased to exist amid the struggle of the Aq Qoyunlu and Qara Qoyunlu for Erzincan.
mutapa-empire: The Mutapa Empire lay on the northern Zimbabwean Plateau, between the Zambezi and Limpopo valleys. The Portuguese term Monomotapa transliterates the royal title Mwenemutapa, from mwene, lord, and mutapa, conquered land; the title came to name the kingdom itself. Shona tradition links its beginnings to Great Zimbabwe: some Karanga migrated north, perhaps after a salt shortage, and an elephant hunter named Mutota became prominent, took an interest in Zambezi trade and found salt in Dande.

Early in the fifteenth century Angoche traders had opened a route along the Zambezi to the goldfields near Khami, and the Karanga intermarried with the Tonga and Tavara and influenced their succession disputes. Mutota led the militaristic Nzou Samanyanga clan to conquer Dande, built a stone enclosure, called a zimbabwe, as capital at Chitako-Changonya Hill and gave land and posts to his allies.

After Mutota and his successor Matope, a son named Nyahuma Mukombero conquered Uteve, valuable because Kilwa and Sofala traded with the interior through it. Tradition says Changamire I, governor of the southern province of Guruuswa, helped him. The Tonga of the Lower Zambezi rebelled from about 1550. Portugal sent Francisco Barreto to conquer the gold, but his army reached Sena by 1571 and returned empty-handed, and his successor Vasco Homem's force was destroyed at Chikova.

After Mwenemutapa Gatsi Rusere died, his son Nyambo Kapararidze killed a Portuguese ambassador and declared war on the Portuguese. A Portuguese army, mostly of African soldiers, defeated him at Masapa in 1629 and placed Mavhura on the throne. Mavhura accepted terms of vassalage, including the Portuguese king's suzerainty, the expulsion of Muslims and open mines, and was baptised. In the 1680s Changamire Dombo, who had used the royal cattle to gain followers, defeated the Portuguese and Mukombwe's forces and went south to conquer Butua. Later reigns saw civil war and a capital in Chidima, in present-day Mozambique.

The ruler, the mambo, took the title Mwenemutapa and held court in a zimbabwe, a walled stone enclosure; later courts were of mud and wood. His wives, hundreds in number, were daughters of vassals, divided into nine houses. The economy rested on farming and cattle, lent out under the kuronzera system, which acted as vassalage. Religion centred on spirits and ancestors: mhondoro mediums, said to have begun with Matope, were consulted on war, succession and rain.
mutara-iii-rudahigwa: Rudahigwa was born at Nyanza, the royal capital, to King Yuhi V Musinga and Queen Kankazi, the first of his eleven wives, and belonged to the Tutsi Abanyiginya clan. He began his education in 1919 at the Colonial School for Chiefs' Sons in Nyanza, became his father's secretary in 1924 and in January 1929 was made a chief over a province. From 1929 Bishop Léon Classe instructed him in Christianity, and the Belgians groomed him to replace his father.

He took the throne on 16 November 1931, four days after the Belgians deposed Yuhi V Musinga for alleged contact with German agents. In 1943 he became the first Rwandan king to convert to Catholicism, baptised Charles Léon Pierre, and his conversion led a wave of baptisms. The famine years of 1941 to 1945 fell in his reign, among them the Ruzagayura famine of 1943–1944, in which 200,000 of a population of around two million died.

In 1935 the Belgian administration issued identity cards fixing the categories Tutsi, Hutu and Twa. After World War II a Hutu emancipation movement grew, and although he abolished the ubuhake system of indentured service in 1954, this had little practical effect. In 1956 he demanded independence from Belgium. The Bahutu Manifesto of 1957 denounced Tutsi rule, and Hutu parties formed under Gregoire Kayibanda and Joseph Gitera.

On 25 July 1959, the day after arriving in Usumbura for a meeting with Belgian officials, he died at the colonial hospital after visiting his Belgian doctor. The Belgians gave conflicting explanations, a cerebral haemorrhage or a reaction to penicillin, and no autopsy was done after the Queen Mother objected. Rumours that the Belgians had killed him spread, and Rwandans stoned Europeans' cars. His half-brother Jean-Baptiste Ndahindurwa succeeded him as Kigeli V. His widow, Rosalie Gicanda, was killed in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi.
mutare: Mutare lies near the border with Mozambique, about 290 kilometres from the Mozambican port of Beira, which has earned it the title Zimbabwe's Gateway to the Sea. The town lies north of the Bvumba Mountains and south of the Imbeza Valley, and it is also called the Gateway to the Eastern Highlands. Christmas Pass, a winding road with views of the highlands, leads into the city from the west and was named by colonial pioneers who camped at its foot on Christmas Day 1890. Many Zimbabweans call the city Kumakomoyo, place of many mountains.

The region had a long history of trading caravans passing through on the way between Indian Ocean ports such as Sofala and inland settlements such as Great Zimbabwe. The British archaeologist E. M. Andrews found a large hoard of soapstone carvings, jewellery, weapons and other objects near Mutare early in the twentieth century; they were donated to the British Museum in 1905. The area was the site of Chief Mutasa's kraal. In 1890 A. R. Coquhoun was given concessionary rights and Fort Umtali was established between the Tsambe and Mutare Rivers. The name Mutare is said to derive from utare, meaning iron or possibly gold, probably given to the river after gold was found in the Penhalonga valley.

In 1891 the settlement was moved to a site now known as Old Mutare, about 14 kilometres north of the city centre. The construction of the railway between Beira and Bulawayo led to a third move, closer to the line, and the British South Africa Company paid compensation to the townspeople for the cost. A tramway carried passengers from the railway station up to the Umtali Club from 26 January 1897 until 23 May 1921. The town was proclaimed a municipality on 11 June 1914 and was granted city status in 1971. The name was officially changed from Umtali to Mutare in 1982. The population was 46,000 in 1965, 69,621 in 1982 and 131,367 in 1992.

Mutare is the capital of Manicaland Province, a centre of trade on the Beira-Bulawayo railway, with road and pipeline links between the coast and the interior. The population is predominantly Shona, most of them speaking the Manyika dialect. Industries include timber, forestry, farming and food processing, and gold is mined in the area. Its attractions include the Mutare Museum, the National Gallery of Zimbabwe and Murahwa Hill, known for its rock paintings and an Iron Age village.
mutesa-i-of-buganda: Muteesa was born at the Batandabezaala Palace at Mulago, a son of Kabaka Ssuuna II and of Nabakyala Muganzirwazza, one of his father's 148 recorded wives. The historian MSM Kiwanuka called him an insignificant, obscure prince beside his brothers Prince Kajumba, his father's preferred heir, and Prince Kiyimba. On Ssuuna's death in October 1856 the chiefs, led by the Katikkiro Kayiira, chose Muteesa because they thought Kajumba would be hard to control. Rival princes were imprisoned on Kisimi Island, and after a plot to replace the new king with Kiyimba was foiled, the conspirators and both princes were executed.

Muteesa fought wars to expand Buganda, guard its trade routes and defend it against Bunyoro Kitara, the Khedivate of Egypt, armed slave traders and Buvuma. Buganda traded ivory, barkcloth and slaves for firearms, salt, cloth and copper wire from the East African coast and Zanzibar, and control of the routes let him limit the firearms that reached Bunyoro. He enlarged the kingdom's fleet on Lake Nnalubaale and backed Ruyonga with troops in Bunyoro's succession war after the death of the Omukama Kamurasi.

The first Europeans, John Hanning Speke and James Augustus Grant, arrived in 1862. Charles George Gordon, governor of Egypt's Equatoria province, sent envoys to divert Buganda's ivory from Zanzibar to Egypt; Charles Chaillé-Long claimed that Muteesa signed an agreement making Buganda a vassal of Egypt, which other historians dispute. Seeking a stronger ally, Muteesa had Stanley write an open letter inviting missionaries, published in the Daily Telegraph in November 1875. Missionaries of the Church Missionary Society arrived in 1877 and the White Fathers in 1879.

Muteesa died at Kasubi Nabulagala on 9 October 1884 and was the first kabaka buried at Kasubi. He is reported to have had 87 wives and 98 children, among them the later kabakas Mwanga II, Kiweewa Nnyonyintono and Kalema. Ugandan historians judge him variously: some regard him as the most important king of Buganda for his vision and diplomacy, while others hold that he welcomed foreign influence that undermined Buganda's sovereignty. Muteesa I Royal University was opened in his name in 2007.
mutesa-ii-of-buganda: Mutesa was born on 19 November 1924 at Makindye, Kampala, the fifth son of the Kabaka Daudi Cwa II and of Lady Irene Drusilla Namaganda of the Nte clan. He was educated at King's College Budo and then at Magdalene College, Cambridge, and was commissioned as a captain in the Grenadier Guards. When his father died on 22 November 1939 the Lukiiko elected him Kabaka at the age of 15, and he reigned under a Council of Regents until he came of age. He was crowned at Buddo on 19 November 1942, his eighteenth birthday.

In the early 1950s the British government floated a federation of Uganda, Kenya and Tanganyika. The Baganda feared that they would lose the limited autonomy they had under British rule, and Mutesa opposed the plan, which brought him into conflict with the governor, Sir Andrew Cohen. In 1953 the Lukiiko sought independence for Buganda from the Uganda Protectorate, and on 30 November Cohen deposed and exiled the Kabaka. The deportation made him a martyr in the eyes of the Baganda, and after two years of hostility he returned to Kampala on 17 October 1955 under a settlement that made him a constitutional monarch.

After independence in 1962 Mutesa's Kabaka Yekka party formed a governing coalition with Milton Obote's Uganda People's Congress, and on 4 October 1963 Parliament elected him president, a non-executive post, with the support of over two thirds of its members. The coalition collapsed in 1964 over a referendum on the lost counties, whose residents voted to return from Buganda to Bunyoro. In February 1966 Obote suspended the constitution and declared himself president. When the Buganda parliament demanded that the federal government leave the capital, Obote attacked the Kabaka's palace, and Mutesa went into exile. A new constitution in 1967 abolished all of Uganda's kingdoms.

In exile Mutesa wrote an autobiography, The Desecration of My Kingdom. He died in his London flat in Rotherhithe in 1969 of alcohol poisoning. The Metropolitan Police identified the death as suicide, while others have viewed it as assassination by agents of the Obote government. His body was buried provisionally at Kensal Green Cemetery and returned to Uganda in 1971, after Obote was overthrown, for a state funeral ordered by Idi Amin, who as army commander had led the assault on his palace in 1966.
mutimir-of-serbia: Mutimir was the eldest son of Knez Vlastimir, a great-great-grandson of the unnamed 7th-century ruler who had united the Serb tribes into a state. Between 839 and 842 Vlastimir fought off an invasion by Khan Presian I of Bulgaria in a three-year war and then extended his rule west into south-eastern Bosnia and Hum. When Vlastimir died, sometime between 845 and 850, his lands were divided among his three sons, Mutimir, Strojimir and Gojnik. The brothers ruled together, but Mutimir held the supreme rule and the other two acted as his vassals.

In 853 or 854 a Bulgar army led by Vladimir, son of Boris I of Bulgaria, invaded Serbia to avenge the earlier defeat. Mutimir and his brothers defeated it and captured Vladimir and 12 boyars. Boris and Mutimir agreed to end hostilities, and Mutimir's sons Bran and Stefan escorted the prisoners to the border, where gifts were exchanged: Boris gave rich gifts and received two slaves, two falcons, two dogs and 80 furs. A later quarrel among the brothers, perhaps over treachery, ended with Mutimir banishing Strojimir and Gojnik to the Bulgarian court. He kept Gojnik's son Petar at his court, but Petar soon fled to Croatia.

By 878 Byzantine rule had been restored over Dalmatia after Emperor Basil I sent a fleet to relieve Ragusa from the Saracens in 866. Constantine VII later credited missionaries sent by Basil I with baptising the Serbs, and Basil probably sent at least one embassy to Mutimir. In a letter dated to May 873, Pope John VIII urged Mutimir to return to the jurisdiction of the Pannonian diocese of Sirmium, complaining of wandering priests without a bishop. Mutimir seemingly kept the Church in Serbia in communion with the Patriarchate of Constantinople, and the Serbs adopted the Old Slavonic liturgy rather than the Greek.

Mutimir died in 891 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Pribislav. He and Pribislav appear to have been entered in the Cividale Gospels, which may point to contacts with Aquileia. The Christian names of the next generation of the dynasty, Petar Gojniković, Stefan Mutimirović and Pavle Branović, show a lasting Christian identity. Alexis P. Vlasto argued that the Eparchy of Ras was founded in his reign, but Predrag Komatina and Tibor Živković found no evidence of a bishopric in Serbia at the time. His peace with Boris I is shown in the 1985 Bulgarian film Boris I.
mutsamudu: Mutsamudu, also written Moutsamoudou, was likely founded in 1482. It grew into a prosperous Swahili port that funnelled traffic between the Swahili ports of Mozambique and Madagascar. Later, Arab, Persian, Indian, Somali and Malagasy sailors and traders settled in the town. By the 1700s it was the most prosperous town in the Comoros archipelago.

In 1773 the commissioner Frederick Holtzappel visited it during an expedition along the Swahili Coast and recorded his admiration. He noted that the houses were built of stone, whitewashed inside and out, with painted plank ceilings and roofs thatched with coconut leaves. He saw several two-storey houses belonging to the elite, whom he called Turkified. There were numerous public baths in the town, and every elite household had its own. The men wore white linen gowns and turbans, as well as silk clothing and daggers with silver sheaths. The citadel was built in 1786 with British help to protect the town from Malagasy slave raisers, and it was badly damaged in 1950 at the landfall of a cyclone.

Mutsamudu has two parallel main streets, with the medina of the 15th century lying between them, and narrow streets with many shops and small crafts. It is the capital and largest city of the island of Anjouan and the second-largest city in the Comoros. Its deep-water port, built in 1982, is the only one in the Union of the Comoros; three quarters of its cargo is containerised goods transhipped to the other two islands. Rice, cement, sugar, flour and petroleum products come in through it, and ylang-ylang, cloves and vanilla go out. The climate is marine tropical, with temperatures from 27°C to 32°C throughout the year.
mutsu-munemitsu: Mutsu was born on 20 August 1844 in Wakayama domain in Kii Province, the sixth son of Date Munehiro, a samurai retainer of the Kii Tokugawa Clan who was active in the Sonnō jōi movement. Mutsu joined Sakamoto Ryōma and Itō Hirobumi in the movement to overthrow the Tokugawa shogunate.

After the Meiji Restoration he governed Hyōgo and then Kanagawa prefectures, both of which held foreign settlements, headed the Land Tax Reform of 1873–1881 and sat on the Genrōin. He was imprisoned from 1878 until 1883 for conspiring to help Saigō Takamori in the Satsuma Rebellion, and in prison he translated Jeremy Bentham's Utilitarianism into Japanese. Rejoining the government in the Foreign Ministry, he was sent to Europe for studies in 1884 and was Minister to Washington D.C. from 1888 to 1890, when he established diplomatic relations between Japan and Mexico and partially revised the unequal treaties with the United States.

Back in Japan in 1890 he became Minister of Agriculture and Commerce and won a seat in the House of Representatives for the 1st Wakayama District. As Foreign Minister in the cabinet of Itō Hirobumi from 1892, he was the lead Japanese negotiator of the Treaty of Shimonoseki. After a Japanese fanatic attempted to kill the Chinese negotiator Li Hongzhang, the government reduced the indemnity it meant to claim, and Mutsu remarked that Li's misfortune was the good fortune of the Great Ch'ing Empire.

When the Triple Intervention of France, Germany and Russia reversed the gains of Shimonoseki, the Japanese public blamed Mutsu. He resigned all government posts in May 1896 and moved to Ōiso, Kanagawa, where he wrote his diplomatic memoir Kenkenroku; because of the secrets it contained, it could not be published until 1923. He had been made a count at the end of the war and received the Grand Cordon of the Order of the Rising Sun in 1895. He died of tuberculosis in Takinogawa, Tokyo Prefecture, on 24 August 1897.
mutsu-province: Mutsu lay in northern Honshū, in what is now Fukushima, Miyagi, Iwate and Aomori prefectures and the municipalities of Kazuno and Kosaka in Akita Prefecture. It was also called Ōshū or Michinoku, and the early forms of the name varied between Mutu and Miti. Together with the neighbouring Dewa Province it makes up the Tōhoku region, known also as Ōu from the Chinese readings of the two names.

Mutsu was one of the last provinces to be formed, as land was taken from the indigenous Emishi, and it grew to be the largest as it expanded northward. The regional capital of the Kinai government was Tagajō, in present-day Miyagi Prefecture. In 709 an uprising against the government broke out in Mutsu and in nearby Echigo Province, and troops were sent to put it down. In 712 Mutsu was separated from Dewa Province, and in 718 several of its districts were joined with others to form Iwaki Province. Sakanoue no Tamuramaro conquered Mutsu in 801. In 869 a severe earthquake struck it and killed more than 1,000 people.

In 1095 the Ōshū Fujiwara clan settled at Hiraizumi under Fujiwara no Kiyohira, who hoped to build a city rivalling Kyoto as a centre of culture. Their legacy survives in the temples Chūson-ji and Mōtsū-ji in Hiraizumi and in the Shiramizu Amidadō in Iwaki. In 1189 Minamoto no Yoritomo invaded Mutsu with three great forces, killed Fujiwara no Yasuhira and took the entire domain. In the Sengoku period clans ruled parts of the province: the Nanbu at Morioka in the north, the Date at Iwadeyama and Sendai, the Sōma at Nakamura, the Iwaki at Iinodaira and the Uesugi, who had a castle town at Wakamatsu, in the south.

After the Boshin War the Meiji government divided Mutsu into five provinces: Iwashiro, Iwaki, Rikuzen, Rikuchū and Rikuō. The last, corresponding roughly to today's Aomori Prefecture, was written with the same two characters as the old province but read differently, so it has sometimes also been called Mutsu.
muwatalli-ii: Muwatalli II, whose name means mighty, was the eldest son of Mursili II and Queen Gassulawiya. His wife was Tanu-Ḫepa, and he had at least two children. One was Urhi-Teshup, who became king as Mursili III until his uncle Hattusili III, Muwatalli's younger brother, deposed him. Another was Kurunta, who became the vassal ruler of Tarhuntassa. Egyptologists suspect that before Ramesses II came to the throne, Muwatalli had reached an informal understanding with Seti I over Kadesh, by which Seti effectively ceded the city so as to focus on affairs at home.

Early in his reign Muwatalli moved the Hittite capital from Hattusa to a new city he named Tarhuntassa, and appointed his brother Hattusili governor at Hattusa. No document gives the reason. One theory holds that after stabilising the northern frontier against the Kaska and Piyamaradu's rebellion, he moved south for a better position in the coming fight with Egypt over Syria. Itamar Singer argues instead for a religious reform. The move eventually led to a bitter civil war after his death. He also made treaties with Alakšandu of Wiluša and with Talmi-Šarrumma of Aleppo.

At the Battle of Kadesh against Ramesses II, Muwatalli's spies, posing as deserters, convinced Ramesses that the Hittite army was far away at Aleppo, and Hittite chariots then attacked the Egyptian army as it marched towards Kadesh. Both sides claimed victory, but scholars generally believe that it went badly for both, and especially for Ramesses. Afterwards Muwatalli continued to expand into Syria, and Egyptian expansion was halted in the area of Palestine.
muyeol-of-silla: Kim Ch'un-ch'u was born into the sacred bone (seonggol) rank. His father, Kim Yong-su, was a son of King Jinji, Silla's 25th ruler, and his mother, Princess Cheonmyeong, was a daughter of King Jinpyeong. When Jinji was overthrown, his line was deemed unfit to rule, and Kim Yong-su, having lost his power to Kim Paek-ban, the king's brother, accepted demotion to the true bone (jingol) rank just below, which removed his own and his son's right to the throne.

On the death of his aunt, Queen Seondeok, Ch'un-ch'u was passed over in favour of Jindeok of Silla, the last verifiable seonggol. When she died no sacred bone was left, so a jingol of royal blood had to succeed. The favourite was Alcheon, who held the highest post of government, Sangdaedeung, but Kim Yu-sin backed Ch'un-ch'u, and Alcheon stood aside and supported his claim.

The tie with Kim Yu-sin was also a family one. Yu-sin arranged a meeting between Ch'un-ch'u and his sister Munhee, and when she became pregnant he spread word that he might burn her, until Queen Seondeok, seeing the smoke from his house, ordered Ch'un-ch'u to marry her. Munhee became his wife after his first wife, Boryang, died in childbirth, and queen when he was crowned in 654. Their son was the future King Munmu, and Kim Yu-sin became the most powerful man at court.

Muyeol had been a friend of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty before Gaozong took the throne, and he repeatedly asked the Tang for troops against Baekje. In 660 the Tang sent 130,000 men under General Su Dingfang, while Kim Yu-sin led 50,000 soldiers from Silla and fought the Battle of Hwangsanbeol. King Uija of Baekje surrendered, leaving Goguryeo as Silla's only rival on the peninsula.

Muyeol died in June of the following year and was succeeded by Munmu. He is credited with leading the unification of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, which his son completed. His tomb in Gyeongju is the only Silla-era tomb whose owner is known with certainty.
muzaffar-al-din-gokbori: Gökböri, whose name means Blue-wolf in Old Turkic, was born on 13 April 1154 into a Turcoman family, the Begtegīnids, associated with the Seljuk Turks. When his father died in August 1168 the fourteen-year-old succeeded to the lordship of Erbil, but the atabeg Kaimaz deposed him in favour of his younger brother. In exile he took service with the Zengid prince Sayf al-Din Ghazi II of Mosul, who granted him Harran as a fief. He commanded the right wing of the Zengid army that Saladin defeated at the Horns of Hama on 13 April 1175.

Seeing Zengid power wane, he defected to Saladin in 1182 and invited him across the Euphrates into the Jazira, and his support helped reduce Zengid rule to little more than Mosul and Aleppo. Briefly arrested in 1185 on suspicion of collusion with Izz ad-Din Mas'ud of Mosul, he nursed Saladin through a grave illness at his castle in Harran and was given Edessa and Samsat.

At the Battle of Cresson in 1187 he led the army that destroyed a Christian force and killed Roger de Moulins, master of the Knights Hospitaller; his Christian enemies knew him as Manafaradin. At Hattin he commanded the Ayyubid left, and according to Ibn Khallikan he and Saladin's nephew Taqi ad-Din stood firm when the rest of the army was fleeing and led the counter-attack that decided the battle.

During the Siege of Acre in 1190 his brother Zain ad-Din Yusuf died, and Gökböri gave up Edessa, Harran and Samsat in return for Erbil and Shahrozur. After Saladin's death in 1193 he was in effect independent, acknowledging only the caliph. Erbil became a centre of Sunni learning: he patronised Ibn Khallikan and the vizier Ibn al-Mustawfi, who wrote a history of the city in four volumes, and he founded the Dar al-Hadith al-Muzaffariya in 1198.

He kept his position through alliances, joining al-Muazzam of Damascus in an attack on Mosul in 1226. Without a male heir, he willed Erbil to the Abbasid Caliph al-Mustansir. He fell ill while campaigning against the Mongols and died on 28 June 1233, and he was buried in Kufa.
muzaffar-shah-i: Zafar Khan was born on 30 June 1342, the son of Wajih-ul-Mulk; his paternal aunt was married into the Tughluq family. The Mirʾāt-i-Sikandarī tells that the saint Jahaniyan Jahangasht, in return for food given to fakirs at his house, handed him a handful of dates and foretold that his descendants, as many as the seeds, would rule Gujarat. In 1391 Sultan Nasir ud-Din Muhammad Shah III appointed him governor of Gujarat with the title Muzaffar Khan, replacing Farhat-ul-Mulk, who was rumoured to be seeking independence.

Farhat-ul-Mulk was defeated and killed in battle near Anhilwada Patan, and Zafar Khan founded Jitpur, the city of victory, on the battlefield. He forced tribute from the Rao of Idar in 1393 and from the Rao of Junagadh in 1394, then destroyed the Somnath temple, built a mosque and posted Muslim officials there. He besieged Mandu for a year without taking it and fought the chiefs of Sambhar and Dandwana and the Rajputs of Delvada and Jhalavada.

After Timur sacked Delhi, Sultan Mahmud II came to Patan seeking an alliance, which Zafar Khan refused. In 1403 his son Tatar Khan, whose call to march on Delhi he had also refused, imprisoned him at Ashawal, the future Ahmedabad, and took the title Muhammad Shah. Tatar Khan died on the march to Delhi, poisoned, some say, by his uncle Shams Khan Dandani, and Zafar Khan was freed in 1404. In 1407 he proclaimed himself Sultan Muzaffar Shah at Birpur and issued coins in his own name.

When Hushang Shah was rumoured to have poisoned his father Dilawar Khan of the Malwa Sultanate, Muzaffar Shah besieged him in Dhar and took him captive. A year later, after a kinsman, Musa Khan, had usurped Malwa, he sent his grandson Ahmed Khan with an army to restore Hushang, and the fortress of Mandu was taken. He also marched towards Delhi in support of Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Shah Tughluq, forestalling an attack on the city by Sultan Ibrahim of Jaunpur.

Accounts of his end differ. The Mirat-i-Ahmadi says he abdicated in favour of his grandson because of failing health and died some months later. The Mirat-i-Sikandari says that Ahmad Shah, after seeking the opinion of the ulema on avenging his father's unjust death, forced him to drink poison. He was buried at Patan.
muzaffar-shah-i-of-perak: Muzaffar Shah I was born Raja Muzaffar in 1505, the son of Mahmud Shah of Malacca and Putri Onang Kening, a daughter of Mansur Shah of Kelantan. When the Malacca Sultanate fell to the Portuguese in 1511, Mahmud Shah retreated with his family to Ulu Muar, then to Pahang and Pulau Bintan, where he ruled again. There Raja Muzaffar married Tun Terang, the daughter of Tun Fatimah by her first husband Tun Ali, and they had a son, Raja Mansur, who would succeed him.

After his defeat by the Portuguese in 1526, Mahmud Shah withdrew to Kampar in Sumatra, where he died around 1528 and was succeeded by Raja Ali. Raja Muzaffar was driven out by the Bendahara and chiefs, and he left Kampar with his wife and son, stopping at Klang before going on to Perak.

The Malay Annals say that the people of Perak made him their first sultan. The Sejarah Raja Perak tells a different story: Perak sent Tun Saban and Nakhoda Kasim to Kampar to ask Mahmud Shah for his son as ruler, and the old sultan agreed. Guided by Nakhoda Tumi of Manjong, Raja Muzaffar was welcomed at Beting Beras Basah, taken up the Perak River and installed as Sultan Muzaffar Shah at Tanah Abang, in the Lambor Kanan area.

According to the Malay Annals he invited Tun Mahmud, son of Tun Isap Berakah, from Selangor to be the first Bendahara of Perak, but Tun Mahmud was later summoned to Johor by Alauddin Riayat Shah II. The Sejarah Raja Perak records a war with Tun Saban after Tun Saban refused to give his daughter Tun Merah to the sultan. Muzaffar Shah offered the office of Bendahara to whoever killed Tun Saban. Megat Terawis, who had come with him from Kampar, did so and was made Bendahara, and his descendants held the office until the reign of Sultan Iskandar Zulkarnain, the fifteenth sultan.

Muzaffar Shah I ruled Perak until his death in 1549, after 21 years on the throne, and was buried at Tanah Abang, which had been the centre of his government once Tun Saban was dead. His son Raja Mansur, born to Tun Terang during the family's years at Pulau Bintan, succeeded him.
muzaffar-shah-of-malacca: Born Raja Kassim, he was a son of Sultan Muhammad Shah and Tun Wati, and the History of Ming records him as Sulutan Wudafona Sha. He became the fifth ruler of Malacca on the death of his half-brother, Raja Sri Parameswara Dewa Shah. His uncle Tun Ali, an influential Tamil Muslim leader, allegedly conspired to have the previous ruler assassinated so that his nephew could take the throne.

On his installation Raja Kassim took the name Muzaffar Shah and ordered his senior officers to keep all the customs, traditions and prohibitions his father had introduced. He married a daughter of the bendahara, the chief minister, and had a son, Raja Abdullah. When the bendahara Seri Wak Raja I died, the sultan gave the office to his son Tun Perpatih Sedang, who took his own life by poison after wrongly believing the sultan displeased with him.

Custom would have passed the office to Tun Perpatih Sedang's son Tun Perak, but the sultan, grateful for help in gaining the throne, made his uncle Tun Ali bendahara instead, married Tun Perak's sister Tun Kudu and sent Tun Perak away to be chieftain of Klang. In 1456, during the reign of King Trailok, Siam planned an attack on Malacca by sea. Malacca's fleet, led by Tun Perak, with the warrior Tun Hamzah, known as Datuk Bongkok, met the Siamese at Batu Pahat and drove them back to Singapore in what was counted as Malacca's first battle.

The victory raised Tun Perak's standing and brought him into rivalry with Tun Ali. To keep the peace, Tun Ali agreed to step down if he could marry Tun Kudu, and the sultan divorced her so that she could marry him. The two ministers became friends, and around 1456 the sultan appointed Tun Perak bendahara with the title Paduka Raja.
muzaka-family: The family came from the lower Opar region, where many of its ancestral burial grounds lie around the village of Lavdar; ethnographic sources name Lal Muzaka as its earliest known member. Gjon Muzaka claimed that the name came from the Myzeqë region, itself named after the Molossians through a corruption of Molossi. The earliest mention of the family is in the work of the Byzantine historian Anna Komnene, who around 1090 describes a Muzaka as a loyal commander of Alexios I Komnenos. The family's coat of arms was a two-headed eagle.

At the turn of the 14th century the Muzaka held the land between the rivers Devoll and Vjosë. Some served Byzantium while others took titles such as sebastokrator from Charles of Anjou; Gjon I Muzaka, loyal to the Byzantines, was captured by Angevin forces in 1279 and released under pressure from Albanian nobles. Andrea II Muzaka became despot in 1335 but then backed an anti-Byzantine revolt and in 1336 became a vassal of Robert, Prince of Taranto. Around 1340 he defeated a Serbian army at the Pelister mountain. Stefan Dušan took the family's domains in the 1340s, but after his death in 1355 they regained Berat and took Kastoria.

Andrea II's descendants divided his lands at his death in 1372, Theodor II holding Myzeqe and Berat. With Stoya Muzaka he built the Church of St Athanasius of Mouzaki in Kastoria in 1383-84, and the family chronicle has him fall at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. After the Battle of Savra in 1385 the region came under Ottoman control, and the annexation of Vlorë and Berat ended the family's rule.

Some of the family converted to Islam and served the Ottomans: Yakup Bey Muzaka was sanjakbey of the Sanjak of Albania until he was killed in 1442 by forces under Janos Hunyadi. In 1444 Theodor Corona Musachi joined Skanderbeg's rebellion, and when the Ottomans crushed it many of the family withdrew to Italy, while those who stayed lost their feudal rights. Theodor is remembered in South Slavic epic poetry as Korun Aramija, enemy of Prince Marko. According to some sources the last member of the line in Italy died at Naples in 1600, but in the 18th century Ahmet Pasha Kurt of the family was sanjakbey of Avlona.
muziris: Muziris lay near the mouth of the Periyar River in the Chera country of Tamilakam. Its Tamil name, Muciṟi, is said to come from the Old Tamil word for a cleft lip, for the Periyar branches in two there. The Periplus places it 20 stadia up a river from the shore. Because the shallows kept deep-hulled ships from sailing upriver, Roman freighters waited at the edge of the lagoon while smaller craft carried their cargoes to and from the port. The site was once placed near Mangalore and later at Kodungallur; excavations at Pattanam since 2007 have led some experts to favour that village, though the identification is disputed.

Sangam poems describe Yavana ships arriving with gold and leaving with pepper, and Pliny the Elder called Muziris the first emporium of India, though he warned of pirates nearby. Besides black pepper and malabathron it exported beryl, pearls, diamonds, ivory, Chinese silk and tortoise shell, while Roman traders brought gold coins, textiles, metals, coral, raw glass and wine. The 2nd-century Muziris papyrus records a cargo worth around 9 million sesterces carried on the ship Hermapollon, and the Peutinger Map marks a temple of Augustus near the port. A Tamil poem tells of a Pandya prince besieging it, and after Roman trade declined from the 5th century Persians, Chinese and Arabs traded there.

The port is thought to have vanished after floods on the Periyar in 1341, which opened the harbour at Kochi and formed the island of Vypin. The historians Rajan Gurukkal and Dick Whittakker see this as only the most dramatic of the changes along the coast, where the regular silting of the river mouth finally ended the port's life.

Excavations by the Kerala Council for Historical Research at Pattanam, in seven seasons from 2007 to 2014, found amphora shards, Roman glass, beads, Chera coins and a brick wharf with teak bollards and a 6-metre canoe; occupation there reaches back to the 10th century BCE. The Kerala Tourism Department's Muziris Heritage Project covers Pattanam and other historic sites of central Kerala.
muzo: Muzo is a town and municipality in the Western Boyacá Province of the department of Boyacá, Colombia. It is widely known as the world capital of emeralds, for mines that hold what are described as the world's highest-quality gems of this type. The urban centre stands at 815 metres above sea level, 178 kilometres from the departmental capital Tunja and 118 kilometres from Chiquinquirá, the capital of the province. The median temperature is 26 °C and the annual rainfall 3,152 millimetres. When the Spanish first founded the settlement it was called Villa de la Santísima Trinidad de los Muzos, or simply Trinidad; Muzo is the name the indigenous people used for themselves.

Before the Spanish conquest the region was inhabited by the Muzo, who extracted emeralds in pre-Columbian times and were called the Emerald People. They used poles of hard tropical wood and water to peel the stones from the rock formations. Historians estimate that they settled the area around 1000 CE. The Cariban-speaking Muzo, like their Chibcha neighbours, adored the Sun and Moon as deities but, unlike them, built no temples.

After the conquest of the Muisca to the east, Spanish expeditions pressed into Muzo territory. Luis Lanchero arrived first, in 1539, with the expedition of Nikolaus Federmann; the Muzo used the rugged terrain and poisoned arrows against his forty men, and he withdrew to Bogotá in 1541. Diego Martínez found the rich emerald deposits in a second invasion in 1544, and Pedro de Ursúa failed to conquer the Muzo in 1552. On a fourth attempt Lanchero defeated them and founded the town on 20 February 1559. Juan de los Barrios led the first evangelisation in 1566. The Spanish set up encomiendas to guard the gemstones and used the indigenous people as forced labour in the extraction.

Emerald mining provides about 75 per cent of the municipality's income, and agriculture and livestock the rest, with sugarcane, cacao, yuca, avocados and citrus fruits. The mines lie on the western flank of the Eastern ranges of the Colombian Andes. The Devonshire emerald, an uncut stone of 1,383.95 carats, comes from them; Emperor Dom Pedro I of Brazil gave it to the 6th Duke of Devonshire in 1831.
mwai-kibaki: Emilio Stanley Mwai Kibaki was born on 15 November 1931 in Gatuyaini village, Othaya division of the then Nyeri District, the youngest son of Kikuyu peasants Kibaki Gĩthĩnji and Teresia Wanjikũ. Italian missionaries baptised him Emilio Stanley, but he was known as Mwai Kibaki throughout his public life. He attended the Karima mission school and Mathari School, where he also learned carpentry and masonry, and at Mang'u High School from 1947 to 1950 he gained the highest grade in his O Level examinations.

In early 1960 Kibaki left his post at Makerere to become an executive officer of the Kenya African National Union (KANU), at the request of Thomas Joseph Mboya, and helped draft the independence constitution. In 1963 he was elected Member of Parliament for Doonholm in Nairobi and appointed Permanent Secretary for the Treasury. He became Minister of Commerce and Industry in 1966 and Minister of Finance and Economic Planning in 1969, and was Vice-President under Daniel arap Moi from 1978 to 1988.

He sat as an opposition member from 1992, ran unsuccessfully for the presidency in 1992 and 1997 and led the official opposition in Parliament from 1998 to 2002. For the 2002 election his Democratic Party joined other opposition parties in the National Alliance of Kenya, which merged with the Liberal Democratic Party to form the National Rainbow Coalition. On 14 October 2002 Raila Odinga declared him its candidate with the words "Kibaki Tosha!".

Kibaki was sworn in on 30 December 2002, ending four decades of KANU rule. His administration introduced free primary education in January 2003. In the referendum of 21 November 2005, 58 per cent of voters rejected a draft constitution he supported, and two days later he dismissed his entire cabinet. After the disputed election of 2007, in which he stood for the Party of National Unity against Odinga's ODM, mediation led by Kofi Annan produced a national accord in February 2008. Kibaki remained president, and on 17 April 2008 Odinga was sworn in as Prime Minister. A new constitution was promulgated in 2010. Kibaki handed the presidency to Uhuru Kenyatta on 9 April 2013 and died on 21 April 2022, aged 90.
mwambutsa-iv: Born Prince Bangiricenge at Nyabiyogi in the chiefdom of Buyenzi, he was one of two sons of Mwami Mutaga IV and Ngenzahayo and, like other Burundian kings, an ethnic Ganwa. He became king as a child on 16 December 1915, after his father died in a family dispute, and a regency was formed in which family members including Queen Mother Ririkumutima served; a full regency council followed in 1925 with Belgian approval. Belgium had taken Burundi from German East Africa in 1916. He attended a primary school opened for him at Muramvya, but never converted to Catholicism.

He was declared of age on 28 August 1929, and on 24 December 1930 he married Thérèse Kanyonga, a Catholic Tutsi of the Abasine clan. The Belgians kept the monarchy under their policy of indirect rule, and Mwambutsa held aloof from party politics, declaring on 8 February 1960 that he belonged to no party. Burundi became independent as a kingdom on 1 July 1962, with Mwambutsa as head of state with wide powers. While the monarchy of Rwanda had been overthrown, he tried to balance Hutu and Tutsi by choosing prime ministers from each group in turn.

After Hutu officers attempted a coup in October 1965, he went into exile and eventually settled in Switzerland. In March 1966 he delegated his powers to his only surviving son, Charles Ndizeye, who was brought to power as Ntare V by a coup on 8 July 1966; a further coup in November abolished the monarchy and brought Michel Micombero to power.

Mwambutsa spent the rest of his life in Switzerland and died there in 1977. His remains were exhumed in 2012 so that they could be taken home for a state funeral in Burundi, but after a legal battle they were reburied in Switzerland in 2016, in accordance with his family's wishes.
mwanga-ii: Mwanga II was born at Nakawa on 3 June 1868, a son of Kabaka Muteesa I and of Abakyala Abisagi Bagalayaze, the tenth of his father's 85 wives. He came to the throne at sixteen on 18 October 1884 and set up his capital on Mengo Hill. His father had played Catholics, Protestants and Muslims off against one another, and so balanced the foreign powers behind each; Mwanga saw the missionaries as the chief threat to his rule and took a far harsher course.

The killing of the converts alarmed the British, who backed Christian and Muslim groups that defeated him at Mengo in 1888 and raised his brother Kiweewa Nnyonyintono, who lasted a month, and then Kalema Muguluma. Mwanga escaped and, by ceding some sovereignty to the British East Africa Company, won British backing and removed Kalema in 1889. He later became a Protestant. On 26 December 1890 he signed a treaty with Lord Lugard granting the company powers over revenue, trade and justice, and on 27 August 1894 he accepted a British protectorate. On 6 July 1897 he declared war on the British and was defeated at Buddu on 20 July.

Interned by the German colonial authorities at Bukoba, he was deposed in his absence on 9 August 1897 and succeeded by his son Daudi Chwa II. He escaped, returned with a rebel army and was beaten again on 15 January 1898, then captured and sent to the Seychelles in April 1899, where he was received into the Anglican Church as Danieri. He died there on 8 May 1903, and his remains were buried at the Kasubi Tombs on 2 August 1910.

Historians have judged him variously. Samwiri Karugire held him unequal to the foreigners subverting his kingdom, yet right to claim the authority of his forefathers; Kabaka Mutesa II wrote in 1967 that he deserved some sympathy, and Morris Twaddle that for sheer tyranny his father and forebears easily outclassed him.
my-country-tis-of-thee: Smith gave Lowell Mason the words he had written, and the song was first performed in public on 4 July 1831, at a children's Independence Day celebration at Park Street Church in Boston. Setting new words to the tune of the British royal anthem made it a contrafactum: it took up a symbol of the British monarchy and turned it to a statement about American democracy. Before the adoption of The Star-Spangled Banner as the official national anthem of the United States in 1931, it served as one of the country's de facto anthems, along with songs such as Hail, Columbia.

The five stanzas address the country as a sweet land of liberty, the land where the singer's fathers died and of the pilgrims' pride, and the first ends with the call to let freedom ring from every mountainside. Later verses praise its rocks and rills, woods and templed hills, look to a time when tyrants and soldier bands shall no more appear, and close with a prayer to the God of the singers' fathers, the author of liberty. An abolitionist version was written by A. G. Duncan in 1843, with lyrics mentioning white and black races, and a further verse was added for the centennial of Washington.

The singer Marian Anderson performed the song at the Lincoln Memorial on Easter Sunday, 9 April 1939, after she had been barred from the DAR Constitution Hall because of its whites-only policy. With the support of Eleanor Roosevelt, the concert drew a crowd of more than 75,000 and a national radio audience of millions. Martin Luther King Jr. recited its first verse near the end of his I Have a Dream speech at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom on 28 August 1963. Aretha Franklin sang it at the first inauguration of Barack Obama on 20 January 2009.
myanmar-civil-war-2021-present: Insurgencies have been ongoing in Myanmar since 1948, largely along ethnic lines, with communists and the Karen National Union opposing the central government and groups such as the Kachin Independence Army forming after the 1962 coup. On 1 February 2021 the Tatmadaw overthrew the elected government, formed a State Administration Council under Min Aung Hlaing and detained the leaders of the National League for Democracy. It claimed that the 2020 election had 8.6 million voter irregularities but presented no evidence. The violent repression of anti-coup demonstrations led to armed groups, which aligned with the National Unity Government, formed by ousted parliamentarians, as the People's Defence Force; in September 2021 they declared a defensive war against the council's rule.

Ethnic armed organisations were strengthened by the unrest: the Kachin Independence Army took the base of Alaw Bum on 25 March 2021, and the Karen National Liberation Army attacked a base the next day. By 2022 the opposition held substantial, though sparsely populated, territory, and the Arakan Army and the junta agreed a temporary ceasefire in November 2022. On 27 October 2023 the Three Brotherhood Alliance launched Operation 1027 near Lashio, taking 57 bases within days, and other offensives followed, among them Operation 1111 at Loikaw. By October 2023 the Tatmadaw controlled under 40 per cent of the country, though it maintained that it held about two thirds of the 330 townships.

In 2024 anti-junta forces captured Demoso, Papun and Matupi, and on 3 August the MNDAA took Lashio, headquarters of the Northeastern Command; on 20 December the Arakan Army took the Western Command headquarters at Ann. After the earthquake of 28 March 2025 both sides declared ceasefires. On 31 July 2025 the council announced its dissolution and transferred power to a National Defence and Security Council under Min Aung Hlaing. The junta retook Kyaukme on 2 October 2025, and the MNDAA withdrew from Lashio under Chinese pressure.

By March 2023 the United Nations estimated that 17.6 million people needed humanitarian assistance, 1.6 million were internally displaced and over 55,000 civilian buildings had been destroyed. The military was accused of war crimes, among them murder, torture, sexual violence and attacks on civilians, and its aerial bombing campaign was reported to have displaced nearly three million people. The economy contracted by more than 18 per cent in 2021, according to the French ambassador, and the Burmese kyat lost over 60 per cent of its value by September 2022. Resistance groups made their own weapons and set up an Interim Central Bank.
mycenae: Mycenae stands on a hill 274 metres above sea level in the north-east corner of the Argive plain, about 120 kilometres south-west of Athens and 11 kilometres north of Argos. From there it overlooked the whole plain and commanded all easy routes to the Isthmus of Corinth, and it also had good farmland and an adequate water supply. The name is thought not to be Greek but one of the many pre-Greek place names inherited by later speakers. Pausanias ascribed it to its founder in myth, Perseus, who named it either after the cap, mykēs, of his sword sheath or after a mushroom he plucked there.

The site was continuously occupied from the Early Neolithic. The shaft graves that Heinrich Schliemann found in 1876 are called Grave Circle A and date to the sixteenth century BCE. They show extensive Cretan influence. The earlier and less wealthy Grave Circle B, found in 1951, dates from about 1650 to 1550 BCE. Mycenae became a major power from about 1550 BCE and the main centre of Aegean civilisation through the fifteenth century, and it gave its name to the Mycenaean Age. Mycenaeans occupied Knossos until its destruction about 1370 BCE. At its peak in 1350 BCE the citadel and lower town had a population of 30,000. Linear B tablets show that a king, the wanax, ruled the Mycenaean state.

Mycenae was among the sites destroyed in the Bronze Age Collapse around 1200 BCE. The causes are unknown, though enemy attack, internal strife and earthquakes have been proposed. It was partly rebuilt, but no longer as the centre of a centralised literate bureaucracy, and it was sparsely populated until the Hellenistic period. A temple of Hera was built on the summit in the Archaic Period. A Mycenaean contingent fought at Thermopylae and Plataea, but in 468 BCE troops from Argos captured the place, expelled the inhabitants and razed the fortifications. In the second century CE Pausanias saw the walls and the Lion Gate still standing.

Francesco Vandeyk, a Venetian engineer, correctly identified the ruins in 1700 using Pausanias's description of the Lion Gate, and he also identified the Treasury of Atreus. Schliemann, who believed Homer's stories were historically true, hoped to find Agamemnon's grave. He labelled a gold death mask from Grave Circle A the Mask of Agamemnon, but it dates more than 300 years before the events of the Trojan War. Christos Tsountas cleared much of the citadel between 1884 and 1902.

Mycenae and nearby Tiryns were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1999. Its notable architecture includes the Lion Gate, the Treasury of Atreus and the walls of the citadel, and it is strongly connected with the Homeric epics.
myitnge-river: The Myitnge is a major tributary of the Irrawaddy, or Ayeyarwady. Its Burmese name and the Pali name Dokhtawaddy both mean little river, in contrast with the Ayeyarwady, the big river. It rises on the watershed between the Irrawaddy and the Salween, not far from the Salween itself, and flows west through the northern Shan Plateau, where it is called the Namtu River, past towns such as Namtu, Hsenwi and Hsipaw.

Near its mouth the river divides. The Myittha branch leaves it to the west, while the eastern stream keeps the name Myitnge and enters the Ayeyarwady at Amarapura; the old capital of the Ava Kingdom was built between the two. The Zawgyi River joins it about 20 km north of Kyaukse at Nyaungbintha, and the Panlaung River near Ava.

On its north bank stands the Shwe Sar Yan Pagoda, built in 1053 by the Shan princess Sao Mon Hla on her way home after marrying and then leaving King Anawrahta of Bagan; its festival begins each year just before the full moon of Tabaung, in March. Anawrahta built weirs and canals on the Panlaung and Zawgyi rivers but found the Myitnge too wild to tame. Three centuries later Thado Minbya founded Ava at the confluence, within easy reach of the rice granary of Kyaukse.

In the Second World War the railway bridge over the Myitnge, on the main line from Mandalay to Rangoon, was a target of B-25s and B-24s of the USAAF from New Year's Day 1943 to late April, and again that December together with the rail yards at nearby Paleik. Two years later RAF Thunderbolts attacked it.

A new road bridge over the river, 700 feet long and 27 feet wide with a footpath on each side, was opened in 1999. A hydroelectric project, the Yeywa Dam, was begun with assistance from China on the Myitnge about 50 km south-east of Mandalay.
mykhailo-hrushevsky: Mykhailo Hrushevsky was born on 29 September 1866 in Chełm, then in Congress Poland, within the Russian Empire, to a Ukrainian noble family. His mother taught the children Ukrainian. He studied history at Kyiv University under Volodymyr Antonovych, and in 1894 was appointed to the new chair of Ukrainian history at the University of Lviv. In Austrian Galicia he became president of the Shevchenko Scientific Society in 1897 and turned it into an institution resembling an academy of sciences. In 1899 he co-founded the National Democratic Party, which looked towards Ukrainian independence.

After the Russian Revolution of 1905 he returned to Russian-ruled Ukraine and co-founded the Ukrainian Scientific Society in Kyiv. Soon after the First World War began he was arrested, accused of Mazepinism and Austrophilia, and in 1915 exiled to Simbirsk, later to Kazan and Moscow. On 17 March 1917 he was elected head of the Central Rada in Kyiv. He guided it from autonomy within a democratic Russia to full independence, and its government drafted a constitution of the Ukrainian People's Republic, adopted on 29 April 1918. After the coup of Pavlo Skoropadskyi he went into hiding. In 1919 he emigrated to Vienna.

Hrushevsky wrote the first detailed scholarly synthesis of Ukrainian history, the ten-volume History of Ukraine-Rus', which covers the period from prehistory to the 1660s. He also wrote a History of Ukrainian Literature and an Illustrated History of Ukraine, and his bibliography has over 2,000 titles. The work broke with the Russocentric view that saw direct continuity from Rus' to Muscovy and the Russian Empire. He regarded the Principality of Galicia–Volhynia as the legitimate heir of Kievan Rus', stressed the role of the common people, and saw the Cossack revolt of Bohdan Khmelnytsky as largely national and social. Omeljan Pritsak criticised him for neglecting the political elite.

Hrushevsky returned to Soviet Ukraine in 1924, was elected to the All-Ukrainian Academy of Sciences and went on writing his History. In 1931, after a long press campaign against him, he was exiled to Moscow and soon arrested on a charge of belonging to a Ukrainian nationalist centre. He died on 24 November 1934 at Kislovodsk, of sepsis after minor surgery, and was buried at Baikove Cemetery in Kyiv. The speed with which an obituary was approved led to suspicion about his death.

He is regarded as one of Ukraine's most prominent scholars and statesmen of the 20th century. Museums in Kyiv and Lviv are devoted to him, and the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences has published his Collected Works.
mykola-skrypnyk: Skrypnyk was born in the village of Yasynuvata in the Yekaterinoslav Governorate of the Russian Empire, the son of a railway telegraph operator and a midwife. At school he came to know the works of Taras Shevchenko and Panteleimon Kulish. He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1898, and after his arrest in 1901 while studying at the Saint Petersburg State Institute of Technology he became a full-time revolutionary.

Over the next years he was arrested between fifteen and seventeen times, exiled seven times and at one point sentenced to death. He escaped from exile more than once, once covering 1,200 versts by boat and on foot, and worked as a party organiser in Tsaritsyn, Saratov, Odesa, Saint Petersburg, Riga and Moscow. In 1914 he sat on the editorial board of Pravda.

Amnestied after the February Revolution, he sat on the Military Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet during the October Revolution. In March 1918 he replaced Yevhenia Bosch as head of the Soviet Ukrainian government, which German troops soon drove out. He led the Kyiv faction of the Ukrainian Bolsheviks, who wanted a separate Ukrainian party; a Moscow congress overturned that in July 1918. He then worked for the Cheka and, back in Ukraine, led the suppression of the rebellion of Danylo Terpylo.

In the debates of 1922 before the formation of the Soviet Union he opposed Joseph Stalin's plan to absorb the republics into the Russian SFSR, calling it thinly disguised Russian chauvinism. After this defeat he turned to culture. As head of education from 1927 he pressed the Ukrainization policy despite a lack of teachers and textbooks, and he convened the Kharkiv Orthographic Conference of 1927, whose spelling, the Skrypnykivka, was adopted in 1928. He nonetheless opposed Ukrainian nationalism and testified against Mykola Khvylovy and Oleksandr Shumsky.

In January 1933 Stalin sent Pavel Postyshev to Ukraine to reverse Ukrainization and purge the party. Skrypnyk was removed from his post and his followers were condemned as counter-revolutionary nationalists. Rather than recant in a show trial, he shot himself at his desk in his Kharkiv apartment on 7 July 1933. His second wife, Raisa Khavina, was executed in 1938. He was rehabilitated in 1962.
mykonos: Mykonos lies in the Cyclades, 150 kilometres east of Athens, between Tinos, Syros, Paros and Naxos. It has an area of 85.5 square kilometres and rises to 341 metres. The island is mostly granite, with a rocky terrain eroded by strong winds, which give it the nickname Island of the Winds. It has no rivers but many seasonal streams. Its largest town, Mykonos, also called Chora, stands on the west coast. Clay and baryte were mined on the eastern side until the late 1900s.

Herodotus names Carians as the original inhabitants, and Ionians from Athens seem to have followed in the early 11th century BCE. The island lay only 2 km from Delos, which made it a place of supplies and transit, but in antiquity it was poor, with limited agricultural resources. After the death of Alexander the Great it belonged to the League of the Islanders, then to the Romans and the Byzantine Empire. With the fall of Constantinople in the Fourth Crusade it was occupied by Andrea Ghisi, and a castle was built by the Ghisi family in 1207.
