The Catalans ravaged it at the end of the 13th century, and in 1390 it passed to direct Venetian rule.

In 1537 the Ottoman admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa attacked the island, and an Ottoman fleet established itself there. Mykonos was Ottoman for almost three centuries, governed by a governor and an appointed council of syndics. The last Venetians withdrew from the region when the castle of Tinos fell in 1718. Until the end of the 18th century Mykonos prospered as a trading centre, attracting immigrants and regular pirate raids, and in June 1794 British and French ships fought in its harbour.

When the Greek Revolution began in 1821 the island was important to the cause under the heroine Manto Mavrogenous, who gave her family's fortune to it. Greece became independent in 1830. The island's economy declined in the late 19th century, especially after the Corinth Canal opened in 1904, and many Mykonians emigrated. In September 1944 the Greek Sacred Squadron raided the German garrison, and the island was liberated on 30 September.

The island had 10,704 inhabitants at the 2021 census, most of them in Chora. Excavations by the French School of Archaeology at Delos from 1873 and the tourism that followed came to dominate the economy; the island became popular with international visitors in the 1960s. Landmarks include the windmills of Kato Mili, built by the Venetians in the 16th century, the church of Panagia Paraportiani, whose construction ran from the 15th to the 17th century, and the Archaeological Museum, built in 1905 for finds from the Purification Pit of Rheneia.
myles-coverdale: John Bale gives Yorkshire as his birthplace. He became a bachelor of canon law at Cambridge in 1513 and was ordained priest in Norwich in 1514. Among the Augustinian friars of Cambridge he came under the influence of their prior, Robert Barnes, who had studied under Erasmus at Louvain, and in 1526 he went with other friars to London when Barnes was tried for heresy before Cardinal Thomas Wolsey. By Lent 1528 he was preaching in Essex against transubstantiation, the veneration of images and confession to a priest, views that were then very dangerous.

In Antwerp he probably helped William Tyndale with his translations. His Bible of 1535 was most likely printed there, financed by Jacobus van Meteren, and dedicated to Henry VIII. In 1538 Thomas Cromwell sent him to Paris to oversee the printing of the Great Bible by François Regnault, but English bishops and theologians of the Sorbonne interfered, and Coverdale rescued sheets and type and brought them to London, where Richard Grafton and Edward Whitchurch finished the work.

When Cromwell, who had protected him, was executed in 1540, Coverdale left England with his wife, the Scotswoman Elizabeth Macheson. He lived in Strasbourg, took a doctorate at Tübingen, and from 1543 was assistant minister and schoolmaster at Bergzabern, where he learned Hebrew. Returning in 1548, he became almoner to Catherine Parr and in 1549 went as chaplain with Lord John Russell to put down the Prayer Book Rebellion in Devon and Cornwall, staying on to preach there.

Back in London from 1559, he lodged with the Duchess of Suffolk. His opposition to vestments was one reason he was not given back his bishopric, and from 1564 to 1566 he was rector of St Magnus the Martyr. He died in poverty in London on 20 January 1569. Besides his Psalter, used in musical settings such as Handel's Messiah, he compiled Ghostly Psalms and Spiritual Songs, which Celia Hughes calls the first English hymn book; it was banned in 1539, and one complete copy survives at Queen's College, Oxford. The Episcopal Church (USA) honours him with Tyndale on 6 October.
myocheong: At the court of King Injong of Goryeo the monk argued that the kingdom had been weakened by Confucian ideals. His views clashed directly with those of the leading Confucian officials, represented by Kim Pusik, and the dispute formed part of a longer struggle between Confucian and Buddhist factions at the Goryeo court.

As a geomancer he held that the capital, Kaegyong, was depleted of virtue, and that Sogyong, the Western Capital, now Pyongyang, was the right place for a revival of the dynasty. Sogyong had been a capital of Goguryeo, the state Goryeo saw as its predecessor, and moving there was tied to the aim of reclaiming the former Goguryeo lands in Manchuria.

At the time the Jin dynasty was pressing on Goryeo. Relations had soured partly because Goryeo underestimated the new state and mistreated its envoys, killing them and humiliating their corpses; the Jurchens had once been a subject people of Goguryeo, and their claim to equality offended the Goryeo court. He proposed attacking Jin and claimed that moving the capital to Sogyong would assure success.

King Injong was persuaded, but the rest of the court and the bureaucracy opposed the move, and the king had to go back on his commitments. The southern elites feared losing their dominant position if the capital moved north. Frustrated, he led a rebellion against the Goryeo government and set up a breakaway state at Sogyong, which he named Daewi. The rising was crushed by forces under the scholar-general Kim Pusik.
myra: Myra was probably founded by Lycians and lay on the river Myros, now the Demre Çay, in the fertile alluvial plain between the Massikytos range and the sea. By the 3rd century BCE it was Hellenized, and after the wars of the Diadochi the area came under the loose control of the Ptolemies, the Seleucids and finally the Romans. Alluvial silt mostly covers the ruins of the Lycian and Roman towns. Its harbour, Andriake, silted up later; a granary built under Hadrian survives there.

No firm written reference to Myra exists before it appears as a member of the Lycian League, which lasted from 168 BCE to 43 CE; according to Strabo it was one of the largest towns of the alliance. The citizens worshipped Artemis Eleutheria as their protective goddess and also venerated Zeus, Athena and Tyche. Pliny the Elder records a spring of Apollo where fish, summoned by a pipe, gave oracular responses. In Roman times Myra belonged to the Greek speaking world that quickly embraced Christianity, and one of its early bishops was Saint Nicholas. Its bishops also included Nicander, said to have been martyred under Domitian in 95.

Abbasid troops besieged and sacked the city in 809, but it soon returned to Roman control. Early in the reign of Alexius I Comnenus the Seljuk Turks overran it, and sailors from Bari stole the relics of Saint Nicholas in 1087 and took them to their city. Myra was recovered under the Komnenian restoration and lost for good some time after the Fourth Crusade. Under Ottoman rule the small Turkish town of Kale grew up in the area, renamed Demre in 2005. The Greek inhabitants had to leave in 1923, under the population exchange between Greece and Turkey.

Two necropoleis hold Lycian rock-cut tombs carved as temple fronts into cliffs. The best known is the Lion's tomb, or Painted Tomb, which the traveller Charles Fellows in 1840 found still coloured red, yellow and blue. The semicircular Roman theatre was destroyed by an earthquake in 141 and rebuilt. The church of Saint Nicholas was first built in the 6th century and the present building mainly from the 8th. Its floor is of opus sectile, and the granary at Andriake now houses the Museum of Lycian Civilizations.
myrrh: Myrrh is a gum-resin from a few small, thorny species of the genus Commiphora, in the family Burseraceae. The tree secretes it when a cut penetrates the bark into the sapwood, and it is harvested by repeatedly cutting the trees. The gum is waxy and coagulates quickly, then hardens and turns glossy. It is yellowish, clear or opaque, and darkens as it ages. Commiphora myrrha is native to Somaliland, Somalia, Oman, Yemen, Eritrea, the Somali Region of Ethiopia and parts of Saudi Arabia. The word comes from a Semitic root m-r-r, meaning bitter, and entered English through the Hebrew Bible, where it is mōr.

The earliest attested expedition to Punt, recorded by the 5th-dynasty king Sahure, brought back large quantities of myrrh and frankincense along with malachite, electrum, ebony, ivory and animals. A relief from his mortuary temple shows Sahure tending a myrrh tree in his palace garden, the only Egyptian relief that shows a king gardening. The Egyptians used myrrh with natron to embalm mummies. In the first century BCE Diodorus Siculus recorded that Nabataean caravans and ports carried it from southern Arabia to Petra, which controlled the Incense Route and taxed the trade.

The Hebrew Bible names myrrh as a rare perfume. Exodus 30:23 to 25 prescribes 500 shekels of liquid myrrh for the sacred anointing oil, it was an ingredient of the incense of the Jerusalem temples, and Esther 2:12 gives six months of oil of myrrh to the women prepared for King Ahasuerus. In medicine it served as an antiseptic in mouthwashes and salves and as a painkiller for toothache and bruises, and mixed with wine it was used to dull pain.

The New Testament lists myrrh among the three gifts of the magi, with gold and frankincense, and says Jesus was offered wine mixed with myrrh at his crucifixion and that Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes for his burial. Myrrh is still burned as incense with frankincense in Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, traditional Roman Catholic and Anglican churches, is added to egg tempera in icon painting, and is used to prepare the chrism for chrismation. In Islam a hadith advises fumigating houses with mugwort, myrrh and thyme.
mysia: Mysia lay on the south coast of the Sea of Marmara, in the north-west of ancient Asia Minor. It was bounded by Bithynia on the east, Phrygia on the south-east, Lydia on the south, Aeolis on the south-west and the Troad on the west. Its inhabitants in ancient times included Mysians, Phrygians and Aeolian Greeks. Its precise limits are hard to fix, since the Phrygian frontier fluctuated and the Troad was only sometimes included.

The chief physical features were Mount Olympus in the north and Mount Temnus in the south, which for some distance separated Mysia from Lydia. The rivers Macestus and Rhyndacus drained the north, and the Caïcus flowed west from Temnus to the Aegean past Pergamon. The most important cities were Pergamon and Cyzicus on the Propontis, and the coast was studded with Greek towns such as Parium, Lampsacus, Abydos, Assos, Adramyttium, Elaea, Myrina and Cyme.

In Greek myth the Greek fleet landed in Mysia by mistake, taking it for Troy, and Achilles wounded its king, Telephus. In the Iliad, Homer makes the Mysians allies of Troy, led by Ennomus and Chromius. Homeric Mysia seems to have been much smaller than the historical region. Some Mysian inscriptions survive in a dialect of Phrygian, and a few references in Aeolic Greek sources point to a Lutescan language native to Mysia. Under the Persian Achaemenid Empire the north-west corner of Asia Minor, mainly Aeolian though still Phrygian in part, was called Phrygia Minor, and by the Greeks Hellespontos.

After Rome defeated Antiochus the Great in the war of 192 to 188 BCE, the area passed from the Seleucid Empire to Rome's ally, the Attalid kingdom, and on the death of King Attalus III in 133 BCE to Rome itself, which made it part of the province of Asia and later a separate province called Hellespontus. In later times the region was also called Hellespontine Phrygia, and Acquired Phrygia after it was annexed to the Attalid kingdom. According to the Acts of the Apostles, Paul, Silas and Timothy came to or passed by Mysia on Paul's second journey, shortly before he had a vision of a man of Macedonia.

Remains of several Roman bridges can still be found in the region, among them the Aesepus Bridge across the Gönen Çayı, Constantine's Bridge across the Adırnas Çayı and the Makestos Bridge across the Susurluk Çayı. The area lies in the north-west of modern Turkey.
mysore: Mysore stands at the foot of the Chamundi Hills at an altitude of 770 metres, about 140 kilometres south-west of Bangalore, between the Kaveri River to the north and its tributary the Kabini to the south. The name is an anglicised form of Mahiṣūru, the abode of Mahiṣa. Mahiṣa is Mahishasura, a mythical demon who, in Hindu belief, ruled the area and was killed by the goddess Chamundeshwari, whose temple stands on Chamundi Hill. The city was officially renamed Mysuru on 1 November 2014.

At the start of the 16th century a village named Puragere occupied the site where Mysore Palace now stands. Chamaraja Wodeyar III (1513–1553) built the Mahishūru Fort in 1524. The Kingdom of Mysore, governed by the Wodeyar family, was at first a vassal of the Vijayanagara Empire. After that empire declined following the Battle of Talikota in 1565, Mysore gradually became independent, and by the time of King Narasaraja Wodeyar in 1637 it was a sovereign state. Seringapatam, the present-day Srirangapatna, was its capital from 1610. In the 17th century, under Narasaraja Wodeyar I and Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar, the kingdom annexed large areas of what is now southern Karnataka and parts of Tamil Nadu.

Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, who held power briefly in succession, promoted the planting of mulberry trees and silk in the region and fought four wars against the British. Most of the city's modern development is attributed to the Wodeyar maharajas, patrons of art and culture. A municipality was established in 1888, and a railway from Bangalore opened in 1882. The first free English school was founded in 1833, Maharaja's College in 1864 and the Mysore Sanskrit Pāthaśhāla in 1876. The Mysore economic conference of 1911 planned industrial growth, which led to the Mysore Sandalwood Oil Factory in 1917 and the Sri Krishnarajendra Mills in 1920.

Mysore is the administrative headquarters of Mysore district and is known as the City of Palaces, with Mysore Palace, also called the Amba Vilas Palace, at the centre of its Dasara festival. King Raja Wodeyar I introduced the ten days of Dasara in 1610. On the tenth day, Vijayadashami, the idol of Chamundeshwari is carried on an elephant in procession from the palace to Bannimantapa. Mysore also gives its name to Mysore painting, the sweet Mysore pak and Mysore silk saris.
mysore-dasara: Navaratri and Vijayadashami celebrate the victory of good over evil, and in Hindu belief they commemorate the day the goddess Chamundeshwari, a form of Durga, killed the demon Mahishasura, whose name is also held to have given the city of Mysuru its name. The festival falls on the tenth day of the month of Ashvina, usually in September or October. Its exact origin is unknown. Under the Vijayanagara Empire it was called Mahanavami and is shown in reliefs on the outer wall of the Hazara Rama temple at Hampi; the Italian traveller Niccolò de' Conti described it as a great religious and martial event with athletic contests, fireworks and a military parade.

After the fall of Vijayanagara the celebrations lapsed under the Deccan Sultanates, until Raja Wodeyar I revived them at Srirangapatna in mid-September 1610. In 1805 Krishnaraja Wodeyar III began a special durbar in the Mysore Palace during the festival, and in 1880 Chamarajendra Wadiyar X founded the Dasara exhibition.

The Mysuru tradition honours the warriors and the state: the state sword, weapons, elephants and horses are worshipped and displayed with the goddess in her warrior form, and the king of Mysuru presides. On Mahanavami, the ninth day, the royal sword is worshipped and carried in procession. Each evening the palace is lit with nearly 100,000 bulbs, and concerts, dance and wrestling bouts are held across the city.

On Vijayadashami the procession known as the Jumbo Savari carries the image of Chamundeshwari on a golden mantapa of about 750 kilograms on an elephant from the palace to Bannimantap, where the banni tree is worshipped; in the Mahabharata the Pandavas hid their weapons in such a tree, and kings worshipped it before going to war. The day ends with a torchlight parade. Activists have campaigned against the use of elephants after deaths of animals and mahouts and footage of an elephant in distress in 2018.
mystras: Mystras stands on a slope of the Taygetos mountains above ancient Sparta, among pines and cypresses. The steep ground shaped its plan, with distinct upper and lower city zones, and many streets are footpaths. The Palace of the Despots occupies the main terrace; its last main building follows the form of the Tekfur saray in Constantinople, with three storeys and a large audience hall on top.

In late 1248 William II of Villehardouin, ruler of the Frankish Principality of Achaea, captured Monemvasia and completed the conquest of Laconia. Near his residence of Lacedaemon, on a spur of Mount Taygetos, he built the fortress that became known as Mystras. In September 1259 he was defeated and captured at the Battle of Pelagonia by the Nicaean emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos, and was freed in exchange for an oath of fealty and the cession of Monemvasia, Grand Magne and Mystras. The handover took place in 1262. The people of Lacedaemon later abandoned their exposed city and settled in a new town below the fortress.

In 1349 the Byzantine Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos made the Morea an appanage for his son, the Despot Manuel Kantakouzenos, and from then until 1460 Mystras was the residence of a despot. The Palaiologos dynasty took the Morea after Manuel's death in 1380, and Theodore I Palaiologos, despot from 1383 to 1407, recognised Ottoman suzerainty. The philosopher Gemistos Plethon lived at Mystras until his death in 1452 and accompanied the emperor John VIII Palaiologos to Florence in 1439. The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, was despot there before he took the throne.

Demetrios Palaiologos, the last despot, surrendered the city to Sultan Mehmed II in 1460. The Venetians held it from 1687 to 1715, and otherwise the Ottomans held it until 1821. It was looted in 1770 after joining the Orlov revolt, and in 1825 Egyptian forces under Ibrahim massacred its population. The town of Sparta was built about 9 km away in 1831.

The ruins, including the fortress, palace, churches and monasteries, were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1989. Many of the most important churches still stand, among them St Demetrios, the Hagia Sophia, St George and the Monastery of Peribleptos, and some of their frescoes survive. The only residents are nuns at the Pantanassa Monastery.
myzeqe: The Myzeqe is a wide alluvial plain in the Western Lowlands of Albania, crossed by the Shkumbin, Seman and Vjosë rivers. It stretches about 65 km from north to south and 50 km from east to west, around 1,350 square kilometres in all, and falls mainly within the districts of Lushnjë and Fier. The toponym is first recorded as Musachia in 1417. Its oldest recorded inhabitants are the Albanian tribe of the Lalë, to whom the Muzaka family was related.

In classical antiquity the Illyrian Taulantii controlled much of the plain and lived alongside the Greek colonists of Apollonia. In the Middle Ages local families such as the Skuraj and the Muzaka ruled it, at times as vassals of Byzantium or Bulgaria. In the late 13th century it came under the Angevin Kingdom of Albania, and in 1318 Andrea I Muzaka became the first Orthodox Albanian to command the kingdom's army. Stefan Dushan of Serbia conquered the region in the mid-14th century, and the Battle of Savra, fought on one of its plains, marked the rise of the Ottomans.

The Muzaka joined Skanderbeg's League of Lezhë, but the plain fell under Ottoman rule until the early 20th century. It was one of the few large regions of Albania where most people stayed Orthodox Christian. Malaria was common in the wet late Ottoman years, and risings in 1835 and 1837 failed. In the mid-20th century many Cham Albanian refugees from Greece settled there.

Most of today's fields were swamps until after World War II, when the communist government drained them and the plain became known as the granary of Albania. Gheg, Tosk and Lab Albanians meet there, with Vlachs around Divjake and the Bosniaks of Libofshë. Besides farming, the plain is an important region for Albania's petroleum industry.
mzilikazi: Mzilikazi kaMashobane was born near Mkuze in present-day KwaZulu-Natal, the son of Mashobane kaMangeth, chief of the Northern Khumalo clan, and of Cikose Ndiweni. The Khumalo lived on the Black Mfolozi River between the rival Ndwandwe and Mthethwa confederacies. After Zwide killed Mashobane for helping Shaka escape, Mzilikazi became chief in the 1820s and swore allegiance to Shaka, serving as his lieutenant. A rift opened after Shaka killed the twins of Mzilikazi's sister, and in 1823, during the Mfecane, Mzilikazi left with a large herd of cattle, whether taken from Shaka or raided from neighbours is unclear.

He moved first into present-day Mozambique and in 1826 west into the Transvaal, absorbing members of the peoples he defeated. For some ten years he dominated the Transvaal, defeating the Griqua in 1831 and using scorched-earth methods to keep a distance from the surrounding kingdoms; the death toll has never been satisfactorily determined. The arrival of the Voortrekkers brought two years of fighting, and by early 1838 he and his people had been driven north across the Limpopo River, his following split in two.

After moving into present-day Botswana and towards what is now Zambia, where the tsetse fly made the land unfit for cattle, he settled in Matabeleland in 1840 and rejoined the group led by his son Nkulumane and Gundwane Ndiweni. Having been given up for dead, he reasserted control; by one account Nkulumane and the chiefs who had chosen him were put to death, by another the son was sent south and lived near Rustenburg until 1883. Organised in regimental kraals like Shaka's, the Matabele repelled Boer attacks between 1847 and 1851, and the South African Republic signed a peace treaty with him in 1852.

His capitals were Inyathi, abandoned in 1859 after the death of Queen Loziba, and then Mhlahlandlela, where he is buried. He died at eNqameni near Gwanda in September 1868 and was succeeded by his son Lobengula. Gold had been found a year before his death, which drew Cecil Rhodes and the British South Africa Company to the region; within thirty years the British had conquered Matabeleland. A memorial was raised to him in 1941, and every September people gather at Mhlahlandlela to commemorate him.
mzimba-district: Mzimba, formerly Kathibi in the original Chitumbuka name, covers 10,473 square kilometres and is the largest district in Malawi. Its capital is Mzimba, and its biggest town is Mzuzu, which is also the administrative headquarters of the Northern Region. The Viphya Mountains stretch across its southern and eastern parts, and the central area is the Mzimba Plain, through which the South Rukuru River and its tributaries flow. A low divide, separating the South Rukuru basin from the Luangwa River basin, marks its western border with Zambia. The Vwaza Marsh Game Reserve lies within the district.

The district had a population of 1,017,701 in 2023. It is divided into 13 sub-divisions, which include the areas of traditional authorities and senior chiefs such as Senior Chief Jaravikuba Munthali, Senior Chief Kampingo Sibande and Senior Chief Khosolo Gwaza Jere, and it has twelve National Assembly constituencies since 2009. Its towns are Mzimba, Mzuzu and Ekwendeni.

Chitumbuka is the predominant language. At the 2018 census, 78.3 per cent of the district's people were Tumbuka, 9.1 per cent Chewa and 6.3 per cent Ngoni. The Tumbuka are known for the cultural dance Vimbuza, while descendants of Ngoni people from South Africa perform the dance Ingoma. Mzimba is the centre of netball in Malawi, and most players of the national team, including Mwayi Kumwenda, were born and raised there.

On 10 June 2024 a Malawian Defence Force aircraft carrying Vice-President Saulos Chilima, the former First Lady Patricia Shanil Muluzi and seven others crashed in the Chikangawa Forest Reserve in Nkhata Bay District on its way from Lilongwe to Mzuzu, and all on board died.
